# Retrieval-Augmented Methods for LLM Planning, Agents, Tool-Use, and Decision-Making

_A curated map of methods that RETRIEVE demonstrations, cases, trajectories, skills, tools, experiences, or guidelines to augment large language models for task-solving and acting. It spans in-context-learning demonstration retrieval, retrieval-augmented reasoning and code generation, LM planning, case-based reasoning, tool-use agents, and agent memory / in-context RL, deliberately distinct from vanilla single-shot RAG-for-QA._

**Corpus:** 181 researched items across 7 sub-topics (37 seed · 140 supplemental · 4 gap-fill). Generated from validated per-item research JSON. Fields marked uncertain during research are omitted.

_TOC tags: year · retrieved-unit · retriever · when-to-retrieve._

## A — Retrieval-Augmented In-Context Learning / Demonstration Selection

<a id="item-kate"></a>
### 1. KATE (KNN-Augmented in-conTExt Example selection) - What Makes Good In-Context Examples for GPT-3?

2021  ·  DeeLIO@ACL 2022  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.06804)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2021
- **venue**: DeeLIO@ACL 2022 (Workshop on Knowledge Extraction and Integration for Deep Learning Architectures); first released as arXiv:2101.06804 (Jan 2021). ACL Anthology 2022.deelio-1.10, DOI 10.18653/v1/2022.deelio-1.10.
- **authors affiliation**: Jiachang Liu (Duke University; intern at Microsoft), Dinghan Shen (Microsoft), Yizhe Zhang (Microsoft), Bill Dolan (Microsoft), Lawrence Carin (Duke University), Weizhu Chen (Microsoft). Work done while Jiachang Liu (intern) and Yizhe Zhang were at Microsoft.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.06804
- **code url**: https://github.com/jiachangliu/KATEGPT3

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: NLP in-context learning: sentiment analysis (text classification), table-to-text generation, and open-domain question answering (QA). Demonstration/example selection for few-shot prompting of GPT-3.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-model (GPT-3 via API, no fine-tuning), single-turn in-context few-shot learning. A labeled training set is available from which in-context examples are selected; GPT-3's parameters are frozen and inaccessible. The work addresses the sensitivity of GPT-3's few-shot performance to the choice of in-context examples and asks whether selecting semantically similar examples (vs random sampling) improves results. Single-agent, non-interactive prompt construction; the GPT-3 API is called once per test query with temperature 0.
- **what is retrieved**: In-context demonstrations (labeled training examples / demos, i.e. (x, y) input-output pairs) to be placed in the GPT-3 prompt.
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus: retrieval is over the fixed labeled training set of the target task (and, for QA, the question-answer training pairs). No growing/episodic memory written by the model.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k ranking: for each test query, retrieve the k nearest-neighbor training examples by embedding similarity, where k is a preset hyperparameter (3 for sentiment, 2 for ToTTo due to token limit, 64 for NQ/WQ, 10 for TriviaQA). Not a completeness-recovery or variable-size precision objective.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: Retrieve (yes) / Reuse (yes, verbatim as ICL exemplars) / Revise (no) / Retain (no) — only Retrieve and Reuse are implemented.
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False: the work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is framed as retrieval-augmented in-context example selection (kNN over sentence embeddings); it does reference retrieve-and-edit literature (Hashimoto et al. 2018) and kNN-LM/kNN-MT.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: Single demonstration (one training (source, target) example / (x_i, y_i) pair); the query key is the source sentence x_i embedding. For QA, a retrieved unit is a question-answer pair.
- **index source**: Static, offline corpus = the target task's training set. Sentence embeddings of all training sources are precomputed offline; the test source is encoded on the fly. No online/test-time induction of new store entries.
- **index structure topology**: Flat vector index over sentence-embedding vectors of training sources; nearest neighbors found by Euclidean distance (for KATE_roberta) or cosine similarity (for KATE_nli / KATE_nli+sts-b). No graph or hierarchy.
- **retriever type**: Dense retriever: off-the-shelf pretrained/fine-tuned sentence encoders (RoBERTa-large CLS embeddings; Sentence-BERT-style encoders fine-tuned on NLI / STS-B / SST-2) used for kNN search. No BM25, no LLM-as-retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None for the core method (off-the-shelf encoders, no retriever training against downstream task). The retriever is a frozen pretrained sentence encoder. The paper additionally studies encoders that were independently fine-tuned (with contrastive/similarity objectives) on auxiliary datasets (NLI, STS-B, SST-2), showing task-related fine-tuning of the encoder helps, but this fine-tuning is not driven by GPT-3 / LM-feedback or downstream-task reward — it is supervised similarity training on external datasets.
- **query construction**: Raw test input (test source sentence x_test) is encoded directly by the sentence encoder; no decomposition, expansion, or thought-conditioning. The embedding of the raw query is used for nearest-neighbor search.
- **query granularity**: Task-level / one-shot at t=0: a single retrieval is performed per test instance before the single GPT-3 call. No step-level or trajectory-level retrieval.
- **when to retrieve**: One-shot: retrieval happens once per test query to build the prompt, then GPT-3 is called a single time. No iterative or uncertainty-triggered retrieval.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule: retrieval is always performed once per test example before prompt construction; there is no confidence-, attention-, or classifier-based trigger.
- **reranking**: No dedicated reranking stage. Retrieved neighbors are ordered by similarity score; the only ordering study is whether default vs reverse vs random permutation of the selected k examples in the prompt matters (found to have small effect, data-dependent).
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> None (beyond similarity ordering). No decomposition, distillation, distractor filtering, or compression of retrieved examples; a minor ToTTo-specific preprocessing deletes closing angle brackets to fit the 2048-token limit, but this is input formatting, not refinement of retrieved content.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tools).
- **index content separation**: N/A: examples are short text pairs; no separation of a lightweight index from heavy on-demand content.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index/protocol).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tools, no inter-tool dependencies).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation: the k retrieved (x_i, y_i) demonstrations are concatenated, ordered by similarity, to form the context C, then C is prepended to the test source x_test and fed to GPT-3 ([C; x_test]) to generate the answer. Verbatim in-context exemplars; no adaptation, no training signal.
- **planning integration**: N/A for planning/acting in the agentic sense. KATE provides one-shot exemplars at prompt-construction time for a single forward generation; there is no planner, no per-step interleaving, no tree search.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer: retrieval occurs once and the entire answer is generated in a single GPT-3 call; retrieval is not interleaved with reasoning steps, sentences, or tool calls.
- **adaptation mechanism**: Verbatim ICL exemplar: retrieved training examples are inserted unchanged into the prompt; no LLM-prompted adaptation, execution-feedback revision, or critic-guided revision.
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw demonstration text: the surface (source, target) pairs of retrieved training examples inserted verbatim into the prompt (e.g. table-to-text pairs, question-answer pairs, sentence-label pairs). No distillation, workflow, program, or latent token form.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Single raw demonstration (concrete labeled training instance); no distilled strategy, guideline, workflow, or skill abstraction.
- **noise robustness mechanism**: None explicit. The implicit robustness mechanism is semantic-similarity selection itself (closer examples give better results, shown via closest-vs-farthest study). No relevance evaluator, self-reflection, retriever-aware training, or distractor-aware SFT.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (static training set used as a fixed example pool; no episodic/skill/workflow/procedural/graph/latent memory).
- **write back**: False: the system never writes new experiences/cases/skills back into any store; the training set is fixed and read-only.
- **online growth**: False: the retrievable store (training set) does not grow during deployment/test time; it is frozen offline.
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back occurs).
- **failure experience usage**:
> None: only the labeled training examples (treated as positive demonstrations) are used; no storage or contrastive use of failed/negative experiences. A separate kNN-only baseline (predict via neighbor labels / majority voting) is studied but it is a baseline, not a memory mechanism.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A / none: no stored entries are mutated (store is static, append-only is not even used).
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No: retrieval is a fixed similarity top-k (nearest neighbors by Euclidean/cosine distance in a frozen embedding space), not a learned/RL-optimized selection policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No: single-model, single-agent prompting; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> SST-2 (train) -> IMDB (test) for sentiment analysis; ToTTo (table-to-text generation, dev set, incl. overlap and nonoverlap subsets); Natural Questions (NQ), WebQuestions (WQ), and TriviaQA for open-domain QA. Backbone LLM: GPT-3 (via OpenAI API, temperature 0). Sentence encoders: RoBERTa-large, and RoBERTa-large fine-tuned on SNLI+MultiNLI (nli), then STS-B (nli+sts-b), and SST-2.
- **benchmark family**: QA (open-domain: NQ, WQ, TriviaQA), text classification / sentiment (SST-2 -> IMDB), and table-to-text generation (ToTTo). Not in the agentic/web/embodied/tool/code/memory families.
- **baselines**:
> Random (random sampling of in-context examples from the training set, averaged over 5 trials with std); kNN_roberta (non-parametric kNN classifier/predictor using retrieved neighbors' targets via top-1 or majority voting, same RoBERTa-large embedding space, no GPT-3); GPT-3 (64 examples) figures from Brown et al. 2020; and fine-tuned reference systems for context: T5 (fine-tuned, 11B / closed-book T5, T5+SSM), and RAG (open-domain) for QA.
- **key metrics**: Accuracy (sentiment/IMDB); BLEU and PARENT (ToTTo, overall/overlap/nonoverlap); Exact Match (EM) score (NQ, WQ, TriviaQA).
- **ablations**:
> (1) Closest vs farthest neighbors on NQ subset of 100 (EM 46.0 closest vs 31.0 farthest) — motivates similarity-based selection. (2) kNN_roberta baseline (no GPT-3) performs near random guessing / much worse, showing the retrieval module is complementary to GPT-3, not sufficient alone. (3) Choice of sentence encoder: encoders fine-tuned on task-similar data help (KATE_sst-2 best on IMDB; KATE_nli / KATE_nli+sts-b best on QA), while fine-tuning on a dissimilar objective (NLI/STS-B for IMDB/ToTTo) slightly hurts. (4) Number of in-context examples (5/10/20/35/64 on NQ): both KATE and random improve with more examples, but KATE dominates even with as few as 5. (5) Training-set size (retrieval pool size): larger pool improves KATE EM but barely changes random. (6) Order of in-context examples (default / reverse / 3 random permutations on NQ): small effect, data-dependent (reverse best on NQ; default slightly better on WQ/TriviaQA).
- **evaluation decoupling**: No: only end-to-end task metrics (Accuracy, BLEU/PARENT, EM) are reported; no separate intrinsic retrieval metrics such as Recall@k or nDCG. The closest-vs-farthest study is reported via downstream EM, not retrieval IR metrics.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Outcome only: evaluation scores final task output (answer correctness, generation quality). Qualitative case studies of retrieved examples are shown but no quantitative intermediate/process metrics.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> KATE calls the GPT-3 API only once per test query (contrasted with contextual calibration which repeats per token), framed as inference-efficient. Using fewer in-context examples (e.g. 5) still beats random, enabling cheaper/shorter prompts. ToTTo uses only 2 examples due to the GPT-3 2048-token limit. No detailed latency/dollar-cost numbers reported.
- **context budget and selection count**: Fixed-k per task, budget-capped by GPT-3's 2048-token input limit: k=3 for sentiment (more did not help), k=2 for ToTTo (token-limit constrained), k=64 for NQ/WQ, k=10 for TriviaQA (64 retrieved examples would exceed the token limit). Selected examples are ordered by similarity.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (not a benchmark paper; uses existing datasets SST-2/IMDB, ToTTo, NQ, WQ, TriviaQA).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> GPT-3 in-context learning (Brown et al. 2020); retrieve-and-edit / retrieval-augmented generation literature (Hashimoto et al. 2018); kNN-augmented LM/MT methods (kNN-LM Khandelwal et al. 2019, kNN-MT Khandelwal et al. 2020, BERT-kNN Kassner & Schutze 2020); Sentence-BERT (Reimers & Gurevych 2019) and RoBERTa (Liu et al. 2019) sentence encoders.
- **contrasts with**:
> Random sampling of in-context examples (the GPT-3 default in Brown et al. 2020); contextual calibration (Zhao et al. 2021, which must repeat per generated token); prompt-based fine-tuning of smaller LMs LM-BFF (Gao et al. 2020) and AutoPrompt (Shin et al. 2020); fine-tuned models T5 / T5+SSM and RAG (used as reference upper bounds); the kNN-only non-parametric baseline (kNN modifies the prediction whereas KATE modifies the conditional context).
- **lineage**:
> Group A (ICL demonstration retrieval). KATE is the founding similarity-based / kNN demonstration retriever for in-context learning: it established the dense-embedding nearest-neighbor demo-selection paradigm that later learned/retriever-trained demo selectors (e.g. EPR, learning-to-retrieve-prompts) build upon and contrast against.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- headline_result

<a id="item-epr"></a>
### 2. EPR (Efficient Prompt Retrieval) - Learning To Retrieve Prompts for In-Context Learning

2022  ·  NAACL 2022  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.08633)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2022
- **venue**: NAACL-HLT 2022 (Proceedings of the 2022 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies); preprint arXiv:2112.08633
- **authors affiliation**: Ohad Rubin, Jonathan Herzig, Jonathan Berant — The Blavatnik School of Computer Science, Tel Aviv University.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.08633
- **code url**: https://github.com/OhadRubin/EPR (author implementation; built on the DPR codebase; ~64 stars).
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (single-paper author repo with a single initial commit Aug 2022; no continuously-updated leaderboard or paper list).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: In-context learning / few-shot demonstration (prompt) retrieval for structured NLP tasks; specifically semantic parsing (mapping natural-language utterances to meaning representations). QA-adjacent (sequence-to-sequence structured prediction).
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, supervised, single-model (no multi-agent) setting. Given a labeled training set D of input-output pairs and a scoring LM, the goal is to train a retriever R(x_test, D) that selects training examples (prompts) for a frozen inference LM that does in-context learning with no parameter updates. Supervision is available (gold y is used at training-data-construction time to retrieve high-quality candidates and to LM-score them). Two evaluation regimes: (a) LM-as-a-service (scoring LM == inference LM, e.g. both GPT-Neo, used as a black-box service) and (b) LM-as-a-proxy (small scoring LM, e.g. GPT-Neo, used to train a retriever later applied to larger inference LMs GPT-J/GPT-3/Codex). Retrieval is one-shot at test time; the retriever and index are frozen after offline training.
- **what is retrieved**: Demonstrations (training input-output pairs / examples) used as in-context prompts. Each retrieved unit is a single labeled training example (utterance + meaning representation).
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus: the fixed annotated training set D is the retrieval store. It is not a growing/episodic agent memory; the index is built offline once and frozen.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Variable-size top-L ranking subject to a context budget: the retriever returns examples sorted by inner-product similarity, and the number actually used (L') is the largest set that fits in the inference LM's context window (C=2,048 tokens). Objective is similarity-style ranking (each candidate scored independently), not recovery of a minimal complete set; selection count is dynamic/budget-capped rather than a fixed k.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: Retrieve (yes) / Reuse (yes, verbatim demonstrations injected into the prompt) / Revise (no) / Retain (no). Effectively [Retrieve, Reuse].
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False as self-framing: EPR frames itself as prompt/demonstration retrieval, not case-based reasoning. However it explicitly includes a CASE-BASED REASONING (CBR) baseline adapted from Das et al. (2021) (KB-QA CBR), which it positions against. It does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner as its own framework.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: Single demonstration (one training input-output pair: utterance + meaning representation). Granularity = single demo / case (problem-solution).
- **index source**: Static corpus, offline-induced: the annotated training set D is encoded offline with the trained prompt encoder E_P(.) and indexed with FAISS. No online/test-time growth.
- **index structure topology**: Flat dense vector index (FAISS, maximum inner-product search over dense BERT-CLS embeddings of training examples).
- **retriever type**: Learned dense retriever (dual-encoder: input encoder E_X and prompt encoder E_P, both BERT-base, trained contrastively a la DPR). An unsupervised retriever (BM25 or SBERT) is used only to build the candidate set for training-data construction.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> LM-feedback / contrastive on LM-scored labels. For each training example, candidate prompts are scored by the probability the scoring LM assigns to the gold output y given x and the candidate (s(e_l)=Prob_g_hat(y | e_l, x)); top-k candidates labeled positive, bottom-k labeled negative; a dense retriever is then trained with the DPR contrastive (in-batch negatives) objective. The signal is LM utility for decoding the target, argued to be a better proxy than surface-similarity heuristics.
- **query construction**: At test time the raw input utterance x_test is encoded by E_X to form the query (no decomposition/expansion). At training-data construction time the candidate set is retrieved using the target output y (using y, i.e. R_u(y, D), found slightly better than using the full pair).
- **query granularity**: Task-level / instance-level, one-shot at t=0: a single query is formed once per test instance from x_test; no per-step or trajectory-level re-querying.
- **when to retrieve**: One-shot: retrieval happens once per test instance before decoding; no iterative or uncertainty-triggered retrieval.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule (retrieve once per test instance, unconditionally, before LM decoding). No confidence/uncertainty/learned-router trigger.
- **reranking**: No dedicated reranking stage at test time; retrieved examples are simply sorted by inner-product similarity. (A two-stage candidate-then-LM-score pipeline exists only during offline training-data construction, not at inference.)
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> None beyond similarity ordering and context-budget truncation: the L most similar examples are sorted high-to-low and the largest prefix L' that fits the context window C is kept; examples are placed in reverse order (lowest-scoring first, highest-scoring nearest to x_test). No decomposition, distillation, compression, or distractor filtering.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tools/skills; demonstrations are raw training examples, not engineered tool/skill descriptions).
- **index content separation**: N/A / No: the full demonstration text is what is both indexed (via dense embedding) and loaded into the prompt; no lightweight-index-then-content progressive-disclosure split.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index or live protocol; static FAISS index over a fixed training set).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tools; no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation: retrieved training examples are concatenated (as in-context demonstrations) with the test input and passed as a prefix to the frozen inference LM, which greedily decodes the output. The examples are also a training signal for the retriever itself (LM-scored positives/negatives), but at use-time they are verbatim in-context exemplars.
- **planning integration**: One-shot exemplars at inference time (retrieve-then-generate). Not interleaved with planning/search; there is a single retrieval call followed by a single greedy decode. No MCTS/tree-search/hierarchical integration.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer / per-instance: a single retrieval feeds a single decode of the full output; retrieval is not woven per-CoT-step or per-token.
- **adaptation mechanism**: Verbatim ICL exemplar: retrieved demonstrations are used as-is in the prompt; there is no explicit case adaptation/revision step (the inference LM may implicitly compose/generalize, analyzed via the 'prompt copying' study, but no algorithmic revision).
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw demonstration text: the surface form of each retrieved unit is the concatenation of the training example's input utterance and its gold meaning representation (a raw problem-solution pair), injected directly into the prompt.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Single demonstration (raw, un-distilled training example / problem-solution pair); not a distilled strategy, workflow, or skill.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Retriever-aware training via hard negatives: the contrastive objective uses LM-scored bottom-k candidates (drawn from the same high-similarity BM25 candidate set) as hard negatives plus in-batch negatives, training the retriever to distinguish examples that actually help the LM decode the target from superficially similar but unhelpful ones. No test-time relevance evaluator, self-reflection, or distractor filtering.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (static training-set index; no episodic/skill/workflow memory).
- **write back**: False: the system does not store new experiences/cases into a memory during deployment; the retrievable store is the fixed offline training set.
- **online growth**: No: the index is frozen after offline construction; it does not grow at test time.
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back; memory is static).
- **failure experience usage**:
> Not stored as deployment memory, but failure-style signal is used during offline retriever training: bottom-k LM-scored candidates (prompts that lead to LOW probability of the gold output) are used as negative examples in the contrastive objective (success+failure contrastive labeling of the candidate set). No storage/retrieval of test-time failures.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A / append-only-none: stored entries are never mutated; the training-set index is fixed.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: Partially: the retriever is a learned (contrastively trained) dense scorer rather than a fixed off-the-shelf similarity, but it is NOT an RL/value-based policy. Selection at test time is fixed top-L by learned inner-product similarity (not an MDP/RL policy).
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No: single-model, single private retriever/index. (One cross-model transfer is shown — a retriever trained with a small scoring LM, GPT-Neo, is applied to larger inference LMs GPT-J/GPT-3/Codex — but there is no shared multi-agent memory.)

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: BREAK (low-level subset; 44K/7K/8K train/dev/test), MTOP (English subset; 16K/2K/4K), SMCALFLOW (15K dev examples, 134K train sampled to 44K). Tasks map utterances to meaning representations (QDMR steps, nested intent-slot queries, and dataflow programs respectively).
- **benchmark family**:
> Semantic parsing / structured sequence-to-sequence (utterance-to-meaning-representation). Not in the standard agent/web/embodied/tool benchmark families; closest normalized grouping is QA/structured-parsing (BREAK is a question-understanding/decomposition benchmark; MTOP and SMCALFLOW are task-oriented dialogue semantic parsing).
- **baselines**:
> Unsupervised: RANDOM, SBERT (paraphrase-mpnet-base-v2), BM25, BRUTEFORCE (test-time LM prompt-selection from Shin et al. 2021). Supervised (same BM25 candidate template, differ in scoring function): DR-BM25 (BM25 scores label positives/negatives), CBR (Case-Based Reasoning, adapted from Das et al. 2021 using token-F1 between outputs). Oracles: BM25-ORACLE (BM25 on gold y_test), LM-ORACLE (LM scoring at test time, upper bound for EPR), ANYCORRECT-ORACLE (any BM25 candidate yields correct output).
- **key metrics**: Exact-match-style accuracy: LF-EM (logical-form exact match) for BREAK dev; NEM (normalized EM, the official metric) for BREAK test; EM (exact match) for MTOP and SMCALFLOW.
- **headline result**:
> When the scoring LM and inference LM are identical (GPT-Neo), EPR improves over the best baseline from 26.0 to 31.9 (LF-EM) on BREAK, from 57.0 to 64.2 (EM) on MTOP, and from 51.4 to 54.3 (EM) on SMCALFLOW (dev set, LM-as-a-service). EPR also outperforms BM25-ORACLE on BREAK and MTOP.
- **ablations**:
> 1) Hyperparameter robustness (Table 8): varying k in {1,5,10} and candidate-set size L in {50,100} yields stable performance (e.g. BREAK 31.0-32.3, MTOP 63.0-64.2). 2) Unsupervised candidate retriever: BM25 > SBERT, so BM25 is used to build candidate sets. 3) Scoring-LM vs inference-LM mismatch: using GPT-Neo as scoring LM vs GPT-J itself only changes GPT-J BREAK from 31.5 to 33.6; Codex scoring itself 29.5 vs 29.3 — small LM as proxy is effective. 4) One-shot vs full-context (Table 4): EPR 23.0 (one-shot) vs 31.9 (full-context) LF-EM on BREAK; EPR beats BM25-ORACLE one-shot. 5) Prompt-copying analysis (Table 7): higher accuracy on exactly/abstractly copied patterns, but non-negligible accuracy on novel structures (generalization). 6) Cross-LM generalization (Table 5): consistent EPR gains across GPT-3, Codex, GPT-J, GPT-Neo as inference LMs.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No: only end-to-end downstream task accuracy (LF-EM/EM/NEM) is reported. No separate intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k/nDCG); oracles (LM-ORACLE, ANYCORRECT-ORACLE) bound achievable end-task accuracy rather than measuring retrieval recall directly.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome (final decoded-output exact match). Some process-level analysis is added qualitatively: prompt-copying analysis (exact vs abstract copying, copy-distance distribution) and t-SNE/OPTICS clustering of learned representations, but these are diagnostic, not scored process metrics.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Efficiency is a central motivation: training a light-weight BERT-base dense retriever lets a small scoring LM (GPT-Neo) serve as a cheap proxy for large inference LMs, avoiding expensive per-test-instance LM calls. Test-time retrieval is a single FAISS MIPS lookup (cheap) vs BRUTEFORCE which scores 200 examples with the LM at test time (slow, and worse). No explicit latency/$ numbers reported; training used 8x RTX 3090, batch size 120, lr 1e-4, 30 epochs (DPR defaults).
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Budget-capped, dynamic k: maximum inference-LM context C=2,048 tokens. After retrieving the top-L examples sorted by similarity, the largest prefix L' fitting within C (reserving room for x_test and the desired output length) is kept; the number of in-context examples therefore varies per instance (App. Figure 5 shows the distribution). Candidate-set size for training L=50 (also tried 100); k=5 positives/negatives.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (method paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (uses existing benchmarks rather than constructing a new one). Datasets used: BREAK (~60K examples low-level subset), MTOP (~22K English subset), SMCALFLOW (~148K, sampled to 44K train + 15K dev).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> DPR (Karpukhin et al. 2020) contrastive dual-encoder training with in-batch negatives; BERT-base encoders (Devlin et al. 2019); FAISS (Johnson et al. 2017) for indexing; GPT-style in-context learning (Brown et al. 2020 / GPT-3); GPT-Neo (Black et al. 2021) as scoring/inference LM; BM25 (Robertson & Zaragoza 2009) and SBERT (Reimers & Gurevych 2019) as candidate/unsupervised retrievers.
- **contrasts with**:
> Liu et al. (2021a) KATE — unsupervised nearest-neighbor (SBERT) prompt selection; Das et al. (2021) CBR — supervised retriever for KB-QA relying on formal-query surface similarity (adapted as the CBR baseline); Shin et al. (2021) BRUTEFORCE — test-time LM prompt selection (slow); plain BM25/SBERT/RANDOM example selection. EPR's distinction: train the retriever from LM-utility labels rather than surface similarity, and do the LM scoring offline rather than at test time.
- **lineage**:
> Group A (ICL demonstration retrieval). A foundational early (2021/2022) learned dense demonstration retriever: it moves the field from unsupervised similarity-based example selection (KATE) toward LM-feedback-trained retrievers, and is a direct predecessor of later learned/reranking ICL retrievers (e.g. CEIL, UDR, LLM-R, dr.icl) and reward/feedback-trained prompt retrievers.

<a id="item-dr-icl"></a>
### 3. Dr.ICL: Demonstration-Retrieved In-context Learning

2023  ·  Data Intelligence 2024  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14128)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2023
- **venue**: Data Intelligence, Vol. 6, Issue 4, pp. 909-922 (2024 acceptance; published 2025-03-03; DOI 10.3724/2096-7004.di.2024.0012); originally arXiv:2305.14128 (May 2023)
- **authors affiliation**: Man Luo (Arizona State University), Xin Xu, Zhuyun Dai, Panupong Pasupat, Mehran Kazemi, Vaiva Imbrasaite, Vincent Y. Zhao (Google Research), Chitta Baral (Arizona State University). Lead author Man Luo; primary affiliations Arizona State University and Google Research.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14128
- **code url**: N/A (no official code repository is linked in the paper or arXiv listing; no public release found)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: QA and NLP reasoning: free-form question answering, natural language inference, mathematical reasoning, and boolean/commonsense QA. This is an in-context-learning / demonstration-retrieval study, not an agent/tool-use/planning system.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-turn in-context learning (ICL) with frozen large LLMs (no parameter updates). For each test query the system retrieves query-specific few-shot demonstrations from the labeled training set of the same task and prepends them to the prompt. Supervision is available in the form of the task's training data (used both as the demonstration pool and to mine training signal for a learned retriever). Settings cover one-shot and few-shot ICL, with both a general LLM (PaLM) and an instruction-finetuned LLM (Flan-PaLM), and with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting for reasoning tasks. Single-agent; no interactive environment.
- **what is retrieved**: Demonstrations (few-shot exemplars), i.e. labeled (input, answer) pairs from the task training data; for CoT tasks the demonstrations contain intermediate reasoning chains.
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus: the fixed, labeled task training set (Dtrain) is the demonstration pool. No growing/episodic memory; the store does not change during inference.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: Retrieve: yes; Reuse: yes (verbatim in-context exemplars); Revise: no; Retain: no. [Retrieve, Reuse]
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The work frames itself as retrieval-based in-context learning (Dr.ICL) and does not cite or invoke case-based reasoning (Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner). Verbatim exemplar reuse loosely resembles CBR Retrieve+Reuse but is not framed as CBR.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: Single demonstration = a (problem, solution) / (input, answer) pair; for CoT tasks the demonstration also includes a step-by-step reasoning chain. Granularity is one full labeled example per retrieved item.
- **index source**:
> Static corpus built offline from the existing task training data (Dtrain). The retrievable store is the same labeled training pool used at train time; it is frozen at test time (no online/test-time induction). For the trained retriever, additional offline mining produces positive/hard-negative pairs, but the demonstration pool itself stays static.
- **index structure topology**: Flat index. BM25 uses a sparse bag-of-words inverted index; GTR / the trained Demo-GTR use a flat dense vector index (dual-encoder embeddings with inner-product / nearest-neighbor search). No graph, hierarchy, or clustering.
- **retriever type**: Three variants: (1) BM25 (sparse, off-the-shelf), (2) GTR (dense dual-encoder based on T5, off-the-shelf), and (3) Demo-GTR, a learned dense retriever fine-tuned from GTR. Hybrid in the sense that both sparse and dense off-the-shelf retrievers are studied plus a trained one.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Two regimes. Off-the-shelf BM25/GTR: none (no task-specific training). Trained Demo-GTR: LM-feedback / downstream-task-effectiveness signal — for each training query, GTR retrieves 100 candidate demonstrations, PaLM-62B scores each by the LM probability p_LM(y_q | d, x_q) of the gold answer, the top-n are positives and bottom-n hard negatives, and GTR is fine-tuned with a contrastive (InfoNCE) loss using in-batch and hard negatives.
- **query construction**:
> Raw input query used directly as the retrieval key: the test question/input x_q is matched against candidate demonstrations in the training pool. No decomposition, sub-queries, or synthetic query expansion. For CoT tasks demonstrations carry reasoning chains and retrieval is based on the query (and, per the published version, retrieving based on reasoning chains gives improvements).
- **query granularity**: Task-level / one-shot at t=0: a single retrieval is performed per test query before generation; there is no per-step or trajectory-level re-querying.
- **when to retrieve**: One-shot (single retrieval per query before the LLM call). Not iterative, active, or adaptively routed.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule: retrieval always happens once per test query prior to prompting. No confidence-, uncertainty-, classifier-, or agent-initiated trigger.
- **reranking**:
> For the off-the-shelf inference pipeline, no separate reranking stage at test time (top-n nearest demonstrations are used directly). During training-data construction for Demo-GTR, an LLM (PaLM-62B) reranks the GTR-retrieved 100 candidates by gold-answer probability to mine positives/hard-negatives — a training-time reranking, not an inference-time reranker.
- **retrieved context refinement**: None. Retrieved demonstrations are inserted into the prompt as-is (linearized as 'question: x \n answer: y', with reasoning chains for CoT). No decomposition, distillation, compression, or distractor filtering.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tools; demonstrations are raw labeled examples, not engineered tool/skill descriptions).
- **index content separation**: N/A / No. There is no lightweight-index-then-heavy-content separation; demonstrations are both the index entries and the injected content.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index, no live synchronization, no MCP/RapidAPI/function-calling protocol).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tools; no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation: the retrieved demonstrations are prepended to the test query as few-shot in-context exemplars; the frozen LLM conditions on them to predict the answer. For Demo-GTR, retrieval feedback (LM scores) is also used as a training signal to learn the retriever, but at inference the retrieved demos are used purely as prompt context.
- **planning integration**:
> N/A for planning/acting. The closest mapping is one-shot exemplars injected at prompt/generation time (retrieve-then-generate). There is no MCTS, tree search, hierarchical subtask planning, or per-step interleaving; for reasoning tasks, retrieved CoT demonstrations guide a single forward generation.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer: retrieval occurs once and the full answer (including any CoT) is generated in a single pass. Retrieval is not interleaved per CoT step or per token.
- **adaptation mechanism**: Verbatim ICL exemplar: retrieved cases are reused as-is in the prompt with no adaptation/revision step. (CBR-style 'Revise' is absent.)
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw demonstration text: linearized (input, answer) pairs, including raw step-by-step reasoning chains for CoT tasks. No distillation into strategies, programs, or latent tokens.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Single demonstration (concrete labeled example). For CoT tasks the demonstration includes a raw reasoning trajectory, but it is still a concrete worked example rather than a distilled strategy, workflow, or skill.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Limited. The main mechanism is training a task-specific retriever (Demo-GTR) on LM-feedback with hard negatives so that more task-representative (less merely query-overlapping) demonstrations are retrieved, reducing unhelpful exemplars. The paper also analyzes label/answer overlap (Table 3) to confirm gains are not due to trivial label copying. No explicit relevance evaluator, self-reflection, or reason-in-documents filtering at inference.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (static labeled training pool; no episodic/skill/workflow/procedural/graph/latent memory).
- **write back**: False. The system never writes new experiences/cases/skills back into a memory store; the demonstration pool is the fixed training set.
- **online growth**: No. The retrievable store is frozen after offline construction; it does not grow during deployment/test-time.
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back mechanism exists).
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success-only at inference (only gold labeled demonstrations are retrieved/used). During offline training of Demo-GTR, low-utility demonstrations (lowest LM-probability candidates) are used as HARD NEGATIVES in the contrastive loss, so 'unhelpful' examples inform retriever training, but there is no storage/retrieval of failed agent trajectories.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A / append-only static (no entries are mutated; the pool is fixed and not updated post hoc).
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Partially: Demo-GTR is a learned (contrastively trained) retriever optimized via LM-feedback-derived labels, which is more than fixed similarity top-k. However it is a learned similarity/relevance scorer, NOT an RL/value-based sequential policy (no M-MDP, soft Q-learning, or interactive preference optimization). The BM25/GTR variants are fixed similarity top-k.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: N/A / No. Single-LLM, single-task setting; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> NQ (Natural Questions, free-form QA), ANLI round 3 / ANLI-r3 (natural language inference), GSM8k (grade-school math word problems, with CoT), AQuA (algebraic word problems with multiple choice, with CoT), StrategyQA (boolean/multi-hop commonsense QA, with CoT). Five datasets total.
- **benchmark family**: QA (NQ, StrategyQA), NLI (ANLI-r3), and math reasoning (GSM8k, AQuA). No web/embodied/tool/code/memory/decision-RL agent benchmarks.
- **baselines**:
> Random demonstrations and no-demonstration (zero-shot) prompting; off-the-shelf retrievers BM25 and GTR. The trained Demo-GTR retriever is compared against off-the-shelf GTR. Related-work methods (KATE, EPR, CEIL, UPRISE) are discussed for positioning but not all directly re-run as head-to-head baselines.
- **key metrics**: Exact-match accuracy on all five tasks (downstream task accuracy). No separate Recall@k / nDCG retrieval metrics are reported.
- **headline result**:
> Retrieved demonstrations (BM25 or GTR) beat random demonstrations for both PaLM-540B and Flan-PaLM across one-shot and few-shot settings; and the trained Demo-GTR retriever further beats off-the-shelf GTR, e.g. PaLM one-shot average accuracy rises from 49.8 (GTR) to 51.1 (Demo-GTR, +1.3), with per-task one-shot gains NQ 37.8->39.2 (+1.4), ANLI-r3 54.0->54.8 (+0.8), GSM8k 57.7->59.3 (+1.6); improvements are largest in the one-shot setting.
- **ablations**:
> Comparison of demonstration source (no-demo vs random vs BM25 vs GTR) across one-shot and few-shot for both PaLM and Flan-PaLM (Figures 3-4), isolating that retrieval (vs random) drives gains and that even sparse BM25 helps. Off-the-shelf GTR vs trained Demo-GTR (Table 2) isolates the value of the learned retriever, especially in one-shot. Answer-overlap analysis (Table 3) ablates whether gains come from trivial label/answer leakage, finding overlap ratios near/below the uniform-label baseline for four of five datasets (NQ is the exception, with notable answer overlap explained by near-duplicate questions). The retriever-training recipe uses GTR to fetch 100 candidates, PaLM-62B to score, and top-5 reranked as positives.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No. Only end-to-end exact-match accuracy is reported; intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k/nDCG) are not reported separately.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (this is an empirical method paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (uses existing public datasets; not a new benchmark). Datasets are standard NQ, ANLI-r3, GSM8k, AQuA, StrategyQA.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Retrieval-based ICL line: KATE (Liu et al. 2022), EPR (Rubin et al. 2022), CEIL (Ye et al. 2023); GTR dense retriever (Ni et al. 2021); BM25 (Robertson et al. 2009); Chain-of-Thought prompting (Wei et al. 2022b; Wang et al. 2022); base models PaLM (Chowdhery et al. 2022) and Flan-PaLM (Chung et al. 2022). The trained retriever extends EPR-style LM-feedback retriever training.
- **contrasts with**:
> Random/fixed-demonstration ICL and zero-shot (no-demo) prompting; off-the-shelf QA/IR retrievers (BM25, GTR) that capture query-specific knowledge but not task-nature; prior retrieval-ICL work focused on general LLMs (e.g., GPT-3) without instruction-tuned models or CoT, and cross-task retrieval methods like UPRISE (Cheng et al. 2023). Also contrasted with implicit-demonstration approaches like RetroPrompt.
- **lineage**:
> Group A (icl_demonstration_retrieval): a foundational empirical study in the retrieval-augmented in-context-learning lineage, extending retrieval-of-demonstrations from general LLMs to instruction-finetuned LLMs and CoT, and adding a learned (LM-feedback-trained) demonstration retriever. Predecessor-adjacent to EPR/CEIL; precursor to later learned demo-retriever and diverse-coverage selection work.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- completeness_vs_topk_objective
- context_budget_and_selection_count
- cost_efficiency_tradeoff
- process_vs_outcome_metrics

<a id="item-llm-r"></a>
### 4. LLM-R (Learning to Retrieve In-Context Examples for Large Language Models)

2024  ·  EACL 2024  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.07164)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **authors affiliation**: Liang Wang, Nan Yang, Furu Wei — all at Microsoft Research (Microsoft).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.07164
- **code url**: https://github.com/microsoft/LMOps/tree/main/llm_retriever
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/microsoft/LMOps (parent repo; the llm_retriever subdirectory hosts code and data).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> In-context example (demonstration) retrieval for LLMs across a broad suite of NLP tasks (Closed-book QA, commonsense reasoning, coreference, NLI, paraphrase, reading comprehension, sentiment, data-to-text, summarization). This is ICL demonstration retrieval, not agentic planning/tool-use.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline supervised setting: a single dense retriever is trained from frozen-LLM feedback to select few-shot in-context examples that maximize ICL performance. Supervision is available because each training example has a ground-truth output used to compute LLM log-likelihood feedback. Single-model (non-agent, non-interactive) setting; the trained retriever is then applied at test time to pick k-shot demonstrations from a static pool. A mixture of 30 tasks (9 categories) is trained jointly; 4 tasks are held out to test generalization to unseen tasks, and the retriever (trained with LLaMA-7B) is also tested for transfer to other LLMs (GPT-Neo-2.7B, LLaMA-13B, GPT-35-Turbo).
- **what is retrieved**: Demonstrations (in-context examples) — i.e., (input x_i, output y_i) training pairs used as few-shot ICL exemplars.
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus: a fixed retrieval pool of ~6.3M labeled training examples (union of all training-task examples). The pool is frozen after construction; it is not a growing/episodic agent memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k ranking objective: retrieve top-k (k=8 in main experiments) demonstrations by retriever similarity score. Candidates are treated independently (no minimal-set completeness or combinatorial selection); the paper notes in Limitations that joint/combinatorial selection of mutually-influencing examples is left to future work.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: [Retrieve: yes, Reuse: yes (verbatim ICL exemplar), Revise: no, Retain: no]. Only Retrieve + Reuse phases are realized; no case adaptation/revision and no retention of new cases.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: false — The work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is framed as dense-retriever training for in-context example selection via reward-model knowledge distillation.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: Single demonstration: one (input, output) example pair. The query is the test input x; each candidate key is the string concatenation of input x_i and output y_i.
- **index source**: Static corpus, offline-induced: the retrievable store is the union of all training examples (~6.3M) across the 30-task mixture, built once offline. No online/test-time growth.
- **index structure topology**: Flat vector index: bi-encoder embeddings of candidate (x_i,y_i) pairs retrieved by cosine similarity (kNN). BM25 inverted index is used only as the initial/first-iteration retriever. No graph/hierarchical/cluster topology.
- **retriever type**:
> Learned dense bi-encoder (initialized from E5-base), trained via knowledge distillation from a cross-encoder reward model. BM25 (unsupervised) is the initial retriever for the first training iteration. So: hybrid pipeline (BM25 bootstrap) but the final deployed retriever is a learned dense bi-encoder.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> LM-feedback + downstream-task-effectiveness via reward distillation. Pipeline: (1) BM25 retrieves top-n candidates; (2) a frozen LLM (LLaMA-7B) ranks candidates by log p(y | x, x_i, y_i) — the LM-feedback signal; (3) a cross-encoder reward model (ELECTRA-base) is trained with a softmax cross-entropy (1 positive vs N_neg hard negatives) over LLM-ranked candidates; (4) the bi-encoder retriever is trained by KL-divergence knowledge distillation from the reward model plus an InfoNCE contrastive loss (L = alpha*L_cont + L_distill). Trained iteratively (retriever from iter i mines candidates for iter i+1). Not RL; not a sequential decision policy.
- **query construction**: Raw test input x is used directly as the query (no decomposition, no synthetic/expanded query, no thought conditioning). At training time the query is the training input x and itself is excluded from retrieval results.
- **query granularity**: Task-level / instance-level, one-shot at t=0: a single query is formed from the test input and retrieval happens once before generation. No step-level or trajectory-level re-querying.
- **when to retrieve**: One-shot: retrieve top-k demonstrations once per test input before the single LLM forward pass. (The 'iterative' aspect refers to iterative offline retriever TRAINING, not iterative test-time retrieval.)
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule: retrieval is always performed once per test input (always-on, k=8). No confidence/uncertainty/learned-router trigger.
- **reranking**: No test-time reranking stage. A cross-encoder reward model is used only during training (as a teacher for distillation, with access to ground-truth label y); it is not applied at inference. At test time the bi-encoder directly produces the top-k.
- **retrieved context refinement**: None at test time: retrieved demonstrations are concatenated verbatim as k-shot prompt context. No decomposition, distillation, distractor filtering, or compression of retrieved items.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A — no tool/skill descriptions; retrieved units are labeled NLP demonstrations, indexed as raw concatenated (x_i,y_i) strings (no synthetic-query augmentation or weighted-field embeddings).
- **index content separation**: N/A — no separation of a lightweight index from heavy on-demand content; embeddings index the full (x_i,y_i) pairs directly.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A — not a tool-retrieval system; static example pool, no live tool index or integration protocol (RapidAPI/REST/MCP/function-calling).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A — no inter-tool dependency modeling; demonstrations are treated independently.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation: the top-k retrieved (input, output) pairs are concatenated as few-shot in-context examples in front of the test input and fed to the frozen LLM, which generates the prediction. The retrieved examples are also a training signal for the retriever offline, but at inference they are pure prompt exemplars.
- **planning integration**:
> N/A for planning — this is ICL demonstration retrieval, not a planner/agent. Integration pattern: one-shot retrieve-then-prompt (retrieve top-k exemplars at prompt-construction time, then a single LLM forward pass for the answer). No interleaving with planning, MCTS, or a search loop.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer: a single retrieval informs a single LLM prediction for the whole test instance. No per-step / per-token / per-tool-call interleaving.
- **adaptation mechanism**: Verbatim ICL exemplar: retrieved demonstrations are reused as-is in the prompt with no adaptation/revision (consistent with CBR Retrieve+Reuse only).
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw demonstration text: each injected item is the verbatim (input, output) training pair rendered with the task template. No distilled strategy, workflow, executable program, or latent/soft tokens.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Single demonstration (raw, concrete input-output example). Not a distilled strategy, guideline, workflow, or skill.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Retriever-aware training via reward-model distillation and hard-negative mining: the cross-encoder reward model provides fine-grained, lower-variance supervision (vs raw LLM log-likelihood) and iterative training mines better positives/hard-negatives, improving the retriever's ability to discriminate helpful vs unhelpful examples. No explicit test-time relevance evaluator, self-reflection, or distractor filtering.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none — static labeled example pool used as a retrieval corpus; no episodic/skill/workflow/procedural/graph/latent memory that the system writes to.
- **write back**: false — the system does not store new experiences/cases/skills; the retrieval pool is fixed (the union of training examples) and is not augmented at deployment.
- **online growth**: No — the retrievable store is frozen after offline construction; it does not grow during deployment/test-time.
- **write back trigger**: never — no write-back mechanism exists; nothing is added to the pool during or after inference.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success-only / label-driven (no failure-experience memory). During TRAINING, hard NEGATIVE (low-LLM-feedback) candidates are mined and used contrastively to train the reward model and retriever, so negative/less-helpful examples shape the retriever; but there is no storage or retrieval of failed task trajectories as experiences. The retrieval pool contains only ground-truth labeled examples.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A / append-only-at-train-time only: the example pool is static (no mutation). The only iterative update is offline retriever-parameter refinement across training iterations (mining better positives/negatives), not mutation of stored entries.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Partially: retrieval is a LEARNED scoring function (dense bi-encoder distilled from a reward model trained on LLM feedback), so selection is learned rather than a fixed off-the-shelf similarity. However it is NOT an RL/sequential-decision policy (no M-MDP, no soft Q-learning); it is a learned top-k similarity retriever with independent candidate scoring.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: N/A — single-retriever, single-model setting; no multi-agent or cross-framework memory sharing. (The retriever does generalize/transfer across different evaluation LLMs, but that is model transfer, not shared memory.)

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> 30 publicly available datasets across 9 categories (collection based on FLAN and UPRISE): Closed-book QA (CQA), Commonsense reasoning, Coreference, NLI, Paraphrase, Reading Comprehension, Sentiment, Data-to-text (D2T), Summarization. Specific datasets mentioned include NQ, ARC (easy/challenge), HellaSwag, COPA, PAWS, OpenBookQA, WSC, Winogrande, MultiRC, SNLI, MNLI, SQuAD v1, Sentiment140; 4 held-out tasks: QNLI, PIQA, WSC273, Yelp.
- **benchmark family**: QA / general NLP (FLAN-style task suite) — closed-book QA, commonsense, coreference, NLI, paraphrase, reading comprehension, sentiment, data-to-text, summarization. Not web/embodied/tool/code/memory/decision-RL families.
- **baselines**:
> Zero-shot prompting, Random selection, K-means clustering, BM25, off-the-shelf dense retrievers E5-base and SBERT (all-mpnet-base-v2), and EPR (Efficient Prompt Retrieval, Rubin et al. 2022; re-implemented for fair comparison). A REPLUG-style variant (LLM log-likelihood as distillation reward) is compared as an ablation.
- **key metrics**:
> Task-specific metrics averaged per category and overall (accuracy for classification/multiple-choice; ROUGE/BLEU-style for generation tasks like D2T/summarization). Reported as average score across the 30 tasks (and per-category averages). Std dev over 3 runs reported for the Random baseline.
- **headline result**:
> On the 30-task suite with LLaMA-7B and 8 in-context examples, LLM-R reaches an average score of 66.5 (2 iterations), vs 63.5 for the best baseline EPR and 61.3 for BM25 — i.e., +3.0 over the strongest retrieval baseline (EPR) and roughly +8.6 over Random (57.9). On the 4 held-out unseen tasks it averages 81.7, surpassing the second-best (E5-base, 76.3) by +5.4 points.
- **ablations**:
> Training-pipeline ablations (Table 2, 1-iter LLM-R = 65.7): (1) 'w/o reward model' (contrastive loss only on LLM-ranked candidates) drops to 64.9 (-0.8), showing the reward model is crucial; (2) 'reward model w/o label y+' (reward model lacks ground-truth label) drops to 63.8 (-1.9), the largest drop, showing label access for the teacher matters; (3) 'LLM score as reward' (REPLUG-style log-likelihood as distillation target) gives 65.2 (-0.5), worse because raw LLM log-likelihood is high-variance/not a proper distribution; (4) initializing retriever with BERT-base instead of E5-base gives 65.2 (-0.5). Iterative training: 1 iter 65.7 -> 2 iter 66.5 -> 3 iter 66.4 (converges after 2). Generalization to LLMs: GPT-Neo-2.7B +7.4, LLaMA-13B +4.2, GPT-35-Turbo +0.4 over BM25 (gains larger for smaller LLMs). Ranking-LLM vs eval-LLM (Table 6): eval LLM quality is the primary determinant; ranking-LLM choice has minor impact; merging both training sources is marginally best. Scaling: gains diminish after ~4 in-context examples; large-size retriever boosts more than small/base.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No — only end-to-end downstream ICL task metrics are reported; intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG) are not reported separately. Retrieval quality is assessed indirectly via downstream task performance and qualitative retrieved-example analysis.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Outcome-only: evaluation scores the final task prediction. There is qualitative analysis of retrieved examples (similar input patterns; when LLM-R helps vs hurts, e.g., low diversity on SQuAD) but no quantitative process/faithfulness metric.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Efficiency motivations: bi-encoder used for fast inference; computing LLM feedback log p(y|x,x_i,y_i) needs only one forward pass per candidate (no task-specific metric). Scaling analysis shows gains diminish after ~4 examples (more examples => longer prompts, higher inference cost); small-size retriever is comparable to base-size (cheaper deployment option). No explicit latency/API-cost numbers reported.
- **context budget and selection count**: Fixed-k: 8 in-context examples retrieved per test input in main experiments (k held constant). Scaling experiment varies k (gains saturate after ~4). No adaptive/budget-capped/precision-driven selection.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A — primary method paper, not a survey.
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A — not a benchmark-construction paper; it reuses 30 public datasets (collection based on FLAN and UPRISE). Pool ~6.3M examples; up to 30k train / 10k eval sampled per dataset.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> EPR (Efficient Prompt Retrieval, Rubin et al. 2022) for LLM-feedback-trained ICL retrieval; E5 (Wang et al. 2022) retriever initialization; ELECTRA (Clark et al. 2020) reward-model init; iterative dense-retrieval training (ANCE/Xiong et al. 2021; Li et al. 2023); knowledge distillation from a cross-encoder teacher; InfoNCE contrastive learning (Chen et al. 2020 / SimCLR). REPLUG (Shi et al. 2023) is the inspiration for the LLM-log-likelihood-reward variant. Task collection based on FLAN (Wei et al. 2022) and UPRISE (Cheng et al. 2023).
- **contrasts with**:
> Contrasts with off-the-shelf / unsupervised retrievers (BM25, SBERT, E5, K-means, Random) that use similarity only; with EPR which distills directly from LLM scores per task; with REPLUG-style direct LLM-log-likelihood distillation (shown suboptimal because the signal is high-variance and not a proper distribution); with UPRISE (cross-task retrieval) and FLAN (instruction fine-tuning) whose objectives differ. Distinguished from ad-hoc retrieval re-rankers since the reward model uses the ground-truth label y unavailable at test time.
- **lineage**:
> Group A — ICL demonstration retrieval. A learned, LLM-feedback-trained dense retriever for selecting in-context examples; a successor to KATE/EPR-style learned demonstration retrievers, adding a cross-encoder reward model + iterative knowledge distillation for multi-task, generalizable ICL example retrieval.

<a id="item-cbr-kbqa"></a>
### 5. CBR-KBQA (Case-based Reasoning for Natural Language Queries over Knowledge Bases)

2021  ·  EMNLP 2021  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08762)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2021
- **venue**: EMNLP 2021 (Proceedings of the 2021 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, pages 9594-9611; ACL Anthology 2021.emnlp-main.755)
- **authors affiliation**:
> Rajarshi Das, Manzil Zaheer, Dung Thai, Ameya Godbole, Ethan Perez, Jay-Yoon Lee, Lizhen Tan, Lazaros Polymenakos, Andrew McCallum. Lead/primary affiliation: University of Massachusetts, Amherst (Das, Thai, Godbole, Lee, McCallum); other affiliations: New York University (Perez), Google Research (Zaheer), Amazon (Tan), EY Greece (Polymenakos).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08762 (peer-reviewed: https://aclanthology.org/2021.emnlp-main.755/ , DOI 10.18653/v1/2021.emnlp-main.755)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: QA -- knowledge base question answering (KBQA) / semantic parsing: mapping complex natural language questions to executable SPARQL logical forms over Freebase.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-agent, supervised semantic parsing for KBQA. Given a natural language query q and a symbolic KB K (full Freebase, ~45M entities / ~3B facts), generate an executable SPARQL logical form whose execution returns the answer set A. Supervision is gold (question, logical-form) pairs in a training set D. Setting is non-interactive at inference (one-shot retrieve-reuse-revise per query), but supports test-time addition of new human-labeled cases to the case memory without retraining. Weakly-supervised (question-answer only) baselines are also compared.
- **what is retrieved**: cases -- specifically (question, logical-form/SPARQL-program) pairs (k-nearest-neighbor similar training queries and their gold logical forms) stored in a nonparametric case memory.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> HYBRID leaning growing-memory: the primary store is a case memory seeded from the training set (offline), but it is explicitly designed to grow at inference by injecting new human-labeled or SimpleQuestions-derived cases without retraining (write-able episodic case memory). The revise step additionally grounds to the static external KB (Freebase relation neighborhood / TransE KB embeddings).
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k retrieval objective: retrieve top-k=20 similar cases, optimized so that the union of their logical-form relations covers (recall@k) the relations needed by the target query. The retriever is evaluated by percentage of gold LF relations present in the top-k retrieved cases (recall@k), i.e. a coverage/completeness flavor of relation recall rather than a single-best ranking; downstream the reuse module composes from multiple retrieved cases.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve, Reuse, Revise, Retain] -- all four canonical CBR phases are implemented: Retrieve (RoBERTa KNN case retrieval), Reuse (BigBird seq2seq reuses LF components to generate an intermediate LF), Revise (align generated relations to KB neighborhood via TransE/RoBERTa to make LF executable), Retain (human-in-the-loop / SimpleQuestions cases are added to the KNN case memory at test time without retraining).
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> True. The work explicitly frames itself as case-based reasoning, cites Aamodt & Plaza (1994) for the Retrieve/Reuse/Revise CBR cycle and Schank (1982)/Kolodner for CBR origins, and defines a 'case' as an abstract problem-solution representation (question paired with executable logical form).

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: case (problem-solution): a (natural-language-question, executable-SPARQL-logical-form) pair. The query key is the question; the retrieved payload includes the full SPARQL program.
- **index source**:
> Hybrid construction: the retrievable case store is offline-induced from the training set D of (question, LF) pairs (precomputed and cached query representations), and is online/test-time-extendable by appending new cases (human-labeled simple cases or SimpleQuestions edges) to the KNN index without retraining.
- **index structure topology**: Flat dense vector index (KNN index over normalized RoBERTa [CLS] question embeddings; inner-product / cosine similarity). The downstream revise step additionally consults the KB graph neighborhood, but the case index itself is a flat vector store.
- **retriever type**: Dense (learned bi-encoder): a RoBERTa-base encoder produces independent [CLS] embeddings per question; retrieval is inner-product / cosine top-k (DPR-style dense passage-retrieval design).
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Contrastive / weighted similarity supervision derived from downstream logical forms: fine-tuned with a weighted negative-log-likelihood (in-batch) loss where the weight w_ij between a query pair is the F1 overlap between the sets of KB relations in their gold logical forms (distant supervision from LFs). Entity spans are masked with probability p_mask (0.2 for CWQ, 0.5 otherwise) to emphasize relational rather than entity similarity. Initialized from pre-trained RoBERTa-base; trained ~10 epochs, selected by recall@20 on validation.
- **query construction**:
> Raw natural language question is encoded directly; named entities are detected by an NER tagger and masked with a [BLANK] symbol (probability p_mask) during retrieval to emphasize relational similarity. For the reuse step, the query string is augmented by appending each entity's KB id after its surface mention (e.g. 'What do Jamaican m.03_r3 people speak?').
- **query granularity**: Task-level (one-shot at t=0): a single retrieval per input question; the whole question is the query, retrieved once before generation. No per-step or trajectory-level re-retrieval.
- **when to retrieve**: One-shot: retrieve top-k cases once per query before generation. (The only iterative aspect is the offline/human-in-the-loop addition of cases to the index, not per-inference iterative retrieval.)
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule: retrieval is always performed once per incoming query at the start of the pipeline (no confidence/uncertainty/learned-router trigger).
- **reranking**: None. No explicit reranking stage; the top-k=20 cases by dense similarity are passed directly to the reuse module.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> None at the retrieval stage (top-k cases are concatenated directly into the BigBird encoder). A post-generation refinement exists in the separate Revise step (relation alignment to KB), but no decompose/distill/compress/filter operation is applied to the retrieved cases themselves.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tools/APIs; retrieved units are question-LF cases, not tool documents).
- **index content separation**: N/A -- cases (question + full SPARQL program) are stored and loaded together; no lightweight-index-then-heavy-content progressive-disclosure separation. Query vectors are precomputed/cached but the case content is loaded directly.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index / external API protocol). The case index is static-after-training but manually extendable by appending cases; no CRUD auto-sync, RapidAPI/MCP/function-calling protocol.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no inter-tool dependency modeling; no tools).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Case adaptation / prompt(context) augmentation for generation: the retrieved (question, LF) cases are concatenated with the input query and fed to a BigBird seq2seq generator (Reuse) which composes/reuses components of the retrieved logical forms to produce an intermediate LF; the LF is then revised by aligning generated relations to the KB. Retrieved cases also serve as a parametric training signal (model learns to reuse) and at test time enable copying unseen relations from injected cases.
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-plan/generate (one-shot exemplars at generation time): retrieval happens once up front; the k cases condition a single seq2seq generation of the full logical form (the 'plan'), followed by a post-hoc revise/alignment step. Not interleaved per-step, not inside tree search.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer / per-query: a single retrieval and a single conditioned generation produce one logical form per query; retrieval is not woven per CoT-step or per token.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> LLM/seq2seq-prompted adaptation plus execution-grounded revision: (1) Reuse -- a BigBird seq2seq model conditioned on the retrieved cases generates a new (intermediate) logical form, reusing/recombining components of the retrieved LFs (a learned, non-verbatim adaptation, regularized by a KLD term toward the no-case prediction); (2) Revise -- a non-learned alignment that replaces generated relations with the most semantically similar relation edge that actually exists in the query entity's local KB neighborhood (via pre-trained TransE KB embeddings, or RoBERTa surface-form similarity) to make the LF executable.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Surface form injected is the raw case text: the retrieved question string plus its executable SPARQL program, concatenated with [SEP] separators on the encoder side (q [SEP] q1' [SEP] l1' ... qk' [SEP] lk'). No distillation/compression; it is the literal (question, logical-form) pair.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Single demonstration / case at the level of a problem-solution pair (question + executable logical form). Not a distilled strategy or abstracted workflow -- the literal prior solved cases are retrieved and their LF components reused.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> (1) Reuse-step KL-divergence regularization term forcing the with-cases prediction not to deviate too far from the no-case prediction (guards against over-reliance on possibly-irrelevant retrieved cases); (2) entity masking during retrieval so similarity reflects relational structure rather than entity overlap; (3) the Revise step corrects relations that do not execute (domain mismatch / KB incompleteness) by aligning to existing KB edges. No explicit relevance-evaluator/self-reflection on retrieved cases.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: episodic case memory (nonparametric KNN case store of (question, logical-form) pairs); the knowledge for revision is also a graph (KB) but the retrievable memory is episodic/case-based.
- **write back**:
> True (limited / manual): new cases (human-labeled simple cases, or SimpleQuestions-derived single-relation cases) can be written into the KNN case memory at inference time to fix erroneous predictions or cover unseen relations, without any retraining. There is no automatic self-generated experience write-back during normal inference.
- **online growth**:
> Yes -- the case memory can grow at test/deployment time: an expert or curated source adds new cases to the KNN index (0 gradient steps, ~2 seconds), which the retriever can then surface. This is the paper's central controllability/point-fix contribution. Growth is human/curation-driven, not autonomous.
- **write back trigger**: Human-validated / on-demand: writes are triggered by a human-in-the-loop point-fix (an expert injects a simple case to correct a wrong prediction) or by curated import from SimpleQuestions; not automatic, not on every success/failure, not reflective.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success-only / positive cases: the memory stores correct (question, gold-LF) cases. Failed/negative trajectories are not stored as retrievable items; the point-fix mechanism responds to a detected failure by adding a new correct case, not by storing the failure itself. (Negatives appear only transiently as in-batch negatives during contrastive retriever training.)
- **memory evolution update**: Append-only: new cases are added to the KNN index; existing stored cases are not mutated, merged, deltas-updated, or pruned.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No -- retrieval is a fixed similarity top-k (dense cosine KNN). The retriever encoder is learned (contrastive on LF-relation-overlap weights), but case selection at inference is a fixed top-k nearest-neighbor rule, not an RL/learned selection policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No -- single-model private case memory; no multi-agent or cross-framework experience sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> WebQSP (WebQuestionsSP), ComplexWebQuestions (CWQ), Compositional Freebase Questions (CFQ; MCD1/MCD2/MCD3 splits). Underlying KB: full Freebase (~45M entities, ~3B facts). Also a held-out unseen-relation generalization split of WebQSP and a human-in-the-loop (HITL) OOV-relation experiment; SimpleQuestions used as a source of simple cases. Entity linking via ELQ + FACC1.
- **benchmark family**: QA / multi-hop KBQA (semantic parsing to SPARQL over a knowledge base); CFQ specifically targets compositional generalization.
- **baselines**:
> Supervised: T5-11B (Raffel et al. 2020), T5-11B+Revise (their revise step applied to T5), STAGG (Yih et al. 2016). Weakly-supervised: GraftNet, PullNet, EmbedKGQA (WebQSP); KBQA-GST, QGG, PullNet, DynAS/Alibaba (CWQ). On CFQ, T5-11B (Furrer et al. 2020). Generalization/point-fix experiments compare against a baseline (BigBird/BART-style) transformer that must be fine-tuned.
- **key metrics**:
> Strict exact-match accuracy (Acc; predicted answer list from executing generated SPARQL must exactly match gold answer list), plus Precision/Recall/F1 of answer entities. Retriever evaluated intrinsically by recall@k (fraction of gold LF relations covered by top-k cases). CFQ reported as accuracy per MCD split.
- **headline result**:
> On the hidden CWQ test set, CBR-KBQA reaches 67.1% accuracy (P 70.4 / R 71.9 / F1 70.0), outperforming the prior state-of-the-art (the abstract states 'by 11% on accuracy'; vs the best reported prior weakly-supervised system DynAS 50.0 and T5-11B 52.4). On WebQSP it reaches 69.9% accuracy (F1 72.8), >6 points over the best baseline; on CFQ MCD-mean 78.1 vs T5-11B 67.7.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Cases ablation (Table 9): baseline K=0 (no cases) vs CBR-KBQA K=20 -- 67.2->69.9 on WebQSP and 65.8->67.1 on CWQ, showing retrieved cases help; removing the KL-divergence regularization term drops to 68.1 (WebQSP) / 66.7 (CWQ). (2) Revise-step ablation (Table 5): +Revise(TransE) improves accuracy 69.43->70.00 (WebQSP, +0.57) and 65.95->67.11 (CWQ, +1.16); TransE alignment beats RoBERTa surface-form alignment; revise also improves the T5 baseline (>3 F1 points on CWQ). (3) Unseen-relation generalization (Table 6): adding cases to the index (0 gradient steps) lifts held-out accuracy from 0 to 70.6% with no forgetting on the initial set (69.4), whereas a fine-tuned transformer suffers catastrophic forgetting. (4) HITL OOV experiment (Table 7): adding cases raises OOV-question performance from 0 to ~36 F1 / 32.89 Acc without retraining. (5) Novel-combination analysis: CBR-KBQA answers more compositional-reasoning questions correctly than T5 (CWQ 270 vs 205; CFQ 3886 vs 3351).
- **evaluation decoupling**: Yes -- intrinsic retriever quality is reported separately (recall@k of gold LF relations in top-k cases; retriever selected by recall@20) and entity-linking P/R/F1 (Table 2) is reported separately, in addition to end-to-end answer accuracy/F1.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome (answer exact-match accuracy / F1 from executing the generated SPARQL). Some intermediate/process signals are reported: retriever recall@k, entity-linking P/R/F1, and analysis of how many compositional-reasoning questions are answered correctly; but no per-step reasoning-faithfulness scoring.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Argues a strong parameter-efficiency tradeoff: CBR-KBQA uses orders-of-magnitude fewer parameters than T5-11B (generator is BigBird with 6+6 sparse-attention layers initialized from BART-base) yet outperforms it on all benchmarks, with lower carbon footprint. Controllability efficiency: a point-fix (adding a case to the index) takes 0 gradient steps / ~2 seconds vs fine-tuning a transformer (100-300 gradient steps) which causes catastrophic forgetting. Query representations are precomputed/cached. No explicit per-query latency/API-cost numbers reported.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k: k=20 retrieved cases concatenated into the BigBird encoder; BigBird's sparse attention is the enabling lever for the long concatenated context (BART/T5 512-token full-attention encoders cannot fit as many cases). Decoding uses beam size 5. k is fixed (not adaptive/precision-driven).
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A (not a benchmark paper). For reference, datasets used: WebQSP ~4737 questions, 56 domains, 661 unique relations, up to 2-hop; CWQ extends WebQSP to up to 4-hop multi-hop (composition 45% / conjunction 45% / comparative 5% / superlative 5%); CFQ targets compositional generalization (MCD1/2/3). KB is full Freebase (~45M entities, ~3B facts).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Dense passage retrieval / DPR (Karpukhin et al. 2020; Das et al. 2019); BigBird sparse-attention transformer (Zaheer et al. 2020); BART (Lewis et al. 2020); RoBERTa; TransE KB embeddings (Bordes et al. 2013) for revise alignment; entity-independent relational representations via entity masking (Soares et al. 2019); ELQ entity linker (Li et al. 2020) + FACC1; classical CBR (Schank 1982; Aamodt & Plaza 1994; Kolodner); the authors' earlier CBR for KB completion (Das et al. 2020 'A Simple Approach to Case-Based Reasoning in Knowledge Bases', AKBC).
- **contrasts with**:
> Retrieve-and-edit (Hashimoto et al. 2018) -- conditions on a single retrieved example and lacks an explicit revise step, unlike CBR-KBQA which reuses partial logic from multiple cases and revises against the KB. REALM (Guu et al. 2020) and RAG (Lewis et al. 2020) -- retrieve relevant text passages from a nonparametric memory, whereas CBR-KBQA retrieves similar queries and reuses relational structure of their logical forms. Massive parametric seq2seq models (T5-11B) that memorize patterns in parameters and cannot add new relations without retraining (catastrophic forgetting). KB-traversal/weakly-supervised models (GraftNet, PullNet, EmbedKGQA, STAGG).
- **lineage**:
> Group A (in-context-learning / demonstration retrieval). Foundational neuro-symbolic CBR-with-retrieval: a nonparametric (question, logical-form) case memory plus a retrieve-and-reuse(-revise) pipeline usable with new cases without retraining -- a lineage origin for case/demonstration retrieval and CBR-style retrieve-reuse-revise in later LLM agent / KBQA work (e.g. its own follow-up CBR-SUBG, ICML 2022).

<a id="item-fantastically-ordered"></a>
### 6. Fantastically Ordered Prompts and Where to Find Them: Overcoming Few-Shot Prompt Order Sensitivity (GlobalE / LocalE probing)

2021  ·  ACL 2022  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08786)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2022
