- **venue**: ACL 2022 (Proceedings of the 60th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, Volume 1: Long Papers, pp. 8086-8098, Dublin, Ireland); Outstanding Paper Award. First posted on arXiv April 2021 (arXiv:2104.08786).
- **authors affiliation**: Yao Lu, Max Bartolo, Sebastian Riedel, Pontus Stenetorp (University College London); Alastair Moore (Mishcon de Reya LLP / MDR Research). Lead author: Yao Lu (UCL).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08786
- **code url**: https://github.com/mdrresearch/mdr-research/tree/main/Fantastically_ordered_prompts (official MDR Research repo hosting paper materials/illustrative code; not a full standalone training repo)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: QA / NLP text classification under few-shot in-context learning (ICL); demonstration ordering/selection for prompt construction.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-model, single-turn in-context learning (no fine-tuning). A small fixed set of n labeled training samples (typically 4-shot; 1-shot for DBPedia, 2-shot for AGNews due to GPT-2 1024-token context limit) is given. The paper studies sensitivity of few-shot ICL accuracy to the ORDER (permutation) of these demonstrations and proposes a true-few-shot method (no held-out labeled dev set, following Perez et al. 2021) to pick performant orderings. Supervision beyond the few training samples is unavailable; an artificial unlabeled 'probing set' is self-generated by the LM. No interaction with an environment; no multi-agent setting.
- **what is retrieved**: Demonstration permutations (orderings of the same fixed set of few-shot demos). The method selects/ranks candidate orderings rather than retrieving demos from a corpus; it also self-generates an artificial probing set used for scoring orderings.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> Neither a static external corpus nor a growing episodic memory in the classic RAG sense: the 'candidate pool' is the n! permutations of one fixed small training set, and the scoring data (probing set) is generated on the fly by the LM itself. Best characterized as self-generated / internal grounding (LM as data source), not external-corpus retrieval.
- **completeness vs topk objective**: Fixed top-k selection over candidate orderings: from the up-to-24 (n!) candidate permutations, rank by entropy probing metric and keep the top k (k=4 used; K=1 also works). Objective is selecting a small set of performant orderings, not completeness recovery.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based reasoning method).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False - the work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is positioned as prompt-order selection for ICL.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: A full prompt = an ordered concatenation (permutation) of the few-shot demonstrations (single demos linearized via a template and concatenated). The selectable unit is a demonstration ordering/permutation, not an individual document or trajectory.
- **index source**:
> Test-time-induced and ephemeral: candidate orderings are enumerated from one fixed training set, and the artificial probing set used to score them is generated online by sampling from the LM (temperature t=2, max generation length 128, with block n-gram repetition to encourage diverse generation). No persistent offline index.
- **index structure topology**: Flat enumeration of permutations (up to 24 = 4! candidate orderings); no vector index, graph, or hierarchy. The probing set is a flat collection of LM-generated, label-discarded sentences.
- **retriever type**:
> Not a conventional retriever. Selection is done by an LM-as-scorer / generative-probing mechanism: the same LM generates a probing set and produces predicted-label distributions, then candidates are ranked by an entropy statistic (GlobalE / LocalE). No BM25/dense embedding retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None (no trained retriever). Selection uses an unsupervised, training-free statistic over self-generated probes: GlobalE (entropy of the predicted category-label distribution over the probing set) and LocalE (mean per-example prediction entropy). Higher entropy is preferred (avoids degenerate, highly unbalanced or over-confident predictions). No similarity contrastive learning, no RL.
- **query construction**:
> Each candidate prompt c_m is the concatenation of one permutation of the linearized training samples (template T(x,y) = 'input: x ... label: y'). To build the probing set, each candidate prompt is itself used as context to sample a continuation g_m ~ P(.|c_m; theta); the generated probes (T^{-1}(g_m), labels discarded) form the unlabeled dev set against which all candidates are scored.
- **query granularity**: Task-level / one-shot: ordering selection happens once at prompt-construction time (t=0) for the fixed demo set; not per-step or per-test-instance.
- **when to retrieve**: One-shot: the performant orderings are selected once before inference, then reused for all test examples of the task.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule (no dynamic trigger): probing-set generation and entropy ranking are performed once during prompt construction; not confidence/uncertainty/agent-triggered.
- **reranking**: Yes - the core mechanism is a (re)ranking of candidate orderings by an entropy probing metric (GlobalE or LocalE), then selecting the top-k (k=4). It is an entropy-statistic ranker, not a cross-encoder; no RRF.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Selection/ranking only. Probes generated by the LM have their predicted labels discarded (kept as unlabeled inputs because label validity is not guaranteed); candidate orderings are then ranked and truncated to top-k. No document distillation or compression of the demos themselves.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tools).
- **index content separation**: N/A.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index/protocol).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**: Prompt augmentation: the selected performant ordering(s) of the few-shot demonstrations are placed in the LM context as the in-context-learning prompt; no training signal, no skill reuse, no latent injection.
- **planning integration**: One-shot exemplars at prompt/inference time. Selected orderings serve directly as the few-shot context; there is no planner, no tree search, no per-step retrieval.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer: a single classification prediction is produced from the fixed selected prompt; no interleaving of retrieval with multi-step reasoning.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (no case adaptation; selected demos are used verbatim as ICL exemplars).
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw few-shot demonstrations (template-linearized sentence+label pairs) injected verbatim in a chosen order; surface form is plain natural-language exemplars.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw single demonstrations (ordered set thereof); no distilled strategy, skill, or workflow abstraction.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> The entropy-based selection itself acts as a guard against degenerate prompts: GlobalE penalizes orderings that yield highly unbalanced predicted-label distributions and LocalE penalizes overconfident/poorly-calibrated predictions, thereby filtering 'bad' orderings. No retriever-aware training or self-reflection module.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (no persistent memory; the probing set is transient and discarded after selection).
- **write back**: False - nothing is written back to a persistent store; the artificial probing set is generated, used for ranking, and not retained as reusable memory.
- **online growth**: False - no store grows during deployment; the candidate pool is fixed (permutations of one training set) and probes are regenerated per selection, not accumulated.
- **write back trigger**: never - no write-back of experiences/cases/skills occurs.
- **failure experience usage**: N/A - no explicit storage of failed experiences. (Indirectly, degenerate/non-performant orderings are identified and discarded via low/abnormal entropy, but they are not stored.)
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (no stored entries to mutate).
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No - selection is a fixed unsupervised entropy statistic over self-generated probes, not a learned/RL-optimized policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No - single-model, no shared memory across agents. Notably, the paper shows performant orderings are NOT transferable across model sizes (e.g., Spearman correlation 0.05 between GPT-3 2.7B and 175B), arguing against cross-model sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: Eleven text-classification tasks: SST-2, SST-5, MR, CR, MPQA, Subj, TREC, AGNews, DBPedia, CB, RTE. Models: GPT-2 (0.1B/base, 0.3B/medium, 0.8B/large, 1.5B/XL) and GPT-3 (2.7B and 175B via OpenAI API).
- **benchmark family**: QA / text classification (sentiment: SST-2, SST-5, MR, CR, MPQA; subjectivity: Subj; question type: TREC; topic: AGNews, DBPedia; NLI: CB, RTE). Not a planning/agentic/embodied/tool benchmark family.
- **baselines**:
> Baseline = mean accuracy over all candidate prompt orderings (no probing/selection); Majority baseline (always predict majority label, lower bound); Oracle (top-4 orderings selected using the true validation set, upper bound); Split Training Set (split the 4-shot training samples into train/dev and select orderings by dev-set performance); calibration along the lines of Zhao et al. 2021 (contextual calibration) discussed in analysis. Compared GlobalE vs LocalE against these.
- **key metrics**: Classification accuracy (mean and standard deviation across orderings/sample sets); relative improvement over the no-selection baseline; Spearman's rank correlation (for the transferability analysis of orderings across models).
- **headline result**:
> GlobalE yields on average a 13% relative improvement in accuracy over the no-probing baseline across the eleven text-classification tasks and across all model sizes (GPT-2 0.1B to GPT-3 175B); LocalE gives ~9.6% average relative improvement. Variance across orderings is also substantially reduced; up to ~30% relative improvement on high-variance tasks/models, and +4.9% for GPT-3 175B on CB.
- **ablations**:
> GlobalE vs LocalE comparison (GlobalE > LocalE: 13% vs 9.6% avg relative gain). Top-K selection sweep (Figure 8): K from 1..24, K=24 equals the all-orderings baseline; negative-sloped curves confirm entropy ranks performant orderings well; K=4 chosen for stability though K=1 often works. Robustness across 4 different prompt templates on SST-2 (Tables 3-4): selection helps across templates. Comparison to 'Split Training Set' (Table 5): both GlobalE and LocalE beat splitting the few-shot set into train/dev across all GPT-2 sizes, supporting the true-few-shot claim. Analysis ablations: order sensitivity persists across model sizes, varying number of shots, sample subsets, and label patterns; good orderings are non-transferable across models (low pairwise Spearman, e.g., 0.05 between 2.7B and 175B); calibration (Zhao et al. 2021) raises mean accuracy but leaves variance high.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> No separate intrinsic retrieval metric (no Recall@k/nDCG). The entropy probing score (GlobalE/LocalE) is the internal ranking signal; effectiveness is validated end-to-end via downstream classification accuracy of selected orderings (and via Top-K-vs-accuracy curves), not via a decoupled retrieval-quality metric.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Primarily outcome (final classification accuracy and its variance). Process-level analysis is qualitative/diagnostic (predicted-label distribution balance, calibration, Spearman correlations of orderings) rather than a scored intermediate-process metric.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k selection: k=4 performant orderings kept (out of up to 24). Prompt size constrained by GPT-2's 1024 word-piece context window, hence 4-shot generally, 2-shot for AGNews, 1-shot for DBPedia; probing-set generation capped at 128 tokens. Not budget-adaptive beyond these fixed shot counts.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (not a benchmark paper). For context, evaluation uses subsets of standard validation sets across 11 established classification datasets; an LM-generated artificial 'probing set' is constructed at test time (examples shown in Table 9), with predicted labels discarded.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> GPT-3 / in-context learning (Brown et al. 2020); GPT-2 (Radford et al. 2019); true-few-shot evaluation without a held-out dev set (Perez et al. 2021); contextual calibration (Zhao et al. 2021); prompt/template design work (Shin et al. 2020 AutoPrompt; Gao et al. 2020 LM-BFF; Jiang et al. 2020; Schick & Schutze 2020).
- **contrasts with**:
> Liu et al. 2021 (KATE: kNN demo retrieval over a standard-size training set, which concluded ordering has little effect after relevance retrieval) - this paper, using only a few-shot set without a large pool, reaches the opposite conclusion that order matters greatly. Also contrasts with using a held-out/split validation set for ordering selection (shown inferior to entropy probing) and with template-quality-focused prompt-design work that ignored ordering. Contrasts fine-tuning (order-insensitive, <1% std per Gao et al. 2020) with ICL (highly order-sensitive).
- **lineage**:
> Group A (ICL demonstration retrieval/selection): a foundational ordering-sensitivity work. It establishes few-shot prompt-order sensitivity and introduces an entropy-statistic probing method over an LM-generated artificial dev set to select performant permutations - a precursor/sibling to demonstration-selection and ordering-optimization methods (e.g., later many-shot order-optimization work that critiques GlobalE/LocalE as heuristic).

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- cost_efficiency_tradeoff

<a id="item-selective-annotation-votek"></a>
### 7. Selective Annotation Makes Language Models Better Few-Shot Learners (vote-k)

2022  ·  ICLR 2023  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.01975)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2022
- **venue**: ICLR 2023 (Eleventh International Conference on Learning Representations); preprint arXiv:2209.01975 (submitted 5 Sep 2022). DBLP key conf/iclr/SuKWSWX0OZS023 confirms acceptance at ICLR 2023.
- **authors affiliation**:
> Hongjin Su, Jungo Kasai, Chen Henry Wu, Weijia Shi, Tianlu Wang, Jiayi Xin, Rui Zhang, Mari Ostendorf, Luke Zettlemoyer, Noah A. Smith, Tao Yu. Affiliations: The University of Hong Kong (Su, Yu); University of Washington (Kasai, Shi, Zettlemoyer, Smith, Ostendorf); Allen Institute for AI; Carnegie Mellon University (Wu); Penn State University (Zhang); Meta AI (Wang). Corresponding/lead: Hongjin Su and Tao Yu (HKU).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.01975
- **code url**: https://github.com/HKUNLP/icl-selective-annotation (official; now redirects to https://github.com/xlang-ai/icl-selective-annotation).
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (single-paper author/lab repo; no continuously-updated leaderboard or paper list).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> In-context learning / few-shot demonstration (prompt) retrieval for diverse NLP tasks, with a focus on annotation efficiency. Tasks span classification (paraphrase, sentiment, topic, NLI), commonsense reasoning (multiple-choice), dialogue state tracking, and text/code generation (semantic parsing, open-domain QA, summarization). QA-adjacent; not an agent/tool/embodied setting.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, supervised-budget, single-model (no multi-agent) setting. Departing from prior ICL work that assumes a large fully-annotated training set is available for prompt retrieval, the paper formulates a two-step annotation-efficient framework: (1) selective annotation - before test time, choose a small subset L (size = annotation budget M, e.g. M=18 or 100) from an unlabeled pool X to annotate; (2) prompt retrieval - at test time, retrieve similar in-context examples from the annotated pool L for each test instance. The vote-k selection method itself is UNSUPERVISED (uses Sentence-BERT embeddings plus the inference LM's own prediction confidence on unlabeled data; no labels needed during selection). Supervision enters only when the selected pool is then annotated. The inference LM is frozen (no parameter updates). Selection is deterministic given a fixed unlabeled pool; variance is simulated by subsampling 3K unlabeled instances three times. Two regimes by budget: M=18 (all fit in context, no retrieval step) vs M=100 (similarity-based prompt retrieval at test time).
- **what is retrieved**:
> Demonstrations (annotated input-output training examples) used as in-context prompts. At test time, similar annotated examples are retrieved from the selectively-annotated pool L. (The upstream 'selective annotation' step is itself a selection/coreset procedure that builds the pool, not a per-instance retrieval.)
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus: the fixed selectively-annotated pool L is the retrieval store. It is built offline once (via vote-k selection + annotation) and frozen; it is not a growing/episodic agent memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Two-stage objective. (a) Selective annotation optimizes COVERAGE/representativeness-plus-diversity of the annotated pool (a set-coverage-style goal: pick a diverse, representative subset so many future test instances find a similar demonstration) rather than a fixed top-k ranking. (b) Prompt retrieval at test time is similarity-style top-k ranking (most-similar examples by cosine similarity), with k effectively budget-capped (fill the LM context). It is not framed as recovering a minimal complete tool/demo set.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> Retrieve (yes, similarity-based prompt retrieval from the annotated pool) / Reuse (yes, retrieved demonstrations injected verbatim as in-context exemplars) / Revise (no) / Retain (no). Effectively [Retrieve, Reuse]. The distinctive contribution is the upstream construction of the case base (which cases to annotate), not the CBR adaptation loop.
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False: the work frames itself as in-context learning with selective annotation + prompt retrieval; it does not present itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is conceptually adjacent (building a small high-quality case base for reuse) but not explicitly CBR-grounded.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: Single demonstration (one annotated training input-output pair / example), e.g. an utterance-label pair, a multiple-choice context-continuation, a dialogue-state pair, or an utterance-SQL pair. Granularity = single demo / case (problem-solution).
- **index source**:
> Static corpus, offline-induced. The retrievable store is the selectively-annotated pool L, built offline by the unsupervised graph-based vote-k method (Sentence-BERT embeddings + LM confidence over an unlabeled pool) and then annotated. No online/test-time growth. The unlabeled pool itself is subsampled (3K) from the original training data.
- **index structure topology**:
> Two layers. (1) Selection-time: a directed k-nearest-neighbor GRAPH G=(V,E) over Sentence-BERT embeddings of unlabeled instances (each vertex connects to its k=150 nearest neighbors by cosine similarity), used by the vote-k scoring. (2) Retrieval-time: a flat dense embedding store over the annotated pool L (Sentence-BERT embeddings, cosine-similarity nearest-neighbor lookup). So selection uses a kNN graph; test-time retrieval uses a flat vector index.
- **retriever type**:
> Off-the-shelf dense / similarity retriever (no learned/trained retriever). Sentence-BERT (all-mpnet-base-v2, averaged token embeddings) is used both to build the selection graph and to compute test-time cosine-similarity nearest neighbors. The novelty is in the SELECTION objective (vote-k graph algorithm), not in a learned retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None / off-the-shelf for the retriever itself (frozen Sentence-BERT cosine similarity; no contrastive or RL training of a retriever). However, the SELECTION step uses an unsupervised graph degree score combined with the inference LM's own confidence (average log-probability of the LM's generation over unlabeled instances) to pick diverse, representative examples - i.e. selection is LM-confidence-informed but not a trained retriever and not label-supervised. 'Fast vote-k' drops the LM-confidence component entirely (pure graph score).
- **query construction**: At test time the raw test input is encoded by Sentence-BERT to form the query (no decomposition/expansion/intent-extraction); nearest annotated examples by cosine similarity are retrieved. No query rewriting.
- **query granularity**: Task-level / instance-level, one-shot at t=0: a single query is formed once per test instance; no per-step or trajectory-level re-querying. (When M=18 there is no per-instance query at all - the same 18 selected examples are fixed in the prompt for every test instance.)
- **when to retrieve**: One-shot: retrieval happens once per test instance before generation (only in the M=100 / large-pool regime). In the M=18 regime there is no test-time retrieval - the fixed annotated pool is used directly as the prompt. No iterative or uncertainty-triggered retrieval.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule (retrieve once per test instance, unconditionally, before LM decoding, when a retrieval step is used). No confidence/uncertainty/learned-router trigger at test time. (LM confidence is used only at offline selection time, not as a test-time retrieval trigger.)
- **reranking**: No dedicated reranking stage. Retrieved annotated examples are simply ordered by cosine similarity. (At selection time there is an iterative confidence-bucketing procedure, but that builds the pool, not a test-time rerank.)
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> None beyond similarity ordering and context-budget truncation. As many retrieved examples as fit in the LM's maximum token length are kept (on average 13.4 in-context examples across experiments), concatenated in ASCENDING order of similarity so the most similar example is nearest the test input (exploiting recency bias, Lu et al. 2022). No decomposition, distillation, compression, or distractor filtering.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tools/skills; retrieved units are raw annotated demonstrations).
- **index content separation**: N/A / No: the full demonstration text is both indexed (via Sentence-BERT embedding) and loaded into the prompt; no lightweight-index-then-content progressive-disclosure split.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index or live protocol; static dense store over a fixed annotated pool).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tools; no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation: retrieved (or, at M=18, fixed selected) annotated examples are concatenated as in-context demonstrations before the test input and fed to the frozen inference LM. For classification/multiple-choice the LM scores each candidate label (max average log-probability); for generation it does beam-search decoding. No parameter updates; verbatim exemplar use.
- **planning integration**: One-shot exemplars at inference time (select-then-annotate offline, then retrieve-then-generate). Not interleaved with planning/search; a single retrieval (or fixed prompt) feeds a single decode. No MCTS/tree-search/hierarchical integration.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer / per-instance: a single retrieval (or fixed prompt) feeds one decode of the full output; retrieval is not woven per-CoT-step or per-token.
- **adaptation mechanism**: Verbatim ICL exemplar: retrieved/selected demonstrations are used as-is in the prompt; no explicit case adaptation/revision step.
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw demonstration text: the surface form of each retrieved unit is the concatenation of the annotated example's input and gold output (a raw problem-solution pair), injected directly into the prompt. No distillation into strategies/workflows.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Single demonstration (raw, un-distilled annotated example / problem-solution pair); not a distilled strategy, workflow, or skill.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Stability and outlier-robustness come from the SELECTION design plus similarity retrieval rather than a test-time relevance filter. Vote-k jointly optimizes diversity + representativeness, reducing variance across unlabeled-data subsamples; the paper argues similarity-based prompt retrieval is robust to outliers/small annotation sizes because each test instance retrieves only its most similar examples (evidenced by the random-prompt-retrieval ablation in 4.4 and the outlier-removal finetuning analysis in Appendix E/Table 9). No learned relevance evaluator, self-reflection, or distractor-aware SFT.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (static selectively-annotated pool; no episodic/skill/workflow memory).
- **write back**: False: the system does not store new experiences/cases into memory during deployment; the annotated pool is fixed after offline selection + annotation.
- **online growth**: No: the annotated pool / index is frozen after offline construction; it does not grow at test time.
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back; the annotated pool is static after offline selection).
- **failure experience usage**:
> Not used as deployment memory. The selection procedure uses the inference LM's confidence (average log-probability) over unlabeled instances to bucket and diversify the pool, but it does not store labeled failures/negatives as a contrastive memory; selection is unsupervised and there is no success/failure trajectory store.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A / append-only-none: the annotated pool is built once and never mutated after annotation.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No: neither selection nor retrieval is an RL/value-based learned policy. Selection is a deterministic graph + LM-confidence heuristic (vote-k); test-time retrieval is fixed top-k by off-the-shelf Sentence-BERT cosine similarity.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No: single-model, single private annotated pool / retriever. (Cross-LM transfer is studied descriptively - the same selected pool is evaluated with GPT-Neo 2.7B, GPT-J 6B, GPT-3 175B, OPT-175B, Codex - but there is no shared multi-agent memory.)

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> 10 datasets across 9 tasks: MRPC (paraphrase detection), SST-5 (sentiment), DBpedia (topic classification), MNLI (NLI), RTE (NLI), HellaSwag (commonsense multiple-choice), MWoZ 2.4 (dialogue state tracking), GeoQuery (semantic parsing / text-to-SQL), NQ / Natural Questions (open-domain QA), XSUM (summarization). Domain-shift analysis adds two WILDS datasets: CivilComments (toxicity) and Amazon (review classification), each with random vs domain splits.
- **benchmark family**:
> Primarily classic NLP/QA: classification + NLI (GLUE-style: MRPC, MNLI, RTE, SST-5, DBpedia), commonsense reasoning (HellaSwag), dialogue (MWoZ), semantic parsing/code (GeoQuery), open-domain QA (NQ), summarization (XSUM), plus distribution-shift (WILDS: CivilComments, Amazon). Not in the agent/web/embodied/tool benchmark families; closest normalized grouping is QA + classification/NLI (GLUE) with some structured generation.
- **baselines**:
> (1) Selective-annotation baselines (the core comparison): RANDOM selection (averaged over 3 trials), Maximizing Facility Location (MFL; Lin & Bilmes 2009, submodular greedy, representativeness), Diversity (max embedding diversity), Least-confidence (Lewis & Gale 1994, active learning), and Fast vote-k (vote-k without the LM-confidence step). (2) Prompt-retrieval baseline: Random prompt retrieval vs similarity-based retrieval (Liu et al. 2022). (3) Paradigm baseline: supervised finetuning of strong PLMs - RoBERTa-large for MRPC and HellaSwag, DS2-T5 (Shin et al. 2022) for MWoZ - under FT-random and FT-vote-k.
- **key metrics**:
> Accuracy for classification and multiple-choice; joint accuracy (Budzianowski et al. 2018) for MWoZ dialogue state tracking; test-suite accuracy (Zhong et al. 2020) for GeoQuery; exact match (Rajpurkar et al. 2016) for NQ; ROUGE-L (Lin 2004) for XSUM. Aggregate reporting uses average absolute gain and relative gain over random selection; stability via min/max across 3 trials.
- **headline result**:
> Averaged over 10 datasets, vote-k selective annotation beats random selection by +5.2 absolute / +11.4% relative at an annotation budget of 100, and by +5.8 absolute / +12.9% relative at budget 18 (where no prompt retrieval is needed). In-context learning with only 18 vote-k-selected examples beats 100 randomly selected examples on 6/10 tasks, and matches strong supervised finetuning with 10-100x less annotation cost (e.g. finetuning needs ~1000 examples on HellaSwag and ~800 on MWoZ to match vote-k at 18-100).
- **ablations**:
> 1) Main Table 2: vote-k vs random at L=18 and L=100 across all 10 datasets (consistent gains, e.g. MRPC 63.5->70.7, SST-5 44.2->53.0, MNLI 37.4->47.3, HellaSwag 65.2->70.7, MWoZ 47.2->51.4 at L=100). 2) ICL vs finetuning (4.1, Fig.2): ICL-vote-k > finetuning of SOTA PLMs; selective annotation helps ICL but NOT finetuning (consistent with active-learning-vs-finetuning literature), attributed to outliers/instability; Appendix E/Table 9 shows removing 10% outliers lets finetuning benefit from vote-k. 3) Model size (4.2, Fig.3): gains larger for smaller models (HellaSwag: +7.5 with GPT-Neo 2.7B vs +2.6 with GPT-3), but consistent across GPT-Neo/GPT-J/GPT-3/OPT-175B. 4) Domain shift (4.3, Table 3, WILDS): vote-k gain larger under domain splits (CivilComments +9.9 domain vs +5.5 random; Amazon +8.3 domain vs +6.0 random). 5) Random prompt retrieval (4.4, Table 4): with random (not similarity) retrieval, vote-k no longer beats random selection (HellaSwag 62.5 vs 63.2) - selection + similarity retrieval are jointly necessary. 6) Alternative selection methods (4.5, Table 5): vote-k > Fast vote-k > Least-confidence/Diversity > MFL > Random (e.g. HellaSwag 70.7 vote-k vs 65.2 random; Fast vote-k 69.5 with 10x+ speedup). 7) Diversity/representativeness analysis (Appendix F, Table 10): vote-k selected sets score higher on DIV-I, DIV-F, and REPR. than random.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> No: only end-to-end downstream task metrics are reported (accuracy / joint accuracy / test-suite accuracy / EM / ROUGE-L). No intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k/nDCG). The closest decoupled diagnostics are the diversity/representativeness measurements of the SELECTED pool (Appendix F), not retrieval recall.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome (final task accuracy/score). Process-style diagnostics are added: stability (min/max over 3 unlabeled subsamples), diversity/representativeness scores of selected sets, and the random-vs-similar retrieval decomposition, but these characterize the selection/retrieval pipeline rather than scoring intermediate reasoning steps.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Annotation efficiency is the central thesis: vote-k matches SOTA finetuning with 10-100x less annotation (e.g. finetuning needs ~800-1000 labels to match vote-k at 18-100); 18 vote-k examples beat 100 random examples on 6/10 tasks. Compute trade-off: full vote-k runs the inference LM over all unlabeled instances to compute confidence (expensive); 'Fast vote-k' drops this for a 10x+ speedup with near-identical accuracy. Test-time retrieval is a single cheap Sentence-BERT nearest-neighbor lookup; on average 13.4 demonstrations are fed per prompt. No explicit dollar/latency numbers; GPT-J 6B is the default ICL model for budget reasons, Codex-davinci-002 for MWoZ/GeoQuery/NQ.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Two budgets. (a) Annotation budget M (the labeled pool size): main experiments use M in {18, 100}; analysis uses {18, 100, 300, 800} (and up to ~1000 for the finetuning comparison). M=18 is chosen because all 18 examples fit in the LM context (no retrieval needed). (b) Prompt context: at M=100, retrieve as many similar examples as fit within the LM's max token length (avg 13.4 in-context examples), ordered ascending by similarity. Vote-k hyperparameters: k=150 nearest neighbors, rho=10 (the discount exponent rho>1 penalizing closeness to already-selected examples); 9M/10 confidence buckets used in the second phase.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (method paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A (uses existing benchmarks rather than constructing a new one). Selection is performed over a 3K-instance unlabeled subsample of each dataset's training split (resampled 3x for stability); evaluation uses standard test splits where public (SST-5, XSUM, MWoZ, DBpedia) and dev splits otherwise, following prior work.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> In-context learning / prompt retrieval: Liu et al. 2022 (KATE, similarity-based demonstration retrieval) and Rubin et al. 2022 (EPR, learned prompt retrieval) for the prompt-retrieval step; Brown et al. 2020 (GPT-3) for the ICL paradigm. Embeddings: Sentence-BERT (Reimers & Gurevych 2019, all-mpnet-base-v2). Selection/active-learning lineage: facility location (Lin & Bilmes 2009), least-confidence active learning (Lewis & Gale 1994). LMs used: GPT-J (Wang & Komatsuzaki 2021), GPT-Neo (Black et al. 2021), GPT-3 (Brown et al. 2020), OPT-175B (Zhang et al. 2022), Codex (Chen et al. 2021). Recency-bias ordering from Lu et al. 2022.
- **contrasts with**:
> Recent ICL methods that assume a LARGE fully-annotated training set is available for retrieval (Liu et al. 2022 KATE; Rubin et al. 2022 EPR) - this work instead minimizes total annotation cost via a two-step framework. Active-learning / coreset selection baselines for supervised finetuning (facility location/MFL, diversity, least-confidence) - vote-k beats them for ICL, and active learning is shown ineffective for finetuning (Karamcheti et al. 2021; D'Arcy & Downey 2022). Supervised finetuning of strong PLMs (RoBERTa-large, DS2-T5) - ICL-vote-k matches/beats them at far lower annotation cost. Random selection and random prompt retrieval.
- **lineage**:
> Group A (ICL demonstration retrieval). A foundational 2022/ICLR-2023 work that reframes demonstration retrieval around ANNOTATION EFFICIENCY: it adds an upstream unsupervised graph-based selective-annotation stage (vote-k) before the now-standard similarity-based prompt retrieval (KATE/EPR), establishing the select-pool-then-retrieve paradigm. Sits between unsupervised similarity retrieval (KATE) and learned demonstration retrievers (EPR, CEIL, UDR, LLM-R), and connects ICL demonstration selection to the active-learning/coreset-selection literature.

<a id="item-ceil"></a>
### 8. CEIL (Compositional Exemplars for In-context Learning)

2023  ·  ICML 2023  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.05698)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2023
- **venue**: ICML 2023 (Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR v202)
- **authors affiliation**:
> Jiacheng Ye, Zhiyong Wu, Jiangtao Feng, Tao Yu, Lingpeng Kong. Affiliations (per PMLR v202): (1) Department of Computer Science, The University of Hong Kong (Jiacheng Ye, Tao Yu, Lingpeng Kong); (2) Shark-NLP, Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (Zhiyong Wu, Jiangtao Feng).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.05698
- **code url**: https://github.com/HKUNLP/icl-ceil

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> In-context demonstration retrieval / exemplar selection for NLP in-context learning (ICL), spanning text classification (sentiment analysis, paraphrase detection, NLI, commonsense reasoning) and generation (open-domain QA, code generation, semantic parsing). Not an agent/planning task.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, non-interactive, single-pass in-context example selection. A frozen black-box LM performs ICL; the goal is to select a subset of K demonstrations from a training set (index) to maximize the LM's likelihood of the correct answer for a given test input. Supervision is the LM's own score over candidate subsets (no human labels for the optimal subset). The retriever (a learnable conditional-DPP / metric-learning encoder) is trained offline per task; at inference the LM weights are never updated.
- **what is retrieved**: demos (in-context examples, i.e., input-output exemplar pairs from the training set), selected jointly as a SUBSET rather than independently.
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus: the retrievable store is the task's fixed training set (deduplicated). No growing/episodic agent memory is written; the store is frozen.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Subset-completeness oriented rather than independent top-k: in-context example selection is recast as a SUBSET selection problem, modeling the joint probability of the whole exemplar set with a conditional DPP and selecting via MAP inference to jointly optimize relevance and inter-example diversity (compositional coverage). K is still a fixed budget per task, but the selection objective is set-level (det of the kernel sub-matrix) not per-item top-k.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not framed as CBR; only a Retrieve-then-Reuse pattern would apply: Retrieve = yes, Reuse = verbatim ICL exemplars, Revise = no, Retain = no).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. CEIL does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it frames demo selection as DPP subset selection / metric learning.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: single demonstration (input-output example) as the atomic item, but the retrieved/selected unit is a SUBSET (set) of such demonstrations jointly modeled by a conditional DPP.
- **index source**: Static corpus: the task training set, deduplicated (truncated to ~44,000 instances following Rubin et al. 2022 to reduce scoring cost). Offline-induced; not online/test-time-induced.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat vector index over training-set examples encoded by a learnable BERT-based dual encoder (dot-product kernel). A two-stage scheme is used: a KNN/dense retriever first narrows N candidates to n (e.g., n=100), then the DPP kernel (PSD matrix L over those candidates) defines set probabilities; no graph or hierarchy.
- **retriever type**:
> Learned dense retriever instantiated as a conditional Determinantal Point Process (DPP) with learnable BERT-based embedders (metric learning); dot-product (linear) kernel as relevance/similarity function. Initialized from EPR. Baselines include BM25 (sparse), TopK-BERT/Contriever/SimCSE (off-the-shelf dense), DPP-BERT (DPP on frozen BERT), and EPR (learned).
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Downstream-task-effectiveness / LM-preference via contrastive learning. Each sampled candidate subset is scored by the frozen inference LM as s_ij = P_LM(y_i | S_ij, x_i) (probability of the correct answer given the subset). A fine-grained pair-wise margin (ranking) loss trains the DPP so that 'better' subsets get higher det-probability than 'worse' ones; margin is scaled by the LM-score rank difference. (InfoNCE is also studied as an alternative loss.) No RL.
- **query construction**:
> Raw test input is encoded by the input embedder; the conditioned (relevance-modulated) DPP kernel is L_tilde = Diag(r) L Diag(r) where r_i = g(a_i, x) is the relevance of candidate i to the test input x. Candidate examples are encoded by concatenating all instance texts except labels.
- **query granularity**: task-level (one-shot at t=0): a single retrieval/selection of the exemplar subset per test input before generation; no iterative or step-level querying.
- **when to retrieve**: one-shot: select the exemplar subset once per test instance, then the frozen LM generates the answer in a single pass.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule (always retrieve once per test input before inference); no confidence/uncertainty-triggered or learned-router triggering.
- **reranking**:
> MAP inference acts as a joint selection/ranking step: after a KNN retriever narrows N to n candidates, an exact greedy DPP-MAP algorithm (O(nK) per iteration via incremental Cholesky updates) greedily selects K examples by maximal incremental log-det gain, jointly balancing relevance and diversity. This effectively replaces top-k with a set-level DPP rerank/selection (DPP-MAP vs TOPK is ablated, Table 6).
- **retrieved context refinement**: Selected exemplars are sorted by similarity to the input in ascending order before being concatenated into the prompt (common practice); otherwise no decomposition/compression/distillation. The DPP diversity term itself reduces redundancy/distractors within the selected set.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tools).
- **index content separation**: N/A (full example texts are both indexed and loaded; two-stage KNN->DPP narrows candidates for efficiency but not an index/content separation).
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tools / no live index).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tools).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation: the selected exemplar subset is concatenated as the in-context demonstration prompt for a frozen black-box LM (GPT-Neo 2.7B primarily; also GPT2-XL 1.5B and Codex 175B). For classification, tasks are reframed as multiple choice (compare LM likelihood of each labeled option); for generation, greedy decoding. The LM-score over subsets is also used as the training signal for the retriever.
- **planning integration**: N/A for planning/acting; integration is one-shot exemplars at prediction time (retrieve-then-predict). Not embedded in any search/MCTS or multi-step plan.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: per-answer: a single retrieval feeds one LM forward pass per test instance; no per-step or per-token interleaving.
- **adaptation mechanism**: verbatim ICL exemplar (retrieved examples are used as-is in the prompt; no case adaptation/revision).
- **retrieved item representation**: raw demonstrations (input-output example pairs) injected verbatim as prompt text; for classification, candidate label names are appended as options.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: raw single demonstrations (concrete input-output examples), but selected as a composed set; not distilled strategies, rules, workflows, or programs.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Retriever-aware training (contrastive learning aligns embeddings/DPP-score with actual LM usefulness) plus the DPP diversity term that suppresses redundant/overlapping exemplars; selecting a compact, mutually-diverse subset reduces uninformative/duplicate context. No explicit self-reflection or distractor-filtering module.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (static training-set index; no episodic/skill/workflow memory).
- **write back**: False. The system does not store new experiences/cases/skills; the retriever is trained offline and the index is the frozen training set.
- **online growth**: False. The retrievable store does not grow during deployment/test-time; it is frozen after offline induction.
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back).
- **failure experience usage**: No explicit storage of failed experiences. Training uses a contrastive pair-wise margin over candidate subsets ranked by LM score, so relatively 'worse' (lower-LM-score) subsets serve as negatives within the contrastive loss, but failures are not retained in any memory.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (no memory; store is append-free/static after offline construction).
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Partially: subset selection is a LEARNED conditional-DPP scorer trained by contrastive LM-preference (metric learning), and selection uses DPP-MAP greedy inference rather than fixed similarity top-k. It is not an RL/value-based policy (no M-MDP or Q-learning); the learned object is a DPP probability model over subsets.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> No multi-agent sharing. However the paper demonstrates transferability: a retriever trained for one LM (e.g., GPT-Neo) transfers to other LMs (GPT2-XL, Codex), and a retriever trained on one dataset partially transfers to related datasets (e.g., across NLI tasks, and among code/semantic-parsing tasks).

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: 12 datasets across 7 NLP tasks: SST-5, MRPC, QNLI, MNLI, CMSQA (CommonsenseQA), HellaSwag, WebQs, GeoQuery, NL2Bash, Break, MTOP, SMCalFlow. Compositional splits: GeoQuery (Standard/Template/TMCD/Length) and SMCalFlow-CS (0-S, 0-C, 8-C, 16-C, 32-C).
- **benchmark family**:
> QA / NLU+generation: sentiment (SST-5), paraphrase (MRPC), NLI (QNLI, MNLI), commonsense reasoning (CMSQA, HellaSwag), open-domain QA (WebQs), code generation (GeoQuery, NL2Bash), semantic parsing (Break, MTOP, SMCalFlow). Not agent/web/embodied/tool benchmarks. Includes compositional-generalization splits.
- **baselines**:
> Learning-free: RANDOM, TOPK-BM25, TOPK-BERT, DPP-BERT, TOPK-CONTRIEVER, TOPK-SIMCSE. Learning-based: EPR (Rubin et al. 2022, singleton example scorer). Compositional comparisons (Table 3): T5-Base+CSL-Aug (Qiu et al. 2022a), Cover-LS (Levy et al. 2022), PaLM 540B and PaLM 540B (Oracle) (Qiu et al. 2022b).
- **key metrics**: Accuracy for classification tasks; Exact Match (EM) for WebQs/GeoQuery/NL2Bash/MTOP/SMCalFlow; LF-EM for Break. Also MRR of top-K candidates (training-data construction ablation) and retrieval latency (seconds).
- **headline result**:
> Using GPT-Neo 2.7B as inferencer, CEIL achieves an average of 56.76 across the 12 datasets vs 53.37 for EPR (the strongest learned baseline), a +3.39 absolute average gain (state-of-the-art over all baselines); especially strong on NLI (>20% absolute over learning-free baselines, e.g., QNLI 85.41 and MNLI 71.74).
- **ablations**:
> (1) Inference algorithm (Table 6): DPP-MAP vs TOPK on BERT/EPR/CEIL; DPP-MAP helps more for learned retrievers (DPP-CEIL avg gains over TOPK-CEIL), showing the value of aligning embedding similarity to LM usefulness. (2) Initialization & loss (Table 5): EPR-init >> BERT-init; pair-wise margin loss beats InfoNCE notably on generation tasks (~+4% GeoQuery, ~+6% MTOP). (3) Training-data construction (Table 4): TOP100+RAND sampling with C=50 candidates best; k-DPP sampling worse. (4) Number of in-context examples (Fig 3 Left): classification benefits from fewer/compact sets; CEIL matches EPR/TOPK-BERT-with-32-examples using merely ~4 / ~1 example. (5) Trade-off factor lambda (Fig 3 Right): diversity matters more for harder tasks (NLI, semantic parsing), relevance more for simpler tasks (sentiment). (6) Transferability across LMs and datasets (Fig 2).
- **evaluation decoupling**: Mostly end-to-end task metrics. Intrinsic retrieval quality is reported in a limited way (MRR of top-K candidates in the training-data construction ablation, Table 4) but not as a primary decoupled Recall@k/nDCG evaluation; main results are downstream task accuracy/EM.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Primarily outcome metrics (final task accuracy/EM/LF-EM). Some process-oriented signals: MRR of candidate ranking and compositional-split performance, but no reasoning-faithfulness or step-wise process scoring.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> DPP-MAP adds negligible latency over KNN top-k because n and K are small (e.g., n=100, K=16); measured retrieval latency for 50 in-context examples on SST5 is 30s (TOPK) vs 36s (DPP-MAP), ~1.2x. The pair-wise ranking loss avoids computing the O(N^3) DPP normalization det(L+I). Training: 30 epochs, batch 128, lr 1e-5 on 2x NVIDIA A100 GPUs; greedy DPP-MAP is O(nK) per iteration via incremental Cholesky. Compactness benefit: CEIL matches 32-example baselines using ~1-4 examples, cutting quadratic attention cost.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k budget capped by LM context length: nominal 50 in-context examples, truncated to the LM max context (1,024 for GPT2-XL, 2,048 for GPT-Neo, 8,001 for Codex), giving average #ICE per task ~22-50 (e.g., SST-5 40, MRPC 27, SMCalFlow 22). Candidate narrowing n (e.g., 100) then DPP-MAP greedily selects K (e.g., 16 during training subsets).
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (uses existing datasets, not a newly constructed benchmark; dataset sizes are reported in Table 1, e.g., MNLI 392,568 train, SMCalFlow 102,491 train).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> EPR (Rubin et al. 2022, Efficient Prompt Retrieval / learning-to-retrieve singleton in-context examples via contrastive LM-feedback) which CEIL extends from single-example to set-level selection and uses as encoder initialization; Determinantal Point Processes (Kulesza & Taskar; Chen et al. 2018 greedy MAP); KATE / kNN dense demo retrieval (Liu et al. 2022).
- **contrasts with**:
> EPR and other independent top-k demo retrievers (TOPK-BERT/BM25/Contriever/SimCSE) that select examples independently without modeling inter-example interaction; Cover-LS (Levy et al. 2022) which uses a specially-trained subphrase predictor + task-specific DPP diversity not aligned with the LM; compositional data-augmentation methods (Qiu et al. 2022a CSL-Aug); multi-pass ICL aggregation methods (Shi et al. 2022; Li et al. 2022) which need multiple test-time inferences.
- **lineage**:
> Group A (ICL demonstration retrieval): a learning-based, set-level demonstration retriever that advances the lineage from heuristic/similarity top-k selection (KATE) -> learned singleton retrieval (EPR) -> learned compositional subset retrieval (CEIL via conditional DPP + contrastive LM preference), establishing joint relevance+diversity demo selection.

<a id="item-self-adaptive-icl"></a>
### 9. Self-Adaptive In-Context Learning: An Information Compression Perspective for In-Context Example Selection and Ordering

2023  ·  ACL 2023  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10375)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2023
- **venue**: ACL 2023 (Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the ACL, Volume 1: Long Papers, pp. 1423-1436). First posted to arXiv Dec 2022 (arXiv:2212.10375).
- **authors affiliation**: Zhiyong Wu (Shanghai AI Lab), Yaoxiang Wang (Xiamen University), Jiacheng Ye (The University of Hong Kong), Lingpeng Kong (The University of Hong Kong). Equal contribution among Wu/Wang/Ye; Wu led the project.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10375
- **code url**: https://github.com/Shark-NLP/self-adaptive-ICL
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (single-paper repo, last pushed 2023-05-05, ~45 stars, not a maintained leaderboard/paper list)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: QA / NLP classification and reasoning: in-context-learning (ICL) demonstration selection and ordering for text classification (sentiment, topic), natural language inference, and multi-choice commonsense QA.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-model, single-turn ICL with a frozen causal PLM (no parameter updates). The goal is per-test-instance ('self-adaptive') selection AND ordering of k in-context examples, framed as an NP-hard combinatorial optimization / search problem. A key assumption is that NO labeled validation set is required at test time (validation-free); only an unlabeled annotated retrieval pool of candidate examples is available. Supervision: none for the selection/ranking algorithm itself (the retrieval pool provides labeled exemplars but the ranker is unsupervised). Contrasted explicitly with corpus-level methods that pick one universal prompt for all test samples.
- **what is retrieved**: In-context demonstrations (labeled input-output examples) from an annotated candidate/training pool, then organized (selected and permuted) per test sample.
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus: a fixed annotated pool of labeled training examples. No growing/episodic memory is written; the pool is frozen.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed-size selection (top-k / fixed candidate-set then fixed-size organization, e.g. 8 examples per prompt). Not a completeness or precision-driven variable-size objective; the contribution is ranking/ordering of fixed-k organizations rather than recovering a minimal complete set.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based-reasoning method). At most realizes a Retrieve phase (no Reuse-as-adaptation, Revise, or Retain).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: false. The paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is grounded in information theory (MDL) and ICL example-selection literature.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: Single demonstration (a labeled input-output example); the operative unit for ranking is an 'organization' = an ordered set/permutation of k single demos.
- **index source**: Static corpus (annotated training/retrieval pool); offline-fixed. No online or test-time induction of the store; the pool is built once and frozen. Selection (e.g. TopK candidates) is computed per test sample at inference but the underlying store does not grow.
- **index structure topology**: Flat vector index over example embeddings (semantic-similarity nearest-neighbor search via a sentence encoder). VoteK adds diversity-aware graph-style penalization and DPP imposes a determinantal-set structure, but the base index is flat dense.
- **retriever type**: Two-stage: (1) selection module is dense embedding-based nearest-neighbor (TopK), or diversity-aware variants VoteK and DPP; (2) ranking module is LLM-as-scorer (the frozen PLM itself scores candidate organizations via an MDL/codelength criterion). No learned/trained retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None (off-the-shelf). The selection retriever uses fixed semantic similarity (and optionally diversity heuristics). The ranking criterion is an unsupervised information-theoretic objective (Minimum Description Length / codelength, instantiated as the entropy of the PLM's predictive distribution over labels) computed from the frozen PLM's own confidence — no contrastive training, no LM-feedback fine-tuning, no RL, no downstream-label supervision.
- **query construction**: Raw test input x is used directly as the query for nearest-neighbor selection. For ranking, each candidate organization c is concatenated with the test input and scored by the PLM; the 'query' for MDL is the model's predictive distribution p(y_i | c, x) over candidate labels.
- **query granularity**: Task/instance-level, one-shot at t=0 (a single per-test-sample query for selection and a single per-test-sample ranking pass; no step-wise or trajectory-level retrieval).
- **when to retrieve**: One-shot: a single selection + ranking pass per test instance before generating the prediction. No iterative or uncertainty-triggered re-retrieval during decoding.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule (always retrieve once per test sample). No dynamic trigger.
- **reranking**:
> Yes. The core contribution is the ranking (rerank) stage: after the selection module returns a small candidate set, a window of W candidate organizations (default 10 sampled permutations of 8 examples drawn from ~30 retrieved candidates) is reranked by the MDL/codelength criterion; the lowest-codelength (minimum-entropy) organization is chosen. It is an LLM-confidence-based reranker, not a trained cross-encoder.
- **retrieved context refinement**: Rerank (MDL-based selection of the best organization among sampled permutations). No decomposition, distillation, distractor filtering, or compression of the demonstration content itself.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tools; demonstrations are raw labeled examples wrapped in task templates, not engineered tool descriptions).
- **index content separation**: N/A (no lightweight-index-then-content separation; embeddings index the same examples used as content).
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index or integration protocol).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tools; no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**: Prompt augmentation: the chosen organization (ordered concatenation of input-output examples wrapped in a template) is prepended to the test input as the ICL context; the frozen PLM then generates/scores the label. No training signal, no skill reuse, no latent injection.
- **planning integration**: One-shot exemplars at plan/prediction time. No planning, tree search, or interleaving; retrieval+ranking happens once, then a single forward pass produces the answer.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer (one retrieval-and-rank pass per final prediction; no CoT-step or token-level interleaving).
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (no case adaptation; retrieved examples are used as verbatim ICL exemplars without revision).
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw input-output demonstration pairs wrapped in a task template (verbatim ICL exemplars). No distillation into strategies/guidelines/programs.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw single demonstrations (concrete labeled examples), assembled into a raw ordered exemplar sequence; no abstraction into distilled strategy/workflow/skill.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Implicit via the MDL/minimum-entropy ranking objective, which selects the organization making the PLM most confident, thereby down-weighting organizations that produce a flat/uncertain (noisy) predictive distribution. Diversity-aware selection (VoteK, DPP) also reduces redundant/biased candidates. No retriever-aware training, self-reflection module, or distractor-aware SFT.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (static annotated retrieval pool; no episodic/skill/workflow memory).
- **write back**: false. No new experiences/cases/skills are written back; the candidate pool is fixed.
- **online growth**: No. The retrievable store does not grow during deployment/test time; it is frozen after the annotated pool is fixed.
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back mechanism).
- **failure experience usage**: Not applicable / none stored. The method does not store failed or negative experiences. (Note: a separate analysis section studies the effect of corrupting demonstration labels on accuracy, but this is diagnostic, not a stored-failure-retrieval mechanism.)
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (no memory entries are written or mutated; the pool is append-free and frozen).
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No. Selection is fixed similarity/diversity heuristics (TopK/VoteK/DPP) and ranking is a fixed unsupervised MDL criterion; neither is an RL-/value-learned policy. The paper explicitly leaves learned selection (e.g. Rubin et al. 2022 EPR) as future work to close the gap to finetuning.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-model, single-instance use; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: Eight NLP datasets: SST-2 and SST-5 (sentiment classification); SNLI, MNLI, QNLI (natural language inference); CommonsenseQA / CMS QA (multi-choice commonsense QA); TREC and AgNews (topic classification).
- **benchmark family**: QA / NLP-classification (sentiment + topic classification, natural language inference, multi-choice commonsense QA). Not an agentic/web/embodied/tool benchmark; these are GLUE-style and SST/TREC/AgNews/CommonsenseQA classification tasks.
- **baselines**:
> Three groups. Prompting (zero-shot, no in-context examples). Corpus-level: Random, Random&Validation, MI / Mutual Information (Sorensen et al. 2022, validation-free), GlobalE (Lu et al. 2022, needs validation set). Instance-level: Random (8 random examples per test sample), TopK (Liu et al. 2022), Majority vote (over 8 TopK-retrieved examples), TopK+LocalE (Lu et al. 2022). Proposed: TopK+MDL (Ours).
- **key metrics**: Accuracy (classification accuracy averaged over 3 random seeds). Also reports average MDL/codelength per method (intrinsic ranking-criterion value) and an oracle upper-bound accuracy.
- **headline result**:
> TopK+MDL (Ours) achieves an average accuracy of 60.16 over the eight datasets, a 40% relative improvement over the common-practice Random baseline (corpus-level Random AVG 42.78 / instance-level Random AVG 43.06); and ~17% relative improvement over the instance-level TopK+LocalE baseline (AVG 51.36).
- **ablations**:
> Multiple analyses: (1) Selection-method comparison — TopK vs VoteK vs DPP; TopK best on average for small-label-space classification, but VoteK/DPP outperform TopK on large-label-space CommonsenseQA. (2) Ranking accuracy vs an oracle (if any of the sampled organizations yields the correct answer): large gap between oracle and TopK+MDL, motivating better rankers/supervised retrieval. (3) Window size W (number of permutations ranked per sample) from 2 to 50: accuracy steadily increases with W (even W=2 gives +3.19 acc on SST-2 over TopK), trading efficiency for effectiveness. (4) Number of in-context examples N from 0 to 32: increasing N helps on average; Random plateaus at N=8 while organization matters. (5) Model scale (OPT 350M to 175B): larger is not always better (plateau on simple tasks; 30B beats 175B on SNLI) but the method improves consistently over baselines at all scales. (6) Generality across PLMs and across prompt templates: consistently beats TopK. (7) Average MDL table showing lower codelength correlates with higher accuracy. (8) Label-corruption / bias-rate analysis on the role of labels.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Partially. The paper reports the intrinsic ranking criterion (average MDL/codelength per method) and an oracle ranking-accuracy upper bound separately from end-to-end task accuracy, but does not report standard Recall@k/nDCG retrieval metrics (the selection retriever is off-the-shelf).
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Primarily outcome (final task accuracy). Process-side signals reported are the average MDL/codelength of organizations and an oracle upper bound on ranking quality, used to argue that the ranker is the bottleneck.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Explicitly discussed as an efficiency-effectiveness trade-off: the ranking window size W equals the number of forward passes over the test set (W=50 means 50x inference forward passes), so larger W boosts accuracy but multiplies inference cost. Default W=10. Selection reduces the combinatorial search space (e.g. 8-of-10 permutations = A(10,8) ~ 1.8M choices) by retrieving ~30 candidates and sampling 10 permutations to rank. No latency-in-seconds or API-dollar numbers reported.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k: default 8 in-context examples per organization; selection retrieves ~30 nearest candidates, then a window of W=10 randomly sampled 8-example permutations is reranked by MDL and the best chosen (reranked-then-selected, fixed-k). N varied 0-32 and W varied 2-50 in ablations. No explicit token-budget cap.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (research method paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A (uses existing public datasets, not a newly constructed benchmark). Dataset splits are documented (e.g. SST-2 6920/872/1821; SNLI 550152/10000/10000; AgNews 120000/0/7600; CMS QA 9471/1221/1140); for datasets with restricted test access (MNLI, QNLI, CMS QA) a 10% held-out training subset is used for corpus-level validation and results are reported on the validation set.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> TopK semantic-similarity demonstration retrieval (Liu et al. 2022, 'What makes good in-context examples for GPT-3?'); VoteK selective annotation (Su et al. 2022); determinantal point processes / k-DPP (Kulesza & Taskar 2011) for diverse selection; Minimum Description Length principle (Grunwald 2007) and Solomonoff's theory of inductive inference (1964); description-length-of-deep-learning view (Blier & Ollivier 2018); ICL-as-implicit-Bayesian-inference (Xie et al. 2021).
- **contrasts with**:
> Corpus-level prompt/order search methods: GlobalE / LocalE (Lu et al. 2022, 'Fantastically ordered prompts'), Mutual Information prompt selection (Sorensen et al. 2022). Contrasted because those operate at corpus level (one universal prompt for all samples), suffer majority bias, and (GlobalE) require a labeled validation set, whereas this work is per-instance and validation-free. Also contrasts with template-search methods (Gao et al. 2021 LM-BFF, AutoPrompt/Shin et al. 2020, RLPrompt/Deng et al. 2022) that search templates rather than example organization. Positioned against learned-retrieval (Rubin et al. 2022 EPR) as a future complement.
- **lineage**:
> Group A (ICL demonstration retrieval). An early (2022/2023) instance-level, training-free demonstration selection-AND-ordering method that introduces an information-compression (MDL) criterion; a predecessor in the lineage of per-query demonstration organization that later learned/RL-based demonstration retrievers build upon.

<a id="item-udr"></a>
### 10. UDR (Unified Demonstration Retriever for In-Context Learning)

2023  ·  ACL 2023  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.04320)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2023
- **venue**: ACL 2023 (Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, Volume 1: Long Papers, pages 4644-4668)
- **authors affiliation**:
> Xiaonan Li, Kai Lv, Hang Yan, Tianyang Lin, Wei Zhu, Yuan Ni, Guotong Xie, Xiaoling Wang, Xipeng Qiu. Primary affiliation: Fudan University (Shanghai Key Laboratory of Intelligent Information Processing / School of Computer Science); also East China Normal University and Pingan Health Tech. Corresponding authors: Hang Yan / Tianyang Lin and Xipeng Qiu.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.04320
- **code url**: https://github.com/KaiLv69/UDR

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: NLP in-context learning (ICL) demonstration retrieval spanning classification, multi-choice, NLI, semantic parsing, summarization, code summarization, data-to-text, text simplification, story/commonsense generation; QA-style and generation tasks. Not agent/planning/tool-use.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-turn (non-interactive) in-context learning: given a test input x_test, retrieve a few relevant labeled (input,output) demonstrations from an annotated training set D_train of the same task so a frozen inference LM conditions on them and directly outputs the prediction. Supervision is available as ground-truth training labels, and the training signal is the inference LM's feedback (conditional likelihood of the gold output given a candidate demonstration). Single-agent, no environment interaction. The goal is a SINGLE multi-task retriever covering 30+ tasks instead of one task-specific retriever per task.
- **what is retrieved**: Demonstrations (labeled input-output example pairs {x', y'}) drawn from the task's training set.
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus: the (frozen) annotated training set of each task serves as the demonstration pool indexed with FAISS at inference time. No growing/episodic memory written during deployment.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k ranking objective: retriever ranks training examples by learned similarity and selects the top demonstrations (k determined by LM context budget for generation tasks, fixed k=8 for classification/multi-choice). The training objective is list-wise ranking (LambdaRank-style) over candidates, not minimal-set completeness or precision-driven variable-size selection.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: Retrieve only (Reuse=verbatim ICL exemplar injection but no explicit case adaptation; no Revise; no Retain). Effective flags: [Retrieve: yes, Reuse: partial/verbatim, Revise: no, Retain: no]
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The paper frames itself as demonstration retrieval for in-context learning and list-wise ranking from LM feedback; it does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner or frame itself as case-based reasoning.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: Single demonstration (a problem-solution / input-output example pair) from the training set.
- **index source**: Static corpus, offline-induced: each task's training set is encoded offline by the demonstration encoder E_d after training; candidates for training are mined iteratively offline (BM25/Elasticsearch initialization then retriever-self-mining). No online/test-time growth.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat dense vector index per task (FAISS over the task's training-set embeddings). Task identity is handled by prepending a task instruction to each example before encoding (context/metadata-keyed) rather than a separate structural index; each task has its own flat index searched at inference.
- **retriever type**: Learned dense bi-encoder (DPR-style, two BERT-base-uncased encoders E_q and E_d with CLS pooling); single multi-task model. BM25 (Elasticsearch) is used only to initialize candidates during training.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> LM-feedback / downstream-task-effectiveness ranking. Candidates are scored by the inference LM's likelihood of the gold output conditioned on the candidate demonstration (s_gen = p_G(y|z,x) for generation; s_cls = normalized p_G(y|z,x) over the label set for classification), then ranked, and the retriever is trained with a list-wise LambdaRank-inspired pairwise ranking loss plus an in-batch (InfoNCE-style) negative loss. Trained multi-task across all tasks. Not contrastive on surface-similarity labels; not RL.
- **query construction**: Raw test input x prepended with the task's short natural-language task instruction I_i (e.g., 'Summarize the text'), encoded by query encoder E_q(I_i ⊕ x). Demonstration keys are encoded as E_d(I_i ⊕ z). No query decomposition or expansion.
- **query granularity**: Task-level / one-shot at t=0: the query is the single test input formed once before answering; retrieval happens once per test example.
- **when to retrieve**: One-shot: retrieval is performed once per test input before the inference LM generates the answer.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule (always retrieve once per test example before inference). No confidence/uncertainty/learned-router trigger.
- **reranking**: No separate reranking stage at inference (single dense bi-encoder retrieval). During TRAINING, an iterative candidate-mining loop effectively re-ranks/re-mines candidates with the updated retriever each iteration, but the deployed inference pipeline is single-stage FAISS top-k.
- **retrieved context refinement**: None beyond ordering: retrieved demonstrations are concatenated into the prompt (ascendingly sorted by similarity, most similar nearest to the test input). No decomposition, distillation, compression, or distractor filtering.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tools; for demonstrations, each example/key is augmented with a short task-instruction prefix before embedding, but no synthetic-query/summary expansion).
- **index content separation**: N/A (no progressive disclosure / index-then-content separation; full demonstrations are both indexed and injected).
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index or external protocol; static per-task FAISS index).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tools / no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation: the top-L retrieved demonstrations are concatenated with the test input and fed to a frozen inference LM which decodes the output greedily (G([z_1; z_2; ...; z_L; x_test])). Demonstrations are used verbatim as ICL exemplars; the retriever (not the LM) is what is trained.
- **planning integration**: N/A for planning/acting; one-shot exemplars at inference time. Retrieval is decoupled from any planning loop: retrieve-then-generate in a single forward pass.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer: one retrieval per test input, demonstrations injected once before a single LM generation. No per-CoT-step or per-token interleaving.
- **adaptation mechanism**: Verbatim ICL exemplar (retrieved demonstrations used as-is in the prompt); no LLM-prompted adaptation or execution-feedback revision of the retrieved case.
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw labeled example pairs (input-output demonstrations) injected verbatim as text into the prompt.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Single demonstration (raw labeled training example); lowest abstraction level, no distilled strategy/guideline/workflow/skill.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Retriever-aware/effectiveness-aware training: training on LM-feedback list-wise ranking with iterative hard-negative mining teaches the retriever to down-rank unhelpful candidates, improving the quality (helpfulness) of retrieved demonstrations. No explicit relevance evaluator, self-reflection, or distractor-filtering module at inference. The paper also reports robustness to demonstration ordering (high-quality demonstrations are order-insensitive, gap within ~1 point).

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (static training-set index; no episodic/skill/workflow memory).
- **write back**: False. No new experiences/cases are stored back into a memory during deployment; the retrievable store is the fixed training set encoded offline.
- **online growth**: False. The index is frozen after offline training/encoding; it does not grow at test time.
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back to memory).
- **failure experience usage**:
> No stored failure memory at deployment. During TRAINING, low-scoring mined candidates act as hard negatives (contrastive negative signal) in the list-wise ranking loss, so negative/less-helpful examples shape the retriever, but they are not retrieved/stored as failure experiences for the agent.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A / append-only at most during offline candidate mining (each training iteration re-mines candidates with the updated retriever); no deployment-time mutation of stored entries.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Partially: the retriever is a LEARNED ranking model trained from LM feedback (list-wise LambdaRank loss), so selection is learned rather than fixed similarity top-k. However it is not an RL/value-based sequential policy (no MDP, no soft Q-learning); at inference it reduces to learned-similarity top-k.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: Single shared multi-task retriever across 30+ tasks (one model serves all tasks instead of per-task retrievers), but it is not multi-agent experience sharing; no cross-agent memory.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> 30+ tasks across 13 task families: Sentiment Classification (SST-2, SST-5, Amazon, Yelp, MR, CR); Topic Classification (AGNews, Yahoo, TREC, DBPedia); Multi-Choice (COPA, Cosmos QA, ComE, ComV); NLI (MNLI, SNLI, RTE); Subjectivity (Subj); Linguistic Acceptability (COLA); Semantic Parsing (BREAK, MTOP, SMCalFlow); Text Summarization (CNN/DailyMail, PubMed, Reddit); Commonsense Generation (CommonGen); Story Generation (RocStory, Roc Ending); Code Summarization (Go, Python, Java, PHP); Text Simplification (WikiAuto, Turk, ASSET); Data-to-Text (DART, E2E). Unseen-dataset evaluation: Twitter sentiment, QNLI, Ruby and JavaScript code summarization.
- **benchmark family**: QA / NLU+NLG ICL task suite (classification, multi-choice, NLI, semantic parsing, summarization, code, data-to-text). Not in the standard web/embodied/tool/SWE/memory benchmark families; closest to a broad multi-task NLP ICL benchmark family.
- **baselines**:
> Random, BM25 (Elasticsearch/off-the-shelf), SBERT (Sentence-BERT paraphrase-mpnet-base-v2), Instructor (instruction-tuned text embedder, base size), DR-Target (task-specific target-similarity retriever trained with DPR using BM25 target-similarity positives), and EPR (Efficient Prompt Retriever, Rubin et al. 2022) trained per-task with the same hyper-parameters. Single-task UDR is also compared in ablations.
- **key metrics**:
> Per-task task-specific metrics (accuracy for classification/multi-choice/NLI; task metrics such as exact-match/structured-match for semantic parsing, ROUGE for summarization, BLEU/CIDEr-style metrics for generation, SARI for simplification, code-summarization metrics, etc. - exact per-task metrics listed in the paper's Appendix A), reported as task scores and per-family / overall averages. Headline comparison is the overall average task score across families.
- **headline result**:
> A single UDR model outperforms all baselines across 30+ tasks. Overall averages (GPT-Neo-2.7B as scoring+inference LM): on classification/multi-choice tasks UDR reaches 73.2 overall vs EPR 68.8, Instructor 63.2, SBERT 61.6, BM25 57.7, Random 47.3; on generation tasks UDR reaches 30.9 overall vs EPR 27.7, Instructor/BM25 24.2, SBERT 23.7, Random 15.8. UDR improves over the strongest prior task-specific retriever EPR by ~4.4 (classification) and ~3.2 (generation) average points while using a single multi-task model.
- **ablations**:
> Table 3 ablation on SMCalFlow / SST-2 / Java (avg in parentheses): full UDR 60.8/91.3/23.2 (58.4); -w/o Task Prompt 60.1/90.8/21.9 (57.6, small drop -> task instructions help distinguish tasks); -w/o MultiTask 60.9/91.0/22.9 (58.3, single-task UDR nearly matches full -> multi-task sharing gives small gains and single-task UDR still beats EPR); -w/o Rank Loss 56.7/89.2/21.1 (55.7, largest drop -> list-wise ranking from LM feedback is the key driver); -w/o Self-Guided 59.5/90.2/19.7 (56.5 -> iterative candidate mining is important, especially for generation/code). Additional analyses: transferability across inference LMs (1.3B-175B, Table 4), unseen-dataset zero-shot transfer (Table 5), demonstration ordering robustness (Table 6), and demonstration-quantity effect (Figure 3, UDR with 2 demos beats BM25/EPR with 8).
- **evaluation decoupling**: No: only end-to-end downstream task metrics (ICL task scores) are reported; intrinsic retrieval metrics like Recall@k / nDCG are not reported separately. Retrieval quality is measured indirectly through downstream ICL performance.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Outcome only: final ICL task performance is scored; no intermediate process/faithfulness or step-wise retrieval metrics.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Parameter/deployment efficiency is the central efficiency argument: one shared UDR model replaces N task-specific retrievers, reducing parameter-storage and deployment cost as tasks scale. Training efficiency: Elasticsearch/BM25 used to initialize candidates and FAISS for fast inference search; iterative mining adds 3 training iterations (iter0/1/2). Demonstration-quantity analysis shows UDR with 2 demonstrations beats BM25/EPR with 8, i.e., fewer, higher-quality demos lower token cost. No explicit API-cost/latency numbers reported.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed/budget-capped: for generation tasks the number of demonstrations L is set by the inference LM's max input length C (sum of demo lengths + |x_test| + reserved |y| <= C); for classification and multi-choice tasks L is fixed to 8 (increasing L gives negligible gains). Demonstrations are ascendingly sorted by similarity (most similar closest to the test input).
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
