### 15. Self-Generated In-Context Examples / Traj-Bootstrap (Self-Generated In-Context Examples Improve LLM Agents for Sequential Decision-Making Tasks)

2025  ·  arXiv 2501.00750 (OpenReview 2025)  ·  [paper](https://openreview.net/forum?id=WdL3O58gde)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**:
> NeurIPS 2025 (poster; accepted). Earlier presented at the ICML 2025 PUT (Programmatic representations for agent learning) Workshop poster. Preprint: arXiv:2505.00234 (v1 May 2025; v3 16 May 2025). NOTE: the task brief listed 'arXiv 2501.00750 (OpenReview 2025)', but arXiv:2501.00750 is a different, unrelated paper ('Beyond Text: ... No-Code Platform' by Cheonsu Jeong); the correct identifier for this work is arXiv:2505.00234, OpenReview id WdL3O58gde.
- **authors affiliation**: Vishnu Sarukkai, Zhiqiang Xie, Kayvon Fatahalian (all Stanford University). Project supported by Roblox and Meta; API credits from OpenAI and together.ai.
- **paper url**: https://openreview.net/forum?id=WdL3O58gde (NeurIPS 2025 poster). arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00234
- **code url**: https://github.com/VSAnimator/llm_self_improvement (linked as [Code] on the author homepage). Project page/blog: https://vsanimator.github.io/self_improvement/

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: LLM agents for multi-step sequential decision-making: embodied/text-game (ALFWorld), interactive code/SQL (InterCode-SQL), and compositional crafting (Wordcraft). Framed as agentic decision-making, not single-shot QA.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent ReAct-style decision-making in sparse-reward POMDPs (S,O,A,T,R,gamma) where reward is binary success only at episode end (R=1 success, R=0 otherwise). The agent autonomously bootstraps its own performance via in-context learning without human knowledge engineering (no custom prompts, no curated examples, no specialized observation/action spaces). Assumptions: (1) the trajectory database D is initialized with a small (possibly empty) set of human-provided exemplars, (2) a descriptor of the action space is given, (3) the agent has access to a set of training tasks it can attempt. Two-phase: a training/collection phase where the agent attempts training tasks and grows the database, then a frozen test-time phase. The +DB-Curation and +Exemplar-Curation variants run N=5 parallel database instances (each driven by a separate agent), but the deployed agent itself is single-agent (population-based training is a training-time mechanism, not a multi-agent deployment).
- **what is retrieved**:
> trajectories / experiences: the agent's own past successful trajectories (and trajectory segments / state windows). Each trajectory tau = (goal g, plan p, sequence of (observation o_t, reasoning r_t, action a_t), success s). Retrieved as in-context examples (demonstrations) at plan and per-step decision points.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> GROWING / episodic memory the agent writes: retrieval targets a self-built database of the agent's own successful trajectories that grows during the training/collection phase. It is seeded by a small human-provided set, so the construction is hybrid (offline seed + online/test-time-induced growth), but the dominant grounding is a growing experience store, not a static external corpus.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k ranking at each decision point (k=6 examples retrieved by averaged cosine distance). However the work elevates a database-construction objective beyond per-item top-k: D* = argmax_D E_{g~T}[Success(Agent(g,D,E,T))], i.e. it optimizes the COLLECTION's emergent quality (coverage, diversity, complementarity) via population-based DB-curation and value-function-like exemplar selection, rather than just ranking individual items. Retrieval itself is still fixed-size top-k; the curation operates on which items populate the index.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> Retrieve + partial Retain. Retrieve: dense top-k of past trajectories at each decision point. Reuse: trajectories used as verbatim ICL exemplars (no explicit case adaptation). Revise: not implemented (retrieved trajectories are not adapted/edited per case). Retain: yes - successful trajectories are stored, and exemplar-level curation selectively retains high-utility trajectories. So coverage is approximately [Retrieve: yes, Reuse: yes (verbatim), Revise: no, Retain: yes].
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False - the paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner. It is framed via in-context learning, reward-weighted regression, population-based training (PBT), and value-function analogies from RL. It nonetheless realizes Retrieve/Reuse/Retain CBR mechanisms under another name.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Two-level: (1) full trajectory (problem-solution episode: goal, plan, and the (obs, reasoning, action) sequence) selected by trajectory-level keys; (2) sub-trajectory / state-window: within the top trajectories, a windowed slice of states (window of 5 steps around the most similar state) is selected for state-level retrieval. Thus the retrieved unit ranges from full trajectory (for plan-level retrieval) to a sub-trajectory/state-window segment (for per-step retrieval).
- **index source**:
> Growing, online/test-time-induced store seeded by a small offline human-provided exemplar set. The database D is built by the agent itself during the training/collection phase as it successfully completes tasks (online growth). Hybrid construction: human-seed (offline) + self-generated successful trajectories (online).
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat dense vector index over example embeddings, implemented with FAISS (exact nearest-neighbor search). Multi-key/context-keyed: separate keys per field (goal, plan, observation, reasoning) with hybrid search returning top-k by averaged cosine distance across keys, plus a sliding-window state-level index within trajectories. No graph or category hierarchy.
- **retriever type**: Dense retriever using off-the-shelf sentence embeddings (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, Sentence-BERT) with FAISS exact nearest-neighbor search and cosine similarity. Not learned/RL-trained; not BM25; not generative.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None for the retriever itself (off-the-shelf frozen all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings; fixed cosine top-k). The LEARNING/selection signal is applied to the index contents, not the retriever: (a) +DB-Curation uses downstream-task effectiveness (recent training-task success rate) in a population-based-training loop to propagate good databases; (b) +Exemplar-Curation computes a retrieval-weighted quality metric Q(tau) (analogous to a value function) measuring each trajectory's empirical contribution to successful outcomes when retrieved, to keep high-utility exemplars. So the curation signal is downstream-task-effectiveness / value-based, but the embedding retriever has no learning signal.
- **query construction**:
> Raw, decision-point-conditioned keys. At plan time the key is the raw goal g. At step t, retrieval keys are [g, p, o_t] (goal, plan, current observation) for the pre-reasoning retrieval and [g, p, r_t] (goal, plan, current reasoning) for the pre-action retrieval, embedded directly with the same sentence encoder. Queries are the agent's own current context strings (no synthetic query generation, no decomposition).
- **query granularity**:
> Both task-level and step/state-level (two-level retrieval): a task-level retrieval at plan time (key=goal), and fresh per-step retrievals at each decision point conditioned on current observation/reasoning, plus a within-trajectory state-level (windowed) retrieval. This dynamic per-decision retrieval is contrasted with using the same fixed examples throughout an episode.
- **when to retrieve**: Iterative / per-step: retrieval is performed on a fixed schedule at every decision point of the ReAct loop (once for the plan, and at each timestep before reasoning and before action). It is not uncertainty-triggered or learned-router-gated.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed schedule tied to the agent control loop: retrieve once at plan generation (key=goal), then at every timestep t retrieve before reasoning (keys=[g,p,o_t]) and before acting (keys=[g,p,r_t]). No confidence/attention/uncertainty/reflection-token trigger; retrieval frequency is determined by the agent's reason-act steps.
- **reranking**: None - no separate reranking stage (no cross-encoder, no RRF). Candidates are scored by averaged cosine similarity across keys and the top-k are taken directly; for state-level retrieval a sliding window is added around the single most-similar state.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Light structural refinement rather than content distillation: (1) multi-key averaged-similarity selection of trajectories; (2) a sliding-window extraction of a coherent +/-window-5 state segment around the most relevant state to provide coherent episode fragments. No decompose-recompose, distillation into rules, distractor filtering, or compression of the trajectory text itself.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A - no tools/skill descriptions are indexed; the retrieved items are natural-language trajectory strings encoded with off-the-shelf embeddings (no docstring/synthetic-query/weighted-field engineering).
- **index content separation**: N/A - no progressive-disclosure / lightweight-index-then-heavy-content split; the embedded keys and the in-context example content are drawn from the same trajectory records. (A sliding window does limit how much of a trajectory's state content is injected.)
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A - not a tool-retrieval system; no live tool index or RapidAPI/REST/MCP/function-calling protocol. The store is an internally-managed FAISS index that grows as the agent solves tasks.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A - no inter-tool dependency modeling (no tools retrieved).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation: retrieved trajectories / state-window segments are inserted verbatim into the LLM prompts as in-context demonstrations at three call sites - LLM_plan(g, C_p), LLM_reason(tau, o_t, C_t), and LLM_act(tau, o_t, r_t, C_{t+1}) - formatted as goal->plan, goal,plan,observation,reasoning,action exemplars matching the requested output. The same self-collected data is also (in an appendix study) usable as fine-tuning data, but the core method is in-context (no weight updates at deployment).
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-act, interleaved per decision point within a ReAct loop: a plan is first generated using goal-conditioned retrieved exemplars, then at each timestep the agent retrieves fresh examples before reasoning and before acting (Algorithm 1). No MCTS/tree search; the planning step is optional and omitted on short-horizon benchmarks (InterCode-SQL, Wordcraft) following RAP, and kept for long-horizon ALFWorld (~30 steps).
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-CoT-step / per-decision-point: retrieval is woven in at the plan step and at each reason and act step of the rollout (i.e., per reasoning step and per action within an episode), not merely once per final answer.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> Verbatim ICL exemplar - retrieved trajectories/segments are used as-is as demonstrations; there is no LLM-prompted case rewriting, execution-feedback revision, or critic-guided adaptation of the retrieved case. (Curation operates on which cases are stored/retained, not on adapting an individual retrieved case.)
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Raw trajectory (and raw state-window segment) injected as natural-language goal/plan/(observation,reasoning,action) text. No distillation into strategies, rules, or guidelines; no executable program/skill abstraction; no latent/soft tokens. (This is explicitly contrasted with rule-distilling baselines like AutoGuide.)
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw trajectory / raw sub-trajectory (concrete past episode text), at the low (least-abstracted) end of the spectrum - deliberately NOT a distilled strategy/insight, state-aware rule, reusable workflow, or procedural skill.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Curation-based data quality control rather than retriever-side noise handling: (1) success-only filtering (only s=1 trajectories are stored, akin to reward-weighted regression); (2) +Exemplar-Curation drops trajectories whose retrieval-weighted utility Q(tau) is low (those that 'succeed in spite of bad decisions' that would be harmful to repeat), keeping only top-1 utility trajectory per task; (3) +DB-Curation removes underperforming whole databases. The retrieval step itself has no relevance evaluator, self-reflection, or distractor-aware training.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: Episodic experience memory (a database of self-generated successful trajectories). Stored as raw episodic trajectories, not a distilled skill-library/workflow/graph/latent memory.
- **write back**: True - successful trajectories generated by the agent are written into the database D and become retrievable in-context examples for future tasks, creating a positive feedback loop (successful examples help solve new tasks, generating more successful examples).
- **online growth**:
> True - the retrievable store grows during the training/collection phase as the agent attempts and solves training tasks (database scaling is a central studied axis; performance improves with more training tasks, with diminishing returns after ~25% of tasks). The database is then frozen for the reported test-time evaluation (test-time cost is identical across methods).
- **write back trigger**:
> On-success only: a trajectory is written to the database iff the episode succeeds (s=1). Failed trajectories are NOT stored, due to the credit-attribution problem of identifying good vs bad sub-segments. For the curation variants, additional write-time selection occurs: +DB-Curation events fire at size thresholds (10, 20, 40, 80, ... doublings) replacing the bottom-20% database with copies of the top-20%; +Exemplar-Curation selects the top-1 utility trajectory per task into a composite database after training.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success-only. Failed trajectories are explicitly excluded from the database (paper notes failures are harder to operationalize due to credit attribution and leaves leveraging them for exploration to future work). Negative/contrastive failure storage is not used. Implicitly, exemplar-level curation down-weights/removes 'successful' trajectories that empirically lead to downstream failures (low Q), but it does not store failed trajectories as corrective cases.
- **memory evolution update**:
> Append-only growth plus prune/replace curation. Base Traj-Bootstrap is append-only (successful trajectories accumulate). +DB-Curation does forget-and-propagate at the database level (replace worst databases with copies of best in a population-based-training loop). +Exemplar-Curation does forget-prune at the exemplar level (retain only top-1 utility trajectory per task into a composite DB). Individual stored trajectories are not mutated/rewritten in place (no delta-update or refine-overwrite of an entry's content).
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No for the retrieval step itself (fixed off-the-shelf cosine top-k, not a learned/RL retrieval policy). However, index curation is cast in RL-analogy terms: +DB-Curation = population-based training (selection of database 'genomes' by recent success), +Exemplar-Curation = a value-function-like quality metric Q(tau) estimating each trajectory's contribution to success. These are selection heuristics inspired by RL, not a trained soft-Q/M-MDP retrieval policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Within a training run, N=5 parallel database instances (each with its own agent) share/propagate experience via population-based DB-curation (copying high-performing databases) and via exemplar-curation that pools trajectories across all N databases into a composite DB. This is collective memory across parallel agent instances of the SAME framework, not cross-heterogeneous-framework sharing. The method is also model-agnostic/portable (same database usable across LLMs; demonstrated improving even a fine-tuned agent in an appendix).

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: ALFWorld (text-based embodied navigation/object manipulation), InterCode-SQL (interactive SQL coding environment), and Wordcraft (Little-Alchemy-style compositional element-crafting). Comparison baselines drawn from ALFWorld evaluations of AutoGuide and AutoManual.
- **benchmark family**: Embodied (ALFWorld) + code/interactive-coding (InterCode-SQL) + compositional-reasoning game (Wordcraft). Spans the embodied and code families (with a game/decision benchmark), under sparse-reward sequential decision-making.
- **baselines**:
> Fixed-DB (the same ReAct agent with a fixed human-provided initial example database and no growth) is the primary internal baseline. External/contextual comparisons on ALFWorld: AutoGuide (Fu et al. 2024, converts successful trajectories into explicit rules + retrieves rules, gpt-3.5-turbo+gpt-4-turbo) and AutoManual (Chen et al. 2024, hand-crafted task-specific observation/action spaces + manual generation, gpt-4o-mini and gpt-4-turbo+gpt-4o-mini). Also contextualized against test-time scaling (Fixed-DB pass@k, k=1..5) and against LLM upgrade (gpt-4o-mini -> gpt-4o). Conceptually positioned against ExpeL, RAP, TRAD.
- **key metrics**:
> Task success rate (binary, averaged over test tasks, mean +/- std over 5 trials) on all three benchmarks; pass@k of the Fixed-DB baseline for the test-time-scaling comparison; AUROC of a success-prediction classifier in the diagnostics analysis (0.77 InterCode-SQL, 0.71 Wordcraft).
- **headline result**:
> On ALFWorld, +DB+Exemplar-Curation reaches 93% success (0.93 +/- 0.03) with gpt-4o-mini, surpassing AutoManual (0.91, which uses gpt-4-turbo+gpt-4o-mini and hand-crafted observation/action spaces) and AutoGuide (0.79*). Even naive Traj-Bootstrap raises ALFWorld 73%->89%, Wordcraft 55%->64%, InterCode-SQL 75%->79%; the ALFWorld gain exceeds the boost from upgrading gpt-4o-mini->gpt-4o and matches Fixed-DB pass@3 (single attempt).
- **ablations**:
> (1) Method decomposition (Table 1): Fixed-DB vs Traj-Bootstrap vs +DB-Curation vs +Exemplar-Curation vs +DB+Exemplar-Curation across all three benchmarks - shows naive accumulation gives the largest single jump, +Exemplar-Curation best on Wordcraft (0.72), +DB+Exemplar-Curation best on ALFWorld (0.93) and InterCode-SQL (0.82). (2) Database scaling (Fig.2): success rises with number of training tasks (100 -> 3500) with diminishing returns past ~25%, since each new example is retrieved less often as DB grows. (3) 'Best vs worst' exemplar selection (Fig.4): selecting top-1 vs bottom-1 trajectory by Q(tau) confirms the utility metric - 'best' (=+Exemplar-Curation) beats 'worst' on ALFWorld and Wordcraft. (4) Test-time-scaling comparison (Table 3): Traj-Bootstrap ~= Fixed-DB pass@2-3, +DB+Exemplar-Curation ~= pass@3-5. (5) LLM-upgrade comparison (Table 2). (6) Appendix: fine-tuning on self-collected data; success-prediction classifier (AUROC).
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> No - the paper reports end-to-end task success rate (and pass@k, AUROC for diagnostics), but does not report intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG / retrieval completeness) decoupled from task performance. The exemplar-utility metric Q(tau) is a curation signal, not a reported retrieval-quality benchmark.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome-focused (final binary task success). Some process-adjacent analyses: training-task rolling success used for curation, the retrieval-weighted exemplar quality Q(tau), and the success-prediction classifier (AUROC) that probes whether outcomes are predictable from goal/observation embeddings. No step-wise retrieval-accuracy or reasoning-faithfulness scoring.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k retrieval: k=6 examples retrieved per decision point (stated as k=6). State-level retrieval uses a sliding window of 5 steps around the most-similar state to bound injected content. No explicit token-budget cap stated; selection is fixed-k top-k by averaged cosine distance (not adaptive/precision-driven, not reranked-then-truncated).
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A - not a survey/taxonomy paper.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> ReAct (Yao et al. 2023) as the base agent loop; retrieval-augmented agent example-selection from RAP (Kagaya et al. 2024) and TRAD (Zhou et al. 2024, step-wise thought retrieval); reward-weighted regression (Peters & Schaal) for success-only filtering; population-based training (Jaderberg et al. 2017) for DB-curation; value-function learning (RL) analogy for the exemplar quality metric; many-shot ICL scaling (Agarwal et al. 2024; Bertsch et al.); Sentence-BERT / all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (Reimers & Gurevych) and FAISS (Douze et al.) for retrieval; DSPy (Khattab et al.) for automatic example curation context; ExpeL (Zhao et al. 2024) as an experiential-learning predecessor.
- **contrasts with**:
> AutoManual (hand-crafted task-specific observation/action spaces + generated manuals) and AutoGuide (distills trajectories into explicit context-aware rules) - both use task-specific knowledge engineering and/or rule abstraction; this work instead retains RAW self-generated trajectories with no abstraction or task-specific engineering. Also contrasted with: test-time sampling / multiple-attempt (pass@k) methods (shifts compute to train-time instead), LLM upgrades, RL/fine-tuning-based self-improvement (DPO, RLHF, o1), and methods using fixed per-task examples throughout an episode (vs dynamic per-decision-point retrieval).
- **lineage**:
> Group A (ICL demonstration retrieval) intersecting experiential/episodic-memory agent self-improvement. Lineage: ReAct -> retrieval-augmented exemplar agents (RAP, TRAD) and experiential learners (ExpeL, AutoGuide, AutoManual) -> Traj-Bootstrap, which pushes toward fully self-generated, raw-trajectory in-context databases with population-level (PBT) and exemplar-level (value-function-style) utility curation, emphasizing data-centric scaling of test-time-collected experience over architectural or task-specific engineering.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- benchmark_construction_and_size
- cost_efficiency_tradeoff

### 16. CIRCLES (Composed Image Retrieval for Causal Learning Example Selection)

2026  ·  arXiv:2603.16737 (2026-03, verified)  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.16737)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2026
- **venue**: CVPR 2026 (IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition); preprint arXiv:2603.16737 (2026-03-17)
- **authors affiliation**: Guangzhi Xiong, Sanchit Sinha, Zhenghao He, Aidong Zhang -- University of Virginia
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.16737
- **code url**: https://github.com/gzxiong/CIRCLES
- **maintained repo url**: https://gzxiong.github.io/CIRCLES/ (project homepage). N/A as a continuously-updated leaderboard/paper-list; the GitHub repo (https://github.com/gzxiong/CIRCLES) is the maintained code repo.

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Multimodal reasoning with vision-language models (VLMs): fine-grained image classification (CUB, Flowers) and visual question answering (OK-VQA, VizWiz), plus ScienceQA in the appendix. Framed as demonstration selection for visual in-context learning (ICL).
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-query inference-time in-context learning. A frozen VLM answers a query (image, question) conditioned on a set of retrieved in-context demonstrations drawn from a fixed training/demonstration corpus. Training-free (no retriever or VLM fine-tuning); CLIP encoders and the VLM are frozen. Single-agent, no interactive/multi-turn environment. Supervision is the labeled training corpus from which demonstrations (with their gold answers) are retrieved.
- **what is retrieved**: Labeled demonstration examples (image, question, answer triples) from a VQA/classification corpus. Two complementary pools: (1) correlational similarity-based image neighbors, and (2) counterfactual-style demonstrations retrieved via attribute-guided composed image retrieval.
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus -- a fixed labeled training/demonstration corpus K = {(I_j, Q_j, A_j)}; no growing or episodic memory written during deployment.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed-budget top-k construction. The injected context is a fixed budget of 32 demonstrations, split 16 causal (composed/counterfactual) + 16 correlational (standard image-retrieval) examples; each pool is a TopK selection by a similarity score. Not framed as recovering a minimal complete set, but the paper does study budget allocation (breadth across attributes vs depth per attribute) under tight #CIR budgets.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: [Retrieve] only. No Reuse-as-adaptation, no Revise, no Retain. Retrieved demonstrations are injected verbatim as ICL exemplars; the system neither adapts cases nor stores new ones.
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False. The work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is positioned as counterfactual/causal demonstration selection for visual ICL via composed image retrieval, citing causality (Pearl-style do-intervention notation) rather than CBR.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: Single demonstration (a complete image-question-answer example). Causal-pool items are demonstrations surfaced by matching counterfactual captions; correlational-pool items are nearest-image-neighbor demonstrations.
- **index source**: Static corpus, offline-precomputed. CLIP image embeddings z^I_j and text (question) embeddings z^Q_j for every candidate are precomputed once over the fixed training corpus; the store is frozen at test time.
- **index structure topology**: Flat vector index over CLIP embeddings (L2-normalized image and text embeddings), scored by inner-product similarity; no graph or hierarchical structure.
- **retriever type**:
> Dense, off-the-shelf CLIP (ViT-g/14) embeddings used for cosine/inner-product similarity. Composed image retrieval is a training-free CIR pipeline (OSrCIR) where the VLM generates counterfactual captions whose CLIP text embeddings are matched against candidate image embeddings (LLM-as-query-generator + dense matching). Hybrid in the sense that causal retrieval combines image-caption similarity with question-question (text-text) similarity.
- **retriever learning signal**: None (off-the-shelf). The retriever is a frozen CLIP model; no contrastive, LM-feedback, or RL training of the retriever. Demonstration selection is a fixed similarity ranking (top-k), augmented by VLM-generated counterfactual captions but with no learned retrieval policy.
- **query construction**:
> Two-track query construction. (1) Correlational: raw query image embedding z^I_q used for image-image similarity. (2) Causal: the VLM Phi extracts decisive attribute-value pairs from (I_q, Q_q), samples an alternative value v_i' for each attribute, and prompts the VLM to generate a counterfactual caption c^{do(a_i=v_i')} describing I_q under the atomic intervention do(a_i=v_i'); this synthetic caption embedding plus the query question embedding z^Q_q form the composed query. Score S_j = s^img (image-caption similarity) + s^txt (question-question similarity).
- **query granularity**: Task/query-level, one-shot at t=0. All retrieval happens once per query before answer generation (no per-step re-querying), but uses two-level signals: per-attribute counterfactual sub-queries are aggregated into the causal pool.
- **when to retrieve**: One-shot. Retrieval is performed once per query (correlational + causal pools assembled up front), then a single VLM answer-generation call consumes the combined context.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule -- retrieval always runs once per query before answering; there is no confidence/uncertainty/learned trigger deciding whether or when to retrieve.
- **reranking**: No explicit reranking stage in the main CIRCLES pipeline; selection is a single TopK by the combined similarity score S_j (causal) or s^corr (correlational). Note: the MMICES baseline does two-stage image-then-text reranking, but CIRCLES itself does not rerank.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Light filtering via the scoring design rather than a separate refinement module: the question-question similarity term s^txt acts as a semantic constraint to prune counterfactual matches that are visually faithful but semantically off-topic. No decompose-recompose, distillation, or compression of retrieved items.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tool/skill items retrieved).
- **index content separation**: N/A. Precomputed CLIP embeddings serve as a lightweight index while full demonstration content (image+question+answer) is loaded for injection, but the paper does not frame this as a progressive-disclosure index/content separation pattern.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index or external API/MCP integration).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tools / inter-tool dependencies).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation. The combined set R = R_causal U R_corr (32 demonstrations) is injected as in-context exemplars; the VLM generates the answer A_q = Phi(I_q, Q_q, R). Demonstrations are used verbatim (raw image-question-answer exemplars), with counterfactual examples implicitly teaching attribute->outcome causal contrasts.
- **planning integration**: One-shot exemplars at inference time (retrieve-then-answer). No planning, tree search, or multi-step acting; retrieval directly conditions a single answer-generation pass. No interleaving of retrieval with reasoning.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer. All retrieval is completed before the single answer-generation call; retrieval is not woven into per-CoT-step or per-token reasoning.
- **adaptation mechanism**: Verbatim ICL exemplar (no case adaptation). Retrieved demonstrations -- both correlational neighbors and counterfactual examples -- are inserted as-is; CIRCLES does not rewrite or adapt cases. Causal benefit comes from contrastive composition, not adaptation.
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw demonstrations: actual demonstration images paired with their questions and gold answers/labels, shown in-context. Counterfactual examples are real corpus images surfaced by synthetic intervention captions (not synthesized images).
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Single demonstration (raw exemplar). Counterfactual-style demonstrations expose attribute-level variations but are still concrete labeled examples, not distilled strategies, rules, or workflows.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Combined-pool design and a semantic constraint: pairing counterfactual (causal) demonstrations with standard correlational neighbors guards against spurious correlations; the question-question similarity term filters counterfactual matches that drift off the original query context. The retrieval-budget analysis (breadth-vs-depth across attributes) also mitigates imperfect CIR ranking. No retriever-aware training or self-reflection relevance evaluator.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none -- static external corpus only; no episodic, skill-library, workflow, procedural, graph, or latent memory.
- **write back**: False. No new experiences/cases/skills are written back; the demonstration corpus is fixed and read-only.
- **online growth**: False. The retrievable store is frozen (offline precomputed embeddings); it does not grow during deployment/test time.
- **write back trigger**: never -- nothing is written to memory.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success-only in effect: demonstrations carry their gold (correct) answers. There is no storage/retrieval of the system's own failed trajectories. Counterfactual examples surface contrastive class transitions (attribute change -> different correct label) but are themselves correctly-labeled examples, not failure records.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A -- no memory is mutated (store is frozen, append-only changes do not occur during inference).
- **retrieval as learned policy**: False. Selection is fixed similarity top-k over frozen CLIP embeddings plus VLM-generated counterfactual captions; no learned/RL-optimized retrieval or case-selection policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: N/A / No. Single-agent, single-VLM inference; no memory or experience shared across agents or frameworks. (Method is evaluated across multiple VLM backbones independently, but no cross-agent sharing.)

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: CUB (Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011), Oxford Flowers, OK-VQA, VizWiz; plus ScienceQA (appendix). Backbones: Gemma3-4B/12B (and 27B in appendix) and Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B; CLIP ViT-g/14 retrieval encoder.
- **benchmark family**: QA (knowledge-based VQA: OK-VQA; real-world VQA: VizWiz; multimodal science QA: ScienceQA) and fine-grained image classification (CUB, Flowers). Not part of the agentic web/embodied/tool/code benchmark families.
- **baselines**:
> None (zero-shot, no in-context examples); Random (randomly sampled in-context examples); RICES (Retrieval-based In-Context Example Selection, image-image nearest-neighbor); MUIER (joint image-image + image-text multimodal retrieval); MMICES (two-stage: image-image candidate retrieval then text-image reranking). Appendix adds RICES* (compute-matched RICES with K=3 generations + self-consistency).
- **key metrics**: Classification: Accuracy (Acc) and weighted F1 (CUB, Flowers). VQA: Exact Match (EM) and word-level F1 (OK-VQA, VizWiz). Average computed by treating Acc as EM for classification and averaging EM and F1 across datasets. ScienceQA: test accuracy (%).
- **headline result**:
> CIRCLES consistently outperforms all example-selection baselines across four datasets and multiple VLM backbones, with average relative EM improvements ranging from 0.76% to 94.02% over the strongest selection baseline. Concrete example: on Gemma3-4B, average EM/F1 rises from RICES 58.71/64.54 to CIRCLES 63.54/68.53; on CUB (Gemma3-4B) accuracy 65.40 -> 71.97. Gains are most pronounced for small models and under information scarcity.
- **ablations**:
> (1) IR vs CIR vs IR+CIR (Table 9, Gemma3-4B): CIR-only lags on fine-grained classification (CUB 25.16 vs IR 65.40) but is competitive on VQA; IR+CIR is best on all four datasets (+6-7 acc pts over IR on CUB/Flowers), showing complementary roles. (2) IR vs IR+Attr vs IR+CIR (Table 7): attribute text alone helps classification but hurts OK-VQA/VizWiz; CIR grounding gives the best overall, so attributes help most when grounded via counterfactual visual examples. (3) Question-question similarity term (Table 2): consistent OK-VQA gains (+5.16% to 14.32% relative EM), modest/robust on VizWiz; no effect on CUB/Flowers (identical question templates). (4) CIR implementation (Fig 5): OSrCIR > CIReVL by 5.39-5.56% relative accuracy. (5) Attribute quality (Table 6): dataset ground-truth attributes beat VLM-extracted by a modest margin (CUB Gemma3-4B 72.44 vs 71.97 acc). (6) Information scarcity (Fig 4): CIRCLES advantage over RICES grows as training data is removed (Gemma3-4B relative gain 10.05% at 0% removal -> 16.28% at 75% removal). (7) Retrieval budget (Fig 6): more #CIR helps; under tight budget spread interventions across attributes (breadth), with larger budget concentrate on fewer attributes (depth). (8) Compute-matched RICES* (Table 4): CIRCLES still wins, so gains are not just from extra generations. (9) IR similarity variants (Table 8): image-image+text-text gives small consistent VQA gains.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Partly. Primarily end-to-end task metrics (Acc/F1/EM). No standard intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k/nDCG) are reported, but qualitative retrieval-quality analysis (diversity, counterfactual informativeness; Fig 3) and a retrieval-budget analysis are provided as proxies for retrieval behavior separate from final accuracy.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Mostly outcome-only (final answer Acc/F1/EM). Process insight is qualitative: case studies showing how counterfactual demonstrations expose decisive attributes and class transitions (Fig 3, Fig 7 failure/success modes), but no quantitative step-wise/process metrics.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> CIRCLES adds VLM calls (one attribute-extraction call + one counterfactual-caption call per selected attribute, plus the shared final answer call) but only ~10% token overhead vs RICES (Table 3: e.g., Gemma3-4B CUB 12.2k vs 11.1k tokens/question). A compute-matched RICES* (K=3 self-consistency) still underperforms CIRCLES (Table 4). Budget analysis (Fig 6) shows adding composed examples improves accuracy even at a lower total example count than IR-only.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed budget of 32 in-context demonstrations for all methods (k=32); CIRCLES splits this as 16 causal (R_causal, composed/counterfactual) + 16 correlational (R_corr). Defaults in code: default_k=16, num_attributes=1, attribute_k=16. Budget-allocation ablations vary #IR, #CIR, and #attributes.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> RICES (Retrieval-based In-Context Example Selection; Yang et al. GPT-3 few-shot KB-VQA, Flamingo) for the standard image-retrieval / correlational component; OSrCIR (Reason-before-Retrieve one-stage reflective CoT zero-shot composed image retrieval) and CIReVL (Vision-by-Language training-free CIR) for the composed-image-retrieval module; CLIP for embeddings; Pearl-style do-intervention / counterfactual reasoning notation.
- **contrasts with**:
> Similarity-only / passive multimodal demonstration selection: RICES (image-image nearest neighbors), MUIER (image-image + image-text), MMICES (two-stage image-then-text rerank). CIRCLES argues these select correlated-but-non-causal examples that amplify spurious associations; it instead actively constructs counterfactual demonstrations. Also contrasts with CIR work that treats composed image retrieval as an end task rather than a tool for counterfactual demonstration construction.
- **lineage**:
> Group A (ICL demonstration retrieval). Extends retrieval-based in-context demonstration selection from text/single-modality settings into multimodal VLM ICL, and introduces a causal/counterfactual selection objective (via composed image retrieval) rather than pure similarity ranking.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- benchmark_construction_and_size

## B — Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning & Generation for Task-Solving

<a id="item-dsp"></a>
### 17. DSP (Demonstrate-Search-Predict) - Composing retrieval and language models for knowledge-intensive NLP

2022  ·  arXiv 2212.14024  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.14024)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2022
- **venue**: arXiv preprint arXiv:2212.14024 (v1 28 Dec 2022, v2 23 Jan 2023; cs.CL / cs.IR). Not peer-reviewed; this report is the precursor to the peer-reviewed DSPy paper (ICLR 2024).
- **authors affiliation**: Omar Khattab, Keshav Santhanam, Xiang Lisa Li, David Hall, Percy Liang, Christopher Potts, Matei Zaharia — all Stanford University. (Correspondence: Omar Khattab, okhattab@cs.stanford.edu.)
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.14024
- **code url**: https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dsp (released with the paper; the framework was subsequently renamed/evolved into DSPy at https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy, ~34.9k stars, MIT license, actively maintained).
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy (the continuously-maintained successor framework; 100+ releases, 410+ contributors as of 2026). The original DSP repo redirects into this line of work.

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: QA (knowledge-intensive NLP): open-domain question answering, multi-hop QA, and conversational QA. Framed as programmatic retrieval-augmented in-context learning (programmatic RAG) for knowledge-intensive tasks.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-agent (single LM + single RM), in-context-learning setting with FROZEN models and NO fine-tuning of either the LM (GPT-3.5 / text-davinci-002) or the RM (ColBERTv2). The developer writes a Python program that orchestrates natural-language messages (and scores) passed between a frozen LM and a frozen RM through composable transformations grouped into three stages: DEMONSTRATE, SEARCH, PREDICT. Supervision is limited to a small k-shot set of end-task (question, answer) labels (e.g. 16 demonstrations for open/multi-hop QA, 4 conversations for conv-QA); intermediate transformations (hop queries, decompositions, query rewrites) are NOT labeled and are bootstrapped automatically via weak supervision in DEMONSTRATE. Inference is interactive within a single example in the sense that retrieval and generation are interleaved across multiple hops, but there is no environment/agent loop and no cross-episode memory. Evaluation uses subsampled validation sets (1000 questions / 400 conversations) averaged over five seeds.
- **what is retrieved**:
> (1) Passages/documents from a knowledge corpus (Wikipedia), retrieved by the RM to ground predictions during SEARCH and to support demonstrations during DEMONSTRATE; and (2) demonstrations (training examples) selected from the small k-shot train set to be programmatically augmented (bootstrapped) into pipeline-aware in-context exemplars. The primary 'retrieval' grounding the answer is passages.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus: a large pre-defined knowledge corpus (a Wikipedia dump, aligned per dataset — Dec 2016 / Nov 2017 abstracts / Dec 2018) indexed by ColBERTv2. It is not a growing/episodic agent memory; the index is fixed (though the paper notes the framework makes the search index a first-class construct that can be changed/updated over time). The small train set used for demonstration selection is also static.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed/scheduled top-k retrieval per query (e.g., k=2, 5, or 7 passages depending on program/stage), but the OVERALL objective across a multi-hop SEARCH is iterative completeness-oriented: the program decomposes a complex question and gathers supporting evidence over multiple hops (e.g., two hops for HotPotQA, fusing across n=10 generated queries per hop with CombSUM) rather than a single fixed top-k. Not a precision-driven variable-size recommendation; selection counts are developer-set per stage.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve, Reuse] primarily. Retrieve (yes — passages and demonstrations). Reuse (yes — bootstrapped demonstrations and retrieved passages injected into prompts). Revise (partial/no — DEMONSTRATE bootstraps and self-filters candidate annotations by correctness, a weak form of validation, but does not revise/adapt a stored case to a new problem in the CBR sense). Retain (no — bootstrapped demonstrations are cached per program run, not retained into a persistent growing case base).
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False: DSP does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is positioned within retrieval-augmented in-context learning and 'programming' frozen LMs/RMs. (It does realize CBR-like Retrieve+Reuse mechanisms via demonstration selection/bootstrapping, but under different terminology.)

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Two units: (a) text passage / document (the SEARCH unit — passages from a Wikipedia corpus retrieved by ColBERTv2, top-k per query); and (b) single demonstration / case (a (question, answer) training example, programmatically augmented with bootstrapped intermediate fields in DEMONSTRATE). The grounding retrieval unit is the passage.
- **index source**:
> Static corpus, offline-induced: a fixed Wikipedia passage index built with ColBERTv2 (late-interaction). No online/test-time growth of the corpus. (DSP notes retrieval is a first-class construct so the index could be swapped/updated, but in the experiments it is fixed per dataset.)
- **index structure topology**: Flat passage index over a large corpus, retrieved via ColBERTv2 late-interaction (token-level MaxSim) search (efficient via PLAID). No graph/hierarchical/cluster topology over the corpus. (Multi-query result fusion uses CombSUM across retrieval lists, not a structured index.)
- **retriever type**:
> Dense neural retriever: ColBERTv2 (late interaction / contextualized token-level MaxSim over BERT), used off-the-shelf zero-shot. DSP is described as agnostic to the retriever, so essentially any RM can be substituted. The LM additionally acts as a query generator (generating hop queries / rewrites that are fed to the RM), making the combined SEARCH stage an LM-guided dense retrieval pipeline.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None for the retriever itself — the RM (ColBERTv2) is used FROZEN / off-the-shelf with no fine-tuning, and the LM is also frozen. There is no retriever training in DSP; the only 'learning' is in-context: DEMONSTRATE bootstraps demonstrations using end-task labels (weak supervision) — keeping intermediate annotations only when the zero-shot pipeline produces a correct answer — which programmatically shapes the prompts that condition the frozen LM's query generation, but this does not update retriever parameters.
- **query construction**:
> LM-generated, thought-conditioned queries: in SEARCH the LM is prompted (via templates) to generate hop queries and intermediate summaries, conversational query rewrites that resolve dialogue dependencies, and decompositions; multiple queries (e.g., n=10) can be generated and fused. For the simplest open-QA program, the raw question is used directly to retrieve k=7 passages. Demonstrations are selected via sample / knn / crossval primitives.
- **query granularity**: Both task-level and step/hop-level (two-level): a query is constructed per retrieval hop within SEARCH (step-level, conditioned on prior hops' summaries), and demonstration selection is done at the example/task level. Multi-hop programs re-query iteratively across hops.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Iterative (multi-hop) for the multi-hop/conversational programs: SEARCH performs a fixed or bounded number of hops (e.g., 2 hops for HotPotQA, up to max_hops=3 with an 'N/A' termination condition in the v2 search transformation), retrieving anew each hop conditioned on accumulated summaries. For the simplest open-QA program, retrieval is one-shot (retrieve k=7 then predict). Retrieval is also invoked during DEMONSTRATE bootstrapping.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Programmatic / fixed-schedule with an LM-generated termination signal: retrieval is triggered by the explicit control flow of the DSP program (each hop in a loop), not by token-confidence or a learned router. In multihop_search_v2 the LM can emit a query of 'N/A' to terminate hopping (an agent-/LM-initiated stop condition); otherwise the schedule is a developer-fixed number of hops.
- **reranking**:
> No dedicated learned reranking stage over retrieved passages. Instead DSP uses multi-query RESULT FUSION (a fused_retrieval primitive with a default CombSUM variant summing per-passage probabilities across retrieval lists from n generated queries). For PREDICTions, candidate answers can be re-scored/compared (self-consistency majority vote, RM-based 'rank' to find the most grounded prediction, or MCQ-style comparison), which is answer-level selection rather than passage reranking.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Decompose-then-recompose and summarize: in multi-hop SEARCH the LM summarizes the context retrieved in earlier hops (a per-hop summary is carried forward together with the final-hop passages), effectively distilling/compressing intermediate evidence; multi-query fusion (CombSUM) recombines lists. DEMONSTRATE filters out examples where search/predict fails (distractor/failure filtering during bootstrapping). No cross-encoder reranking or explicit distractor-removal model.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tools/skills; retrieval is over text passages and demonstrations, not engineered tool/API descriptions).
- **index content separation**: N/A / No: the corpus passages are both indexed (ColBERTv2) and loaded into the prompt; there is no lightweight-index-then-content progressive-disclosure split.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index or live protocol). The RM is invoked as a first-class construct via the 'retrieve' primitive; the paper notes the search index can be changed/updated over time, but there is no CRUD auto-sync, RapidAPI/REST/MCP/function-calling tool protocol.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tools; DSP composes a single LM and a single RM over text passages, so there is no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation: retrieved passages and bootstrapped demonstrations are inserted into LM prompt templates (Context / Question / Rationale / Answer fields) to generate grounded chain-of-thought rationales and answers. Demonstrations additionally serve as in-context exemplars that adapt the frozen LM to each transformation. Retrieval is woven into a multi-stage program (DEMONSTRATE -> SEARCH -> PREDICT) rather than a single retrieve-then-read step.
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-plan-then-retrieve interleaved within an explicit program: the DSP program assigns control flow to code (not to the LM completions, contrasting self-ask), composing small transformations (generate query -> retrieve -> summarize -> next hop -> predict). SEARCH realizes incremental, multi-hop 'research path' planning where the LM proposes next-step queries and the RM gathers evidence; PREDICT can branch into n pipelines-of-transformations (PoT) and aggregate by majority vote. No MCTS/tree search; planning is programmatic/iterative.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Per-hop / per-transformation within a rollout: retrieval is interleaved at the granularity of each SEARCH hop (each hop = generate query + summarize + retrieve), and CoT reasoning is generated per PREDICT step; not per-token. Self-consistency operates per-answer across n=20 sampled chains; PoT branching samples n=5 full pipeline paths.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> Bootstrapping with correctness self-filtering (weak supervision): DEMONSTRATE runs the zero-shot pipeline on train examples and RETAINS the intermediate annotations (generated queries, retrieved passages) only when the produced answer matches the gold label (e.g., EM/F1/precision thresholds), turning end-task labels into pipeline-aware demonstrations. Retrieved demonstrations are then reused largely verbatim as in-context exemplars; there is no per-test-case LLM-prompted case adaptation or RL reuse-finetuning.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Mixed surface forms injected as text: (a) raw retrieved passages plus LM-generated per-hop free-text summaries (distilled context), and (b) bootstrapped demonstrations rendered as structured prompt fields (question, generated hop queries, summaries, rationale, answer). All passed as natural-language text between LM and RM (no latent/soft tokens).
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Two levels: passages are raw evidence (with LM-distilled per-hop summaries adding a light abstraction layer), and demonstrations are single examples augmented with intermediate reasoning/query annotations (raw-to-lightly-structured exemplars). Not distilled strategies, reusable workflows, or procedural skills.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Decomposition + correctness-filtered bootstrapping + aggregation: breaking problems into small, individually reliable transformations reduces error propagation (explicitly contrasted with self-ask's 'self-distraction'); DEMONSTRATE discards demonstrations whose search or predict fails (filtering bad/distracting annotations); PREDICT uses self-consistency / majority vote over many sampled chains and RM-grounded answer selection to suppress unreliable single generations. No retriever-aware training (RM is frozen).

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (no persistent cross-episode memory). The only stateful store is the static Wikipedia passage index plus a per-program-run cache of bootstrapped demonstrations; neither is an episodic/skill/workflow/graph memory that grows across tasks.
- **write back**:
> False (no test-time write-back to a persistent memory). DEMONSTRATE caches bootstrapped intermediate annotations for the current program/seed (the 'annotate' primitive caches successful intermediate predictions), but these are demonstrations for the run, not experiences retained into a growing store.
- **online growth**: No: the retrievable corpus index is frozen during evaluation and does not grow at test time. (The framework permits swapping/updating the index, but no online growth is implemented in the experiments.)
- **write back trigger**:
> on-success only (within the bootstrapping/annotation step): 'annotate' caches an example's intermediate predictions only if the zero-shot pipeline answered it correctly (returns the example when pred matches answer, else None). This is offline demonstration construction, not deployment-time experiential write-back; there is no per-step or reflective write to a persistent memory.
- **failure experience usage**: Success-only: failed bootstrap attempts (examples where search or predict does not produce a correct answer) are discarded (return None) rather than stored as negative/corrective experiences. No failure memory or success-vs-failure contrastive store is used.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A / append-and-discard within a run: bootstrapped demonstrations are cached (append) when successful and dropped when not; stored entries are not mutated, merged, refined, or pruned over time, and there is no persistent evolving memory.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No: retrieval/demonstration selection is NOT a trained/RL policy. The RM is frozen off-the-shelf and selection is via fixed similarity (knn), random sampling, or cross-validation primitives, with multi-query fusion. The LM (frozen) generates queries via prompting, but no policy parameters are learned (no M-MDP/RL/value-based optimization).
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No: single LM + single RM, single program; no multi-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing. (DSP is a framework for composing one LM and one RM via programs.)

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> Open-SQuAD (open-domain version of SQuAD over Wikipedia 2016, processed per Khattab et al. 2021b), HotPotQA (open-domain 'fullwiki', 'hard' split, over Wikipedia 2017 abstracts), and QReCC (conversational open-domain QA over Wikipedia 2018). Validation-set results reported, subsampled to 1000 questions (or 400 conversations) across five seeds. Held-out tasks mentioned for future versions: Open-NaturalQuestions, FEVER claim verification.
- **benchmark family**: QA: open-domain QA (Open-SQuAD), multi-hop QA (HotPotQA), and conversational/multi-turn QA (QReCC). All in the QA / multi-hop family; not in web/embodied/tool/code/memory/decision-RL families.
- **baselines**:
> Vanilla LM (few-shot in-context GPT-3.5, no retrieval; 16-shot for open/multi-hop QA, 4 conversations for conv-QA); Retrieve-then-Read (RM supports each example with retrieved passage(s) then LM reads — emulates SoTA open-domain QA pipelines); Self-ask (Press et al. 2022, contemporaneous; reconfigured to query the same ColBERTv2 index, evaluated with original prompt and with a Refined Prompt). Qualitative reference points (from related work, not apples-to-apples): No-retrieval LM SoTA (Si et al. 2022, code-davinci-002) and Retrieval-augmented LM SoTA (Si et al. 2022; ReAct / Yao et al. 2022 on HotPotQA).
- **key metrics**: Answer Exact Match (EM) and F1 for Open-SQuAD and HotPotQA; F1 and novel-F1 (nF1, Paranjape et al. 2022) for QReCC. Relative gains reported against vanilla LM, retrieve-then-read, and self-ask.
- **headline result**:
> On HotPotQA (open-domain, GPT-3.5 + ColBERTv2, 16-shot, no fine-tuning), the task-aware DSP program reaches 51.4% EM / 62.9 F1, vs Vanilla LM 28.3 EM, Retrieve-then-Read 36.9 EM, and Self-ask 25.2 EM — exceeding these baselines by 82% / 39% / 80% relative in EM respectively. Open-SQuAD: DSP 36.6 EM / 49.0 F1 (vs vanilla 16.2 EM, RtR 33.8 EM, self-ask 9.3 EM). QReCC: DSP 35.0 F1 / 25.3 nF1 (vs vanilla 29.8 F1 / 18.4 nF1, RtR 31.6 F1 / 22.2 nF1). Aggregate abstract claim: 37-120%, 8-39%, and 80-290% relative gains over vanilla LM, retrieve-then-read, and self-ask respectively across the three tasks.
- **ablations**:
> Not a controlled component-ablation study; rather component-level design analyses and comparisons. (1) Open-SQuAD: DSP's self-consistency over many retrieved passages gives +8% EM / +6% F1 over retrieve-then-read, attributing gains to aggregating information across passages. (2) Reference comparison to fine-tuned systems: DPR 29.8 EM and FiD-base ~36% (5 passages) up to 48% (100 passages) on Open-SQuAD, suggesting DSP's PREDICT could gain further by aggregating more passages. (3) Self-ask 'self-distraction' failure analysis (it decomposes questions tangentially, e.g. answering 1997 vs 1858) motivates DSP's program-controlled control flow over LM-controlled flow. (4) Self-ask Refined Prompt vs original (e.g., HotPotQA 25.2->28.6 EM) shows prompt engineering helps self-ask but it still trails DSP. (5) Program design choices: multi-hop fusion across n=10 queries/hop, choosing summary by largest avg log-prob, fixed 2 hops for HotPotQA, k=5 passages split across hops; conv-QA fuses n=10 rewritten queries.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No: only end-to-end downstream task metrics (EM/F1/nF1) are reported. No separate intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG / retrieval completeness) are reported.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Primarily outcome (final answer EM/F1/nF1). Process quality is examined only qualitatively (e.g., the self-ask 'self-distraction' error analysis and example decompositions), not scored with step-wise/process metrics.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Efficiency motivations stated qualitatively rather than with full $/latency numbers: uses FROZEN LM+RM (no fine-tuning, lower annotation/deployment overhead); ColBERTv2 chosen for efficient zero-shot search (via PLAID). Cost-control measures: subsample eval to 1000 questions over 5 seeds, each seed processing one-fifth of examples to limit LM API spend. Programs make multiple LM calls (e.g., generate n=20 chains for self-consistency, n=10 queries per hop, n=5 PoT branches) and multiple retrieval calls per hop — increased inference cost is traded for large accuracy gains. No explicit latency/token-count/dollar figures reported.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Developer-set, fixed selection counts per stage rather than an adaptive budget: open-QA uses 16 sampled demonstrations, annotate keeps k=3 bootstrapped demos, retrieves k=7 passages, generates n=20 CoT chains (self-consistency); multi-hop uses 2 hops with k=5 passages split across hops and n=10 fused queries per hop; conv-QA uses 4 conversations as demos, 5 retrieved passages, n=10 rewritten queries, n=20 predict candidates. Constrained by GPT-3.5's context window but k is mostly fixed by the program, not precision-driven.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (framework/method paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (uses existing benchmarks rather than constructing a new one). Existing datasets used: Open-SQuAD, HotPotQA (open-domain 'fullwiki', 'hard' subset), QReCC; eval subsampled to 1000 questions / 400 conversations over 5 seeds.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Retrieve-then-read / open-domain QA pipelines (Lee et al. 2019; Khattab et al. 2021b ColBERT-QA; Izacard & Grave 2020 FiD); ColBERT / ColBERTv2 late-interaction retrieval (Khattab & Zaharia 2020; Santhanam et al. 2022b) and PLAID (Santhanam et al. 2022a); GPT-3-style in-context learning (Brown et al. 2020) on GPT-3.5/text-davinci-002 (Ouyang et al. 2022); chain-of-thought (Wei et al. 2022; Kojima et al. 2022) and self-consistency (Wang et al. 2022c); bootstrapping/self-generated rationales (STaR, Zelikman et al. 2022; Auto-CoT, Zhang et al. 2022; Huang et al. 2022); multi-hop dense retrieval and condensed/iterative retrieval (Xiong et al. 2020; Khattab et al. 2021a Baleen; Qi et al. 2020 IRRR); query-rewriting/decomposition for conversational and multi-hop QA (Anantha et al. 2020; Geva et al. 2021); retrieval fusion / CombSUM (Fox & Shaw 1994); language model cascades (Dohan et al. 2022); RAG for knowledge-intensive NLP (Lewis et al. 2020); Hindsight (Paranjape et al. 2022).
- **contrasts with**:
> Self-ask (Press et al. 2022) — contemporaneous LM-controlled follow-up-question prompting that delegates control flow to the LM completions and suffers 'self-distraction'; DSP outperforms it by 80-290% and instead assigns control flow to an explicit program. Standard retrieve-then-read pipelines (Lazaridou et al. 2022; Izacard et al. 2022) — rigid single-shot retrieve-then-read that fails when simple search cannot directly answer. ReAct (Yao et al. 2022, reference comparison on HotPotQA, 35.1 EM). Fine-tuned weakly-supervised multi-hop systems (Baleen, IRRR) that require labeled intermediate hops/decompositions, whereas DSP bootstraps these from end-task labels only.
- **lineage**:
> Group B (RAG task-solving / programmatic RAG pipelines). DSP is a foundational framework that generalizes 'retrieve-then-read' into composable multi-stage LM<->RM programs and is the direct conceptual+codebase predecessor of DSPy (Khattab et al., 'DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines', ICLR 2024), which adds automatic prompt/weight optimization (compilers). It sits in the lineage from RAG (Lewis et al. 2020) / retrieve-then-read toward agentic, programmatic, and self-improving retrieval-augmented LM pipelines, and is contemporaneous with self-ask and ReAct.

<a id="item-docprompting-repocoder"></a>
### 18. DocPrompting / RepoCoder - Retrieval-Augmented Code Generation

2022  ·  ICLR 2023 / EMNLP 2023  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05987)


**Basic Info**

- **authors affiliation**:
> DocPrompting: Shuyan Zhou, Uri Alon, Frank F. Xu, Zhiruo Wang, Zhengbao Jiang, Graham Neubig (Language Technologies Institute, Carnegie Mellon University; Inspired Cognition). RepoCoder: Fengji Zhang, Bei Chen, Yue Zhang, Jacky Keung, Jin Liu, Daoguang Zan, Yi Mao, Jian-Guang Lou, Weizhu Chen (City University of Hong Kong; Microsoft Corporation; Wuhan University).
- **paper url**: DocPrompting: https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05987 (ICLR 2023, OpenReview ZTCxT2t2Ru). RepoCoder: https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.12570 (EMNLP 2023, DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2303.12570).
- **code url**: DocPrompting: https://github.com/shuyanzhou/docprompting . RepoCoder: https://github.com/microsoft/CodeT/tree/main/RepoCoder
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (per-paper code repos only; no maintained leaderboard list).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: code (NL-to-code generation and repository-level code completion).
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-agent, supervised code generation grounded by retrieval, with no multi-agent interaction. DocPrompting: natural-language-intent-to-code generation across PLs (Python, Bash) where the model must generalize to libraries/functions and arguments unseen in training by reading retrieved documentation from an external, updatable documentation pool; the retriever is trained with supervision (oracle docs per example) plus weak supervision, and the generator is finetuned (or few-shot for Codex). RepoCoder: repository-level code completion (continue unfinished in-file code) where useful context is scattered across other files of the same repo; an iterative retrieve-then-generate loop uses the model's own previous prediction to re-query the repo. Both keep retriever and generator parameters frozen at inference (RepoCoder fully frozen; DocPrompting trains components offline).
- **what is retrieved**: DocPrompting: documentation pieces (per-function / per-library / per-argument doc paragraphs from manuals or DevDocs). RepoCoder: code snippets (fixed-size sliding-window contiguous line spans extracted from other files in the same repository).
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus in both. DocPrompting: an external, frequently-updatable documentation pool D (treated as static at inference, can be swapped with new-library docs without retraining). RepoCoder: the target repository's own files indexed as a static (per-repository) snapshot; the retrieval database is rebuilt per repository but is not a growing episodic agent memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**: Fixed top-k ranking in both. DocPrompting selects top-k docs (default k=10) by similarity. RepoCoder selects up to K (=10) most-similar snippets filling the available prompt budget. Neither targets minimal-complete-set recovery nor precision-driven variable-size selection.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: Retrieve=yes; Reuse=yes (retrieved docs/snippets injected and conditioned on); Revise=no (no case adaptation/revision step); Retain=no (no write-back of new cases). [Retrieve, Reuse] only.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False - neither work frames itself as case-based reasoning nor cites Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; both are framed as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for code.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> DocPrompting: document (single doc per function/library/argument; in tldr a two-level scheme - first retrieve a whole Bash manual, then top-10 paragraphs within it). RepoCoder: token/snippet - a fixed-size code snippet of contiguous lines defined by sliding-window size Sw with stride Ss.
- **index source**:
> Static, offline-constructed store in both. DocPrompting: a global documentation pool shared across all examples (tldr ~400k paragraphs from 1,879 Bash manuals; CoNaLa 35,763 function docs from DevDocs). RepoCoder: a per-repository retrieval database built offline by sliding-window partitioning of repo files (no online/test-time growth).
- **index structure topology**: DocPrompting: flat similarity index over documents (in tldr a 2-level hierarchy: manual -> paragraph). RepoCoder: flat index of sliding-window code snippets (bag-of-words / dense vectors), keyed by file path; no dependency/knowledge graph.
- **retriever type**:
> DocPrompting: both sparse (Elasticsearch BM25) and dense (contrastively-trained dense retriever initialized from SimCSE/RoBERTa or CodeT5-base encoder); BM25 best on tldr, CodeT5 dense best on CoNaLa. RepoCoder: main experiments use a sparse bag-of-words retriever scored by Jaccard index over token sets; also tested a dense UniXcoder retriever (equivalent performance).
- **retriever learning signal**:
> DocPrompting: dense retriever trained with contrastive loss on similarity labels (oracle docs as positives, in-batch negatives) MIXED with weak self-supervision (SimCSE-style dropout-masked sentence pairs over the doc pool); sparse BM25 is off-the-shelf (none). RepoCoder: none - the similarity-based retriever (Jaccard/UniXcoder) is fixed/off-the-shelf with no training; learning signal is absent (parameters of R and M unchanged throughout).
- **query construction**:
> DocPrompting: raw NL intent n used directly as the query. RepoCoder: iteration 1 uses the last (Sw-Ss) lines of the unfinished in-file code X; iteration i>1 augments the query by concatenating those last (Sw-Ss) lines of X with the first Ss lines of the model's previous prediction Y_hat^{i-1} (self-generated query expansion / pseudo-completion).
- **query granularity**: DocPrompting: task-level (one-shot at t=0 from the intent). RepoCoder: trajectory/step-level via iteration - the completion position query is re-formed each iteration using the latest generated draft.
- **when to retrieve**: DocPrompting: one-shot (single retrieval before generation). RepoCoder: iterative (fixed number of retrieval-generation iterations; 2 iterations is the recommended/best setting, with the prior prediction grounding the next retrieval).
- **retrieval trigger signal**: DocPrompting: fixed schedule (retrieve once before generating). RepoCoder: fixed schedule / fixed iteration count - retrieval re-triggered each iteration deterministically; no confidence/uncertainty/learned trigger.
- **reranking**: No dedicated reranking stage in either. DocPrompting takes top-k by retriever similarity. RepoCoder orders retrieved snippets in ascending similarity within the prompt but applies no separate reranker (cross-encoder/RRF).
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Largely none. DocPrompting: top-k docs concatenated (with FiD encoding each (intent, doc) pair separately for T5/CodeT5 to fit length). RepoCoder: snippets concatenated with file-path headers up to a token budget (retrieved content set to half the prompt length); no decompose/distill/compression beyond truncation to budget.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tool/skill descriptions). DocPrompting indexes raw documentation paragraphs / function docs as-is (oracle docs built via string/function-name matching for training supervision, not as runtime augmentation).
- **index content separation**: DocPrompting (tldr) uses a coarse-to-fine separation: a lightweight manual-level index retrieved first, then paragraph-level content within the top manual. Otherwise no progressive-disclosure / index-then-content split.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A - no live tool index or integration protocol (no RapidAPI/RESTful/MCP/function-calling). DocPrompting's doc pool is described as updatable with new-library docs but is not auto-synced.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A - no inter-tool dependency modeling.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation in both. DocPrompting: retrieved docs concatenated with the NL intent as the generator prompt (or FiD fusion in the decoder); generator finetuned to maximize p(code | intent, docs) (few-shot ICL for Codex). RepoCoder: retrieved code snippets prepended (with originating file paths) to the unfinished code in a prompt template; the frozen code LM completes the code.
- **planning integration**: DocPrompting: retrieve-then-generate (one-shot exemplars/docs at generation time). RepoCoder: iterative retrieve-then-generate loop where each generated draft conditions the next retrieval (generate-then-retrieve-then-regenerate); no MCTS/tree search and no explicit planner.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: DocPrompting: per-answer (single retrieval, single generation). RepoCoder: per-iteration / per-draft-completion - retrieval interleaved at the granularity of whole completion attempts (each iteration produces a full candidate completion that re-grounds retrieval).
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A for DocPrompting (no case adaptation). RepoCoder's iterative loop functions as an execution-free, prediction-driven query refinement rather than a CBR case-revision step.
- **retrieved item representation**: DocPrompting: raw natural-language documentation text (function/argument descriptions) injected into the prompt. RepoCoder: raw code snippets (verbatim line spans) with file-path comments injected into the prompt.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: DocPrompting: documentation/manual (descriptive reference text, more abstract than code) - a hint/usage description. RepoCoder: raw code (single demonstration-like snippet of concrete repo code).
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> DocPrompting: retriever finetuned on the target programming language plus weak supervision improves doc relevance (better alignment reduces noise); generator finetuned to condition on retrieved docs. RepoCoder: relies on similarity-based filtering and iterative re-grounding (using the generated draft to fetch more on-target snippets) plus ascending-similarity ordering; no explicit relevance evaluator or distractor-aware training.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none - no persistent episodic/skill/workflow memory. DocPrompting uses a static external doc pool; RepoCoder uses a per-repository static snippet index. Neither maintains an evolving agent memory.
- **write back**: False - neither stores new experiences/cases/skills back into a memory store. RepoCoder's previous prediction is used transiently as the next query, not persisted.
- **online growth**: False - retrievable stores are frozen after offline construction; they do not grow during deployment. (DocPrompting's doc pool can be manually updated with new docs but does not self-grow at test time.)
- **write back trigger**: never - no write-back event in either system.
- **failure experience usage**: Not used as stored experience. RepoCoder reuses its own (possibly incorrect) intermediate prediction only as a query-expansion signal within the same instance loop; failed completions are not stored or contrastively retrieved.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A - no stored entries are mutated (no memory). RepoCoder's transient query is regenerated, not an evolving memory record.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No - retrieval/selection is fixed similarity top-k (BM25/dense/Jaccard), not an RL/learned selection policy. (DocPrompting trains the dense retriever's representations contrastively, but selection remains fixed top-k; no policy over when/what to retrieve.)
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No - single-model pipelines; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> DocPrompting: tldr (new Bash NL-to-command benchmark, 1,879 unique commands / 9,187 NL-Bash pairs, train/dev/test with disjoint commands; doc pool ~400k paragraphs) and a new re-split of CoNaLa (Python; 2,135/201/543 train/dev/test, doc pool 35,763 DevDocs function docs; +100 examples with manual unit tests for pass@k). RepoCoder: RepoEval (new benchmark, latest GitHub repos created after 2022-01-01, >100 stars, >80% Python, with unit tests; three granularities: line completion 1,600 samples, API invocation completion 1,600 samples, function body completion 373 samples with unit-test execution).
- **benchmark family**: code (NL-to-code generation: CoNaLa, tldr; repository-level code completion: RepoEval, related to RepoEval/CrossCodeEval family). Not QA/web/embodied/tool.
- **baselines**:
> DocPrompting: base generators without retrieval (GPT-Neo-125M, GPT-Neo-1.3B, T5-base, CodeT5-base, Codex code-davinci-001 3-shot); ExPrompting (retrieving NL-code pairs/examples instead of docs, following Parvez et al. 2021 / Pasupat et al. 2021); oracle-docs and oracle-command-name upper bounds; multiple retrievers (BM25, RoBERTa off-shelf/finetuned, CodeT5 off-shelf/finetuned). RepoCoder: In-File completion (no retrieval), vanilla single-iteration RAG, and an Oracle method (single retrieval using the ground-truth completion as query, an upper bound); also GT-Code (static-analysis-located ground-truth-API snippets) in analysis; generators GPT-3.5-Turbo, CODEGEN-Mono 6B/2B/350M.
- **key metrics**:
> DocPrompting: pass@k (execution), exact match (EM), token-level F1, character-level BLEU / BLEU-4, command-name accuracy (CMD Acc), function-name recall and unseen-function recall; retrieval recall@k. RepoCoder: Exact Match (EM), Edit Similarity (ES), unit-test Pass Rate (PR) for function bodies, and retrieval Recall (fraction of retrieved snippets containing ground-truth API invocations).
- **ablations**:
> DocPrompting: (1) retriever comparison (Table 4) - BM25 matches dense retrievers on tldr but is far weaker on CoNaLa (recall@10 9.73% vs CodeT5 55.81%), showing dataset-dependent retriever choice; (2) PL-pretrained retrievers (CodeT5 on Python) beat text-pretrained (RoBERTa); (3) mixing supervised + weak (SimCSE-style) supervision improves the retriever vs supervised-only; (4) docs-vs-examples: DocPrompting >> ExPrompting; (5) oracle-docs and oracle-command-name give large additional gains (e.g. Codex EM 22.44%->32.43% with oracle command). RepoCoder: (1) number of iterations - 2 iterations consistently beat 1-iteration vanilla RAG, with Recall of ground-truth-API snippets rising (e.g. GPT-3.5-Turbo API recall 86.04%->90.34% from iter1->iter2); (2) sparse Jaccard vs dense UniXcoder retriever - roughly equivalent (robustness); (3) restricting retrieval to specific file locations degrades performance; (4) GT-Code/Oracle upper bounds show retrieval quality drives completion accuracy.
- **evaluation decoupling**: Yes - both report intrinsic retrieval metrics separately from end-to-end task metrics. DocPrompting reports retrieval recall@k (Table 4) independent of generation quality. RepoCoder reports retrieval Recall (ground-truth-API snippet recall) alongside EM/ES.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Primarily outcome-focused (final code correctness: pass@k/EM/ES/PR), but both add a process-quality lens via retrieval recall (whether the needed doc/snippet was retrieved), and RepoCoder analyzes per-iteration recall improvement.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> DocPrompting: minimal added cost - single retrieval pass; FiD used to fit multiple docs within length limits; few-shot (3-shot) for Codex. RepoCoder: extra cost from iterative generation+retrieval (multiple LM calls per completion); paper notes 2 iterations gives best accuracy/cost balance and that performance is not highly sensitive to hyper-parameters; CODEGEN-350M+RepoCoder approaches GPT-3.5-Turbo In-File, implying a cost-quality lever. No explicit latency/$ numbers reported.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> DocPrompting: top-k = 10 retrieved docs (default) used in all main results; FiD encodes docs separately to handle T5/CodeT5 512-token limit. RepoCoder: prompt budget 4,096 tokens (GPT-3.5-Turbo) / 2,048 (CODEGEN); retrieved snippets capped at half the prompt length; max K=10 snippets; sliding window Sw=20, stride Ss=10 (line/API), Sw=50/Ss=10 (function body); max generated tokens 100 (line/API) / 500 (function).
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> DocPrompting tldr: human-written NL intents from community tldr pages, 1,879 commands / 9,187 pairs, disjoint-command splits, oracle docs via string matching, doc pool ~400k paragraphs. DocPrompting CoNaLa: re-split of StackOverflow-mined pairs (2,135/201/543) guaranteeing >=1 unseen function per dev/test example, doc pool 35,763 DevDocs function docs, 100 manually-unit-tested examples for execution eval. RepoCoder RepoEval: reverse-engineered from real GitHub repos created after 2022-01-01 (avoid leakage), >100 stars, >80% Python, with unit tests; line (1,600), API invocation (1,600), function body (373, unit-test verifiable). Answer verifiability: similarity-based (EM/ES) for line/API, execution-based (unit-test Pass Rate) for function body.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Retrieval-augmented generation / retrieval-conditioned generation (Lewis et al. RAG; REALM; Fusion-in-Decoder, Izacard & Grave 2021); dense retrieval (DPR Karpukhin et al., SimCSE Gao et al.) and BM25; code LMs (CodeT5, GPT-Neo, Codex, CODEGEN, UniXcoder, GPT-3.5-Turbo). RepoCoder builds on similarity-based code retrieval (Lu et al. ReACC 2022) and the In-File completion paradigm; query-shifting idea from Lu et al. 2022. DocPrompting builds on NL-to-code generation (CoNaLa, Yin et al.).
- **contrasts with**:
