> DocPrompting contrasts with example/snippet-retrieval methods (ExPrompting; Parvez et al. 2021 REDCODER; Pasupat et al. 2021) by retrieving documentation instead of NL-code examples, and with parametric-only code LMs that cannot generalize to unseen libraries/functions. RepoCoder contrasts with: In-File-only completion; single-pass vanilla RAG for code; static-analysis/heuristic completion (Raychev et al.; Svyatkovskiy et al.) and classifier-based prompt construction (Shrivastava et al. RLPG 2022, Repository-Level Prompt Generation) by being training-free and iterative.
- **lineage**:
> Group B (RAG for task-solving): static-corpus retrieval-augmented code generation. DocPrompting = documentation-grounded one-shot retrieve-then-generate (lineage of doc/knowledge-grounded code LMs). RepoCoder = iterative self-grounded retrieval-generation for repository context (lineage of iterative RAG and repository-level code completion, predecessor to RLCoder, CrossCodeEval, and repo-level agentic code methods).

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- headline_result
- venue
- year

<a id="item-react"></a>
### 19. ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models

2022  ·  ICLR 2023  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2022
- **authors affiliation**: Shunyu Yao (work partly done at Google Brain), Jeffrey Zhao, Dian Yu, Nan Du, Izhak Shafran, Karthik Narasimhan, Yuan Cao. Primary affiliations: Department of Computer Science, Princeton University (Yao, Narasimhan) and Google Research / Brain team (Zhao, Yu, Du, Shafran, Cao).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629 (DOI: https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2210.03629; OpenReview/ICLR 2023; project site https://react-lm.github.io/)
- **code url**: https://github.com/ysymyth/ReAct (official GPT-3 prompting code for the ICLR 2023 paper)
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (single research repo; no continuously-maintained leaderboard. The README points users to LangChain's ReAct agent implementation for broader use)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Multi-domain: knowledge-intensive QA (HotpotQA), fact verification (FEVER), embodied/text-based decision making (ALFWorld), and web navigation / online shopping (WebShop). The method is a general reasoning-and-acting prompting paradigm spanning QA, tool-use (Wikipedia API), embodied, and web tasks.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent, few-shot (in-context) prompting setting with a frozen LLM (primarily PaLM-540B; also GPT-3 text-davinci-002). The agent operates in a closed loop with an external environment: at each step the LLM generates either a free-form reasoning trace (thought) or a task-specific action; actions are executed against an external source (a Wikipedia search API for QA/fact-verification, or the ALFWorld/WebShop environment) which returns an observation appended to the context, and the loop continues until a finish/answer action. Supervision is only 1-6 hand-written ReAct-format exemplars per task (no gradient updates at inference). The paper also reports an optional bootstrapped finetuning setting using 3,000 ReAct trajectories with correct answers to finetune smaller PaLM-8B/62B models.
- **what is retrieved**:
> docs / external knowledge: for QA and fact verification, the agent retrieves short Wikipedia passages (first 5 sentences of an entity page) and lookup hits via a simple Wikipedia web API; the actions also gather environment observations (state descriptions) in ALFWorld and product/page text in WebShop. Few-shot ReAct exemplars (human-written reasoning+action trajectories) are provided in the prompt but are fixed, not retrieved per query.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus: retrieval (via the Wikipedia search/lookup API) targets a fixed external knowledge base (Wikipedia) / the external environment state. There is no agent-written, growing episodic memory store that retrieval indexes into; the LLM is frozen and the corpus is static.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Neither a learned top-k ranking nor a completeness objective in the retriever sense. Retrieval is a single deterministic API lookup per action: search[entity] returns the first 5 sentences of the matching page (or top-5 similar entity name suggestions if no exact match), and lookup[string] returns the next sentence containing the string. The 'completeness' of evidence is driven by the LLM's iterative reasoning deciding which entities to search next, not by a ranking objective. The paper explicitly notes this API is deliberately weaker than SOTA lexical/neural retrievers.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based-reasoning method; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain case cycle is implemented).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is positioned as a reasoning-and-acting prompting paradigm.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> document / snippet: a short Wikipedia passage (first 5 sentences of an entity page) or a single lookup sentence per action; in decision-making tasks the retrieved unit is an environment observation (text state description, product listing/option text). The retrievable in-context exemplars are full human-written ReAct trajectories (thought-action-observation sequences).
- **index source**:
> Static external corpus: Wikipedia accessed live through a simple search/lookup web API (no offline-induced or test-time-grown private index). For decision tasks, observations come from the static ALFWorld simulator and the WebShop environment (1.18M real-world products). No growing/learned retrievable store.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat / API-keyed: the Wikipedia API is keyed by exact entity/page name (search) and by substring match within a page (lookup); it is not a vector index, graph, or hierarchical store built by the authors. WebShop is a website search index (keyword search over product catalog). No custom index topology is constructed.
- **retriever type**:
> Off-the-shelf keyword/exact-match API (lexical lookup): the Wikipedia search engine + a Ctrl+F-style substring lookup; for WebShop a built-in keyword product search. There is no dense, learned, or generative retriever trained by the authors; the LLM acts as the policy that issues queries.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None (off-the-shelf). The retrieval API itself is not trained. The LLM's decision of WHAT to search/look up is shaped only by the few-shot in-context ReAct exemplars (no gradient training of a retriever). In the optional finetuning variant, the whole trajectory generator (including action/query choices) is bootstrap-finetuned on 3,000 self-generated correct trajectories, but this trains the policy LM, not a separate retriever.
- **query construction**:
> Thought-conditioned, LLM-generated queries: the model emits a reasoning thought (e.g. 'I need to search x, find y, then find z') and then issues a search[entity] or lookup[string] action whose argument is generated by the LLM. Queries can be reformulated across steps ('maybe I can search/look up x instead'). The query is composed online from the model's evolving reasoning, not from the raw input alone.
- **query granularity**: Step/state-level: a new query (search or lookup action) can be constructed at each step of the interleaved reasoning-acting loop, conditioned on the current thought and prior observations, rather than once at t=0.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Iterative / agent-initiated: retrieval happens whenever the LLM decides to emit an action (vs. a thought) during the reasoning-acting loop; the model itself chooses when to think and when to act/retrieve. Multiple retrieval steps per task instance (up to a step cap, e.g. 7 steps on HotpotQA, 5 on FEVER).
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Agent-initiated request: the LLM-generated decision to output an action (search/lookup) rather than a thought is the trigger. There is no explicit token-confidence, attention-uncertainty, or learned-classifier trigger; the model's prompted policy interleaves thoughts and retrieval actions freely. (At the task level, a heuristic backoff exists: ReACT->CoT-SC switches to internal-knowledge reasoning if no answer is returned within the step budget, and CoT-SC->ReAct switches to acting when CoT-SC majority confidence is below n/2.)
- **reranking**: None. No reranking stage; the Wikipedia API returns a fixed-format result (first 5 sentences, or top-5 similar entity name suggestions) consumed directly as the observation.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> None / minimal: retrieved Wikipedia text is returned in a truncated form by design (first 5 sentences via search, single next sentence via lookup), which acts as a coarse built-in truncation, but there is no learned distillation, decompose-recompose, distractor filtering, or compression of the retrieved content. The LLM's own reasoning then extracts/interprets the relevant facts in subsequent thoughts.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A: the action set (search/lookup/finish) is described directly in the few-shot prompt via exemplar trajectories rather than indexed tool documents; no synthetic-query augmentation, expanded summaries, or instruction-tuned tool embeddings.
- **index content separation**: N/A: no separation of a lightweight retrievable index from heavy on-demand content; the Wikipedia API simply returns truncated page text on each call.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A: a single fixed Wikipedia web API (custom search/lookup/finish) and the WebShop/ALFWorld environment interfaces; no live-synchronized tool index, RapidAPI/RESTful catalog, MCP, or function-calling registry, and no CRUD auto-sync.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A: no modeling of inter-tool dependencies; the small fixed action space (search, lookup, finish, or environment-specific actions) has no dependency graph or prerequisite modeling beyond the LLM's reasoning.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation in a closed loop: each retrieved observation (Wikipedia passage, environment state, product text) is appended to the running context, and the LLM reasons over the accumulated thought-action-observation stream to decide the next thought/action and ultimately the final answer. The few-shot ReAct exemplars are used as in-context demonstrations of the reason-act-observe format. Retrieved/observed information directly grounds the model's reasoning and final answer synthesis.
- **planning integration**:
> Per-step interleaved retrieve-and-act within a single closed-loop trajectory: reasoning traces induce, track, and update the action plan, handle exceptions, and decide search reformulation, while actions interface with external sources; retrieval/acting and planning are woven together step by step (no separate plan-then-retrieve phase, no tree search/MCTS). Reasoning helps plan acting; acting (retrieval) supplies information that updates the plan.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Per-tool-call / per-step within a rollout: thoughts (reasoning) and actions (incl. search/lookup tool calls) are interleaved at the step level. For QA the prompt uses 'dense' thoughts (a thought before nearly every action); for decision-making tasks (ALFWorld/WebShop) the prompt uses 'sparse' thoughts (the LM decides when to think vs. act), so reasoning is woven per-action rather than per-token.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (no case adaptation; not a CBR method). The few-shot ReAct exemplars are used as verbatim in-context demonstrations of format/strategy, and the LLM generalizes from them in-context.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Surface form is raw text: retrieved Wikipedia passages and environment observations are injected as raw text observations interleaved with the model's free-text thoughts and actions. In-context exemplars are raw human-written reason-act-observe trajectories. No distilled strategy, executable program, or latent token representation.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw text evidence/observation (low abstraction): short raw Wikipedia passages / raw environment state descriptions, not distilled strategies or workflows. The in-context exemplars are raw demonstration trajectories.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> LLM self-reflection via reasoning, plus a hybrid-backoff strategy: free-form thoughts let the model recognize non-informative searches and reformulate queries; the paper analyzes that non-informative search derails reasoning (23% of error cases). To combat both hallucination (CoT) and unhelpful retrieval (ReAct), the authors propose combining ReAct with CoT-SC (ReAct->CoT-SC and CoT-SC->ReAct) so the model falls back to internal knowledge when retrieval fails and to retrieval when internal-knowledge confidence is low. No retriever-aware training or learned relevance evaluator.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (within a task instance, the running context window acts as transient working memory of the thought-action-observation stream; there is no persistent episodic store, skill library, or graph memory that carries across tasks).
- **write back**:
> False: the system does not store new experiences/cases/skills into a persistent retrievable memory at inference. (The optional offline finetuning bootstraps 3,000 self-generated correct trajectories into model weights, but this is offline training, not an inference-time write-back memory.)
- **online growth**: No: no retrievable store grows during deployment/test-time; the LLM is frozen and the Wikipedia corpus is static. The only growth-like step is offline bootstrapped finetuning on pre-collected trajectories.
- **write back trigger**:
> Never (at inference): no memory write occurs during the reasoning-acting loop. In the optional finetuning pipeline, trajectory collection is on-success-only (only ReAct trajectories that reached correct answers are used to finetune), but this is an offline training-data step, not an online write-back.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success-only: the optional finetuning uses only trajectories with correct final answers (3,000 correct-answer trajectories); failed/negative trajectories are not stored or retrieved. At inference there is no failure memory; the model can react to a failed/non-informative search only within the current context window via reasoning.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A / not applicable (no persistent stored entries to mutate). Within a task, context is append-only (each thought/action/observation is appended), but there is no cross-task memory evolution, dedup, or pruning.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Partially: retrieval is not a fixed similarity top-k. The LLM acts as the policy deciding when and what to retrieve, driven by in-context few-shot prompting (not an RL/value-based learned selection policy). The optional finetuning bootstraps this acting policy into smaller models via supervised imitation on self-generated correct trajectories, but it is not RL or a learned ranking policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No: single-agent, single-model; no memory/experience sharing across multiple agents or frameworks.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> HotpotQA (multi-hop QA, 500-question validation subset), FEVER (fact verification), ALFWorld (text-based embodied household game, 134 unseen evaluation games, 6 task types), WebShop (online shopping web navigation, 1.18M products, 12k instructions, 600 test instructions). Base LLMs: PaLM-540B (main) and GPT-3 text-davinci-002 (confirmatory). Finetuning uses PaLM-8B/62B.
- **benchmark family**: QA / multi-hop (HotpotQA), fact-verification (FEVER), embodied (ALFWorld), web (WebShop). Spans the QA, embodied, and web families.
- **baselines**:
> Prompting baselines (systematic ablations of ReAct): Standard (no thoughts/actions/observations), CoT (chain-of-thought, reasoning-only), CoT-SC (self-consistency over CoT samples), Act (acting-only, no thoughts), and hybrids ReAct+CoT-SC and CoT-SC+ReAct. Decision-making baselines: BUTLER and BUTLER_R (imitation-learning agents) on ALFWorld; ReAct-IM (Inner Monologue style dense-feedback ablation) on ALFWorld; imitation learning (IL) and imitation+RL (IL+RL) agents, plus expert Human, on WebShop. Reference SOTA fine-tuned methods are cited (e.g. on HotpotQA/FEVER) as context but not directly beaten by the prompting methods.
- **key metrics**:
> HotpotQA: exact match (EM). FEVER: accuracy. ALFWorld: task-specific success rate (%). WebShop: average score (% of desired attributes covered) and success rate (% of episodes satisfying all requirements). Also qualitative human-labeled success/failure mode analysis (e.g. hallucination/false-positive rates).
- **headline result**:
> On the two interactive decision-making benchmarks, ReAct outperforms imitation and reinforcement learning methods by an absolute success-rate improvement of 34% on ALFWorld and 10% on WebShop, while being prompted with only one or two in-context examples (ICLR camera-ready abstract). Concretely on ALFWorld the best ReAct trial reaches 71% average success vs. best Act 45% and BUTLER 37%; on WebShop ReAct gives an absolute +10% success rate over the previous best. (Note: the arXiv v3 abstract states 34% for ALFWorld; the older PDF body text in one place states 44% — the canonical/camera-ready figure is 34%.)
- **ablations**:
> Extensive systematic ablations: (1) ReAct vs. Act (removing thoughts) shows reasoning helps acting on all tasks; on ALFWorld ReAct (71% best) >> Act (45% best), with relative gains 33%-90% (avg 62%) across six controlled trials. (2) ReAct vs. CoT on QA/FEVER: ReAct beats CoT on FEVER (60.9 vs 56.3) but slightly trails CoT on HotpotQA (EM 27.4 vs 29.4); human analysis shows CoT hallucinates more (false-positive 14% vs 6%; 56% of CoT failures are hallucination) while ReAct's failures are more from non-informative search (23% of errors). (3) ReAct+CoT-SC / CoT-SC+ReAct hybrids are best overall and reach 21-sample CoT-SC performance with only 3-5 samples. (4) Finetuning ablation: with 3,000 examples, finetuned ReAct is the best format across sizes; finetuned PaLM-8B ReAct beats all PaLM-62B prompting, and finetuned PaLM-62B ReAct beats all 540B prompting methods. (5) ReAct vs. ReAct-IM (Inner-Monologue-style dense external feedback) on ALFWorld: ReAct (71) >> ReAct-IM (53), confirming the value of flexible internal reasoning over reactive feedback.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No: there are no separate intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG) reported. Evaluation is end-to-end task performance (EM, accuracy, success rate, score); the retrieval quality is examined only qualitatively (e.g. fraction of non-informative searches in error analysis).
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both outcome and process: primary metrics are outcome-based (EM / accuracy / success rate / score), but the paper adds substantial process analysis -- human-labeled success/failure modes on 50 sampled trajectories (hallucination vs reasoning error vs non-informative search) and explicit discussion of interpretability/trustworthiness of the reasoning-acting trajectories.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Few-shot efficiency emphasized: ReAct uses only 1-2 (decision tasks) or 3-6 (QA/FEVER) in-context exemplars yet beats IL/RL baselines trained on 10^3 to 10^9 task instances. Hybrid ReAct+CoT-SC matches 21-sample CoT-SC accuracy using only 3-5 samples (large sampling-cost saving). Step budgets are small (7 steps HotpotQA, 5 steps FEVER; trajectories needing the full budget are <2% of correct cases). No explicit token/API-dollar latency table is reported.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed small prompt budget: 6 ReAct exemplars for HotpotQA, 3 for FEVER, and 1-2 for the decision-making tasks (ALFWorld uses 2 of 3 annotated trajectories per task type via permutation; WebShop one/two-shot). Retrieval per action returns a capped amount (first 5 sentences for search, one sentence for lookup, top-5 similar entity suggestions on miss). Step caps bound the trajectory length (e.g. 7/5 steps). Selection count is fixed/heuristic, not adaptive or reranked-then-truncated.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (not a benchmark-construction paper; it evaluates on existing benchmarks -- HotpotQA, FEVER, ALFWorld, WebShop).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Chain-of-Thought prompting (Wei et al., 2022) and CoT self-consistency (Wang et al., 2022) for the reasoning side; action-generation / LLM-as-policy work such as WebGPT (Nakano et al., 2021), SayCan, and Inner Monologue (Huang et al., 2022) for the acting side; STaR (Zelikman et al., 2022) for the bootstrapped self-generated-trajectory finetuning. Built on frozen PaLM-540B and GPT-3 (text-davinci-002). Evaluation environments build on HotpotQA, FEVER, ALFWorld/ALFRED, and WebShop.
- **contrasts with**:
> Reasoning-only methods (CoT, CoT-SC, zero-shot-CoT, Selection-Inference, Faithful Reasoning, Scratchpad) that do not interact with external sources and hallucinate; acting-only / decision-making LLM policies (WebGPT, BlenderBot, Sparrow, SimpleTOD) that do not explicitly model reasoning and rely on expensive human feedback / RL; Inner Monologue (ReAct-IM ablation) whose 'inner monologue' is limited to environment-state observations rather than flexible reasoning; imitation/RL agents (BUTLER, IL, IL+RL) trained on large datasets.
- **lineage**:
> Foundational paradigm in the B (RAG / agentic task-solving) lineage: ReAct establishes the interleaved reason-act-observe loop that grounds LLM reasoning in external retrieval/tool calls, a precursor to subsequent retrieval-augmented planning, tool-use agents, and reflection/memory methods (e.g. Reflexion, Toolformer-style tool agents, and agent frameworks like LangChain's ReAct agent).

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- venue

<a id="item-flare"></a>
### 20. FLARE (Forward-Looking Active REtrieval augmented generation) - Active Retrieval Augmented Generation

2023  ·  EMNLP 2023  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.06983)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2023
- **venue**: EMNLP 2023 (Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, pages 7969-7992); preprint arXiv:2305.06983 (v1 11 May 2023, v2 22 Oct 2023).
- **authors affiliation**: Zhengbao Jiang, Frank F. Xu, Luyu Gao, Zhiqing Sun, Yiming Yang, Jamie Callan, Graham Neubig (Language Technologies Institute, Carnegie Mellon University); Qian Liu (Sea AI Lab); Jane Dwivedi-Yu (FAIR, Meta). First four authors are equal-contribution.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.06983
- **code url**: https://github.com/jzbjyb/FLARE (official author implementation, MIT license, Python; ~667 stars, 60 forks; uses Elasticsearch/BM25 over the DPR Wikipedia dump and Bing search; includes code + datasets + few-shot configs).
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (single-paper author repo; last pushed 2023-11-20; not a continuously-updated leaderboard or paper list).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Long-form, knowledge-intensive text generation with LLMs: multihop QA, commonsense reasoning, long-form QA, and open-domain summarization. Framed as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over the course of long-text generation rather than agentic tool-use.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-model, inference-time (test-time) setting with a frozen black-box LLM (GPT-3.5 text-davinci-003 accessed via API; gpt-3.5-turbo used to generate explicit questions). No training/fine-tuning of the LM or retriever; off-the-shelf retrievers (BM25 over a Wikipedia dump, or the Bing search engine for open-web tasks). Few-shot in-context learning with task-specific exemplars. Single agent, no multi-agent interaction. The core problem is deciding WHEN and WHAT to retrieve during long-form generation, so that retrieval is interleaved with generation. FLARE generalizes single-time retrieve-and-generate to active retrieval triggered by the LM's own token-level confidence, querying with an anticipated (forward-looking) next sentence.
- **what is retrieved**: Documents / passages (Wikipedia passages via BM25, or open-web pages via Bing search) that provide factual knowledge to ground the next sentence being generated. Not demonstrations, tools, cases, or agent experiences.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus: a fixed Wikipedia dump (psgs_w100 from Karpukhin et al. 2020, indexed with BM25/Elasticsearch) for Wikipedia-grounded tasks, and the live open web via the Bing search engine for the open-domain summarization (WikiAsp) task. There is no growing/episodic agent memory; the knowledge store is external and not written to by the system.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k document ranking per retrieval call, with k set per dataset (top-2 for 2WikiMultihopQA, top-3 for StrategyQA and ASQA, top-5 for WikiAsp). The objective is similarity-style top-k document retrieval to ground each sentence, not recovery of a minimal complete set nor a precision-driven variable-size set. (For the explicit-question variant, documents retrieved by multiple generated questions are interleaved into a single ranking list.)
- **cbr cycle coverage**: [Retrieve] only. FLARE retrieves documents; there is no case Reuse/Revise/Retain in the CBR sense (no case library, no case adaptation, no retention of solved cases). Not a CBR method.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False: FLARE does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is a retrieval-augmented generation method.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: Document / passage (a retrieved document or web page snippet). The decision/iteration unit of generation is the sentence (a temporary next sentence), but the retrieved unit itself is a document/passage.
- **index source**:
> Static corpus, offline-induced for Wikipedia tasks (BM25/Elasticsearch index over the fixed DPR Wikipedia dump); live web index for WikiAsp (Bing search engine, with several Wikipedia-related domains excluded to avoid leakage). No online/test-time growth of the store driven by the agent.
- **index structure topology**: Flat inverted/lexical index: BM25 over Elasticsearch for Wikipedia passages, and the Bing web-search backend for open-web retrieval. No graph, hierarchy, or cluster topology.
- **retriever type**: Off-the-shelf sparse/lexical retriever (BM25, Robertson & Zaragoza 2009) over Wikipedia, and the Bing search engine (a black-box web search API) for open-web tasks. No dense or learned retriever; the retriever is fixed and not trained.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None (off-the-shelf): the retriever (BM25 / Bing) is not trained or fine-tuned. FLARE focuses on the integration of retrieval and generation, deliberately using off-the-shelf retrievers; the novelty is in query construction and trigger timing rather than in learning a retriever. The only learned signal is the LM's own token probabilities/calibration used as a trigger, not a retriever-training objective.
- **query construction**:
> Forward-looking, generation-conditioned query. At each step the LM first generates a temporary next sentence s_hat_t = LM([x, y_<t]) WITHOUT retrieval; this anticipated sentence becomes the basis of the query. Two query-formulation methods over s_hat_t: (1) implicit -- mask out low-confidence tokens (probability below threshold beta) to remove distractions; (2) explicit -- prompt gpt-3.5-turbo to generate targeted questions for each low-confidence span. FLARE-instruct alternatively prompts the LM to emit [Search(query)] queries via retrieval-encouraging instructions. The initial query (t=1) is the raw user input x.
- **query granularity**:
> Step/sentence-level: a new query is constructed at each generation step (per sentence) from the anticipated next sentence, interleaving retrieval and generation throughout long-form output. Not a single task-level query at t=0 (except the initial bootstrap query which is the user input).
- **when to retrieve**:
> Active (uncertainty/confidence-triggered) and iterative: retrieval is triggered during generation only when the anticipated next sentence contains a low-probability (low-confidence) token; otherwise the sentence is accepted without retrieval. This interleaves retrieval and generation adaptively across the course of long-text generation.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Token-level confidence (LM probability). Retrieval is triggered if ANY token of the anticipated next sentence s_hat_t has a generation probability below a threshold theta in [0,1] (theta=0 never retrieves, theta=1 retrieves every sentence). Motivated by the observation that large LMs are well-calibrated and low probability indicates lack of knowledge (Kadavath et al. 2022). FLARE-instruct uses an alternative agent-initiated trigger: the LM emits a [Search(query)] token sequence.
- **reranking**: No dedicated reranking stage. Retrieved documents are linearized in their retriever ranking order. For the explicit-question variant, documents from multiple generated questions are interleaved into a single ranking list, but no learned/cross-encoder reranker is applied.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Query-side refinement rather than document-side: low-confidence tokens are masked out of the query (implicit) or converted into targeted questions (explicit) to improve retrieval accuracy and remove distractions. Retrieved documents themselves are used with light processing (linearized by rank, prepended to the input; only current-step documents are kept and previous retrieved documents are discarded to fit the context limit). No document distillation, compression, or relevance filtering of returned documents.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tools/skills; documents are raw retrieved passages/web results, not engineered tool descriptions).
- **index content separation**: N/A / No: retrieved documents are linearized and prepended directly; there is no lightweight-index-then-content progressive-disclosure separation.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index/protocol). Retrieval uses a static BM25 Wikipedia index and the live Bing web-search API; no MCP/RapidAPI/function-calling tool integration.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tools; no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation: retrieved documents D_qt are linearized by rank and prepended before the user input x and previous generation y_<t, then the LM regenerates the next sentence s_t = LM([D_qt, x, y_<t]). Only the current step's documents are used (previously retrieved documents are discarded) to avoid exceeding the input length limit. No fine-tuning; pure in-context conditioning.
- **planning integration**:
> Per-step interleaved retrieve-then-generate inside a generation loop (no explicit planner, MCTS, or tree search). Generation proceeds sentence by sentence; at each step the LM looks forward (generates a temporary sentence), conditionally retrieves, then regenerates, until the end of the long-form answer. For multihop QA / commonsense it operates over chain-of-thought generation, so retrieval is woven into the CoT reasoning chain.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Per-sentence: retrieval is interleaved at the granularity of each generated sentence (the iteration unit), which for CoT tasks corresponds to per-CoT-step. The trigger decision is informed at the token level (any low-probability token in the sentence), but the interleaving/regeneration granularity is the sentence.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not a CBR method; no case adaptation). The closest analog is regeneration of the next sentence conditioned on newly retrieved documents when low confidence is detected.
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw retrieved document/passage text, linearized by rank (format: 'Search results: [1] Document 1 [2] Document 2 ... The user input x') and prepended to the prompt. No distilled strategy, workflow, or latent representation.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw document/passage (un-distilled factual text from Wikipedia or the web). Not a distilled strategy, guideline, workflow, skill, or demonstration.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Query-side noise reduction: low-confidence tokens (likely erroneous/hallucinated) are masked out of the query (implicit) or replaced by targeted questions (explicit) so they do not distract the retriever; ablations confirm masking low-probability tokens (beta=0.4) beats using the full sentence (beta=0). Confidence-gated retrieval also avoids unnecessary retrieval when the LM is confident, since the ablation shows over-retrieval can introduce noise and hurt performance (e.g., StrategyQA drops past ~50% retrieval). No retriever-aware training, relevance evaluator, or reason-in-documents distillation of returned passages.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (no episodic/skill/workflow/graph/latent memory; the external Wikipedia/web corpus is a static knowledge source, not an agent memory).
- **write back**: False: FLARE does not store new experiences, cases, or skills into any memory; it only reads from a fixed external corpus / web.
- **online growth**: No: the retrievable store (Wikipedia BM25 index / Bing web) does not grow as a function of the system's own generation; it is a fixed/external knowledge source.
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back; no memory is maintained or updated).
- **failure experience usage**: N/A / none: no storage or retrieval of failed experiences. The only use of 'failure-like' signal is at query time -- low-confidence (likely-wrong) tokens trigger retrieval and are masked from the query -- but nothing is stored.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (no stored memory entries to mutate; append-only-none).
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No: retrieval/triggering is a fixed, hand-set rule (token-probability threshold theta plus off-the-shelf BM25/Bing), not an RL- or value-trained policy. Selection is threshold-gated top-k, not a learned MDP policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No: single-model, single private retrieval pipeline; no memory/experience shared across agents or frameworks.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> 2WikiMultihopQA (multihop QA, 500 examples), StrategyQA (commonsense yes/no QA, 229 examples), ASQA and ASQA-hint (long-form/ambiguous QA, 500 examples), WikiAsp (open-domain aspect-based summarization, 500 examples). FLARE was also tried on Wizard of Wikipedia and ELI5 (reported in Limitations as showing no significant gains).
- **benchmark family**: QA / multi-hop (2WikiMultihopQA), commonsense QA (StrategyQA), long-form QA (ASQA), and open-domain summarization (WikiAsp). Knowledge-intensive long-form generation family; not in the standard web/embodied/tool/code/memory-agent benchmark families.
- **baselines**:
> No retrieval (parametric LM only); Single-time retrieval (retrieve once on the input, retrieve-and-generate, a la REPLUG/IC-RALM style); and three multi-time retrieval categories reimplemented in the same framework: Previous-window (retrieve every l=16 tokens using the last window as query; representing RETRO/IC-RALM/KNN-LM), Previous-sentence (retrieve every sentence using the previous sentence; representing IRCoT, Trivedi et al. 2022), and Question decomposition (manually annotated sub-question exemplars; representing self-ask, Press et al. 2022). FLARE has two variants compared: FLARE-instruct (retrieval-instruction prompting, inspired by Toolformer) and FLARE-direct (confidence-based forward-looking, the main method).
- **key metrics**:
> 2WikiMultihopQA: Exact Match (EM, primary), token-level F1, Precision, Recall. StrategyQA: EM. ASQA / ASQA-hint: EM (str-EM, primary), Disambig-F1 (D-F1), ROUGE-L (R-L), and DR (Disambig-ROUGE composite). WikiAsp: UniEval (factual consistency, primary), named entity-based F1 (E-F1), ROUGE-L.
- **headline result**:
> On 2WikiMultihopQA, FLARE-direct achieves EM 51.0 / F1 59.7 / Prec. 59.1 / Rec. 62.6 with GPT-3.5 (text-davinci-003), substantially beating no-retrieval (EM 28.2), single-time retrieval (EM 39.4), and the strongest multi-time baseline question-decomposition (EM 47.8). Across all 4 tasks/datasets FLARE achieves superior or competitive performance over single-time and multi-time retrieval baselines (e.g., StrategyQA EM 77.3 vs 72.9 no-retrieval; WikiAsp UniEval 37.2 vs 36.0 single-time).
- **ablations**:
> 1) Forward-looking (next-sentence) vs past (previous-sentence) query (Table 3): retrieving with the NEXT sentence clearly beats the previous sentence (2WikiMultihopQA EM 48.8 vs 39.0; ASQA-hint EM 45.9 vs 42.5), confirming forward-looking queries reflect future intent. 2) Active-retrieval threshold theta (Figure 5): varying the % of sentences with retrieval -- on 2WikiMultihopQA performance plateaus past ~60% retrieval (confident-step retrieval is unnecessary); on StrategyQA performance DROPS past ~50% (over-retrieval injects noise); triggering retrieval for 40-80% of sentences works well. 3) Previous-window query length (Table 4): 16-32 tokens best (EM 43.2-43.6), 'All' tokens worst (EM 39.0). 4) Masking threshold beta (Table 5): beta=0.4 best (EM 51.0) vs beta=0 full sentence (EM 48.8), confirming low-confidence tokens distract the retriever. 5) Implicit vs explicit query formulation (Table 6): roughly comparable performance on ASQA-hint and WikiAsp. FLARE-direct strongly outperforms FLARE-instruct, indicating teaching the LM to emit search queries via generic retrieval instructions is hard.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No: only end-to-end downstream generation metrics (EM/F1/UniEval/ROUGE/Disambig-F1) are reported. No separate intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k/nDCG) for the retriever.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome metrics (final answer/summary quality: EM, F1, UniEval, ROUGE). Process aspects are studied indirectly via the active-retrieval ablation (proportion of steps with retrieval vs performance) and the next-vs-previous-sentence comparison, but there is no scored reasoning-faithfulness or step-wise retrieval-accuracy metric.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Efficiency discussed qualitatively: FLARE triggers retrieval for ~30-60% of sentences on average (vs KNN-LM every token, RETRO/IC-RALM every 4-32 tokens, IRCoT every sentence), so it retrieves less than fixed-schedule multi-time baselines. However, the authors note in Limitations that interleaving generation and retrieval with a naive (caching-free) implementation increases overhead: the LM is activated multiple times (once per retrieval) and previous activations must be recomputed after each retrieval; experiments are 'relatively expensive' due to repeated OpenAI API calls per example. No explicit latency/dollar numbers reported. Forward-looking + confidence gating is the efficiency lever (retrieve only when uncertain).
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed top-k per dataset capped by the LM context window: top-2 documents for 2WikiMultihopQA, top-3 for StrategyQA, top-3 for ASQA/ASQA-hint, top-5 for WikiAsp (max that fits within text-davinci-003's input length limit). Only the current step's retrieved documents are kept (previous retrieved documents discarded each step) to stay within the context budget. Trigger threshold theta and masking threshold beta are dataset-specific (e.g., 2WikiMultihopQA theta=0.8, beta=0.4, implicit; StrategyQA theta=0.4; ASQA/WikiAsp theta=0.8, explicit).
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (method paper, not a survey). It does, however, present a generalized framework of active retrieval (when and what to retrieve) and re-casts prior multi-time methods within it.
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (uses existing benchmarks; does not construct a new dataset). Evaluation subsets: 2WikiMultihopQA 500, StrategyQA 229, ASQA 500, WikiAsp 500 examples.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Single-time RAG (Lewis et al. 2020 RAG, REALM Guu et al. 2020, REPLUG Shi et al. 2023, Atlas Izacard et al. 2022); fixed-interval/passive multi-time retrieval (KNN-LM Khandelwal et al. 2020, RETRO Borgeaud et al. 2022, IC-RALM Ram et al. 2023); interleaved CoT retrieval IRCoT (Trivedi et al. 2022); question-decomposition self-ask (Press et al. 2022); generated-query/hypothetical-document retrieval (HyDE Gao et al. 2022, GAR Mao et al. 2021, recitation Sun et al. 2022, GenRead Yu et al. 2022); Toolformer (Schick et al. 2023, inspires FLARE-instruct); LM calibration (Jiang et al. 2021, Kadavath et al. 2022). Base LM GPT-3.5 text-davinci-003 (Ouyang et al. 2022) and gpt-3.5-turbo; BM25 (Robertson & Zaragoza 2009); DPR Wikipedia dump (Karpukhin et al. 2020).
- **contrasts with**:
> Passive fixed-interval multi-time retrieval (KNN-LM, RETRO, IC-RALM -- previous-window) which may retrieve at inappropriate points; previous-sentence retrieval (IRCoT) which uses past context not reflecting future intent; question-decomposition (self-ask) which needs task-specific manual sub-question annotation limiting generalizability; single-time retrieve-and-generate which retrieves only once on the input. FLARE's distinctions: (1) retrieve only when the LM is uncertain (token-confidence trigger), and (2) query with the forward-looking anticipated next sentence rather than past context, with no task-specific annotation.
- **lineage**:
> Group B (RAG for task solving) -- active/adaptive retrieval-augmented generation. A foundational token-confidence-triggered, forward-looking active RAG method for long-form generation; sits between fixed-schedule iterative RAG (IRCoT, IC-RALM) and later adaptive/self-reflective RAG (e.g., Self-RAG, Adaptive-RAG), pioneering the 'retrieve only when uncertain, query with anticipated content' pattern.

<a id="item-ircot"></a>
### 21. IRCoT - Interleaving Retrieval with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning

2023  ·  ACL 2023  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10509)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2023
- **venue**: ACL 2023 (Long Paper; ACL Anthology 2023.acl-long.557). Preprint arXiv:2212.10509 (submitted Dec 2022, v2 Jun 2023).
- **authors affiliation**: Harsh Trivedi, Niranjan Balasubramanian (Stony Brook University); Tushar Khot, Ashish Sabharwal (Allen Institute for AI / AI2).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10509
- **code url**: https://github.com/StonyBrookNLP/ircot

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: QA - knowledge-intensive multi-step (multi-hop) open-domain question answering.
- **problem setting**:
> Few-shot (in-context, no additional training) open-domain multi-step QA over a large external corpus, following a retrieve-and-read paradigm. Single-agent, offline non-interactive inference. The key observation is that for multi-step QA, what to retrieve depends on what has already been derived, which in turn depends on what was previously retrieved, so one-step question-based retrieve-and-read is insufficient. Supervision is limited to ~20 hand-written CoT exemplars per dataset (used as in-context demonstrations); no parameter updates are made to the LLM or retriever.
- **what is retrieved**: Documents/paragraphs (Wikipedia passages) from an external knowledge corpus.
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus (Wikipedia paragraph corpus per dataset indexed in Elasticsearch/BM25). No agent-written growing memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed-budget recovery of the complete set of gold supporting paragraphs: a maximum of 15 paragraphs is allowed for every retriever system and recall of gold paragraphs within that capped set is measured, i.e. fixed-budget optimal recall rather than a single fixed top-k ranking; the per-step K is tuned for best dev recall.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A - not a case-based reasoning method (no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain case cycle over solved cases; retrieves documents, not cases).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: false - the work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite CBR literature (Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner).

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: document (Wikipedia paragraph/passage).
- **index source**: Static corpus, constructed offline (per-dataset Wikipedia paragraph corpus indexed in Elasticsearch); not test-time induced and does not grow online.
- **index structure topology**: Flat BM25 inverted index (Elasticsearch); no graph or hierarchical structure.
- **retriever type**: BM25 (sparse lexical), implemented in Elasticsearch; off-the-shelf, no learning.
- **retriever learning signal**: None - the base retriever (BM25) is off-the-shelf and not trained; retrieval is steered entirely by the frozen LLM's generated CoT sentences used as queries (no contrastive/RL/preference training of the retriever).
- **query construction**:
> Two-phase: (i) initial query is the raw question Q; (ii) thereafter the query is the most recently generated CoT sentence (thought-conditioned query). The LLM generates one CoT sentence at a time conditioned on the question, paragraphs collected so far, and CoT generated so far; only the first generated sentence per reason-step is kept and used as the next retrieval query.
- **query granularity**: Both task-level and step-level: one task-level query at t=0 (the question), then step/CoT-sentence-level queries at each subsequent iteration.
- **when to retrieve**: Iterative - retrieval and reasoning are interleaved on a fixed alternating schedule until a termination criterion (CoT emits 'answer is:' or a max-step threshold, set to 8, is reached).
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule: a retrieve-step is invoked after every reason-step (each newly generated CoT sentence). There is no confidence/uncertainty/learned-classifier trigger; termination is rule-based ('answer is:' string detected or max steps = 8).
- **reranking**: None - no reranking stage; BM25 top-K paragraphs are added directly (collected paragraphs are capped at 15 total to fit context).
- **retrieved context refinement**: None beyond accumulation and capping: paragraphs from all retrieve-steps are collected and de-duplicated/capped at a fixed budget (15); no decompose-recompose, distillation, or distractor filtering of retrieved text.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A - no tools/skills are retrieved; only Wikipedia paragraphs are indexed (raw text via BM25).
- **index content separation**: N/A - single flat BM25 paragraph index; no lightweight-index-then-content / progressive-disclosure separation.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A - no tool index or tool-integration protocol; static document corpus only.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A - no inter-tool dependency modeling (no tools).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**: Prompt augmentation: collected paragraphs are concatenated into the LLM prompt to (a) guide generation of the next CoT sentence in the retriever loop and (b) be read by a separate QA reader that produces the final answer (CoT Prompting for GPT-3, Direct Prompting for Flan-T5).
- **planning integration**:
> Per-step interleaved retrieve-then-reason inside a fixed reasoning loop: alternate reason-step (generate next CoT sentence) and retrieve-step (retrieve K more paragraphs using that sentence) until termination; this is reasoning-guided iterative retrieval rather than tree-search or hierarchical subtask planning.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-CoT-step (per-sentence): retrieval is performed after each generated chain-of-thought sentence.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A - not a CBR method; retrieved paragraphs are used verbatim as in-context evidence, not adapted as cases.
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw retrieved paragraphs (verbatim Wikipedia passage text) injected into the prompt; not distilled, summarized, or converted to structured notes.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw document/paragraph (no abstraction or distillation of the retrieved unit).
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Implicit/none-trained: robustness comes from step-by-step CoT-guided retrieval (retrieving after each reasoning step reduces early factual errors that derail the CoT) and from including M randomly sampled distractor paragraphs alongside gold paragraphs in the in-context demonstrations so the LLM learns to read amid distractors. No retriever-aware training, relevance evaluator, or self-reflection module.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (no episodic/skill/workflow/procedural/graph/latent memory; only an accumulating per-question paragraph buffer that resets each question).
- **write back**: false - the system does not store new experiences/cases/skills; no persistent memory is written across questions.
- **online growth**: false - the retrievable store (BM25 corpus) is fixed/frozen; it does not grow during deployment.
- **write back trigger**: never - no write-back to any persistent store occurs.
- **failure experience usage**: N/A - no failure or success experiences are stored or retrieved (no memory). Failures are only analyzed qualitatively (factual-error counts in CoTs), not fed back.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A - no stored entries to mutate (no memory).
- **retrieval as learned policy**: false - retrieval/selection is fixed BM25 top-K steered by LLM-generated queries; it is not an RL- or value-optimized retrieval policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: N/A - single-model, single-agent; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue, IIRC (used in open-domain settings; 100 dev questions for tuning and 500 test questions sampled per dataset).
- **benchmark family**: QA / multi-hop (open-domain multi-step QA).
- **baselines**:
> One-step Retriever (OneR) and OneR QA; No-Retrieval reader (NoR QA, parametric-only). Leaderboard-style (not head-to-head) comparison against recent few-shot ODQA LLM systems: Internet-Augmented QA (Lazaridou et al. 2022), RECITE (Sun et al. 2022), ReAct (Yao et al. 2022), SelfAsk (Press et al. 2022), and DecomP (Khot et al. 2023). CoT generators: GPT-3 (code-davinci-002, 175B) and Flan-T5 of various sizes (base 0.2B, large 0.7B, XL 3B, XXL 11B).
- **key metrics**: Retrieval recall of gold paragraphs (fixed-budget, max 15 paragraphs) for the retriever; Answer F1 (and EM) for downstream QA; number of CoTs with >=1 factual error for the hallucination analysis.
- **headline result**:
> IRCoT with GPT-3 substantially improves retrieval (up to 21 points recall) and downstream QA (up to 15 points F1) over one-step retrieve-and-read across HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue, and IIRC; e.g., for Flan-T5-XXL IRCoT QA beats OneR QA by +15.3 F1 on 2WikiMultihopQA, and Flan-T5-XL (3B) with IRCoT outperforms the 58x larger GPT-3 with one-step question-based retrieval.
- **ablations**:
> Model-size scaling study (Flan-T5 base/large/XL/XXL and GPT-3 175B): IRCoT beats OneR on retrieval at all sizes including 0.3B, with the gap roughly growing with model size; IRCoT QA beats OneR QA at all sizes except the smallest 0.3B. Out-of-distribution (OOD) study: using demonstrations from one dataset to evaluate on another preserves the IRCoT advantage in both retrieval and QA. Reader-strategy ablation: Flan-T5 readers do better with Direct Prompting, GPT-3 with CoT Prompting (App. E). Separate reader vs. extracting the answer from the retrieval-time CoT: a separate reader is better (App. F). Hallucination ablation: IRCoT reduces CoT factual errors by ~50% on HotpotQA and ~40% on 2WikiMultihopQA vs OneR (NoR > OneR > IRCoT errors). Hyperparameters: per-step retrieved K and number of distractors M (M in {1,2,3}) tuned on dev.
- **evaluation decoupling**: Yes - intrinsic retrieval recall is reported separately (Fig. 3/5/8) from end-to-end QA F1/EM (Fig. 4/6/9, Table 1), allowing the retrieval gain to be distinguished from the QA gain.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Both: final-outcome QA metrics (F1/EM) plus intermediate process quality via retrieval recall and a CoT factual-error (hallucination) analysis over the generated reasoning chains.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed paragraph budget: collected paragraphs capped at 15 across all retrieve-steps; per-step K tuned over {2,4,6,8} (and OneR's K over {5,7,9,11,13,15}); number of demonstration distractor paragraphs M tuned over {1,2,3}. Context limits: GPT-3 code-davinci-002 ~8K word pieces, Flan-T5 limited to 6K word pieces (memory-bound on 80G A100); demonstrations packed to fill the context.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A - this is a method paper, not a survey/taxonomy.
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A - this is a method paper, not a benchmark paper; it reuses existing datasets (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue, IIRC), sampling 100 dev and 500 test questions per dataset for its experiments.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Chain-of-Thought prompting (Wei et al. 2022); few-shot in-context learning / GPT-3 (Brown et al. 2020); the retrieve-and-read open-domain QA paradigm; BM25 (Robertson et al.) in Elasticsearch; Flan-T5 (Chung et al. 2022). Conceptually extends iterative/multi-step retrieval ideas (e.g., GoldEn retriever, multi-hop DPR) to the few-shot prompting setting.
- **contrasts with**:
> One-step retrieve-and-read (OneR) and no-retrieval parametric QA (NoR); few-shot ODQA decomposition/action systems SelfAsk, DecomP, ReAct, RECITE, and Internet-Augmented QA, which decompose questions or generate reasoning+action steps but are not developed to improve retrieval via CoT and often need larger models or fine-tuning; supervised iterative-retrieval ODQA methods that require large-scale training (Das et al. 2019, Xiong et al. 2021 multi-hop DPR, GoldEn retriever).
- **lineage**:
> Group B (retrieval-augmented task solving): an early, influential method establishing CoT-guided iterative/interleaved retrieval for multi-step open-domain QA, a predecessor to later adaptive/iterative RAG (e.g., FLARE, Self-RAG, Adaptive-RAG) that condition when/what to retrieve on the model's intermediate reasoning.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- cost_efficiency_tradeoff

<a id="item-self-rag"></a>
### 22. Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection

2023  ·  ICLR 2024  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11511)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2023
- **venue**: ICLR 2024 (The Twelfth International Conference on Learning Representations; accepted as Oral, top 1%). OpenReview id hSyW5go0v8 / DBLP conf/iclr/AsaiWWSH24. Preprint arXiv:2310.11511 (submitted 17 Oct 2023).
- **authors affiliation**:
> Akari Asai (University of Washington / Allen Institute for AI; lead author, IBM Fellowship), Zeqiu Wu (University of Washington), Yizhong Wang (University of Washington), Avirup Sil (IBM Research AI), Hannaneh Hajishirzi (University of Washington / Allen Institute for AI). Primary affiliations: University of Washington, Allen Institute for AI (AI2), and IBM Research AI.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11511
- **code url**: https://github.com/AkariAsai/self-rag (MIT license; ~2.4k stars). Models: HuggingFace selfrag/selfrag_llama2_7b and selfrag/selfrag_llama2_13b; training data: selfrag/selfrag_train_data (150K instances); project site https://selfrag.github.io/.
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/AkariAsai/self-rag (original research repo; last substantive update Mar 2024; not a continuously-maintained leaderboard/paper-list). Community fine-tune: SciPhi/SciPhi-Self-RAG-Mistral-7B-32k.

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> QA / knowledge-intensive NLG. Open-domain QA (PopQA, TriviaQA-unfiltered), closed-set tasks (fact verification PubHealth, multiple-choice reasoning ARC-Challenge), and long-form generation (biography generation / FactScore, ASQA long-form QA with citations). Not an agent/tool-use/planning setting.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-agent, non-interactive generation. A single arbitrary LM (Llama2-7B / 13B) is trained to interleave on-demand retrieval, generation, and self-critique by emitting special 'reflection tokens', evaluated zero-shot (no few-shot demonstrations) across six tasks. Supervision is available but synthetic: reflection-token labels are distilled offline from GPT-4 into an in-house Critic model C, which then annotates a 150K-instance instruction-following + knowledge-intensive corpus that trains the Generator M via standard next-token prediction. The retriever (Contriever-MSMARCO) is frozen off-the-shelf; only the Critic and Generator LMs are trained. At inference the model itself decides whether/when to retrieve (via a [Retrieve] token, optionally thresholded) and ranks passage-conditioned segment candidates using its own critique-token probabilities in a segment-level beam search.
- **what is retrieved**: docs (text passages from a Wikipedia corpus) retrieved on-demand to provide factual grounding. No demos/cases/trajectories/skills/tools/experiences are retrieved.
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus (Wikipedia passages, plus Google Programmable Search intro paragraphs for some open-ended tasks). No agent-written growing/episodic memory; the corpus is fixed at test time.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k document retrieval per retrieval call (top-5 by default, top-10 for PopQA), but the operative selection is precision-driven over GENERATED SEGMENTS rather than over documents: for each retrieved passage the model generates a candidate continuation and selects/ranks via critique-token (IsRel/IsSup/IsUse) scores in a segment-level beam search. The objective is on-demand, quality-controlled use of retrieval, not recovery of a complete minimal document set and not a fixed document ranking.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A - not a case-based-reasoning method; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain case cycle over a case base. [Retrieve: no (retrieves passages, not cases), Reuse: no, Revise: no, Retain: no].
- **explicit cbr grounding**: false. The work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is framed as self-reflective retrieval-augmented generation with reflection tokens.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: document/passage. Contriever-MSMARCO retrieves Wikipedia text passages (DPR-style psgs_w100 100-word chunks / 2020 preprocessed Wikipedia for PopQA). Retrieval granularity is the passage; generation is organized at the segment (sentence) level.
- **index source**:
> Static corpus, offline-built. By default the official Contriever Wikipedia embeddings over 2018 English Wikipedia; for PopQA the December 2020 preprocessed Wikipedia; bio-generation and open-domain QA additionally retrieve via Google Programmable Search (Wikipedia introductory paragraphs). Store is frozen at test time; nothing is induced online.
- **index structure topology**: Flat dense vector index (Contriever passage embeddings, nearest-neighbor / FAISS-style search). No graph or hierarchical structure.
- **retriever type**:
> Dense (off-the-shelf Contriever-MSMARCO bi-encoder, Izacard et al. 2022). Optionally augmented with the Google Programmable Search API for some open-ended tasks. The novel 'retrieve-on-demand' decision is made by the GENERATIVE LM emitting a [Retrieve] reflection token, but document scoring itself is dense retrieval.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> none for the retriever (Contriever-MSMARCO is frozen off-the-shelf, not fine-tuned). The LM's retrieve-or-not [Retrieve] token IS learned, via supervised next-token prediction on Critic-distilled labels (Critic data distilled from GPT-4), but this trains the decision policy inside the LM, not the document retriever. The authors explicitly leave instruction-tuned/jointly-trained retrievers to future work.
- **query construction**:
> Raw input prompt plus preceding generation. The retrieval query is (x, y_{<t}): the original input x together with the previously generated segment y_{t-1}, so retrieval at a later segment is conditioned on what has already been generated. No explicit decomposition/expansion; the [Retrieve] token gates whether the query is issued.
- **query granularity**: Step/segment-level (interleaved). The model can retrieve at the start and again at each subsequent segment (sentence) during generation, conditioning each retrieval on x and the preceding generation; it can also skip retrieval entirely. Not a single task-level one-shot query.
- **when to retrieve**:
> adaptive (learned, model-initiated) and on-demand: the LM emits a [Retrieve] = {yes, no, continue} reflection token to decide per segment whether to retrieve. A soft threshold on the normalized P([Retrieve]=Yes) probability can additionally tune retrieval frequency at inference. Can be forced to no_retrieval / always_retrieve / adaptive_retrieval modes.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Reflection token: the model-generated [Retrieve] token (values yes / no / continue), produced by the LM as part of decoding. Optionally a confidence threshold on the normalized probability of [Retrieve]=Yes over the retrieval-token vocabulary triggers retrieval (larger threshold -> less retrieval). This is a learned, self-reflective signal rather than a fixed schedule, token-perplexity heuristic (FLARE), or external classifier (Adaptive-RAG).
- **reranking**:
> Segment-level critique-guided reranking rather than a document cross-encoder. When retrieval fires, K passages are processed in parallel to produce K candidate continuations; a segment-level beam search (default beam width B=2) ranks candidates by a critic score S = linear weighted sum of normalized desirable-critique-token probabilities (IsRel, IsSup, IsUse). No separate cross-encoder/RRF/instruction-tuned reranker over documents.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Relevance/support self-evaluation and selection (a self-reflection filter): the model emits IsRel (relevant/irrelevant) to judge each passage and IsSup (fully/partially/no support) to judge whether its own segment is grounded, and can hard-filter undesirable continuations (e.g., IsRel=Irrelevant) or down-weight them softly. No decompose-recompose, summarization/compression (contrasted with Recomp), or reason-in-documents distillation; refinement is critique-token-based selection.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (retrieves plain Wikipedia passages, not tool/skill descriptions; no docstring/synthetic-query/weighted-field engineering).
- **index content separation**: N/A. No lightweight-index-then-content / progressive-disclosure separation; full passages are embedded and retrieved directly.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A. Static document index; no tool API / RapidAPI / RESTful / MCP / function-calling integration (the only API is Google Programmable Search used as a retrieval source, not a live tool index).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A. No tools and no inter-tool dependency modeling.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation with self-critique: retrieved passages are inserted (wrapped in <paragraph>...</paragraph> markup) into the LM input, and the LM generates a passage-conditioned continuation plus reflection tokens (IsRel/IsSup/IsUse) that are used to score and select the output segment. Reflection tokens are also a TRAINING signal (the LM is trained to predict them as ordinary next tokens from the expanded vocabulary), making them both an inference-time controller and a learned latent-control mechanism.
- **planning integration**:
> Per-segment interleaved retrieve-generate-critique inside a segment-level beam (tree) search. At each segment step t the model decides to retrieve (or not); if retrieving, K passages are expanded in parallel into K continuations and the top-B continuations are kept by critique-weighted score, returning the best full sequence at the end. No external planner/MCTS over actions; the 'search' is over output segments conditioned on passages.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-segment (sentence-level). Retrieval, generation, and critique are interleaved at the granularity of each generated segment/sentence, not per-token, per-CoT-step, or per-tool-call.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not CBR; no retrieved case is adapted/revised). The analogue is that the LM conditions generation on retrieved passages and self-critiques via reflection tokens, but there is no case adaptation step.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Raw retrieved passages injected as text (delimited by <paragraph> context markup), accompanied by model-generated reflection tokens. What is injected is concrete passage text, not distilled strategies, workflows, programs, or soft/latent tokens (reflection tokens are discrete special vocabulary tokens, not the retrieved content).
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw passage/document (single concrete Wikipedia passage). No distilled strategy, state-aware guideline, reusable workflow, or procedural skill.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Self-reflection relevance/support evaluation: the model is trained to predict and act on IsRel (passage relevance) and IsSup (whether its segment is supported by the passage), enabling it to discount irrelevant retrieved passages via soft weighting or hard filtering in the segment-level beam search. The ablation shows that naively using the top passage regardless of relevance ('Retrieve top1', as in standard RAG) causes large drops on PopQA and ASQA, evidencing the robustness benefit of critique-based selection.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (no episodic/skill/workflow/graph/latent memory). The only persistent learned artifacts are the trained Critic and Generator LMs and the expanded reflection-token vocabulary; the retrievable store is a fixed external Wikipedia corpus.
- **write back**: false. No new experiences/cases/passages are written back to any store at deployment; the retrieval corpus is static and the model weights are fixed after offline training.
- **online growth**: false. The retrievable corpus is frozen after offline construction; nothing grows at test time.
- **write back trigger**: never. There is no memory write-back at inference; reflection-token supervision is created once offline (GPT-4 -> Critic -> annotated 150K corpus -> Generator) and then frozen.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Not as stored retrievable experience. During offline TRAINING the Critic learns to emit negative/undesirable reflection tokens (e.g., IsRel=Irrelevant, IsSup=No support, low IsUse) so the Generator learns to recognize unsupported/irrelevant cases, but these are token-level supervision signals, not a stored failure memory retrieved at test time. At inference, undesirable critique tokens are used to filter/down-weight continuations within the current query, not stored.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (no stored memory entries to mutate). Model weights are fixed after offline training; no online update.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Partial. The WHEN-to-retrieve decision is a learned policy embedded in the LM (the [Retrieve] reflection token, trained via supervised next-token prediction on Critic-distilled labels), and segment selection is driven by learned critique-token probabilities. However, this is supervised distillation, NOT RL / value-based / M-MDP policy learning, and the document retriever itself remains a fixed off-the-shelf dense top-k.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: N/A. Single-agent, single private model; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> Six tasks: (1) PopQA (long-tail open-domain QA, accuracy/match), (2) TriviaQA-unfiltered (TQA, open-domain QA, accuracy), (3) PubHealth (Pub, public-health fact verification, accuracy), (4) ARC-Challenge (ARC, multiple-choice scientific reasoning, accuracy), (5) Biography generation / FactScore (Bio, factual precision FS), (6) ASQA (long-form QA with citations; metrics: str-em (em), rouge (rg), MAUVE (mau), citation precision (pre), citation recall (rec)).
- **benchmark family**: QA (open-domain single-hop: PopQA, TriviaQA) + closed-set fact verification/reasoning (PubHealth, ARC-Challenge) + long-form knowledge generation with attribution (FactScore/Bio, ASQA). Not multi-hop / web / embodied / tool / code / memory / decision-RL families.
- **baselines**:
> Without retrieval: Llama2-7B/13B, Alpaca-7B/13B, CoVE-65B*, plus proprietary ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo-0301). With retrieval: Toolformer*-6B, retrieval-augmented Llama2-7B/13B and Alpaca-7B/13B, Llama2-FT-7B (same instruction-output data as Self-RAG but no retrieval/reflection in training, retrieval-augmented only at test time), SAIL*-7B, retrieval-augmented Llama2-chat-13B (Ret-Llama2-c13B), retrieval-augmented ChatGPT (Ret-ChatGPT), and Perplexity.ai. (* numbers cited from original papers.)
- **key metrics**: Accuracy/match (PopQA, TQA, PubHealth, ARC); FactScore (FS) for Bio; for ASQA: str-em (em), rouge (rg), MAUVE (mau, fluency), citation precision (pre) and citation recall (rec). Analyses also report retrieval frequency vs accuracy.
- **headline result**:
> Self-RAG (7B and 13B) outperforms ChatGPT and retrieval-augmented Llama2-chat on most of the six tasks. Self-RAG-7B: PopQA 54.9, TQA 66.4, PubHealth 72.4, ARC 67.3, Bio FactScore 81.2, ASQA em 30.0 / rg 35.7 / MAUVE 74.3 / citation precision 66.9 / recall 67.8. Self-RAG-13B: PopQA 55.8, TQA 69.3, PubHealth 74.5, ARC 73.1, Bio FactScore 80.2, ASQA em 31.7 / rg 37.0 / MAUVE 71.6 / citation prec 70.3 / recall 71.3. For comparison, ChatGPT: PopQA 29.3, PubHealth 70.1, ARC 75.3, Bio 71.8; Ret-ChatGPT: PopQA 50.8, ASQA citation prec 65.1 / rec 76.6; Ret-Llama2-chat-13B: PopQA 51.8, PubHealth 52.1, Bio 79.9, ASQA citation prec 19.8 / rec 36.1. Most-cited single claim: Self-RAG substantially improves factuality (FactScore) and citation accuracy in long-form generation over ChatGPT and retrieval-augmented Llama2-chat.
- **ablations**:
> Table 3a (7B model, trained on a 50k subset; PopQA acc / PubHealth-Med acc / ASQA em). Full Self-RAG(50k): 45.5 / 73.5 / 32.1. Training ablations: No Retriever (standard instruction-tuning without retrieved passages) 43.6 / 67.8 / 31.0; No Critic (trained on input-output always augmented with top-1 retrieved doc, no reflection tokens, similar to SAIL) 42.6 / 72.0 / 18.1 - large ASQA drop. Inference ablations: No retrieval 24.7 / 73.0 / - (PopQA collapses, ~40% relative drop); Hard constraints (retrieve whenever IsRel triggers, no adaptive threshold) 28.3 / 72.6 / -; Retrieve top1 (always use top passage, standard RAG) 41.8 / 73.1 / 28.6 - large PopQA/ASQA drop; Remove IsSup (drop IsSup from beam-search score) 44.1 / 73.2 / 30.6 - hurts ASQA. Conclusion: all training and inference components matter; critique-based fine-grained selection beats naive top-passage use. Additional analyses: (b) increasing IsSup weight raises ASQA citation precision but lowers MAUVE/fluency (test-time customization); (c) raising the retrieval threshold reduces retrieval frequency with small loss on PubHealth (~2%) but large loss on PopQA (~40% relative); training-data-scale analysis (5k/10k/20k/50k vs 150k) shows upward trajectories, larger gains on PopQA/ASQA; human evaluation finds reflection-token predictions (IsRel, IsSup) mostly align with annotators (S&P PopQA 92.5 / Bio 70.0; IsRel 95.0/90.0; IsSup 90.0/85.0). Critic agreement with GPT-4 >90% (e.g., Llama2-7B critic: Retrieve 93.8, IsSup 93.5, IsRel 80.2, IsUse 73.5).
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Partial. Self-RAG reports task-level end-to-end metrics (accuracy/FactScore/ASQA suite) and, separately, intrinsic reliability of the reflection-token predictions via Critic-vs-GPT-4 agreement (>90%) and human-vs-model agreement for IsRel/IsSup, and retrieval-frequency-vs-accuracy curves. It does not report standard retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG) for the document retriever.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both. Outcome: task accuracy, FactScore, ASQA str-em/rouge/MAUVE/citation precision/recall. Process: reliability/agreement of predicted reflection tokens (IsRel, IsSup) against human and GPT-4 judgments, citation precision/recall as attribution-process quality, and retrieval frequency.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k retrieval per call: top-5 documents by default (Contriever-MSMARCO), top-10 for PopQA, with max_new_tokens ~100 (short-form) / 300 (long-form, max_depth T up to 6-7); segment-level beam width B=2. k is fixed, not adaptive/precision-driven at the document level; the adaptive lever is WHETHER to retrieve (the [Retrieve] token / threshold) plus critique-based segment selection rather than variable document k.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (method paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A (uses existing benchmarks; no new benchmark constructed). Training data: 150K instances annotated with reflection tokens, sourced from instruction-following data (GPT-4 Alpaca 26,168; Stanford Alpaca 25,153; FLAN-V2 17,817; ShareGPT 13,406; Open Assistant 1 9,464 - via Open-Instruct) and knowledge-intensive data (Wizard of Wikipedia 17,367; Natural Questions 15,535; FEVER 9,966; OpenBookQA 4,699; ARC-Easy 2,147; ASQA 3,897 - via KILT/HF/ASQA). Critic training collected via GPT-4 (e.g., ~19,317 relevance, ~11,181 utility, ~1,294 IsRel, ~3,831 utility-type instances per the appendix counts).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Lewis et al. 2020; Guu et al. 2020; Ram et al. 2023 in-context RAG); Contriever-MSMARCO dense retriever (Izacard et al. 2022); Llama2-7B/13B (Touvron et al. 2023) as base LMs; GPT-4 (OpenAI 2023) as the Critic teacher; Open-Instruct instruction-tuning data and KILT knowledge-intensive datasets; controllable/fine-grained feedback learning (Wu et al. 2023 fine-grained RLHF) and attribution work (Menick et al. 2022; Bohnet et al. 2022; Liu et al. 2023a ALCE; Min et al. 2023 FactScore).
- **contrasts with**:
> Standard fixed RAG that always retrieves a fixed number of passages (Ram et al. 2023; Lewis et al. 2020); SAIL (Luo et al. 2023, instruction-tuned with top-1 retrieved doc, no reflection) - approximated by the No-Critic ablation; Toolformer (Schick et al. 2023, learns to call tools/retrieval via special tokens but without fine-grained relevance/support critique); RLHF/PPO feedback learning (Ouyang et al. 2022; Wu et al. 2023) which needs retraining to change behavior; Recomp (Xu et al. 2023) and robustness-to-irrelevant-context (Yoran et al. 2023) which refine context differently; CoVE (self-verification). Later positioned against by Adaptive-RAG (Jeong et al. 2024) as either too simple or too complex per-query.
- **lineage**:
> Group B (RAG for task solving) - the active / self-reflective / adaptive-retrieval lineage. Self-RAG is a foundational 'learned when-and-whether-to-retrieve plus self-critique' framework: it advances from fixed RAG and token-confidence-triggered active retrieval (FLARE) toward model-emitted reflection-token control, and is a key predecessor/contrast for learned-router adaptive retrieval (Adaptive-RAG), corrective/agentic RAG (CRAG, Self-Reflective RAG recipes in LangGraph/LlamaIndex), and self-critique RAG pipelines.
