### 23. Iter-RetGen - Iterative Retrieval-Generation Synergy (ITER-RETGEN)

2023  ·  EMNLP 2023 Findings  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.15294)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2023
- **venue**: Findings of EMNLP 2023 (ACL Anthology 2023.findings-emnlp.620). Preprint arXiv:2305.15294 (cs.CL), v1 submitted 24 May 2023, v2 revised 23 Oct 2023.
- **authors affiliation**:
> Zhihong Shao (lead; The CoAI Group, DCST, Institute for Artificial Intelligence / State Key Lab of Intelligent Technology and Systems, Tsinghua University, Beijing), Minlie Huang (corresponding; Tsinghua University); Yeyun Gong, Nan Duan (Microsoft Research Asia); Yelong Shen, Weizhu Chen (Microsoft Azure AI). Primary affiliations: Tsinghua University and Microsoft.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.15294

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: QA and knowledge-intensive reasoning - multi-hop open-domain question answering, fact verification, and commonsense reasoning (all cast as retrieval-augmented generation tasks).
- **problem setting**:
> Few-shot (3-shot in-context), single-agent, offline non-interactive inference with a fixed black-box LLM (text-davinci-003 / InstructGPT; also open-source Llama-2 in appendix). The setting is retrieve-and-read open-domain reasoning where retrievers struggle to capture relevance for queries with complex information needs (semantic gaps between the original question and its supporting knowledge). No LLM parameter updates; supervision is limited to 3 shared in-context demonstrations per dataset. An optional generation-augmented retrieval adaptation stage fine-tunes only the dense retriever's query encoder using ~9,000 train / 1,000 validation questions per dataset (HotPotQA, Feverous) and a re-ranker as teacher.
- **what is retrieved**: Documents/paragraphs (Wikipedia passages) from an external knowledge corpus.
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus (per-dataset Wikipedia dumps indexed for dense retrieval). No agent-written growing/episodic memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k retrieval per query (top-5 paragraphs each iteration), but iteration is explicitly motivated by progressively accumulating a more comprehensive and relevant set of supporting knowledge across iterations (the authors note retrieval recall of gold paragraphs increases with iterations) - i.e., approximate completeness pursued via repeated fixed top-k retrieval rather than a single fixed ranking or a variable-size precision-driven recommendation.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A - not a case-based reasoning method (no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain case cycle over solved problem-solution cases; it retrieves documents, not cases).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: false - the work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite CBR literature (Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner).

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: document (Wikipedia paragraph/passage); top-5 paragraphs per retrieval call.
- **index source**:
> Static corpus constructed offline: per-dataset Wikipedia dumps (October 2017 dump for HotPotQA, December 2018 dump for 2WikiMultiHopQA, December 2021 dump for MuSiQue/Bamboogle/Feverous/StrategyQA), encoded for dense retrieval. Not test-time induced and does not grow online. (The retriever's query encoder can be optionally fine-tuned offline via generation-augmented adaptation, but the document store itself is static.)
- **index structure topology**: Flat dense vector index (inner-product similarity over Contriever-MSMARCO embeddings); no graph or hierarchical structure.
- **retriever type**: Dense retriever (Contriever-MSMARCO, Izacard et al. 2022) - off-the-shelf bi-encoder; optionally adapted via distillation from a re-ranker (TART) in the generation-augmented retrieval-adaptation experiments.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Default: none (off-the-shelf Contriever-MSMARCO). Optional generation-augmented retrieval adaptation: the query encoder is trained by KL-divergence distillation from a re-ranker (TART) whose relevance scores are conditioned on the first-iteration LLM output y1 (i.e., LM-generation-conditioned re-ranker supervision distilled into the retriever). This is a distillation / LM-feedback signal, not contrastive similarity labels, RL, or human preference.
- **query construction**:
> First iteration: the raw question q is the query. Later iterations t>=2: the query is the concatenation of the previous-iteration LLM output y_{t-1} with the question q (y_{t-1} || q) - a full generation-augmented (generation-as-query) reformulation. The generated output is a Chain-of-Thought response that signals what knowledge is needed, used verbatim as retrieval context.
- **query granularity**: Iteration/trajectory-level (one query per iteration, formed from the whole previous generation plus the question), not per-CoT-step or per-token; one task-level query at t=1, then full-generation-conditioned queries at each subsequent iteration.
- **when to retrieve**: Iterative on a fixed schedule: retrieval and a full generation alternate for a fixed number T of iterations (each iteration = retrieve-then-generate). No uncertainty trigger or learned router; T is a fixed hyperparameter (experiments report T=1..5, up to 7 iterations).
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed schedule: exactly one retrieval at the start of each of the T iterations (retrieve top-5 using y_{t-1}||q, then generate a full output). No token-level confidence, attention/uncertainty, learned complexity classifier, reflection tokens, or agent-initiated request; the number of iterations T is preset.
- **reranking**:
> No reranking stage in the main inference loop (top-5 dense-retrieved paragraphs are used directly). A re-ranker (TART, Asai et al. 2022) is used only as a teacher during the optional offline generation-augmented retrieval-adaptation experiments (to distill into the retriever), not to rerank at inference.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> None at inference: all retrieved paragraphs are processed as a whole and prepended to the question; the paper explicitly contrasts this with DSP, deliberately NOT summarizing retrieved documents (to avoid summarization errors), and imposing no structural constraints / decomposition. No distractor filtering or compression.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A - no tools/skills are retrieved; only Wikipedia paragraphs are indexed (raw passage text encoded by a dense retriever).
- **index content separation**: N/A - single flat dense paragraph index; no lightweight-index-then-content / progressive-disclosure separation.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A - no tool index or tool-integration protocol; static document corpus only.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A - no inter-tool dependency modeling (no tools).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**: Prompt augmentation: the top-k retrieved paragraphs (D_{y_{t-1}||q}) are prepended to the question q in a Chain-of-Thought prompt, and the LLM generates a full reasoning+answer output y_t. All retrieved knowledge is processed as a whole within a single generation per iteration.
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-generate per iteration in a fixed alternating loop (generation-augmented retrieval across iterations): each iteration produces a complete CoT output that is then reused as retrieval context for the next iteration. This is full-generation/whole-output interleaving, distinct from per-step (IRCoT), per-token (FLARE), or action-loop (ReAct) interleaving; no tree search, MCTS, or hierarchical subtask planning.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Per-answer / per-full-generation: retrieval is interleaved at the granularity of an entire model output (one complete CoT response per iteration), NOT per-CoT-step, per-sentence/token, or per-tool-call. This is the paper's defining distinction from token-level (FLARE) and CoT-step-level (IRCoT) interleaving.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A - not a CBR method; retrieved paragraphs are used verbatim as in-context evidence, not adapted as cases. (The closest 'adaptation' is the offline retriever query-encoder distillation, which adapts the retriever, not a retrieved case.)
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw retrieved paragraphs (verbatim Wikipedia passage text with titles) injected into the prompt; not distilled, summarized, or converted to structured notes.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw document/paragraph (no abstraction or distillation of the retrieved unit).
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Implicit/architectural rather than a dedicated module: processing all retrieved knowledge as a whole within a flexible CoT generation, and iterating, lets later iterations correct factual errors and override distractive paragraphs (case study shows distractor paragraphs in iteration 1 being corrected in iteration 2). The error analysis acknowledges that iteration-1 reasoning can be misled by noisy/distractive retrieved knowledge (65% of errors are retrieval-related). No retriever-aware SFT, explicit relevance evaluator, self-reflection, or distractor-aware training in the main method (the optional retrieval adaptation improves relevance but is not a noise-filtering module).

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (no episodic/skill/workflow/procedural/graph/latent memory; only a per-question accumulation of retrieved paragraphs and the prior generation, which resets each question).
- **write back**: false - no new experiences/cases/skills are stored to a persistent memory across questions. (The optional retrieval-adaptation stage updates retriever parameters offline using generated outputs, but this is offline training, not online experience write-back.)
- **online growth**: false - the retrievable document store is fixed/frozen; it does not grow during deployment/test time.
- **write back trigger**: never - no write-back to any persistent experience/case store occurs during inference. (Retriever adaptation is a separate, offline, one-time training procedure, not a per-deployment write trigger.)
- **failure experience usage**: N/A - no failure or success experiences are stored or retrieved (no memory). Failures are only examined qualitatively in a manual error analysis (e.g., iteration-1 reasoning misleading retrieval), not fed back into any store.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A - no stored experience entries to mutate (no memory). The only parameter update is the optional offline distillation of the retriever query encoder.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> false - retrieval is fixed dense top-5 (steered by the LLM's generated output as query). The optional generation-augmented adaptation trains the retriever's relevance/embedding (via KL distillation) but is not an RL/value-optimized retrieval-selection policy; selection remains similarity top-k.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: N/A - single-model, single-agent; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> HotPotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue (2-hop subset only), Bamboogle (multi-hop QA); Feverous (fact verification); StrategyQA (commonsense reasoning). Evaluated on 125 Bamboogle questions, first 500 StrategyQA train questions, and first 500 dev questions of the other datasets; 3-shot.
- **benchmark family**: QA / multi-hop (HotPotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, Bamboogle); fact verification (Feverous); commonsense reasoning (StrategyQA).
- **baselines**:
> Without retrieval: Direct Prompting (Brown et al. 2020), CoT Prompting (Wei et al. 2022). With retrieval: Direct+retrieval, ReAct (Yao et al. 2022), Self-Ask (Press et al. 2022), and DSP (Khattab et al. 2022, on HotPotQA). Backend LLM: text-davinci-003 (InstructGPT); also Llama-2 in Appendix A. Retriever: Contriever-MSMARCO. Conceptually positioned against IRCoT (Trivedi et al. 2022) as another reasoning-retrieval synergy method.
- **key metrics**:
> Exact Match (EM) and F1 for multi-hop QA; Accuracy for fact verification (Feverous) and commonsense (StrategyQA); plus Acc-dagger, an LLM-judged (text-davinci-003) correctness metric that checks whether a prediction implies the gold answer (used because EM severely underestimates performance). Efficiency: average number of LLM API calls (#API) and number of retrieved paragraphs (#Doc). Retrieval recall of gold paragraphs is reported for the retrieval-recall analysis.
- **headline result**:
> ITER-RETGEN is superior to or competitive with state-of-the-art retrieval-augmented baselines (ReAct, Self-Ask, DSP) while incurring fewer retrieval and generation overheads. E.g., on HotPotQA ITER-RETGEN reaches EM 45.8 / F1 61.1 / Acc-dagger 73.4 (T=4) vs Self-Ask EM 36.8 / F1 55.2 / Acc-dagger 64.8; and ITER-RETGEN with only T=2 (2 API calls, 10 retrieved paragraphs total) is superior to or competitive with ReAct and Self-Ask (which use ~3 API calls and ~15 paragraphs). Generation-augmented retrieval adaptation further raises HotPotQA Acc-dagger to 75.7 at T=2 (vs 71.2 with the original retriever).
- **ablations**:
> (1) Iteration count: increasing T from 1->5 (up to 7) generally improves all metrics, with the largest single boost at the second iteration; performance then plateaus (Table 2). (2) Generation-augmented retrieval adaptation (Table 4): distilling re-ranker (TART) knowledge into the dense query encoder using the first-iteration generation y1 improves Acc-dagger (HotPotQA T=2: 71.2 original -> 75.7 distilled w/ y1; Feverous T=1: 67.0 -> 70.7), and 'distilled w/ y1' beats 'distilled w/o y1', isolating the value of conditioning on the generation. (3) Parametric vs non-parametric knowledge breakdown (Table 5): on CoT-correct vs CoT-incorrect and answer-retrieved vs answer-not-retrieved subsets, ITER-RETGEN better preserves CoT-solvable cases and is consistently more accurate than Self-Ask whether or not retrieved knowledge mentions the answer - attributing Self-Ask's weakness to its structural (follow-up-question) constraints and inability to process all retrieved knowledge as a whole. (4) Efficiency comparison (Table 3): #API and #Doc vs ReAct/Self-Ask. (5) Metric analysis: manual check shows EM is 0 while Acc-dagger=1 for 98.75% of sampled cases, i.e., EM underestimates true correctness. (6) Error analysis: 65% of T=2 errors are retrieval-related (76.9% of those caused by wrong iteration-1 reasoning misleading retrieval), 10% correct-retrieval-but-wrong-reasoning, 25% false negatives. Appendix A reports Llama-2 results.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Partially: a separate retrieval-recall analysis reports that LLM generations help achieve significantly higher recall of gold supporting paragraphs (intrinsic retrieval metric), reported apart from end-to-end EM/F1/Acc-dagger task metrics; however the headline tables are end-to-end task metrics and no full Recall@k/nDCG table across all datasets is the primary report.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome (EM/F1/Acc/Acc-dagger), but with process-oriented analyses: retrieval recall of gold paragraphs, a manual error analysis of where the retrieve-then-reason loop fails, and subset breakdowns by CoT-solvability and answer-retrieval - giving partial insight into intermediate retrieval/reasoning quality.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed top-k = 5 retrieved paragraphs per query/iteration (10 total at T=2, growing linearly with T as each iteration re-retrieves top-5 using the updated query). 3-shot demonstrations shared across methods. All retrieved paragraphs for the current iteration are prepended whole (no truncation/reranking budget). Backend models: text-davinci-003 and Llama-2.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A - this is a method paper, not a survey/taxonomy.
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A - this is a method paper, not a benchmark paper; it reuses existing datasets (HotPotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue 2-hop, Bamboogle, Feverous, StrategyQA), evaluating 125 Bamboogle questions, first 500 StrategyQA train questions, and first 500 dev questions of the other datasets under a shared 3-shot setting.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Chain-of-Thought prompting (Wei et al. 2022); few-shot in-context learning / GPT-3 / InstructGPT (Brown et al. 2020; Ouyang et al. 2022); retrieve-and-read open-domain QA; dense retrieval with Contriever-MSMARCO (Izacard et al. 2022); generation-augmented retrieval ideas - GAR (Mao et al. 2021), HyDE (Gao et al. 2022), and RepoCoder (Zhang et al. 2023, a 2-iteration retrieval-generation paradigm for code); re-ranking with TART (Asai et al. 2022) for the retrieval-adaptation distillation.
- **contrasts with**:
> Methods that interleave retrieval with generation WHILE producing a single output under structural constraints: Self-Ask (Press et al. 2022) and ReAct (Yao et al. 2022) (follow-up-question / action-observation decomposition), IRCoT (Trivedi et al. 2022, per-CoT-step retrieval), and FLARE-style token/sentence-level interleaving; and DSP (Khattab et al. 2022), which summarizes retrieved documents (risking summarization errors) - whereas ITER-RETGEN processes all retrieved knowledge as a whole, preserves generation flexibility without structural constraints, and uses the entire previous output as the next-iteration retrieval context.
- **lineage**:
> Group B (retrieval-augmented task solving): an influential 2023 method establishing whole-generation-augmented iterative retrieval (generation-as-query at the full-output level) for knowledge-intensive multi-step reasoning, sitting alongside IRCoT (CoT-step interleaving) and FLARE (token-level active retrieval) and contrasting with action-loop ReAct/Self-Ask; a predecessor/comparison point for later iterative and adaptive RAG that condition retrieval on the model's own generations.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

### 24. Self-Ask (+ Search) — Measuring and Narrowing the Compositionality Gap in Language Models

2023  ·  EMNLP 2023 Findings  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03350)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2023
- **venue**: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2023 (ACL Anthology 2023.findings-emnlp.378, pages 5687-5711); originally arXiv Oct 2022
- **authors affiliation**: Ofir Press, Muru Zhang, Sewon Min, Ludwig Schmidt, Noah A. Smith, Mike Lewis. Primary affiliation: Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, University of Washington; with MosaicML, Meta AI Research, and Allen Institute for AI (AI2).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03350
- **code url**: https://github.com/ofirpress/self-ask
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/ofirpress/self-ask

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: QA — compositional multi-hop open-domain question answering (factual reasoning).
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-agent, few-shot prompting of a frozen large language model (GPT-3 family, e.g. InstructGPT text/code Davinci-002 and vanilla Davinci) with no fine-tuning. The work first measures the 'compositionality gap' (the fraction of multi-hop questions answered wrong even though the model answers all sub-questions correctly) and then narrows it. Self-Ask prompts the LM to explicitly emit and answer follow-up sub-questions before the final answer; Self-Ask + Search Engine (SA+SE) routes each emitted follow-up sub-question to an external internet search engine API instead of the LM, inserting the returned answer back into the prompt. No supervised training; only few-shot in-context demonstrations.
- **what is retrieved**: Search-engine answers (featured snippets / first-result extracted text) for the LM-generated follow-up sub-questions. In SA+SE the retrieved item is the search engine's answer to a natural-language sub-question.
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus — a live internet search engine API over the web (no agent-written growing memory). Retrieval grounds against an external, web-scale, continuously-updatable source.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Effectively top-1: for each follow-up sub-question the search engine returns a single answer (featured snippet, else the first search result's extracted text); the objective is to answer each decomposed sub-question correctly rather than to retrieve a fixed top-k document ranking.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A — not a case-based reasoning method (no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain case cycle).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False — the work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: snippet — a search-engine answer string (featured snippet or first-result extracted text) per LM-generated follow-up sub-question.
- **index source**: Static external web index served by a popular internet search engine API; no offline-induced or test-time-induced store is built by the method.
- **index structure topology**: flat — an external search-engine web index queried by natural-language sub-questions; no method-side graph/hierarchical/cluster structure.
- **retriever learning signal**: none (off-the-shelf) — the search engine is used as-is with no training; query generation is produced by the frozen LM via few-shot prompting, not by a trained retriever.
- **query construction**: Decomposed sub-queries: the LM emits explicit follow-up sub-questions (after the trigger phrase 'Follow up:'); each full sub-question is sent verbatim as the query to the search engine.
- **query granularity**: step-level — one query per follow-up sub-question step within the decomposition (iterative, multiple sub-queries per main question), not a single task-level query.
- **when to retrieve**: iterative — retrieval is triggered each time the LM emits a follow-up sub-question, repeating until the LM outputs the final answer; agent-initiated (the LM decides how many follow-ups to ask).
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Agent-initiated request: the LM's emission of a 'Follow up:' sub-question (terminated by the 'Intermediate answer:' cue) triggers a search-engine call. The number and timing of retrievals are decided by the LM's own generated decomposition (not a fixed schedule or token-confidence signal).
- **reranking**: None — no reranking stage; the search engine's featured snippet (or first result) is taken directly.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Largely none for SA+SE (the returned answer is inserted back into the prompt). A separate baseline 'Search Engine + LM postprocessing' uses Davinci-002 to extract the short final answer from full-sentence search results, but in SA+SE itself no explicit refinement/compression/distractor-filtering is applied.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A — no tool/skill descriptions are indexed; the search engine is a single fixed tool invoked with the natural-language sub-question.
- **index content separation**: N/A — no separate lightweight index vs heavy content; queries go straight to a web search engine.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Live external search-engine web index (continuously updatable), accessed via a search-engine API (e.g. SerpAPI/Google in the released code). No MCP/RapidAPI/function-calling formalism; integration is a few lines of code feeding sub-questions to the API and inserting results back into the prompt.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A — a single search tool; no inter-tool dependency modeling.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation: the search engine's answer to each follow-up sub-question is inserted back into the prompt (as if the LM had produced 'Intermediate answer: ...'), and the LM continues generating the next sub-question or the final answer. Retrieved evidence is consumed in-context, not used as a training signal or latent injection.
- **planning integration**:
> Inside a decompose-then-search loop: the LM plans by decomposing the question into follow-up sub-questions; retrieval is interleaved per sub-question within the reasoning chain (retrieve-then-continue), repeating until a final answer. This is per-step interleaved retrieval inside a self-generated decomposition, not one-shot plan-time exemplars or tree search.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: per-sub-question (per decomposition step): one search-engine call per LM-emitted follow-up question within a single rollout.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A — not CBR; no retrieved case is adapted. (The closest analogue is that the search answer is spliced verbatim into the in-context decomposition.)
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw text answer (featured snippet or extracted first-result text) inserted as 'Intermediate answer:' into the free-text decomposition transcript; surface form is a short natural-language answer string.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw factual answer to a single sub-question (atomic fact / snippet), not a distilled strategy, workflow, or skill.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Minimal/none explicit. The structured Self-Ask scaffolding (clear sub-question demarcation) plus the optional LM-postprocessing baseline to extract short answers mitigate format/noise issues, but there is no retriever-aware training, relevance evaluator, or reason-in-documents refinement in SA+SE.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none — the method uses no episodic/skill/workflow memory; it relies on a stateless external search engine plus the in-context prompt transcript.
- **write back**: False — no experiences/cases/skills are written back to any memory store.
- **online growth**: False — no method-side store grows during deployment (the underlying web index updates externally, but the method itself maintains no growing memory).
- **write back trigger**: never — nothing is written back to a memory.
- **failure experience usage**: N/A — no storage or reuse of failed/negative experiences (no memory).
- **memory evolution update**: N/A — no stored entries to mutate (no memory).
- **retrieval as learned policy**: False — retrieval is not a learned/RL policy; sub-question emission is produced by a frozen few-shot-prompted LM and queries go to an off-the-shelf search engine.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: N/A — single-agent, single-LM; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> Compositional Celebrities (CC, ~8.6k automatically generated 2-hop questions, 17 templates, introduced by this paper); Bamboogle (125 hand-written 2-hop questions, introduced by this paper, filtered so a search engine's featured snippet is wrong); 2WikiMultiHopQA (Ho et al., 2020); MuSiQue / Musique (Trivedi et al., 2022).
- **benchmark family**: QA / multi-hop (compositional open-domain multi-hop QA).
- **baselines**:
> Direct Prompting (few-shot, Brown et al. 2020); Chain of Thought (Wei et al. 2022b); plain Search Engine (question sent directly to search engine); Search Engine + LM postprocessing (Davinci-002 extracts the short answer from search results); 'Let's think step by step' zero-shot CoT (Kojima et al. 2022) is discussed but not extensively run. Self-Ask is also compared against these; Self-Ask + Search is the proposed extension.
- **key metrics**: Accuracy (%). For Bamboogle, accuracy is manually judged by the authors; for 2WikiMultiHopQA and MuSiQue, exact match (EM). Also reports speed as average number of tokens in the generated answer.
- **headline result**:
> On Bamboogle with Davinci-002, Self-Ask + Search Engine reaches 60.0% accuracy vs 57.6% Self-Ask, 46.4% Chain of Thought, 17.6% Direct Prompting, and 0.0% for plain search. Self-Ask + Search also leads on 2WikiMultiHopQA (40.1% EM) and MuSiQue (15.2% EM). Separately, the paper's central measurement is that the compositionality gap stays roughly constant at ~40% across GPT-3 model sizes (1B–175B), not shrinking with scale.
- **ablations**:
> Table 1 (Davinci-002): Direct prompting 17.6/25.4/5.6, Chain of Thought 46.4/29.8/12.6, plain Search 0.0/2.2/1.5, Search+postproc. -/26.3/6.5, Self-ask 57.6/30.0/13.8, Self-ask+Search 60.0/40.1/15.2 on Bamboogle/2Wiki/MuSiQue respectively — isolating the marginal gains of (a) elicitive decomposition (Self-ask over CoT/Direct) and (b) plugging in the search engine (SA+SE over Self-ask). On CC, Self-Ask obtains 79.6%/54.2% with InstructGPT-Davinci-002/Davinci vs 45.7%/1.1% for 'Let's think step by step', showing decomposition prompting strongly beats zero-shot CoT. Format ablation: 40% of CoT final answers were not short-form vs 17% for Self-ask and 3% for Self-ask+search, showing the scaffolding improves answer parseability. Trigger-phrase ablation: appending 'Are follow up questions needed here:' slightly improves results (more so for smaller models).
- **evaluation decoupling**: Partly. The compositionality gap is an intrinsic decomposition metric (sub-question correctness vs full-question correctness) reported on CC, separate from end-to-end accuracy; but no Recall@k/nDCG retrieval metrics are reported (the retriever is an external search engine).
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Both. Final-answer accuracy/EM is the outcome metric; the compositionality gap measures intermediate sub-question vs final reasoning quality (a process-level metric), and the short-form-answer-rate analysis assesses process/format quality.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Reports speed as average number of generated answer tokens (Table 2) and notes the search-engine integration is implementable in only a few lines of code and requires no fine-tuning or architecture change. SA+SE makes one search-engine API call per follow-up sub-question (typically a few per 2-hop question). No detailed dollar/latency cost study beyond token-count speed.
- **context budget and selection count**: Few-shot prompting with task-specific demonstrations (e.g. a 4-shot prompt for Bamboogle); the SA+SE prompt is identical to the Self-Ask prompt. Retrieval selection count is top-1 per sub-question (featured snippet, else first result). No fixed token budget cap reported.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A — this is a method/measurement paper, not a survey.
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Compositional Celebrities: ~8.6k automatically generated 2-hop questions composed from frequently stated facts combined in improbable ways, covering 17 templates; designed to estimate the compositionality gap at scale, answers programmatically verifiable. Bamboogle: 125 hand-crafted 2-hop questions written by the authors, each verifiable from Wikipedia but filtered so a popular search engine returns an incorrect featured snippet; designed for diverse, high-variation evaluation with less statistical power. (2WikiMultiHopQA and MuSiQue are pre-existing automatically generated multi-hop datasets.)

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Few-shot in-context prompting (GPT-3, Brown et al. 2020); Chain-of-Thought prompting (Wei et al. 2022b); scratchpad/elicitive prompting (Nye et al. 2021); zero-shot CoT 'Let's think step by step' (Kojima et al. 2022). Uses GPT-3 family models (InstructGPT/Davinci) off-the-shelf and a commercial internet search engine API.
- **contrasts with**:
> Direct (naive) few-shot prompting; Chain-of-Thought prompting (Self-Ask disentangles question decomposition from sub-answer generation and yields more parseable answers); plain search-engine QA (which fails on these composed questions, 0.0% on Bamboogle); 'Let's think step by step' zero-shot CoT (much weaker on CC).
- **lineage**:
> Sub-topic B (RAG for task solving): an early (2022/2023) decompose-then-search / interleaved reasoning-and-retrieval method for compositional multi-hop QA, alongside contemporaneous work like ReAct and IRCoT; a foundational predecessor for agentic retrieval-augmented reasoning where an LM emits sub-questions answered by an external search tool.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- retriever_type

<a id="item-adaptive-rag"></a>
### 25. Adaptive-RAG: Learning to Adapt Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models through Question Complexity

2024  ·  NAACL 2024  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.14403)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: NAACL 2024 (Proceedings of the 2024 Conference of the North American Chapter of the ACL, pages 7036-7050; ACL Anthology 2024.naacl-long.389)
- **authors affiliation**: Soyeong Jeong, Jinheon Baek, Sukmin Cho, Sung Ju Hwang, Jong C. Park (corresponding author). All affiliated with KAIST (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology), School of Computing and Graduate School of AI.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.14403
- **code url**: https://github.com/starsuzi/Adaptive-RAG
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (single-author research repo, last pushed 2024-05; not a continuously-updated leaderboard/paper-list)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: QA (open-domain question answering, spanning single-hop and multi-hop / multi-step reasoning QA)
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-agent, non-interactive open-domain QA over a fixed Wikipedia-style document corpus. The system must, per incoming query, dynamically choose one of three retrieval-augmented LLM strategies (no-retrieval, single-step retrieval, or iterative multi-step retrieval) to balance accuracy and computational cost. No human-annotated complexity labels are available; supervision for the routing classifier is automatically constructed from (a) the actual prediction outcomes of the three strategies (silver labels) and (b) inductive dataset biases (single-hop datasets -> single-step, multi-hop datasets -> multi-step). The off-the-shelf LLM and retriever are frozen; only a small external classifier is trained.
- **what is retrieved**: docs (Wikipedia passages / external knowledge-base documents relevant to the query)
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus (Wikipedia passages for single-hop datasets, and the preprocessed multi-hop document corpus from Trivedi et al. 2023 IRCoT). No agent-written growing memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**: Fixed top-k document ranking per retrieval call (standard BM25 top-k). The novel adaptive lever is over the NUMBER of retrieval STEPS (0 / 1 / iterative), not over recovering a complete minimal document set; not a precision-driven variable-size set.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based-reasoning method; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain case cycle).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: false. The work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is an adaptive retrieval-routing framework.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: document (Wikipedia / KB passage). Retrieval granularity is the standard passage/document returned by BM25; the adaptive component routes WHEN/HOW MANY TIMES to retrieve.
- **index source**: Static corpus, offline-built. Documents indexed offline in Elasticsearch/BM25 (HotpotQA 5,233,329; 2WikiMultihopQA 430,225; MuSiQue 139,416; Wiki 21,015,324 indexed documents). Store is frozen at test time.
- **index structure topology**: Flat term-based inverted index (BM25 over Elasticsearch 7.10.2). No graph or hierarchical structure.
- **retriever type**: BM25 (term-based sparse retrieval, Robertson et al. 1994), used off-the-shelf and shared across all compared methods for fair comparison.
- **retriever learning signal**: none (off-the-shelf BM25, not trained). The learned component is the separate query-complexity ROUTER classifier, not the document retriever.
- **query construction**:
> For single-step: raw input query q. For multi-step (label C): the IRCoT-style interleaved process where each retrieval step uses the original query plus accumulated Chain-of-Thought context (q, c_i) to issue the next retrieval. A separate T5-Large classifier consumes the raw query q to produce a complexity label (A/B/C) that selects the strategy.
- **query granularity**: Task-level for the routing decision (one classification at t=0 over the raw query). Within the chosen multi-step path, retrieval is step/CoT-step-level (iterative).
- **when to retrieve**: adaptive (learned router): a trained complexity classifier selects no-retrieval (A) / single-step retrieval (B) / iterative multi-step retrieval (C) per query.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Learned query-complexity classifier (a smaller T5-Large LM outputs label o in {A,B,C}). Trained on automatically-collected labels from (1) silver data = which of the three strategies actually answered correctly, with ties broken toward the simpler strategy, and (2) inductive dataset bias (single-hop->B, multi-hop->C) for queries left unlabeled by silver labeling.
- **reranking**: None. Standard BM25 top-k results are used directly; no cross-encoder or RRF reranking stage is introduced.
- **retrieved context refinement**: None beyond strategy selection. Retrieved documents are injected directly into the LLM prompt; no decompose-recompose, distillation, distractor filtering, or compression is applied (within the multi-step path it follows IRCoT's interleaving of CoT and retrieval).
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tool/skill retrieval; retrieves plain documents).
- **index content separation**: N/A (no lightweight-index-then-content separation; standard BM25 index over full passages).
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (static document index; no tool API / RapidAPI / MCP / function-calling integration).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tools, no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**: prompt augmentation: retrieved documents are concatenated into the LLM input. Single-step uses LLM(q,d); multi-step iteratively uses LLM(q,d_i,c_i) with accumulated documents/CoT context; no-retrieval uses LLM(q) only.
- **planning integration**:
> retrieve-then-plan / per-step interleaved depending on routed strategy. Label A: direct LLM answer (no retrieval). Label B: one-shot retrieve-then-answer. Label C: iterative interleaving of Chain-of-Thought reasoning and retrieval inside a search loop (IRCoT, Trivedi et al. 2023), repeating until the reasoning chain yields the answer.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer for labels A and B (single response). Per-CoT-step for label C (multi-step IRCoT interleaves a reasoning/Chain-of-Thought step with a retrieval step each round).
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (no case adaptation; retrieved documents are used verbatim as prompt context).
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw retrieved documents (Wikipedia/KB passages) inserted as text into the LLM prompt; no distillation into strategies/guidelines/programs.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw document/passage (no distilled strategy, workflow, or skill abstraction).
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> None explicit. The implicit robustness mechanism is the routing classifier itself: by routing simple queries to no-retrieval, it avoids injecting partially-irrelevant retrieved documents (the case study shows Adaptive Retrieval pulling distracting 'Microsoft' docs whereas Adaptive-RAG answers from parametric knowledge). No dedicated relevance evaluator, self-reflection, or distractor-aware training.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (no episodic/skill/workflow memory; the only learned artifact is the static query-complexity classifier).
- **write back**: false. No new experiences, cases, or documents are written back into any store during deployment.
- **online growth**: false. The document index is frozen after offline construction; nothing grows at test time.
- **write back trigger**: never (no memory write-back; the classifier is trained once offline and then frozen at inference).
- **failure experience usage**:
> Partially, only at classifier TRAINING time (offline), not as stored retrievable experience: the silver-labeling uses which strategies succeed/fail to assign complexity labels (success of the simplest strategy -> A, etc.). Queries that all three strategies fail are left to inductive-bias labeling. There is no failure memory stored or retrieved at test time.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (no stored memory entries to mutate). The classifier weights are fixed after offline training; no online update.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Partial: the WHEN/HOW-MANY-STEPS routing decision is a learned classifier (supervised cross-entropy on automatically-collected silver+binary labels), not RL. The document-selection within each step remains fixed similarity top-k BM25. So routing-as-policy is a supervised classifier, not an RL/value-based policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: N/A (single-agent, single private system; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory sharing).

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: Single-hop: SQuAD v1.1, Natural Questions (NQ), TriviaQA. Multi-hop: MuSiQue, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA. 500 test samples per dataset, evaluated jointly to simulate mixed-complexity workloads.
- **benchmark family**: QA (open-domain single-hop) + multi-hop QA. Single-hop family: SQuAD/NQ/TriviaQA; multi-hop family: MuSiQue/HotpotQA/2WikiMultiHopQA.
- **baselines**:
> No Retrieval (LLM only); Single-step Approach (one-shot retrieve-then-read); Multi-step Approach (IRCoT, Trivedi et al. 2023, iterative CoT+retrieval, the most sophisticated SOTA); Adaptive Retrieval (Mallen et al. 2023, entity-frequency-based binary retrieve-or-not); Self-RAG (Asai et al. 2024, self-reflective adaptive retrieval, with LLaMA2-7B/13B base); plus Adaptive-RAG w/ Oracle (upper-bound oracle classifier).
- **key metrics**: Effectiveness: EM (Exact Match), F1, Acc (accuracy = answer contains ground truth). Efficiency: Step (number of retrieve-and-generate steps) and Time (average per-query answering time relative to the single-step approach).
- **headline result**:
> Averaged over all 6 datasets with FLAN-T5-XL (3B): Adaptive-RAG F1 46.94 / EM 37.17 / Acc 42.10 at 2.17 steps (relative time 3.60), versus the Multi-step Approach F1 48.85 / EM 39.00 / Acc 43.70 at 4.69 steps (relative time 8.81) and the Single-step Approach F1 44.31 / Acc 38.87 at 1.0 step. Adaptive-RAG nearly matches the expensive multi-step accuracy while roughly halving the number of steps, and beats the adaptive baselines (Adaptive Retrieval F1 32.24; Self-RAG* F1 20.79). With GPT-3.5 it reaches Acc 48.97 at only 1.03 steps.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Classifier training data ablation (Table 4, FLAN-T5-XL): full (silver+binary) gives F1 46.94 / 1084 steps / overall classifier Acc 54.52; w/o Binary (silver only) F1 43.43 / 640 steps / Acc 60.30 but Multi-class Acc collapses to 39.55; w/o Silver (binary/inductive-bias only) F1 48.79 / 1464 steps / overall Acc 40.00 with No-retrieval Acc 0.00 - showing silver labels are needed to recover the no-retrieval (A) class and binary labels are needed for multi-hop (C) accuracy/efficiency balance. (2) Classifier size (Table 6): Small 60M (F1 45.83), Base 223M (F1 45.97), Large 770M (F1 46.94) - little sensitivity, so a small classifier suffices. (3) Adaptive-RAG w/ Oracle classifier as an upper bound (avg F1 56.28 / Acc 49.90 at 1.28 steps for FLAN-T5-XL), showing headroom for classifier improvement. (4) Confusion-matrix analysis of misclassification across A/B/C labels.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Yes, partially. The query-complexity CLASSIFIER is evaluated intrinsically (classification accuracy overall and per A/B/C label, plus confusion matrix in Figure 3 and Table 4) separately from the end-to-end QA metrics (EM/F1/Acc). However, this is classifier accuracy, not retrieval Recall@k/nDCG (retrieval quality itself is not separately scored).
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Both. Outcome: QA EM/F1/Acc. Process: number of retrieval-and-generate steps, per-query time, classifier complexity-prediction accuracy, and per-label classification breakdown - i.e., the routing/process quality is explicitly measured alongside final answer quality.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Central focus. Reports Step count and relative Time per query, plus exact per-query latency (Table 3): No(A) 0.35s, One(B) 3.08s, Multi(C) 27.18s, with predicted label distribution 8.60% A / 53.33% B / 38.07% C. Adaptive-RAG cuts steps from the multi-step approach's 4.69 to 2.17 (FLAN-T5-XL) while retaining near-multi-step accuracy; with GPT-3.5 it uses only 1.03 steps vs 2.81 for multi-step.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (this is a method paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (uses existing benchmarks rather than constructing a new one). Note: 500 test samples per dataset are subsampled following Trivedi et al. 2023; classifier training uses ~400 sampled queries per dataset annotated via silver + inductive-bias labels.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> IRCoT (Trivedi et al. 2023, used as the multi-step strategy and as the skeleton code base); standard single-step retrieve-then-read RAG; BM25 (Robertson et al. 1994); FLAN-T5 (Chung et al. 2022) and GPT-3.5 as frozen reader LLMs; T5-Large (Raffel et al. 2020) as the classifier; DPR Wikipedia corpus (Karpukhin et al. 2020).
- **contrasts with**:
> Adaptive Retrieval (Mallen et al. 2023, binary entity-frequency retrieve-or-not - too coarse, ignores multi-hop); Self-RAG (Asai et al. 2024, single self-reflective model that retrieves/critiques/generates - argued to be either overly simple or overly complex for all queries); Qi et al. 2021 (fixed retrieve-read-rerank loop on BERT-like LMs needing task-specific training); always-multi-step and always-single-step one-size-fits-all RAG.
- **lineage**:
> Sits in the lineage of adaptive / when-to-retrieve RAG (Group B: RAG for task solving). It is a router-based bridge between no-retrieval, single-step RAG, and iterative multi-step RAG (IRCoT/FLARE/Self-RAG family), pioneering the use of a learned query-complexity classifier to select retrieval depth; widely featured downstream in LlamaIndex/LangGraph adaptive-RAG recipes.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- context_budget_and_selection_count

<a id="item-agentless"></a>
### 26. Agentless (Agentless: Demystifying LLM-based Software Engineering Agents)

2024  ·  arXiv 2407.01489  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01489)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: arXiv:2407.01489 (v1 Jul 2024, v2 Oct 2024). Peer-reviewed version published as 'Demystifying LLM-Based Software Engineering Agents' in Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering (PACMSE), Vol. 2, FSE 2025, pp. 801-824, DOI 10.1145/3715754.
- **authors affiliation**: Chunqiu Steven Xia, Yinlin Deng, Soren Dunn, Lingming Zhang — all at University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (UIUC). First two authors contributed equally.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01489
- **code url**: https://github.com/OpenAutoCoder/Agentless
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/OpenAutoCoder/Agentless (MIT license; ~2.1k stars; v1.5.0 release with artifacts for SWE-bench Lite/Verified runs and preprocessed repo structures; Dec 2024 update adds Claude 3.5 Sonnet reaching 40.7%/50.8% on Lite/Verified).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Code / automated software engineering — automatically resolving real-world GitHub issues (repository-level bug fixing and feature implementation) on SWE-bench. Explicitly positioned as an 'agentless' alternative to autonomous LLM software agents.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, non-interactive, single-pass pipeline (no autonomous agent loop): given a GitHub issue description and the project codebase, produce a patch. Agentless uses a fixed three-phase process — (1) hierarchical fault localization, (2) repair (multi-sample patch generation), (3) patch validation (regression + generated reproduction tests for selection) — without letting the LLM decide future actions or use complex tools. Single-agent (no multi-agent), no training of the LLM (off-the-shelf GPT-4o gpt-4o-2024-05-13); supervision is NOT used to train any component. The realistic SWE-bench setup provides only regression tests from the repo, not bug-triggering reproduction tests (which Agentless synthesizes).
- **what is retrieved**:
> Source-code context: relevant repository files / code snippets (chunks) localized as candidate edit sites for the issue. Retrieval here is fault-localization retrieval (issue description -> suspicious code locations), NOT retrieval of demonstrations/cases/skills/experiences. No external demos or memory are retrieved.
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus: the target project's own codebase (the repository under repair) is the corpus from which relevant files/chunks are retrieved. There is no growing/episodic agent memory and no external knowledge base; the corpus is the per-issue repository snapshot.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Mixed/completeness-oriented within a top-k frame: file-level uses top-N (default top-3 suspicious files); related-element and edit-location steps are unrestricted in count (localize an unrestricted number of suspicious classes/functions, then fine-grained edit locations). The objective is to RECOVER the complete minimal set of edit locations needed to fix the issue (multi-location repository edits), measured by whether ground-truth locations are contained ('Contains GT'), rather than a single fixed ranking.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A — Agentless is not a case-based-reasoning system; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain over a case base. [Retrieve: no (retrieves code context, not cases), Reuse: no, Revise: no, Retain: no].
- **explicit cbr grounding**: false — the work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is framed as fault localization + automated program repair + patch validation.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Code at multiple granularities across the hierarchy: (1) file-level (whole files, top-N), (2) related elements = classes/functions/variables (via a 'skeleton format' of each file), (3) fine-grained edit locations (specific lines/code snippets). The embedding-based retriever indexes code CHUNKS (segments, 512 tokens). So retrieval units are document/file and code-snippet/element.
- **index source**:
> Static corpus, per-issue online-constructed: for each issue the repository is parsed into a tree-like structure and (after filtering irrelevant folders) divided into code chunks that are embedded on the fly. The index is built at test time per repository snapshot but is not a learned/offline-induced store and does not grow during deployment beyond the single issue.
- **index structure topology**:
> Hybrid: (a) a hierarchical tree-like repository structure (file paths) given to the LLM for prompting-based localization; (b) a flat vector index of code chunk embeddings (cosine similarity) for embedding-based retrieval; plus a per-file 'skeleton' (class/function signatures) representation. No dependency/knowledge graph (contrasted with Aider's call-graph repo map and RepoGraph).
- **retriever type**:
> Hybrid: LLM-as-retriever (prompting-based localization: LLM reads repo tree + issue and ranks top-N suspicious files; also localizes elements and edit locations) combined with dense embedding-based retrieval (OpenAI text-embedding-3-small via LlamaIndex, cosine similarity over code chunks). BM25 is used only in the RAG baseline, not in Agentless itself.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None (off-the-shelf): both retrieval mechanisms use frozen, untrained models. The LLM (GPT-4o) localizer is prompted zero/few-shot with no fine-tuning; the dense retriever uses a pretrained off-the-shelf embedding model (text-embedding-3-small) with no contrastive/LM-feedback/RL training. There is no learned retriever and no learned selection policy.
- **query construction**:
> Raw issue description is the query. For prompting-based localization the query is the issue text plus the repository tree structure (and, in later steps, the skeleton format / localized elements). For embedding-based retrieval the query is the embedding of the original issue description, matched against code-chunk embeddings. No query decomposition, expansion, or thought-conditioning.
- **query granularity**: Task-level, one-shot at t=0 per phase: a single query (the issue) drives localization; localization itself is hierarchical/multi-step (file -> element -> edit location) but each step is a fixed prompt, not a state/step-conditioned re-query within an agent loop.
- **when to retrieve**:
> One-shot (per phase) within a fixed pipeline: retrieval/localization happens once at the start (file localization via prompting + embedding, then element localization, then edit-location localization). It is NOT iterative/active/agent-triggered — the LLM never decides to retrieve more based on intermediate observations.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule: localization and embedding retrieval are always executed in the predetermined three-phase order. No confidence/uncertainty signal, learned router, reflection token, or agent-initiated retrieval request triggers retrieval.
- **reranking**:
> Light combination/merging rather than a learned reranker: prompting-localized files and embedding-retrieved files are combined by selecting the top-N most common files localized by both methods. There is no cross-encoder or instruction-tuned reranking stage. (A separate 'patch re-ranking/selection' via tests exists in the validation phase, but that ranks PATCHES, not retrieved context.)
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Decompose/compress via hierarchical localization: instead of feeding whole files, Agentless compresses each file to a concise 'skeleton format' (class/function signatures with bodies elided), then narrows to fine-grained edit locations with a +/-10-line context window. This progressively reduces context to essential parts; irrelevant folders are filtered before embedding. No distractor-classifier or reason-in-documents distillation.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A — Agentless retrieves source code, not tool/skill descriptions. Code is processed via the 'skeleton format' (signature-level summary of each file) before being shown to the LLM, but this is code-context engineering, not tool-document engineering.
- **index content separation**:
> Yes (progressive disclosure): a lightweight repository-tree/skeleton representation is used for early localization, and the heavy full source content is only loaded for the narrowed edit locations (+/-10 lines). The skeleton format separates a concise index-like view from on-demand detailed code, an explicit cost-reduction design.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A — not a tool-retrieval system. No live tool index or integration protocol (no RapidAPI/REST/MCP/function-calling); the codebase is a static per-issue snapshot.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A — no inter-tool dependency modeling. (Code-level dependencies such as call graphs are explicitly NOT modeled; Agentless contrasts with Aider's call-graph repo map and RepoGraph's repository graph, deliberately using a simpler tree + embedding approach.)

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation: localized code (file skeletons, related elements, then code snippets at edit locations with +/-10-line context) plus the issue description are placed in the LLM prompt, which samples candidate patches in a simple search/replace diff format. Retrieved code is context for generation, not a training signal or reused skill.
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-repair fixed pipeline (no planning/search loop): hierarchical localization (a structured retrieval cascade) feeds the repair phase, which feeds patch validation. There is no MCTS/tree search, no per-step interleaving with an agent policy, and the LLM does not plan future actions. The 'plan' is the hard-coded three-phase process.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-phase / per-answer: localization, repair, and validation are distinct stages; within repair the whole patch is generated per sample (not interleaved per token/step with retrieval). There is no per-CoT-step or per-tool-call retrieval interleaving.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not a CBR system) — no retrieved case is adapted. The closest analogue is that the LLM generates patches conditioned on retrieved code context (LLM-prompted generation), but there is no case/exemplar being revised.
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw code surface forms at varying compression: repository tree (file paths), per-file skeleton (signatures), and raw code snippets at edit locations (+/-10 lines). What is injected is concrete source code, not distilled strategies, workflows, programs-as-skills, or latent tokens.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw, concrete code (single repository's source), shown at multiple abstraction granularities (file path -> signature skeleton -> raw edit-location snippet). Not a distilled strategy, guideline, reusable workflow, or procedural skill.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Hierarchical narrowing + combination + test-based filtering: (1) irrelevant-folder filtering before embedding reduces distractors; (2) combining prompting- and embedding-localized files (intersection/most-common) reduces spurious files; (3) skeleton format limits context; (4) crucially, generated reproduction tests + regression tests filter out incorrect candidate patches at validation time. No retriever-aware training or self-reflection module.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none — no episodic/skill-library/workflow/procedural/graph/latent memory. Each issue is solved independently from the static repository snapshot; nothing persists across issues.
- **write back**: false — the system stores no experiences/cases/skills. Generated patches and reproduction tests are produced per issue and not written to any reusable store.
- **online growth**: No — there is no retrievable store that grows during deployment. The per-issue code index is rebuilt for each problem and discarded; no cross-issue accumulation.
- **write back trigger**: never — no write-back mechanism exists; nothing is added to any persistent memory during or after solving an issue.
- **failure experience usage**: No failure-experience memory. Within a single issue, candidate patches that fail regression or reproduction tests are filtered out (negative signal used transiently for selection), but failed trajectories/patches are never stored or retrieved as experiences for future issues.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A — no stored entries exist to mutate (no append/dedup/delta/refine/prune); memory is absent.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No — retrieval/localization is NOT a learned or RL-optimized policy. It is a fixed pipeline using off-the-shelf LLM prompting plus untrained dense-embedding cosine similarity (top-N). No M-MDP, soft Q-learning, or learned selection.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> SWE-bench Lite (300 real GitHub issues) is the primary benchmark. The authors also construct SWE-bench Lite-S (249 problems, filtering out issues with exact ground-truth patch leaked in the description, misleading solutions, or insufficient information). The peer-reviewed/extended version and repo also report SWE-bench Verified (with Claude 3.5 Sonnet reaching >50% solve rate).
- **benchmark family**: code (SWE-bench family: SWE-bench Lite / SWE-bench Lite-S / SWE-bench Verified). Repository-level issue resolution / automated program repair.
- **baselines**:
> Open-source and closed-source software agents on the SWE-bench Lite leaderboard, including: SWE-agent, AutoCodeRover / AutoCodeRover-v2, Aider, Moatless, OpenDevin+CodeAct, AppMap Navie, RepoGraph, SpecRover, CodeR, MASAI, RepoUnderstander, and commercial systems (CodeStory Aide, Bytedance MarsCode, Honeycomb, MentatBot, Gru, Isoform, SuperCoder2.0, Alibaba Lingma Agent, Factory Code Droid, Amazon Q Developer, IBM Research Agent-101, OpenCSG StarShip, SIMA). Also a simple RAG agentless baseline (BM25-retrieved files + direct LLM patch generation, from the SWE-bench paper) across Claude-2/3 Opus, GPT-4, GPT-3.5.
- **key metrics**:
> (1) % Resolved (percentage of issues resolved); (2) Avg. $ Cost (average inference cost per issue); (3) Avg. # Tokens (input+output tokens per issue); (4) % Correct Location at file / function / line levels (localization quality); plus 'Contains GT' (fraction of issues whose ground-truth locations are recovered) and LoC (lines of code in context) for localization ablations.
- **headline result**:
> On SWE-bench Lite with GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-05-13), Agentless resolves 96/300 = 32.00% of issues at an average cost of $0.70 and 78,166 tokens per issue — the highest performance and among the lowest cost vs all existing open-source software agents at submission time. Later (Dec 2024) Agentless with Claude 3.5 Sonnet reaches 40.7% on SWE-bench Lite and 50.8% on SWE-bench Verified.
- **ablations**:
> Localization (Table 2, % Contains GT / LoC / cost): file-level Prompting-based 78.67%, Embedding-based w/o irrelevant filtering 67.67% vs w/ filtering 70.33%, Combined 81.67%; related-element Complete file 53.67% vs Skeleton format 58.33% (skeleton both better and ~7x cheaper, $0.02 vs $0.15); edit-location Greedy 50.67% vs Direct-from-file 47.00% vs Multi-samples-merged 56.33%. Repair (Table 3): Greedy location 88 (29.33%), Multi-samples merged 85 (28.33%), Multi-samples (4x10) 96 (32.00%); just 1 greedy sample already fixes 80; performance plateaus around 40 samples; the upper bound if ANY sampled patch counted is 126 (42.0%). Patch validation (Table 4): Majority voting alone 77 (25.67%, $0.00 extra); +Regression test 81 (27.00%, +$0.01); +Reproduction test 96 (32.00%, +$0.25) — reproduction-test filtering is the largest single driver. Irrelevant-folder filtering improves both cost and accuracy for embedding retrieval.
- **evaluation decoupling**: Yes — intrinsic localization metrics are reported separately from end-to-end resolution: % Correct Location at file/function/line levels (Table 1) and 'Contains GT' / LoC / cost per localization step (Table 2) are decoupled from the % Resolved end-to-end metric.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both — beyond the final % Resolved (outcome), the paper reports process-level metrics: localization correctness at line/function/file granularity, ground-truth-containment of localized context, reproduction-test plausibility/selection counts, and patch-sample scaling (issues fixed vs number of samples).
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Strong efficiency emphasis: Agentless costs only $0.70 and 78,166 tokens per issue on SWE-bench Lite (vs e.g. SWE-agent $1.62-$2.53 and ~500k tokens), while resolving more issues than all open-source agents. Skeleton format cuts related-element localization cost ~7x ($0.15 -> $0.02). Reproduction-test filtering adds ~$0.25 for the largest accuracy gain. v1.0 originally reported $0.34 per issue. Component costs are itemized per phase.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed/budget-capped counts: top-3 suspicious files (file level); unrestricted number of suspicious classes/functions (element level); 4 sampled sets of edit locations with +/-10 lines context each; repair samples 10 patches per set (1 greedy + 9, total ~40); 40 reproduction-test samples (1 greedy + 39). Embedding chunk size 512, overlap 0. Context is progressively truncated via skeleton format and edit-location windows.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A — primary method paper, not a survey/taxonomy.
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> SWE-bench Lite-S: a 249-problem subset of SWE-bench Lite (300) constructed by manual classification, excluding problems whose description leaks the exact ground-truth patch, gives misleading solutions, or provides insufficient/misleading information — to normalize difficulty and enable more rigorous comparison. Answers are verifiable via test execution (PASS_TO_PASS regression + FAIL_TO_PASS). This filtering anticipated OpenAI's human-validated SWE-bench Verified. Rankings on Lite vs Lite-S are largely stable (Agentless ranks 9 on both); top system reaches 45.78% on Lite-S.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> SWE-bench (Jimenez et al. 2024) benchmark and its RAG baseline; Aider's simple search/replace diff format and repo-map idea (Gauthier 2024); IR-based static fault localization (Zhou et al. 2012 'Where Should the Bugs Be Fixed?'; Singhal et al. 2001); LLM-based fault localization (Yang et al., Wu et al., Qin et al., Kang et al.); LLM-based APR with multi-sample patch generation (Xia et al. 2023); reproduction-test-guided selection inspired by SpecRover (Ruan et al. 2024) and CodeR (Chen et al. 2024); LlamaIndex + OpenAI text-embedding-3-small for embedding retrieval.
- **contrasts with**:
> Autonomous LLM software AGENTS — SWE-agent, AutoCodeRover/SpecRover (code-search APIs, iterative retrieval), Aider (call-graph repo map), Moatless (LLM-query retrieval + search tools), OpenDevin+CodeAct, RepoGraph/RepoUnderstander (repository graphs) — which let the LLM use tools, run commands, observe feedback, and plan future actions. Agentless deliberately removes agentic decision-making, tool use, and iterative control in favor of a fixed three-phase pipeline, arguing it is simpler, more interpretable, cheaper, and competitive or better.
- **lineage**:
> Group B (RAG / retrieval for task-solving) — specifically retrieval-grounded code repair on SWE-bench. A landmark 'agentless' baseline using hierarchical LLM- and IR/embedding-based fault localization (issue -> file -> class/function -> edit location) followed by sample-and-validate repair; it reset the SWE-bench baseline and was widely adopted (OpenAI GPT-4o/o1, DeepSeek V3/R1) and extended (RepoGraph, Isoform, MarsCode).

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing

<a id="item-crag"></a>
### 27. CRAG: Corrective Retrieval Augmented Generation

2024  ·  arXiv 2401.15884  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.15884)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **authors affiliation**:
> Shi-Qi Yan (National Engineering Research Center of Speech and Language Information Processing, University of Science and Technology of China, USTC, Hefei, China), Jia-Chen Gu (Dept. of Computer Science, University of California, Los Angeles / UCLA; equal contribution), Yun Zhu (Google DeepMind), Zhen-Hua Ling (USTC). Lead authors Shi-Qi Yan and Jia-Chen Gu (equal contribution); primary affiliations USTC and UCLA, with Google DeepMind.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.15884
- **code url**: https://github.com/HuskyInSalt/CRAG (official; releases inference of CRAG/Self-CRAG, retrieval-evaluator fine-tuning, evaluator weights and training data; ~460 GitHub stars, last updated Oct 2024).
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (the official repo HuskyInSalt/CRAG is a frozen artifact repository, not a continuously-maintained leaderboard/paper-list).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> QA / knowledge-intensive generation (open-domain RAG). Tasks span short-form entity QA (PopQA), long-form generation (Biography), true-or-false fact verification (PubHealth), and multiple-choice reasoning (Arc-Challenge). Not an agent/tool-use/planning system; it is a corrective RAG inference framework.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-turn, single-agent retrieval-augmented generation with a frozen generator LLM. The core problem is robustness of generation when retrieval 'goes wrong', i.e. when retrieved documents from a static, limited corpus are irrelevant or misleading and degrade the answer. CRAG is plug-and-play at inference and is coupled to standard RAG and Self-RAG. Supervision used: a separate lightweight retrieval evaluator (T5-large) is fine-tuned offline using relevance signals derived from datasets (e.g. PopQA's golden subject Wikipedia title) before deployment; the generator itself is not retrained. At test time the same Contriever retrieval results provided by Self-RAG are reused for comparability, plus an external web-search fallback (Google Search via the serper.dev API).
- **what is retrieved**: Documents/passages (text). From the static corpus: top-k retrieved passages (Wikipedia-style, via Contriever). From the web-search fallback: web pages (Wikipedia preferred) returned by a commercial Google Search API, transcribed and refined into knowledge strips.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> HYBRID, but predominantly STATIC: the primary source is a static external corpus (Wikipedia passages via Contriever); when retrieval is judged Incorrect/Ambiguous, large-scale live web search (Google/serper.dev) is added as a corrective external source. No agent-written growing/episodic memory; the web search is an external static-world query, not a memory the system accumulates.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based-reasoning system). Loosely: Retrieve yes (corpus + web), Reuse yes (knowledge strips injected as context); no Revise/Retain of cases. [Retrieve, Reuse]
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The paper frames itself as corrective retrieval-augmented generation / self-correction for RAG and does not cite or invoke case-based reasoning (Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner).

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Document/passage as the retrieval unit, then a finer 'knowledge strip' as the refined unit. Each retrieved passage is segmented into internal strips (a strip is one or a few sentences, an independent piece of information); strips are scored, filtered and recomposed. So the effective injected unit is a sentence-level knowledge strip, derived from document-level retrieval.
- **index source**:
> Static corpus constructed offline (Wikipedia passages, the same Contriever-retrieved results provided by Self-RAG) plus a live external web index queried at test time (Google Search / serper.dev). No online-induced growing store; the corpus is frozen and the retrieval evaluator is fine-tuned offline.
- **index structure topology**: Flat. The static corpus is a flat passage index queried by a dense retriever (Contriever); the web search returns a flat list of URLs/pages. No graph, hierarchy, or clustering of the index.
- **retriever type**:
> For the static corpus: dense retriever (Contriever, off-the-shelf, inherited from Self-RAG). For the fallback: a commercial web search engine (Google Search API via serper.dev) acting as an external retriever. CRAG itself does not introduce a new trained retriever; its novel learned component is the retrieval EVALUATOR (a fine-tuned T5-large), not the retriever. Hybrid (dense corpus retriever + web search engine).
- **retriever learning signal**:
> The underlying corpus retriever (Contriever) is off-the-shelf (none / pretrained). CRAG's distinctive learned signal is for the lightweight retrieval EVALUATOR: T5-large (0.77B) is fine-tuned on relevance labels per (question, passage) pair, where positive relevance signals are derived from dataset metadata (e.g. PopQA's golden subject Wikipedia title used to identify high-quality passages) and negative samples are drawn from other retrieved/random passages. This is supervised relevance classification (LM-feedback-style relevance labels), not RL or contrastive interactive preference; the web search trigger is then threshold-based on the evaluator score.
- **query construction**: Two-stage. For corpus retrieval, the raw input query is used (the same retrieval results as Self-RAG are reused). For the web-search fallback, the input is rewritten by ChatGPT into a keyword-style search query (intent/keyword extraction) to mimic typical search-engine usage.
- **query granularity**: Task-level / one retrieval per query (t=0) for the corpus. The web-search query is also formed once per input (after rewriting). No per-step or trajectory-level re-querying; it is single-shot with a conditional corrective branch.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Adaptive/active in a single corrective pass: corpus retrieval happens once per query, then a learned retrieval evaluator decides (Correct / Incorrect / Ambiguous) whether to refine the retrieved docs, discard-and-web-search, or combine both. So the corrective web-search retrieval is uncertainty/confidence-triggered (one-shot base retrieval + confidence-gated corrective retrieval), not iterative looping.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Learned relevance-evaluator confidence with two thresholds. The fine-tuned T5-large evaluator produces a relevance/confidence score per retrieved document; an upper and a lower threshold map scores to three actions: Correct (at least one doc above the upper threshold), Incorrect (all docs below the lower threshold -> trigger web search), and Ambiguous (in between -> combine refined corpus knowledge and web knowledge). The web-search corrective action is thus gated by this confidence signal, not by a fixed schedule or token-level confidence of the generator.
- **reranking**:
> No explicit cross-encoder reranking of the document list. Instead, the retrieval evaluator scores each document/strip for relevance and these scores (i) trigger actions and (ii) drive knowledge-strip filtering. The scoring-then-filtering of strips functions as a relevance-based selection rather than a classic listwise reranker.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Decompose-then-recompose knowledge refinement: retrieved documents are segmented into knowledge strips (one-to-few sentences), each strip is scored by the retrieval evaluator, irrelevant strips are filtered out, and relevant strips are recomposed (concatenated in order) into 'internal knowledge'. The same refinement is applied to transcribed web pages to form 'external knowledge'. This is distractor filtering + decompose-then-recompose distillation, central to CRAG.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tool/skill descriptions; the system retrieves text documents/web pages, not tool APIs).
- **index content separation**: N/A / No explicit lightweight-index-then-content separation. Documents are retrieved and then refined into strips; there is no progressive-disclosure SOP-index-then-content design.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Partially relevant: the corpus index is static, but a live web-search integration via a commercial Google Search API (serper.dev) provides a dynamic external knowledge source at query time. Integration protocol is a REST web-search API (URL retrieval + page transcription), not MCP/RapidAPI/function-calling, and there is no tool CRUD auto-sync.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tools; no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation: the refined knowledge (internal corpus knowledge and/or external web knowledge) is concatenated and prepended to the query as context for the frozen generator LLM (standard RAG or Self-RAG generation). No training-signal injection into the generator; retrieval purely conditions generation. The retrieval evaluator additionally acts as a control/router determining which knowledge is assembled.
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-(evaluate/correct)-then-generate, single-pass. There is no multi-step planner, MCTS, or tree search. The 'planning' is a fixed corrective decision tree: retrieve from corpus -> evaluate relevance -> branch into {refine, web-search, combine} -> generate. When coupled with Self-RAG, Self-RAG's own reflection-token generation runs on top of the CRAG-corrected context.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Per-answer. Retrieval/correction occurs once before the answer is generated; it is not interleaved per CoT step, per sentence/token, or per tool-call. (When wrapped around Self-RAG, Self-RAG may still do segment-level reflection, but CRAG's correction itself is per-query/per-answer.)
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (no CBR case adaptation). The closest analogue is the decompose-then-recompose refinement that adapts raw retrieved documents into filtered knowledge strips, but this is content filtering, not case revision.
- **retrieved item representation**: Free-text knowledge: refined 'knowledge strips' (relevant sentence-level fragments concatenated in order) drawn from corpus passages (internal knowledge) and/or transcribed web pages (external knowledge). Raw-text, not distilled strategies, programs, or latent tokens.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw factual text at sentence/strip granularity (filtered passage fragments). Not a distilled strategy, workflow, skill, or hint; it is concrete evidence text selected for relevance.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Core contribution. (1) A learned lightweight retrieval evaluator (relevance scorer) that detects when retrieval is wrong; (2) confidence-thresholded corrective actions {Correct, Incorrect, Ambiguous}, with the Ambiguous action explicitly added to reduce dependence on evaluator accuracy; (3) web-search fallback to replace irrelevant corpus knowledge; (4) decompose-then-recompose strip filtering to remove irrelevant/distractor content within retrieved documents. Together these guard against irrelevant/incorrect retrieved context.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (no episodic/skill/workflow/procedural/graph/latent memory; static corpus + live web search only).
- **write back**: False. The system does not store new experiences, cases, or knowledge back into any memory store; web-search results are used transiently for the current query and not persisted.
- **online growth**: No. The retrievable corpus and the fine-tuned evaluator are frozen after offline setup; nothing grows during deployment (web search is a transient external query, not an accumulating store).
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back mechanism exists).
- **failure experience usage**:
> N/A / success-oriented. CRAG corrects per-query retrieval failures at inference (discard-and-web-search when retrieval is judged Incorrect) but does not store failed experiences/trajectories for later retrieval. During offline evaluator fine-tuning, irrelevant/negative (question, passage) pairs serve as negative training labels, but no failure experiences are retained at deployment.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (no stored entries; nothing is mutated, merged, or pruned post-write).
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Partially. The decision of WHICH corrective action to take is governed by a learned (fine-tuned T5-large) relevance evaluator with fixed thresholds, which is more than fixed similarity top-k routing. However, it is a supervised relevance classifier driving a hand-designed threshold/decision rule, NOT an RL/value-based sequential retrieval policy (no M-MDP, soft Q-learning, or interactive preference optimization). The underlying corpus retrieval is fixed top-k.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: N/A / No. Single-system, single-generator setting; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing. (CRAG is, however, plug-and-play across different RAG frameworks/generators, e.g. standard RAG and Self-RAG, but it does not share an experience store across agents.)

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> PopQA (short-form entity QA), Biography / Bio (long-form generation), PubHealth / Pub (true-or-false health fact verification), Arc-Challenge / ARC (multiple-choice science QA). Four datasets total. Retrieval uses the same Contriever results provided by Self-RAG; web search via Google Search API (serper.dev).
- **benchmark family**: QA / knowledge-intensive generation: PopQA (open-domain short-form QA), Biography (long-form generation/factuality), PubHealth (fact verification / true-or-false), Arc-Challenge (multiple-choice reasoning QA). No web-agent, embodied, tool, code, memory, or decision-RL benchmarks.
- **baselines**:
> Without retrieval: LLaMA2-7B/13B, Alpaca-7B/13B, CoVE-65B, LLaMA2-chat-13B, ChatGpt.
