With retrieval / standard RAG: LLaMA2-7B/13B (RAG), Alpaca-7B/13B (RAG), and the Self-RAG-instruction-tuned LLaMA2-7B as standard RAG; Ret-LLaMA2-chat-13B; cited private-data baselines Ret-ChatGPT, Ret-LLaMA-chat, and perplexity.ai. Advanced RAG: Self-RAG (Asai et al., ICLR 2024). CRAG/Self-CRAG are compared head-to-head against standard RAG and Self-RAG on the same inputs; also a ChatGPT (zero-shot / CoT / few-shot) relevance-judge baseline for evaluator quality.
- **key metrics**:
> Accuracy for PopQA, PubHealth, and Arc-Challenge; FactScore for Biography (long-form). Plus evaluator-quality accuracy (relevance-judgment accuracy on PopQA), computational overhead (TFLOPs per token, execution time per instance), and a robustness curve vs degraded retrieval performance.
- **headline result**:
> Coupled with the SelfRAG-LLaMA2-7B generator, CRAG outperformed standard RAG by +7.0% accuracy on PopQA, +14.9 FactScore on Biography, +36.6% accuracy on PubHealth, and +15.4% accuracy on Arc-Challenge; and Self-CRAG outperformed the state-of-the-art Self-RAG by +20.0% accuracy on PopQA, +36.9 FactScore on Biography, and +4.0% accuracy on Arc-Challenge when based on the original LLaMA2-hf-7B (and by +6.9 PopQA, +5.0 Bio, +2.4 PubHealth on SelfRAG-LLaMA2-7B). Main results table: Self-CRAG reaches PopQA 61.8 / Bio 86.2 / Pub 74.8 / ARC 67.2 (vs Self-RAG 54.9 / 81.2 / 72.4 / 67.3) on SelfRAG-LLaMA2-7B.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Removing each action {Correct, Incorrect, Ambiguous} on PopQA: every removal drops accuracy (e.g. CRAG 54.9->53.2 w/o Correct, 54.4 w/o Incorrect, 54.0 w/o Ambiguous on LLaMA2-hf-7b; Self-CRAG 49.0 drops to 43.6/47.7/48.1), showing each action contributes, with Ambiguous reducing dependence on evaluator accuracy. (2) Removing each knowledge-utilization operation {document refinement, search-query rewriting, external-knowledge selection} on PopQA: all hurt (CRAG 54.9->49.8 w/o refinement, 51.7 w/o rewriting, 50.9 w/o selection; Self-CRAG 49.0->35.9 / 37.2 / 24.9 on LLaMA2-hf-7b). (3) Retrieval-evaluator accuracy on PopQA: T5-based evaluator 84.3% vs ChatGPT 58.0 / ChatGPT-CoT 62.4 / ChatGPT-few-shot 64.7. (4) Consistent web-search supplementation: adding web knowledge to plain RAG/Self-RAG helps only marginally (e.g. RAG 50.5->52.2 w. web), confirming gains stem from the self-correction mechanism, not merely extra web data. (5) Robustness: as retrieval quality is artificially degraded, Self-CRAG degrades more gracefully than Self-RAG.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Yes, partially. End-to-end task metrics (accuracy/FactScore) are reported, and the intrinsic quality of the retrieval evaluator (relevance-judgment accuracy 84.3% on PopQA) is reported separately (Table 4). However, standard IR metrics like Recall@k / nDCG of the retriever itself are not reported.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Both. Primarily outcome metrics (final accuracy/FactScore), but process-level evaluation is included: the relevance-judgment accuracy of the retrieval evaluator (an intermediate component) and a robustness study of how generation quality tracks degraded retrieval performance.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Reported. The retrieval evaluator is lightweight (T5-large, 0.77B) vs Self-RAG's critic (instruction-tuned LLaMA2-7B). Computational overhead (generation-phase estimate, retrieval/data-processing excluded): RAG 26.5 TFLOPs/token & 0.363 s/instance vs CRAG 27.2 TFLOPs/token & 0.512 s; Self-RAG 26.5~132.4 TFLOPs/token & 0.741 s vs Self-CRAG 27.2~80.2 TFLOPs/token & 0.908 s. Self-CRAG's upper bound is lower because only three passages (correct/incorrect/ambiguous) are provided. The web-search fallback adds external API latency/cost not fully quantified. Conclusion: modest overhead for substantial accuracy gains.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (empirical method paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (uses existing public datasets PopQA, Biography, PubHealth, Arc-Challenge; not a new benchmark). Retrieval results and eval splits are reused from Self-RAG for comparability.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Standard RAG (Lewis et al., 2020) and Self-RAG (Asai et al., ICLR 2024) as the host frameworks; Contriever (Izacard et al., 2022) as the corpus retriever; T5-large (Raffel et al., 2020) as the retrieval evaluator backbone; web-search-augmentation lines (Piktus et al., 2021; Komeili et al., 2022); FactScore (Min et al., 2023) for long-form evaluation; LLaMA2 (Touvron et al., 2023) generators.
- **contrasts with**:
> Self-RAG (which instruction-tunes the LLM to emit reflection/critic tokens and needs a 7B critic, and degrades when the underlying LLM is not specially tuned) - CRAG argues its external lightweight evaluator is plug-and-play and does not require retraining the generator; standard RAG (which always uses raw top-k documents regardless of relevance); CoVE (chain-of-verification, no retrieval); naive web-search supplementation (shown to help only marginally without the self-correction mechanism); using ChatGPT as a relevance judge (underperforms the fine-tuned T5 evaluator).
- **lineage**:
> Group B (rag_task_solving): a robust/corrective RAG method in the adaptive-RAG lineage. It sits alongside Self-RAG (self-reflective retrieval) and active-/adaptive-retrieval work, introducing a confidence-gated corrective controller (relevance evaluator -> {refine, web-search, combine}) and decompose-then-recompose refinement. A foundational 'Corrective RAG' (CRAG) reference frequently cited by later agentic/corrective RAG and graph-based RAG systems.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- completeness_vs_topk_objective
- context_budget_and_selection_count
- venue

<a id="item-codrag-bench"></a>
### 28. CodeRAG-Bench: Can Retrieval Augment Code Generation?

2024  ·  NAACL 2025 Findings  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.14497)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: NAACL 2025 (arXiv preprint June 2024, v2 Feb 2025; published NAACL 2025 Findings, pages 3199-3214)
- **authors affiliation**: Zora Zhiruo Wang, Akari Asai, Xinyan Velocity Yu, Frank F. Xu, Yiqing Xie, Graham Neubig, Daniel Fried. Primary affiliations: Carnegie Mellon University; University of Washington; University of Southern California. (Wang and Asai contributed equally.)
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.14497
- **code url**: https://github.com/code-rag-bench/code-rag-bench
- **maintained repo url**: https://code-rag-bench.github.io/ (project page; HuggingFace datasets/datastore at https://huggingface.co/code-rag-bench)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: code (retrieval-augmented code generation, RACG), spanning basic programming, open-domain coding, repository-level code generation/issue-solving, and code retrieval.
- **problem setting**:
> A holistic benchmark and empirical study of retrieval-augmented code generation. The setting is offline, single-turn, single-agent generation: a code LM is given a natural-language problem plus retrieved documents and produces a program evaluated by execution (pass@1). Two retrieval setups are studied: canonical retrieval (retrieve only from a manually annotated canonical datastore) and open retrieval (retrieve from any of five aggregated sources). Supervision exists in the form of manually annotated canonical/gold documents per task, enabling decoupled evaluation of retrieval quality (NDCG@10/Recall/Precision) separately from end-to-end generation quality. No model training is proposed; the work evaluates 10 off-the-shelf retrievers and 10 LMs.
- **what is retrieved**: docs (Python library documentation), programming solutions (competition/canonical problem-solution pairs), online tutorials, StackOverflow posts, and GitHub repository files/code snippets. These serve as external contexts to augment code generation.
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus. Retrieval targets a fixed, pre-built 25M-document datastore aggregated from five sources plus per-task canonical documents; there is no growing/episodic agent memory written at test time.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k ranking objective. Retrieval is evaluated as a ranking task (NDCG@10 primary, plus Precision/Recall) against annotated canonical documents, and generation prepends a fixed number of top-k documents (top-5 default; top-1 from each source for mixed retrieval). It is not a completeness/minimal-set or precision-driven variable-size recommendation objective.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based reasoning system; if forced: Retrieve only, no Reuse-as-adaptation/Revise/Retain)
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The work is framed as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG/RACG) and does not frame itself as case-based reasoning or cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> document / snippet. Concretely: a problem-solution document (NL problem concatenated with canonical solution) for programming-solutions; a library documentation entry; a StackOverflow post; an online tutorial page; a GitHub file or 20-line code snippet; and CodeSearchNet Python functions for the code-retrieval task. Documents are optionally chunked to 200-800 tokens (first 500 tokens used as default).
- **index source**:
> Static corpus, offline-constructed. A diverse open datastore aggregated offline from five sources (programming solutions, online tutorials, Python library docs, StackOverflow posts, GitHub files) totaling 25 million documents, plus manually annotated per-task canonical documents. The store is frozen, not online/test-time-induced.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat vector index (dense embeddings via sentence-transformers) and a sparse inverted index (BM25 via Pyserini). Documents are organized/separable by source pool (programming solutions, tutorials, docs, StackOverflow, GitHub), but retrieval is over flat per-source or aggregated indices; no dependency graph or hierarchical/cluster topology.
- **retriever type**:
> hybrid across the benchmark (the study evaluates sparse + dense + proprietary-API retrievers): sparse BM25; dense open models (BGE-base/large, GIST-base/large, SFR-Embedding-Mistral, Codesage-small, Jina-v2-code); proprietary APIs (voyage-code-2, openai-text-embedding-3-small). All are off-the-shelf; 10 retrievers total.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> none (off-the-shelf). Retrievers are used as-is without task-specific training. Underlying models were pretrained with contrastive similarity objectives (e.g., MTEB-leaderboard dense models, code-specific contrastive models like Jina-v2-code/Codesage), but CodeRAG-Bench does not train or fine-tune any retriever on its tasks; it evaluates them with no learned downstream/RL signal.
- **query construction**: Raw input. The natural-language problem description (and, for repo-level tasks, the in-file context / issue) is used directly as the retrieval query against the datastore. No query decomposition, expansion, or intent extraction is introduced.
- **query granularity**:
> task-level (one-shot at t=0). A single query is formed per coding problem at the start; retrieval is not interleaved per reasoning step. (Exception: SWE-bench-Lite uses the Agentless n=21-way sampling + majority-vote localization pipeline for context, but the benchmark's core RACG protocol is one-shot task-level retrieval.)
- **when to retrieve**: one-shot. Documents are retrieved once before generation and prepended to the prompt; there is no iterative or uncertainty-triggered retrieval in the core protocol.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: fixed schedule (always retrieve once before generation). No token-confidence, attention/uncertainty, learned complexity classifier, reflection tokens, or agent-initiated trigger is used.
- **reranking**:
> Yes, optionally. A cross-encoder reranking stage with BGE-reranker-base is applied on top-100 OpenAI-embedding results before generation, and as a post-retrieval chunk-reranking strategy. The paper reports that reranking within the optimal 200-800-token chunk range greatly degrades results, showing limited utility of current rerankers.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Chunking/compression and optional rerank. Post-retrieval processing studied includes: (i) post-retrieval chunking (first N tokens of each document), (ii) post-retrieval reranking to find the most relevant N-token chunk (BGE-reranker-base), and (iii) pre-retrieval chunking (chunk then retrieve N-token pieces). Default uses first 500 tokens per document; chunking to 200-800 tokens is found best. No reason-in-documents distillation or learned distractor filtering.
- **tool document engineering**:
> N/A (this is a code-document RAG benchmark, not a tool-retrieval setting). Documents are processed only by source-specific formatting (e.g., concatenating NL problem with solution for programming-solution docs) and chunking; no synthetic-query augmentation or instruction-tuned tool embeddings.
- **index content separation**: N/A. No lightweight-index-then-content / progressive-disclosure separation is used; documents are chunked (default first 500 tokens) but there is no separated lightweight retrievable index over heavy on-demand content.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A. Static, offline-built datastore; no live-synchronized tool index, RapidAPI/RESTful/MCP/function-calling protocol, or CRUD auto-sync.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A. No inter-tool dependency modeling (this is document retrieval for code generation, not tool/API retrieval).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**: prompt augmentation. Top-k retrieved documents (default top-5; top-1 per source for mixed retrieval) are prepended to the original coding problem in the LM context window; no training signal, latent-token injection, or explicit case adaptation.
- **planning integration**:
> one-shot exemplars/context at generation time (retrieve-then-generate). Retrieved documents are inserted into the prompt before the model generates the full program in a single pass; there is no per-step interleaving, MCTS/tree search, or hierarchical subtask planning in the core RACG protocol.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: per-answer. Retrieval happens once and conditions the single end-to-end code generation; it is not woven per-CoT-step, per-sentence/token, or per-tool-call.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not CBR). Retrieved documents are used verbatim as in-context augmentation; no case adaptation/revision mechanism.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> raw document text injected into the prompt: raw problem-solution pairs, raw library-documentation entries, raw StackOverflow posts, raw tutorial text, and raw GitHub code snippets (optionally truncated/chunked to the first ~500 tokens). No distilled strategy/guideline, executable skill abstraction, or latent-soft tokens.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Mostly raw artifacts (raw code snippets, raw documentation, raw posts/tutorials, single problem-solution demonstrations). Programming-solution documents act as single demonstrations; library docs act as reference/hint material. No distilled strategy or procedural-skill abstraction.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> None built-in. The study explicitly analyzes (does not fix) noise: it shows models are easily distracted by irrelevant/distracting retrieved contexts and that adding more low-ranked documents introduces noise and degrades generation. No retriever-aware training, relevance evaluator, self-reflection, or distractor-aware SFT is proposed; robustness is left as an identified open challenge.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none. The system uses a static external datastore, not an episodic/skill-library/workflow/procedural/graph/latent memory that the agent writes to.
- **write back**: False. No new experiences/cases/skills are stored back into the datastore; the store is fixed offline.
- **online growth**: False. The retrievable store is frozen after offline construction; it does not grow during deployment/test-time.
- **write back trigger**: never. No write-back events occur (no success/failure/per-step/reflective/human-validated writes).
- **failure experience usage**: N/A / none. No storage or retrieval of failed/negative experiences; failure cases are only analyzed qualitatively (e.g., distraction by irrelevant contexts, over-complicated generations) but not written to any memory.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A / none. No stored entries are mutated (no append-only/dedup-merge/delta-update/refine-overwrite/forget-prune/link-and-evolve); the datastore is static.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: False. Retrieval/document-selection is fixed similarity top-k (or BM25 ranking), not a learned/RL-optimized policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: N/A / none. Single-pass, single-generator evaluation with a shared static datastore; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> HumanEval (164), MBPP (500), LiveCodeBench (400; generation-only, no gold docs), DS-1000 (1000), ODEX (945) plus an ODEX-hard subset (20 least-common libraries), RepoEval function split (373), SWE-bench-Lite (300), and CodeSearchNet-Python (CSN, 22,177; code-retrieval task). Retrieval datastore: 25 million documents from five sources (programming solutions, online tutorials ~79.4k, Python library docs, StackOverflow posts ~23.5M, GitHub files).
- **benchmark family**: code. Spans code generation (basic: HumanEval/MBPP/LiveCodeBench; open-domain: DS-1000/ODEX; repository-level: RepoEval, SWE-bench-Lite) and code retrieval (CodeSearchNet-Py). SWE-bench and RepoEval are code/repo-level benchmarks; CodeSearchNet is the code-retrieval benchmark.
- **baselines**:
> Retrievers (10): BM25; GIST-base/large; BGE-base/large; SFR-Embedding-Mistral; Codesage-small; Jina-v2-code; OpenAI-text-embedding-3-small; voyage-code-2; plus BGE-reranker-base reranking. Generators (10): StarCoder2-7B, CodeGemma-7B, CodeLlama-7B/34B, DeepSeekCoder-7B/33B, Llama3, Command-R, GPT-3.5-turbo-0125, GPT-4o (also GPT-4, Claude-3-haiku/sonnet, Gemini-1.5-flash/pro in appendix). Reference conditions: no-context (w/o), gold/canonical documents, and RACG (retrieved) settings.
- **key metrics**: Retrieval: NDCG@10 (primary), plus Precision and Recall. Generation: pass@1 via execution-based evaluation (functional correctness; SWE-bench resolve rate). Retrieval efficiency: indexing/search latency and index storage size.
- **headline result**:
> Retrieving high-quality (canonical/gold) contexts yields notable RACG gains, e.g., GPT-4o improves by 27.4% (absolute, resolve rate) on SWE-bench-Lite and 6.9% on the harder ODEX subset when given canonical documents; some RACG settings even surpass the gold-document setting. However, current retrievers struggle to fetch useful contexts (especially with low lexical overlap, e.g., DS-1000/ODEX NDCG@10 as low as ~5-37), and weaker/long-context generators improve less, revealing substantial room for improvement.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Retriever comparison (Table 3): dense models frequently surpass BM25; code-specific retrievers (Jina-v2-code, voyage-code-2) outperform comparable general models (Jina-v2-code beats GIST-base/BGE-base by 7.4/6.6 avg NDCG@10); larger models help (GIST-large > GIST-base, SFR-Mistral 7B strong). (2) Retrieval efficiency vs accuracy (Table 4): BM25 is orders of magnitude cheaper; SFR-Mistral needs >5x index storage and ~100x encode latency. (3) Number of documents (Appendix E): top-5 is the sweet spot across context-length budgets; more docs add noise. (4) Chunking strategy (Fig 2/Table 9): 200-800-token chunks are best; reranking within that range degrades results. (5) Source comparison (Table 7): StackOverflow/tutorials help HumanEval; programming solutions most help ODEX. (6) ODEX-hard (least-common libraries): documentation augmentation improves 20.3-40.1%, verifying RACG helps for less-popular libraries. (7) Does RACG help stronger models (Appendix F): mixed results; models often distracted by non-canonical contexts.
- **evaluation decoupling**: Yes. Intrinsic retrieval metrics (NDCG@10/Precision/Recall) are reported separately (Table 3) from end-to-end execution-based generation metrics (pass@1, Tables 5-7), and the benchmark explicitly provides reproducible evaluation of both retrieval and end-to-end generation.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Both, in a decoupled way: an intermediate process metric (retrieval quality, NDCG@10) is reported alongside the final outcome metric (execution-based pass@1 / resolve rate). It does not score reasoning faithfulness or step-wise trajectory quality (single-pass generation).
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Reported (Table 4). On sampled CodeSearchNet-Python (10k queries, 100k docs), BM25 indexing/search takes only seconds (0.15ms/0.02ms per query, 141MB); GIST-base 3.7ms/9.7ms encode/search, 440MB+307MB; SFR-Mistral 316ms/113ms, 14220MB index (>5x storage, ~100x encode latency vs GIST-base), 1638MB model; Voyage-code/OpenAI-03 ~22-47ms with ~1172MB. The paper argues retrieval efficiency must be weighed against accuracy in RAG pipelines.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k with budget-capped chunking. Default prepends top-5 retrieved documents (top-1 per source for 5-source mixed retrieval), each truncated to the first 500 tokens (optimal per ablation), to fit all model context limits. Number-of-documents ablation (top-1/2/5/10) finds 5 best; chunk-size ablation finds 200-800 tokens best.
- **survey scope and axes**:
> N/A (benchmark/empirical study, not a survey). Organizing axes of the benchmark: four task categories (basic programming, open-domain, repository-level, code retrieval) x two retrieval setups (canonical vs open) x five datastore sources; evaluation across 10 retrievers and 10 LMs. References: 52.
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> 9k coding tasks across 6-8 datasets and a 25M-document retrieval datastore (StackOverflow ~23.5M posts, online tutorials ~79.4k, plus library docs/programming solutions/GitHub). Construction: aggregates existing datasets (HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench, DS-1000, ODEX, RepoEval, SWE-bench-Lite, CodeSearchNet) and manually annotates canonical documents per task (e.g., avg 1.4/1.2 doc entries for DS-1000/ODEX; 20-line snippets for RepoEval; gold edited files for SWE-bench). Answers are execution-verifiable (test-case execution; NDCG@10 for retrieval). Difficulty signal: SWE-bench-Lite remains very hard (only GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4o achieve non-trivial results; GPT-4o ~2.3% w/o, ~30.7% with gold docs).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Aggregates and extends existing code-generation datasets (HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench, DS-1000, ODEX, RepoEval, SWE-bench-Lite, CodeSearchNet) and RAG/retrieval infrastructure (Pyserini/BM25, sentence-transformers, MTEB-leaderboard dense retrievers, code retrievers Jina-v2-code/Codesage, voyage-code-2, OpenAI embeddings). For SWE-bench it uses the Agentless localization pipeline (Xia et al., 2024). Conceptually builds on text-RAG benchmarks BEIR and KILT.
- **contrasts with**:
> Positioned against prior RACG work that relied largely on BM25 alone (e.g., DocPrompting/Zhou et al. 2023, SWE-bench/Jimenez et al. 2024) without comprehensive multi-retriever comparison, and against text-centric RAG benchmarks (BEIR, KILT) that do not cover code; contrasts the assumption that neural retrievers underperform BM25 out-of-domain by showing dense retrievers frequently surpass BM25 on code.
- **lineage**:
> Group B (retrieval-augmented task solving) - belongs to the benchmark/evaluation lineage of retrieval-augmented code generation; a holistic RACG testbed providing decoupled retrieval + end-to-end evaluation, intended to standardize and advance code-oriented RAG methods (Surveys/Benchmarks branch).

<a id="item-dragin"></a>
### 29. DRAGIN - Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the real-time Information Needs of Large Language Models

2024  ·  ACL 2024  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.10081)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: ACL 2024 (Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, Main Conference, Long Paper, Oral; pages 12991-13013). Preprint arXiv:2403.10081 (v1 Mar 2024, v3 Sep 2024).
- **authors affiliation**: Weihang Su, Yichen Tang (equal contribution), Qingyao Ai (corresponding author), Yiqun Liu - Department of Computer Science and Technology, Tsinghua University; Zhijing Wu - School of Computer Science and Technology, Beijing Institute of Technology.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.10081
- **code url**: https://github.com/oneal2000/DRAGIN/tree/main
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/oneal2000/DRAGIN (actively maintained; rebranded 'DRAGIN & Dynamic RAG Toolbox' with updated reproducibility guide and bug fixes through 2025).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: QA / knowledge-intensive text generation - multi-hop QA (2WikiMultihopQA, HotpotQA), reading comprehension (IIRC), and commonsense reasoning (StrategyQA), all framed as knowledge-intensive multi-step generation with chain-of-thought.
- **problem setting**:
> Single-agent, offline non-interactive inference with a frozen, training-free LLM (no fine-tuning, no prompt engineering, no additional parameters). DRAGIN is a dynamic/active RAG framework that, during the LLM's left-to-right autoregressive generation of a CoT-style answer, decides in real time WHEN to pause generation and trigger retrieval and WHAT query to issue, then injects retrieved passages and continues generation. It can be plugged into any open-source Transformer-based LLM whose token-probability distribution and self-attention scores are accessible (a stated limitation is that closed APIs without attention access are not supported). Supervision is limited to few-shot CoT in-context exemplars (fewshot = 6); the only tunable knobs are the RIND threshold theta and top-k token-keep budget. Greedy decoding is used for reproducibility.
- **what is retrieved**: Documents/passages (100-token Wikipedia passages) from a static external corpus.
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus: Wikipedia (DPR psgs_w100 dump, ~21M 100-token passages) indexed once offline in Elasticsearch (BM25) or encoded by SGPT. No agent-written growing/episodic memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k ranking: each retrieval call returns a fixed retrieve_topk = 3 passages (the three most relevant passages replace the previous retrieved set). There is no notion of recovering a complete minimal set or precision-driven variable-size selection; only the number of retrieval EVENTS varies (driven by RIND triggers), not k per event.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A - not a case-based reasoning method (retrieves documents, not solved cases; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain case cycle).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: false - the work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite CBR literature (Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner).

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: document (100-token Wikipedia passage). The retrieval QUERY is built at token granularity (a bag of self-attention-selected content tokens), but the retrieved unit is a passage/document.
- **index source**: Static corpus, constructed offline (Wikipedia DPR dump indexed once in Elasticsearch/BM25, or SGPT-encoded). Not test-time-induced and does not grow online.
- **index structure topology**: Flat index: BM25 inverted index in Elasticsearch (main setting), or a flat dense-vector store of SGPT passage embeddings (alternative). No graph, hierarchy, or cluster structure.
- **retriever type**: Off-the-shelf retriever, retriever-agnostic by design: BM25 (sparse lexical, default, Elasticsearch) is the main retriever; a SOTA dense retriever SGPT (Muennighoff 2022) is tested as an alternative. BM25 consistently outperforms SGPT inside DRAGIN.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None - the retriever (BM25 or SGPT) is entirely off-the-shelf and is not trained, fine-tuned, or selected via any learning signal (no contrastive, LM-feedback, preference, RL, or value-based training). DRAGIN's contribution is in WHEN and WHAT to query, not in learning the retriever; the LLM's self-attention determines the query content without any retriever-side training.
- **query construction**:
> QFS (Query Formulation based on Self-attention): when RIND triggers retrieval at token position i, QFS extracts the self-attention scores of the LAST Transformer layer that token t_i assigned to all preceding tokens {t_1..t_{i-1}}, sorts them descending, selects the top-n highest-attention tokens, maps them back to words, re-orders the words by their original position in the text, and concatenates them into the retrieval query. This pulls the query from the LLM's information needs across the ENTIRE generated context rather than just the last sentence/last few tokens. (Code option `query_formulation: real_words`; `retrieve_keep_top_k` ~35-40 tokens.)
- **query granularity**: Step/token-level (trigger-position-level): a fresh query is formulated dynamically at each retrieval-trigger token position during generation, conditioned on the entire preceding context via self-attention. Not a single task-level query at t=0.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Active (uncertainty-triggered) and iterative: retrieval is triggered dynamically during generation whenever the real-time information-need signal exceeds a threshold, and this can fire multiple times within one answer (multi-round). Distinct from one-shot retrieval and from fixed-schedule iterative retrieval.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Attention + uncertainty + semantics combined (RIND - Real-time Information Needs Detection). For each generated token t_i a score S_RIND(t_i) = H_i * a_max(i) * s_i is computed, where H_i is the entropy of the token's output probability distribution over the vocabulary (uncertainty), a_max(i) is the maximum self-attention this token receives from all FOLLOWING tokens in the last Transformer layer (its influence on subsequent generation), and s_i is a binary semantic indicator that is 0 for stopwords (filtered via spaCy en_core_web_sm) and 1 otherwise. Retrieval activates when any token's S_RIND exceeds a predefined threshold theta (default ~0.6-1.2 depending on config). This is a richer signal than FLARE's pure next-token-probability rule.
- **reranking**: None - no reranking stage; the retriever returns the top-3 passages directly for the QFS-formulated query.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> None - retrieved passages are used verbatim; no rerank, decompose-recompose, distillation, distractor filtering, or compression. At a new trigger position j the newly retrieved 3 passages simply REPLACE the previously injected ones (the generation is also truncated back to the trigger position before re-generating with new evidence).
- **tool document engineering**: N/A - no tools/skills are retrieved; only Wikipedia passages are indexed (raw 100-token text via BM25/SGPT, no description engineering).
- **index content separation**: N/A - single flat passage index; no lightweight-index-then-content / progressive-disclosure separation.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A - no tool index or tool-integration protocol; static document corpus only.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A - no inter-tool dependency modeling (no tools).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation: the 3 retrieved passages are inserted via a fixed prompt template ('Below are the external knowledge references: [1].. [2].. [3].. Please answer the question based on the external knowledge: Question: ... Answer: T'') and the LLM continues generation from the truncated output T' (the prefix up to the trigger token). No training signal or latent injection.
- **planning integration**:
> Per-step interleaved retrieve-during-generation inside a single autoregressive decoding loop: generate -> RIND detects an information need at a token -> truncate output at that token -> QFS forms a query -> retrieve top-3 -> prepend evidence -> resume generation, repeating whenever RIND fires. It is reasoning/generation-guided iterative retrieval, not tree search, MCTS, or hierarchical subtask planning.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-sentence-or-token: retrieval is woven in at the token position where RIND's real-time-information-need score crosses the threshold, which is finer-grained than FLARE's per-sentence rule and the fixed per-n-token / per-sentence baselines.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A - not a CBR method; retrieved passages are used verbatim as in-context evidence, not adapted as cases.
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw retrieved passages (verbatim 100-token Wikipedia text) injected into the prompt; not distilled, summarized, or converted to structured notes.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw document/passage (no abstraction or distillation of the retrieved unit).
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Largely none/implicit: DRAGIN adds no retriever-aware training, relevance evaluator, self-reflection, or distractor-aware SFT. Robustness comes only from (a) RIND firing retrieval only when truly needed (avoiding low-value retrieval that the paper shows can hurt, e.g., FL-RAG/FS-RAG sometimes below single-round), and (b) QFS issuing more targeted queries. The paper's case study explicitly notes a failure mode: weaker long-context LLMs (e.g., LLaMA-7B) can get confused by multiple injected passages, so noise robustness is acknowledged as a limitation, not solved.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none - no episodic, skill, workflow, procedural, graph, or latent memory; only a transient per-question generation buffer (the in-progress output and the currently injected passages, which are replaced on each new trigger and reset per question).
- **write back**: false - DRAGIN does not store any new experiences, cases, or skills; nothing is written to a persistent store across questions.
- **online growth**: false - the retrievable store (Wikipedia BM25/SGPT index) is fixed/frozen after offline construction and does not grow during deployment.
- **write back trigger**: never - no write-back to any persistent store occurs.
- **failure experience usage**: N/A - no success or failure experiences are stored or retrieved (no memory). Failures are only analyzed qualitatively in a case study, not fed back.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A - no stored entries to mutate (no memory).
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> false - the WHEN-to-retrieve decision is a fixed thresholded heuristic over a hand-designed score (entropy * max-attention * semantic indicator), and the WHAT (query) is a fixed top-attention token selection; neither the trigger policy nor the query/passage selection is an RL- or value-learned policy. The retrieval itself is fixed BM25/SGPT top-3.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: N/A - single-model, single-agent inference; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: 2WikiMultihopQA, HotpotQA, StrategyQA, IIRC (top-1000 questions sampled per dataset). External corpus: Wikipedia (DPR psgs_w100, ~21M 100-token passages). LLMs evaluated: LLaMA-2-7B-Chat, LLaMA-2-13B-Chat, Vicuna-13B-v1.5.
- **benchmark family**: QA / multi-hop (2WikiMultihopQA, HotpotQA) plus reading comprehension (IIRC) and commonsense reasoning (StrategyQA) - all knowledge-intensive open-domain QA.
- **baselines**:
> wo-RAG (no retrieval / direct answer); SR-RAG (single-round RAG, retrieve once from initial question); FL-RAG (fix-length RAG, retrieve every n tokens using last token window as query); FS-RAG (fix-sentence RAG, retrieve every sentence using last sentence as query); FLARE (retrieve when a token's probability is below threshold, query = last sentence minus low-probability tokens). Ablation comparisons also include 'Full Context' as query. All multi-round baselines re-implemented under FLARE's protocol so only the when/what differs.
- **key metrics**: Exact Match (EM), token-level F1, and token-level Precision for 2WikiMultihopQA / HotpotQA / IIRC; Accuracy for StrategyQA (yes/no exact match). Efficiency measured as the average number of retrieval-module activations (retrieval calls) per question.
- **headline result**:
> DRAGIN achieves the best results on most LLM x dataset cells across all four benchmarks. Most-cited example: on HotpotQA with LLaMA2-13B-Chat, DRAGIN reaches EM 0.314 / F1 0.4238, vs the best baseline FS-RAG 0.267 / 0.3715 and single-round SR-RAG 0.263 / 0.3706 (and wo-RAG 0.223 / 0.3097). On 2WikiMultihopQA (LLaMA2-13B-Chat) DRAGIN gets EM 0.304 / F1 0.3931 vs FS-RAG 0.270 / 0.3610. Gains are largest on multi-hop QA and smaller on StrategyQA commonsense reasoning.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Timing-of-retrieval ablation (Table 4, IIRC): with query formulation fixed to the last sentence, RIND timing beats FLARE/FL-RAG/FS-RAG triggers (LLaMA2-13B EM 0.187 vs FS-RAG 0.171; Vicuna-13B EM 0.196 vs FS-RAG 0.103). (2) RIND threshold sensitivity (Table 5, HotpotQA, LLaMA2-13B): performance is stable across theta in [0.3,1.0] (EM 0.293-0.304, peak F1 ~0.394), and higher theta reduces retrieval frequency (efficiency-accuracy knob). (3) Query-formulation ablation (Table 6, HotpotQA): with timing fixed to RIND, QFS beats FLARE, FS-RAG, FL-RAG, and even Full-Context queries (LLaMA2-13B EM 0.314 vs FLARE 0.262, Full-Context 0.252), showing full context adds redundancy. (4) Retriever ablation (Table 7): BM25 consistently beats SGPT inside DRAGIN (e.g., HotpotQA LLaMA2-13B EM 0.314/F1 0.424 BM25 vs 0.264/0.371 SGPT). (5) Efficiency (Table 3): DRAGIN uses fewer retrieval calls than FS-RAG/FL-RAG (e.g., ~2.6-3.5 on multi-hop) though more than FLARE.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> No - only end-to-end task metrics (EM/F1/Precision/Accuracy) are reported. No intrinsic retrieval-quality metric (Recall@k / nDCG / gold-passage recall) is reported separately; retrieval quality is only argued indirectly via downstream gains and a qualitative QFS-vs-FLARE query case study.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Primarily outcome metrics (final-answer EM/F1/Precision/Accuracy). The only process-level signal is the retrieval-activation frequency (efficiency) and a qualitative case study of the generated query; no quantitative reasoning-faithfulness or step-wise retrieval-accuracy score.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k injection: retrieve_topk = 3 passages per retrieval event, each ~100 tokens; on a new trigger these replace the prior 3 (not accumulated). Query token budget: top-n (retrieve_keep_top_k ~35-40) highest-attention content tokens. generate_max_length = 64; fewshot = 6 demonstrations. k is fixed (not adaptive/precision-driven); the variable quantity is the NUMBER of retrieval events, governed by the RIND threshold.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A - this is a method paper, not a survey/taxonomy.
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A - this is a method paper, not a benchmark paper; it reuses existing datasets (2WikiMultihopQA, HotpotQA, StrategyQA, IIRC), evaluating the top-1000 questions per dataset over a Wikipedia DPR corpus of ~21M 100-token passages.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> FLARE (Jiang et al. 2023) - the closest active/dynamic RAG predecessor that triggers retrieval on low next-token probability and queries with the last sentence; fixed-schedule iterative RAG (FS-RAG following IRCoT/Trivedi et al. 2022; FL-RAG following kNN-LM Khandelwal et al. 2019, RETRO Borgeaud et al. 2022, In-Context RALM Ram et al. 2023); the retrieve-and-read RAG paradigm (Lewis et al. 2020, REALM/Guu et al. 2020, REPLUG/Shi et al. 2023); BM25 (Robertson et al.); SGPT (Muennighoff 2022); Transformer self-attention; chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al. 2022). Base LLMs: LLaMA-2-Chat (Touvron et al. 2023b), Vicuna-13B-v1.5 (Chiang et al. 2023).
- **contrasts with**:
> FLARE (static next-token-probability trigger; query = last sentence minus low-prob tokens) - DRAGIN argues this trigger is suboptimal (good query strategy but poor timing) and that the query should span the whole context; fixed-rule multi-round RAG (FL-RAG per-n-tokens, FS-RAG per-sentence) which retrieve at fixed positions regardless of need; single-round SR-RAG (retrieve once from the question); no-retrieval wo-RAG; and using the Full Context as the query (shown to add redundancy).
- **lineage**:
> Group B (retrieval-augmented task solving): a 2024 advance in the active/dynamic-RAG lineage of when-and-what-to-retrieve methods, directly succeeding FLARE and the IRCoT/FS-RAG line of CoT-guided iterative retrieval, and a frequently-reproduced predecessor to later step-wise/learned dynamic-RAG methods (e.g., DeepRAG, dynamic strategy planning, TC-RAG).

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- cost_efficiency_tradeoff

### 30. GraphRAG (From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization)

2024  ·  arXiv 2404.16130  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16130)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **authors affiliation**:
> Darren Edge and Ha Trinh (co-first authors), Newman Cheng, Joshua Bradley, Alex Chao, Apurva Mody, Steven Truitt, Dasha Metropolitansky, Robert Osazuwa Ness, Jonathan Larson. Affiliations: Microsoft Research; Microsoft Strategic Missions and Technologies; Microsoft Office of the CTO.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16130
- **code url**: https://github.com/microsoft/graphrag
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/microsoft/graphrag (actively maintained official Microsoft open-source implementation; documentation at https://microsoft.github.io/graphrag/)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: QA / query-focused summarization (global sensemaking question answering over private text corpora).
- **problem setting**:
> Offline-indexed, single-agent, non-interactive QA over a fixed private text corpus (~1 million token range). The goal is to answer global 'sensemaking' questions about an entire corpus (e.g., 'What are the main themes in the dataset?') that conventional vector RAG cannot handle because such questions are query-focused summarization (QFS) tasks rather than explicit retrieval tasks. No task-level supervision/labels; evaluation uses LLM-as-judge head-to-head comparisons plus claim-based metrics. Indexing is done once offline with an LLM; queries are answered at test time via map-reduce over precomputed community summaries.
- **what is retrieved**:
> Pregenerated community summaries (report-like summaries of groups of closely related entities) derived from an LLM-built entity knowledge graph; the underlying graph index spans nodes (entities), edges (relationships), and covariates (claims). For the vector RAG baseline (SS), raw source text chunks are retrieved.
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus: an LLM-derived entity knowledge graph plus hierarchical community summaries built offline from the source documents. The store is frozen after offline indexing; it is not a growing/episodic agent memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Completeness/exhaustive-coverage objective rather than fixed top-k ranking. The hierarchical Leiden community partition is described as mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive (MECE), enabling divide-and-conquer global summarization in which ALL community summaries at a chosen level are processed (map-reduce over the whole partition), not a small top-k retrieved subset. At reduce time, partial answers are filtered/ranked by a 0-100 helpfulness score and added until the token budget is reached.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based reasoning system; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain case cycle).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is positioned as graph-based RAG / query-focused summarization.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: Community summary (report-like summary over a group of closely related entities = a graph community). Underlying graph index units are KG entities (nodes), relationships (edges), and claims (covariates). Baseline SS retrieves document text chunks (600-token chunks).
- **index source**:
> Static corpus, offline-induced: an LLM derives an entity knowledge graph from source documents, then community detection partitions it and the LLM pregenerates community summaries at all hierarchy levels at indexing time. The store is frozen after offline construction (no test-time growth).
- **index structure topology**:
> Knowledge GRAPH plus HIERARCHICAL community structure: entities/relationships/claims form a graph; hierarchical Leiden community detection recursively partitions it into a nested hierarchy of communities (root level C0 -> C1 -> C2 -> leaf level C3), each level a MECE partition. Community summaries are organized bottom-up along this hierarchy.
- **retriever type**:
> LLM-as-retriever / generative (no learned dense or BM25 retriever in the global pipeline). At query time a map-reduce process uses the LLM to read all community summaries (generate partial answers + helpfulness scores) rather than a similarity-based retriever; relevance filtering is done by the LLM's 0-100 helpfulness score. The vector RAG baseline (SS) uses a conventional dense semantic-search retriever over text chunks.
- **retriever learning signal**: None (off-the-shelf). The global GraphRAG pipeline uses no trained retriever; community selection is via LLM-generated helpfulness scores, not a learned similarity model. Graph construction relies on prompted LLM extraction (with self-reflection/gleaning), not retriever training.
- **query construction**:
> Raw user query used directly. The query is applied unchanged against each community summary in the map step (each summary independently produces a partial answer to the raw query); no query decomposition, expansion, or intent extraction is performed. (Separately, for benchmark construction, an LLM generates user personas, tasks, and high-level global questions, but this is evaluation-set generation, not query-time processing.)
- **query granularity**: Task-level (one-shot at query time): a single global query is answered in one map-reduce pass over a chosen community level; no per-step or trajectory-level query construction.
- **when to retrieve**: One-shot (single map-reduce pass per query over precomputed community summaries at a fixed chosen level). Indexing-time summarization is precomputed offline; there is no iterative or uncertainty-triggered retrieval loop at query time.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed schedule: retrieval/use of context is not conditionally triggered. Every query deterministically runs the map step over all community summaries at the selected level; the only filtering signal is the LLM-assigned 0-100 helpfulness score per partial answer (answers scored 0 are filtered out).
- **reranking**:
> Yes, a lightweight LLM-score-based ranking at the reduce step: intermediate community answers are sorted in descending order of LLM-generated helpfulness score (0-100) and iteratively added to the reduce context window until the token limit is reached. No cross-encoder or learned reranker is used.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Map-reduce summarization with helpfulness-score filtering: in the map step the LLM produces partial answers with 0-100 helpfulness scores; answers scored 0 are filtered out; remaining answers are ranked and concatenated up to a token budget, then summarized into the global answer in the reduce step. Community summaries themselves are a form of pre-retrieval distillation/compression of the underlying graph elements.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tool retrieval).
- **index content separation**:
> Partial: the hierarchical community structure separates lightweight higher-level (more abstract, fewer/shorter) summaries from heavier lower-level (more detailed, more numerous) summaries, allowing a user/query to scan general themes at one level then drill into linked lower-level reports; community summaries also act as a lightweight index over the heavier raw source text. Not a formal progressive-disclosure index-then-content protocol.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index/protocol).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tools).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation via map-reduce query-focused summarization: each community summary is independently placed in the LLM context to generate a partial (community) answer with a helpfulness score (map); selected partial answers are then combined in a final context window and summarized into the global answer (reduce).
- **planning integration**:
> Plan-free; retrieve(precompute)-then-summarize. No agentic planning, tree search, or step-wise acting. The pipeline is a fixed two-stage map-reduce over precomputed community summaries: divide-and-conquer global summarization that decomposes the corpus by graph community (indexing time) and aggregates partial answers (query time).
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer (no interleaving of retrieval with reasoning steps). A single map-reduce pass produces one global answer per query; there is no per-CoT-step, per-sentence, or per-tool-call retrieval.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not CBR; no retrieved-case adaptation).
- **retrieved item representation**: Distilled free-text report-style community summaries (natural-language summaries that aggregate node/edge/claim element summaries). Underlying injected information is abstractive LLM summaries of graph elements; the global answer is itself a generated free-text summary.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Distilled abstractive summaries at multiple abstraction levels: hierarchical community summaries range from highly abstract corpus-wide themes (root C0) to fine-grained subtopic detail (leaf C3). These are abstractive summaries of concepts (entities, relationships, claims) rather than raw trajectories or single demonstrations.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Helpfulness-score filtering in the map step (LLM rates each partial answer 0-100; score-0 answers are dropped before the reduce step). At indexing time, a self-reflection 'gleaning' loop (iterative LLM re-prompting to detect missed entities/relationships) increases extraction completeness and reduces noise/omission. Random shuffling of community summaries across reduce chunks mitigates 'lost in the middle' positional bias.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: graph (entity knowledge graph) plus hierarchical community-summary store. Static after offline indexing; not an episodic or skill-library agent memory.
- **write back**: False (no test-time write-back). New experiences/cases are not stored during deployment; the graph index and community summaries are built once at indexing time and frozen. (The index can be rebuilt/extended offline, but the system does not write back from query answering.)
- **online growth**: No. The retrievable store (graph + community summaries) does not grow during deployment/test time; it is constructed offline and frozen.
- **write back trigger**: Never (at query/test time). Index construction is an offline batch process, not triggered by query-time events; there is no on-success/on-failure/reflective write-back of answers into the store.
- **failure experience usage**: Not applicable / not used. The system does not store or retrieve failed or negative experiences; there is no experience memory. (The only failure-like signal is filtering of score-0 partial answers within a single query, which are discarded, not stored.)
- **memory evolution update**:
> Not applicable at runtime: the store is effectively static/append-built offline. Within indexing, repeated element instances of the same entity/relationship are aggregated/deduplicated and summarized (dedup-merge during construction), but no post-write mutation occurs during deployment.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No. Retrieval/selection is not a learned or RL-optimized policy; community-answer selection is governed by LLM-generated helpfulness scores and a fixed map-reduce schedule, not a trained retrieval policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single, monolithic indexing+query pipeline; no multi-agent or cross-framework memory sharing (parallelism in map step is independent LLM calls, not cooperating agents with shared memory).

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> Two ~1M-token real-world datasets: (1) Podcast transcripts of 'Behind the Tech with Kevin Scott' (1669 x 600-token chunks, ~1M tokens); (2) News articles from the MultiHop-RAG news corpus (Tang & Yang, 2024), published Sept 2013-Dec 2023 (3197 x 600-token chunks, ~1.7M tokens). Evaluation set: LLM-generated global sensemaking questions (personas x tasks x questions), 125 questions per comparison. HotPotQA used only for a self-reflection/chunk-size ablation in the appendix.
- **benchmark family**: QA / query-focused summarization over long private corpora (global sensemaking). Not one of the standard agent/embodied/tool families; closest normalized grouping is long-document/corpus-level QA & summarization. News corpus is sourced from MultiHop-RAG.
- **baselines**:
> Conventional vector RAG 'semantic search' (SS, retrieves text chunks up to a token budget); global text summarization without a graph index (TS, map-reduce applied directly to shuffled/chunked source texts). GraphRAG is evaluated at four community levels C0 (root), C1, C2, C3 (leaf). All six conditions (C0-C3, TS, SS) share the same context-window size and answer-generation prompts; they differ only in how the context window is populated.
- **key metrics**:
> LLM-as-judge head-to-head win rate (%) on four criteria: Comprehensiveness, Diversity, Empowerment, and Directness (a control criterion). Plus claim-based validation metrics (Experiment 2): Comprehensiveness = average number of unique factual claims per answer (extracted via Claimify); Diversity = average number of claim clusters per answer. Cost: context tokens per query.
- **headline result**:
> Using GPT-4 (gpt-4-turbo), global GraphRAG conditions substantially outperformed conventional vector RAG (SS): comprehensiveness win rates 72-83% (p<.001) on Podcast and 72-80% (p<.001) on News; diversity win rates 75-82% (p<.001) on Podcast and 62-71% (p<.01) on News. Root-level GraphRAG (C0) retained 72% comprehensiveness and 62% diversity win rates over vector RAG while requiring ~9x-43x fewer context tokens per query (>97% fewer tokens than source-text summarization TS).
- **ablations**:
> Community level comparison (C0/C1/C2/C3): community summaries gave a small consistent comprehensiveness/diversity gain over source-text summarization (TS) except at root level (e.g., intermediate-level on Podcast 57% comprehensiveness win, low-level on News 64%); no statistically significant differences among global conditions or vs TS otherwise. Token-cost vs level tradeoff: C3 used 26-33% fewer context tokens than TS, C0 used >97% fewer. Self-reflection ('gleaning') ablation (Appendix A.2, on HotPotQA): iterative self-reflection lets larger chunk sizes recover entity references lost at 600 vs 2400 token chunks (GPT-4 extracted nearly 2x more entity references at 600 vs 2400 token chunks without reflection). Claim-based validation (Experiment 2) corroborates LLM-judge comprehensiveness/diversity findings.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> No standard intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG) are reported, since the global pipeline is not a top-k retrieval task. Instead, end-to-end answer-quality metrics (LLM-judge win rates) are validated by an independent claim-based intrinsic measure (claim count and claim-cluster count via Claimify) reported separately (Experiment 2).
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome-focused (final answer comprehensiveness/diversity/empowerment/directness). Claim-based measures add a finer-grained outcome decomposition (factual-claim coverage and diversity of an answer), but there is no step-wise retrieval/planning-accuracy or reasoning-faithfulness scoring.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Token cost reported per condition (Table 2): map-reduce over source texts (TS) is most expensive (e.g., ~1.01M Podcast / ~1.71M News context tokens); root-level community summaries (C0) need dramatically fewer (~26.7k Podcast / ~39.8k News), i.e. ~9x-43x fewer tokens than TS and >97% reduction. Offline indexing cost: ~281 minutes for the Podcast dataset on a 16GB-RAM Xeon VM using a public gpt-4-turbo endpoint (2M TPM, 10k RPM). Tradeoff: root-level GraphRAG (C0) trades a modest quality drop for large query-time token savings.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed context window of 8k tokens for community summaries, community answers, and global answers; 600-token chunks (100-token overlap) for indexing and for the SS/TS text. At reduce time, community answers are reranked-then-truncated: sorted by helpfulness score and added until the token limit is reached (budget-capped). All six conditions share the same context-window size and prompts.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Evaluation questions are LLM-synthesized for global sensemaking: given a short corpus description, the LLM generates N user personas, K tasks per persona, and M high-level questions per (user,task) pair (K*N*M questions) that require global corpus understanding and explicitly avoid retrieval of specific low-level facts; 125 questions per head-to-head comparison, each repeated 5 times and averaged. Datasets are two ~1M-token corpora (Podcast ~1M tokens / 1669 chunks; News ~1.7M tokens / 3197 chunks). Answers are open-ended (no single gold answer); difficulty is assessed via LLM-judge win rates and claim-based metrics rather than exact-match accuracy.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al., 2020); hierarchical/recursive summarization indexing (RAPTOR, Sarthi et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2023); graph community detection (Leiden, Traag et al., 2019; Louvain, Blondel et al., 2008; graph modularity, Newman, 2006) implemented via the graspologic library; LLM self-reflection/gleaning (Reflexion-style, Shinn et al., 2024; Madaan et al., 2024); LLM-based persona generation for evaluation; Claimify (Metropolitansky & Larson, 2025) for claim extraction; MultiHop-RAG news corpus (Tang & Yang, 2024).
- **contrasts with**:
> Conventional vector/semantic-search RAG ('vector RAG', SS), which fails on global sensemaking queries; prior query-focused summarization (QFS) methods that do not scale to RAG-scale corpora; non-graph hierarchical-summary indexing methods (e.g., RAPTOR / Sarthi et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2023), from which GraphRAG differs by building a graph index and using graph-community detection for thematic partitioning; fact-retrieval benchmarks (HotPotQA, MultiHop-RAG, MT-Bench) and vector-RAG-oriented evaluation frameworks (e.g., RAGAS criteria).
- **lineage**:
> Group B (RAG for task solving) / static-corpus document-graph RAG. A foundational 2024 work establishing the graph + community-summary (graph/community retrieval unit) line of 'GraphRAG' methods for global/sensemaking QA, distinct from experience/case-memory agent lines; spawned a large family of follow-up graph-based RAG systems.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- venue

<a id="item-ra-dit"></a>
### 31. RA-DIT (Retrieval-Augmented Dual Instruction Tuning)

2024  ·  ICLR 2024  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01352)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: ICLR 2024 (The Twelfth International Conference on Learning Representations, Vienna, Austria, May 7-11, 2024; OpenReview id 22OTbutug9). Preprint arXiv:2310.01352 (v1 2 Oct 2023; v4 ICLR 2024 camera-ready, 6 May 2024). DBLP: conf/iclr/Lin0CSL00KSLZY24.
- **authors affiliation**:
> Xi Victoria Lin, Xilun Chen, Mingda Chen (equal contribution), Weijia Shi, Maria Lomeli, Rich(ard) James, Pedro Rodriguez, Jacob Kahn, Gergely Szilvasy, Mike Lewis, Luke Zettlemoyer, Wen-tau (Scott) Yih. Affiliation: FAIR at Meta (Weijia Shi is also affiliated with the University of Washington). Corresponding/lead emails: {victorialin,xilun,mingdachen,scottyih}@meta.com.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01352
- **code url**:
> https://github.com/facebookresearch/RA-DIT (official data-preparation artifact release, ICLR 2024; CC-BY-NC license; Python 99.5%; releases fine-tuning dataset processing scripts and the DRAGON+ embeddings of the Wiki-2021 index, plus prompt-generation code. It is a partial/WIP artifact: retriever setup and training are marked WIP and full LM/retriever training code is not included.)
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (single-paper official artifact repo; not a continuously-updated leaderboard or paper list).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> QA / knowledge-intensive NLP. Retrieval-augmented language modeling (RALM) for knowledge-intensive zero- and few-shot tasks: open-domain QA (Natural Questions, TriviaQA), multiple-choice knowledge (MMLU), multi-hop QA (HotpotQA), fact verification (FEVER), entity linking (AIDA CoNLL-YAGO), slot filling (Zero-Shot RE, T-REx), long-form QA (ELI5), and knowledge-grounded dialogue (Wizard of Wikipedia). Not an agentic/planning/tool-use/embodied setting.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-model (single-agent), non-interactive setting. The goal is to retrofit any pre-trained auto-regressive LLM (Llama 7B/13B/65B) with retrieval capability via a lightweight two-step fine-tuning recipe, as a cheaper alternative to expensive end-to-end RALM pre-training (REALM, RETRO, Atlas) and to suboptimal post-hoc/off-the-shelf fusion (REPLUG, In-Context RALM). Supervision is available: multi-task instruction-tuning data (20 datasets across dialogue, open-domain QA, reading comprehension, summarization, chain-of-thought) plus unsupervised corpus text. Two decoupled fine-tuning steps: (1) LM-ft (RA-IT) updates the LLM to better use retrieved 'background' context and to ignore distractors; (2) R-ft updates the retriever's query encoder via LM-Supervised Retrieval (LSR) so retrieved chunks better match LLM preferences. Evaluation is primarily zero-/few-shot on held-out knowledge-intensive benchmarks not seen during fine-tuning. The retrieval corpus is a fixed external store (Wikipedia + CommonCrawl); there is no test-time interaction or growing agent memory.
- **what is retrieved**: Documents / text chunks (passages, max 200 words each) from an external corpus that provide factual 'background' knowledge to ground the LLM's prediction. Not demonstrations, tools, cases, trajectories, skills, or agent experiences.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus: a fixed retrieval data store of 399M text chunks combining the Dec 20, 2021 Wikipedia dump (from Izacard et al. 2022, Atlas) with the 2017-2020 CommonCrawl dumps. There is no growing/episodic agent memory; the store is read-only and not written to by the system during deployment.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k document ranking. The retriever returns top-k relevant text chunks (k tuned: top-1/3/10 studied, with performance improving as k grows; k-tilde=3 used to build LM-ft data). The objective is similarity/effectiveness-style top-k retrieval whose chunks are then ensembled (weighted by relevance score), not recovery of a minimal complete set nor a precision-driven variable-size set. The R-ft (LSR) objective trains the retriever to rank chunks by how much they improve the LLM's likelihood of the correct answer.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: [Retrieve] only. RA-DIT retrieves documents to ground generation; there is no case Reuse/Revise/Retain in the CBR sense (no case library, no case adaptation, no retention of solved cases). Not a CBR method.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False: RA-DIT does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is a retrieval-augmented LM fine-tuning method.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: Document / text chunk (a passage of up to 200 words) retrieved by dense similarity. Each retrieved chunk is the unit prepended as a 'Background:' field to the LLM prompt.
- **index source**:
> Static external corpus, offline-induced. A 399M-chunk dense index built from Wikipedia 2021 (Atlas snapshot) + 2017-2020 CommonCrawl, encoded with the DRAGON+ document encoder; ANN search via FAISS / Atlas distributed index (the released embeddings use an IVF65536/PQ256 index). No online/test-time growth driven by the model.
- **index structure topology**: Flat dense vector index (single-vector dual-encoder embeddings, dot-product / nearest-neighbor search; FAISS IVF-PQ in the released index). No graph, hierarchy, or cluster topology.
- **retriever type**:
> Dense dual-encoder retriever (single-vector bi-encoder). Initialized with DRAGON+ (Lin et al. 2023), a state-of-the-art dense retriever trained with contrastive learning and data augmentation. Then made LEARNED via R-ft: the query encoder is fine-tuned with LM supervision (LSR). So overall: dense + learned (LM-feedback-trained query encoder).
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Two-fold. Initialization: contrastive similarity training (off-the-shelf DRAGON+). Then RA-DIT's R-ft uses LM-feedback / downstream-effectiveness supervision: a generalized LM-Supervised Retrieval (LSR, from REPLUG) objective. For each (x,y), the LSR target distribution p_LSR(c|x,y) is the softmax over LM likelihoods p_LM(y | c o x)/tau of the correct answer given each candidate chunk; the retriever score distribution p_R(c|x) is trained to minimize KL(p_R || p_LSR). A higher LSR score means a chunk more improves the LLM's chance of predicting the correct answer, so the retriever is aligned to LLM preferences. Generalized beyond REPLUG by mixing unsupervised corpus data with multi-task instruction (MTI) data; best mixture is 95% corpus + 5% MTI. Only the query encoder is updated (fine-tuning both encoders hurt performance). Not RL/value-based.
- **query construction**:
> The retrieval query/key is the language model prompt x, formed from task inputs via manually constructed templates (e.g., the standalone question for QA). At LM-ft and inference time, the top-k chunks retrieved on x are prepended to x. The paper notes automatically generating task-specific retrieval queries is left to future work; queries are template-built from the raw task input, not decomposed or expanded.
- **query granularity**: Task-level (one-shot at t=0): a single retrieval is performed on the full task prompt; there is no per-step / per-sentence / iterative query reconstruction. (A preliminary iterative dual-tuning variant was tried but yielded no gains.)
- **when to retrieve**: One-shot: retrieval is performed once on the input prompt (top-k chunks), both during LM-ft data construction and at inference. No iterative, active (uncertainty-triggered), or learned-router retrieval scheduling.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed schedule / always-on: retrieval is always invoked once per prompt (no confidence/uncertainty trigger, no learned classifier, no reflection tokens, no agent-initiated request). The only learned 'when/what' signal is offline in R-ft, where LM likelihood (LSR score) supervises which chunks the retriever should prefer; but the decision to retrieve is unconditional at runtime.
- **reranking**:
> No explicit separate reranking stage. Retrieved top-k chunks are kept; their retriever similarity scores are re-normalized (softmax over the top-k) and used as ensemble mixture weights p_R(c|x). R-ft implicitly improves ranking by aligning retriever scores to LM-preference (LSR), but there is no cross-encoder/hierarchy-aware reranker.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Minimal / none in the classic sense. Each retrieved chunk is prepended verbatim as a 'Background:' field (demarcated by 'Background:' ... '\n\n'). No decomposition, distillation, compression, or distractor filtering of returned text. Robustness to distracting chunks is instead handled at the LLM side via retrieval-augmented instruction tuning (training the LM to ignore irrelevant chunks and fall back on parametric knowledge), and via parallel ensembling rather than concatenation. The SQuAD-2.0 'I don't know' training also helps the model abstain on wrong passages.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tools/skills; retrieved items are raw Wikipedia/CommonCrawl text chunks, not engineered tool descriptions).
- **index content separation**: N/A / No: the dense vector index maps directly to passage text; there is no lightweight-index-then-content progressive-disclosure separation (chunks are retrieved and prepended directly).
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index/protocol). The retrieval corpus is a static, offline-built dense index (Wikipedia 2021 + CommonCrawl, 399M chunks); no MCP / RapidAPI / RESTful / function-calling tool integration or live sync.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tools; no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation PLUS training signal (dual). (a) Utilization: each of the top-k retrieved chunks is prepended to the prompt as a 'Background:' field; the LLM computes predictions for each augmented prompt in PARALLEL and the final output probability is a relevance-weighted mixture: p_LM(y|x,C') = sum_{c in C'} p_LM(y | c o x) * p_R(c|x) (parallel in-context retrieval-augmentation, following REPLUG). (b) Training: retrieval augmentation is baked into LM fine-tuning (RA-IT, minimize -sum_i sum_j log p_LM(y_i | c_ij o x_i)), and LM likelihood feeds back as the LSR training signal for the retriever. No latent-token injection or cross-attention; pure in-context conditioning + fine-tuning.
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-generate (one-shot), no planning/search loop. There is no explicit planner, MCTS, tree search, or per-step interleaving. For a prompt: retrieve top-k once, build k parallel augmented prompts, ensemble the LM outputs. Both LM-ft and R-ft are offline training stages; inference is a single retrieve-then-predict pass.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer: a single retrieval per input prompt grounds the full answer; retrieval is not interleaved per CoT-step, per-sentence, per-token, or per-tool-call. (CoT-reasoning datasets appear in the LM-ft training mix, but retrieval at inference is still one-shot per prompt.)
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not a CBR method; no case adaptation). The nearest analog is parallel ensembling of multiple retrieved chunks weighted by relevance, plus LM fine-tuning to integrate/ignore retrieved content.
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw retrieved document/passage text, injected as a natural-language 'Background:' field prepended to the instruction prompt. No distilled strategy, workflow, executable program, structured note, or latent/soft-token representation.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw document/passage (un-distilled factual text chunk from Wikipedia/CommonCrawl). Not a distilled strategy/insight, state-aware guideline, reusable workflow, procedural skill, demonstration, or hint.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Retriever-aware LM training plus abstention. (1) Retrieval-augmented instruction tuning (RA-IT) deliberately trains the LLM on (correct chunk, sometimes incorrect chunk) -> correct answer, so the model learns to exploit relevant context and to ignore distracting/misleading chunks by leaning on parametric knowledge (cites Shi et al. 2023a 'large language models can be easily distracted'). (2) The SQuAD-2.0 reading-comprehension data trains the model to answer 'I don't know' when the passage is irrelevant, inducing abstention when the retriever errs. (3) Preserving parametric knowledge (commonsense-reasoning eval shows no degradation) is framed as a safety net for retriever mistakes. (4) Parallel ensembling weighted by relevance reduces reliance on any single noisy chunk. No separate relevance-evaluator/self-reflection module or reason-in-documents distillation.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (no episodic/skill/workflow/procedural/graph/latent agent memory). The external 399M-chunk corpus is a static knowledge source, not an agent-written memory.
- **write back**: False: RA-DIT does not store new experiences, cases, or skills into any memory at deployment; it only reads from a fixed external corpus. (The retriever's query encoder is updated offline during R-ft training, but that is parameter learning, not memory write-back.)
- **online growth**: No: the retrievable store (399M Wikipedia + CommonCrawl chunks) is fixed/offline-built and does not grow during deployment/test-time.
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back; no episodic memory is maintained or updated at runtime).
- **failure experience usage**:
> Partial, training-time only and not stored as memory. RA-IT exposes the LLM to imperfect/incorrect retrieved chunks during fine-tuning (and trains 'I don't know' abstention via SQuAD 2.0) so it is robust to failed retrievals, and the LSR signal down-weights chunks that lower answer likelihood. But there is no stored/retrieved repository of failed experiences; this is a static training behavior, not success+failure memory contrast at inference.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (no stored runtime memory entries to mutate; append-only-none). Model/retriever parameters are updated only during offline fine-tuning, not as evolving memory.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Partially: the retriever (query encoder) is LEARNED via LM-supervised LSR (KL to the LM-preference distribution), so 'what to retrieve' is trained from LM feedback rather than fixed similarity. However, it is an offline-trained dense scoring function, not an RL/value-based or M-MDP soft-Q retrieval policy, and the decision of WHEN to retrieve remains a fixed top-k schedule.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No: single-model, single private retriever+LM pipeline; no memory/experience shared across agents or heterogeneous frameworks.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> Knowledge-intensive (held out from fine-tuning): MMLU; Natural Questions (NQ); TriviaQA (TQA); ELI5; and a 7-task KILT subset: HotpotQA (HoPo), FEVER (FEV), AIDA CoNLL-YAGO (AIDA), Zero-Shot RE (zsRE), T-REx, Wizard of Wikipedia (WoW) (and ELI5). Commonsense reasoning (no retrieval): BoolQ, PIQA, SIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, OpenBookQA (OBQA). Comparison setting also uses Atlas's 64-shot KILT-style fine-tuning on 8 tasks (NQ, TQA, HoPo, FEV, AIDA, zsRE, T-REx, WoW).
- **benchmark family**:
> QA / multi-hop / knowledge-intensive NLP. Spans MMLU (multiple-choice knowledge), open-domain QA (NQ, TQA), multi-hop QA (HotpotQA), fact verification (FEVER), entity linking (AIDA), slot filling (zsRE, T-REx), long-form QA (ELI5), knowledge-grounded dialogue (WoW) -- i.e., the KILT family -- plus a standard commonsense-reasoning suite. Not in the web/embodied/tool/code/memory-agent/decision-RL benchmark families.
- **baselines**:
> Primary: base Llama (7B/13B/65B) and Llama+REPLUG (Llama 65B + off-the-shelf DRAGON+, parallel in-context RA but no fine-tuning), in 0-shot and 5-shot in-context settings. Cross-architecture: Atlas 11B (encoder-decoder RALM jointly pre-trained with its retriever) in a 64-shot fine-tuning setting. Internal ablation baselines: IT (conventional instruction tuning, no retrieval), RA-IT (retrieval-augmented IT), LM-ft-only, R-ft-only; retriever ablations vs Contriever and Contriever-MSMARCO; also referenced/compared qualitatively to InstructRetro 48B and SAIL.
- **key metrics**:
> Exact Match / accuracy for QA and classification tasks (NQ, TQA, HoPo, FEV, AIDA, zsRE, T-REx EM-style; MMLU accuracy), task-appropriate KILT metrics for WoW and ELI5 (e.g., F1/ROUGE-style scoring per KILT), and averages: Avg-diamond (MMLU, NQ, TQA, ELI5) and overall Avg across the 10 knowledge-intensive tasks. Commonsense tasks use accuracy. Improvements reported as average percentage-point gains.
- **headline result**:
> RA-DIT 65B sets state-of-the-art on knowledge-intensive zero-/few-shot benchmarks, outperforming the un-tuned in-context RALM REPLUG (Llama 65B + DRAGON+) by +8.9% on average 0-shot and +1.4% 5-shot (averaged over MMLU, NQ, TQA, ELI5). Per-task 0-shot vs REPLUG: MMLU +8.2% (64.6 vs 59.7), NQ +22% (relative; 35.2 vs 28.8), e.g. zsRE 73.7 vs 50.8, T-REx 53.1 vs 36.3. In the 64-shot fine-tuned setting, a single RA-DIT 65B model beats task-specific Atlas 11B by +4.1 points on average (60.9 vs 56.8) over 8 KILT tasks, winning on 6/8.
- **ablations**:
> 1) Dual instruction tuning ablation (Table 6, 5-shot dev): both LM-ft (RIT 65B + Dragon+, Avg 53.9) and R-ft (Llama 65B + FTed Dragon+, Avg 54.4) alone beat the REPLUG baseline (Llama 65B + Dragon+, Avg 53.8); combining both (RA-DIT, RIT 65B + FTed Dragon+, Avg 54.6) is best (+0.8 over baseline). 2) LM fine-tuning strategy (Table 4): RA-IT > IT > base Llama with retrieval; at 0-shot top-10 chunks RA-IT 65B 51.0 vs IT 65B 47.7; instruction tuning alone helps 0-shot but is marginal/hurts 5-shot; performance rises monotonically with more retrieved chunks (top-1<top-3<top-10). 3) Retriever fine-tuning data (Table 5): corpus data alone +0.4, MTI data alone +0.1; best is 95% corpus + 5% MTI (Avg 58.0 vs 57.4 base Dragon+); fine-tuning BOTH encoders hurts (54.0) vs query-encoder only -> only the query encoder is updated. 4) Retriever choice (Table 7): Dragon+ (Avg 53.4) > Contriever-MSMARCO (51.8) > Contriever (47.5) > Llama no-retrieval (45.0). 5) Commonsense reasoning (Table 3): RA-DIT 65B improves over Llama 65B on 7/8 tasks (Avg 74.5 vs 72.1), showing parametric knowledge is preserved. 6) Appendix: RA-IT gives even larger boosts on smaller Llama 7B/13B (scaling-laws analysis); retrieval-corpora ablation shows Wiki-2021-only retains most of the benefit vs full Wiki+CC. Iterative/multi-step RA-DIT was tried but gave no further gains.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> No: only end-to-end downstream task metrics (EM/accuracy/KILT scores and their averages) are reported. No separate intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG) for the retriever are reported; retriever quality is assessed indirectly through downstream task gains (e.g., the retriever-choice and R-ft ablations).
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Outcome only: final-answer task metrics. There is no scored intermediate process metric (no reasoning-faithfulness or step-wise retrieval-accuracy scoring). The number of retrieved chunks (top-1/3/10) ablation and qualitative appendix examples (model ignoring wrong chunks / answering 'I don't know') touch on process behavior but are not quantified as process metrics.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Framed as a 'lightweight' alternative: RA-DIT avoids the expensive end-to-end RALM pre-training of REALM/RETRO/Atlas, needing only two short fine-tuning steps over downstream data. A single multi-task RA-DIT 65B model beats task-specific Atlas 11B (which needs joint pre-training + per-task fine-tuning). Inference uses parallel in-context augmentation over k chunks (k=1/3/10), adding moderate cost that scales with k; accuracy rises with more chunks. The released artifact notes the Wiki-2021-only index retains most performance vs the full 399M Wiki+CC index, reducing storage. No explicit GPU-hour, dollar, or latency numbers are reported.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed top-k, capped by context window.
