### 41. Search-o1: Agentic Search-Enhanced Large Reasoning Models

2025  ·  EMNLP 2025  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.05366)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**: EMNLP 2025 (Main Conference); preprint arXiv:2501.05366 (Jan 2025). DOI 10.18653/v1/2025.emnlp-main.276
- **authors affiliation**: Xiaoxi Li, Guanting Dong, Jiajie Jin, Yuyao Zhang, Yutao Zhu, Peitian Zhang, Zhicheng Dou (Gaoling School of Artificial Intelligence, Renmin University of China); Yujia Zhou (Tsinghua University). Corresponding author: Zhicheng Dou (RUC).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.05366
- **code url**: https://github.com/RUC-NLPIR/Search-o1 (originally referenced as https://github.com/sunnynexus/Search-o1 in v1 abstract). Project page: https://search-o1.github.io/
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/RUC-NLPIR/Search-o1

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Complex multi-step reasoning (PhD-level science QA, mathematics, code generation) plus open-domain QA (single-hop and multi-hop). Augments o1-style large reasoning models (LRMs) with on-demand web retrieval.
- **problem setting**:
> Inference-time / test-time framework (no training of the backbone LRM). A single LRM (QwQ-32B-Preview) reasons autonomously and, when it hits a knowledge gap during its long chain-of-thought, emits a search query, retrieves documents from a live web search engine, refines them, and continues reasoning. Single-agent (one reasoning model that also doubles as the Reason-in-Documents refiner via a separate generation pass). No fine-tuning or supervision; the backbone is frozen and used in a prompting/inference-only manner. Supports batch inference over multiple questions in parallel.
- **what is retrieved**: External web documents/pages (open-web knowledge) retrieved on demand to fill knowledge gaps in the reasoning chain.
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus (the open web via Bing Web Search API; Wikipedia-backed corpora for open-domain QA benchmarks). No agent-written/episodic memory; retrieval targets a fixed external knowledge source.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k ranking objective (top-10 documents per search query, configurable k); the system issues multiple retrievals across reasoning steps to incrementally cover the diverse knowledge needs, but each retrieval is a fixed top-k call rather than a completeness-driven variable-size set.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A — not a case-based reasoning method. Implements only a Retrieve-like step (web retrieval); no Reuse/Revise/Retain of cases.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is positioned as agentic RAG for large reasoning models.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: document / web page (top-k retrieved documents per query; in the RAgent baseline top-10 snippets first, then full documents fetched by URL via Jina Reader API). After refinement the injected unit is a distilled text passage.
- **index source**: Static external store: live web index queried through the Bing Web Search API (and Wikipedia-based corpora for open-domain QA). Not offline-induced and not grown by the agent at test time.
- **index structure topology**: Flat external search index (commercial web search engine inverted index / Wikipedia dense or sparse index). No graph or hierarchical structure imposed by the method.
- **retriever type**: Off-the-shelf web search engine (Bing Web Search API) as the retriever; for open-domain QA benchmarks a standard retriever over Wikipedia is used. Effectively BM25/dense-style search engine, not learned by the method.
- **retriever learning signal**: None (off-the-shelf). The retriever is not trained or fine-tuned; the LRM only learns nothing here either (frozen). Retrieval quality depends on the underlying search engine.
- **query construction**:
> Thought-conditioned: the LRM autonomously generates a targeted natural-language search query (e.g., 'structure of trans-Cinnamaldehyde') based on the current reasoning state and previously retrieved knowledge, emitted between special symbols <|begin_search_query|> and <|end_search_query|>.
- **query granularity**: Step/state-level: queries are generated at the reasoning step where the model encounters uncertainty (mid-chain), not a single task-level query at t=0. Multiple queries can be issued within one reasoning session.
- **when to retrieve**: Iterative and agent-initiated (agentic / active): the model decides when to retrieve, triggering retrieval whenever it emits a search-query special token; can iterate multiple times within a single reasoning chain.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Agent-initiated request via generated special tokens. When the model decodes the <|end_search_query|> symbol, generation is paused and the enclosed query triggers retrieval. The trigger is the model's own decision (driven by knowledge uncertainty during reasoning, motivated by high frequency of uncertain words like 'perhaps'), not a fixed schedule, external confidence threshold, or trained classifier.
- **reranking**: No dedicated reranking stage described. The search engine returns top-k; the Reason-in-Documents module performs analysis/extraction rather than learned reranking.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Reason-in-Documents distillation: a separate generation pass (using the same reasoning model) analyzes the top-k retrieved documents conditioned on the current search query and prior reasoning steps, producing a concise 'Final Information' refined snippet (or 'No helpful information found.'). This minimizes noise/redundancy and preserves coherence before injection. Two-stage: intermediate analysis reasoning r_docs then refined output r_final.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A — Search-o1 retrieves web documents, not tools/APIs; no tool-description engineering. (The Reason-in-Documents module post-processes retrieved documents but this is query-time refinement, not pre-indexing tool-document engineering.)
- **index content separation**:
> Partial/related: in the RAgent baseline, lightweight top-10 snippets are retrieved first and full documents are fetched by URL on demand (progressive disclosure). Search-o1 itself relies on the Reason-in-Documents module to condense full retrieved content rather than a separate lightweight index.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A — no tool index. Retrieval uses the live Bing Web Search API and Jina Reader API for page content; integration is via API calls within the inference loop (not MCP/RapidAPI tool registries).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A — no inter-tool dependency modeling (the only external tool is web search).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**: Prompt augmentation: the refined knowledge r_final is injected back into the ongoing reasoning chain between special symbols <|begin_search_result|> and <|end_search_result|>, and the LRM continues reasoning. Not used as a training signal.
- **planning integration**:
> Per-step interleaved inside the reasoning/search loop: the reasoning chain is paused at the point a search query is emitted, retrieval + Reason-in-Documents refinement runs, the refined result is inserted, and reasoning resumes. This is a retrieve-within-reasoning loop (agentic RAG) rather than plan-then-retrieve or tree search.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-CoT-step / per-search-step within a single rollout: retrieval is woven in at each point where the model decodes a search-query special token during its long reasoning chain (can be multiple times per question).
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A — not CBR; no retrieved-case adaptation/revision. (The closest analog is the Reason-in-Documents distillation that adapts raw documents into context-fit refined knowledge.)
- **retrieved item representation**: Distilled free-text knowledge (the 'Final Information' refined passage produced by the Reason-in-Documents module), injected as text between search-result special tokens. Raw documents are not injected directly in Search-o1 (they are in the RAgent baseline).
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Distilled, query-and-context-conditioned factual snippet derived from raw web documents (an extracted/condensed insight rather than a raw trajectory or a single demonstration).
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Reason-in-Documents refinement module: it filters redundant/irrelevant content from verbose retrieved documents and outputs only concise relevant information (or explicitly 'No helpful information found.'), guarding the main reasoning chain against noise and incoherence introduced by directly inserting long documents. No retriever-aware training or distractor-aware SFT (inference-only).

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (no persistent episodic/skill/workflow memory). The framework is stateless across questions; retrieved knowledge lives only within the current reasoning session.
- **write back**: No. The system does not store new experiences/cases/skills into any memory for later retrieval; refined knowledge is used only in-context for the current question.
- **online growth**: No. The retrievable store (web search index) is external and not grown by the agent at deployment/test time.
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back to a memory store).
- **failure experience usage**: N/A — no experience storage. Failed or successful reasoning trajectories are not retained or retrieved; there is no success/failure memory.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A — no stored memory entries to mutate (no append/merge/refine/prune).
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No. Retrieval/when-to-search is an emergent prompting behavior of the frozen LRM via special tokens, not an RL-optimized or learned retrieval policy. (Search-o1 is inference-only; trained-policy successors such as Search-R1 came later.)
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent private reasoning; no memory or experience shared across agents or frameworks. (Batch inference processes multiple independent questions in parallel but they do not share knowledge.)

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> Challenging reasoning: GPQA (diamond 198 / extended 546, PhD-level science MCQA in physics/chemistry/biology), MATH500, AMC2023 (40 q), AIME2024 (30 q), LiveCodeBench (112 problems, Aug-Nov 2024). Open-domain QA: Natural Questions (NQ), TriviaQA (single-hop); HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA (2WIKI), MuSiQue, Bamboogle (multi-hop).
- **benchmark family**: QA (GPQA science MCQA; NQ, TriviaQA single-hop), multi-hop (HotpotQA, 2WIKI, MuSiQue, Bamboogle), math (MATH500, AMC2023, AIME2024), code (LiveCodeBench).
- **baselines**:
> Direct Reasoning w/o retrieval: Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, QwQ-32B-Preview, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, Llama3.3-70B-Instruct, and (reference) DeepSeek-R1-Lite-Preview, GPT-4o, o1-preview. Retrieval-augmented: Standard RAG (top-10 docs for the original question, RAG-Qwen2.5-32B / RAG-QwQ-32B) and RAG Agent (RAgent, ReAct-style top-10 snippets then URL fetch, RAgent-Qwen2.5-32B / RAgent-QwQ-32B). Also human experts on GPQA extended set.
- **key metrics**: Pass@1 (reported for all challenging reasoning tasks: GPQA, math, LiveCodeBench). Exact Match (EM) and F1 for open-domain QA. GPQA also broken down by Physics/Chemistry/Biology and Overall.
- **headline result**:
> On the GPQA diamond set Search-o1 (QwQ-32B-Preview backbone) reaches 63.6 overall Pass@1, exceeding RAgent-QwQ-32B (61.6) and direct QwQ-32B (58.1); on the GPQA extended set it surpasses human experts overall (57.9). Averaged across the five challenging reasoning datasets, Search-o1 exceeds RAgent-QwQ-32B by 4.7%, QwQ-32B by 3.1%, and non-reasoning Qwen2.5-32B / Llama3.3-70B by 44.7% / 39.3%.
- **ablations**:
> Reason-in-Documents ablation: Search-o1 vs RAgent-QwQ-32B (agentic RAG that injects raw documents) isolates the Reason-in-Documents refinement (+4.7% avg on reasoning tasks; +5.3% avg EM on multi-hop QA). Agentic-RAG vs Standard-RAG ablation: agentic RAG (RAgent) gives +23.2% avg EM over standard RAG on multi-hop QA for QwQ-32B, while single-hop QA shows little change (47.8 vs 47.6 EM). Scaling analysis on number of retrieved documents (top-k): retrieving even one document with Search-o1 surpasses Direct Reasoning and standard RAG using ten documents. Non-reasoning model (Qwen2.5-32B) with agentic RAG performs no better or worse than standard RAG, showing ordinary LLMs cannot effectively use search as a tool.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No. Only end-to-end task metrics (Pass@1, EM, F1) are reported; intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG / retrieval completeness) are not reported separately.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome metrics (final-answer Pass@1 / EM / F1). Process quality is illustrated qualitatively via case studies (Appendix B on GPQA, AMC2023, HotpotQA) showing coherent interleaving of search queries and refined results, and via a preliminary analysis counting uncertain words ('perhaps', etc.) in reasoning chains, but no quantitative step-wise process score.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Discusses efficiency via a batch inference mechanism that parallelizes both token generation and Reason-in-Documents refinement across multiple questions to improve throughput. Scaling analysis shows Search-o1 with a single retrieved document can beat baselines using ten documents (more cost-effective use of retrieval). Hardware: eight NVIDIA A800-80GB GPUs. No explicit per-question API-cost or latency numbers reported.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k retrieval: top-k = 10 documents per search query by default (Bing region US-EN), with a scaling analysis over k. Generation budget: up to 32,768 max tokens, temperature 0.7, top_p 0.8, top_k 20, repetition penalty 1.05. Reason-in-Documents compresses the top-k documents into a short refined snippet before injection, capping injected context.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A — this is a method paper, not a survey/taxonomy.
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A — uses existing benchmarks (does not construct a new benchmark). Sizes of evaluation sets noted: GPQA diamond 198 / extended 546; MATH500 500; AMC2023 40; AIME2024 30; LiveCodeBench 112 (Aug-Nov 2024).

**Relations**

- **builds on**: Large reasoning models (OpenAI-o1, Qwen QwQ-32B-Preview as backbone, DeepSeek-R1); agentic RAG / ReAct-style tool-use; chain-of-thought prompting; retrieval-augmented generation. Uses Bing Web Search API and Jina Reader API.
- **contrasts with**:
> Standard (one-shot, problem-oriented) RAG that retrieves once and injects raw top-k documents; plain agentic RAG / RAgent (ReAct-style) that injects lengthy raw retrieved documents and disrupts reasoning coherence; direct reasoning without retrieval (knowledge-insufficient); MCTS-based o1 reproductions that rely on external policy/reward models without internalized reasoning.
- **lineage**:
> Group B (retrieval-augmented task solving / agentic RAG for reasoning). An inference-time agentic-RAG-for-reasoning framework that bridges o1-style LRMs with on-demand web retrieval plus document distillation; a direct precursor to later RL-trained search-augmented reasoning models (e.g., Search-R1, R1-Searcher, ReSearch) that train the search policy rather than prompt it.

### 42. ZeroSearch: Incentivize the Search Capability of LLMs without Searching

2025  ·  NeurIPS 2025  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.04588)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **authors affiliation**:
> Hao Sun, Zile Qiao, Jiayan Guo, Xuanbo Fan, Yingyan Hou, Yong Jiang, Pengjun Xie, Yan Zhang, Fei Huang, Jingren Zhou. Affiliation: Tongyi Lab, Alibaba Group (lead author Hao Sun also affiliated with Peking University, per contact email sunhao@stu.pku.edu.cn). Corresponding authors: Jiayan Guo and Yan Zhang.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.04588
- **code url**: https://github.com/Alibaba-NLP/ZeroSearch
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/Alibaba-NLP/ZeroSearch (Apache-2.0; ~1254 stars; homepage https://alibaba-nlp.github.io/ZeroSearch; models/datasets on Hugging Face under sunhaonlp/Alibaba-NLP, e.g. https://huggingface.co/datasets/sunhaonlp/ZeroSearch_dataset)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: QA (open-domain single-hop and multi-hop question answering); RL-trained agentic search / retrieval-augmented reasoning. The core contribution is a training methodology (search-engine simulation for RL) rather than a new task.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, multi-turn, single-agent setting where an LLM policy model is trained with reinforcement learning to interleave reasoning (<think>), search queries (<search>), and answers (<answer>). The key problem: prior RL-for-search methods (e.g., Search-R1) train against live search engines, which suffer from (1) uncontrolled/unpredictable document quality and (2) prohibitively high API costs over hundreds of thousands of rollout queries. ZeroSearch replaces the live search engine during training with a frozen, lightly SFT-tuned simulation LLM that generates documents, while still using a real engine (Google/SerpAPI) at inference/evaluation. Supervision is outcome-based (rule-based F1 reward on final answer); no step-level supervision.
- **what is retrieved**:
> Documents (passages) in response to a search query. During training these documents are GENERATED by a simulation LLM (5 short docs of ~30 words each per query, controllable as 'useful' or 'noisy'); during inference the policy retrieves real documents from Google Web Search via SerpAPI.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus at inference (real web/Google via SerpAPI; a Wikipedia-compatible variant is also released). During training, retrieval is grounded in a frozen simulation LLM's parametric knowledge that mimics a search engine rather than any external corpus. No agent-written growing/episodic memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**: Fixed top-k ranking style: a fixed k=5 documents are returned per query (both for the simulation LLM and the real engine). The objective is end-to-end answer accuracy (F1 reward / EM eval), not retrieval completeness or a variable-size precision-driven set.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based reasoning method).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is an RL-for-search framework.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: document / passage (short ~30-word documents during simulated training; standard web search snippets/passages at inference). Top-5 documents are concatenated into the <information> block.
- **index source**:
> Hybrid by phase. Training-time 'index' is a frozen simulation LLM (offline lightly-SFT-tuned to generate useful vs noisy documents; parametric, not a stored corpus). Inference-time index is a static external corpus = the live web via Google/SerpAPI (or Wikipedia in the released variant). The store is not induced/grown online during deployment.
- **index structure topology**: Flat. During training the 'search engine' is a generative LLM (no explicit index structure). During inference a standard flat web-search ranking is used (top-k by the search engine). No graph/hierarchical/cluster topology.
- **retriever type**:
> LLM-as-retriever (generative): a fine-tuned simulation LLM generates documents during RL training (the paper's core novelty). At inference, an off-the-shelf real search engine (Google Web Search via SerpAPI) is used. The trained policy model itself is the query generator, not the retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> For the simulation LLM (the 'retriever'): lightweight supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on query-document pairs harvested from real-search interaction trajectories, with an LLM-as-judge labeling each document useful or noisy; document quality is then controlled at rollout by adjusting a few prompt words. The simulation LLM is frozen during RL. The retriever is NOT trained with RL or contrastive similarity labels. (The policy model that issues queries is trained with RL / outcome F1 reward, but it is the agent, not the retriever.)
- **query construction**:
> Thought-conditioned, agent-generated free-text search queries. The policy model first reasons inside <think>...</think>, then if it needs evidence emits a query inside <search>...</search>; queries can be reformulated/decomposed across turns (e.g., first search the person, then their birthplace).
- **query granularity**: Step/turn-level: queries are generated iteratively at each reasoning step during a multi-turn rollout (not a single one-shot query at t=0). Multiple searches per question are allowed (MAX_TURNS=5 in the released code).
- **when to retrieve**: Iterative / agent-initiated. The model searches on demand whenever its own reasoning decides external knowledge is needed, across multiple turns, until it chooses to answer.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Agent-initiated request: the policy model itself decides when to emit a <search> query based on its internal reasoning (<think>), with no fixed schedule, confidence threshold, or learned external router. The decision behavior emerges from RL training on the outcome reward.
- **reranking**: None. No explicit reranking stage; the top-5 documents (generated or retrieved) are used directly.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> None (no rerank, distillation, compression, or distractor filtering of returned documents). Training-time robustness instead comes from deliberately injecting noisy documents via the curriculum, and document tokens are loss-masked during the RL update (not a context-refinement step but a gradient-masking step).
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tool/skill descriptions are indexed; retrieval target is documents, not tools).
- **index content separation**: N/A (no separate lightweight index vs heavy content; documents are generated/retrieved directly).
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A for a tool index. For completeness: inference uses Google Web Search via the SerpAPI HTTP API; training uses a locally served simulation LLM (sglang/vLLM server). No MCP/RapidAPI/function-calling tool registry.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation: retrieved/generated documents are inserted into the rollout between <information> and </information> tags and conditioned on for the next reasoning step. Retrieval is embedded inside the RL training loop, so the (simulated) retrieved context also indirectly shapes the training signal, but it is not itself a learned latent injection.
- **planning integration**:
> Inside a search loop / per-step interleaved retrieve-then-reason. The agent follows a think -> search -> read information -> think -> ... -> answer loop within a single multi-turn rollout (retrieve-as-you-reason), rather than plan-then-retrieve or tree search. Curriculum noise scheduling is applied across training steps, not within a single rollout's plan.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-reasoning-step / per-search-call within a rollout: each <think> step may trigger one <search> call whose returned <information> conditions the next step. Interleaving granularity is at the level of individual search turns, not per-sentence or per-token.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not a CBR case-adaptation method).
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw textual documents (short passages) injected verbatim into the <information> block of the prompt; no distillation into strategies/guidelines or programs.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw document/passage (lowest abstraction). No distilled strategy, guideline, workflow, or skill.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Retriever-aware / curriculum training: the simulation LLM can be prompted to emit 'noisy' documents, and a curriculum rollout schedule progressively raises the probability of noisy documents (per the exponential schedule p_i = p_s + (b^{i/m}-1)/(b-1)*(p_e-p_s), default b=4), exposing the policy to increasingly hard/noisy retrieval and forcing it to learn robust reasoning. Document tokens are loss-masked so externally-generated (potentially noisy) tokens do not destabilize the gradient. No explicit relevance evaluator / self-reflection / reason-in-documents module.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (no episodic store, skill library, workflow memory, or graph memory). The only persistent learned artifact is the RL-updated policy weights plus the frozen SFT'd simulation LLM.
- **write back**: False. The system does not store new experiences/cases/skills into any retrievable memory during deployment; knowledge is internalized in policy weights via RL, not written to an external store.
- **online growth**: False. No retrievable store grows at test time; the simulation LLM and (inference) search corpus are fixed. Curriculum difficulty changes during training, but that is a schedule, not store growth.
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back to an external memory store; learning is via on-policy RL weight updates rather than memory writes).
- **failure experience usage**:
> No persistent storage/retrieval of failed experiences. Indirectly, 'noisy' (often answer-lacking) documents are deliberately generated during the curriculum to harden the policy, and the outcome-based F1 reward naturally penalizes wrong answers, but failures are not stored as retrievable negative cases.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (no stored memory entries to mutate). The policy is updated by REINFORCE/PPO/GRPO gradient steps.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Partial. The decision of WHEN/WHAT to search is a learned RL policy (the policy model emits search queries, trained with outcome reward). However the retriever/document source itself is NOT a learned/RL retrieval policy: at training it is a frozen SFT'd simulation LLM, and at inference it is a fixed top-k web search engine.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent private training; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing. (The paper notes one simulation server could be shared across multiple RL training jobs to cut cost, but that is infrastructure sharing, not experience sharing.)

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: NQ (Natural Questions), TriviaQA, PopQA (single-hop QA); HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, Bamboogle (multi-hop QA). Training set is the merged NQ + HotpotQA train splits (NQ and HotpotQA are in-domain; the other five are out-of-domain).
- **benchmark family**: QA: single-hop (NQ, TriviaQA, PopQA) and multi-hop (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, Bamboogle).
- **baselines**:
> Vanilla prompting: Direct Answer, Chain-of-Thought (CoT), standard RAG. Advanced RAG: RAgent (RAG-Agent style iterative search) and Search-o1. RL tuning: R1 (reasoning on internal knowledge only) and Search-R1 (RL with a real search engine). Search-R1 with a real search engine is the primary head-to-head comparison. Ablation comparisons also include prompt-based vs SFT simulation engines (3B/7B/14B) and Google Search itself.
- **key metrics**:
> Exact Match (EM) for end-to-end QA accuracy (primary, following Search-R1). F1 score is used as the rule-based RL reward (and as the reward across all RL baselines for fair comparison). Cost metrics: API cost vs GPU cost in USD; reward curves and number of interaction turns are tracked as training dynamics.
- **headline result**:
> Using Qwen-2.5-3B-Base as the policy model, ZeroSearch with a fine-tuned 14B simulation engine (SFT-14B) reaches average EM 34.47 across the 7 datasets, surpassing the same policy trained with real Google Search (avg EM 32.81); a fine-tuned 7B simulation engine (SFT-7B, avg 33.53) matches Google. Headline claim: a 7B retrieval module matches a real search engine and a 14B module surpasses it, at zero API cost. Cost: ~64,000 queries cost $70.8 (GPU, SFT-14B) vs $586.7 (Google/SerpAPI API).
- **ablations**:
> (1) Choice of simulation LLM (Table 4, Qwen-2.5-3B-Base policy): Base-no-RL 8.82 avg; prompt-based Prompt-3B/7B/14B = 29.44/31.39/31.50; SFT-3B/7B/14B = 30.47/33.53/34.47; Google = 32.81 -> SFT engines beat prompt engines, larger is better, SFT-7B ~= Google, SFT-14B > Google. (2) RL algorithm (Table 5): REINFORCE 34.47 > GRPO 33.17 > PPO 32.67 (REINFORCE best/most stable). (3) Curriculum vs random noise=0.5 (Table 6): Curriculum 34.47 vs Random 32.59 on Qwen-2.5-3B-Base; 36.07 vs 34.84 on LLaMA-3.2-3B-Base -> curriculum helps. (4) Document-token loss masking (Table 7, LLaMA-3.2-3B): w/ mask 36.07 vs w/o mask 34.53 -> masking improves stability/performance. (5) Base vs Instruct and reward-curve comparisons vs Search-R1 (Figs 2-4).
- **evaluation decoupling**: No. Intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG / completeness) are not reported separately; evaluation is end-to-end QA EM only. Simulation document quality is shown qualitatively (useful vs noisy case studies) rather than via intrinsic retrieval scores.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome (final-answer EM / F1 reward). Some process-level training-dynamics analysis is reported (reward curves, number of interaction turns over training, base-vs-instruct curves, effect of loss masking), but no formal step-wise retrieval-accuracy or reasoning-faithfulness metric.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Central claim of the paper. For ~64,000 search requests over a ~12h / batch 64 / 5 rollouts / 200-step run: API cost with Google/SerpAPI = $586.7 vs GPU cost for SFT-3B/7B/14B simulation = $17.7 / $35.4 / $70.8 (API cost $0). So ZeroSearch removes API cost entirely at the price of GPU deployment, achieving equal-or-better accuracy than the real engine. REINFORCE/GRPO involve repeated rollouts that would multiply real-engine API cost.
- **context budget and selection count**: Fixed-k: exactly 5 documents returned per search query for all methods (TOPK=5); MAX_TURNS=5 search turns per question in released code. Simulated documents are short (~30 words each). No adaptive/budget-capped selection or truncation reranking.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Search-R1 (Jin et al., 2025, arXiv:2503.09516) for the multi-turn think/search/answer RL template, F1-reward choice, dataset setup (NQ+HotpotQA train), and EM evaluation; DeepSeek-R1 / OpenAI-o1 for reward-driven reasoning without step supervision; 'Generate rather than retrieve' (Yu et al., 2022) for the insight that LLMs can generate relevant documents; RL algorithms REINFORCE (Williams 1992), PPO (Schulman et al. 2017), GRPO (DeepSeekMath, Shao et al. 2024). Implementation builds on Search-R1, veRL, and RAGEN codebases.
- **contrasts with**:
> Search-R1, R1-Searcher, ReSearch (RL-for-search against static local corpora or real engines), and DeepResearcher / WebThinker (RL with live commercial search engines). ZeroSearch contrasts by simulating the search engine with a frozen SFT'd LLM to remove API cost and gain controllable, curriculum-degraded document quality. Also contrasts with prompt-based / SFT RAG (Self-RAG, RetroLLM, Adaptive-RAG) and MCTS test-time-scaling RAG (RAG-Star, AirRAG, Marco-o1).
- **lineage**:
> Part of the RL-for-search / agentic-RAG lineage (group B: RAG for task solving). A 2025 sibling of Search-R1 / R1-Searcher / ReSearch / DeepResearcher, distinguished by replacing the live retriever with a simulation LLM during RL training (search-engine simulation for cost-free, quality-controllable RL). Has inspired follow-ups such as SSRL (Self-Search Reinforcement Learning).

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- benchmark_construction_and_size
- venue

## C — Retrieval-Augmented Planning (LM Planners)

<a id="item-adaplanner"></a>
### 43. AdaPlanner: Adaptive Planning from Feedback with Language Models

2023  ·  NeurIPS 2023  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16653)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2023
- **venue**: NeurIPS 2023 (Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36); preprint arXiv:2305.16653 (cs.CL)
- **authors affiliation**: Haotian Sun, Yuchen Zhuang, Lingkai Kong, Bo Dai, Chao Zhang. All from Georgia Institute of Technology (Sun and Zhuang contributed equally).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16653
- **code url**: https://github.com/haotiansun14/AdaPlanner

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: LLM-agent sequential decision-making / planning in interactive grounded environments (embodied text-game ALFWorld and web-interaction MiniWoB++).
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent, closed-loop sequential decision-making. An LLM agent is given a task goal, a list of admissible actions, and (optionally) a small number of expert demonstrations, then must generate and execute a plan in an environment that returns natural-language observations. The setting is online/test-time: the agent acts, observes feedback, and adaptively revises its plan within an episode. Supervision is limited to a few human demonstrations (or none), with no gradient training of the LLM; environment feedback (observations and assertion checks) supplies the refinement signal. Evaluated on ALFWorld (embodied household tasks) and MiniWoB++ (web GUI tasks).
- **what is retrieved**: Successful plans/skills (full code-style solution() programs together with their environment interactions) stored as few-shot exemplars; at plan time these discovered skills plus human-written demonstrations are injected into the prompt.
- **retrieval grounding**: HYBRID: a static set of human-written task demonstrations plus a GROWING episodic skill memory that the agent writes during deployment via skill discovery (successful trajectories archived after a filtering step).
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> Retrieve (reuse skills for resembling tasks), Reuse (skills as few-shot exemplars), Revise (in-plan/out-of-plan plan refinement from feedback), Retain (skill discovery archives successful plans after filtering). 4-flag: [Retrieve: yes (lightweight, task-resemblance), Reuse: yes, Revise: yes, Retain: yes]. Note: the work does not frame itself as CBR.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The paper does not explicitly frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it realizes CBR-like mechanisms (skill reuse + revise + retain) under the terms skill discovery and closed-loop plan refinement.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: skill-or-program: a full code-based plan (a Pythonic solution() function) representing a successful trajectory for a task, plus the corresponding human demonstrations; effectively a full-trajectory/case unit expressed as executable code.
- **index source**: Hybrid: offline human-written demonstrations (one example per task) combined with an online/test-time-induced skill memory grown via the trial-and-error skill discovery loop during deployment.
- **retriever learning signal**: none (no trained retriever). Which skill is retained is decided by a downstream-task-effectiveness filter (skill filtering: keep the discovered skill only if it improves success rate), but skill selection at plan time is not a learned retrieval policy.
- **query construction**: The query/key is the current task goal plus the list of admissible actions (and current state for refinement); resembling tasks trigger reuse of stored skills as exemplars. Raw task description is used; no synthetic query expansion.
- **query granularity**: task-level (skills/demonstrations are selected once at initial plan generation, t=0, conditioned on the task goal). Refinement operates at sub-goal/step level but the skill retrieval itself is task-level.
- **when to retrieve**: one-shot for skill/demonstration retrieval (assembled into the prompt at initial planning). Plan refinement is iterative/active but it re-prompts the same exemplars rather than retrieving new ones.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Skill/demonstration injection is on a fixed schedule at plan generation. The separate plan-refinement trigger is an assertion-failure / out-of-plan signal: each sub-goal ends with an assertion checked at N checkpoints; assertion failure (misaligned observation vs prediction) triggers out-of-plan refinement, while aligned feedback triggers in-plan refinement via ask_LLM().
- **reranking**: None. No reranking stage over retrieved skills/demonstrations.
- **retrieved context refinement**: None at retrieval time. (A skill-filtering step occurs at write/storage time, discarding skills that do not boost success rate, but retrieved exemplars are injected verbatim into the prompt without post-retrieval reranking, compression, or distillation.)
- **index content separation**: N/A (skills stored as full code plans; no separate lightweight index vs heavy content described).
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (not a tool-retrieval method; environment interaction via ALFWorld/MiniWoB++ action APIs and a code-execution interface, not a tool index/MCP).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**: prompt augmentation / skill reuse: discovered skills and human demonstrations are placed into the code-style LLM prompt as few-shot exemplars to ground initial plan generation and refinement.
- **planning integration**:
> one-shot exemplars at plan time combined with a closed-loop plan-then-refine loop: AdaPlanner first generates a complete code-based plan (decomposed into sub-goals with assertions), executes it, and applies in-plan refinement (ask_LLM extracts info, integrated into current plan) or out-of-plan refinement (regenerate/revise the whole plan via refine-then-resume from a saved breakpoint). Retrieved skills serve as initial-plan exemplars.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> per-sub-goal / per-checkpoint: refinement is woven in at N sub-goal assertion checkpoints within a rollout (in-plan refinement is a one-step ask_LLM action; out-of-plan refinement revises the whole plan at a checkpoint). Skill retrieval itself is per-answer (per-episode, at plan time).
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> execution-feedback-driven revision: a reused skill/plan is adapted via in-plan refinement (ask_LLM extracts info integrated into the plan) and out-of-plan refinement (LLM regenerates/revises the whole plan from an assertion-failure feedback message, then refine-then-resume from a saved breakpoint). Not verbatim ICL only; the plan is actively revised.
- **retrieved item representation**: executable program / skill: the injected item is a Pythonic code-based solution() function (a successful plan plus interactions), used as a free-text/code exemplar in the prompt.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: procedural skill / reusable code plan derived from a successful full trajectory (a code-style plan that decomposes the task into sub-goals); above raw trajectory, framed as a reusable skill exemplar.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Code-style (Pythonic) prompting constrains the LLM generation space to mitigate hallucination; assertion-based self-checking detects misaligned (out-of-plan) feedback and triggers correction; skill filtering discards non-generalizing skills before they enter memory, guarding against episode-specific noise.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: skill-library (skill memory module archiving successful code-based plans/trajectories as reusable few-shot skills).
- **write back**: Yes. Successful plans discovered during deployment are written into the skill memory (after a filtering check) and reused as few-shot exemplars for resembling tasks.
- **online growth**: Yes. The skill memory grows at test time via skill discovery; e.g., in MiniWoB++ AdaPlanner starts with 38 human demonstrations and automatically discovers 21 additional skill examples, yielding 59 examples for 53 tasks.
- **write back trigger**: on-success only, gated by an effectiveness filter: a candidate skill is created when AdaPlanner successfully completes a task (skill acquisition); it is retained (written to memory) only if including it improves success rate during skill filtering, otherwise discarded.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success-only for memory: only successful plans are archived as skills (failed trajectories are not stored as reusable skills). Within an episode, failed assertions/out-of-plan feedback drive immediate plan revision but are not persisted as negative cases. Contrasts with Reflexion, which stores past-failure reflections.
- **memory evolution update**: append-only with a filtering gate (discovered skills are appended if they improve success rate, discarded otherwise); no described merge/delta-update/refine-overwrite of already-stored skills.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No. Skill/demonstration selection is not an RL- or value-optimized retrieval policy; it is task-resemblance-based reuse. The only optimization is a success-rate filter at storage time.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent private skill memory; no cross-agent or cross-framework experience sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: ALFWorld (134 tasks across 6 task types: Pick, Clean, Heat, Cool, Examine, Pick two) and MiniWoB++ (53 tasks: 9 with feedback, 44 without feedback).
- **benchmark family**: embodied (ALFWorld) and web (MiniWoB++).
- **baselines**:
> ALFWorld: BUTLER (training-based), ReAct, Reflexion (implicit closed-loop). MiniWoB++: CC-Net and WGE (training-based), WebN-T5-3B (finetuning-based), RCI (implicit closed-loop). DEPS is discussed as a related strict closed-loop method. Backends: GPT-3 (text-davinci-002), GPT-3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo / text-davinci-003).
- **key metrics**: Success rate (%); sample efficiency measured as number of expert demonstrations/samples used.
- **headline result**: AdaPlanner outperforms SOTA baselines by 3.73% on ALFWorld and 4.11% on MiniWoB++ while using 2x and 600x fewer samples respectively; overall success rate 91.79% on ALFWorld (GPT-3) and 91.11% on MiniWoB++ tasks with feedback (92.87% over all 53 MiniWoB++ tasks).
- **ablations**:
> (1) Number of closed-loop refinements: success rate rises monotonically with each refinement and AdaPlanner beats Reflexion at every iteration, even with as few as 2 total demonstrations across six tasks. (2) Code interface ablation: removing the code interface (natural-language plans) drops ALFWorld from 81% to 46% and MiniWoB++ from 93% to 66%. (3) Skill discovery ablation: with vs without skill discovery; success rate nearly doubles on ALFWorld and rises ~15% on MiniWoB++. (4) GPT-3 vs GPT-3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo) showing AdaPlanner's resilience to hallucination via code prompts.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No. Only end-to-end task success rates are reported; no intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k/nDCG/completeness) are reported separately (retrieval here is skill reuse, not ranked retrieval).
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Primarily outcome (task success rate). Process-level insight is given indirectly via success rate vs number of closed-loop refinements (showing intermediate refinement quality) and sample-efficiency curves, but no formal step-wise/faithfulness metrics.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Strong efficiency focus: 2x fewer samples on ALFWorld, ~600x fewer samples on MiniWoB++ vs CC-Net; the refine-then-resume mechanism resumes from a saved breakpoint instead of restarting episodes, reducing the number of LLM/API calls; assertions are checked only at N crucial sub-goal checkpoints to cut API-call count. gpt-3.5-turbo noted as ~10x cheaper than text-davinci-002/003 but with more hallucination.
- **context budget and selection count**: Fixed, small exemplar count: ALFWorld uses one demonstration per task (6 total, half of what ReAct/Reflexion use); MiniWoB++ uses 38 human demos + 21 discovered skills (59 examples for 53 tasks). Selection count is fixed/budget-capped per task rather than adaptive top-k.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> ReAct (action grounding from feedback), Reflexion (self-revision from trials), RCI (plan-then-act), code-as-prompt / program-of-thought ideas (e.g., code-generation prompting reduces ambiguity), Chain-of-Thought and Zero-Shot Planner as earlier open-loop LLM planners; ALFWorld and MiniWoB++ as environments.
- **contrasts with**:
> Open-loop planners (Chain-of-Thought, Zero-Shot Planner, HuggingGPT, Chameleon); implicit closed-loop methods that fix the initial plan and only adjust the current action (ReAct, Inner Monologue, Reflexion, RCI); and DEPS, which needs a trained plan selector and task-specific data; AdaPlanner instead refines the whole plan purely via LLM prompting.
- **lineage**:
> Group C (RAG planning): LLM planners that adaptively refine plans from environment feedback and reuse self-discovered skills, in the lineage of feedback-driven closed-loop LLM agents (ReAct -> Reflexion -> AdaPlanner) with an experience/skill-memory (growing episodic store) component.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- completeness_vs_topk_objective
- index_structure_topology
- retriever_type

### 44. LLM-MCTS (Large Language Models as Commonsense Knowledge for Large-Scale Task Planning)

2023  ·  NeurIPS 2023  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14078)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2023
- **venue**: NeurIPS 2023 (Thirty-seventh Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems)
- **authors affiliation**: Zirui Zhao, Wee Sun Lee, David Hsu — National University of Singapore (NUS), School of Computing.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14078
- **code url**: https://github.com/1989Ryan/llm-mcts (project page: https://llm-mcts.github.io/)
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (single-paper code repo, not a continuously-maintained leaderboard/paper-list)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Embodied / decision-making: large-scale, long-horizon household object-rearrangement task planning (robot task planning under partial observation), with additional analysis tasks (multiplication, multi-hop air-travel planning).
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, online, single-agent sequential decision-making in a partially observable, large object-centric domain (VirtualHome). The agent receives a natural-language instruction plus partial observations and must output executable actions to rearrange objects. Modeled as a POMDP solved online by MCTS. Supervision is available only as a small dataset D of expert trajectories/observations used for few-shot prompting and (for one baseline) fine-tuning; no gradient updates to the LLM itself. The LLM (GPT-3.5-turbo, or GPT-2 for a fine-tuned baseline) is used both to induce a commonsense prior belief over states (world model) and a heuristic action policy.
- **what is retrieved**:
> Few-shot demonstrations (expert trajectories): instruction-conditioned (instruction + corresponding expert trajectory) demos retrieved from the expert dataset D to build the K-shot prompt for the LLM heuristic policy. Object/location lists (Dobj) are also drawn from D, and sentence-BERT embeddings are used to map free-form LLM outputs to canonical names.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus: a fixed offline dataset D of expert trajectories/observations in similar household environments (200 prompt-candidate instances selected from 2000 generated tasks). The retrievable store does not grow during deployment; the per-episode belief is updated but is not a retrievable memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**: Fixed top-k ranking: the K most similar expert instructions/trajectories (by sentence-BERT cosine similarity to the current instruction) are retrieved as the K-shot prompt. No notion of recovering a complete minimal set or precision-driven variable-size selection.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not framed as case-based reasoning). If forced to map: only a weak Retrieve phase (similarity-based exemplar retrieval) is present; no Reuse-as-adaptation, Revise, or Retain. Flags: [Retrieve=partial, Reuse=no, Revise=no, Retain=no].
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False: the paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. Retrieval is incidental few-shot prompt selection, not CBR.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: Single demonstration / full expert trajectory: an (instruction, expert-trajectory) demo used as a K-shot exemplar for the policy prompt. (Auxiliary: object-name strings from Dobj for state/goal grounding.)
- **index source**: Static, offline-induced store: the expert dataset D (generated offline via regression planning with handcrafted heuristics, following Watch-And-Help). A 200-instance subset of D serves as prompt candidates. Frozen after offline construction.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat embedding index of instructions/demonstrations (sentence-BERT vectors over which cosine similarity is computed). The per-episode state belief is maintained as an object-centric graph (nodes=objects, edges=Inside/On relations), but that is the world-model belief, not the retrieval index.
- **retriever type**: Dense (off-the-shelf sentence-BERT embeddings + cosine similarity top-K). No BM25, no learned/generative retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**: None (off-the-shelf): sentence-BERT (Reimers & Gurevych 2019) is used as a fixed encoder; retrieval is pure cosine-similarity top-K with no training, no contrastive fine-tuning, no LM-feedback or RL signal.
- **query construction**:
> Raw natural-language instruction l of the current task is embedded with sentence-BERT and compared (cosine similarity) to embedded instructions l_i in D; the most similar are selected as exemplars. Surface forms of LLM outputs (object positions, actions) are likewise embedded and matched to canonical names in Dobj / admissible action set.
- **query granularity**: Task-level: the prompt-exemplar retrieval is done once per task using the task's natural-language instruction (one-shot at t=0). The retrieved K-shot prompt is then reused across the LLM policy queries within that task's tree search.
- **when to retrieve**: One-shot (per task): exemplars are retrieved once at the start of an episode based on the instruction. Within MCTS the same retrieved K-shot prompt is reused for repeated LLM policy/world-model queries; sentence-BERT matching of LLM responses to canonical names recurs throughout.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule (no learned trigger): exemplar retrieval is triggered once per task by the arrival of the instruction; there is no uncertainty/confidence/reflection-based retrieval trigger.
- **reranking**: None: top-K by cosine similarity is used directly with no reranking stage (no cross-encoder, no RRF, no hierarchy-aware rerank).
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> None of the rerank/distill/compress kind for the retrieved demos. The only post-processing is sentence-BERT embedding + cosine-similarity mapping of free-form LLM outputs to canonical object names / admissible actions (a normalization/translation step, not refinement of retrieved exemplars).
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tools/APIs are retrieved; not a tool-use method).
- **index content separation**: N/A (no lightweight-index-then-content / progressive-disclosure separation; flat demo index only).
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index or integration protocol; not a tool-use method).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no inter-tool dependency modeling; not a tool-use method).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation (in-context few-shot): retrieved (instruction, expert-trajectory) pairs are concatenated as a K-shot prompt that conditions the LLM when it acts (a) as the heuristic policy pi(a|h) inside PUCT and (b) as the commonsense world model sampling initial object positions. The LLM outputs are then used as a search heuristic (prior policy) and as a state prior belief, not committed directly as actions.
- **planning integration**:
> Inside MCTS / tree search: retrieval-conditioned LLM outputs are embedded inside Monte Carlo Tree Search. The LLM-induced commonsense belief b(s0) provides the prior over states that MCTS samples from at each simulation root; the LLM-induced heuristic policy provides the prior pi(a|h) in the PUCT action-selection rule. Goals and observations are translated to/from natural language. MCTS does look-ahead simulation, expansion, random rollout, and backup; the LLM policy biases exploration but final action choice depends on Q-values and visit counts.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Per-tool-call/per-node within a rollout: the LLM heuristic policy is queried (and sampled M times) at action-selection / node-expansion points during the tree search to form the empirical policy distribution; the world-model belief sampling occurs per simulation at the root. So retrieval-conditioned LLM calls are woven in per simulation/per node rather than once per final answer.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A / verbatim ICL exemplar: retrieved expert trajectories are used as verbatim in-context examples with no case adaptation/revision (not a CBR adaptation pipeline).
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw expert trajectory / natural-language demonstration: the injected exemplars are raw (instruction, action-sequence) trajectories rendered as English sentences (observations and goals translated to natural language), used verbatim as in-context few-shot examples.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw trajectory / single demonstration (verbatim expert (instruction, trajectory) examples). Not distilled strategies, guidelines, or reusable skills.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Primarily MCTS itself: the LLM policy is used only as a soft heuristic prior in PUCT, so action selection is also governed by Q-values and visit counts, tolerating an imperfect/hallucinated policy. A randomness hyper-parameter lambda is mixed into the empirical policy distribution to avoid over-deterministic LLM samples; M-sample averaging approximates the policy distribution; sentence-BERT mapping forces LLM outputs into admissible actions/objects. No retriever-aware training or explicit relevance-evaluator/self-reflection module.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (no persistent cross-task learned memory). A per-episode object-centric belief over states (a graph/probability-vector) is maintained and updated online, but it is reset per task and is not a retrievable experience memory.
- **write back**: False (no): the system does not store new experiences/cases/skills back into a retrievable store. The expert dataset D is fixed; only the within-episode state belief is updated from observations (transient, not written back to D).
- **online growth**: No: the retrievable store (expert dataset D / prompt candidates) is frozen after offline construction; it does not grow during deployment/test time.
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back to a retrievable memory). The per-episode belief is updated per-step from observations, but that is transient state-estimation, not memory writing.
- **failure experience usage**: Not used: failed trajectories are analyzed qualitatively in the paper (policy/model/translation errors) but are not stored or retrieved; the few-shot prompt corpus is expert (success) trajectories only. No success+failure contrastive or failure-only corrective storage.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (no persistent memory store is mutated). The transient per-episode belief is delta-updated by Bayesian-style observation updates within an episode but is not a stored/evolving memory.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No: case/exemplar selection is fixed sentence-BERT cosine top-K, not a learned or RL-optimized retrieval policy. (The action policy guidance comes from the LLM heuristic + MCTS, not from a learned retriever.)
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No: single-agent private setting; no sharing of memory/experience across multiple agents or frameworks.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> VirtualHome (3D household simulator) object-rearrangement tasks across difficulty splits: Simple, Compositional (Comp.), NovelSimple, NovelComp.(2), NovelComp.(3), each in Seen and Unseen apartment/item settings (2000 tasks generated, 200 used as prompt candidates, 800 for evaluation). Analysis tasks: arithmetic multiplication; multi-hop air-travel planning (Kaggle World Cities + Virtual Radar Server flight routes, 68 large + 62 mid-size cities, 400+400 city-pair tests).
- **benchmark family**: embodied (VirtualHome) — household object rearrangement / task planning; plus auxiliary symbolic/decision-making analysis tasks (multiplication, multi-hop travel-planning).
- **baselines**:
> UCT (vanilla MCTS with uniform state prior and ground-truth reward, no commonsense knowledge); Fine-tuned GPT-2 policy (Li et al., trained on 10000 trajectories); GPT-3.5 Policy (LLM-as-policy few-shot, Huang et al. language-planner style). Also referenced: L-Model (LLM as world model only) and L-Policy (LLM as policy only) as conceptual baselines. Ablations: No Heuristic Policy, Uniform State Prior, Fully Observable.
- **key metrics**: Success rate (%) of completing the task within the step limit (30 steps in main eval), reported as mean ± standard error across difficulty splits and Seen/Unseen settings. Travel-planning uses path/flight-route accuracy.
- **headline result**:
> On VirtualHome, GPT3.5-MCTS outperforms both MCTS-alone (UCT: 0% across all splits) and LLM-as-policy baselines by a wide margin, with the largest gains on novel/complex tasks: on the hardest split NovelComp.(3)-Seen it reaches 33.6±3.1% vs GPT3.5 Policy 5.4±2.0% and fine-tuned GPT-2 2.3±1.5%; on NovelComp.(2)-Seen 72.6±6.9% vs 48.2% (GPT3.5 Policy); on Simple-Seen 91.4±3.3% vs 83.4% (GPT3.5 Policy).
- **ablations**:
> Three ablations on the GPT3.5-MCTS framework: (1) No Heuristic Policy (UCT with LLM-induced commonsense belief but NO LLM PUCT guidance) collapses to 0.0±0.0% on all splits — the LLM heuristic policy is essential to make the search tractable. (2) Uniform State Prior (replace LLM commonsense belief with uniform prior) drops to ~0-3% — the LLM world-model prior is essential. (3) Fully Observable (give MCTS perfect state knowledge) raises success only modestly above the partial-observation LLM-MCTS (e.g. Simple-Seen 94.0 vs 91.4; NovelComp.(3)-Unseen 76.6 vs 70.4), indicating the LLM-induced belief is already fairly accurate and partial observability is not the main bottleneck. Together these show both components (commonsense world model + heuristic policy) are necessary, with search-space reduction via the policy heuristic being the dominant driver.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Not decoupled in the RAG sense: no intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k/nDCG) are reported. Evaluation is end-to-end task success rate; the travel-planning analysis adds a separate path/flight-accuracy intrinsic measure for the world-model-vs-policy comparison, and a failure-mode breakdown (policy/model/translation errors) is given.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome (task success rate within a step budget). Some process-level analysis is provided qualitatively: failure analysis attributing errors to policy/model/translation, and the MDL/travel-planning analysis examining intermediate world-model accuracy vs policy generalization.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Compute is driven by MCTS rollouts and repeated LLM sampling: default run uses simulation_num=100 simulations, simulation_per_act=2, M samples per LLM policy/world-model query, max_depth=20, max_episode_len=50 (per the released config). The central efficiency argument is that the LLM heuristic policy drastically reduces the effective search space (vanilla UCT is intractable, scoring 0%), trading extra LLM API calls for vastly fewer effective rollouts; explicit wall-clock/latency/token-cost numbers are not the headline (no quantified token/$ budget reported).
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (this is a method/empirical paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A (not a benchmark-contribution paper). Note for context: 2000 VirtualHome tasks generated (following Watch-And-Help), 200 selected as prompt candidates, 800 used for evaluation; expert trajectories collected via regression planning with handcrafted heuristics under full observation; travel-planning ground truth from Virtual Radar Server flight routes over Kaggle World Cities.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Monte Carlo Tree Search / PUCT (Kocsis & Szepesvari UCT; Silver et al. AlphaGo-style PUCT with policy prior); LLM-as-policy task planners (Huang et al. language-planner / 'Language Models as Zero-Shot Planners', SayCan-style line); fine-tuned GPT-2 interactive-decision policy (Li et al., Pre-Trained LMs for Interactive Decision-Making); VirtualHome and Watch-And-Help (Puig et al.) for environment/data; sentence-BERT (Reimers & Gurevych) for embedding-based name/exemplar matching; LLM-to-formal-goal translation (Xie et al.). MCTS implementation adapted from MC-LAVE-RL.
- **contrasts with**:
> L-Policy (using the LLM directly as the committed policy, e.g. GPT-3.5 Policy / fine-tuned GPT-2 policy) and L-Model (using the LLM only as a world model with planning, which performs poorly alone due to search-space size); vanilla UCT/MCTS without commonsense knowledge (intractable, 0%). Also contrasts with prior work using LLMs only as MCTS heuristics or transition functions on small-scale reasoning/coding (e.g., LLM-as-heuristic, LLM-as-transition), arguing those did not exploit LLMs as a full commonsense world model for large-scale planning.
- **lineage**:
> Group C (RAG/LLM planning): sits in the lineage of LLM-guided search/planning that injects LLM knowledge into a classical search algorithm (MCTS). It bridges LLM-as-policy planners (SayCan/Zero-Shot-Planner) and model-based search; a precursor to later LLM+MCTS/tree-search reasoning-and-planning methods (e.g., RAP/Reasoning-via-Planning, LATS, ToT-style search). Retrieval here is light (similarity-based few-shot exemplar selection) rather than a central RAG memory component.

### 45. RAP: Retrieval-Augmented Planning with Contextual Memory for Multimodal LLM Agents

2024  ·  arXiv 2402.03610  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03610)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2402.03610 [cs.LG], submitted 6 Feb 2024). Subsequently presented as a Poster at the NeurIPS 2024 Workshop on Open-World Agents (OWA-2024), OpenReview id=Xf49Dpxuox. No full-conference / journal peer-reviewed venue.
- **authors affiliation**:
> Tomoyuki Kagaya*, Thong Jing Yuan*, Yuxuan Lou*, Jayashree Karlekar, Sugiri Pranata, Akira Kinose, Koki Oguri, Felix Wick, Yang You (*equal contribution). Affiliations: Panasonic Connect Co., Ltd. (Japan); Panasonic R&D Center (Singapore); National University of Singapore (Singapore); Panasonic R&D Center Germany (Germany). Correspondence: Tomoyuki Kagaya (Panasonic Connect), Thong Jing Yuan (Panasonic R&D Singapore), Yuxuan Lou (NUS).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03610 (DOI: https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2402.03610; OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=Xf49Dpxuox; NeurIPS 2024 OWA workshop page: https://neurips.cc/virtual/2024/100937)
- **code url**: https://github.com/PanasonicConnect/rap (official implementation, MIT License; READMEs per benchmark for ALFWorld, WebShop, Franka Kitchen, Meta-World; ~24 stars, last push 2024-08-23)
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (single research repository, not a continuously-maintained leaderboard or paper list; last push 2024-08-23)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Embodied / decision-making and web interaction for LLM agents. Spans text-based embodied household tasks (ALFWorld), web navigation / online shopping (WebShop), and multimodal robotic manipulation (Franka Kitchen, Meta-World). General retrieval-augmented planning framework for sequential decision-making in both text-only and multimodal embodied environments.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent, closed-loop sequential decision-making over a finite horizon of H timesteps. A frozen LLM/VLM acts as the agent (no gradient training of the policy); the only learning is offline construction of an episodic memory of past SUCCESSFUL task executions. At each timestep the agent forms an action plan, picks an action, and receives an observation (textual world-state for ALFWorld/WebShop; fixed-viewpoint camera images for Franka Kitchen/Meta-World). RAP augments the standard ReAct loop with four modules (Memory, Reasoner, Retriever, Executor): the Reasoner generates overall plan, action plans, and retrieval keys; the Retriever selects the most relevant memory logs by a weighted similarity score; the Executor consumes the retrieved past experiences via in-context learning to choose the next action. Supervision is the bank of self-collected successful trajectories (no labeled retrieval data; off-the-shelf embedders). For multimodal benchmarks, a small MLP policy network trained on 25 D4RL expert demonstrations per task maps high-level VLM plans to low-level control actions. Evaluation runs recursively for up to 3 trials (d_max=3), with memory growing from successes in earlier trials (and optionally a 1000-task training set in RAP_train).
- **what is retrieved**:
> Past experiences = episodic logs of prior SUCCESSFUL task executions. Each log L_i stores the task information T_i, the overall plan p_i, and the full trajectory tau (sequences of action plans, actions, and observations). Retrieved units are windows of these trajectories (action-observation sub-trajectories) centered on the most similar action; for multimodal tasks the observations are stored images.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> GROWING / episodic memory the agent writes. The retrievable store is a memory database of the agent's own past successful trajectories, built offline from prior attempts/training tasks and grown across recursive trials. It is not a static external knowledge corpus (no Wikipedia/KB/API docs); retrieval targets self-generated experience.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k similarity retrieval (no completeness or precision-driven variable-size objective). A constant number of experiences and a fixed window of actions are extracted per retrieval, e.g. ALFWorld action-based: 4 experiences x 10 actions before/after the most similar action; observation-based: 8 experiences x 5 actions; WebShop: 3 experiences x 5 actions. There is no notion of recovering a complete minimal set; k and window sizes are fixed hyperparameters tuned per environment.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> Retrieve: yes (similarity-based retrieval of past cases). Reuse: yes (in-context analogy-making / ICL adaptation by the Executor, incl. WebShop intra-task 'A:B::C:D' analogy). Revise: no (no execution-feedback revision of a retrieved case; the LLM adapts implicitly but there is no explicit case-revision step). Retain: partial (new SUCCESSFUL trajectories are written back to memory across recursive trials / training, so [Retrieve, Reuse, partial-Retain]; Revise not implemented).
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False. The paper frames itself as Retrieval-Augmented Planning / memory-augmented RAG for LLM agents and emphasizes LLM 'analogy-making'; it does NOT cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner and does not call itself case-based reasoning, though it realizes CBR-like Retrieve/Reuse/Retain mechanisms under the RAG-with-memory framing.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Sub-trajectory: a window of an action-observation trajectory centered on the most similar action (rather than the full trajectory, to reduce noise). The stored case is a full episodic log (task + overall plan + trajectory), but at retrieval time only a centered action/observation window from each of k experiences is injected. For multimodal tasks the unit includes the visual observation(s) of the windowed sub-trajectory.
- **index source**:
> Growing episodic memory induced from the agent's own runs. Built offline by having agents attempt tasks and saving streams of successful episodes; expanded online across recursive trials (successes from earlier trials and, in RAP_train, 1000 training-set tasks are added). Test-time / deployment growth across trials; not a static offline-frozen corpus.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat similarity store with metadata/context keys: logs are embedded (sentence-transformers all-MiniLM-L6-v2 for text; CLIP ViT-B/32 for images) and retrieved by cosine similarity. Keyed by task information, overall plan, and a Reasoner-generated retrieval key; in constrained-task environments (e.g. Franka Kitchen with 5 tasks) retrieval is filtered to same task type, and WebShop adds product-category keying. No graph or hierarchical index; effectively a flat vector index with adaptive, context-keyed weighting.
- **retriever type**:
> Dense (off-the-shelf embedding similarity). Cosine similarity over frozen sentence-transformer (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) text embeddings and CLIP-based ViT image embeddings; a hand-designed weighted average of task, overall-plan, and retrieval-key similarities. No BM25, no learned/generative retriever; an LLM (Reasoner) only constructs the retrieval key, not the matching function.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None (off-the-shelf, no training). The retriever uses fixed pretrained embedders (sentence-transformers, CLIP) with cosine similarity; component weights (w_t, w_p, w_k) and which similarity equation to use (observation-based vs action-based) are hand-set/adaptive heuristics per environment, not learned. There is no contrastive training, LM-feedback, preference, or RL signal optimizing the retriever.
- **query construction**:
> Two-level, Reasoner-generated. (1) At task start the overall plan is generated from the task and used (with task info) as the query. (2) During the loop, whenever the Reasoner emits an action plan, it derives a concise retrieval key from it (e.g. action plan 'I need to find the watch' -> retrieval key 'search watch'; 'put' -> 'action put'). The key is matched against logged observations (search/locate) or logged actions (interact), and in multimodal settings the key corresponds to the current visual observation.
- **query granularity**: Both task-level and step/state-level (two-level retrieval). An initial task-level retrieval at t=0 using task + overall plan, then step-level re-retrieval each time the Reasoner produces a new action plan and corresponding retrieval key during the trajectory.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Iterative / agent-initiated. Retrieval happens once at task start, then again at every step where the Reasoner generates an action plan (which triggers a new retrieval-key-based query). Per Algorithm 1, retrieval is re-invoked inside the while-loop whenever an action plan (vs. a directly-executable action) is produced.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Agent-initiated by plan type: a re-retrieval is triggered whenever the Reasoner outputs an 'action plan' (rather than a directly executable environment action), at which point a retrieval key is generated and the Retriever is called again. No token-confidence, attention-uncertainty, or learned-complexity-classifier trigger; the schedule is determined by the ReAct-style think/act branching in the Reasoner.
- **reranking**: None. A single weighted-similarity scoring step selects the top experiences; there is no second-stage reranker (no cross-encoder, RRF, or instruction-tuned reranking). The only refinement is selecting a centered trajectory window from each retrieved log.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Windowing / truncation: for each retrieved experience only a window of the trajectory centered around the most similar action is passed to the agent (e.g. 10 or 5 actions before/after), explicitly to avoid the noise of full trajectories. No learned distillation, decompose-recompose, distractor classifier, or compression model.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A. RAP retrieves past experience trajectories, not tool/API documents; no docstring processing, synthetic-query augmentation, or tool-embedding tuning.
- **index content separation**:
> Partial / implicit: lightweight embedded keys (task, overall plan, retrieval key embeddings) are matched first, then only a centered window of the heavier full trajectory log is loaded into the prompt on demand. This is not framed as a formal progressive-disclosure / SOP-index-then-content design, but functions as index-then-windowed-content.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A. No tool index or integration protocol (no RapidAPI/RESTful/MCP/function-calling registry); the 'store' is an experience memory, grown across trials but not a live-synchronized tool catalog with CRUD.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A. No inter-tool dependency modeling. (The closest analogue is WebShop intra-task relationship reasoning between a task's scenario and its actions, but this concerns task-action correspondence, not tool dependencies.)

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation via in-context learning (case reuse). The Executor (an LLM/VLM) receives the retrieved past-experience windows together with the task, overall plan, and current trajectory, and generates the next action by analogy-making/ICL, mirroring how humans reuse past experience. No weight updates, no latent-token injection; retrieved trajectories are injected as in-context exemplars.
- **planning integration**:
> Per-step interleaved retrieve-then-act within a closed loop, on top of ReAct. The Reasoner first produces an overall plan and an initial retrieval; then in the loop the Executor generates either an action (executed in the environment) or an action plan; an action plan triggers retrieval-key generation and re-retrieval of relevant experiences, which then condition the next Executor action. Retrieval is woven step-by-step into planning/acting (no MCTS/tree search, no single plan-then-retrieve phase).
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-step / per-action-plan within a rollout: retrieval is interleaved at the granularity of each Reasoner-generated action plan (think step) inside the ReAct-style think-act loop, i.e. roughly per-reasoning-step, not per-token and not only per-final-answer.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> LLM-prompted in-context adaptation (verbatim-window ICL exemplars + analogy). Retrieved trajectory windows are presented as exemplars and the Executor LLM adapts them to the current situation by analogy-making; WebShop additionally uses an explicit intra-task analogy ('A is to B as C is to D') relating each memory action to its scenario to project onto the current scenario. No execution-feedback-driven case revision, critic, or RL-reuse finetuning.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Raw trajectory windows (action-observation text, and stored images for multimodal tasks) injected as in-context exemplars. Not distilled into strategies/guidelines, not converted to executable programs, not latent/soft tokens. The agent draws implicitly from raw experiences without an extra insight-extraction step (contrasted with ExpeL).
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Raw trajectory (low abstraction): windows of action-observation sequences from past successful episodes, deliberately kept as raw experience rather than distilled insights, strategies, or reusable workflows. The paper relies on the LLM's analogy-making over raw patterns rather than on abstracted rules.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> (1) Trajectory windowing: only a window centered on the most similar action is passed, explicitly to reduce noise from full trajectories. (2) Memory contains only SUCCESSFUL executions, so retrieved exemplars are prototypical/correct. (3) Adaptive similarity routing: switching between observation-based and action-based similarity (and constrained-task / category filtering) to retrieve more contextually relevant logs. No retriever-aware training, learned relevance evaluator, or self-reflection over retrieved content.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: Episodic (experience memory of past successful task trajectories), text and multimodal (images stored for embodied tasks).
- **write back**:
> True. The system stores new successful task executions into the memory database: initial logs are collected by attempting tasks and saving successful episodes, and the database is expanded with successes from subsequent recursive trials (and, in RAP_train, from the 1000-task training set).
- **online growth**:
> Yes (across trials at evaluation/deployment). The memory grows over recursive trials (d_max up to 3): successful tasks from preceding trials are added to memory for later trials. It is not frozen after a single offline induction. (Within a single trial the store is fixed; growth occurs between trials.)
- **write back trigger**: On-success only. A trajectory is written to memory only when the task is solved successfully (e.g. in WebShop, tasks with reward = 1 are counted as successful and added). Failed trajectories are not stored; there is no per-step or reflective write of failures.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success-only. Only successful executions are stored and retrieved; failed/negative experiences are not added to memory (contrasting with Reflexion which reflects on failures within a task). RAP avoids past failures indirectly by retrieving prototypical successful executions, not by storing failure cases.
- **memory evolution update**: Append-only. New successful trajectories are appended to the memory database across trials; existing stored entries are not mutated, merged, refined, or pruned (no dedup/forget/link-and-evolve described).
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No. Retrieval is fixed similarity top-k with hand-set adaptive weights and routing rules; it is not an RL/value-based or otherwise learned selection policy. The LLM Reasoner only constructs the retrieval key; the matching/selection is deterministic cosine-similarity ranking.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Cross-model memory transfer (a form of sharing). Because experiences are model-independent, memory built with one model can be reused by another: the paper shows memory constructed with GPT-3.5 improves a Llama2-13b agent (and GPT-3.5 itself) in a transfer-learning ablation. This is cross-model sharing of a single shared memory store, not concurrent multi-agent collective memory.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> ALFWorld (134 unseen games, six task types: Pick/Clean/Heat/Cool/Look/Pick2), WebShop (1.18M Amazon products; 100 evaluation instructions), Franka Kitchen (5 selected tasks: cabinet, microwave, burner, light, kettle), Meta-World (5 selected tasks: assemble, button, drawer, hammer, bin). LLMs/VLMs: GPT-3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct), GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613), Llama2-13b-chat for text; LLaVA-v1.5-13B and CogVLM-17B for multimodal. Embedders: sentence-transformers all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (text), CLIP ViT-B/32 (images).
- **benchmark family**: Embodied (ALFWorld; and robotic-manipulation Franka Kitchen / Meta-World) + web (WebShop). Multimodal embodied robotics (Franka Kitchen, Meta-World) plus text-based embodied (ALFWorld) and web-navigation (WebShop).
- **baselines**:
> Act, ReAct (Yao et al. 2023), Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023), ADaPT (Prasad et al. 2023) on textual benchmarks (ALFWorld, WebShop). For multimodal benchmarks, the base VLMs without RAP (LLaVA, CogVLM) serve as the baselines (LLaVA vs LLaVA+RAP; CogVLM vs CogVLM+RAP). RAP is also compared across base models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama2-13b) vs ReAct.
