- **key metrics**: Task success rate (%) for ALFWorld (per task type and overall), Franka Kitchen, and Meta-World; for WebShop both Success Rate (%) and average reward/overall Score (%). Reported per base model and across trials.
- **headline result**:
> RAP improves over ReAct by 33.6% (ALFWorld), 13.0% (WebShop), 18.2% (Franka Kitchen), and 12.7% (Meta-World). On ALFWorld with GPT-3.5, RAP reaches 85.8% overall success vs ReAct 52.2%, Reflexion 74.6%, ADaPT 71.6%; RAP_train (memory from 1000 training tasks) reaches 91.0%; RAP with GPT-4 reaches 94.8%. RAP with GPT-3.5 matches ReAct with GPT-4 (85.8%) and RAP_train (GPT-3.5) surpasses ReAct-GPT-4. The paper claims SOTA in textual scenarios.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Retriever-type on ALFWorld (GPT-3.5, d_max=3): RAP_act (action-only) 82.1%, RAP_obs (observation-only) 84.3%, full adaptive RAP 85.8%, and RAP_clip (using CLIP image observations instead of text) 86.6% (slightly best), showing direct image retrieval can beat text-converted observations and that adaptively switching action/observation info helps. (2) WebShop retriever components on Llama2-13b: ReAct 31.0% / 64.6 score -> RAP_act 33.0/68.6 -> RAP_obs 33.0/69.0 -> RAP_intra (intra-task analogy) 34.0/69.3 -> RAP_cat (product-category retrieval) 35.0/69.9 -> full RAP 36.0/71.1 (overall +5.0% success, +6.5 score on Llama2; +13.0% success, +14.3 score on GPT-3.5). (3) Transfer learning (ALFWorld, d_max=1): GPT-3.5 44.0% -> 63.4% with GPT-3.5-built memory; Llama2-13b 20.9% -> 27.6% with GPT-3.5-built memory, showing model-independent memory transfer. (4) Multimodal: LLaVA 43.4 Franka / 65.4 MetaWorld -> +RAP 61.6 / 79.2; CogVLM 44.2 / 61.5 -> +RAP 56.9 / 68.8.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No. Only end-to-end task metrics (success rate, score) are reported; there are no separate intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k, nDCG, retrieval precision). Retriever quality is assessed only indirectly via end-task success in the retriever ablations.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome-based (final task success rate / reward score). Process quality is examined only qualitatively via example ReAct-vs-RAP trajectories in the appendix (showing RAP reaches success in fewer / correct steps where ReAct fails); no quantitative step-wise or trajectory-quality metric.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Efficiency is addressed mainly via a fixed, small injected context (constant number of experiences and a fixed trajectory window) to bound prompt size and avoid noise; and by showing RAP-GPT-3.5 matching/surpassing ReAct-GPT-4 (cheaper model reaching a stronger model's performance via memory). Max steps are capped (ALFWorld 50, WebShop 15) and trials at d_max=3. No explicit token-count, dollar-cost, latency, or number-of-retrieval-calls measurements are reported.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k, budget-capped by windowing. ALFWorld: action-based retrieval extracts 4 experiences with 10 actions before/after the most similar action; observation-based extracts 8 experiences with 5 actions before/after. WebShop: 3 experiences with 5 actions before/after. A constant number of current-trajectory steps is also kept. k and window sizes are fixed hyperparameters per environment (not adaptive/precision-driven); only same-task-type or category filtering narrows the candidate pool in constrained environments.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (not a benchmark-construction paper; evaluates on existing benchmarks ALFWorld, WebShop, Franka Kitchen, Meta-World).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> ReAct (Yao et al. 2023) — RAP explicitly extends the ReAct reason-act loop with memory retrieval; Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Lewis et al. 2020) for the retrieve-then-generate paradigm; Chain-of-Thought (Wei et al. 2022) for reasoning; the 'LLMs as general pattern machines' analogy-making idea (Mirchandani et al. 2023); sentence-transformers/Sentence-BERT (Reimers & Gurevych 2019) and CLIP (Radford et al. 2021) as off-the-shelf retrievers; VLM foundations LLaVA (Liu et al. 2023) and CogVLM (Wang et al. 2023c); D4RL demonstrations and policy-network mapping for embodied control.
- **contrasts with**:
> Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023) — reflects on FAILED trajectories within a task, insights restricted to that task; ADaPT (Prasad et al. 2023) — decomposes into sub-tasks and re-executes but still reflects only within-task; ExpeL (Zhao et al. 2023) — passes all generated experiences to the LLM to explicitly extract text-based insights. RAP instead implicitly draws from a diverse range of successful experiences across tasks via similarity retrieval + in-context analogy, without an extra insight-extraction step, and extends from textual to multimodal contexts (a first for memory-retrieval multimodal agents per the authors).
- **lineage**:
> Sub-topic B/F lineage of memory-/experience-augmented LLM-agent planning (RAG-with-memory for agentic decision-making). Sits in the ReAct -> Reflexion/ExpeL line of experiential agents, distinguished by cross-task similarity retrieval of raw successful trajectories and by pioneering multimodal (VLM) experience retrieval for embodied robotics tasks.

<a id="item-rada"></a>
### 46. RaDA: Retrieval-augmented Web Agent Planning with LLMs

2024  ·  ACL 2024 Findings  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07607)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2024 (ACL Findings 2024), Bangkok, Thailand, pages 13511-13525. ACL Anthology ID 2024.findings-acl.802; DOI 10.18653/v1/2024.findings-acl.802; DBLP conf/acl/KimBKGH24.
- **authors affiliation**: Minsoo Kim (Seoul National University), Victor S. Bursztyn (Adobe Research), Eunyee Koh (Adobe Research), Shunan Guo (Adobe Research), Seung-won Hwang (Seoul National University, corresponding author). Primary affiliations: Seoul National University and Adobe Research.
- **paper url**:
> https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-acl.802/ (DOI https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2024.findings-acl.802; PDF https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-acl.802.pdf). NOTE: the arXiv URL supplied in the task (https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07607) is INCORRECT -- that arXiv ID resolves to an unrelated paper 'On Graph Grammars and Games' (Vijayakumar & Mathew, cs.FL). The canonical/verified source for RaDA is the ACL Anthology / Adobe Research page.
- **code url**:
> https://github.com/ldilab/RaDA (official repo; the paper footnote states 'Code is available at: https://github.com/ldilab/RaDA', and the repo is titled '[ACL 2024-findings] RaDA: Retrieval-augmented Web Agent Planning with LLMs' linking to the ACL Anthology page. Note: as of retrieval the public repo contains only a README placeholder -- 1 commit, no released code files).
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (no continuously-updated leaderboard or paper-list maintained by the authors; the work is a single research repo).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: web (LLM-based Web/computer-control agents performing task automation via planning and grounded action generation on web environments).
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent, exemplar-free (no human-engineered few-shot prompts) Web-agent planning with a frozen LLM backbone (GPT-3.5-turbo-0613 and GPT-4-0613 via the OpenAI API). Given a natural-language task instruction, the agent must produce a sequence of grounded actions (e.g., click/type/select over HTML elements) executed in a web environment. Supervision comes only from a retrieval corpus of previously collected successful trajectories (48 base MiniWoB tasks for CompWoB; the Mind2Web training-set trajectories for Mind2Web) -- no gradient training of the LLM or the retriever, and no manually authored task-specific exemplars. The setting explicitly targets unseen and compositional (complex) tasks and the compositional-generalization failure of LLM agents. RaDA disentangles planning into Retrieval-augmented Task Decomposition (RaD) and Retrieval-augmented Action Generation (RaA), with a subtask-completion verifier closing the loop step by step.
- **what is retrieved**:
> demos / trajectories: dynamically retrieved exemplars, i.e., (partial) trajectory demonstrations of similar previously-seen tasks/subtasks (each exemplar is a task/subtask description plus its demonstrated action trajectory). These exemplars are retrieved both for task decomposition (queried by the overall task T) and for per-subtask action generation (queried by a subtask-compositional query).
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus: retrieval targets a fixed, pre-collected corpus of successful trajectories (48 MiniWoB base-task trajectories for CompWoB; Mind2Web training-set trajectories for Mind2Web). The corpus is constructed offline and is NOT grown/written by the agent at test time. The paper lists collecting new exemplars during deployment as future work, confirming the store is static/frozen.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k ranking: the dense retriever outputs the top-k exemplars with k set to 3 (a fixed hyperparameter). There is no completeness/minimal-set recovery objective or precision-driven variable-size recommendation for the retriever; RaDA's contribution is reformulating the QUERY (subtask-compositional) and the granularity of retrieval rather than the ranking objective.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> Partial: Retrieve (yes -- dense retrieval of exemplars), Reuse (yes -- retrieved exemplars are reused as in-context demonstrations to ground decomposition and action generation), Revise (partial -- a subtask-completion verifier re-formulates the query and tracks plan state, but retrieved cases are not explicitly edited/repaired into new solutions), Retain (no -- nothing is written back to the corpus). Flags: [Retrieve: yes, Reuse: yes, Revise: partial, Retain: no].
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False. The work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is framed as retrieval-augmented planning / in-context learning with exemplar retrieval, inspired by human cognitive abstraction and memory reuse (Lachmy et al. 2022; Zhao et al. 2022; Sumers et al. 2023).

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> single demo / (sub-)trajectory: a retrieved exemplar is a task- or subtask-level trajectory demonstration (task/subtask description plus its action sequence in the web environment). RaDA's key distinction from Synapse is that it can retrieve PARTIAL (subtask-level) trajectories rather than whole-task trajectories, enabling the use of partial/sub-trajectory exemplars per subtask.
- **index source**: Static, offline-induced corpus: the retrievable store is built from successful trajectories collected offline (48 MiniWoB base tasks for CompWoB; Mind2Web training-set trajectories for Mind2Web). It is not test-time-induced and does not grow during deployment.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat vector index: a dense embedding index over exemplar task/subtask descriptions (and additional state/task metadata) encoded with pre-trained sentence embeddings (text-embedding-ada-002), ranked by cosine similarity. No graph, hierarchical, or cluster topology is imposed on the index itself (though planning over subtasks is hierarchical, the retrieval index is a flat embedding store).
- **retriever type**: Dense retriever: dense passage-retrieval-style retrieval using pre-trained sentence embeddings (OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002), with cosine similarity, following the Synapse (Zheng et al., 2024b) retriever setup. Off-the-shelf, not BM25 / not generative / not LLM-as-retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None (off-the-shelf): the retriever uses frozen pre-trained embeddings (text-embedding-ada-002) with cosine similarity; it is NOT trained with contrastive similarity labels, LM-feedback, downstream-task effectiveness, or RL. The paper's Limitations explicitly note that retriever finetuning was not considered and is left to future work. RaDA's novelty is in query construction/granularity, not retriever learning.
- **query construction**:
> Two distinct query formulations: (1) for RaD (decomposition) the query is the raw overall task instruction T; (2) for RaA (action generation) the query is a 'subtask-compositional query' Q_T formed by concatenating the currently relevant/remaining subtasks (Q_T = gamma_1 (+) gamma_2 (+) ... (+) gamma_m), where subtasks are produced by the decompositional planner and updated by the verifier. This composed query can range from a single focused subtask to all remaining subtasks. So the query is decomposition-derived and dynamically reformulated, not just the raw input.
- **query granularity**:
> Both task-level and subtask/step-level (two-level retrieval): retrieval is done once at the task level with T for decomposition (RaD), and then repeatedly at the subtask level with the subtask-compositional query Q_T during iterative action generation (RaA). The subtask-level query is reformulated each iteration via the verifier.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Iterative: one task-level retrieval at decomposition time (RaD), then iterative subtask-level retrieval during the RaA action-generation loop (a new retrieval per reformulated subtask-compositional query until all subtasks are completed). A 'decomposition trigger' gates whether decomposition is invoked (always on for CompWoB; on Mind2Web triggered when task length exceeds the minimum-length exemplar by 50%).
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed schedule plus a length-based decomposition trigger: retrieval is invoked on a deterministic schedule (at decomposition, then once per remaining-subtask iteration). The decision to DECOMPOSE (and thus enter the subtask-retrieval loop) uses a simple rule/trigger: always triggered on CompWoB; on Mind2Web triggered if the task length exceeds the minimum-length exemplar by 50% (an oracle decomposition trigger is also used in some reported full-set runs). There is no token-confidence, attention-uncertainty, learned-complexity-classifier, or reflection-token trigger.
- **reranking**: None: the dense retriever produces a cosine-similarity ranking and the top-k (k=3) exemplars are taken directly; no cross-encoder, hierarchy-aware, RRF, or instruction-tuned reranking stage is applied.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Decompose-then-recompose plus light deduplication: rather than refining the retrieved text itself, RaDA refines WHAT is retrieved by decomposing the task and issuing subtask-scoped (compositional) queries, so each LLM call sees only the relevant subtask exemplars (reducing context). For the RaA ablation baseline, redundant exemplars are removed (deduplicated) before concatenation. No learned distillation, reason-in-documents compression, or distractor-filtering model.
- **tool document engineering**:
> N/A: RaDA does not retrieve tool/skill documents; exemplars are trajectory demonstrations encoded by their task/subtask description (plus state/task metadata) with off-the-shelf embeddings. No synthetic-query augmentation, expanded summaries, weighted-field, or instruction-tuned tool embeddings.
- **index content separation**:
> Partial / implicit: the index keys are lightweight task/subtask descriptions and metadata embeddings, while the heavier exemplar trajectory content is loaded into the prompt only for the retrieved top-k. The subtask decomposition further limits how much exemplar content is loaded per call (driving the 4x token efficiency), but the paper does not frame this as a formal progressive-disclosure / SOP-index-then-content mechanism.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> N/A: the retrieval corpus is static (no live-synchronized tool index, no RapidAPI/RESTful/MCP/function-calling registry, no CRUD auto-sync). The agent's action space is a fixed programmatic interface (action_type(ID, text) with click/move/type for CompWoB and click/select/type for Mind2Web).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A: RaDA does not model inter-tool dependencies; it retrieves trajectory exemplars, not tools. Subtask ordering/sequencing is handled by the decompositional planner and verifier, not by a tool-dependency graph.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation (in-context demonstrations): retrieved exemplars are injected into the LLM prompt as demonstrations -- for RaD they contextualize the decomposition prompt (P_piD = [instructional prompt, phi(T,E)]); for RaA they implement each subtask function pi_{Q_T} by serving as the demonstrations conditioning grounded action generation (a_1..a_t <- pi_{Q_T}(.|phi(Q_T,E))). The retrieved exemplars replace human-engineered few-shot prompts; no training signal is derived from them.
- **planning integration**:
> Hierarchical, retrieve-then-plan-then-(retrieve-then-act): planning is disentangled into two stages -- (1) Retrieval-augmented Task Decomposition (RaD) uses task-level retrieved exemplars to produce a high-level set of subtasks; (2) Retrieval-augmented Action Generation (RaA) iterates over subtasks, at each step reformulating a subtask-compositional query, retrieving subtask-scoped exemplars, generating grounded actions, executing them, and using a subtask-completion verifier to update plan state. Retrieval is interfaced at both the plan (decomposition) level and the per-subtask grounded-action level (subtask-level interleaving), not inside MCTS/tree search.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Per-subtask within a rollout: retrieval is woven in at the subtask granularity -- one retrieval for decomposition (per-task) and then one retrieval per subtask iteration during action generation (the subtask-compositional query is reformulated and re-retrieved each loop iteration, after the verifier checks completion). It is not per-CoT-step, per-token, or per-individual-tool-call below the subtask level.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> Verbatim ICL exemplar with compositional re-querying: retrieved exemplars are reused as in-context demonstrations (not edited). 'Adaptation' to a new/complex task is achieved structurally -- by decomposing the task into subtasks and dynamically re-composing the retrieval query per subtask (subtask-compositional query) and tracking completion via the verifier -- rather than by an LLM rewriting/repairing a retrieved case. No execution-feedback case-revision, critic-guided rewrite, or RL-reuse finetuning of cases.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Raw trajectory demonstrations injected as text: retrieved exemplars are surfaced as raw (sub-)trajectory demonstrations of interactions in the web environment (task/subtask description plus action sequences/HTML interactions) placed in the prompt. Not distilled strategies, executable skills, or latent tokens.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Raw (sub-)trajectory / single demonstration: the retrieved unit is a concrete demonstration trajectory (task- or subtask-level). The ABSTRACTION in RaDA comes from the planner's high-level subtask decomposition, but the retrieved items themselves are raw demonstrations, not distilled strategies/insights or rules.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Structural / compositional decomposition plus a subtask-completion verifier: by retrieving subtask-scoped exemplars and grounding actions per subtask, RaDA reduces irrelevant whole-trajectory context (vs. Synapse), and the verifier (an instruction-prompted LLM over the last-k steps + remaining subtasks) checks subtask completion before reformulating the next query, mitigating drift. There is no retriever-aware training, learned relevance evaluator/self-reflection model, or reason-in-documents refinement.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: episodic (static): a pre-collected episodic store of past task/subtask trajectories used as the retrieval corpus. It is read-only at inference (no skill-library induction, no graph, no latent memory).
- **write back**: False: RaDA does not store new experiences/cases/skills into memory at inference. The retrieval corpus is fixed (offline-collected successful trajectories); the Limitations section explicitly notes that a framework which also collects new exemplars is future work.
- **online growth**: No: the retrievable store does not grow during deployment/test-time; it is frozen after offline construction. The verifier-maintained set of completed subtasks C is transient per-task state, not a persistent growing memory.
- **write back trigger**: Never: no write-back event occurs. The corpus is constructed offline from successful trajectories and remains static during inference; no on-success, on-failure, per-step, reflective, or human-validated write is performed at test time.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success-only: the retrieval corpus is built exclusively from SUCCESSFUL trajectories (48 successful MiniWoB base-task trajectories for CompWoB; Mind2Web training-set trajectories). Failed/negative experiences are not stored or retrieved; there is no failure-contrastive or corrective-rule memory.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A / append-only-offline: stored entries are not mutated after writing (the corpus is fixed offline). No dedup-merge (beyond the RaA-baseline's prompt-time exemplar deduplication), delta-update, refine-overwrite, forget-prune, or link-and-evolve at the memory level.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No: retrieval/exemplar-selection is a fixed dense-similarity top-k (k=3) over frozen embeddings, not a learned/RL-optimized policy. RaDA's learned/dynamic element is the LLM-driven decomposition and subtask-compositional query reformulation, but the retriever itself is fixed similarity ranking (the paper notes retriever finetuning as future work).
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No: single-agent, single-model private memory; no memory/experience sharing across multiple agents or heterogeneous frameworks.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> CompWoB (50 compositional web-automation tasks built by combining 2-8 base MiniWoB easy tasks, categorized as two-way (20), three-way (10), n-way (5), transition (5), easy-medium two-way (10); evaluated in Original and Reverse orderings; full-set runs use 912 examples via official Synapse logs) and Mind2Web (crowdsourced human interaction tasks on diverse real websites; cross-domain generalization split and a complex subset selected by task-complexity rank). Retrieval corpora: 48 base MiniWoB-task trajectories (CompWoB) and Mind2Web training-set trajectories (Mind2Web). Backbones: GPT-3.5-turbo-0613, GPT-4-0613 (RaA ablation and Mind2Web use gpt-3.5-turbo-16k-0613).
- **benchmark family**: web (CompWoB is MiniWoB-derived compositional web automation; Mind2Web is a real-website generalist web-agent benchmark). Both fall under the web-agent / web-navigation family.
- **baselines**:
> RCI (Recursive Criticism and Improvement; Kim et al., 2023 -- prior SOTA reported in Furuta et al. 2023), AdaPlanner (Sun et al., 2023 -- adaptive post-hoc plan repair), Synapse (Zheng et al., 2024b -- trajectory-as-exemplar prompting with retrieval; closest baseline / pure RaA), and MindAct (Deng et al., 2023 -- the Mind2Web baseline agent, multiple-choice action formulation; used on Mind2Web). Internal ablation baselines: RaA (RaD ablated) and RaD (RaA ablated).
- **key metrics**:
> CompWoB: task success rate (%) in Original and Reverse settings, broken down by compositional task type. Mind2Web: element accuracy (Element Acc.), operation F1 (Operation F1), and step success rate (Step SR), macro-averaged across tasks. Statistical significance via paired t-test (P<.001, marked with asterisks). Also context-token efficiency (average/max tokens per LLM call, for exemplars-only and total).
- **headline result**:
> On CompWoB, RaDA significantly outperforms all baselines: with GPT-3.5-turbo it reaches 63.6% success (Original) and 49.0% (Reverse) vs. the best baseline RCI at 28.7% / 19.2% (Synapse 25.4% / 16.0%); with GPT-4 RaDA reaches 68.6% (Original) and 57.8% (Reverse) vs. RCI 56.0% / 43.5%. All RaDA improvements are statistically significant (P<.001, paired t-test). On Mind2Web's complex subset (GPT-3.5) RaDA reaches Element Acc. 30.13 / Operation F1 58.18 / Step SR 26.71 vs. Synapse 24.73 / 37.78 / 21.34 and MindAct 9.76 / 55.43 / 8.46.
- **ablations**:
> Component ablations on CompWoB (GPT-3.5): RaDA (full) = 63.6 (Original) / 49.0 (Reverse); RaA (ablate RaD, subtask-level retrieval but grounds all steps simultaneously) = 38.0 / 23.8; RaD (ablate RaA, decompositional planner with a FIXED set of 5 exemplars: 3 easy + 1 medium + 1 hard) = 50.0 / 37.8 -- showing subtask decomposition and dynamic exemplar retrieval are complementary and both necessary. Per-task-type breakdown (Table 5) shows baselines collapse on n-way/transition/easy-medium and in the Reverse setting (e.g., Synapse Transition 0.0), while RaDA stays robust. Context-token efficiency ablation (Table 6): RaDA uses 1259.8 avg exemplar tokens / 1969.4 avg total tokens per call vs. RaA 3483.5 / 4110.1 (~4x per-call computational efficiency); RaA's long context forces use of the 16k model.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No: only end-to-end task metrics are reported (success rate; element accuracy / operation F1 / step SR). No intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG / completeness) are reported separately for the retriever.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Mostly outcome, with some process: primary metrics are outcome-based (task/step success rate, element accuracy, operation F1). Some process-level signal is reported via the CompWoB per-compositional-task-type breakdown (Table 5), the Mind2Web action-step-count complexity analysis (Fig. 2), and qualitative analysis; but there is no formal reasoning-faithfulness or step-wise retrieval-accuracy metric.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Strong efficiency emphasis: an LLM inference call in RaDA uses on average < half the tokens of RaA (1969.4 vs 4110.1 total; 1259.8 vs 3483.5 exemplar tokens), giving ~4x per-call computational efficiency (due to quadratic attention scaling), while RaA's long concatenated exemplars exceed the 4096-token turbo limit and require gpt-3.5-turbo-16k. Per-task total tokens are ~2x higher for RaDA (7285.76 vs 4582.31) because it makes one call per subtask, but RaDA is still more compute-efficient per call and far more accurate. The full-set CompWoB (912 examples) was run on official Synapse logs due to high API costs.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k selection: top-k = 3 exemplars retrieved per query (a fixed hyperparameter, following Synapse). Context budget is managed structurally via subtask decomposition so each call loads only subtask-scoped exemplars (avg ~1260 exemplar tokens per call, fitting within the 4096-token turbo limit), in contrast to whole-trajectory concatenation that exceeds it. The RaD ablation uses a fixed static set of 5 exemplars. No adaptive/precision-driven k or reranked-then-truncated budget.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A (RaDA is a method paper, not a benchmark-construction paper; it evaluates on existing benchmarks). For context: CompWoB (Furuta et al., 2023) systematically combines 2-8 MiniWoB easy base tasks into 50 compositional tasks (full set 912 examples) with Original/Reverse orderings; Mind2Web (Deng et al., 2023) is crowdsourced human demonstrations on real websites with a cross-domain split and a complexity-ranked subset.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Synapse (Zheng et al., 2024b -- trajectory-as-exemplar retrieval prompting; RaDA reuses its dense retriever setup and corpora and treats it as the pure-RaA baseline); ReAct (Yao et al., 2023 -- interleaved reasoning/acting for agents) and Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023); decomposition prompting line: Least-to-Most (Zhou et al., 2023), DecomP (Khot et al., 2023), Plan-and-Solve (Wang et al., 2023), Drozdov et al. (2022); demonstration retrieval / DSP (Khattab et al., 2022), UDR (Li et al., 2023), Dr.ICL (Luo et al., 2023); Dense Passage Retrieval (Karpukhin et al., 2020) for the retriever; in-context learning (Brown et al., 2020). Cognitive inspiration: Lachmy et al. (2022), Zhao et al. (2022), Sumers et al. (2023, cognitive architectures for language agents).
- **contrasts with**:
> Synapse (whole-trajectory retrieval that fails on unseen/complex tasks and overflows context); RCI (high human-annotation effort, self-refinement, no compositional generalization -- prior SOTA); AdaPlanner (few-shot post-hoc plan repair, high human effort); DecomP (compositional generalization but requires extensive manual decomposition exemplars and is hard to apply to interactive tasks); MindAct (Mind2Web few-shot multiple-choice baseline). Positioning summarized in Table 1: RaDA targets compositional generalization with NO manual annotation and SHORT input length, unlike DECOMP (high effort), RCI (high effort, no comp. gen.), and Synapse (no effort but long input, no comp. gen.).
- **lineage**:
> Sits in the retrieval-augmented agent-planning lineage (RAG-for-planning / agentic task-solving, group C_rag_planning): it extends the trajectory-as-exemplar retrieval paradigm of Synapse by introducing retrieval-augmented task DECOMPOSITION plus subtask-level (compositional-query) retrieval-augmented action generation, fusing the decomposition-planning lineage (Least-to-Most / DecomP) with exemplar-retrieval ICL (DSP / UDR / Dr.ICL) to attack compositional generalization in web agents. Precursor/sibling to step-wise / sub-trajectory retrieval agents (e.g., TRAD).

<a id="item-trad"></a>
### 47. TRAD - Step-Wise Thought Retrieval and Aligned Decision

2024  ·  arXiv 2403.06221  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.06221)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: SIGIR 2024 (Proceedings of the 47th International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval); preprint arXiv:2403.06221
- **authors affiliation**: Ruiwen Zhou, Yingxuan Yang, Muning Wen, Ying Wen, Yong Yu, Weinan Zhang (Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Wenhao Wang, Chunling Xi, Guoqiang Xu (China Pacific Insurance). Lead author Ruiwen Zhou (Shanghai Jiao Tong University).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.06221
- **code url**: https://github.com/skyriver-2000/TRAD-Official

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: LLM-agent sequential decision-making: embodied/text-game household tasks (ALFWorld) and web navigation (Mind2Web), plus real-world robotic process automation (RPA) on enterprise insurance websites.
- **problem setting**:
> Tuning-free in-context learning (ICL) LLM agents for sequential decision-making. The setting assumes access to a large memory of near-optimal expert trajectories (collected by humans or expert policies). The agent is interactive (multi-step, environment in the loop), single-agent, and not fine-tuned. Supervision is available only as expert trajectories (no reward); ground-truth actions are available offline for the memory but NOT at inference time. The core problem is automatic, per-task, per-step selection and effective utilization of in-context demonstration examples, addressing the failure modes of trajectory-level retrieval (plausible examples, LLM context limit, irrelevant context noise).
- **what is retrieved**:
> Step-level expert demonstrations (individual decision steps from expert trajectories), each pre-labeled with a pseudo-golden 'thought' (CoT reasoning) used as the retrieval key. A coarse trajectory-level retrieval (Synapse-style, keyed on task meta-data) is also used as a first stage to enable thought generation.
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external memory of expert trajectories (a fixed offline corpus). The memory is enriched once offline with pseudo-golden thoughts but does not grow during deployment.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-K ranking objective: TRAD retrieves the top-K most thought-similar steps (K in {1..5}, default 3 on Mind2Web, 2 on ALFWorld) belonging to mutually different trajectories. It is not framed as completeness/minimal-set recovery nor as precision-driven variable-size recommendation.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: Retrieve: yes (thought-based step retrieval). Reuse: yes (retrieved steps + temporal neighbors used as ICL exemplars). Revise: no (no case adaptation/revision of stored cases). Retain: no (no write-back of new experiences). Flags: [Retrieve, Reuse, ~Revise(no), ~Retain(no)].
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The work frames itself as step-wise demonstration/in-context-example retrieval and retrieval-augmented decision-making; it does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner or describe itself as case-based reasoning.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: thought-step (a single decision step represented by its pseudo-golden thought). Sub-trajectory context is added afterward via temporal expansion, but the retrieval unit itself is a single step's thought.
- **index source**: Static, offline-induced memory of expert trajectories. Pseudo-golden thoughts for every memory step are induced offline by an LLM (prompted with ground-truth actions and a small human-thought-annotated seed subset). No online/test-time induction of the store.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat dense vector index over thought embeddings (cosine-similarity search). A coarse trajectory-level index keyed on task meta-data (Synapse-style) is also maintained for first-stage trajectory retrieval; retrieved steps are constrained to come from mutually different trajectories.
- **retriever type**: Dense retriever using off-the-shelf pretrained sentence/passage encoders (Sentence-BERT, DPR). For the first-stage trajectory retrieval, Synapse's task-meta-data similarity is reused.
- **retriever learning signal**: None (off-the-shelf). The dense encoder is a frozen pretrained retriever (Sentence-BERT / DPR); it is not trained on similarity labels, LM feedback, downstream-task signals, or RL. Selection is fixed cosine-similarity top-K over thought embeddings.
- **query construction**:
> Thought-conditioned query: at each timestep the LLM is prompted (with first-stage trajectory-retrieved demonstrations as exemplars) to generate a CoT 'thought' abstracting the current state; this thought is encoded as the dense query. Keys are the precomputed pseudo-golden thoughts of memory steps.
- **query granularity**: Two-level retrieval: (1) trajectory-level retrieval with task meta-data (one-shot, used only to generate the thought), then (2) step/state-level retrieval where the per-step generated thought is the query.
- **when to retrieve**: Iterative (per-step). Thought retrieval is performed at every decision timestep of the rollout.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule: retrieval is triggered at every timestep (one thought-retrieval per decision step). No uncertainty/confidence/learned-router trigger.
- **reranking**: No dedicated reranking stage. Selection is plain cosine-similarity top-K with a constraint that retrieved steps belong to mutually different trajectories.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Decompose-then-recompose / context shaping rather than rerank or compression: each retrieved step is temporally expanded into a short sub-sequence (B previous + F subsequent steps), annotated with relative-order marks ([Step -1], [Step 0], [Step 1] ...), and the current episode is history-aligned to match demonstration format. The overall effect is noise reduction by keeping only step-relevant context instead of full trajectories.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tool/skill descriptions; demonstrations are expert decision steps). Thought Preparation does synthesize pseudo-golden thoughts as retrieval keys for each memory step, which is an index-side text-engineering step.
- **index content separation**: Partial: lightweight thought embeddings serve as the retrievable index/key, while the heavier step content (observation, action, neighboring steps) is loaded on demand for the chosen top-K steps. Not framed as progressive disclosure but functions similarly.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (static memory; no live tool index, RapidAPI/REST/MCP protocol, or CRUD sync).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation: the retrieved step demonstrations, after temporal expansion + relative-order marking, are inserted into the LLM prompt as in-context exemplars; the LLM then predicts the next action conditioned on the current (history-aligned) observation. Retrieval is not a training signal and not latent.
- **planning integration**: Per-step interleaved retrieve-then-act. At each timestep: generate thought -> step-wise thought retrieval -> aligned-decision context shaping -> LLM predicts next action. No tree search / MCTS; integration is a per-step retrieval-augmented action policy.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-CoT-step / per-decision-step: one thought generation and one thought retrieval per action step within the rollout.
- **adaptation mechanism**: Verbatim ICL exemplar usage with context augmentation (no case revision). Retrieved steps are used as demonstrations and complemented by their temporal neighbors and order marks; the retrieved cases themselves are not adapted/edited.
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw expert step demonstrations (observation-action pairs) augmented with pseudo-golden thoughts, temporally-neighboring steps, and relative-order position marks; injected as structured text exemplars in the prompt.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Single demonstration step (raw step), with a distilled CoT-thought abstraction used as its retrieval handle; expanded into a short raw sub-trajectory for decision. Not a distilled strategy, workflow, or skill.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Two complementary mechanisms: (1) step-wise thought retrieval reduces irrelevant context by selecting only step-relevant demonstrations (vs full noisy trajectories), mitigating plausible examples and context-limit/forgetting; (2) Aligned Decision (temporal expansion + relative-order mark + history alignment) provides tolerance for imperfect thoughts by supplying neighboring-step context, so an inaccurate query thought is used for retrieval rather than direct prediction.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: Episodic expert-trajectory memory (static), enhanced offline with pseudo-golden thoughts to support both trajectory-level and step-level retrieval.
- **write back**: False. No new experiences/cases are written back to memory during inference; the thought-enhanced memory is built once offline and remains fixed.
- **online growth**: No. The retrievable store does not grow during deployment/test-time; it is frozen after offline thought induction.
- **write back trigger**: Never (no write-back). Offline, thoughts are added to memory steps once via LLM labeling, but there is no runtime write event triggered by success/failure/reflection.
- **failure experience usage**: None. The memory contains only near-optimal expert (success) trajectories; failed/negative experiences are neither stored nor retrieved.
- **memory evolution update**: Append-only at construction time (thoughts appended to memory steps offline); no runtime mutation, dedup, delta-update, refine-overwrite, or pruning.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No. Retrieval/case-selection is a fixed similarity top-K over a frozen pretrained encoder, not a learned/RL-optimized policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent private memory; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> ALFWorld (134 out-of-distribution tasks, 6 task types: Put/Examine/Clean/Heat/Cool/PutTwo); Mind2Web (3 subsets: Cross-Task, Cross-Website, Cross-Domain); plus real-world deployment on 4 enterprise insurance websites (20 unseen tasks each) at a global business insurance company (China Pacific Insurance).
- **benchmark family**: embodied (ALFWorld) and web (Mind2Web); plus real-world RPA/web-navigation deployment.
- **baselines**:
> ReAct (Fixed), ReAct (Random), ReAct (Relevant) [Mind2Web]; Synapse (trajectory-level retrieval with task meta-data); Synapse + ReAct combination (ALFWorld); Synapse w/o Retrieval; MindAct (Mind2Web, no reasoning/retrieval). Real-world: ReAct-RD (random demo), ReAct-RV (relevant-trajectory demo), TR (TRAD w/o aligned decision).
- **key metrics**: ALFWorld: task Success Rate (SR). Mind2Web: Element Accuracy (Ele. Acc), Step Success Rate (Step SR), trajectory Success Rate (SR). Real-world deployment: Step SR and SR; plus inference time overhead (efficiency).
- **headline result**:
> On ALFWorld, TRAD reaches 96.77% average SR, a +2.99% improvement over the strongest baseline Synapse+ReAct (93.78% -> 96.77%), with GPT-4 and 2 in-context examples. On Mind2Web (GPT-3.5-turbo, 3 examples) TRAD improves over Synapse by +2.1% Ele.Acc, +1.4% Step SR, +0.5% SR overall (All: 32.5/28.0/2.1). Real-world deployment raises average Step SR 90.2%->98.1% and SR 65.0%->92.5%.
- **ablations**:
> Aligned Decision component ablation on Mind2Web (GPT-3.5-turbo): removing Temporal Expansion (TE) hurts most across all subsets (it is the basic structure); removing History Alignment (HA) and Relative Order Mark (ROM) hurts the harder Cross-Website/Cross-Domain subsets but slightly helps Cross-Task (in-distribution). Hyper-parameter studies: expansion steps B (backward) and F (forward) varied 0->4 one-sided — both improve over no expansion; forward expansion (F) helps more than backward (B); best at F=2, B=0; large B/F adds no further gain (far context is noisy). Number of retrieved demonstrations K in {1..5}: K has mild effect and TRAD's advantage over Synapse is stable for K in {1..4} (Synapse exceeds context limit at K=5). Real-world TR vs TRAD ablation confirms both thought retrieval and aligned decision contribute.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No. Only end-to-end task metrics (SR / Step SR / Ele. Acc) are reported; no intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG / completeness) are reported separately.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Both outcome and intermediate process: trajectory Success Rate (outcome) plus step-level process quality via Step SR and Element Accuracy (Mind2Web), which capture per-step decision correctness.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Reported efficiency: at inference TRAD adds only ~11.7% more time than ReAct-RD (the extra thought-retrieval step). Step-wise retrieval substantially reduces input context vs full-trajectory prompting, alleviating context-limit failures (Synapse exceeds the LLM context limit at K=5 while TRAD does not). Authors note ALFWorld/Mind2Web baseline choices were constrained by API cost limits.
- **context budget and selection count**: Fixed-K selection with context-shaping: top-K steps (K=3 default on Mind2Web, K=2 on ALFWorld), each expanded to at most B+1+F steps (best F=2,B=0). Step-wise retrieval is explicitly motivated by staying within the LLM context budget where trajectory-level prompting overflows it.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (not a new benchmark; uses ALFWorld 134 OOD tasks and Mind2Web 3 subsets). The real-world deployment dataset (100 expert trajectories per website over 4 websites for memory; 20 unseen eval tasks per website) is author-collected but proprietary.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Synapse (Zheng et al., 2024b — trajectory-level retrieval with task meta-data, ICL exemplars); ReAct (Yao et al., 2023b — reason-then-act CoT for agents); Chain-of-Thought (Wei et al., 2022); dense retrievers Sentence-BERT (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019) and DPR (Karpukhin et al., 2020); IRCoT (Trivedi et al., 2023 — closest prior, retrieval with reasoning steps for QA).
- **contrasts with**:
> Synapse (trajectory-wise retrieval/prompting — criticized for plausible examples, context-limit overflow, and irrelevant-context noise); IRCoT (retrieves with full historical trajectory and accumulates documents over time for QA, uses thoughts only as queries with raw docs as keys — TRAD instead retrieves distinct single steps across timesteps, uses single-step thoughts as both query and key, and adds temporal alignment for sequential decision-making); ReAct (Fixed/Random) which use non-retrieved or randomly retrieved demonstrations.
- **lineage**:
> Group C (RAG planning): retrieval-augmented in-context demonstration selection for LLM-agent sequential decision-making. Advances the lineage from trajectory-level retrieval (Synapse) toward step-level / thought-aligned retrieval, and is the first to bring thought-based retrieval to sequential decision-making (extending IRCoT's QA-only reasoning-retrieval).

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- compute_cost
- evaluation_protocol_standardization
- provenance_and_leakage_controls
- reproducibility

<a id="item-davis"></a>
### 48. DAVIS: Planning Agent with Knowledge Graph-Powered Inner Monologue

2024  ·  arXiv 2410.09252  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.09252)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: EMNLP 2025 Findings (Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2025, pages 16490-16505; DOI 10.18653/v1/2025.findings-emnlp.895). Preprint arXiv:2410.09252 (cs.CL), submitted 11 Oct 2024 (v1), last revised 17 Sep 2025 (v2).
- **authors affiliation**:
> Minh Pham-Dinh (Davis Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Colby College), Munira Syed (University of Notre Dame), Michael Yankoski (Colby College / William & Mary), Trenton W. Ford (William & Mary). Correspondence: mhpham26@colby.edu. Funded in part by DARPA / Accelerate Foundation Models Research.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.09252
- **code url**: https://github.com/minhphd/DAVIS
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/minhphd/DAVIS (official code + prompts, MIT license; 6 commits, last updated Sep 2025; noted as potentially unstable due to dependency drift, cleanup ongoing). Not a leaderboard/paper-list; minimally maintained.

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Embodied/interactive decision-making and planning (text-based scientific agent in ScienceWorld), plus multi-hop QA (HotpotQA, MusiqueQA) used to evaluate the World Model component.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent, model-based planning in a partially observable text environment, formalized as a POMDP P=(S,A,T,R,Omega,O,gamma). The agent must complete grade-school science tasks in ScienceWorld (e.g., melting/boiling, building circuits, growing plants) requiring multi-hop scientific reasoning, temporal/structured understanding of an evolving environment, safety/interpretability, and operation under partial observability. Supervision is provided as golden trajectories used offline to populate memory: all RAG-based agents (DAVIS, RAP) are initialized with five episodes of golden-trajectory rollouts per task variation (a total of 150 training variations); evaluation uses three randomly sampled test variations per task (90 test variations total). The agent maintains an approximate belief state b_hat_t = f(trajectory history) updated recurrently, and plans inside a learned/retrieval-augmented World Model before acting in the environment. The World Model alone is also evaluated as a standalone multi-hop QA system on HotpotQA and MusiqueQA (400 sampled instances each).
- **what is retrieved**:
> Past experiences/transitions stored as a temporal knowledge graph (TKG): retrieved units are temporally-ordered subgraphs of (entity, relation, entity, timestamp) tuples extracted from past (observation, action, next-observation) transitions. During the inner monologue, the agent retrieves relevant subgraphs via graph QA to predict next observations/rewards and to fill knowledge gaps for planning.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> HYBRID toward GROWING/episodic structured memory. The retrievable store is a Temporal Knowledge Graph (World Model) that the agent itself constructs from its own past experience transitions; it is populated offline from golden-trajectory rollouts (training phase) and is intended to evolve with the agent's interactions ('continuously evolves with the agent's interactions'). It is not a static external document/KB corpus; it is an agent-built experiential memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Not a fixed top-k ranking objective. Retrieval narrows to relevant entity types, selects the two most relevant entities, then iteratively expands their neighbors to form a maximal subgraph (aiming for a feasible/complete temporal path rather than a ranked list), reordering edges by timestamp to recover the complete sequence of events. The objective is coverage of the causally/temporally relevant subgraph (a feasible path), not a fixed-size ranked retrieval; entity scope is capped at two seed entities for tractability.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> N/A (not framed as case-based reasoning). If mapped loosely: Retrieve (subgraph retrieval via graph QA) and Retain (writing transitions into the TKG) are present; there is no discrete case Reuse/Revise of stored cases as case-based-reasoning units. Use a 4-flag interpretation: [Retrieve: yes (subgraph), Reuse: partial (informs transition/reward prediction), Revise: no (no case adaptation), Retain: yes (TKG write of transitions)].
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False. The work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is positioned as model-based planning with a temporal-knowledge-graph World Model and an agentic multi-turn (inner-monologue) retrieval system, contrasted against vector-based RAG (Reflexion, RAP).

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: KG-subgraph: a temporally-ordered maximal subgraph of (entity, relation, entity, timestamp) tuples retrieved from a Temporal Knowledge Graph. The underlying stored units are quadruples (v_i, e_j, v_k, tau) extracted from concatenated transitions (o_t || a_t || o_{t+1}).
- **index source**:
> Growing experiential memory, offline-induced then evolving: the TKG World Model is built from the agent's own past transitions. It is populated during a training phase from five episodes of golden-trajectory rollouts across 150 task variations (offline construction), and is designed to continuously evolve with interactions. Not a static external corpus.
- **index structure topology**:
> Knowledge GRAPH (temporal knowledge graph). Entities are nodes; typed relations are edges; each edge carries a timestamp tau encoding when the fact was introduced. Stored in PostgreSQL (per the code). Retrieval first restricts to relevant entity types (e.g., PER, LOC), then does neighbor expansion to form a maximal subgraph, then temporal edge reordering.
- **retriever type**:
> LLM-as-retriever / graph QA (agentic). Retrieval is performed by a graph-QA function (graphQA(q)) that an LLM drives: it selects entity types, picks the two most relevant entities, expands neighbors into a subgraph, temporally reorders edges, and passes the temporal sequence to an LLM as in-context examples for extrapolation/summarization. No dense vector or BM25 retriever over the experience store; explicitly contrasted with vector-based retrieval (RAP, Reflexion). KG construction uses LLaMA3-70B-Instruct + Stanford CoreNLP coreference resolution.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None (off-the-shelf / prompted). The retriever is not trained; it is a prompted LLM graph-QA process. There is no contrastive, RL, or preference-learning signal for retrieval. Entity-type narrowing, entity selection, neighbor expansion, and temporal reordering are heuristic/prompt-driven; the LLM extrapolates over temporal patterns in-context (citing Lee et al. 2023 on TKG forecasting with in-context learning).
- **query construction**:
> Thought-conditioned / agent-initiated queries. During transition prediction the World Model's transition/reward predictors emit a query q (e.g., 'Where can I find water?') when they detect a knowledge gap; this question is the retrieval query. The query is then expanded inside graph QA (entity-type narrowing -> two-entity selection -> subgraph neighbor expansion -> temporal reordering). Belief state b_hat_t = f(trajectory history) is maintained and conditions the queries.
- **query granularity**:
> Step/state-level with an inner inner-loop: queries are generated per planning step during transition prediction (Algorithm 2), and multiple queries can be issued within a single transition prediction via the multi-turn inner monologue (up to Maximum QA Turns = 5). Effectively two-level: per-step planning plus per-monologue-turn sub-queries.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Iterative / active (agent-initiated, multi-turn). Retrieval is triggered as an inner monologue loop during transition/reward prediction: while i<k or not predicted, the transition and reward models may emit a query q; if q is non-empty, graph QA is invoked and the (q, answer) pair is appended to the running monologue M. This continues up to k=5 maximum QA turns or until a prediction is reached.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Agent-initiated request driven by detected knowledge gaps. In Algorithm 2 the transition/reward predictors return a query q together with a tentative prediction; a non-empty q (i.e., the LLM signals it still needs information / a remaining knowledge gap) triggers another graph-QA retrieval turn. The loop also terminates on a fixed budget (k = Maximum QA Turns = 5) or once a confident prediction ('predicted') is produced. So: hybrid of self-detected uncertainty/knowledge-gap signal plus a fixed turn-budget cap.
- **reranking**:
> No explicit learned reranking stage. Within retrieval, edges of the retrieved maximal subgraph are temporally reordered (sorted by timestamp) to establish a coherent event sequence before being passed to the LLM; this is temporal ordering rather than relevance reranking. Entity selection ('two most relevant entities') is a coarse relevance filter performed by the LLM, not a cross-encoder reranker.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Decompose-then-recompose + summarization: the retrieved maximal subgraph is temporally reordered into a coherent event sequence, then passed to an LLM as in-context examples for extrapolation and summarization to generate a structured, interpretable natural-language response. Multi-turn inner monologue accumulates (query, answer) pairs that progressively refine the predicted transition/reward before planning. The Critic additionally refines plans post-execution via reflection.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tool/skill retrieval; retrieval is over an experiential temporal knowledge graph, not tool documentation).
- **index content separation**:
> Partial: the lightweight retrievable index is the temporal knowledge graph (entities/relations/timestamps); the heavier raw transition text is summarized at write time into KG tuples, so retrieval operates over a compact structured graph rather than raw trajectory text. Not a formal progressive-disclosure SOP-index-then-content protocol.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no external tool index/integration protocol such as RapidAPI/MCP/function-calling for tools). The TKG is built and queried via an internal graph-QA pipeline (LLaMA3-70B extraction + Stanford CoreNLP coreference, PostgreSQL store).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no inter-tool dependency modeling). The graph models inter-entity relations and temporal ordering of events/transitions, not tool-to-tool dependencies.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation for model-based planning. Retrieved temporal subgraphs (summarized via graph QA into the inner monologue M_t) are injected as context into the World Model's policy pi(a_t | b_hat_t, M_t), transition model T_hat(o_{t+1} | b_hat_t, a_t, M_t), and reward model R_hat(r_t | b_hat_t, a_t, M_t). The WM uses them to approximate future observations/rewards and to generate a high-level natural-language plan/trajectory tau_{t:t+L}, which the Actor decomposes into executable low-level commands and the Critic validates against actual outcomes.
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-plan inside a model-based planning loop with replanning. The agent runs Algorithm 1 (Planning with Retrieval-Augmented World Model): estimate state -> select action via policy -> predict next observation/reward via Transition Prediction (Algorithm 2, which itself runs the multi-turn inner-monologue retrieval) -> append to trajectory -> optional safety check. A predicted trajectory of length L (=5) is generated, then handed to an Actor (decomposes into low-level executable commands and executes step by step) and a Critic (compares predicted vs actual transitions; on significant deviation updates a reflection list and triggers replanning of the subtask). Retrieval is woven into per-step transition prediction during planning.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Per-step (per planning/transition-prediction step), with a nested per-monologue-turn granularity: within each transition prediction the inner monologue interleaves up to 5 query/answer retrieval turns with reasoning before committing a predicted (observation, reward). Plan-level retrieval feeds into per-step actor execution and critic-triggered replanning.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> N/A as CBR case adaptation. Closest mechanism: execution-feedback-driven revision via the Critic, which compares predicted vs actual (o,r,o') transitions, produces a qualitative discrepancy score Delta_t, appends reflections to R_t, and triggers replanning of the subtask (e.g., 'find an alternative heating method' when a stove is broken). This is plan revision via reflection, not retrieved-case adaptation.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Structured note distilled into free text: the retrieved temporal subgraph is summarized by an LLM into a coherent, structured, interpretable natural-language answer that becomes a (query, answer) entry in the inner monologue. The World Model's output plan is itself a high-level, interpretable natural-language trajectory. Underlying stored form is structured KG quadruples (entity, relation, entity, timestamp).
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> State-aware / temporally-structured experiential knowledge: retrieved units are temporally-ordered subgraphs of past transitions (causal/temporal event sequences), more abstract and structured than a raw trajectory but grounded in concrete past experience. They are extrapolated by the LLM into predicted next states, i.e., reusable temporal patterns rather than verbatim demonstrations or distilled high-level strategies.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Critic-based self-reflection/validation: the LLM Critic checks semantic consistency between predicted and actual transitions and triggers replanning on significant deviation, guarding against erroneous WM predictions. Retrieval scope is constrained (two seed entities, relevant entity types) to limit irrelevant context, and temporal reordering enforces feasible event sequences. No retriever-aware training or distractor-aware SFT. Limitations section notes the agent can still be biased toward TKG contents and struggle on novel scenarios / incomplete knowledge.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: graph (temporal knowledge graph World Model) serving as structured episodic/experiential memory; plus a transient within-episode reflection list (R_t) and an inner-monologue working memory (M_t).
- **write back**:
> True. Executed transitions (o_t || a_t || o_{t+1}) are summarized, coreference-resolved (Stanford CoreNLP), parsed by an LLM into entity/relation tuples, and added to the TKG as quadruples (v_i, e_j, v_k, tau): G_{t+1} = G_t U {(v_i, e_j, v_k, tau)}. Primary population is during the training phase from golden-trajectory rollouts.
- **write back trigger**:
> On observed transition (per-step append during experience collection): each executed action and its resulting observation are encoded and written to the TKG. Primary writes occur during training-phase golden-trajectory rollouts. Separately, the Critic's reflection list R_t is updated on detected prediction/observation discrepancies (failure-triggered) within an episode, but that is transient replanning context, not a permanent TKG write. Not human-validated.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Experience storage in the TKG is transition-based (observation/action transitions from golden trajectories), not labeled success-vs-failure. Failure handling is via the Critic's within-episode reflection: discrepancies (Delta_t) between predicted and actual outcomes are stored in a reflection list R_t and used as additional context to trigger and guide replanning within the current execution. So failures drive corrective replanning but are not retained as persistent failure cases in the long-term memory.
- **memory evolution update**:
> Append-only growth of the TKG (union of new quadruples with timestamps; coreference resolution merges entity mentions during extraction). No explicit delta-update/forget-prune/refine-overwrite of existing stored facts is described; temporal information is added as timestamped edges so the graph accumulates time-ordered facts. The within-episode reflection list R_t is appended to and reset across executions.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No. Retrieval/subgraph selection is a fixed prompted graph-QA + heuristic-expansion process (LLM-driven), not a trained or RL-optimized retrieval policy. The agent's action policy itself is an LLM-prompted model-based planner, not an RL-learned retrieval policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent private World Model / temporal knowledge graph; no multi-agent or cross-framework memory sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> (1) ScienceWorld (Wang et al., 2022): 30 tasks across 9 grade-school science subjects (Matter, Thermodynamics, Electricity, Biology, Botany, Chemistry, Lifespan/Life Stages, Physics, Genetics); 10 interconnected locations, ~200 object types, 25 high-level actions; >100 variations per task; max steps 80 (hyperparameter table lists 100). (2) HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018) and MusiqueQA / MuSiQue (Trivedi et al., 2022) for multi-hop QA, 400 randomly sampled instances each, following GraphReader (Li et al., 2024)'s protocol.
- **benchmark family**: embodied/interactive (ScienceWorld) + multi-hop QA (HotpotQA, MusiqueQA). Per the survey's normalized grouping: embodied (ScienceWorld) and QA / multi-hop (HotpotQA, MuSiQue).
- **baselines**:
> ScienceWorld: SayCan (Ahn et al., 2022), ReAct (Yao et al., 2023), Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023), RAP (Kagaya et al., 2024). SwiftSage (Lin et al., 2023), the prior ScienceWorld SOTA, was excluded from replication baselines due to code/eval-method discrepancies. For fairness, both RAP and DAVIS used memory built from five episodes of golden trajectories. Multi-hop QA (World Model comparison): GPT-4o, GPT-4-turbo (raw LLM), GraphReader (GPT-4), HOLMES (GPT-4), GraphRAG (GPT-4o-mini); QA baseline numbers are taken from the original papers (best-reported configs), not re-run.
- **key metrics**: ScienceWorld: task progress score (0-100, % progress toward completion before failure/timeout), averaged across subjects/variations; plus average steps per replanning cycle (steps/replan) in ablations. Multi-hop QA: Exact Match (EM) and F1.
- **headline result**:
> On ScienceWorld, DAVIS outperforms all four baselines on 8 of 9 science subjects, achieving an overall average score of 65.06 (~1.8x higher than competing methods). For the World Model on multi-hop QA, DAVIS (GPT-4o) reaches HotpotQA F1 73.8 / EM 56.25 and MusiqueQA F1 48.5 / EM 33.8, surpassing GraphReader and GraphRAG on HotpotQA and approaching the SOTA HOLMES (HotpotQA EM 66.0 / F1 78.0).
- **ablations**:
> Two ablation tables on representative short/medium/long tasks (3 variations each). (1) World Model ablation (Table 1, DAVIS without WM 'D' vs with WM 'D+W'): WM consistently and often dramatically improves performance, e.g., Melt 1-2 3.00 -> 70.00, Determine Melting Point Unknown 2-3 5.00 -> 92.33, Find Living Thing 4-1 25.00 -> 100.00, Lifespan Longest-Lived 7-1 66.67 -> 100.00; on Mix Paint Secondary 6-1 the WM did not help (40.00 -> 36.37). (2) Actor/Critic ablation (Table 2, full D+W vs no-Actor D-A vs no-Critic D-C): removing the Actor causes invalid-command struggles, low scores, and near-1.0 steps/replan (constant replanning); removing the Critic loses error recovery on long tasks (gap widens on longer tasks needing adaptive reasoning). E.g., long task 2-3: 92.3 (full) vs 79.7 (no-Actor) vs 33.3 (no-Critic); short 4-1: 100 vs 44.7 vs 25. Conclusion: WM supplies temporal/multi-hop grounding, Actor enables valid structured execution, Critic enables adaptivity.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Partial. For multi-hop QA the World Model is evaluated with intrinsic QA metrics (EM/F1) separately from the end-to-end ScienceWorld task scores, effectively decoupling the retrieval/QA component's quality. However, no standard top-k retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG) are reported for the experience-retrieval step within planning.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both. Primary ScienceWorld metric is outcome (task progress score), but the ablation also reports a process metric: average steps per replanning cycle (steps/replan), interpreted as planning coherence/efficiency (higher steps/replan with strong scores = coherent, cost-efficient planning). Multi-hop QA uses outcome metrics (EM/F1).
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> High operational cost is explicitly reported as a limitation: each action involves ~43,000 tokens sent/received due to the structured multi-turn inner-monologue interaction with the TKG, averaging ~$0.43 per action; a 100-action task can scale to ~$43 per episode, totaling over $3,000 across the 90 experimental variations (the GitHub README states the full 90 variations over 30 tasks with GPT-4-turbo cost over $2,000 in credits). Inner-monologue is capped at Maximum QA Turns = 5 and predicted trajectory length = 5 to bound cost. Authors frame this as a deliberate depth-of-reasoning vs efficiency trade-off and propose future distillation/fine-tuning onto smaller open-source models. DAVIS also reportedly converged in fewer steps than SayCan/ReAct/Reflexion.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Bounded by fixed loop/scope caps rather than a token-truncation budget: Maximum QA Turns = 5 (inner-monologue retrieval turns per transition prediction), predicted trajectory length L = 5, retrieval scope limited to two most relevant entities per query (then neighbor-expanded into a maximal subgraph), max steps per task = 80 (hyperparameter table lists 100). Per-action footprint ~43k tokens.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (DAVIS is a method, not a benchmark contribution). It evaluates on existing benchmarks: ScienceWorld (30 tasks / 9 subjects / >100 variations each; 150 training and 90 test variations used), and HotpotQA & MusiqueQA (400 sampled instances each).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Model-based planning / world models (Sutton & Barto, 1998; Dreamer-style latent imagination, Hafner et al., 2020; MuZero, Schrittwieser et al., 2020); knowledge-graph world models of textual environments (Ammanabrolu & Riedl, 2021; Ammanabrolu & Hausknecht, 2020), generalized to temporal KGs; temporal-KG forecasting via in-context learning (Lee et al., 2023); graph QA / graph-based retrieval (GraphReader, Li et al., 2024; HOLMES, Panda et al., 2024; GraphRAG, Edge et al., 2024); RAG agentic planning with memory (RAP, Kagaya et al., 2024; Reflexion, Shinn et al., 2023); ReAct (Yao et al., 2023), SayCan (Ahn et al., 2022), SwiftSage (Lin et al., 2023); Stanford CoreNLP (Manning et al., 2014); ScienceWorld (Wang et al., 2022).
- **contrasts with**:
> Vector/semantic-search RAG agents with unstructured episodic memory: Reflexion and RAP (nearest-neighbor retrieval of past experiences), which DAVIS argues fragment information and cannot support multi-hop/causal/temporal reasoning and use static (single-shot) retrieval. CoT-only agents (ReAct, SayCan, SwiftSage) lacking long-term structured memory. Static graph-QA systems (HOLMES's static hyper-relational graph) that cannot update during inference, unlike DAVIS's dynamically updating TKG. Positioned as the first RAG agent to employ an interactive (agentic multi-turn) retrieval method within a RAG pipeline.
- **lineage**:
> Group C (RAG for planning): experience/memory-based planning agents. DAVIS sits in the experience/episodic-memory planner line but replaces flat vector experience retrieval (Reflexion/RAP) with agentic multi-turn graph QA over a temporal knowledge-graph world model, bridging the GraphRAG / graph-QA retrieval line (GraphReader, HOLMES, GraphRAG) with model-based interactive agent planning.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- online_growth

<a id="item-exrap"></a>
### 49. ExRAP (Exploratory Retrieval-Augmented Planning)

2024  ·  NeurIPS 2024  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.08222)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: NeurIPS 2024 (Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37, pp. 67034-67060). arXiv:2509.08222 posted 2025-09-10 is a later mirror of the same paper.
- **authors affiliation**: Minjong Yoo, Jinwoo Jang, Honguk Woo (Dept. of Computer Science and Engineering, Sungkyunkwan University); Wei-jin Park (Acryl Inc.). Corresponding author: Honguk Woo.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.08222 (NeurIPS proceedings / OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=LpXV29Ggl3)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Embodied instruction following / LLM-based task planning for embodied agents (home robotics in VirtualHome and ALFRED, skill-based autonomous driving in CARLA).
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent embodied planning in dynamic, non-stationary environments. Introduces 'continual instruction following': a set of M conditional instructions (e.g. 'If the temperature is high, open the window') that are conducted continuously and simultaneously, where conditions may become satisfied/unsatisfied over time, requiring ongoing environment exploration. No agent fine-tuning is performed; planning uses a frozen LLM (LLaMA-3-8B default) with in-context learning. An expert planning demonstration dataset D_e is assumed available for in-context exploitation-value estimation. Objective combines task success rate (SR) and average pending step (PS).
- **what is retrieved**:
> Two retrieval targets: (1) environmental-context quadruples (se, re, te, t) from a temporal embodied knowledge graph (TEKG) accumulated from agent observations, retrieved for query evaluation; (2) expert planning demonstrations from an offline dataset D_e, retrieved by graph similarity to the current observation for exploitation-value (skill-value) estimation.
- **retrieval grounding**: HYBRID. The TEKG environmental-context memory is a GROWING/episodic store the agent writes online from observations; the expert demonstration dataset D_e for in-context skill-value estimation is a STATIC external corpus.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k retrieval for both stores: k=12 quadruples per query and 3 demonstrations per instruction are retrieved via similarity sampling/ranking. There is no completeness or precision-driven variable-size objective; selection of which executions to act on is governed by a probability threshold theta=0.5 on query satisfaction rather than a retrieval-completeness criterion.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The paper frames itself as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for embodied planning and never invokes case-based reasoning or cites Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: (1) (source-entity, relation, target-entity, timestep) quadruple from the temporal embodied knowledge graph (a (state) tuple / KG-subgraph unit); (2) full expert planning demonstration (trajectory) for in-context skill valuation.
- **index source**:
> Hybrid: the TEKG environmental-context memory is online/test-time-induced (built and updated from streaming observations during deployment); the expert demonstration dataset D_e is an offline static corpus (100 trajectories across 10 settings in VirtualHome, 50 trajectories each in ALFRED and CARLA).
- **index structure topology**:
> Dependency/knowledge GRAPH: the environmental context memory is a temporal embodied knowledge graph (TEKG) of timestamped quadruples representing objects, relations, states, and room adjacencies. Retrieval over the graph is performed via sentence-embedding similarity (effectively a flat similarity index over quadruples linearized as text). The demonstration store is similarity-keyed by observation graph.
- **retriever type**:
> Dense/hybrid. Quadruple and demonstration retrieval uses sentence-embedding similarity (DPR: dpr-ctx_encoder-single-nq-base) combined with BM25 for in-context example retrieval. Quadruple sampling uses a multinomial softmax over highest sentence-embedding similarity between a quadruple and any task directive.
- **retriever learning signal**: None (off-the-shelf). Retrievers are pre-trained/frozen (DPR + BM25); no retriever training, contrastive fine-tuning, LM-feedback, or RL signal is applied to the retriever itself.
- **query construction**:
> Instructions are decomposed by an LLM-based instruction interpreter Phi_I into queries Q (conditions to be checked, e.g. 'TV is off') and executions E (manipulations), with a conditional function C mapping each query to its execution. Queries and executions then serve as the retrieval keys against the TEKG and demonstration store.
- **query granularity**: Both task-level and step/state-level. Instruction decomposition into query/execution is task-level (done once via Phi_I), but query evaluation against the memory and skill-value-based retrieval are re-run at every timestep (step-level) as the memory and observations change.
- **when to retrieve**: Iterative / per-step. At each timestep the agent re-evaluates queries against memory (retrieving fresh quadruples) and retrieves demonstrations for skill-value estimation; retrieval is woven into the per-step planning loop (Algorithm 1).
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed schedule (per-timestep loop). Query re-evaluation by the LLM is additionally gated by a change detector: if the retrieved subgraph is unchanged (G_hat_{1:t} == G_hat_{1:t-1}) the prior response R(q|G_{t-1}) is reused, otherwise the LLM re-evaluates - an efficiency-driven staleness/change trigger rather than a confidence-based one.
- **reranking**: No explicit learned reranking stage. Quadruples are sampled by a multinomial softmax over embedding similarity; in-context examples use DPR + BM25 scoring. Temporal-consistency refinement filters (not reranks) query-response priors by an entropy-monotonicity constraint.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Distractor/staleness filtering via temporal-consistency refinement: multiple query-response priors are sampled (10 iterations) using the LLM over retrieved memory, and any response whose entropy does not increase relative to the previous step (violating the information-decay constraint H(R(q|G_{t-1})) > H(P(q|G_{t-1}))) is discarded; surviving responses are averaged. Memory update function mu also removes semantically contradictory/outdated quadruples.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tool/skill-description retrieval; skills are a fixed primitive action set per environment).
- **index content separation**: Partial: a lightweight similarity index over linearized quadruples retrieves only 12 quadruples on demand from a potentially large TEKG, separating the heavy full graph from the small injected context, but not a formal SOP-index-then-content scheme.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no external tool API store; skills are environment-native primitives such as walk/grab/switch/open/close, goto/toggle, turn/go-straight/load-offload).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation. Retrieved quadruples plus demonstrations are linearized into the LLM prompt: (a) for memory-augmented probabilistic query evaluation Phi_M estimating P(q|G_t), and (b) for in-context exploitation skill-value estimation v_T. Retrieval is not used as a training signal.
- **planning integration**:
> Per-step interleaved, retrieve-then-plan within a continuous loop. Each step: (a) evaluate queries via retrieved memory to select active executions E_t (threshold theta=0.5); (b) score each candidate skill z by a weighted sum of an LLM-derived exploitation value v_T (using retrieved demonstrations + memory) and an information-gain exploration value v_R, then execute argmax skill; update memory; repeat.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-tool-call / per-skill within the rollout: retrieval and value estimation are performed for every skill-selection step in the continual loop, and per-query for the evaluation stage.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (see CBR fields; demonstrations used as verbatim in-context exemplars, not adapted cases).
- **retrieved item representation**: Structured note / linearized knowledge-graph text: retrieved TEKG quadruples are injected as linearized relational facts (e.g. '(TV, is, off, 27)'); demonstrations are injected as raw in-context trajectory exemplars.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Low-level/raw: timestamped state quadruples (raw environmental facts) and raw demonstration trajectories; no distilled strategy, guideline, or reusable workflow abstraction.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Entropy-based temporal-consistency refinement on query evaluation (discards stale/inconsistent LLM responses whose entropy fails to grow with time, modeling information decay) and a memory update function mu that removes contradictory and outdated quadruples (e.g. conflicting object states/positions). No retriever-aware training or distractor-aware SFT.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: Graph + episodic: a temporal embodied knowledge graph (TEKG) of timestamped quadruples serving as the environmental-context memory, accumulated episodically from observations.
- **write back**: True. Each observation o_{t+1} is integrated into the memory via update function mu (G_{t+1} = mu(G_t, o_{t+1})), which adds new quadruples and removes contradicting/outdated ones.
- **online growth**: Yes. The TEKG environmental-context memory grows and is continuously synchronized during deployment as the agent observes the changing environment. (The offline expert demonstration store D_e is frozen.)
- **write back trigger**: Per-step: memory is updated at every timestep from the new observation produced by executing the selected skill (Algorithm 1 line: G_{t+1} = mu(G_t, o_{t+1})). Writes are observation-driven, not success/failure- or reflection-gated.
- **failure experience usage**: Not used. Memory stores environmental-state observations, not success/failure planning outcomes; there is no storage or contrastive retrieval of failed planning experiences. (Baseline LLM-Planner uses execution-error feedback, but ExRAP's memory does not store failure cases.)
- **memory evolution update**:
