> DQA (Decision QA benchmark), introduced by this paper, with two scenarios: Locating (from the game Europa Universalis IV) and Building (from the game Victoria 3). 301 (Q, D) pairs total (200 Locating, 101 Building); each question provided in both RDB and GDB versions, giving 602 databases. Compared against Tabular QA / Table NLI benchmarks (HybridQA, TAT-QA, FinQA, WikiTableQA, TabFact, ToTTo-TNLI) only to contrast database size (avg rows per table), not as evaluation tasks.
- **benchmark family**:
> decision-making over structured databases (a new benchmark family proposed here, DQA). Not in the standard QA/web/embodied/tool/code/memory/decision-RL families; closest neighbor is structured-data reasoning (Tabular QA / Table NLI), but DQA adds business rules R and large database querying (SQL/Cypher) for best-decision selection.
- **baselines**:
> SingleRAG-LM (single-turn RAG); IterRAG-LM (iterative RAG, treated as the state-of-the-art iterative RAG technique, implemented with a ReAct Thought-Action-Observation prompt structure following Yao et al. 2023); and PlanRAG-LM w/o RP (PlanRAG without re-planning, internal ablation). All built on GPT-4 (zero temperature, zero-shot, LangChain). Additional model-variation baselines in the appendix: IterRAG-LM vs PlanRAG-LM implemented with GPT-3.5-turbo-0125, Llama-2 (70B), Llama-2 (13B), and Phi-2.
- **key metrics**:
> Accuracy (%) - an answer is correct only if it is semantically identical to the ground-truth best decision; reported as the average of RDB and GDB accuracies per scenario. Supporting/process metrics: rate of missed data analysis (%), SR (single-retrieval) vs MR (multiple-retrieval) accuracy breakdown, failure-case category distribution (CAN/MIS/DEEP/QUR/OTH), and number of re-plannings vs accuracy.
- **headline result**:
> PlanRAG-LM (GPT-4) achieves 64.3% accuracy on Locating and 45.0% on Building, outperforming the SOTA iterative RAG (IterRAG-LM: 48.5% / 37.6%) by 15.8 percentage points on Locating and 7.4 percentage points on Building (the paper states '15.8%' and '7.4%' improvements). SingleRAG-LM scores 30.5% / 2.5%.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Re-planning ablation (Table 4): removing re-planning (PlanRAG-LM w/o RP) drops accuracy to 53.5% Locating / 44.1% Building, i.e., -10.8% Locating and -0.9% Building vs full PlanRAG, showing re-planning is important (especially for Locating). (2) RDB vs GDB (Table 5): PlanRAG best in both; PlanRAG more effective for GDB than RDB on Building (40.6% RDB vs 49.5% GDB) due to longer traversals. (3) SR vs MR difficulty split (Figure 5; 84 SR pairs, 518 MR pairs): PlanRAG's gain over IterRAG is larger on SR questions (questions IterRAG underestimated as single-retrieval). (4) Rate of missed data analysis (Table 6): PlanRAG 1.3%/21.8% vs IterRAG 3.3%/33.2%. (5) Failure-case analysis (Figure 6): PlanRAG sharply reduces CAN and MIS errors, with slightly more DEEP errors as a side effect. (6) Prompt-structure ablation (Table 10, 10% subset): Plan-Thought-Action-Observation-Re-plan (57.5/50) beats IterRAG Thought-Action-Observation (37.5/30) and the variants Plan-Action-Observation-Re-plan (40/40) and Thought-Plan-Action-Observation-Re-plan (27.5/30), showing the planning step's placement matters and 'Thought' must precede the action. (7) Re-planning frequency vs accuracy (Table 7): accuracy declines as the number of re-plannings rises; Building re-plans far more often (38% of questions) than Locating (6%). (8) Model ablation (Table 11): with GPT-3.5, Llama-2 70B/13B, Phi-2, both methods collapse - Llama-2/Phi-2 solve 0; under GPT-3.5 IterRAG slightly beats PlanRAG because the PlanRAG prompt is too complex; GPT-4 is required.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Partially. The primary metric is the end-to-end decision accuracy, but the paper also reports an intrinsic process metric - the 'rate of missed data analysis' (whether the critical values were ever queried/computed) - decoupled from final accuracy (e.g., PlanRAG could in principle reach 98.7% on Locating given its 1.3% miss rate, vs 64.3% actual), separating retrieval/analysis completeness from reasoning quality. Standard IR metrics (Recall@k / nDCG) are not used because retrieval is exact DBMS querying.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both. Outcome: decision accuracy (semantic match to ground-truth best decision). Process: rate of missed data analysis, SR/MR breakdown, failure-category analysis (CAN/MIS/DEEP/QUR/OTH), and number-of-re-plannings vs accuracy - all probing intermediate planning/retrieval quality, not only the final answer.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Not a primary focus; no token/latency/API-cost numbers are reported. The closest cost-related observation is the re-planning distribution (Table 7): Building re-plans more (38% of questions; 14.85% re-plan >4 times) than Locating (6%; 1.75% >4 times), and SingleRAG fails to retrieve any results in over 60% of Locating and 95% of Building questions (so extra iterative/planning steps are needed for correctness). The trade-off framing is accuracy/correctness vs prompt complexity (the complex PlanRAG prompt only works with a strong model like GPT-4 and breaks weaker models such as GPT-3.5/Llama-2/Phi-2).
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Not explicitly budgeted as a fixed-k. The LM is given <Q, S, R> (question, full DB schema, business rules) plus the running plan and Observations; retrieved data are exactly what the generated SQL/Cypher queries return (variable size). The DB is too large to fit in context, motivating selective querying. Token-limit overflow is acknowledged only as an 'OTH' failure category. No reranked-then-truncated or fixed-k passage budget is defined.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (method + benchmark paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> DQA is reverse-engineered/transformed from two Paradox Interactive grand-strategy games (Europa Universalis IV for Locating, Victoria 3 for Building), chosen because they imitate real business decision situations. Size: 301 (Q, D) pairs (200 Locating, 101 Building); each question in both RDB and GDB -> 602 databases. Avg DB scale far exceeds prior Tabular QA/NLI (Locating RDB 2038.8 avg rows/table, Building 579.0, vs e.g. FinQA 6.26, HybridQA 15.7, TabFact 14.5). Construction: parse game savefiles into D per a fixed schema; generate Q from templates (Locating: 'Where should I locate my merchant? ... maximizing {COUNTRY_NODE}'s profit on home node {HOME_NODE}'; Building: 'Which building ID should we increase a level by 5 to maximally decrease the market price of {GOODS}?'); answers are deterministically annotated by purpose-built game SIMULATORS that apply business rules to every decision candidate and pick the best (verifiable ground-truth d_best). Quality control: Locating omits low-trading-power countries; Building filters questions with multiple answers. Released under MIT license (per Paradox EULA UGC clause); nation names anonymized to 3-letter codes for ethics. Best system (GPT-4 PlanRAG) reaches only 64.3% Locating / 45.0% Building, signaling the benchmark is hard.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> ReAct (Yao et al. 2023, Thought-Action-Observation backbone, extended with Plan/Re-plan instructions); iterative RAG (Trivedi et al. 2023 IRCoT; Jiang et al. 2023b FLARE; Shao et al. 2023) and single-turn RAG (Lewis et al. 2020; Guu et al. 2020 REALM; Izacard & Grave 2021; Izacard et al. 2023 Atlas); GPT-4 (OpenAI 2023) as the frozen base LM; LangChain and LlamaIndex as RAG/DB interfaces; Neo4j (Cypher/CQL, Francis et al. 2018) and MySQL as the DBMSs; structured-data reasoning benchmarks (Tabular QA / Table NLI) as conceptual predecessors.
- **contrasts with**:
> Existing single-turn and iterative RAG methods (IRCoT/FLARE-style, and the ReAct-based IterRAG baseline) that focus on knowledge-based QA and lack an explicit planning step - the paper argues they perform Steps (2) retrieval and (3) answering but not Step (1) planning, leading to disorganized querying and missed/improper data analysis. Also contrasts with prior Tabular QA / Table NLI benchmarks (HybridQA, TAT-QA, FinQA, WikiTableQA, TabFact, ToTTo-TNLI) which ignore business rules and use far smaller tables.
- **lineage**:
> Group C (RAG + planning): a plan-then-retrieve / retrieve-then-plan agentic-RAG method. It sits in the lineage of iterative RAG (single-turn RAG -> IRCoT/FLARE iterative RAG -> ReAct agentic loop) and extends the ReAct family with explicit Plan and Re-plan reasoning for LLM-as-decision-maker over structured databases, simultaneously introducing the DQA decision-making benchmark.

<a id="item-asi"></a>
### 54. Agent Skill Induction (ASI) - Inducing Programmatic Skills for Agentic Tasks

2025  ·  COLM 2025  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.06821)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**: COLM 2025 (Second Conference on Language Modeling), accepted (Accept; submission #603; published on OpenReview 07 Jul 2025). Preprint: arXiv:2504.06821 (v1 9 Apr 2025; v2 29 Aug 2025).
- **authors affiliation**: Zora Zhiruo Wang, Apurva Gandhi, Graham Neubig, Daniel Fried - all Carnegie Mellon University ({zhiruow,apurvag,gneubig,dfried}@cs.cmu.edu). (Zora supported by CMU Presidential Fellowship and Fujitsu Research; Apurva supported by Amazon.)
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.06821 (OpenReview COLM 2025: https://openreview.net/forum?id=lsAY6fWsog; DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2504.06821)
- **code url**: https://github.com/zorazrw/agent-skill-induction (linked in the paper footnote and abstract)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> web - LLM-based web navigation agents. Online, adaptive digital agents that solve natural-language web tasks (e-commerce, social forum, software development, content management, travel) by inducing and reusing programmatic skills. Framed as agentic decision-making / tool-use, not single-shot QA.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent online adaptation in a web browser environment with transition function T(s'|s,a). The agent policy pi_L(.|M,A) consists of an LM backbone L, a memory M, and a skill library A (both M and A are provided as input context to the LM). Given a sequence of NL queries Q={q1,...,qN} specifying tasks (presented in a fixed WebArena order), the agent generates an action trajectory tau=(s0,a0,...,sH) of up to H_max steps, receiving observation o_h (webpage accessibility tree) at each step and emitting an action a_h in A. CRITICAL assumption: NO demonstration trajectories and NO ground-truth rewards are available - the agent learns online purely from test queries (supervision-free), using an LM-based evaluator V_L(e)->0/1 to judge episode correctness. It updates M and A non-parametrically (no LM weight updates) and reuses them across episodes. Skills are induced per-website. Backbone LM is claude-3.5-sonnet for all components (policy, evaluator, induction); implemented in BrowserGym.
- **what is retrieved**:
> skills - reusable programmatic skills represented as executable Python functions (e.g., search_product(name), navigate_to_address_settings()). These verified skill programs are integrated into the agent action space (skill library A) and are directly callable as higher-level actions. (Contrasted with the AWM baseline which retrieves free-text workflow skills stored in memory.)
- **retrieval grounding**:
> GROWING / online-induced skill library (procedural memory the agent writes during deployment). The skill library A starts as the fixed WebArena primitive action space (click, fill, etc.) and grows online as the agent induces, verifies, and adds new program-based skills from its own successful episodes. No static external corpus / KB / API docs are retrieved; the store is self-built at test time.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Neither a fixed top-k ranking nor a completeness-recovery objective. ASI does not perform similarity-based top-k retrieval of skills at all; instead, the entire verified skill library A is provided in the LM context (action space) and the LM itself decides which skill to call. The selection objective is the agent autonomously choosing the appropriate higher-level action; quality is governed by execution-based verification at induction time (only skills passing correctness + usage + validity checks enter A), not by a ranking/completeness metric.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve: partial (no similarity search; the whole skill library is exposed and the LM selects which skill program to call), Reuse: yes (skill programs are invoked as actions to solve new tasks - 42.5% of cases reuse >=1 skill), Revise: yes (incompatible skills on new websites are updated/extended, e.g., adding a has_popup_window() check, or rewritten), Retain: yes (verified skills are added to the action space A_t U D_called -> A_t+1)]. So approximately Retrieve(partial)/Reuse/Revise/Retain.
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False - the paper does NOT frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner. It is framed as online adaptive agents, skill induction, program synthesis / tool-making, and non-parametric memory augmentation (building on AWM and TroVE). It nonetheless realizes Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain CBR-like mechanisms under another name (skill induction + verification + reuse + update).

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> skill-or-program - the retrieved/usable unit is an executable Python program function representing a reusable skill (a workflow-routine abstracted as a callable, e.g., search_product(name), open_marketing_reviews(), navigate_and_sort_category(category_id, subcategory_id)). Each wraps multiple primitive actions or prior skills into one higher-level action call. Skills have mediocre complexity (>=2-3 actions, <=5-10 lines) and may include control flow (if-else, for/while loops).
- **index source**:
> Online/test-time-induced store. The skill library is grown online from the agent's own successful episodes during the same online run on the target website; it starts only from the fixed primitive action space (no offline skill mining, no pre-collected demonstrations). Skills are induced per-website. Explicitly contrasted with offline skill-mining methods (e.g., SkillWeaver, RL roll-outs) that need supervision/offline compute and may suffer offline-online distribution mismatch.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat skill library / toolkit: a growing set of callable Python functions provided in the LM context as the agent action space. Skills are organized per-website (some skills are website-tailored with hard-coded link constants; others are versatile). No vector index, no dependency graph, no category hierarchy is used to organize or retrieve skills; the LM reads the full library as context.
- **retriever type**:
> LLM-as-selector / generative - there is no separate dense/BM25/learned retriever module. The induced skill programs are placed directly in the agent action space, and the LM backbone (claude-3.5-sonnet) generates actions that call the relevant skill, i.e., skill 'retrieval' is the LM emitting a function call (tool-as-action / generative selection). No embedding similarity search.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None for any retriever (there is no trained retriever). Skill ENTRY into the action space is gated by execution-based verification (downstream-task-effectiveness): a candidate skill program is admitted only if the verification trajectory passes (1) Correctness (LM-evaluator judges the task solved), (2) Skill Usage (>=1 new skill is called), and (3) Skill Validity (skill-calling actions cause environment changes). So the selection/admission signal is execution + LM-feedback verification, not contrastive similarity or RL-trained retrieval.
- **query construction**:
> No explicit query is constructed for skill selection - the agent simply conditions on the current observation/action history (o_0:h, a_0:h-1) plus the in-context skill library and memory, and the LM generates the next action (which may be a skill call). At induction time, the 'query' to the induction module I is a cleaned successful episode e (CoT thoughts simplified from 87.9 to 13.4 tokens/step, error steps removed); for verification a rewritten skill-using trajectory prefix tau_D is constructed by replacing sub-trajectories with skill calls and truncating trailing primitive actions.
- **query granularity**:
> step/state-level for skill invocation: at every decision step the LM may emit a skill-call action conditioned on the current observation and history. There is no separate task-level similarity retrieval; skill use is decided per action step within the ReAct-style observe-act loop.
- **when to retrieve**:
> iterative / per-step (agent-initiated) - at each step of the rollout the agent (LM) may choose to call an available skill action; skills become available as soon as they are induced and verified online. Induction/verification of NEW skills is triggered per successful episode (after V_L marks an episode correct).
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Agent-initiated, fixed control loop: skill use is triggered whenever the LM decides to emit a skill-call action at a decision step (no confidence/attention/uncertainty/reflection-token gating for using skills). Skill INDUCTION is triggered by an event signal: an episode being predicted correct by the LM-based evaluator V_L (V_L(e)=1) -> the cleaned episode is passed to the induction module; addition to the action space is then triggered by passing the three-way verification check.
- **reranking**: None - no reranking stage of any kind (no cross-encoder, no RRF). Skills are exposed in the action space and selected directly by the LM; admission is by execution verification, not by re-scoring a candidate list.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Induction-side refinement rather than post-retrieval reranking: (1) episode cleaning - removing action steps that caused execution errors and LM-summarizing verbose CoT thoughts (87.9 -> 13.4 tokens/step); (2) trajectory rewriting - replacing sub-trajectories with new skill calls to form a skill-using prefix tau_D; (3) trailing-action truncation - removing primitive actions after the last skill call to avoid spurious verification successes; (4) explored but rejected an observe() function for intermediate-state access (caused instability). No distractor filtering / compression of a retrieved candidate set (there is no candidate set).
- **tool document engineering**:
> Skill programs are induced with structured docstrings: the induction module is prompted to include 'Args', 'Returns', and 'Examples' in each function's documentation, plus inline comments, so each skill carries a self-describing docstring used by the LM when deciding to call it. Skill functions are constrained to mediocre complexity (>=2-3 actions, no try-except, no undefined actions). No synthetic-query augmentation or learned tool embeddings (no embedding-based tool retrieval is used).
- **index content separation**: N/A - no lightweight-index-then-heavy-content / progressive-disclosure separation; the full skill programs (with docstrings) are loaded directly into the agent action-space context.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Dynamic, live-synchronized skill library that grows during the online run via CRUD-like updates (add verified skills A_t U D_called -> A_t+1; update/extend incompatible skills on new websites). Integration protocol is function-calling / executable-program actions over BrowserGym primitives (click, fill, hover, select_option, etc.); no RapidAPI/RESTful/MCP. Skills execute as Python functions composing primitive browser actions.
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> Partial - skills can call prior skills (newly induced skills 'wrap primitive actions or prior skills'), so inter-skill composition/dependency is supported in the action space. However there is no explicit dependency-graph modeling, shared-auth tracking, or dependency-aware retrieval/reranking; composition emerges from the LM and the induction module.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> skill reuse - induced skill programs are integrated INTO the agent action space (A_t U {d_t} -> A_t+1) and are directly CALLED/EXECUTED as higher-level actions to solve subsequent tasks, composing multiple primitive steps into one. This is explicitly contrasted with AWM, which only adds textual skills to memory (M_t U {d_t} -> M_t+1) for reference/prompt augmentation. ASI's ablation shows that using verified program skills in the action space (40.1 SR) beats placing the same verified programs only in memory (36.4 SR) on the shopping site.
- **planning integration**:
> Per-step interleaved within an online observe-act (ReAct-style) loop, plus an offline-style induction/verification phase after each successful episode. The agent acts step-by-step; whenever a higher-level skill is available it can be invoked, enabling better/easier planning over fewer, more abstract steps (the paper attributes long-horizon success gains to easier planning with higher-level skills). No MCTS/tree search. The skill induction-verification-reuse cycle runs continuously online.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: per-tool-call within a rollout - skill (tool) calls are interleaved at the level of individual action steps in the agent's trajectory; each step is an action that may be a primitive or a composed skill call. Not per-answer; reasoning CoT precedes each action step.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> execution-feedback-driven revision plus LM-prompted adaptation - retrieved/induced skills are reused largely as-is (called by name), but when a skill is incompatible with a new website, the agent (a) detects the mismatch (from web-design vs skill-implementation discrepancy or from execution error messages in context) and rarely calls the deprecated skill, and (b) updates/extends the prior skill or induces a new skill on the new website (+update setting), e.g., adding a has_popup_window() guard. Skill programs are also rewritten/cleaned during induction.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> executable program-or-skill - the injected/usable unit is an executable Python function (with docstring, Args/Returns/Examples, optional control flow) integrated as a callable action. This is explicitly the central contribution vs AWM's free-text workflow representation in memory.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> procedural skill / reusable workflow - a higher-level abstraction over primitive actions (e.g., search_product composes click+fill+click), at the procedural-skill end of the spectrum, deliberately MORE abstract than raw trajectories and MORE verifiable/composable than free-text workflows (AWM) or single-state guidelines (AutoGuide).
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Execution-based verification + LM-evaluator filtering as the primary quality guard: (1) episodes are filtered by an LM evaluator V_L before induction (only predicted-correct episodes are used); (2) only ~15.6% of induction turns produce skills that pass the three-way verification (correctness, skill usage, skill validity) and get added; (3) episode cleaning removes error-causing steps and noisy CoT; (4) trailing-action truncation prevents spurious verification successes; (5) on new websites, execution errors and design discrepancies steer the agent away from incompatible skills and toward updating them. No retriever-side relevance evaluator (no retriever).

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: procedural / skill-library (a growing library of executable program skills in the agent action space). Compared against the AWM baseline's free-text workflow memory; ASI's skills live in the action space A rather than the textual memory M.
- **write back**: True - verified skill programs are written into the agent skill library (A_t U D_called -> A_t+1) and become callable actions for future tasks; on new websites the agent can also write updated/new skills (+update).
- **online growth**:
> True - the skill library grows online during the same deployment run as the agent solves WebArena/scaled-up/cross-website tasks (skills are created from ~7.6% of tasks and reused in 42.5% of cases). There is no separate frozen offline-induction stage; growth happens at test time as queries arrive (in the fixed WebArena order).
- **write back trigger**:
> on-success only, with verification gating: a skill is written to the action space only after (1) the source episode is judged correct by the LM evaluator V_L, AND (2) a rewritten skill-using verification trajectory tau_f passes all three checks - Correctness (LM-evaluator success), Skill Usage (>=1 new skill called), and Skill Validity (skill calls cause environment changes). Failed/unverified inductions are discarded (none added). On new websites, updates are triggered when prior skills are incompatible.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success-only for storage: only episodes evaluated as correct (and skills passing execution verification) are retained; failed episodes are filtered out and not stored as cases. However, failure signals are used REACTIVELY at use-time: execution error messages from calling an incompatible skill are fed back into context so the agent avoids reusing that skill and instead refines/induces a new one (a corrective, non-stored use of failure). No contrastive failure database is maintained.
- **memory evolution update**:
> append-and-refine: verified skills are appended to the library (append-only growth), and existing skills can be refined-overwrite / extended on new websites (the +update setting rewrites incompatible skills, e.g., adding pop-up handling, or composes new skills referencing prior ones). No forget-prune of skills is described; incompatible skills are simply left unused rather than deleted.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No - skill selection is performed by the (frozen, non-finetuned) LM backbone emitting function-call actions, not by a learned/RL-optimized retrieval policy. There is no trained retriever, no soft-Q/M-MDP, and no LM weight update (purely non-parametric memory/action-space augmentation). Skill admission is rule-based execution verification.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Single-agent private skill library (no multi-agent or cross-framework memory sharing). The only cross-context transfer studied is the SAME agent transferring its induced skills from sandboxed WebArena websites to real-world counterparts (OneStopMarket->Target, PostMill->Reddit, OpenStreetMap->Google Maps), i.e., cross-website skill generalization by one agent, not sharing across heterogeneous agents/frameworks.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> WebArena (812 examples across 5 domains: e-commerce/shopping, social forum/Reddit, software development/GitLab, content management/admin, travel/maps); a curated set of scaled-up long-horizon browsing tasks (multi-subtask, with intermediate checkpoints, ~10 examples per website across shopping/admin/Reddit/GitLab/maps); and cross-website real-world tasks (10 information-seeking queries each on Target, Reddit, Google Maps, mapped from OneStopMarket/PostMill/OpenStreetMap).
- **benchmark family**: web (WebArena and WebArena-derived scaled-up + real-world cross-website tasks). Sandbox-to-real transfer pairs cover shopping (OneStopMarket->Target), online forum (PostMill->Reddit), and travel/maps (OpenStreetMap->Google Maps).
- **baselines**:
> Vanilla static agent (Claude/claude-3.5-sonnet + BrowserGym, no adaptation; also a GPT/gpt-4o vanilla in Table 1) and AWM (Agent Workflow Memory, Wang et al. 2024b), the prior top-performing online adaptive web agent that induces free-text workflow skills into memory (run with both gpt-4o and, for fair comparison, claude-3.5-sonnet + episode cleaning). Ablation conditions: (unverified,text in memory), (verified,program in memory), (verified,text in memory), (verified,program as actions = ASI). Rebuttal-added baseline: trajectory-as-prompt (previous episodes directly in context) = 35.6 SR / 6.3 steps. Positioned against (not run) SkillWeaver (concurrent, offline), TroVE, AutoGuide, AutoManual, Voyager, Synapse.
- **key metrics**:
> Success rate (SR; WebArena program-based binary 0/1 evaluator, averaged over examples; scaled-up uses percentage of intermediate checkpoints achieved); number of steps (#Steps, efficiency, lower is better); LLM input/output token counts (efficiency, from rebuttal); statistical significance (paired t-test |t|>2, p<0.05).
- **headline result**:
> On WebArena with claude-3.5-sonnet, ASI reaches 40.4% overall SR, surpassing the static vanilla agent by 23.5% relative (32.7 -> 40.4) and the AWM text-skill agent by 11.3% relative (36.3 -> 40.4), while using fewer steps (5.0 vs 5.6 vanilla / 5.9 AWM, i.e., 15.3% / 10.6% fewer). The ASI vs AWM SR gain is statistically significant (paired t-test t=-2.21, p=0.027). In scaled-up long-horizon tasks ASI outperforms vanilla and AWM by 38.9% and 20.7% on average and is markedly more efficient (e.g., shopping 100.0% SR / 16.3 steps vs AWM 68.3% / 21.5; up to 85.2% horizon reduction in the multi-address case study).
- **ablations**:
> (1) Verification + format ablation on the shopping site (Table 3): Add-to-Memory (unverified,text)=32.6 -> (verified,program)=36.4 (+4.2 from execution-verified induction) -> (verified,text)=39.0 (+2.6, text suits memory better); Add-as-Actions (verified,program)=ASI=40.1 (program format suits action space). So both verification quality AND action-space integration drive the gain. (2) Episode-cleaning ablation (rebuttal): without cleaning AWM=35.5, ASI=38.5 (cleaning adds +0.8/+1.9; not necessary, still beats vanilla). (3) Trajectory-as-prompt baseline (rebuttal): 35.6 SR / 6.3 steps, 4.8 below ASI and 26% more steps. (4) Skill induction/reuse analysis (Table 8): skills created from 7.6% of tasks, reused in 42.5% of cases (e.g., shopping 21 attempted / 8 successful / 96 reuse). (5) Token-efficiency (rebuttal): ASI cuts input tokens 8.0% (301190->277208) and output tokens 12.9% (761->663) vs vanilla. (6) Significance testing on scaled-up and cross-web tasks (Tables 17-18). (7) Cross-website +update ablation (Table 6).
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> No - the paper reports end-to-end task success rate and efficiency (steps, tokens) but does NOT report intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG) decoupled from task performance (there is no top-k retrieval to evaluate). The closest decoupled signals are skill induction/reuse rates (attempted/successful/reuse counts) and the ~15.6% verification pass rate, which are induction-quality diagnostics rather than retrieval-quality metrics.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both outcome and process: outcome = success rate (with checkpoint-level partial credit on scaled-up tasks, giving intermediate-progress granularity); process/efficiency = number of steps and input/output token counts (trajectory quality / adherence to the optimal route), induction and reuse frequencies, and qualitative case studies of trajectory quality. WebArena's program-based evaluator scores functional correctness of the trajectory.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A - not a survey/taxonomy paper.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> AWM - Agent Workflow Memory (Wang et al. 2024b): the direct predecessor that induces and reuses workflows from online experiences via non-parametric memory augmentation; ASI changes the skill representation from free-text-in-memory to verifiable-executable-program-in-action-space. Also builds on TroVE (Wang et al. 2024a, inducing verifiable/efficient toolboxes for programmatic tasks), program-synthesis/library-learning (DreamCoder, LILO, LLMs-as-Tool-Makers), ReAct-style observe-act agents, BrowserGym (Chezelles et al. 2024) and WebArena (Zhou et al. 2024a), and embodied skill-as-program work (Voyager, Code-as-Policies).
- **contrasts with**:
> AWM (free-text, non-executable, unverifiable skills in memory) - the primary contrast; AutoGuide (single-state textual guidelines) and CLIN (causal abstractions); offline skill-mining methods such as SkillWeaver (concurrent; offline API creation needing supervision and offline compute, with offline-online mismatch), RL-rollout web-skill methods (WebRL, Agent Q, PAE), and SFT/contrastive self-improvement (NNetscape Navigator, Patel et al.). Also contrasts step-counting efficiency with token-based efficiency raised in review.
- **lineage**:
> Group A/experiential-memory agent self-improvement lineage, on the procedural-skill / programmatic-tool branch. Lineage: ReAct -> non-parametric experiential memory (Reflexion, Synapse, ExpeL) and workflow induction (AWM) -> programmatic, execution-verified skill induction integrated into the action space (ASI), as the executable-program successor to text-workflow-memory approaches; sibling to TroVE (programmatic toolboxes) and Voyager (skill library) and concurrent with SkillWeaver (offline API induction).

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- benchmark_construction_and_size
- context_budget_and_selection_count
- cost_efficiency_tradeoff

<a id="item-cfgm"></a>
### 55. CFGM - Coarse-to-Fine Grounded Memory for LLM Agent Planning

2025  ·  EMNLP 2025  ·  [paper](https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-main.659/)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**: EMNLP 2025 (Main Conference); Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, pp. 13029-13056, Suzhou, China, ACL. Also arXiv:2508.15305.
- **authors affiliation**: Wei Yang, Jinwei Xiao, Hongming Zhang (corresponding), Qingyang Zhang, Yanna Wang, Bo Xu (corresponding). All from the National Key Laboratory of Cognition and Decision Intelligence for Complex Systems, Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CASIA).
- **paper url**: https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-main.659/ (arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.15305 ; DOI: 10.18653/v1/2025.emnlp-main.659)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: LLM-agent planning / decision-making in interactive (text-based) environments: embodied household tasks (AlfWorld), web shopping (WebShop), and scientific reasoning (ScienceWorld).
- **problem setting**:
> Training-free, memory-augmented LLM agents for complex long-horizon interactive planning. Single-agent setting. CFGM uses an offline phase over a training task set (experience collection with trial-and-error reflection plus tips extraction) and an online inference phase over a held-out evaluation task set. No agent/model parameter training is performed; the LLM is enhanced purely via grounded memory injected as context. Four-fold cross-validation is used (train on one half, evaluate on the other half, and vice versa) so supervision is limited to the offline-collected trajectories generated by the agent itself, not human-labeled targets.
- **what is retrieved**:
> Two types of memory: (1) the successful trajectory content of past task experiences (full successful trajectories), and (2) the experience-wise hybrid-grained 'tips' dictionary entries (high-level principles plus fine-grained scene-specific techniques) associated with the retrieved experiences. Both are grounded/distilled by the LLM from collected experiences.
- **retrieval grounding**: GROWING/episodic memory the agent writes offline (experience pool B and tips dictionary TD are induced from the agent's own trial-and-error trajectories over training tasks). The store is frozen after the offline induction phase; it is not a static external corpus (docs/KB/APIs).
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k similarity ranking (Faiss kNN top-k over task-description embeddings). The k is small and fixed (k=2 in main experiments); ablation shows k=2 or 3 is optimal and larger k (5) hurts due to conflicting tips. Objective is relevance-driven top-k retrieval of similar experiences, not minimal-set completeness recovery.
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False. The paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner; it frames its work as memory grounding / experience-based and feedback-based optimization for LLM agents. It realizes CBR-like mechanisms (retrieve similar experiences, reuse, revise via reflection, retain) under the 'grounded memory' framing.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Full successful trajectory (problem-solution experience) plus its associated hybrid-grained tips set (guideline-rules + fine-grained techniques). The retrievable key is the task description; the retrieved payload is the experience's successful trajectory and the corresponding tips dictionary entry TD[t_h].
- **index source**:
> Growing/episodic memory built offline (test-time-induced relative to deployment but offline relative to evaluation): the agent collects experiences via Reflexion-style trial-and-error over a training task set, guided by LLM-grounded coarse focus points; experiences are stored in pool B and distilled into a tips dictionary TD. The store is frozen for online evaluation (no online growth).
- **index structure topology**: Flat vector index keyed by task description embedding (Faiss kNN), with experiences re-indexed by their associated task t_n; tips are organized as a dictionary keyed per-task (TD[t_n]). No graph or hierarchical topology.
- **retriever type**: Dense retrieval: kNN over textual embeddings using Faiss with the all-mpnet-base-v2 embedder (off-the-shelf sentence embedding).
- **retriever learning signal**: None (off-the-shelf). The retriever uses a fixed pretrained text embedder (all-mpnet-base-v2) with Faiss kNN over task-description similarity; no contrastive/LM-feedback/RL training of the retriever is performed.
- **query construction**: Raw task description of the current evaluation task t_m is embedded and used as the query for top-k similar-experience retrieval (prior analysis based on task-description retrieval before inference).
- **query granularity**: Task-level (one-shot at the start of each evaluation task t=0): the top-k similar experiences and tips are retrieved once before the rollout begins and held fixed as context for the whole episode.
- **when to retrieve**:
> One-shot for the experience/tips retrieval (done once per task before inference). Separately, online reflection is active/anomaly-triggered: when an abnormal observation is detected, the agent performs fine-grained key-information extraction and self-QA reflection (this is a reflection trigger, not an additional memory-retrieval call).
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Experience/tips retrieval: fixed schedule (once per task at episode start). Online self-QA reflection: agent/environment-driven anomaly detection - real-time monitoring of observations o_{i+1}; a trigger fires on specific abnormal observations (e.g., 'Nothing happens', mismatch/error), after which key-information extraction (LLM_KIE) and key-information reflection (LLM_KIR) are invoked.
- **reranking**: None. A single Faiss kNN top-k similarity stage is used with no reranking stage.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Offline distillation rather than post-retrieval refinement: experiences are converted offline into hybrid-grained tips (compare success-vs-failure trajectories to extract error-avoidance tips, then refine success-specific tips). At retrieval time the successful trajectory content and tips are concatenated into context (ST and ET) without further reranking/compression. Online, key-information extraction structures the current trajectory but does not refine the retrieved memory.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tool/skill retrieval; memory items are trajectories and LLM-distilled tips, not tool docstrings).
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index or integration protocol; memory store is a static Faiss index after offline induction).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tool retrieval or inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation / case reuse: retrieved successful trajectories (ST) and experience tips (ET) are concatenated into the policy LLM's (LLM_CFGM) context to guide ReAct-style planning. On anomalies, retrieved successful trajectories also serve as context for the key-information self-QA reflection that produces a corrective plan (ref_i) injected back into the current trajectory.
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-plan with per-step interleaved correction: top-k experiences and tips are retrieved once and prepended as exemplars/guidelines for the whole ReAct rollout; within the rollout, anomaly-triggered fine-grained key-information self-QA reflection produces in-line plan corrections appended to the trajectory step. No tree search / MCTS.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-tool-call/per-step within a rollout for the reflection correction (triggered at the step where an abnormal observation occurs); experience+tips context is per-answer (once at episode start). Underlying policy is ReAct (per think-act step).
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> Execution-feedback-driven revision via self-QA: retrieved successful cases/tips are reused largely verbatim as ICL exemplars/guidelines; when execution feedback signals an anomaly, the LLM grounds the current state into fine-grained key information (LLM_KIE) and performs self-reflective question-answer (LLM_KIR) over the current trajectory, key information, and similar successful trajectories to derive a corrective plan ref_i.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Mixed surface forms injected as text: (1) raw successful trajectory content (ST) and (2) distilled hybrid-grained tips (ET) which are free-text high-level principles plus fine-grained scene-specific techniques (structured note-like guidelines). Online corrections are free-text reflection/plan adjustments.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Hybrid: raw successful trajectory (low abstraction) combined with distilled hybrid-grained tips spanning high-level coarse principles (cross-task strategy/insight) and fine-grained scene-specific techniques (hint/rule). Coarse focus points additionally guide collection offline.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Relevance/self-reflection-based: (a) restricting retrieval to a small focused top-k (k=2/3) to avoid conflicting tips (ablation shows k=5 degrades performance), (b) hybrid-grained tips distilled by comparing success vs failure trajectories to encode error-avoidance, and (c) online fine-grained key-information self-QA reflection that detects environmental anomalies and corrects derailed plans. No retriever-aware training or distractor-aware SFT (training-free).

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: Episodic experience pool (successful/failed trajectories) plus a distilled tips dictionary (guideline/insight memory). Combination of episodic memory and a workflow/guideline-style distilled memory; no skill-library program store or graph memory.
- **write back**: True (offline only). The agent stores collected trajectories (successful and failed) into the experience pool B during offline collection, and writes LLM-distilled hybrid-grained tips into the tips dictionary TD. No write-back occurs during online evaluation.
- **online growth**: No. The experience pool and tips dictionary are induced offline over the training tasks and frozen for online evaluation; the store does not grow at test/deployment time. Online reflection corrections are appended to the current trajectory only, not persisted to memory.
- **write back trigger**:
> Offline, on-success-and-failure: during experience collection both successful and failed trajectories of a (eventually) solved task are stored in B; tips are then written reflectively after offline self-critique comparing success vs failure trajectories (and from single-success trajectories). No online/human-validated write-back.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success+failure contrastive (offline): failed trajectories paired with successful ones (C_compare) are fed to LLM_Tips to extract error-prevention tips; success-only trajectories (C_success) yield success-specific tips. At online retrieval, only successful trajectory content (tau_h^success) plus the distilled tips are injected as context (failures are used to derive tips, not surfaced directly).
- **memory evolution update**:
> Append-only with offline refinement: trajectories are appended to the pool; tips per task are generated then expanded/refined (compare-trajectory tips, then success-specific tips appended). No online mutation, dedup-merge, forgetting, or link-and-evolve of stored entries after the offline phase.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No. Retrieval is fixed similarity top-k (Faiss kNN over off-the-shelf embeddings); it is not an RL/learned case-selection policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent private memory; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> AlfWorld (134 solvable tasks across 6 task types), WebShop (100 tasks; success rate and mean reward), ScienceWorld (100 tasks sampled from test set across diverse task types, up to 80 env steps). WebArena-Shopping (90/98 tasks) used in the out-of-distribution transfer ablation; WebArena referenced for ablation.
- **benchmark family**: embodied (AlfWorld), web (WebShop; WebArena-Shopping for OOD transfer), science/embodied-text (ScienceWorld).
- **baselines**: ReAct, ExpeL, AutoGuide, QuBE, and ExpeL + QuBE (combination baseline). For the OOD transfer ablation: ReAct, ExpeL, AutoGuide. For the reflection ablation: template-free Self-QA Reflection and QA Reflection with fixed-question template (QuBE-style).
- **key metrics**: Success Rate (SR) as the primary metric across all environments; WebShop additionally reports mean Reward (attribute/option matching quality). Efficiency reported via offline tokens, online tokens-per-step, and average interaction turns.
- **headline result**:
> On AlfWorld CFGM reaches 91.00% +/- 0.82% SR vs ReAct 80.60% (+10.40 pts) and best memory baseline ExpeL+QuBE 85.07%. Also WebShop 85.0 +/- 1.3 mean reward and 57% SR, ScienceWorld 74% SR; CFGM consistently outperforms all baselines (using GPT-4-Turbo as policy model, GPT-4o as knowledge-extraction model).
- **ablations**:
> (1) Component ablation on AlfWorld: ReAct 80.60 -> +FP 85.82 -> +ET 86.57 -> +KIR 85.82 -> ET+KIR 88.06 -> FP+ET+KIR (full CFGM) 91.00; removing FP drops SR to 88.06, showing FP improves collected-memory quality. (2) Top-k experience retrieval scope on tips quality (ReAct+ET): k=0 80.60%, k=1 82.09%, k=2 86.57%, k=3 86.57%, k=5 81.34% (peak at k=2/3). (3) OOD transfer WebShop->WebArena-Shopping: CFGM 25.1% SR vs AutoGuide 20.4%, ExpeL 18.5%, ReAct 10.2%. (4) Online reflection comparison on AlfWorld: Key Information Reflection 85.82% vs Self-QA Reflection 84.33% vs fixed-question QA Reflection 84.33%. (5) Generalizability across models (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct to GPT-4.1) - CFGM beats ReAct and ExpeL across all. (6) Efficiency: CFGM has lowest online tokens/step (4681.4) and fewest online turns (14.32) among memory baselines.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No. Only end-to-end task metrics (SR, reward) and efficiency are reported; no intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG / completeness) are reported separately. The top-k ablation reports downstream SR vs k, not retrieval quality directly.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Primarily outcome-based (SR, reward). Some process-adjacent signals: efficiency in interaction turns and tokens-per-step, and qualitative trajectory examples showing error recovery; no quantitative step-wise reasoning-faithfulness or retrieval-accuracy metrics.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Reported on AlfWorld. Offline tokens per training sample: CFGM 4068.5 (comparable to ExpeL 3888.2, more efficient than AutoGuide 4873.4). Online tokens-per-step: CFGM 4681.4 (lowest among memory baselines: ExpeL 5125.5, AutoGuide 4809.4, QuBE 4752.3; ReAct 1734.6 with no memory). Online interaction turns: CFGM 14.32 (fewest; ReAct 19.01, ExpeL 17.32, AutoGuide 16.55, QuBE 17.21), implying lower latency/cost.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k retrieval: Experience Retrieval Scope = 2 and Top-k Experience's Tips Selection = 2 (Faiss kNN). Max tips from compare trajectories = 5, max tips from success trajectory = 3. Max reflection retries (offline collection) = 3. Per-environment max env steps: AlfWorld 20, WebShop 15, ScienceWorld 80, WebArena-Shopping 20. No explicit token-budget cap or reranked-then-truncated selection beyond the fixed k. SR is binary task completion; WebShop reward is the attribute/option matching score (Eq.1-2).
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (this is a method paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (uses existing benchmarks; AlfWorld 134 tasks/6 types, WebShop 100 tasks from a 1.18M-product/12,087-instruction catalog, ScienceWorld 100 tasks across 30 task types/10 topics, WebArena-Shopping ~90 tasks). Not a new benchmark contribution.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> ReAct (reasoning-acting interleaving, used as the underlying policy), Reflexion (trial-and-error self-reflection used in offline experience collection), ExpeL (experience recall + insight extraction), AutoGuide (context-aware guideline extraction), QuBE (question-based belief-state reflection). Uses Faiss for retrieval and all-mpnet-base-v2 as the embedder.
- **contrasts with**:
> Single-granularity memory methods: ExpeL (holistic insight extraction), AutoGuide (scenario-specific guidelines), QuBE (fixed human-curated question templates for reflection), and the ExpeL+QuBE combination. CFGM argues these use single-granularity memory and fixed-question reflection; CFGM instead grounds coarse-to-fine (focus points, hybrid-grained tips) memory and uses flexible fine-grained self-QA reflection.
- **lineage**:
> Experience/memory-augmented LLM-agent planning lineage (experience-based and feedback-based optimization for agents); sub-topic of growing-memory experience/case planners (Group C: RAG planning / experience-grounded agent memory). Successor in the ReAct -> Reflexion -> ExpeL/AutoGuide/QuBE line, adding LLM-grounded coarse-to-fine multi-granularity memory.

### 56. CR-Planner (Critic-guided planning with Retrieval-augmentation)

2025  ·  ACL 2025  ·  [paper](https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.1244.pdf)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**: ACL 2025 (Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, Long Papers, pp. 25589-25604). Preprint arXiv:2410.01428 (Oct 2024). Also reviewed on OpenReview (id=4JfFW7d1gu).
- **authors affiliation**:
> Xingxuan Li (MiroMind; Nanyang Technological University — work done mainly at DAMO Academy, Alibaba Group, under the Alibaba-NTU Joint PhD Program), Weiwen Xu (DAMO Academy, Alibaba Group; Hupan Lab, Hangzhou), Ruochen Zhao (NTU), Fangkai Jiao (NTU), Shafiq Joty (NTU; Salesforce Research), Lidong Bing (MiroMind, corresponding author). Lead/primary affiliations: MiroMind, NTU, DAMO Academy (Alibaba Group).
- **paper url**: https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.1244.pdf (arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.01428)
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (single-paper code repo, not a continuously-maintained leaderboard/paper-list).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Reasoning-heavy and domain-knowledge-intensive problem solving that couples reasoning with retrieval: competitive programming / code (USACO), theorem-driven math reasoning (TheoremQA-Math), and reasoning-intensive document retrieval (BRIGHT StackBio/StackEcon). Spans code, math QA, and retrieval/IR; cast as planning/decision-making over a {REASON, GENQUERY, RETRIEVE} action space.
- **problem setting**:
> Single-agent, interactive test-time planning framed as a Markov Decision Process (S, A_s, P, R, T). A state s_t is the action-observation history (o_0,a_0,...,o_t); observations are sub-goal types (REASON/GENQUERY/RETRIEVE) or execution outputs (RATIONALE/QUERY/DOC). At each step a policy pi(s_t)=argmax_a R(s_t,a) selects the action with highest expected reward, where R is estimated by fine-tuned critic models. A large general generator (GPT-4) produces candidates and a BM25 retriever produces documents; small fine-tuned critics (Skywork-Reward-Llama-3.1-8B) score them. Supervision: step-wise reward training data is collected offline via Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) over generator/retriever rollouts (no human step annotations; final-answer correctness / test-case signals drive MCTS simulation scoring). The base generator is NOT fine-tuned (plug-and-play with closed-source LLMs); only the external critics are trained. Inference is online step-by-step planning; the external knowledge corpus is fixed/static.
- **what is retrieved**:
> External knowledge documents grounding the reasoning: for USACO, algorithm textbook chapters and a problem bank of other USACO problems; for TheoremQA-Math, processed documents from high-quality STEM datasets (GSM8K, GSM8K-RFT, MATH, AQuA-RAT, TheoremQA, CAMEL-MATH); for BRIGHT StackBio/StackEcon, web-derived StackExchange-cited documents/articles/tutorials. The retrieval action (RETRIEVE) returns DOC observations; the GENQUERY action produces search QUERY strings. No demos/cases/trajectories/skills are retrieved as reusable units — only knowledge documents.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus. Retrieval targets fixed, pre-gathered knowledge sources (USACO textbooks + problem bank; BRIGHT STEM document collections; StackExchange documents). The store does not grow during deployment, and the agent does not write experiences/cases back into a retrievable memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k ranking. The RETRIEVE action surfaces top-k candidate documents (k=10 for the final retrieval in BRIGHT nDCG@10 evaluation; top-k candidates per Table 9), and the execution critic g^e_DOC ranks/selects among them. No notion of recovering a complete minimal evidence set; selection is critic-driven single-best (or top-10 for nDCG) rather than precision-driven variable-size.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A — not framed as case-based reasoning. If force-mapped: a weak Retrieve phase (BM25 documents, not cases) and no Reuse-as-adaptation/Revise/Retain. Flags: [Retrieve=partial(documents,not-cases), Reuse=no, Revise=no, Retain=no].
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False: the paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It retrieves knowledge documents, not prior solved cases as adaptable units.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Document (knowledge passage): a textbook chapter / problem-bank problem / STEM-corpus document / StackExchange-cited document, surfaced as a DOC observation. Query strings (GENQUERY->QUERY) are an intermediate conceptual-query unit, not a retrieved unit. Reasoning is at the rationale-step granularity (REASON->RATIONALE).
- **index source**: Static, offline-constructed store: benchmark-provided external corpora (USACO textbooks + full problem bank; BRIGHT processed STEM documents; StackExchange web content already gathered into BRIGHT). Indexed once and frozen; not online/test-time-induced and not hybrid.
- **index structure topology**: Flat term-based (BM25/inverted-index) document store. No graph, hierarchy, or cluster/toolkit organization is described; documents are retrieved by lexical relevance to the generated query.
- **retriever type**:
> BM25 (sparse, term-based, off-the-shelf). The paper chooses BM25 for efficiency in both MCTS training-data collection and inference across all three domains. No dense/learned/generative retriever is trained; relevance selection among retrieved DOCs is delegated to the fine-tuned execution critic g^e_DOC rather than a learned dense retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None for the retriever itself (off-the-shelf BM25, untrained). The learned signal lives in the CRITIC models, not the retriever: an execution critic g^e_DOC is trained (pairwise ranking loss, Burges 2005 / Ouyang 2022) on MCTS-collected, long-term-reward-labeled trajectories to select among BM25-retrieved documents, and the sub-goal critic g^g learns when RETRIEVE (vs REASON/GENQUERY) maximizes downstream task reward. So the effective retrieval/selection signal is downstream-task-effectiveness (MCTS-estimated long-term reward) realized through trained critics, not retriever contrastive training.
- **query construction**:
> Thought-conditioned synthetic query generation. When GENQUERY is selected, the generator (GPT-4) produces conceptual search queries derived from the current reasoning step/state; multiple (3) candidate queries are sampled via temperature sampling and the execution critic g^e_QUERY selects the best. Queries are required to be conceptual/relevant to the reasoning step and to avoid specific numbers/entities of that step (per the prompt). The first retrieval may also use the problem itself; subsequent queries are reasoning-conditioned.
- **query granularity**: Step/state-level. A query is constructed per planning step when GENQUERY is chosen (conditioned on the current RATIONALE/state), not once at t=0. Retrieval is interleaved across steps, so queries are formed at the reasoning-step granularity within the trajectory.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Adaptive (learned router) + iterative. WHEN to retrieve is decided at every step by the sub-goal critic g^g, which scores REASON vs GENQUERY vs RETRIEVE and routes to the highest-reward action; retrieval can occur multiple times across a trajectory (iterative) and only when the critic judges it beneficial (not a fixed schedule).
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Learned critic reward score (a trained sub-goal critic g^g acting as a learned router). At each state the sub-goal critic assigns reward scores to {REASON, GENQUERY, RETRIEVE}; RETRIEVE (or GENQUERY) is triggered when its critic score is highest. The critic is trained on MCTS-estimated long-term rewards, so the trigger is a learned-complexity/utility signal rather than token confidence, attention, or reflection tokens.
- **reranking**:
> Yes, via the execution critic acting as a learned reranker/selector. For RETRIEVE, BM25 returns top-k candidate DOCs and the fine-tuned execution critic g^e_DOC scores each (first-logit reward) and selects the optimal document — a critic-based reranking stage rather than a cross-encoder/RRF reranker. (For nDCG@10 evaluation the top-10 are kept.)
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Critic-based selection/filtering: among the top-k retrieved DOCs the execution critic picks the most useful one (distractor/irrelevant-document filtering), and the sub-goal critic can choose to REASON again over a retrieved doc (e.g., decide retrieval is insufficient and trigger a second-level retrieval). No compression, summarization, or decompose-then-recompose; refinement is per-step critic-driven selection plus optional reasoning-over-documents.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A — no tools/APIs are retrieved; the retrieved items are knowledge documents. Documents are used as-is (no synthetic-query augmentation/expanded summaries/weighted-field embeddings of the corpus); queries (not documents) are engineered to be conceptual.
- **index content separation**: N/A / No: a single flat BM25 document index is used; there is no lightweight-index-then-heavy-content progressive-disclosure separation.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A — not a tool-use method; no live tool index, no RapidAPI/RESTful/MCP/function-calling protocol or CRUD auto-sync. The document corpus is static.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A — no inter-tool dependency modeling; not a tool-use method.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation within an iterative plan. The selected DOC is appended to the action-observation history (state) and conditions subsequent REASON steps and the final generator answer/code; retrieved knowledge grounds rationales to improve factuality. Critic scores are used as a search/selection signal (not injected into the prompt). Retrieved content is used as in-context grounding, not as a training signal or latent token.
- **planning integration**:
> Per-step interleaved critic-guided planning over a {REASON, GENQUERY, RETRIEVE} action space (retrieve-and-reason interleaving). At inference the framework alternates Sub-Goal Selection (critic g^g picks the next sub-goal) and Execution Selection (critic g^e picks the best sampled candidate), forming a step-by-step plan; MCTS is used OFFLINE only to collect critic-training data (it explores action sequences and back-propagates long-term rewards), not at inference. (A 'Vanilla MCTS at inference' variant is studied as a baseline and underperforms CR-Planner.)
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Per-CoT-step / per-sub-goal: retrieval (and query generation) is woven in at the granularity of individual reasoning sub-goals within a trajectory — each step the planner may REASON, GENQUERY, or RETRIEVE, so search is interleaved per reasoning step rather than per final answer or per token.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not CBR). Retrieved documents are used verbatim as in-context grounding; the closest mechanism is critic-guided selection/revision of which rationale/query/document to keep at each step (critic-guided revision of the plan), but there is no case-adaptation pipeline.
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw free-text knowledge document (textbook chapter / problem-bank problem / STEM passage / StackExchange document) injected verbatim into the planning state/prompt. Not distilled into a strategy/guideline, workflow, executable skill, or latent token.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw knowledge document / passage (concrete reference content). Not a distilled strategy/insight, state-aware guideline, reusable workflow, or procedural skill — though queries are deliberately made conceptual, the retrieved unit itself is raw document text.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Fine-tuned critic models as the central noise guard: the execution critic g^e_DOC filters out irrelevant/misleading retrieved documents by scoring usefulness, and the sub-goal critic can decline retrieval (route to REASON) when retrieval is unhelpful, directly attacking the 'retrieving error / irrelevant retrieval' failure mode. The reason-then-retrieve interleaving and conceptual-query constraint also reduce off-topic retrieval. No retriever-aware SFT of the base model and no reflection-token mechanism.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> none (no persistent cross-task experience memory). The framework relies on a static external knowledge corpus plus trained critic models; it does not maintain an episodic/skill/workflow memory that is read and written during deployment. The MCTS-collected trajectories are training data for critics, not a queryable memory.
- **write back**: False. The system does not store new experiences/cases/skills into a retrievable memory at test time. MCTS trajectories are collected offline once to train critics; nothing is written back during inference.
- **online growth**: No. The retrievable knowledge store is frozen after offline construction and does not grow at deployment/test time.
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back to a retrievable memory). Offline, MCTS produces pairwise (chosen, rejected) preference data used solely to train the critic models; this is training-data generation, not test-time memory writing.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Indirect, success-vs-suboptimal contrastive at TRAINING time only: MCTS yields pairwise data where a chosen observation (highest long-term-reward score) is contrasted against a rejected sibling observation (lower score) sharing the same parent, and critics are trained via pairwise ranking loss on these (chosen, rejected) pairs. So suboptimal/failed action branches inform critic training contrastively, but failed experiences are not stored or retrieved at inference.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Yes (partially): the decision of whether/when to RETRIEVE and which retrieved DOC to keep is governed by LEARNED critic models (sub-goal critic g^g and execution critic g^e_DOC) trained on MCTS-estimated long-term rewards via pairwise ranking — i.e., a learned selection/routing policy rather than fixed similarity top-k. The underlying retriever (BM25) is itself fixed; the learned policy sits at the action-selection/reranking layer (value/reward-based selection, not RL-finetuned retriever).
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> No. Single-agent private setting; no sharing of memory/experience across multiple agents or heterogeneous frameworks. (The trained critic models are reusable plug-and-play across different base generators — GPT-4, Claude-3.5, Llama-3.1 — but this is critic portability across base LLMs, not cross-agent experience sharing.)

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> USACO (USA Computing Olympiad competitive-programming benchmark; 123 bronze, 100 silver, 63 gold, 21 platinum problems; Shi et al. 2024); TheoremQA-Math (206 solvable theorem-driven math problems, the Math subset of TheoremQA rewritten in BRIGHT; Chen et al. 2023 / Su et al. 2024); BRIGHT StackBio and StackEcon (103 biology + 103 economics reasoning-intensive retrieval questions from StackExchange; Su et al. 2024).
- **benchmark family**: code (USACO — competitive programming / Olympiad), QA-math (TheoremQA-Math — theorem-driven math reasoning), and reasoning-intensive retrieval/IR (BRIGHT StackBio/StackEcon). Cross-cutting: knowledge-intensive + reasoning-heavy benchmarks.
- **baselines**:
> Standard prompting (Ouyang et al. 2022); Chain-of-Thought (CoT, Wei et al. 2022); Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023); standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG, Lewis et al. 2020); Chain-of-Knowledge (CoK, Li et al. 2024, SoTA CoT+retrieval-with-rationale-postedit); Retrieval+Reflexion (from Shi et al. 2024, USACO) reported on USACO; BM25 baseline for BRIGHT retrieval; Claude-3.5 zero-shot for BRIGHT. Additional analysis baselines: Vanilla MCTS at inference; LoRA-fine-tuned Llama-3.1-70B base model on the same MCTS data; GPT-4 (in-context) as critic; single unified critic vs task-specific critics. Self-RAG is explicitly excluded as a baseline because it requires fine-tuning the base model.
- **key metrics**: USACO: Pass@1 (%) overall and per difficulty tier (Bronze/Silver/Gold/Platinum). TheoremQA-Math: accuracy (%). BRIGHT StackBio/StackEcon: nDCG@10. Improvements reported as absolute percentage-point gains over baselines.
- **headline result**:
> CR-Planner outperforms the baseline by 10.06% on average across the three tasks (key contribution claim). On USACO Pass@1 it reaches 17.59% overall vs 10.10% standard prompting (+7.49 pts) and beats CoT 12.38, RAG 8.47, CoK 8.14; CR-Planner+Reflexion reaches 22.80% overall (vs Retrieval+Reflexion 18.05). On TheoremQA-Math, 53.40% vs 39.81% standard (+13.59 pts). On BRIGHT, nDCG@10 improves over BM25 by +10.31 on StackBio and +7.9 on StackEcon.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Fine-tuned critics vs GPT-4-as-critic (Fig 3): fine-tuned domain-specific critics beat GPT-4 in-context critics, especially on domain-specific StackBio, validating domain fine-tuning. (2) Various base generators (Table 4): CR-Planner improves Claude-3.5 by 4.56% and Llama-3.1-70B by 2.61% (smaller than the 7.49% GPT-4 gain, since critics were trained on GPT-4 data) — shows plug-and-play across open/closed models. (3) Fine-tuning critics vs fine-tuning the base model (Table 5, TheoremQA-Math): LoRA-fine-tuned Llama-3.1 reaches 34.10 (> Standard 31.43) but CR-Planner reaches 38.62, i.e., training external critics beats fine-tuning the base model and costs less. (4) Retrieve-or-not (Table 6, USACO): CR-Planner w/o Retrieval 14.33 vs full CR-Planner 17.59 vs Standard 10.10 — retrieval contributes ~3.3 pts; reasoning critic alone already helps. (5) Vanilla MCTS at inference (Table 7, USACO): 12.42 vs CR-Planner 17.59 — learned critics beat raw test-time MCTS (which overfits to local test cases). (6) Execution sampling count (Fig 4): gains rise sharply from 1->2 candidates, converge ~3; 3 chosen for main experiments. (7) Single-unified vs task-specific critics (Table 8, USACO): task-specific 17.59 vs single unified 12.38 — task-specific critics generalize better.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Partially decoupled by task: for the BRIGHT StackBio/StackEcon retrieval tasks an intrinsic retrieval metric (nDCG@10) is reported, separate from the end-to-end task metrics (Pass@1 on USACO, accuracy on TheoremQA-Math). There is no per-step Recall@k / completeness metric isolating the retriever from the end-to-end pipeline within the code/math tasks; the retrieval-or-not ablation (Table 6) indirectly isolates retrieval's end-to-end contribution.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome metrics (Pass@1, accuracy, nDCG@10). Process quality is examined qualitatively and via ablations rather than a dedicated step-wise score: Fig 3 (critic quality), Fig 4 (execution-sampling effect), and the Vanilla-MCTS / retrieve-or-not / unified-vs-task-specific-critic analyses probe intermediate selection quality, but no formal reasoning-faithfulness or step-wise retrieval-accuracy metric is reported.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (this is a method/empirical paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A (not a benchmark-contribution paper). For context, evaluation reuses existing benchmarks: USACO (307 problems: 123 bronze/100 silver/63 gold/21 platinum), TheoremQA-Math (206 solvable problems), BRIGHT StackBio (103) and StackEcon (103) StackExchange questions with gold = documents cited in answers. External corpora: USACO 30 human-written textbook chapters + full problem bank; BRIGHT STEM document collection (GSM8K, GSM8K-RFT, MATH, AQuA-RAT, TheoremQA, CAMEL-MATH).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Chain-of-Thought (Wei et al. 2022) and RAG (Lewis et al. 2020) as the reason+retrieve foundation; process-supervision / planning-based reasoning (Lightman et al. 2024 'Let's verify step by step'; RAP-style reward estimation; Jiao et al. 2024 planning-based reasoning via DPO on process-reward-ranked trajectories); Monte Carlo Tree Search (Browne et al. 2012) for trajectory simulation and long-term reward estimation; learning-to-rank pairwise ranking loss (Burges et al. 2005) and RLHF-style reward modeling (Ouyang et al. 2022); Skywork-Reward-Llama-3.1-8B reward model + LoRA (Hu et al. 2021); GPT-4 / Claude-3.5 / Llama-3.1 generators; BM25 retriever.
- **contrasts with**:
> Self-RAG (Asai et al. 2024) and variants (CRAG/Yan et al. 2024, Open-RAG/Islam et al. 2024) — which fine-tune the base LLM with reflection tokens to decide when/how to retrieve; CR-Planner instead trains external critics and leaves the base model untouched (works with closed-source LLMs). Chain-of-Knowledge (Li et al. 2024) and ReAct/Verify-and-Edit-style step-wise RAG that optimize retrieval sub-tasks locally (pre-retrieval analysis, query gen, doc selection) rather than learning global step rewards. Self-ask (Press et al. 2023), RePlug (Shi et al. 2023, fine-tuned retriever), Reflexion (linguistic-feedback self-correction). Also contrasts with applying Vanilla MCTS at inference (overfits to local test cases) and with fine-tuning the base model on the same data.
- **lineage**:
> Group C (RAG + LLM planning). Sits in the lineage of critic/reward-guided step-wise reasoning-and-retrieval planners: it generalizes iterative RAG (FLARE/IRCoT/Self-RAG style 'when-to-retrieve') by replacing reflection-token / confidence triggers with trained sub-goal+execution critics over a unified {REASON, GENQUERY, RETRIEVE} action space, and combines this with MCTS-collected process rewards (RAP / 'Let's verify step by step' lineage). Distinct from experience/case-memory planners in that retrieval grounds against a static knowledge corpus and no episodic memory is written; the learned component is the critic policy, not the retriever or the base model.

<a id="item-dma-mcts"></a>
### 57. DMA-MCTS (Dynamic Memory-Augmented Monte-Carlo Tree Search for LLM Task Planning)

2025  ·  IEEE SMC 2025  ·  [paper](https://doi.org/10.1109/SMC58881.2025.11343701)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics (SMC), Vienna, Austria, October 5-8, 2025, pages 6377-6382 (IEEE). Added to IEEE Xplore 28 January 2026. DOI 10.1109/SMC58881.2025.11343701.
- **paper url**: https://doi.org/10.1109/SMC58881.2025.11343701 (IEEE Xplore: https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11343701/)
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (single-paper conference work; no continuously-maintained repo/leaderboard).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Embodied / decision-making: long-horizon household object-rearrangement task planning for LLM-based agents in a partially observable, dynamic environment (VirtualHome), framed as POMDP planning.
- **what is retrieved**:
> Past experiences / historical trajectory information: prior planning experiences (episodic trajectory experiences and reflection-distilled knowledge) plus historical Q-value statistics, retrieved context-aware from a dual-layer semantic memory repository to guide subsequent planning.
- **retrieval grounding**: GROWING / episodic memory the agent writes: a dynamic memory repository populated from the agent's own past trajectories and reflections (not a static external corpus/KB/API store). The memory is built and grown from experience and queried context-aware during planning.
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False: the paper frames itself as memory-augmented / reflection-based MCTS, not as case-based reasoning, and (per the visible reference list) does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It realizes CBR-style mechanisms (retrieve-reuse-revise-retain over experiences) under the 'dynamic memory + reflection' framing.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **index source**: Growing memory induced online at test/deployment time: the dual-layer semantic memory repository is dynamically built and updated from the agent's own trajectories and reflections across episodes (not an offline-frozen static corpus).
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tools/APIs are retrieved; not a tool-use method).
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index or integration protocol; not a tool-use method).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no inter-tool dependency modeling; not a tool-use method).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation + search-bias: retrieved past experiences and reflection-distilled knowledge condition the LLM's reasoning/planning, and historical Q-values bias the MCTS UCT/PUCT selection (memory-enhanced UCT) to guide exploration toward promising actions informed by experience. Retrieval thus informs both the LLM heuristic and the tree-search value estimates rather than being committed directly as actions.
- **planning integration**:
> Inside MCTS / tree search: retrieval is embedded in Monte Carlo Tree Search via (1) a memory-enhanced UCT selection strategy biased by historical Q-values from memory, and (2) context-aware retrieval of past experiences and reflection knowledge that condition the LLM used within the search. This extends the LLM-as-world-model + LLM-as-policy MCTS pattern of LLM-MCTS with an experience memory and reflection loop.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Two abstraction levels: raw episodic trajectory experiences AND distilled strategies/insights (reflection-extracted generalizable knowledge from successful and failed trajectories), consistent with the 'dual-layer' memory design. Plus numeric value statistics (historical Q-values) at the search-node level.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: episodic + distilled-knowledge (dual-layer semantic memory): an episodic experience layer plus a reflection-distilled generalizable-knowledge layer, augmented with historical Q-value statistics. It is a growing, cross-episode memory (not 'none').
- **write back**: True: the system stores new experiences/trajectories and LLM-reflection-distilled knowledge back into the dual-layer semantic memory repository, and accumulates historical Q-values, so memory grows from the agent's own planning experiences.
- **online growth**:
> Yes: the dynamic memory repository is built and grown during deployment/test time from the agent's trajectories and reflections (the work is explicitly framed around 'dynamic memory' and accumulating decision-making experience), in contrast to LLM-MCTS's frozen offline prompt corpus.
- **failure experience usage**: Success + failure (differentiated): the reflection mechanism is explicitly 'differentiated' to extract generalizable knowledge from both successful and failed trajectories, so failed/negative experiences are stored and reflected upon (not success-only).

**Evaluation**

- **benchmark family**: embodied (VirtualHome) — household object rearrangement / long-horizon task planning.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (method/empirical paper, not a survey).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> LLM-MCTS (Zhao, Lee, Hsu, NeurIPS 2023 — LLM as commonsense world model + heuristic policy in MCTS on VirtualHome); classical MCTS/UCT and POMDP planning (Kaelbling et al. 1998); reflection/self-improvement for LLM agents (Reflexion [Shinn et al.], Self-Refine [Madaan et al.]); LLM reasoning-as-planning and tree search (RAP / 'Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model' [Hao et al.], Tree of Thoughts [Yao et al.], LATS / Language Agent Tree Search [Zhou et al.]); long-term memory for LLMs (MemoryBank [Zhong et al.], MemGPT [Packer et al.]); VirtualHome and Watch-And-Help [Puig et al.] for the environment/task setting; ReAct, Chain-of-Thought, least-to-most prompting (per the visible reference list).
- **contrasts with**:
> Standard LLM-MCTS (named explicitly as a baseline) and prior LLM planners with overly simplistic memory structures, inadequate retrieval of relevant past information, and underdeveloped reflection/experience-accumulation frameworks (as criticized in the introduction). Also implicitly contrasts with reflection-only or tree-search-only approaches (Reflexion, RAP/LATS, ToT) by combining dynamic experience memory + reflection + memory-biased MCTS.
- **lineage**:
> Group C (RAG / LLM planning): sits in the LLM-guided-search lineage that injects LLM knowledge into MCTS, directly extending LLM-MCTS (NeurIPS 2023) by adding a growing dual-layer experience memory + reflection (success/failure) and a memory-enhanced UCT. It bridges LLM+MCTS planning (LLM-MCTS, RAP, LATS) with experience/memory-augmented agents (Reflexion, MemoryBank/MemGPT), moving from a static offline prompt corpus toward an online-growing episodic+distilled memory for long-horizon embodied planning.
