<a id="item-skill-rag"></a>
### 61. Skill Retrieval Augmentation (SRA) / SR-Agents and SRA-Bench

2026  ·  arXiv:2604.24594 (2026-04, verified)  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.24594)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2026
- **authors affiliation**:
> Weihang Su, Jianming Long, Qingyao Ai (corresponding), Qiaozhi He, Yichen Tang, Changyue Wang, Yiteng Tu, Yingbo Wang, Yiqun Liu. Primary affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Technology, Tsinghua University; several authors (Weihang Su, Qiaozhi He, Yingbo Wang) also ByteDance Inc.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.24594
- **code url**: https://github.com/oneal2000/SR-Agents (MIT license; ships SRA-Bench under data/bench/; dataset mirror at https://huggingface.co/datasets/WeihangSu/SRA-Bench; project site https://sr-agents.github.io)
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/oneal2000/SR-Agents (78 stars / 9 forks at retrieval time; last commit 2026-05-21; release v1.0.0 2026-05-13). Project site: https://sr-agents.github.io

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Agentic AI / tool-use, but evaluated as a capability-augmentation pipeline spanning theorem-based reasoning (TheoremQA), formal logic (LogicBench), tool-interleaved QA (ToolQA), medical calculation (MedCalc-Bench), competition mathematics (CHAMP), and code generation (BigCodeBench). Core problem is retrieving and applying reusable 'skills' (capability packages) for LLM agents.
- **problem setting**:
> Defines Skill Retrieval Augmentation (SRA): a single LLM agent must, on demand, retrieve relevant reusable skills from a large external skill corpus (26,262 skills, only 2.4% gold), decide whether/which to incorporate, and apply them to solve a task. Setting is largely offline/single-pass per query (a 'direct' engine statically prepends retrieved skills) but also includes interactive/iterative agentic engines (Progressive Disclosure with up to 10 load rounds; ReAct and ReAct+Progressive-Disclosure for ToolQA). Single-agent, no agent memory write-back; supervision = gold-skill annotations + ground-truth answers, used for decomposed evaluation (retrieval / incorporation / application), not to train models. Models are used zero-shot off-the-shelf (no fine-tuning of the LLM or retriever). The paper is primarily a paradigm formulation + benchmark + systematic empirical study (SR-Agents as a baseline family) rather than a single new method.
- **what is retrieved**:
> skills: modular reusable capability packages. Each skill s=(name n, short description r, main content c [NL instructions, usage constraints, procedural guidance, SKILL.md-style markdown], executable payload pi [code/tools/auxiliary resources]). Distinct from declarative documents (RAG) and isolated tool APIs (function calling).
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus: a fixed, large, noisy skill corpus (26,262 skills) collected from the web (GitHub, Skills.sh, Hugging Face Hub) plus 636 manually-constructed gold skills. The agent does NOT write back new skills; the corpus is frozen for evaluation. (The paper discusses lifelong/growing skill libraries and skill evolution only as future-agenda directions, not implemented.)
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Mixed. Retrieval is evaluated as fixed top-k ranking (Recall@K, nDCG@K; K in {1,10}). For multi-label datasets (CHAMP, BigCodeBench) an instance maps to MULTIPLE gold skills, so coverage of the complete needed set matters (instances grouped by whether at least one gold appears in top-50). The paper argues retrieval should ultimately be judged by downstream UTILITY (whether retrieved candidates close the agent's capability gap) rather than ranking alone, and floats utility-aware / set-retrieval objectives as future work. Practical configs mostly inject top-1 (Full-Skill Injection) or select 1 from top-50 (LLM Selection).
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> N/A (not framed as CBR). Mapping to CBR phases: Retrieve = yes (skill retrieval); Reuse = yes (skill incorporation + application); Revise = no (skills are not adapted to the instance beyond the agent reading them; the paper deliberately preserves an 'application gap'); Retain = no (no write-back of new/used skills). So effectively [Retrieve, Reuse] only.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it positions SRA as a capability-centric counterpart to RAG ('RAG retrieves knowledge; SRA retrieves capabilities') and a generalization beyond tool-use/function-calling.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> skill (capability package): name + short description + procedural content + optional executable code/resources. Granularity is a reusable skill artifact (markdown SKILL.md-style), coarser than a single tool-API and richer than a passage. In Progressive Disclosure / LLM Selection, a compact index unit (name + description) is retrieved/exposed first, then the full skill content is loaded on demand.
- **index source**:
> Static corpus, offline-induced. 636 gold skills built via two-stage process (LLM draft then expert revision) from six source benchmarks, plus 25,626 web-collected distractor skills crawled from GitHub / Skills.sh / Hugging Face Hub, normalized to a unified document format. No online/test-time induction of the store.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat index over independently-indexed skills (sparse: BM25/TF-IDF term index; dense: BGE / Contriever vector index; plus a round-robin hybrid fusing BM25 and BGE ranked lists). No graph/hierarchy/cluster structure is used. (Structured organization—graphs, hierarchies, dependency structures over skills—is explicitly proposed only as future-agenda direction in §7.)
- **retriever type**:
> Compares sparse (BM25, TF-IDF), dense (BGE = BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5; Contriever = facebook/contriever-msmarco), hybrid (round-robin interleaving of BM25 and BGE ranked lists), and LLM-as-reranker (the target LLM reranks BM25 top-50). BM25 is the default first-stage retriever in the main experiments.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None / off-the-shelf. All first-stage retrievers are used without task-specific training (BM25, TF-IDF, pretrained BGE and Contriever checkpoints). The LLM reranker is a frozen, zero-shot prompted LLM (no fine-tuning). The paper proposes utility-aware / end-task-feedback-trained retrieval only as a future direction; it is not implemented here.
- **query construction**:
> Raw user query / task prompt is used directly as the retrieval query against skill descriptions and content. For LLM Selection and Progressive Disclosure, the LLM is additionally given the candidate metadata (name + description) and selects/loads skills (an LLM-driven selection over the retrieved pool), but the first-stage retrieval query is the raw input. No query decomposition or synthetic expansion in the main method (intermediate-reasoning-state-conditioned retrieval is future work).
- **query granularity**:
> Primarily task-level (one-shot at t=0): retrieval is issued once per query for Full-Skill Injection / LLM Selection. For agentic engines (Progressive Disclosure with up to 10 load rounds; ReAct / ReAct+Progressive-Disclosure on ToolQA), skill incorporation/loading is decided step/turn-level, but the underlying skill RETRIEVAL is typically the single top-50 pool; loading from that pool is interleaved with reasoning.
- **when to retrieve**: Retrieval (first-stage) is one-shot per query. Skill loading/incorporation is one-shot (direct injection) for Full-Skill Injection, and agent-initiated / iterative for Progressive Disclosure and ReAct-style engines (the model issues LOAD_SKILL actions on demand across turns).
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> First-stage retrieval: fixed schedule (always retrieve a candidate pool per query). Skill incorporation/loading trigger: agent-initiated request — in Progressive Disclosure the model decides whether and when to emit a 'LOAD_SKILL: <index>' action; in Full-Skill Injection injection is unconditional. A key empirical finding (RQ5/RQ6) is that this agent-initiated trigger is poorly calibrated: loading is neither reliably relevance-aware (independent of whether a gold skill is in the pool) nor need-aware (independent of whether the task exceeds native capability).
- **reranking**:
> Yes — LLM-based reranking as an optional second stage: given BM25 top-50 candidates, the target LLM reranks them by relevance (listwise LLM reranker, following Sun et al. 2023). 'BM25 + Rerank' is consistently the strongest retrieval strategy in both intrinsic retrieval (Tables 3/4) and end-to-end (Table 5). No trained cross-encoder; hybrid uses round-robin list interleaving (not RRF-weighted) of BM25+BGE.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Progressive disclosure / index-content separation: candidates are first exposed as compact metadata (name + description) and only the selected/loaded skill's full content is injected, limiting distractor exposure. LLM Selection narrows top-50 to a single skill before full injection. LLM reranking reorders candidates. No decompose-recompose, reason-in-documents distillation, or compression of skill content itself.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Gold skills are engineered offline: standardized markdown artifacts with name, one-line description, and procedural content stating what the capability is, when it applies, how to use it, and common pitfalls; executable resources (e.g., Python implementations of medical calculators) attached when needed. Construction enforces generality, correctness, and leakage control (preserving an 'application gap'). Web distractor skills are normalized to a unified document format. Retrievers index over this raw/normalized skill text; no synthetic-query augmentation or instruction-tuned skill embeddings are used.
- **index content separation**:
> Yes — a core design lever. LLM Selection and especially Progressive Disclosure separate a lightweight index (skill name + description catalog) from the heavy full skill content, which is loaded only on demand (OpenClaw-style progressive disclosure). This is shown to be more robust to distractors and to large top-k than Full-Skill Injection.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Static skill corpus (frozen for evaluation); no live tool sync / CRUD. Integration protocol for skill use is in-context injection plus an explicit LOAD_SKILL action protocol (Progressive Disclosure) and a ReAct tool-call loop for ToolQA. Models are served via OpenAI-compatible endpoints. Not MCP/RapidAPI-based; live-synchronized tool indices are future work.
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> No. Skills are treated as independently-indexed units with no modeling of inter-skill dependencies (prerequisites, alternatives, composition). The paper explicitly flags dependency/graph/hierarchy structure over skills as an open future-agenda direction (§7 'From unstructured skill collections to structured skill libraries').

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation / skill reuse: the full content of selected retrieved skill(s) is prepended to the task prompt ('Relevant Skill: {skill content} {original user prompt}'), and the agent applies the skill's methodology. Three practical strategies: Full-Skill Injection (inject top-1 / top-k full content), LLM Selection (pick 1 from top-50 metadata then inject), Progressive Disclosure (compact catalog + on-demand LOAD_SKILL). Oracle Skill (inject gold) is the upper bound; LLM Direct (no skill) is the lower baseline. No training-signal or latent-token injection (parametric skill augmentation is proposed as future work).
- **planning integration**:
> Mostly retrieve-then-solve with one-shot exemplar-style injection at solve time (direct engine). For Progressive Disclosure and ReAct-based engines, skill loading is interleaved per-step/per-turn within the reasoning/acting loop (the model can load skills across up to 10 rounds; ReAct interleaves tool calls). Not embedded in MCTS/tree search; no explicit hierarchical subtask decomposition of retrieval.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Per-answer for Full-Skill Injection and LLM Selection (single retrieval+injection then generate). Per-turn / per-tool-call for the agentic engines: Progressive Disclosure interleaves skill-loading decisions across reasoning turns; ReAct (ToolQA) interleaves tool calls with reasoning.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> N/A (not CBR). Retrieved skills are used as verbatim in-context procedural guidance (prepended) and applied by the LLM; there is no explicit case-adaptation/revision step (the benchmark deliberately preserves an application gap so the agent must still instantiate the procedure to the instance).
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Free-text procedural skill artifact (markdown: name, description, when/how-to-use, pitfalls) optionally bundled with executable program/code (e.g., Python calculator implementations). Injected verbatim as prompt text once loaded; in catalog form, represented as a compact name+description line.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Procedural skill / reusable capability package: distilled, generalized 'how-to-solve-a-class-of-problems' procedures (theorem application method, logic-pattern, tool-use workflow, medical-calculator procedure, math concept, software-library usage) rather than raw trajectories or single demonstrations. Deliberately written above the instance level (leakage control preserves an application gap so the agent must still instantiate the procedure).
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Controlled skill exposure / selective loading: Progressive Disclosure (expose only metadata, load full content on demand) and LLM Selection (narrow to one skill) reduce distractor interference and are shown markedly more robust than Full-Skill Injection under hard-negative distractors and large top-k. LLM reranking improves top-rank precision. However, the paper's central negative finding is that current LLMs lack reliable relevance-aware and need-aware loading, so robustness remains limited; no retriever-aware training or distractor-aware SFT is applied (these are proposed as future work).

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (with respect to a growing agent memory). The skill corpus is a static external skill-library used for retrieval, not an episodic/working memory the agent updates. No procedural/graph/latent memory is maintained across tasks.
- **write back**: False. The system does not store new experiences/cases/skills during evaluation; the skill corpus is fixed. Lifelong skill accumulation, offline skill refinement, and skill evolution are discussed only as future-agenda directions (§7).
- **online growth**: False. The retrievable store is frozen after offline construction; it does not grow at test time.
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back is implemented).
- **failure experience usage**:
> Not used. Failed trajectories/experiences are not stored or retrieved (no memory). The paper does analyze failure modes diagnostically (skill-loading hallucination; lack of need-awareness) and proposes feedback-driven skill debugging/refinement as future work, but does not implement failure-experience storage or contrastive success/failure retrieval.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A — the skill store is static (append-free after offline construction); no dedup-merge/delta-update/refine-overwrite/prune is performed at runtime. (Offline skill optimization/evolution is future-agenda only.)
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No. Retrieval/selection is a fixed similarity top-k (BM25/TF-IDF/BGE/Contriever/hybrid) plus an optional zero-shot LLM reranker and LLM-based selection; none is trained/RL-optimized. The skill-loading decision is made by a frozen LLM via prompting (not a learned policy). Training retrievers from end-task utility feedback and learned controlled-exposure policies are proposed as future research.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Single-agent; no cross-agent shared memory. However, the skill corpus is a SHARED external resource and skills are framed as plug-and-play reusable capabilities portable across agents/models. The benchmark is evaluated across multiple heterogeneous LLM families (Qwen3, Llama, Mistral, GLM-5.1, GPT-5.4) using the same corpus, but this is cross-model evaluation, not collaborative shared memory among concurrently running agents.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> SRA-Bench (newly introduced) = six capability-intensive source datasets re-purposed with gold-skill annotations: TheoremQA (747 inst / 320 skills), LogicBench (760 / 19), ToolQA (1,430 / 14), MedCalc-Bench (1,100 / 55), CHAMP (223 / 89, multi-label), BigCodeBench (1,140 / 139, multi-label). Total 5,400 instances, 636 unique gold skills, mixed with 25,626 web distractor skills into a 26,262-skill retrieval corpus (2.4% gold).
- **benchmark family**:
> Composite capability benchmark spanning QA/reasoning (TheoremQA, CHAMP competition math, LogicBench formal logic), tool-use (ToolQA), domain calculation (MedCalc-Bench), and code (BigCodeBench). Plus a skill-retrieval IR benchmark over a 26k-skill corpus (Recall@K / nDCG@K). Not aligned to a single prior family (Mind2Web/WebArena/ALFWorld/ToolBench/etc.).
- **baselines**:
> Skill-use strategies: LLM Direct (no skill, lower bound), Oracle Skill (gold injected, upper bound), Full-Skill Injection (BM25 top-1 full content), LLM Selection (pick 1 from BM25 top-50 metadata), Progressive Disclosure (OpenClaw-style on-demand loading from top-50). Retrievers compared: BM25, TF-IDF, BGE, Contriever, Hybrid (BM25+BGE round-robin), BM25+LLM Rerank. Models: Qwen3-4B/32B/235B-A22B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, Mistral-Small-3.1-24B-Instruct-2503; behavioral analyses (RQ5/RQ6) also include GLM-5.1 and GPT-5.4.
- **key metrics**:
> Retrieval: Recall@K and nDCG@K (K in {1,10}). End-task: rule-based exact-match/accuracy for TheoremQA/LogicBench/ToolQA/CHAMP/MedCalc-Bench; pass@1 via unit-test execution for BigCodeBench. Behavioral: skill-loading rate (% of instances where the agent incorporates >=1 valid skill before answering), and load-rate differences between gold-covered vs not (RQ5) and skill-free-correct vs skill-free-wrong (RQ6).
- **headline result**:
> Retrieval-based skill augmentation substantially improves agents but lags the oracle. Example (Llama-3.3-70B average over 6 datasets): LLM Direct 47.8 -> LLM Selection 59.2 -> Oracle Skill 64.4. The strongest practical config is LLM Selection (most stable retrieval-to-task transfer) and BM25+Rerank (best retriever); e.g. for Qwen3-235B, BM25+Rerank averages 62.6 vs BM25 56.2 and LLM Direct 53.3. Central negative finding: skill-loading rates are nearly identical regardless of whether a gold skill was retrieved (RQ5) or whether the task exceeds native capability (RQ6; Overall Delta Load = +0.1pp), revealing missing relevance- and need-awareness.
- **ablations**:
> RQ2 robustness: (a) controlled hard-negative distractors N in {0,2,4,8} with gold always present — Full-Skill Injection degrades sharply, Progressive Disclosure stays stable; brittleness does not vanish with model scale. (b) BM25 top-k sweep k in {1,2,4,8} — Full-Skill Injection improves only at small k then declines (inter-skill interference), Progressive Disclosure stable. RQ3: retriever comparison (Recall@1/10, nDCG@1/10) — no universal winner among sparse/dense; BGE generally > Contriever; hybrid mainly raises top-10 recall; LLM rerank strongest, not monotonic in scale. RQ4: end-to-end under 5 retrievers — BM25+Rerank most consistent gains but retrieval gains not strictly monotonic into task gains. RQ5/RQ6: relevance- and need-awareness of skill loading (gold-in-top-50 vs not; skill-free-correct vs wrong) — weak/absent for most models, sharper relevance-awareness only at 235B scale and in GLM-5.1/GPT-5.4.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Yes — a central contribution. SRA-Bench decomposes evaluation into skill retrieval (intrinsic Recall@K/nDCG@K, Tables 3/4), skill incorporation (skill-loading rate and relevance/need-awareness, Tables 6/7/8), and end-task execution (accuracy/pass@1, Tables 2/5), reported separately, enabling diagnosis of where the pipeline fails.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both. Outcome: end-task accuracy / pass@1. Process: intrinsic retrieval quality (Recall/nDCG), and especially incorporation-process metrics — skill-loading rate, relevance-awareness (load-rate gap for gold-in-top-50 vs not), and need-awareness (load-rate gap for skill-free-wrong vs correct). These process metrics drive the paper's main diagnostic findings.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Motivation is context-budget efficiency: enumerating all skills in-context fails to scale (context limits + selection-accuracy degradation), so retrieval narrows N=26,262 to k<<N. Progressive Disclosure / index-content separation reduce token exposure by loading full content only on demand (up to 10 load rounds). No explicit latency/API-cost/token-count numbers are reported; models served with 128K context, temperature 0.7. Parametric Skill Augmentation (turning head skills into plug-in parameters to amortize repeated injection cost) is proposed as future efficiency work.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Practical configs: Full-Skill Injection injects BM25 top-1 (or top-k in the sweep, k in {1,2,4,8}) full skill content; LLM Selection and Progressive Disclosure operate over a BM25 top-50 candidate pool but inject only the selected/loaded skill's full content (catalog = name+description). Distractor study uses gold + N in {0,2,4,8} hard negatives. Models served with 128K-token context. k is largely fixed per config; selection is precision-driven (pick 1) for LLM Selection.
- **survey scope and axes**:
> N/A (not a survey). It is a paradigm-formulation + benchmark + systematic empirical study organized around six research questions (RQ1 usefulness, RQ2 noise robustness, RQ3 retriever effectiveness, RQ4 retrieval->task transfer, RQ5 relevance-aware loading, RQ6 need-aware loading).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Size: 5,400 test instances, 636 manually-constructed gold skills, 26,262-skill retrieval corpus (636 gold + 25,626 web distractors; 2.4% gold). Construction: reverse-engineered — start from capability-intensive instances in six existing benchmarks, abstract source signals (theorem/logic-pattern/calculator/concept/library names) into standardized markdown gold skills via LLM draft + expert revision (principles: generality, correctness, leakage control with preserved application gap); distractors crawled from GitHub/Skills.sh/HF and normalized. Answer verifiability: rule-based exact-match for five datasets, unit-test execution (pass@1) for BigCodeBench. Difficulty signal: even strongest models stay well below Oracle Skill (e.g., best practical averages ~62-63 vs oracles ~64-68), and skill retrieval Recall@1 is low on several datasets (e.g., LogicBench/ToolQA/CHAMP), showing the benchmark is far from saturated.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Lewis et al. 2020) and its retrieve-then-read pipeline; classic retrievers BM25 (Robertson et al.), TF-IDF (Sparck Jones), Contriever (Izacard et al.), BGE/C-Pack (Xiao et al.); hybrid fusion (Bruch et al. 2023); LLM-as-reranker (Sun et al. 2023); agent-skill systems, esp. Voyager (Wang et al. 2023, growing skill library of executable programs) and OpenClaw-style SKILL.md progressive disclosure; tool-use/function-calling (Toolformer, Gorilla, ToolLLM, BFCL). Source datasets: TheoremQA, LogicBench, ToolQA, MedCalc-Bench, CHAMP, BigCodeBench.
- **contrasts with**:
> Classical knowledge-centric RAG (retrieves declarative evidence) — SRA retrieves executable capabilities judged by downstream utility, not just semantic relevance. Conventional tool-use/function-calling (assumes a small visible API set; e.g., Toolformer, Gorilla, ToolLLM/BFCL) — SRA retrieves from an open-ended out-of-context corpus of richer skill packages. In-context skill enumeration (OpenClaw/Codex/Claude Code SKILL.md injection) — shown not to scale. SkillsBench (Li et al. 2026) — evaluates whether curated skills help, but does not decompose retrieval/incorporation/application; SRA-Bench does.
- **lineage**:
> Group C (RAG + planning / agentic): a 2026 reframing of retrieval-augmentation as capability augmentation for agents — sits at the intersection of RAG, tool retrieval, and agent skills. Extends the static-corpus RAG/tool-retrieval line (BM25/dense/hybrid/rerank) to executable skill packages, introduces a decomposed retrieval/incorporation/application evaluation, and points toward utility-aware skill retrieval, structured skill libraries, and parametric skill augmentation as the forward lineage.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- venue

## D — Case-Based Retrieval for LM Planning (CBR + LLM)

<a id="item-generative-agents"></a>
### 62. Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior

2023  ·  UIST 2023  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03442)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2023
- **venue**: UIST 2023 (36th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology, UIST '23, San Francisco, CA). arXiv:2304.03442 (v1 submitted 7 Apr 2023, v2 6 Aug 2023). DOI 10.1145/3586183.3606763.
- **authors affiliation**: Joon Sung Park, Joseph C. O'Brien, Carrie J. Cai, Meredith Ringel Morris, Percy Liang, Michael S. Bernstein. Primary affiliation: Stanford University (Park, O'Brien, Liang, Bernstein); Google Research / Google DeepMind (Cai, Morris).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03442 (DOI: https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2304.03442; ACM proceedings DOI: https://doi.org/10.1145/3586183.3606763)
- **code url**: https://github.com/joonspk-research/generative_agents (official, Apache-2.0; the 'reverie' simulation backend + Django 'Smallville' frontend). ~21.5k stars.
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (single research repo, last updated Aug 2023; no continuously-maintained leaderboard or paper list).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Interactive multi-agent simulation of believable human behavior (embodied/social agents in a sandbox world). Not a QA/tool-use/code benchmark task; the agent must remember, reflect on, and plan day-to-day behavior in a Sims-like town (Smallville) and engage in social interaction.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, open-ended, MULTI-AGENT setting: 25 generative agents populate a sandbox game world (Smallville) and run continuously for two simulated days. Each agent is a frozen LLM (gpt-3.5-turbo / ChatGPT) wrapped with a memory-stream architecture; there is no task reward or ground-truth label and no model training. Supervision is essentially absent (no gradient updates); behavior is driven entirely by prompting the LLM with retrieved natural-language memories. Agents perceive each other and the environment, write every experience to a private growing memory stream, and use retrieval to condition planning and reaction. End users can also inject natural-language interventions (e.g. 'throw a Valentine's Day party').
- **what is retrieved**:
> experiences / memories: natural-language memory records from a per-agent 'memory stream'. These are (a) observations (events the agent directly perceives), (b) reflections (higher-level synthesized inferences the agent generates about itself/others), and (c) plans (intended future action sequences). The retrieved units are passed into LLM prompts to ground reactions, conversations, planning, and reflection.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> GROWING / episodic memory the agent writes. Retrieval targets each agent's own continuously-growing memory stream (a complete first-person natural-language log of experiences) rather than a static external corpus, KB, or API set. No fixed document corpus is indexed; the store expands at every time step of the simulation.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Top-k ranking by a composite relevance score, but k is budget-driven rather than a fixed rank: the highest-scoring memories are retrieved and as many as fit within the LLM context window are included. The objective is to surface the most pertinent memories for the current situation/query, not a learned ranking metric (no Recall@k/nDCG objective is optimized); there is no explicit minimal-set-completeness objective.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It describes a 'memory stream' + retrieval + reflection + planning architecture for believable agents, not a CBR cycle.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> experience record / memory object: a single natural-language memory entry in the memory stream. Each is a typed record (observation, reflection, or plan) with a timestamp, a most-recent-access timestamp, a natural-language description, and a precomputed embedding. Reflections are higher-abstraction memory objects that point to the evidence memories they were synthesized from (forming a tree of citations).
- **index source**:
> Growing memory, online/test-time-induced: the retrievable store is the agent's memory stream, which is constructed entirely online during the simulation (each perceived event, generated reflection, and plan is appended). Optionally seeded with an authored 'seed memory'/agent-history paragraph at initialization, but the bulk of the index grows at deployment time. Not an offline-induced static corpus.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat append-only list (a chronological 'memory stream') with per-record metadata (creation timestamp, last-access timestamp, importance score, embedding). Reflections add a shallow tree/citation structure (a reflection links to the lower-level memories it abstracts), but the primary store is a flat time-ordered log scored at query time. No external vector DB / graph DB / hierarchical category index.
- **retriever type**:
> Hybrid heuristic scorer (not a trained retriever): a hand-designed weighted combination of (i) dense relevance via cosine similarity between memory embeddings and the query embedding, (ii) recency via exponential time decay, and (iii) importance via an LLM-generated salience score. The dense-similarity component uses off-the-shelf LLM-produced embeddings; recency and importance are non-learned signals fused with the similarity score.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None (off-the-shelf / hand-designed). The retriever is not trained: relevance uses frozen pretrained embeddings; recency uses a fixed exponential-decay factor (0.995); importance uses the LLM's own 1-10 rating prompt. The three normalized components are combined with equal weights (alpha_recency = alpha_importance = alpha_relevance = 1) in the released implementation. No contrastive, LM-feedback, RL, or downstream-effectiveness training of the retriever.
- **query construction**:
> The query is a natural-language description of the agent's current situation. For reactions, the agent's current observation/situation is used as the query memory. For reflection, the agent first generates (via the LLM) a small set of salient high-level questions about its recent experiences, and each question becomes a retrieval query. Queries are embedded with the same embedding model used for memories. Query construction is thus situation-conditioned and, for reflection, LLM-synthesized.
- **query granularity**: Step/state-level (situation-level): a fresh retrieval query is constructed at each decision point as the agent's current situation/observation changes, and again whenever reflection is triggered or a plan must be (re)generated. Not a single one-shot query at t=0.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Iterative / event-driven: retrieval is invoked repeatedly throughout the simulation whenever the agent must (a) decide how to react to a newly perceived observation, (b) hold a conversation, (c) generate or revise a plan, or (d) reflect. Triggering is by the simulation loop and by the importance-sum reflection threshold, not by a learned router or token-confidence signal.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Event/schedule-driven plus a threshold heuristic for reflection: (i) for reaction/conversation/planning, retrieval is triggered when a new observation is perceived or a plan step is needed (agent/environment-initiated); (ii) reflection-triggered retrieval fires when the sum of importance scores of the agent's most-recent perceived events exceeds a fixed threshold (150 in the implementation, yielding ~2-3 reflections per day). No token-level confidence, attention-uncertainty, or learned complexity classifier.
- **reranking**: No separate second-stage reranker (no cross-encoder / RRF / instruction-tuned reranker). The single composite score (normalized recency + importance + relevance, equal weights) directly ranks memories; the top-scoring set within the context budget is selected.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Minimal: top-ranked memories are selected by the composite score and truncated to fit the LLM context window; there is no learned distillation, decompose-recompose, or distractor filtering of the retrieved memories themselves. Higher-level synthesis happens upstream via reflection (which compresses raw observations into abstract statements that are then stored and later retrievable), not as a post-retrieval refinement step.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tool/skill documents are indexed; the store holds natural-language experience memories, not API/tool descriptions).
- **index content separation**:
> Partial / implicit: each memory's natural-language description and its precomputed embedding serve as a lightweight retrievable key, and the full record text is loaded into the prompt only when selected. There is no explicit progressive-disclosure SOP-index-then-content design; it is a single-tier memory stream.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (not a tool-retrieval system; no RapidAPI/RESTful/MCP/function-calling tool registry or CRUD auto-sync). The 'live' aspect is that the memory stream is continuously appended during simulation.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tools/APIs and thus no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation: retrieved memories are inserted as natural-language context into LLM prompts that produce the agent's next action/reaction, conversation utterances, daily plan and its recursive decomposition, and reflection statements. Memory thus grounds moment-to-moment behavior, dialogue, and planning. No training signal or latent-token injection; the frozen LLM consumes retrieved memories as text.
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-plan with hierarchical, recursive top-down decomposition, plus retrieval-conditioned reactive replanning. At plan time the agent retrieves its summary description and prior-day summary to generate a broad-stroke daily agenda, then recursively decomposes it into hour-long chunks and then 5-15 minute fine-grained actions. During execution, each new observation triggers retrieval to decide whether to continue the plan or react/replan (and reflections feed back into subsequent planning). Retrieval is woven in at multiple planning levels (subtask/situation level), not a single one-shot exemplar injection and no tree search/MCTS.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-action / per-situation within the ongoing simulation rollout: retrieval is interleaved at each perceive-retrieve-act decision point and at each (re)planning and reflection event, rather than per-CoT-token. Effectively per-step over a long-horizon multi-day rollout.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> N/A for classic CBR adaptation. Retrieved memories are used as in-context natural-language evidence; the LLM synthesizes new behavior/reflections from them (LLM-prompted synthesis) rather than adapting a retrieved solution case verbatim. No execution-feedback case revision, critic-guided revision, or RL reuse-finetuning.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Raw natural-language memory text. Observations are raw event descriptions; reflections are LLM-distilled higher-level statements (still natural language); plans are natural-language future-action descriptions. Injected as plain text into prompts. No executable program/skill, structured note schema, or latent/soft tokens.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Mixed: raw observation records (low abstraction) AND distilled reflections/insights (high abstraction) coexist in the same stream and are retrieved together. Reflections are LLM-synthesized abstract inferences about self/others; observations are concrete single events; plans are procedural future-action descriptions.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Implicit only: the composite recency+importance+relevance score is intended to surface salient, pertinent memories and down-weight stale/irrelevant ones, reducing distractors in the prompt. There is no retriever-aware training, learned relevance evaluator, self-reflection-as-filter, or reason-in-documents refinement to explicitly guard against incorrect retrieved context.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: episodic (per-agent 'memory stream' of observations) augmented with a synthesized semantic/abstract layer (reflections) and a procedural layer (plans). Long-term, natural-language, persistent within a simulation; private per agent.
- **write back**: True. Every perceived observation is appended to the memory stream; the LLM-generated reflections and plans are also stored back as new memory objects, so the store accumulates both raw experience and synthesized abstractions during the simulation.
- **online growth**: Yes. The memory stream grows continuously at test/deployment time as the simulation runs (every observation, reflection, and plan is appended). The store is not frozen after any offline induction.
- **write back trigger**:
> Per-step / continuous for observations (every perceived event is written immediately). Reflections are written reflectively, triggered when the summed importance of recent events crosses the threshold (150), producing ~2-3 reflections/day. Plans are written when generated/decomposed and updated when the agent replans in reaction to observations. Writes are not conditioned on task success/failure (there is no task reward).
- **failure experience usage**:
> N/A in the success/failure sense: the simulation has no task-level success/failure signal, so memories are not labeled success vs. failure. All experiences (including socially 'unsuccessful' interactions) are stored uniformly as observations; there is no failure-specific corrective rule store or success-vs-failure contrastive retrieval.
- **memory evolution update**:
> Primarily append-only, with two evolving dynamics: (1) reflection creates new higher-level memory objects abstracted from existing ones (link-and-evolve / abstraction over time), and (2) each memory's 'last-access' recency timestamp is updated when retrieved, which mutates its future recency score. Existing memory descriptions are not overwritten, deduped, or pruned/forgotten in the released system.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No. Retrieval is a fixed, hand-weighted heuristic top-k over recency+importance+relevance (no M-MDP, soft Q-learning, RL, or any learned selection policy). The only 'learned' component is the pretrained embedding model used for the relevance term.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> No shared memory store: each of the 25 agents has its own PRIVATE memory stream. Information spreads between agents only via in-world social interaction (one agent's utterance becomes another agent's observation), i.e. emergent diffusion through conversation, not a shared retrievable index or cross-framework memory.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> No standard ML benchmark. Two custom human-grounded evaluations on the Smallville sandbox: (1) a controlled individual-agent evaluation in which agents are interviewed with questions across 5 categories (self-knowledge, memory, plans, reactions, reflections; five questions per category) and human raters rank believability via TrueSkill; (2) an end-to-end two-game-day community simulation of 25 agents measuring emergent social behaviors (information diffusion, relationship/network formation, coordination around a Valentine's Day party). Base LLM: gpt-3.5-turbo (ChatGPT).
- **benchmark family**:
> Custom interactive multi-agent social-simulation / believability evaluation (embodied-sandbox flavor, Sims-inspired 'Smallville'). Does not fit the standard QA / web / embodied-RL / tool / code / memory-benchmark families; closest descriptor: human-evaluated believability of LLM agent behavior in an open-ended simulated society.
- **baselines**:
> Internal ablations of the architecture serve as the comparison conditions, plus a human upper-bound: (a) Full architecture (observation + planning + reflection); (b) No reflection; (c) No reflection, no planning; (d) No observation, no planning, no reflection (minimal LLM agent); (e) Human Crowdworker condition (crowdworkers author the agent's responses given the same memory/role information) as a human-authored baseline.
- **key metrics**:
> Controlled study: TrueSkill skill rating (mean mu, std sigma) of believability from human pairwise comparisons over interview responses. End-to-end study: emergent social-behavior measures: information-diffusion counts/percentages, social-network density, and coordination success (fraction of invitees who attend). Qualitative behavior/believability analysis and failure-mode discussion.
- **headline result**:
> In the controlled believability evaluation (TrueSkill, human pairwise ranking), the full generative-agent architecture ranked highest (mu = 29.89, sigma = 0.72), and ablating components monotonically reduced believability: No reflection mu = 26.88; No reflection + no planning mu = 25.64; No observation + no planning + no reflection (memory-less) mu = 21.21. The full architecture also outperformed the Human Crowdworker condition (mu = 22.95, sigma = 0.69). End-to-end, from a single user-seeded intent the agents autonomously spread a Valentine's-party invitation to 13 of 25 agents (4% to 52%), spread Sam's mayoral candidacy to 8 of 25 (4% to 32%), grew network density from 0.167 to 0.74, and coordinated so that 5 of 12 invited agents actually showed up to the party.
- **ablations**:
> The central result IS an ablation: a TrueSkill comparison of Full architecture (mu=29.89) vs. No reflection (mu=26.88) vs. No reflection + no planning (mu=25.64) vs. No observation + no planning + no reflection (mu=21.21), demonstrating that observation/memory, planning, and reflection each contribute critically and additively to believability; the memory-less condition is worst and even below the human-crowdworker baseline (mu=22.95). Qualitative failure analysis notes issues such as memory retrieval missing relevant records, embellishment/hallucination of memories, and overly formal/cooperative ChatGPT-style speech. (No intrinsic Recall@k retrieval ablation.)
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> No. Intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG / completeness) are not reported separately. Evaluation is entirely on downstream behavior quality (TrueSkill believability ranking) and emergent social outcomes; retrieval quality is only discussed qualitatively in the failure analysis.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both, in a behavior-quality sense: the controlled study scores the quality/believability of the agent's responses (a process/behavior judgment via interviews) rather than a single task outcome, and the end-to-end study measures emergent process outcomes (diffusion, relationship formation, coordination). There is no reasoning-faithfulness or step-wise retrieval-accuracy metric.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Discussed qualitatively rather than tabulated: the authors note that running the simulations with many agents over multiple days was time-consuming and costly (each agent issues many LLM calls per simulated step; 'could be somewhat costly, especially when there are many agents'). No explicit per-call token cost, latency table, or accuracy-vs-cost curve is reported.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Budget-capped top-k: memories are ranked by the composite score and the highest-ranked are included up to the LLM's context-window limit (no fixed numeric k is mandated by the method; selection is reranked-then-truncated to fit the prompt). Recursive planning produces fixed-grain decompositions (daily -> hour-long -> 5-15 minute chunks). No adaptive precision-driven k.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A as a released benchmark, but for completeness: the evaluation world is a custom Sims-inspired sandbox ('Smallville') with 25 agents simulated over two game days; the controlled study uses interview questions in 5 categories (5 questions each) with human TrueSkill ranking; the released repo ships base simulations (base_the_ville_n25 with 25 agents and a 3-agent base) and authored seed-memory CSV history files.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Large language models as the cognitive core (ChatGPT / gpt-3.5-turbo); chain-of-thought and LLM prompting; prior LLM-agent and reasoning-and-acting work (e.g. ReAct-style reason-act loops, social-simulacra / interactive-agent work by the same group); cognitive-architecture notions of memory, retrieval, and reflection; cosine-similarity dense retrieval over text embeddings; TrueSkill ranking for human-judgment aggregation; The Sims as the interaction/world-design inspiration.
- **contrasts with**:
> Rule-based / scripted NPC and finite-state-machine game agents (which lack open-ended believable behavior); cognitive-architecture agents requiring hand-built symbolic procedures; and plain LLM agents without long-term episodic memory, retrieval, planning, or reflection (its own ablated memory-less condition, which performs worst). Also contrasts with reinforcement-learned game agents that optimize a task reward, whereas this work has no reward and targets believability.
- **lineage**:
> Foundational work in the experience/episodic-memory lineage of retrieval-augmented LLM agents (group D, case-based / experience-based planning): it popularized the 'memory stream' with retrieval scored by recency + importance + relevance plus reflection, a template later adopted/extended by many memory-augmented and experience-replay agent frameworks (e.g. reflection/insight-distillation agents, generative-agent simulations, and LLM agent memory modules). Sits upstream of works that turn experience retrieval into a learned policy or add success/failure-contrastive memory.

<a id="item-autoguide"></a>
### 63. AutoGuide (Automated Generation and Selection of Context-Aware Guidelines for LLM Agents)

2024  ·  NeurIPS 2024  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.08978)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: NeurIPS 2024 (Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems); preprint arXiv:2403.08978
- **authors affiliation**:
> Yao Fu (University of Michigan), Dong-Ki Kim (LG AI Research; equal contribution), Jaekyeom Kim, Sungryull Sohn, Lajanugen Logeswaran, Kyunghoon Bae (LG AI Research), Honglak Lee (University of Michigan and LG AI Research). Primary affiliations: University of Michigan and LG AI Research.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.08978

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Sequential decision-making for LLM agents: embodied household tasks (ALFWorld), web navigation / web shopping (WebShop, WebArena-Reddit), and multi-modal real-world web navigation (GitHub, Google Flights, Coursera).
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive sequential decision-making (POMDP) with prompt-based (closed-source) LLM agents. AutoGuide operates in two phases: (1) an OFFLINE knowledge-distillation phase that mines a fixed set of context-aware guidelines from a pre-collected offline dataset of trajectories (collected via ReAct/Reflexion runs or human demonstrations); and (2) an interactive TEST-time phase where the frozen guideline store is retrieved per state to augment the agent prompt. Single-agent. Supervision is weak/automatic: trajectory returns (rewards/success) are used to form contrastive success/failure pairs; no gradient training of the agent or a retriever is performed. Train and test tasks are non-overlapping.
- **what is retrieved**: State-conditional natural-language guidelines (conditional 'when context X, do Y' rules) distilled from contrasting success/failure trajectory pairs; each guideline is keyed by a generated natural-language 'context' (a concise description of the agent's current state).
- **retrieval grounding**:
> GROWING/episodic memory that is induced offline then FROZEN. The retrievable store (the context-aware guideline dictionary G) is constructed from the agent's own offline experiences (not a static external KB/docs/API corpus), but it is fixed before test time and does not grow during deployment.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k selection: after keying into the guideline dictionary by the matched context, an LLM selection module returns the top-k most relevant guidelines (k held fixed, e.g. k=2 in main experiments; k=3 best in the WebShop ablation). Not a completeness-recovery or precision-driven variable-size objective.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> Retrieve: yes (context-keyed dictionary lookup + LLM top-k selection). Reuse: yes (selected guidelines injected into the action-generation prompt). Revise: no (no per-case adaptation/revision of a retrieved guideline at test time; guidelines used as-is, though an optional grounding module re-aligns guidelines for the out-of-domain transfer experiment). Retain: no at test time (the store is frozen; retention only happens once during offline induction). Flags: [Retrieve=yes, Reuse=yes, Revise=no, Retain=no(at test time)].
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False. The paper frames itself around 'context-aware guidelines' distilled from contrastive offline experiences and does not explicitly cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner or describe itself as case-based reasoning; it realizes CBR-like retrieve-and-reuse mechanisms under the 'guideline' framing. (Included in group D_case_based_planning by the survey, not by the authors.)

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> guideline-rule: a single concise conditional natural-language guideline ('When on the Reddit main page, if you want to navigate to a specific forum, you should click ...'), organized in a dictionary under a generated state 'context' key. Effectively a state-aware rule abstracted from contrastive (success vs failure) sub-trajectories.
- **index source**:
> Growing memory, offline-induced then frozen: guidelines are induced offline from contrastive trajectory pairs in a training task set (e.g., first 100 ALFWorld training tasks; 50 sampled WebShop training tasks) and stored in a context-keyed dictionary; the store is not extended at test time.
- **index structure topology**:
> Metadata/context-keyed dictionary: a dictionary G mapping a generated natural-language 'context' (key) to the set of guidelines applicable in that context (value). An LLM-based context-matching step deduplicates/merges semantically equivalent contexts during construction. No vector index, no graph; a context-keyed associative store.
- **retriever type**:
> LLM-as-retriever. Retrieval is performed entirely by LLM modules: a context-identification module abstracts the current trajectory into a context, an LLM context-matching check maps it to an existing dictionary key, and an LLM guideline-selection module ranks/selects the top-k guidelines. No BM25/dense embedding retriever is used.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None (off-the-shelf / prompted LLM). No retriever is trained. The guideline-generation pipeline is supervised only indirectly by trajectory return labels used to form contrastive success/failure pairs (R(tau+) > R(tau-)); the context-identification, context-matching, and selection modules are zero/few-shot-prompted LLMs, not learned retrievers.
- **query construction**:
> Thought/state-conditioned: at each timestep the context-identification module M_context summarizes the current partial trajectory tau_:t (observations + actions so far) into a concise natural-language 'context'. That generated context is used as the lookup key; the selection module additionally conditions on the full current trajectory tau when ranking candidate guidelines.
- **query granularity**: Step/state-level: a query (context) is constructed at each timestep of the test trajectory (per-state retrieval), not once at t=0.
- **when to retrieve**: Iterative: retrieval (context identification + dictionary lookup + top-k guideline selection) is performed at every timestep of the test episode (fixed per-step schedule).
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed schedule: retrieval is triggered at each timestep. The only gating is whether the generated current context matches an existing context key in the dictionary (if no match, an empty guideline set is returned and the agent proceeds without guidelines); there is no uncertainty/confidence/learned-router trigger.
- **reranking**:
> Yes (LLM-based selection acts as a reranker): when more than k guidelines exist under the matched context, the LLM guideline-selection module M_select is prompted to choose the top-k most relevant guidelines for the current trajectory. It is an LLM/instruction-based selector, not a cross-encoder.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Rerank/select only: the LLM selection module filters the candidate guideline set down to top-k relevant ones conditioned on the context and current trajectory. No decomposition, compression, or reason-in-documents distillation at test time (the distillation into concise guidelines happens earlier, during offline induction).
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tool/skill descriptions are indexed; retrieved units are distilled guidelines, not tool docs).
- **index content separation**: Partial: the dictionary uses a lightweight generated 'context' key to index into heavier guideline content, so context matching acts as a coarse index before the LLM selects the actual guideline text. Not a formal progressive-disclosure / SOP-index-then-content design.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no live tool index or integration protocol; static frozen guideline store).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation: the matched context and the selected top-k context-aware guidelines are inserted into the LLM agent's action-generation prompt so the agent conditions its next action on the retrieved guidance. No training-signal use, no skill execution, no latent-token injection.
- **planning integration**:
> Per-step interleaved retrieve-then-act within the interactive rollout: at each timestep the agent identifies the current context, retrieves/selects relevant guidelines, and then generates an action conditioned on them (built on a ReAct/SoM base agent). Not inside MCTS/tree search; not one-shot plan-time exemplars.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-tool-call / per-action within a rollout (each environment step): retrieval and guideline injection occur once per agent action step (each ReAct think-act decision).
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> Verbatim ICL reuse of the retrieved guideline (injected as-is into the prompt); no per-case revision at test time. Exception: in the out-of-domain transfer experiment (WebShop->WebArena-Shopping) an additional GPT-4-Turbo grounding module re-aligns the WebShop guidelines to the new domain's observations (LLM-prompted adaptation).
- **retrieved item representation**: Distilled strategy-as-guideline: concise free-text conditional natural-language rules (a context description plus an actionable guideline), injected as text into the prompt.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: State-aware guideline/rule: a distilled, context-conditional natural-language rule (higher abstraction than a raw trajectory or single demonstration), describing the state/context in which a recommended action applies.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Context-conditioned selection as the primary robustness mechanism: by retrieving only guidelines whose generated context matches the current state and then LLM-selecting top-k relevant ones, AutoGuide avoids flooding the agent with irrelevant guidelines (the failure mode of ExpeL's all-guidelines prompting). The top-k cap also limits distractor overload (ablation shows k too large causes 'overthinking'). No dedicated retriever-aware training or self-reflection relevance evaluator.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: workflow/procedural-style guideline library (a context-keyed dictionary of distilled natural-language guidelines). Not episodic raw-trajectory memory, skill-library of executable programs, graph, or latent memory.
- **write back**: False at deployment. The guideline dictionary is written once during the offline induction phase and is frozen at test time; the system does not store new experiences/guidelines online during evaluation.
- **online growth**: No: the retrievable guideline store does not grow during test-time deployment; it is fixed after offline induction (test tasks are non-overlapping with the offline/training tasks).
- **write back trigger**:
> Offline induction only (effectively 'never' during deployment): guidelines are written during the offline phase from contrastive success/failure trajectory pairs; no per-step, on-success, reflective, or human-validated write-back occurs at test time. (Reflexion, when combined, adds intra-task feedback to the prompt but is not written into the guideline store.)
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success+failure contrastive: guidelines are extracted by contrasting a higher-return (success) trajectory tau+ against a lower-return (failure) trajectory tau- for the same task, identifying the deviation timestep and generating a guideline that captures the desirable vs undesirable action in that context. Failures are used contrastively (not stored as standalone corrective rules and not success-only).
- **memory evolution update**:
> Dedup-merge during construction: an LLM context-matching step merges contexts describing the same situation expressed differently (reuse existing key) before appending the new guideline; otherwise append-only. No delta-update, refine-overwrite, or forgetting/pruning after writing.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No: retrieval/guideline selection is prompted LLM-based context-keyed lookup plus LLM top-k selection, not a learned/RL-optimized retrieval policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: Single-agent private store. The guideline dictionary is built and used by one agent pipeline. (It generalizes/transfers across domains in the out-of-domain experiment, but there is no multi-agent or cross-framework shared-memory mechanism.)

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: ALFWorld; WebShop; WebArena (focused on the Reddit domain for main experiments; WebArena-Shopping for out-of-domain transfer); real-world multi-modal websites: GitHub, Google Flights, Coursera.
- **benchmark family**: embodied (ALFWorld); web (WebShop, WebArena / WebArena-Reddit / WebArena-Shopping, and real-world multi-modal websites GitHub/Google Flights/Coursera).
- **baselines**:
> ReAct; ExpeL (non-contextual all-guidelines prompting; guidelines-only variant); Reflexion (and ReAct+Reflexion, ExpeL+Reflexion, AutoGuide+Reflexion combinations); ReAct with varying numbers of in-context examples (1/2/4/6-shot); Set-of-Marks (SoM) GPT-4V agent for the multi-modal real-world web tasks.
- **key metrics**: Task success rate (SR, %) and, for WebShop, average reward; multi-modal real-world web results reported as success counts (e.g., x/30).
- **headline result**: On WebArena-Reddit (GPT-4-turbo base), AutoGuide reaches 47.1% success rate vs ExpeL 21.8% and ReAct 8.0%. Also: ALFWorld SR 79.1% (vs ExpeL 59.0%, ReAct 54.5%) and 88.1% with Reflexion; WebShop reward 73.4 / SR 46% (vs ReAct 66.4/30%, ExpeL 60.9/35%).
- **ablations**:
> (1) Component ablation on WebShop: ReAct 30% -> ReAct+CI (context identification only) 36% -> ReAct+GES (guideline extraction+selection without contexts) 37% -> full AutoGuide (CI+GES) 46%, showing both context summaries and contextual guideline selection are needed. (2) Top-k ablation on WebShop: k=0 (ReAct) 30%, k=1 42%, k=2 46%, k=3 47% (best), k=5 43% (degrades from overthinking). (3) ReAct in-context-example count on WebShop (1/2/4/6-shot: 30%/35%/37%/38%; AutoGuide 46% beats all and avoids token-limit blowup). (4) Out-of-domain transfer: guidelines from WebShop applied to WebArena-Shopping raise SR from 10.2% (ReAct) to 20.4% (AutoGuide, with a GPT-4-Turbo grounding module). (5) AutoGuide+Reflexion complementarity (inter-task vs intra-task knowledge).
- **evaluation decoupling**: No: only end-to-end task metrics (success rate / reward) are reported. No intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k, nDCG, context-match accuracy, or guideline-completeness) are reported separately.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Primarily outcome metrics (final task SR / reward). Process is examined only qualitatively via trajectory case studies (Figure 4 comparing ReAct/ExpeL/AutoGuide action selection) rather than quantitative step-wise retrieval/planning accuracy.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k: top-k guideline selection with k=2 in the main ALFWorld and WebShop experiments (Tables 7-8); WebShop ablation sweeps k in {0,1,2,3,5} with k=3 best. Budget is implicitly capped by selecting a small k and by injecting only the matched context's guidelines rather than the whole store.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (primary method paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A as a benchmark contribution; evaluation sizes noted: ALFWorld extracted from first 100 training tasks; WebShop induced from 50 sampled training tasks and evaluated on 100 test tasks (max 15 actions, top-3 search results); WebArena-Reddit and WebArena-Shopping (98 shopping tasks with a product in the intent template); real-world web: GitHub 30 tasks, Google Flights 20, Coursera 20.

**Relations**

- **builds on**: ReAct (reasoning+acting base agent); ExpeL (offline natural-language guideline extraction from experiences); Reflexion (test-time self-feedback, used complementarily); Set-of-Marks (SoM) prompting for multi-modal GPT-4V agents.
- **contrasts with**:
> ExpeL (explicitly positioned against: ExpeL provides ALL guidelines non-contextually whereas AutoGuide retrieves only state/context-relevant guidelines; AutoGuide reports substantial improvements over ExpeL's non-contextual all-guidelines prompting); demonstration-based in-context learning / many-shot ReAct (raw-trajectory exemplars hit context limits and plateau); plain ReAct (no offline knowledge); Reflexion (intra-task self-feedback vs AutoGuide's inter-task guideline knowledge, shown complementary).
- **lineage**:
> Group D (case-based / experience-distillation planning). Sits in the lineage of experience/guideline-distillation methods for LLM agents (ExpeL -> AutoGuide), advancing from non-contextual all-guidelines prompting to state-conditional retrieval of distilled guidelines; complementary to self-reflection lines (Reflexion) and ReAct-style interactive agents.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- code_url
- cost_efficiency_tradeoff

<a id="item-cbr-rag"></a>
### 64. CBR-RAG (Case-Based Reasoning for Retrieval Augmented Generation in LLMs for Legal Question Answering)

2024  ·  ICCBR 2024  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.04302)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**:
> ICCBR 2024 -- 32nd International Conference on Case-Based Reasoning (Merida, Mexico, July 1-4, 2024). Proceedings published as 'Case-Based Reasoning Research and Development', Springer LNCS/LNAI vol. 14775, pp. 445-460 (DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-63646-2_29). arXiv:2404.04302 (submitted 4 Apr 2024).
- **authors affiliation**:
> Nirmalie Wiratunga, Ramitha Abeyratne, Lasal Jayawardena, Kyle Martin, Stewart Massie, Ikechukwu Nkisi-Orji (Robert Gordon University, Aberdeen, UK -- primary affiliation); Lasal Jayawardena, Ruvan Weerasinghe (Informatics Institute of Technology, Sri Lanka); Anne Liret, Bruno Fleisch (BT France). Lead author: Nirmalie Wiratunga (Robert Gordon University). Funded by SFC International Science Partnerships Fund.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.04302 (peer-reviewed: Springer LNCS vol. 14775, pp. 445-460, DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-63646-2_29)
- **code url**: https://github.com/rgu-iit-bt/cbr-for-legal-rag (official; Jupyter Notebook code + datasets; created 2024-04-01, last push 2025-02-20; contains code/ and code/resources/ with the ALQA-derived casebase and 32-case test set).
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (the official code repo above is the only maintained artifact; no separate leaderboard/paper-list).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: QA -- legal question-answering (generative legal QA over Australian legislation/case-law), framed as a knowledge-intensive, expert-reliant RAG task requiring evidence to validate generated answers.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-agent, non-interactive RAG for legal QA. Given a user legal question Q, retrieve contextually relevant prior cases from a fixed casebase (built from the Australian Open Legal QA dataset) and augment the LLM prompt with that context to generate a validated answer. The case is formalised as a tuple c=<Q,S,E,A> (Question, Support/evidence snippet, Entities extracted from S, Answer). Supervision: the casebase is GPT-4-synthesised QA-support triplets (weak/synthetic supervision); embedding encoders are off-the-shelf (not fine-tuned to the ALQA corpus). Inference is one-shot retrieve-then-generate; the generator (Mistral-7B) is deliberately distinct from the GPT-4 used to build the casebase, simulating consulting an alternative expert.
- **what is retrieved**: cases -- prior legal QA cases represented as <Question, Support snippet, Entities, Answer> tuples (problem-solution-support cases). The retrieved context can be either the support text only or the full case (Q,S,E,A).
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus / casebase: a fixed offline-built casebase of 2,084 cases derived from the Australian Open Legal QA (ALQA) dataset. The casebase is not written to or grown during inference (no episodic write-back). It is framed as CBR's non-parametric memory but is effectively a static evidence base for this work.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k ranking objective: similarity-based k-Nearest-Neighbors retrieval returns the top-k cases (k swept over prime numbers 1-37; k=3 selected as best, k=1 as comparative baseline). Retrieval quality is measured by F1-score for retrieval@k against a ground-truth relevant set (each test case derived from a known pair of parent cases). It is a ranking/relevance objective rather than minimal-set completeness or precision-driven variable-size recommendation, though the parent-pair design gives it a 2-relevant-case recall flavor.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve, -, -, -] -- only the Retrieve phase of the CBR cycle is operationalised. The paper explicitly states it integrates 'the initial retrieve-only stage of the CBR cycle' with its indexing vocabulary and similarity knowledge containers. Reuse is realised loosely as injecting retrieved cases as LLM context (the paper calls it 'case reuse'), but there is no explicit Revise (adaptation) or Retain (write-back) phase implemented.
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> True. The work explicitly frames itself as Case-Based Reasoning and is built on CBR knowledge-container theory (indexing vocabulary, similarity knowledge containers -- Richter/Aamodt-Plaza lineage), citing classical legal CBR systems HYPO (Ashley 1991) and CATO (Aleven & Ashley 1997), textual CBR (Bruninghaus & Ashley 2001; Wiratunga et al. 2004), and the hybrid CBR-IR legal retrieval work of Rissland & Daniels (1995). Published at ICCBR.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: case (problem-solution-support): a structured tuple c=<Q,S,E,A> (Question, Support evidence snippet, Entities, Answer). The query key is the question Q (encoded as intra and inter embeddings); the retrieved payload is the support text (rho=1) or the full case Q,S,E,A (rho=2).
- **index source**:
> Static, offline-induced casebase: built once from the ALQA dataset (2,124 GPT-4-generated question-support-answer triplets; 40 removed for offensive content -> 2,084 cases). Each case is expanded with GPT-3.5-turbo-extracted named entities. No online/test-time induction; the store is frozen after offline construction.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat vector index with multi-field (dual) embeddings: each case is indexed by several neural embedding vectors -- intra-embedding f(Q) of the question, and inter-embeddings g(Q), g(S), g(E) of question/support/entities. Retrieval is kNN over cosine similarity, optionally a weighted combination across these fields (hybrid). No graph/hierarchical topology; it is a flat metadata-keyed (per-attribute) vector store.
- **retriever type**:
> Dense (off-the-shelf embedding kNN). Three encoders compared: BERT, LegalBERT (BERT further pre-trained on 12GB UK/EU/US legal text), and AnglEBERT (AnglE angle-optimized contrastive embeddings on top of BERT). Retrieval is cosine-similarity top-k (kNN). No BM25/sparse, no learned re-ranker, no generative tool-as-token retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None for this work's training -- all three encoders are used off-the-shelf and are NOT fine-tuned to the ALQA legal corpus. The encoders' own pre-training signals differ: BERT/LegalBERT use self-supervised MLM + NSP (LegalBERT additionally pre-trained on legal documents); AnglEBERT uses a contrastive (Siamese-style, angle-optimized) loss on positive/negative text pairs. The hybrid similarity weights (w1=0.25, w2=0.40, w3=0.35) are hand-set, not learned. The paper notes contrastive (AnglE) embeddings outperform self-supervised LegalBERT and flags fine-tuning with contrastive self-supervision as future work.
- **query construction**:
> Raw user question encoded directly. Dual encoding of the same query Q: (1) intra embedding f(Q) = encode the question text as-is (empty prompt cue) for attribute-to-attribute (question-to-question) matching; (2) inter embedding g(Cue(Q)) where a fixed prompt cue 'Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: {Q}' is prepended to bias the embedding toward IR-style matching against support/entity fields. No query decomposition or sub-query generation.
- **query granularity**: Task-level (one-shot at t=0): a single retrieval per input question; the whole question is the query, encoded once (as intra and inter forms) before generation. No per-step or trajectory-level re-retrieval.
- **when to retrieve**: One-shot: retrieval is performed once per query before answer generation (retrieve-then-generate). No iterative/active/adaptive re-retrieval.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule: retrieval is always performed once per incoming question at the start of the pipeline (no confidence/uncertainty/learned-router/reflection trigger). The No-RAG baseline simply skips retrieval entirely.
- **reranking**: None. The top-k=3 cases by (possibly weighted) cosine similarity are passed directly to the generator; no cross-encoder/RRF/instruction-tuned reranking stage. The hybrid weighting is a fusion of similarity scores at retrieval time, not a second-stage reranker.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Minimal / selection only: post-retrieval the system selects what part of each retrieved case to inject -- support-text-only (rho=1) vs full-case Q,S,E,A (rho=2). No decompose-recompose, distillation, distractor filtering, or compression of the retrieved cases. The paper notes combining multiple neighbours into a coherent prompt is challenging and defers case-aggregation strategies to future work.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tools/APIs; retrieved units are legal QA cases, not tool documents).
- **index content separation**:
> Partial: lightweight embedding vectors (the indexing vocabulary) are separated from heavy case content (the full Q/S/E/A text) which is loaded into the prompt only after the kNN match. This follows CBR's knowledge-container separation (indexing vocabulary vs case content) but it is not a progressive-disclosure SOP-index-then-content mechanism in the agentic-tool sense.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index / external API protocol; static casebase, no CRUD auto-sync / RapidAPI / MCP / function-calling).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tools; no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation ('case reuse'): the top-k retrieved cases (support text only, or full Q,S,E,A tuples) are concatenated into the LLM prompt as context C, forming the enriched prompt p=(Q,C). Mistral-7B then generates the answer conditioned on this context. The paper terms this CBR-style 'case reuse', but adaptation is implicit/LLM-internal (no explicit case-revision step).
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-generate (one-shot exemplars at generation time): retrieval happens once up front; the k retrieved cases condition a single answer generation. No planning loop, no per-step interleaving, no tree search; legal QA is single-turn answer generation rather than multi-step planning.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer / per-query: a single retrieval and a single conditioned generation produce one answer per question; retrieval is not woven per CoT-step or per token.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> Verbatim ICL exemplar injection (implicit adaptation only): retrieved cases are inserted into the prompt as context and the LLM (Mistral-7B) implicitly 'reuses'/adapts them when generating the answer. There is no explicit CBR Revise step (no execution-feedback revision, critic-guided revision, or RL reuse-finetuning); adaptation is whatever the frozen LLM does internally with the injected cases.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Raw case text injected into the prompt: either the support evidence snippet only, or the full case as a (Question, Citation/Support, Answer) tuple set, concatenated as context. No distilled strategy, workflow, executable program, or latent-soft tokens -- the literal prior cases are injected.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Single demonstration / case at the problem-solution-support level (question + supporting evidence + entities + answer). Not a distilled strategy, abstracted workflow, or procedural skill -- literal prior solved legal QA cases are retrieved and shown as exemplars.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Limited / representation-level: robustness is pursued through better case-matching representations rather than explicit noise filtering. (1) Dual intra/inter embeddings and hybrid weighting [0.25,0.40,0.35] aim to surface the most on-point cases across question/support/entity fields; (2) AnglE contrastive embeddings mitigate cosine-similarity saturation to better discriminate relevance; (3) dataset validation (manual review, removing 40 offensive/hallucinated cases) cleans the casebase. There is no per-retrieval relevance evaluator, self-reflection, reason-in-documents refinement, or distractor-aware training.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (in the experiential/learning sense). The casebase is a static non-parametric case memory used for retrieval only; it is not an episodic/skill/workflow memory that grows or is updated. Best characterised as a static CBR case store.
- **write back**: False -- the system does not store new experiences/cases/answers back into the casebase during inference. The Retain phase of the CBR cycle is explicitly out of scope (retrieve-only integration).
- **online growth**: No -- the casebase is frozen after offline construction (2,084 cases) and does not grow at deployment/test time.
- **write back trigger**: Never -- no write-back mechanism is implemented (Retain phase not realised).
- **failure experience usage**:
> None / success-only context: only the curated (synthetic, validated) positive QA cases form the retrievable store. No failed/negative trajectories are stored or retrieved. (AnglE's contrastive pre-training used positive/negative pairs, but that is encoder pre-training, not failure-experience memory in this system.)
- **memory evolution update**: None -- the casebase is static/append-nothing at runtime; stored cases are never mutated, merged, delta-updated, refined, or pruned during deployment (the only pruning, removing 40 offensive cases, occurs once during offline casebase construction).
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No -- retrieval is a fixed similarity top-k (kNN cosine over fixed embeddings) with hand-set hybrid weights. Case selection is not an RL/learned policy; the encoders are off-the-shelf (not even fine-tuned for this task).
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No -- single-system private casebase; no multi-agent or cross-framework experience sharing. (The casebase author GPT-4 and the answer generator Mistral-7B are different models, but this is a generator/expert separation, not shared memory across agents.)

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> Australian Open Legal QA (ALQA) dataset (umarbutler/open-australian-legal-qa on HuggingFace), synthesised by GPT-4 from the Open Australian Legal Corpus; 2,124 question-support-answer triplets -> 2,084-case casebase after removing 40 offensive cases. A bespoke 32-case test set was created by pairing casebase cases sharing common legal acts and generating new questions with Mistral-7B (released as Ramitha/open-australian-legal-qa-test). Underlying corpus: Open Australian Legal Corpus (785 unique legal acts; e.g. Federal Court Rules, Civil Aviation Regulations 1998, Corporations Act 2001).
- **benchmark family**: QA -- domain-specific (legal) open-ended generative question answering with evidence grounding. Not in the standard multi-hop/web/embodied/tool/code/memory/decision-RL families; it is a single-domain legal QA evaluation on a self-constructed casebase + test set.
- **baselines**:
> No-RAG (LLM with no case retrieval; Mistral-7B answering from parametric memory only) is the primary baseline comparator. Within CBR-RAG, ablative comparisons across encoders (BERT vs LegalBERT vs AnglEBERT), weighting schemes (question-only [1,0,0], support-only [0,1,0], entities-only [0,0,1], hybrid [0.25,0.40,0.35]), context type (support-only vs full-case), and k (k=1 vs k=3). No external system baselines beyond No-RAG.
- **key metrics**:
> (1) Retrieval: F1-score for retrieval@k (relevant set = the parent pair of cases each test case was derived from), swept over prime k in 1-37. (2) Generation: cosine similarity between the Mistral-embedding of the generated answer and the reference answer (semantic similarity to ground truth). Statistical significance via ANOVA + one-tailed paired T-tests.
- **headline result**:
> Hybrid AnglEBERT with weights [0.25,0.40,0.35] and k=3, injecting full cases, achieved the best generation quality at 0.9141 mean cosine similarity to the reference answer, vs 0.8967 for the No-RAG baseline -- a 1.94% average improvement.
