This setting significantly outperforms both No-RAG and Hybrid LegalBERT (k=3) at the 95% confidence level (and Hybrid BERT k=1 at 90%) by one-tailed T-test. For retrieval, Hybrid AnglEBERT [0.25,0.40,0.35] at k=3 was the best-performing retrieval configuration by F1@k.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Encoder comparison: AnglEBERT > BERT and LegalBERT for both retrieval and generation; notably AnglEBERT (general contrastive embeddings) beats LegalBERT (domain-pre-trained, self-supervised), suggesting contrastive optimisation matters more than legal-domain pre-training when not fine-tuned to ALQA. LegalBERT embeddings were more densely clustered (higher baseline similarity), suggesting weaker discrimination. (2) Weighting/component ablation: question-only [1,0,0], support-only [0,1,0], entities-only [0,0,1] vs hybrid [0.25,0.40,0.35]; hybrid weighting gives the best retrieval F1. (3) Context type: full-case context (Q,S,E,A) generally outperforms support-text-only context in hybrid setups. (4) k ablation: k=3 outperforms k=1; all hybrid variants beat No-RAG. (5) Generation table (Table 4): No-RAG 0.8967; best Hybrid AnglEBERT k=3 full-case 0.9141.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Yes -- intrinsic retrieval quality (F1-score for retrieval@k, with a separately constructed parent-pair relevance ground truth, visualised as a heat-map over encoders/weights/k) is reported and analysed separately from the end-to-end generation quality (answer-to-reference cosine similarity). k=3 was selected from the retrieval analysis before the generation experiments.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Mostly outcome-oriented but with a decoupled retrieval-process metric: the final outcome is answer semantic similarity (cosine to reference); the intermediate retrieval process is scored by F1@k. There is no reasoning-faithfulness or step-wise reasoning-quality metric; a qualitative domain-expert evaluation of answers is named as a future step.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Not quantified in cost/latency terms. The method adds one kNN retrieval over a small 2,084-case casebase plus prompt augmentation per query; no API-cost, latency, or token-count numbers are reported. The accuracy gain is modest (~1.94% mean cosine over No-RAG) and the No-RAG baseline is already high (0.8967) because Mistral's parametric memory covers many legal questions. Encoders are off-the-shelf (no fine-tuning cost).
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k: k=3 retrieved cases injected (k=1 as comparative baseline), selected from a retrieval sweep over prime k in 1-37. Context is either support-text-only or the full Q/S/E/A tuple per case. No explicit token budget or budget-capped truncation is reported; the paper notes that combining multiple neighbours into a coherent prompt is challenging (motivating future case-aggregation work).
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Casebase: ALQA -> 2,084 cases (from 2,124 GPT-4-synthesised question-support-answer triplets, minus 40 offensive cases), each augmented with GPT-3.5-turbo-extracted entities; 785 unique legal acts, 57% of cases reference no legal act. Test set: 32 questions (from 35 generated, pruned to 32), constructed by selecting casebase case pairs sharing common legal acts and using Mistral-7B to synthesise new questions answerable only by combining both parent cases (so test questions are reasonably disjoint from any single casebase case); manually reviewed; released as Ramitha/open-australian-legal-qa-test. Answers are open-ended free text (verified by cosine similarity to a reference answer, not exact-match). Best-system signal: best generation cosine 0.9141 vs No-RAG 0.8967, indicating a relatively narrow improvement margin / difficult-to-beat parametric baseline.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Lewis et al. 2020); CBR knowledge-container theory and the CBR cycle (Aamodt & Plaza / Richter; HYPO -- Ashley 1991; CATO -- Aleven & Ashley 1997; textual CBR -- Bruninghaus & Ashley 2001, Wiratunga et al. 2004); hybrid CBR-IR legal information retrieval (Rissland & Daniels 1995); ensemble CBR-neural for content planning (Upadhyay & Massie 2022); BERT (Devlin et al. 2018); LegalBERT (Chalkidis et al. 2020); AnglE angle-optimized embeddings (Li & Li 2023) and Siamese networks (Bromley et al. 1993); Mistral-7B (Jiang et al. 2023); ALQA / Open Australian Legal Corpus (Butler 2024).
- **contrasts with**:
> No-RAG (LLM relying solely on parametric memory, prone to hallucination and lacking provenance). Standard RAG whose retrieval does not exploit CBR's varying matching strategies across content segments (the paper's central critique -- conventional RAG retrieval ignores CBR indexing-vocabulary / similarity-knowledge-container structure). Self-RAG (Asai et al. 2023) and other sophisticated fact-identifying RAG mechanisms are cited as related retrieval approaches. Domain-pre-trained LegalBERT is contrasted against contrastive AnglEBERT (contrastive optimisation found more important than domain pre-training when not fine-tuned).
- **lineage**:
> Group D (case-based planning / case-based reasoning lineage). A concrete CBR-RAG reference: operationalises the CBR Retrieve stage (indexing vocabulary + similarity knowledge containers; intra/inter/hybrid dual embeddings) inside an LLM RAG pipeline for legal QA. Sits in the CBR-for-RAG sub-lineage alongside CBR-KBQA (retrieve-reuse-revise for semantic parsing) but is retrieve-only, explicitly ICCBR-grounded, and a touchstone for later case-based agentic-RAG work; followed by the authors' own ensemble-LLM CBR legal follow-up (Abeyratne, ICCBR 2025).

<a id="item-expel"></a>
### 65. ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners

2024  ·  AAAI 2024  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10144)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: AAAI 2024 (Proceedings of the 38th AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, vol. 38 no. 17, pp. 19632-19642; Oral). Preprint arXiv:2308.10144 (cs.LG/cs.AI/cs.CL), submitted 20 Aug 2023, last revised 20 Dec 2024 (v3).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10144
- **code url**: https://github.com/LeapLabTHU/ExpeL

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: LLM-agent sequential decision-making / planning across knowledge-intensive QA (HotpotQA), embodied household tasks (ALFWorld), web interaction/shopping (WebShop), and fact verification (FEVER, transfer). Spans QA, embodied, and web/decision-making domains.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent, gradient-free (no parameter updates) experiential learning. Two phases: (1) an offline TRAINING phase where the agent (a ReAct planner wrapped with Reflexion) autonomously gathers success/failure experiences via trial-and-error over a collection of training tasks, storing trajectories in an experience pool and distilling natural-language insights; (2) an EVALUATION phase where, on unseen tasks, the agent makes a single attempt (no retries) augmented with the extracted insights plus top-k retrieved similar successful trajectories. Deterministic, text-observation environments. Supervision is limited to a few manual fewshot demonstrations per environment (taken from ReAct/Reflexion); environment success/failure signals drive experience collection and insight extraction. A transfer-learning variant moves insights from a source domain (HotpotQA) to a target domain (FEVER) via insight 'finetuning' with a few target demos.
- **what is retrieved**:
> (1) Successful past trajectories (full ReAct trajectories) from the agent's own experience pool, retrieved as semantically similar fewshot in-context demonstrations; and (2) extracted natural-language insights (cross-task guidelines/best-practices) which are not retrieved per-query but concatenated wholesale into the task specification. So retrieval proper targets self-generated successful experiences/trajectories; insights are abstracted experiences injected directly.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> GROWING/episodic memory the agent writes itself: the experience pool is populated by the agent's own trial-and-error trajectories during the training phase (seeded with manual fewshot examples). It is a self-generated episodic store rather than a static external corpus. Note: the pool is grown offline during training and then frozen for the single-attempt evaluation phase, so growth is offline-induced, not test-time streaming.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k ranking objective: a fixed number k of most task-similar successful trajectories is retrieved (k set per environment, e.g. HotpotQA k=6, ALFWorld k=2, WebShop k=2, FEVER k=3). No completeness/minimal-set objective and no variable-size precision-driven recommendation; selection is fixed-k maximum-inner-product nearest-neighbor.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve: yes (task-similarity kNN recall of successful trajectories), Reuse: yes (trajectories as fewshot exemplars; insights as guidelines), Revise: partial (insights are revised/edited via ADD/EDIT/UPVOTE/DOWNVOTE during training, but retrieved trajectories themselves are reused verbatim and not adapted per-case at solve time), Retain: yes (writes successful trajectories to the experience pool and abstracted insights to the insight store during training)].
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False. The paper frames itself as experiential learning / experience-replay / off-policy learning (citing Lin 1992, Watkins & Dayan 1992, Sutton & Barto) and does NOT cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner or use the term case-based reasoning; it realizes CBR-like Retrieve/Reuse/Retain mechanisms under experiential-learning and RAG framing.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> full trajectory: a complete successful ReAct trajectory (thought-action-observation sequence for a whole task) stored in the experience pool and retrieved as a fewshot exemplar. The complementary insight unit is a guideline-rule (natural-language insight), but that is injected directly rather than retrieved per-query.
- **index source**:
> Growing memory, offline-induced: the retrievable store (Faiss experience pool) is built from the agent's self-collected successful trajectories during the offline training phase (initialized with manual fewshot examples F_manual), then used during the single-attempt evaluation phase. Not a static external corpus; not online/test-time-grown during evaluation.
- **index structure topology**: Flat vector index: a Faiss vectorstore of trajectory embeddings (all-mpnet-base-v2) queried by kNN maximum-inner-product task similarity. No graph or hierarchical/cluster organization. Insights are kept as a separate flat list with importance counts (not a vector index).
- **retriever type**: Dense (embedding-based) kNN retriever: all-mpnet-base-v2 sentence embeddings over a Faiss vectorstore, ranked by maximum inner-product (task-description) similarity. Off-the-shelf, not learned.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> none (off-the-shelf): the retriever uses a pretrained all-mpnet-base-v2 embedder with a fixed kNN/maximum-inner-product similarity over task descriptions; there is no contrastive fine-tuning, LM-feedback, RL, or downstream-task-effectiveness training of the retriever. (Insights, by contrast, evolve via LLM-driven ADD/EDIT/UPVOTE/DOWNVOTE operations, but that is not retriever training.)
- **query construction**:
> Raw task input: the evaluation task specification/description is embedded and used as the query key to find maximum-inner-product similar successful training trajectories. No query decomposition, intent extraction, or synthetic expansion for retrieval. (Insights are not query-conditioned; the full insight list is concatenated.)
- **query granularity**:
> task-level (one-shot at t=0): similar-trajectory retrieval is performed once per evaluation task at the start, conditioned on the task description; the retrieved fewshot exemplars are fixed for the whole episode. (The paper notes that in the reason-similarity ablation, retrieval could be done per-reasoning-step, but the default ExpeL uses task-level retrieval.)
- **when to retrieve**:
> one-shot: retrieval of similar successful trajectories happens once at the beginning of each evaluation task and the result is used as fixed fewshot exemplars; the agent does a single attempt with no retries during deployment. Insights are likewise applied once (concatenated into the prompt).
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> fixed schedule: retrieval is triggered unconditionally at the start of every evaluation task (top-k similar successful trajectories are fetched and inserted into the prompt). There is no confidence/uncertainty/learned-classifier/reflection-token trigger; retrieval is not agent-initiated mid-episode in the default setup.
- **reranking**: None. After kNN maximum-inner-product retrieval the top-k trajectories are used directly as fewshot examples; no cross-encoder, RRF, or instruction-tuned reranking stage.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> None at retrieval time: retrieved successful trajectories are injected verbatim as fewshot exemplars without compression, decomposition, distillation, or distractor filtering. (Separately, insights undergo an LLM-managed importance-count voting/EDIT process at write/extraction time, but that is abstraction of experiences into insights, not post-retrieval refinement of fetched trajectories.)
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (not a tool-retrieval method; the only tool is a fixed Wikipedia Docstore search API for HotpotQA/FEVER, not a retrievable tool index).
- **index content separation**: N/A. No separation of a lightweight retrievable index from heavy on-demand content; full successful trajectories are both indexed (via embeddings) and loaded as exemplars; the full insight list is loaded wholesale.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (not a tool-retrieval system; environment interaction via ReAct action APIs and a Wikipedia Docstore API, not MCP/RapidAPI/RESTful tool stores).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> prompt augmentation: the evaluation prompt is the base ReAct prompt augmented by (1) the concatenated list of extracted natural-language insights appended to the task specification, and (2) the top-k dynamically-retrieved similar successful trajectories used as fewshot in-context demonstrations. No fine-tuning / latent injection; everything is in-context.
- **planning integration**:
> one-shot exemplars at plan time: ExpeL augments a base ReAct planning agent. At evaluation, insights + top-k similar successful trajectories are assembled once into the ReAct prompt, and the agent then runs ReAct (think-act-observe) for a single attempt. Retrieval is plan-/task-level (retrieve-then-plan); there is no per-step re-retrieval, no MCTS/tree search, and no hierarchical subtask decomposition in the default method.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: per-answer (per-task/per-episode): retrieval and insight injection occur once per task before the ReAct rollout; the retrieved exemplars and insights remain fixed throughout the multi-step ReAct reasoning of that episode. Not per-CoT-step or per-tool-call (default).
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> Mostly verbatim ICL exemplar reuse for retrieved trajectories (retrieved successful trajectories are injected as-is as fewshot demonstrations). The abstraction/adaptation happens at the insight level: an LLM extracts/edits cross-task insights via ADD/EDIT/UPVOTE/DOWNVOTE from success/failure comparisons, providing LLM-prompted generalization rather than per-case solution adaptation. No execution-feedback case revision at solve time in the default single-attempt setting.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Two surface forms: (a) raw successful ReAct trajectories (thought/action/observation text) injected as fewshot exemplars; and (b) distilled natural-language guidelines/insights (free-text rules such as 'consider the answer might be in the observations already made') concatenated into the task specification.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Mixed: retrieved trajectories are raw full trajectories (concrete demonstrations), while the injected insights are distilled cross-task strategies/guidelines (high-level abstractions). The paper explicitly frames these as the two complementary human learning modes: storing/recalling specific successful trajectories vs. extracting high-level generalizable insights.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Insight-level robustness via an importance-count voting mechanism: each insight starts with importance count 2 and is incremented by UPVOTE/EDIT and decremented by DOWNVOTE, with insights removed at count zero, so that suboptimal/misleading insights (even from suboptimal successful trajectories) are pruned. Using gpt-4-0613 (vs gpt-3.5-turbo) for insight extraction reduces hallucination. Retrieval-side robustness comes from selecting maximum-task-similarity successes (ablation shows random sampling significantly hurts). The paper also found that adding raw reflections into insight extraction hurt performance due to hallucination, so reflections are excluded.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: episodic (experience pool of successful trajectories in a Faiss vectorstore) combined with a distilled natural-language insight/guideline store (a semantic/procedural-knowledge list). Primarily episodic-experience memory plus an abstracted-insight memory.
- **write back**:
> Yes. During the training phase the agent writes its trial-and-error trajectories into the experience pool B (all attempt trajectories are ingested; only successful ones are retrievable as demonstrations) and writes/edits cross-task insights into the insight list. No new entries are written during the single-attempt evaluation phase.
- **online growth**:
> No (not at deployment/test-time): the experience pool and insight list grow only during the offline training phase via trial-and-error; they are frozen for the single-attempt evaluation. The paper notes that for truly lifelong learning, extra retrieval over a growing insight set might be needed, framing test-time growth as future work.
- **write back trigger**:
> on-success-and-failure (during training): the experience pool ingests every finished trajectory (both successes and failures) at each Reflexion trial; successful trajectories become retrievable demonstrations and success/failure pairs feed insight extraction. Insight writes are reflective/comparison-driven: the insight-extraction LLM ADDs/EDITs/UPVOTEs/DOWNVOTEs insights when shown fail/success pairs or lists of L successes. No writes during evaluation.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success+failure used, but differently: (1) for retrieval/demonstrations, only SUCCESSFUL trajectories are recalled; (2) for insight extraction, FAILED trajectories are explicitly contrasted with successful ones for the same task (success/failure pairs) to surface mistakes and best practices, so failures are leveraged to derive corrective guidelines rather than retrieved as exemplars. Reflexion reflections on failures drive re-attempts during training but are deliberately NOT fed into insight extraction (found to hurt).
- **memory evolution update**:
> Insight store: link-and-evolve / refine via LLM operators ADD, EDIT, UPVOTE, DOWNVOTE with an importance count; insights are edited/merged/upvoted/downvoted and pruned (forget) when count hits zero, i.e. dynamic mutation beyond append-only. Experience pool: append-only (trajectories are added during training; no described merge/overwrite of stored trajectories).
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No. Trajectory selection is fixed dense kNN top-k by maximum-inner-product task similarity using an off-the-shelf embedder; it is not an RL/value-optimized or learned retrieval policy. The agent is described as analogous to off-policy/experience-replay learning, but the selection rule itself is a fixed similarity heuristic.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent private memory (one ExpeL agent's own experience pool and insights). The work does demonstrate cross-TASK and cross-DOMAIN transfer (HotpotQA->FEVER insight transfer) but not sharing across multiple agents or heterogeneous agent frameworks.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> HotpotQA (100 distractor dev-split validation tasks, Wikipedia Docstore API search), ALFWorld (134 solvable household tasks across 6 types: put, clean, heat, cool, look, puttwo), WebShop (100 tasks, online-shopping environment with reward score r in [0,1]), and FEVER (fact verification, used as transfer-learning target from HotpotQA). Same task subsets as ReAct/Reflexion; four-fold validation (train on one half, evaluate on the other and vice versa).
- **benchmark family**: QA / multi-hop (HotpotQA), fact-verification QA (FEVER), embodied (ALFWorld), web (WebShop).
- **baselines**:
> ReAct and Act (Yao et al. 2023) as the main prompt-based planning agents (all use gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 at evaluation); Imitation Learning (IL) results taken from the ReAct paper (gradient-based); Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023) for the cross-task / task-reattempt comparisons (R0-R3); plus internal restricted variants ExpeL (insights-only) and ExpeL (retrieve-only). Transfer baselines: Act, ReAct, and ExpeL Transfer w/o Task Demos.
- **key metrics**:
> Success rate (%) - exact match for HotpotQA and FEVER, task completion within step budget for ALFWorld, purchasing item matching all attributes for WebShop; WebShop also reports mean reward score r in [0,1]; ALFWorld reports per-task-type success-rate breakdown. Auxiliary statistics: average thoughts/actions/observations, invalid actions, and token counts per trajectory.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Learning-mode synergy (Fig.5/Tab.5): insights-only vs retrieve-only success rates are 36%/31% on HotpotQA and 50%/55% on ALFWorld (37%/38% SR and 0.675/0.67 reward on WebShop), with full ExpeL beating both, showing insight extraction and similarity retrieval are complementary and synergistic (insights dominate on HotpotQA, retrieval on ALFWorld). (2) Amount/diversity of experience (Fig.6): an agent extracting insights only from the initial fewshots has no advantage over ReAct; more autonomously-gathered experience helps, and Reflexion-gathered success/failure diversity beats ReAct-only gathering. (3) Insight-extraction ablations (Tab.3, HotpotQA): LLM-learned insights > hand-crafted insights > ReAct; adding raw reflections into insight extraction HURTS (hallucination); gpt-4-0613 insight extractor > gpt-3.5-turbo-0613. (4) Retrieval ranking (Tab.3, ALFWorld): task-similarity (ExpeL, 59.0) > reason-similarity > random sampling (significant drop), justifying task-similarity ranking. (5) Task reattempts (Tab.2): ExpeL+Reflexion improves with rounds (ALFWorld 59.0->64.2 over R0-R3) and beats ReAct+Reflexion at every round.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No. Only end-to-end task success rates (and WebShop reward) are reported; no intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG / retrieval completeness) are reported separately, since retrieval here is trajectory recall for fewshot prompting rather than a ranked retrieval benchmark.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome (success rate / reward). Some process-level statistics are reported in the appendix (average number of thoughts, actions, observations, invalid actions, and tokens per trajectory) and qualitative behavioral analyses (hypothesis formulation, world-model belief update, self-correction), but no formal step-wise reasoning-faithfulness or trajectory-quality metric.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Reports token overhead vs accuracy in the appendix (Tab.6): ExpeL uses more tokens per trajectory than ReAct due to injected insights+exemplars (e.g. HotpotQA ~4310 vs ReAct ~1320 tokens; ALFWorld ~2857 vs ~2051; WebShop ~3291 vs ~2575), trading extra context tokens for higher success. Emphasized efficiency angles: no parameter updates / no GPU finetuning, no need for large human-labeled datasets, and a single evaluation attempt with no test-time retries (unlike Reflexion's repeated trials). No explicit dollar/latency figures given.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k, budget-capped: max fewshot examples k per environment - HotpotQA k=6, ALFWorld k=2, WebShop k=2, FEVER k=3 (plus k_reflections=2); number of success examples L per insight-extraction batch is 8 (HotpotQA, ALFWorld) or 4 (WebShop). The full extracted insight list is concatenated (kept under the LLM token limit; paper notes insight retrieval may be needed for lifelong settings). Selection is fixed-k retrieved-then-used (no adaptive/precision-driven k).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (uses existing benchmarks: HotpotQA 100 distractor-dev tasks; ALFWorld 134 solvable tasks (6 types); WebShop 100 tasks; FEVER for transfer; four-fold validation, same subsets as ReAct/Reflexion).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> ReAct (Yao et al. 2023, base think-act-observe planning agent and fewshot prompts/templates) and Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023, used to gather diverse success/failure experiences via self-reflective retries during training); semantic-similarity in-context example selection (Liu et al. 2022 KATE-style); experience replay / off-policy RL framing (Lin 1992; Watkins & Dayan 1992; Sutton & Barto 2018); Faiss vectorstore (Johnson et al. 2019) and all-mpnet-base-v2 embeddings (Song et al. 2020); RAG for decision-making (Humphreys et al. 2022).
- **contrasts with**:
> Finetuning-based LLM-agent learning (resource-heavy, needs parametric access, can hurt generalization); Reflexion (intra-task self-improvement via repeated retries on the SAME task, lacks cross-task memory) - ExpeL emphasizes inter-task/cross-task learning with a single evaluation attempt and no retries; standard RAG that retrieves gold/external examples - ExpeL instead retrieves its OWN self-generated experiences; imitation-learning baselines.
- **lineage**:
> Group D (case-based / experience planning): an experience/insight-memory LLM agent in the lineage of feedback-driven planning agents (ReAct -> Reflexion -> ExpeL), pioneering gradient-free cross-task experiential learning that retrieves self-generated successful trajectories plus distilled natural-language insights at inference. A canonical predecessor for later experience/case-based retrieval-augmented agents (e.g., trajectory-bootstrapping and guideline/insight-distillation methods).

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- authors_affiliation
- headline_result

<a id="item-synapse"></a>
### 66. Synapse: Trajectory-as-Exemplar Prompting with Memory for Computer Control

2024  ·  ICLR 2024  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.07863)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: ICLR 2024 (The Twelfth International Conference on Learning Representations); also accepted at NeurIPS 2023 Foundation Models for Decision Making Workshop; preprint arXiv:2306.07863 (cs.AI), v1 Jun 2023 / v3 Jan 2024.
- **authors affiliation**: Longtao Zheng, Rundong Wang, Xinrun Wang, Bo An. All from Nanyang Technological University (NTU), Singapore.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.07863
- **code url**: https://github.com/ltzheng/Synapse (project page: https://ltzheng.github.io/Synapse ; OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=Pc8AU1aF5e ; trajectories released on Google Drive).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: web / computer-control LLM agents: in-context-learning agents that perceive computer states (HTML of webpages) and emit keyboard/mouse actions to complete tasks; evaluated on GUI/web-navigation suites MiniWoB++ and Mind2Web.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent sequential decision-making for computer control. An LLM agent receives a natural-language task plus raw computer states (HTML), and outputs actions (code-style on MiniWoB++: click_xpath/type/press/click_option/move_mouse; CLICK/TYPE/SELECT on Mind2Web). The LLM is frozen and used purely via in-context learning (no gradient training). Supervision is a fixed offline pool of human demonstrations (MiniWoB++: demos for 48 of the tested 64 tasks; Mind2Web: the 1,009-task training set). MiniWoB++ is interactive/closed-environment with 50 episodes per task; Mind2Web is a static offline dataset scored against human-annotated ground truth across cross-task / cross-website / cross-domain generalization splits. No self-correction loop is used (unlike RCI/AdaPlanner). The exemplar memory is built once offline from the demo/training pool and is frozen at test time.
- **what is retrieved**: demos / trajectories: complete demonstration trajectories (sequences of abstracted-state + action pairs) plus their associated state-abstraction prompts, retrieved as few-shot exemplars; keyed by task metadata embeddings.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> GROWING/episodic-style memory in form but functionally STATIC at deployment: the exemplar memory is an episodic store of demonstration trajectories that the agent constructs offline from the demonstration/training pool and then retrieves from; it does NOT grow during test-time deployment (no write-back of new trajectories). Effectively a static, offline-induced experience corpus.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k ranking by similarity (arg top-n over memory by Euclidean distance). On MiniWoB++ it retrieves the top-3 metadata matches then takes the most-common matched task and uses all of that task's exemplars (a small task-keyed set, ~3.45 exemplars/task avg). Not a completeness or precision-driven variable-size objective; selection size is largely fixed/budget-driven.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve: yes (similarity search over trajectory memory), Reuse: yes (trajectories injected as few-shot exemplars), Revise: no (no case adaptation/self-correction; exemplars used largely verbatim), Retain: no (no online write-back of new cases)]. Implements the Retrieve+Reuse half of the CBR cycle only.
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False. The paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it presents trajectory-as-exemplar prompting + exemplar memory under in-context-learning / retrieval-augmented prompting terminology. It nonetheless realizes CBR-style Retrieve+Reuse over full-trajectory cases.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> full trajectory: a complete demonstration trajectory expressed as <task, observation, action, ..., observation, action> over abstracted states, together with the matching state-abstraction prompt. The injected unit is a whole multi-step trajectory (case), not a single demo or step.
- **index source**:
> Static, offline-induced store. The memory D=(K,V) is built once by encoding all task metadata (K = embedding vectors) with their corresponding state-abstraction prompts and exemplary trajectories (V) from the human demonstration pool (MiniWoB++ 48 tasks) / Mind2Web training set (1,009 tasks). It is not grown at test time.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat vector index: a fixed-size array of metadata embeddings stored in a vector database (Faiss), each metadata key mapped to its corresponding exemplars (state-abstraction prompts + trajectories). Metadata-keyed flat similarity index; no graph or learned hierarchy. (Implicit task-level grouping on MiniWoB++ via most-common-match heuristic.)
- **retriever type**: dense (off-the-shelf): embed task metadata with OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 and perform nearest-neighbor similarity search (Euclidean distance) over the Faiss vector index. No BM25, no learned/generative retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**: none (off-the-shelf). The embedding model (text-embedding-ada-002) is fixed/pretrained and not fine-tuned; retrieval is fixed top-n similarity over task-metadata embeddings with no contrastive/LM-feedback/RL training of the retriever.
- **query construction**:
> Intent/metadata extraction: the query key is the embedding of task metadata. On MiniWoB++ the metadata = task description concatenated with the initial state (from five random seeds of the 48 selected tasks); on Mind2Web the metadata = website name + domain + task description. Raw metadata is encoded directly (no synthetic query expansion or decomposition).
- **query granularity**: task-level (one-shot at t=0): exemplars are retrieved once per task at the start, conditioned on the task metadata; the same retrieved exemplars are then reused across all steps of the episode (state abstraction itself is per-step but uses the already-retrieved prompts).
- **when to retrieve**: one-shot: a single similarity-search retrieval is performed per task at the beginning; no iterative or uncertainty-triggered re-retrieval during the rollout.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: fixed schedule: retrieval is triggered once, deterministically, when a new task arrives (Synapse first retrieves relevant exemplars from memory by similarity search before acting). No confidence/attention/learned-classifier/reflection trigger.
- **reranking**: None (beyond the similarity top-n itself). On MiniWoB++ there is a lightweight majority-vote heuristic over the top-3 retrieved metadata matches (take the most common matched task, then use all its exemplars), but no cross-encoder or learned reranking stage.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> None at retrieval time. Retrieved trajectories are injected as few-shot exemplars largely verbatim. (Refinement happens at the STATE level, not the retrieval level: state abstraction filters task-irrelevant content from raw states before/within prompting, but it processes the current state, not the retrieved exemplars.)
- **index content separation**:
> Partial: the index stores lightweight task-metadata embeddings (K) separated from the heavier content (V = state-abstraction prompts + full trajectories) loaded on retrieval. This is a metadata-key vs content separation rather than a progressive-disclosure SOP-index-then-content scheme.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (not a tool-retrieval method; environment interaction is via MiniWoB++/Mind2Web action APIs and code execution, not a live tool index/MCP).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> prompt augmentation: retrieved complete trajectories (plus their state-abstraction prompts) are placed into the LLM prompt as few-shot exemplars; the LLM is then prompted with these exemplary trajectories together with the current trajectory (task + previous observation-action pairs) to generate the next action (or temporally abstracted multi-action block).
- **planning integration**:
> one-shot exemplars at plan/act time with per-step interleaved acting: retrieved trajectory exemplars condition a closed-loop act loop. At each step the LLM (1) abstracts the raw state into a clean observation (few-shot, explicit <state,observation> or implicit <task,code>), then (2) given the exemplary trajectories + current history generates the next action(s); the action is executed, the new observation appended, and the loop continues until task completion or max steps. Trajectory-as-exemplar prompting lets the LLM emit temporally abstracted multi-action blocks (e.g., type(ls)+press(enter)) before querying a new state. No tree search / MCTS / self-correction.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> per-tool-call / per-action-block within a rollout: action generation is interleaved per environment step, but TaE prompting encourages temporally abstracted blocks of consecutive actions emitted between state queries (querying a new state only when necessary). Exemplar retrieval itself is per-task (per-answer), done once.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> Verbatim ICL exemplar: retrieved trajectory cases are reused as few-shot exemplars without explicit adaptation/revision (no LLM-prompted case rewriting, no execution-feedback revision, no critic). Generalization to novel tasks relies on the LLM implicitly adapting similar retrieved trajectories rather than an explicit Revise step.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> raw trajectory (state-abstracted): the injected exemplar is a free-text/code interleaved trajectory <task, observation, action, ...> where observations are the abstracted (cleaned) states and actions are code-style calls (agent.type(...), agent.click_xpath(...)) on MiniWoB++ or CLICK/TYPE/SELECT on Mind2Web. Not a distilled strategy or latent token; it is the demonstration trajectory itself.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> raw (state-abstracted) full trajectory / single demonstration of the matched task: the retrieved unit is a complete demonstration trajectory over abstracted states (a worked example), not a distilled strategy, guideline, skill, or workflow. State abstraction reduces per-state verbosity but the trajectory remains a concrete example.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> (1) State abstraction filters task-irrelevant information from raw HTML states (explicit <state,observation> pairs, implicit <task,code> parsing, or zero-shot fallback if code errors), reducing distractor content and the 'lost-in-the-middle' long-context degradation; (2) code-style action grounding constrains generation; (3) the most-common-match retrieval heuristic on MiniWoB++ guards against a single mismatched metadata neighbor. No retriever-aware training or self-reflection relevance evaluator. A 2% failure on click-tab-2-hard is attributed to exemplar mismatch.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: episodic exemplar memory: a vector store D=(K,V) of demonstration-trajectory exemplars (with state-abstraction prompts) keyed by task-metadata embeddings; episodic/demonstration store rather than skill-library, workflow, procedural, graph, or latent memory.
- **write back**:
> No (effectively read-only at deployment). The memory is populated once offline from the human demonstration pool / Mind2Web training set; the agent does not write newly generated successful trajectories back into memory during test-time. (The paper notes future-work human-in-the-loop additions for customization, but no automatic online write-back is implemented.)
- **online growth**: No. The retrievable store is frozen after offline construction from the demonstration/training pool; it does not grow during deployment/test-time.
- **write back trigger**:
> never (no online write-back). Memory is built offline by encoding all demonstration metadata and storing the corresponding exemplars; no per-episode success/failure/reflective write occurs at test time. Discussed as future work: combining the memory module with human intervention for user customization and task adaptation.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success-only / not stored as negative cases. Only successful human demonstration trajectories are stored as exemplars; failed trajectories are neither stored nor retrieved. Synapse explicitly avoids self-correction (unlike RCI/Reflexion/AdaPlanner), so it does not accumulate or reuse failure experiences. A text-transform failure case is analyzed qualitatively in the appendix but not fed back.
- **memory evolution update**: append-only at construction time / static thereafter: all metadata-to-exemplar entries are written once during offline memory construction; stored entries are not merged, delta-updated, refined, pruned, or evolved during deployment.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No. Case/exemplar selection is fixed similarity top-n over frozen task-metadata embeddings (plus a deterministic majority-match heuristic on MiniWoB++); it is not an RL- or value-optimized retrieval policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent private exemplar memory; no cross-agent or cross-framework experience sharing. (The prompting technique is described as broadly applicable/composable with other methods, but memory itself is not shared across agents.)

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> MiniWoB++ (legacy branch; 64 tested tasks, demos from 48 tasks, 16 unseen tasks; 50 episodes/task). Mind2Web (real-world web navigation; >2,000 tasks from 137 websites in 31 domains; training set 1,009 tasks/73 sites; test splits Cross-Task 252 tasks/69 sites, Cross-Website 177 tasks/10 sites, Cross-Domain 912 tasks/73 sites).
- **benchmark family**: web / GUI computer-control: MiniWoB++ (web GUI task suite) and Mind2Web (real-world web navigation; same family as Online-Mind2Web/WebArena).
- **baselines**:
> MiniWoB++: RCI (ICL SOTA, recursive self-correction), AdaPlanner (concurrent, feedback self-correction), Pix2Act (concurrent, tree search + BC), CC-Net (BC+RL human-level, 2.4M demos), WebN-T5 and WebGUM (fine-tuned T5), plus the human-performance reference. Mind2Web: MindAct (MCQ-formatted ICL SOTA with element-ranking model), with both GPT-3.5 and CodeLlama-7B backbones. Backbone LLMs: gpt-3.5-turbo-0301 (MiniWoB++), gpt-3.5-turbo-16k-0613 (Mind2Web), CodeLlama-Instruct-7B; embeddings via text-embedding-ada-002; GPT-4 used to sample state-parsing code offline.
- **key metrics**:
> MiniWoB++: average task success rate (%). Mind2Web: Element selection accuracy (Ele. Acc), step success rate (Step SR), and whole-task success rate (SR) against human ground truth. Also reported: number of exemplars per task (data efficiency), recall of clean observations (target-element coverage).
- **headline result**:
> MiniWoB++: 99.2% average success rate across 64 tasks using demonstrations from only 48 tasks (a ~10% relative improvement; first ICL method to reach human-level performance and the first ICL method to solve book-flight), without self-correction. Mind2Web: 56% relative improvement in average step success rate over MindAct (the prior SOTA ICL prompting scheme) on GPT-3.5 across three generalization levels; ~2.5x step success rate over MindAct with CodeLlama-7B.
- **ablations**:
> Incremental Mind2Web ablation (Table 1, both CodeLlama-7B and GPT-3.5) adding components one at a time: (a) state abstraction alone (direct generation with top-5 elements) beats MCQ-with-top-50 MindAct by 32% avg Step SR (e.g., GPT-3.5 Cross-Task Step SR 17.4 -> 25.2); (b) + TaE prompting adds +19% (to 50% over MindAct; Cross-Task Step SR -> 29.2); (c) + exemplar memory reaches 56% over MindAct (Cross-Task Step SR -> 30.6). Memory helps cross-task/cross-website but is marginal cross-domain (unseen domains -> larger retrieval distance, Table 2). MiniWoB++ ablations: state abstraction enables complex-state tasks (book-flight) and lifts email-inbox-nl-turk 52% -> 100%; TaE prompting fixes long-horizon/repeated-action tasks (guess-number 20%->100%, use-spinner 88%->100%, use-autocomplete 58%->98% vs RCI); exemplar memory gives ~100% avg on the 16 unseen tasks. Reducing top-k elements drops recall 86% -> 53% yet improves Step SR. RCI loses ~50% success rate if any of its three self-correction stages is removed.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Partially. Mind2Web reports element selection accuracy (Ele. Acc) and the recall of clean observations (86% at k=50 vs 53% at k=5) as intrinsic-style measures alongside end-to-end Step SR / SR, and reports retrieval-distance (similarity) statistics across test splits (Table 2). No standard ranked-retrieval metrics (Recall@k/nDCG) of the exemplar retriever itself are reported separately; retrieval quality is assessed mainly via downstream task gains.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Both. MiniWoB++ uses outcome (task success rate); Mind2Web adds intermediate process metrics: per-step Step SR and per-action Element Accuracy in addition to whole-task SR, giving step-wise process quality beyond final outcome.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Efficiency is a central motivation. State abstraction shrinks per-state tokens, enabling more exemplars within context. TaE prompting produces temporally abstracted multi-action blocks, reducing the number of LLM queries -> lower latency and cost (and higher long-horizon success). Sample efficiency: 64 tasks solved with demos from only 48 tasks; avg exemplars/task 3.45 (Synapse) vs 1.52 (RCI), vs CC-Net's 2.4M demos / WebGUM's 346,827 demos. Faiss used for efficient large-scale similarity search. Stated limitation: high inference latency due to LLM use (proposed remedy: distill a task-specific agent).
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Budget-driven, mostly fixed small k. MiniWoB++: retrieve top-3 metadata matches then use all exemplars of the most-common matched task (avg 3.45 exemplars/task; up to 5 for hard tasks like book-flight). Mind2Web: retrieve exemplars of matched metadata; element budget set to k=3 for memory trajectories and previous observations and k=5 for the current observation (vs MindAct's k=50), deliberately trading recall (86%->53%) for shorter context and higher Step SR. Greedy decoding (temperature 0).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> RCI (Kim et al., 2023; high-level-plan ICL computer agent, recursive self-correction), MindAct/Mind2Web (Deng et al., 2023; MCQ + element-ranking model), ReAct (Yao et al., 2022a), Code-as-Policies / ProgPrompt (code-as-action grounding), Chain-of-Thought / least-to-most prompting, in-context learning (Brown et al., 2020), Faiss (Johnson et al., 2019) for similarity search, OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002; concurrent skill-memory work Voyager (skill library) cited as complementary.
- **contrasts with**:
> RCI and AdaPlanner (self-correction-based ICL agents that rely on task-specific exemplars and recursive correction; Synapse drops self-correction and uses task-similarity memory), MindAct (MCQ-formatted step-wise prompting with top-50 elements; Synapse uses trajectory-as-exemplar direct generation with aggressive state abstraction), CC-Net / WebN-T5 / WebGUM / Pix2Act (BC+RL or fine-tuning on huge demonstration datasets; Synapse is data-efficient ICL), and prior agents that hard-code the task->exemplar mapping (Synapse retrieves exemplars from memory).
- **lineage**:
> Group D (case-based planning): a trajectory-as-exemplar, retrieval-augmented computer-control agent that stores abstracted full-trajectory cases in an episodic memory and retrieves them as few-shot prompts, in the lineage of ICL web/computer agents (ReAct -> RCI/MindAct -> Synapse) and adjacent to skill-/experience-memory agents (Voyager, AdaPlanner). Realizes CBR Retrieve+Reuse over trajectory cases without explicit Revise/Retain.

<a id="item-leake-cbr"></a>
### 67. Augmenting LLMs with Cases and Prompting Them to Perform CBR (Wilkerson & Leake; paper title: "On Implementing Case-Based Reasoning with Large Language Models")

2024  ·  ICCBR 2024 (tech report)  ·  [paper](https://homes.luddy.indiana.edu/leake/papers/p-24-02.pdf)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**:
> ICCBR 2024 -- 32nd International Conference on Case-Based Reasoning (Case-Based Reasoning Research and Development), Merida, Mexico, July 1-4, 2024. Published in Springer LNCS vol. 14775, pp. 404-417, DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-63646-2_26. The provided paper_url (homes.luddy.indiana.edu/.../p-24-02.pdf) is the authors' technical-report / preprint version of this peer-reviewed conference paper.
- **authors affiliation**: Kaitlynne Wilkerson and David Leake. Primary affiliation: Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA ({kwilker, leake}@indiana.edu).
- **paper url**: https://homes.luddy.indiana.edu/leake/papers/p-24-02.pdf (tech-report version). Peer-reviewed version: https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-63646-2_26 (Springer LNCS 14775, pp. 404-417); DBLP: dblp.org/rec/conf/iccbr/WilkersonL24.

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Decision-making / classification (QA-style single-label prediction): medical triage classification -- assigning a Korean Triage and Acuity Scale (KTAS) level 1-5 to emergency-room patients from their vital signs and chief complaint. Framed as a case-based classification process implemented with LLMs.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-agent, supervised classification with a small curated case base. Given a current patient's status (7 attribute-value features: sex, age, heart rate, respiratory rate, mental state, blood pressure, chief complaint), the LLM must output a KTAS triage number 1-5. A k-NN retrieval component first selects a small subset of prior labeled cases from a 102-case case base; that subset is injected into the LLM prompt. There is no model training/fine-tuning -- the study only varies prompting strategy (Direct Solution baseline vs Implicit-CBR vs Explicit-CBR) and the number/type of provided cases (1NN / 2NN / NUN). Interaction is one-shot per test case (ECBR uses a short multi-turn similarity-then-adapt prompt sequence). It is an empirical/exploratory study (the paper's stated purpose is to open the door to future investigation), testing whether LLMs benefit from being given cases and from being guided through CBR sub-processes (similarity assessment, adaptation, nearest-unlike-neighbor reasoning). 25 test cases (5 per class), 7 prompt/formulation types each = 175 prompts per LLM, run on ChatGPT 3.5 and Llama 2 70b-chat.
- **what is retrieved**:
> cases -- prior labeled patient cases (problem-solution pairs: patient feature vector + expert-assigned KTAS triage number) drawn from the case base. The paper explicitly contrasts retrieving cases (concrete prior episodes aimed at the task) versus RAG-style text snippets of general facts.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus: retrieval targets a fixed, offline-constructed case base (102 cases sampled from a public Kaggle triage dataset). The case base is not written to or grown by the agent during deployment; it functions as a static external experience store (case base) rather than a growing/episodic memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k retrieval objective: the k-NN component returns a fixed small set of nearest cases (k=1 for 1NN; k=2 for 2NN; NN + nearest-unlike-neighbor for NUN; for ECBR a fixed pool of 10 candidate cases is provided and the LLM is asked to select 1 or 2). The objective is a fixed-size top-k selection feeding a classification decision, not minimal-set completeness recovery or precision-driven variable-size recommendation.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve, Reuse, Revise] -- Retrieve (k-NN nearest-neighbor case retrieval, and in ECBR the LLM additionally performs similarity assessment / case selection); Reuse + Revise (the LLM adapts/combines the retrieved case(s) -- the ICBR/ECBR adaptation step -- to produce a triage number for the new patient, i.e. reuse of the prior solution plus revision in light of similarities/differences). Retain is NOT implemented (no new cases are written back to the case base). So Retrieve=yes, Reuse=yes, Revise=yes, Retain=no.
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> True. The work explicitly frames itself as implementing Case-Based Reasoning with LLMs, cites Watson (CBR is a methodology not a technology), Leake, and the CBR literature on cases as explanations, and is published at ICCBR (the CBR conference). It explicitly invokes the CBR cycle phases (similarity assessment, adaptation) and CBR concepts (nearest neighbor, nearest unlike neighbor). It does not center on the Aamodt & Plaza four-R formalism in this preprint text but is unambiguously grounded in CBR.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> case (problem-solution): a single prior patient case = attribute-value feature vector (sex, age, heart rate, respiratory rate, mental state, blood pressure, chief complaint) paired with its expert KTAS triage label. Retrieved as 1-2 full cases (ICBR) or selected from a 10-case candidate pool (ECBR).
- **index source**: Static corpus, offline-induced: the retrievable case base is a fixed set of 102 cases sampled once (random sample with >=1 case per class) from a public Kaggle emergency-triage dataset; missing-value instances were removed. Not online/test-time-induced and not hybrid.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat case base queried by a weighted-Euclidean-distance k-NN over the 7 attribute features (categorical distance 1/0; textual chief-complaint compared by semantic similarity via sentence-transformer all-mpnet-base-v2 + cosine). No graph, hierarchy, or cluster structure; a flat metric-space index with per-feature weights tuned by hill climbing.
- **retriever type**:
> Hybrid/classical: a weighted-Euclidean k-NN retriever (numeric/categorical features) augmented with dense semantic similarity (all-mpnet-base-v2 sentence embeddings + PyTorch cosine similarity) for the textual chief-complaint feature. In the ECBR condition, the LLM itself acts as a second-stage retriever/selector (LLM-as-retriever for similarity assessment) over a 10-case pool provided by k-NN.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Mostly none (off-the-shelf) plus a lightweight weight-tuning step: the k-NN feature weights were selected by hill climbing to maximize k-NN training accuracy (best weighted-1-NN accuracy 48%; final weights Respiratory Rate=1.0, Mental State=0.25, Chief Complaint=0.25, all others=0.001). The sentence-transformer (all-mpnet-base-v2) is used off-the-shelf. The LLMs are not trained/fine-tuned for retrieval; LLM similarity assessment is pure zero-shot prompting (no learning signal).
- **query construction**:
> Raw current-patient status in textual attribute-value form (e.g. 'Patient Status: Sex: Female, Age: 50, Chief complaint: ..., Mental state: Pain Response, Heart Rate: 37, Respirations: 28, Blood Pressure: 50/33'). The same patient description serves as the k-NN query and as the LLM prompt context. No query decomposition, expansion, or intent extraction.
- **query granularity**: Task-level (one-shot at t=0): a single query per test case (the whole patient description), used once to retrieve cases before the LLM produces a classification. No per-step or trajectory-level re-querying.
- **when to retrieve**:
> One-shot: cases are retrieved once per test case (via k-NN) before prompting the LLM. In the ECBR condition there is a fixed, scripted two-stage prompt (first similarity assessment to select case(s) from the provided pool, then adaptation), but retrieval is not iterative/active/uncertainty-triggered.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule: retrieval is always performed once per incoming test case (k-NN selects the case subset). For ECBR, the similarity-assessment selection step is likewise always performed on a fixed schedule, not gated by confidence/uncertainty or a learned router.
- **reranking**:
> None as a dedicated module. The k-NN ordering by weighted distance provides the nearest neighbor(s); for ECBR the LLM re-selects/reorders by picking the most-similar case(s) from the 10-case pool (an LLM-as-selector step that loosely acts as reranking), but there is no cross-encoder/RRF/instruction-tuned reranker.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> None: retrieved cases are passed verbatim (as attribute-value text) into the prompt with no decomposition, distillation, compression, or distractor filtering. The only post-hoc processing is a manual hallucination check on the LLM output (responses where the LLM hallucinated case information were discarded and re-run), which is a sanity check on output rather than refinement of retrieved context.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tools/APIs; retrieved units are patient cases, not tool documents).
- **index content separation**: N/A -- cases are small attribute-value records stored and loaded together; no lightweight-index-then-heavy-content progressive-disclosure separation.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index or external API protocol; the case base is a static local store).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tools or inter-tool dependencies).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation + case adaptation: retrieved prior case(s) are concatenated into the LLM prompt, and the LLM is instructed to use the similarities and differences between the current patient and the prior case(s) to assign a triage number -- i.e. the LLM performs case reuse/adaptation in natural language. In ICBR the adaptation is implicit (LLM given the case and asked to solve); in ECBR the LLM is explicitly guided through similarity assessment (select case(s) from a pool) then adaptation. No training-signal or latent-token use.
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-solve with one-shot exemplar(s) at decision time: k-NN retrieves case(s), which are injected as prompt context, and the LLM produces a single classification (the 'solution'). For ECBR there is a short fixed plan-like sequence (similarity-assessment prompt -> adaptation prompt). There is no tree search, MCTS, hierarchical subtask decomposition, or per-step interleaving -- this is a single classification decision, not multi-step planning.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer (per-case): one retrieval and (for ICBR) one conditioned generation produce one triage label per test case. ECBR uses two scripted turns (similarity assessment then adaptation) but retrieval is not interwoven per CoT-step or per token.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> LLM-prompted adaptation: the retrieved case's solution (a prior patient's KTAS number) is adapted by prompting the LLM to weigh similarities and differences between the current patient and the prior case(s) and to assign a (possibly different) triage number. The paper operationally defines 'adaptation occurred' as the LLM output differing from the retrieved nearest neighbor's label, and measures adaptation rates per model (e.g. ChatGPT adapted >50% of the time across most prompts; Llama 2 adapted much less often). For NUN formulations a counterfactual (nearest-unlike-neighbor) is provided to help delineate class boundaries during adaptation. No execution-feedback, critic, or RL-based revision.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Raw case in attribute-value text form: the prior patient's feature values plus its triage label, presented verbatim as structured text in the prompt (e.g. 'Sex: ..., Age: ..., Heart Rate: ..., ... ,' with the KTAS number). No distillation to a strategy/guideline, no program/skill, no latent tokens.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Single demonstration / concrete prior case (problem-solution pair): a literal prior solved patient case, not a distilled strategy, abstracted rule, or reusable workflow. The NUN formulation additionally supplies a counterfactual concrete case.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Limited / largely manual: (1) a post-generation hallucination sanity check -- because the original case is available, responses in which the LLM hallucinated case attributes were detected and discarded/re-run (the paper highlights this case-grounded sanity check as a robustness benefit of CBR over plain generation); (2) providing multiple cases (2NN) and a counterfactual (NUN) is motivated as increasing robustness of the response. No retriever-aware training, learned relevance evaluator, reason-in-documents refinement, or distractor-aware SFT.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> none (static case base) -- the retrievable store is a fixed external case base used at inference; it is not an agent-written episodic memory, skill-library, workflow, graph, or latent memory. (Closest descriptor: a static case base, i.e. an external experience corpus that is read-only at test time.)
- **write back**: False -- the system does not store new experiences/cases/solutions back into the case base; the 102-case case base is fixed and read-only during the experiment. (Retain phase of the CBR cycle is not implemented.)
- **online growth**: No -- the case base does not grow during deployment/test-time; it is frozen after the offline sampling step.
- **write back trigger**: Never -- no write-back mechanism exists; nothing is written to the case base on success, on failure, per-step, reflectively, or via human validation.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success-only cases (positive labeled cases) are stored/retrieved; failed or negative LLM trajectories are not stored or reused. The NUN (nearest-unlike-neighbor / counterfactual) formulation does inject a contrasting case of a DIFFERENT class to help delineate decision boundaries, but this is a correctly-labeled contrastive case from the static case base, not a stored failure experience.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A -- the case base is static (read-only); stored entries are never mutated, merged, delta-updated, refined, or pruned during the experiment (other than the one-time offline removal of missing-value instances and sampling to 102 cases).
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No -- case selection is fixed: weighted k-NN nearest-neighbor retrieval (weights set once by hill climbing). In ECBR the LLM selects cases via zero-shot prompting, which is not a trained/RL retrieval policy. No M-MDP / soft Q-learning / RL retrieval.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No -- single-agent, single-model use of a private static case base; no memory/experience sharing across multiple agents or frameworks. (Two LLMs, ChatGPT and Llama 2, are compared but each is run independently on the same case base, not sharing experience.)

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> A custom medical-triage classification testbed built from a public Kaggle emergency-service triage dataset (originally 1,267 patients, 24 vital signs/assessments, KTAS labels 1-5 assigned by 3 triage experts). The authors narrowed to 7 features, removed missing-value instances, used a 102-case case base and a 25-case test set (5 per class). No standard public benchmark suite; LLMs tested: ChatGPT 3.5 and Llama 2 70b-chat.
- **benchmark family**: decision-making / single-label classification (medical triage). Not part of standard QA / web / embodied / tool / code / memory / decision-RL benchmark families; it is a custom small-scale classification testbed.
- **baselines**:
> (1) Unweighted 1-NN classifier (full 102-case case base); (2) Weighted 1-NN classifier (hill-climbing-optimized feature weights, full case base); (3) Direct Solution LLM prompt (no case provided) as the non-CBR LLM baseline, for each of ChatGPT and Llama 2. The CBR prompting conditions (ICBR / ECBR x 1NN/2NN/NUN) are compared against these.
- **key metrics**:
> Classification accuracy on the 25-case test set under three correctness criteria: Strict Accuracy (exact KTAS match); Correct-within-1-class-higher (accepting safe near-misses that over-triage); Correct-within-1-class-higher-or-lower. Secondary diagnostic metrics: similarity-assessment accuracy (rate at which the LLM-selected case matches the k-NN-selected case) and adaptation analysis (rate of adaptation, % of adapted cases that were correct, % of adaptations where the NN was already correct i.e. unnecessary adaptation).
- **headline result**:
> Providing cases improved LLM triage accuracy over the no-case Direct Solution baseline. The best prompt type overall was ICBR with the single nearest neighbor (ICBR 1NN): strict accuracy 60% with ChatGPT and 56% with Llama 2, versus the Direct Solution baseline of 28% for both LLMs, and outperforming the optimized weighted-1-NN classifier (48%) and unweighted 1-NN (28%) for both models.
- **ablations**:
> The study is structured as a set of controlled comparisons (effectively ablations) over prompt type and case formulation: (1) Direct Solution (no case) vs ICBR vs ECBR -- ICBR/ECBR generally match or beat the no-case baseline, showing cases provide useful knowledge. (2) Number/type of cases: 1NN vs 2NN vs NUN -- ICBR 1NN best overall; a second similar case (2NN) helps in some settings (ICBR 2NN strong on Llama 2: 44% strict; ECBR 2NN strong on ChatGPT, e.g. 44% strict / 72% within-1-higher); the counterfactual NUN formulation generally did not help and ECBR NUN was the weakest (28% strict on both LLMs). (3) Implicit vs Explicit CBR: ICBR (k-NN-selected case) >= ECBR (LLM-selected case), attributed to poor LLM similarity assessment. (4) Similarity-assessment diagnostic (Table 3): LLM-vs-k-NN agreement was low for both models (e.g. ECBR 1NN: ChatGPT 20%, Llama 2 28%; ECBR 2NN second-case: ChatGPT 4%, Llama 2 16%), with Llama 2 slightly better at selecting 2NN/NUN. (5) Adaptation diagnostic (Table 4): ChatGPT adapts much more often than Llama 2 (ICBR 1NN adaptation rate 56% vs 64%; ECBR 2NN 84% vs 32%); Llama 2's lower and less-correct adaptation likely explains its weaker ECBR 2NN results. Conclusion: adaptation ability is LLM-specific and drives which prompt/case formulation is best.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Partially yes: the LLM's intrinsic similarity-assessment quality (agreement with k-NN-chosen cases, Table 3) and its adaptation behavior (Table 4) are reported separately from end-to-end triage accuracy (Table 2). However these are diagnostic process metrics, not standard IR metrics (no Recall@k / nDCG); the k-NN retriever's own retrieval quality is not separately scored beyond k-NN classification accuracy.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both: the primary metric is the outcome (triage classification accuracy under three criteria), but the paper also reports intermediate process quality -- similarity-assessment correctness (does the LLM pick the same case as k-NN) and adaptation analysis (how often adaptation occurs, whether it is correct, whether it was unnecessary). These process metrics are used to explain the outcome differences between ChatGPT and Llama 2.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Not quantified in terms of latency/API cost/tokens. The study is small-scale (25 test cases x 7 prompt types = 175 prompts per LLM); ChatGPT prompts were entered by hand via the web interface over a single day (noted as not parameter-controllable and not replicable), while Llama 2 70b-chat was run locally (temperature 0, top_p 0.9) on IU's Big Red 200 supercomputer for replicability. The motivation includes a knowledge-acquisition-cost argument: using LLM knowledge to bypass costly manual CBR knowledge engineering in knowledge-rich domains. No explicit cost/accuracy tradeoff numbers.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k, small budget driven by prompt-size limits: the authors explicitly note prompt-size limitations prevented presenting the whole case base, so an initial k-NN retrieval selects a small subset. ICBR injects 1 case (1NN) or 2 cases (2NN/NUN). ECBR presents a fixed pool of 10 candidate cases and asks the LLM to select 1 (1NN) or 2 (2NN / NN+NUN). k is fixed per formulation (not adaptive/precision-driven). Llama 2 generation used temperature 0, top_p 0.9.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Custom testbed (not a released benchmark): source = public Kaggle emergency-service triage dataset (1,267 patients, 24 features, KTAS 1-5 expert labels). Construction: narrowed to 7 commonly-used triage features (sex, age, heart rate, respiratory rate, mental state, blood pressure, chief complaint), removed missing-value instances, randomly sampled a 102-case case base (>=1 per class) and a 25-case test set (5 per class). Answer verifiability: KTAS labels assigned by three triage experts in the original dataset serve as ground truth. Difficulty signal: triage is noisy/subjective; best baseline (weighted 1-NN) reaches only 48% strict accuracy and the best LLM condition (ICBR 1NN, ChatGPT) reaches 60% strict accuracy.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLMs (Lewis et al. 2020; Gao et al. survey 2023); generated/external-knowledge prompting for commonsense reasoning (Liu et al. 2021); classical CBR as a methodology not a technology (Watson 1996) and CBR knowledge/explanation work (Leake; Cheetham & Watson 2005; Cunningham et al. 2003; Gates, Leake & Wilkerson 2023 'Cases are King' user study); CBR-RAG for legal QA (Wiratunga et al. 2024) as the prior example of giving LLMs cases. Uses Llama 2 (Touvron et al. 2023), ChatGPT 3.5, sentence-transformers all-mpnet-base-v2, llama.cpp / llama-cpp-python.
- **contrasts with**:
> Standard RAG (text-snippet retrieval): the paper explicitly contrasts providing LLMs with cases (concrete prior episodes aimed at the task, prompting CBR sub-processes) against RAG, which retrieves general fact snippets and merely adds context. It also contrasts implicit case use (ICBR) vs explicitly guiding the LLM through CBR steps (ECBR / similarity assessment + adaptation), and contrasts LLM similarity assessment against k-NN similarity, and CBR-augmented prompting against a knowledge-light k-NN classifier and a no-case Direct Solution LLM baseline.
- **lineage**:
> Group D (case-based planning / case-based reasoning with LLMs). An exploratory ICCBR-2024 study positioned at the intersection of CBR and LLMs: it advances the case-augmented-generation lineage (cases instead of RAG snippets) and specifically probes whether prompting LLMs through CBR sub-processes (similarity assessment, adaptation, nearest-unlike-neighbor) helps. Sits alongside CBR-RAG (Wiratunga et al. 2024) and feeds the authors' subsequent CBR-LLM reliability / hallucination-feedback work (CBR-LLM workshop papers, CEUR Vol-3708, Vol-3993).

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):
