### 68. CaseGPT: A Case Reasoning Framework Based on Language Models and Retrieval-Augmented Generation

2024  ·  arXiv 2407.07913  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.07913)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **authors affiliation**: Rui Yang (single author), University of California, Riverside, USA
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.07913
- **code url**: N/A (no official code repository released; the paper provides no code link and no GitHub repo could be located)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Domain-specific case retrieval + decision-support / insight generation for case-based reasoning (CBR) in healthcare (medical diagnosis) and legal (precedent retrieval) domains; framed as semantic information retrieval (cs.IR) rather than agentic planning.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-agent retrieval-and-generation system over a static curated case repository. Given an imprecise / natural-language professional query (e.g., symptom description or legal fact pattern), the system performs semantic ('fuzzy') retrieval of relevant historical cases and then generates insights/recommendations. Supervision: experiments use a held-out 20% test split with generated test queries; no interactive/online learning is tested (the paper explicitly notes it did not test learning/adaptation over time). Two domains evaluated separately (medical: 100,000 cases; legal: 50,000 case summaries).
- **what is retrieved**: Full cases (problem-solution records): medical cases (symptoms, diagnostic procedures, final diagnoses, treatment outcomes) and legal court-case summaries (facts, relevant statutes, court decisions, outcomes). Treated as CBR cases.
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus (a curated dense-vector-indexed case database). The paper mentions incremental/dynamic index updates to add new cases, but no agent-written episodic memory of its own experiences is used during reasoning; effectively static-corpus RAG.
- **completeness vs topk objective**: Fixed top-k ranking objective (retrieve top-N most semantically relevant cases, evaluated at Precision@10 / Recall@10 / NDCG@10), augmented with a Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) diversity step; not a minimal-complete-set or precision-driven variable-size objective.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve, Reuse]; Revise and Retain are not implemented (no case adaptation/revision loop and no learned retain step are evaluated). Reuse is realized as LLM-based insight generation conditioned on retrieved cases. Flags: Retrieve=yes, Reuse=partial (insight generation, not explicit solution transfer), Revise=no, Retain=no.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: Partial. The work explicitly frames itself as 'case-based reasoning' and uses CBR terminology and keywords, and was submitted to ICCBR, but it does NOT cite the canonical CBR foundations (Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner); it realizes CBR Retrieve/Reuse mechanisms under a RAG framing.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: case (problem-solution record / full case document): a complete medical case or a complete legal case summary, encoded as a single dense vector.
- **index source**: Static curated corpus, offline-induced (cases encoded once into a dense vector index). Supports incremental real-time index updates to add new cases, but is not an online experience/episodic memory grown from the agent's own outputs.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat dense vector index built with the Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graph for approximate nearest-neighbor search; vectors of ~768-1024 dimensions; FAISS used for similarity search. (HNSW is internally a navigable-small-world graph used as an ANN index, not a semantic/dependency knowledge graph.)
- **retriever type**: Dense retriever (BERT-variant embeddings fine-tuned on domain corpora; e.g., LEGAL-BERT/BioBERT-style domain encoders) with cosine similarity over a FAISS/HNSW index; not BM25, not generative, not LLM-as-retriever.
- **query construction**:
> Raw user query is parsed and encoded by a pre-trained LLM (e.g., GPT-3 or domain variant) into high-dimensional semantic vectors (tokenize-and-encode). Query expansion is applied in the insight-generation stage to capture related concepts not explicitly mentioned. Encoding is per-word/per-token then aggregated into an encoded query.
- **query granularity**: Task-level (one-shot at query time): a single query is encoded and used to retrieve cases once; there is no per-step or trajectory-level re-querying loop.
- **when to retrieve**: One-shot (single retrieval pass per query before insight generation).
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule: retrieval is always triggered once per incoming user query; no confidence/uncertainty/learned-router trigger.
- **reranking**: Yes. Initial cosine-similarity ranking followed by a multi-factor re-ranking step incorporating domain-specific factors (case recency, citation frequency, jurisdictional relevance), inspired by learning-to-rank; plus an MMR diversity-aware selection step. Not a cross-encoder.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Rerank + diversity filtering (MMR) + context aggregation/summarization. After retrieval, a hybrid summarization aggregates retrieved cases and query into a weighted context (attention-inspired weighting scheme) before LLM generation; no explicit distractor-filtering or reason-in-documents distillation is described.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tools/skills; items are cases). Cases are encoded with a domain-fine-tuned BERT-variant encoder; no synthetic-query or weighted-field tool engineering.
- **index content separation**: N/A (no separation of a lightweight index from heavy on-demand content is described; the dense vector index points to full cases).
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index / external API protocol). The case index does support incremental/real-time updates for new cases, but there is no MCP/RapidAPI/function-calling tool integration.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tools; no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**: Prompt augmentation: retrieved cases are aggregated into context and injected into an LLM prompt for conditional generation (case adaptation in the loose sense of generating insights/recommendations grounded in retrieved cases). Insights are then iteratively refined by the LLM.
- **planning integration**: Retrieve-then-generate (one-shot retrieve-then-reason): retrieval happens once, then the LLM generates insights conditioned on retrieved cases. No planning/tree-search/MCTS, no per-step interleaving; this is a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline, not a planner.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer: a single retrieval feeds a single generation/insight pass per query (with internal iterative refinement of the generated insight, but no additional retrieval interleaving).
- **adaptation mechanism**: LLM-prompted adaptation: retrieved cases are used as context for LLM conditional generation of insights/recommendations, then iteratively refined by the LLM (IterativeRefine). No execution-feedback-driven or critic-guided revision, no RL reuse-finetuning.
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw retrieved case text aggregated/summarized into a weighted free-text context that is injected into the generation prompt; output insights are free-text recommendations.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw cases (full problem-solution case records); no distillation into strategies/guidelines/workflows/skills before retrieval. Abstraction (pattern discernment) happens only downstream in the insight-generation LLM.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Limited / mostly implicit: MMR diversity-aware retrieval and multi-factor re-ranking aim to surface more relevant/diverse cases, and an attention-inspired context weighting prioritizes pertinent information; there is no explicit relevance evaluator, self-reflection, retriever-aware training, or distractor-aware SFT for noise robustness.

**Memory & Learning**

- **write back**: No (false). The system does not store new experiences/cases/skills generated from its own reasoning back into memory; the index can be updated by adding externally-provided new cases (incremental indexing) but the system does not write back its own outputs/experiences.
- **online growth**: Largely no for the evaluated setting. The index supports incremental real-time updates to integrate newly supplied cases, but the paper explicitly did not test learning/adaptation over time and the agent does not grow the store from its own deployment experiences.
- **write back trigger**: Never (for the agent's own experiences). New cases may be added via external incremental indexing, but there is no success/failure/reflective write-back of generated insights or solved queries.
- **failure experience usage**: Not used. The corpus contains historical cases with outcomes, but failed/negative experiences are not specifically stored or retrieved as a contrastive/corrective mechanism; retrieval is success-agnostic similarity matching.
- **memory evolution update**: Append-only at most (new cases can be incrementally added to the index); stored case entries are not mutated, deduped, refined, or pruned. No experience-memory evolution.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No. Case selection is fixed cosine-similarity top-k plus heuristic multi-factor re-ranking and MMR; it is not a learned/RL-optimized retrieval policy (no M-MDP, no soft Q-learning, no preference/value-based retrieval training).
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent system with a single shared static case database; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing (federated/collaborative learning is only listed as future work).

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> Two private real-world datasets assembled by the author: (1) Medical dataset of 100,000 anonymized medical cases from a large urban hospital network (symptoms, diagnostics, diagnoses, outcomes; ICD-10 standardized); (2) Legal dataset of 50,000 court-case summaries across criminal/civil/administrative law (facts, statutes, decisions, outcomes). No public/standard benchmark is used.
- **benchmark family**: Domain-specific information retrieval (medical IR and legal case retrieval) on private custom datasets; does NOT map to standard agentic-RAG families (not QA/multi-hop/web/embodied/tool/code/memory/decision-RL benchmarks). Closest normalized label: domain IR / CBR retrieval.
- **baselines**: TF-IDF + BM25; BERT-based dense retrieval; GPT-3 zero-shot (retrieval + insight generation); LEGAL-BERT (legal domain); BioBERT (medical domain). For insight-generation human evaluation, only GPT-3 zero-shot is compared.
- **key metrics**: Precision@10 (P@10), Recall@10 (R@10), F1, Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR), NDCG@10, Response Time (s); plus human evaluation of generated insights on a 5-point Likert scale across Quality, Relevance, Actionability.
- **headline result**:
> Medical domain: CaseGPT reaches P@10=0.90, R@10=0.88, F1=0.89, MRR=0.92, NDCG@10=0.91 at 0.5s, vs best baseline BioBERT (F1=0.81), reported as a ~15% F1 improvement over traditional methods. Legal domain: P@10=0.93, R@10=0.90, F1=0.91, MRR=0.94, NDCG@10=0.93 at 0.8s, vs best baseline LEGAL-BERT (P@10=0.87), reported as a ~12% precision improvement. Insight quality (Likert): CaseGPT 4.3/4.5/4.4 vs GPT-3 zero-shot 3.6/3.4/3.5.
- **ablations**:
> No controlled component ablations are reported. The paper provides baseline comparisons (TF-IDF+BM25, BERT, GPT-3 zero-shot, domain BERTs) and a separate human evaluation of insight generation vs GPT-3 zero-shot, but it does not isolate the contribution of individual modules (e.g., MMR diversity, multi-factor re-ranking, domain fine-tuning, iterative refinement) via ablation.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Yes (partially). Intrinsic retrieval-ranking metrics (P@10, R@10, F1, MRR, NDCG@10) are reported separately from the downstream insight-generation quality (human Likert evaluation of Quality/Relevance/Actionability); however there is no separate end-to-end task-success metric beyond retrieval and the human insight assessment.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Mixed: retrieval ranking quality (MRR/NDCG, a process/ranking signal) and final insight quality (human Quality/Relevance/Actionability) are both measured; no step-wise reasoning faithfulness or trajectory-quality metrics (single-pass system).
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**: Reports response time as the efficiency metric: CaseGPT 0.5s (medical) and 0.8s (legal), faster than baselines (BioBERT 0.8s, LEGAL-BERT 0.9s, TF-IDF+BM25 1.0-1.2s, GPT-3 zero-shot 1.2-1.3s). No API cost, token-count, or rollout/retrieval-call counts are reported.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (this is a system/method paper, not a survey).

**Relations**

- **builds on**: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG, Lewis et al.); BERT and domain-adapted encoders (LEGAL-BERT, BioBERT); GPT-3 / LLMs; FAISS for ANN similarity search; HNSW indexing; Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) for diversity; learning-to-rank for re-ranking.
- **contrasts with**:
> Traditional exact keyword/database query systems (TF-IDF + BM25); plain BERT-based dense retrieval; GPT-3 zero-shot used directly for retrieval+generation; standalone domain encoders (LEGAL-BERT, BioBERT). Positioned as semantic, context-aware fuzzy retrieval + insight generation that outperforms keyword-based and simple LLM-based systems.
- **lineage**:
> Group D (case-based planning / case-based reasoning). An early, lightweight LLM+RAG-for-CBR application paper: it implements the Retrieve (and a loose Reuse via insight generation) phases of the CBR cycle using dense-vector RAG, applied to healthcare and legal case retrieval; sits in the CBR-meets-RAG line of work but without learned retrieval policy, case adaptation/revision, or experiential memory growth.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- benchmark_construction_and_size
- context_budget_and_selection_count
- memory_type
- retriever_learning_signal
- venue

<a id="item-ds-agent"></a>
### 69. DS-Agent: Automated Data Science by Empowering Large Language Models with Case-Based Reasoning

2024  ·  ICML 2024  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17453)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: ICML 2024 (Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR vol. 235, pp. 16813-16848); preprint arXiv:2402.17453 (cs.LG)
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17453
- **code url**: https://github.com/guosyjlu/DS-Agent

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> code / decision-making: LLM-agent automated data science (automated machine learning) - comprehending a task description, then building, training, and validating the best-fit ML model via generated and executed Python code. Spans three data modalities (text, time series, tabular) and two ML task types (regression, classification).
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent, closed-loop automated data science. A task is a tuple (task description tau, D_train, D_valid, D_test, evaluation metric M); the agent comprehends tau, generates code to train an ML model on D_train, evaluates on D_valid via M, and is scored on D_test. Two distinct stages: (1) a high-resource Development stage that runs a full CBR automatic iteration pipeline with code execution feedback (multiple iterations per task, T=5); (2) a low-resource Deployment stage that uses a simplified one-shot CBR (retrieve one past successful case, adapt, generate code directly, no execution loop). 30 tasks total (12 development, 18 deployment); datasets mostly released after Sep 2021 to avoid pretraining contamination. No gradient finetuning of the LLM - the only 'learning' is retaining successful cases into the case bank. Supervision: expert knowledge cases crawled from Kaggle (winners' technical reports + top public-leaderboard code summarized by GPT-3.5).
- **what is retrieved**:
> cases: in the development stage, human-insight cases from a Kaggle-derived case bank C (cleaned winner technical reports + GPT-3.5-summarized textual solution insights from top public code) plus retained successful (task description, Python script) solution cases; in the deployment stage, past successful (tau_0, s_0) solution-code case pairs from the agent experience case bank B.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> HYBRID: an initially offline-induced static human-insight case bank C crawled from Kaggle, which also GROWS at test time (development stage retains new successful cases into both C and the agent case bank B). Deployment retrieves from the grown agent case bank B (which was filled during development; frozen at deployment time).
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Two-level objective. The dense retriever returns a fixed top-k (k=5) candidate set by cosine similarity (a fixed top-k ranking). The ReviseRanker (LLM) then re-orders these k cases and selects a single best case for reuse. The reuse process is centered on adapting ONE example case; ablation shows adding more than one case in context hurts performance, so effectively the objective is a precision-driven single-case selection rather than a completeness/minimal-set objective.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve: yes (dense top-k + LLM ReviseRank), Reuse: yes (Planner/Adapter adapts the chosen case into an experiment plan / code), Revise: yes (execution-feedback-driven Revise loop iteratively re-ranks cases and revises the plan over T iterations), Retain: yes (improved successful cases archived into both case banks C and B)]. All four canonical CBR phases are explicitly implemented in the development stage; deployment uses a simplified Retrieve+Reuse subset.
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> True. The paper explicitly frames itself as case-based reasoning, names the method as integrating CBR into LLMs, and cites the canonical CBR literature including Aamodt & Plaza (1994), Kolodner (1992), and Watson & Marir (1994); it formally contrasts CBR-based LLMs against RAG-based LLMs (the defining feedback/revise/retain distinction).

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> case (problem-solution): a (task description, solution) pair. In the development case bank these are human-insight cases (textual expert solution insights extracted from Kaggle reports/code) and retained (task, Python script) pairs; in deployment they are (task description, successful Python solution code) pairs. Effectively a full-solution/case unit expressed as textual insight or executable code.
- **index source**:
> Hybrid construction: offline-induced human-insight case bank C crawled from 12 recently-completed Kaggle competitions (4 per modality; top-10 winner technical reports + top-10 public-leaderboard Jupyter notebooks summarized into textual insights by GPT-3.5). The store then grows online during the development stage as successful solution cases are retained into both C and the agent experience case bank B. Deployment retrieves from B (induced during development, then fixed).
- **index structure topology**: Flat vector index keyed by task-description embeddings (cosine similarity over llm-embedder embeddings). No graph or hierarchical topology is described; cases are organized as a flat case bank (the human insight bank C and the agent experience bank B).
- **retriever type**:
> dense (off-the-shelf): a pretrained embedding model (llm-embedder, Zhang et al. 2023b) computes embeddings and cosine similarity sim(tau,c)=cos(E(tau),E(c)) for top-k retrieval, followed by an LLM-as-reranker (ReviseRank) stage that uses the LLM to re-order candidates - so the overall pipeline is dense-retriever + LLM-as-reranker (a form of hybrid dense + generative reranking).
- **retriever learning signal**:
> none for the dense retriever (off-the-shelf llm-embedder, not trained on task feedback). The ReviseRank stage is LM-feedback / execution-feedback driven but not gradient-trained: the paper explicitly notes that finetuning the retriever on execution feedback is too expensive (requires code execution), so instead the LLM estimates each candidate case's utility conditioned on the prior iteration's execution feedback l^{t-1} and revises the ranking via prompting (zero-shot LLM permutation generation). So the selection signal is downstream-task / execution-effectiveness, realized through an LLM reranker rather than a trained retriever.
- **query construction**:
> Raw task description tau is the retrieval key/query for the dense retriever. For ReviseRank, the query is the task description tau plus the previous iteration's execution feedback l^{t-1} (initialized empty), used by the LLM to estimate per-case utility and re-rank. No synthetic query expansion or decomposition.
- **query granularity**:
> task-level for the dense retrieval (one cosine-similarity retrieval at the task level), then iteration/trajectory-level for ReviseRank: the case selection is refined once per development iteration step (t=1..5) conditioned on the latest execution feedback. Deployment is purely task-level (single retrieval, no loop).
- **when to retrieve**: Development: iterative - dense top-k retrieval at the start, then per-iteration LLM ReviseRank re-selection within the T=5 iteration loop driven by execution feedback (a Revise loop). Deployment: one-shot - a single retrieval of the most similar past case, no iteration.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed schedule tied to the CBR iteration loop. Initial dense retrieval is triggered once at the start of a task. The ReviseRank re-selection is triggered each iteration step by the arrival of new execution feedback l^{t-1} (experiment log produced after code execution and debugging); the loop runs for a predetermined maximum number of iteration steps (T=5) rather than via an uncertainty/confidence trigger.
- **reranking**:
> Yes - ReviseRank: an LLM-as-reranker (instruction-prompted, inspired by Sun et al. 2023 RankGPT-style listwise relevance ranking) that takes the top-k candidates with identifiers ([1],[2],...), the task tau, and the prior execution feedback l^{t-1}, and generates a descending utility permutation (e.g. [2]>[1]>[3]); the top-ranked case is selected for reuse. This is execution-feedback-aware listwise reranking.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Rerank (ReviseRank re-orders the top-k candidates conditioned on execution feedback and keeps only the single top-ranked case for reuse). At case-bank-construction time, raw Kaggle code is also distilled by GPT-3.5 into textual solution insights (a content-preparation step). No distractor-filtering, compression, or decompose-then-recompose is applied to retrieved items beyond selecting one case.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (not a tool-retrieval method). The closest analogue is case-document engineering: raw Kaggle winner code is summarized by GPT-3.5 into distilled textual solution insights, and technical reports are cleaned, before being embedded and indexed in the case bank.
- **index content separation**: N/A / not explicitly separated. Cases (insight text or code) are embedded by task description and the full case content is loaded into context on retrieval; no separate lightweight-index-then-heavy-content (progressive disclosure) scheme is described.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A. Not a tool/API-retrieval system; no RapidAPI/REST/MCP/function-calling tool index. The agent interacts with the environment via Python code execution within the MLAgentBench framework, not a tool registry.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tool/API retrieval; no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> prompt augmentation + case adaptation (case reuse): the selected top-ranked case is given to the Planner (development) or Adapter (deployment), which analyzes the case's human insights / solution code and adapts/reuses it to produce a new experiment plan y^t (development) or directly generate the solution Python code s (deployment). The plan is then executed; execution feedback drives the next revision.
- **planning integration**:
> retrieve-then-plan inside an iterative CBR loop. Development pipeline per step: Retrieve (dense top-k) -> ReviseRank (LLM re-rank using feedback) -> Reuse (Planner adapts the chosen case into an experiment plan y^t) -> Execute (Programmer writes Python, runs it, Debugger fixes bugs Reflexion-style, Logger summarizes feedback l^t) -> Retain (archive improved solutions) -> loop back to ReviseRank. Deployment: single retrieve-then-adapt-then-generate-code, no loop. Planning and retrieval are tightly interleaved at the per-iteration level in development.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: per-iteration (per experiment-plan revision within a task). Retrieval/reranking is woven in once per CBR iteration step (T=5 steps), each tied to one plan-generate-execute-feedback cycle; not per-CoT-token or per-tool-call. Deployment is per-answer (single shot).
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> execution-feedback-driven revision (development) plus LLM-prompted adaptation: the Planner reuses the selected case to draft an experiment plan, the plan is executed, and the resulting execution feedback drives both the next-iteration ReviseRank case re-selection and the plan revision (Revise loop). In deployment, an Adapter performs LLM-prompted adaptation of a single retrieved past solution case to the new task to directly generate code (no execution loop).
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Mixed: in the development human-insight bank, items are distilled free-text strategy/insight (cleaned technical reports and GPT-3.5-summarized textual solutions describing model architecture, hyper-parameters, objective, tricks); retained solution cases and deployment cases are executable Python programs paired with task descriptions. So injected items range from distilled strategy/guideline text to executable program/skill code.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> distilled strategy/insight (textual expert solutions summarizing design choices, architectures, hyper-parameters, tricks) for human-insight cases, and reusable procedural solution (executable Python code) for retained/deployment cases. The ablation explicitly contrasts learning from a homogeneous case (example task + one of its solutions) vs heterogeneous textual human insights, finding the homogeneous (concrete solution) case more effective in deployment.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> (1) ReviseRank uses execution feedback to discard misleading candidates and promote the empirically-useful case, mitigating retrieval noise from pure similarity. (2) The reuse process is restricted to a single best case - the paper shows adding extra cases injects interference/noise and degrades performance, so limiting k-in-context to 1 is itself a noise-control choice. (3) Retain only archives solutions with improved test performance, keeping the case bank high-quality. (4) Debugger (Reflexion-style self-reflection on execution errors) corrects buggy generated code before feedback is logged.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: episodic / skill-library: two case banks - a human-insight case bank C (expert knowledge) and an agent experience case bank B that stores successful (task, solution-code) cases retained during development for reuse in deployment.
- **write back**: Yes. At each development iteration's Retain step, if the trained model achieves improved test performance, DS-Agent archives the task description tau and its Python script s into BOTH the human-insight case bank C and the agent experience case bank B for future reuse.
- **online growth**: Partially. During the development stage the case banks grow at test/run time as successful cases are retained. The agent case bank B used in the deployment stage is grown during development and then fixed (frozen) for deployment; deployment itself does not write new cases back.
- **write back trigger**:
> on-success only, gated by performance improvement: a case (tau, s) is retained into C and B only when the trained ML model shows improved performance on the test set at the end of an iteration step. Failed or non-improving solutions are not stored as cases. (Within-iteration debugging from failures occurs but is not persisted as a stored case.)
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success-only for memory: only performance-improving solutions are retained as reusable cases. Failures/errors are handled transiently within an iteration - the Debugger reflects on execution errors (Reflexion-inspired) and the ReviseRanker uses the execution feedback log (which can reflect poor results) to re-select cases - but negative/failure cases are not stored in the case bank as retrievable contrastive items.
- **memory evolution update**: append-only with a quality gate: new successful cases are appended to C and B when they improve performance; the paper does not describe dedup-merge, delta-update, refine-overwrite, or forgetting/pruning of already-stored cases.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No. The dense retriever is off-the-shelf top-k cosine similarity (not RL/value-optimized). The ReviseRank re-selection is an LLM prompting policy conditioned on execution feedback, but it is not a trained/RL-optimized retrieval policy (the paper explicitly avoids finetuning the retriever due to the cost of execution feedback).
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> No. Single-agent (multi-role: Retriever, ReviseRanker, Planner, Programmer, Debugger, Logger, Adapter are sub-modules of one DS-Agent system, not independent collaborating agents) with private case banks. No cross-agent or cross-framework memory sharing is described, though knowledge does transfer across the two stages (development cases reused in deployment).

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> A purpose-built suite of 30 data science tasks (12 development: FB, AR, TE, CP, ETT, ILI, HW, EC, MCS, WBY, ST, ES; 18 deployment: JS, HR, BPP, WR, DAG, BQ, TFC, WTH, ELE, SRC, UGL, HB, CA, CS, MH, SS, CO, SD), spanning text/time-series/tabular modalities and regression/classification, with metrics including accuracy, AUROC, NLL, MCRMSE, MSE, RMLSE, MAE, RMSE, MedAE. Built on top of the MLAgentBench framework. Human-insight cases crawled from 12 recently-completed Kaggle competitions.
- **benchmark family**: Automated data science / AutoML over Kaggle-style ML tasks (code + decision-making); built on the MLAgentBench (Huang et al. 2023) framework. Not one of the standard QA/web/embodied/tool/SWE-bench families - it is a custom Kaggle-derived data-science benchmark.
- **baselines**:
> Development stage: ResearchAgent (Huang et al. 2023, the MLAgentBench SOTA language agent for ML research tasks), on GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. Deployment stage: Zero-shot (direct prompting) and One-shot (a random case from the agent case bank in context), each on GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and the open-source Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1. Ablations: DS-Agent w/o ReviseRank (= a RAG-based LLM agent) and DS-Agent w/o CBR.
- **key metrics**: Development: success rate (bug-free model build within a fixed number of steps) and mean rank / best rank w.r.t. task-specific metrics. Deployment: one-pass rate (build a working ML model in a single trial) and mean rank. Resource cost: USD per run.
- **headline result**:
> DS-Agent with GPT-4 achieves a 100% success rate in the development stage and a near-100% (GPT-3.5: 85%) one-pass rate in deployment, with a 36% average one-pass-rate improvement across alternative LLMs in deployment; it achieves the best rank in both stages, costing $1.60 per run (development) and $0.13 per run (deployment) with GPT-4 (deployment GPT-4 single run $0.1350, GPT-3.5 $0.0045 - over 90% cheaper than development).
- **ablations**:
> (1) w/o ReviseRank (= RAG-based agent using the top-1 similarity case without feedback-driven re-ranking): average best rank degrades from 2.08 to 2.58 on 12 development tasks (GPT-4), showing feedback-aware reranking matters. (2) w/o CBR (prompt LLM to plan without human insights): worst, average best rank 3.41, confirming the Kaggle expert-knowledge cases are the main driver. (3) Deployment: learning from past successful (homogeneous) cases vs textual human insights (heterogeneous) - homogeneous solution cases win on nearly all tasks. (4) Hyper-parameter on number of in-context example cases: best with a single case; performance declines rapidly as more cases are added (extra cases inject interference). (5) Performance improves monotonically with CBR iteration steps (T) for both GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> No. Intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG / completeness) are not reported. Evaluation is end-to-end (success rate, one-pass rate, mean/best rank on ML task metrics); the value of the retrieval/reranking components is shown via ablations rather than standalone retrieval metrics.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Mostly outcome (final ML model performance via mean/best rank; build success/one-pass rate). Some process insight is provided: the success/one-pass rate captures whether the pipeline can build a bug-free model (intermediate process quality), and the performance-vs-iteration-step curve shows step-wise improvement, but no formal reasoning-faithfulness or step-wise retrieval-accuracy metric.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Strong cost emphasis. Development with GPT-4 costs $1.60 per run; deployment $0.13 (GPT-4) / $0.0045 (GPT-3.5) per run - over 90% cheaper than development, by design (deployment drops the iteration loop and uses a single retrieved case for direct code generation). Hyper-parameters: T=5 iterations and k=5 retrieved candidates, n_debug=5 debugging attempts in development. The two-stage split (expensive exploration once, cheap reuse many times) is the core efficiency lever; deployment runs even on open-source Mixtral-8x7B.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-then-pruned: dense retrieval returns k=5 candidates, ReviseRank re-ranks them, and exactly ONE top case is injected for reuse (in both stages). The single-case budget is deliberate - the hyper-parameter study shows that injecting more than one case in context degrades performance, so selection count is effectively capped at 1 case in the prompt.
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> 30 human-curated data science tasks (12 development + 18 deployment) across 3 modalities (text, time series, tabular) and 2 task types (regression, classification); each task has a natural-language description, train/valid/test split, a random-guess baseline script, and a task-specific metric. Datasets sourced from varied platforms and mostly released after Sep 2021 to avoid LLM pretraining contamination; answers are verifiable via the task-specific evaluation metric on a held-out test set. Built on MLAgentBench. Best system (DS-Agent + GPT-4) attains 100% development success and best rank, indicating headroom remains on harder text/time-series tasks vs easy tabular tasks.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Case-Based Reasoning (Aamodt & Plaza 1994; Kolodner 1992; Watson & Marir 1994); the MLAgentBench / ResearchAgent framework (Huang et al. 2023) it is implemented on top of and compared against; Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023) for the self-reflective Debugger; RankGPT-style LLM relevance ranking (Sun et al. 2023) for ReviseRank; llm-embedder (Zhang et al. 2023b) as the dense embedding retriever; RAG / in-context example selection (Lewis et al. 2020; Rubin et al. 2022) as the conceptual retrieval baseline.
- **contrasts with**:
> RAG-based LLMs (formalized as retrieve-then-generate with a single latent retrieved case and NO feedback-driven case adjustment or retain step - DS-Agent's w/o ReviseRank ablation is exactly a RAG agent); plain LLM planning without expert cases (w/o CBR ablation); ResearchAgent (high reasoning/coding demand, no CBR); AutoML techniques (HPO/NAS search-based, contrasted in Appendix C as lacking LLM flexibility and case reuse); Zero-shot / One-shot (random case) prompting baselines; complementary-but-distinct concurrent work Data Interpreter (Hong et al. 2024a).
- **lineage**:
> Group D (case-based planning / experience-grounded LLM planners). DS-Agent is a canonical, explicitly CBR-grounded instantiation of the full 4R cycle (Retrieve-Reuse-Revise-Retain) for ML experiment-plan generation, sitting in the lineage of CBR-augmented LLM agents and growing-memory experience planners, and explicitly positioned as a generalization of RAG (which lacks Revise + Retain).

<a id="item-ical"></a>
### 70. ICAL (In-Context Abstraction Learning) — "VLM Agents Generate Their Own Memories: Distilling Experience into Embodied Programs of Thought"

2024  ·  NeurIPS 2024  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.14596)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: NeurIPS 2024 (Spotlight)
- **authors affiliation**: Gabriel Sarch, Lawrence Jang, Michael J. Tarr, William W. Cohen, Kenneth Marino, Katerina Fragkiadaki. Carnegie Mellon University; Google DeepMind (Cohen and Marino).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.14596
- **code url**: https://github.com/Gabesarch/ICAL
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (project website https://ical-learning.github.io/; no maintained leaderboard/paper-list)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Multimodal/embodied agents and decision-making: dialogue-based household instruction following (embodied), multimodal autonomous web navigation, and egocentric video action forecasting.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, continual learning of a single VLM agent that transforms noisy/suboptimal demonstrations (from humans or its own policy) into high-quality, generalizable examples. Two phases: (1) an offline-style abstraction phase where a VLM corrects action errors and writes language+visual 'programs of thought'; (2) a human-in-the-loop phase where annotations are refined via natural-language feedback during execution in similar environments. Supervision is available as suboptimal demos plus non-expert human feedback. The learned example library is then used either for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) at test time or for supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Single-agent, private growing memory. (Ego4D is a passive setting using the abstraction phase only, no human-in-the-loop.)
- **what is retrieved**:
> Abstracted experiences / cases: optimized trajectories paired with multimodal 'programs of thought' (generalized strategies, causal/task abstractions, object state changes, temporal subgoals, task-relevant visual elements / construals) plus the corresponding action sequence — stored as in-context demonstrations.
- **retrieval grounding**: GROWING/episodic memory the agent writes to itself (memory set M of self-distilled abstracted examples that grows during continual learning), rather than a static external corpus.
- **completeness vs topk objective**: Fixed top-k ranking objective: retrieve the top-K (K=5) most similar abstracted examples by aggregated similarity to inject into the prompt; no notion of recovering a complete minimal set or variable-size precision-driven recommendation.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: Retrieve, Reuse, Revise, Retain (all four). Retrieve = top-K similar abstracted examples; Reuse = inject as in-context exemplars / SFT data; Revise = VLM self-refinement + human-in-the-loop correction of trajectory and thoughts; Retain = store successful refined example into M.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> A full abstracted example (case = problem-solution): an optimized trajectory plus its language/visual programs of thought. At deployment in VisualWebArena/Ego4D the in-context example is built around a single time step (image input + abstracted textual state + summary + step-by-step reasoning + predicted next state + abstraction comments + predicted action); an appendix variant uses the full trajectory.
- **index source**:
> Growing memory built online/at learning-time: examples are induced by abstracting noisy human or agent demonstrations and stored into memory set M, which grows continually as more demonstrations are processed; frozen at deployment when used purely for RAG/SFT (but grows during the learning loop).
- **index structure topology**: Flat similarity index over example embeddings; retrieval by aggregated cosine similarity over three components (input instruction text, textual state, visual state). No graph/hierarchical/cluster topology.
- **retriever type**: Dense embedding retriever (off-the-shelf): OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 for text and CLIP ViT-B/32 for images, combined via a weighted multi-modal cosine-similarity score. A reranking variant is also explored.
- **retriever learning signal**: None (off-the-shelf frozen embedders); the only tuned parameters are the per-domain similarity-weighting coefficients (lambda_I, lambda_textual, lambda_visual) chosen on a held-out validation set. The retriever itself is not contrastively trained or RL-optimized.
- **query construction**:
> Query is formed from the current context: the new task instruction I, the current textual state description (objects/attributes for embodied, HTML elements for web), and the current visual state (webpage image / video frames, Set-of-Marks annotated). Matched against stored example embeddings.
- **query granularity**: Both task-level and step/state-level: retrieval is conditioned on the instruction (task-level) and the current scene/state. In VisualWebArena/Ego4D deployment, top-5 examples are retrieved at each time step (step/state-level).
- **when to retrieve**: Iterative / per-step at deployment (retrieve top-5 at each time step for web/embodied execution); also retrieves during the learning loop (abstraction and human-in-the-loop phases) to condition new abstractions on prior examples. Fixed schedule, not uncertainty-triggered.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule: retrieval happens deterministically at every decision step (and at each abstraction-generation step during learning); there is no learned router, confidence threshold, reflection token, or agent-initiated retrieval request.
- **reranking**: Optional reranking stage explored as an ablation ('w/ retrieval re-ranking' on TEACh gave 35.3 SR / 51.7 GC vs 35.1 / 49.3 without); the main pipeline uses weighted multi-modal cosine similarity top-K without a dedicated cross-encoder reranker.
- **retrieved context refinement**: None at retrieval time beyond the optional reranking; the retrieved items are themselves already-distilled/refined abstractions (refinement happens at write-time via self-refinement + human feedback, not as a post-retrieval step).
- **tool document engineering**: N/A — ICAL retrieves experience examples, not tool/API documents.
- **index content separation**: N/A — no lightweight-index-then-load-content / progressive-disclosure separation; embeddings index full abstracted examples directly.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A — not a tool-retrieval system; agent acts via a fixed action API (e.g., go_to(X), pickup(X)) / Python code, no RapidAPI/RESTful/MCP tool index.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A — no inter-tool dependency modeling.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Two utilization modes: (1) prompt augmentation — the top-K retrieved abstracted examples are injected as in-context demonstrations for retrieval-augmented generation with a VLM (GPT-4V/GPT-4o/GPT-3.5); (2) training signal — the abstracted examples form a dataset for supervised fine-tuning (LoRA on GPT-3.5; full SFT of Qwen2-VL). The two can be combined (SFT + retrieval).
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-act with per-step interleaving: at each step the agent retrieves the top-5 abstracted examples and prompts the VLM to emit the next action (or a Python program over the action API) for embodied/web tasks; one-shot conditioning for the passive Ego4D forecasting. No MCTS/tree-search integration.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-tool-call / per-action-step within a rollout for interactive tasks (retrieve and re-prompt each step); per-answer for the passive Ego4D action-forecasting setting.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> Execution-feedback-driven and human-in-the-loop revision at write-time, then mostly verbatim ICL reuse at deployment: a retrieved example is used as an in-context exemplar; the agent does not run an explicit per-query case-adaptation step at test time (adaptation/revision is what produced the stored example).
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Distilled multimodal 'programs of thought': free-text strategy/causal abstractions, subgoal decomposition, predicted state changes and abstraction comments, task-relevant visual elements, plus the optimized action sequence (which can be executable code over the action API). Structured-note + executable-action hybrid.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Distilled strategy/insight and state-aware guideline level (causal abstractions, object state changes, temporal subgoals/decomposition, visual construals) layered on an optimized trajectory — explicitly contrasted against raw, unabstracted demonstrations.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Robustness comes from the abstraction/refinement pipeline rather than retrieval-time filtering: a VLM self-corrects action inefficiencies/errors in noisy trajectories, and human-in-the-loop natural-language feedback iteratively refines abstractions; only successful refined examples are retained, filtering bad experiences out of memory. Paper notes it can handle noisy demos but not extremely misleading ones.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: Episodic example library / skill-and-experience memory (memory set M of abstracted trajectory examples). Episodic-with-procedural-content.
- **write back**: True — successful refined trajectories and their thoughts are stored into the memory set M (M <- M ∪ {(xi_optimized, L)}); this self-generated memory is the core contribution ('VLM agents generate their own memories').
- **online growth**:
> True — the example library grows continually as new demonstrations are processed; the paper shows continual-learning/meta-learning effects (later examples require fewer environment steps and less human feedback). At pure test-time deployment the store is used as-is, but during the learning loop it grows online.
- **write back trigger**: On-success only: after the human-in-the-loop phase, if the trajectory succeeds it is stored; if still unsuccessful after N_feedbacks iterations it is discarded and the agent moves on. (Appendix S4.5 explores relabeling partially-successful demos, which helps weaker models.)
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success-only storage in the main method: failed/unsuccessful trajectories (after exhausting feedback iterations) are NOT stored or retrieved. Failures are used transiently as feedback signal to drive revision, not retained as negative cases. (An appendix variant relabels partially-successful demonstrations.)
- **memory evolution update**:
> Append-only: successful abstracted examples are added to M (M <- M ∪ {...}); stored entries are not subsequently mutated, merged, pruned, or overwritten. (Earlier examples are retrieved to help abstract later ones, improving future abstractions, but already-stored entries themselves are not edited.)
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No — case selection is a fixed weighted-cosine-similarity top-K, not a learned/RL-optimized retrieval policy (only the per-domain similarity weights are tuned on validation).
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: Single-agent private memory — the agent builds and uses its own example library; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: TEACh (dialogue-based household instruction following, validation unseen/seen); VisualWebArena (multimodal autonomous web navigation; classifieds/Reddit/shopping); Ego4D v2 (egocentric long-term video action anticipation/forecasting).
- **benchmark family**: embodied (TEACh) + web (VisualWebArena) + video/embodied forecasting (Ego4D).
- **baselines**:
> HELPER (hand-written domain-expert examples; prior TEACh SOTA); Zero-Shot CoT; Raw Visual Demos (inverse-dynamics-labeled) and Raw Kinesthetic Demos (GT-action labeled); GPT-4V + Set-of-Marks (Koh et al., prior VisualWebArena SOTA), GPT-4o + SoM, Gemini-Pro-1.5, CogVLM, IDEFICS-80B-Instruct, base Qwen2-VL-7B; for Ego4D: few-shot GPT-4V with CoT and the fully-supervised SlowFast+Transformer baseline (Grauman et al. 2022).
- **key metrics**:
> TEACh: Success Rate (SR) and Goal-Condition success (GC). VisualWebArena: task success rate (seen/unseen/average). Ego4D: edit distance (Damerau-Levenshtein) over predicted verbs/nouns/actions. Plus efficiency metrics: environment steps and human feedbacks per example; scaling vs #examples.
- **headline result**:
> Across benchmarks ICAL sets SOTA: TEACh +12.6% goal-condition success over HELPER (and combined SFT+retrieval on ICAL examples beats raw human/expert demos by 17.5% GC); VisualWebArena task success improved 1.6x with retrieval-augmented GPT-4V (14.3% -> 22.7% avg) and fine-tuned Qwen2-VL 2.8x over base (2.9% -> 8.2%); Ego4D surpasses few-shot GPT-4V and is competitive with supervised models using 639x less in-domain training data; scales 2x better than raw demonstrations.
- **ablations**:
> TEACh ablations (GPT-3.5): full ICAL retrieval 35.1 SR / 49.3 GC; w/o programs-of-thought (abstraction) phase 29.4 / 44.9; w/o human-in-the-loop 29.9 / 41.0; w/ retrieval re-ranking 35.3 / 51.7; w/ GPT-4 41.7 / 63.6; ICAL SFT 23.2 / 40.3; ICAL SFT + retrieval 35.8 / 54.2. VisualWebArena ablations (GPT-4V, 257-episode subset): ICAL 28.0/21.6/22.2 (seen/unseen/avg) vs GPT-4V 11.5/12.9/12.7; w/o image 28.0/17.3/19.0; w/ full text trajectory 57.7/21.6/25.5 (helps seen but not unseen, and costs more, so single-step+image used for final). Ablations show both the offline abstraction (programs-of-thought) phase and the human-in-the-loop phase are important.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No — only end-to-end task metrics (SR/GC, web success, edit distance) are reported; intrinsic retrieval metrics like Recall@k/nDCG are not reported separately (retrieval quality is assessed only via downstream task performance and a reranking ablation).
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome metrics (final task success / goal-condition success / action-forecasting edit distance), plus learning-process/efficiency metrics (environment steps per example, human feedbacks per example, scaling vs number of learned examples) that characterize the continual-learning dynamics rather than per-step reasoning faithfulness.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Continual-learning efficiency: in TEACh, the second half of examples required 38.8% fewer environment steps (436±88 -> 267±43, p=0.0143) and 71.6% less human feedback (0.74±0.17 -> 0.21±0.08, p=0.0089) per example; scales 2x better than raw demonstrations; only ~10 learned examples give +14.7% SR over zero-shot CoT; Ego4D competitive with supervised models using 639x less in-domain data. Appendix shows full-trajectory in-context examples raise cost (context length) without improving unseen success, so single-step+image retrieval is used. Uses K=5 retrieval.
- **context budget and selection count**: Fixed-k: top-K = 5 abstracted examples injected at each step (k=5 for example retrieval). Single time-step representation (image + abstracted state + reasoning + action) chosen over full-trajectory to bound context length / cost; not adaptive or budget-capped beyond the fixed k.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A — primary research paper, not a survey.
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A — uses existing benchmarks (TEACh, VisualWebArena, Ego4D v2) rather than introducing one. (Data-efficiency note: ICAL learns from ~30 non-expert human demos in VisualWebArena and uses 639x less in-domain training data than the supervised Ego4D baseline.)

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> HELPER (Sarch et al., embodied LLM agent with memory-augmented prompting / retrieval — extended as the TEACh execution backbone and baseline); VisualWebArena + GPT-4V + Set-of-Marks prompting (Koh et al.); set-of-marks visual prompting; in-context learning / chain-of-thought and self-reflection lines (e.g., Reflexion-style introspection); CLIP and OpenAI text embeddings for retrieval; LoRA fine-tuning; Qwen2-VL.
- **contrasts with**:
> Methods that only store/retrieve successful raw action plans or trajectories without distilled abstractions (HELPER, AdaPlanner-style, Synapse/trajectory-as-exemplar); text-only experience/insight methods that focus on reward signals or store human corrections only after failures; expert-hand-written example pipelines (HELPER requires 48-107 lines of expert text per example) and pure prompt-engineering approaches.
- **lineage**:
> Group D (case-based / experience planning): a multimodal experience-distillation / self-generated-memory line that converts raw suboptimal trajectories into abstracted, retrievable insights stored in a growing example library for RAG or fine-tuning — sits between trajectory-memory agents (HELPER, Synapse, ExpeL) and procedural skill-library agents (Voyager), distinguished by cognitive abstractions (causal, state-change, subgoal, visual construal) and human-in-the-loop refinement.

<a id="item-mart"></a>
### 71. MART (MLLM As ReTriever): Interactively Learning Multimodal Retrieval for Embodied Agents

2024  ·  arXiv 2410.03450  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.03450)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: ICLR 2025 (preprint arXiv:2410.03450, submitted Oct 2024; DBLP conf/iclr/YueXK025)
- **authors affiliation**:
> Junpeng Yue (School of Computer Science, Peking University), Xinrun Xu (Institute of Software, Chinese Academy of Sciences), Borje F. Karlsson (Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence / BAAI), Zongqing Lu (Peking University, corresponding author). Yue and Xu work as interns at BAAI.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.03450

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Embodied agents / embodied household task execution (multimodal MLLM agents performing fine-grained control in 3D simulated home environments).
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent setting: a retrieval-augmented MLLM agent (frozen GPT-4o policy) must complete long-horizon embodied tasks drawn from a task distribution by conditioning on one retrieved expert reference trajectory. Supervision comes from environment interaction: for training tasks, candidate expert trajectories are fed to the agent and their induced task success rates serve as effectiveness feedback. Train and test task distributions (and their memories) are disjoint, so evaluation measures generalization to unseen tasks/scenes. The agent outputs fine-grained control actions directly (not teleportation), with observations being egocentric images (plus natural-language feedback in AI2-THOR).
- **what is retrieved**: Multimodal expert trajectories (sequences of task instruction + egocentric observation images + actions + environment feedback), used as in-context reference/grounding for the embodied MLLM agent. After Trajectory Abstraction these become condensed milestone summaries.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> Hybrid leaning toward a fixed/offline-induced episodic memory of expert trajectories. The retrievable store is built offline from planner-collected successful executions (separate train and test memories); it is not grown online during deployment. It is grounded in agent-environment experience (episodic trajectory memory) rather than a static document/KB corpus.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Single-best (top-1) selection: the fine-tuned MLLM retriever scores candidate trajectories for effectiveness and the single highest-scoring trajectory is injected as the reference (one-shot, single-trajectory due to MLLM context-window limits). Not a completeness/minimal-set objective; effectively a precision-driven top-1 selection.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> Retrieve: yes (effectiveness-based retrieval of an expert trajectory). Reuse: yes (retrieved trajectory used as in-context grounding for the agent). Revise: partial/implicit (Trajectory Abstraction condenses/re-represents trajectories into milestones and inferred rules conditioned on the current task, but the agent does not adapt the case into a new stored solution). Retain: no (memory is fixed offline; no write-back of new cases). Flags: [Retrieve=yes, Reuse=yes, Revise=partial, Retain=no].
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False. The paper frames itself as multimodal trajectory retrieval / memory retrieval with interactive preference learning; it does not cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner or explicitly invoke case-based reasoning terminology, though it realizes Retrieve/Reuse mechanisms of CBR under another name.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: Full multimodal expert trajectory (task instruction + observation/image sequence + action sequence + feedback), represented at retrieval/use time as a Trajectory Abstraction (a small set of key milestones, avg 3.13 milestones from avg 11.51 input steps).
- **index source**:
> Offline-induced growing-free memory: expert trajectories collected offline via a classical planner-based method (PDDL/FF-style planner) from successful task executions, then redundancy-filtered. Distinct training memory and testing memory are constructed offline (AI2-THOR: 170 train / 118 test sub-task trajectories; LEGENT: 40 train / 32 test trajectories). No online/test-time growth.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat memory pool of trajectories (no graph or hierarchy). Retrieval is performed by scoring each candidate trajectory in the (small) pool with the MLLM retriever rather than via a vector ANN index. For the Similarity+LLaVA and RAP baselines a flat embedding similarity index is used to pre-select top-K candidates.
- **retriever type**:
> LLM-as-retriever / learned generative scorer: a fine-tuned MLLM (LLaVA-7B) augmented with a Bradley-Terry scalar score head acts as the retriever, directly scoring trajectory effectiveness for the current task+observation. (Baselines use dense embedding similarity; MART itself is the learned MLLM scorer.)
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Downstream-task-effectiveness / interactive preference learning via a Bradley-Terry reward-modeling loss. For each training task, K candidate trajectories are fed to the agent; their induced task success rates produce a partial order; pairwise comparisons (C(K,2) pairs) form positive (higher success) / negative (lower success) preference pairs used to fine-tune the MLLM retriever's score head. This is effectiveness/interaction-based preference learning, not similarity-label contrastive training.
- **query construction**:
> The query is the current task instruction plus the current (initial) egocentric observation. The MLLM retriever takes (current task instruction l^c, current observation o_1^c, candidate trajectory abstraction A(tau_i^e)) plus a judging prompt, and outputs a scalar effectiveness score per candidate.
- **query granularity**: Task-level / one-shot at t=0: a single retrieval is performed at the start of each (sub-)task using the initial observation and task instruction; the retrieved reference trajectory is then used throughout that (sub-)task.
- **when to retrieve**: One-shot per (sub-)task (retrieve once at the beginning of each task or sub-task, before execution). In AI2-THOR, tasks are decomposed into sub-tasks and retrieval occurs per sub-task.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule: retrieval is triggered deterministically at the start of each task (or each sub-task after task decomposition in AI2-THOR); there is no uncertainty-, confidence-, or agent-initiated trigger.
- **reranking**:
> MART itself functions as a one-stage effectiveness scorer/selector (no separate rerank stage in the full method). The Similarity+LLaVA (SL) baseline uses a two-stage retrieve-then-rank (embedding similarity top-K then plain LLaVA Yes/No scoring), and the Sim.+FTM ablation uses similarity retrieval then MART's fine-tuned model as a reranker; both underperform the unified MART.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Trajectory Abstraction: a separate MLLM (GPT-4o, zero-shot) condenses each trajectory into key milestones (description + image + feedback + overarching actions between milestones), removing redundant/irrelevant steps and reducing token count while preserving task-relevant grounding (e.g., reduces a 73-step trajectory to 5 milestones; 13 transitions to 6 inferred rules). This is a decompose-then-distill/compression refinement applied before both retriever scoring and agent use.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tools/APIs; the analogous step is Trajectory Abstraction which summarizes trajectories into milestone form before scoring and use).
- **index content separation**: Partial: trajectories are stored in full but a lightweight Trajectory Abstraction (milestones) is what is fed to the retriever and agent, reducing context load. Not a formal index-then-content progressive-disclosure scheme; abstraction is the on-demand condensed representation.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index or external API protocol; memory is a static offline trajectory pool).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tools / no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**: Prompt augmentation / in-context grounding: the single highest-scored expert trajectory abstraction is injected into the frozen MLLM agent's prompt as a reference to ground its fine-grained action planning for the current embodied (sub-)task.
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-act with one-shot exemplar at plan time: one reference trajectory is retrieved per (sub-)task and used as a single in-context exemplar; in AI2-THOR long-horizon tasks are first decomposed into sub-tasks (ALFRED-style) and retrieval+execution proceed hierarchically per sub-task. The agent then directly outputs control actions over the finite horizon.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-(sub)task: retrieval is interleaved at the granularity of a whole task (LEGENT) or sub-task (AI2-THOR), not per-CoT-step, per-token, or per-action within a rollout.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> LLM-prompted abstraction/condensation rather than explicit case adaptation: the retrieved trajectory is re-represented via GPT-4o Trajectory Abstraction (milestones / inferred implicit rules conditioned on the current task) and used as a verbatim in-context exemplar; the agent does not edit the case into a new solution. Effectively a distilled-exemplar reuse.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Distilled milestone summary of a trajectory: each milestone contains a textual description, the corresponding key image, the corresponding feedback, and the overarching actions between milestones. Some cases yield an abstract set of inferred rules. (Surface form: condensed multimodal trajectory abstraction injected as in-context text+images.)
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Distilled/condensed trajectory: between a raw trajectory and a reusable workflow. Trajectory Abstraction turns the raw multimodal trajectory into key milestones (and sometimes inferred implicit rules), i.e., a state-aware milestone/strategy representation rather than the raw step-by-step trajectory.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Two mechanisms: (1) the retriever is fine-tuned on interactive effectiveness preferences so it prioritizes trajectories that actually help (filtering out trajectories that are similar but ineffective/misleading, addressing the observed weak correlation between similarity and success); (2) Trajectory Abstraction removes redundant/distracting steps and irrelevant information before the trajectory is used, reducing distractor noise and context overflow.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: Episodic (a memory pool of expert trajectories / past task executions); no skill-library, graph, or latent memory.
- **write back**: False (no write-back): the expert trajectory memory is constructed offline via a planner and frozen; the agent does not store new experiences/cases during deployment. The only transformation is the offline/at-use Trajectory Abstraction of existing trajectories.
- **online growth**: No: the retrievable store is fixed after offline induction (separate train/test memories); it does not grow at test time.
- **write back trigger**: Never (no test-time write-back). Memory entries are populated offline from planner-collected successful trajectories prior to training/evaluation.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success-only for the stored memory (only successful planner-collected trajectories are retained as expert references). However, the retriever's TRAINING signal is contrastive over effectiveness: trajectories yielding lower task success (relatively 'failed/less-effective' references) become negative items in Bradley-Terry preference pairs, so relative ineffectiveness is used as a learning signal (not stored as corrective rules).
- **memory evolution update**: Append-only at construction with offline dedup/redundancy filtering (about one-third of redundant AI2-THOR trajectories are filtered out). No post-write mutation, delta-update, or forgetting during deployment.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Partially: case-selection is a LEARNED scorer (an MLLM fine-tuned with a Bradley-Terry preference/reward-modeling objective from interactive feedback) rather than fixed similarity top-k. It is a learned effectiveness ranker, but not an RL/value-based sequential retrieval policy (no soft Q-learning / M-MDP).
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No: single-agent private memory; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: AI2-THOR (with an ALFWorld+ALFRED-inspired custom embodied task setting, task decomposition into sub-tasks; 45 train tasks / 260 sub-tasks, 28 test tasks / 158 sub-tasks) and LEGENT ('Come Here' and 'Where Is' tasks, each One-room/Two-room; 40 train tasks, 32 test tasks).
- **benchmark family**: Embodied (AI2-THOR household manipulation/navigation, adapting ALFWorld/ALFRED; LEGENT embodied home navigation). RAP baseline references ALFWorld/WebShop/Franka-Kitchen/Meta-World, but MART's own evaluation is on AI2-THOR and LEGENT.
- **baselines**:
> Plain-Agent (PA): GPT-4o agent with no reference trajectories/no memory. LLaVA-Plain (LP): pre-trained LLaVA, no head/no fine-tuning, scored via Yes/No token probability. Similarity+LLaVA (SL): embedding-similarity top-K retrieval then plain-LLaVA ranking (retrieve-then-rank). RAP (Kagaya et al., 2024): per-modality plain-similarity retrieval (most similar prior method).
- **key metrics**: Success Rate (SR), and in AI2-THOR also sub-task Success Rate (SR-Sub); Average Steps (AS), and sub-task Average Steps (AS-Sub) (lower is better; failed cases counted at the step limit). Each task tested 5 times.
- **headline result**:
> In AI2-THOR, MART achieves SR 0.40 vs best baseline 0.26 (LLaVA-Plain) -- a >10 percentage-point (over 50% relative) gain; SR-Sub 0.75 vs 0.69; AS 123.19 vs 144.18. In LEGENT, MART achieves SR 0.87 vs best baseline 0.75 (SL/RAP); AS 13.81 vs ~20.6. The paper summarizes MART as 'consistently surpasses baselines by over 10% across different environments.'
- **ablations**:
> Table 4 ablates two components. (1) w/o Abstraction: removing Trajectory Abstraction drops AI2-THOR SR from 0.40 to 0.31 (9-pt drop) and LEGENT SR from 0.87 to 0.77. (2) Sim.+FTM: decomposing the unified MART into similarity-based retrieval + MART's fine-tuned model as a separate ranker drops AI2-THOR SR to 0.34 and LEGENT SR to 0.77, showing the unified effectiveness-scoring retriever outperforms a retrieve-then-rank pipeline; notably Sim.+FTM still beats SL and RAP, isolating the value of MART's learned trajectory-utility scoring. Case studies show on a 73-step task MART reaches 80% SR / 28 avg steps vs 40% / ~70-75 steps for similarity and no-memory baselines, and 80% SR vs 0% for others on an implicit-rule task.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No: only end-to-end task metrics (SR/SR-Sub, AS/AS-Sub) are reported. No intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG) are reported separately; the paper instead shows scatter plots of success rate vs embedding similarity vs effectiveness score to motivate the approach.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome-oriented (task success rate). Average Steps gives a partial efficiency/process proxy, and case studies qualitatively examine milestone selection and trajectory quality, but there is no formal step-wise retrieval/planning accuracy or reasoning-faithfulness metric.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Efficiency is reported chiefly via Average Steps (MART reduces steps to success, e.g., AI2-THOR AS 123.19 vs 144-160 for baselines; LEGENT AS 13.81 vs ~20-25) and via token reduction from Trajectory Abstraction (avg 11.51 input steps condensed to avg 3.13 milestones), which lowers required context-window length. No explicit API-cost, latency, or retrieval-call-count accounting is given.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (this is a method paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Custom embodied task suites built on existing simulators rather than a new released benchmark: AI2-THOR setting integrates ALFWorld+ALFRED characteristics with task decomposition (45 train / 28 test tasks; 260 / 158 sub-tasks; memory 170 train / 118 test sub-task trajectories after redundancy filtering); LEGENT uses 'Come Here'/'Where Is' x One-room/Two-room (40 train / 32 test tasks; one trajectory per task in memory). Expert trajectories collected by a PDDL/FF-style planner; success verified by environment feedback / agent self-detection. Best system (MART) reaches only 0.40 full-task SR in AI2-THOR, signaling high task difficulty.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> LLaVA-7B (base MLLM retriever) with a Bradley-Terry (1952) reward-modeling preference loss / reward-model score head; GPT-4o as the agent policy and as the Trajectory Abstraction summarizer; AI2-THOR and LEGENT simulators; ALFWorld/ALFRED task design; classical PDDL/FF planner for expert trajectory collection; the general MLLM-agent-with-memory paradigm (Voyager, DEPS, Cradle, LLM-Planner, RAP).
- **contrasts with**:
> Similarity-based multimodal retrievers that select trajectories by surface-level text/image embedding similarity (the paper's central foil), the RAP method (Kagaya et al., 2024) of per-modality similarity retrieval, Similarity+LLaVA retrieve-then-rank, plain LLaVA scoring (LP), and memoryless agents (Plain-Agent / GPT-4o). Also contrasted with VLA models (PaLM-E, RT-2, Gato, VIMA) that train end-to-end policies without explicit memory.
- **lineage**:
> Group D (case-based / experience / trajectory retrieval for planning agents): an embodied, multimodal instance where the retriever itself is a learned effectiveness scorer (MLLM fine-tuned with interactive Bradley-Terry preferences) and retrieved trajectories are distilled (Trajectory Abstraction) before in-context reuse. Sits in the lineage moving from similarity-only memory retrieval to effectiveness/preference-learned, task-grounded trajectory retrieval for MLLM embodied agents.
