<a id="item-mcbr-rag"></a>
### 79. MCBR-RAG (A General Retrieval-Augmented Generation Framework for Multimodal Case-Based Reasoning Applications)

2025  ·  arXiv 2501.05030  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.05030)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **authors affiliation**: Ofir Marom (sole author), Independent Researcher (ofiremarom@gmail.com). Acknowledges Prof. Benjamin Rosman (University of the Witwatersrand) for discussions, but Rosman is not a co-author.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.05030 (PDF: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.05030; HTML: https://arxiv.org/html/2501.05030v1)
- **code url**: https://github.com/OfirMarom/Math24 (official; Python implementation of the Math-24 application only -- pipeline/, experiments/, processing/, llm_api.py, solutions.csv; initial commit 26 Dec 2024). The Backgammon application code/data is NOT released.
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (single-application demo repo above is the only artifact; no leaderboard or maintained paper-list).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Decision-making / problem-solving framed as multimodal case-based reasoning. Two demonstrator applications: (1) Math-24 puzzle solving (text+image; arithmetic reasoning) and (2) Backgammon move analysis (text+image; game-playing expert commentary generation). Both are knowledge-intensive generation tasks where the case problem has non-text (image) components.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-agent, non-interactive RAG over a fixed case repository, generalized to MULTIMODAL cases. A case is a tuple C=(P,S,R) where the problem P=(p_1,...,p_n) has components of arbitrary modality (e.g., image), the solution S is text, and R is the result/outcome. A general framework (MCBR-RAG) converts each non-text problem component into (a) a text-based representation (for LLM context) and (b) a learned application-specific latent representation (for retrieval indexing). At inference: given a new case problem P~, retrieve the top-k most similar solved cases via weighted-average cosine similarity over per-component latent representations, then build an augmented query containing the textified problem + retrieved (textified) cases and prompt a frozen LLM to generate the solution. Supervision: application-specific text-generation models (CNNs) and latent-representation models (FFNNs) are trained on synthetic/labeled data (40,000 Math-24 card images; 100,000 simulated Backgammon board images; GNU Backgammon value labels); the generator LLM is off-the-shelf and frozen. The framework explicitly covers only the Retrieve and Reuse CBR phases; Revise and Retain are left application-specific and not implemented in the experiments.
- **what is retrieved**:
> cases (problem-solution-result tuples). For Math-24: prior solved puzzle cases (card image -> solution set). For Backgammon: prior solved lesson cases (board position image + player + dice + move -> expert textual analysis). Retrieved cases supply both a precise execution plan/strategy (Math-24) and expert analysis exemplars (Backgammon) as LLM context.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus / case repository. The repository is built offline from curated sources (466 Math-24 puzzles in the chosen solution form; 1015 Backgammon cases collected from three expert books) and is frozen at inference time -- no episodic write-back during the experiments. (The CBR Retain phase that would grow the store is acknowledged but deliberately left out of the general framework / experiments.)
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k ranking objective: retrieval returns the arg-top_k most similar cases by a weighted-average cosine similarity (Eq. 7). Math-24 generation uses the single Top Context (TC, k=1) case; Backgammon generation uses the top-3 (k=3) most similar cases. Retrieval quality is reported as Precision@k/Recall@k/F1@k/NDCG@k/MRR@k averaged over k in {1,2,3,4,5}. It is a ranking/relevance objective, not minimal-set completeness or a precision-driven variable-size recommendation.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve, Reuse, -, -] -- the framework explicitly implements only the Retrieve (RAG retrieval, Eq. 7) and Reuse (RAG generation, Eq. 8) phases. Revise (Eq. 3) and Retain (Eq. 4) are formalized in the CBR background but stated to be application-specific and NOT handled generally (the paper notes DS-Agent could implement Revise/Retain via test-set evaluation, but MCBR-RAG itself does not).
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> True. The work explicitly frames itself as Case-Based Reasoning, defines the four-phase CBR pipeline (Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain), and cites the canonical CBR foundations Aamodt & Plaza (1994) and Gilboa & Schmeidler's case-based decision theory (1995). It positions RAG as supporting the Retrieve and Reuse CBR stages and cites prior LLM-CBR works (CBR-RAG, CaseGPT, DS-Agent, logical-fallacy CBR).

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> case (problem-solution-result tuple). The query key is the new-case problem P~ converted to per-component latent representations; the retrieved payload is the full solved case (problem textified + solution S + result R). For Backgammon a case = (board-position image z, player p, dice r, move m, expert analysis S, accuracy R); for Math-24 a case = (card image P, solution set S, results R).
- **index source**:
> Static, offline-induced repository. Math-24: 466 puzzles (subset of 1362 solvable puzzles restricted to the (x1 o x2) x (x3 o x4)=24 form). Backgammon: 1015 cases collected from three expert books (Magriel 'Backgammon' 1977/X-22; Robertie '501 Essential Backgammon Problems'; Trice 'Backgammon Bootcamp'); ~90% retention after legality validation of CNN-extracted positions. No online/test-time induction; the store is frozen.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat vector index with per-component (multi-field) embeddings. Each case is indexed by application-specific learned latent vectors (64-unit FFNN embeddings). Retrieval is kNN over a WEIGHTED AVERAGE of per-component cosine similarities (Eq. 7, sum_j w_j CosineSim(L_j(p~_j), L_j(p_{i,j})), weights >0 summing to 1). For Backgammon the latent key averages the position latent and the post-move position latent ( (l_z + l_z')/2 ). No graph/hierarchical/cluster topology.
- **retriever type**:
> Dense (learned-embedding kNN). Retrieval uses cosine similarity over application-specific latent representations produced by trained FFNNs (Math-24: multi-label classifier FFNN; Backgammon: multi-task FFNN with a value head + a decoder/reconstruction head). No BM25/sparse, no LLM-as-retriever, no generative tool-as-token retrieval. A 'Features'/'Encoding' baseline uses hand-crafted/raw-encoding cosine similarity instead of the learned latent.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Learned, but via SUPERVISED PROXY tasks rather than retrieval/contrastive labels or downstream LLM feedback. Math-24: the latent FFNN is trained as a multi-label classification task predicting solution category + decomposition (40 engineered features + 4 puzzle numbers as input, 4x5 sigmoid outputs), so the embedding clusters puzzles with similar solution structure. Backgammon: the latent FFNN is trained multi-task to predict (a) position value (win/loss probability, from GNU Backgammon labels) and (b) reconstruct the encoded position (decoder), so the embedding captures both strategic value and checker configuration. There is no contrastive similarity-label training, no LM-feedback, no RL, and the retrieval weights w_j (Math-24) / value-vs-decoder weights (Backgammon, swept e.g. (1,0.01)) are hand-tuned/grid-searched, not learned end-to-end.
- **query construction**:
> Raw new-case problem converted by application-specific functions. For retrieval: each problem component p~_j is mapped to its latent representation L_j(p~_j) (image -> text via CNN text-generator -> latent FFNN). For generation: the textified problem T(P~) plus the textified top-k retrieved cases T(C_k) are assembled into an augmented query q_RAG=Query(T(P~), T(C_k)). Math-24 uses a fixed parsing-convention system prompt; for the Top Context query the retrieved case is converted into a precise step-by-step execution plan (solution category + decomposition). No query decomposition into sub-queries.
- **query granularity**:
> Task-level (one-shot at t=0): a single retrieval per new case, with the whole (multimodal) problem as the query, followed by a single conditioned generation. No per-step or trajectory-level re-retrieval. (Backgammon optionally averages two related latent vectors -- current and post-move position -- but this is still one retrieval per case.)
- **when to retrieve**: One-shot: retrieval is performed once per new case before generation (retrieve-then-generate). No iterative/active/adaptive re-retrieval.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed schedule: retrieval always occurs once per incoming case at the start of the Reuse/generation pipeline. The No Context (NC) baseline simply skips retrieval; the General Context (GC, Math-24) baseline injects a fixed generic tip instead of a retrieved case. No confidence/uncertainty/learned-router/reflection trigger.
- **reranking**:
> None. The arg-top_k cases by weighted-average cosine similarity are passed directly to the generator. The Backgammon similarity-weight sweep ((value, decoder) weights such as (1,0.01) chosen as best) is a tuning of the single-stage similarity score, not a second-stage reranker. No cross-encoder/RRF/instruction-tuned reranking.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Minimal / selection + reformatting only. Math-24: the single top case (TC) is reformatted into an explicit step-by-step execution plan (solution category + decomposition) before injection; the GC variant injects a generic tip rather than a retrieved case. Backgammon: the top-3 cases are injected verbatim as (position JSON, player, dice, move, expert analysis). There is no decompose-recompose, distillation across multiple cases, distractor filtering, or compression. A legality-validation filter discards ~10% of Backgammon cases, but that happens during offline index construction, not post-retrieval.
- **tool document engineering**:
> N/A (no tools/APIs; retrieved units are CBR cases, not tool documents). The closest analogue is the bespoke text-generation pipeline (CNNs) that converts image components into text strings for both indexing-input and context, and the engineered aggregate features (Math-24's 40 pair-counting features) feeding the latent model.
- **index content separation**:
> Partial: lightweight learned latent vectors (the retrieval index) are separated from the heavier full case content (textified problem + solution + analysis) that is loaded into the prompt only after the kNN match. This mirrors CBR's index-vs-content separation but is not an agentic progressive-disclosure / SOP-index-then-content mechanism.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index / external API protocol; static case repository, no CRUD auto-sync / RapidAPI / MCP / function-calling).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tools; no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation / case reuse: the textified top-k retrieved cases are concatenated into the LLM query as additional context (q_RAG=Query(T(P~), T(C_k))), and a frozen LLM generates the solution S~=L(q_RAG) (Eq. 8). For Math-24 the retrieved case is converted into an explicit execution plan the LLM follows; for Backgammon the retrieved analyses serve as exemplars to imitate. Adaptation is implicit/LLM-internal -- there is no explicit case-revision step.
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-generate (one-shot exemplars at generation time). Retrieval happens once up front; the k retrieved cases condition a single answer/analysis generation. There is no multi-step planning loop, tree search, or per-step interleaving. For Math-24, the retrieved case essentially supplies a one-shot solution plan (use pair to make {1,24}/{2,12}/{3,8}/{4,6} then multiply) that the LLM executes in a single pass.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer / per-case: a single retrieval feeds a single conditioned generation producing one solution/analysis per new case. Retrieval is not woven per CoT-step or per token.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> LLM-prompted adaptation (implicit). Retrieved cases are injected as context and the frozen LLM reuses/adapts their solutions when generating the new solution; for Math-24 the retrieved case is templated into an execution plan that the LLM applies to the new puzzle. There is no explicit CBR Revise step (no execution-feedback revision, critic-guided revision, or RL reuse-finetuning) -- Revise is explicitly left application-specific and unimplemented.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Textified case content injected into the prompt. Math-24: a step-by-step execution-plan tip derived from the retrieved case's solution category + decomposition (or a generic tip for GC). Backgammon: the retrieved cases' position (JSON-encoded), player, dice, move, plus the expert free-text analysis. Underlying images are first converted to text strings (e.g., '4 5 9 10' for Math-24; '1X2 2X3 3O2 ...' for Backgammon). No latent-soft tokens or executable programs are injected.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Single demonstration / case at the problem-solution level, with light strategy abstraction. Backgammon retrieves literal prior solved cases (board + expert analysis) as exemplars. Math-24 retrieves a single case but presents it as a distilled, state-aware execution plan (solution category + decomposition strategy) rather than a verbatim worked example. Not a reusable workflow library or procedural skill.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Limited / representation-level + filtering. (1) Application-specific learned latent spaces (multi-label-classification FFNN for Math-24; value+decoder multi-task FFNN for Backgammon) are designed so retrieved cases share solution structure / strategic value, improving relevance over raw features (latent similarity beats feature similarity on all metrics). (2) Offline legality validation discards ~10% of Backgammon cases whose CNN-extracted positions are illegal. (3) Backgammon excludes from retrieval all cases originating from the same source analysis as the test case (anti-leakage). There is NO per-retrieval relevance evaluator, self-reflection, reason-in-documents refinement, or distractor-aware training; the paper notes that incorrect context can mislead the LLM (low Negative Rejection on Math-24).

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (static case repository used for retrieval only). It is a non-parametric CBR case store, not an episodic/skill/workflow memory that grows or self-updates during deployment.
- **write back**: False -- the implemented framework does not store newly solved cases back into the repository at inference. The CBR Retain phase (Eq. 4) is formalized but explicitly left application-specific and not realized in the experiments.
- **online growth**: No -- the repository is frozen after offline construction (466 Math-24 cases; 1015 Backgammon cases) and does not grow at deployment/test time.
- **write back trigger**: Never -- no write-back is implemented (Retain phase not realized in MCBR-RAG; the paper only describes, in a footnote, how an application like DS-Agent could retain cases that improve test-set performance).
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success-oriented context. Cases carry a result R (e.g., R=24 if correct for Math-24; a binary accuracy flag for Backgammon), but the framework retrieves similar cases regardless and relies on them being valid expert/solved cases; failed/negative trajectories are not specifically stored or contrastively retrieved. The experiments analyze the LLM's behavior under correct vs incorrect retrieved context (Faithfulness vs Negative Rejection) but do not maintain a failure memory.
- **memory evolution update**: None -- the repository is static at runtime; stored cases are never mutated, merged, delta-updated, refined, or pruned during deployment (the only pruning -- discarding illegal Backgammon positions -- occurs once during offline construction).
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No -- retrieval is fixed similarity top-k (kNN cosine over learned latent embeddings) with hand-tuned component/objective weights. Case selection is not an RL/learned policy; while the latent encoders are trained (supervised proxy tasks), the selection rule itself is fixed arg-top_k similarity, not a trained retrieval policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No -- single-system private case repository; no multi-agent or cross-framework experience sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> Two self-constructed CBR applications: (1) Math-24 -- 466 puzzles (from 1362 solvable, restricted to (x1 o x2)x(x3 o x4)=24 form); text-generation CNN trained on 40,000 synthetic card images; 10 runs each holding out 30 test cases. (2) Backgammon -- 1015 cases collected from three expert books (Magriel; Robertie; Trice); landmark-CNN trained on 100,000 simulated board images; GNU Backgammon value-labeled dataset used for the latent value head; 10 runs each holding out 30 test cases. No standard public benchmark is used.
- **benchmark family**:
> Other / bespoke multimodal-CBR tasks (not in the standard QA/multi-hop/web/embodied/tool/code/memory/decision-RL families). Math-24 is an arithmetic-reasoning puzzle benchmark; Backgammon is a game-analysis text-generation benchmark. Both are author-constructed multimodal (text+image) case repositories.
- **baselines**:
> Primary baseline: No Context (NC) -- the LLM solves/analyzes with no retrieved context (parametric-only). Math-24 also includes a General Context (GC) baseline (a fixed generic execution tip instead of a retrieved case). The proposed conditions are Top Context (TC, Math-24, k=1 retrieved case as plan) and With Context (WC, Backgammon, top-3 retrieved cases). Retrieval baselines: 'Features' (Math-24 hand-crafted feature cosine) and 'Encoding'/'Latent(0,1)' (Backgammon raw-encoding / decoder-only latent) vs the learned 'Latent' similarity. Six LLMs are evaluated as the frozen generator: Llama-3.1-405B-Instruct-Turbo, Qwen2-72B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct-Turbo, Llama-3-70b-chat-hf, Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-Turbo. No external system baselines (e.g., a competing CBR/RAG method) are compared.
- **key metrics**:
> Retrieval: Precision@k, Recall@k, F1-Score@k, NDCG@k, MRR@k (averaged over k in {1..5}), reported as percentages. Generation (Math-24): Accuracy (final expression evaluates to 24 using all 4 numbers), plus Faithfulness (correct given context contains >=1 correct solution) and Negative Rejection (correct given context contains no correct solution). Generation (Backgammon): BERTScore-F1 plus sentence-transformer cosine similarity to the reference expert analysis using all-mpnet-base-v2 (MPNet), all-roberta-large-v1 (RoBERTa), all-MiniLM-L12-v1 (MiniLM), and their average (Avg).
- **headline result**:
> MCBR-RAG context consistently improves generation over the no-context baseline. Math-24: Top Context (TC, retrieved-case-as-plan) yields the highest accuracy for every LLM -- e.g., Llama-3.1-405B-Instruct-Turbo 61.3% TC vs 34.0% NC (and 30.0% GC); Qwen2-72B-Instruct 47.3% TC vs 16.7% NC (a +30.6% absolute gain over NC and +25.3% over GC). Backgammon: With Context (WC, top-3 cases) improves the average sentence-transformer score for all LLMs -- best LLM Meta-Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct-Turbo reaches 63.8% Avg with context vs 58.3% without. Retrieval: learned latent similarity beats raw-feature similarity (e.g., Math-24 SCD NDCG 65.1% latent vs 46.5% features; Backgammon best Latent(1,0.01) NDCG 45.6% vs Encoding 36.6%).
- **ablations**:
> (1) Retrieval representation -- learned Latent similarity > raw Features (Math-24: SCO Latent 82.0%/SCD Latent 64.2% precision vs Features 71.9%/45.4%; SCD NDCG 65.1% vs 46.5%) and > raw Encoding (Backgammon). (2) Backgammon latent objective weighting -- sweeping (value, decoder) weights: Latent(1,0) value-only (NDCG 45.5%) >> Latent(0,1) decoder-only (NDCG 38.0%) ~ raw Encoding (36.6%), showing value is a stronger similarity signal than checker configuration; combined Latent(1,0.01) is best (NDCG 45.6%, MRR 54.2%) and is used for generation. (3) Math-24 labeling schemes -- SCO (solution-category-only) vs SCD (category+decomposition): SCD lowers precision but raises recall. (4) Query-type ablation -- TC > GC > NC for accuracy in most models, but GC does not consistently beat NC (e.g., Llama-3.1-405B NC 34.0% > GC 30.0%), indicating generic context can cause fixation. (5) Faithfulness >> Negative Rejection across all LLMs (e.g., Llama-3.1-70B 56.2% vs 18.8%), showing the LLM follows correct context well but cannot recover from incorrect context. (6) Metric ablation -- BERTScore improves inconsistently with context while all three sentence-transformer metrics improve consistently, with qualitative examples (Appendix C) showing BERTScore can be high yet semantically wrong.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Yes -- intrinsic retrieval metrics (Precision/Recall/F1/NDCG/MRR@k, Tables 1 and 3) are reported and analyzed separately from end-to-end generation metrics (accuracy/faithfulness/negative-rejection for Math-24, Table 2; BERTScore + sentence-transformer similarities for Backgammon, Table 4). The best retrieval configuration is selected from the intrinsic metrics before the generation experiments.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Mixed. Math-24 has a verifiable outcome metric (Accuracy: does the expression equal 24 using all four numbers) plus process-flavored diagnostics (Faithfulness / Negative Rejection conditioned on retrieved-context correctness). Backgammon has no verifiable outcome (move quality is not auto-graded); generation quality is proxied by semantic similarity to the reference expert analysis (sentence-transformer cosine), with qualitative examples arguing this captures strategic-concept match better than token-level BERTScore. No step-wise reasoning-faithfulness metric.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Not quantified in cost/latency/token terms. Overheads include training the application-specific CNN text-generators (Math-24 CNN reaches 100% test accuracy on 10,000 cards; Backgammon two CNNs over 100,000 simulated images with ~90% case-retention) and the FFNN latent models, plus one kNN retrieval and one augmented LLM call per case. No API-cost, latency, speedup, or token-count numbers are reported. The accuracy gains (e.g., Math-24 +30.6% absolute for Qwen2-72B) come at the cost of building bespoke per-application text/latent models.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k. Math-24 generation injects the single Top Context case (k=1) reformatted as an execution plan (or one generic tip for GC). Backgammon generation injects the top-3 (k=3) most similar cases (position JSON + player + dice + move + expert analysis each). Retrieval metrics are averaged over k in {1,2,3,4,5}. No explicit token budget, budget-cap, or reranked-then-truncated selection is reported.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Both repositories are author-constructed. Math-24: 466 cases (subset of the 1362 solvable puzzles, restricted to solutions of form (x1 o x2)x(x3 o x4)=24); supporting CNN trained on 40,000 synthetic card images (4 random numbers 1-13), reaching 100% test accuracy on 10,000 held-out cards; answers are verifiable (expression must equal 24 using all four numbers). Backgammon: 1015 cases reverse-engineered from three expert books by OCR/CNN extraction of board images (landmark CNN trained on 100,000 simulated boards; part CNN predicts checker count/owner; ~90% case-retention after legality validation), with value labels from the public GNU Backgammon training dataset; answers are free-text expert analyses (not exactly verifiable -- scored by semantic similarity). Difficulty signal: best Math-24 accuracy 61.3% (Llama-3.1-405B TC); Backgammon best Avg similarity 63.8% with context. Cases are labeled for retrieval relevance via solution category/decomposition (Math-24) or grouped book chapter names (~75% of Backgammon cases labelable).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Lewis et al., NeurIPS 2020); the CBR cycle / case-based decision theory (Aamodt & Plaza 1994; Gilboa & Schmeidler 1995); prior LLM+RAG-for-CBR works -- CBR-RAG (Wiratunga et al., ICCBR 2024), CaseGPT (Yang 2024), DS-Agent (Guo et al., ICML 2024), CBR for logical-fallacy classification (Sourati et al., IJCAI 2023); multimodal RAG -- retrieval-augmented multimodal LM (Yasunaga et al., ICML 2023), BLIP-2 (Li et al., ICML 2023), RECAP audio captioning (Ghosh et al. 2023), retrieval-augmented egocentric video captioning (Xu et al., CVPR 2024); transformer encoders BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) and GPT-2 (Radford et al. 2019); TD-Gammon position encoding (Tesauro 1995) and GNU Backgammon value data; sentence-transformer / scoring models MPNet, RoBERTa, MiniLM, BERTScore; Dense Passage Retrieval (Karpukhin et al., EMNLP 2020) for the relevance-vs-recall argument.
- **contrasts with**:
> No Context (LLM parametric-only generation) -- the primary comparator; General Context (Math-24 generic fixed tip, shown to be unreliable / sometimes worse than NC); raw-feature / raw-encoding retrieval similarity (vs the learned latent similarity); token-level evaluation (BERTScore, criticized as rewarding jargon overlap) vs semantic sentence-transformer similarity. Positioned against prior CBR-RAG works (CBR-RAG, CaseGPT, DS-Agent, logical-fallacy CBR) that are TEXT-ONLY, whereas MCBR-RAG generalizes the Retrieve+Reuse RAG-for-CBR recipe to MULTIMODAL cases via application-specific text-generation and latent-representation functions.
- **lineage**:
> Group D (case-based planning / case-based reasoning lineage). Directly extends the CBR-RAG line (Wiratunga et al. 2024) to the multimodal setting: it abstracts the Retrieve (RAG retrieval) + Reuse (RAG generation) recipe and adds per-component text-generation and learned latent-representation functions so non-text case components can be indexed and injected. Sits alongside CaseGPT and DS-Agent in the LLM-RAG-for-CBR sub-lineage, distinguished by (a) explicit multimodal-case formalization, (b) weighted per-component latent retrieval, and (c) leaving Revise/Retain application-specific.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- venue

### 80. Memento (Agent-on-the-Fly / AgentFly) - Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs

2025  ·  arXiv 2508.16153  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.16153)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **authors affiliation**:
> Huichi Zhou, Yihang Chen, Siyuan Guo, Xue Yan, Kin Hei Lee, Zihan Wang, Ka Yiu Lee, Guchun Zhang, Kun Shao, Linyi Yang, Jun Wang. Primary affiliations: AI Centre, University College London (UCL) and Huawei Noah's Ark Lab (UK); also Jilin University and Institute of Automation, CAS. Corresponding authors: Linyi Yang (SUSTech) and Jun Wang (UCL).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.16153
- **code url**: https://github.com/Agent-on-the-Fly/Memento (MIT license; ~2.4k stars; both non-parametric CBR and parametric memory/neural retriever code released)
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/Agent-on-the-Fly/Memento (actively maintained; related survey list at https://github.com/ai-agents-2030/awesome-deep-research-agent)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Deep-research LLM agents: long-horizon tool-use, planning, and decision-making over open-domain QA and web research (spans QA / web / tool-use / planning).
- **problem setting**:
> Adaptive generalist LLM agents that must continually adapt from environmental feedback without fine-tuning (no gradient updates to) the underlying LLMs. Interactive, online/test-time setting: an agent solves complex long-horizon tasks by iteratively planning, invoking external tools, and processing heterogeneous data. Single-agent (planner-executor) architecture; supervision is sparse binary task-level reward (success/failure) rather than dense step labels. Both successful and failed trajectories are stored. Continual/online learning: the case bank is built from scratch and grows during deployment.
- **what is retrieved**: Past experiences stored as cases: case triplets (state s = task, action a = plan, reward r = success/failure label). At planning time the planner retrieves the K nearest/highest-value past cases (problem-solution-outcome episodes) from the Case Bank.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> GROWING / episodic memory the agent writes (an online-growing Case Bank built from the agent's own trajectories), explicitly contrasted with classic RAG over a STATIC document corpus. Note: tool-level execution also uses live web search/crawl over external sources, but the case retrieval that defines the method targets the agent's own episodic memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-K case selection (K nearest cases by similarity, or top-K by learned Q-value). The objective is a precision/utility-driven small selection: ablations show performance peaks at K=4 and plateaus or declines for larger K (small, high-quality memory preferred over many exemplars), so it is closer to a precision-driven selection than a recall/completeness objective.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve, Reuse, Revise, Retain] - all four canonical CBR phases are implemented. Eq. 2 explicitly labels the trajectory factorization as (1) Retrieve, (2) Reuse & Revise, (3) Evaluation, (4) Retain, (5) Transition. Reuse/Revise = LLM adapts the retrieved plan; Retain = append new case to Case Bank.
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> True. The work explicitly frames itself as case-based reasoning (CBR), citing Aamodt & Plaza (1994), Kolodner-lineage CBR, and prior CBR agents (DS-Agent, Guo et al. 2024/2025). It states it is 'the first to cast case-based continual learning for LLM agents' and contrasts CBR with modern RAG.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> case (problem-solution tuple): a triplet (s, a, r) where s = task/state, a = plan, r = binary success reward. Effectively a (state, action/plan, reward) experience tuple stored as episodic memory; only the final-step (s_T, a_T, r_T) of each trajectory is written to keep the bank compact.
- **index source**: Growing episodic memory induced online/at test-time (Case Bank Mt built from scratch and incrementally appended during deployment); not an offline static corpus. For OOD experiments the bank is pre-populated from training-split trajectories, then queried at inference.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat vector index: states are encoded with a frozen text encoder (SimCSE) and stored as vectors keyed by their (a, r) payload; retrieval is nearest-neighbour over this flat embedding store (cosine similarity for non-parametric; Q-value scoring over the same flat bank for parametric).
- **retriever type**:
> Non-parametric variant: dense embedding nearest-neighbour (SimCSE encoder + cosine similarity, off-the-shelf). Parametric variant: learned retriever - a neural case-selection policy (Q-function as a two-layer MLP over SimCSE state representations) realising a learned soft-Q retrieval policy. So: dense (off-the-shelf) and/or learned value-based retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Non-parametric: none (off-the-shelf similarity). Parametric: RL / value-based - a neural case-selection policy trained via online soft Q-learning in a maximum-entropy RL framework. The optimal retrieval policy is a softmax over the optimal Q-value; Q is learned by TD learning (kernel/episodic-control estimate) or, in the single-step deep-research instantiation, by supervised binary cross-entropy regression of Q(s,c;theta) onto the binary task reward r in {0,1} (downstream-task-effectiveness signal).
- **query construction**:
> The query/key is the current task instruction encoded as the state s_t (raw task text passed through the frozen SimCSE encoder). No sub-query decomposition for case retrieval; the raw task state is the query. (Task decomposition into subtasks happens downstream in the planner after case retrieval.)
- **query granularity**:
> Task-level: case retrieval is performed at the planning step keyed on the task/state. Because CBR is applied only for planning, the deep-research instantiation collapses to a single-step (per-task) setting; retrieval is essentially one-shot at the task/plan level (re-issued on replanning).
- **when to retrieve**: One-shot per planning step (retrieve relevant cases when the planner forms/refines a plan). The planner can replan if a task is unfinished, so retrieval can recur across plan-replan iterations, but it is not token-level or uncertainty-triggered active retrieval.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule tied to the planning stage: the planner queries Case Memory at the start of planning (and again on replanning when the task is judged incomplete). No learned router, token-confidence, or reflection-token trigger for case retrieval.
- **reranking**:
> For case retrieval: no separate cross-encoder reranking stage; the parametric Q-function effectively reranks candidate cases by learned Q-value (TopK over Q). For tool-level web search, retrieved candidate web results are re-ranked by semantic similarity to the query context (a tool-internal reranking, distinct from case retrieval).
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Case side: minimal - retrieved case triplets are concatenated verbatim with the current task instruction to form the planner prompt (no decompose/compress of cases). Tool side: a query-aware crawler (ai_crawler) performs content compression to reduce token cost, and search results are filtered/re-ranked; these refine tool outputs rather than retrieved cases.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Tools are exposed via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) as a suite of MCP servers (search, crawl, code, document/image/video/audio/excel/math). Tool selection is performed by the LLM executor at execution time from MCP tool descriptions; no special synthetic-query augmentation or instruction-tuned tool embeddings are reported for tool indexing.
- **index content separation**:
> Partial: memory stores compact case triplets (only final-step s,a,r; state vectorised, action/reward kept as text) so a lightweight retrievable representation is kept; heavy per-subtask tool logs are kept in separate Tool Memory and subtask results in Subtask Memory (text-based), separating high-level case index from per-step execution content.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Tools integrated via a live, model-agnostic MCP (Model Context Protocol) layer; executor acts as an MCP client invoking MCP servers (SearxNG metasearch, SerpAPI, Crawl4AI, code sandbox, etc.). Tool index is the configured MCP server list (extensible by adding FastMCP servers); not a CRUD-auto-synced live registry.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A - retrieval does not explicitly model inter-tool dependency graphs; the LLM executor composes tools per subtask using Tool Memory, but there is no dependency-graph/bipartite-KG modeling of tool prerequisites.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation + case adaptation: retrieved case triplets (s_i, a_i, r_i) are concatenated with the current task instruction and fed to the planner LLM, which reuses and revises (adapts) the retrieved plans to generate a new plan (in-context, no weight updates). Mixes successful and failed cases so the agent can prospectively reuse successes and retrospectively avoid past mistakes.
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-plan within a plan-and-act loop: the CBR planner retrieves cases, generates a plan / decomposes the task into subtasks; a tool-enabled executor (MCP client) runs each subtask; the planner then assesses completion and replans with updated context. CBR is applied at the planning stage (one-shot exemplar-style case conditioning at plan time), looped with execution.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Case retrieval is per-plan (per-task / per-replan) rather than per-token. Tool calls are per-subtask within the executor's autonomous episode (per-tool-call within a rollout). So two granularities: case retrieval at plan level; tool invocation at subtask/step level.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> LLM-prompted adaptation of retrieved cases (Reuse & Revise): the planner LLM conditions on retrieved (s,a,r) cases to produce an adapted plan; execution-feedback-driven revision via replanning when subtasks are incomplete. Case selection itself is additionally RL-shaped by the learned Q-function in the parametric variant, but the case content adaptation is LLM in-context (no LLM fine-tuning).
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Structured case triplet injected as text: (state/task, plan/action, success-or-failure reward). The state is also stored as a SimCSE embedding for retrieval; the surface form injected into the planner is the natural-language task + plan + outcome (raw trajectory final-step), i.e. a structured note rather than a distilled rule or executable skill.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw (final-step) trajectory case = a single past problem-solution-outcome episode, including both successes and failures. Not a distilled strategy/guideline, not an executable skill/program, not a reusable abstract workflow - it is a concrete past case used analogically.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Two mechanisms: (1) the learned value-based (parametric) case-selection policy prioritises high-utility cases, mitigating noise from irrelevant cases (soft-Q / maximum-entropy retrieval); (2) deliberately small K (peak at K=4) to limit injected noise (ablation shows large K hurts). Storing failure cases also provides corrective signal. No retriever-aware SFT of the base LLM or explicit relevance evaluator/self-reflection module for cases.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: episodic (an episodic Case Bank of past trajectory cases). Has both non-parametric (vector NN store) and parametric (Q-function-shaped) variants; auxiliary Subtask Memory and Tool Memory are text-based working memories.
- **write back**:
> True. The system stores new experiences as cases: Write appends (s_t, a_t, r_t) to the Case Bank; in the parametric variant Write also online-updates the Q-function (and an episodic memory D of (s,c,Q) tuples). Case bank grows incrementally into a transferable experience repository.
- **online growth**: True. The Case Bank is an online-growing store that expands during deployment/test-time (built from scratch over iterations); it is not frozen after an offline induction phase. Continual-learning curves show monotonic improvement across iterations as cases accumulate.
- **write back trigger**:
> On both success and failure - both successful and failed trajectories are written to the case bank (enabling prospective reuse of successes and retrospective avoidance of mistakes). In the planner-executor implementation a case is written upon task completion (final-step s_T,a_T,r_T of each trajectory), with the binary outcome as reward; parametric variant additionally updates the Q-function on each write.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success + failure: the memory accumulates both successful and failed cases; retrieval returns a mixture of successful and failed cases, and the binary reward (r in {0,1}) lets the value/policy down-weight failure cases while the LLM can use failures to avoid past mistakes. Not success-only.
- **memory evolution update**:
> Append-only for case content (cases are added each step; only final-step tuples stored to keep the bank compact, deduplicating redundant intermediate states). The retrieval policy evolves: in the parametric variant the Q-function/kernel is continually refined (delta-update via TD/CE learning and target-network soft updates), reshaping the retrieval distribution over the growing bank. No explicit forgetting/pruning of stored cases is implemented (noted as future work / memory-compression TODO).
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Yes (in the parametric variant). Retrieval/case-selection IS a learned policy: a neural case-selection policy over the episodic case bank, formalised in a Memory-augmented MDP (M-MDP) and optimised via online soft Q-learning (maximum-entropy RL; optimal policy = softmax over learned Q). The non-parametric variant uses fixed similarity top-K. This is the paper's defining contribution and matches the field's M-MDP soft-Q-learning exemplar.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Single-agent private episodic memory (one growing Case Bank for the agent). The bank is transferable across tasks/datasets (e.g. OOD transfer from training to test datasets) but the paper does not implement shared memory across multiple distinct agents or heterogeneous frameworks.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: GAIA (validation 150 / test 300, 3 difficulty levels); DeepResearcher suite of 7 open-domain QA datasets - Natural Questions (NQ), TriviaQA (TQ), HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA (2Wiki), MuSiQue, Bamboogle, PopQA; SimpleQA (4,330 fact-seeking Qs); Humanity's Last Exam (HLE, 2,500 Qs).
- **benchmark family**: tool/long-horizon agentic (GAIA); multi-hop & open-domain QA / web research (DeepResearcher = NQ/TQ/HotpotQA/2Wiki/MuSiQue/Bamboogle/PopQA); factual QA (SimpleQA); frontier/long-tail academic reasoning QA (HLE). Overall: web/tool-use + multi-hop QA families.
- **baselines**:
> GAIA leaderboard agents: Alita, Skywork Super Agents, Langfun Agent, AWorld/Aworld, Manus, OWL-Workforce/OWL-Roleplaying, OpenAI DeepResearch, Open Deep Research, Su Zero Ultra, h2oGPTe Agent. DeepResearcher table: CoT, CoT+RAG, Search-o1, Search-r1 (base/instruct), R1-Searcher, DeepResearcher (training-based SOTA). SimpleQA: WebSailor, WebDancer, WebThinker, DeepSeek-r1-React. HLE: GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, o3-high, o4-mini-high. Internal ablation baselines: Offline Executor, Online Executor, Memento w/o CBR.
- **key metrics**: GAIA: accuracy / Exact Match (and Pass@3 on validation), reported per level and average. DeepResearcher/SimpleQA/HLE: macro-F1 and PM (Partial Match, GPT-4o-mini-judged semantic match). Plus token cost / cost-per-task analysis on GAIA.
- **headline result**:
> Top-1 on GAIA validation with 87.88% (Pass@3) and 79.40% on the GAIA test set (open-source agent frameworks, as of June 26 2025). On the DeepResearcher 7-dataset suite: 66.6% F1 / 80.4% PM (weighted avg), surpassing the training-based SOTA DeepResearcher (51.8 F1 / 60.5 PM); case-based memory adds +4.7 to +9.6 absolute points on OOD tasks; 95.0% on SimpleQA; 24.4% PM on HLE.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Component-wise (Table 5): Offline Executor -> Online Executor (live tools) -> +planning (Memento w/o CBR) -> +CBR; CBR gives consistent additive gains (HLE +4.5 F1/+7.0 PM, SimpleQA +3.7/+5.3, DeepResearcher +6.7/+8.2). Planning alone gives large gains; live tools help on SimpleQA/HLE but hurt DeepResearcher F1 (-18.0, attributed to contamination). (2) K sweep (Table 3): peak at K=4 (64.5 F1/78.5 PM), plateau/decline for larger K -> small high-quality memory beats more exemplars. (3) Continual-learning over 5 iterations (Table 4): Parametric CBR (80.46->85.44) > Non-Parametric CBR (79.84->84.85) > w/o CBR (78.65->84.47). (4) OOD generalisation: +4.7-9.6 absolute on MuSiQue/Bamboogle/PopQA when bank trained on NQ/TQ/HotpotQA/2Wiki. (5) Token-cost analysis on GAIA by difficulty level.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome metrics (final-answer EM/F1/PM/success). Process is examined only indirectly: continual-learning curves over iterations, token-cost-per-task by GAIA level, and per-task-type statistics (code/search/crawl). No formal step-wise reasoning-faithfulness or retrieval-precision scoring.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Core claim is low-cost continual adaptation with no LLM fine-tuning / no gradient updates to the base LLM (only a small two-layer MLP Q-function is trained in the parametric variant). Token-cost analysis on GAIA: per-task input/output tokens scale with difficulty - Level 1 ~26k/4.7k, Level 2 ~48k/6.9k, Level 3 ~121k/9.8k; main cost is integrating multi-step tool outputs. A query-aware compression crawler is added to reduce token cost. Small K=4 keeps retrieval cost low.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A - this is a method/system paper, not a survey.
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A - this is a method paper, not a benchmark paper. (It uses existing benchmarks: GAIA 450 Qs across 3 levels; DeepResearcher 7 datasets at 512 examples each except Bamboogle 125; SimpleQA 4,330; HLE 2,500.)

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Case-Based Reasoning (Aamodt & Plaza 1994); episodic / neural episodic control (Pritzel et al. 2017); maximum-entropy / soft Q-learning RL (Haarnoja et al. 2017, 2018); plan-and-act paradigm (Erdogan et al. 2025); prior CBR agents DS-Agent and Guo et al. (2024/2025); deep-research agent setting (Huang et al. 2025); Model Context Protocol (MCP) for tooling; SimCSE sentence encoder; tool stack (SearxNG, Crawl4AI, Camel-AI toolkit).
- **contrasts with**:
> Contrasts with (a) parametric continual-learning agents that fine-tune the LLM via SFT/RL (e.g. Search-r1, R1-Searcher, DeepResearcher, START) - high compute, catastrophic forgetting; (b) static handcrafted-workflow / reflection agents (Reflexion, ReAct-style) lacking lifelong learning; (c) classic RAG over static document corpora (Lewis et al. 2020) which lacks continual adaptation; (d) memory agents that append cases without curation (swamping problem) and other memory systems (MemoryBank, SAGE, Mem0, A-MEM, MemInsight, ExpeL, AutoGuide, Agent Workflow Memory, Agent-KB, Alita).
- **lineage**:
> Group D: case-based planning / experience-and-memory-augmented agents. Sits in the lineage of CBR-for-LLM-agents and memory-augmented continual-learning agents, distinguished by formalising planning as a Memory-augmented MDP (M-MDP) with retrieval/case-selection AS a learned soft-Q policy over a growing episodic case bank (vs fixed similarity top-k), bridging episodic/neural-episodic-control RL with deep-research LLM agents.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- context_budget_and_selection_count
- evaluation_decoupling

### 81. Meta-Policy Reflexion (MPR)

2025  ·  arXiv 2509.03990  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.03990)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2509.03990, cs.AI); not peer-reviewed as of writing
- **authors affiliation**: Chunlong Wu, Ye Luo, Zhibo Qu, Min Wang — Tongji University (corresponding: wuchunlong@tongji.edu.cn)
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.03990
- **code url**: N/A (no public code repository released; the paper repeatedly refers to 'the provided implementation' and an 'uploaded spreadsheet' but supplies no GitHub/Zenodo link)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Embodied / interactive text-based agent decision-making (household task completion). Single-agent sequential decision-making framed as an MDP.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent, text-based embodied environment (AlfWorld) modeled as an MDP M=(S,A,P,r,gamma). A frozen LLM (Qwen3-32b) acts as the base policy generating natural-language actions under deterministic/low-temperature decoding. Supervision is via environment success/failure signals (no ground-truth action labels, no model weight updates). The setting separates a training phase (memory is updated after failed episodes on a 60-task train set) from an inference phase (memory frozen, used to guide decoding plus hard admissibility, evaluated on a 74-task held-out test set). Goal: distill ephemeral per-episode reflections into reusable cross-task corrective knowledge without RL/fine-tuning.
- **what is retrieved**: Structured, predicate-like corrective rules ('meta-policy' rules with confidence weights) distilled from hindsight reflections of past failed trajectories; stored in a Meta-Policy Memory (MPM). At each step a state-relevant subset of these rules is retrieved.
- **retrieval grounding**: GROWING / episodic agent-written memory. The Meta-Policy Memory (MPM) is built and grown online from the agent's own failed trajectories during the training phase, then frozen at inference. It is not a static external corpus (no docs/KB/API store).
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> Retrieve (state-relevant rule subset), Reuse (soft memory-conditioned decoding), Retain (write distilled rules from failed episodes into MPM). Revise is partial: the LLM reflection function f(τ) generalizes/abstracts new rules, and HAC enforces constraints, but there is no explicit per-case adaptation/repair loop. Flags: [Retrieve: yes, Reuse: yes, Revise: partial, Retain: yes]
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False. The work does NOT frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner; it is positioned as reflective memory / verbal-RL extension (Reflexion lineage). It realizes CBR-like retain-and-reuse mechanisms under the 'meta-policy memory' framing rather than CBR terminology.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: guideline-rule: a predicate-like, generalized corrective rule (with confidence weight) distilled from a failed trajectory's reflection. Not a raw trajectory or single demo — an abstracted rule.
- **index source**:
> Growing memory, online/test-time-induced (during training rounds). MPM is initialized empty (M ← ∅) and accumulates rules via M ← M ∪ f(τ) after failed episodes; it is frozen for the inference/evaluation phase. Construction is online during the training phase, then static at deployment.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None (no trained retriever). Rule extraction is driven by environment success/failure (failed episodes trigger LLM reflection f(τ)); rules carry confidence weights, but rule selection/retrieval itself is not a learned/optimized retriever — it is off-the-shelf state-relevance matching. The improvement signal is downstream-task failure feedback used to grow memory, not to train a retriever.
- **query construction**: The query/key is the current environment state s_t; a state-relevant rule subset M_t is retrieved and the LLM conditions on (s_t, M_t). No decomposed sub-queries or synthetic query expansion described.
- **query granularity**: Step/state-level: retrieval of the relevant rule subset M_t occurs at each step t conditioned on the current state s_t.
- **when to retrieve**: Iterative / per-step: at every decision step the agent retrieves a state-relevant rule subset before generating the action.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule (per-step, every step): retrieval of M_t happens at each step conditioned on s_t. There is no uncertainty- or confidence-triggered gating; memory WRITE (not retrieval) is triggered by episode failure.
- **reranking**: None. No reranking stage is described; a state-relevant subset is selected and injected directly.
- **retrieved context refinement**: None explicit beyond selecting the state-relevant subset. Rules are distilled/abstracted at write time (via LLM reflection), not refined post-retrieval; no compression/decompose/distractor-filtering stage at retrieval time is described.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tool/skill descriptions are indexed; retrieved units are corrective rules, not tools).
- **index content separation**: N/A — no separation of a lightweight index from heavy on-demand content; MPM stores compact predicate-like rules directly.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no external tool index or integration protocol such as RapidAPI/MCP/function-calling).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Two complementary mechanisms: (1) SOFT prompt augmentation — memory-conditioned decoding where the retrieved rule subset M_t is injected into the LLM prompt to bias decoding toward memory-supported actions, a_t = π_θ(s_t, M_t), with no logit/weight changes; (2) HARD rule admissibility check (HAC) — the generated action a_t is validated post-hoc against a constraint set C(s_t); if a_t ∉ C(s_t) the agent resamples with adjusted memory/context or falls back to a safe action.
- **planning integration**:
> Per-step interleaved retrieval-augmented acting: at each step the agent retrieves state-relevant rules, conditions decoding on them (soft guidance), generates an action, then applies hard admissibility filtering before executing in the environment. No tree search/MCTS; it is a retrieve-then-act loop within an MDP rollout, with offline memory growth between episodes.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-tool-call / per-action-step within a rollout: retrieval and admissibility checking occur at each environment action step.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> LLM-prompted soft adaptation plus post-hoc constraint validation: retrieved rules bias the frozen LLM's decoding (verbatim-rule-in-prompt soft guidance), and HAC enforces hard constraints with resample/safe-fallback. New rules are produced by execution-feedback-driven (failure-triggered) LLM reflection f(τ), not by per-case revision of a retrieved case.
- **retrieved item representation**: Distilled strategy/guideline injected as structured, predicate-like text rules (with confidence weights) into the prompt. Not raw trajectories, not executable programs, not latent tokens.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: State-aware guideline/rule (distilled, generalized corrective rule), more abstract than a raw trajectory or single demonstration; predicate-like form derived from failure analysis.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Hard rule admissibility check (HAC): post-generation validation of actions against an environment/user constraint set C(s_t), with resample or safe-fallback for inadmissible actions — guards against invalid/unsafe actions. Confidence weights on rules and the predicate-like format aim to improve quality/interpretability, but the paper notes LLM-generated rules may contain redundancies/inconsistencies (no learned relevance evaluator or distractor-aware training).

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: episodic-derived structured rule memory (Meta-Policy Memory, MPM): an external, predicate-like rule store distilled from episodic failures; closest to a guideline/rule library rather than a skill-library, graph, or latent memory.
- **write back**: True. The system writes distilled corrective rules into MPM after failed episodes: M ← M ∪ f(τ), where f is an LLM reflection function over a failed trajectory τ.
- **online growth**:
> Partial / phase-dependent: the store grows online during the training phase (rounds where meta-policy update is enabled) but is FROZEN at inference/test time (no memory update on the held-out test set). So it grows during training-time interaction, not during deployment evaluation.
- **write back trigger**: On-failure only (reflective): a write occurs only when an episode fails, after which the LLM reflects on the failure and extracts corrective rules. Successful episodes do not trigger writes.
- **failure experience usage**: Failure-only corrective rules: only failed trajectories are reflected upon to extract corrective predicate-like rules; there is no success-based or success+failure contrastive storage.
- **memory evolution update**: Append-only (set union M ← M ∪ f(τ)). No dedup-merge, delta-update, refine-overwrite, or pruning is implemented; the paper lists automatic rule management (confidence weighting, redundancy detection, abstraction, pruning) only as future work.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No. Retrieval/rule-selection is not a learned or RL-optimized policy; it is state-relevance-based selection over the rule set. The base LLM policy is frozen and not fine-tuned. MPR explicitly contrasts itself with RL approaches that require parameter updates.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No — single-agent private memory. Multi-agent / graph-based shared-and-negotiated rule memory is proposed only as future work.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: AlfWorld (text-based embodied agent environment). Train set: 60 tasks; held-out test set: 74 tasks.
- **benchmark family**: embodied (ALFWorld)
- **baselines**: Reflexion (verbal reinforcement learning / textual self-reflection). ReAct is discussed as related background but the quantitative comparison is against Reflexion. Ablation-style internal comparison: MPR vs. MPR+HAC.
- **key metrics**: Execution accuracy (% of tasks completed correctly), reported per training round (Rounds 1-5) and as a sixth-round held-out comparison.
- **headline result**:
> On the 74-task held-out test set: MPR+HAC reaches 91.4% accuracy vs. Reflexion 86.9% (6 reflection rounds on test set) and MPR-without-HAC 87.8% (trained 5 rounds on train set, single evaluation). On the 60-task training set MPR reaches 100% by Round 3 vs. Reflexion's 88.3% by Round 5.
- **ablations**:
> HAC ablation is the central one: MPR (memory-conditioned decoding only) = 87.8% vs. MPR + HAC (hard admissibility at test time) = 91.4% on the 74-task test set, isolating the +3.6-point contribution of hard admissibility checks on top of soft memory-guided decoding. Per-round training-set curve (Reflexion 70.0->88.3 over Rounds 1-5 vs. MPR 83.9->100.0, reaching 100% by Round 3) isolates the value of consolidated reusable rules vs. ephemeral reflection. No retriever/rule-selection ablation reported.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No. Only end-to-end task execution accuracy is reported; no intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG / rule-selection precision) are reported separately.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Outcome-only: evaluation scores final task execution accuracy; no intermediate process-quality metrics (reasoning faithfulness, step-wise retrieval accuracy, trajectory quality) are quantified. The paper recommends per-task inspection but does not report process metrics.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (this is a method paper, not a survey/benchmark).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (uses existing AlfWorld; not a benchmark-construction paper). For reference: 60 train tasks + 74 test tasks; best reported system MPR+HAC = 91.4% on the 74-task test set.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023, verbal reinforcement learning / textual self-reflection) as the primary predecessor; ReAct (Yao et al., 2022/2023, reasoning+acting interleaving); AlfWorld (Shridhar et al., 2020) as the environment. Related memory work cited: A-Mem, G-Memory, Memory-R1, SAGE, and Zhang et al.'s memory-mechanism survey.
- **contrasts with**:
> Reflexion / ReAct (ephemeral, task-specific reflective traces not reused across tasks) and RL / RLHF policy-adaptation methods (transferable but requiring substantial parameter updates and compute). MPR positions itself as keeping the lightweight flexibility of textual reflection while distilling reusable, structured, transferable rules without weight updates.
- **lineage**:
> Group D — case-based / experience-based planning (reflective experiential memory for agents). Sits in the reflective-memory lineage extending Reflexion toward persistent, cross-task reusable corrective rules plus hard admissibility constraints; CBR-like Retain/Reuse realized without explicit CBR framing.

- context_budget_and_selection_count
