### 82. ReAP (Reflection-Augmented Planning); paper titled "Reflection-Based Memory For Web navigation Agents"

2025  ·  arXiv 2506.02158  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02158)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **authors affiliation**: Ruhana Azam (UIUC); Aditya Vempaty (Emergence AI); Ashish Jagmohan (Emergence AI). Lead author Ruhana Azam.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02158

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: web (web navigation agents)
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent LLM web navigation in the WebArena simulated environment (shopping, shopping_admin, map, Reddit, GitLab). The agent (AgentOccam built on gpt-4o-2024-08-06) is augmented with a persistent reflection memory built offline from prior trajectory rollouts. No additional training is required; reflections are induced from prior trajectories (successful and failed) and injected at inference. Two settings tested: (H1) re-doing previously attempted tasks where memory holds reflections of the same tasks; (H2) transfer to similar-but-distinct tasks via an 80-20 train-test split of AgentOccam WebArena trajectories. Reward labels (success/failure) for prior trajectories are available as supervision when constructing reflections.
- **what is retrieved**:
> experiences / reflections: key-value pairs mapping a past user task (key) to a learned reflection/insight gained during navigation (value); three knowledge-type variants tested - One-shot (raw trajectory + reward), Summary (LLM high-level plan summary + reward + failure reason), and Web-Reflection (structured reflection + reward).
- **retrieval grounding**: GROWING/episodic memory the agent writes from its own prior experiences (offline-induced knowledge base of reflections from past trajectory rollouts); not a static external doc/KB/API corpus.
- **completeness vs topk objective**: Fixed top-k ranking: the system retrieves the k=5 most relevant reflections via cosine similarity; no completeness or precision-driven variable-size objective.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> Retrieve: yes; Reuse: yes (reflections injected into prompt for adaptation to new task); Revise: no (no execution-feedback-driven case revision of stored entries); Retain: partial/offline (reflections are stored once during offline BuildMemory from prior trajectories, not continuously retained online during deployment). Flags: [Retrieve=yes, Reuse=yes, Revise=no, Retain=partial-offline].
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The work does not explicitly frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it frames itself as reflection-based memory / retrieval-augmented planning, realizing retrieve-and-reuse mechanisms under a different name.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> guideline-rule / distilled insight: a task-keyed reflection (free-text key insight about the website/task, e.g., 'Allrecipes.com does not have a filter for preparation time'). Variants also include full-trajectory (One-shot raw (s,a,...,r) sequence) and high-level summary units, but the headline ReAP unit is the distilled reflection.
- **index source**:
> Growing memory, offline-induced: the retrievable store is built offline (BuildMemory) from prior trajectory rollouts of the base agent (AgentOccam); in H1 from a single rollout per task, in H2 from 80% training-split trajectories. Frozen at inference (not grown online at test time).
- **index structure topology**: Flat vector index keyed by task-instruction embeddings (each entry stores task text, reflection R(tau), and Embed(task)); retrieval is over flat cosine-similarity nearest neighbors.
- **retriever type**: Dense (off-the-shelf text-embedding model with cosine similarity). Selected embedding model: gte-Qwen2-7B-instruct (also evaluated llama8b-nnetnav-wa, text-embedding-3-large/small, all-MiniLM-L6-v2).
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None (off-the-shelf). The retriever uses a pretrained embedding model with cosine similarity; no contrastive, LM-feedback, task-effectiveness, or RL training of the retriever. Embedding model choice (gte-Qwen2-7B-instruct) was selected by qualitative inspection of task-cluster separation, not trained.
- **query construction**: Raw task-instruction query, lightly templated as "Go to {start_url}, {intent}" (e.g., 'Go to MAP, Which US states border Illinois?'), then embedded.
- **query granularity**: Task-level (one-shot at t=0): a single query is formed from the new task instruction and used to retrieve reflections before/at planning time; not per-step or trajectory-level.
- **when to retrieve**: One-shot: retrieval is performed once per task at the start (top-5 reflections injected into the prompt before the agent acts).
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule: retrieval is triggered once at task start by the ReAPPrompt routine; no confidence/uncertainty/learned-router/reflection-token trigger.
- **reranking**: None. A single dense cosine-similarity ranking selects the top-5; no separate reranking stage (cross-encoder, RRF, etc.).
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> None at retrieval time (top-5 reflections concatenated directly into the prompt). Note: the reflections themselves are pre-distilled/compressed at memory-construction time (Summary and Web-Reflection variants), but no post-retrieval rerank/decompose/distill/filter step is applied.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tool/skill descriptions; the indexed items are task-keyed reflections, not tool docs).
- **index content separation**: No explicit progressive-disclosure / index-then-content separation; the embedding key (task) and the stored content (reflection) are co-stored in the same entry and the reflection is loaded directly when retrieved.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index or integration protocol; WebArena environment, no RapidAPI/RESTful/MCP/function-calling tool store).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tool retrieval; no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**: Prompt augmentation: the top-5 retrieved reflections (K1...Kk) are concatenated with the current task instruction and fed to the base agent (Agent(t_i (+) K1 (+) ... (+) Kk)), guiding planning/acting without any fine-tuning. Functions as case-adaptation via in-context insights.
- **planning integration**: One-shot exemplars/insights at plan time: reflections are injected once into the agent prompt before the agent plans and acts; the base AgentOccam agent then runs its standard multi-step planning/acting loop conditioned on these insights (retrieve-then-plan).
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer / per-task: retrieval happens once per task before the navigation rollout; reflections are not re-retrieved per CoT-step or per action within the rollout.
- **adaptation mechanism**: LLM-prompted adaptation: retrieved reflections/insights are provided in-context and the LLM agent adapts its plan to the new task; for the One-shot variant a verbatim trajectory+reward exemplar is used. No execution-feedback-driven revision of stored cases or RL reuse-finetuning.
- **retrieved item representation**: Distilled strategy/insight as free text (Web-Reflection and Summary variants: high-level insights, plan summaries, failure reasons, shortcuts, feedback). The One-shot variant instead injects a raw trajectory with reward label.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Primarily a distilled strategy/insight (state-aware reflection/guideline about the site and task), contrasted in ablations with raw-trajectory (One-shot) and plan-summary representations.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Limited/none explicit. The reflections are pre-distilled to key insights (rather than full noisy trajectories) which the authors argue transfers better, but there is no dedicated relevance-evaluator, retriever-aware training, reason-in-documents refinement, or distractor-aware SFT. The paper notes some negative transfer on previously successful tasks.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: episodic (reflection-based key-value memory of past task->insight pairs); functions as a persistent reflection memory across sessions/tasks.
- **write back**: True (offline). The system writes reflections derived from prior trajectories into the knowledge base during the BuildMemory phase; however, it does not write back new experiences online during test-time deployment in the reported experiments.
- **online growth**: No. The retrievable store is built offline from prior rollouts / the 80% training split and is frozen at inference; the paper does not grow memory during test-time evaluation.
- **write back trigger**:
> On-success-and-failure (reflective): reflections are generated and stored from BOTH successful and failed prior trajectories, with reward labels and reasons-for-failure captured. The write happens offline during memory construction (after self-reflection over a completed trajectory), not per-step and not human-validated; it is not triggered online during deployment.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success + failure (both stored): a central contribution is leveraging both successful and failed past experiences. Reflections from failed trajectories drive the largest gains (+20 points H1, +28 points H2 on previously-failed tasks). Reward labels mark success/failure; not purely contrastive but both polarities are stored and retrieved.
- **memory evolution update**: Append-only: entries are added during BuildMemory and not subsequently mutated, deduped, refined, or pruned.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No. Retrieval/case-selection is a fixed cosine-similarity top-k over off-the-shelf embeddings; not a learned/RL-optimized policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: Single-agent private memory. No sharing across multiple agents or heterogeneous frameworks; one base agent (AgentOccam) uses its own reflection store.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: WebArena (70-task subset for H1 with single rollout per task; for H2, publicly available AgentOccam WebArena trajectories split 80-20 train/test). Sites: shopping, shopping_admin, map, Reddit, GitLab.
- **benchmark family**: web (WebArena).
- **baselines**:
> AgentOccam (base agent, gpt-4o-2024-08-06, no memory) - reported as the 'N/A'/baseline. Knowledge-type variants compared internally: One-shot & Reward Label, Summary & Reward Label, Web-Reflection & Reward Label. Prior memory approaches discussed (ICAL, AgentWorkflow, WILBUR) are positioned against but not run as quantitative baselines.
- **key metrics**: Success Rate (SR, primary); plus cost-efficiency metrics: total tokens, prompt tokens, task-completion time (Tct, seconds), and average number of steps.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No. Only end-to-end task metrics (SR) and cost are reported; intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k/nDCG) are not reported. Embedding quality is assessed only qualitatively via t-SNE and cosine-similarity matrices (Appendix C), not as decoupled retrieval scores.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Mostly outcome (SR), augmented with process/efficiency proxies: number of steps, re-prompt reductions, tokens, and completion time, which reflect trajectory quality. No reasoning-faithfulness or step-wise retrieval-accuracy metric.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Reported in detail. ReAP reduces steps by ~15.4% (H1) and 29.1% (H2) overall, up to 37.1% on previously failed tasks; Summary cuts H1 token usage ~74% (221k->58k total) and time 51% (682s->334s); H2 Reflection uses 83k vs 221k baseline tokens. Tradeoff: Summary best for tokens, Reflection best for SR with reduced steps; One-shot can increase tokens (up to 1095k in negative-only H2).
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k: top k=5 reflections retrieved by cosine similarity and concatenated into the prompt. No adaptive/precision-driven k or explicit token budget cap; injected reflection size varies by knowledge type (distilled reflections/summaries are far smaller than raw One-shot trajectories).
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (not a benchmark paper; reuses WebArena, a 70-task subset for H1 and an 80-20 split of public AgentOccam trajectories for H2).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> AgentOccam (Yang et al. 2024a, base web agent + AgentOccam-Judge); WebArena (Zhou et al. 2023, environment); self-reflection methods (Reflexion - Shinn et al. 2023; Self-Refine - Madaan et al. 2023); insight/strategy-memory methods (Suzgun et al. 2025, the most conceptually similar; Thought-Retriever - Feng et al. 2024; Buffer-of-Thoughts - Yang et al. 2024b); RAG (Lewis et al. 2020). Authors' prior work: Azam et al. 2024 (multimodal auto-validation / self-refinement in web agents).
- **contrasts with**:
> Prior trajectory-storing memory systems that store complete workflows/trajectories rather than distilled insights: ICAL (Sarch et al. 2025, iteratively improving in-context examples), AgentWorkflow (Wang et al. 2024b, parses/stores trajectory sub-goals), and WILBUR (Lutz et al. 2024, stores trajectory summaries). ReAP contrasts by focusing on key reflections/insights (not full workflows) and by explicitly using both successful and failed experiences.
- **lineage**:
> Group D (case-based / experience-based planning): an experience/reflection-memory web-navigation method in the lineage of self-reflection (Reflexion) + memory-augmented agents, positioned among insight-distillation memory approaches (Suzgun et al. 2025, Buffer-of-Thoughts) and trajectory-memory web agents (ICAL, AgentWorkflow, WILBUR).

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- ablations
- code_url
- headline_result
- venue

<a id="item-reasoningbank"></a>
### 83. ReasoningBank: Scaling Agent Self-Evolving with Reasoning Memory

2025  ·  arXiv 2509.25140 (ICLR 2026)  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25140)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**: ICLR 2026 (The Fourteenth International Conference on Learning Representations; OpenReview id jL7fwchScm). Preprint arXiv:2509.25140 (cs.AI/cs.CL), submitted 29 Sep 2025 (v1), last revised 16 Mar 2026 (v2).
- **authors affiliation**:
> Siru Ouyang (lead; work done during an internship at Google Cloud AI Research), Jun Yan (corresponding), I-Hung Hsu, Yanfei Chen, Ke Jiang, Zifeng Wang, Rujun Han, Long T. Le, Samira Daruki, Xiangru Tang, Vishy Tirumalashetty, George Lee, Mahsan Rofouei, Hangfei Lin, Jiawei Han, Chen-Yu Lee (corresponding), Tomas Pfister. Affiliations: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (Ouyang, J. Han), Google Cloud AI Research, Yale University (Tang), Google Cloud AI (Rofouei, H. Lin).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25140
- **code url**: https://github.com/google-research/reasoning-bank
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/google-research/reasoning-bank (Apache-2.0; releases code for WebArena and SWE-Bench; OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=jL7fwchScm)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: LLM-agent sequential decision-making in interactive environments: web browsing (WebArena, Mind2Web) and software engineering / repository-level issue resolution (SWE-Bench-Verified). Spans web and code agent domains.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent, gradient-free test-time learning. A stream of task queries Q={q1..qN} arrives sequentially and must be solved one at a time without access to future queries and WITHOUT any ground-truth labels at test time (proxy correctness comes from an LLM-as-a-Judge). The agent policy is a backbone LLM (Gemini-2.5-Flash/Pro, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, also Gemma-3-12B) conditioned on a memory module M (ReasoningBank), initialized empty, acting via a ReAct-style loop over web-navigation operations (BrowserGym, max 30 steps) or bash commands (mini-SWE-Agent, bash-only). The agent must self-evolve across the stream by extracting and reusing memory from its own past successful AND failed trajectories. Supervision: no test-time ground truth; an LLM-as-a-Judge (same backbone, temperature 0.0) provides binary success/failure signals. A second contribution, memory-aware test-time scaling (MaTTS), allocates more inference compute per task (parallel: multiple rollouts; sequential: iterative self-refinement) with scaling factor k.
- **what is retrieved**:
> Self-distilled reasoning-strategy memory items extracted from the agent's own past successful and failed experiences. Each item is a structured unit with (i) a title (concise strategy identifier), (ii) a one-sentence description, and (iii) content recording distilled reasoning steps, decision rationales, or operational insights/pitfalls. These are generalizable reasoning strategies and guardrails, NOT raw trajectories or success-only workflows.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> GROWING/episodic self-written memory: ReasoningBank starts empty and is populated online during the test-time stream from the agent's own trajectories (both successes and failures). No static external corpus/KB/API store; the retrievable store is entirely self-generated and grows during deployment (closed-loop retrieve -> extract -> consolidate).
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k ranking objective: the agent retrieves the top-k most relevant past experiences (and their associated memory items) by embedding similarity. There is no minimal-complete-set or variable-size precision-driven objective. The number-of-retrieved-experiences ablation (WebArena-Shopping, Gemini-2.5-flash) finds k=1 best (49.7), with success rate declining as k grows (46.0 at k=2, 45.5 at k=3, 44.4 at k=4), so the default uses a small fixed k (k=1 in the ablated best setting).
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve: yes (embedding-similarity top-k recall of past experiences/items), Reuse: yes (retrieved memory items injected into the system instruction to guide acting), Revise: partial (no per-case verbatim-then-adapt step; instead experiences are re-distilled and strategies evolve over the stream, and MaTTS self-contrast/self-refinement revises which strategies are curated), Retain: yes (new memory items extracted from successes and failures are consolidated/appended after every task)].
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False. The paper frames itself as agent memory / experiential learning / self-evolving agents and test-time learning; it does NOT cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner or use the term 'case-based reasoning'. It realizes CBR-like Retrieve/Reuse/Retain mechanisms under memory and experience-learning framing (related to ExpeL, Synapse, AWM, AutoGuide).

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> guideline-rule / distilled reasoning-strategy memory item (title + description + content). Retrieval is keyed on past experiences; each retrieved experience carries its associated structured memory items (high-level transferable reasoning patterns), not full raw trajectories or executable programs.
- **index source**:
> Growing memory, online/test-time-induced: the retrievable store is built incrementally during the streaming test-time evaluation from the agent's own successful and failed trajectories (distilled via an LLM extractor). Initialized empty; not offline-induced and not a static external corpus.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat vector index: memory items / experiences are embedded and retrieved by embedding-based similarity search (cosine/inner-product nearest-neighbor). No graph, hierarchy, or cluster organization (the paper deliberately keeps retrieval simple; modular/compositional and hierarchical organization are explicitly flagged as future work).
- **retriever learning signal**:
> none (off-the-shelf): retrieval is a fixed embedding-similarity top-k using pretrained Gemini embeddings; there is no contrastive fine-tuning, LM-feedback, RL, or downstream-task-effectiveness training of the retriever. The paper intentionally keeps retrieval simple to isolate the contribution of the reasoning-oriented memory CONTENT.
- **query construction**: Raw query context: the agent queries ReasoningBank with the current task query/context, embedded and matched against stored experiences via similarity search. No query decomposition, intent extraction, or synthetic query expansion.
- **query granularity**: task-level (one-shot at t=0): retrieval is performed once per incoming task query using the current query context, and retrieved memory items are injected into the agent's system instruction for the whole episode. Not per-step or per-state.
- **when to retrieve**: one-shot: memory retrieval happens once at the start of each task (top-k relevant experiences/items), then the agent runs its ReAct loop using the injected memory. There is no mid-episode iterative or uncertainty-triggered re-retrieval.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> fixed schedule: retrieval is triggered unconditionally at the beginning of every new task query (the agent queries ReasoningBank with the current query context). No token-confidence, attention/uncertainty, learned complexity classifier, reflection-token, or agent-initiated mid-episode trigger.
- **reranking**: None. After embedding-similarity top-k retrieval, the retrieved experiences' memory items are injected directly into the system instruction; no cross-encoder, RRF, hierarchy-aware, or instruction-tuned reranking stage.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> None at retrieval time: retrieved memory items are injected verbatim as additional system instructions without post-retrieval compression, decomposition, distillation, or distractor filtering. (Distillation/abstraction happens at WRITE time during memory extraction, not on the fetched items.) The k-ablation notes excessive retrieved experiences can introduce conflicts/noise, motivating a small k rather than a refinement stage.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (not a tool-retrieval method; the agent interacts with environments via BrowserGym web actions or bash commands, not a retrievable tool/API index).
- **index content separation**:
> Partial: each memory item stores a lightweight title + one-sentence description for identification alongside heavier content (distilled reasoning steps). However, there is no progressive-disclosure mechanism that retrieves a light index first and loads heavy content on demand; retrieval returns whole items injected into the prompt.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index or integration protocol such as MCP/RapidAPI/RESTful/function-calling; the memory store is an internally-managed growing pool, not a live external tool registry).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> prompt augmentation: retrieved top-k memory items are injected into the agent's system instruction so that action prediction is grounded in past reasoning strategies, allowing the agent to recall effective insights and avoid previously observed pitfalls. No fine-tuning or latent-token injection; everything is in-context.
- **planning integration**:
> retrieve-then-plan, one-shot at plan time: relevant memory items are retrieved once per task and prepended to the system instruction; the agent then runs a ReAct (reason-act-observe) loop for the episode using that fixed memory context. No per-step re-retrieval, no MCTS/tree search inside the loop (default). MaTTS adds an outer test-time-scaling wrapper (parallel multi-rollout self-contrast or sequential self-refinement) around this retrieve-then-plan pipeline to generate richer experiences for memory curation.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: per-answer / per-task (per-episode): retrieval and memory injection occur once before the ReAct rollout and remain fixed throughout the multi-step reasoning of that task. Not per-CoT-step, per-token, or per-tool-call.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> LLM-prompted distillation/generalization rather than per-case verbatim reuse: an LLM extractor (temperature 1.0) converts each trajectory into up to 3 generalized strategy items; retrieved items are reused as injected guidance (not copied as a solution to be edited). MaTTS adds self-contrast (parallel) and self-refinement (sequential) to adapt which strategies are curated. No execution-feedback per-case revision of a single retrieved solution, no RL reuse-finetuning.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Distilled strategy / structured note: a structured, human-interpretable and machine-usable memory item with title + one-sentence description + content (distilled reasoning steps, decision rationales, operational insights, or failure pitfalls/guardrails) in Markdown. Not a raw trajectory, executable program, or latent token.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Distilled high-level reasoning strategy / state-aware guideline. The memory schema deliberately abstracts away low-level execution details while preserving transferable reasoning patterns and strategies; the paper contrasts this against prior memory that stores raw trajectories (Synapse) or success-only procedural workflows (AWM). A case study shows items evolving from procedural action rules -> adaptive self-reflections -> adaptive checks -> compositional strategies over time.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> (1) Self-verification via LLM-as-a-Judge to gate which trajectories are labeled success vs failure; the paper shows ReasoningBank is robust to judge noise: success rate is stable for simulated judge accuracy in the 70%-90% range (Figure 8). (2) Failure-aware extraction turns failed trajectories into corrective guardrails/pitfalls rather than noise. (3) Keeping retrieval k small (k=1 best) avoids conflicting/noisy retrieved context. (4) In MaTTS parallel scaling, self-contrast across multiple trajectories filters out spurious solutions and keeps consistent reasoning patterns.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> episodic-experience-derived strategy memory: a growing pool of distilled reasoning-strategy memory items (semantic/procedural knowledge) induced from the agent's episodic trajectories. Stored as plain structured text (title/description/content), not latent embeddings of content, not a graph.
- **write back**:
> Yes. After each task completes, the trajectory is processed by an LLM extraction pipeline (same backbone, temperature 1.0) that distills up to 3 structured memory items, which are then consolidated (added) into ReasoningBank, forming a closed-loop retrieve -> extract -> consolidate cycle.
- **online growth**: Yes. The memory store grows continuously during the streaming test-time deployment: starts empty and accumulates new memory items after every task, enabling sustained self-evolution (no offline freeze).
- **write back trigger**:
> on-success-and-failure, per-task (reflective): after every completed task, an LLM-as-a-Judge assigns a proxy success/failure label, then memory items are extracted from BOTH successful trajectories (validated transferable strategies) and failed trajectories (counterfactual pitfalls / preventive guardrails) and appended. Writing is human-label-free (self-judged). In MaTTS, the abundant trajectories from scaling additionally feed contrastive memory curation.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success + failure, contrastively used. Distinct from baselines (Synapse, AWM) that build memory only from successful trajectories: ReasoningBank extracts reasoning patterns from successes AND distills lessons/pitfalls/preventive strategies from failures. Ablation (Figure 7, WebArena-Shopping, Gemini-2.5-flash) shows adding failures raises ReasoningBank from 46.5 (success-only) to 49.7, whereas baselines stagnate or degrade (Synapse 40.6->41.7; AWM 44.4->42.2).
- **memory evolution update**:
> append-only by default: memory consolidation is a 'simple addition' of newly extracted items into the pool with no pruning, merging, or overwriting (deliberately minimal to isolate the content contribution). Although individual stored strategies are observed to evolve in EFFECT over time via successive additions (emergent strategy refinement in the case study), the consolidation operator itself is append-only; merging/forgetting are flagged as future work.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No. Memory selection is fixed embedding-similarity top-k using off-the-shelf Gemini embeddings, not an RL- or value-optimized learned retrieval policy. (MaTTS scaling and the agent loop are not framed as a learned retrieval policy; the paper draws an analogy to RL learning dynamics but the retrieval itself is fixed similarity.)
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> No. Single-agent private memory: one agent maintains and evolves its own ReasoningBank across the task stream. The work demonstrates cross-task / cross-website / cross-domain transfer of memory (e.g., Mind2Web cross-domain, WebArena Multi subset) but not sharing across multiple agents or heterogeneous frameworks.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> WebArena (684 instances across Shopping 187, Admin 182, Gitlab 180, Reddit 106, Multi 29; Map domain excluded due to website issues, following Miyai et al. 2025); Mind2Web (1341 instances: Cross-Task 252, Cross-Website 177, Cross-Domain 912); SWE-Bench-Verified (500 human-verified repository-level issue-resolution instances). Open-source-model study on WebArena-Shopping with Gemma-3-12B-Instruct.
- **benchmark family**: web (WebArena, Mind2Web) and code/software-engineering (SWE-Bench-Verified). No QA/multi-hop, embodied, or decision-RL benchmarks.
- **baselines**:
> No Memory / Vanilla (backbone LLM agent, no memory); Synapse (Zheng et al. 2024, trajectory-as-exemplar in-context memory from successful trajectories); AWM = Agent Workflow Memory (Wang et al. 2025d, abstracts reusable workflows/routines from successful trajectories). For SWE-Bench-Verified, only No Memory and Synapse are compared (AWM excluded because mini-SWE-Agent's open-ended bash action space precludes fixed workflows). MaTTS is also compared against vanilla TTS (test-time scaling without memory aggregation) and MaTTS-w/o-memory. All baselines share the SAME retrieval and consolidation; only the extraction (memory formulation) differs.
- **key metrics**:
> Web browsing: Success Rate (SR, %) for effectiveness and Average number of Steps (AS / Step) for efficiency on WebArena; Mind2Web reports Element Accuracy (EA), Action F1 (AF1), Step Success Rate (SSR), and task-level Success Rate (SR). SWE-Bench-Verified: issue Resolve/Resolution Rate (%) and Average Steps (AS). Scaling analyses report Pass@1, Best-of-N (BoN/Best-of-5), and Pass@k. Inference cost reported as average total token consumption per task.
- **headline result**:
> ReasoningBank consistently outperforms No-Memory, Synapse, and AWM across all backbones/datasets, with up to ~20% relative effectiveness improvement and up to 16% fewer interactions; MaTTS amplifies the gains. On WebArena overall SR it improves over memory-free agents by +8.3 (Gemini-2.5-flash 40.5->48.8), +7.2 (Gemini-2.5-pro 46.7->53.9), and +4.6 (Claude-3.7-sonnet 41.7->46.3); +MaTTS (parallel, k=5) further raises these (e.g., flash 48.8->51.8, pro 53.9->56.3, sonnet 46.3->48.8). On SWE-Bench-Verified, resolve rate rises from 34.2->38.8 (Gemini-2.5-flash) and 54.0->57.4 (Gemini-2.5-pro). The inference-cost study reports total tokens increase only ~4.3% over No-Memory while overall performance improves ~20.5%.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Failure trajectories (Figure 7, WebArena-Shopping, Gemini-2.5-flash): ReasoningBank 46.5 (success-only) -> 49.7 (with failures), while Synapse 40.6->41.7 and AWM 44.4->42.2 (degrades), showing only ReasoningBank turns failures into constructive signals. (2) Number of retrieved experiences (Figure 13): k=1 best (49.7) vs No-Memory 39.0; SR declines with more retrieved items (46.0 at k=2, 45.5 at k=3, 44.4 at k=4), indicating relevance/quality over quantity. (3) MaTTS scaling factor k (Figures 4/5/14): parallel scaling 49.7 (k=1) -> 55.1 (k=5); sequential 49.7 -> 54.5; MaTTS w/o memory only fluctuates 39.0-42.2 (parallel) / 37.4-40.6 (sequential). (4) MaTTS vs vanilla TTS at k=5: 55.1 vs 52.4 (parallel), 54.5 vs 51.9 (sequential). (5) Memory-scaling synergy (Figure 5, BoN, k=5): BoN climbs from 49.7->55.1 with ReasoningBank vs No-Memory 39.0->42.2; Pass@1 rises 49.7->53.0 for ReasoningBank while weaker memories barely move (Synapse 40.6->41.2, AWM 44.4->45.5). (6) Judge-noise robustness (Figure 8): SR stable for simulated judge accuracy 70%-90%. (7) Step breakdown on successful vs failed cases (Table 4): larger step reductions on successful instances (up to 2.1 fewer, 26.9% relative). (8) Open-source model (Gemma-3-12B, Table 6): SR 17.1->24.1, fewest steps (11.8). (9) Inference cost (Table 5): ReasoningBank total ~53054 tokens vs No-Memory ~50847, Synapse ~58515, AWM ~59373.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> No. Only end-to-end task metrics (SR / resolve rate / EA / AF1 / SSR) plus efficiency (steps, tokens) and scaling metrics (Pass@1/BoN/Pass@k) are reported. No intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k, nDCG, retrieval completeness) are reported separately, since retrieval here is memory recall for prompting rather than a ranked-retrieval benchmark; the closest decoupled signal is the k-ablation on number of retrieved experiences.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Mixed. Primary metrics are outcome-level (SR, resolve rate). The paper also reports process-relevant signals: efficiency via average interaction steps (overall and split by successful vs failed instances, Table 4), token-consumption breakdown (Table 5), Mind2Web step-level metrics (Step Success Rate, element accuracy, action F1), and qualitative analysis of emergent strategy evolution and per-step behavior in case studies.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Strongly reported. Effectiveness gains come with reduced interaction steps (up to 1.4 fewer steps vs No-Memory and 1.6 vs other memory baselines on WebArena; 2.8/1.3 fewer steps on SWE-Bench; up to 16% fewer interactions overall). Token cost (Table 5): ReasoningBank ~53054 total tokens (Action 49306 + Judge 2186 + Extraction 1562) vs No-Memory 50847, Synapse 58515, AWM 59373 - i.e., only ~4.3% more tokens than No-Memory for ~20.5% performance gain, and CHEAPER than Synapse/AWM. MaTTS trades extra rollouts/refinement compute (scaling factor k up to 5) for higher SR and better Pass@k sample efficiency (e.g., 62.1 Pass@5 with MaTTS vs 52.4 without memory).
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed small-k, budget-conscious: retrieve top-k relevant experiences/items (k=1 found best in the ablation; small k chosen because more retrieved items add conflict/noise). At most 3 memory items extracted per trajectory at write time. Web agents capped at 30 steps per query (BrowserGym). Retrieved items injected into the system instruction; no adaptive/precision-driven k or reranked-then-truncated budget cap beyond the small fixed k.
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (uses existing benchmarks: WebArena 684 instances over 5 domains with Map excluded; Mind2Web 1341 instances over cross-task/website/domain splits; SWE-Bench-Verified 500 human-verified instances). No new benchmark constructed.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Agent memory / experience-as-memory line: Synapse (Zheng et al. 2024) and AWM/Agent Workflow Memory (Wang et al. 2025d) as the direct memory baselines extended; ReAct (Yao et al. 2023) agent loop; ExpeL (Zhao et al. 2024) and AutoGuide (Fu et al. 2024) for insight/guideline distillation; LLM-as-a-Judge (Gu et al. 2024) and autonomous trajectory evaluation (Pan et al. 2024) for self-verification; test-time scaling (Snell et al. 2025; Zhu et al. 2025), best-of-N (Chow et al. 2025), self-refine (Madaan et al. 2023), self-contrast/contrastive learning (Chen et al. 2020) for MaTTS; Gemini Embedding (Lee et al. 2025) for retrieval; BrowserGym (de Chezelles et al. 2025) and mini-SWE-Agent (Yang et al. 2024) execution environments. Code adapts agent-workflow-memory, webarena, and mini-swe-agent repos.
- **contrasts with**:
> Memory mechanisms that store RAW trajectories (Synapse, RAP/Kagaya 2024, MapAgent) or SUCCESS-ONLY procedural workflows/routines/skills (AWM, Memp/Fang 2025, skill-set optimization/Nottingham 2024, ICE/Qian 2024) and instance-level concepts (Dynamic Cheatsheet, ExpeL) - ReasoningBank instead stores distilled high-level reasoning strategies and learns from BOTH successes and failures. Also contrasts with vanilla test-time scaling that ignores memory (Zhu et al. 2025; ExACT/Yu 2025b; Thinking-vs-Doing/Shen 2025; multi-agent TTS/Jin 2025), which MaTTS shows is suboptimal without memory-aware aggregation.
- **lineage**:
> Group D (case-based / experience planning): a 2025-2026 self-evolving agent-memory method advancing the ExpeL -> Synapse -> AWM -> AutoGuide lineage of experience/insight memory. Its distinctive contributions are (a) storing distilled, transferable REASONING STRATEGIES (not raw trajectories or success-only workflows), (b) learning from FAILURES via self-judged contrastive signals in a label-free streaming test-time-learning setting, and (c) introducing memory-aware test-time scaling (MaTTS) that couples memory curation with inference-time compute scaling as a new scaling dimension for self-evolving agents.

<a id="item-exprag"></a>
### 84. EXPRAG / Retrieval-Augmented LLM Agents: Learning to Learn from Experience (incl. EXPRAG-LoRA)

2026  ·  OpenReview 2026 (arXiv:2603.18272, 2026-03, verified)  ·  [paper](https://openreview.net/forum?id=HXTOSwUwF6)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2026
- **venue**:
> ICLR 2026 Workshop on Memory for LLM-Based Agentic Systems (MemAgents), OpenReview id=HXTOSwUwF6, published 03 Mar 2026 (CC BY 4.0). A preprint exists at arXiv:2603.18272 (2026-03, NAVER LABS Europe). The PDF header reads 'Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026', but the OpenReview venue listing is the ICLR 2026 MemAgents workshop. The term 'EXPRAG' itself was coined by contemporaneous work Wei et al. 2025 (Evo-Memory, arXiv:2511.20857) and adopted by this paper.
- **authors affiliation**: Thomas Palmeira Ferraz, Romain Deffayet, Vassilina Nikoulina, Hervé Déjean, Stéphane Clinchant. All authors at NAVER LABS Europe, Meylan, France. Correspondence: thomas.palmeira@naverlabs.com, stephane.clinchant@naverlabs.com.
- **paper url**: https://openreview.net/forum?id=HXTOSwUwF6

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> LLM-agent sequential decision-making in text-based interactive environments (embodied/decision-making). Evaluated on embodied household manipulation (ALFWorld) and science-experiment tasks (ScienceWorld). Not QA/tool-use; the work explicitly distinguishes itself from Agentic RAG (knowledge-intensive QA) and positions itself as retrieval-augmented AGENTS retrieving experience to improve decisions.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent, multi-turn decision making in fixed text-based environments where dynamics are fixed but required action sequences differ across tasks. The central goal is robust generalization to UNSEEN tasks within the same environment, including action types not observed during training (e.g., trained to clean an object but tested on heating one). Supervision is available as scripted expert trajectories from the environment-provided policy (these include failures/suboptimal segments). The agent is a moderately-sized open LLM adapted with supervised LoRA fine-tuning. The work systematically studies three settings: (1) training-free experience retrieval at inference (EXPRAG), (2) supervised LoRA fine-tuning (LoRA baseline), and (3) retrieval-augmented fine-tuning (EXPRAG-LoRA) that injects the retrieved memory block into each training context. The memory is intentionally a FIXED, read-only bank of full trajectories (no online write/update/reflection). For out-of-distribution (hard) tasks, a small set of in-domain reference trajectories (expert demos or strong-model rollouts) is assumed collectable for the index.
- **what is retrieved**:
> Past full interaction TRAJECTORIES (experiences). Each retrieved item is a complete agent trajectory tau = (T, o1, a1, ..., o_{T-1}, a_{T-1}, o_T) serialized as a multi-turn chat. Stored as raw chat-formatted data (including successful and unsuccessful episodes), and retrieved as in-context exemplars. No documents, skills, guidelines, or reflective summaries are retrieved.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> GROWING/episodic memory in spirit, but operationally a FIXED read-only episodic experience bank built offline. Retrieval targets prior interaction trajectories (episodic memory) rather than a static semantic corpus of documents/KB/APIs. The paper explicitly contrasts classic RAG (external semantic memory = corpus) with its episodic-memory view (retrieve prior trajectories to guide action selection). The bank is built offline from expert trajectories of the relevant task split and NOT updated online during deployment.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-K nearest-neighbor ranking objective. The agent retrieves the top-K most relevant trajectories by dot-product similarity (K in {1,2,4}; K=2 chosen as default efficiency-effectiveness tradeoff). No completeness/minimal-set objective and no variable-size precision-driven recommendation; selection is fixed-K and the study analyzes how K affects performance ('more experiences vs. context rot').
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve: yes (dense top-K nearest-neighbor recall of past trajectories), Reuse: yes (trajectories injected verbatim as in-context exemplars / memory block, and via EXPRAG-LoRA the policy is trained to reuse them), Revise: no (retrieved trajectories are not adapted/revised per case; no execution-feedback case revision), Retain: no (fixed read-only bank; no online write-back of new cases)]. Effectively a Retrieve+Reuse system without Revise/Retain.
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False. The paper frames itself as experience retrieval / episodic RAG / retrieval-augmented agents (citing classic RAG: Lewis 2020, Guu 2020, Ram 2023, RETRO, Atlas, RAFT, and RAP/Kagaya 2024) and adopts the term EXPRAG from Wei et al. 2025. It does NOT cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner or use 'case-based reasoning'; it realizes CBR-like Retrieve/Reuse under a RAG/episodic-memory framing.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> full trajectory: a complete agent rollout (task description + observation/action turns) stored as raw chat-formatted data. Trajectories are stored without filtering or aggregation; the retrieval and injection unit is the whole trajectory (one trajectory per retrieved item, K of them assembled into a memory block).
- **index source**:
> Growing-in-spirit but FIXED episodic memory, offline-induced: the retrieval index is built from scripted expert trajectories generated by the environment-provided policy on the training split (including failures unless stated otherwise). For fine-tuning, only successful trajectories from the training split are used as supervision; the index includes both successful and unsuccessful episodes. Index is split-specific (easy/hard/all) and not grown online at test time. For OOD tasks, a small in-domain reference set (expert demos or strong-model rollouts) is assumed collectable.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat vector index: a Sentence-Transformers embedding store of trajectory key embeddings e_i = phi(tau_i), queried by nearest-neighbor (dot-product) search. No graph, hierarchical, or cluster organization. The index can be composed by task-type partition (easy/hard/all) but within a partition it is a flat embedding index. Trajectories stored as raw chat-formatted (OpenAI message) data.
- **retriever type**:
> Dense (embedding-based) nearest-neighbor retriever using the Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B model (Zhang et al. 2025c) via the Sentence-Transformers library; top-K retrieved by dot-product similarity in embedding space. Off-the-shelf, frozen embedder (no other embedding model was tried). Not BM25/learned/generative/LLM-as-retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> none (off-the-shelf): the trajectory encoder phi is a fixed pretrained Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B model and is kept frozen throughout the paper; the authors found retrieved trajectories satisfactory given the simplicity of the retrieval task. There is no contrastive fine-tuning, LM-feedback, RL, preference, or downstream-task-effectiveness training of the retriever. (The POLICY is trained via LoRA, and EXPRAG-LoRA trains the policy to better USE retrieved context, but the retriever itself is never trained.)
- **query construction**:
> Two regimes. Static: the query q_t is built from the current task description (raw task text) once at episode start. Dynamic: the query is rebuilt at every step from the current agent context = task description + partial interaction history h_t, requiring re-encoding the prompt with updated retrieved examples. No query decomposition, intent extraction, or synthetic expansion; the query is the formatted text of the (task / task+history).
- **query granularity**:
> Both task-level and step/state-level depending on mode. Static retrieval = task-level (one-shot at t=0 using the task description). Dynamic retrieval = step/state-level (re-query at every decision step using the growing interaction history). The fine-tuning experiments adopt static (task-level) retrieval as the default.
- **when to retrieve**: one-shot (static, default) OR iterative/per-step (dynamic). Static retrieves once at episode start and keeps the memory block fixed for the whole episode; dynamic re-retrieves on a fixed schedule at every step. Both are FIXED-schedule, not uncertainty-triggered or learned-router.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> fixed schedule: retrieval fires unconditionally either once at t=0 (static) or at every decision step (dynamic). There is no token-confidence, attention/uncertainty, learned-complexity classifier, reflection-token, or agent-initiated trigger; the WHEN is a hard-coded static-vs-dynamic schedule chosen as an experimental variable.
- **reranking**: None. After dense top-K nearest-neighbor (dot-product) retrieval, the K trajectories are assembled directly into the memory block; no cross-encoder, RRF, hierarchy-aware, or instruction-tuned reranking stage is applied.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Light formatting only, no semantic refinement. Retrieved trajectories are inserted verbatim into a memory block (prepended to the system prompt) that separates successful from unsuccessful demonstrations; within it they are serialized in 'chat JSON' format by default (ablated against agentic JSON, compact JSON, and textual). No compression, decomposition-recompose, reason-in-documents distillation, or distractor filtering is performed; the model itself must learn to identify which retrieved actions are relevant (failures are deliberately kept in the index).
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (not a tool-retrieval method; no tool/skill documents are indexed - the retrieved items are agent trajectories).
- **index content separation**: N/A / No. No lightweight-index-then-content progressive disclosure; the trajectory key embeddings index the same full trajectories that are loaded verbatim into the memory block (no separation of a light retrievable index from heavy on-demand content).
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (not a tool-retrieval system; environment interaction is via fixed text action grammars for ALFWorld/ScienceWorld, not MCP/RapidAPI/RESTful/function-calling tool stores; the retrieval index is a static read-only trajectory bank).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> prompt augmentation (in-context) plus, in EXPRAG-LoRA, a training signal. At inference, the top-K trajectories are formatted into a memory block m_t = system(tau^1,...,tau^K) prepended to the policy prompt, and the LLM policy pi_theta samples the next action a_t ~ pi_theta(.| m_t, chat(h_t), a_t^{<i}). In EXPRAG-LoRA, the same retrieval pipeline injects the memory block into EACH training context so the model learns to leverage retrieved trajectories rather than memorize targets (retrieval becomes part of the supervised fine-tuning input). No latent-token injection; everything is text in-context.
- **planning integration**:
> retrieve-then-act with two variants. Static = one-shot exemplars at plan time: retrieve once, then run the multi-turn ReAct-style act loop with the fixed memory block. Dynamic = per-step interleaved: re-retrieve and refresh the memory block at every decision step using the partial history. No MCTS/tree search and no explicit hierarchical subtask decomposition; the policy directly outputs actions conditioned on retrieved experience + history. EXPRAG-LoRA additionally folds retrieval into the fine-tuning loop (retrieval-augmented training) so the trained policy natively conditions on retrieved trajectories at act time.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: per-answer/per-episode for static retrieval (memory block fixed across the whole multi-turn rollout) and per-step (per agent decision step / per tool-call-equivalent action) for dynamic retrieval, which re-queries and rebuilds the retrieved context at every environment step.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> verbatim ICL exemplar reuse plus RL-free retrieval-augmented fine-tuning. Retrieved trajectories are reused verbatim as in-context demonstrations (no per-case LLM-prompted adaptation or execution-feedback revision). The key adaptation lever is EXPRAG-LoRA: supervised LoRA fine-tuning with the retrieved memory block in the training context, which trains the policy to adapt retrieved experience in-context to the new task (learn-to-learn) rather than memorizing targets.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> raw trajectory injected as text: full multi-turn chat trajectories (observation->user turn, action->assistant turn) serialized in chat JSON (default) / agentic JSON / compact JSON / textual formats and placed in a memory block in the system prompt, treated as plain text by the model. No distilled strategy/guideline, executable program/skill, or latent-soft tokens; the surface form is the verbatim trajectory.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> raw trajectory (lowest abstraction): the agent retrieves complete past interaction trajectories, not distilled strategies, insights, guidelines, reusable workflows, or procedural skills. The paper deliberately keeps memory as full unprocessed trajectories (read-only bank) rather than reflective summaries/abstractions used by methods like Reflexion/A-MEM.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Learned in-context robustness via training, not a dedicated filter. The index intentionally includes failures and suboptimal segments, and EXPRAG-LoRA (retrieval-augmented fine-tuning) trains the policy to learn which retrieved actions are relevant, so the model becomes robust to imperfect retrieved context through training rather than via a relevance evaluator, self-reflection, or distractor-aware preprocessing. The work also studies robustness to lack of relevant trajectories (Empty / Mismatched index stress tests) showing EXPRAG-LoRA degrades but, with a mismatched (training) index, remains often more robust than alternatives. No explicit retriever-aware contrastive training or reason-in-documents refinement.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: episodic (a fixed read-only experience bank of full agent trajectories). Explicitly framed as episodic memory in contrast to RAG's semantic memory. No skill-library, workflow, procedural, graph, or latent memory; no memory controller.
- **write back**:
> No (within the studied pipeline). Memory is a FIXED, read-only bank of full trajectories built offline from expert/recorded rollouts; the system does not write new experiences into memory during inference. The paper explicitly states it does NOT propose a new memory controller, online memory update rule, or reflection mechanism, and lists read-write memories as future work.
- **online growth**:
> No. The retrievable store is frozen after offline construction (from training-split expert trajectories or a small collected OOD reference set); it does not grow during deployment/test-time. Self-evolving / read-write memory with consolidation is named as a promising future direction.
- **write back trigger**:
> never: no write events occur during inference. The index is constructed offline once (built from scripted expert trajectories of the relevant split, including failures), then used read-only. There is no on-success, on-failure, per-step, reflective, or human-validated write-back loop in the proposed method.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success+failure stored, but used as-is rather than contrastively. The retrieval index deliberately includes both successful AND unsuccessful (failed/suboptimal) episodes 'unless stated otherwise', so the policy can learn to identify which retrieved actions are relevant; the memory-block template separates successful from unsuccessful demonstrations. For LoRA/EXPRAG-LoRA supervised fine-tuning, only SUCCESSFUL trajectories are used as training targets. There is no explicit failure-only corrective-rule extraction; failures are retained in-context as negative/noisy examples.
- **memory evolution update**: append-only / static: the bank is constructed once offline and never mutated, merged, refined, or pruned at runtime. No dedup-merge, delta-update, refine-overwrite, forget-prune, or link-and-evolve dynamics; this is an explicit design simplification (fixed read-only memory).
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No. Retrieval/trajectory-selection is a fixed dense top-K nearest-neighbor rule (dot-product over frozen Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B), not an RL/value-optimized or learned retrieval policy. The novelty is training the POLICY (via EXPRAG-LoRA) to better USE retrieved trajectories, not learning the retrieval/selection policy itself.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Single-agent private memory in the main experiments. The framework allows experience to come from the agent's own rollouts, OTHER agents, or expert demonstrations, and in practice uses scripted expert (environment-policy) trajectories as the shared source. But there is no mechanism for sharing/evolving memory across multiple cooperating agents or heterogeneous agent frameworks; cross-agent sourcing is mentioned as a possibility, not a contribution.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> ALFWorld (Shridhar et al. 2021; household manipulation, binary success/failure, official held-out valid-unseen split, 6 task-types) and ScienceWorld (Wang et al. 2022; elementary-school science tasks, dense episode score in [-1,1] converted to binary success, official test split, 10 topics; subsampled to 5 variations per task except in the cross-paper Table 1). Each split partitioned into Easy (training/in-distribution) and Hard (held-out/out-of-distribution) task groups to probe generalization.
- **benchmark family**: embodied (ALFWorld, ScienceWorld) - text-based interactive embodied/decision-making environments.
- **baselines**:
> Prompting baselines: Zero-shot, ReAct (Yao et al. 2023), ITP (Liu et al. 2026b, imagine-then-plan). Training-free memory-augmented: Mem0 (Chhikara et al. 2025), A-MEM (Xu et al. 2025), AgeMem-noRL (Yu et al. 2026), Memory Bank (Zhong et al. 2024), Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023). Supervised fine-tuned: NAT+ReAct (Wang et al. 2024c), IWM and Self-Reflection (Zhang et al. 2025b), ETO+ReAct (Song et al. 2024), SFT+ReAct, SAND (Xia et al. 2025), ITP_R (Liu et al. 2026b), Rule-based Expert. The paper's own baselines: EXPRAG (training-free retrieval), LoRA (SFT), LoRA+EXPRAG (inference-time), EXPRAG-LoRA. Internal No-RAG ablation. Backbones: Ministral 3-8B (main), Gemma 3-4B, Qwen 2.5-7B, Qwen 2.5-7B-1M (plus Qwen 2.5-3B in appendix).
- **key metrics**:
> Success rate (%) is the primary metric for both ALFWorld (binary episode outcome) and ScienceWorld (dense [-1,1] score converted to binary success at 1). Reported as mean over 3 seeds (2025,2026,2027) with std. Efficiency metrics (Appendix F): average prompt tokens/step, steps/sample, total generation time, time/step.
- **headline result**:
> On ALFWorld official valid-unseen, the simple LoRA baseline reaches 94.1% success (Qwen 2.5-7B), surpassing rule-based expert (89.6) and prior pipelines (SAND 85.0, ITP_R 85.1), and the training-free 'Best EXPRAG' reaches 83.6 vs <=42.7 for elaborate training-free memory systems. The flagship EXPRAG-LoRA result is on OUT-OF-DISTRIBUTION (hard) tasks: e.g., Ministral 3-8B ALFWorld hard goes from LoRA 34.4 -> LoRA+EXPRAG 67.2 -> EXPRAG-LoRA 88.5 (with EXPRAG training-free at 47.5); Qwen 2.5-7B-1M ALFWorld hard 23.0 (LoRA) -> 91.8 (EXPRAG-LoRA); ScienceWorld hard for Ministral 15.6 (LoRA) -> 42.2 (EXPRAG-LoRA). Core takeaway: retrieval-augmented fine-tuning avoids the OOD collapse of standard LoRA while preserving high in-distribution success.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Top-K sweep (K in {1,2,4}, Table 2/Tables 9-14): more retrieved trajectories generally help on ALFWorld (best all-task 41.04% at K=1 -> 64.18% at K=4 for Ministral) but saturate earlier on ScienceWorld (26.62 -> 34.67 -> 35.24); large K can hurt on hard tasks with mismatched index ('context rot'); K=2 chosen as default. (2) Static vs dynamic retrieval: dynamic helps when index is matched but is less stable under mismatch ('context churn'), can reverse at large K. (3) Index composition (easy/hard/all): mismatched index (esp. easy-index on hard tasks) degrades sharply; 'all' is the strongest overall compromise; benchmark asymmetry (ALFWorld benefits more from hard index, ScienceWorld opposite). (4) Backbone scaling: bigger/long-context backbones (Qwen 2.5-7B-1M) exploit larger K better; smaller models (Gemma 3-4B, Qwen 2.5-3B) noisier. (5) Trajectory formatting (Table 16): chat JSON robust default; textual hurts Qwen sharply at large K. (6) Prolonged fine-tuning / 'delayed generalization' (Sec 4.4.1, App D): OOD success keeps improving for many epochs after validation loss starts rising (grokking-like), best OOD checkpoints often near epoch 50; 9 epochs (ALFWorld)/29 epochs (ScienceWorld) used for main runs. (7) Robustness stress test (Table 4): Empty index makes EXPRAG-LoRA drop most (distribution shift); Mismatched (training) index is preferable to empty. (8) Caveat: Qwen 2.5-7B suspected ALFWorld data contamination (29.85% zero-shot vs 5.22% for 1M variant), so it is not treated as a main backbone.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No. Only end-to-end task success rate is reported; no intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG / retrieval completeness) are reported separately, since the retriever is fixed/off-the-shelf and the contribution is on using retrieved experience, not on ranking quality.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome (success rate). Some process-adjacent diagnostics are reported: average steps/sample (Table 17, where higher K reduces steps, i.e., the agent solves faster), prompt-token growth, and the training-dynamics analysis correlating (poorly) validation loss with downstream agent success. No formal step-wise reasoning-faithfulness or trajectory-quality scoring.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Reported in Appendix F (Table 17, Ministral 3-8B / ALFWorld): average prompt tokens scale ~linearly with K (No-RAG 489.6 -> top1 1851.9 -> top2 3096.7 -> top4 5597.7 -> top5 6866.4), while steps/sample DECREASE with K (48 -> 34.4 -> 29.8 -> 25.7 -> 25), so total wall-clock time grows much more slowly (2769.59s No-RAG -> 2927.81s top2 -> 3556.04s top4 for 134 episodes); time/step rises (0.43 -> 0.73 -> 1.03s). K=2 chosen as best efficiency-effectiveness tradeoff. EXPRAG-LoRA incurs higher TRAINING cost (longer context) but preserves high in-distribution success. No dollar/API-cost figures (open models on a single 80GB A100).
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-K, budget-capped by K: K in {1,2,4} studied, K=2 the default (captures most zero-shot gain while limiting prompt length/latency vs K=4); long-context Qwen 2.5-7B-1M benefits from larger K. The memory block of K trajectories is prepended to the system prompt; selection is fixed-K nearest-neighbor (no adaptive/precision-driven or reranked-then-truncated budget).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A (uses existing benchmarks). Data statistics (Table 5): ALFWorld easy train=1748/test=73 (look_at_obj_in_light, pick_clean_then_place_in_recep, pick_and_place_simple), hard train=1805/test=61 (pick_cool_then_place_in_recep, pick_heat_then_place_in_recep, pick_two_obj_and_place); ScienceWorld easy train=2335/test=1183, hard train=1254/test=636, with the test set subsampled to 5 variations per task (Table 6).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Classic RAG (Lewis et al. 2020; Guu et al. 2020; Ram et al. 2023 in-context RALM; RETRO/Borgeaud 2022; Atlas/Izacard 2023; RAFT/Zhang 2024) reframed from semantic to episodic memory; RAP (Kagaya et al. 2024, retrieval-augmented planning with contextual memory); the EXPRAG term from contemporaneous Wei et al. 2025 (Evo-Memory); LoRA / PEFT (Hu et al. 2022; Han et al. 2024); agent SFT/behavior-cloning (FireAct/Chen et al. 2023, Agent-FLAN/Chen et al. 2024); multi-turn agent serialization (Wang & Ammanabrolu 2025; RAGEN/Wang et al. 2025; Search-R1/Jin et al. 2025); Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (Zhang et al. 2025c) + Sentence-Transformers (Reimers & Gurevych 2019); environments ALFWorld (Shridhar et al. 2021), ScienceWorld (Wang et al. 2022); grokking/delayed-generalization literature (Wang et al. 2024a; Liu et al. 2022; Kumar et al. 2024).
- **contrasts with**:
> Standard LoRA/SFT fine-tuning (strong in-distribution but collapses on OOD/unseen tasks); RL/preference-based agent training (ETO, GiGPO/Feng 2025, IWM, Self-Reflection/Zhang 2025b) - the paper argues simple PEFT can already outperform these; complex training-free memory systems (Mem0, A-MEM, Memory Bank, Reflexion) - shown to add limited or even negative improvement vs simple episodic retrieval; self-evolving read-write memory and memory controllers (MemGPT, Memento, A-MEM) - the paper deliberately keeps a fixed read-only bank and does not propose a memory controller; Agentic RAG (Singh et al. 2025) - explicitly distinguished (Appendix A): Agentic RAG orchestrates multi-step retrieval over external KNOWLEDGE for QA, whereas this retrieves EXPERIENCE for policy generalization. Closest contemporaneous work: Wei et al. 2025 (inference-only episodic retrieval vs self-evolving memory on proprietary models) - this paper instead studies weaker open models under inference-time AND fine-tuning retrieval augmentation.
- **lineage**:
> Group D (case-based / experience planning): an episodic experience-retrieval agent that retrieves full past trajectories in-context and, crucially, folds experience retrieval into LoRA fine-tuning (EXPRAG-LoRA). In the lineage of feedback/experience-driven planning agents (ReAct -> Reflexion -> ExpeL/RAP -> EXPRAG), it differs by (i) retrieving raw full trajectories rather than reflective summaries/insights, (ii) keeping memory fixed/read-only, and (iii) studying retrieval DURING TRAINING to teach the policy to learn from retrieved experience, positioning a simple read-only episodic RAG as a strong baseline that should be beaten before adding complex memory/RL machinery.
