## E — Retrieval-Augmented Tool-Use Agents

<a id="item-gorilla"></a>
### 85. Gorilla: Large Language Model Connected with Massive APIs

2023  ·  NeurIPS 2024  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.15334)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2023
- **venue**: NeurIPS 2024 (38th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems, poster; OpenReview id tBRNC6YemY, accepted 25 Sept 2024). Originally arXiv:2305.15334 (cs.CL), submitted 24 May 2023.
- **authors affiliation**: Shishir G. Patil (UC Berkeley), Tianjun Zhang (UC Berkeley) [equal contribution], Xin Wang (Microsoft Research), Joseph E. Gonzalez (UC Berkeley). Project from the UC Berkeley Sky Computing Lab / RISELab.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.15334
- **code url**: https://github.com/ShishirPatil/gorilla (project site https://gorilla.cs.berkeley.edu/; HuggingFace gorilla-llm)
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/ShishirPatil/gorilla (continuously maintained; now also hosts the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard / BFCL, the Gorilla API Zoo, OpenFunctions, GoEx, and RAFT). Leaderboard at https://gorilla.cs.berkeley.edu/leaderboard.html

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: tool-use (LLM tool/API calling): given a natural-language request, select and write the correct fully-qualified ML API call from a massive, overlapping, and changing set of APIs. Also touches code (single-line API-call program synthesis).
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-agent, non-interactive single-turn API-call generation. The model receives a natural-language user intent and must emit one correct, fully-qualified API call (e.g. torch.hub.load(...)) drawn from a large corpus of ML APIs scraped from TorchHub, TensorFlow Hub, and HuggingFace. Supervision is self-instruct: GPT-4 synthesizes ~10 instruction-API pairs per API from 18 hand-written seed examples; a LLaMA-7B base model is finetuned on these (instruction -> reference API) pairs. Two inference modes are supported: zero-shot (no retriever) and retrieval-augmented (a retriever appends the most relevant API documentation to the prompt). The key novelty is Retriever-Aware Training (RAT): during finetuning the retrieved (oracle) API document is appended to the prompt so the model learns to ground its answer in provided documentation, enabling test-time adaptation to changed/updated API docs. No environment execution or multi-step planning is part of the evaluated task (an execution engine exists but is out of scope).
- **what is retrieved**:
> tools / docs: API documentation (model cards converted to structured JSON with fields domain, framework, functionality, api_name, api_call, api_arguments, environment_requirements, example_code, performance, description) for candidate ML APIs from TorchHub / TensorFlow Hub / HuggingFace.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus: a fixed API documentation database (APIBench, 1,645 ML API model cards). Retrieval targets this static doc store; the method explicitly stresses that the store can be UPDATED at test time (version/document changes) but is not an agent-written growing episodic memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**: Fixed top-1 ranking objective: the retriever fetches the single most relevant API document (top-1) and appends it to the prompt. Not a complete-minimal-set or precision-driven variable-size recommendation; a single API call is generated and evaluated.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: [Retrieve: yes (top-1 API document retrieval), Reuse: partial (retrieved doc used as grounding context, not a prior solved case), Revise: no, Retain: no]. Not a case-based-reasoning method; it retrieves documentation, not prior problem-solution cases.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False: the paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is retrieval-augmented finetuning for tool calling, not CBR.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: tool-API document: one API's documentation (a model card rendered as a JSON object) is treated as a single retrievable document; each API is indexed as a separate document.
- **index source**:
> Static corpus, offline-built from scraped public model hubs: 95 TorchHub APIs, 696 TensorFlow Hub APIs (after filtering low-information cards), and 925 HuggingFace APIs (top-20 most-downloaded per domain), totaling 1,645 API documents. The store is designed to be editable/updatable at test time (documentation change experiments) but does not grow via agent self-writing.
- **retriever type**:
> hybrid set of off-the-shelf retrievers evaluated: BM25 (sparse term-based), GPT-Index (dense retrieval using OpenAI text-davinci-003 embeddings), plus an Oracle retriever (ground-truth document, upper bound). The retriever is external/frozen; Gorilla itself is the generator, not a learned retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> none (off-the-shelf retrievers: BM25, GPT-Index/text-davinci-003, Oracle are not trained). The learning happens in the GENERATOR via Retriever-Aware Training: the LLaMA-7B model is finetuned with the (oracle) retrieved document appended, i.e. supervised next-token loss conditioned on retrieved documentation, teaching the model to parse and ground on retrieved docs. There is no contrastive or RL training of the retriever component.
- **query construction**:
> Raw natural-language user instruction is used as the query to the retriever; the top-1 retrieved API documentation is concatenated to the user prompt with the fixed string 'Use this API documentation for reference:' before being fed to Gorilla. No query decomposition, expansion, or intent extraction.
- **query granularity**: task-level: a single retrieval is performed once per user request (t=0) using the raw instruction; one API call is produced.
- **when to retrieve**: one-shot: a single retrieval call per query (in retrieval mode). Zero-shot mode performs no retrieval at all. No iterative or uncertainty-triggered retrieval.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed schedule / mode switch: retrieval is either always-on (retrieval mode, one retrieval per query) or always-off (zero-shot mode). There is no learned router, confidence signal, or agent-initiated trigger deciding when to retrieve; the mode is set by the user/system configuration.
- **reranking**: None. The top-1 document from BM25 / GPT-Index is used directly; no cross-encoder, RRF, or hierarchy-aware reranking stage.
- **retrieved context refinement**: None. The retrieved API documentation is appended verbatim to the prompt (prefixed by 'Use this API documentation for reference:'); no decompose-recompose, distillation, distractor filtering, or compression is applied.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Tool/API descriptions are engineered into a uniform structured JSON schema before indexing: each scraped model card is converted into fields {domain, framework, functionality, api_name, api_call, api_arguments, environment_requirements, example_code, performance, description}, chosen to generalize beyond ML APIs to RESTful APIs. Low-information cards are filtered out. This is curated/normalized documentation rather than raw docstrings, but no synthetic-query augmentation or weighted-field tool embeddings are used for the index itself (self-instruct queries are used to train the generator, not to expand the index).
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> The API documentation database is designed to be UPDATED at test time (the paper demonstrates adapting to changed API docs, e.g. backbone upgrades ResNet-50 -> ResNet-101 and registry moves pytorch/vision -> NVIDIA/DeepLearningExamples:torchhub), so it supports manual/user updates of documents. Integration protocol in the paper is ML model-hub API calls (TorchHub/TensorFlow Hub/HuggingFace) with structured fields extensible to RESTful APIs; no automatic CRUD live-sync or MCP. (The broader follow-on Gorilla ecosystem adds the community API Zoo, OpenFunctions function-calling, and GoEx execution, but those are outside this paper.)
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A: the paper considers single, independent API calls (one API call per query) and explicitly does not model inter-tool dependencies, prerequisites, or chaining. It does model intra-call CONSTRAINTS (e.g. parameter size, minimum accuracy) that the chosen API must satisfy.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> prompt augmentation + retriever-aware training signal: at inference the retrieved API doc is concatenated to the user prompt to ground generation; during training the same retrieved (oracle) doc is appended so the model learns to read and use retrieved documentation (Retriever-Aware Training). The output is a single API call to be invoked.
- **planning integration**:
> retrieve-then-generate (one-shot, no planning loop): in retrieval mode the retriever fetches the top-1 API document, which is appended to the prompt, then Gorilla generates the API call in a single forward pass. There is no MCTS/tree search, no per-step interleaving, and no multi-step plan; the task is single-call API selection.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: per-answer: one retrieval and one generation per user query; retrieval is not interleaved with multi-step reasoning, CoT steps, or multiple tool calls.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> N/A (not framed as case-based reasoning). The closest analogue: the retrieved API document is used as grounding context that the retriever-aware-finetuned model conditions on to produce a correctly-instantiated API call (verbatim documentation injection + learned grounding), not case adaptation/revision.
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw structured API documentation (the JSON model card text) injected into the prompt; the surface form is the documentation string, not a distilled strategy, workflow, or latent token.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw documentation / single reference item: the retrieved unit is the concrete API's documentation (a single candidate tool's spec), not a distilled strategy, guideline, reusable workflow, or procedural skill.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Retriever-aware training (RAT): by finetuning with the retrieved document appended (and demonstrating that a non-optimal retriever can sometimes hurt), the model learns to ground on documentation and substantially reduce hallucination; AST sub-tree matching is used to detect/define hallucinations (an API call not matching any subtree in the database). The paper explicitly notes retrieval is not always beneficial (BM25/GPT-Index can mislead vs zero-shot), so robustness comes from finetuning-with-retrieval and from the zero-shot fallback rather than a relevance evaluator or self-reflection.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none: no episodic/skill/workflow/graph/latent memory. The retrievable store is a static (editable) external API documentation database, not an agent-written memory.
- **write back**: false: the system does not write new experiences/cases/skills into a memory during deployment. (The API documentation store can be manually updated by users/maintainers, but the model does not self-write.)
- **online growth**: false: the API documentation index is frozen after offline construction; it can be manually edited/updated to reflect doc changes (the central test-time-adaptation feature) but it does not autonomously grow from the agent's own outputs at test time.
- **write back trigger**:
> never: there is no automatic memory write-back. The only updates to the store are external/manual (human or maintainer editing API documents to reflect version/registry changes), demonstrated as the test-time documentation-change capability, not triggered by model success/failure or reflection.
- **failure experience usage**: N/A / none: no experiences (success or failure) are stored or retrieved. Hallucinations and errors are measured and reduced via finetuning and AST matching, but failed outputs are not persisted as negative cases for retrieval.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A: no stored experience entries to mutate. The external documentation store is updated only by manual/external editing (overwrite documents to new versions); there is no append/dedup/refine of model-written memory.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No: retrieval/document selection uses fixed off-the-shelf top-1 retrievers (BM25 / GPT-Index) or the Oracle; it is not an RL- or value-learned selection policy. The learned component is the document-grounded GENERATOR (retriever-aware finetuning), not the retrieval policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No: single-model setup with a private/shared static API store; no cross-agent or cross-framework experience sharing. (Gorilla can be plugged into agent frameworks like LangChain, but the paper does not study shared memory across agents.)

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> APIBench (introduced by this paper): 1,645 ML APIs across three model hubs - TorchHub (95 APIs, 6 domains), TensorFlow Hub (696 APIs, 57 domains), HuggingFace (925 APIs, 37 domains), each with ~10 self-instruct instruction-API pairs (held-out train/test split). Also a constraint-aware subset of TorchHub (the 65.26% of TorchHub entries with accuracy defined in their model card).
- **benchmark family**: tool (tool/API-use benchmark): APIBench is an ML-API tool-calling benchmark, predecessor in the same lineage that later grew into the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL). Functional correctness verified via AST sub-tree matching (verifiable answers).
- **baselines**: Zero-shot SOTA LLMs: GPT-4 (gpt-4-0314), GPT-3.5-turbo (gpt-3.5-turbo-0301), Claude (claude-v1), and LLaMA-7B (base). Each is also evaluated under the same BM25, GPT-Index, and Oracle retrievers for fair comparison against Gorilla.
- **key metrics**:
> Overall AST functional-correctness accuracy (%, higher better); hallucination rate (%, lower better, defined via AST: an API call not a subtree of any DB API = imagined tool); error rate (%, wrong-but-real API). Constraint-aware setting additionally reports accuracy-constraint satisfaction. No latency/cost metrics in this paper (added later to BFCL).
- **headline result**:
> Lightly finetuned Gorilla (LLaMA-7B-based) in the zero-shot setting beats GPT-4 by 20.43% and GPT-3.5 by 10.75% in overall AST accuracy on APIBench, and outperforms LLaMA by ~83%, while substantially reducing hallucination. Per-hub zero-shot overall accuracy: TorchHub 59.13%, HuggingFace 71.68%, TensorFlow Hub 83.79%. Retriever-aware training with an oracle retriever pushes HuggingFace to 91.26% and TensorFlow Hub to 94.16% (Table 2).
- **ablations**:
> (1) Finetuning vs retrieval: zero-shot finetuned Gorilla > adding off-the-shelf retrievers at test time; a non-optimal retriever (BM25/GPT-Index) at eval time can HURT, dropping accuracy by 21.50% on TorchHub and 47.57% on HuggingFace vs zero-shot. (2) Retriever-Aware Training (RAT): finetuning WITH the (oracle) retriever incorporated improves over finetuning without it by 12.37% on TorchHub and 23.46% on HuggingFace; but at eval time current retrievers still trail the ground-truth oracle (GPT-Index -29.20%, BM25 -52.27% accuracy gap). (3) Retriever quality sweep (zero-shot / BM25 / GPT-Index / Oracle) in Table 2 quantifies the accuracy-vs-hallucination tradeoff and the oracle upper bound. (4) Constraint-aware API invocation (Table 3): Gorilla matches the best model (GPT-3.5) with retrievers and has highest zero-shot accuracy under accuracy constraints. (5) RLHF/hallucination observation: GPT-3.5 hallucinates less than GPT-4 across all retriever settings.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Partial: results are reported as end-to-end overall AST accuracy decomposed into hallucination rate and error rate (an intrinsic-style breakdown of failure modes), and separately swept across retriever types (zero-shot/BM25/GPT-Index/oracle). However, standalone retriever metrics (Recall@k / nDCG) are NOT reported; the oracle retriever serves as the upper-bound proxy instead.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Primarily outcome: correctness of the single generated API call (overall accuracy), with a process-relevant decomposition into hallucination vs error and a constraint-satisfaction metric. No step-wise reasoning-faithfulness or trajectory-quality metrics (single-call task).
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Efficiency angle is model-size, not retrieval-call count: a small finetuned LLaMA-7B beats much larger GPT-4 zero-shot, and avoids costly retraining by adapting to updated docs via retrieval at test time. Training cost reported: 5 epochs, lr 2e-5 cosine decay, batch size 64, max seq length 2048, on 8xA100 (40GB). No explicit latency/API-cost/token-savings numbers in this paper (cost and latency metrics were added later to BFCL, 04/2024).
- **context budget and selection count**: Fixed top-1 selection: exactly one API document is retrieved and appended per query in retrieval mode; max sequence length 2048 tokens caps the prompt budget. Selection count is fixed (k=1), not adaptive or reranked-then-truncated.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> APIBench size: 1,645 ML APIs (TorchHub 95, TensorFlow Hub 696, HuggingFace 925) with ~10 self-instruct instruction-API pairs each (~16,450 instruction-API datapoints). Construction: scrape public model-hub model cards -> filter low-information cards -> convert to structured JSON -> GPT-4 self-instruct generation from 18 hand-written seeds (3 hubs x 6 examples). Answer verifiability: AST sub-tree matching against the reference API (checks specific arguments, ignores optional/default args), which also defines hallucination. Difficulty signal: best zero-shot SOTA (GPT-4/GPT-3.5) reach only ~40% overall on TorchHub/TensorFlow Hub; oracle-retriever upper bounds reach ~67-94%.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Self-Instruct (Wang et al. 2022) for synthetic instruction generation; LLaMA-7B (Touvron et al. 2023) as the finetuned base; instruction-tuned chat models Alpaca/Vicuna lineage; retrieval-augmented LM ideas (WebGPT, internet-augmented LMs); tool-use LLMs (Toolformer). Distinct claim: first to finetune a base model by supplementing it with information retrieval (retriever-aware training).
- **contrasts with**:
> Prompting-only tool-use methods that inject a small, well-documented API set into the context (Toolformer, HuggingGPT, TaskMatrix.AI) which cannot scale to millions of overlapping/changing APIs; and zero-shot prompting of GPT-4/GPT-3.5/Claude, which hallucinate API calls. Gorilla instead finetunes a small model with retrieval awareness over a large, updatable API documentation corpus.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use): retrieval-augmented tool/API calling. A foundational static-corpus tool-retrieval-grounded method (retriever-aware finetuning over large API documentation) that selects/writes a single correct API call; predecessor of the Gorilla ecosystem (OpenFunctions, Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard / BFCL, API Zoo) and a reference point for later large-scale tool-retrieval work (e.g. ToolLLM/ToolBench, ToolRet).

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- index_content_separation
- index_structure_topology

<a id="item-tool-documentation"></a>
### 86. Tool Documentation Enables Zero-Shot Tool-Usage with Large Language Models

2023  ·  arXiv 2308.00675  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.00675)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2023
- **authors affiliation**:
> Cheng-Yu Hsieh (University of Washington), Si-An Chen (National Taiwan University), Chun-Liang Li, Chen-Yu Lee (Google Cloud AI Research), Yasuhisa Fujii (Google Research), Alexander Ratner (University of Washington), Ranjay Krishna (University of Washington), Tomas Pfister (Google Cloud AI Research). Primary affiliations: University of Washington, National Taiwan University, Google Cloud AI Research, Google Research.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.00675

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: tool-use (LLM tool/API planning) across language and vision modalities; multi-modal QA, tabular math reasoning, compositional visual reasoning, image editing, and video tracking
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-agent, zero-shot/in-context tool-use planning. An LLM planner (primarily ChatGPT/gpt-3.5-turbo, also text-davinci-002) is given a task and a set of available tools/APIs and must produce an executable tool-use plan WITHOUT few-shot demonstrations. No model fine-tuning is performed; tools (including just-released, unseen vision models) are introduced solely by their documentation. The central assumption tested is that tool documentation (per-tool descriptions / docstrings) can replace input-output demonstrations, including in plug-and-play settings where new unseen tools are added at test time.
- **what is retrieved**:
> tool documentation (per-tool descriptions / docstrings: tool functionality descriptions and how to invoke each tool). In the large-tool-set setting (LLM-Cloud CLI with 200 tools) the relevant tool documents are retrieved per question; in the small-tool-set benchmarks the docs for all tools are simply placed in the prompt.
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus: a fixed store of tool documentation (e.g., GCP CLI manuals scraped and renamed, VisProg module docs, original Chameleon tool docs). The store does not grow from the agent's own experience; new tools are added manually by inserting their documentation.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Mixed. For small tool sets, all tool docs are provided (no ranking needed). For the 200-tool LLM-Cloud CLI, retrieval uses a fixed top-k (top-10 TF-IDF documents) truncated to a length budget; the downstream objective is task completeness, since each question requires at least two commands and is scored by command-line-level F1 measuring recovery of the needed command set, not a single ranking.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based reasoning method; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain case cycle is implemented)
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it contrasts documentation-based zero-shot tool use against demonstration-based (in-context example) tool use.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: tool-API / tool documentation document (per-tool description / docstring; for the CLI benchmark, a per-command documentation page)
- **index source**:
> Static corpus constructed offline: tool documentation collected from original benchmark tool docs (ScienceQA/Chameleon, TabMWP/Chameleon), author-written module docs for VisProg tools, and scraped+renamed GCP CLI manuals for the LLM-Cloud CLI benchmark. No online/test-time induction; new tool docs are added manually.
- **index structure topology**: Flat document store. For the 200-tool LLM-Cloud CLI, a flat TF-IDF index over tool documents; for small tool sets, docs are simply concatenated into the prompt with no special structure.
- **retriever type**: Sparse lexical: TF-IDF search (used only for the 200-tool LLM-Cloud CLI benchmark, querying with the question to retrieve relevant tool docs). For all other tasks no retriever is used (all tool docs fit in the prompt).
- **retriever learning signal**: none (off-the-shelf, unlearned TF-IDF; no training of the retriever)
- **query construction**: Raw input question used directly as the TF-IDF query to retrieve relevant tool documentation (no decomposition, expansion, or thought-conditioning).
- **query granularity**: task-level (one query formed from the input question at the start; one-shot retrieval at t=0)
- **when to retrieve**: one-shot (retrieve relevant tool docs once before planning, only in the large-tool-set CLI setting; no retrieval for small tool sets)
- **retrieval trigger signal**: fixed schedule / driven only by prompt-length constraints: retrieval is triggered when the full set of tool documentation cannot fit in the prompt (200 tools); otherwise all docs are included with no trigger.
- **reranking**: None. A single TF-IDF top-10 retrieval is used with no reranking stage.
- **retrieved context refinement**: Length truncation/compression only: retrieved documents are truncated to a maximum of ~600 words to fit the prompt budget; no rerank, distillation, or distractor filtering. The authors deliberately keep unrelated content (terms, hyperlinks) to test robustness.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Mostly raw docstrings/manuals: original tool docs are reused (ScienceQA/TabMWP via Chameleon); for VisProg modules the authors write docs containing the module functionality description plus the function signature; for LLM-Cloud CLI, GCP manuals are scraped with BeautifulSoup, HTML tags removed and commands renamed, but content is deliberately NOT curated/engineered (unrelated terms/hyperlinks kept) to assess robustness.
- **index content separation**: Partial: in the 200-tool CLI setting, a lightweight TF-IDF index over docs selects which tool documents to load into the prompt, separating selection from the full documentation content; for small tool sets there is no separation.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Static tool index (no live synchronization, no CRUD auto-sync). Integration is via prompt-based plan generation; for vision tasks tools are invoked through the VisProg program-execution framework, and for CLI via generated command-line strings. No RapidAPI/MCP/function-calling protocol.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> prompt augmentation: retrieved/provided tool documentation is inserted into the LLM prompt, and the LLM zero-shot generates a tool-use plan (a sequence of tool calls / a VisProg program / CLI commands) by reading the docs. No fine-tuning; docs guide the model's internal planning and reasoning.
- **planning integration**:
> retrieve-then-plan / one-shot exemplar-free plan time: documentation is provided up front and the LLM produces a complete tool-use plan in a single zero-shot pass (no per-step interleaved retrieval, no tree search). For vision tasks the plan is a VisProg program executed afterwards.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: per-answer (the LLM generates the full multi-tool plan in one shot from the provided documentation; retrieval is not interleaved per reasoning step)
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (no case adaptation; documentation is used verbatim as prompt context and the LLM directly generates plans)
- **retrieved item representation**: raw free-text tool documentation (natural-language tool descriptions plus function signatures / CLI manuals) injected into the prompt
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: tool-level descriptive documentation (a hint/manual describing each individual tool's functionality and invocation), not raw trajectories or distilled strategies; it is per-tool capability description rather than task-level demonstration
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Tested-not-engineered: the authors intentionally do NOT curate documentation (keeping unrelated terms/hyperlinks, varying doc length) to assess the LLM's robustness to realistic/noisy docs; they report a length ablation showing degradation past ~600 words. No explicit retriever-aware training or relevance evaluator is used.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (no episodic, skill-library, or procedural memory that the system writes to; only a static, manually-maintained documentation store)
- **write back**: False. The system does not store new experiences/cases/skills; the tool documentation store is static and only manually extended with new tools' docs.
- **online growth**: No. The retrievable store does not grow from deployment experience; new tools are added by humans inserting their documentation (plug-and-play), not by the agent writing back.
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back of agent experience)
- **failure experience usage**: N/A (no experience/memory storage, so no use of failed or successful trajectories)
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (no stored memory entries; the static doc store is not mutated by the system)
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No. Retrieval (where used) is a fixed off-the-shelf TF-IDF top-k, not a learned/RL-optimized policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent, single-framework use; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing. (Tool docs themselves are shareable artifacts, but there is no shared experience memory.)

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: ScienceQA; TabMWP; NLVRv2; LLM-Cloud CLI (newly collected, 200 commands renamed from GCP CLI, 50 questions); image editing and video tracking with VisProg expanded by GroundingDINO + Segment Anything (SAM) + XMem (qualitative, re-inventing Grounded-SAM and Track Anything).
- **benchmark family**:
> Tool-use / multi-modal tool planning. ScienceQA = multi-modal QA; TabMWP = tabular math reasoning; NLVRv2 = compositional visual reasoning (VisProg); LLM-Cloud CLI = realistic large tool-set API/CLI tool-use (new benchmark, GCP-derived); image editing + video tracking = vision tool pipelines.
- **baselines**:
> Few-shot demonstration prompting (varying number of demos, with and without docs); demos+docs combinations. Task-specific: ScienceQA - CoT, Chameleon (few-shot) and finetuned models (e.g., UnifiedQA, others on the SQA training set); TabMWP - UnifiedQA, TAPEX (finetuned), Chain-of-Thought (CoT), Program-of-Thoughts (PoT), Chameleon (few-shot); NLVRv2 - ViLT-NLVR (finetuned), VisProg (few-shot, varying demos); LLM-Cloud CLI - zero-shot LLM, few-shot demos without docs, and docs+demos, on text-davinci-002 and gpt-3.5-turbo.
- **key metrics**: Accuracy (ScienceQA, TabMWP, NLVRv2); command-line-level F1 averaged over 50 examples (LLM-Cloud CLI); qualitative success of generated pipelines (image editing, video tracking).
- **headline result**:
> Zero-shot tool-documentation prompting matches few-shot performance on existing benchmarks and far outperforms demonstrations on the 200-tool LLM-Cloud CLI: with gpt-3.5-turbo, 0-shot with docs reaches F1 0.45 vs 0.13 zero-shot no-doc and best few-shot no-doc F1 0.19; with text-davinci-002, 0-shot with docs F1 0.37 vs 0.02 zero-shot no-doc and best few-shot no-doc 0.05. On benchmarks, 0-shot with docs achieves 79.91 (ScienceQA), 92.69 (TabMWP), and 63.40 (NLVRv2, vs 0.00 without docs), competitive with or better than CoT/PoT few-shot and some finetuned models.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Number of demonstrations: stripping demos away barely changes accuracy when docs are present (0-shot+docs on par with 16-shot on TabMWP, 12-shot on NLVRv2, and better than 10-shot on ScienceQA), while without docs performance drops sharply and shows high variance to which demos are chosen (e.g., 2-shot std up to 16.1 points on NLVRv2). (2) Docs vs docs+demos: adding demos to docs does not help and can slightly hurt (text-davinci-002 docs-only 0.37 vs docs+demos avg 0.35; gpt-3.5-turbo docs-only 0.45 vs 0.44/0.44/0.42), showing demos are redundant given docs. (3) Documentation quality/length: truncating docs to first n words; performance degrades after document length exceeds ~600 words, attributed to long-context comprehension limits. (4) Different LLM planners (text-davinci-002 vs gpt-3.5-turbo) on LLM-Cloud CLI confirm docs >> demos at large tool counts.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No. Retrieval quality (the TF-IDF doc retrieval) is not evaluated with intrinsic metrics (Recall@k/nDCG); only end-to-end task metrics (accuracy / command-line F1) are reported.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome metrics (final accuracy / F1). Some process-level insight via command-line-level F1 (which credits partial recovery of the needed commands/flags) and qualitative inspection of generated plans/pipelines, but no formal reasoning-faithfulness or step-wise planning metric.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Efficiency framed as avoiding combinatorial demo-selection cost and human curation: documentation is 'organically available' and zero-shot, eliminating few-shot demo curation and the combinatorial search over which/how-many demos to include as tool counts scale. Prompt-length is the binding cost: docs are truncated (~600 words/tool; top-10 docs in the 200-tool setting) and performance degrades past ~600 words. No explicit latency/API-cost numbers reported.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> For the 200-tool LLM-Cloud CLI: fixed top-10 TF-IDF documents, each truncated to a maximum of ~600 words to fit the prompt (token count varies by tokenizer, typically >600). For small tool sets: all tool docs included (no k selection). Documentation-length ablation shows ~600 words is roughly the effective budget before long-context degradation.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (empirical study, not a survey)
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> LLM-Cloud CLI: newly collected; 200 command-line tools renamed from the Google Cloud Platform (GCP) CLI to be unseen to LLMs while preserving semantics (e.g., 'gcloud compute create NAME' -> 'llmvm compute make NAME'); 50 questions, each requiring at least two commands; docs scraped from real GCP manuals via BeautifulSoup with HTML removed and renaming applied, deliberately not over-curated. Answer verifiability via command-line-level F1 against reference commands. Best system (gpt-3.5-turbo, 0-shot with docs) reaches F1 0.45, signaling the benchmark is far from saturated.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> VisProg (Gupta & Kembhavi) and Chameleon (Lu et al.) tool-use frameworks (tool sets reused); in-context learning / few-shot prompting (Brown et al.); DocPrompting (Zhou et al., retrieving docs for code generation) as the closest documentation-based predecessor; uses GroundingDINO, Segment Anything (SAM), XMem, and Stable Diffusion as plug-in tools.
- **contrasts with**:
> Demonstration/few-shot-based tool-use methods (VisProg, Chameleon, MM-REACT, HuggingGPT, ART, Visual ChatGPT/TaskMatrix); instruction-tuning-on-synthetic-tool-data approaches (Gorilla, ToolLLM/ToolBench-style works that finetune LLaMA/OPT on GPT-4-generated tool-use data); ViperGPT (concurrent, function implementations/specs as docs for visual programming); AutoGPT (anecdotal doc reading). The paper argues documentation alone, zero-shot, suffices and avoids demo-selection and finetuning costs.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use). An early (Aug 2023) position/empirical work establishing that tool documentation (static external doc grounding) can substitute for few-shot demonstrations for zero-shot tool/API usage, including unseen tools; a conceptual predecessor to later tool-retrieval and tool-documentation-engineering lines (e.g., Gorilla, ToolBench/ToolLLM, and doc-augmented tool-retrieval works).
