<a id="item-toolllm"></a>
### 87. ToolLLM / ToolBench - Facilitating LLMs to Master 16000+ Real-World APIs (ToolLLaMA + API Retriever + DFSDT + ToolEval)

2023  ·  ICLR 2024  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.16789)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2023
- **venue**: ICLR 2024 (spotlight). Preprint arXiv:2307.16789 (cs.AI; cs.CL; cs.LG), v1 submitted 31 Jul 2023, v2 revised 3 Oct 2023; published at the International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR) 2024 (OpenReview id dHng2O0Jjr).
- **authors affiliation**:
> Yujia Qin, Shihao Liang, Yining Ye, Kunlun Zhu, Lan Yan, Yaxi Lu, Yankai Lin (corresponding), Xin Cong, Xiangru Tang, Bill Qian, Sihan Zhao, Lauren Hong, Runchu Tian, Ruobing Xie, Jie Zhou, Mark Gerstein, Dahai Li, Zhiyuan Liu (corresponding), Maosong Sun (corresponding). Affiliations: Tsinghua University (THUNLP, 1); ModelBest Inc. (2); Renmin University of China (Yankai Lin, 3); Yale University (Xiangru Tang, Bill Qian, Mark Gerstein, 4); WeChat AI, Tencent Inc. (Ruobing Xie, Jie Zhou, 5); Zhihu Inc. (6).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.16789
- **code url**: https://github.com/OpenBMB/ToolBench (official; codes, ToolLLaMA models, API retriever, ToolBench data and ToolEval). Models on HuggingFace (ToolBench/ToolLLaMA-2-7b-v2 etc.).
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/OpenBMB/ToolBench (actively maintained; ICLR'24 spotlight). Successor/stabilized evaluation: StableToolBench (https://github.com/THUNLP-MT/StableToolBench) which adds an API simulator/caching to address RapidAPI temporal instability.

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> tool-use (LLM tool learning): instructing LLMs to call external real-world RESTful APIs to fulfill natural-language instructions, including single-tool and multi-tool, multi-step solution paths. Also touches planning/decision-making (DFSDT tree search) and retrieval (API retriever) over a 16k+ API pool.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent tool use. Given a user instruction and a (large) pool of RapidAPI tools/APIs, an LLM must select and call APIs over multiple turns to produce a solution path (chain of API calls). Two operational settings: (a) ORACLE setting where the ground-truth relevant API subset is given to the model (simulating a user who specifies preferred APIs); (b) RETRIEVER setting where, from the full 16,464-API pool, a trained neural API retriever supplies top-5 candidate APIs (practical setting; no manual API recommendation). Supervision: instruction-tuning data (ToolBench) is auto-generated by ChatGPT (instructions + DFSDT-annotated solution paths); ToolLLaMA is obtained by SFT on LLaMA. The retriever is trained with contrastive learning on instruction->relevant-API pairs. Evaluation is reference-free via ChatGPT-based ToolEval (pass rate, win rate) because ground-truth solution paths are not fixable (RapidAPI APIs change over time; infinitely many valid paths). Generalization is tested to unseen instructions, unseen tools, and unseen categories.
- **what is retrieved**: tools / APIs (real-world RESTful API endpoints from RapidAPI Hub), represented by their API documents. The neural API retriever recommends a small set (top-5) of relevant APIs for an instruction from the 16,464-API pool.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus: a fixed pool of 16,464 real-world RESTful APIs (with documentation) crawled from RapidAPI Hub, spanning 49 categories. The retrievable store is frozen (constructed offline); the agent does not write new tools/experiences back into it. (Note RapidAPI itself is live/temporally variable, which motivates ToolEval's reference-free evaluation, but the indexed API corpus used for retrieval/training is a static snapshot.)
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k ranking objective. The API retriever returns the top-5 APIs and is evaluated as a ranking task with NDCG@1 and NDCG@5. For multi-tool instructions (I2/I3) the relevant set has multiple APIs, so recovering the needed API set matters, but it is operationalized as a ranking metric (NDCG) and a fixed k=5 candidate feed to ToolLLaMA, not a variable-size precision-driven recommendation nor an explicit minimal-set-completeness objective.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> N/A (not framed as CBR). Loose mapping: Retrieve = yes (API retriever); Reuse = partial (retrieved APIs are used as the candidate action space for the solver, not retrieval of prior solution cases); Revise = no; Retain = no. So effectively only a Retrieve phase over tools, not a case-based reasoning cycle.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is framed as tool learning / instruction tuning for tool use + API retrieval + tree-search reasoning.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: tool-API: a single real-world RESTful API endpoint, indexed via its API document (tool name, API name, description, parameters/category). Granularity is the API/function level (each API is a retrievable item; a 'tool' on RapidAPI may expose multiple APIs).
- **index source**:
> Static corpus, offline-constructed. 16,464 RESTful APIs (and their documents) crawled from RapidAPI Hub across 49 categories (filtered from a larger initial crawl, retaining APIs that respond reliably). The retriever's training labels (positive APIs per instruction) come from the ChatGPT-generated ToolBench instructions. No online/test-time growth of the index.
- **index structure topology**:
> Underlying RapidAPI has a natural hierarchy (category -> collection -> tool -> API) which ToolBench exploits for instruction generation (intra-category I2, intra-collection I3) and generalization splits. The retriever itself, however, uses a FLAT dense vector index: each API document is encoded into an embedding and ranked by cosine similarity to the instruction embedding (no graph/dependency structure in the retriever). So: hierarchical metadata over tools used for data construction; flat embedding index used for retrieval.
- **retriever type**:
> Dense retriever (bi-encoder). Sentence-BERT (Reimers & Gurevych 2019) initialized from BERT-BASE (Devlin et al. 2019), encoding instruction and API document into embeddings and scoring by embedding similarity. Compared against BM25 (sparse) and OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 (off-the-shelf dense) baselines.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Contrastive learning on similarity labels. For each instruction, the relevant APIs (from the ChatGPT-generated ToolBench instruction-API pairs) are positives and a few other sampled APIs are negatives; the Sentence-BERT bi-encoder is trained to pull instruction and relevant-API embeddings together. This is supervised-contrastive (relevance-label) training, not LM-feedback, RL, or downstream-task-effectiveness signal.
- **query construction**: Raw user instruction used directly as the query, encoded by the trained retriever and matched against API-document embeddings. No query decomposition, synthetic expansion, or intent extraction; no thought-conditioning.
- **query granularity**: Task-level (one-shot at t=0): a single retrieval is issued per instruction to obtain the top-5 candidate APIs, which then form the action space for the entire DFSDT solving process. Retrieval is not re-issued per reasoning step.
- **when to retrieve**:
> One-shot. The API retriever is invoked once per instruction (returning top-5 APIs) before/at the start of solving. The subsequent multi-step solving (DFSDT) operates over this fixed candidate set; APIs are selected/called per step from the retrieved set but no new retrieval is triggered mid-trajectory.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule: always retrieve once per instruction (in the retriever setting) before solving. There is no confidence/uncertainty/reflection-token trigger and no learned router deciding when to retrieve.
- **reranking**: No explicit second-stage reranker. The dense retriever produces the ranked top-5 directly via embedding similarity. (DFSDT can be seen as a downstream selection/search over the retrieved/oracle APIs, but it is a solver, not a retrieval reranker.)
- **retrieved context refinement**: None beyond top-5 truncation. The top-5 retrieved API documents are passed to ToolLLaMA as the available tool set; there is no decompose-recompose, distillation, compression, or distractor filtering of the retrieved API documents.
- **tool document engineering**:
> API documents are used largely as structured RapidAPI metadata (tool name, API name, description, required/optional parameters, category, example responses). For solving, the prompt presents the available APIs' documentation (a system prompt of API definitions). No synthetic-query augmentation, expanded-summary generation, or instruction-tuned tool embeddings beyond the contrastive Sentence-BERT training; the retriever embeds the API document text.
- **index content separation**:
> Partial / implicit. The retriever first narrows 16,464 APIs to a top-5 candidate set, and only those API documents are loaded into the solver's prompt (lightweight retrieval over the full pool, then heavier per-API documentation injected only for selected candidates). There is no formal progressive-disclosure / SOP-index-then-content protocol; it is a standard retrieve-then-feed-top-k pattern.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Integration protocol = RapidAPI: APIs are real RESTful endpoints called live via RapidAPI during solution-path execution. The retrievable API index is a STATIC crawled snapshot (16,464 APIs), not live-synchronized with CRUD auto-sync. Not function-calling-schema or MCP based; tool calls are emitted in the ReAct/DFSDT format and executed against RapidAPI. (RapidAPI's runtime temporal variability motivated the later StableToolBench API simulator/cache.)

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation defining the action space. Retrieved (top-5) or oracle API documents are placed in the solver prompt as the set of callable tools; ToolLLaMA then plans and emits API calls over these tools, executes them against RapidAPI, and reasons over returned responses to produce a final answer. Retrieval thus supplies the candidate toolset; it is not used as a training signal or latent-token injection at inference.
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-plan/act, with planning realized by a depth-first search-based decision tree (DFSDT). After one-shot retrieval supplies the candidate APIs, the LLM performs DFSDT: it expands a tree of reasoning/action nodes (each node = a thought + an API call + observation), can evaluate multiple traces, backtrack from dead-ends/failed calls, and expand the search space beyond a single ReAct chain. Retrieval is one-shot at plan time; the search/tree exploration is internal to the solver over the fixed retrieved toolset.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Per-tool-call within a rollout. Within DFSDT, reasoning (thought) and acting (API call) alternate per node/step, and the tree explores multiple such per-step branches with backtracking. Retrieval itself is per-answer (one retrieval per instruction), but tool-use reasoning is interleaved per API call inside the tree search.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not CBR). No retrieved-case adaptation step; retrieved APIs are used directly as the callable toolset and the LLM solves via DFSDT.
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw API documentation (structured text: tool/API name, description, parameters, category) injected verbatim into the solver prompt as the available tools. Not a distilled strategy, workflow, or latent token.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Single tool/API specification (a reusable callable action with its documentation), i.e., the action/affordance level. Not a raw trajectory, demonstration, distilled strategy, or workflow; it is the executable tool interface to be invoked.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Limited / implicit. ToolLLaMA is instruction-tuned on DFSDT-annotated trajectories that include handling failed API calls (errors, invalid responses), and DFSDT's backtracking lets the solver recover from dead-ends and irrelevant/non-functional APIs. Empirically, feeding retriever top-5 (which may include APIs not in the oracle set) slightly OUTPERFORMS the oracle set, indicating robustness to and even benefit from broadened candidates. There is no explicit retriever-aware distractor-filtering, relevance evaluator, or self-reflection module dedicated to retrieved-context noise.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (no persistent agent memory). The system uses a static external API corpus for retrieval and the in-context DFSDT search tree as transient working state; nothing is stored across tasks/episodes. No episodic, skill-library, workflow, procedural, graph, or latent memory.
- **write back**: False. No experiences/cases/skills/tools are written back into a memory or the index during deployment. (Offline, ChatGPT-generated solution paths form the SFT training data, but this is dataset construction, not runtime write-back.)
- **online growth**: False. The API index and the model are frozen after construction/training; the retrievable store does not grow at test time.
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back mechanism). During offline DATA construction, only successfully-passed DFSDT solution paths are RETAINED as training data (a success-filtered dataset-building step), but this is not runtime memory write-back.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success-filtered for training data (only passed/valid DFSDT solution paths are kept as ToolLLaMA training trajectories; failed search branches are discarded rather than stored as negative experiences for retrieval). At inference, DFSDT uses failed/invalid API responses transiently to backtrack within the current tree, but failures are not persisted or contrastively retrieved. No failure-memory.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (no memory store to evolve). The API index is static; no dedup-merge/delta-update/refine/prune at runtime.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Partially: the API retriever is a TRAINED (contrastive Sentence-BERT) model, so retrieval is learned rather than off-the-shelf, but it is a fixed similarity-based top-k retriever, NOT an RL/value-based or interactively-optimized retrieval policy. Selection is supervised on relevance labels, not optimized via downstream task reward.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: Single-agent; no cross-agent/cross-framework memory sharing. The ToolBench dataset, API retriever, and ToolEval are shared community resources reused by later work, but at runtime there is no shared memory among multiple agents.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> ToolBench (introduced here): test sets across three scenarios and three generalization levels, instantiated as six test subsets - I1 (single-tool): I1-Instruction, I1-Tool, I1-Category; I2 (intra-category multi-tool): I2-Instruction, I2-Category; I3 (intra-collection multi-tool): I3-Instruction. (Repo labels these G1/G2/G3 x {Instruction, Tool, Category}; ~200 sampled test instructions per subset.) Also: APIBench (Gorilla; TorchHub, TensorHub, HuggingFace) for OOD generalization. Underlying corpus: 16,464 RapidAPI RESTful APIs across 49 categories.
- **benchmark family**: tool (ToolBench/RapidAPI) - the canonical real-world API tool-use benchmark; plus tool (APIBench/Gorilla, ML model-hub APIs) for OOD. ToolBench is the origin of the 'ToolBench' family (later stabilized as StableToolBench) referenced throughout tool-retrieval/tool-use literature.
- **baselines**:
> Reasoning strategies: ReAct, ReACT@N (cost-matched repeated ReAct), vs DFSDT. Models (each with ReAct and/or DFSDT): ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo, teacher), Text-Davinci-003, GPT-4, Claude-2, Vicuna, Alpaca, and ToolLLaMA (fine-tuned LLaMA). API-retriever baselines: BM25 and OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 vs the trained Sentence-BERT retriever. OOD baseline: Gorilla (LLaMA-7B fine-tuned on APIBench) in zero-shot (ZS) and retrieval-aware (RS) settings.
- **key metrics**:
> Tool use (ToolEval, ChatGPT-based): Pass Rate (proportion of instructions completed within a limited budget; executability) and Win Rate (ChatGPT preference vs the reference ChatGPT-ReACT solution; >50% means better than ChatGPT-ReACT). API retrieval: NDCG@1 and NDCG@5. OOD (APIBench): hallucination rate and AST accuracy. ToolEval human-agreement: 87.1% (pass rate), 80.3% (win rate).
- **headline result**:
> ToolLLaMA matches ChatGPT and, with its trained API retriever, performs best among the open framework variants. In ToolBench main experiments (Table 4): ToolLLaMA-DFSDT-Retriever achieves average Pass Rate 67.3 and Win Rate 63.1 (vs ChatGPT-ReACT reference); ToolLLaMA-DFSDT with oracle APIs gets Pass 66.7 / Win 60.0; ChatGPT-DFSDT 64.8 / 64.3; GPT-4-DFSDT highest pass among baselines (~67.0). Using the retriever's top-5 even slightly beats the oracle API set. DFSDT >> ReAct: preliminary pass rate (Table 3, ChatGPT) ReAct 35.3 -> ReACT@N 44.5 -> DFSDT 63.8 (average over I1/I2/I3). API retriever (Table 2) average NDCG@1 78.0 / NDCG@5 84.9 vs Ada 49.6/45.4 and BM25 18.5/17.0.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Reasoning-strategy comparison (Table 3): DFSDT vs ReAct vs ReACT@N (cost-matched) on ChatGPT pass rate - DFSDT 63.8 avg >> ReACT@N 44.5 >> ReAct 35.3, isolating the depth-first tree-search/backtracking as the driver of improved decision-making and motivating its use for solution-path annotation. (2) Retriever comparison (Table 2): trained Sentence-BERT retriever vs BM25 vs ada-002 across I1/I2/I3 (NDCG@1/@5); the trained retriever wins everywhere; single-tool (I1) retrieval easier than multi-tool (I2/I3). (3) Retriever-vs-oracle integration (Table 4): top-5 retrieved APIs match/slightly exceed oracle-API performance, showing the retriever can substitute (and improve upon) ground-truth API specification. (4) Generalization ablation: pass/win across unseen-instruction / unseen-tool / unseen-category splits shows ToolLLaMA generalizes to unseen APIs. (5) OOD ablation: ToolLLaMA on APIBench vs Gorilla-ZS/RS (hallucination rate, AST accuracy).
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Yes. Intrinsic retrieval quality is reported separately (NDCG@1/@5, Table 2) from end-to-end tool-use task metrics (Pass/Win Rate via ToolEval, Table 4). DFSDT is also evaluated intrinsically (pass-rate-only preliminary study, Table 3) before being integrated into the end-to-end pipeline.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Mostly outcome-oriented (Pass Rate = task completion; Win Rate = solution-path quality preference, which partly reflects process/usefulness of the action sequence). Intermediate retrieval quality (NDCG) is a separate process-style metric. There is no per-step reasoning-faithfulness or step-wise accuracy metric; Win Rate's pairwise preference is the main proxy for solution-process quality.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> DFSDT trades more OpenAI API calls / compute for higher pass rate; the paper explicitly cost-matches with the ReACT@N baseline (repeat ReAct until cost equals DFSDT) and still finds DFSDT superior, indicating the gain is not merely from more compute. Retrieval narrows 16,464 APIs to top-5, drastically reducing the prompt/context and call space versus presenting all APIs. No detailed latency/token/dollar-cost tables are reported; cost is discussed qualitatively (API-call budget for pass rate; DFSDT consumes more calls than single ReAct).
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed k. The API retriever feeds top-5 APIs to ToolLLaMA (k=5) in the practical setting; the oracle setting feeds the ground-truth relevant API subset. Pass rate is computed under a 'limited budget' of API calls / search steps. ~200 test instructions sampled per subset. k is fixed (5), not adaptive/precision-driven.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey; a framework + dataset + method + benchmark/evaluator paper).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> ToolBench is LLM-SYNTHESIZED (auto-constructed with ChatGPT) in three stages: (i) API collection - crawl 16,464 real-world RESTful APIs across 49 categories from RapidAPI Hub (filtered for reliability); (ii) instruction generation - prompt ChatGPT to produce diverse single-tool and multi-tool instructions, using RapidAPI category/collection hierarchy (sample 2-5 tools, <=3 APIs each) to form I1/I2/I3; (iii) solution-path annotation - ChatGPT runs DFSDT to find valid API-call chains, keeping only passed paths. Answer verifiability: NOT fixed ground-truth (RapidAPI temporal variability + infinite valid paths), so evaluated reference-free via ChatGPT-based ToolEval (pass/win rate), validated at 87.1%/80.3% human agreement. Difficulty signal: even GPT-4-DFSDT and ToolLLaMA-DFSDT-Retriever reach only ~67 average pass rate, and ReAct alone ~35, showing the benchmark is far from saturated. ~200 test instances per subset; six test subsets.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> ReAct (Yao et al. 2023, reasoning+acting) as the reasoning-strategy predecessor extended by DFSDT; Self-Instruct / Alpaca-style automatic instruction generation with ChatGPT; AlpacaEval (Li et al. 2023) for the model-based pairwise evaluator design (ToolEval); LLaMA (Touvron et al. 2023) as the base model; Sentence-BERT (Reimers & Gurevych 2019) and BERT-BASE (Devlin et al. 2019) for the dense API retriever; BM25 and OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 as retrieval baselines; Gorilla/APIBench (Patil et al. 2023) for OOD evaluation; broader tool-learning line (Toolformer, HuggingGPT, WebGPT, etc.).
- **contrasts with**:
> ReAct / single-chain reasoning (DFSDT adds tree search + backtracking + multi-trace evaluation); closed-source tool-use LLMs (ChatGPT/GPT-4) that ToolLLaMA aims to match with an open model; Gorilla / APIBench (single-domain ML-hub APIs, retrieval-aware fine-tuning) - ToolBench covers 16k+ multi-domain RapidAPI APIs and multi-tool multi-step instructions; prior tool benchmarks with small/limited API sets, real-API instability, and missing multi-tool/multi-step scenarios.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool use). A foundational large-scale real-world tool-use framework/benchmark: introduces ToolBench (16,464 RapidAPI APIs, 49 categories), the DFSDT decision-tree solver, a trained dense API retriever over the full pool, and the ChatGPT-based ToolEval (pass/win rate). Sits at the intersection of tool retrieval (API retriever), agentic tree-search planning (DFSDT), and instruction tuning (ToolLLaMA). Directly seeds the 'ToolBench' lineage (later StableToolBench, and many tool-retrieval works, e.g., ToolRet/ToolGen/Re-Invoke/ToolScaler benchmark against it).

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- tool_dependency_awareness

<a id="item-toolformer"></a>
### 88. Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools

2023  ·  NeurIPS 2023  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.04761)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2023
- **venue**: NeurIPS 2023 (Thirty-seventh Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems; poster, https://neurips.cc/virtual/2023/poster/71288; OpenReview id Yacmpz84TH). arXiv preprint arXiv:2302.04761 submitted 9 Feb 2023.
- **authors affiliation**:
> Timo Schick, Jane Dwivedi-Yu, Roberto Dessì, Roberta Raileanu, Maria Lomeli, Luke Zettlemoyer, Nicola Cancedda, Thomas Scialom. Primary affiliation: Meta AI Research (FAIR); Roberto Dessì is also affiliated with Universitat Pompeu Fabra. Lead author: Timo Schick (Meta AI Research).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.04761 (DOI: https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2302.04761; OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=Yacmpz84TH; NeurIPS 2023 poster: https://neurips.cc/virtual/2023/poster/71288)
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (no authors-maintained repository, leaderboard, or paper list).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> tool-use (self-supervised tool/API learning for language models), evaluated on QA / factual lookup (LAMA), math word problems, open-domain QA, multilingual QA, and temporal reasoning. Cross-cutting: it teaches a general LM to decide which API to call, when, with what arguments, and how to use the result.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-model, self-supervised setting. A frozen base LM (GPT-J 6.7B; also GPT-2 family 124M-1.6B for scaling) is given only a handful (3-5) of hand-written demonstrations per API. The LM in-context annotates a plain-text corpus (a subset of CCNet) with candidate API calls; the calls are executed against external tools; a self-supervised perplexity-reduction filter (does the API call+result reduce the LM's loss on subsequent tokens) keeps only useful calls; the LM is then finetuned on the API-call-augmented corpus C* with a standard LM objective. At inference the finetuned LM autonomously emits API calls during decoding (interrupting generation when it produces the response token), and downstream tasks are evaluated zero-shot (no in-context task examples). Supervision is only the per-API demonstrations plus the model's own perplexity feedback; no human-annotated tool-use traces and no task-specific tuning.
- **what is retrieved**:
> tools / external API results: at inference the LM invokes external tools (a question-answering system, a Wikipedia/BM25 search engine, a calculator, a calendar, and a machine-translation system) and incorporates their returned text results. For the Wikipedia Search tool specifically, the retrieved unit is short Wikipedia text snippets. The 'retrieved' content the model conditions on is the tool's textual output, not a ranked set of documents per se.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus / external tools. Tools target fixed external resources: a BM25 retriever over the KILT Wikipedia dump (search engine), an Atlas QA model finetuned on Natural Questions, a Python calculator, a 600M NLLB translation model, and a calendar. There is no agent-written growing episodic memory; the augmented training corpus C* is built offline once and the base LM is frozen aside from finetuning.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Neither a ranking nor a completeness objective in the retriever sense. The driving objective is perplexity reduction on future tokens: an API call is kept only if L_i^- - L_i^+ >= tau_f (the call+result reduces the LM's weighted cross-entropy loss by at least a threshold). At inference the model issues at most ONE API call per input (a deliberate restriction to avoid loops), so there is no top-k document set and no multi-tool completeness target; tool selection is a single autonomous decision per example.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based-reasoning method; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain case cycle).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The work is framed as self-supervised tool learning / model bootstrapping; it does not cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner and does not describe itself as case-based reasoning.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> tool-API call and its returned text result. Concretely: a single API call c=(a_c, i_c) (tool name + textual input) linearized with special tokens <API> a_c(i_c) -> r </API>. The returned unit varies by tool: a short answer string (QA), short Wikipedia text snippets (BM25 search over KILT Wikipedia), a numeric result (calculator), the current date string (calendar), or an English translation (NLLB). For the few-shot annotation phase, the in-context unit is 3-5 human-written demonstrations of API usage per tool.
- **index source**:
> Offline-induced static construction. The retrievable/usable knowledge is reached through fixed external tools; the central artifact is the augmented corpus C* induced offline by annotating CCNet text with API calls and filtering by perplexity reduction. The base LM is frozen and then finetuned once on C*; nothing is induced or grown at test time. For the search tool, the index is a static BM25 index over the KILT Wikipedia dump.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat / tool-keyed. The five tools are independent APIs invoked by name (no graph, hierarchy, or clustering of tools). The Wikipedia Search tool uses a flat BM25 lexical index over the KILT Wikipedia dump. There is no learned vector index, no inter-tool dependency graph, and no hierarchical category->tool organization.
- **retriever type**:
> Hybrid of off-the-shelf tools plus the LM-as-controller. The LM itself is the generative 'retriever/router' that decides which tool to call and with what argument (tool invocation emitted as special-token text during decoding). The underlying tools include a BM25 lexical retriever (Wikipedia Search over KILT), a retrieval-augmented QA model (Atlas, finetuned on Natural Questions; Atlas-large for data creation, Atlas-xxl at inference), a Python calculator, the fastText language detector + 600M NLLB translator, and a calendar. No dense neural retriever is trained by the authors for tool selection.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Self-supervised perplexity/LM-feedback. The decision of when/which/how to call a tool is learned by finetuning the LM on API calls that were kept by a self-supervised filter: a call is retained only if including its input and result reduces the weighted cross-entropy loss over subsequent tokens by at least tau_f (L_i^- - L_i^+ >= tau_f). There is no contrastive similarity training, no human relevance labels, no RL, and no downstream-task reward; the only learning signal is the model's own next-token loss reduction (bootstrapping in the STaR / self-training tradition).
- **query construction**:
> LM-generated, in-context-conditioned. During data creation, for each API a fixed prompt P(x) instructs the LM to insert API calls into a text x; the LM samples candidate positions (where p_M(<API>) >= tau_s) and then samples up to m candidate calls (tool argument text) at each position. At inference the LM generates the API call argument autonomously as part of decoding, conditioned on the text generated so far. The query (tool argument) is thus composed by the model from its evolving context, not from the raw input verbatim.
- **query granularity**:
> Step/position-level within a single text, but capped at one effective call. During corpus annotation, candidate calls are sampled at up to k positions per document (top-k by <API>-token probability, default k=5; k=20 for calculator/MT). At inference, the model can in principle emit a call at any decoding position, but is restricted to AT MOST ONE API call per input. So effectively task-level (one tool decision per example) at test time, position-level during offline data generation.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Adaptive / model-decided (learned router emergent from finetuning). The finetuned LM itself decides when to emit an API call during decoding; there is no fixed schedule. In practice it is one-shot per input (at most one call). The propensity to call is tuned via a modified greedy-decoding rule (emit <API> if it is among the top-k most likely tokens; default k=10 at inference).
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Token-level model decision: the model triggers a call when the special <API> token is among the k most likely next tokens (k=10 used at inference vs k=1 = ordinary greedy). During offline annotation, a candidate position is considered only if p_M(<API> | prefix) >= tau_s (default tau_s=0.05; relaxed to 0.0 for calculator/MT). The model is somewhat calibrated at k=1 (it calls APIs preferentially on examples it would otherwise do badly on), though this calibration is lost at higher k.
- **reranking**:
> None. No reranking stage over tool outputs. During data creation, candidate API calls are filtered by the perplexity-reduction criterion (L_i^- - L_i^+ >= tau_f), which is a thresholded keep/drop filter rather than a learned reranker. The Wikipedia BM25 search returns snippets directly with no second-stage reranker.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Minimal / filtering at training-data level. There is no inference-time distillation, decomposition, or compression of tool outputs. The key refinement is the offline self-supervised filter that removes API calls (and results) that do not reduce future-token loss (keeping only useful calls in C*). The authors note that leaving some non-perfectly-filtered noise can be beneficial so the finetuned model does not blindly follow every call result. Tool outputs are inserted into the context as-is at inference.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Per-tool hand-written demonstration prompts (few-shot exemplars), not indexed tool docstrings. Each tool is specified by a natural-language instruction prompt with 3-5 worked input/output examples of how to insert that tool's calls (full prompts in Appendix A.2). There is no synthetic-query augmentation, no expanded summaries, no weighted-field or instruction-tuned tool embeddings; tool 'descriptions' are consumed in-context only during the offline annotation phase, and tool-use ability is then internalized into the LM weights via finetuning.
- **index content separation**: N/A. No separation of a lightweight retrievable tool index from heavy on-demand content; tools are invoked directly and return their results inline.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Static, custom text-API protocol. Each tool is a fixed custom API whose input and output are text sequences, invoked via special <API>...</API> tokens with an explicit ' -> ' result marker; there is no live-synchronized tool catalog, no RapidAPI/RESTful registry, no MCP, and no function-calling schema or CRUD auto-sync. The set of five tools is fixed in advance.
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> No. Tools are sampled and called independently; the method explicitly cannot chain tools (use the output of one tool as input to another) because API calls in the finetuning data are generated independently and at most one call per input is allowed. The paper names this lack of tool chaining and interactivity as a key limitation.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Training signal + prompt augmentation (latent-into-weights). Useful API calls are interleaved into the training text and the LM is FINETUNED on this augmented corpus, internalizing tool use into its weights. At inference the model autonomously generates an API call, the system executes the tool, inserts the result back into the decoding context (after the ' -> ' token), and the LM continues generation conditioned on the tool's returned text. Thus the retrieved tool result directly grounds subsequent token prediction / the final answer.
- **planning integration**:
> Inline, per-decoding-step tool invocation within a single generation pass (no explicit planner, no tree search). Tool use is woven into ordinary autoregressive decoding: the model decides during generation to emit a call, the tool result is spliced in, and decoding resumes. There is no separate plan-then-retrieve phase, no multi-step planning loop, and (by design) no chaining of tool calls; effectively a single tool call augments one generation.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Per-tool-call within a single generation, capped at one call per input. The tool call is interleaved at the token/position where the model emits <API>; decoding is interrupted, the tool runs, and the result is inserted before continuing. Because of the at-most-one-call restriction, this is effectively per-answer (one interleaving point per example) rather than dense per-step interleaving.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not a CBR method; no case adaptation). The closest analog is that the finetuned LM internalizes when/how to call tools from the self-generated, perplexity-filtered API-call data.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Raw text inserted inline. Tool inputs and outputs are linearized as text: <API> tool(argument) -> result </API> (e.g. [QA("...")] -> answer, [Calculator(...)] -> number, [WikiSearch(...)] -> snippet). The model conditions on this raw textual result; there is no distilled strategy, executable program object, or latent-soft-token representation of the tool output.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Low / raw factual result. The retrieved unit is a concrete tool output (a fact, a number, a date, a translation, or a short Wikipedia snippet) inserted verbatim, not a distilled strategy, workflow, or guideline.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Self-supervised perplexity filtering of training data plus deliberate retention of mild noise. Only API calls whose results reduce future-token loss are kept in C*, removing most useless/irrelevant calls before finetuning. The authors also observe that not over-filtering (leaving some imperfectly useful calls) helps prevent the finetuned model from blindly trusting every tool result. There is no inference-time relevance evaluator, self-reflection, retriever-aware adversarial training, or distractor-aware SFT; the Wikipedia search results can be poor and the model cannot reformulate/browse (a noted limitation).

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (no persistent episodic/skill/workflow/graph memory). Tool-use competence is stored in the finetuned LM weights (parametric), not in an external retrievable memory store that grows or is queried at test time.
- **write back**:
> False (no test-time memory write-back). New experiences/cases are not stored into an external memory during deployment. (Offline, useful API calls are written into the training corpus C* and then baked into weights via finetuning, but this is a one-time offline data-construction step, not online write-back.)
- **online growth**: No. The augmented corpus C* is constructed once offline and the model is finetuned once; nothing grows at test time. The base LM is frozen apart from the single finetuning pass, and the tool index (e.g. BM25 Wikipedia) is static.
- **write back trigger**:
> Never at deployment. During offline data construction, the 'write' (keeping an API call in C*) is triggered when the call+result reduces future-token loss by at least the threshold (perplexity-improvement / on-usefulness trigger), i.e. a self-supervised keep criterion, not a deployment-time memory write or a success/failure or reflective trigger.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success/usefulness-only, no failure memory. The filter keeps only API calls that DECREASE perplexity (useful calls); calls that do not reduce loss are discarded, not stored as negative/failure examples. There is no contrastive use of failed calls and no corrective failure-rule store. (The retained mild noise is incidental, not an explicit failure-experience mechanism.)
- **memory evolution update**:
> N/A / append-only at the data-construction level. The augmented corpus C* is assembled once (useful calls appended/interleaved into texts) and never mutated, deduped, or refined after writing; tool-use knowledge is then frozen into the finetuned weights. No delta-update, refine-overwrite, or forget-prune of stored entries.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Partially. Tool invocation is NOT a fixed similarity top-k; the LM learns (via self-supervised finetuning on perplexity-filtered data) an emergent policy for when/which/how to call a tool. However, it is not an RL/value-based or M-MDP policy and not a trained ranking retriever; it is a generative decision internalized by language-model finetuning, with the trigger modulated at decode time by the top-k <API>-token rule.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single model, single-agent; tool-use ability is private to the finetuned LM. No memory or experience sharing across agents or frameworks.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> LAMA (SQuAD, Google-RE, T-REx subsets; factual cloze completion); math word problems ASDiv, SVAMP, MAWPS; open-domain QA WebQS (Web Questions), Natural Questions (NQ), TriviaQA; multilingual QA MLQA (Es, De, Hi, Vi, Zh, Ar); temporal datasets TEMPLAMA and a newly introduced DATESET (~9,400 templated date-reasoning queries). Language-modeling perplexity on WikiText(-103) and a CCNet validation subset. Base models: GPT-J 6.7B (main) and GPT-2 family (124M/355M/775M/1.6B) for scaling.
- **benchmark family**:
> QA (LAMA factual lookup, WebQS, NQ, TriviaQA), multilingual QA (MLQA), math word problems (ASDiv/SVAMP/MAWPS), temporal/knowledge reasoning (TEMPLAMA, DATESET), and language modeling perplexity (WikiText, CCNet). Spans the QA and tool-augmented-reasoning families; not the agentic web/embodied/tool-retrieval (ToolBench-style) benchmark families.
- **baselines**:
> Same-size GPT-J variants: GPT-J (vanilla, no finetuning), GPT-J + CC (GPT-J finetuned on the same CCNet subset C WITHOUT API calls), Toolformer (disabled) (the Toolformer model but with API calls turned off at decoding), and Toolformer (full). Larger LM baselines: OPT (66B) and GPT-3 (175B, text-davinci-002 era). For MLQA, additional 'AllEn' upper-bound rows give GPT-J and GPT-3 English contexts+questions. Related self-supervised tool-learning method TALM (Parisi et al., 2022) is discussed as the closest prior work but not directly tabulated.
- **key metrics**:
> Zero-shot downstream accuracy: for LAMA/TEMPLAMA, whether the correct word is in the first 5 predicted words; for QA datasets, whether the correct answer is in the first ~20 (10 for MLQA) predicted words; for math benchmarks, whether the predicted number matches. Language-modeling perplexity on WikiText and CCNet. Plus diagnostic statistics: fraction of examples where each tool is called.
- **headline result**:
> Toolformer (based on a 6.7B GPT-J) substantially improves zero-shot performance and, on several tasks, outperforms the much larger OPT (66B) and GPT-3 (175B). Examples from the paper: LAMA T-REx 53.5 vs GPT-3 (175B) 39.8 and vs best same-size baseline ~34.9 (+18.6 over best GPT-J baseline); LAMA SQuAD 33.8 vs GPT-3 26.8; math MAWPS 44.0 / ASDiv 40.4 / SVAMP 29.4, each more than doubling the no-tool baselines and clearly beating GPT-3 (19.8/14.0/10.0) and OPT-66B. Tool calls are issued autonomously (e.g. QA tool used for 98.1% of LAMA examples, calculator for 97.9% of math examples), and adding API calls does not increase language-modeling perplexity.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Toolformer vs Toolformer(disabled) isolates the value of actually calling tools at inference: e.g. math performance more than doubles when calls are enabled; LAMA T-REx jumps from 34.9 (disabled) to 53.5 (enabled). (2) GPT-J + CC vs Toolformer(disabled) shows finetuning on API-augmented text (even without calling tools) gives modest gains (the model internalizes some skill, especially math). (3) Decoding-strategy ablation (Table 9): varying k in the top-k <API> rule from k=1 (greedy, calls on 40.3% of T-REx / 8.5% of WebQS examples) to k=10 (98.1% / 100%); higher k increases call frequency and performance but loses the k=1 calibration. (4) Scaling-laws ablation (Sec 4.4, GPT-2 124M-1.6B + GPT-J): the ability to benefit from tools EMERGES only around 775M parameters; smaller models gain little, and a large with-vs-without-tool gap persists even for the largest model. (5) Data-quality analysis (Table 10): high L_i^- - L_i^+ filter scores correspond to intuitively useful calls. (6) Filtering-threshold tau_f statistics (Table 2) show the number of retained examples per tool.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No. The paper does not report intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG / completeness) separately. Evaluation is end-to-end zero-shot task accuracy plus perplexity; retrieval/tool quality is examined only via tool-call frequencies and qualitative data-quality analysis.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome metrics (zero-shot task accuracy, perplexity). Some process-level diagnostics are reported: the fraction of examples each tool is called on (e.g. 98.1% QA, 97.9% calculator, 0.2% calendar on TEMPLAMA, 54.8% calendar on DATESET), calibration analysis at k=1, and qualitative inspection of the usefulness of generated API calls.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Emphasizes parameter efficiency: a 6.7B GPT-J Toolformer matches or beats OPT-66B and GPT-3-175B on tool-amenable tasks, and adding tool calls does not increase LM perplexity. The method is sample-INefficient at data-creation time: processing more than a million documents yields only a few thousand useful calculator API examples (Table 2: e.g. 994 calculator examples at tau_f=1.0). Training uses up to 25k examples per API, max seq length 1,024, effective batch size 128, DeepSpeed ZeRO-3, 8x NVIDIA A100 40GB (BF16), up to 2k steps. At inference at most one API call per input is allowed; decoding is interrupted once to run the tool. No explicit per-query API-dollar/latency table is reported.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Few-shot per-tool demonstrations (3-5 hand-written examples per API) in the annotation prompt. Data-creation hyperparameters: top k=5 candidate positions per text (k=20 for calculator/MT), up to m=5 candidate calls per position (m=10 for calculator/MT), tau_s=0.05 (0.0 for calculator/MT), tau_f=1.0 (0.5 for calculator/MT). Inference: emit <API> if among top k=10 tokens; AT MOST ONE API call per input. Tool outputs are inserted inline with no explicit token-budget cap or truncation beyond the tool's own short return (e.g. Wikipedia snippets).
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Introduces DATESET, a new temporal-reasoning benchmark: ~9,400 queries generated from 7 template families (Table 11) populated by randomly selecting 500 'current dates' and associated random past/future dates within a four-year range (plus US federal holidays), where knowing the current date is required to answer; verifiability is exact (templated, deterministic answers). Toolformer scores 27.3 on DATESET (using the calendar tool for 54.8% of examples) vs <=5.9 for all baselines including GPT-3 (175B) at 0.8, signaling the task isolates calendar-tool utility. Other benchmarks are pre-existing (LAMA, ASDiv/SVAMP/MAWPS, WebQS/NQ/TriviaQA, MLQA, TEMPLAMA, WikiText, CCNet).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Self-training / bootstrapping for self-improvement, especially STaR (Zelikman et al., 2022) and dataset-generation-from-LMs (Schick & Schütze 2021b; Honovich et al. 2022 Unnatural Instructions; Wang et al. 2022 Self-Instruct); in-context learning of GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020). Base LM GPT-J 6B (Wang & Komatsuzaki, 2021) and GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019). Tools build on the Atlas retrieval-augmented QA model (Izacard et al., 2022) finetuned on Natural Questions, a BM25 retriever (Robertson et al., 1995) over the KILT Wikipedia dump (Petroni et al., 2021), the 600M NLLB translator (Costa-jussà et al., 2022), and the fastText classifier (Joulin et al., 2016). Training corpus CCNet (Wenzek et al., 2020).
- **contrasts with**:
> Closest prior work TALM (Parisi et al., 2022), which uses a similar self-supervised objective but only in task-specific finetuned settings; tool-use approaches relying on large human supervision (WebGPT, Nakano et al. 2021; Komeili et al. 2022; LaMDA/Thoppilan et al. 2022) or on task-specific few-shot prompting that presupposes which tool to use (PAL/Gao et al. 2022; Lazaridou et al. 2022; ReAct/Yao et al. 2022). Also contrasted with retrieval-augmented pretraining methods (REALM/Guu et al. 2020, RETRO/Borgeaud et al. 2021, Atlas/Izacard et al. 2022) that always inject retrieved text regardless of usefulness, whereas Toolformer learns to ask for the right information for itself.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool use). A foundational self-supervised tool-learning method: it teaches a general LM to autonomously decide when/which/how to call external APIs by bootstrapping training data via perplexity-filtered self-annotation, in contrast to prompt-based interleaved tool-use agents (ReAct) and human-supervised tool agents (WebGPT). A direct precursor to subsequent tool-augmented LMs and function-calling / tool-retrieval lines of work.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

<a id="item-anytool"></a>
### 89. AnyTool: Self-Reflective, Hierarchical Agents for Large-Scale API Calls

2024  ·  ICML 2024  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.04253)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: ICML 2024 (also arXiv:2402.04253, submitted Feb 2024; DBLP: conf/icml/DuW024)
- **authors affiliation**: Yu Du (Tsinghua University); Fangyun Wei (Microsoft Research Asia, equal contribution); Hongyang Zhang (University of Waterloo, corresponding author).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.04253
- **code url**: https://github.com/dyabel/AnyTool

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Tool-use: LLM-agent tool/API retrieval and invocation to answer user queries over a large-scale (16k+) real-world API pool (RapidAPI).
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, training-free (plug-and-play) tool-use. Given a user query and a pool of 16,000+ RapidAPI APIs, an agent must (1) retrieve a small relevant API-candidate set from the full pool and (2) solve the query by calling those APIs. The system is a multi-agent hierarchy (meta-agent -> category agents -> tool agents) plus a single solver agent, all driven by GPT-4 function calling with no external module training. Operates under the assumption that some subset of APIs can resolve the query; supervision is limited to GPT-4 self-evaluation of solvability/solved (96.5% alignment with human evaluators).
- **what is retrieved**: Tools / APIs (RapidAPI tool-API documents): the hierarchical retriever selects a set of relevant API candidates from the 16k+ pool, organized as category -> tool -> API.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus: the 16k+ RapidAPI API pool (as collected by ToolLLM/ToolBench) and its RapidAPI category->tool->API taxonomy. No growing/episodic memory persists across queries; the per-query API-candidate pool and agent histories are transient within a single query's reflection loop.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Completeness-oriented (recovery of the minimal needed set), NOT fixed top-k ranking: the retriever grows a variable-size API-candidate pool until a tool agent's 'check_if_request_solvable' returns True or a max-pool-size cap (default 64) is reached; self-reflection then re-expands the pool until the query is solved, aiming to recover the complete set of APIs needed (often multiple APIs across 2-5 categories).
- **cbr cycle coverage**: Not framed as CBR. If forced to map: [Retrieve: partial - retrieves APIs not prior cases; Reuse: no; Revise: yes via self-reflection re-activation; Retain: no - nothing persisted across queries]. N/A as a CBR work.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it frames itself as a self-reflective hierarchical tool-retrieval agent.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> tool-API (individual RapidAPI API endpoint, defined by category_name/tool_name/api_name plus its documentation: purpose, required/optional parameters, output types). The hierarchy also exposes coarser units: categories (tier 1) and tools (tier 2), but the retrieved/added candidates are individual APIs.
- **index source**:
> Static corpus, offline-defined: the 16k+ RapidAPI API pool from ToolLLM/ToolBench plus its fixed RapidAPI category->tool->API taxonomy. Not online-induced; the store is frozen. (Preprocessing scripts extract api/category/tool details and a tool 'database' for the agents to query.)
- **index structure topology**:
> Hierarchical (3-tier): category -> tool -> API, mirroring the RapidAPI taxonomy. Realized as a divide-and-conquer agent hierarchy: a meta-agent dynamically spawns category agents, which spawn tool agents (each managing up to K=5 tools by default); tool agents add individual APIs to a shared global API-candidate pool. No flat vector index for the retriever itself (baselines like ToolLLM's retriever and AutoGen-RAG use flat dense indices).
- **retriever type**:
> LLM-as-retriever (generative agentic retrieval): GPT-4 function-calling agents directly explore the taxonomy and select APIs, with NO trained dense/sparse retriever and no external embedding model. (Contrasts with ToolLLM's fine-tuned dense retriever and AutoGen-RAG's embedding-based retriever used as baselines.)
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None (off-the-shelf): the retriever is not trained or fine-tuned. It relies entirely on GPT-4's pretrained function-calling/linguistic comprehension. The only feedback signal is the in-context self-reflection 'fail reason' fed back to agents (LM-feedback at inference time), not a learned retriever objective.
- **query construction**:
> Raw user query Q is passed (with a bootstrap prompt and the function list) to the meta-agent; each tier-agent reasons over Q against the categories/tools/APIs it can see. No explicit query decomposition or synthetic-query expansion; intent handling is implicit via GPT-4 reasoning. On self-reflection, the query context is augmented with the identified failure reason.
- **query granularity**: Task-level: retrieval is driven by the whole user query Q (one query at a time), not per-reasoning-step. The hierarchical decomposition is over the API space (category/tool/API), not over sub-queries; multiple agents process Q in parallel (multi-threaded).
- **when to retrieve**:
> Iterative / active (reflection-triggered): an initial retrieval+solve pass, then the self-reflection mechanism re-activates the retriever-and-solver loop whenever the solver fails (avg 4.6 self-reflections per query). Within the retriever, agents iteratively explore and add APIs until a solvability check passes.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Agent-initiated / reflection-triggered failure signal: re-retrieval is triggered when (1) the solver issues 'Give Up', or (2) the solver returns 'Give Solution' but GPT-4's evaluator judges the query still unsolved. The concrete signal is the GPT-4-/solver-provided 'fail reason', which is injected into agents' histories to re-activate them. Initial retrieval termination is triggered by a tool agent's 'check_if_request_solvable'=True or the API-candidate pool reaching max size.
- **reranking**:
> No explicit reranking stage. Selection is via agentic decisions (tool agents call add_API_into_API_pool); a solvability check gates termination rather than scoring/reranking a ranked list. Self-reflection in the solver instead prunes APIs deemed irrelevant from the candidate pool.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Yes, via self-reflection pruning: when the solver gives up it must name the irrelevant/non-working APIs; these are removed from the expanded API-candidate pool and the history items invoking them are excluded from the solver's context before re-activation. Otherwise no compression/distillation; agents fetch on-demand tool descriptions and API details (progressive disclosure of documentation).
- **tool document engineering**:
> Raw RapidAPI documentation, accessed on demand and progressively: agents call get_tool_descriptions and get_API_detail to fetch tool/API descriptions, parameters, and output specs only when needed. No synthetic-query augmentation, expanded summaries, or instruction-tuned tool embeddings (those are absent because there is no trained retriever). Preprocessing extracts API/category/tool details into a queryable database.
- **index content separation**:
> Yes (progressive disclosure): a lightweight navigable index (category names -> tool names -> API names) is separated from heavy content (full tool descriptions and API details) which agents load on demand via get_tool_descriptions / get_API_detail. This keeps each agent's context within GPT-4's max context length.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: Static tool index (frozen 16k+ RapidAPI pool from ToolBench); integration protocol is RapidAPI (real RapidAPI calls via ToolBench's StableToolBench-style RapidAPI keys / function-calling). No live CRUD auto-sync, no MCP.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation for tool invocation: the retrieved API-candidate pool is supplied (with a bootstrap prompt and a 'finish' function) to the solver agent, which calls the APIs via GPT-4 function calling using DFSDT (or CoT) to produce the final answer. Retrieved APIs are executable functions, not just text exemplars.
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-plan (dual-phase), wrapped in a closed reflection loop: (phase 1) hierarchical retriever produces an API-candidate pool; (phase 2) the solver plans/acts over those APIs with DFSDT (depth-first search-based decision tree, allowing backtracking) or CoT. On failure, self-reflection re-activates retriever then solver, expanding/pruning the candidate pool. Planning is at the level of API-call sequences within the solver, not a tree search over retrieval itself.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Per-tool-call within a rollout (solver phase) and per-reflection-round at the system level. Retrieval is decoupled from per-CoT-step reasoning: retrieval happens in a dedicated phase and is re-invoked per self-reflection round (avg 4.6 rounds) rather than woven into every reasoning step.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not a CBR/case-adaptation method). The closest analogue is execution-feedback-driven revision: the self-reflection loop revises the API-candidate pool and re-runs the solver using the GPT-4/solver failure reason.
- **retrieved item representation**: Executable tool/API functions injected into the solver's function list (GPT-4 function-calling schema with name, parameters, output spec), plus their RapidAPI documentation as context. Not raw trajectories or distilled strategies.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Procedural tool / executable API (single RapidAPI endpoint). Retrieval operates at concrete tool-API granularity, navigated via a coarser-to-finer abstraction (category -> tool -> API).
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Self-reflection / relevance evaluation: a GPT-4 solvability+solution evaluator (96.5% human alignment) gates outcomes; the solver must identify and the system removes irrelevant/non-working APIs from the candidate pool before re-activation, reducing distractor APIs. Hierarchical decomposition also narrows each agent's search scope to reduce irrelevant context. No retriever-aware training or distractor-aware SFT (no training at all).

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: None (no persistent cross-query memory). Within a single query it maintains transient per-agent historical contexts and a global API-candidate pool; these are not retained across queries.
- **write back**: False: the system does not store new experiences/cases/skills into any persistent memory for reuse on future queries. (Within-query: it does append failure reasons and explored APIs into transient agent histories, but this is discarded after the query.)
- **online growth**: No: the retrievable store (16k+ API pool and taxonomy) is frozen and does not grow during deployment. Only the transient per-query API-candidate pool grows within a query.
- **write back trigger**:
> Never (no persistent write-back). For the transient within-query expansion, the trigger is reflective: after self-critique/failure (solver 'Give Up' or GPT-4 judging the solution unsolved), the failure reason is written into agent histories and new APIs are added to the candidate pool. Nothing is written to a durable store.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Failures are used corrective and within-query only: the failure reason and the names of irrelevant/non-working APIs drive pruning (remove bad APIs) and re-expansion (add unexplored categories/tools/APIs). Failure experiences are NOT stored for retrieval on future queries (no cross-query failure memory).
- **memory evolution update**: N/A for persistent memory. Within-query candidate-pool dynamics: append (add new APIs on re-activation) plus forget/prune (remove APIs flagged irrelevant by the solver), with agent histories augmented by the failure reason. No durable entries are mutated.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No: retrieval/API-selection is NOT a learned/RL-optimized policy. It is performed by frozen GPT-4 function-calling agents (zero training of external modules), guided by prompts and in-context feedback rather than a trained selection policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Within-query multi-agent sharing only: meta/category/tool agents share a single global API-candidate pool and pass failure reasons across the hierarchy during one query. There is no cross-query or cross-framework memory sharing; nothing persists for other queries or external frameworks.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> ToolBench (filtered, six subsets: G1-Instruction, G1-Tool, G1-Category, G2-Instruction, G2-Category, G3-Instruction; filtered counts 115/132/142/107/98/38 after manual removal of non-solvable queries), original ToolBench (Table 9), and AnyToolBench (new benchmark introduced here, 400 GPT-4-synthesized solvable instances).
- **benchmark family**: tool (ToolBench / RapidAPI tool-use); AnyToolBench is a new tool-use benchmark in the same RapidAPI family.
- **baselines**:
> ToolLLM (ToolLLaMA w/ DFSDT, with ToolLLM's trained API retriever or OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 retriever) and its variants (GPT-4 w/ DFSDT as solver; reference-API-only no-retriever); GPT-4 with reference APIs (w/ CoT and w/ DFSDT); GPT-4 with a Plain Agent retriever; GPT-4 with AutoGen-RAG retriever (text-embedding-ada-002 and all-mpnet-base-v2); GPT-3.5 with reference APIs (w/ CoT and w/ DFSDT).
- **key metrics**:
> Pass rate (PR). The paper uses a revised pass rate R = #(Solved) / (#(Solved) + #(Unsolved)) on filtered ToolBench (Eq. 2 / Fig. 4(b)), correcting ToolLLM's R = (#(Non-solvable)+#(Solved)) / (#(Non-solvable)+#(Solved)+#(Unsolved)) which inflates pass rate (random APIs yield 99.0%). GPT-4 is the evaluator (96.5% human alignment).
- **headline result**:
> On filtered ToolBench, AnyTool reaches 58.2% average pass rate vs ToolLLM 22.9% (ToolLLM's retriever + ToolLLaMA w/ DFSDT), i.e. +35.4% (abstract) / +32.6 over original ToolLLM and +19.3 over GPT-4-with-reference-APIs (text). On AnyToolBench, AnyTool 73.8% vs best ToolLLM variant 36.6% and GPT-4 plain-agent 14.0%.
- **ablations**:
> Component ablation (Table 3, G2-I/G3-I): full AnyTool 58.9/63.2; -Hierarchical Structure (flat retriever) 22.4/15.8; -Self-Reflection 19.6/15.8; -DFSDT/+CoT 50.5/60.3 (drop of 8.4/2.9). Self-reflection re-activation scope (Table 4): tool agents only 43.9/44.7; +category agents 55.2/55.3; all agents 58.9/63.2. API pool size (Table 5): 1k=18.6/7.9, 5k=26.3/23.7, 10k=38.1/36.8, all=58.9/63.2 (larger pool helps). Max API-candidate pool size (Table 6): 16=49.5/42.1, 32=58.9/55.3, 64=58.9/63.2 (saturates ~64). Max tools per tool agent K (Table 7): K=3 -> 48.6/42.1, K=5 -> 58.9/57.9, K=10 -> 52.3/39.5 (trade-off, best K=5). Plain-agent info ablation (Table 10) and AutoGen-RAG embedding ablation (Table 11) show all near 13-16%, far below AnyTool.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No: the paper reports only end-to-end pass rate. It does NOT report intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG / retrieval completeness) separately; retrieval quality is assessed indirectly through end-task pass rate and the API-pool/candidate-pool ablations.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome (pass rate). Some process-level statistics are reported (avg self-reflection rounds, avg agent quantity, avg API-candidate count, token/call counts), and a solvability-vs-solved decomposition exists, but there is no step-wise reasoning-faithfulness or trajectory-quality score.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Reported consumption (Table 12, avg over datasets): ~13.5-13.6 x 10^4 tokens per query, 14.1 API candidates, 43.3 OpenAI API calls, and 4.6 self-reflections per query. With only 4-6 self-reflection rounds pass rate improves by up to 20% across datasets. Wall-clock latency deemed infeasible to measure due to unstable GPT-4 server response. Self-reflection reduces 'over-search' on simple queries while enabling deeper search on complex ones.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Completeness-/saturation-driven variable-size selection, budget-capped: the API-candidate pool grows until a solvability check passes or a maximal pool size is reached (default max_api_number=64; performance saturates ~64, with 32 also strong). Hierarchy + progressive disclosure keep each agent within GPT-4's max context length; actual avg APIs used per query ~14.1.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> AnyToolBench: 400 instances, LLM-synthesized by prompting GPT-4 to freely explore the API pool (get_tools_in_category/get_tool_descriptions/get_APIs_in_tool/get_API_detail), add real APIs via add_API_into_API_pool, synthesize parameters, and formulate queries from actual API responses (composing 2-5 categories), with GPT-4-generated reference solutions verified to truly resolve the query (ensuring solvability and reducing hallucination). Also constructs a filtered ToolBench via manual review removing non-solvable queries (115/132/142/107/98/38 per subset). Answers verified via GPT-4 evaluation (96.5% human alignment). Difficulty signal: best system (AnyTool) reaches 73.8% PR on AnyToolBench and 58.2% avg on filtered ToolBench.

**Relations**

- **builds on**: ToolLLM / ToolBench (Qin et al., 2023b; 16k+ RapidAPI pool, dual-phase retrieve-then-solve, DFSDT solver, ToolLLaMA) which AnyTool reuses and extends; GPT-4 function calling (Achiam et al., 2023); DFSDT and CoT (Wei et al., 2022); self-reflection literature in LLMs.
- **contrasts with**:
> ToolLLM's trained dense API retriever and ToolLLaMA solver; embedding-based retrieval (OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002, all-mpnet-base-v2 via AutoGen-RAG); flat GPT-4 plain-agent retrieval; and ToolLLM's evaluation protocol (which inflates pass rate by counting non-solvable queries as passes). AnyTool argues against trained retrievers (low accuracy, no feedback) in favor of training-free hierarchical GPT-4 retrieval with self-reflection.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use). Lineage: large-scale real-world API tool-use after ToolLLM/ToolBench; pioneers training-free, LLM-as-retriever hierarchical (category/tool/API) retrieval with a self-reflective re-activation loop, and introduces AnyToolBench plus a corrected pass-rate evaluation protocol. A precursor to later tool-retrieval works emphasizing tool-document engineering, dependency-aware and MCP/live tool indices.
