<a id="item-toolnet"></a>
### 91. ToolNet: Connecting Large Language Models with Massive Tools via Tool Graph

2024  ·  arXiv 2403.00839  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.00839)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: arXiv:2403.00839 [cs.AI; cs.CL] (preprint, submitted 29 Feb 2024, v1). Not a peer-reviewed venue; an OpenReview submission PDF exists (openreview.net/pdf/b978cbbfe6c59f7fcb3631e0313b3254f3ef860e.pdf) but no accepted-venue record was found.
- **authors affiliation**:
> Xukun Liu (Northwestern University), Zhiyuan Peng (North Carolina State University), Xiaoyuan Yi (Microsoft Research Asia), Xing Xie (Microsoft Research Asia), Lirong Xiang (NC State University), Yuchen Liu (NC State University), Dongkuan Xu (NC State University). Lead author: Xukun Liu; senior/corresponding: Dongkuan Xu (NC State). Collaboration between NC State, Northwestern, and Microsoft Research Asia.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.00839
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (no maintained leaderboard/paper-list repo for this work; it is indexed in third-party survey lists such as github.com/quchangle1/LLM-Tool-Survey and github.com/AngxiaoYue/awesome-llm-tool-learning).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: tool-use (LLM tool/API learning at scale): selecting and chaining the correct tool/API from a massive library (up to ~3992 APIs) to solve multi-hop tasks; evaluated on tool-augmented QA (science QA, table math, math) and large-scale multi-task tool-calling.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent, in-context (training-free) tool use. At each step the LLM (gpt-3.5-turbo) takes the current observation o_s and a bounded interaction history C_s (a queue of size K of past observation-thought-action tuples), produces a thought t_s, then emits an action a_s = (tool, args), receives a new observation from the environment, and iterates up to a maximum of 8 steps until an Answer/Finish tool is called. The central problem is that prompting all tools as a plain-text list does not scale to thousands of tools: token consumption explodes and the LLM hallucinates/mis-selects as |T| grows. ToolNet is a plug-and-play framework (no LLM finetuning) that, instead of exposing the full tool set T at every step, exposes only a small successor subset T_s = pi(T, a_{s-1}) defined by a weighted directed tool graph G under a Markov (last-tool) assumption. Supervision: no model training; the graph is built from tool-use trajectories (static, 2-gram-style transition counts) and/or refined online by an LLM tool Evaluator that scores each used tool in [-3,3], whose accumulated scores reweight edges. The setting includes adversarial/noisy tools (deliberately broken tools) and sudden tool failures to test robustness.
- **what is retrieved**:
> tools (the candidate set of next tool/API nodes). At step t=0 a semantic similarity retriever (or ToolBench's fine-tuned BERT tool retriever) retrieves the K most relevant starting tools from the full library; at every subsequent step the 'retrieval' is graph traversal returning the out-neighbor successor tools of the previously used tool, each annotated with a transition weight. Tool descriptions (and weights) are the retrieved content injected into the prompt.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> HYBRID. The retrievable store is the tool graph G over a (largely static) external tool/API library, but the edge weights form a GROWING/episodic structure: in dynamic construction an LLM Evaluator's per-tool scores accumulate over iterations and continuously update transition weights online, so the structure the agent navigates evolves with experience (down-weighting broken/noisy tools, raising backup tools). The tool nodes themselves come from a static API corpus (ToolBench/APIBank etc.); the graph edges are an agent-written, online-updated overlay.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Variable, neighborhood-constrained selection rather than a fixed global top-k over all tools. At t=0 a fixed-K top-K retrieval seeds the starting tool(s) (K=8 for ToolBench baselines, K=5 for APIBank; ToolNet/ToT use only the single most-recommended starting tool). Thereafter each step exposes the (small) set of graph successors (typically <6 by the sparsity analysis) and the LLM picks one. The implicit objective is to recover the correct multi-hop tool SEQUENCE (task completion / win rate), not a single global ranking; per-step candidate sets are precision-driven and small.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve: yes (graph-successor candidate retrieval + t=0 semantic retrieval), Reuse: partial (transition-weight preference reused to guide selection, not a prior solution reused), Revise: yes-as-weights (Evaluator-driven online reweighting revises the navigation structure), Retain: yes-as-weights (updated weights persisted in the graph)]. It realizes a retrieve-evaluate-update loop over tool transitions rather than over problem-solution cases.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False: the paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is framed as graph-based tool organization with reflection-driven weight updates, not CBR.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> tool-API (one tool/API = one graph node). The retrievable/injected unit is a tool node together with its transition-weight-annotated successor set (out-neighbors). At t=0 the unit is a single tool's description (semantic-retrieval candidate). There is no document/snippet/trajectory unit; the unit is the tool node and its outgoing edges.
- **index source**:
> Hybrid: tool nodes come from a static external tool corpus (ToolBench 3451/3992 APIs, APIBank tools, or 16 hand-set tools for the task-specific QA datasets). The GRAPH (edges/weights) is built two ways: (1) static / offline-induced from existing completed tool-use trajectories via 2-gram transition counting (Eq. 5), available for ToolBench/APIBank/ToolAlpaca-style data; and (2) dynamic / online/test-time-induced, initialized either from static counts or as a fully-connected uninformative graph and then updated each iteration by an LLM Evaluator's tool scores (Eqs. 6-7). The task-specific QA experiments use purely dynamic construction (no public trajectories), starting from a fully-connected equal-weight graph.
- **index structure topology**:
> Dependency/transition GRAPH: a weighted directed graph G=(V,E) with V = T plus special 'start' and 'end' nodes. Each tool is a node; a directed edge (v_i, v_j, w_{i,j}) encodes the transition preference from tool i to tool j (estimated from trajectory transition statistics, i.e. P(next=v_j | cur=v_i)). 'start' connects to all tools (the t=0 candidate pool), every non-special node has a self-loop, and all nodes can transition to 'end'/Finish. Sparsity is the design goal (most tools have <6 successors), so each node's out-neighborhood is the small candidate set surfaced to the LLM. This is a flat (non-hierarchical) tool-transition graph, distinct from category->tool hierarchies or bipartite dependency KGs.
- **retriever type**:
> Hybrid / two-stage: (a) the next-tool selection at each step is effectively LLM-as-retriever constrained by the graph — the graph deterministically yields the successor candidate set and the LLM picks among them (the 'retriever' is the graph traversal policy pi plus the LLM); (b) the t=0 starting-tool retrieval uses dense semantic similarity search (tool-description embeddings ranked vs the task-description embedding) or, on ToolBench, the provided fine-tuned BERT Tool Retriever. No BM25 reported.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> LM-feedback / interactive experience (not contrastive or RL-policy training). The traversal 'retriever' (the graph) is learned in two ways: (1) static construction is unsupervised frequency estimation — transition weights = empirical 2-gram transition probabilities from completed trajectories (Eq. 5), no learning of a model; (2) dynamic construction uses LM feedback: an LLM Evaluator scores each used tool as a discrete integer in [-3,3] based on whether the final answer was correct and which tools were helpful/noisy/erroneous; accumulated scores s_i^{(n)} are mapped by f(x) and normalized into edge-weight gradients (Eqs. 6-7) that interpolate (via beta) with the static prior. The t=0 semantic retriever / ToolBench BERT retriever is off-the-shelf (BERT fine-tuned in ToolBench, not by this paper). No gradient training of the underlying LLM.
- **query construction**:
> Two query types: (1) t=0 starting-tool query = the raw initial task/question description o_1, embedded and matched against tool-description embeddings (or fed to the ToolBench BERT retriever). (2) Per-step 'query' is implicit and structural: the previously used tool a_{s-1} indexes its successor set in the graph (Markov assumption), so no semantic query is formed at intermediate steps — the prior tool itself is the key. The LLM's thought t_s and weights are then used to pick among the surfaced successors. No sub-query decomposition or query expansion.
- **query granularity**:
> Both task-level and step-level (two-level). Task-level: a single semantic retrieval at t=0 selects the starting tool(s) from the whole library. Step/state-level: at every subsequent step the candidate set is regenerated as the graph successors of the last-used tool (per-step, last-action-conditioned), so candidate selection is interleaved with each action.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Iterative (per-step). Candidate-set generation happens at every reasoning step: t=0 semantic retrieval for the starting tool, then graph-successor lookup at each subsequent step until Finish/end or the max of 8 iterations. Not one-shot; not uncertainty-triggered (retrieval is on a fixed per-step schedule, deterministically driven by the previous action).
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed schedule (per-step, deterministic). The next-candidate set is produced every step as a function of the last action (T_s = oneigh(v_{s-1})); there is no learned router, token-confidence, attention/uncertainty, or reflection-token trigger gating WHEN to retrieve. (The separate Evaluator that UPDATES the graph is invoked reflectively after a trajectory completes, but that governs memory writing, not retrieval triggering.)
- **reranking**:
> Yes, lightweight weight-based ordering: within each step the successor tools are sorted by their transition weights and formatted in that order as input context, so higher-weight tools are presented as 'more recommended'. This is a preference-weighted ordering / soft rerank of the candidate set rather than a cross-encoder or RRF reranker. The ablation (Table 5) shows the numeric format of these weights matters (integer / x10 best).
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Candidate-set restriction + weight annotation: instead of refining retrieved documents, ToolNet prunes the candidate set to the small successor neighborhood (token reduction) and annotates each candidate with a confidence/transition weight that is sorted into the prompt. The interaction history C_s is also a bounded size-K queue (FIFO) to cap context. No distillation, decompose-recompose, or distractor-filtering of retrieved text content.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Minimal: tool descriptions are used largely as provided by the source datasets (e.g. ToolBench API docstrings), formatted as input text alongside the transition weight. The key engineering is (a) compressing each tool description into a semantic embedding for t=0 retrieval and (b) attaching a numeric transition/confidence score to each surfaced tool, with the score's numeric formatting (integer vs decimal, scaling x10) shown (Table 5) to materially affect performance. No synthetic-query augmentation or instruction-tuned tool embeddings.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Live-updated graph with RapidAPI/RESTful tool backends. The tool graph supports online updates so it adapts to tools being added, updated, or crashing (a tool that breaks at iteration 50 is rapidly down-weighted and a backup revived). The underlying tools are real-world RapidAPI / RESTful APIs (ToolBench, drawn from RapidAPI; APIBank tools), called via function-calling style actions (tool name + JSON arguments). No MCP and no automatic CRUD schema sync are described; updates are to edge weights, not to a live-synchronized tool schema registry.
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> Yes — central. ToolNet explicitly models inter-tool dependency as the weighted directed transition graph: the edge weight w_{i,j} captures how often / how preferably tool j follows tool i (output-of-A-feeds-B style chaining observed in multi-hop trajectories). The motivating analysis (Fig. 2) shows tools have a sparse set of successor tools. This is dependency-as-transition-statistics (Markovian last-tool conditioning), not a typed prerequisite/auth dependency graph, and edge weights are dependency-aware via both 2-gram counts and Evaluator feedback.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation with candidate restriction + preference signal. At each step the LLM prompt contains the bounded history, the current observation/thought, and only the successor tool subset (tool names/descriptions) sorted by transition weight, with an explicit instruction that 'tools with higher scores are more recommended.' The LLM then chooses one tool to call. The retrieved structure thus both constrains the action space (token-efficient) and injects a learned preference prior to guide selection; it is not used as a training signal for the LLM (no finetuning).
- **planning integration**:
> Per-step interleaved retrieve-and-act within a sequential ReAct-style loop, where the retrieval (candidate generation) is the navigation step of a graph walk. The LLM 'plans' implicitly by traversing G: thought -> choose successor tool -> act -> observe -> next successors, up to 8 steps. Reflexion can be layered on top (ToolNet+Reflexion) to add trajectory-level self-reflection. No MCTS/explicit tree search inside ToolNet itself (ToT is a baseline, not the integration); planning is a guided sequential graph walk rather than plan-then-retrieve.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-tool-call (per-step): retrieval/candidate-generation is interleaved at the granularity of each tool call / each ReAct step within the rollout (one successor-set lookup and one tool choice per step), not per-CoT-token or per-answer.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> N/A (not case-based reasoning; no retrieved prior case is adapted). The closest analogue is that accumulated tool-use experience (Evaluator scores) adapts the transition weights, which in turn changes which candidates are surfaced — an execution-feedback-driven adaptation of the retrieval structure, not adaptation of a retrieved solution.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Surface form injected = tool names/descriptions plus a numeric transition/confidence weight per candidate, sorted by weight, embedded in the ReAct-style prompt (thought-action format). The 'start' candidate set is the K semantically retrieved tool descriptions. No distilled strategy text, executable program, or latent token; the injected representation is structured tool-list-with-scores.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Low abstraction / concrete tool: the retrieved unit is a concrete tool/API (single candidate tool) plus its transition-preference score. The graph encodes a procedural transition prior over tools, but each retrieved item is a raw tool, not a distilled strategy, guideline, reusable workflow, or full trajectory.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Experience-driven down-weighting via the LLM Evaluator: failed/incorrect trajectories cause noisy or broken tools to be scored low (in [-3,3]), reducing their transition weights so they are surfaced less or not at all; backup/redundant tools are correspondingly up-weighted. Demonstrated by (a) deliberately injected noisy tools on the QA datasets whose scores stay ~0 while effective tools rise (Fig. 3), and (b) a tool crashing at iteration 50 being swiftly supplanted by a fallback (Fig. 4). Robustness thus comes from online graph reweighting and tool redundancy, plus the candidate-set restriction that limits exposure to irrelevant tools — not from retriever-aware SFT or a separate relevance evaluator on retrieved docs.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: graph (a weighted directed tool-transition graph) functioning as procedural/experiential memory. Experience is encoded into edge weights rather than stored as episodic trajectories; the graph is the persistent memory across tasks/iterations.
- **write back**: true: the LLM Evaluator writes accumulated tool scores back into the graph as updated transition weights (Eqs. 6-7) during dynamic construction, so experience is persisted into the structure. (No raw trajectory or case store is written; the write-back target is the edge weights.)
- **online growth**:
> true (for the graph weights/structure): in dynamic construction the graph is updated online at every iteration as new trajectories are generated and scored, allowing it to accommodate new tasks, new tools, and tool failures at test time. The node set (tool library) is largely fixed, but the navigable structure (edges/weights, effectively which successors are reachable/preferred) grows and adapts during deployment.
- **write back trigger**:
> Reflective, after-trajectory (and per-iteration in dynamic construction): once a tool-use trajectory completes, the LLM Evaluator inspects the whole trajectory and scores each used tool conditioned on whether the final answer was valid/incorrect and which tools were helpful or noisy/erroneous; these scores then update the weights. Writes happen on both successful and failed trajectories (success raises helpful tools, failure lowers noisy/broken ones). In static construction, weights are written once offline from completed (successful) trajectories. Not per-step and not human-validated.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Both success and failure are used (contrastive-style reweighting). The Evaluator explicitly assigns higher scores to tools that helped produce a valid final answer and lower (negative, down to -3) scores to noisy, erroneous, or unhelpful tools when the answer is wrong or absent; broken tools are detected and down-weighted. Failure experience is thus stored implicitly as reduced transition weights (corrective signal) rather than as explicit failed-case exemplars.
- **memory evolution update**:
> Delta-update / interpolation: edge weights evolve via w_{i,j}^{(n)} = beta * w_{i,j}^{(0)} + (1-beta) * Delta w_{i,j}^{(n)}, where the prior (static) weight is blended with a normalized gradient derived from accumulated Evaluator scores (f(x): alpha*x+1 for x>=0, e^{alpha*x} for x<0). Scores accumulate across iterations (s_i^{(n)} = sum of Delta_i^{(k)}), so weights are continuously refined/overwritten rather than append-only; alpha controls update speed, beta the prior-vs-learned trade-off. Edges can be effectively pruned by down-weighting.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Partially. Tool selection is governed by a graph-defined policy pi(T, a_{s-1}) whose edge weights are LEARNED from experience (frequency statistics + LLM-Evaluator-driven weight updates), so the candidate-surfacing/preference is a learned-from-feedback policy rather than fixed cosine top-k. However it is not an RL/value-learned action policy (no soft Q-learning / M-MDP / policy-gradient training); the final tool choice among surfaced candidates is still made by the frozen LLM conditioned on the weights. So: learned retrieval STRUCTURE, heuristic/LM-driven update rule, no RL.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> Five datasets (subsets used due to cost): (1) SciQA / ScienceQA (1,000 randomly sampled questions, 16 tools incl. noisy); (2) TabMWP (test1k subset, 16 tools); (3) MATH (level-5 only, geometry excluded, 675 questions, 16 tools); (4) API-Bank (lv1-lv2-samples subset, 212 questions, 49 APIs); (5) ToolBench (random 1,000 questions from the G1 set; reports 3992 APIs available). gpt-3.5-turbo as the LLM; max 8 iterations.
- **benchmark family**: tool (ToolBench, API-Bank) plus tool-augmented QA / math (ScienceQA, TabMWP, MATH used as tool-use environments with injected noisy tools). Primary family = tool-use benchmarks; the three QA/math sets are repurposed as controlled tool-selection-with-noise testbeds.
- **baselines**:
> ReAct (Yao et al. 2022), Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023), and Tree-of-Thought / ToT (Yao et al. 2023). Also ReAct (clean) — ReAct with all deliberately-noisy tools removed — as a reference/upper-bound on the QA datasets. On the multi-task datasets, baselines are augmented with the ToolBench fine-tuned BERT tool retriever (K=8 candidates per step; K=5 for APIBank). A combined ToolNet+Reflexion variant is also reported.
- **key metrics**:
> Answer quality + efficiency: Exact Match (EM) on SciQA, TabMWP, MATH, and API-Bank; Win Rate (via ToolBench's built-in ToolEval, powered by gpt-3.5-turbo) on ToolBench (no unique ground truth). Efficiency: number of tokens consumed (input + generated) for task completion, and number of reasoning steps (#Steps).
- **headline result**:
> ToolNet matches or beats baselines while using far fewer tokens. On TabMWP and MATH it uses only 16.4% and 22.8% of Reflexion's tokens; on SciQA/TabMWP it improves EM by >=10% absolute over the best competitor (SciQA EM 0.61 vs ReAct 0.45 / Reflexion 0.48; TabMWP EM 0.67 vs ToT 0.57). On the massive-tool sets it is on par with Reflexion in win rate while using only 38.5% (APIBank) and 49.7% (ToolBench) of Reflexion's tokens; ToolNet+Reflexion gives the highest scores (APIBank EM 0.83, ToolBench Win Rate 0.75). The paper headlines up to 2.6x greater token efficiency.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Noisy-tool robustness: ReAct vs ReAct(clean) shows large degradation when noisy tools are present, while ToolNet's tool scores keep effective tools rising and noisy tools near 0 (Fig. 3). (2) Sudden tool failure (Fig. 4, APIBank GetUserToken): a primary tool crashed at iteration 50 is rapidly down-weighted and a functionally identical fallback tool revived — demonstrating dynamic-construction resilience. (3) Transition-weight format ablation (Table 5, APIBank): removing weights (EM 0.70) or scaling to decimals (/100 EM 0.70, /10 EM 0.71) is worst; integer weights (EM 0.75) and x10 (EM 0.75) are best, with token use also dropping as weights scale up — LLMs are more sensitive to integer/large-number differences than to small decimals; performance saturates at x10. (4) Complementarity: layering Reflexion onto ToolNet further raises win rate / EM.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> No: only end-to-end task metrics (EM, win rate) plus efficiency (tokens, steps) are reported. There are no standalone intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG) for the tool retriever or graph navigation; retrieval quality is observed only indirectly via tool-score trajectories (Figs. 3-4) and final task performance.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Mixed, mostly outcome with some process signals. Outcome: EM / win rate. Process/efficiency: number of reasoning steps (#Steps) and tokens per task (a process-efficiency measure), plus qualitative per-tool score trajectories (Figs. 3-4) and a reasoning-process visualization (Appendix B) illustrating step-wise tool selection quality; but no quantified step-wise selection accuracy or trajectory-quality score.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Token efficiency is the headline tradeoff. ToolNet attains comparable/better answer quality with markedly fewer tokens and steps: e.g. TabMWP 4,062 tokens / 3.7 steps vs Reflexion 6,594 / 5.3 and ToT 24,710 / 11.3; MATH 6,602 vs ToT 28,886; APIBank 1,649 tokens vs Reflexion 4,286; ToolBench 6,575 vs Reflexion 13,217 and ToT 10,167. Reported up to 2.6x token efficiency. Cost of the approach: extra LLM Evaluator calls for dynamic construction and the need for multi-hop tool-use trajectories to build the graph (named as a limitation). No wall-clock latency / dollar-cost numbers.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Budget-capped via two mechanisms: (a) the interaction history C_s is a fixed-size-K FIFO queue (oldest tuple popped at capacity); (b) the per-step candidate set is the sparse successor neighborhood (typically <6 successors per the Fig. 2 sparsity analysis), so far fewer than |T| tool descriptions are ever in context. At t=0 the starting-tool count is fixed-K: K=8 for ReAct/Reflexion/ToT on ToolBench, K=5 on APIBank, while ToolNet/ToT receive only the single top-recommended starting tool. Successors are reranked by transition weight before being placed in the prompt.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A: ToolNet introduces no new benchmark; it evaluates on subsets of existing datasets (ScienceQA 1,000; TabMWP test1k; MATH level-5 non-geometry, 675; API-Bank lv1-lv2 subset, 212; ToolBench G1, 1,000 of 3992 APIs). Answer verifiability: EM against ground truth for the QA/math/API-Bank sets; LLM-judged win rate (ToolEval) for ToolBench, which has no unique ground-truth answer.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> ReAct (Yao et al. 2022) as the underlying step-by-step tool-calling loop; Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023) for trajectory-level self-reflection (used as baseline and as a complementary add-on); ToolBench/ToolLLM (Qin et al. 2023) for the massive RapidAPI tool corpus, trajectories, BERT tool retriever, and ToolEval; Shao et al. 2023 (prompting LLMs with candidate answer scores) and Shinn et al. 2023 (verbal reflection) motivate the score-annotated prompting and tool-level reflection. Graph weights are a 2-gram language-modeling analogue over tool transitions.
- **contrasts with**:
> Methods that prompt LLMs with all tools as a flat plain-text list (ReAct, Chameleon, HuggingGPT) which do not scale and ignore inter-tool dependency; finetuning-to-master-tools approaches (Toolformer, ToolkenGPT, Gorilla, ToolLLM) which are costly and poorly adaptable to new/updated tools; beam-search tool exploration (Xie et al. 2023 self-evaluation) which multiplies token cost and lacks an explicit reusable memory; and naive semantic tool retrieval, argued to be coarse/inaccurate when |T| is large and when the thought t_s is generated without full knowledge of T. Table 1 contrasts #APIs (ToolNet 3992), adaptability, token efficiency, planning style (NL+Graph), and plug-and-play.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use), large-scale tool-retrieval/organization sub-lineage. Positioned as a training-free, structure-based alternative to (a) finetuned massive-tool models (Gorilla, ToolLLM/ToolBench, ToolkenGPT) and (b) flat-list in-context tool prompting (ReAct/Chameleon/HuggingGPT). It introduces a tool-transition GRAPH as the index/organization, presaging later graph- and dependency-aware tool-retrieval work; sibling to dependency/graph-structured tool-retrieval methods.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- code_url
- cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing
- index_content_separation

<a id="item-toolrerank"></a>
### 92. ToolRerank: Adaptive and Hierarchy-Aware Reranking for Tool Retrieval

2024  ·  LREC-COLING 2024  ·  [paper](https://aclanthology.org/2024.lrec-main.1413/)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: LREC-COLING 2024 (Proceedings of the 2024 Joint International Conference on Computational Linguistics, Language Resources and Evaluation), pages 16263-16273, Torino, Italia, ELRA and ICCL; preprint arXiv:2403.06551 (cs.IR)
- **authors affiliation**:
> Yuanhang Zheng (Dept. of Computer Science and Technology, Tsinghua University), Peng Li (Institute for AI Industry Research (AIR), Tsinghua University; Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory; corresponding author), Wei Liu (Xiaomi AI Lab; corresponding author), Yang Liu (Tsinghua University / AIR / Shanghai AI Lab), Jian Luan (Xiaomi AI Lab), Bin Wang (Xiaomi AI Lab). Lead/first author affiliated with Tsinghua University; work supported in part by Xiaomi AI Lab.
- **paper url**: https://aclanthology.org/2024.lrec-main.1413/
- **code url**: https://github.com/XiaoMi/ToolRerank

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: tool-use / tool learning for LLMs; specifically tool (API) retrieval, framed as an information-retrieval reranking problem to supply suitable APIs to an LLM that calls them.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline (non-interactive) retrieval pipeline for tool learning. Given a user query and a large tool library (ToolBench, >16,000 APIs organized hierarchically as category -> tool -> API), the goal is to retrieve the k=5 most suitable APIs whose documents are then placed in the LLM's input context so the LLM can call them. Single-agent setting; supervision is available (a labeled training set of 169,287 queries with golden API annotations, plus a 600-query dev set). A key assumption is the seen-vs-unseen tool distinction: some test queries involve tools/categories deliberately removed from the retriever's training data (I1-Tool, I1-Cat, I2-Cat are unseen; I1-Inst, I2-Inst, I3-Inst are seen). Retrieval must generalize to unseen tools without retraining the LLM. ToolRerank is a reranking stage inserted after a first-stage dual-encoder retriever and a cross-encoder reranker.
- **what is retrieved**: tools: specifically APIs (tool documents) from a hierarchical tool library; the retrieved API documents are passed to the LLM as context for tool calling.
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus: a fixed tool library of API documents (ToolBench, >16,000 APIs). No agent-written growing/episodic memory; the index is built once over the static tool corpus.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Hybrid of fixed top-k and completeness-aware/precision-driven selection. The final output is a fixed top-k=5 list given to the LLM, but the core contribution targets the completeness of the needed set: Adaptive Truncation tunes how many candidates feed the reranker (more for unseen tools to recover correct APIs that fall outside the top-10), and Hierarchy-Aware Reranking makes results concentrated (single-tool queries, where ideally all needed APIs come from one tool) vs diverse (multi-tool queries, where the minimal needed set spans functionally different tools). Thus the objective is recovering the complete minimal needed set within a fixed k budget, not merely a similarity-ordered top-k.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based-reasoning method; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain case cycle).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is positioned within information-retrieval reranking for tool learning.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: tool-API: a single API document (within a hierarchical tool library where a tool may have multiple APIs and a category contains multiple tools).
- **index source**: Static corpus, offline-induced: a fixed tool/API library indexed offline; the dual-encoder retriever, cross-encoder reranker, and single/multi-tool classifier are all trained offline on the ToolBench training split. No online/test-time index growth.
- **index structure topology**:
> Hierarchical (category -> tool -> API). The retriever produces a flat dense vector index over API documents, but ToolRerank explicitly exploits the library hierarchy: each API carries a tool(c_i) parent-tool label, and reranking algorithms operate over tool-membership groupings. For multi-tool queries a graph is built over candidate APIs (nodes = candidates; edges connect APIs sharing the same tool or with semantic similarity above threshold tau_m) and connected components are used to select diverse results.
- **retriever type**:
> Two-stage hybrid: first-stage dense dual-encoder retriever (DPR-style, bert-base-uncased) producing m coarse-grained candidates, followed by a cross-encoder reranker (bert-base-uncased, BERT-style query-document concatenation a la Nogueira & Cho 2019). ToolRerank itself is a reranking/post-processing layer (Adaptive Truncation + Hierarchy-Aware Reranking) wrapping the cross-encoder reranker. BM25 is used only as a baseline, not in the proposed pipeline.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Contrastive on similarity labels with supervised positives and hard negatives. The dual-encoder retriever and the single/multi-tool classifier are trained directly on the ToolBench training set. The cross-encoder reranker is trained on sampled positive pairs (from golden annotations) and hard-negative pairs (sampled from the dual-encoder's coarse-grained retrieval results). No RL / no LM-feedback / no interactive preference signal; reranking thresholds (m_s, m_u, tau_s, tau_m, n) are set by grid search on the dev set, not learned end-to-end.
- **query construction**:
> Raw user query is used directly as the retrieval/rerank key (encoded by the dual encoder and concatenated with each candidate document for the cross-encoder). No decomposition, intent extraction, or synthetic query expansion. A separate trained classifier maps the raw query to a single-tool vs multi-tool label to choose the reranking algorithm.
- **query granularity**: task-level (one-shot at t=0): a single retrieval+rerank pass is performed per user query; no per-step or trajectory-level re-querying.
- **when to retrieve**: one-shot: a single retrieve-then-rerank pipeline is executed per query before the LLM acts; retrieval is not interleaved with the LLM's tool-calling/reasoning loop.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed schedule: retrieval and reranking always run once per query at the start of the pipeline. There is no dynamic/uncertainty trigger for WHEN to retrieve. (Within reranking, the seen-vs-unseen tool flag and the single/multi-tool classifier decision are the adaptive control signals, but they govern HOW to truncate/rerank, not whether to retrieve.)
- **reranking**:
> Yes - reranking is the central contribution. Two-level: (1) a cross-encoder reranker (Nogueira & Cho 2019, BERT-based) scores the (query, API) pairs; (2) ToolRerank adds Adaptive Truncation (truncate candidates at position m_s for seen tools and m_u for unseen tools, with m_s < m_u) plus Hierarchy-Aware Reranking (hierarchy/diversity-aware reordering: a concentration algorithm pinning APIs from the seed/lump tool set X for single-tool queries, and a graph-based diversification algorithm for multi-tool queries). This is an adaptive, hierarchy-aware reranking stage.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> rerank (multi-stage) plus adaptive truncation and diversity/concentration reordering. Pipeline: dual-encoder coarse retrieval -> Adaptive Truncation (drop candidates beyond a seen/unseen-dependent cutoff) -> cross-encoder rerank -> Hierarchy-Aware Reranking (concentrate for single-tool via a seed lump set X of tools containing a confidently-scored API; diversify for multi-tool via graph connected components keeping at most n per component) -> top-k=5 sent to LLM. For single-tool unseen queries an extended F1 list is built by searching the whole library for sibling APIs of seed tools and re-reranking them.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Raw API/tool documents are used (no synthetic-query augmentation, summary expansion, or instruction-tuned tool embeddings). The dual encoder and cross-encoder operate over the original API documents; the only document-side processing is hard-negative sampling at reranker training time.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: Static tool index built offline over ToolBench's RapidAPI-derived API library; no live synchronization/CRUD auto-sync and no MCP/function-calling integration protocol described. Downstream API calling is handled by the ToolLLaMA/ToolBench framework (RapidAPI-based).
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> Partial / hierarchy-aware rather than dependency-aware. ToolRerank models the category->tool->API hierarchy and semantic similarity among candidate APIs (via a graph whose edges link same-tool or high-similarity APIs, used to diversify multi-tool results and concentrate single-tool results), but it does not model functional inter-tool dependencies such as output-of-A-feeds-B, shared authentication, or prerequisite chaining.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**: prompt augmentation: the documents of the top-k=5 reranked APIs are placed in the LLM's input context so the LLM (ToolLLaMA-7b) can call those APIs to produce an execution result.
- **planning integration**:
> retrieve-then-plan / plan-decoupled: retrieval+reranking is a standalone front-end stage that selects k=5 API documents; these are then handed to a separate downstream LLM agent (ToolLLaMA-7b with the DFSDT search algorithm) which does the multi-step tool-call planning/execution. ToolRerank does not interleave with the LLM's planning loop; it improves the tool set the planner sees.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: per-answer / per-query: retrieval and reranking are performed once per user query, decoupled from the LLM's downstream per-tool-call reasoning (DFSDT). Retrieval is not woven per-CoT-step or per-tool-call.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (no case adaptation; retrieved API documents are used as-is in the prompt).
- **retrieved item representation**: raw API documents (tool/API descriptions) injected verbatim into the LLM prompt; the reranker reorders them but does not distill, compress, or rewrite the API documents.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: single tool-API document (an executable API specification). It is a concrete tool specification rather than a distilled strategy, workflow, or trajectory.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Adaptive Truncation reduces injected noise by limiting candidates fed to the reranker (the paper notes that for seen tools 91.9% of correct APIs are in the top-10, so extra candidates only add noise; for unseen tools only 70.2% are in the top-10, so more candidates help recall). Hierarchy-Aware diversification suppresses redundant functionally-similar candidates (e.g., many near-duplicate QR-code APIs) for multi-tool queries. The reranker is trained on hard-negative pairs to improve discrimination. A trained single/multi-tool classifier (93.3% accuracy) routes queries to the matching reranking algorithm.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (no episodic/skill/workflow memory). The retrievable store is a static, offline tool library.
- **write back**: No. The system does not write new experiences/cases/skills back into any store; the tool library and trained models are fixed at deployment.
- **online growth**: No. The tool index is frozen after offline construction; it does not grow at test time.
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back mechanism exists).
- **failure experience usage**: No storage/retrieval of failed experiences. (Hard-negative pairs sampled from coarse retrieval are used at reranker training time, but these are training-time negatives, not stored runtime failure cases.)
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (no memory entries are stored or mutated; the store is static).
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No. Retrieval/reranking is not an RL- or value-optimized policy. The retriever/reranker/classifier are supervised models and the truncation/reranking thresholds are chosen by grid search on a dev set; the final selection remains a (hierarchy-/adaptivity-modified) similarity-and-score ranking rather than a learned sequential policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-pipeline, single downstream agent; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> ToolBench (Qin et al., 2023b). Test split into 6 subsets of 100 queries each: seen = I1-Inst, I2-Inst, I3-Inst; unseen = I1-Tool, I1-Cat, I2-Cat. Train = 169,287 queries; Dev = 600 queries. Tool library >16,000 APIs. Downstream LLM execution evaluated with ToolLLaMA-7b (v1) using the DFSDT algorithm.
- **benchmark family**: tool (ToolBench).
- **baselines**:
> BM25 (Robertson & Zaragoza 2009); DPR (dual-encoder retriever, Karpukhin et al. 2020 / Qin et al. 2023b); Rerank-m (cross-encoder reranking of top-m coarse candidates, Nogueira & Cho 2019) with m in {10, 30, 50} (Rerank-10, Rerank-30, Rerank-50). For execution-result evaluation an Oracle (ground-truth APIs) upper bound is also reported. LLM-based retrievers are explicitly NOT compared due to inefficiency over 16,000+ APIs.
- **key metrics**: Retrieval quality: NDCG@5 and Recall@5 (per the 6 test subsets and averages). Downstream execution quality: Pass Rate and Win Rate (Win Rate vs a ChatGPT+ReAct baseline solution).
- **headline result**:
> On average over all six ToolBench test subsets, ToolRerank reaches 84.2 Recall@5 and 82.1 NDCG@5, outperforming Rerank-10/30/50 by 5.0/3.9/4.8 Recall@5 points respectively and beating DPR (75.2 Recall@5 / 71.0 NDCG@5). End-to-end with ToolLLaMA-7b + DFSDT, ToolRerank achieves Pass Rate 61.5 and Win Rate 57.0, the best among retrieval methods and exceeding even the Oracle Pass Rate (61.0) while remaining below the Oracle Win Rate (68.3).
- **ablations**:
> (1) Adaptive Truncation (Table 5, Recall@5): m_s<m_u (best: m_s=10, m_u=50 -> 84.2 All) beats fixed m_s=m_u (best 82.0) and m_s>m_u (worst 78.5), confirming truncation must be looser for unseen than seen tools. (2) Hierarchy-Aware Reranking (Table 6, Recall@5): removing it (ToolRerank_none 82.8) drops performance; applying a single algorithm to all queries hurts when it mismatches query type (ToolRerank_single 83.5, ToolRerank_multi 82.6); the oracle classifier (ToolRerank_oracle 84.5) is only +0.3 over the trained-classifier ToolRerank (84.2), and the classifier has 93.3% accuracy. (3) Extended API list for single-tool queries (Table 7): adding the extended F1 only for unseen tools is best (88.3 avg); building it for seen tools injects noise (only 2.6% of correct seen-tool APIs lie outside T vs 7.7% for unseen). (4) Shuffling APIs given to the LLM drops NDCG@5 by 16.5 points but barely affects Pass/Win Rate, motivating reporting only Recall@5 in ablations.
- **evaluation decoupling**: Yes. Intrinsic retrieval metrics (NDCG@5, Recall@5) are reported separately (Table 3) from end-to-end downstream LLM execution metrics (Pass Rate, Win Rate; Table 4), explicitly decoupling retrieval quality from task outcome.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both. Retrieval-process quality is measured intrinsically (NDCG@5/Recall@5, plus analyses of where correct APIs fall in the candidate list and a single/multi-tool classifier accuracy of 93.3%), while final task outcome is measured by downstream Pass Rate and Win Rate. The paper also notes that final execution outcome is largely insensitive to API ordering (shuffling cuts NDCG@5 by 16.5 but not Pass/Win Rate).
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Efficiency is a stated motivation: ToolRerank deliberately avoids LLM-based retrievers because using an LLM to rank over 16,000+ APIs is too slow, opting for an efficient dual-encoder + cross-encoder cascade. Adaptive Truncation also limits the number of candidates passed to the (more expensive) cross-encoder, reducing reranking cost while improving accuracy. No explicit latency/throughput numbers or API-cost figures are reported.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed k=5 final APIs given to the LLM (following Qin et al. 2023b). Reranked-then-truncated: the candidate count fed to the reranker is adaptively truncated (m_s in {10,30,50} for seen tools, m_u in {10,30,50} for unseen tools, with chosen m_s<m_u, e.g. m_s=10, m_u=50); after reranking and hierarchy-aware reordering only the top-5 are kept for the prompt. Thresholds tau_s, tau_m in {0.6..0.9} and n in {2,3,4} are grid-searched on the dev set.
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A (ToolRerank reuses the existing ToolBench dataset; it does not construct a new benchmark). It does re-derive a seen/unseen split following Qin et al. (2023b): train 169,287 queries, dev 600, six 100-query test subsets (3 seen, 3 unseen), over a >16,000-API hierarchical tool library.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> ToolBench / ToolLLaMA (Qin et al., 2023b) for the dataset, tool hierarchy, single/multi-tool query notion, DFSDT, and Pass/Win Rate metrics; DPR dual-encoder retrieval (Karpukhin et al., 2020); cross-encoder reranking (Nogueira & Cho, 2019); BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) backbone for retriever/reranker/classifier; classic IR reranking literature (Guo et al. 2016; Xiong et al. 2017; Yan et al. 2019).
- **contrasts with**:
> Fixed-candidate cross-encoder reranking (Rerank-m, Nogueira & Cho 2019) that ignores seen/unseen differences and tool hierarchy; plain dual-encoder retrieval (DPR) and BM25; LLM-based tool retrievers (e.g., Paranjape et al. 2023 / ART) which are rejected as too inefficient at >16,000-API scale; fine-tuning LLMs to internalize tools (Hao et al. 2023; Gao et al. 2023b Confucius) which cannot easily support new/unseen tools.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use). Sits in the tool-retrieval sub-lineage: a dedicated, hierarchy-aware and seen/unseen-adaptive reranking stage layered on the ToolBench/ToolLLaMA retrieval pipeline, advancing tool retrieval beyond generic dense retrieval + fixed cross-encoder reranking toward tool-library-structure-aware reranking.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- index_content_separation

<a id="item-api-bank"></a>
### 93. API-Bank: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Tool-Augmented LLMs

2023  ·  EMNLP 2023  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.08244)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2023
- **venue**: EMNLP 2023 (Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, main/long paper, pages 3102-3116; ACL Anthology 2023.emnlp-main.187, DOI 10.18653/v1/2023.emnlp-main.187). Preprint arXiv:2304.08244 (cs.CL), submitted 14 Apr 2023, v2 25 Oct 2023.
- **authors affiliation**:
> Minghao Li (Alibaba Group) and Yingxiu Zhao (HKUST) [equal contribution]; Bowen Yu (Alibaba Group, corresponding); Feifan Song (Peking University); Hangyu Li, Haiyang Yu, Fei Huang, Yongbin Li (Alibaba Group); Zhoujun Li (Shenzhen Intelligent Strong Technology Co., Ltd.). Primary affiliation: Alibaba Group (DAMO Academy / Conversational AI).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.08244
- **code url**: https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-ConvAI/tree/main/api-bank
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-ConvAI (official Alibaba DAMO Conversational AI repo hosting the api-bank subdirectory; the benchmark is integrated into downstream harnesses such as CAMEL's apibank.py). No standalone live leaderboard is maintained by the authors.

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: tool-use (tool-augmented LLM benchmark): evaluating an LLM's ability to plan, retrieve, and call external API tools within multi-turn dialogues, with a runnable execution system. Touches decision-making/planning over API call sequences.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent, multi-turn tool-use evaluation with a runnable (executable) system. The LLM converses with a user; when it decides a tool is needed it must emit an API-Request in a fixed format [ApiName(key='value', ...)], which the API-Bank system actually executes against initialized databases/external-info stubs and returns an Observation, after which the model generates a natural-language Response. The benchmark grades three escalating ability levels: (1) Call - call the correct API when the relevant API descriptions are given in context (small API pool, slot-filling style); (2) Retrieve+Call - the API pool is hidden/large so the model must first invoke a meta-API 'ToolSearcher'/API Search to retrieve the right API before calling it, with the complex requirement pre-decomposed into single-API simple queries; (3) Plan+Retrieve+Call - the model must autonomously plan and chain multiple Retrieve-then-Call steps within a single turn to satisfy a complex requirement (no pre-decomposition). Evaluation is primarily zero-shot prompting of off-the-shelf LLMs; supervision also exists as a training set (1,888 dialogues from 2,138 APIs over 1,000 domains) used to fine-tune the open model Lynx (initialized from Alpaca-7B / LLaMA-7B). The test set (314 dialogues, 753 API calls, 73 implemented APIs, 8 test domains) is human-annotated and intentionally distribution-shifted from the LLM-synthesized training set to assess generalization.
- **what is retrieved**: tools (APIs): API meta-information (name, description, input/output parameters) of candidate tools in a private API Pool/library, retrieved via the special meta-API 'ToolSearcher' (a.k.a. API Search) so the LLM can identify which tool to call.
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus: retrieval targets a fixed API Pool / tool library (the set of implemented APIs and their meta-information). The store is not an agent-written growing/episodic memory; it is a predefined library of tools the user/system has registered.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-1 ranking objective per retrieval call: ToolSearcher returns the single API with the highest cosine similarity to the query keywords ('best_matchs', the best match tool). For the Plan+Retrieve+Call ability the agent must, across multiple ToolSearcher calls, recover the complete minimal set of APIs needed to satisfy a multi-step requirement (multi-call completeness emerges from repeated top-1 retrievals), but each individual retrieval is top-1 rather than a variable-size recommendation list.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve: yes (ToolSearcher top-1 retrieval of the needed API from the library), Reuse: partial (retrieved API spec is reused to format the call, but it is tool documentation, not a prior solved problem-solution case), Revise: no, Retain: no]. Not a case-based-reasoning system; it retrieves tools, not prior cases.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False: the paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is a tool-augmented-LLM benchmark with embedding-similarity tool retrieval.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: tool-API: one tool's API meta-information record (name + description + input/output parameter specs) is the retrievable unit; ToolSearcher returns the best-matching API record from the library.
- **index source**:
> Static corpus built offline: the API Pool/library of registered tools. In the runnable evaluation system 73 APIs are implemented (with initialized databases and hard-coded external-info responses for reproducibility); the training set spans 2,138 APIs over 1,000 domains. The retrievable index is constructed from the meta-information of these predefined APIs; it is not induced online from the agent's own trajectories.
- **retriever type**:
> dense (embedding) retriever exposed as a meta-API tool: ToolSearcher obtains sentence embeddings of query keywords and of all API meta-information, computes cosine similarity, and returns the top match. It is an off-the-shelf embedding-similarity retriever invoked by the LLM as a callable API; the LLM acts as the query generator (deciding keywords and when to call ToolSearcher).
- **retriever learning signal**:
> none (off-the-shelf embedding similarity): the ToolSearcher/API Search retriever is a fixed sentence-embedding + cosine-similarity matcher; it is not trained with contrastive, LM-feedback, preference, or RL signals. The only learning in the work is in the GENERATOR side (Lynx is fine-tuned on API-Bank training data, which teaches it to issue ToolSearcher calls and parse retrieved API info), not in the retriever itself.
- **query construction**:
> Intent-keyword extraction by the LLM: when an API is needed, the model condenses the user's demand into a few keywords and passes them as the 'keywords' argument to ToolSearcher (e.g. ToolSearcher(keywords='add reminder')). The query is thus an LLM-generated keyword string, not the raw full utterance and not a decomposed sub-query tree.
- **query granularity**:
> step/sub-task level: a ToolSearcher query is issued per needed tool. In Retrieve+Call each simple query maps to one retrieval+call; in Plan+Retrieve+Call multiple step-level ToolSearcher queries are issued within a single turn as the plan unfolds. Not a single task-level one-shot retrieval at t=0.
- **when to retrieve**: iterative / agent-initiated: the model decides when to call ToolSearcher; an API Search is required before every other (non-search) API call. In Plan+Retrieve+Call, retrieval is interleaved repeatedly across the multi-step rollout (retrieve, call, observe, retrieve again).
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Agent-initiated request governed by a fixed protocol rule: the prompt instructs that before using any tool the model must first search for it via ToolSearcher, so retrieval is triggered whenever the model decides it needs a (new) tool to make progress. There is no learned router, token-confidence, or uncertainty signal; the trigger is the agent emitting a ToolSearcher API-Request, constrained by the rule 'an API Search is required before every other API call'.
- **reranking**: None: ToolSearcher returns the single highest-cosine-similarity API ('best_matchs'); there is no second-stage cross-encoder, RRF, or hierarchy-aware reranking.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> None / minimal: the retrieved API meta-information (name, description, input/output parameters) is returned as an Observation and used directly by the model to format the subsequent API call. No decompose-recompose, distillation, distractor filtering, or compression is applied to the retrieved record.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Tool descriptions are engineered into a uniform structured schema {name, description, input_parameters, output_parameters}, and each API additionally has a 'desc_for_search' field (name + description concatenation) that serves as the embedding key for ToolSearcher. No synthetic-query augmentation, expanded summaries, or instruction-tuned tool embeddings are applied to the index; retrieval uses off-the-shelf sentence embeddings over this curated meta-information.
- **index content separation**:
> Partial / progressive disclosure by design: the lightweight API meta-information (name/description/parameter schema) is what is retrieved and injected on demand via ToolSearcher, deliberately because the full API Pool cannot fit in the prompt when many APIs are defined; the heavy runnable API implementation/execution is invoked separately when the model issues the actual API call. So a lightweight searchable index is separated from the executable tool, though the same meta-record is both indexed and shown.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Static, custom function-calling protocol: API-Bank uses its own bespoke API-Request format [ApiName(key='value', ...)] executed by a self-contained runnable system (73 APIs implemented in-house), with ToolSearcher as a built-in retrieval meta-API. The tool index is static/predefined (no live RapidAPI/REST/MCP sync, no automatic CRUD live-sync); external-info APIs are hard-coded to fixed responses to guarantee reproducibility.
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> Implicit, not modeled in retrieval: Plan+Retrieve+Call dialogues require chaining where one API's output feeds another (e.g., GetUserToken -> AddReminder; GetOccupationSalary -> TaxCalculator) and some calls require prerequisite auth tokens, so inter-tool dependencies exist in the tasks. However, ToolSearcher itself does not model dependencies (no dependency graph or dependency-aware reranking); the planning/chaining is left to the LLM agent to infer.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> prompt augmentation within an interactive loop: the retrieved API meta-information (returned as an Observation from ToolSearcher) is read by the model to construct the correct subsequent API-Request (correct name and input parameters), which the system then executes. For Lynx, the same retrieve-then-call pattern is also a fine-tuning training signal (the model learns the ToolSearcher -> API-call pipeline).
- **planning integration**:
> retrieve-then-call interleaved inside an agentic ReAct-style loop. Call: no retrieval (APIs given). Retrieve+Call: one retrieve-then-call per pre-decomposed simple query. Plan+Retrieve+Call: the model plans a chain of API calls within a single turn, performing ToolSearcher retrieval before each tool use, executing it, observing the result, and proceeding to the next step until the requirement is met (plan-and-act with per-step retrieval; no MCTS/tree search).
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: per-tool-call within a rollout: each tool the agent needs triggers its own ToolSearcher retrieval, so retrieval is interleaved at the granularity of individual API calls across the multi-step Plan+Retrieve+Call rollout (and once per simple query in Retrieve+Call).
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not framed as CBR): the closest analogue is that the model reads the retrieved API specification and instantiates a correctly-formatted call from it (parameter slot-filling grounded in the retrieved doc), rather than adapting a prior solved case.
- **retrieved item representation**: Structured API meta-information record injected as an Observation: a JSON-like dict with fields {name, description, input_parameters, output_parameters} (the tool's specification). It is raw tool documentation, not a distilled strategy, workflow, program, or latent token.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw documentation / single reference item: the retrieved unit is one candidate tool's concrete API specification (name + description + parameter schema), not a distilled strategy, guideline, reusable workflow, or procedural skill.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none: there is no episodic/skill/workflow/graph/latent memory. The API Pool is a static external tool library, not an agent-written memory; dialogue history is passed in-context but not a retrievable learned memory store.
- **write back**: false: the system does not write new experiences/cases/skills back into a retrievable memory during evaluation. (A separate offline training set is synthesized by the Multi-agent pipeline, but that is dataset construction, not test-time write-back.)
- **online growth**: false: the API Pool / retrievable tool library is fixed during evaluation; it does not grow from the agent's own outputs at test time.
- **write back trigger**: never: no automatic memory write-back exists. API and dialogue data are created offline (human annotation for the test set; LLM Multi-agent synthesis for the training set), not triggered by model success/failure or reflection at inference time.
- **failure experience usage**:
> N/A / none: failed experiences are not stored or retrieved. The paper does perform a manual error-type analysis (e.g., No API Call, API Hallucination, Failed API Retrieval, False API Call Format, Invalid/Missing Input Parameters) to characterize failures, but errors are not persisted as negative cases for retrieval or learning.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A: there is no model-written memory to mutate. The static API library is updated only by human/system registration (e.g., hard-coding external-info responses for reproducibility), not via append/dedup/refine of agent memory.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No: tool selection uses a fixed embedding-similarity top-1 retriever (ToolSearcher) invoked by the agent; it is not an RL- or value-learned retrieval policy. The decision of WHEN/WHAT keywords to search is made by the (possibly fine-tuned) LLM via prompting, but the ranking function itself is fixed cosine similarity.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No: single-agent evaluation with a private/user-defined API Pool; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing. (The Multi-agent method uses five collaborating ChatGPT agents, but that is for offline DATA GENERATION, not shared retrievable memory at inference.)

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> API-Bank (introduced by this paper): runnable evaluation system with 73 implemented APIs, 314 human-annotated tool-use dialogues, 753 API calls, across 8 test domains; split by ability into Call (214 calls), Retrieve+Call (50), Plan+Retrieve+Call (50). Plus an LLM-synthesized training set: 1,888 dialogues, 2,138 APIs, 1,000 domains, 4,149 API calls (broader synthesized corpus reported as 1,008 domains / 2,211 APIs / 2,202 dialogues / 6,135 turns). Also a dataset-quality comparison against ToolAlpaca (Call-only).
- **benchmark family**: tool (tool/API-use benchmark): API-Bank is a canonical entry in the tool-use benchmark family (alongside ToolBench, APIBench/Gorilla, ToolAlpaca, ToolQA), and is the named tool benchmark in retrieval-augmented tool-use surveys.
- **baselines**:
> Zero-shot LLMs evaluated on the API-Bank evaluation system: GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613), GPT-3.5-turbo (gpt-3.5-turbo-0613), GPT-3 Davinci (text-davinci, 175B), ChatGLM-6B, Alpaca-7B (instruction-tuned LLaMA-7B). The authors' fine-tuned model Lynx-7B (LLaMA-7B initialized from Alpaca, fine-tuned on API-Bank training data) is compared against these. A dataset-quality baseline fine-tunes Alpaca on the ToolAlpaca training set vs Lynx on API-Bank.
- **key metrics**:
> (1) Correctness / Accuracy of API calls = #correct predictions / #total predictions, where correctness is judged by whether the predicted API call produces the same database queries/modifications and the same returned results as the annotated call (execution-state consistency in the runnable system). (2) ROUGE-L for the quality of the LLM's post-call natural-language Response. Reported per ability (Call / Retrieve+Call / Plan+Retrieve+Call) and as a Total. No latency/token-cost metrics.
- **headline result**:
> On the API-Bank evaluation system (Total, Correctness): GPT-4 60.24%, GPT-3.5-turbo 47.16%, Lynx-7B (fine-tuned) 39.58%, ChatGLM-6B 16.42%, Alpaca-7B 15.19%, GPT-3 Davinci 0.57%. Lynx surpasses Alpaca-7B by 26 points in API Call correctness (49.87% vs 24.06%) and approaches GPT-3.5, while a ~21% Total gap from GPT-4 remains. GPT-4 excels especially at Plan+Retrieve+Call (70.00% vs GPT-3.5's 22.00%).
- **ablations**:
> (1) Per-ability decomposition (Table 3): correctness drops as required ability escalates (Call > Retrieve+Call > Plan+Retrieve+Call) for most models, exposing planning/retrieval as the bottleneck; GPT-4 is the exception, far stronger on Plan+Retrieve+Call. (2) Instruction-tuning matters: GPT-3 Davinci (175B, not instruction-tuned) scores ~0.5% on Call vs ~20-24% for much smaller instruction-tuned Alpaca-7B/ChatGLM-6B. (3) Fine-tuning effect: Lynx fine-tuned on API-Bank improves Call correctness by 26 pts over base Alpaca-7B and largely eliminates the 'No API Call' and 'False API Call Format' errors, and removes the 'Failed API Retrieval' failure that dominates GPT-4. (4) Error-type analyses (Tables 4-6): Alpaca dominated by 'No API Call' (36.77%); Lynx dominated by 'API Hallucination' (61.38%); GPT-4 dominated by 'Failed API Retrieval' (67.86%). (5) Dataset-quality ablation (Table 7): Lynx fine-tuned on API-Bank data (6,184 samples) beats Alpaca fine-tuned on ToolAlpaca data (10,366 samples) on Call accuracy (54.64 vs 53.88) and Rouge (39.80 vs 39.75) despite fewer samples. (6) Multi-agent vs self-instruct data synthesis: self-instruct yields only 5% usable data (ChatGPT) / 25% (GPT-4), whereas the 5-agent decomposed pipeline produces compliant data at ~98% lower cost ($0.1 vs $8 per dialogue).
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Partial: retrieval quality is assessed indirectly rather than via standalone Recall@k/nDCG. The benchmark grades end-to-end execution-state correctness, and retrieval competence surfaces through (a) the separate Retrieve+Call ability score and (b) the 'Failed API Retrieval' error category in the error analysis. No intrinsic ToolSearcher Recall@k/nDCG numbers are reported separately from task success.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both outcome and process: outcome is per-API-call execution-state Correctness and final Response ROUGE-L; process is captured via the ability-graded breakdown (planning vs retrieving vs calling) and a six-category error analysis (No API Call, API Hallucination, Failed API Retrieval, False API Call Format, Invalid/Missing Input Parameters, Has Exception) that localizes where in the plan-retrieve-call pipeline models fail.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Reported as data-construction and model-size efficiency rather than retrieval-call counts: Multi-agent synthesis costs ~$0.1/dialogue vs ~$8/dialogue human annotation, a 98% reduction; Lynx-7B approaches GPT-3.5 with far fewer parameters and beats ToolAlpaca-fine-tuned Alpaca with fewer training samples (6,184 vs 10,366). Lynx fine-tuning: LLaMA-7B base, 3 epochs, batch size 256, lr 2e-5. API implementation cost 98 person-days; annotation $8/dialogue; 21.5% of 400 annotated dialogues discarded. No inference latency/token-cost metrics.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Per-retrieval selection is top-1 (ToolSearcher returns the single best-matching API; the example also shows it can return a short candidate list). Total tools surfaced per dialogue grows with the number of ToolSearcher calls the agent issues in Plan+Retrieve+Call. The ability grading is explicitly motivated by input-length limits: when many APIs are defined, all cannot fit in context, so retrieval (top-1 per call) is used instead of injecting the whole pool. No fixed token budget figure is reported.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Evaluation set: 73 runnable APIs implemented in a common framework (98 person-days) with initialized databases and hard-coded external-info responses for reproducibility; 314 human-annotated multi-turn dialogues with 753 API calls over 8 domains, split Call (214) / Retrieve+Call (50) / Plan+Retrieve+Call (50). Annotation: CS-student annotators pair-annotate each dialogue with two extra QA annotators; $8/dialogue; 400 annotated, 21.5% discarded, 314 retained. Training set: synthesized by a novel Multi-agent pipeline of 5 ChatGPT agents (domain -> API (grounded with Public-APIs examples) -> query+ability -> API call & simulated response -> tester agent that discards ~35% non-compliant instances), yielding 1,888 dialogues, 2,138 APIs, 1,000 domains, 4,149 calls (broader run: 1,008 domains / 2,211 APIs / 2,202 dialogues / 6,135 turns); ~$0.1/dialogue (98% cheaper than human). Answer verifiability: high - API-call correctness checked by execution-state consistency in the runnable system; responses scored by ROUGE-L. Difficulty signal: best system GPT-4 reaches only 60.24% Total correctness (vs 80-90% that GPT-3.5 reaches on the concurrent self-instruct-built APIBench/ToolAlpaca), reflecting deliberate real-world difficulty and train/test distribution shift.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Self-instruct (Wang et al., 2022) as the data-generation point of departure (extended into the Multi-agent decomposed pipeline because self-instruct under-produces compliant tool-use data); Alpaca-7B / LLaMA-7B (Taori et al., 2023; Touvron et al., 2023) as the base for fine-tuning Lynx; tool-augmented LLM line including Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023), ReAct (Yao et al., 2022), WebGPT (Nakano et al., 2021), and large-scale API integration (TaskMatrix.AI, ChatGPT Plugins).
- **contrasts with**:
> Concurrent tool-use benchmarks it positions against in Table 1: APIBench/Gorilla (Patil et al., 2023; single-call, no planning, no multi-turn), ToolAlpaca (Tang et al., 2023; Call-only, self-instruct, narrow domains), ToolBench-1/ToolLLM (Qin et al., 2023b), ToolBench-2 (Xu et al., 2023), ToolQA (Zhuang et al., 2023), and DATESET/Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023). API-Bank claims highest diversity (1,000 domains, 2,138 APIs), highest realism (multi-turn + multi-call), and highest coverage (evaluates Call, Retrieve, and Plan with a runnable execution system and response scoring). It explicitly contrasts its human-annotated, distribution-shifted, harder test set against the self-instruct-generated, narrow-domain test sets where GPT-3.5 already reaches 80-90%.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use): a foundational tool-use BENCHMARK with an integral static tool-library retrieval component (the ToolSearcher / API Search meta-API). It sits alongside Gorilla/APIBench and precedes ToolBench/ToolLLM-scale and later tool-retrieval benchmarks (e.g., ToolRet); it is a standard reference benchmark for evaluating retrieve-then-call tool-augmented LLMs and is cited in retrieval-augmented tool-use surveys as the canonical planning+retrieving+calling benchmark.
