- index_structure_topology
- noise_robustness_mechanism

<a id="item-protip"></a>
### 94. ProTIP: Progressive Tool Retrieval Improves Planning

2023  ·  arXiv 2312.10332  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.10332)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2023
- **authors affiliation**: Raviteja Anantha, Bortik Bandyopadhyay (equal contribution), Anirudh Kashi, Sayantan Mahinder, Andrew W Hill, Srinivas Chappidi -- all at Apple.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.10332

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: tool-use / multi-step planning (LLM agent that selects APIs/tools from an external toolbox to fulfill complex multi-step requests).
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-agent setting on the ToolBench dataset. The goal is to retrieve the correct top-k tools for a complex multi-step query and then generate a step-by-step plan (next-API prediction) with a fine-tuned LLM planner. Supervision is available: each request has ground-truth tool and plan labels. The work decouples Tool Retrieval (TR) evaluation from progressive planning. It explicitly notes that true end-to-end interactive step-by-step planning (executing each predicted API and feeding its output back) is deferred to future work; experiments use a tool-interleaving strategy rather than live execution.
- **what is retrieved**: tools / APIs (specifically tool descriptions from an external toolbox).
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus -- a fixed toolbox of ~16,000 tool descriptions indexed in a vector database; no agent-written growing memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Recovery of the complete minimal set of tools needed across all subtasks of a multi-step query, measured via Recall@K (K from 6 to 20). Retrieval is progressive/iterative per subtask, with the union (interleaving) of per-step retrieved tools forming the top-K set; objective is completeness over the multi-tool plan rather than a single fixed top-k ranking.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based reasoning method).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False -- the work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is a contrastive-learning embedding retrieval method.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: tool-API (a single tool, represented by its tool description / name + description). Retrieval is performed one tool per planning subtask.
- **index source**: Static corpus: the ToolBench toolbox (16,000 tools, 49 categories) is encoded offline into a vector database of tool-description embeddings; the store is frozen, not grown at test time.
- **index structure topology**: Flat vector index (vector database of tool-description embeddings); cosine/L2 similarity over a flat embedding space. No graph or hierarchical organization of the index itself.
- **retriever type**: Dense / learned: a fine-tuned BERT-base-uncased bi-encoder for ProTIP. Baselines include BM25 (text-based) and GTR-T5-XL dense semantic search (off-the-shelf).
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Contrastive learning on similarity labels: margin-based contrastive loss (Hadsell et al. 2006), margin m=0.3, L2 distance. Positive pairs = (progressively transformed query embedding, ground-truth next-tool description); negatives = randomly drawn irrelevant tools (in-batch). The query embedding for step i>1 is formed by element-wise subtracting embeddings of previously retrieved tool descriptions from the full-query embedding, so the retriever implicitly learns task decomposition without explicit subtask labels.
- **query construction**:
> Progressive/iterative query transformation in vector space: initial retrieval uses E_w(q) (the full-query embedding); for subsequent steps the query key is E_w(q) minus the element-wise sum of embeddings of previously retrieved tool descriptions, approximating an embedding for the remaining (i+1..n) subtasks. No explicit text decomposition is generated.
- **query granularity**: Step/subtask-level: a distinct query embedding is constructed per planning step (conditioned on execution history), in contrast to single-step full-query retrieval or explicit task-decomposition into text subqueries.
- **when to retrieve**: Iterative -- retrieval is performed progressively, once per subtask/planning step, up to the number of subtasks in the query (max 6 in ToolBench).
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule tied to the multi-step plan structure: one retrieval per subtask step, iterating until the subtasks are exhausted (the number of steps is bounded by the plan length / top-k budget). Not uncertainty- or confidence-triggered.
- **reranking**: No dedicated reranking stage. Final top-K is assembled via a tool-interleaving strategy that merges per-step (per-subtask) retrieved tools into the final candidate set for Recall@K evaluation.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Interleaving of per-subtask retrieved tools to form the final top-K set; otherwise no explicit distillation/compression/distractor-filtering of retrieved tool descriptions (the embedding-subtraction operation that removes already-addressed subtasks happens on the query side, not on retrieved context).
- **tool document engineering**:
> Tool descriptions are used largely as-is (raw tool name + description encoded by BERT-base for ProTIP, GTR-T5-XL for SS, or BM25 over description text). No synthetic-query augmentation or expanded summaries; the paper notes (as future work) that enriching tool metadata could improve generalization to unseen tools.
- **index content separation**:
> No explicit lightweight-index-then-content (progressive-disclosure) separation; tool-description embeddings are the index and the retrieved tool metadata is loaded into the prompt directly. (Top-k truncation to fit the 2048-token budget is a budget mechanism, not index/content separation.)
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Static tool index (frozen ToolBench toolbox); no live synchronization, RapidAPI/MCP/RESTful auto-sync, or CRUD updates implemented. The motivation mentions toolboxes can evolve dynamically (creating subtask-tool atomicity-alignment problems), which ProTIP's implicit-TD design aims to be robust to, but the evaluated index itself is static.
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> Yes (implicitly): a primary motivation is handling 'inter-tool dependency' across multi-step plans. ProTIP conditions each retrieval step on execution history by subtracting previously retrieved tool-description embeddings, so the next-tool retrieval depends on prior tool selections. However, dependencies are modeled implicitly in embedding space, not via an explicit dependency graph or bipartite KG.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation for planning: the retrieved top-k tool candidates (with metadata, e.g., tool name) are inserted into the LLM planner's prompt (alongside the instruction, the request, and optional execution history) so the planner selects the next API to execute. Retrieval itself is also a learned-embedding signal (contrastive fine-tuning).
- **planning integration**:
> Per-step interleaved retrieve-then-plan: tools are retrieved progressively per subtask and supplied to a supervised fine-tuned LLM planner (OpenLLaMA-7B-v2) that predicts the next API per step. Note the authors evaluate planning by unrolling each interaction into per-step prompts and use tool interleaving for candidate sets rather than a fully live execution loop (true end-to-end step-by-step execution is deferred to future work).
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-tool-call / per-subtask step: retrieval is woven in once per plan step (next-API prediction), not per CoT token or per sentence.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not a CBR case-adaptation method).
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw tool metadata injected as text into the planner prompt -- primarily the tool name (and optionally tool description/metadata); the planner selects from this candidate list. On the retrieval side the unit is a tool-description embedding.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Single tool/API specification (tool name + description) -- a concrete actionable unit, not a distilled strategy, workflow, or trajectory.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Contrastive/retriever-aware training: ProTIP is fine-tuned with negatives, and the planner is trained with (K-p) randomly sampled distractor tools added to the p ground-truth tools per step so it learns to pick the correct tool amid distractors. The paper discusses (as a limitation) that random-distractor training versus semantically-similar test-time distractors causes a train/test mismatch and proposes using TR-retrieved tools during training as future work. No explicit relevance-evaluator or self-reflection module.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (static toolbox index; no episodic/skill/workflow memory).
- **write back**: False -- the system does not write new experiences, cases, or skills into a memory store; the toolbox index is fixed.
- **online growth**: False -- the retrievable store (toolbox) is frozen after offline encoding and does not grow during deployment/test-time.
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back mechanism).
- **failure experience usage**: Success-only with respect to retrieval supervision (positive = ground-truth next tool; negatives are randomly sampled irrelevant tools used contrastively, not stored failed trajectories). No storage/retrieval of failed execution experiences.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (no stored memory entries to mutate; index is append-only at construction and otherwise static).
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Partially: retrieval is a learned dense embedding model (contrastive fine-tuning that implicitly performs task decomposition) rather than off-the-shelf top-k similarity, but it is NOT an RL-optimized or value-based selection policy -- selection is still nearest-neighbor in the learned (progressively transformed) embedding space.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: N/A -- single-agent, single-framework; no cross-agent memory or experience sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> ToolBench (Qin et al. 2023b). 16,000 tools across 49 categories, ~27,000 complex requests; after cleaning (removing hallucinated/invalid-tool annotations) ~25,489 train / 274 test requests, and after TD-outlier filtering 25,124 train / 268 test data points. Max subtasks per query = 6; avg ~2.93 subtasks.
- **benchmark family**: tool (ToolBench / tool-retrieval and tool-use planning).
- **baselines**:
> Full-query BM25; Task-Decomposition (TD, via ChatGPT) BM25 with tool interleaving; Full-query Semantic Search (SS) with GTR-T5-XL; TD-based Semantic Search with tool interleaving; Oracle TR (ground-truth tools, plus a variant with GT + random tools). Planner backbone: supervised fine-tuned OpenLLaMA-7B-v2.
- **key metrics**: Tool Retrieval: Recall@K (K=6,10,15,20). Planning: Tool Accuracy (TA, %), Tool Hallucination (TH, %), Exact Match (EM), ROUGE-LSum (RLSum).
- **headline result**:
> On ToolBench, ProTIP outperforms the ChatGPT task-decomposition-based TR approach by ~24% in Recall@K=10 (ProTIP 81.36 vs TD-based Semantic Search 65.57, i.e. ~15.79 absolute points) and yields ~41% enhancement in Tool Accuracy for plan generation (ProTIP planner setting [T+H] TA=36.49% vs TD-based SS [T+H] TA=25.88%).
- **ablations**:
> Reported as comparative settings rather than a single ablation table. (1) TR ablation across retrievers: full-query BM25 < TD-BM25 < full-query SS < TD-SS < ProTIP (Recall@10: 41 / 47 / 60.86 / 65.57 / 81.36). (2) Prompt-content ablation for the planner: tools-only [T] vs tools+history [T+H] -- adding execution history gives large TA gains (PTR [T] 19.82% -> [T+H] 36.49%, ~80%+ relative; Oracle-GT [T] 46.59% -> [T+H] 80.3%, ~70%+ relative), at the cost of higher Tool Hallucination and truncation risk. (3) Oracle upper bounds: GT+random tools vs only-GT tools (TA 77.53% vs 80.3% at [T+H]), quantifying headroom of TR-based planners vs oracle retrieval. The Recall@K of the retriever correlates with downstream Tool Accuracy (BM25 < SS < PTR).
- **evaluation decoupling**: Yes -- intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@K, Table 1) are reported separately from end-to-end planning metrics (TA/TH/EM/RLSum, Table 2), and the paper explicitly correlates retrieval recall with downstream tool accuracy.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both, partially: outcome-style plan metrics (EM, ROUGE-LSum over full predicted output incl. parameters) plus process-oriented per-step tool-selection quality (Tool Accuracy, Tool Hallucination) and step-wise retrieval Recall@K. Planning is evaluated on unrolled per-step prompts rather than a fully executed end-to-end trajectory.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> ProTIP is positioned as lightweight: a fine-tuned BERT-base-uncased bi-encoder that avoids expensive LLM (ChatGPT) task decomposition at inference, while outperforming the LLM-augmented TD baseline. Planner fine-tuning is resource-heavy: each configuration needs 8 A100 GPUs on AWS; context window 2048 tokens; ~12.3% of train and ~12.25% of test inputs exceed 2048 tokens causing truncation. No explicit latency/API-cost numbers reported.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Planner context window = 2048 tokens. Top-k fixed at K=10 (chosen to balance the 2048-token budget against max plan length p<=6), with p ground-truth tools plus (K-p) random/retrieved tools per step during training; Recall@K reported for K=6,10,15,20. Inputs exceeding 2048 tokens are truncated.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Uses (does not construct) ToolBench: an LLM(ChatGPT)-synthesized instruction-tuning dataset, 16,000 tools / 49 categories / ~27,000 requests, with tool and plan labels. The authors note ToolBench is susceptible to hallucinated tool annotations and perform cleaning (removing imaginary-tool requests, manual correction), yielding ~25,124 train / 268 test points. Best-system (Oracle, only-GT, [T+H]) Tool Accuracy ~80.3%, signaling substantial difficulty for TR-based planners (best non-oracle TA 36.49%).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Word/embedding-space arithmetic and analogy regularities (Mikolov et al. 2013; Pennington et al. 2014 GloVe; Levy & Goldberg 2014); contrastive loss for metric learning (Hadsell et al. 2006); dense dual-encoder retrieval GTR-T5-XL (Ni et al. 2021) and BM25 (Robertson et al. 1995); BERT-base-uncased encoder; ToolBench / ToolLLM (Qin et al. 2023b); OpenLLaMA-7B-v2 (Geng & Liu 2023 / LLaMA Touvron et al. 2023) planner; Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Lewis et al. 2021); Decomposed Prompting (Khot et al. 2022).
- **contrasts with**:
> Single-step full-query tool retrieval (cannot model inter-tool dependency) and explicit task-decomposition (TD) retrieval -- in particular ChatGPT-based TD (requires subtask-tool atomicity alignment, costly LLM rewrites, operates in text space susceptible to OOV/semantic issues). Also contrasts with Gorilla (Patil et al. 2023) and ToolLLM/ToolBench retrieval as standard tool-retrieval baselines.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use). Early (Dec 2023) step-wise / progressive tool-retrieval method: introduces per-subtask progressive tool retrieval via contrastive embedding-space query transformation, sitting in the lineage between single-step and explicit-task-decomposition tool retrieval, and a precursor to later tool-dependency-aware and graph-based tool-retrieval work.

**Other Info**

- **how retrieved used note**: Retrieved tools are placed in the LLM planner prompt for per-step API selection; ProTIP's embedding transformation conditions retrieval on execution history.

### 95. RestGPT: Connecting Large Language Models with Real-World RESTful APIs

2023  ·  arXiv 2306.06624  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.06624)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2023
- **venue**: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2306.06624, cs.CL). Submitted 11 Jun 2023 (v1), last revised 27 Aug 2023 (v2, which adds RestBench). DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2306.06624. No peer-reviewed conference/journal venue identified; it remains an arXiv preprint.
- **authors affiliation**:
> Yifan Song, Weimin Xiong, Dawei Zhu, Wenhao Wu, Han Qian, Mingbo Song, Hailiang Huang (Peking University), Cheng Li, Ke Wang, Rong Yao, Ye Tian (Huawei Technologies), Sujian Li (Peking University, corresponding author). Primary affiliation: School of Computer Science, Peking University (PKU-TANGENT lab), with Huawei Technologies. {yfsong, lisujian}@pku.edu.cn.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.06624
- **code url**: https://github.com/Yifan-Song793/RestGPT (MIT license; project page https://restgpt.github.io/). Built on LangChain; prompts inspired by the LangChain OpenAPI agent.
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/Yifan-Song793/RestGPT (1.4k stars, 16 commits, last meaningful commit 2023; not a continuously-updated leaderboard. Also hosts the RestBench datasets under /datasets and OAS specs under /specs).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> tool-use (LLM agent calling real-world RESTful APIs) with strong planning/decision-making component; touches web-service control and code (the parser generates Python parsing code). Builds an autonomous agent that controls real-world applications (movie database, music player) via RESTful APIs.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent, online (test-time) tool-use: given a complex natural-language user instruction, the agent must decompose it into sub-tasks and select/execute the correct sequence of real RESTful API endpoints (which follow the OpenAPI Specification / Swagger and return JSON), parsing responses to feed the next step. Closed-source LLMs (text-davinci-003 primary; also ChatGPT, Llama2-13B, Vicuna-13B) are used purely via prompting with in-context examples; no training/fine-tuning of the LLM or any retriever. The agent interacts with LIVE APIs (TMDB movie database, Spotify music player), so it must be robust to real API feedback, errors, and unforeseen situations. Supervision: none for the model; evaluation uses human-annotated gold API solution paths. The challenge is API understanding under a limited context window (cannot fit all API docs), planning under inter-API dependencies, parameter formulation, and parsing lengthy/complex JSON responses.
- **what is retrieved**:
> tools / docs: real-world RESTful API endpoints and their OpenAPI Specification (OAS) documentation. The API Selector 'retrieves' (selects) which endpoint(s) to call for the current sub-task by reading endpoint names+descriptions of all available APIs; the Caller then loads the full detailed OAS doc of the chosen endpoint(s); the Parser reads the OAS response schema.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus: a fixed set of real-world RESTful API endpoints described by their OpenAPI Specification (TMDB 54 / Spotify 40 endpoints in RestBench v2). The store of API documentation is external and static (not an agent-written growing episodic memory); selection/retrieval is performed online over this fixed API set.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Completeness of a minimal multi-API solution path rather than a fixed top-k ranking: the goal across a full instruction is to recover the complete (minimal) sequence of API endpoints (the gold solution path, scored by Correct Path rate as a subsequence match). At each individual step the API selector picks the needed API(s) (one or a few) for the current sub-task; there is no fixed-k retrieved set and no precision/recall@k ranking objective. The headline objective is end-to-end task completion via the correct ordered set of APIs.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: [Retrieve: partial (LLM-as-retriever API selection over endpoint descriptions, not retrieval of prior solved cases), Reuse: no, Revise: partial (online re-planning via 'continue' feedback revises the plan, but not a retrieved case), Retain: no]. Not a case-based-reasoning system.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False: the paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner. It is a coarse-to-fine online planning tool-use agent over RESTful APIs.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> tool-API endpoint (a single RESTful API endpoint, e.g. GET /movie/{movie_id}/credits) is the retrievable/selectable unit. Its associated documentation is the OAS entry (API path, description, request method, parameter list, response schema, response example, errors). The API selector keys on endpoint name + description; the caller then consumes the full per-endpoint OAS document.
- **index source**:
> Static corpus, offline-curated: the authors filter the official OAS of each application down to a fixed set of commonly-used endpoints (TMDB 54, Spotify 40 in RestBench v2; v1 used the full 135 TMDB / 71 Spotify endpoints). The retrievable store of API endpoints/docs is built once and does not grow at test time. The underlying applications are live (real API calls return real, changing data), but the API index itself is static.
- **retriever type**:
> LLM-as-retriever: API selection is done by an LLM (the API Selector module) that reads the endpoint names and descriptions of all available APIs and chooses the appropriate endpoint(s) for the current natural-language sub-task. It is NOT a BM25/dense/learned embedding retriever; no trained retrieval model is used. Table 1 of the paper marks its API use as 'API selection with retrieval' but the realized mechanism is prompted-LLM selection over the full API-description list.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> none: the API selector LLM is used off-the-shelf via prompting with a few in-context examples; there is no contrastive training, no LM-feedback fine-tuning, no RL, and no learned retrieval policy. Selection quality comes entirely from the frozen LLM's text comprehension of endpoint descriptions plus the coarse-to-fine prompt design.
- **query construction**:
> Two-level, thought-conditioned: (1) the Planner produces a high-level natural-language sub-task p_t conditioned on the user query q and the history of prior NL plans and execution results (p_1,r_1,...,p_{t-1},r_{t-1}); (2) this NL sub-task is used as the query to the API Selector, which maps it to a finer API calling plan a_t (conditioned also on prior execution results / background such as resolved ids). No embedding query vector is built; the 'query' is the natural-language sub-task plus accumulated background context.
- **query granularity**: step/sub-task level (online, per iteration) and effectively two-level: a coarse NL sub-task query (planner) refined into a finer API-selection query (API selector). Retrieval/selection happens once per planning step within the iterative plan-and-execute loop, not once at t=0.
- **when to retrieve**:
> iterative (online): API selection occurs at every planning step in the coarse-to-fine online plan-and-execute loop until the planner emits an 'end' signal. The planner can also emit a 'continue' signal that triggers re-selection of a new API plan for the same sub-task based on the latest execution result. Selection is thus interleaved with execution rather than one-shot.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Agent/planner-driven schedule: retrieval (API selection) is triggered each step by the planner generating a new NL sub-task; a special 'continue' signal (planner judging the current executor output has not fulfilled the sub-task) re-triggers selection of a new API plan, and an 'end' signal terminates the loop. The trigger is the planner's LLM-judged progress/feedback state, not a token-confidence, attention-uncertainty, learned complexity classifier, or reflection-token mechanism.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Progressive disclosure / content separation plus response distillation: (1) only the chosen endpoint's full OAS document is loaded for the caller (docs for non-selected APIs are filtered out to fit the context window); (2) the Parser generates Python code from the OAS response schema to extract just the required fields from lengthy JSON responses (with a direct-LLM-parse backup if the code errors), distilling the API response into a short natural-language execution result returned to the planner. This is decompose-then-load and reason-in-response-schema distillation rather than rerank/compress of retrieved candidates.
- **tool document engineering**:
> API/tool descriptions are taken from the OpenAPI Specification (OAS / Swagger) and split by field across modules: the API selector consumes endpoint names + short descriptions, the caller consumes the full per-endpoint doc (path, parameters, request body), and the parser consumes the response schema. The authors curate/filter the official OAS to a commonly-used subset, but do not perform synthetic-query augmentation, summary expansion, weighted-field embeddings, or instruction-tuned tool embeddings; documentation is used largely as-is (raw OAS) and routed by field.
- **index content separation**:
> Yes, central design: a lightweight retrievable index (endpoint names + descriptions seen by the API selector) is separated from heavy content loaded on demand (the caller loads the full OAS doc only for endpoints in the current API plan; the parser loads the response schema). This OAS-field-routed progressive disclosure is explicitly motivated by the limited LLM context window so the framework can scale to 100+ APIs.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Integration protocol is RESTful (HTTP GET/POST/PUT/DELETE/PATCH over URIs, via the Python Requests library), with API definitions standardized through the OpenAPI Specification (OAS/Swagger). This enables plug-and-play connection to any RESTful application. The API index is static per scenario (curated OAS subset); there is no automatic live CRUD synchronization of the index, no RapidAPI integration, and no MCP (predates MCP).
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> Implicit/handled by online planning rather than an explicit dependency model: inter-API dependencies (e.g., output id of one call feeding the in-path parameter of the next, such as getting a user_id before creating a playlist for that user) are resolved by the iterative coarse-to-fine planner+executor passing accumulated 'background' results forward. The paper's case study highlights that offline/ReAct baselines fail precisely because they ignore such dependencies, whereas RestGPT's online planning respects them. There is NO explicit dependency graph, bipartite KG, or dependency-aware reranker; dependencies are managed via context/state carried across steps.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> prompt augmentation within an agentic plan-and-execute loop: the selected endpoint's OAS documentation grounds the Caller's prompt to formulate correct parameters/request body and call the live API; the response schema grounds the Parser's code generation; the distilled execution result is fed back to the Planner as natural-language context to plan the next step. No training signal and no latent-token injection; retrieval is used purely as in-context grounding.
- **planning integration**:
> retrieve(select)-then-execute interleaved per step inside an iterative coarse-to-fine online planning loop: Planner generates a coarse NL sub-task -> API Selector maps it to a finer API plan (the selection step) -> Executor (Caller+Parser) calls the API and returns a parsed result -> Planner re-plans the next sub-task online from feedback. 'Continue'/'end' control signals govern re-selection and termination. Not a one-shot exemplar, MCTS/tree search, or plan-then-execute offline scheme; it is a per-step coarse-to-fine plan/select/act/feedback loop.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> per-sub-task / per-planning-step (which corresponds to per-tool-call or per-few-tool-calls within the rollout): API selection and execution are interleaved with the planner's reasoning at each step, with possible intra-sub-task re-selection on a 'continue' signal. Coarser than per-token; finer than per-answer.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> N/A (not framed as case-based reasoning). The closest analogue is execution-feedback-driven online re-planning: when an API call result is judged insufficient, the planner issues 'continue' and the API selector regenerates the API plan from the latest feedback. This adapts the PLAN, not a retrieved prior case.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Raw OpenAPI Specification documentation injected as prompt context: endpoint name+description (for selection), full endpoint doc with parameters and request body (for the caller), and response schema (for the parser). Surface form is structured/raw API documentation text, not a distilled strategy, free-text workflow, executable skill, or latent token.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw documentation of a concrete tool: each retrieved/selected unit is a single concrete API endpoint and its specification (a tool spec), not a distilled strategy, state-aware guideline, reusable workflow, procedural skill, or demonstration.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Coarse-to-fine online planning with execution feedback provides robustness: dividing planning (planner) from API selection (selector) lets the LLM handle one of API-understanding/selection/planning at a time; the planner monitors executor output via 'continue'/'end' signals to recover from incomplete/erroneous results; the parser has a direct-LLM-parse fallback when generated parsing code errors. The paper demonstrates robustness to NOISE APIs (adding distractor/noise endpoints from official TMDB barely degrades RestGPT while baselines deteriorate). No retriever-aware training, learned relevance evaluator, or distractor-aware SFT (everything is prompting-based).

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> none (no persistent learned memory). The system carries within-episode working context (prior NL plans p_1..p_{t-1} and execution results r_1..r_{t-1}) across steps to enable online planning, but this is transient per-instruction context, not an episodic store, skill library, workflow memory, graph, or latent memory that persists across tasks.
- **write back**:
> false: RestGPT does not write new experiences, cases, or skills into any persistent memory. Each instruction is solved fresh; nothing learned from one instruction is stored for future instructions. (Note: a baseline, Reflexion, does maintain reflective episodic memory across trials, but RestGPT itself does not.)
- **online growth**: false: the retrievable store (curated set of RESTful API endpoints / OAS docs) is fixed per scenario and does not grow during deployment. The agent does not add new tools, cases, or skills to its store at test time.
- **write back trigger**: never: there is no memory write-back mechanism. The only persistence within an episode is the running plan/result history used as context for the next planning step, which is discarded after the instruction completes.
- **failure experience usage**:
> N/A / none: failed API calls or wrong plans are handled within the current episode via online re-planning ('continue' signal) and the parser's fallback, but no failure (or success) experiences are stored or later retrieved. There is no success-only vs success+failure memory; nothing is retained across instructions.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A: no stored memory entries exist to mutate. Within an episode the context is append-only (each step's plan and result is appended to the running history), but there is no cross-episode memory to update, dedup, refine, or prune.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No: API selection is a frozen prompted-LLM decision, not a learned/RL-optimized retrieval or case-selection policy. There is no M-MDP, soft Q-learning, value function, or trained ranker; selection is LLM-as-retriever over endpoint descriptions.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No: single-agent system with private within-episode context; no memory or experience sharing across multiple agents or heterogeneous frameworks. (RestGPT is itself plug-and-play across RESTful applications, but that is tool/API portability, not shared experience.)

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> RestBench (introduced by this paper): two real-world scenarios - TMDB movie database (54 commonly-used API endpoints; 100 test instructions; gold solution-path lengths 1-4, avg 2.3) and Spotify music player (40 endpoints; 57 test instructions; lengths 1-4, avg 2.6), each with 10 development instructions. Human-annotated instructions with gold API solution paths. (Paper v1 reported the full OAS scale of 135 TMDB / 71 Spotify endpoints; v2 RestBench uses the filtered 54 / 40 subsets.) Plus an auxiliary noise-API scaling experiment: 10 hand-picked TMDB APIs + 15 instructions, with increasing numbers of added noise APIs.
- **benchmark family**:
> tool (tool/API-use agent benchmark over real RESTful APIs). RestBench is a real-application RESTful-API tool-use benchmark with human-annotated gold solution paths, distinct from synthetic tool benchmarks; it is an early member of the tool-use benchmark family alongside API-Bank and ToolBench/ToolLLM.
- **baselines**:
> Four planning/tool baselines, all equipped with RestGPT's proposed API executor for fair comparison and all run with text-davinci-003: (1) Offline introspective method (plan-then-execute, as in HuggingGPT/Chameleon); (2) DEPS (Describe, Explain, Plan and Select; max 10 steps); (3) ReAct (interleaved reasoning+acting); (4) Reflexion (verbal reflection in episodic memory, max 2 trials). Plus internal ablations (w/o Planner = ReAct + executor; w/o Parser) and base-LLM variants (ChatGPT/gpt-3.5-turbo-0301, Llama2-13B-chat, Vicuna-13B-v1.5).
- **key metrics**:
> Success Rate (%, human-judged whether the result fulfills the query), Correct Path rate (CP, %; model's API-call path contains the gold path as a subsequence), and Delta Solution Length (mean number of EXTRA API calls beyond gold for successfully completed instructions; lower/closer-to-0 is better, measures planning efficiency).
- **headline result**:
> On RestBench with text-davinci-003, RestGPT achieves 75.0% Success / 79.0% CP / +0.55 Delta Solution Length on TMDB and 72.7% Success / 74.5% CP / +0.25 on Spotify, outperforming the best baseline Reflexion (TMDB 52.0% Success / 59.0% CP; Spotify 59.6% / 61.4%) and ReAct (TMDB 44.0% / 57.0%; Spotify 54.5% / 49.1%), with the smallest Delta Solution Length (most efficient planning).
- **ablations**:
> (1) Remove Planner (= ReAct equipped with the proposed executor): large drop to TMDB 44.0% Success / 57.0% CP, Spotify 54.5% / 49.1% - shows current LLMs cannot simultaneously plan, understand and select APIs, so the coarse-to-fine planner is the key driver. (2) Remove schema-based Parser (LLM directly parses raw JSON): drop to TMDB 46.0% Success / 53.0% CP, Spotify 47.3% / 52.7% - the OAS-schema-grounded code parser materially helps comprehension of complex responses. (3) Base-LLM swap: ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo) slightly worse than text-davinci-003 (TMDB 68.0% / 65.0%; Spotify 69.1% / 72.3%; ChatGPT over-plans/too verbose); Llama2-13B fails completely (0.0% on both, cannot follow the prompts); Vicuna-13B partially works (TMDB 9.0% / 15.0%; Spotify 12.7% / 20.6%). (4) Scaling analyses: success rate degrades with longer gold paths but RestGPT stays >40% at gold length 4 while all baselines collapse; adding noise APIs barely affects RestGPT while baselines deteriorate (robustness/extensibility). (5) Error breakdown: most errors arise in the planning stage (planner losing track / early exit, and API selector picking wrong APIs or hallucinating in-path parameters).
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Partial: Correct Path rate is a path/selection-level (intrinsic-ish) metric reported separately from human-judged Success Rate (end-to-end outcome), and Delta Solution Length separately measures planning efficiency; the gap (CP slightly above Success) is interpreted as correct plans that fail at execution. However, no standalone retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG) are reported, since selection is LLM-driven rather than ranked.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both: outcome via human-judged Success Rate, plus process-level metrics - Correct Path rate (whether the intermediate API-call trajectory matches the gold solution path as a subsequence), Delta Solution Length (planning efficiency / extra calls), and a per-module error breakdown (planner vs API selector vs caller vs parser).
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Planning efficiency reported via Delta Solution Length (extra API calls beyond gold): RestGPT is most efficient (TMDB +0.55, Spotify +0.25) vs e.g. Reflexion (+1.37 / +1.68) and Offline (+1.52 / +1.10); the case study shows RestGPT solving a task in 4 API calls vs ReAct's 6. Max generation length 256, temperature 0. No explicit dollar/API-cost, wall-clock latency, or token-count numbers are reported.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Variable, budget-driven selection rather than fixed-k: the API selector picks the one-or-few endpoints needed for the current sub-task; to respect the limited LLM context window the framework filters API docs so only endpoints in the current API plan a_t have their full OAS loaded into the caller (progressive disclosure). Generation capped at 256 tokens. The number of selected/called APIs per instruction is set by the plan (gold avg 2.3-2.6; RestGPT adds ~0.25-0.55 extra), not a preset k.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> RestBench size: TMDB 54 APIs / 100 test + 10 dev instructions (gold path lengths 1-4, avg 2.3); Spotify 40 APIs / 57 test + 10 dev instructions (lengths 1-4, avg 2.6). Construction: bottom-up, human-curated - 6 NLP-expert annotators brainstorm realistic instructions over different API combinations and annotate gold API solution paths; 2 additional experts verify solvability and path correctness. Answer verifiability: API solution paths are largely stable so correctness is checked by gold-path-as-subsequence (Correct Path rate); because some instructions are time-dependent, final-answer success is judged by humans (Success Rate). Difficulty signal: best baselines reach only ~52-60% Success while all baselines fail at gold-path length 4; RestGPT reaches 72.7-75% Success and stays >40% at length 4.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Coarse-to-fine online planning over an LLM agent built on LangChain (prompts inspired by the LangChain OpenAPI agent). Conceptually builds on ReAct (interleaved reasoning+acting), DEPS (interactive planning), Reflexion (feedback/reflection), and the offline plan-then-execute introspective method (Tool Learning with Foundation Models / HuggingGPT / Chameleon). Uses the OpenAPI Specification (Swagger) as the API-documentation standard and shares the autonomous-agent spirit of AutoGPT.
- **contrasts with**:
> Tool-augmented LLMs limited to a small set of specially-designed tools and inflexible planning: Toolformer, Visual ChatGPT, ViperGPT (offline program plans), HuggingGPT and Chameleon (offline natural-language plan-then-execute over fixed model/tool sets), API-Bank, GPT4Tools, and Gorilla (large API set but single-call, no online planning). RestGPT contrasts these with (a) standardized RESTful/OAS integration and plug-and-play extensibility to 100+ real APIs, and (b) an online coarse-to-fine plan-with-feedback loop instead of offline/static or pure-ReAct planning.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use): an LLM-agent that selects and executes real-world RESTful API endpoints via online coarse-to-fine planning, with retrieval realized as LLM-as-retriever API selection over OAS endpoint descriptions and progressive-disclosure document loading. Sits between single-call API-grounding work (Gorilla) and large-scale tool-retrieval/agent benchmarks (API-Bank, ToolLLM/ToolBench, ToolRet); introduces RestBench as an early real-RESTful-API agent benchmark and emphasizes online planning + inter-API dependency handling over static tool retrieval.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- index_structure_topology
- reranking

<a id="item-colt"></a>
### 96. COLT (COllaborative Learning-based Tool Retrieval)

2024  ·  CIKM 2024  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.16089)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: CIKM 2024 (Proceedings of the 33rd ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management, pp. 1930-1940); arXiv:2405.16089 (v1 May 2024, v2 Jul 2024)
- **authors affiliation**:
> Changle Qu, Sunhao Dai, Jun Xu, Ji-Rong Wen (Gaoling School of Artificial Intelligence, Renmin University of China); Xiaochi Wei, Shuaiqiang Wang, Dawei Yin (Baidu Inc.); Hengyi Cai (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences). Corresponding/lead institution: Renmin University of China.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.16089
- **code url**: https://github.com/quchangle1/COLT (also HuggingFace https://huggingface.co/Tool-COLT for processed ToolBench data and first-stage checkpoints; ToolLens dataset released in the repo)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: tool-use (tool retrieval for tool-augmented LLMs); information retrieval (cs.IR / cs.CL)
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-step tool retrieval for tool-augmented LLMs: given a (typically short, multifaceted) user query and a large static tool set, retrieve a top-K subset of tools so that the LLM can answer. Supervision is available (query-to-ground-truth-tool-set labels) and the retriever is trained in two supervised stages (semantic learning then graph collaborative learning). It is not an interactive agent loop; retrieval happens once per query before LLM tool use. Single-agent. The work emphasizes recovering the COMPLETE set of diverse tools a multifaceted query needs rather than ranking similar tools.
- **what is retrieved**: tools (tool/API descriptions). Each tool is a (tool, description) pair; ground truth for a query is a small complete set of 1-4 collaborative tools.
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus of tools/APIs (a fixed tool set of size N, e.g. 464 tools for ToolLens). No agent-written growing memory; the retrievable store is frozen after offline training.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Completeness-oriented: the explicit goal is to recover the complete minimal set of multiple diverse collaborative tools a query needs (multi-tool completeness), not a fixed semantic top-k of similar tools. The paper introduces the COMP@K metric measuring whether the full ground-truth tool set is contained in the top-K, and a list-wise multi-label loss that treats the whole ground-truth tool set as one entity. Output is still a top-K list (K in {3,5}), but optimized for set completeness.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based reasoning method; only Retrieve-like behavior, no Reuse/Revise/Retain of cases)
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is a graph-collaborative-learning dense tool retriever.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: tool-API (a single tool described by its textual description). Ground-truth target is a complete set of such tool-API units (a 'scene' = the group of collaborative tools for a query).
- **index source**: Static corpus: a fixed tool set indexed offline. Query/tool/scene embeddings are induced offline via two-stage training (PLM semantic fine-tuning + LightGCN graph collaborative learning on training-set bipartite graphs); no online/test-time growth of the store.
- **index structure topology**:
> Graph-structured: three bipartite graphs among queries, scenes, and tools - Query-Scene (Q-S), Query-Tool (Q-T), and Scene-Tool (S-T). A 'scene' node aggregates the ground-truth tool set of a query, giving a hierarchical query->scene->tool topology that captures high-order inter-tool collaborative relationships. Underlying tool embeddings live in a flat dense vector space; the collaborative structure is the bipartite-graph overlay.
- **retriever type**: Hybrid learned dense retriever: PLM bi-encoder (dense) backbone + graph neural network (LightGCN) collaborative-learning layer on top. Model-agnostic over dense backbones (ANCE, TAS-B, coCondenser, Contriever). BM25 is used only as a baseline, not a component.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Learned/supervised in two stages: (1) Semantic learning - contrastive InfoNCE on query-positive-tool vs negative-tool pairs (similarity labels). (2) Collaborative learning - a list-wise multi-label loss (cross-entropy between ideal vs predicted selection distributions over a sampled tool list, treating the whole ground-truth set jointly) plus a cross-view InfoNCE contrastive loss aligning scene-centric and tool-centric query/scene representations. No RL, no LM-feedback reward; trained on ground-truth tool-set labels.
- **query construction**:
> Raw user query is encoded directly (mean-pooled PLM embedding) as the query key; no decomposition, expansion, or thought-conditioning. Collaborative refinement of the query representation is then done via graph message propagation (the query node aggregates from its scene/tool neighbors during training).
- **query granularity**: task-level (one query, one-shot at retrieval time). The dual-view design retrieves via two representations (scene-centric e_q^S and tool-centric e_q^T) but both are computed at the single-query level.
- **when to retrieve**: one-shot (single retrieval pass per query before LLM tool use; no iterative or uncertainty-triggered re-retrieval).
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule: retrieval is performed once per query unconditionally before tool use; there is no learned or confidence-based trigger.
- **reranking**:
> No separate cross-encoder reranking stage. Final ranking is by a combined matching score y_hat(q,t) = sim(e_q^S, e_t^T) + sim(e_q^T, e_t^T) that fuses the scene-centric and tool-centric views; this dual-view scoring is collaborative/scene-aware but is the primary scorer, not a second-stage reranker.
- **retrieved context refinement**: none (no post-retrieval distillation/compression of tool descriptions). Refinement happens in the representation space during training (graph propagation, contrastive alignment), not as a post-retrieval filtering step on the returned list.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Tool descriptions are used largely as raw text encoded by the PLM bi-encoder (mean pooling of the final layer). The novelty is not in document expansion but in the 'scene' abstraction: ground-truth tool sets are grouped into scene nodes whose embedding is the mean pooling of member-tool embeddings. ToolLens construction uses GPT-4 scene mining and query rewriting to build queries, but tool docs themselves are not synthetically augmented.
- **index content separation**: N/A (no progressive-disclosure / index-then-content separation; tool descriptions are the retrievable units directly).
- **dynamic index and protocol**: Static tool index (fixed tool set, e.g. 464 tools filtered from ToolBench/RapidAPI for ToolLens). No live CRUD synchronization or MCP integration; tools originate from the RapidAPI-based ToolBench collection but the retrieval index is offline/static.
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> Yes - this is the central contribution. COLT models inter-tool collaborative relationships (tools that must be used together to fully answer a multifaceted query) via the 'scene' concept and three bipartite graphs (Q-S, Q-T, S-T) with LightGCN message propagation, capturing high-order collaborative/dependency structure rather than treating tools independently. It models collaborative co-usage rather than explicit data-flow dependencies (output-of-A feeds B) or shared-auth prerequisites.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation: the retrieved top-K tools (their descriptions) are provided to the LLM, which then uses them to generate a response (validated in the downstream tool-learning study where retrieved top-3 tools feed GPT-4). The retriever itself is trained with the list-wise + contrastive objective; the retrieved tools are not adapted/revised before use.
- **planning integration**: retrieve-then-plan / one-shot at plan time: tools are retrieved once up front and supplied to the LLM, which then plans and acts with them. No interleaving of retrieval inside a planning/search loop; tool retrieval is a front-end module decoupled from the LLM's reasoning.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: per-answer (retrieval done once for the whole query/answer; not woven per CoT step or per tool call).
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (no case adaptation; retrieved tools are passed to the LLM as-is).
- **retrieved item representation**: Surface form injected to the LLM is the raw tool/API descriptions of the top-K retrieved tools (plus implicitly their callable signatures for downstream tool use). Internally tools are dense embeddings refined by graph collaborative learning.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Single tool/API (a concrete callable function with its description); the retrieval target is the complete set of such tools, conceptually grouped under a higher-level 'scene' abstraction during learning.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Indirect: the cross-view graph contrastive learning and list-wise multi-label loss promote balanced, scene-aware representations so that semantically-similar-but-redundant tools are not over-retrieved and complementary tools are recovered; semantic learning stage uses contrastive negatives. There is no explicit relevance-evaluator, self-reflection, or distractor-filtering module on the retrieved output.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (no episodic/skill/workflow memory; static tool corpus with learned embeddings).
- **write back**: False. The system does not store new experiences/cases; it is trained offline and the tool store is fixed at inference.
- **online growth**: No. The retrievable tool store and learned graphs are frozen after offline training; no growth during deployment.
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back mechanism).
- **failure experience usage**: N/A / success-only-style supervision: training uses ground-truth positive tool sets and (randomly sampled / contrastive) negative tools, but there is no storage or retrieval of failed execution experiences; failures are not used as a corrective memory.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (no stored memory entries to mutate; embeddings are fixed after training).
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Partially: retrieval is a learned model (trained dense + GNN retriever with list-wise/contrastive objectives) rather than off-the-shelf top-k similarity, but it is NOT an RL/Q-learning policy - it is a supervised ranking model. Selection at inference is still argtop-K over the learned matching score.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-retriever, single-agent setting; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> ToolLens (newly introduced; 18,770 queries, 464 tools, 1-3 tools/query); ToolBench subsets I2 (82,507 queries-ish stats: 74,257 train / 8,250 test, 11,473 tools, 2-4 tools/query) and I3 (21,361 train / 2,373 test, 1,419 tools, 2-4 tools/query). TOOLE is discussed as a prior dataset (used in dataset-quality comparison, not as a retrieval test set).
- **benchmark family**: tool (ToolBench / ToolLens) - tool retrieval benchmarks.
- **baselines**: BM25 (lexical); dense PLM retrievers ANCE, TAS-B, coCondenser (coCondensor), Contriever - each evaluated Zero-shot and +Fine-tune; COLT is applied on top of each dense backbone (+COLT). Backbone-size study spans BERT-mini to BERT-large.
- **key metrics**:
> Recall@K (R@K), NDCG@K (N@K) for K in {3,5}; and the newly proposed COMP@K (C@K) completeness metric = fraction of queries whose full ground-truth tool set is contained in the top-K. Further analysis also uses Recall@|N| and COMP@|N| (K set to the number of ground-truth tools). Downstream: GPT-4 pairwise Elo ratings over Coherence/Relevance/Comprehensiveness/Overall.
- **headline result**:
> On ToolLens, Contriever+COLT reaches R@3 93.64 / R@5 97.75 / N@3 94.53 / C@3 84.55 (vs Contriever+Fine-tune R@3 83.58 / C@3 59.46), i.e. ~+25 absolute on COMP@3. Most-cited headline: BERT-mini (11M) equipped with COLT outperforms BERT-large (340M, 30x larger) without COLT. Largest gains are on the COMP (completeness) metric across all backbones and datasets.
- **ablations**:
> Table 5 ablates four components on ToolLens and ToolBench(I3) using R@|N| and C@|N|: (1) w/o semantic learning -> catastrophic drop (e.g. ANCE+COLT C@|N| 78.36 -> 6.84), confirming semantic fine-tuning is the foundation; (2) w/o collaborative learning (semantic only) -> large drop (78.36 -> 49.01), showing graph collaborative learning drives completeness; (3) w/o list-wise learning (pairwise instead) -> notable drop (78.36 -> 52.68), showing list-wise multi-label loss is key to completeness; (4) w/o contrastive learning (no cross-view InfoNCE) -> drop (78.36 -> 63.87), especially impactful for Contriever. Also: model-size study (BERT-mini..BERT-large), per-tool-count subset analysis (gains largest for 3-4 tool queries), and hyperparameter analysis on tau, lambda, list length L.
- **evaluation decoupling**: Yes. Intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@K, NDCG@K, and the completeness metric COMP@K) are reported separately from the downstream end-to-end tool-learning quality (GPT-4 pairwise Elo on generated responses), explicitly decoupling retrieval quality from generation quality.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both: intrinsic retrieval-process quality (Recall/NDCG/COMP completeness of the retrieved tool set) plus downstream outcome quality of LLM responses (Elo over Coherence/Relevance/Comprehensiveness/Overall). The completeness metric itself is a process-quality measure of the retrieved set.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k: top-K with K in {3,5} for main retrieval evaluation, and K=|N| (number of ground-truth tools) in the further analysis. The downstream study uses top-3 retrieved tools fed to GPT-4. The list-wise loss samples a tool list of length L (containing N_q positives + L-N_q sampled negatives) during training. No adaptive/precision-driven variable-size selection at inference.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> ToolLens: 18,770 queries over 464 callable tools (filtered from ToolBench/RapidAPI, excluding auth/test tools), each query mapped to 1-3 verified tools; 10% held out as test (1,877 test queries). Constructed via a 5-step GPT-4 pipeline with human verification at each step: tool selection, scene mining, query generation, tool aggregation (multi-tool), and query rewriting - designed to produce concise, natural, multifaceted queries (verified superior to ToolBench/TOOLE by GPT-4 and human eval). ToolBench (I2, I3) reused as additional benchmarks. Best-system difficulty signal: on ToolLens COMP@3 only reaches ~84.55 (Contriever+COLT) and on ToolBench(I3) COMP@3 ~52, showing complete multi-tool retrieval remains hard.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Dense retrieval bi-encoders (ANCE, TAS-B, coCondenser, Contriever) and the BEIR framework for semantic learning; LightGCN graph collaborative filtering for the collaborative-learning stage; InfoNCE contrastive learning; ToolBench / RapidAPI tool collection for tools and as a benchmark. Tool-learning context: ToolLLaMA, ToolBench (Qin et al. 2023b).
- **contrasts with**:
> Standard semantic-matching dense tool retrievers that rank tools by query-description similarity (the paper argues these retrieve redundant/similar tools and miss complementary ones), BM25 lexical retrieval, and traditional retrieval metrics (Recall, NDCG) that ignore set completeness. Also contrasts with recommendation/semantic-search settings that select any relevant items without modeling collaborative tool utility.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use): tool retrieval line. A 2024 milestone reframing tool retrieval from per-tool semantic ranking to completeness/collaboration-oriented set recovery (introduces 'scene', bipartite-graph collaborative learning, the COMP@K metric, and the ToolLens benchmark); precursor to later dependency-aware / completeness-aware tool retrieval and to the authors' subsequent tool-learning survey work.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

<a id="item-pluto"></a>
### 97. PLUTO (Planning, Learning, and Understanding for TOols) - Plan-and-Retrieve (P&R) / Edit-and-Ground (E&G) tool retrieval

2024  ·  NAACL 2024 Findings  ·  [paper](https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-naacl.61.pdf)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: NAACL 2024 (pages 975-988, Mexico City, Mexico, June 2024); DOI 10.18653/v1/2024.findings-naacl.61. Preprint: arXiv:2404.00450 (v1 Mar 30 2024).
- **paper url**: https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-naacl.61/ (arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.00450)
- **code url**: https://github.com/tenghaohuang/PLUTo (Python; 3 stars, 4 commits, last updated Dec 2024; contains faiss_rm.py retriever, modules.py, descripton_optimization.py for E&G, DSP_functions.py).
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (the GitHub repo is a frozen code release, not a continuously-updated paper list or leaderboard; last commit Dec 2024).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: tool-use (tool retrieval for tool-augmented LLMs); also framed as LLM tool learning / NLP retrieval (cs.CL).
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-query tool retrieval for tool-augmented LLMs over a large static tool pool (ToolBench / RapidAPI, 3,000+ tools across 49 categories, intra-category setting). Given a complex multi-faceted user query and an index of human-written tool descriptions, the system must shortlist the COMPLETE set of relevant tools (multiple tools per query; average ground-truth solution-path length is 4 tools). Single-agent. The framework is execution-free at retrieval time (it does not actually run tools to verify, leveraging the LLM's internal world knowledge instead). It is evaluated in both a Non-Finetuned setting (off-the-shelf dense retriever) and a Finetuned setting (retriever fine-tuned with in-batch negatives on domain data). Supervision is available via ToolBench annotated solution paths used as ground truth. 500 user queries evaluated per setting.
- **what is retrieved**: tools (tool/API descriptions). Each retrievable unit is a tool description d(t); ground truth for a query is the complete set of tools on its solution path (avg ~4 tools).
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus of tool/API descriptions (a fixed ToolBench/RapidAPI tool index). However, the corpus is NOT immutable: the Edit-and-Ground paradigm rewrites (edits) under-informative tool descriptions during an offline optimization phase, so the retrievable store is a static tool set whose textual content is LLM-edited offline before inference. No agent-written episodic memory of past tasks; can be characterized as static-corpus with offline content editing (mildly HYBRID in that the index content is regenerated, not just indexed as-is).
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Completeness-oriented: the explicit goal is to recover the complete set of diverse, complementary tools a complex query needs (the paper stresses that one-time similarity retrieval 'falls short of retrieving diverse types of tools'). The query planner decomposes the query into n sub-queries and the final tool set is the UNION of per-sub-query shortlists (T = union of T_i), giving a variable-size, completeness-driven result rather than a fixed top-k of similar tools. Recall (over the full ground-truth tool set) is the primary metric. Internally a fixed top-5 candidate pool per sub-query is used before LLM selection.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based reasoning method; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain of past problem-solving cases - 'editing' here refers to tool-description optimization, not case adaptation).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is a plan-decompose + dense-retrieve + LLM-selection + tool-description-editing framework.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: tool-API (a single tool represented by its textual description d(t)). The retrieval target per query is the union of such tool units across decomposed sub-queries.
- **index source**:
> Static tool corpus indexed offline (ToolBench/RapidAPI tool descriptions encoded by a dense encoder into a tool index corpus D). Construction is hybrid in content: the base index is offline, but tool descriptions are offline-edited/enriched by the Edit-and-Ground optimizer (multi-round, dev-set-recall-gated) before inference; the index is then frozen at test time.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat dense vector index of tool-description embeddings (dense encoder + FAISS, per repo faiss_rm.py). No dependency graph or explicit hierarchy is used in retrieval; the ToolBench intra-category structure provides a category grouping of tools but PLUTO retrieves over a flat embedding space.
- **retriever type**:
> Hybrid: a dense neural retriever (DPR / Contriever bi-encoder) for first-stage candidate shortlisting, followed by LM-likelihood re-ranking and an LLM-as-selector (predictor) stage. BM25 is used only as a baseline, not as a PLUTO component. So PLUTO = dense retrieval + LM-likelihood scoring + LLM-based predictor (retriever-agnostic / plug-and-play over DPR or Contriever).
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Two modes. Non-Finetuned: off-the-shelf dense retriever (no training, 'none'). Finetuned: contrastive in-batch-negatives training (DPR-style cross-entropy/softmax over a positive tool d_j+ vs n sampled negative tools d_ij-) on domain query-tool pairs (similarity labels). The LM-likelihood re-ranker and the LLM planner/predictor/optimizer are prompted (no gradient training; they leverage the LLM's pretrained world knowledge). No RL / preference / value-based learning signal.
- **query construction**:
> Decomposed sub-queries: an LLM-based query planner autoregressively decomposes the complex user query Q into focused sub-queries q_1...q_n. Generation uses 'furthest reasoning with plan assessment' (Zhu et al. 2023): at each step a batch of hypothesis sub-queries is generated, clustered with prior sub-queries via K-means (TF-IDF vectors), and the sub-query most distinct from previous ones is selected, encouraging diverse, non-redundant sub-queries. Each sub-query is then encoded as the dense retrieval key. Tool-side keys are the (E&G-enriched) tool descriptions.
- **query granularity**:
> Sub-task / step-level: the query is decomposed and retrieval is performed per sub-query q_i, then unioned. This is a decomposition-driven multi-query retrieval (not a single task-level one-shot query, and not per-token); effectively trajectory/plan-level decomposition into sub-query steps.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Iterative / adaptive within an execution-free planning loop: the planner autoregressively emits sub-queries and retrieves per sub-query, evaluating after each whether the original query Q has been satisfied (self-evaluation) and stopping when the goal is judged met. So retrieval is interleaved across the auto-generated sub-query sequence rather than a single one-shot pass, but it is execution-free (no tool execution between steps).
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Planner self-assessment: after generating each sub-query q_t and its shortlist, the LLM planner evaluates (based on the current planning history) whether the original query Q has been satisfactorily achieved; if not, it proposes the next sub-query q_{t+1}, triggering another retrieval. The loop is agent-initiated/LLM-judged completion rather than a fixed schedule, token-confidence, or learned-classifier trigger.
- **reranking**:
> Yes - LM-likelihood re-ranking: the first-stage dense candidate pool T_i' for each sub-query is re-ranked by an LM-likelihood score LM-likelihood(q_i, t_j) = -log P(q_i, d(t_j)). The top-5 re-ranked tools are then passed to an LLM-based predictor that selects the final relevant subset T_i. This is a generative-LM-scoring re-ranker (not a trained cross-encoder), followed by LLM selection.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Rerank + LLM selection/filtering: candidate tools are LM-likelihood re-ranked, truncated to top-5 per sub-query, then an LLM predictor filters to the relevant subset (distractor filtering by the LLM). Separately, the Edit-and-Ground paradigm refines the tool DESCRIPTIONS themselves (offline enrichment) before they ever enter retrieval, which is an index-side refinement rather than a post-retrieval one.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Central contribution (Edit-and-Ground). Tool descriptions are LLM-rewritten/expanded BEFORE indexing: an Evaluator flags under-informative tools (those whose retrieval failure count exceeds a threshold on dev set); an Optimizer then prompts an LLM with (1) the base description d(t), (2) a batch of entity-filtered relevant user queries U (LLM removes specific entities to avoid overfitting to a local batch), and (3) LLM-generated reasons R explaining why the tool is helpful for those queries, producing an enriched description d'(t) = E&G(t, d(t), U, R). Done in multiple rounds, keeping the new description only if dev-set recall improves. This is query-grounded synthetic description expansion (expanded summaries grounded in user scenarios), substantially lengthening abstract human docstrings (see Table 4 examples: Magisto, Bing Image Search, LANDR Mastering).
- **index content separation**: N/A / No explicit progressive-disclosure index-vs-content split (the enriched tool description serves as both the retrievable key and the content). Tools are still represented by full (enriched) descriptions.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Static tool index sourced from ToolBench / RapidAPI Hub (real-world RESTful APIs). No live CRUD synchronization, no MCP; downstream execution-pass-rate evaluation does call real RapidAPI RESTful APIs, but the retrieval index is offline/static. The paper motivates handling 'ever-evolving tool environments' but does not implement a live-synced index.
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> Partial / implicit. PLUTO targets multi-tool completeness for complex queries (tools that jointly address a query) via query decomposition and union of per-sub-query results, but it does NOT explicitly model inter-tool data-flow dependencies (output-of-A feeds B), shared auth, prerequisites, or a tool dependency graph. Complementarity is captured through diverse sub-query decomposition rather than an explicit dependency model.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation for downstream tool use: the final shortlisted tool set T (union over sub-queries) is provided to an LLM (ChatGPT) which then executes/uses the tools to address the query (validated via ToolBench execution pass rate against real RESTful APIs). Within PLUTO itself, retrieved candidates are consumed by the LLM predictor for selection and by the planner for next-step planning. Tool descriptions are also (offline) edited to improve retrieval, an index-side use of the LLM.
- **planning integration**:
> Plan-then-retrieve interleaved in a feedback loop: an LLM query planner decomposes the query, retrieval is performed per sub-query, the planner selects suitable tools from the retrieved set, evaluates their effectiveness, and proposes the next action - a dynamic feedback loop interlinking retrieval with refinement, evaluation, and planning. It is execution-free (no real tool execution during planning, unlike ReAct). Retrieval is woven per sub-query step within this planning loop.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-sub-query (per planning step): retrieval is interleaved at the granularity of each autoregressively-decomposed sub-query within the plan, not per-CoT-token, per-sentence, or per executed tool-call (execution-free).
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A for case adaptation. The only 'adaptation' is index-side: the Edit-and-Ground Optimizer adapts/rewrites tool descriptions via LLM-prompted enrichment grounded in user queries and generated reasons (a description-optimization adaptation, not retrieved-case reuse).
- **retrieved item representation**: Surface form injected is the raw (LLM-enriched) tool/API descriptions of the shortlisted tools, plus their callable signatures for downstream execution. Internally tools are dense embeddings of these descriptions.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Single tool/API (a concrete callable function with its - now LLM-enriched - description). The query side is abstracted into sub-tasks, but the retrieved unit itself stays at the individual-tool level.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Several: (1) furthest-reasoning plan assessment (K-means-based selection of the most distinct sub-query) enforces goal-oriented, non-redundant decompositions and guards against faulty planning loops / hallucinating non-existent tools; (2) LM-likelihood re-ranking plus an LLM predictor that filters the top-5 candidates to relevant tools (rejecting surface-level-similar distractors - e.g. avoiding the 'all tools contain the word Love' failure of plain similarity retrieval); (3) Edit-and-Ground enrichment narrows the semantic gap between abstract human docstrings and user queries, reducing mismatch noise. No retriever-aware adversarial SFT or explicit reflection-token mechanism.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (no episodic/skill/workflow/graph memory; a static, offline-edited tool corpus). The only persistent artifact is the optimized tool-description store produced by E&G.
- **write back**:
> False for task experiences. The system does NOT store solved-task trajectories/cases. There is an offline 'write' of edited tool descriptions back into the tool index during the optimization phase, but this is index curation, not experiential memory write-back; no writes occur at inference.
- **online growth**: No. The tool store does not grow at deployment/test time; Edit-and-Ground description editing happens during an offline optimization phase and the (enriched) index is frozen at inference. No new tools or experiences are added online.
- **write back trigger**:
> For tool-description editing: dev-set-recall-gated / on-improvement-only - the Evaluator flags a tool as under-informative when its retrieval failure count exceeds a threshold, the Optimizer rewrites it, and the new description is committed only if dev-set retrieval recall improves over the previous round (otherwise the original is kept), across multiple rounds until a (loose, cost-bounded) stop criterion. For task/experience memory: never (no experiential write-back).
- **failure experience usage**:
> Yes, in a limited index-curation sense: retrieval FAILURE cases drive Edit-and-Ground - tools with retrieval failure counts above a threshold are selected for description optimization, and the LLM is prompted to reason about why a tool could be relevant to the failing queries. This uses retrieval failures to correct tool descriptions; it does not store failed task trajectories as retrievable negative experiences.
- **memory evolution update**:
> Refine-overwrite (for tool descriptions): under-informative descriptions are iteratively rewritten across rounds and overwritten only when dev-set recall improves (monotonic-improvement keep/revert), i.e. delta-refinement with a quality gate. No append-only experience log, dedup-merge, or forgetting of task memories (there is no task memory).
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No. Tool selection is not an RL/learned policy; it is dense similarity retrieval + LM-likelihood re-ranking + prompted LLM selection within a heuristic planning loop. The optional finetuning is supervised contrastive training of the dense retriever, not a learned retrieval/selection policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent, single-framework; the optimized tool index could in principle be reused, but no cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing is proposed or evaluated.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> ToolBench (Qin et al. 2023), intra-category setting, built on the RapidAPI Hub (3,000+ tools across 49 categories; annotated solution paths, avg length 4, used as ground truth). 500 user queries evaluated per setting. Downstream evaluation uses ToolBench's automatic execution pass rate against real-world RESTful APIs.
- **benchmark family**: tool (ToolBench - tool retrieval / tool-use benchmark).
- **baselines**:
> BM25 (lexical); ToolRetriever (the prior SOTA tool retriever from ToolBench/Qin et al. 2023, a DPR-based dense retriever) - reported with DPR and Contriever backbones, in both Non-Finetuned and Finetuned settings. PLUTO is applied on top of DPR and Contriever to show retriever-agnostic gains. Plan-and-Retrieve is also compared across LLM backbones (Llama2 vs ChatGPT variants).
- **key metrics**: Recall (Rec) over the ground-truth tool set; NDCG (relevance-graded, 0/1/2 human-annotated relevance scale); and downstream Pass Rate (ToolBench automatic execution metric against real RESTful APIs, using ChatGPT).
- **headline result**:
> On ToolBench intra-category, Non-Finetuned PLUTO with Contriever reaches Recall 46.57 / NDCG 82.93, outperforming the best baseline (Contriever 31.78 Rec) by +9.92 Recall points; Finetuned PLUTO with Contriever reaches Recall 48.47 / NDCG 84.73 (+5.7 Rec over the Contriever baseline 42.77). With DPR, PLUTO improves Recall from 19.58 (ToolRetriever non-finetuned) toward 36.65 (PLUTO+DPR non-finetuned). PLUTO significantly surpasses the previous SOTA (ToolRetriever) on both Recall and NDCG across settings.
- **ablations**:
> Component ablation (Table 2, Recall/NDCG, both settings): PLUTO-full 46.57/82.93 (NF), 48.47/84.73 (FT). Removing Edit-and-Ground (-w/o E&G) drops to 42.55/80.70 (NF) and 44.90/81.10 (FT), showing E&G's role in enhancing what is retrieved. Removing Plan-and-Retrieve (-w/o P&R) drops to 38.12/77.60 (NF) and 47.07/81.90 (FT); P&R matters most in the Non-Finetuned setting (largest Recall hit), highlighting its importance when the retriever is off-the-shelf. The full model combining both is consistently best, evidencing synergy. Additional studies: retriever-agnostic generalization across DPR and Contriever (Table 1); LLM-backbone generalization for P&R (Fig. 3, Llama2 vs ChatGPT both improve over baselines); qualitative tool-retrieval case studies (Table 3) and before/after E&G description examples (Table 4).
- **evaluation decoupling**: Yes. Intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall, NDCG) are reported separately from the downstream end-to-end execution Pass Rate, decoupling retrieval quality from tool-use task success.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Both: retrieval-process quality (Recall / NDCG of the retrieved tool set, with graded 0/1/2 human relevance for NDCG) plus downstream outcome quality (execution Pass Rate of actually addressing the user query via real RESTful API calls).
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Per-sub-query: a fixed top-5 re-ranked candidate pool (T'_{i,top-5}) is fed to the LLM predictor, which selects a relevant subset T_i; the final tool set is the union over the n sub-queries (variable, completeness-driven total size). Retrieval evaluation uses Recall/NDCG over the retrieved set. No fixed global top-k token budget is stated beyond the per-sub-query top-5 candidate cap.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Uses the existing ToolBench dataset (Qin et al. 2023) rather than introducing a new benchmark: 3,000+ real RapidAPI tools across 49 categories, multi-tool queries with annotated executed solution paths (avg length 4) taken as ground truth; PLUTO focuses on the high-quality intra-category subset and evaluates 500 queries per setting. NDCG relevance labels (0/1/2) were annotated by hired graduate students. Difficulty signal: best system (PLUTO+Contriever) reaches only ~46-48 Recall, indicating complete multi-tool retrieval over this large tool space remains hard.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Dense passage retrieval (DPR; Karpukhin et al. 2020) and Contriever (Izacard et al. 2022) as retriever backbones; LM-likelihood scoring (Song/RestGPT et al. 2023); furthest reasoning with plan assessment (Zhu et al. 2023) for sub-query decomposition; adaptive/active retrieval-augmented generation (FLARE - Jiang et al. 2023; Yoran et al. 2023 robustness to irrelevant context) for the adaptive planning idea; ToolBench / ToolLLM (Qin et al. 2023) for the tool set, benchmark, and the ToolRetriever SOTA baseline; tool-documentation insights (Hsieh et al. 2023) and LLM-as-optimizer (Yang et al. 2023) motivating Edit-and-Ground.
- **contrasts with**:
> Conventional one-time 'Retrieve-and-Read' tool retrieval relying solely on similarity matching (Gorilla/Patil et al. 2023; ToolLLM/Qin et al. 2023), which the paper argues retrieves surface-similar but functionally incomplete tools and cannot handle complex multi-tool queries; ReAct (Yao et al. 2022) and execution-based planning that run/verify tools at retrieval time (expensive); and approaches that finetune on static tool sets (brittle in evolving tool environments). PLUTO instead is execution-free, plan-driven, and edits tool descriptions.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use): tool-retrieval line. A 2024 work advancing tool retrieval from one-shot similarity matching toward (a) query-decomposition + iterative planning retrieval (Plan-and-Retrieve) and (b) LLM-based tool-documentation enrichment (Edit-and-Ground) to close the query-tool semantic gap. Sits alongside completeness/diversity-oriented tool retrieval (e.g. COLT) and tool-documentation works (Hsieh et al. 2023), and is a precursor to later query-planning + document-engineering tool-retrieval methods; builds on the ToolBench/ToolLLM ecosystem and adaptive-RAG ideas.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):
