<a id="item-ptr"></a>
### 98. PTR: Precision-driven Tool Recommendation for LLMs (paper title later revised to 'Task-Aligned Tool Recommendation for Large Language Models'; method still named PTR / Precision-driven Tool Recommendation)

2024  ·  IJCNLP-AACL 2025  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.09613)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**:
> IJCNLP-AACL 2025 Main (Findings/Main long paper track); ACL Anthology 2025.ijcnlp-long.110, pages 2023-2045; DOI 10.18653/v1/2025.ijcnlp-long.110; DBLP conf/ijcnlp/GaoZ25. Preprint arXiv:2411.09613 (v1 submitted 14 Nov 2024 as 'Precision-driven Tool Recommendation'; v2 revised 21 Nov 2025 renamed 'Task-Aligned Tool Recommendation for Large Language Models').
- **authors affiliation**: Hang Gao (Rutgers University; h.gao@rutgers.edu) and Yongfeng Zhang (Rutgers University; yongfeng.zhang@rutgers.edu).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.09613

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Tool-use: pre-execution tool-set recommendation for LLMs (recommend a precise, variable-size set of external tools/APIs to equip an LLM before it executes a query).
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-step, pre-execution tool recommendation (the system supplies a toolset before any tool is invoked, distinct from execution-time/iterative tool use). Single-agent, model-agnostic pipeline driven by an off-the-shelf unsupervised retriever plus a backbone LLM (open-mistral-7b / GPT-3.5-turbo / GPT-4o) prompted for matching and decomposition; no module is trained. The paper newly defines the 'tool recommendation' problem (Appendix A): given a tool set T and query Q with a ground-truth toolset T_ground subset of T, recommend T_recommend such that T_recommend = T_ground exactly (both quantity |T_recommend|=|T_ground| and identity), avoiding under-selection (omissions) and over-selection (redundant tools). Supervision: historical (query, tool-bundle) usage data D={(Q_i,B_i)} is available as a memory of past tool combinations; ground-truth toolsets exist for evaluation. Tests on 20% held-out splits of each dataset.
- **what is retrieved**: Tools / tool-API descriptions. Specifically: (stage 1) a historical tool bundle (a previously-used set of tools) most relevant to the query; (stage 3) individual tools drawn from the full tool set and from tools used in similar historical queries, to fill unsolved sub-problems.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> HYBRID leaning STATIC. The full available tool set T (tool descriptions, from MetaTool/OpenAI plugin list and ToolLens) is a static external corpus; additionally a store of historical tool-bundle usage D={(Q_i,B_i)} (past queries paired with the tool bundles used) is leveraged as an offline-curated experience/memory. This historical store is fixed/offline (not grown online during deployment), so retrieval grounds on a static tool corpus plus an offline-induced usage memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Precision-driven variable-size recommendation (the paper's central thesis). The objective is to recover the complete-yet-minimal ('minimal sufficient') toolset T_recommend = T_ground with matching cardinality, explicitly rejecting fixed top-k packaging. PTR dynamically grows/shrinks the toolset (delete redundant tools in stage 2, add tools for unsolved sub-problems in stage 3) so different queries get different numbers of tools (1-10). The new TRACC metric jointly rewards content sufficiency (intersection accuracy) and size fidelity (penalizes |set-size deviation|), unlike Recall@k/NDCG@k which assume k=|A| is known.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> Not framed as CBR. Loose mapping: [Retrieve: partial - retrieves a historical tool bundle and tools from similar past queries; Reuse: partial - reuses tools previously used in similar contexts (Historical Query Correlation view); Revise: yes - functional coverage mapping prunes/keeps tools and multi-view re-ranking adds tools, revising the bundle to fit the new query; Retain: no - nothing is written back to the historical store at test time]. N/A as a formal CBR work.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner; it frames the work as 'tool recommendation' (a recommendation problem for LLMs) using historical tool-bundle usage, retrieval, and multi-view re-ranking.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Two granularities: (1) tool-bundle / toolkit (a set of tools used together for a past query) in Tool Bundle Acquisition (stage 1); (2) single tool-API (an individual tool with its description) in Multi-view Based Re-ranking (stage 3). Historical queries are also retrieved as keys to surface their associated tools (Historical Query Correlation).
- **index source**:
> Hybrid, offline-constructed/static: (a) a static index over the full tool set T (tool descriptions) used for Direct Semantic Alignment and Contextual Tool Expansion; (b) an offline-curated store of historical (query, tool-bundle) usage D (the collection of unique tool bundles B and historical queries Q) used for Tool Bundle Acquisition and Historical Query Correlation. Not online/test-time-induced; the stores are frozen during evaluation.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat embedding/lexical similarity indices over tools and over historical queries, plus a metadata-keyed historical store (query -> tool bundle mapping). Tool bundles are implicit clusters/toolkits of co-used tools, but there is no explicit dependency graph or hierarchical category->tool taxonomy; co-usage synergy is captured statistically via historical bundles rather than a built graph.
- **retriever type**:
> Hybrid / pluggable off-the-shelf retrievers: sparse (BM25) or dense (Contriever, SBERT all-mpnet-base-v2, TAS-B, SimCSE) for stage-1 bundle acquisition and stage-3 similarity; the backbone LLM (open-mistral-7b / GPT-3.5-turbo / GPT-4o) acts as an LLM-based matcher/decomposer (functional coverage mapping) rather than as the core retriever. SimCSE + GPT-4o is the best configuration.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None (off-the-shelf, unsupervised). All retrievers are used zero-shot/unsupervised (BM25, Contriever, SBERT, TAS-B, SimCSE); none are fine-tuned for this task. The paper explicitly addresses 'potential performance issues of these models in zero-shot scenarios' by adding the LLM-driven matching and multi-view re-ranking stages rather than by training the retriever. The backbone LLM is also used without task-specific training (prompted).
- **query construction**:
> Multi-stage query forming. Stage 1: the raw query Q is matched against historical tool bundles. Stage 2 (Functional Coverage Mapping): the LLM decomposes Q into discrete key functionalities F={F_1..F_m}, matches each to tools, assesses completeness (Exact/Over/Partial solving), and emits unsolved sub-problems U={U_1..U_y} (extracted directly from Q without further decomposition, retaining query context). Stage 3: each unsolved sub-problem U_j becomes its own query for multi-view retrieval (semantic alignment to tools, similarity to historical queries, and expansion from the top tool).
- **query granularity**: Two-level: task-level (whole query Q for bundle acquisition) and sub-problem-level (per unsolved functionality U_j for multi-view re-ranking). It is one-shot/pre-execution overall (no per-execution-step querying), but internally decomposes the task into sub-problem queries.
- **when to retrieve**:
> One-shot, pre-execution (a single recommendation pass before query execution, not iterative test-time retrieval interleaved with tool execution). Internally the pipeline is staged/sequential (bundle -> coverage mapping -> per-unsolved-problem re-ranking) but it does not retrieve adaptively based on execution feedback.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed pipeline schedule conditioned on the functional coverage assessment. Stage 1 always runs (bundle acquisition). Stage 2 classifies the bundle as Exact Solving / Oversolving / Partial Solving; the toolset is pruned of redundant tools, and only in the Partial Solving case (unsolved functionalities remain) is stage-3 multi-view re-ranking triggered to add tools for each unsolved sub-problem. So the concrete WHEN-to-add signal is the LLM-judged presence of unsolved functionalities (a coverage/completeness gap), not token confidence or a learned router.
- **reranking**:
> Yes: a multi-view frequency-based re-ranking (stage 3). For each unsolved sub-problem U_j, three candidate lists are built - Direct Semantic Alignment (L_DSA: tools most similar to U_j), Historical Query Correlation (L_HQC: tools used in the top-K historical queries most similar to U_j, deduplicated), and Contextual Tool Expansion (L_CTE: tools most similar to the top DSA tool) - then combined and ranked by occurrence frequency across the three views; the single top-ranked tool is added per unsolved problem. This is an ensemble/voting (frequency-aggregation) reranker, not a cross-encoder.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Decompose-then-recompose plus pruning. Stage 2 prunes redundant/irrelevant tools from the acquired bundle (keeps only tools mapped to required functionalities) and decomposes the query into unsolved sub-problems; stage 3 recomposes the toolset by adding minimally-needed tools via multi-view aggregation/deduplication. No document compression or distillation of tool descriptions beyond this set-level pruning/addition.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Raw tool descriptions are used (from MetaTool/OpenAI plugin list and ToolLens). No synthetic-query augmentation, expanded summaries, weighted-field embeddings, or instruction-tuned tool embeddings. Tool descriptions are embedded as-is for similarity and shown verbatim to the LLM for functionality matching ('as long as the tool description can roughly provide the needed information ... ignore the proper nouns').
- **index content separation**: N/A / no explicit progressive-disclosure index-vs-content separation. Tool descriptions are short and loaded directly; there is no lightweight-index-then-heavy-content scheme.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Static tool index (frozen tool corpora from ToolLens, MetaTool, and the constructed RecTools). No live tool synchronization, no MCP/RapidAPI/RESTful/function-calling execution protocol is integrated - PTR is a pre-execution recommender that outputs a toolset rather than invoking tools; it is positioned as a front-end to downstream execution planners.
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> Partial/implicit. Inter-tool synergy is captured implicitly via historical tool-bundle usage (tools that were used together effectively in the past) and via Historical Query Correlation (tools co-used in similar queries), giving 'a more holistic understanding of tool dependencies and synergies.' However, there is no explicit dependency graph, output-of-A-feeds-B modeling, shared-auth or prerequisite reasoning, or dependency-aware reranking.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> The output is a recommended toolset (a precise, variable-size set of tool identifiers/descriptions) intended for prompt augmentation of a downstream LLM/execution planner. Within PTR, retrieved tools are used as candidates that the LLM matches to functionalities and that the multi-view reranker votes on; the final set is the recommendation. It is not used as a training signal or latent injection.
- **planning integration**:
> Plan/decompose-then-retrieve, pre-execution. The pipeline first acquires a bundle, then decomposes the task into functionalities/unsolved sub-problems (a lightweight plan of required capabilities), then retrieves/re-ranks tools per unsolved sub-problem. PTR itself does not plan tool-call sequences or run a search/MCTS; it is explicitly framed as a front-end recommender that supplies a 'lean, capability-complete tool set to downstream execution planners.'
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-sub-problem (per unsolved functionality) within a single pre-execution pass; not per-CoT-step, per-token, or per-tool-call within a rollout. Retrieval/re-ranking is invoked once per identified unsolved sub-problem, then aggregated into the final set.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> N/A (not a CBR/case-adaptation method). The closest analogue is LLM-prompted revision of the retrieved bundle: the functional coverage mapping (LLM) revises the acquired bundle by keeping/discarding tools, and multi-view re-ranking adds tools, adapting the historical bundle to the new query. No execution-feedback-driven revision (it is offline/pre-execution).
- **retrieved item representation**: Surface form is a structured set of tool identifiers with their natural-language tool descriptions (the recommended toolset). Not raw trajectories, executable programs, or latent tokens; tools are represented as name + description strings.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Concrete tool / tool-API (single tool with its description) at the finest level, plus tool-bundle/toolkit (a set of co-used tools) at the coarser level. No distilled strategies, workflows, or procedural skills are retrieved.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Relevance/coverage evaluation via the LLM (functional coverage mapping): the LLM explicitly assesses whether the toolset Exactly/Over/Partially solves the query and removes tools that do not contribute to any required functionality (distractor/redundancy pruning), reducing over-selection. The multi-view frequency aggregation reduces the randomness of selecting tools from the full set (a tool surfacing in multiple views is more trustworthy). No retriever-aware training, self-reflection loop, or distractor-aware SFT.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: Episodic / usage memory of historical (query, tool-bundle) pairs used for retrieval (offline, read-only at test time). Plus the static tool corpus. No skill-library, workflow, procedural, graph, or latent memory.
- **write back**: False. PTR does not store new queries, recommended toolsets, or experiences back into the historical store during deployment; the historical (query, tool-bundle) usage data is a fixed offline resource consumed read-only.
- **online growth**: No. The retrievable stores (tool corpus and historical tool-bundle usage) are frozen; they do not grow at test/deployment time.
- **write back trigger**: Never. There is no write-back mechanism; nothing is added to a durable memory after a recommendation is produced (the system is offline/pre-execution and read-only over its historical store).
- **failure experience usage**:
> Not used. PTR stores no failed/negative experiences and has no failure memory; it is success-only in the sense that the historical store holds previously-used (presumably effective) tool bundles, but it neither records nor retrieves failures. (Within a single query, the 'unsolved problems' from coverage mapping drive tool addition, but these are transient, not stored.)
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (append-only would not apply since there is no write-back). The historical store is static and entries are never mutated, merged, refined, or pruned at deployment.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No. Retrieval/tool-selection is not a learned or RL-optimized policy; it relies on fixed unsupervised similarity (BM25/dense embeddings) plus LLM prompting and a frequency-based multi-view aggregation heuristic. No M-MDP, soft Q-learning, or trained selection policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> No cross-agent/cross-framework memory sharing. PTR is a single-agent pipeline; the historical tool-bundle usage is a shared offline dataset but not memory communicated among multiple agents at runtime. It is positioned to hand its toolset to a downstream execution planner, which is an interface, not memory sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> ToolLens (Qu et al., 2024, COLT), MetaTool (Huang et al., 2023), and RecTools (newly constructed in this paper). 20% of each dataset is held out as test data. RecTools: 10 usage scenarios (queries using 1 to 10 tools), 100 examples per scenario (1000 queries total), 20 tool combinations per scenario, 5 queries per combination; tools and descriptions sourced from MetaTool / OpenAI plugin list.
- **benchmark family**: tool (tool retrieval/recommendation). ToolLens and MetaTool are existing multi-tool benchmarks; RecTools is a new tool-recommendation benchmark in the same family, emphasizing variable-size, exactly-solvable toolsets.
- **baselines**:
> Retriever baselines (each used standalone 'N/A framework' and as the stage-1 retriever fed into +PTR): Random (random selection from historical tools), BM25, Contriever, SBERT (all-mpnet-base-v2), TAS-B, SimCSE. Backbone-LLM variants of PTR: +PTR+open-mistral-7b, +PTR+GPT-3.5-turbo, +PTR+GPT-4o. (Execution-time tool-use frameworks such as Re-Invoke, DRAFT, TECTON, Toolformer are discussed as a distinct paradigm in related work, not run as baselines because converting them to offline pre-execution removes their runtime-feedback learning signal.)
- **key metrics**:
> Recall@K and NDCG@K (with K set to the size of the ground-truth toolset |A|), plus the newly proposed TRACC. TRACC = (|A intersect B| / |A|) * (1 - (| |B| - |A| | / |A union B|)), where A is the ground-truth toolset and B the recommended toolset; the first factor measures content sufficiency (ACC = |A intersect B| / |A|) and the second penalizes size deviation, jointly capturing minimality + completeness (an equivalent form is TRACC = (1 - (1/|A union B|)*||B|-|A||)*ACC). Also reports average length difference ||B|-|A|| (tool-count precision) and per-query token/cost.
- **headline result**:
> Best configuration SimCSE + PTR + GPT-4o achieves the top scores on all three datasets: ToolLens Recall@K=0.368, NDCG@K=0.467, TRACC=0.336; MetaTool Recall@K=0.774, NDCG@K=0.956, TRACC=0.690; RecTools Recall@K=0.609, NDCG@K=0.896, TRACC=0.591. Illustrative gain: on RecTools, SimCSE+PTR+GPT-4o TRACC 0.591 vs SimCSE-alone TRACC 0.523 and Random-alone TRACC 0.097. PTR also markedly lifts weak retrievers, e.g. Random TRACC on MetaTool 0.133 -> 0.562 with PTR+GPT-4o.
- **ablations**:
> Stage ablation (Table 2, using GPT-4o backbone + SimCSE retriever, the strongest config). ToolLens: w/o Stage-1 (Tool Bundle Acquisition) Recall/NDCG/TRACC = 0.283/0.391/0.235; w/o Stage-2 (Functional Coverage Mapping) 0.355/0.455/0.322; w/o Stage-3 (Multi-view Re-ranking) 0.351/0.448/0.318; full PTR 0.368/0.467/0.336. MetaTool: w/o S1 0.745/0.922/0.677; w/o S2 0.762/0.945/0.678; w/o S3 0.759/0.942/0.676; full 0.774/0.956/0.690. RecTools: w/o S1 0.581/0.916/0.439; w/o S2 0.598/0.888/0.552; w/o S3 0.601/0.892/0.566; full 0.609/0.896/0.591. Stage-1 removal causes the largest TRACC drop (e.g. ToolLens 0.336->0.235; RecTools 0.591->0.439), showing historical bundle info is the strongest inductive bias. TRACC-validity ablation (Appendix C): on RecTools, w/o Stage-1 reaches NDCG=0.916 but TRACC only 0.439, while full PTR has comparable NDCG (0.896) yet much higher TRACC (0.591), demonstrating TRACC captures precision/size errors that NDCG misses. Backbone sweep (Table 1): GPT-4o > GPT-3.5-turbo > open-mistral-7b consistently. Average set-length-difference analysis (Figure 4) confirms PTR controls |#tools - #ground-truth|.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Partially yes. Intrinsic retrieval-style metrics (Recall@K, NDCG@K) and the recommendation-precision metric (TRACC) are all reported, but PTR is itself the recommender (the 'task' is the recommendation), so there is no separate downstream end-task execution metric. The paper deliberately separates ranking-quality metrics (Recall/NDCG) from the precision/size-fidelity metric (TRACC) and argues the former are insufficient for tool recommendation. No downstream LLM task-success rate (e.g., final answer correctness with the recommended tools) is measured.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Outcome-of-recommendation focused: metrics score the final recommended set against ground truth (Recall@K, NDCG@K, TRACC) and the set-size accuracy (avg length difference). No intermediate process-quality metric (e.g., functional-decomposition accuracy, per-stage correctness) is independently scored beyond the stage-ablation analysis. No downstream reasoning-faithfulness or trajectory metric.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Resource consumption reported per query under GPT-4o pricing (USD 2.50/M input tokens, USD 10.00/M output tokens; Appendix D): ToolLens ~1,638 input + 139 output tokens => ~USD 0.0055/query; MetaTool ~2,036 in + 194 out => ~USD 0.0070/query; RecTools ~2,657 in + 207 out => ~USD 0.0087/query (all under one cent per query). Motivation also emphasizes efficiency: a precise (not oversized) toolset reduces prompt length / input-length limits and avoids executing redundant tools downstream. No latency/speedup numbers and no retrieval-call count reported.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Adaptive / precision-driven variable-size selection (the core contribution): the number of recommended tools is determined dynamically per query (1-10 in RecTools) by pruning redundant tools (stage 2) and adding tools per unsolved sub-problem (stage 3), rather than a fixed-k cutoff. For Recall@K/NDCG@K evaluation, K is set to the ground-truth size |A|; but the recommendation pipeline does not assume |A| is known and outputs its own set size. Token budgets per query are small (~1.6k-2.7k input tokens; see cost analysis).
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> RecTools (new): ~1000 queries (10 tool-count scenarios x 100 examples; 20 tool combinations per scenario x 5 LLM-generated queries each), with up to 10 tools per query (vs ToolLens 1-3 tools/query, MetaTool fixed 2 tools/query). Construction: LLM-synthesized - GPT-4o is prompted to generate user queries solvable exclusively by a given tool bundle (all tools necessary, no external tools needed), using tools/descriptions from MetaTool / OpenAI plugin list. Verifiability/quality control: two-step GPT-4o(/GPT-4) evaluation - (1) confirm the full toolset yields 'Exact Solving'; (2) after randomly removing one tool, confirm 'Partial Solving'; a query qualifies only if both pass (score=1), plus dedup and validation steps. Difficulty signal: GPT-4o 'Exact Solving' rate is 61.3% for RecTools vs 55.1% MetaTool and 6.34% ToolLens; for 2-tool and 3-tool (query, tools) pairs RecTools success rates reach 76% and 89%. Best-system TRACC on RecTools is 0.591 (SimCSE+PTR+GPT-4o), indicating substantial headroom.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Tool retrieval line: BM25/TF-IDF lexical retrieval (Robertson 2009; Sparck Jones 1972), dense retrievers (Contriever/Izacard 2021, SBERT/Reimers 2019, TAS-B/Hofstatter 2021, SimCSE/Gao 2021, DPR/Karpukhin 2020), and tool-retrieval/selection works (ToolLLM/Qin 2023, MetaTool/Huang 2023, COLT-ToolLens/Qu 2024, Confucius/Gao 2024, ToolRerank/Zheng 2024, Gorilla/Patil 2023). Conceptually builds on the broader 'recommendation for LLMs' framing (memory/knowledge/data/architecture/prompt recommendation) extended to a new 'tool recommendation' axis.
- **contrasts with**:
> Fixed top-k tool retrieval that packages a fixed number of top-ranked tools (e.g., COLT/ToolLens, ToolRerank, Confucius-style ranking) - PTR argues these suffer under-/over-selection and assume the tool count is known. Execution-time tool-use/refinement frameworks driven by runtime feedback or trajectories (Toolformer/Schick 2023, Re-Invoke/Chen 2024, DRAFT/Qu 2024, TECTON/Alazraki 2025) - positioned as a distinct paradigm (runtime feedback) vs PTR's offline pre-execution precision objective. Also contrasts conventional metrics Recall@K/NDCG@K (insufficient for size/precision) with the proposed TRACC.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use), tool-retrieval/selection sub-lineage. PTR shifts the objective from top-k tool retrieval to precision-driven, variable-size pre-execution tool recommendation (minimal sufficient toolset), introduces the tool-recommendation problem definition, the RecTools dataset (variable, exactly-solvable toolsets), and the TRACC metric (sufficiency + size fidelity). Sits alongside COLT/ToolLens and MetaTool as a multi-tool selection work, and is positioned as a front-end recommender feeding downstream execution planners (AnyTool/ToolLLM-style solvers).

<a id="item-re-invoke"></a>
### 99. Re-Invoke: Tool Invocation Rewriting for Zero-Shot Tool Retrieval

2024  ·  EMNLP 2024 Findings  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.01875)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2024 (EMNLP 2024 Findings), pages 4705-4726
- **authors affiliation**:
> Yanfei Chen, Jinsung Yoon, Chen-Yu Lee, Tomas Pfister (Google Cloud AI Research); Devendra Singh Sachan (Google DeepMind); Qingze Wang, Vincent Cohen-Addad, Mohammadhossein Bateni (Google). Primary affiliation: Google (Google Cloud AI Research / Google DeepMind / Google). Correspondence: yanfeichen, jinsungyoon, chenyulee @google.com.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.01875

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: tool-use (tool/API retrieval for tool-augmented LLM agents); the retrieved tools are consumed by a downstream tool-use agent (ToolLLaMA with DFSDT) for task fulfillment
- **problem setting**:
> Offline-indexing + online-inference, single-agent, fully UNSUPERVISED (training-free) tool retrieval. Given a user query and a very large pool of tool documents (16,000+ RapidAPI APIs in ToolBench), the system must retrieve the most relevant tool(s) without any labeled query-tool pairs and without fine-tuning a retriever. Two regimes are addressed: single-tool retrieval and multi-tool retrieval (queries needing several tools/categories). The setting targets three stated challenges: (a) LLM input-token-length limits making it infeasible to list all tools in a prompt, (b) an evolving/dynamic tool pool for which maintaining labels and retraining is impractical, and (c) ambiguous user intents where verbose context obfuscates the underlying tool request. Retrieval is decoupled from the agent and also evaluated end-to-end by plugging Re-Invoke as the retriever in front of a ToolLLaMA+DFSDT agent.
- **what is retrieved**: tools (tool documents / tool-API descriptions). The retrievable store is the set of tool documents (each containing tool name, API description, and parameters); these are indexed and the top-k relevant tools are returned for the user query.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus: a fixed pool of tool documents (ToolBench's 16,000+ RapidAPI APIs; ToolE's 199 tools). The store does not grow from the agent's own experience. Re-Invoke enriches each tool document offline with LLM-generated synthetic queries, but the underlying tool corpus is a static, externally provided document collection.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Both top-k ranking and multi-tool completeness. The primary objective is a fixed top-k ranking (nDCG@5 / recall@5 / nDCG@1 / recall@1). For multi-tool retrieval (ToolBench I2/I3, ToolE multi-tool), the multi-view similarity ranking explicitly aggregates the top tool from each extracted intent so that the complete set of needed tools (one per intent) is recovered, i.e., a completeness-oriented variant of top-k that ensures every distinct intent contributes a retrieved tool.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based reasoning method; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain case cycle is implemented)
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is positioned within tool retrieval, generative document/query expansion, and query-rewriting literature.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: tool-API / tool document (a per-tool document containing the tool name, API description, and parameters). For indexing, the retrievable unit is an augmented tool document = original tool document concatenated with one LLM-generated synthetic query (m such copies per tool).
- **index source**:
> Static corpus enriched offline. Tool documents come from existing benchmarks (ToolBench's RapidAPI APIs; ToolE/MetaTool's 199 tools). During offline indexing, each tool document is expanded with m LLM-generated synthetic queries (generative document expansion) and encoded into the embedding space. No online/test-time induction or write-back; the enriched index is built once offline.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat vector index (dense embeddings via Vertex AI textembedding-gecko@003) or flat sparse BM25 index. Per tool, m augmented-document copies are created (document + one synthetic query each) and their embeddings are averaged into a single per-tool representation E_d; the store is a flat collection of these per-tool vectors with no graph/hierarchy.
- **retriever type**:
> Dense (Google Vertex AI text-embedding, textembedding-gecko@003) OR sparse (BM25, k=1.5, b=0.75); Re-Invoke is applied on top of either. An LLM (text-bison@001 / gpt-3.5-turbo / Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3) is used for query generation and intent extraction, but the matching itself is embedding/lexical similarity, not LLM-as-retriever or generative tool-as-token.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> none (fully unsupervised / training-free). No retriever is trained: off-the-shelf BM25 and off-the-shelf Vertex AI text embeddings are used, and the LLM components (query generator, intent extractor) are used purely in-context (zero/few-shot prompting) with no fine-tuning and no labeled query-tool pairs.
- **query construction**:
> Two-sided rewriting. (Indexing side) Document expansion: LLM reads each tool document and generates m diverse synthetic user queries (high sampling temperature for diversity), each concatenated to the tool document. (Inference side) Intent extraction: LLM rewrites the verbose user query into one or more concise tool-related intents via in-context learning, filtering out extraneous background context; these extracted intents replace the original query for matching.
- **query granularity**: task-level (one-shot at inference time, t=0): a single retrieval pass is done per user query, but the query is decomposed into multiple intents and indexing-time keys are multiple synthetic queries per tool (a two-level / multi-view construction rather than per-step retrieval).
- **when to retrieve**: one-shot (a single retrieval is performed for the user query before the downstream agent acts; no iterative or uncertainty-triggered re-retrieval within the retrieval method).
- **retrieval trigger signal**: fixed schedule: retrieval is always performed once up front for each incoming user query (the standard retrieve-then-act pipeline); there is no confidence/uncertainty/learned-classifier trigger.
- **reranking**:
> Yes, a custom multi-view similarity ranking stage. For each extracted intent, tools are ranked by intent-document cosine similarity; a tuple (reversed rank within intent, similarity score) is formed, and the maximum tuple across intents is taken per tool so that the top tool from each intent is aggregated until k tools are retrieved. It is an intent-aware multi-view aggregation rather than a cross-encoder or RRF reranker.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Query-side refinement via intent extraction (the verbose user query is distilled into clean tool-related intents, removing irrelevant background context), plus document-side enrichment. No post-retrieval distillation/compression of the retrieved tool documents themselves; the multi-view ranking is the main post-similarity processing.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Synthetic-query augmentation (generative document expansion): for each tool document, an LLM generates m diverse synthetic queries the tool could answer, and each is concatenated to the original tool document to create augmented documents. Per-tool embeddings are computed as the mean over the m augmented-document copies. An ablation shows appending synthetic queries to the document beats replacing the document with synthetic queries only, and that more synthetic queries (1->5->10) and mean (vs max) aggregation improve nDCG@5.
- **index content separation**:
> N/A / No explicit lightweight-index-then-content separation. The full augmented tool document is embedded and stored; there is no progressive-disclosure split between a light retrievable index and heavy on-demand content (the tool documents are short, e.g., name+description+parameters).
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Tool corpus drawn from RapidAPI hub (ToolBench's 16,000+ real-world APIs) and ToolE/MetaTool tools; integration in the end-to-end setting is via the ToolLLaMA + DFSDT agent calling RapidAPI tools. The method is motivated by an evolving tool pool and avoids retraining (so it adapts to new tools by indexing their documents), but the indexing itself is offline/static with no live CRUD auto-sync, MCP, or function-calling protocol described.
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> No explicit inter-tool dependency modeling. Retrieval treats tools independently per intent; multi-tool queries are handled by extracting multiple independent intents and retrieving one tool per intent, not by modeling output-of-A-feeds-B dependencies, shared auth, or prerequisite graphs.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> prompt augmentation for a downstream tool-use agent: the top-k retrieved tools are provided to a ToolLLaMA+DFSDT agent which then plans and executes tool calls. The retriever narrows the 16,000+ API search space to a relevant candidate set; the agent uses these retrieved tools to fulfill the instruction. No fine-tuning; retrieved tools enter the agent's prompt/action space.
- **planning integration**:
> retrieve-then-plan: a single retrieval pass selects candidate tools, then the agent (ToolLLaMA with Depth-First Search-Based Decision Tree, DFSDT) plans/searches over those tools to complete the task. Retrieval is a front-end stage, not interleaved per planning step nor embedded inside the agent's tree search.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: per-answer (retrieval is a one-shot front-end stage producing the candidate tool set for the whole query; it is not interleaved per CoT step or per tool-call within the downstream DFSDT rollout).
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not a CBR method; no retrieved case is adapted/revised). The closest analog is intent extraction, which rewrites the query rather than adapting a retrieved case.
- **retrieved item representation**: raw tool documents (structured tool/API descriptions: tool name, API description, parameters in JSON-like form) injected into the downstream agent; on the index side these are augmented documents (tool document + synthetic query) embedded into vectors.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: tool-level descriptive documentation (per-tool capability description / API spec), i.e., a tool-API document rather than a raw trajectory, distilled strategy, or reusable workflow.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Intent extraction as a noise/distractor filter: the LLM intent extractor removes extraneous background context from verbose, ambiguous user queries so the retriever matches on the true underlying tool request (the motivating Fig.1 failure: 'planning a trip to France' masking the real 'improve French language skills' intent). On the index side, document expansion with diverse synthetic queries provides generative pseudo-relevance feedback to better distinguish highly similar tools. No retriever-aware training or learned relevance evaluator.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (no episodic/skill/workflow/procedural memory that the system writes to; only a static, offline-enriched tool-document index).
- **write back**: False. The system does not store new experiences/cases/skills at test time; the enriched tool index is built once offline and is not updated from agent execution.
- **online growth**: No. The retrievable store does not grow during deployment from the agent's own experience; new tools would be incorporated by indexing their documents offline (re-running query generation), not via online write-back.
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back of agent experience). The Limitations section notes that using the downstream agent's execution results as feedback to refine intent extraction is left to future work, confirming no such feedback/write-back exists in the current method.
- **failure experience usage**: N/A (no experience/memory storage, so neither successful nor failed trajectories are stored or retrieved).
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (no stored memory entries; the offline-built index is static and not mutated by the system after construction).
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No. Retrieval is a fixed similarity-based top-k (dense or BM25) with a deterministic multi-view ranking rule; it is not a learned/RL-optimized retrieval policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent, single-retriever pipeline; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing (the tool index is a shared external resource but not a shared experiential memory).

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> ToolBench (Qin et al., 2023; subsets I1, I2, I3) and ToolE (Huang et al., 2023, the MetaTool benchmark; single-tool and multi-tool splits) for retrieval evaluation. End-to-end pass-rate evaluation on six ToolBench subsets: I1-Instruction, I1-Category, I1-Tool, I2-Instruction, I2-Category, I3-Instruction. Data statistics: ToolBench I1 (87,419 queries / 10,439 tools), I2 (84,815 / 13,142), I3 (25,251 / 1,605); ToolE single-tool (20,550 queries / 199 tools), ToolE multi-tool (497 queries / 199 tools).
- **benchmark family**: tool (ToolBench; ToolE/MetaTool). Tool/API retrieval and end-to-end tool-use benchmarks over the RapidAPI ecosystem (16,000+ APIs) and the MetaTool tool set.
- **baselines**:
> Unsupervised retrieval baselines: (a) BM25 sparse retrieval (k=1.5, b=0.75); (b) dense retrieval with Google Vertex AI textembedding-gecko@003; (c) HyDE (Gao et al., 2022) on both sparse (BM25) and dense (Vertex AI) settings, generating a hypothetical tool document per query via text-bison@001. End-to-end baselines: ToolLLaMA+DFSDT agent with (i) the reference tool set without a retriever and (ii) ToolLLM's supervised API retriever (Sentence-BERT trained on labeled query-tool pairs).
- **key metrics**: Retrieval: nDCG@5 (primary), plus nDCG@1, recall@1, recall@5; round-trip consistency recall@10 for the query generator. End-to-end: pass rate (% of instructions completed within budget, per ToolLLM, using gpt-3.5-turbo as evaluator).
- **headline result**:
> On ToolE, Re-Invoke achieves a 20% relative improvement in nDCG@5 for single-tool retrieval and a 39% relative improvement for multi-tool retrieval over the best baseline (fully unsupervised). Concretely (dense, text-bison@001 backbone), ToolE single-tool nDCG@5 0.7821 (Re-Invoke) vs 0.6522 (Vertex AI dense baseline) and ToolE multi-tool 0.7231 vs 0.5296. End-to-end, Re-Invoke as retriever raises average ToolBench pass rate to 56.07% vs 52.63% (ToolLLM's trained retriever) and 52.13% (reference tools, no retriever).
- **ablations**:
> (A) Component ablation (Vertex AI dense): query generator and intent extractor each help individually and combine best (e.g., ToolE single-tool: baseline 0.6522 -> +query generator 0.7813 -> +intent extractor 0.6756 -> both/Re-Invoke 0.7821; ToolBench I2: 0.3880 -> 0.4135 -> 0.5157 -> 0.5379). Intent extractor gives no gain on ToolBench I1 because its APIs are under the same tool so per-intent retrieval overlaps; query generator dominates on ToolE (short docs, names+descriptions only), intent extractor dominates on multi-tool/verbose ToolBench I2/I3. (B) Appending synthetic queries to the document beats using synthetic-query-only (e.g., I1 0.6286 vs 0.4924; ToolE single 0.7813 vs 0.7535), showing replacement causes information loss. (C) More synthetic queries help: 1 -> 5 -> 10 queries (I1 0.5962 -> 0.6242 -> 0.6286; ToolE single 0.7388 -> 0.7777 -> 0.7813). (D) Mean aggregation beats max similarity aggregation across datasets. Backbone-LLM robustness: similar gains with text-bison@001, gpt-3.5-turbo, and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3. Round-trip consistency recall@10 confirms query-generator effectiveness, lower on larger toolsets (I1/I2).
- **evaluation decoupling**: Yes. Intrinsic retrieval metrics (nDCG@1/@5, recall@1/@5, round-trip recall@10) are reported separately from end-to-end task performance (pass rate on the ToolBench agent), explicitly decoupling retrieval quality from downstream task success.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Both. Retrieval-stage (process-level) quality is measured by ranking metrics (nDCG/recall) and round-trip consistency recall; downstream outcome is measured by agent pass rate. No fine-grained per-step reasoning-faithfulness metric beyond these.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Framed as eliminating training/labeling cost: Re-Invoke is fully unsupervised, avoiding the production cost of maintaining labeled query-tool pairs and continuous retraining of a tool retriever as the tool pool evolves. It scales to a vast pool (16,000+ APIs) by narrowing the candidate set before the agent acts, mitigating LLM input-token limits and lost-in-the-middle issues. The added cost is offline LLM calls for synthetic-query generation per tool and one online LLM call for intent extraction per query; no explicit latency or dollar-cost numbers are reported.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Retrieval reported primarily at top-5 (nDCG@5 / recall@5) and top-1; the algorithm retrieves a specified number k of tools via Argmax over the multi-view ranking score, aggregating the top tool per extracted intent until k tools are collected. Indexing uses m synthetic queries per tool (default m=10, ablated over 1/5/10). No explicit token budget for the downstream prompt is stated beyond using the retriever to fit within LLM input-length limits.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (empirical method paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A (Re-Invoke reuses existing benchmarks rather than constructing a new one). It evaluates on ToolBench (Qin et al., 2023; 16,000+ RapidAPI APIs; I1/I2/I3 splits with 87,419 / 84,815 / 25,251 queries and 10,439 / 13,142 / 1,605 tools respectively) and ToolE/MetaTool (Huang et al., 2023; 199 tools; single-tool 20,550 queries, multi-tool 497 queries / 994 labeled pairs), both providing ground-truth query-tool pairs.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Generative document expansion (Nogueira et al., 2019 Doc2Query; Lewis et al., 2021 PAQ; Ma et al., 2023a) for synthetic-query indexing; HyDE (Gao et al., 2022) and Query2doc (Wang et al., 2023) / query-expansion and LLM query-rewriting lines (Jagerman et al., 2023; Mao et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2023b) as the rewriting-pipeline lineage; tool-documentation-for-tool-use (Hsieh et al., 2023; Patil et al., 2023 Gorilla) and ToolBench/ToolLLM (Qin et al., 2023, ToolLLaMA + DFSDT) as the tool-retrieval and downstream-agent substrate; off-the-shelf BM25 (Robertson et al., 2009) and Vertex AI text embeddings as retrievers.
- **contrasts with**:
> Supervised/trained tool retrievers that learn from labeled query-API pairs (ToolLLM's Sentence-BERT API retriever (Qin et al., 2023); Kong et al., 2023 TPTU-v2; Gao et al., 2024 Confucius) -- Re-Invoke is fully unsupervised. Generative query-expansion / pseudo-relevance-feedback methods (HyDE, Query2doc) -- Re-Invoke emphasizes query UNDERSTANDING (intent extraction) rather than query expansion, and combines it with document expansion. LLM-agent-as-retriever approaches that list a limited tool set in-prompt -- Re-Invoke retrieves from a vast (16,000+) pool.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use). A 2024 zero-shot/unsupervised tool-retrieval method that fuses generative tool-document expansion (Doc2Query/PAQ lineage) with LLM intent extraction (query-rewriting lineage) and a multi-view intent-based ranking, positioned against trained tool retrievers (ToolLLM) and HyDE-style query expansion; a tool-document-engineering successor to Tool Documentation (Hsieh et al., 2023) and Gorilla for scalable tool retrieval.

<a id="item-task-aligned-tool"></a>
### 100. Task-Aligned Tool Recommendation for Large Language Models (PTR: Precision-driven Tool Recommendation)

2024  ·  IJCNLP-AACL 2025  ·  [paper](https://aclanthology.org/2025.ijcnlp-long.110/)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**: IJCNLP-AACL 2025 Main (Proceedings of the 14th IJCNLP and 4th AACL); ACL Anthology 2025.ijcnlp-long.110; preprint arXiv:2411.09613 (v1 Nov 2024, v2 Nov 2025)
- **authors affiliation**: Hang Gao and Yongfeng Zhang, Rutgers University.
- **paper url**: https://aclanthology.org/2025.ijcnlp-long.110/

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Tool-use for LLMs (tool selection / tool recommendation prior to query execution).
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-step, pre-execution recommendation of a precise tool set for a given natural-language query, before any tool is invoked. Single-agent, no runtime/execution feedback. The framework is model-agnostic: an off-the-shelf retriever produces a candidate tool bundle and a backbone LLM (open-mistral-7b, GPT-3.5-turbo, or GPT-4o) drives the functional reasoning. Supervision comes from historical (query, tool-bundle) usage data; no retriever fine-tuning is performed. Evaluated against a known ground-truth toolset per query (exact-solving regime).
- **what is retrieved**: tools (external tool/API descriptions), retrieved both as historical tool bundles (sets) and as individual candidate tools; also retrieves similar historical queries to surface their previously-used tools.
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus: a fixed catalog of available tools T plus a fixed set of historical (query, tool-bundle) usage records D. No growing/episodic memory written during deployment.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Precision-driven, variable-size recommendation aimed at recovering the COMPLETE minimal-sufficient tool set (exact solving) rather than a fixed top-k ranking. The paper explicitly argues against fixed top-k packaging and defines the objective as T_recommend = T_ground with |T_recommend| = |T_ground| (no over- or under-selection).
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False. The paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it frames the work as 'tool recommendation' analogous to recommender systems / tool retrieval. It does realize CBR-like reuse of historical (query, bundle) cases under another name.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: tool-API (individual tool description) and tool-bundle (a set of tools co-used in a past query); historical queries are also retrieved as a unit to extract their associated tools.
- **index source**: Static, offline-induced store: a catalog of all available tools and a corpus of historical (query, tool-bundle) pairs D={(Q_i,B_i)} and the derived set of unique bundles B. Not online/test-time-induced; frozen after construction.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat vector / lexical index over (a) unique tool bundles, (b) individual tools, and (c) historical queries. No explicit dependency graph or hierarchy is built; inter-tool 'synergies/dependencies' are captured implicitly via co-occurrence in historical bundles rather than an explicit graph topology.
- **retriever type**:
> Hybrid set of off-the-shelf retrievers evaluated as the Stage-1 component: sparse (BM25) and dense (Contriever, SBERT all-mpnet-base-v2, TAS-B, SimCSE), plus a Random baseline. Stage-3 multi-view re-ranking uses embedding similarity (sigma) over tools/queries. No LLM-as-retriever or generative tool-as-token retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**: None / off-the-shelf. Retrievers are used unsupervised/zero-shot (no contrastive fine-tuning, no LM-feedback, no RL). The 'learning signal' is purely the historical tool-bundle co-usage prior leveraged at retrieval/aggregation time, not retriever parameter training.
- **query construction**:
> Two-level. Stage-1: raw query Q is matched against historical bundles/queries. Stage-2 (Functional Coverage Mapping): the LLM decomposes Q into a set of discrete key functionalities F={F_1,...,F_m} and, after pruning, emits residual unsolved sub-problems U={U_1,...,U_y}. Stage-3: each unsolved sub-problem U_j is used as a sub-query for multi-view re-ranking. So queries are LLM-decomposed/intent-extracted, not just raw.
- **query granularity**: Both task-level and sub-problem level (two-level retrieval): bundle retrieval at task level (t=0), then per-unsolved-sub-problem retrieval in the re-ranking stage.
- **when to retrieve**: One-shot, multi-stage pipeline executed once per query (retrieve bundle -> map/prune -> re-rank to add). It is not iterative over execution and not uncertainty-triggered; all retrieval happens before execution in a fixed 3-stage schedule.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed schedule (deterministic 3-stage pipeline). Stage-3 re-ranking is triggered only when Stage-2 'Assessment of Toolset Completeness' classifies the bundle as 'Partial Solving' (unsolved sub-problems remain); pruning is triggered on 'Oversolving'. The completeness assessment thus acts as an LLM-judged trigger for add/remove operations.
- **reranking**: Yes. Stage-3 'Multi-view Based Re-ranking' aggregates three candidate tool lists per unsolved sub-problem and re-ranks tools by frequency of occurrence across the three views (a frequency/voting-based, multi-view aggregation rather than a cross-encoder).
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Decompose-then-recompose plus distractor filtering: Stage-2 prunes redundant/unused tools (removing tools that fulfill no required functionality) and identifies gaps; Stage-3 recomposes the set by adding tools for unresolved sub-problems via frequency-based voting across three views. Net effect is a minimal-sufficient (non-redundant, complete) tool set.
- **tool document engineering**: Raw tool descriptions/docstrings are used for matching tools to functionalities and for embedding-based similarity; no synthetic-query augmentation, expanded summaries, or instruction-tuned tool embeddings are reported.
- **index content separation**: N/A. No explicit lightweight-index-then-content / progressive-disclosure separation is described; tool descriptions are used directly.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: Static tool index (tools/bundles from ToolLens, MetaTool, RecTools datasets); no live-synchronized tool store, no RapidAPI/MCP/function-calling CRUD auto-sync. Pre-execution recommender, not an execution protocol.
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> Partial / implicit. The method argues it captures 'tool dependencies and synergies' by retrieving historical tool bundles (co-used sets) rather than single tools, but there is no explicit dependency graph, bipartite KG, or dependency-aware reranking; dependency is modeled only through co-occurrence in historical bundles.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation / tool-set provisioning: the recommended toolset is the output, intended to be supplied to a downstream LLM execution planner as the precise set of tools available before execution. Within PTR, the LLM also uses retrieved tools for reasoning (functional matching, completeness assessment).
- **planning integration**:
> Plan-then-retrieve / retrieve-then-refine front-end: a one-shot pre-execution recommender that delivers a lean, capability-complete tool set to downstream execution planners. It is not integrated into MCTS/tree search or per-step interleaved acting; the authors position PTR as a front-end to (distinct from) execution-time tool-use frameworks.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer (one recommendation per query), with internal per-functionality / per-unsolved-sub-problem retrieval inside the single pipeline pass. No per-CoT-step or per-tool-call interleaving during execution.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> LLM-prompted adaptation of the retrieved historical bundle: the LLM matches tools to functionalities, classifies completeness (Exact/Over/Partial Solving), prunes redundant tools, and identifies unsolved sub-problems; new tools are then added via frequency-based multi-view re-ranking. No execution-feedback-driven or RL revision.
- **retrieved item representation**: Surface form is the tool itself (tool identifier/description) packaged into a recommended toolset; intermediate representations include the LLM-extracted functionality list and unsolved-sub-problem text. No latent/soft tokens.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Mix: reusable co-used tool bundles (procedural/usage-pattern abstraction) at Stage-1 and individual procedural tools (single tool-API units) at Stage-3; functionalities/unsolved-problems are LLM-distilled intermediate abstractions of the query.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Functional Coverage Mapping acts as an LLM relevance evaluator that prunes redundant/unsuitable tools (Oversolving case), and multi-view frequency voting reduces the randomness/noise of selecting tools from the full set (the paper states multi-view ranking 'reduces the randomness associated with selecting tools'). No retriever-aware/distractor-aware SFT training.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (no agent-written episodic/skill memory). Uses a static historical (query, tool-bundle) usage corpus as a read-only prior; this is a fixed database, not a growing memory.
- **write back**: False. The system does not store new experiences/cases/skills back into any memory during deployment; the historical-usage store is frozen.
- **online growth**: False. The retrievable store does not grow during deployment/test-time; it is offline-constructed and frozen.
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back mechanism exists in the method).
- **failure experience usage**: Not used. Only successful historical (query, tool-bundle) usage records inform retrieval; no failed/negative experiences are stored or retrieved. (Stage-2's 'unsolved problems' are within-query gaps, not a failure memory.)
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (append-only is not applicable; the store is static and not mutated after construction).
- **retrieval as learned policy**: False. Selection is fixed similarity top-k retrieval plus LLM-prompted reasoning plus frequency-based voting; no learned/RL-optimized retrieval policy (no M-MDP, no soft Q-learning, no RL retriever).
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent private pipeline; no memory/experience sharing across multiple agents or heterogeneous frameworks. (The shared 'historical usage' corpus is a static dataset, not cross-agent runtime sharing.)

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: ToolLens (from COLT, Qu et al. 2024), MetaTool (Huang et al. 2023), and the newly introduced RecTools dataset. 20% of each dataset used as test data.
- **benchmark family**: tool (tool-retrieval/recommendation benchmarks): ToolLens and MetaTool are existing tool benchmarks; RecTools is a new multi-tool (1-10 tools per query) tool-recommendation dataset.
- **baselines**:
> Random (random selection from historical tools), BM25 (sparse), Contriever, SBERT (all-mpnet-base-v2), TAS-B, SimCSE — six standalone retrievers, each also evaluated with +PTR using three backbones (open-mistral-7b, GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4o). The retrievers alone serve as the fixed-top-k tool-retrieval baselines that PTR is compared against.
- **key metrics**:
> TRACC (newly proposed: TRACC = (|A∩B|/|A|) × (1 − ||B|−|A|| / |A∪B|), combining tool-content accuracy/sufficiency and set-size fidelity/minimality), Recall@K, and NDCG@K (with K set to the ground-truth toolset size). Also: average tool-set length difference ||B|−|A|| and per-query API cost.
- **headline result**:
> Best configuration SimCSE + PTR + GPT-4o achieves TRACC 0.336 / Recall@K 0.368 / NDCG@K 0.467 on ToolLens, TRACC 0.690 / Recall@K 0.774 / NDCG@K 0.956 on MetaTool, and TRACC 0.591 / Recall@K 0.609 / NDCG@K 0.896 on RecTools (best across all columns). PTR adds large gains over standalone retrievers, e.g. SimCSE+PTR+GPT-4o gives absolute Recall@K improvements of +0.141 (ToolLens), +0.111 (MetaTool), +0.117 (RecTools) over the Random baseline.
- **ablations**:
> Stage-wise ablation (GPT-4o backbone + SimCSE retriever) removing each of the three stages. w/o Stage-1 (Tool Bundle Acquisition) causes the largest drop (TRACC 0.336->0.235 ToolLens; 0.591->0.439 RecTools), showing historical bundle co-usage is a strong inductive bias. w/o Stage-2 (Functional Coverage Mapping) drops TRACC (e.g. 0.591->0.552 RecTools), key for minimal-sufficient pruning. w/o Stage-3 (Multi-view Re-ranking) drops TRACC (e.g. 0.591->0.566 RecTools), showing multi-view aggregation refines precision. Notably NDCG can stay high while TRACC drops (w/o Stage-1 on RecTools: NDCG 0.916 but TRACC 0.439), validating TRACC.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Yes. Intrinsic retrieval/ranking metrics (Recall@K, NDCG@K) are reported alongside the recommendation-precision metric TRACC; the paper explicitly contrasts them to show Recall/NDCG can be high while TRACC (precision/size fidelity) is low. No separate downstream end-to-end task-success metric (e.g. LLM task pass rate) is reported — evaluation is at the tool-set recommendation level only.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Primarily outcome-of-recommendation (does the recommended set match the ground-truth set), plus an explicit set-size-quality dimension (average length difference, the TRACC size-penalty term). No downstream execution/trajectory process metrics are measured.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Resource Consumption Analysis (GPT-4o pricing, USD 2.50/M input, 10.00/M output): avg per-query ~USD 0.0055 (ToolLens: 1,638 in + 139 out), ~USD 0.0070 (MetaTool: 2,036 in + 194 out), ~USD 0.0087 (RecTools: 2,657 in + 207 out) — under one cent per query. Motivationally, the method also argues precise toolsets reduce downstream LLM computational overhead vs over-selection. No latency numbers reported.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Precision-driven / adaptive selection count: PTR determines the tool-set size dynamically per query rather than a fixed k, explicitly targeting |T_recommend| = |T_ground|. For the rank-based metrics, K is set to the ground-truth toolset size. RecTools allows 1-10 tools per query (variable), unlike ToolLens (1-3) and MetaTool (fixed 2).
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Tool retrieval and recommendation lineage: COLT/ToolLens (Qu et al. 2024), MetaTool (Huang et al. 2023), Confucius (Gao et al. 2024), classic retrievers BM25/TF-IDF, dense retrievers (Contriever, SBERT, TAS-B, SimCSE, DPR), ToolLLM (Qin et al. 2023); broader LLM-recommendation framing (memory/knowledge/architecture/prompt recommendation).
- **contrasts with**:
> Fixed-top-k tool retrieval methods that package a fixed number of top-ranked tools (ToolRerank, COLT, Qu et al. 2024 tool retrieval) and rely on knowing the tool count in advance; ToolkenGPT (tool-as-token). Also explicitly distinguished from execution-time / runtime-feedback tool-use refinement frameworks — Toolformer, Re-Invoke (Chen et al. 2024), DRAFT (Qu et al. 2024), TECTON (Alazraki et al. 2025) — which depend on real tool-execution feedback, whereas PTR is offline pre-execution.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use). Within retrieval-augmented tool-use, PTR sits in the tool-retrieval/selection sub-lineage but reframes the objective from recall-oriented fixed-top-k retrieval to precision-driven, variable-size tool-set recommendation (minimal sufficient set) as a pre-execution front-end to downstream tool-execution planners.
