<a id="item-tool-planner"></a>
### 101. Tool-Planner: Task Planning with Clusters across Multiple Tools

2024  ·  ICLR 2025  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.03807)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: ICLR 2025 (arXiv preprint 2406.03807, first submitted Jun 2024; camera-ready accepted to The Thirteenth International Conference on Learning Representations 2025)
- **authors affiliation**: Yanming Liu, Xinyue Peng, Jiannan Cao, Shi Bo, Yuwei Zhang, Xuhong Zhang, Sheng Cheng, Xun Wang, Jianwei Yin, Tianyu Du. Lead/primary affiliation: Zhejiang University (with Southeast University and Massachusetts Institute of Technology). Corresponding authors at ZJU.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.03807
- **code url**: https://github.com/OceannTwT/Tool-Planner
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/OceannTwT/Tool-Planner (official repo; OpenReview forum: https://openreview.net/forum?id=dRz3cizftU). Not a continuously-updated leaderboard/paper-list; it is the method's own code repository.

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: tool-use (LLM tool learning: task planning and multi-tool/API invocation)
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent LLM tool learning over large real-world API pools (ToolBench/RapidAPI, APIBench). The LLM must plan a multi-step solution and invoke external APIs, observing execution feedback (errors) and re-planning when tools fail. No retriever or planner training: the backbone LLMs (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Claude-3) are used off-the-shelf; the only learned component is an off-the-shelf SimCSE encoder used offline to cluster tools. Supervision for the method itself is none; evaluation uses ToolEval-style judging.
- **what is retrieved**: tools / APIs, organized as toolkits (clusters of same-function APIs). At plan time the model selects toolkits (a set of functionally-equivalent tools per node); at execution/error time it selects an alternative concrete API from within the current toolkit.
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus of tool/API documentation and descriptions (ToolBench RapidAPI APIs, APIBench model-hub APIs). The toolkit clusters are induced offline and remain fixed during task solving; no growing/episodic memory is written back.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Completeness-of-the-needed-set oriented rather than a fixed top-k ranking: each node is a whole toolkit (set of functionally-equivalent APIs) so the planner aims to exhaustively exhaust functionally-equivalent alternatives within a node before abandoning a path, maximizing recovery of a working tool for each subtask rather than ranking one best tool.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not framed as case-based reasoning). If forced to map: [Retrieve: yes (select toolkit/API), Reuse: yes (reuse alternative within toolkit), Revise: partial (re-select tool / replan across toolkits on error), Retain: no (no case stored back)].
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner; it is positioned as tree-search-based task planning over tool clusters.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: tool-API (single API) grouped into a cluster/toolkit. The retrievable/planning unit is the toolkit (cluster of functionally-equivalent APIs); the executable unit is an individual tool-API selected from within that toolkit.
- **index source**: Static corpus, offline-induced. Tool/API documentation and descriptions are summarized by an LLM into functionality explanations, embedded with SimCSE, then clustered offline with k-means++ into toolkits before task solving. No online/test-time growth of the store.
- **index structure topology**:
> cluster-or-toolkit organization: APIs are grouped into k clusters (toolkits) of same/similar function via k-means++ over SimCSE embeddings. During solving, planning forms a decision/behavior tree G(T)=(V_T, E_T) whose nodes are toolkits, so the effective structure is cluster-keyed nodes arranged in a search tree.
- **retriever type**: dense (SimCSE sentence-embedding similarity) for offline tool clustering, combined with LLM-as-selector at plan/execution time (the LLM chooses which toolkit and which API within a toolkit). No BM25/learned-to-rank retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> none (off-the-shelf): SimCSE is a pretrained contrastive sentence encoder used as-is (princeton-nlp/sup-simcse-roberta-base); k-means++ is unsupervised. Tool selection within/across toolkits is performed by the frozen LLM via prompting, not a trained retrieval policy. The contrastive signal exists only inside the pretrained SimCSE encoder, not trained for this task.
- **query construction**:
> Plan-time: the LLM generates a multi-step plan over toolkit functionality descriptions m_{T_h}=f(T_h) given the user instruction x and tool docs/descriptions D,M. Error-time: when an API fails, the current state plus error information E and the retained plan condition the choice of an alternative API within the same toolkit, or a new cross-toolkit plan. Clustering query/key: LLM-generated functionality explanations H={h_i} embedded by SimCSE.
- **query granularity**: Two-level: task-level (initial toolkit-level plan over the whole instruction) and step/state-level (per-node selection of a concrete API within the current toolkit, and per-error re-selection/replanning).
- **when to retrieve**: iterative / active (error-triggered): toolkit clustering is one-shot offline; tool (re)selection is iterative during execution and is actively triggered when a tool invocation error / unavailability occurs.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> agent/execution-feedback-initiated: a tool invocation error (invalid/missing parameters, false API call format, API hallucinated, tool unavailable) triggers reselection of an alternative API within the same toolkit; if all APIs in the toolkit fail, the accumulated error information E triggers cross-toolkit replanning on the subgraph G(T) minus the failed node.
- **reranking**: No explicit learned reranking stage. Within-toolkit alternative selection is done by the LLM among functionally-equivalent APIs; clusters are formed by k-means++ over SimCSE similarity (no cross-encoder / RRF reranker).
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Light: tool documentation and descriptions are summarized by an LLM into brief functionality explanations before embedding/clustering (decompose-then-summarize style). At solving time the planner sees toolkit functionality descriptions rather than full per-API docs (a form of abstraction/compression); no distractor-filtering or reason-in-documents distillation module.
- **tool document engineering**:
> LLM-generated functionality explanations: raw API documentation D and descriptions M are summarized by an LLM into brief functionality explanations H={h_i}, which are then embedded by SimCSE for clustering (a summary/expansion step rather than raw-docstring embedding or instruction-tuned tool embeddings).
- **index content separation**:
> Partial / abstraction-based: at plan time the model reasons over compact toolkit functionality descriptions (the lightweight index), while heavier per-API documentation d_t' is consulted on demand when generating call parameters for a specific selected API — a form of progressive disclosure (functionality-index then per-API content).
- **dynamic index and protocol**: Static tool index built offline via SimCSE+k-means++ clustering (no live CRUD auto-sync). Integration protocol is RapidAPI (ToolBench) plus model-hub APIs (APIBench); execution uses the ToolBench RapidAPI calling interface. Not MCP; no live-synchronized tool store.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> prompt augmentation + tool reuse: toolkit functionality descriptions and candidate APIs are placed in the LLM prompt to drive planning and tool calls; on failure, an alternative API from the same toolkit is reused without altering the plan structure (E_T kept unchanged), keeping plan stability.
- **planning integration**:
> Inside a decision/behavior tree search. Tool-Planner conceptualizes problem solving as a decision tree where each node is a toolkit (set of tools). Plan-then-act with error-driven replanning: (a) within-toolkit reselection on a single tool failure keeps the plan path fixed; (b) cross-toolkit replanning (DFSDT-style depth-first search but at the toolkit level rather than the individual-API level) when all APIs in a toolkit fail, on subgraph G(T)<-G(T)\v.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: per-tool-call within a rollout: retrieval/selection is woven in at each tool invocation step (choose an API for the current toolkit node, and re-select on error), with coarser task-level replanning across toolkits when a node fully fails.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> N/A (not a CBR adaptation). The closest analog: execution-feedback-driven revision — on tool failure the LLM re-selects an alternative API within the toolkit (verbatim swap of equivalent tool) or, if exhausted, prompts the LLM to generate a new cross-toolkit plan using error information while retaining prior states.
- **retrieved item representation**: Surface form injected into the prompt is structured/free-text tool information: toolkit functionality descriptions m_{T_h}=f(T_h) plus candidate API documentation/descriptions; the executable form is the concrete API call (function name + parameters).
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Reusable functional grouping: a toolkit is an abstracted cluster of functionally-equivalent APIs described by a shared functionality explanation (more abstract than a single raw API document but not a distilled strategy/workflow). The unit ranges from this abstracted toolkit (plan level) down to a single procedural tool/API (execution level).
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Functional clustering provides redundancy/robustness: if a chosen API fails or hallucinates, equivalent APIs in the same toolkit serve as fallbacks, reducing the impact of a single bad/unavailable tool. A 'Cluster Incomplete' error (~13.5% of analyzed errors) is acknowledged as a failure mode where clustering misses relevant APIs. No retriever-aware SFT or self-reflection relevance evaluator beyond LLM error handling.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (no persistent learned memory). The toolkit/cluster index is a static offline-built tool library, not an episodic/skill memory that evolves.
- **write back**: False. No new experiences, cases, or skills are written back to a memory store; clusters are fixed after offline induction and intermediate results are used only within the current task's solution tree.
- **online growth**: No. The toolkit store is frozen after offline SimCSE+k-means++ clustering; it does not grow during deployment/test time.
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back mechanism exists).
- **failure experience usage**:
> Within-episode only: failure/error information E={F_t(t_e)} from failed API calls is fed back to the LLM to trigger within-toolkit reselection and cross-toolkit replanning during the same task. Failures are NOT stored persistently across tasks; there is no success+failure contrastive memory or corrective rule database.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (no stored entries are mutated; the cluster index is static after offline construction).
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No. Tool/toolkit selection is performed by the frozen LLM via prompting plus fixed SimCSE-similarity clustering; it is not an RL/value-based or otherwise learned retrieval policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent framework; no memory/experience sharing across multiple agents or heterogeneous frameworks.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: ToolBench (sub-datasets G1-Inst, G1-Tool, G1-Cat, G2-Inst, G2-Cat, G3-Inst; APIs from RapidAPI Hub, 16,464 APIs) and APIBench (TorchHub, HuggingFace, TensorFlow; 1,645 selected APIs).
- **benchmark family**: tool (ToolBench/RapidAPI; APIBench/Gorilla model-hub APIs).
- **baselines**:
> ReAct (Yao et al. 2022), Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023), AdaPlanner (Sun et al. 2023a), DFSDT (Qin et al. 2024, ToolLLM). Ablation also compares ReAct+Toolkit and AdaPlanner+Toolkit. Backbone LLMs: GPT-3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo-0125), GPT-4 (gpt-4-turbo-2024-04-09), Claude-3 (claude-3-sonnet).
- **key metrics**: Pass Rate (%), Win Rate (%) (ToolEval-style LLM judgment vs GPT-3.5+ReAct), Hallucination Rate (%) (APIBench), and efficiency: average running time (sec) / latency and re-planning frequency.
- **headline result**:
> On ToolBench with GPT-4, Tool-Planner improves average Pass Rate by +8.8% and Win Rate by +9.1% over the strongest baseline DFSDT (avg Pass 77.3% vs 68.5%, avg Win 77.5% vs 68.4%); on APIBench with GPT-4 it gains +6.6% pass and +14.5% win. Reported latency only ~2x ReAct/AdaPlanner while DFSDT is 6-8x.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Tool clustering ablation: adding the clustering-derived toolkit to baselines (ReAct+Toolkit, AdaPlanner+Toolkit) on GPT-4 raises pass/win across G1-Tool/G2-Inst/G2-Cat/G3-Inst (e.g., G1-Tool pass +9.0%, G3-Inst win +4.3%); AdaPlanner+Toolkit even slightly exceeds DFSDT, showing the toolkit node design drives gains. (2) Number of clusters k: best when average cluster size ~9 on G1-inst (k=1800 ToolBench, k=65 APIBench); too large k under-clusters (slow, incomplete exploration), too small k mixes functions (wrong tool calls). (3) Text embedding model for clustering: SimCSE > text-embedding-ada-02 > Contriever > RoBERTa-base on pass rate (e.g., G1-inst 66.0 vs 63.5/61.0/60.5). (4) Efficiency: running-time comparison vs ReAct/AdaPlanner/DFSDT. (5) Error analysis: Invalid Input Parameters most frequent; Cluster Incomplete ~13.5%.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> No. Intrinsic retrieval/clustering metrics (e.g., Recall@k / nDCG) are not reported separately; evaluation is end-to-end task metrics (Pass/Win/Hallucination Rate) plus efficiency. Clustering quality is probed only indirectly via downstream pass rate across embedding models and k values.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Both: outcome metrics (Pass/Win/Hallucination Rate) plus process-quality signals — re-planning frequency, average running time/latency, and an error-type distribution analysis (process diagnostics) rather than only final success.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Reported as a core selling point: Tool-Planner reduces re-planning frequency and computation. Latency is only ~2x that of linear methods (ReAct/AdaPlanner) versus DFSDT's 6-8x, because on a tool error it swaps in a same-function API within the toolkit without discarding/re-searching the whole path. Quantified via average running time (sec) per dataset (Figure 4).
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (this is a method paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Uses existing benchmarks: ToolBench (16,464 RapidAPI APIs, G1/G2/G3 = single-tool / intra-category multi-tool / intra-collection multi-tool instructions) and APIBench (1,645 APIs from TorchHub/HuggingFace/TensorFlow). Tool-Planner does not construct a new benchmark; answer verifiability follows ToolEval (Pass Rate) and pairwise Win Rate judging.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> DFSDT / ToolLLM (Qin et al. 2024) — extends DFSDT's depth-first solution-tree search by replacing per-API nodes with toolkit (cluster) nodes; SimCSE (Gao et al. 2021) for tool embeddings; k-means++ (Arthur & Vassilvitskii 2007) for clustering; ToolBench (Qin et al. 2024) and APIBench/Gorilla (Patil et al. 2023) datasets; Tree-Planner (Hu et al. 2023) and tree-of-thought lineage for tree-structured planning.
- **contrasts with**:
> ReAct (linear tool use), Reflexion (verbal feedback re-planning at API level), AdaPlanner (point error correction), DFSDT (API-level depth-first re-planning that discards failing paths). Also contrasts with CRITIC and AnyTool feedback-integration methods and with MCTS/Toolchain* search; key contrast is toolkit-level (cluster) reselection/replanning vs single-API-level search.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use): tree-search task-planning over clustered tool stores. Lineage: ReAct -> Reflexion/AdaPlanner -> DFSDT (ToolLLM) -> Tool-Planner, advancing from single-API tree search to cluster/toolkit-level planning with within-cluster fallback retrieval and cross-cluster replanning.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- context_budget_and_selection_count
- tool_dependency_awareness

<a id="item-tool2vec"></a>
### 102. Tool2Vec + ToolRefiner (Efficient and Scalable Estimation of Tool Representations in Vector Space)

2024  ·  arXiv 2409.02141  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.02141)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **authors affiliation**:
> Suhong Moon* (UC Berkeley), Siddharth Jha* (UC Berkeley), Lutfi Eren Erdogan (UC Berkeley), Sehoon Kim (UC Berkeley), Woosang Lim (POSCO HOLDINGS), Kurt Keutzer (UC Berkeley), Amir Gholami (UC Berkeley / Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, LBNL). *Equal contribution. Primary affiliation: UC Berkeley (SqueezeAILab); with POSCO HOLDINGS and LBNL.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.02141
- **code url**: https://github.com/SqueezeAILab/Tool2Vec (MIT license; ToolBank dataset at https://huggingface.co/datasets/squeeze-ai-lab/ToolBank)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: tool-use / function calling for LLMs; specifically the tool (API) retrieval subproblem - selecting the minimal relevant set of tools to place in an LLM's context for downstream function calling.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, non-interactive multi-tool retrieval. Given a natural-language user query and a large tool/API library (hundreds-to-thousands of tools), efficiently retrieve the relevant subset of tools so that only their descriptions/signatures are placed in the LLM prompt (addressing context-window/latency/cost limits). Single-agent, retrieval-as-front-end setting; supervision is available because domain-specific (query, tool-set) labels are synthesized by LLMs. The paper motivates that LLM-based retrieval (e.g. AnyTool) incurs seconds of latency and fine-tuning LLMs needs frequent retraining, so it instead trains small encoder models (E5-base; DeBERTa-V3 base/xsmall). The setting is multi-label: each query maps to 1-to-several required tools (up to 5 in ToolBank). Retrieval is decoupled from execution; the work does not run the downstream LLM tool-calling, only measures retrieval quality.
- **what is retrieved**: tools (specifically tool/API entries from a tool library). Each retrieved tool is represented by a usage-driven embedding (Tool2Vec) or a classification logit (MLC); the downstream consumer would place the retrieved tool descriptions/signatures into the LLM context.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus: a fixed tool/API library (ToolBench RapidAPI hierarchy; or ToolBank's NumPy/Pandas/Boto3 tool sets). The retrievable store (Tool2Vec embeddings / MLC tool labels) is induced offline from training data and frozen at test time; no agent-written growing/episodic memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Completeness-oriented multi-tool recovery within a top-k budget. The objective is to recover the complete minimal set of tools a query needs (queries require 1-5 tools), measured by Recall@K (K=3,5,7), not just a single best tool. It is framed against COLT's 'completeness-oriented tool retrieval' line; output is a fixed top-K list, so it is a top-k ranking objective aimed at completeness (recall of the full needed set) rather than precision-driven variable-size selection.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based-reasoning method; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain case cycle).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The work is framed as tool retrieval / information retrieval (retrieve-then-rerank, multi-label classification, usage-driven embeddings) and does not invoke case-based reasoning or cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> tool-API: a single tool/function entry (e.g. a RapidAPI endpoint, or a library function like numpy.argmax / pandas.read_csv / boto3 EC2 op). The retrievable unit is one tool, represented either by its usage-driven Tool2Vec embedding (averaged query embeddings) or as one class in a multi-label classifier head.
- **index source**:
> Static corpus, offline-induced. Tool2Vec embeddings are built offline by averaging the embeddings of training-set example queries associated with each tool; MLC and ToolRefiner are encoder classifiers fine-tuned offline per dataset subset. The index/models are frozen at inference; no online/test-time growth. Training labels (query->tools) come either from ToolBench or from LLM-synthesized ToolBank data.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat vector index for the first stage (cosine similarity over Tool2Vec embeddings), or equivalently a flat T-way classification head for MLC. The underlying ToolBench tool library is hierarchical (RapidAPI category->tool->API, reflected in the I1/I2/I3 splits), but Tool2Vec/ToolRefiner explicitly do NOT exploit or assume any tool hierarchy (a stated contrast with ToolRerank). So the method's own index is flat/non-hierarchical.
- **retriever type**:
> Hybrid two-stage: Stage 1 is a fast retriever that is either (a) dense embedding similarity over usage-driven Tool2Vec embeddings (E5 encoder), or (b) MLC - a learned multi-label classifier (fine-tuned DeBERTa-V3 base with an H x T head on the [CLS] token) that directly predicts tool labels from the query (a classification-as-retrieval / generative-classifier style). Stage 2 (ToolRefiner) is a learned cross-encoder-style reranker (fine-tuned DeBERTa-V3 xsmall) that jointly attends over the query plus the Tool2Vec embeddings of the Stage-1 candidates. So: dense + learned-classifier retriever, followed by a learned reranker.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Supervised, with multiple signals. (1) Tool2Vec needs no retriever training - it reuses an off-the-shelf embedding model (E5) and aggregates training-query embeddings per tool (usage-driven construction); the underlying embedding model is not fine-tuned in the main experiments. (2) MLC is trained with multi-label binary cross-entropy: label 1 for required tools, 0 otherwise, over the full tool set. (3) ToolRefiner is trained with per-tool binary cross-entropy on the candidate set (relevant vs not). Thus the learning signal is supervised similarity/relevance labels (query-tool co-occurrence), where the labels themselves can be LLM-synthesized (ToolBank). No RL, no LM-feedback loop, no interactive preference / Bradley-Terry signal.
- **query construction**:
> Raw user query is used directly as the key. For Tool2Vec, the query is embedded by E5 and compared (cosine) to tool embeddings. For MLC, the raw query tokens are fed to DeBERTa-V3 to produce per-tool logits. For ToolRefiner, the raw query is paired with the Tool2Vec embeddings of Stage-1 candidates. No query decomposition, intent extraction, or synthetic query expansion at retrieval time. (Note: LLM 'Query Polish' is applied only when generating the ToolBank training/eval data, not at retrieval time.)
- **query granularity**: task-level (one-shot at t=0): a single retrieval pass per user query produces the tool set; no per-step or trajectory-level re-querying.
- **when to retrieve**:
> one-shot: retrieval is performed exactly once per query as a front-end stage (a fast first-stage retrieve followed by a single ToolRefiner refinement pass). The 'two-stage' / 'staged' / 'iteratively improves' phrasing refers to the retrieve-then-refine cascade, not to repeated test-time retrieval interleaved with reasoning.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule: both the Stage-1 retrieval and the Stage-2 ToolRefiner always run once per query. There is no uncertainty/confidence/agent-initiated trigger deciding whether to retrieve.
- **reranking**:
> Yes - ToolRefiner is the reranking/refinement stage and is a central contribution. It is a learned classifier (fine-tuned DeBERTa-V3 xsmall) that takes the query and the Tool2Vec embeddings of the N Stage-1 candidates and, in a single forward pass, jointly classifies all candidates as relevant/not (binary cross-entropy per tool position). Explicitly likened to BERT passage reranking (Nogueira & Cho 2019), but contrasted with one-by-one cross-encoder rerankers: ToolRefiner reranks all candidates simultaneously, operates directly on precomputed Tool2Vec embeddings (not raw descriptions), and assumes no tool hierarchy (vs ToolRerank).
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> rerank / refine via a second-stage learned classifier (ToolRefiner). Pipeline: fast Stage-1 retriever (Tool2Vec similarity or MLC) returns top-N candidates (N tuned over {8,16,32,64,128}); ToolRefiner then refines this candidate set by jointly re-scoring all N candidates and outputting the final top-K. No distractor-distillation/compression of tool documents; the refinement is candidate re-scoring/pruning. Choosing N is a trade-off: too few hurts recall, too many overwhelms ToolRefiner (peak at N=32 or 64).
- **tool document engineering**:
> Usage-driven tool representation is the key lever: instead of embedding raw tool docstrings, Tool2Vec represents each tool by the AVERAGE embedding of example user queries that use it (closing the query-description semantic gap). MLC and ToolRefiner are trained directly on (query -> tool-label) supervision rather than on tool text. Description-based embeddings serve only as the contrasted baseline. So: usage/query-driven embeddings (a form of synthetic-query-augmented tool representation) rather than raw or summary-expanded docstrings.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Static index built offline; no live synchronization / CRUD auto-sync and no MCP/function-calling protocol integration described. The underlying tools derive from RapidAPI (ToolBench) and from crawled NumPy/Pandas/Boto3 API references (ToolBank), but the retrieval index (embeddings/classifier) is frozen after offline construction.
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> Limited. The method does NOT model explicit inter-tool dependencies (output-of-A-feeds-B, shared auth, prerequisites) and explicitly assumes no tool hierarchy. ToolRefiner does capture inter-tool interactions implicitly by jointly attending over all candidate tool embeddings together with the query in one forward pass (so co-relevance among candidates is modeled), and ToolBank's generation encourages natural tool co-occurrence (M coherent tools whose outputs chain), but no explicit dependency graph or prerequisite modeling is used.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Retrieval-as-front-end for prompt augmentation: the final top-K retrieved tools are intended to be inserted (their descriptions/signatures) into the LLM's context for downstream function calling, reducing prompt length while preserving accuracy. The paper itself evaluates retrieval quality (Recall@K / nDCG@K) and does not run end-to-end LLM execution. ToolRefiner additionally injects Tool2Vec embeddings as inputs to its own classifier (latent tool representations used internally), but the consumer-facing output is the selected tool set for prompt construction.
- **planning integration**:
> retrieve-then-plan / plan-decoupled: tool retrieval is a standalone front-end that selects the tool set; any planning/acting by a downstream LLM happens separately and is out of scope of this paper. Within retrieval itself it is a retrieve-then-rerank (retrieve-then-refine) cascade. No interleaving with an agent planning loop, no MCTS/tree search.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: per-query / per-answer: retrieval (and its two cascaded stages) runs once per user query, decoupled from any downstream per-CoT-step or per-tool-call reasoning. There is no per-step interleaving.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (no case adaptation; retrieved tools are used as-is; refinement is candidate re-scoring, not adaptation of a retrieved solution).
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Two coexisting forms. Internally, tools are represented as Tool2Vec usage-driven dense embeddings (latent vectors = average of associated user-query embeddings), which ToolRefiner consumes directly. The consumer-facing retrieved items are tool/API entries (whose raw descriptions/signatures would be injected into the LLM prompt). No distilled strategy/guideline/workflow text is produced; the surface form is the tool identity (+ its description) plus, internally, a precomputed embedding.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Concrete single tool/API (a procedural skill / executable function), not a distilled strategy, trajectory, or workflow. The key representational novelty is that the INDEXING signal is usage-driven (example queries) rather than the tool description, but the retrieved unit remains a concrete tool.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Two-stage retrieve-then-refine is itself the robustness mechanism: the more powerful ToolRefiner corrects Stage-1 errors and is shown to better separate tools with overlapping/similar functionality (reducing confusion among near-duplicate tools), yielding a more uniform per-tool failure distribution (mean 2.07 vs Tool2Vec's 7.86 mistakes per tool). Candidate-count N is tuned to avoid overwhelming ToolRefiner with distractors (too-large N degrades performance). Tool2Vec embeddings reduce the query-description semantic gap, lowering false matches. No explicit self-reflection / relevance-evaluator / distractor-aware adversarial training beyond the supervised classifier.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (no episodic/skill/workflow/graph/latent memory). The retrievable store is a static, offline-induced set of Tool2Vec embeddings / classifier weights over a fixed tool library.
- **write back**: No. The system does not write new experiences/cases/skills back into a store at deployment; Tool2Vec embeddings and the MLC/ToolRefiner models are fixed after offline training.
- **online growth**: No. The tool index (embeddings/classifier) is frozen after offline construction and does not grow at test time. (Adding a new tool would require recomputing its Tool2Vec embedding from associated queries and, for MLC/ToolRefiner, retraining or expanding the classification head.)
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back/memory-update mechanism exists).
- **failure experience usage**: No storage or retrieval of runtime failed experiences. Training uses positive (required) and negative (unused) tool labels per query as standard multi-label supervision, but these are training-time labels, not stored runtime failure cases retrieved later.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (no stored memory entries are mutated; the store is static after offline induction).
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Partially: retrieval/refinement is realized by LEARNED supervised models (MLC classifier, ToolRefiner reranker) trained on relevance labels, rather than purely fixed similarity top-k (which Tool2Vec alone is). However it is NOT a sequential RL/value-optimized policy (no M-MDP, no Q-learning, no reward optimization); it is supervised classification/ranking. So: learned models, not a learned sequential policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single retrieval pipeline serving a single (hypothetical) downstream agent; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> (1) ToolBench (Qin et al. 2023/2024, ToolLLM; >16,000 RapidAPI APIs), split into I1, I2, I3 (increasing tool-hierarchy level / difficulty). (2) ToolBank - the paper's own LLM-synthesized datasets: NumpyBank (511 NumPy tools, ~20,000 queries), PandasBank (1,655 Pandas tools, ~70,000 queries), AWSBank/Boto3 (1,002 tools across EC2/RDS/IAM/S3/SNS, ~73,000 queries).
- **benchmark family**: tool retrieval (ToolBench family; plus the paper's new ToolBank: NumpyBank / PandasBank / AWSBank).
- **baselines**:
> ToolBench Retriever (Qin et al. 2023/2024 ToolLLM dense retriever; reproduced from original codebase); COLT (Qu et al. 2024, completeness-oriented tool retrieval, Contriever-based; numbers taken from the COLT paper as code unavailable); and for ToolBank a Description-Based Retriever (E5-base fine-tuned on tool descriptions). Within the paper's own methods, Tool2Vec, MLC, ToolRefiner+Tool2Vec, ToolRefiner+MLC are compared against each other. ToolRerank is discussed as related work / conceptual contrast but is not run as a numeric baseline.
- **key metrics**:
> Recall@K (primary) for K=3,5,7; nDCG@K (K=3,5,7) reported as secondary (Appendix A.2). Plus diagnostic metrics: per-tool percentage failure rate (mean/std), and a GPT-4-turbo-judged query-quality win rate (60% win rate of ToolBank queries vs ToolBench queries). No end-to-end Pass Rate / Win Rate execution metric (retrieval-only evaluation).
- **headline result**:
> Up to 27.28 improvement in Recall@K on ToolBench and up to 30.5 (~30%) improvement in Recall@K on ToolBank vs description-based retrieval. Concretely, on ToolBench's hardest split I3, ToolRefiner+Tool2Vec reaches R@5=87.80 / R@7=89.70 vs the ToolBench Retriever's 63.88 / 73.73, and the abstract states 'over 25% higher recall' than ToolBench's retriever on the hardest split. ToolRefiner+MLC is generally the best (e.g. ToolBench I1 R@5=96.83, I2 R@5=87.92).
- **ablations**:
> (1) Tool2Vec vs description embeddings for ToolRefiner inputs (Table A.1, ToolBench I3): ToolRefiner+Tool2Vec embeddings (R@3 80.58) > description embeddings with Tool2Vec retrieval (71.55) > description embeddings with description retrieval (66.00) - usage-driven embeddings clearly help. (2) Number of Stage-1 candidate tools N in {8,16,32,64,128} (Table A.2): recall improves then plateaus/declines; best N=32 or 64 (too-large N confuses ToolRefiner). (3) Embedding-model generality (Table A.3, ToolBench I3, no fine-tuning): Tool2Vec beats description-based retrieval for every model (E5-small/base/large, mxbai-embed-large, text-embedding-3-small), e.g. E5-small Tool2Vec R@3 63.12 vs Descriptions 20.62. (4) nDCG@K (Table A.4) shows the same ranking as Recall@K. (5) Failure analysis (Appendix B): ToolRefiner averages 2.07 mistakes/tool with uniform distribution vs Tool2Vec's 7.86 (skewed); ToolRefiner handles complex/long queries better, Tool2Vec struggles on simpler/shorter queries.
- **evaluation decoupling**: Yes (intrinsic-only). The work reports intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@K, nDCG@K) and explicitly does NOT measure end-to-end downstream task success; retrieval quality is fully decoupled from any execution outcome (execution is not run).
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Process/retrieval-quality metrics only. Evaluation scores the retrieval step (Recall@K, nDCG@K) and diagnostic process analyses (per-tool failure rate distribution, query-length vs failure correlation, query-quality win rate). No final task-outcome (e.g. tool-call success) metric is reported.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Efficiency is the core motivation. The two-stage design lets the expensive ToolRefiner operate only on N pruned candidates (not the whole library), and uses small encoders (E5-base; DeBERTa-V3 base for MLC, xsmall for ToolRefiner) instead of LLM-based retrievers; the paper argues LLM-based retrieval (e.g. AnyTool, iterative-feedback methods) adds latency 'up to several seconds'. ToolRefiner reranks all candidates in ONE forward pass (vs one-by-one cross-encoders like ToolRerank). The N-sweep (Table A.2) frames a recall-vs-latency trade-off (smaller N = faster but lower recall). No concrete wall-clock latency / FLOPs / dollar-cost numbers are reported.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Reported as Recall@K with fixed K in {3,5,7}; final output is a fixed top-K tool list (K up to 5 needed by any ToolBank query). Stage-1 candidate count N is reranked-then-truncated: N swept over {8,16,32,64,128} with best at 32 or 64, then ToolRefiner narrows to the final top-K. The motivation is to cap the LLM prompt's tool budget by retrieving few tools; no explicit token-budget number is given.
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> ToolBank (this paper's contribution) is LLM-synthesized: tools crawled from official API references (NumPy 511 tools, Pandas 1,655, Boto3/AWS 1,002 across EC2/RDS/IAM/S3/SNS). Generation samples T=10 tools and lets Llama-3-70B-Instruct pick M in [2,5] coherent tools (vs ToolBench's random co-occurrence), with 5 in-context examples; then a 'Query Polish' LLM step improves naturalness. Sizes: ~20,000 NumPy queries (19,530 tool combinations), ~70,000 Pandas (69,550 combos), ~73,000 AWS (70,816 combos). Quality validated by GPT-4-turbo judging (ToolBank queries achieve 60% win rate over ToolBench queries on naturalness/fluency/coherence). Train/val split 8:2; test set evaluated once.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> ToolBench / ToolLLM (Qin et al. 2024) for the benchmark, tool hierarchy and the dense ToolBench retriever baseline; COLT (Qu et al. 2024) as completeness-oriented baseline; E5 embeddings (Wang et al. 2022) for Tool2Vec; DeBERTa-V3 (He et al. 2023) for MLC and ToolRefiner; BERT passage reranking (Nogueira & Cho 2019; Yilmaz et al. 2019) as the conceptual basis for ToolRefiner; TinyAgent (Erdogan et al. 2024) and LLM2LLM (Lee et al. 2024) for LLM-driven synthetic tool-retrieval data; Llama-3-70B-Instruct for ToolBank generation; MT-Bench / LLM-as-judge (Zheng et al. 2024) for query-quality evaluation.
- **contrasts with**:
> Description-based dense tool retrieval (ToolBench retriever; EasyTool; ProTIP) which suffers a query-description semantic gap; LLM-as-retriever methods (AnyTool; iterative-feedback retrieval of Xu et al. 2024) which add seconds of latency and need iterative LLM calls; ToolkenGPT (learns tool tokens inside the LLM, needs LLM modification); fine-tuned function-calling LLMs that require frequent retraining; and especially ToolRerank (Zheng et al. 2024) - ToolRefiner differs by assuming NO tool hierarchy, reranking ALL candidates in one forward pass (not one-by-one), and operating on Tool2Vec usage embeddings rather than tool descriptions.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use), tool-retrieval sub-lineage. Sits in the embedding-design / retrieve-then-rerank branch of tool retrieval: it reframes the indexing signal from tool descriptions to usage-driven query embeddings (Tool2Vec), adds a classification-as-retrieval first stage (MLC), and a single-pass learned reranker over latent tool embeddings (ToolRefiner). Advances ToolBench/COLT-style dense tool retrieval toward usage-grounded, completeness-oriented multi-tool retrieval, contemporaneous with and contrasted against ToolRerank.

<a id="item-toolgen"></a>
### 103. ToolGen: Unified Tool Retrieval and Calling via Generation

2024  ·  ICLR 2025  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.03439)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: ICLR 2025 (arXiv:2410.03439, submitted Oct 2024, last revised Mar 2025; DBLP: conf/iclr/WangHJWB025; OpenReview id XLMAMmowdY)
- **authors affiliation**:
> Renxi Wang (LibrAI; MBZUAI - Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence); Xudong Han (LibrAI; MBZUAI); Lei Ji (Microsoft); Shu Wang (UCLA - University of California, Los Angeles); Timothy Baldwin (LibrAI; MBZUAI; The University of Melbourne); Haonan Li (LibrAI; MBZUAI). Primary affiliation: MBZUAI / LibrAI.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.03439
- **code url**: https://github.com/Reason-Wang/ToolGen

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Tool-use: large-scale LLM-agent tool/API retrieval and calling. Unifies tool retrieval and autonomous task completion (tool invocation + argument generation) over a pool of 47k real-world APIs (ToolBench / RapidAPI).
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent tool-use with full-parameter supervised fine-tuning of an open LLM (Llama-3-8B). Given a user query and a tool repository of 16k+ tools / 47k unique APIs, the agent must (1) retrieve the correct tool(s) and (2) iteratively complete the task by generating Thought -> Action (tool) -> Arguments and consuming tool feedback over multiple turns. Supervision comes from ToolBench-derived (query, relevant-API) pairs and trajectory data. Unlike the standard retriever-then-LLM pipeline, ToolGen folds retrieval into the LLM's next-token generation by expanding the vocabulary with one virtual token per tool, so no separate retriever module is needed at inference. Single LLM agent, offline-trained then deployed; no online memory growth.
- **what is retrieved**: Tools / APIs (each ToolBench RapidAPI endpoint, documented with name, description, parameters). Each tool/API is mapped to a unique virtual vocabulary token, and 'retrieval' means the LLM generating that tool token.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus baked into model parameters: the fixed 47k-API ToolBench pool is virtualized into 47k (precisely 46,985) tool tokens learned during three-stage fine-tuning. Tool knowledge is parametric (embedded in the LLM's vocabulary/weights), not an external vector index queried at test time, and not a growing/episodic memory the agent writes during deployment.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Dual: for retrieval evaluation it is a top-k ranking objective scored by NDCG@1/3/5 (generation can produce a ranked list of tool tokens via constrained beam search). For multi-tool queries (I2 intra-category, I3 intra-collection) the model must generate multiple relevant tool tokens, so it also targets recovery of the relevant tool set within the agent trajectory. Primary reported objective is fixed-k NDCG ranking.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: Not a CBR work. If forced to map: [Retrieve: yes - but generative tool-token retrieval, not case retrieval; Reuse: N/A; Revise: N/A; Retain: no]. N/A.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The paper frames itself as generative retrieval / unified tool generation; it does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner and does not describe itself as case-based reasoning.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> tool-API represented as a single virtual token (under the chosen 'atomic' indexing, each of the 47k tools = exactly one new vocabulary token; embedding initialized as the average of the tool-name subtoken embeddings). Alternative indexings (semantic = tool name subtokens, numeric, hierarchical) make a tool span multiple subtokens.
- **index source**:
> Static, offline-induced and parametric: tools come from the fixed ToolBench/RapidAPI corpus (47k APIs); the 'index' is the expanded LLM vocabulary plus weights, created offline via tool memorization + retrieval training. No online/test-time induction; the store is frozen after training (the paper explicitly notes adding new tools is a limitation of generative retrieval, Appendix B).
- **index structure topology**:
> Parametric / flat token vocabulary under atomic indexing (each tool = one independent token, no explicit graph or hierarchy). The paper also studies a HIERARCHICAL indexing variant (recursive Brown-style clustering into a tree, root-to-leaf path encodes a tool) and numeric / semantic variants, but the chosen ToolGen uses flat atomic tokens. No dependency graph; the underlying ToolBench taxonomy (category->tool->API) is not used as a retrieval index.
- **retriever type**: Generative (tool-as-token): the LLM itself IS the retriever, generating tool tokens via next-token prediction with constrained beam search restricted to the tool-token set. No BM25/dense/learned external retriever in the deployed system (those are baselines).
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Next-token-prediction cross-entropy (supervised fine-tuning), in three stages: (1) tool memorization - predict tool token from its documentation; (2) retrieval training - predict relevant tool token(s) from the user query (the key signal for retrieval); (3) end-to-end agent-tuning on trajectories. No contrastive learning, no RL, no preference signal; learning is teacher-forced generation on ToolBench-derived (query, tool-token) and trajectory data.
- **query construction**:
> Raw user query is the input; the model generates tool token(s) directly. In the agent setting the query is consumed within a Thought -> Action -> Arguments conversational template (Agent-Flan-style). No query rewriting, decomposition, or synthetic-query expansion at inference (contrasts with the Re-Invoke and IterFeedback baselines, which do query rewriting / iterative feedback).
- **query granularity**: Two-level: task-level for the standalone tool-retrieval task (one query -> tool tokens), and step/turn-level in the end-to-end agent (at each iteration the model generates a Thought then an Action tool token conditioned on the trajectory so far).
- **when to retrieve**: Retrieval task: one-shot generation per query. Agent task: iterative / per-step - the model generates a tool (Action) token at each agent turn (up to 16 turns / ~5 action rounds + final answer) interleaved with tool feedback, until a 'finish' token or the turn limit.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed/structural schedule driven by the generation template rather than an uncertainty or learned-router signal: the model emits a tool (Action) token whenever the agent paradigm reaches the Action slot after a Thought. There is no token-confidence, attention-uncertainty, or learned complexity classifier deciding whether to retrieve; the LLM autonomously decides which/when tool tokens to generate as part of decoding (and emits 'finish' to stop).
- **reranking**: No separate reranking stage. Ranking emerges directly from constrained beam search over tool tokens (beam scores order the candidate tools for NDCG); no cross-encoder or hierarchy-aware reranker.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> None in the classic sense (no rerank/distill/compress of retrieved documents, because nothing is retrieved into context). The only post-generation processing is constrained beam search, which masks the output distribution to the valid tool-token set, eliminating out-of-vocabulary/nonexistent tool generation (prevents hallucinated tools).
- **tool document engineering**:
> Tool documentation (name, description, parameters) is used as the INPUT in the tool-memorization stage to teach the model the tool->token mapping; at agent inference the predicted tool token fetches that tool's documentation on demand to generate arguments. No synthetic-query augmentation or expanded summaries or weighted-field embeddings; the token embedding is initialized from the average of tool-name subtoken embeddings (atomic indexing).
- **index content separation**:
> Yes (parametric token-as-index + on-demand documentation): the lightweight retrievable unit is the single tool token; the heavy tool documentation is fetched only after the token is generated (used to produce arguments), a progressive-disclosure pattern that avoids putting tool descriptions in the prompt.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Static parametric tool index (frozen after training); the paper explicitly flags adding/maintaining new tools as a limitation of generative retrieval (Appendix B), suggesting continual training / constrained optimization as future work. Integration protocol is ToolBench/RapidAPI API calling (evaluated via StableToolBench, which uses GPT-4 to simulate failed API responses). No live CRUD auto-sync, no MCP.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Latent-token injection + generative invocation: the retrieved tool is the generated virtual token itself (no text injected into the prompt). The token then triggers fetching the tool documentation to generate arguments and execute the call; in pure retrieval mode the generated tokens are the ranked output. Tool knowledge lives in the model's parameters, so retrieval and calling are one generation process.
- **planning integration**:
> Per-step interleaved within an autoregressive agent loop (Agent-Flan-style decomposition of ReAct): the model generates Thought (plan p_i) -> Action tool token (Index(d_si)) -> uses fetched docs to produce Arguments c_i -> receives feedback f_i, iterating until 'finish'. Retrieval is fused INTO acting (retrieve-by-generation), so there is no separate plan-then-retrieve or retrieve-then-plan stage and no external tree search/MCTS over retrieval.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-tool-call within a rollout: a tool token is generated once per agent turn, after a Thought and before Arguments, interleaved with environment feedback. Not per-CoT-step-token-level retrieval and not per-answer only.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not a CBR/case-adaptation method).
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Latent / virtual token: the injected item is a single learned vocabulary token standing for the tool (atomic indexing), whose embedding was initialized from the tool name; the corresponding tool documentation is fetched on demand to instantiate the call. Not a raw trajectory, free-text workflow, or executable program-text injected into the prompt.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Procedural tool / executable API endpoint, encoded at the most compact abstraction possible - a single virtual token per tool. The retrieved unit is concrete (one API), not a distilled strategy, workflow, or trajectory.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Constrained beam search / constrained decoding restricts generation to valid tool tokens, guaranteeing zero nonexistent-tool hallucination (vs ToolLlama/GPT-3.5 which hallucinate; ToolLlama >50% nonexistent tool names when no tools are listed in prompt). Atomic indexing also reduces hallucination relative to semantic/numeric/hierarchical indexing (which generate ~7%+ non-tool tokens without constraints). There is no retrieved-context-noise problem because no external documents are placed in the prompt.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: Parametric / none-explicit: tool knowledge is stored in the LLM's parameters (expanded vocabulary + weights) rather than an external episodic/skill/workflow memory. No retrievable growing memory store.
- **write back**: False: the system does not write new experiences/cases/skills into any memory store during deployment. All learning happens during offline three-stage fine-tuning; at inference the parameters and tool token set are fixed.
- **online growth**: No: the tool token set / parametric store is frozen after training and does not grow at deployment. Adding new tools requires retraining/continual training and is explicitly noted as a limitation of the generative-retrieval design (Appendix B).
- **write back trigger**: Never (no write-back at inference). The only 'writes' are offline gradient updates during the three training stages (tool memorization, retrieval training, agent-tuning).
- **failure experience usage**: Not stored as retrievable memory. Failed agent runs are only handled at inference by a retry mechanism (if the model outputs 'give up' or 'I'm sorry', it is re-prompted to regenerate at higher temperature). No success/failure experiences are retained for future retrieval.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A at inference (parametric store is fixed). During training the embeddings/weights are updated via SGD, but there is no append/dedup/forget/link-and-evolve of any retrievable entries post-deployment.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Partially: retrieval is realized by a fine-tuned generative model (the LLM learns query->tool-token mapping via supervised next-token prediction), so selection is learned rather than a fixed similarity top-k. However it is NOT an RL- or value-optimized policy (no M-MDP / soft Q-learning / reward signal); it is supervised teacher-forced generation.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No: single-agent, single-model. Tool knowledge is private to the one fine-tuned LLM; there is no cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> ToolBench (Qin et al., 2023; 16k+ tool collections, 47k unique APIs) with the standard I1 (single-tool), I2 (intra-category multi-tool), I3 (intra-collection multi-tool) splits for retrieval; StableToolBench (Guo et al., 2024) for end-to-end agent evaluation (solvable-query subset with GPT-4 simulated API outputs).
- **benchmark family**: tool (ToolBench / RapidAPI tool retrieval and tool-use; StableToolBench for stabilized end-to-end agent evaluation).
- **baselines**:
> Retrieval task: BM25 (sparse, unsupervised), Long-Context LLM (gpt-4o over ~2k tools incl. ground truth), Embedding Similarity / EmbSim (OpenAI text-embedding-3-large), Re-Invoke (unsupervised query-rewriting + document expansion), IterFeedback (BERT retriever + gpt-3.5-turbo-0125 iterative feedback, up to 10 rounds), ToolRetriever (BERT retriever trained with contrastive learning, the ToolBench retriever). End-to-end task: GPT-3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo-0613, StableToolBench setup), ToolLlama-2 (Llama-2 fine-tuned on ToolBench), ToolLlama / ToolLlama-3 (Llama-3 fine-tuned on ToolBench, same base model as ToolGen, for fair comparison).
- **key metrics**:
> Retrieval: NDCG@1, NDCG@3, NDCG@5 (per domain I1/I2/I3, in-domain and multi-domain). End-to-end: Solvable Pass Rate (SoPR) and Solvable Win Rate (SoWR, vs GPT-3.5 reference), per category and micro-average, each averaged over 3 runs. Also hallucination rate (% generated tools that do not exist) and number of subtokens per tool (efficiency).
- **headline result**:
> Tool retrieval: ToolGen (single model) is competitive with the multi-model IterFeedback system and clearly beats ToolRetriever; e.g. In-Domain I2 NDCG@1/3/5 = 91.45/88.79/91.13 (best, beating IterFeedback 89.01/85.46/87.10) and I1 NDCG@5 = 92.67 (best). In the harder Multi-Domain setting ToolGen far exceeds ToolRetriever (e.g. I1 NDCG@1 87.67 vs 72.31; I3 NDCG@1 79.00 vs 52.00). End-to-end: best average SoPR (G.T. 54.19, Retriever 53.28) and SoWR (G.T. 49.70, Retriever 51.51), surpassing GPT-3.5 and ToolLlama while using NO external retriever and zero tool hallucination under constrained decoding.
- **ablations**:
> Retrieval training-stage ablation (Table 3, Multi-Domain): removing tool memorization causes a minor drop (e.g. I1 NDCG@1 87.67->84.00); removing retrieval training is catastrophic (I1 NDCG@1 87.67->10.17), confirming retrieval training is the key driver; removing constrained beam search barely changes retrieval NDCG (it matters for hallucination, not ranking). Indexing-method comparison (Tables 2 & 5): semantic indexing slightly best for retrieval NDCG, but ATOMIC indexing is best end-to-end (avg SoPR 55.00 vs semantic 51.87, hierarchical 45.50, numeric 35.45) and is most token-efficient (1 token/tool). Hallucination (Fig. 4): ToolGen w/ constrained decoding = 0% nonexistent tools; w/o constraint ~7% (atomic), more for semantic; ToolLlama >50% without tools in prompt. Generalization (Appendix J): tool memorization improves generalization to unseen tools (e.g. train I1 -> test I2 NDCG@1 11.28 w/o vs 40.86 w/ memorization), though end-to-end on unseen tools ToolGen underperforms ToolLlama (weaker task-completion generalization).
- **evaluation decoupling**: Yes: intrinsic retrieval metrics (NDCG@1/3/5) are reported separately (Section 4) from end-to-end agent task metrics (SoPR/SoWR, Section 5), with dedicated retrieval and end-to-end experimental sections.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Mostly outcome (NDCG ranking quality; SoPR/SoWR task success/win). Some process/diagnostic metrics are reported: tool-hallucination rate (validity of generated actions) and subtokens-per-tool / inference efficiency, but no step-wise reasoning-faithfulness or trajectory-quality scoring.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k for retrieval reporting (k=1/3/5 via constrained beam search). For the agent, no tool descriptions occupy the prompt (tool is a single generated token; documentation fetched on demand), context length truncated to 6,144 tokens; up to 16 agent turns (~5 action rounds + final answer) vs ToolLlama's 6-turn limit. Selection count is generation-driven rather than budget-capped retrieval of top-k documents.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A (ToolGen does not introduce a new benchmark; it reuses ToolBench and StableToolBench). ToolBench: 16k+ tool collections / 47k unique APIs; retrieval data ~200k (query, relevant-API) pairs split I1/I2/I3 with 87,413 / 84,815 / 25,251 instances; ToolGen's retrieval training ~500k samples and end-to-end training ~183k samples (derived/converted from ToolBench).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> ToolBench / ToolLLM (Qin et al., 2023) for the 47k-API tool pool, splits, and ToolRetriever/ToolLlama baselines; generative retrieval (DSI / GENRE / Wang et al. 2022; document-identifier generation); ToolkenGPT (Hao et al., 2023, tool-specific tokens) and Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023, vocabulary expansion for a few tools), which ToolGen extends to 47k real-world tools with full-parameter fine-tuning; Agent-Flan (Chen et al., 2024) inference paradigm (separating Thought/Action/Arguments); StableToolBench (Guo et al., 2024) for evaluation; Llama-3-8B base model.
- **contrasts with**:
> The standard retriever-then-LLM pipeline (BM25, EmbSim, ToolRetriever dense retriever, IterFeedback, Re-Invoke) that uses a separate encoder retriever and puts tool descriptions in the prompt; ToolkenGPT and Toolformer (few-shot prompting / few tools, still list tools in the prompt) - ToolGen handles 47k tools, requires no tools in the prompt, and uses full-parameter fine-tuning. Argues the pipeline suffers from error propagation, context-length limits, and retriever-LLM misalignment.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use). Lineage: generative tool retrieval - reframes the ToolLLM/ToolBench large-scale (47k-API) tool-retrieval problem as next-token generation by virtualizing each tool as a vocabulary token (atomic indexing), unifying retrieval and calling in one LLM with no separate retriever. Bridges generative document retrieval (DSI/GENRE) and tool-token approaches (ToolkenGPT/Toolformer) into a scalable, parametric, end-to-end tool agent; sits alongside dependency-/document-engineering tool-retrieval works (e.g. COLT, AnyTool, ToolRet) but is distinctive as the generative (retriever-free) branch.
