<a id="item-agent-as-a-graph"></a>
### 104. Agent-as-a-Graph: Knowledge Graph-Based Tool and Agent Retrieval for LLM Multi-Agent Systems

2025  ·  arXiv 2511.18194  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.18194)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **authors affiliation**: Faheem Nizar, Elias Lumer, Anmol Gulati, Pradeep Honaganahalli Basavaraju, Vamse Kumar Subbiah — Commercial Technology and Innovation Office, PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC), U.S.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.18194
- **code url**: N/A (no official code repository linked in the arXiv listing or paper; the paper notes the KG is stored in standard graph backends compatible with Cypher/Neo4j but releases no code)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: tool-use / agent routing (tool and parent-agent retrieval for LLM multi-agent systems with MCP servers)
- **problem setting**:
> Offline retrieval/selection problem within a multi-agent system: a single orchestrator must route a user query (or its decomposed sub-steps) to the correct executable subagent among hundreds/thousands of agents, each bundling tens to hundreds of MCP-server tools. The retrievable store is a static, offline-induced bipartite knowledge graph of agents and tools built from existing MCP manifests/schemas; there is no online growth, no agent execution rollout, and supervision is limited to ground-truth agent-tool mappings used only for evaluation (the retriever itself is training-free/non-learned).
- **what is retrieved**: Tools (MCP tool nodes) and their parent agents (MCP server nodes); the final returned set is the top-K executable agents reached via tool-to-agent graph traversal.
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus — a bipartite knowledge graph of agents and tools auto-induced offline from MCP manifests/schemas; no growing/episodic memory written by the agent.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-K ranking objective (top-K unique executable agents); evaluated with Recall@K / mAP@K / nDCG@K at K in {1,3,5,(10)}. It aims to recover the complete set of relevant agents within a fixed K rather than a precision-driven variable-size set, but is not framed as minimal-set completeness recovery.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based reasoning method; only a Retrieve-like step exists, no Reuse/Revise/Retain)
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False — the work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is a knowledge-graph RAG retrieval method.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: tool-API node (tool name + description) and agent/MCP-server node (agent name + description), organized as a bipartite KG-subgraph; the retrieved/returned unit is the parent agent (tool-API granularity at index time, agent granularity at output).
- **index source**: Static corpus, offline-induced: the agent-tool bipartite knowledge graph is automatically constructed offline from existing MCP server manifests and tool schemas; frozen at query time (no online/test-time induction).
- **index structure topology**:
> Bipartite dependency/knowledge GRAPH G=(A,T,E) where tool nodes are linked to their parent agent (owner) nodes via ownership metadata edges; both node types embedded in a shared/unified vector space and stored in standard graph backends (Cypher/Neo4j-compatible). Hierarchical agent->tool ownership relation.
- **retriever type**: Hybrid — dense vector search over a unified embedding space for both tool and agent nodes (eight embedding models evaluated), combined with graph traversal; BM25 used only as a baseline. No learned/LLM reranker.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None (off-the-shelf) — the retriever uses pretrained embedding models with no fine-tuning; ranking uses a training-free, non-learned type-specific weighted Reciprocal Rank Fusion with interpretable, manually-set type priors (alpha_A, alpha_T). The paper explicitly contrasts this with learned/LLM re-rankers.
- **query construction**: Two paradigms: (1) Direct Querying uses the raw user high-level question; (2) Step-wise Querying decomposes the query into sub-tasks and submits each step independently. Step-wise decomposition (reasoning-based retrieval planning) is the primary evaluation setting.
- **query granularity**: Both task-level (Direct Querying, one-shot at t=0) and step/sub-task-level (Step-wise Querying); the step/sub-task level is the primary setting.
- **when to retrieve**: Iterative in the primary (step-wise) setting — retrieval is invoked once per decomposed sub-step; one-shot in the Direct Querying setting. Decomposition is via a fixed schedule of sub-steps, not an uncertainty-triggered or learned router.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule — retrieval fires per decomposed sub-step (one retrieval call per step) or once for the whole task in direct mode; there is no token-confidence, attention, learned-complexity, or reflection-token trigger.
- **reranking**:
> Yes — a type-specific weighted Reciprocal Rank Fusion (wRRF). After forming a unified candidate list with a global base rank r(e), each entity is scored alpha_T/(k+r(e)) for tool nodes or alpha_A/(k+r(e)) for agent nodes (k=60), reranked, then top-K unique agents selected via graph traversal. This is a non-learned, interpretable reranking (not a cross-encoder or instruction-tuned reranker).
- **retrieved context refinement**: Rerank only — type-specific wRRF reranking followed by tool->agent graph traversal and deduplication to the top-K unique executable agents; no decomposition-recompose, distillation, distractor filtering, or compression of retrieved content.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Raw name+description fields — tool nodes index tool names and descriptions; agent nodes index agent/MCP server names and descriptions. No synthetic-query augmentation, expansion, or instruction-tuned tool embeddings; an agent-only baseline dataset is constructed using only MCP server names+descriptions to isolate tool-level information.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: Static index over MCP servers/tools integrated via the Model Context Protocol (MCP); auto-induced from MCP manifests/schemas and stored in Cypher/Neo4j-compatible backends. No live CRUD auto-synchronization is claimed (contrasts with ScaleMCP's dynamic auto-sync).
- **tool dependency awareness**: Models the tool->parent-agent ownership relation as a bipartite KG and traverses tool-to-agent edges to preserve bundle context, but does not model inter-tool dependencies (output-of-A feeds B, shared auth as data-flow, prerequisites) for sequencing.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> The retrieved top-K agents are used for agent routing/selection (which executable subagent the orchestrator delegates to); evaluation is retrieval-only (retrieved agents vs ground-truth agents). Not prompt-augmentation/skill-reuse/training-signal use; it is a selection/routing output.
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-route, interleaved with query decomposition: in the primary step-wise setting the query is decomposed into sub-steps and a retrieval is run per sub-step to identify the relevant agent(s), aligning retrieval with reasoning-based planning; no MCTS/tree search or explicit plan generation is performed by the method itself.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-step (per decomposed sub-task) in the primary setting; per-answer/per-task in the Direct Querying setting.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not a CBR/case-adaptation method; retrieved agents are returned for routing without case revision)
- **retrieved item representation**: Structured graph nodes (agent and tool name+description) surfaced as a ranked set of executable agents; not raw trajectories, distilled strategies, programs, or latent tokens.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Two-level: fine-grained tool-API capability (single tool description) at the node level and coarser agent/MCP-server capability (parent bundle) at the output level; no distilled strategy/insight, workflow, or procedural skill.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Type-specific weighting (alpha_A, alpha_T) as transparent knobs to bias toward agent coverage vs tool specificity, stabilizing top-K routing; RRF's rank-based (calibration-insensitive) fusion is robust across heterogeneous embedding signals. No retriever-aware training, relevance evaluator, self-reflection, or distractor-aware SFT.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: graph (static bipartite agent-tool knowledge graph). No episodic/skill-library/procedural memory that grows.
- **write back**: False — no new experiences/cases/skills are written back; the KG is built offline and frozen during retrieval.
- **online growth**: No — the retrievable store does not grow during deployment/test-time; it is induced offline from MCP manifests and remains static (the paper mentions Cypher/CRUD-compatible backends but no online growth is part of the method).
- **write back trigger**: Never — there is no write-back mechanism; nothing is stored to memory during operation.
- **failure experience usage**: N/A — no experiences (success or failure) are stored or retrieved; the method is a static retrieval over a fixed KG.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A — entries are not mutated after construction (static graph; effectively append-only/none at build time only).
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No — retrieval/selection is a fixed similarity top-N followed by training-free type-specific wRRF and deterministic graph traversal; not an RL/learned policy.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> LiveMCPBench (70 MCP servers, 527 tools, 95 real-world questions annotated with step-by-step breakdowns and relevant agent-tool mappings; avg 2.68 steps, 2.82 tools, 1.40 MCP agents per question). An agent-only baseline dataset (MCP server names+descriptions only) is also constructed.
- **benchmark family**: tool (MCP tool/agent retrieval) — LiveMCPBench (MCP server/tool retrieval benchmark)
- **baselines**: BM25 (lexical, via LlamaIndex BM25 retriever); Q.Retrieval (query/dense retrieval); standard RRF (Reciprocal Rank Fusion); MCPZero (active tool discovery); ScaleMCP (dynamic auto-synchronizing MCP retriever) — the last two are the prior state-of-the-art agent retrievers.
- **key metrics**: Recall@K, mean average precision mAP@K, normalized discounted cumulative gain nDCG@K, for K in {1,3,5} (Table 1 header also references {1,5,10}). Retrieved agents are compared against ground-truth agents.
- **headline result**:
> On LiveMCPBench, Agent-as-a-Graph (optimal type-specific weighting alpha_A=1.5, alpha_T=1.0) achieves Recall@5 = 0.85 and nDCG@5 = 0.48, a 14.9% and 14.6% improvement over prior state-of-the-art retrievers; against MCPZero's Recall@5 0.70 the unweighted variant reaches 0.83 (+18.6%), and on average across 8 embedding models 0.85 vs 0.70 (+19.4%). wRRF type-weighting adds 2.41% over standard RRF.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Type-weighting ratio sweep (Table 3 / Figure 2): unweighted (1,1) gives Recall@5 0.83; optimal modest agent emphasis (alpha_A=1.5, alpha_T=1.0) gives 0.85/nDCG@5 0.47; tool-dominant (1:3) gives 0.80; aggressive agent bias (3:1) degrades to 0.76; type-specific wRRF (Eq.3) beats standard weighted RRF (Eq.2, Recall@5 ~0.79-0.80) by ~2.41%. (2) Cross-architecture generalization across 8 embedding models (Table 2): consistent gains, low variance (std ~0.02 Recall@5, ~0.01 nDCG@5); strongest on Amazon Titan v2 (0.66->0.85, +28.8%); All-MiniLM-L6-v2 0.67->0.80 (+19.4%). (3) Node-source attribution: 39.13% of retrieved top-K items originate from agent nodes; 34.44% of matched tool nodes trace back to agents via graph edges, showing both node types contribute.
- **evaluation decoupling**: Evaluation is intrinsic retrieval-only (Recall@K / mAP@K / nDCG@K of retrieved agents vs ground-truth agents); there is no end-to-end task-execution (e.g., task success) metric, so intrinsic and downstream metrics are not jointly decoupled — only retrieval metrics are reported.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Process/retrieval-quality only — measures retrieval accuracy (Recall/mAP/nDCG) and an analysis of which node types contribute; does not score final task outcome/success of executed agents.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Argues for efficiency qualitatively: training-free, non-learned type-specific wRRF avoids expensive LLM re-ranking and retraining; works with compact open-source embeddings (All-MiniLM-L6-v2 reaches Recall@5 0.80), valuable when embedding choice is constrained by cost/latency/licensing. No concrete latency/throughput/API-cost numbers are reported.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k selection: retrieve top-N (N >> K) nodes by semantic similarity, rerank via type-specific wRRF (k=60 damping constant), then return top-K unique agents (K in {1,3,5}); reranked-then-truncated. No token/prompt budget for injected content is reported (output is the agent set, not prompt-injected content).
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey)
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Uses (does not construct) LiveMCPBench: 70 MCP servers, 527 tools, 95 human-annotated real-world questions with step-by-step breakdowns and ground-truth agent-tool mappings; avg 2.68 steps / 2.82 tools / 1.40 MCP agents per question. The authors additionally build a derived agent-only baseline dataset (server names+descriptions only) to isolate tool-level information.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Reciprocal Rank Fusion (Cormack et al.) and weighted RRF; dense embedding retrievers and BM25; MCP-based tool/agent retrieval (ScaleMCP, MCPZero, ToolShed, MemTool, GraphRAG-Tool Fusion by overlapping authors); Graph RAG literature (graph-retrieval-augmented generation surveys, GraphRAG, G-Retriever, Think-on-Graph, Graph-CoT); tool-graph methods (ToolNet, ControlLLM, Graph-ToolFormer).
- **contrasts with**:
> Agent-only retrievers that match a query against a single agent description and operate only within that agent (e.g., LiveMCPBench's own retriever, AnyTool, MetaTool); tool-only retrievers that treat each tool independently and ignore bundle context (ToolShed, MCPZero-style); ScaleMCP's concatenation of agent+tool descriptions in one vector space (multi-hop limitation); heavy LLM re-rankers and corrective RAG pipelines (replaced by transparent non-learned type-specific weighting).
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use): graph/hierarchical tool-and-agent retrieval for MCP-based multi-agent systems. Positioned in the 2024-2025 tool-retrieval lineage that moved from flat dense tool retrieval to graph/hierarchical and MCP-dynamic indices, extending GraphRAG-Tool Fusion / ScaleMCP / MCPZero by jointly modeling agents and tools as co-equal KG nodes with type-specific wRRF reranking and tool-to-agent traversal.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing
- index_content_separation
- venue

<a id="item-alita-g"></a>
### 105. Alita-G: Self-Evolving Generative Agent for Agent Generation

2025  ·  arXiv 2510.23601  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.23601)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **authors affiliation**:
> Jiahao Qiu, Xuan Qi, Hongru Wang (equal contribution); Xinzhe Juan, Yimin Wang, Zelin Zhao, Jiayi Geng, Jiacheng Guo, Peihang Li, Jingzhe Shi, Shilong Liu (corresponding), Mengdi Wang (corresponding). Affiliations: 1 Princeton University, 2 Tsinghua University, 3 The Chinese University of Hong Kong, 4 Shanghai Jiao Tong University, 5 University of Michigan, 6 King's College London, 7 Hong Kong University. Lead/PI lab: Mengdi Wang (Princeton).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.23601

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: LLM-agent tool-use / deep-research and complex multi-step reasoning (general AI assistant tasks, medical visual QA, and frontier academic reasoning). Framed as automatic agent generation: turning a generalist tool-using agent into a domain-specialist agent.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, multi-component single-agent system (a Manager Agent plus a Web Agent, following the Alita framework). The setting has two phases. (1) An offline-style construction/self-evolution phase: a powerful generalist 'master' agent repeatedly executes a curated suite of target-domain tasks T={(x_i,y_i)} (each task run K times), and from SUCCESSFUL trajectories (where the master's answer matches the gold label) it synthesizes candidate MCP (Model Context Protocol) tools, which are abstracted into parameterized primitives and consolidated into an 'MCP Box'. Supervision here = task labels used only to filter successful runs (no gradient training of the LLM). (2) A test-time inference phase: given a new query, the specialized agent does retrieval-augmented MCP selection from the frozen MCP Box (cosine similarity over embeddings of MCP description+use_case vs. the query), then runs a CodeAct loop with an MCP Executor. The objective is that the specialized policy outperforms the base agent on the target task distribution while reducing compute (tokens).
- **what is retrieved**:
> Tools/skills: parameterized, abstracted MCP tools (executable code modules with FastMCP-standardized interfaces plus a description and a use_case), synthesized from the master agent's successful task trajectories. Effectively reusable procedural skills/tools harvested from past successful experiences.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> HYBRID-leaning toward a GROWING/induced memory: the retrievable store (MCP Box) is not a static external API corpus but is INDUCED offline by the agent itself from its own successful trajectories on the target task suite. After construction it is frozen for inference (no online growth at deployment), so within a single specialized-agent deployment it behaves like a fixed induced store; across construction iterations it grows. Closest to a self-built experiential tool memory rather than a static docs/KB corpus.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Precision-driven variable-size selection (default) with an optional fixed top-k mode. The main/default setting uses threshold-based selection (keep all MCPs with cosine similarity >= tau=0.7), which yields a variable number of tools adapted to task complexity; an alternative top-k mode returns a fixed k. The paper argues threshold selection beats fixed top-k because different tasks need different numbers of MCPs. Not framed as a completeness/minimal-set recovery objective nor as a fixed top-k ranking objective; it is a relevance-threshold-driven variable-size recommendation.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> Retrieve: yes (RAG MCP selection at inference). Reuse: yes (MCP Executor invokes selected tools). Revise/adapt: partial-no (no per-case revision of a retrieved tool at inference; abstraction/refinement happens once at construction). Retain: yes-but-offline (successful trajectories' MCPs are abstracted and retained into the MCP Box during construction, not during deployment). [Retrieve, Reuse, partial-Revise(construction-time abstraction only), Retain(offline)].
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False. The paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It frames the work as MCP abstraction + MCP-level retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for self-evolution / automatic agent generation, though it realizes Retrieve/Reuse/Retain mechanisms that resemble CBR over tools rather than over cases.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: tool-API / skill-or-program: a single abstracted MCP tool = {code, description, use_case}, i.e., a parameterized executable primitive distilled from a successful (sub-)trajectory. The retrieval granularity is one MCP tool per item.
- **index source**:
> Growing memory induced at construction time (not test-time): the store is built offline by running the master agent K times over the target task suite and harvesting MCPs from successful executions, then abstracting/refining them into the MCP Box. It is hybrid in that it requires a curated target task collection as the seed, but the retrievable items themselves are agent-self-generated rather than a pre-existing external corpus. Frozen during inference.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat vector index keyed by a composite text representation (description concatenated with use_case), embedded with text-embedding-3-large and L2-normalized; retrieval is by cosine similarity over this flat set. The paper additionally builds an undirected similarity GRAPH (edges between MCP pairs with sim >= 0.7) purely as an ANALYSIS proxy for redundancy/clusters, not as the retrieval index. No hierarchical category->tool or dependency graph is used for selection.
- **retriever type**:
> Dense (off-the-shelf): semantic embedding retriever using a pre-trained text embedding model (OpenAI text-embedding-3-large by default) with cosine-similarity matching between the query embedding and each MCP's description+use_case embedding. No BM25, no learned/fine-tuned retriever, no generative tool-as-token retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None (off-the-shelf embedding model; no retriever training). The embedding encoder is frozen and pre-trained; selection is fixed cosine-similarity thresholding/top-k. The only 'learning'-like signal in the pipeline is downstream-task-effectiveness used as a FILTER during MCP construction (MCPs are kept only from successful trajectories), but that gates the index contents, not a trained retrieval policy.
- **query construction**: Raw new task query x_new is embedded directly with the embedding model phi to form e_query; no decomposition, no synthetic query expansion, no intent-extraction step is described. The MCP side key is the concatenation context_m = description_m (+) use_case_m.
- **query granularity**: Task-level (one-shot at t=0): a single query embedding is computed for the incoming task and used to filter the MCP Box once before the CodeAct execution loop begins; selection is not re-issued per reasoning step.
- **when to retrieve**:
> One-shot: RAG-based MCP selection is performed a single time at the start of inference (the filtered MCP subset B_filtered is fixed before the while-loop), then the agent reasons/acts and invokes the already-selected MCPs as needed during the CodeAct loop. Not iterative/active/learned-router retrieval.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed schedule: retrieval/selection is triggered once at task initialization (deterministically, before reasoning begins) using the similarity threshold tau (or top-k). Within the loop, tool INVOCATION is agent-initiated (the reasoning engine decides when a tool is required and which MCP to call from the pre-filtered set), but no new RETRIEVAL from the full box is triggered mid-loop; there is no confidence/uncertainty/reflection-token retrieval trigger.
- **reranking**: None. After cosine-similarity scoring, MCPs are filtered by threshold tau>=0.7 (or top-k) directly; no second-stage cross-encoder, hierarchy-aware, RRF, or instruction-tuned reranker is applied.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Rerank/none at retrieval time: only similarity thresholding (or top-k truncation) is applied to produce the focused tool subset; no decompose-then-recompose, reason-in-documents distillation, distractor filtering, or compression of the retrieved tools. (Refinement/abstraction of tool content is done earlier, at MCP Box construction, not post-retrieval.)
- **tool document engineering**:
> Yes, substantial: during MCP abstraction each tool's documentation is engineered before indexing via (i) Parameter Generalization (hard-coded values -> configurable parameters), (ii) Context Removal (strip task-specific references), (iii) Interface Standardization (FastMCP-compatible interfaces), and (iv) Documentation Enhancement (comprehensive docstrings + type annotations). The retrievable text per MCP is the engineered description concatenated with the originating use_case; an ablation shows description+use_case > description-only > use_case-only for retrieval (83.03% vs 81.82% vs 77.57% on GAIA).
- **index content separation**:
> Yes (lightweight index vs heavy content): retrieval is over a lightweight composite text (description (+) use_case) embedding, while the heavy executable MCP code is loaded/invoked on demand only after selection by the MCP Executor. This separates a cheap retrievable index from the on-demand tool code, and is explicitly motivated as mitigating prompt bloat / reducing tokens (~15% token savings).
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Integration protocol: MCP (Model Context Protocol), specifically the FastMCP implementation, with a CodeAct loop and an MCP Executor for dynamic tool invocation; tools are standardized to FastMCP interfaces. The index itself is STATIC at inference (frozen MCP Box, no live CRUD auto-sync during deployment); it is updated only by re-running the offline construction with more iterations.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Skill/tool reuse via prompt-augmented tool provisioning: the filtered, relevant MCP subset is supplied to the specialized agent, which runs a CodeAct loop; when the ReasoningEngine decides a tool is required it selects an MCP from the filtered set and the MCP Executor runs it, feeding the result back into context. Retrieval thus provisions a focused executable toolset rather than injecting demonstrations or training signal.
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-plan/act: a one-shot RAG selection fixes a focused MCP toolset at task start, then a Manager Agent (with Task Analyzer, MCP Retriever, MCP Executor) runs an iterative CodeAct reason-act-observe loop that invokes the pre-selected MCPs. No tree search/MCTS; planning is the agent's standard interleaved reasoning-and-tool-use loop over a retrieval-narrowed action space.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-tool-call within a single rollout for tool USAGE (MCPs invoked as needed across CodeAct steps), but retrieval/selection from the box is per-answer (once per task at t=0). So: retrieval = per-answer; tool invocation = per-tool-call within the reasoning loop.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> Construction-time LLM-prompted abstraction rather than per-case revision: a high-capacity LLM (LLM_abstract) transforms each raw, instance-specific MCP into a generalized parameterized primitive (parameter generalization, context removal, interface standardization, doc enhancement). At inference the retrieved MCP is reused largely as-is (parameters bound at call time by the agent); there is no execution-feedback-driven or critic-guided revision of the retrieved tool itself during deployment.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Executable program/skill: the injected/usable item is a parameterized FastMCP-compatible executable MCP tool (code) with a standardized interface, accompanied by a natural-language description and use_case. Surface form for retrieval is text (description+use_case); surface form for use is callable code.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Procedural, reusable skill/tool abstracted from a successful trajectory: above raw trajectories (hard-coded values lifted to parameters, task-specific context removed), i.e., a generalized parameterized primitive (e.g., the case-study extract_pdf_measurement tool) rather than a raw demonstration, distilled strategy/guideline, or full workflow.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Quality gating + relevance thresholding: (1) MCPs are harvested ONLY from successful master-agent trajectories (success filter) before entering the box; (2) abstraction removes instance-specific context to reduce brittle/overfit tools; (3) threshold-based RAG selection (tau=0.7) excludes low-similarity (likely irrelevant) MCPs at inference, with the ablation showing too-low tau injects irrelevant tools and too-high tau drops useful ones. Behavior analysis reports near-zero Right->Wrong regressions (1/1/0 across 1/2/3 generations), evidence the added tools rarely harm previously-correct answers. No retriever-aware training or explicit distractor-aware SFT.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: skill-library / procedural tool memory: the MCP Box is a curated library of reusable abstracted MCP tools (executable procedural skills). Not episodic-trajectory memory, graph memory, or latent memory.
- **write back**: Yes (during construction/self-evolution): MCPs synthesized from successful trajectories are abstracted and written into the MCP Box. However, write-back occurs in the offline construction loop, not during test-time deployment; the box is frozen at inference.
- **online growth**: No at deployment: the MCP Box is frozen during inference (no test-time growth). It grows only across the offline construction iterations k=1..K (e.g., #MCPs grows 26->46->74->102->128 from k=1 to k=5 on GAIA). So growth is offline/induced, not online/streaming.
- **write back trigger**:
> On-success only, gated by task-label verification: an MCP is retained into the raw pool L only if it was generated during an execution where the master agent's answer matched the gold label (pi_master^(k)(x_i)=y_i). Failed trajectories contribute no MCPs. Retained MCPs are then abstracted into the box. There is no per-step, reflective-after-critique, or human-validated write trigger beyond the success filter.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success-only: only MCPs from SUCCESSFUL trajectories are stored and later retrieved; failed/negative experiences are discarded and not stored as contrastive negatives or corrective rules. (Contrast with experience-replay methods that store failures, e.g., Reflexion/ExpeL, which the paper cites as related but distinct.)
- **memory evolution update**:
> Append-only across iterations (no merge/dedup/overwrite of stored entries): later generation rounds ADD newly harvested abstracted MCPs to the accumulated box; the paper explicitly states it preserves diversity and does NOT cluster/dedup ('Unlike traditional clustering approaches, our method preserves the diversity of MCP implementations'). Redundancy thus accumulates (effective-coverage ratio #Clusters/#MCPs drops from 1.00 at k=1 to 0.51 at k=5), and existing MCPs are not mutated or pruned.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No. Retrieval/MCP selection is a fixed cosine-similarity threshold (or top-k) over frozen pre-trained embeddings; it is not an RL- or value-optimized retrieval policy (no soft Q-learning / M-MDP / learned router).
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Partial/within-framework: the MCP Box is generated by a 'master' generalist agent and then transferred to a separately-instantiated 'specialized' agent (a form of capability transfer from generalist to specialist within the same Alita-based framework), and MCP is a standardized protocol enabling reuse across MCP-compatible agents. The paper contrasts itself with AgentDistill (which shares MCP boxes from strong teacher to weaker student across agents); Alita-G focuses on end-to-end self-specialization of one framework rather than cross-heterogeneous-framework collective memory. No multi-agent shared/collective memory pool.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmark family**: Tool-use / deep-research general-assistant (GAIA), multimodal medical visual QA (PathVQA), and frontier multi-disciplinary reasoning (HLE). GAIA is the headline tool/web-agent benchmark family; PathVQA and HLE are domain-specialization stress tests.
- **baselines**:
> Octotools (tool-augmented agent framework, predefined tool collection); ODR-smolagents (Open Deep Research within HuggingFace Smolagents, strong general-purpose agent baseline); and the 'Original Agent System' = the master/base Alita-style agent (Manager Agent on Claude-Sonnet-4 + Web Agent on GPT-4.1) WITHOUT the specialized MCP Box, reported at both pass@1 and pass@3. Alita-G is also compared against its own variants Alita-G(1x) vs Alita-G(3x) (single vs triple-execution MCP boxes).
- **key metrics**:
> Accuracy (%) per GAIA difficulty level and total, and on PathVQA / HLE; reported at pass@1 and pass@3. Computational efficiency measured by average number of tokens consumed per example. Analysis also reports #MCPs, #clusters (connected components at sim>=0.7), mean/median pairwise MCP similarity, Wrong->Right and Right->Wrong flip counts, and average MCP calls per question.
- **headline result**:
> On GAIA validation, Alita-G (3x) achieves 83.03% pass@1 and 89.09% pass@3 (claimed new state-of-the-art), vs the Original Agent System's 75.15% pass@1 / 87.27% pass@3, while reducing mean tokens per example by ~15% (10,394 vs 12,305 avg tokens on GAIA). Relative gains: +50.5% relative over ODR-smolagents (55.15%) and +10.3% relative over the base agent at pass@1.
- **ablations**:
> (1) RAG content components (Table 2, GAIA, 3x box): description+use_case 83.03% > description-only 81.82% > use_case-only 77.57% -- descriptions are the more generalizable retrieval signal. (2) MCP Box scalability (Table 4, GAIA): average accuracy 80.00 (k=1) -> 81.82 (k=2) -> 83.03 (k=3) -> 83.03 (k=4) -> 83.63 (k=5); #MCPs 26->46->74->102->128, #clusters 26->41->52->60->65, effective-coverage ratio drops 1.00->0.51, confirming diminishing returns with k=3 the cost/utility sweet spot. (3) Selection strategy/threshold (Table 3, 25-question GAIA subset): threshold tau sweep 0.65->0.90 peaks at tau=0.70 (84.0%); top-k sweep peaks at k=2-3 (80.0%); threshold-based generally beats fixed top-k. (4) Embedding encoder (Table 5, 25 questions): text-embedding-3-large 84.0% > text-embedding-3-small 80.0% > Qwen3-Embedding-8B 76.0% > NV-Embed-v2 72.0% = BGE-M3 72.0%. (5) MCP behavior (Table 6): overall acc 80.00/81.52/83.03 for 1/2/3 generations; Wrong->Right flips 9/12/13, Right->Wrong 1/1/0; avg MCP calls/question 1.9/2.2/2.4 and 2.7/3.0/3.4 on improved questions.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> No intrinsic retrieval metrics decoupling: the paper does NOT report Recall@k / nDCG / retrieval completeness separately. Retrieval quality is assessed only indirectly via end-to-end task accuracy (RAG-content ablation, embedding-encoder ablation, threshold/top-k ablation) and via box-statistics proxies (#clusters, similarity), not via gold tool-relevance labels.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome (task accuracy and token cost). Some process-level diagnostics are added: average MCP calls per question (and specifically on 'improved' questions), and Wrong->Right vs Right->Wrong flip counts, which probe whether tool use is targeted and non-regressive. No formal reasoning-faithfulness or step-wise retrieval-accuracy metric.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Adaptive / precision-driven by default: threshold mode (tau=0.7) yields a variable-size MCP subset adapted to task complexity (the paper argues this beats fixed top-k); a top-k mode (k in {1,2,3,5,10,20}) is available for predictable resource use. Selection narrows the toolset to reduce prompt bloat and tokens (~15% savings). No explicit fixed token budget cap is stated; the budget is controlled implicitly via the similarity threshold and the separation of lightweight index from on-demand code.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Alita (Qiu et al., 2025, arXiv:2505.20286) -- the generalist agent with Manager+Web agents and MCP self-generation that Alita-G uses as its master/base architecture (Alita base = 75.15% pass@1 / 87.27% pass@3 on GAIA, matching Alita-G's 'Original' baseline). AgentDistill (Qiu et al., 2025, arXiv:2506.14728) -- training-free MCP-box distillation, whose MCP-abstraction principles Alita-G adopts (parameter generalization, context removal, interface standardization). Model Context Protocol / FastMCP (Anthropic 2024; Lowin 2024) for tool standardization. RAG-MCP (Gan & Sun, 2025, arXiv:2505.03275) for retrieval-augmented MCP/tool selection to mitigate prompt bloat. text-embedding-3-large (OpenAI 2024) for retrieval.
- **contrasts with**:
> Prior self-evolving agents that only do prompt rewriting or failure-retry (Reflexion, ExpeL, SAGE, Agent-Pro, Godel Agent, SELF, RAGEN, EvolveSearch) -- Alita-G instead accumulates and reuses executable tools (capability expansion vs knowledge/reasoning refinement). Auto-agent-generation works (AutoAgents, AutoGenesisAgent, EvoAgent, MetaGPT, AutoAgent, AFlow, AgentSquare, CAMEL, OpenHands) -- Alita-G generates complete deployable task-specific agents rather than isolated components/workflows. AgentDistill -- shares MCP boxes from strong teacher to weaker student, whereas Alita-G targets end-to-end self-specialization of a powerful generalist into a domain expert. Tool-use baselines Octotools (predefined tools) and ODR-smolagents.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use): MCP-tool synthesis + retrieval-augmented tool selection lineage. Sits in the 2024-2025 tool-retrieval / self-evolving-tool-memory line: generalist MCP agent (Alita) -> training-free MCP-box distillation (AgentDistill) -> self-evolving generation of domain-specialist agents via abstracted MCP boxes with MCP-level RAG (Alita-G). Distinct from static API-retrieval tool-use (ToolLLM/Gorilla/ToolBench) by using agent-self-induced, abstracted, retrievable MCP tools.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- benchmarks
- code_url
- cost_efficiency_tradeoff
- tool_dependency_awareness
- venue

<a id="item-appselectbench"></a>
### 106. AppSelectBench: Application-Level Tool Selection Benchmark

2025  ·  arXiv 2511.19957  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.19957)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**: arXiv preprint arXiv:2511.19957 [cs.CL] (Computation and Language). Submitted 25 Nov 2025 (v1), last revised 26 Nov 2025 (v2). DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2511.19957. CC BY 4.0. No peer-reviewed venue as of mid-2026; preprint only.
- **authors affiliation**:
> Tianyi Chen* (corresponding, Tianyi.Chen@microsoft.com) and Michael Solodko* [equal contribution]; Sen Wang, Jongwoo Ko, Junheng Hao, Colby Banbury, Sara Abdali, Saeed Amizadeh, Qing Xiao, Yinheng Li, Tianyu Ding, Kamran Ghasedi Dizaji, Suzhen Zheng, Hao Fan, Justin Wagle, Pashmina Cameron, Kazuhito Koishida. Single affiliation: Microsoft.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.19957

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> tool-use / decision-making for computer-using agents (CUAs): application-level tool selection, i.e., choosing which desktop application to use to accomplish a natural-language user task BEFORE invoking fine-grained tools/APIs within that application. A higher-level inter-application reasoning problem distinct from intra-application API selection.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-step, single-agent evaluation benchmark (not an interactive multi-turn execution loop). The task is formalized as a graph-structured prediction f: U -> G(T) mapping a natural-language user intent U to a directed graph over a candidate application set T={t_1,...,t_n} whose vertices are applications and whose edges encode temporal/logical/data dependencies (singleton, sequential chain, or parallel/branched). In this version the authors deliberately restrict the FOCUS AND SCOPE to the singleton-application setting: each task is solved by a single application or a few interchangeable alternatives; sequential/parallel multi-application scenarios are explicitly left to future versions. Supervision: each user task is paired with a ground-truth set of valid applications (multi-label via an application-equivalence mapping). Evaluation is one-shot prediction of an application name from a fixed candidate list of 100 apps, under deterministic decoding (temperature=0). Five protocols are compared: LLM-free Random Selector and Rule-based Heuristic, and LLM-driven Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, and Retrieval-Augmented Selection (RAS). No tool execution / GUI grounding is performed; the benchmark isolates inter-application reasoning from execution fidelity.
- **what is retrieved**:
> tools (applications): in the Retrieval-Augmented Selection (RAS) protocol the model is provided with structured application descriptions (core capabilities, functionalities, and typical usage scenarios) for each candidate application, retrieved from an external knowledge base; these serve as lightweight factual grounding about the available tools. In the Few-Shot protocol, annotated task->application demonstration examples are provided instead (not framed as retrieval).
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus: RAS retrieves from a fixed external knowledge base of application descriptions (capability/functionality/usage profiles for the 100 desktop applications). It is NOT a growing/episodic agent-written memory; the store is predefined and frozen during evaluation.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Variable-size / membership-based correctness over a multi-valid label set rather than a fixed top-k ranking: because many tasks admit multiple valid applications (grouped via an application-equivalence mapping), a prediction is counted correct if it belongs to the annotated set of valid applications. In the studied singleton setting the model outputs a single application name (effectively top-1) judged against the valid set; the broader graph formulation targets recovery of the complete set/structure of needed applications, but multi-application completeness is left to future versions.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve: partial (RAS retrieves static application descriptions; Few-Shot retrieves demonstration exemplars), Reuse: no (no prior solved case is reused/adapted), Revise: no, Retain: no]. Not a case-based-reasoning system; it grounds selection in tool descriptions/demonstrations, not in prior solved problem-solution cases.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False: the paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is an application-selection benchmark with retrieval-augmented and few-shot grounding protocols.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: tool-API (here at the application granularity): one application's structured description record (name + core capabilities + functionalities + typical usage scenarios) is the retrievable unit in RAS. For Few-Shot, the unit is a single task->application demonstration example.
- **index source**:
> Static corpus built offline: an external knowledge base of structured per-application capability/usage descriptions for the 100 curated desktop applications, plus (separately) the benchmark's own atomic-task database (~3,000 atomic tasks) and >100k generated user task-application pairs used as data, not as a test-time-growing retrievable store. The retrievable RAS index is predefined and not induced online from agent trajectories.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> none (off-the-shelf / no trained retriever): RAS grounding is fixed structured descriptions from a knowledge base; there is no contrastive, LM-feedback, preference, or RL training of a retriever. The Rule-based Heuristic likewise uses fixed predefined application-specific lexicons. No learned retrieval policy is trained.
- **query construction**:
> Raw user task description: the natural-language user intent (e.g., 'I want to know the stock price of Microsoft') is used directly as the query, paired in the prompt with the retrieved application descriptions. No query decomposition, expansion, or intent-extraction stage is described for RAS.
- **query granularity**: task-level (one-shot at t=0): a single retrieval/grounding step per user task; the model makes one application-selection decision for the whole task. No step-level or two-level retrieval (the studied scope is singleton selection).
- **when to retrieve**: one-shot: grounding (application descriptions in RAS, or demonstrations in Few-Shot) is provided once up front before the single selection decision. No iterative, uncertainty-triggered, or learned-router retrieval.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> fixed schedule / protocol-determined: retrieval is not adaptively triggered; it is a fixed property of the RAS evaluation protocol (always provide the external application descriptions for every task). There is no token-confidence, attention, learned-complexity, reflection-token, or agent-initiated retrieval signal.
- **reranking**: None: no reranking stage (no cross-encoder, RRF, or hierarchy-aware reranking) is described; the application descriptions are injected as context and the LLM directly selects.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> None / minimal: the retrieved application descriptions are described as 'lightweight factual grounding' injected directly into the prompt as an application tool list. No decompose-recompose, distillation, distractor filtering, or compression of the retrieved descriptions is reported.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Application descriptions for the RAS knowledge base are engineered into concise structured capability profiles capturing each app's core capabilities, functionalities, and typical usage scenarios (e.g., 'Excel: Supports tabular editing, formulas, data visualization'). No synthetic-query augmentation, expanded summaries, weighted-field embeddings, or instruction-tuned tool embeddings are reported; the Rule-based Heuristic separately uses hand-built application-specific lexicons.
- **index content separation**:
> Partial / lightweight grounding by design: RAS injects 'lightweight factual grounding' (compact capability descriptions) rather than heavy full documentation, and the application identity is decoupled from any (out-of-scope) underlying APIs/execution. But there is no explicit progressive-disclosure index-then-content mechanism; the descriptions are provided directly in-context.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Static, no live tool protocol: the application set (100 apps) and their RAS descriptions are predefined and frozen; there is no live RapidAPI/REST/MCP/function-calling synchronization or CRUD auto-sync. The benchmark evaluates selection in the abstract, decoupled from any live tool-execution protocol.
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> Modeled in the formulation but not in the evaluated scope: the problem is defined as a directed graph whose edges encode temporal/logical/data dependencies between applications (singleton, sequential chain e.g. Browser->PowerPoint, parallel/branched), and the generation pipeline composes inter-application workflows (e.g., ExcelExportChart->PowerPointInsertTable). However, the evaluated FOCUS is the singleton-application setting, so inter-application dependency prediction is largely left to future versions; no dependency-aware retrieval/reranking is used.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> prompt augmentation: the retrieved structured application descriptions (RAS) or annotated demonstration examples (Few-Shot) are concatenated into the LLM prompt alongside the user task to inform a single application-selection decision. There is no skill reuse, case adaptation, training signal, or latent-token injection; retrieval is purely in-context grounding tested against a frozen LLM.
- **planning integration**:
> retrieve-then-select (one-shot exemplars/grounding at decision time): in the studied singleton scope there is no multi-step plan; RAS/Few-Shot context is provided once and the model directly predicts the application. The broader graph formulation envisions selecting a structured set/sequence of applications (plan-like), but multi-application planning is left to future work; no MCTS/tree search or per-step interleaving is used.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: per-answer: a single retrieval/grounding step feeds a single application-selection answer per task; retrieval is not interleaved per-CoT-step, per-token, or per-tool-call.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not framed as CBR): the closest analogue is that the model reads retrieved application descriptions (RAS) or task->app demonstrations (Few-Shot) and uses them as in-context grounding to select an application; no prior solved case is adapted or revised.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Structured note / capability profile injected as free text: for RAS, an 'Application tool list' where each application is paired with a concise capability/functionality/usage description (e.g., 'Excel: Supports tabular editing, formulas, data visualization'). For Few-Shot, raw task->application mapping exemplars (e.g., 'Create a bar chart from a table -> Excel'). Not executable programs, full trajectories, or latent tokens.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Distilled capability description (RAS): a high-level summary of each application's core capabilities, functionalities, and typical usage scenarios, i.e., a structured factual profile rather than a raw trajectory, procedural skill, or reusable workflow. Few-Shot units are single demonstrations (task->app hints).
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> None explicit: no retriever-aware training, relevance evaluator, self-reflection, reason-in-documents refinement, or distractor-aware SFT is built in. The paper instead empirically observes that RAS helps mid-scale/open models (+3-5%) but yields non-monotonic / sometimes negative effects for very small models (e.g., gemma-3-270m drops to chance under RAS), noting retrieval helps only when the model can meaningfully integrate the structured descriptions into its reasoning.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none: there is no episodic, skill-library, workflow, procedural, graph, or latent memory. The external application-description knowledge base is a static reference corpus, not an agent-written memory.
- **write back**: false: the system does not write new experiences/cases/skills into a retrievable memory. The >100k user tasks and atomic-task database are generated offline as benchmark data, not test-time write-back.
- **online growth**: false: the retrievable application-description store (and the benchmark task set) is fixed during evaluation; it does not grow from agent outputs at test time.
- **write back trigger**: never: no automatic memory write-back exists. Tasks and atomic-task/composition databases are created offline via a GPT-5-plus-human-annotation generation pipeline, not triggered by inference-time success/failure or reflection.
- **failure experience usage**:
> N/A / none: failed experiences are not stored or retrieved. The paper performs offline error analysis (category-level confusion matrices, intra- vs cross-category error decomposition, per-application F1) to characterize failure modes, but these are diagnostic analyses, not persisted negative cases used for retrieval or learning.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A: there is no model-written memory to mutate. The static application knowledge base and benchmark data are updated only by the offline curation pipeline (GPT-5 drafting + human refinement), not via append/dedup/refine of agent memory.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No: application selection is performed by a frozen LLM in-context (or by fixed Random/Rule-based baselines); RAS grounding and the retriever are fixed/non-learned. There is no RL- or value-learned retrieval/selection policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No: single-model evaluation against a shared static knowledge base; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing. Multiple LLMs are evaluated independently and confusion patterns are aggregated across models only for diagnostic analysis.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> AppSelectBench (introduced by this paper): 100 widely used desktop applications across 12 high-level categories; an atomic-task database of ~3,000 atomic tasks; >100,000 (one hundred thousand+) realistic user task-application pairs, averaging ~1,000 high-quality tasks per application; an application-equivalence mapping grouping functionally overlapping tools. Evaluation covers all 12 categories under 5 protocols (Random, Rule-based Heuristic, Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, RAS).
- **benchmark family**:
> tool (application/tool-selection benchmark) for computer-using agents (CUAs). Positioned alongside API-level tool benchmarks (API-Bank, ToolBench/ToolLLM, Gorilla/APIBench, ToolAlpaca, ToolQA, MetaTool, StableToolBench) and CUA environments (OSWorld, Windows Agent Arena, WinSpot), but it uniquely targets the application-selection layer rather than API selection or end-to-end GUI execution.
- **baselines**:
> LLM-free baselines: Random Selector and Rule-based Heuristic (semantic lexicon matching). LLM-driven models (closed-source): GPT-5, GPT-4o-mini. Open-source: Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, Llama-3-8B, Phi-4, gemma-3-270m, gemma-3-4b-pt. Each evaluated under Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, and RAS.
- **key metrics**:
> (1) Tool selection accuracy = proportion of user tasks whose predicted application lies within the annotated set of valid solutions (membership-based, multi-valid; not exact-match). (2) Confusion analysis: row-normalized category-level confusion matrices; decomposition of misclassifications into intra-category substitution rate (pi_intra) vs cross-category boundary errors (pi_cross). (3) Per-application precision/recall/F1. Data-quality metrics: 5-point Likert grammatical naturalness, semantic realism, and ground-truth correctness from human evaluation.
- **headline result**:
> On AppSelectBench (overall accuracy averaged across zero-shot/few-shot/RAS), GPT-5 is best at 63.3%, followed by GPT-4o-mini at 60.3%; the Random Selector lower bound is ~1.6% and the Rule-based Heuristic reaches ~56%. Even the strongest model (GPT-5) leaves a large gap to perfect, showing that LLMs still struggle to make consistent application choices. Best single cell: GPT-5 RAS = 0.644 overall.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Protocol/supervision ablation (the core study): Zero-Shot vs Few-Shot vs RAS per model. Few-shot yields consistent but moderate gains (~+2%); RAS delivers the largest improvements for mid-scale/open models (+3-5%, e.g., Qwen-2.5-7B 53.0->55.0->57.4), while high-capacity models (GPT-5/GPT-4o-mini) gain only ~1-2% since semantics are already internalized; very small models (gemma-3-270m) are unstable and degrade under RAS (0.024 zero-shot/RAS vs 0.244 few-shot), showing retrieval helps only when the model can integrate structured descriptions. (2) Error-type decomposition: pi_intra=0.234 vs pi_cross=0.766, i.e., cross-category boundary errors dominate, motivating hierarchical category-then-application selection. (3) Category-difficulty analysis: easiest Streaming & Social Video (0.623), Windows Core Apps & System Utilities (0.581); hardest Gaming & Game Utilities (0.331), Music & Media Players (0.354) due to near-substitutable tools; rankings stable across models. (4) Per-application F1: distinctive apps high (Microsoft Word F1=0.96) vs broad/overlapping apps low (Notepad F1=0.50). (5) Data-quality study: human Likert grammatical 4.7, semantic realism 4.6, ground-truth correctness 99.8% on a 10% (~100/app) sample, 3 annotators each.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> No / not applicable in the standard sense: AppSelectBench's end-to-end task metric IS the retrieval/selection accuracy (selecting the correct application). Intrinsic retrieval metrics like Recall@k/nDCG over the RAS knowledge base are not reported separately; instead application-selection accuracy, per-application precision/recall/F1, and confusion matrices serve as the selection-quality metrics. There is no downstream execution metric to decouple from (execution is intentionally out of scope).
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both outcome and process diagnostics: outcome is application-selection accuracy; process/diagnostic depth is provided via category-level confusion matrices, intra- vs cross-category error decomposition, per-category accuracy, and per-application F1, which localize WHERE inter-application reasoning fails (e.g., Edge<->Chrome, YouTube<->Netflix confusions; Cloud Storage leaking into Windows Core).
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Not a focus: no retrieval-call counts, API cost, latency, token-savings, or rollout numbers are reported. The motivation frames application selection as improving downstream context efficiency (resolving the app first lets a CUA focus on relevant APIs and ignore irrelevant tools), but no quantitative cost/efficiency measurements are given. Inference uses deterministic decoding (temperature=0).
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Size: 100 desktop applications across 12 categories; ~3,000 atomic tasks; >100,000 user task-application pairs (~1,000 per application). Construction: a 4-stage LLM-synthesized + human-refined pipeline -- (1) atomic-task database curated by GPT-5 drafting then human annotation; (2) a composition engine samples/composes atomic tasks into intra- and inter-application workflows (also GPT-5-curated, human-refined); (3) an argument generator instantiates realistic values via rule-based templates, probabilistic sampling, and generative models; (4) an instruction narrator aggregates step instructions, applies step-wise drop-out, then LLM rephrasing to produce fluent natural-language user tasks. An application-equivalence mapping handles multi-valid ground truth. Answer verifiability: high (membership against curated valid-application sets; human-validated 99.8% ground-truth correctness on a 10% sample). Difficulty signal: best system GPT-5 reaches only ~63.3% overall accuracy, indicating substantial headroom and genuine inter-application ambiguity.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> API-level tool-selection benchmarks it extends/contextualizes: API-Bank (Li et al., 2023), ToolBench (Xu et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2023), Gorilla/APIBench (Patil et al., 2024), ToolAlpaca (Tang et al., 2023), ToolQA (Zhuang et al., 2023), MetaTool (Huang et al., 2023), StableToolBench (Guo et al., 2024). Tool-augmented LLM foundations: Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023), ReAct (Yao et al., 2023), PAL (Gao et al., 2023), MINT (Wang et al., 2024). CUA environments it complements: OSWorld (Xie et al., 2024), Windows Agent Arena (Bonatti et al., 2024), WinSpot (Hui et al., 2025), OpenCUA, UI-TARS-2, UltraCUA, Phi-Ground. Models used: GPT-5, GPT-4o-mini, Qwen2.5/Qwen3, Llama-3, Phi-4, Gemma-3.
- **contrasts with**:
> Explicitly contrasts API-LEVEL selection (intra-tool function calls within a pre-selected application, e.g., SUM(range) in Excel; input = user task + pre-selected app; output = sequence of API calls; core challenge = argument binding/sequencing) against its own APPLICATION-LEVEL selection (inter-application choice, e.g., Excel vs Calculator; input = user task only; output = set of suitable applications; core challenge = high-level intent matching) per Table 1. Also contrasts with CUA benchmarks (OSWorld, Windows Agent Arena) that preload the relevant application and thus bypass the application-selection step that AppSelectBench isolates.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use): a 2025 benchmark introducing the application-selection layer for computer-using agents, situated above API-level tool-retrieval/selection benchmarks (API-Bank, Gorilla, ToolBench/ToolLLM, ToolRet) and orthogonal to end-to-end CUA execution benchmarks (OSWorld, WAA). Its retrieval-augmented (RAS) protocol connects to the tool-retrieval line, but its contribution is benchmark + evaluation protocols for inter-application reasoning rather than a new retrieval method.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- code_url
- context_budget_and_selection_count
- index_structure_topology
- maintained_repo_url
- retriever_type

<a id="item-gtool"></a>
### 107. GTool: Graph Enhanced Tool Planning with Large Language Model

2025  ·  arXiv 2508.12725  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.12725)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.12725

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: tool-use (LLM tool planning: selecting, organizing, and sequencing tools/APIs to fulfill a user request)
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-agent, supervised tool planning. Given a tool set, historical user requests and their tool trajectories, the method first induces a tool-dependency graph, then for each new request generates a tool-invocation sequence. A complete tool-dependency graph is NOT assumed available; dependencies are induced from historical trajectories and are typically incomplete. Training is supervised (instruction tuning of a GNN encoder with the LLM frozen); inference performs one-shot planning with a single LLM interaction per request. Supervision is available (ground-truth tool trajectories used as labels).
- **what is retrieved**: tools (a request-specific subgraph of candidate tools and their inter-tool dependencies), encoded into a single <graph token> rather than text passages.
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external store: a tool-dependency graph built offline from a fixed tool set and historical tool trajectories. The graph is not written/grown during deployment; for each request a request-specific subgraph is derived from this static graph.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Recovery of the complete minimal needed set: the objective is to produce the full correct multi-tool dependency-correct plan (sequence) for a request, evaluated by Node-F1 (right tool set), Link-F1 (right dependency topology) and NED (right ordering), rather than a fixed top-k ranking. Naive baselines (BM25/COLT/Graph RAG-Tool Fusion) use top-k retrieval (top-5 / top-3) but GTool itself targets variable-size dependency-complete plans.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based-reasoning method; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain cycle over cases).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: false. The work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is graph-augmented tool planning.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: tool-API node and KG-subgraph: each node is a tool (with a BERT-embedded document attribute) and directed edges are inter-tool dependencies; the retrieved/used unit is a request-specific tool dependency subgraph compressed into one graph-level representation (<graph token>).
- **index source**: Static corpus, offline-induced. The tool graph G={V,E} is constructed once from the tool set T and historical trajectories H (edges added between consecutive tools in each trajectory). It is not grown at test time.
- **index structure topology**: Dependency GRAPH: a directed tool-dependency graph (node=tool, edge=output-of-A-is-precondition-for-B). For each request a request-specific graph G(q) is formed by adding a super node for the request connected to all tool nodes.
- **retriever type**:
> Learned generative graph encoder: a GNN-based encoder (TransformerConv, 3 layers) maps the request-specific tool graph to a graph-level embedding (graph-as-token), aligned with the LLM. Not BM25/dense-text retrieval; the dependency-aware selection is done by the GNN-to-LLM pipeline (BM25/COLT are baselines only).
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Downstream-task-effectiveness plus an auxiliary self-supervised signal: the GNN encoder parameters are trained jointly by (a) the tool-planning autoregressive loss L_TL = p_M(tau_G | w) (supervised on ground-truth trajectories) and (b) a missing-dependency edge-prediction loss L_MDPL (autoregressive yes/no edge existence), combined as L = L_TL + lambda * L_MDPL (lambda=0.1). The LLM is frozen; only the GNN encoder is optimized.
- **query construction**:
> Intent/request node: the raw user request q is embedded by a language model f (BERT) and added as a request-specific super node v_{n+1} with directed edges from all tool nodes to it; the request node's GNN representation h_{n+1}=h_G serves as the query-conditioned graph summary. The textual prompt also lists tool names and the request.
- **query granularity**: task-level (one-shot at t=0): a single request-specific graph and one <graph token> are constructed per user request before planning.
- **when to retrieve**: one-shot: the request-specific tool graph is constructed and the graph token produced once per request, then a single LLM call generates the full plan. (GTool interacts with the LLM only once per request.)
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule (always-on, once per request): graph construction and graph-token generation happen unconditionally for every request before the single planning call; there is no confidence/uncertainty/router trigger.
- **reranking**: No explicit reranking stage. Relevance is handled implicitly by the request-specific super node which lets request-relevant tool/dependency information propagate to the graph token; baselines (BM25/COLT) use similarity sorting but GTool does not apply a separate reranker.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Graph-level compression/distillation: instead of injecting tool descriptions and dependencies as text, GTool distills the entire request-specific dependency subgraph into a single graph-level embedding (<graph token>), reducing irrelevant-tool influence and per-request tokens by over 80-95%. The MDPL task also refines the graph by predicting/imputing masked (missing) edges.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Tool documents d(t) are embedded with a language model f (BERT) and used as node attributes a_i = f(d(t_i)); the request is embedded as the super-node attribute. Descriptions are thus encoded into graph node features (not raw docstrings in the prompt, no synthetic-query augmentation). This is graph-feature engineering rather than text expansion.
- **index content separation**:
> Yes (effectively): heavy tool descriptions are encoded into the graph/node features and compressed into a single graph token, while the LLM prompt carries only lightweight tool names + instruction + the graph token, separating a lightweight injected representation from the heavy content (>80-95% token savings).
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Static tool index (graph built once offline from historical trajectories; not live-synchronized). Integration protocol: tools are APIs/RESTful APIs (ToolBench uses >16k RESTful APIs); no MCP / live CRUD auto-sync. Planning produces a tool sequence consumed via function/tool-calling conceptually but the paper does not implement a live tool-sync protocol.
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> Yes — this is the core contribution. Retrieval/selection explicitly models inter-tool dependencies as a directed dependency graph (output-of-A is precondition for B), with a request-specific super node and a missing-dependency prediction task (MDPL) to handle incomplete dependency edges; the GNN encoder is dependency-aware and the graph token conveys dependency topology to the LLM.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> latent-token injection: the graph representation h_G is injected into the LLM prompt as a special <graph_embed> token (bounded by [/graph]) alongside tool names and the request; the LLM reasons over this latent graph token to autoregressively generate the tool trajectory. (Prompt augmentation via a soft/latent token, not text.)
- **planning integration**:
> retrieve-then-plan, one-shot: build request-specific tool graph -> encode to graph token -> single LLM call generates the full tool-invocation sequence. No tree search, no per-step interleaving, no MCTS; planning is a single autoregressive generation conditioned on the graph token.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: per-answer: the full plan (entire tool trajectory) is produced in one LLM pass with one injected graph token; retrieval is not woven per-CoT-step or per-tool-call.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not CBR; no case adaptation/revision step).
- **retrieved item representation**: latent-soft token: the injected item is a single learned graph-level embedding (<graph token>) representing the request-specific tool dependency subgraph, not raw text/trajectory/program.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Distilled structural summary: a graph-level latent representation aggregating request-specific tool semantics and inter-tool dependency topology (above raw per-tool docstrings, abstracting the dependency subgraph).
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Missing-dependency prediction with LLMs (MDPL): edges are randomly masked with probability rho during training and the model is trained to predict masked/absent edges (balanced positive/negative sampling, size alpha), explicitly modeling edge incompleteness so the graph token stays reliable under incomplete/sparse dependencies. The request-specific super node also suppresses irrelevant-tool noise. Robust down to 90% missing edges in most settings.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: graph (a static tool-dependency graph). No episodic/skill/workflow memory; the graph is induced offline and frozen.
- **write back**: false. No new experiences/cases/trajectories are written back to a memory at inference time; only the offline-induced tool graph is used (graph construction is a one-time preprocessing step, not online write-back).
- **online growth**: No. The tool-dependency store is frozen after offline induction from historical trajectories; it does not grow during deployment/test-time.
- **write back trigger**: never: there is no write-back mechanism; the tool graph is built once offline from historical trajectories and the GNN encoder is trained, after which inference adds nothing to the store.
- **failure experience usage**: Not used as stored experiences. There is no success/failure experience memory. (The closest analogue is MDPL's negative edge candidates (l='no') used contrastively during edge-prediction training, but these are graph-structure negatives, not failed-trajectory experiences.)
- **memory evolution update**:
> append-only / static: edges are added once from trajectories during construction (E <- E ∪ consecutive-tool edges); after offline induction the graph is not mutated, merged, pruned, or refined at deployment. MDPL imputes missing edges only implicitly via the trained encoder, not by editing the stored graph.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Partially: tool selection is driven by a learned (trained) GNN encoder aligned to the LLM rather than a fixed similarity top-k, but it is NOT an RL/MDP-optimized retrieval policy. Training uses supervised planning loss plus a self-supervised edge-prediction loss (no RL, no Q-learning).
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent, single private tool graph per dataset; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory sharing. (The GNN module is backbone-agnostic and can be paired with various LLMs, but memory is not shared across agents.)

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: TaskBench (three sub-datasets: HuggingFace, Daily Life, Multimedia), ToolE (MetaTool), and ToolBench (large-scale, >16,000 RESTful APIs; I2/I3 scenarios used).
- **benchmark family**: tool (tool planning / tool selection): TaskBench and ToolE are tool-planning benchmarks; ToolBench (>16k RESTful APIs) is the large-scale tool benchmark.
- **baselines**:
> Naive: BM25, COLT, Graph RAG-Tool Fusion (GRTF). Tuning-free: HuggingGPT, TaskBench. Tuning-based: GNN4Plan, ToolNet, Tool-Planner. (Backbones: LLaMA-2-7B, Vicuna-13B, Qwen3-14B in main table; plus 7 more backbones in appendix. Methods needing multiple LLM interactions e.g. STE, Toolink, ToolLLaMA are excluded.)
- **key metrics**:
> Node F1-Score (n-F1, correct tool selection, higher better), Link F1-Score (l-F1, dependency-topology preservation, higher better), Normalized Edit Distance (NED, invocation-order correctness, lower better); plus Time/Request (seconds) and per-request token consumption for efficiency.
- **headline result**:
> Over 29.6% performance improvement over SOTA baselines with a light-weight 7B LLM backbone (LLaMA-2-7B). E.g. on HuggingFace/LLaMA-2-7B GTool reaches n-F1=0.7913, l-F1=0.5403, NED=0.2537 vs best baseline GNN4Plan n-F1=0.4853; paper also cites 27.9% n-F1 growth over GNN4Plan. On ToolBench (Qwen3-14B) n-F1=0.6126, l-F1=0.3018 with Time/R=2.02s (~1/10 of baselines).
- **ablations**:
> Four ablations (Table 3): w/o RS (remove request-specific super node, use average pooling), w/o MDPL (remove missing-dependency prediction), w/o Both (remove both but still train for graph token), w/o All (no graph at all, prompt with tool names + brief instruction only). On LLaMA-2-7B: removing RS node drops n-F1 by 9.92%, l-F1 by 17.9%, NED by 22.5%; removing MDPL drops n-F1 3.32%, l-F1 3.83%; w/o Both drops n-F1 22.5%, l-F1 35.7%, NED +60.5%; w/o All collapses (n-F1=0.1566). RS node is the dominant component; effects are larger on weaker backbones (LLaMA-2-7B > Vicuna-13B). Hyperparameter analysis: alpha=4, lambda=0.1, n_l=3 optimal.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Partially. End-to-end planning is reported with n-F1/l-F1/NED (l-F1 captures dependency-topology recovery, a structural/intrinsic-like signal). A separate intrinsic 'accuracy of missing dependency prediction' is reported in Appendix B.3, decoupling the MDPL edge-prediction quality from final planning. Classic Recall@k/nDCG retrieval metrics are not the headline.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Both: outcome is tool selection (n-F1); process/structure quality is also scored via l-F1 (preserves dependency-graph topology) and NED (correctness of invocation order), plus appendix MDPL edge-prediction accuracy and case studies.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Strong efficiency gains: GTool needs only one LLM interaction per request; reduces per-request tokens by over 80% vs HuggingGPT/TaskBench (paper also states >95% pre-task token reduction vs prompt-encoding methods); inference time ~1/10 of SOTA baselines. On ToolBench, Time/R=2.02s vs HuggingGPT 12.77s, Tool-Planner 6.67s, TaskBench 47.24s, GNN4Plan 47.58s. Training cost: ~200 GPU-hours total on 2x NVIDIA A100-80G.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Budget-capped / compressed: tool descriptions are NOT placed in the prompt; instead the entire request-specific dependency subgraph is compressed into one <graph token>, so the prompt holds only tool names + brief instruction + the graph token, achieving >80-95% token reduction. No fixed top-k injected items; the graph token summarizes the request-relevant subgraph. (Naive baselines used top-5/top-3.)
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (primary research paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Not a benchmark paper. Datasets used (Table 4 statistics): HuggingFace (23 tools, 225 edges, 2178/726/726 train/val/test), Multimedia (40 tools, 449 edges, 1788/596/597), Daily Life (40 tools, 1560 edges, 1672/57/558), ToolE (15 tools, 154 edges, 298/99/100); plus ToolBench (>16,000 RESTful APIs, I2/I3 scenarios, invocation chains generated by ChatGPT). Tool graphs are constructed from historical/invocation trajectories (consecutive-tool edges); answer verifiability via ground-truth trajectories (n-F1/l-F1/NED).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> GNN-to-LLM graph-as-token alignment (e.g. GraphGPT-style 'graph as sequence/token', GNN adapters for LLMs), TransformerConv (Shi et al. 2020) as the GNN encoder, BERT for node/request text embeddings, link-prediction / graph autoencoder ideas (Kipf & Welling; Zhang & Chen) for missing-edge prediction, and supervised instruction tuning for LLM tool planning (TaskBench, HuggingGPT).
- **contrasts with**:
> Tuning-free prompt-based planners (HuggingGPT, TaskBench, ControlLLM, ART, ToolFormer) that encode tools/dependencies as long text; graph-traversal retrieval (Graph RAG-Tool Fusion, ToolNet) and clustering (Tool-Planner) that assume complete dependency structures and/or need multiple LLM calls; tuning-based GNN4Plan (requires extra inference to generate textual steps and assumes complete graphs). GTool is positioned as the first to model INCOMPLETE tool dependencies, freeze the LLM, and plan in a single LLM call.
- **lineage**:
> Sub-topic E (tool-use): retrieval/graph-augmented LLM tool planning. Within the tool-retrieval lineage that moved from flat text retrieval -> dependency/knowledge-graph-aware tool retrieval (COLT, ToolNet, Graph RAG-Tool Fusion, GNN4Plan); GTool advances this by compressing a request-specific dependency subgraph into a latent graph token and explicitly handling incomplete dependencies via missing-edge prediction.
