<a id="item-graph-rag-tool-fusion"></a>
### 108. Graph RAG-Tool Fusion

2025  ·  arXiv 2502.07223  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.07223)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **authors affiliation**: Elias Lumer, Pradeep Honaganahalli Basavaraju, Myles Mason, James A. Burke, Vamse Kumar Subbiah - PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC), AI & EmTech Teams
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.07223
- **code url**: https://github.com/EliasLumer/Graph-RAG-Tool-Fusion-ToolLinkOS (MIT license; releases the ToolLinkOS dataset and KG schema; the dataset/benchmark rather than a full method implementation is provided)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: tool-use (tool selection / tool retrieval for LLM agents over hundreds-to-thousands of tools, APIs, or agents-as-tools)
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, retrieval-only tool selection over a predefined static tool knowledge base/graph. Single-agent tool-calling setting: given a natural-language user query, retrieve the complete set of relevant tools including their nested inter-tool dependencies so an LLM agent can execute the task. No model fine-tuning is required (plug-and-play). Evaluation is intrinsic retrieval (mAP/nDCG/Recall@k) and not end-to-end task execution; the tools are non-functional/not-runnable in both benchmarks. The tool knowledge graph is built manually offline from a schema.
- **what is retrieved**: tools (tool/API/agent-as-tool nodes) together with their nested dependency tools (core tools and regular tools connected by dependency edges in a tool knowledge graph)
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus: a predefined, manually-built tool knowledge base/graph (vector index of tool descriptions + Neo4j dependency graph). No agent-written growing/episodic memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Completeness-oriented: the explicit goal is to recover the COMPLETE minimal set of relevant tools plus all of their nested (direct/indirect) dependencies, not just a fixed top-k ranking. Vector search gives an initial top-k of primary tools; graph traversal then expands to recover the full dependent tool set, subject to a final top-K cap.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based reasoning method; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain case cycle)
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False - the work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is positioned as advanced RAG + knowledge-graph tool retrieval.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: tool-API node (a tool/API/agent-as-tool represented as a node in a tool knowledge graph), plus KG-subgraph of its dependency tools recovered via graph traversal; effectively a tool node together with its retrieved dependency subgraph
- **index source**: Static corpus, offline-constructed: a predefined tool knowledge graph built manually (human-in-the-loop with LLM assistance) from a defined schema; frozen at test time (no online/test-time growth).
- **index structure topology**:
> Hybrid of flat vector index (Azure AI Search HNSW over tool-description embeddings) AND a dependency knowledge GRAPH (Neo4j) with two node types (core tool, regular tool) and four directed dependency edge types (tool/parameter x direct/indirect). Hierarchical core-vs-regular tool distinction.
- **retriever type**:
> Hybrid: dense vector search (HNSW over text-embedding-ada-002 embeddings) for first-pass tool retrieval, combined with deterministic graph traversal (depth-first search) over the dependency knowledge graph; baselines also include BM25 lexical and weighted hybrid (alpha=0.8) search. Optional LLM-as-reranker (gpt-4o).
- **retriever learning signal**: None (off-the-shelf): no fine-tuning of the retriever or embeddings; uses pretrained text-embedding-ada-002, off-the-shelf Azure AI Search (HNSW/BM25), deterministic DFS graph traversal, and a prompt-based LLM reranker. Plug-and-play, training-free.
- **query construction**: Raw user query is embedded for vector search; the algorithm optionally applies a query transformation function (QueryTransform, e.g. rewrite/decompose/transform) before vectorization, though the default/main experiments use the raw query without transformation.
- **query granularity**: task-level (one-shot at t=0): a single retrieval is performed for the whole user query/instance to assemble the full tool set with dependencies.
- **when to retrieve**: one-shot: a single two-stage retrieval pass per query (vector search then graph traversal); no iterative or uncertainty-triggered re-retrieval during the experiments.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule: retrieval is invoked once per query at the start (not gated by any confidence/uncertainty/learned-classifier/reflection signal).
- **reranking**:
> Optional reranking stage applied to the initial top-k=3 vector-retrieved tools before graph traversal; implemented as an LLM reranker (gpt-4o-2024-08-06) with a structured (Pydantic) output schema that re-orders the candidate tool names. Reported as the 'w/ RR' variant; 'no RR' omits it.
- **retrieved context refinement**: rerank (LLM reranking of the initial top-k tools) plus deterministic graph traversal expansion; final list is ordered (top vector tool then its dependencies, etc.) and truncated to a final top-K cap. No reason-in-documents distillation or distractor-filtering beyond reranking.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Tools are indexed via their KG-schema JSON descriptions (tool name/description plus schema fields); core vs regular tool node typing and dependency edges (with 'reason' and 'parameter_name' labels) are part of the indexed representation. No synthetic-query augmentation or instruction-tuned tool embeddings; raw schema/description embeddings are used for vector search.
- **index content separation**:
> Partial: a lightweight vector index over tool descriptions is used for first-pass retrieval, while the structured dependency edges (heavy relational content) live in the Neo4j graph and are loaded on demand via traversal only for the retrieved candidate tools. Not framed as progressive-disclosure SOP-index-then-content.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: Static, manually-built tool index (no live synchronization / CRUD auto-sync). Tools are non-functional schema-only entries; ToolSandbox tools (Python-native + selected RapidAPI) were converted into the static KG schema. No MCP/RESTful live integration in the experiments.
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> Yes - this is the central contribution: retrieval explicitly models inter-tool dependencies via a tool knowledge graph with four edge types (tool directly/indirectly depends on; parameter directly/indirectly depends on), recovering nested dependencies (output-of-A feeds B, parameter prerequisites, OS-level/core-tool prerequisites) through DFS graph traversal up to a per-tool dependency limit (d_limit).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> prompt augmentation: the assembled top-K tool set (primary tools + their dependency tools) is equipped/provided to an LLM agent so it can call the relevant tools to solve the user query. The paper's evaluation focuses on the retrieval step itself (which tools are selected), not the downstream execution.
- **planning integration**:
> retrieve-then-plan / one-shot exemplars at plan time: a single retrieval pass assembles the complete dependency-aware tool set up front, which is then handed to the agent for planning/execution. Retrieval is not interleaved per-step or embedded inside a search/MCTS loop in the reported method.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: per-answer / per-query (retrieval is performed once for the whole query, not interleaved per CoT step or per tool-call).
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not a CBR/case-adaptation method; retrieved tools are passed verbatim to the agent, not adapted/revised)
- **retrieved item representation**: structured tool schema entries (tool nodes with their KG-schema JSON descriptions and dependency relationships), injected as the candidate tool set / function definitions for the agent.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: tool-API level (concrete callable tool/API/agent-as-tool plus its dependency tools); not a distilled strategy, workflow, or guideline. Core tools are utility/reusable functions, regular tools are task tools.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Optional LLM reranking of the initial vector candidates to push the most relevant tool to top-1 (reducing dependency-traversal truncation and irrelevant expansions); ordering + final top-K truncation. No retriever-aware training or self-reflection relevance evaluator. Reranking reduced truncation errors by ~52% (ToolLinkOS, mAP@10).

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: graph (a static dependency knowledge graph of tools); no episodic/skill-library/procedural learned memory.
- **write back**: False - the system does not store new experiences/cases/skills; the tool knowledge graph is built offline and is read-only at inference.
- **online growth**: False - the retrievable store (tool KG + vector index) is frozen after offline construction; it does not grow during deployment/test-time.
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back; the tool knowledge graph is static and pre-defined).
- **failure experience usage**: N/A - no experience/failure storage; success and failure trajectories are not stored or retrieved (the system is a stateless retriever over a fixed tool graph).
- **memory evolution update**: N/A - stored entries are not mutated after construction (static append-only-at-build-time graph; no online dedup/delta/refine/prune at inference).
- **retrieval as learned policy**: False - retrieval/selection is fixed similarity top-k vector search plus deterministic DFS graph traversal (with an optional prompt-based LLM reranker); it is not an RL/learned retrieval policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No - single-agent, single shared static tool knowledge base; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing (though the tool KB could in principle serve multiple agents, this is not a studied dimension).

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: ToolLinkOS (new, 573 fictional tools, 1,569 instances, avg 6.3 dependencies/tool, KG schema); ToolSandbox (Lu et al. 2024; 34 tools, 1 omitted -> 33 used; 1,032 instances; converted into the GRTF KG schema).
- **benchmark family**: tool (tool selection / tool retrieval benchmarks). ToolLinkOS is a new dependency-rich tool-retrieval benchmark; ToolSandbox is an existing tool-use benchmark re-indexed for retrieval.
- **baselines**:
> Lexical Search (BM25 via Azure AI Search / Apache Lucene); Naive RAG (dense vector search via Azure AI Search HNSW, text-embedding-ada-002) [primary comparison]; Hybrid RAG (weighted lexical+vector, alpha=0.8). GRTF variants: Graph RAG-Tool Fusion (k=3) no reranking, and (k=3) with reranking.
- **key metrics**: mean Average Precision (mAP) @10/@20/@30 (primary); also nDCG and Recall @10/@20/@30 in the appendix (full retrieval metrics). Reported as intrinsic retrieval-accuracy metrics.
- **headline result**:
> Graph RAG-Tool Fusion achieves absolute improvements of 71.7% and 22.1% over naive RAG on ToolLinkOS and ToolSandbox respectively (mAP@10). Concretely (mAP@10): ToolLinkOS Naive RAG 0.210 -> GRTF w/ RR 0.927 (no RR 0.856); ToolSandbox Naive RAG 0.440 -> GRTF w/ RR 0.661 (no RR 0.521). [Note: the abstract states 22.1% on ToolSandbox while the intro states 21.1%; both numbers appear in the paper - the 0.661 vs 0.440 gap is ~22.1 absolute points.]
- **ablations**:
> Main ablation is reranking vs no reranking on the initial top-k=3 vector retrieval: reranking (LLM gpt-4o reranker) adds absolute +7% (ToolLinkOS) and +14% (ToolSandbox) mAP@10 over default GRTF (no RR), reaching 0.927 and 0.661. Retrieval error analysis (ToolLinkOS, k=3) decomposes errors: (1) primary tool missing from top-k vector search = 8.1% (affects both RR and no-RR equally); (2) correct tool retrieved within top-k but not top-1 then truncated = 91.6% of no-RR cases vs 43.6% of RR cases; (3) correct tool top-1 but excluded by dependency truncation = <0.01% no-RR vs 30% RR. Reranking reduced truncation errors by ~52%. Hybrid RAG vs Naive RAG vs Lexical (BM25) compares the first-pass retriever choice; the gap between Naive RAG and GRTF is much larger on the denser-dependency ToolLinkOS (6.3 deps/tool) than ToolSandbox (1.6 deps/tool), isolating graph traversal as the driver.
- **evaluation decoupling**: Intrinsic retrieval metrics only: the evaluation reports retrieval-quality metrics (mAP, nDCG, Recall@k) and is fully decoupled from end-to-end task/agent success - the tools are non-functional, so no downstream execution accuracy is measured.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Process/retrieval-quality metrics only (mAP/nDCG/Recall@k on tool selection); no final task-outcome (execution success) metric is reported. A retrieval error-type breakdown provides additional process-level analysis.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey)
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> ToolLinkOS: 573 fictional, non-functional tools (523 regular + 50 core) across ~15 industries, avg 6.3 dependencies/tool, 1,569 query instances, with a predefined knowledge-graph schema (2 node types, 4 edge types). Constructed via human-in-the-loop iterative LLM brainstorming + dependency verification (LLMs: gpt-4o-2024-08-06, o1-2024-12-17, o1-mini-2024-09-12), with programmatic verification (3-10 deps/tool). Instances generated with gpt-4o. ToolSandbox (33 used tools, 1,032 instances, 1.6 avg deps) re-indexed into the same KG schema. Answer verifiability is via labeled relevant-tool sets for retrieval (mAP/nDCG/Recall); tools are not runnable. Best system: GRTF w/ RR reaches mAP@10 0.927 (ToolLinkOS) and 0.661 (ToolSandbox), signaling remaining difficulty on real-API-grounded ToolSandbox.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Advanced RAG / GraphRAG (Edge et al. 2024) and knowledge-graph + LLM retrieval; dense vector retrieval (HNSW, text-embedding-ada-002) and hybrid lexical+dense retrieval (Kuzi et al. 2020); Azure AI Search (BM25/HNSW); Neo4j graph store; RAG-based tool selection/retrieval line of work (e.g., ToolBench/ToolE/Seal-Tools/ComplexFuncBench, AnyTool).
- **contrasts with**:
> Naive (vector) RAG tool retrieval, Hybrid RAG, and lexical/BM25 tool retrieval, which retrieve tools by semantic/lexical similarity alone and fail to recover semantically-unrelated but structurally-required tool dependencies; also contrasts with prior tool benchmarks (ToolBench, ToolE, Seal-Tools, ComplexFuncBench) that lack explicit tool dependencies or a KG schema.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use): retrieval-augmented tool selection/retrieval for LLM agents. Positioned in the tool-retrieval sub-lineage that moves from flat vector tool retrieval toward graph/dependency-aware tool retrieval (tools-as-knowledge-graph), emphasizing dependency-completeness over top-k ranking.

<a id="item-livemcpbench"></a>
### 109. LiveMCPBench: Can Agents Navigate an Ocean of MCP Tools?

2025  ·  arXiv 2508.01780  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.01780)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **authors affiliation**:
> Guozhao Mo, Wenliang Zhong, Jiawei Chen, Qianhao Yuan, Xuanang Chen, Yaojie Lu, Hongyu Lin, Ben He, Xianpei Han, Le Sun. Primary affiliation: Chinese Information Processing Laboratory, Institute of Software, Chinese Academy of Sciences (ISCAS), Beijing, China; several authors (Mo, Zhong, Chen, He) also at University of Chinese Academy of Sciences (UCAS). Lead author Guozhao Mo (moguozhao2024@iscas.ac.cn).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.01780
- **code url**:
> https://github.com/icip-cas/LiveMCPBench (Apache-2.0; contains MCP Copilot Agent baseline, LiveMCPEval evaluator, and LiveMCPTool). Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/ICIP/LiveMCPBench . Docker image: https://hub.docker.com/r/hysdhlx/livemcpbench . Project page: https://icip-cas.github.io/LiveMCPBench .
- **maintained repo url**:
> https://github.com/icip-cas/LiveMCPBench (101 stars, 16 forks at access time; last substantive commit Dec 2025 'fix(tools): remove error bing tools') plus a public Google Sheets leaderboard: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1EXpgXq1VKw5A7l7-N2E9xt3w0eLJ2YPVPT-VrRxKZBw . The leaderboard is updated with additional models (e.g. GLM-4.5, GPT-5-Mini, Kimi-K2 added 8/18/2025).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> tool-use (agentic tool retrieval and composition over a large-scale Model Context Protocol (MCP) toolset). Touches planning/decision-making: a multi-step ReAct agent must plan which tools to retrieve and how to compose them to accomplish realistic daily tasks across six domains (Office, Lifestyle, Leisure, Finance, Travel, Shopping).
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent, multi-step tool-use evaluation in a dynamic, large-scale, real (non-simulated) MCP environment. The agent (MCP Copilot Agent) faces 95 multi-step daily tasks and must, from a pool of 70 MCP servers / 527 tools that do NOT fit in context, retrieve relevant tools and compose multiple tool calls to solve each task. The authors formulate tool retrieval+invocation as a POMDP with hidden task states, observations from retrieved tool descriptions and execution feedback, a language action space, transitions, and a task-success reward. The agent is given only a Route action (retrieve k candidate tools), an Execute action (invoke a chosen tool), and a Response action (terminate). Tasks are deliberately dynamic (depend on evolving real-time data such as weather/news/stock prices) and long-horizon (require chaining tools). Supervision: none for the models being benchmarked (zero-shot prompting of off-the-shelf frontier LLMs at temperature 0.7); human annotation supplies 95 tasks with verified key points and serves as ground truth for validating the LLM-as-a-Judge evaluator. This is primarily a BENCHMARK + a baseline agent, not a new learning method.
- **what is retrieved**:
> tools (MCP server-tool entries): the retrievable units are MCP tools, each embedded in a server-tool hierarchy with contextual descriptions. The Route action returns the top-k candidate tools (with their server context and descriptions) from the full LiveMCPTool suite (70 servers, 527 tools); the agent then reads these tool descriptions to decide which to Execute.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus: retrieval targets a fixed, curated tool library (LiveMCPTool: 70 MCP servers, 527 tools), packaged in a frozen, validated Docker environment for reproducibility. It is NOT an agent-written growing/episodic memory; the agent does not add tools to the store at test time. (The framework is described as open/expandable for future benchmark growth, but within an evaluation run the toolset is fixed.)
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k ranking objective per retrieval call (k=5 candidate tools by default), but task success requires multi-tool completeness across the multi-step rollout: each Route call returns a top-k list, and the agent must, over repeated Route+Execute steps, recover and compose the complete minimal set of tools needed for a long-horizon daily task. Retrieval is the dominant failure mode (Retrieve Error = 50% of all errors), and a k-ablation shows k=1 hurts (78.95%->64.21%) while k=10 gives no gain over k=5 (78.95%, p=1.00), indicating that completeness of the candidate set, not just top-1 ranking, matters but saturates due to retriever limits rather than candidate scarcity.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve: yes (Route retrieves top-k tools from the toolset), Reuse: partial (retrieved tool descriptions are reused to format Execute calls, but these are TOOLS, not prior solved problem-solution cases), Revise: no, Retain: no]. Not a case-based-reasoning system; it retrieves tools, not cases.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False: the paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner. It is an MCP tool-use benchmark with dense-embedding tool retrieval (hierarchical server-tool scoring from MCP-Zero).

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> tool-API entry within a server-tool hierarchy: the granularity is one MCP tool (its name, parameters, and description) nested under its parent MCP server. Retrieval scoring (from MCP-Zero) combines a server-level similarity and a tool-level similarity, so the effective retrievable unit is the (server, tool) pair, surfaced as a top-k tool candidate list.
- **index source**:
> Static corpus built offline then warmed up at setup: LiveMCPTool aggregates 5,588 server configurations from the mcp.so MCP Marketplace, filters out key-dependent servers, taxonomically organizes the survivors, manually vets quality, and packages 70 servers / 527 tools into a Docker environment. The retrievable index is built offline from server/tool descriptions; the agent indexes the servers in a warm-up step (repo: 'uv run -m baseline.mcp_copilot.arg_generation') before evaluation. It is not induced online from the agent's own trajectories.
- **index structure topology**:
> Hierarchical server -> tool topology over a dense vector index. The MCP server-tool architecture is explicitly exploited: each server exposes multiple related tools with contextual descriptions. Retrieval uses both a server-level description embedding and a tool-level description embedding (cosine similarities s_server and s_tool combined per the MCP-Zero score). The repo exposes TOP_SERVERS and TOP_TOOLS knobs, confirming a two-level (server-then-tool) hierarchical retrieval index rather than a flat tool list.
- **retriever type**:
> dense (embedding-similarity) retriever, off-the-shelf. Server-level summaries are generated by Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct and embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B; queries are embedded the same way; candidates are ranked by cosine similarity using the MCP-Zero hierarchical score. No learned/contrastively-trained retriever; BM25/sparse not used. An embedding-model ablation swaps Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B for BGE-M3 (minor drop 78.95%->76.84%, p=0.84).
- **retriever learning signal**:
> none (off-the-shelf): the retriever is a frozen dense embedding model (Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, alternatively BGE-M3) with a fixed hierarchical cosine-similarity scoring rule borrowed from MCP-Zero. It is not trained with contrastive similarity labels, LM-feedback, downstream-task-effectiveness/preference, RL, or value-based signals. The paper's analysis explicitly attributes the bottleneck to 'the current tool-retrieval methodology itself rather than a specific embedding model or hyperparameter', motivating (but not implementing) learned retrieval.
- **query construction**:
> LLM-generated structured query produced by the agent at Route time: the prompt requires the query to contain a <tool_assistant> tag with a server-intent field and a tool-intent field, e.g. '<tool_assistant>server: <platform/permission domain> tool: <operation type + target></tool_assistant>'. The agent (the benchmarked LLM) thus constructs an intent-decomposed query specifying the desired server domain and tool operation, rather than passing the raw user task verbatim. Query errors (13.33% of failures) arise from semantic-irrelevance or granularity-mismatch in this generated query.
- **query granularity**:
> step/sub-task level (with a two-level server+tool structure): each Route call issues a query for the tool(s) needed at the current step of the rollout; the agent re-queries as the plan unfolds and after errors. The query itself is internally two-level (server-intent and tool-intent fields), matching the hierarchical index. Not a single task-level one-shot retrieval at t=0.
- **when to retrieve**:
> iterative / agent-initiated within a ReAct loop: there is no fixed retrieve-then-execute pipeline ('always retrieving before executing may fail when outputs must be combined or when re-routing is required after errors'). The agent decides when to emit a Route action versus an Execute or Response action, retrieving repeatedly across the multi-step trajectory as needed (average 1.19-4.35 Route calls per task depending on model).
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Agent-initiated request governed by the ReAct policy / prompt heuristics: the route-tool prompt instructs the LLM to call Route when it cannot solve the task with currently available tools, when a new/unknown task arises, or when the request is vague/complex and feasible tools must first be explored (the 'discovery' phase). There is no learned router, token-confidence, or uncertainty estimator; the trigger is the LLM emitting a Route action under these prompt guidelines, plus re-routing after Execute failures.
- **reranking**:
> No explicit second-stage reranker. Candidate tools are scored once by the MCP-Zero hierarchical formula score=(s_server x s_tool) x max(s_server, s_tool), which fuses server-level and tool-level cosine similarities (a hierarchy-aware scoring rule rather than a cross-encoder rerank), and the top-k=5 are returned directly. No cross-encoder, RRF, or instruction-tuned reranking stage.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Minimal: retrieved tool descriptions (top-k) are passed to the agent largely as-is for it to choose and parameterize an Execute call. A server-summary step (Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct generates concise server-level summaries used as the server-level embedding key) is an index-side, pre-retrieval engineering step rather than post-retrieval refinement. There is no decompose-recompose, reason-in-documents distillation, distractor filtering, or compression applied to retrieved candidates at inference.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Server-level summary generation as an index-side engineering step: Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct generates concise server-level descriptions (via a dedicated 'server summary' prompt) that, together with tool-level descriptions, are embedded by Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B to form the two-level retrieval keys. Beyond this server-summary augmentation, tool descriptions are used largely as collected (curated/vetted during toolset construction); there is no synthetic-query augmentation, weighted-field embedding, or instruction-tuned tool embedding.
- **index content separation**:
> Yes / progressive disclosure by design: the full 527-tool suite is deliberately NOT injected into context; a lightweight retrievable index (server + tool description embeddings) is separated from the heavy executable tools, and only the top-k retrieved candidates are surfaced on demand via Route, with actual execution deferred to the Execute action. This index-then-content pattern is the core motivation for the benchmark (avoiding prompt bloat / context overflow from thousands of tools).
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Protocol: native Model Context Protocol (MCP) with a server-tool architecture; tools invoked through the agent's Execute action over real MCP servers (local and online). Index: STATIC within an evaluation run (a frozen, Docker-packaged validated toolset of 70 servers/527 tools for reproducibility; broken servers are pruned via repo maintenance, not live auto-sync). The framework is designed to be expandable (new servers/tasks can be added and re-indexed), but there is no automatic CRUD live-synchronization of the index during evaluation (contrast ScaleMCP's auto-synchronizing index, which the paper cites). Real-time DATA is dynamic (genuine live weather/news/stock retrieval), even though the tool INDEX is fixed.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> prompt augmentation within an agentic loop: the top-k retrieved tool descriptions (from Route) are injected into the agent's context so it can reason about and select which tool to Execute and with what parameters; the tool's execution output is fed back as an observation. There is no fine-tuning/training signal and no latent-token injection; benchmarked models are used zero-shot.
- **planning integration**:
> retrieve-then-act interleaved inside a ReAct loop over a POMDP. The MCP Copilot Agent unifies reasoning and acting with three actions (Route=retrieve k tools, Execute=invoke a tool, Response=finish). Planning is implicit/dynamic: rather than a fixed plan-then-retrieve pipeline, the agent adaptively alternates Route and Execute, re-routing after errors and composing outputs across tools (per-step interleaved retrieval). No MCTS/tree search; planning emerges from the LLM's ReAct reasoning conditioned on retrieved tool descriptions and execution feedback.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> per-tool-call / per-step within a rollout: each Route is interleaved with the agent's reasoning at the step where a (new) tool is needed, and Execute calls are interleaved between retrievals; retrieval and tool execution are woven into the ReAct reasoning at the granularity of individual agent steps (average ~8-26 dialogue turns per task across models).
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not framed as CBR); see retrieved-item usage: the agent grounds Execute-call parameters in the retrieved tool schema (slot-filling) and can retry/re-route on failure (up to 3 Execute retries), but it does not adapt prior solved cases.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Structured tool documentation injected as text: each retrieved candidate is the tool's name, server context, parameter schema, and natural-language description (server-level summaries generated by Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct feed the server embedding). It is raw tool documentation, not a distilled strategy, free-text workflow, executable program/skill, or latent token.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw documentation / single reference item: the retrieved unit is a concrete MCP tool specification (name + parameter schema + description) within its server context, not a distilled strategy, state-aware guideline, reusable workflow, or procedural skill.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Limited / largely absent in the baseline; the benchmark exposes the lack of robustness as a finding. The agent can re-route and retry Execute (up to 3 repetitions per the prompt) when calls fail, providing rudimentary error recovery, but there is no relevance evaluator, self-reflection module, distractor-aware training, or reason-in-documents refinement. The error analysis shows Retrieve Errors (50%) and Other Errors (18.33%, e.g., abandoning a task on a network timeout without retry) dominate, and the authors explicitly call for future systems with better retrieval robustness, failure recovery, and adaptive tool exploration.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> none: the MCP Copilot Agent has no episodic/skill/workflow/graph/latent memory store. The toolset is a static external library, not an agent-written memory; multi-step dialogue context is kept in-context but not a retrievable learned memory. The error analysis notes a 'need for more sophisticated memory mechanisms' as future work, implying current memory is absent.
- **write back**: false: the agent does not write new experiences, cases, or skills back into any retrievable memory during evaluation. Task/tool/key-point data are created offline (human annotation), not via test-time write-back.
- **online growth**:
> false within an evaluation run: the LiveMCPTool index is fixed (frozen Docker toolset) and does not grow from the agent's outputs at test time. (Separately, the LiveMCPEval framework is designed to allow the BENCHMARK to be expanded with new servers/tasks over time without manual annotation, but that is benchmark maintenance, not agent test-time memory growth.)
- **write back trigger**: never: no automatic memory write-back exists. Tasks and verified key points are produced by a two-stage human proposer/validator pipeline offline; the agent does not persist successes or failures to memory at inference time.
- **failure experience usage**:
> N/A / none for the agent: failed experiences are not stored or retrieved as negative cases. The PAPER does conduct a rich post-hoc human error analysis of agent failure trajectories (Query Error 13.33%, Retrieve Error 50.00%, Tool Error 18.33%, Other Error 18.33% on Claude-family trajectories), but these are diagnostic categories, not a failure-memory the agent learns from.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A: there is no agent-written memory to mutate. The static LiveMCPTool is updated only by maintainers (e.g., removing broken tools, version fixes in the repo), not via append/dedup/refine of agent memory.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No: tool retrieval uses a fixed dense-embedding hierarchical top-k scoring rule (MCP-Zero formula) with frozen embeddings; it is not an RL- or value-learned retrieval policy. The agent's decision of WHEN/WHAT to Route is made by the prompted LLM (ReAct), but the ranking function itself is fixed cosine-similarity scoring, and the agent is run zero-shot without policy training.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> No: single-agent evaluation; each benchmarked LLM operates its own MCP Copilot Agent over a private (per-run) toolset with no cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing. (Multiple human annotators collaborate to BUILD the benchmark, but that is dataset construction, not shared retrievable agent memory.)

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> LiveMCPBench (introduced by this paper): 95 multi-step real-world daily tasks across 6 domains (Office, Lifestyle, Leisure, Finance, Travel, Shopping); LiveMCPTool = 70 MCP servers with 527 tools (taxonomized into ~8 server/tool classes incl. Discovery, Visualization, File Access, Code, Entertainment, Finance, Location, Miscellaneous), packaged in Docker, all retrieving genuine real-time data (no simulation). Annotators used 55/70 servers (78.57%) and 150/527 tools (28.46%). LiveMCPEval = an LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation framework (DeepSeek-V3-0324 default judge) achieving ~81% agreement with human reviewers. Table 1 compares against API-Bank, ToolBench, tau-bench, MCPBench, MCP-RADAR, MCP-Zero (toolset only), MCPEval.
- **benchmark family**:
> tool (tool/MCP-use benchmark). Specifically an MCP-agent benchmark in the lineage of tool-use benchmarks (API-Bank, ToolBench/ToolLLM, tau-bench) and MCP benchmarks (MCPBench, MCP-RADAR, MCPEval); it is the first to stress LARGE-SCALE retrieval + multi-tool composition over a real, plug-and-play MCP toolset of dozens of servers.
- **baselines**:
> Models benchmarked as agents (the 'baselines' are the 12 frontier LLMs driving the single MCP Copilot Agent): Claude-Sonnet-4-20250514, Claude-Opus-4-20250514, GPT-5, GPT-5-Mini, GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1-Mini, Gemini-2.5-Pro, DeepSeek-V3-0324, DeepSeek-R1-0528, Qwen3-235B-A22B, Qwen3-32B, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct (leaderboard adds GLM-4.5, Kimi-K2). The MCP Copilot Agent (ReAct + MCP-Zero hierarchical retrieval) is itself the baseline agent scaffold. Retrieval-config baselines/ablations: k in {1,5,10}; embedding models Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B vs BGE-M3. Evaluator baselines: DeepSeek-V3 vs Qwen2.5-72B vs others as LLM judges, plus majority-vote and human annotation. Prior benchmarks contrasted in Table 1 (API-Bank, ToolBench, tau-bench, MCPBench, MCP-RADAR, MCP-Zero, MCPEval) are positioning baselines, not run head-to-head.
- **key metrics**:
> Primary: task success rate (single-run) under LiveMCPEval's binary LLM-as-a-Judge classification J=Evaluator(Task, KeyPoints, Trajectory, ToolDescriptions) in {Success, Failure}. Efficiency metrics (Table 2): average dialogue Steps, average used Tools, average Execute calls, average Route (retrieval) calls, total Tokens consumed (millions), and monetary cost (for the Pareto frontier). Evaluator-reliability metrics: human-agreement rate, F1 vs human, Kendall's tau-b rank correlation between evaluators. Suggested alternatives: pass@k, pass^k. No standalone Recall@k/nDCG retrieval metrics are reported.
- **headline result**:
> Claude-Sonnet-4 reaches the highest task success rate of 78.95% on LiveMCPBench (DeepSeek-V3 judge), while most other frontier models score only 30-50% (e.g., Claude-Opus-4 70.53%, GPT-5 52.63%, Qwen3-235B-A22B 48.42%, down to Qwen3-32B 30.53%). Retrieval errors account for ~50% of all failures (the single largest error category), establishing tool retrieval as the dominant bottleneck; active tool composition correlates with higher success.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Number of retrieved tools k (Claude-Sonnet-4 agent, DeepSeek-V3 judge): k=5 (main) 78.95%; k=1 drops to 64.21% (exact McNemar p=0.02, significant); k=10 stays at 78.95% (p=1.00, no gain), indicating saturation due to retriever limits, not candidate scarcity. (2) Embedding model: Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (78.95%) vs BGE-M3 (76.84%, p=0.84, not significant) -> result robust to embedding choice, bottleneck is the retrieval methodology itself. (3) Evaluator-bias / single-evaluator analysis: re-evaluating all trajectories with Qwen2.5-72B preserves rankings (Kendall tau-b=0.8837, p=0.00008); majority vote over 10 evaluators gives 77.89% human agreement; max (oracle) agreement 97.89%. (4) Evaluator reliability: DeepSeek-V3 78.95-81.05% human agreement, GPT-4.1-Mini/Qwen2.5-72B ~75%, weaker judges (DeepSeek-R1, Claude-Opus-4, Qwen3-32B) 58.95-70% on long trajectories. (5) Key-points source: LLM-generated vs human-annotated key points -> auto-generated key points often match or improve agreement, showing generalizability. (6) Behavioral analysis: active tool composition (more tools/executions) correlates with success (Claude-Sonnet-4: 2.71 tools), but over-exploration shows diminishing returns (Claude-Opus-4: 3.40 tools -> 70.53%); exploration-exploitation balance, not raw tool count, drives performance.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Partial: intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k/nDCG) are NOT reported as standalone numbers. Retrieval quality is assessed indirectly via (a) the k and embedding-model ablations on end-to-end success, and (b) a human error-attribution analysis where Retrieve Error = 50% of failures. End-to-end task success rate is the headline metric; retrieval competence is diagnosed through error decomposition rather than decoupled IR metrics.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both: outcome is the binary task success rate (LLM-as-a-Judge over key points). Process is captured via (i) behavioral/efficiency metrics (steps, tools used, executions, route calls, tokens), (ii) a four-way agent error taxonomy localizing failures to Query / Retrieve / Tool / Other stages of the retrieve-compose pipeline, and (iii) key-point-based evaluation that checks intermediate critical subtasks (each key point auditable from the tool-call log), plus a separate four-way evaluation-error taxonomy for judge reliability.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Explicitly analyzed via a log-price vs performance Pareto frontier (Figure 5). Token consumption (Table 2) ranges from ~1.93M (Qwen3-32B) to 7.16M (Claude-Opus-4); Claude models and GPT-5 consume 6-7M tokens vs 2-3M for others, driven by more aggressive tool exploration and error-recovery trials. Average Route (retrieval) calls per task range 1.19-4.35; Execute calls 1.29-7.24; steps 8.08-25.53. More aggressive tool exploration buys higher success but at substantially higher token cost; the Pareto frontier identifies the most cost-effective models. Monetary cost computed from OpenRouter prices as of Jan 31, 2026 (input+output tokens).
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed top-k retrieval: k=5 tools returned per Route call in all main experiments (repo exposes two-level knobs TOP_SERVERS=5, TOP_TOOLS=3). The whole-context injection of 527 tools is explicitly avoided (the motivation for retrieval over a large toolset); only the top-k candidates per Route call enter the prompt, with multiple Route calls across a rollout. The k-ablation (1/5/10) shows k=5 is near-optimal (k=1 budget-starves, k=10 plateaus). No fixed token-budget cap figure; budget is governed implicitly by the per-call top-k and number of agent steps.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Tasks: 95 high-fidelity multi-step daily tasks across 6 domains, distilled from 300 candidate tasks via a two-stage pipeline (two groups of 3 CS-student annotators acting as proposers and validators; LLM-assisted ideation permitted but vetted; each task completed against the real toolset with annotated key points; validators de-duplicate and enforce quality and three principles: real-world relevance, temporal dynamics, tool diversity). Toolset: LiveMCPTool = 70 MCP servers / 527 tools, built by aggregating 5,588 server configs from the mcp.so marketplace, filtering out key-dependent servers, taxonomic curation, expert vetting, and Docker packaging for plug-and-play reproducibility (no scattered API keys); all online tools verified to fetch genuine real-time data. Answer verifiability: medium-high but NOT rule-based ground truth -> LiveMCPEval uses an LLM-as-a-Judge over human/LLM-verified key points to handle dynamic data and multiple valid solution paths (binary success), validated at ~81% human agreement (DeepSeek-V3 judge), F1 87.32 (Claude-Sonnet-4 trajectories) / 83.08 (Claude-Opus-4). Difficulty signal: best system Claude-Sonnet-4 reaches only 78.95% success and most models 30-50%, with retrieval errors ~50% of failures, signaling substantial headroom.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> MCP-Zero (Fei et al., 2025) for the hierarchical server-tool retrieval scoring formula score=(s_server x s_tool) x max(s_server, s_tool); ReAct (Yao et al., 2023) for the reasoning+acting agent loop; POMDP / Monte-Carlo planning in large POMDPs (Silver & Veness, 2010) for the formal problem framing; LLM-as-a-Judge (Zheng et al., 2023, MT-Bench) for LiveMCPEval; the Model Context Protocol (Anthropic, 2024) as the underlying tool interface; Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct for server summaries and Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (alt. BGE-M3) for dense embeddings.
- **contrasts with**:
> Prior tool-use benchmarks with simulated/unstable APIs and single-server, in-context tool injection: API-Bank (8 servers/73 tools, rule-based), ToolBench/ToolLLM (unstable, ~55.6% APIs dead), tau-bench (2 servers/28 tools), ToolAlpaca, Seal-Tools, ShortcutsBench, StableToolBench(-MirrorAPI). Prior MCP benchmarks that are small-scale and inject tools directly into context: MCPBench (10 servers, no large-scale retrieval), MCP-RADAR (9 servers/42 tools), MCPEval (12 servers/77 tools, synthetic). Large-scale MCP-retrieval methods it contrasts with on adaptability: RAG-MCP, MCP-Zero, and ScaleMCP (criticized for rigid pipelines lacking adaptive invocation/error recovery; ScaleMCP additionally for a manually-constructed, low-diversity toolset). LiveMCPBench is positioned as the first real + large-scale (70 servers/527 tools) + dynamic + plug-and-play + LLM-judged MCP benchmark requiring genuine large-scale retrieval and multi-tool composition.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use). A 2025 large-scale MCP-agent BENCHMARK (with an integral hierarchical dense tool-retrieval component, the Route action / MCP Copilot Agent). It extends the tool-use benchmark lineage (API-Bank -> ToolBench/ToolLLM -> tau-bench) into the MCP era and the MCP-benchmark lineage (MCPBench/MCP-RADAR/MCPEval), and sits alongside large-scale MCP tool-retrieval work (MCP-Zero, RAG-MCP, ScaleMCP). Its central diagnosis is that tool RETRIEVAL over an ocean of MCP tools, plus multi-tool composition, are the unsolved bottlenecks for agentic tool use.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- tool_dependency_awareness
- venue

<a id="item-mcp-universe"></a>
### 110. MCP-Universe: Benchmarking Large Language Models with Real-World Model Context Protocol Servers

2025  ·  arXiv 2508.14704  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14704)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **authors affiliation**: Ziyang Luo, Zhiqi Shen, Wenzhuo Yang (equal contribution), Zirui Zhao, Prathyusha Jwalapuram, Amrita Saha, Doyen Sahoo, Silvio Savarese, Caiming Xiong, Junnan Li. All affiliated with Salesforce AI Research.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14704
- **code url**: https://github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/MCP-Universe (official; ~588 stars, ~85 forks at time of access). Project website: https://mcp-universe.github.io
- **maintained repo url**:
> https://github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/MCP-Universe - extensible evaluation framework with UI support, allowing community to integrate new agents and MCP servers; hosts all 231 tasks, 84 evaluators, and several in-repo MCP servers (Yahoo Finance, Blender, Google Search, Weather, Date). Project page https://mcp-universe.github.io. No persistent public leaderboard is described in the paper, though the framework is positioned as a living testbed for the evolving MCP ecosystem.

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> tool-use / agentic decision-making benchmark: evaluating LLM agents that plan, select, sequence, and invoke real-world tools exposed by Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers across 6 domains (Location Navigation, Repository Management, Financial Analysis, 3D Designing, Browser Automation, Web Searching). Touches web, code/repo, and embodied-design (3D) sub-domains, but is fundamentally a real tool-use / function-calling benchmark over large, unfamiliar tool spaces.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, multi-turn, single-agent tool-use evaluation grounded in REAL (not simulated) MCP servers connected to authentic external services (Google Maps, GitHub, Yahoo Finance, Blender, Playwright, Google Search, Fetch, plus supporting Notion/Weather/Date/Calculator servers). A task tau is a tuple (G, C, T_available): G is a natural-language goal, C is initial context/background, and T_available is the union of tools from the available MCP servers. The agent must identify, sequence, and invoke appropriate tools from T_available to achieve G given C, reasoning over partial information, adapting to diverse tool interfaces, and handling tool-response ambiguities/failures. Long-horizon multi-turn tool calling is required; input tokens grow rapidly with interaction steps (long-context challenge). The main experiments use a ReAct agent (thought-then-action loop); GPT-OSS, which cannot follow ReAct, uses the OpenAI Agent SDK instead. The benchmark is off-the-shelf evaluation of frontier LLMs (no training/supervision of the models is provided by the benchmark); temperature is set to 1.0 for all LLMs. Evaluation is execution-based and binary (pass/fail) via E: M x A x T -> {0,1}.
- **what is retrieved**:
> tools (MCP server tool APIs). The agent must select and invoke the correct tools from the set of tools exposed by the available real-world MCP servers (133 tools across 11 servers; in the stress test 94 tools across 7 servers). There is no separate document/case/demo retrieval corpus; 'retrieval' here is real tool selection/identification within a large, partly unfamiliar tool space, plus, for Web Searching, agent-initiated web/document content fetching via the Google Search and Fetch MCP servers.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus of real tools/services. The retrievable surface is the fixed set of tools exposed by real-world MCP servers selected per task (their tool schemas/specifications and live data endpoints). It is NOT an agent-written growing/episodic memory; the agent does not persist cases or experiences across tasks. (Within Web Searching tasks, agents query live external web data, but this is task-time data access, not a self-grown memory store.)
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Not a top-k retrieval-ranking objective. The benchmark does not score Recall@k/nDCG over tools; instead the agent is given the full set of available tools per task (all schemas in context) and must select and chain the complete minimal set of correct tool calls to satisfy a multi-step goal (execution-based completeness). Success requires recovering the correct multi-tool plan, not ranking a candidate list. The 'more MCP servers connected' setting (7 servers, 94 tools) tests robustness to a larger candidate tool space rather than introducing an explicit retrieval-ranking metric.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: [Retrieve: partial (the agent selects/identifies the right tools from the available MCP tool set, but this is tool selection, not retrieval of prior solved cases), Reuse: no, Revise: no, Retain: no]. Not a case-based-reasoning system.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False: the paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is a real-world MCP tool-use benchmark with execution-based evaluation.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> tool-API: a single MCP tool (name + description + parameter schema) exposed by an MCP server is the unit the agent must select and invoke. Tools are grouped under servers (server -> tool hierarchy). For Web Searching, the unit additionally includes web search results and fetched URL/document content returned by the Google Search and Fetch MCP servers.
- **index source**:
> Static, offline-defined per-task tool set: for each task the framework selects the directly relevant real-world MCP servers and exposes their tools to the agent (T_available). Tool specifications come from authentic MCP servers (mostly official servers; some re-implemented over official APIs by the authors for quality). The store is fixed at task time and is not induced from the agent's own trajectories. In the stress-test variant, a larger fixed set (7 servers, 94 tools) including unrelated servers is exposed.
- **retriever type**:
> LLM-as-selector (no dedicated retriever): the LLM agent itself selects which tool to call from the in-context tool list at each ReAct step (function-calling / tool-use). There is no BM25/dense/learned tool retriever in the standard setup; tool schemas are placed directly into the prompt and the model chooses among them. This is a key reason the benchmark exposes an 'unknown-tools' challenge.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> none (off-the-shelf). The benchmark evaluates frontier LLMs as-is; no tool retriever is trained, and the models are not fine-tuned on the benchmark. Tool selection emerges from the pretrained/instruction-tuned LLM's own function-calling ability with no contrastive, LM-feedback, preference, or RL signal supplied by the benchmark.
- **query construction**:
> Thought-conditioned action generation: under the ReAct framework the LLM first generates a thought based on the latest observation, then generates the next action (tool call with arguments) based on that thought. The 'query' is thus the model's self-generated tool-call decision and parameters, derived from the goal G, context C, prior observations, and the exposed tool schemas. For Web Searching, the agent additionally formulates search queries and URLs to pass to the Google Search / Fetch tools.
- **query granularity**:
> step/state-level: a tool-selection decision is made at each ReAct interaction step, conditioned on the running observation history. Not a single task-level one-shot retrieval at t=0; tool choices unfold step-by-step over a long-horizon multi-turn trajectory (mean successful-task steps ~5-8 depending on model).
- **when to retrieve**:
> iterative / agent-initiated: the agent decides at each step whether and which tool to invoke within the ReAct thought-action loop until it produces a final answer (or hits step/context limits). Tool use is interleaved across the multi-step rollout; there is no fixed retrieval schedule, learned router, or uncertainty trigger built into the benchmark.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Agent-initiated request governed by the ReAct loop: retrieval/tool-invocation is triggered whenever the model, in its generated action, decides a tool call is needed to make progress toward the goal. No token-confidence, attention-uncertainty, learned-complexity classifier, or reflection-token mechanism is imposed by the benchmark; the trigger is purely the agent emitting a tool-call action. (The optional exploration phase adds an upfront, agent-driven free-interaction stage before the exploitation/ReAct phase, but this is an analysis intervention, not the standard trigger.)
- **reranking**: None. No reranking stage over tools or retrieved content is applied; the agent selects tools directly from the in-context list. (No cross-encoder, RRF, or hierarchy-aware reranking is described.)
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> None by default in the main benchmark; tool outputs (observations) are fed back to the agent verbatim, which contributes to the long-context challenge. As an analysis intervention (Sec 4.3), the authors add an optional per-step Summarization Agent that compresses raw MCP server outputs to reduce context length while preserving essential information; this yields only mixed results (helps Location Navigation for GPT-4.1/Claude-4.0-Sonnet, neutral/negative for Browser Automation and Financial Analysis). Thus compression is studied as a candidate refinement but is not part of the standard pipeline.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Minimal / raw: tools are exposed using their native MCP schemas (name, description, parameter spec) directly in the agent context; the paper does not apply synthetic-query augmentation, expanded summaries, weighted-field embeddings, or instruction-tuned tool embeddings. The 'unknown-tools' challenge is precisely that raw MCP tool docs are often insufficient for correct usage (e.g., Yahoo Finance requiring distinct start/end dates), motivating the optional exploration phase as a remedy rather than offline document engineering.
- **index content separation**:
> Limited: in the standard setup all available tool schemas and their (potentially large) outputs are loaded into context, with no separation of a lightweight index from heavy content - a deliberate stressor producing the long-context challenge. The optional per-step Summarization Agent partially separates essential information from raw heavy tool outputs (a form of on-demand content compression), but it is an analysis intervention, not a default progressive-disclosure / index-then-content design.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> MCP-based, live tool index over REAL servers: tools are accessed through the Model Context Protocol (JSON-RPC 2.0 over STDIO/SSE) against authentic API endpoints with real authentication, so tool outputs reflect live, temporally changing data (handled by dynamic evaluators that fetch real-time ground truth). The framework dynamically configures which servers/tools are exposed per task and is extensible to new servers (researchers can add servers), but it does not perform automatic CRUD live-sync of a tool catalog at agent runtime; the per-task tool set is fixed once configured.
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> Not explicitly modeled by any retrieval/ranking component; inter-tool dependencies are left to the LLM agent to infer. Tasks inherently require multi-tool chaining where one tool's output feeds another (e.g., GitHub: list branches -> create/copy file -> open PR; Finance: fetch institutional-holdings date -> convert to calendar date -> pull closing price for that day; Navigation: compute route polyline -> search place near midpoint -> validate place type). The benchmark thus tests dependency-aware planning, but provides no dependency graph or dependency-aware reranker; correct sequencing is the agent's responsibility.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> prompt augmentation within an interactive agentic loop: selected tool schemas are placed in the prompt, the agent issues tool calls, the real MCP server executes them against live services, and the returned observations are appended to the context to inform subsequent thoughts/actions. Tool outputs are used directly for reasoning and final-answer construction. The benchmark itself provides no training signal; usage is purely inference-time tool invocation and grounding.
- **planning integration**:
> Per-step interleaved plan-and-act via ReAct (thought -> action -> observation, repeated). The agent implicitly plans a sequence of tool calls across a long-horizon multi-turn trajectory; there is no MCTS/tree search and no explicit plan-then-retrieve module in the standard setup. Alternative agent architectures are compared (ReAct, ReAct-with-Exploration, Cursor Agent, OpenAI Agent SDK), showing agent-framework design materially affects planning quality (e.g., o3 + OpenAI Agent SDK 31.60% vs o3 + ReAct 26.41%).
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: per-tool-call within a rollout (equivalently per-ReAct-step): each thought is followed by an action that may be a tool call, and retrieval/tool-use is interleaved at the granularity of individual tool invocations across the multi-step interaction trace.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> N/A (not framed as CBR). The closest analogue is that the agent reads each tool's schema and live outputs and instantiates correctly-formatted, correctly-sequenced tool calls (parameter slot-filling and chaining grounded in the tool docs and observations), optionally informed by a prior exploration phase, rather than adapting a retrieved prior solution case.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Structured tool specifications and live execution results: tools are represented as their MCP schemas (name, description, parameters) injected into the prompt; tool outputs are returned as structured/textual observations (e.g., Google Maps place lists, Playwright HTML/page snapshots, Yahoo Finance time-series, GitHub branch/issue data). For Web Searching, search-result snippets and fetched page content (raw or, optionally, summarized) are injected. No distilled strategy, free-text workflow, executable skill, or latent-token representation is used.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw tool documentation + raw live tool outputs (low abstraction). The retrievable units are concrete tool API specifications and the literal data returned by real services; there is no distilled strategy, guideline, reusable workflow, or procedural skill abstraction.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> None built into the benchmark; robustness to irrelevant tools is instead MEASURED. The 'More MCP Servers Connected' experiment (Sec 4.5) deliberately exposes 7 servers / 94 tools (including unrelated ones), showing consistent performance drops (e.g., Claude-4.0-Sonnet Location Navigation 22.22% -> 11.11%; GPT-4.1 Browser Automation 23.08% -> 15.38%, Financial Analysis 40.00% -> 35.00%), demonstrating brittleness to tool-space noise. The optional summarization agent (context refinement) is the only studied mitigation for noisy long outputs, and it is only partially effective.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none. The agent has no episodic, skill-library, workflow, procedural, graph, or latent memory that persists across tasks. Each task is solved independently; only the within-task conversation trace is retained in context.
- **write back**: false: the system does not store new experiences/cases/skills into any retrievable memory. (The optional exploration phase lets the model accumulate tool knowledge within a single task, but this is in-context and not written to a persistent store; tasks remain independent.)
- **online growth**:
> false: the retrievable tool set is fixed per task and does not grow from the agent's own outputs at test time. The framework is extensible by humans (researchers can add new MCP servers/agents), but this is offline benchmark extension, not online memory growth during agent deployment.
- **write back trigger**: never: no automatic memory write-back exists. Tasks and evaluators are created and cross-checked offline by the authors; no model success/failure/reflection event writes to a persistent memory at inference time.
- **failure experience usage**:
> N/A / none: failed experiences are not stored or retrieved as memory. The paper performs qualitative error analysis (e.g., the 'naive error' where o3 copies format requirements verbatim; the Yahoo Finance identical start/end-date error illustrating unknown-tools failures) to characterize failure modes, but does not persist failures as negative cases for retrieval or learning. The exploration phase can let a model learn correct tool usage within a task, indirectly reducing such errors, but without an explicit failure store.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A: there is no model-written memory to mutate. The benchmark's task/server set is updated only by human curation and framework extension, not via append/dedup/refine of agent memory.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No: tool selection is performed by the off-the-shelf LLM via prompting/function-calling, not by an RL- or value-learned retrieval policy. No M-MDP, soft Q-learning, or trained retrieval policy is involved.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> No shared memory across agents. The benchmark is single-agent per evaluation. However, the framework is explicitly cross-FRAMEWORK at the evaluation level: it standardizes comparison of heterogeneous agent architectures (ReAct, ReAct-with-Exploration, Cursor Agent, OpenAI Agent SDK) over the same MCP servers, and is designed for the community to plug in new agents/servers. There is no shared experience/memory store between agents.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> MCP-Universe (introduced by this paper): 231 tasks across 6 domains and 11 MCP servers with 133 total tools, evaluated by 84 unique execution-based evaluators (4 format / 32 static / 48 dynamic). Domain task counts: Web Searching 55 (23.8%), Location Navigation 45 (19.5%), Financial Analysis 40 (17.3%), Browser Automation 39 (16.9%), Repository Management 33 (14.3%), 3D Designing 19 (8.2%). Real-world MCP servers: Google Maps, GitHub, Yahoo Finance, Blender, Playwright, Google Search, Fetch, plus supporting Notion, Weather, Date, and Calculator servers.
- **benchmark family**:
> tool (real tool-use / function-calling benchmark over MCP servers). Positioned within the agent/tool-calling benchmark family alongside API-Bank, ToolBench/ToolLLM, GAIA, AppWorld, tau-Bench, and BFCLv3, and directly contrasted with contemporary MCP benchmarks (MCPWorld, MCP-RADAR, MCPEval, LiveMCPBench). Spans web (Browser Automation via Playwright, Web Searching), code/repo (GitHub), and design (Blender 3D) sub-domains, but is fundamentally a tool benchmark.
- **baselines**:
> Frontier LLMs evaluated under the ReAct agent (GPT-OSS under OpenAI Agent SDK). Proprietary: GPT-5, Grok-4, Claude-4.0-Sonnet, o3, o4-mini, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Gemini-2.5-Flash, GPT-4.1, GPT-4o. Open-source (>=120B): GLM-4.5, Kimi-K2, Qwen3-Coder (480B-A35B), Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507, DeepSeek-V3-0324, GPT-OSS-120B. Agent-framework comparison baselines: ReAct vs Cursor Agent (Claude-4.0-Sonnet backbone) and ReAct vs OpenAI Agent SDK (o3 backbone). Comparison of MCP benchmarks (MCPWorld, MCP-RADAR, MCPEval, LiveMCPBench) on real-world integration, temporal dynamics, and execution-based evaluation (Table 1).
- **key metrics**:
> (1) Success Rate (SR, %) per domain and overall, from binary execution-based pass/fail E in {0,1}. (2) Average Evaluator score (AE, %): average percentage of evaluators passed per task (finer-grained partial credit). (3) Average Steps (AS): average number of interaction steps for successful tasks (efficiency; not available for GPT-OSS which does not follow ReAct). Also reported: success rate broken down by evaluator type (Format / Static / Dynamic). No Recall@k/nDCG, latency, or dollar-cost metrics are reported.
- **headline result**:
> Even SOTA models struggle: GPT-5 achieves the best overall success rate of 43.72% (AE 60.23%, AS 8.22), followed by Grok-4 at 33.33% and Claude-4.0-Sonnet at 29.44%. Best open-source model GLM-4.5 reaches 24.68%, surpassing some proprietary models (o4-mini 25.97% is close; Claude-3.7-Sonnet 24.24%). The low absolute ceiling (<44%) is the central headline, exposing brittleness of frontier LLM agents on real-world MCP tool use.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Evaluator-type breakdown (Table 4): non-reasoning models pass >90% of Format evaluators (Claude-4.0-Sonnet 98.29%) while reasoning models do worse on format (Gemini-2.5-Flash 51.28%, o3 73.50%); the large gap between Format (often >80%) and Static/Dynamic content evaluators (~40-66%) shows failures stem mainly from content generation, not format. GPT-5 leads Static (61.92%, tied with Claude-4.0-Sonnet) and Dynamic (65.96%). (2) Long-context analysis (Fig 4): tokens grow rapidly with interaction steps (measured on Claude-4.0-Sonnet); adding a per-step Summarization Agent gives mixed results (helps Location Navigation for GPT-4.1/Claude-4.0-Sonnet, neutral/negative elsewhere). (3) Unknown-tools analysis (Fig 5): adding an Exploration phase before exploitation improves some domains (GPT-4.1 Browser Automation +7.69pp to 30.77%; Claude-4.0-Sonnet Financial Analysis +7.50pp to 62.50%) but is not universally beneficial (Claude-4.0-Sonnet Browser Automation declines; GPT-4.1 Financial Analysis flat). (4) More servers connected (Fig 6): exposing 7 servers/94 tools (incl. unrelated) degrades performance (e.g., Claude-4.0-Sonnet Location Navigation 22.22% -> 11.11%). (5) Agent-framework comparison (Table 5): ReAct (29.44%) > Cursor Agent (26.41%) on Claude-4.0-Sonnet; OpenAI Agent SDK (31.60%) > ReAct (26.41%) on o3, with o3+Agent SDK the best agent-backbone combo.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Partial / not in the retrieval sense. The benchmark does NOT report intrinsic retrieval metrics (no Recall@k/nDCG over tools). It does, however, decouple evaluation along orthogonal axes: per-domain success rates, evaluator-type breakdown (Format vs Static vs Dynamic), an Average Evaluator (AE) score giving partial credit on sub-criteria distinct from binary task success, and Average Steps (AS) for efficiency. Tool-selection competence surfaces indirectly through these and through the unknown-tools / more-servers analyses rather than via standalone retrieval metrics.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both. Outcome: binary task Success Rate. Process/intermediate: Average Evaluator (AE) score (fraction of per-task sub-criteria/evaluators satisfied), Average Steps (AS) for successful tasks (trajectory efficiency), Format/Static/Dynamic evaluator breakdown localizing where failure occurs (format compliance vs content correctness vs temporal correctness), and qualitative error analyses (naive format-copying error; unknown-tools parameter misuse) that diagnose process-level failures.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Reported via Average Steps (AS) and the long-context analysis rather than dollar/latency. AS for successful tasks: o3 most efficient among top models at 4.82 steps despite 26.41% SR; GPT-5 8.22 steps, Grok-4 7.75, Gemini-2.5-Flash 8.26; open-source mostly 5-7 (DeepSeek-V3 most efficient at 5.06). The benchmark emphasizes the long-context cost: input tokens grow rapidly with steps (measured on Claude-4.0-Sonnet), often causing context overflow; a summarization agent reduces context but gives mixed accuracy effects. No explicit API-cost, wall-clock latency, or token-count-per-task tables are provided.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> No fixed token budget or fixed-k tool count is set per query; all available tools' schemas are placed in context (133 tools in the standard relevant-server setup; 94 tools in the 7-server stress test), and tool outputs accumulate. This produces a growing, unbounded context that the paper identifies as the long-context challenge (tokens increase rapidly with interaction steps, risking context overflow). The optional per-step summarization agent is the only budget-management mechanism studied, and it is not part of the default protocol.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Size: 231 tasks; 6 domains; 11 MCP servers; 133 tools; 84 unique execution-based evaluators (4 Format, 32 Static, 48 Dynamic). Construction: tasks are MANUALLY designed by the authors to reflect real use cases, with 4-5 sub-task types per domain (e.g., route planning/optimal stops/location/place finding for navigation; portfolio analysis/financial statements/trading strategies/institutional holdings/dividend analysis for finance); a task is rejected as too easy if it can be solved without MCP servers or consistently solved within five retries, prompting brainstorming of a harder one; every task and evaluator is cross-checked by other authors for feasibility, ambiguity, and correctness. Answer verifiability: HIGH and execution-based (not LLM-as-judge) - Format evaluators check strict output formatting, Static evaluators check time-invariant ground truth (manually collected, e.g., historical stock prices, exact goal counts), and Dynamic evaluators automatically fetch real-time ground truth (e.g., live flight prices, current weather, current GitHub issue counts) via tool calls for stable evaluation across timestamps. Difficulty signal: best system GPT-5 reaches only 43.72% overall SR, with several domains (Location Navigation, Repository Management) far lower, indicating high real-world difficulty and an unknown-tools / long-context challenge.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> MCP (Model Context Protocol), introduced by Anthropic (late 2024), as the integration standard (JSON-RPC 2.0 over STDIO/SSE; host/client/server three-layer architecture). The ReAct agent framework (Yao et al., 2023) as the primary agent pipeline; also evaluates ReAct-with-Exploration, the OpenAI Agent SDK, and the Cursor Agent. Uses real official/community MCP servers (Google Maps, GitHub, Playwright, Fetch, Notion, Calculator) and authors' own API-backed servers (Yahoo Finance, Blender, Google Search, Weather, Date). Conceptually builds on the agent/tool-use evaluation lineage (API-Bank, ToolBench/ToolLLM, GAIA, AppWorld, tau-Bench, BFCLv3).
- **contrasts with**:
> Contemporary MCP benchmarks (Table 1): MCPWorld (real-world + exec-eval but GUI-heavy, no temporal dynamics), MCP-RADAR (derivative of HumanEval/GSM8k, not real-world, no temporal dynamics, though exec-based), MCPEval and LiveMCPBench (both rely on LLM-as-a-Judge, unsuitable for real-time tasks and prone to style bias; LiveMCPBench is real-world+temporal but not exec-based). MCP-Universe is the only one combining real-world integration, temporal dynamics, AND execution-based evaluation. Also contrasted with simplistic prior benchmarks focused on isolated abilities (instruction following, math reasoning, function calling) and with enterprise agents (Cursor) which it shows do not beat plain ReAct.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use): a real-world tool-use BENCHMARK for the MCP era. It extends the function-calling/tool benchmark lineage (API-Bank -> ToolBench/ToolLLM -> GAIA/AppWorld/tau-Bench/BFCLv3) into execution-based evaluation over authentic MCP servers with temporal (real-time ground-truth) dynamics, and sits among 2025 MCP benchmarks (MCPWorld, MCP-RADAR, MCPEval, LiveMCPBench). It exposes brittleness in real tool selection over large/unfamiliar tool spaces (the 'unknown-tools' and long-context challenges), serving as a difficulty-defining testbed rather than a retrieval method.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- index_structure_topology
- venue

<a id="item-mcp-zero"></a>
### 111. MCP-Zero: Active Tool Discovery for Autonomous LLM Agents

2025  ·  arXiv 2506.01056  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01056)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2506.01056, cs.AI / cs.SE); not peer-reviewed at time of writing
- **authors affiliation**:
> Xiang Fei (Xiamen University / XMU, xiangf@stu.xmu.edu.cn), Xiawu Zheng (Associate Professor, Institute of Artificial Intelligence, Xiamen University; corresponding author, zhengxiawu@xmu.edu.cn), Hao Feng (University of Science and Technology of China / USTC, haof@mail.ustc.edu.cn). Lead/primary affiliation: Xiamen University.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01056
- **code url**: https://github.com/xfey/MCP-Zero
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/xfey/MCP-Zero (releases code + the MCP-tools dataset of 308 servers / 2,797 tools; dataset distributed via Google Drive; ~486 stars / 52 forks as of mid-2026)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: tool-use (LLM agent tool/MCP-server discovery and selection from large tool ecosystems); cross-domain toolchain construction.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, multi-turn, single-agent setting where an autonomous LLM agent must accomplish tasks requiring external tools/APIs exposed via the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The standard paradigm injects all tool JSON-schemas into the system prompt (e.g. >248k tokens for full ecosystems, 4,600 tokens for one GitHub server), causing massive context overhead and reducing the model to a passive selector. MCP-Zero instead lets the agent proactively decide WHEN it lacks a capability and emit a structured tool request that triggers on-demand retrieval. No model training/fine-tuning is required (off-the-shelf LLMs prompted to author requests). Supervision: human-annotated APIBank test sets + a constructed needle-in-a-haystack benchmark; retriever uses frozen embeddings, no learned retrieval policy.
- **what is retrieved**: tools (MCP tool definitions / JSON-schemas) and, at the coarse stage, MCP servers. Retrieval targets tool/server documentation (descriptions and LLM-generated enhanced summaries).
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus of tool/server documentation (the MCP-tools index of 308 servers / 2,797 tools, or APIBank's 48 tools), built offline; the agent does not write new entries back during deployment. The 'growth' is in the agent's progressively constructed in-context toolchain, not in the retrievable store.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Precision-driven small-k recommendation: top-k retrieval (top-1 used in main experiments; the hierarchical score returns top-k tools with dynamic adjustment when similarity scores are closely clustered, larger k for fault tolerance). Completeness over a full task is achieved not by a single completeness-oriented ranking but by ITERATIVE single-tool requests across turns (each request retrieves one/few tools on-demand).
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based-reasoning method; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain case cycle).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it grounds itself in active learning / information-gain theory and RAG.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: tool-API (a single MCP tool definition / JSON-schema) at the fine stage; MCP-server (a server's description/summary) at the coarse stage. Two-level: server then tool.
- **index source**:
> Static corpus, offline-induced: MCP-tools dataset collected from the official Model Context Protocol servers repo (Tag 2025.4.28, Commit ad2d4e6); 396 servers collected, filtered to 308 servers / 2,797 tools. Embeddings (text-embedding-3-large, 3072-dim) precomputed offline. For APIBank, the level-1 subset's 48 tools form the static index.
- **index structure topology**:
> Hierarchical two-level: server-level (category/platform) -> tool-level, with a flat dense vector index at each level. Each server has description + LLM-generated enhanced summary embeddings; each tool has a description embedding. (APIBank has no server hierarchy, so retrieval is flat over 48 tools.)
- **retriever type**: Dense (off-the-shelf OpenAI text-embedding-3-large embeddings with cosine-similarity matching). No BM25, no learned/trained retriever, no generative tool-as-token retrieval.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> none (off-the-shelf frozen embedding model). The retriever is not trained; the key 'learning-free' lever is that the AGENT authors a request r that is semantically closer to tool documentation than the raw user query q (Alignment(r,t) > Alignment(q,t)), improving matching without any retriever training.
- **query construction**:
> Agent-authored structured request: the LLM emits a <tool_assistant> block with a 'server:' field (platform/permission domain) and a 'tool:' field (operation type + target). This model-generated request replaces the raw user query as the retrieval key, ensuring better semantic alignment with tool docs. Optionally a single ICL example anchors the request style/granularity.
- **query granularity**: Step/state-level (the request is generated at the point a capability gap is identified during task execution) and two-level (separate 'server' and 'tool' fields drive a two-stage retrieval). Multiple requests can be issued across a single conversation.
- **when to retrieve**: Active (agent-initiated, on-demand) and iterative: the agent autonomously decides when it lacks a capability and issues a request; it can re-request iteratively across turns until adequate tools are found or it falls back to parametric knowledge.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Agent-initiated request: the LLM itself detects a capability gap and spontaneously emits a structured <tool_assistant> block (prompted via a system instruction granting 'permission' to declare missing capabilities). Not a fixed schedule, token-confidence, or learned-classifier trigger.
- **reranking**:
> Hierarchy-aware scoring rather than a separate cross-encoder reranker. Final tool ranking combines server- and tool-level cosine similarities via score = (s_server x s_tool) x max(s_server, s_tool); server matching itself takes the higher of original-description vs enhanced-summary similarity (dual-matching). No learned reranking model.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Minimal: top-k selection and injection of the best tool JSON-schema(s) back into context (progressive disclosure of only needed schemas). The main 'refinement' is index-side document engineering (enhanced server summaries). No distractor filtering / compression / reason-in-documents distillation beyond top-k truncation.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Yes, central lever: server descriptions are augmented with LLM-generated 'enhanced summaries' (Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct) emphasizing capabilities and usage patterns; matching takes the higher similarity of original-description vs enhanced-summary (dual-matching). Tool descriptions embedded as-is. This is expanded-summary / capability-summary document engineering, not synthetic-query augmentation.
- **index content separation**: Yes. A lightweight semantic index (server/tool descriptions + summaries + precomputed embeddings) is kept separate from heavy tool JSON-schemas; only the matched tool's full schema is loaded into context on demand (progressive disclosure), keeping per-query tokens near-constant.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Integration protocol is MCP (Model Context Protocol, JSON-RPC), native to the method. The tool index itself is STATIC (offline snapshot at Tag 2025.4.28); no live CRUD auto-sync in the released code (dynamic MCP-server deployment is explicitly future work). So: MCP protocol + static index.
- **tool dependency awareness**: No explicit inter-tool dependency modeling (no dependency graph / bipartite KG / dependency-aware reranking). Cross-tool coordination emerges implicitly via the agent's iterative subtask decomposition (output of one tool informs the next request), not via modeled dependencies.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**: Prompt augmentation: the retrieved tool JSON-schema(s) are injected into the LLM context for immediate invocation (function calling). The agent then either uses the tool or refines its request. Iterative injection builds a cross-domain toolchain in-context.
- **planning integration**:
