> Retrieve-as-you-go inside the agent loop: per-step interleaved / iterative active invocation. The agent decomposes a complex task into subtasks, and at each subtask emits a request -> retrieval -> tool injection -> use, progressively building the toolchain (e.g. filesystem read -> code edit -> command execution). Not one-shot plan-time exemplars and not inside MCTS/tree search.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-tool-call / per-subtask within a rollout: each capability gap during reasoning triggers an independent retrieval request, woven into the multi-turn ReAct-style loop.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not CBR). The closest analog is the agent refining/re-issuing its tool request via execution/adequacy feedback during iterative invocation, but retrieved items are tool schemas used verbatim, not adapted cases.
- **retrieved item representation**: Structured tool definition (JSON-schema with name, description, parameters) injected verbatim into context for function calling; the retrieval KEY is the agent's free-text structured request (server/tool fields).
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Procedural tool/API (executable capability). Retrieved unit is a concrete, invocable MCP tool schema (lowest abstraction: a single tool), grouped under a server-level capability abstraction at the coarse stage.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Two main mechanisms: (1) agent-authored requests reduce the query-document semantic gap, raising matching precision and resisting attention dilution at scale (accuracy stays ~90-96% as the pool scales 40x vs standard injection collapsing to 60-69%); (2) iterative active invocation provides fault tolerance/self-correction (if retrieved tools are inadequate the agent refines and re-requests). Optional single ICL example acts as a schema anchor reducing semantic mismatch. No retriever-aware/distractor-aware training.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (no episodic/skill/workflow memory). A static tool/server vector index is the only persistent store; the in-context toolchain is transient per conversation.
- **write back**: No. The system does not store new experiences, cases, or skills back into any memory; the tool index is fixed offline. (Future work mentions registering newly built tools when combined with Alita, but MCP-Zero itself does not write back.)
- **online growth**:
> No. The retrievable store is frozen after offline construction. Only the agent's transient in-context toolchain grows during a conversation, not the index. (Paper notes the active paradigm scales gracefully as the tool ecosystem grows, but that growth is external dataset expansion, not online self-growth.)
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back mechanism).
- **failure experience usage**: Not stored. Failed/inadequate retrievals are handled in-the-moment by the agent refining and re-issuing its request (iterative fault tolerance), but no failure experience is persisted or retrieved later. No success/failure contrastive memory.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (no stored experiential entries to mutate). The static index is append-only at dataset-construction time only.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No. Retrieval/tool-selection is fixed cosine-similarity top-k over frozen embeddings, not a learned/RL-optimized policy. The 'active' decision of WHEN/WHAT to request is made by the (untrained) LLM via prompting; the paper frames it theoretically as active information acquisition (max mutual-information request) but does not train this policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No (single-agent private use). Cross-agent tool discovery and sharing is listed only as future work (multi-agent orchestration / agents discovering and sharing tools).

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: (1) MCP-tools needle-in-a-haystack test (constructed by the authors: inject 1 to 2,797 tools, retrieve the target tool; 308 servers / 2,797 tools). (2) API-Bank (Li et al. 2023), level-1 subset, 48 unique tools, single-turn and multi-turn, Domain vs Full collection.
- **benchmark family**: tool (tool-retrieval / tool-calling): MCP-tools (new, MCP-domain) and API-Bank. Includes a synthetic large-scale needle-in-a-haystack stress test.
- **baselines**:
> (1) Standard tool-call schema injection (all tools injected into context). (2) Query-based retrieval ('Q.Retrieval' / 'Q.Retrieval', retrieval keyed on the raw user query). (3) MCP-Zero + ICL (one in-context example) as an enhanced variant. Related-work positioning vs RAG-MCP, Tool2Vec/ToolBank, AnyTool, ToolRerank, COLT, Re-Invoke, Gorilla (discussed but not all directly benchmarked).
- **key metrics**: Tool-selection accuracy (%) at top-1 across three LLMs (Claude-3.5-Sonnet, GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash); average token consumption per query (and % token reduction).
- **headline result**:
> 98% reduction in token consumption on APIBank while maintaining high accuracy (specifically: Full single-turn 111 vs 6308.2 tokens = -98.24%, with MCP-Zero accuracy 95.19/95.19/96.63 vs standard injection collapsing to 69.23 on Claude-3.5; needle-in-haystack accurate selection from ~3k candidates spanning 248.1k tokens).
- **ablations**:
> (1) MCP-Zero vs MCP-Zero+ICL: one in-context example improves needle-in-haystack accuracy for Claude-3.5-Sonnet and Gemini-2.5-Flash (acts as stylistic + semantic schema anchor), while GPT-4.1 shows no gain due to already-strong baseline. (2) Domain vs Full collection (40x more APIs): standard injection accuracy collapses (Claude-3.5: 97.60->69.23 single-turn, 100.00->60.22 multi-turn) while MCP-Zero holds (95.19 / 90.32), isolating robustness to attention dilution. (3) Active request vs pure Q.Retrieval: query-only retrieval stalls at 65-72%, showing the agent-authored request is the key driver. (4) Single- vs multi-turn (<=3% drop for MCP-Zero).
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Partially. Retrieval/selection accuracy (top-1 tool selection) IS the primary metric and is reported alongside token cost; a pure 'Q.Retrieval' retrieval-only number is given. No separate Recall@k / nDCG curves and no end-to-end downstream task-completion (e.g. GAIA) metric (GAIA deployment is explicitly future work), so retrieval and full task outcome are not fully decoupled.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Primarily intermediate/process metric (per-step tool-selection accuracy and token cost) rather than full end-to-end task success; multi-turn consistency is reported but final task completion is not evaluated.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Strong efficiency emphasis: 60-98% prompt-token reduction (e.g. 111 vs 6308.2 tokens, -98.24%; 159 vs 6402.2 multi-turn, -97.52%; needle-in-haystack flat ~111-159 tokens vs exponentially growing standard injection). Retrieval is O(m+k) (m servers, k tools/server) vs O(n) passive enumeration. Accuracy maintained/improved while cutting context by up to two orders of magnitude.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Adaptive/precision-driven: top-1 in main experiments (k configurable larger for fault tolerance, with dynamic adjustment when scores are clustered). Only the selected tool schema(s) are injected (progressive disclosure), keeping per-query token budget near-constant (~111-159 tokens) regardless of total pool size.
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> MCP-tools: collected from official MCP servers repo (Tag 2025.4.28, Commit ad2d4e6), 396 servers (20 reference + 114 third-party official + 262 community) filtered to 308 servers / 2,797 tools (mean 9.08, median 5.0, sigma 11.40 tools/server). Structured fields extracted with Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct few-shot (server_summary is an LLM-generated enhanced summary); embeddings precomputed with text-embedding-3-large (3072-dim) for reproducibility. First retrieval-oriented MCP dataset (vs MCPBench's availability/latency focus). Needle-in-a-haystack constructed by injecting 1-2,797 tools; answer verifiability via target-tool match. APIBank level-1 -> 48 tools used as a complementary human-annotated multi-turn reference.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Model Context Protocol (Anthropic, 2024); RAG paradigm (Lewis et al.; REALM; RETRO; In-Context RALM); ReAct observation-action-thought agent loop; tool-retrieval RAG for tool selection (Gorilla, Tool2Vec); OpenAI text-embedding-3-large; Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct for dataset construction.
- **contrasts with**:
> Passive context-based tool injection (ChatGPT function calling, HuggingGPT, ART) that injects all schemas; single-round query-based tool retrieval (RAG-MCP server-level matching, Tool2Vec/ToolBank, Re-Invoke, COLT, ToolRerank); hierarchical retrieval over RapidAPI (AnyTool). Key contrast: those keep the agent a passive selector / use 'query-once retrieve-once'; MCP-Zero makes the agent actively author requests and discover tools iteratively. Positioned as complementary to Alita (tool creation vs MCP-Zero's tool discovery).
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use): retrieval-augmented tool discovery for LLM agents. Within tool-retrieval lineage it advances from flat/query-once dense retrieval (Gorilla, RAG-MCP) and hierarchical retrieval (AnyTool category-tool-API) to agent-initiated, iterative, hierarchical (server-then-tool) coarse-to-fine on-demand retrieval keyed on model-authored requests over an MCP-native tool index.

<a id="item-metaagent"></a>
### 112. MetaAgent - Toward Self-Evolving Agent via Tool Meta-Learning

2025  ·  arXiv 2508.00271  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.00271)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **authors affiliation**: Hongjin Qian (Tommy Chien) and Zheng Liu, both at BAAI (Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence). Corresponding author: Zheng Liu. Contact emails: {chienqhj, zhengliu1026}@gmail.com.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.00271
- **code url**: https://github.com/qhjqhj00/MetaAgent (Apache-2.0 license; ~45 stars / 8 forks as of mid-2025; Python; built on LangGraph; includes search/cache infrastructure with Google Custom Search + Jina Reader + MySQL cache + Elasticsearch/BGE-m3 hybrid retrieval).
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/qhjqhj00/MetaAgent (single-method repo, last updated Sep 2025; not a continuously-updated leaderboard or paper list).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Tool-use / web / agentic information-seeking: deep knowledge discovery with LLM agents (multi-step reasoning + dynamic tool use over web search and code execution). Spans tool-use, web browsing, and QA.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent (single central reasoning agent plus a standalone tool-router agent and an auxiliary summarization model) test-time setting for deep knowledge-discovery / information-seeking tasks. The central LLM is FROZEN (no parameter updates, no post-training); adaptation happens entirely via in-context experience accumulation and a growing in-house knowledge base. Supervision is weak/optional: self-reflection runs without ground truth; verified reflection uses ground-truth answers only when available, and in the reported experiments experience is constructed online from scratch with unilateral (lagged) reflection so the summarized experience from a task is used only for SUBSEQUENT tasks to prevent leakage. The agent starts as a 'novice' (minimal workflow: autonomous reasoning + adaptive help-seeking) and self-evolves to 'expert' through meta tool learning.
- **what is retrieved**:
> Two retrieval streams: (1) distilled task EXPERIENCES / lessons (concise transferable texts capturing planning, tool-selection, and information-integration insights) injected into future task contexts; (2) raw browsed web content / tool-use history stored in a persistent in-house knowledge base, retrieved on demand. Per help request, the tool router also routes to external tools (web search results, code-execution outputs) which return external knowledge.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> HYBRID. The in-house knowledge base 𝒞 is a GROWING/episodic memory the agent writes (raw tool-use interaction history and browsed pages accumulated across episodes and tasks), retrieved via BGE-m3 hybrid search; the accumulated EXPERIENCE ℰ is likewise a growing memory injected into context. Simultaneously, live tool calls retrieve from a STATIC external corpus (the open web via Google Custom Search + Jina Reader, and code execution). So retrieval targets both the agent-written growing store and external live sources.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k retrieval for the memory/in-house tool (search_topk=10 in the repo default; BGE-m3 hybrid top-k). For the overall task objective, BrowseComp-style tasks are framed as completeness-of-constraint problems: the agent must satisfy the INTERSECTION of all task constraints (the experience lesson 'Total Constraint Compliance: never omit any clue' enforces recovering the complete minimal set of constraints), but the retrieval mechanism itself is fixed top-k rather than a learned variable-size completeness objective.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> N/A (not framed as CBR). If mapped loosely: Retrieve (retrieve experiences + memory), Reuse (inject lessons into context), Revise (self-reflection / second-attempt revision) are present; Retain (write distilled experience + raw tool history to persistent store) is present. But the work does not present a CBR case (problem-solution) abstraction; it stores distilled lessons and raw knowledge, not solution cases for analogical adaptation.
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False. MetaAgent does NOT frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner. It grounds itself in metacognitive theory (Schraw & Moshman, 1995) and 'learning-by-doing' / meta tool learning, not CBR. It realizes some CBR-adjacent mechanisms (retain-then-reuse experiences) under a different name.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Mixed granularity: (a) experience unit = a concise distilled guideline/lesson (free-text strategy or pitfall, e.g. 'Total Constraint Compliance', 'Constraint-Driven Filtering'); (b) in-house knowledge-base unit = browsed web page / raw tool-result chunk indexed for retrieval; (c) tool-call unit = web search results and code-execution outputs returned per help request. So units span guideline-rule, document/web-page, and tool-API result.
- **index source**:
> Hybrid, online/test-time-induced growing store: the in-house knowledge base 𝒞 and the experience repository ℰ are both built from scratch online from the agent's own tool-use history and reflections (the in-house tool is initialized by simulating each benchmark's tasks three times to pre-gather web content). The external web/code tools are a static live external source queried on demand. Not an offline-induced fixed corpus.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat hybrid vector+keyword index for the in-house tool: browsed web pages are embedded with BGE-m3 and stored in Elasticsearch, retrieved via hybrid search (dense embeddings + traditional keyword search). A MySQL cache stores raw search results and page contents (metadata-keyed cache). The experience store is an appended free-text context block. No dependency graph or hierarchical category->tool topology.
- **retriever type**:
> Hybrid: dense BGE-m3 embeddings + BM25/keyword search (Elasticsearch hybrid retrieval) for the in-house knowledge base; an LLM-as-router (the tool router agent Γ) maps natural-language help requests to the appropriate external tool (web search vs code executor). Web search itself uses Google Custom Search JSON API + Jina Reader. So: dense+sparse hybrid for memory, LLM-as-router for tool selection.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None (off-the-shelf). The in-house retriever uses a pretrained BGE-m3 embedding model and standard Elasticsearch hybrid scoring with no task-specific training. The tool router Γ is a fixed LLM agent that matches requests to tool descriptions 𝒟 without learned weights. No contrastive, RL, or preference-based retriever training; the 'learning' in MetaAgent is in the in-context experience/memory accumulation, not in retriever parameters.
- **query construction**:
> The central agent generates a natural-language HELP REQUEST t_i describing its unmet information need (intent expressed in NL); the tool router translates this into a concrete tool action (web search query, or code snippet). For memory/in-house-tool retrieval, the (help-request-derived) query is matched against the BGE-m3/ES index. Queries are thus thought-conditioned NL intents decomposed from the reasoning trajectory rather than raw user input.
- **query granularity**:
> Step-level: queries (help requests) are issued at intermediate reasoning steps whenever the agent reaches a knowledge gap (interleaved within the trajectory y_1,t_1,k_1,...). Experience is injected at task-level (one block prepended to the input X_t at the start of each task), so two granularities: task-level experience injection + step-level tool/memory retrieval.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Iterative / agent-initiated: the central agent decides when to retrieve by emitting help requests upon reaching its ability limitation during step-by-step reasoning (adaptive help-seeking), not on a fixed schedule. Experience injection is one-shot at task start; tool/memory retrieval is iterative and agent-triggered within the trajectory.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Agent-initiated request: retrieval is triggered when the central reasoning agent judges it has reached the limit of its own knowledge and generates a natural-language <help> request (an LLM self-assessed knowledge-gap signal). Not token-level confidence, attention/uncertainty, reflection tokens, or a separately trained complexity classifier; the trigger is the LLM's own decision to seek help.
- **reranking**:
> No explicit dedicated learned reranking stage for retrieved items is described. The tool router Γ acts as a selection/filter (chooses the best tool and returns only a distilled task-relevant subset of all retrieved knowledge), and an auxiliary model summarizes web pages, which functions as content filtering/distillation rather than a cross-encoder reranker. Elasticsearch hybrid search produces ranked top-k.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Distillation/compression: the tool router Γ processes all accessible information (e.g., the full set of retrieved web pages) but returns only a distilled, task-relevant subset k_i = Γ(𝒦_i) to the central agent (an auxiliary summarization model condenses crawled page content). The in-house tool 𝒞 additionally preserves the raw full knowledge to bridge the information gap left by this distillation, so the agent can revisit/cross-reference. Reason-in-documents-style filtering is performed by the router/summarizer.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Tools are described by a configurable, extensible tool-description set 𝒟 (raw natural-language tool descriptions) consumed by the tool router agent; an ablation ('w/ tool description') feeds these descriptions directly in-context. No synthetic-query augmentation, weighted-field embeddings, or instruction-tuned tool embeddings; tool selection is done by an LLM router over the descriptions.
- **index content separation**:
> Yes (partial). The tool router returns only a lightweight distilled subset k_i to the central agent, while the heavy raw knowledge (full browsed pages, all intermediate results) is held in the separate persistent in-house knowledge base 𝒞 and retrieved on demand — a progressive-disclosure / index-then-content separation between the distilled working context and the full backing store.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> The external tool index is a small, manually configurable/extensible set 𝒟 (two core tools: a web search tool = Google Custom Search JSON API + Jina Reader; a code executor = Python exec()), integrated via a custom HTTP API service and the LangGraph framework, not via RapidAPI/MCP/function-calling registries. The in-house knowledge base grows live (insert route adds new pages to the ES index), giving the memory store a live-synced character, but tool integration is via REST/HTTP, not a CRUD-auto-synced live tool registry or MCP.
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> N/A. Retrieval/tool-routing does not explicitly model inter-tool dependencies (no dependency graph, bipartite KG, or prerequisite modeling). The central agent composes tools sequentially via successive help requests, but inter-tool dependencies are handled implicitly through reasoning, not by a dependency-aware retriever.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation + experience reuse + memory grounding: distilled experiences ℰ are injected into the input sequence X_t={q,p,ℰ_{t-1}} to steer planning and tool-use; tool-call results k_i are appended into the reasoning trajectory; the in-house knowledge base 𝒞 grounds reasoning with global access to accumulated browsed content. All in-context, with FROZEN model parameters (no training signal, no latent-token injection).
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-plan + per-step interleaved: at task start the accumulated experience is prepended to guide planning; during execution the agent interleaves autonomous reasoning steps y_i with help requests t_i (routed to tools by Γ) and incorporates returned knowledge k_i step by step (single-central-agent unified think-and-call loop, Eq. 4/10). The minimal workflow = reason -> on limitation emit NL help request -> aggregate evidence -> answer, executed iteratively within one trajectory; self-reflection can trigger a full second attempt.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Per-tool-call / per-reasoning-step within a single rollout: reasoning and tool invocation are interleaved at the step level (y_t then optional tool result k_t), with help requests issued mid-trajectory whenever a knowledge gap arises. Reflection/experience operates at the per-task granularity.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> N/A (not a CBR method, no case adaptation). The closest analog is execution-feedback-driven revision: self-reflection (and verified reflection) prompts the agent to reconsider and launch a corrected second attempt, and distilled lessons are reused as in-context guidance — but there is no retrieved-case adaptation step; the central LLM is frozen and only its in-context experience is updated.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Surface forms injected: (a) experiences as concise free-text distilled lessons/guidelines (e.g., 'Total Constraint Compliance', 'Constraint-Driven Filtering', 'Cultural Depth in Symbolism'); (b) tool results as natural-language summaries of web pages or code-execution outputs; (c) in-house-tool hits as retrieved raw/summarized web content. So distilled strategy/guideline text plus raw/summarized document text, all as natural language.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Mixed: distilled, transferable strategies/guidelines (high abstraction — generalizable planning, tool-selection, and pitfall-avoidance principles abstracted via metacognitive reflection) for the experience stream; raw/summarized browsed documents (low abstraction — concrete evidence) for the in-house knowledge base. Not raw trajectories or executable skills/programs.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Multiple in-context safeguards: (1) self-reflection scrutinizes the validity and factual grounding of each reasoning step without ground truth and triggers reconsideration/second attempts when confidence is low; (2) verified reflection (when ground truth available) abstracts which strategies/tool choices succeeded or failed and what cognitive pitfalls emerged, distilling corrective lessons; (3) the tool router + auxiliary summarizer filter retrieved content into a distilled task-relevant subset (distractor filtering); (4) the in-house tool lets the agent cross-reference evidence to catch errors. No retriever-aware SFT or trained relevance classifier.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> Hybrid procedural + episodic, non-parametric: (1) an experience/procedural memory ℰ of distilled lessons (workflow/strategy knowledge) injected into context; (2) an episodic/document memory 𝒞 = a persistent in-house knowledge base of raw browsed content (BGE-m3 + Elasticsearch). No latent/parametric memory (model weights unchanged); a MySQL cache also persists raw tool outputs.
- **write back**:
> True. The system writes back both: (i) distilled experiences ℰ_t / ℰ_self after each task (Eq. 6/7), and (ii) raw tool-use history and all intermediate browsed knowledge into the persistent in-house knowledge base 𝒞 (Eq. 9, 𝒞 <- 𝒞 ∪ (𝒦_1 ∪...∪ 𝒦_T)). Both stores grow over tasks; model parameters are never written.
- **online growth**:
> True. Both the experience repository ℰ and the in-house knowledge base 𝒞 grow during deployment/test-time (experience is built online from scratch in the reported experiments; the knowledge base is initialized by simulating each benchmark's tasks three times and then keeps accumulating browsed content as tasks are solved). Becomes 'progressively richer and more informative' over time.
- **write back trigger**:
> Reflective (after self-critique) and on-both-success-and-failure: distilled experience is written after each task via self-reflection (no ground truth) and verified reflection (compares predicted vs ground-truth answer, analyzing BOTH successes and failures). To prevent leakage, verified reflection is performed only after the answer is finalized and the resulting experience is used exclusively for SUBSEQUENT tasks (unilateral/lagged write). Raw tool knowledge is written to 𝒞 continuously per tool execution.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success + failure: verified reflection explicitly analyzes both successes and failures, abstracting which reasoning strategies/decision frameworks contributed to success or failure, what principles governed effective tool use, and what cognitive pitfalls/errors emerged. Failures yield corrective generalizable lessons (e.g., the case study where a wrong first answer triggers a 'check all constraints' lesson and a corrected second attempt). Not success-only.
- **memory evolution update**:
> Experience store: incremental refine/append — ℰ_t = Ω(X,Y,A*,ℰ_{t-1}) updates and accumulates distilled lessons across tasks (transformed, not purely appended verbatim; distilled into concise transferable texts that are incrementally enriched). In-house knowledge base 𝒞: append-only union of accumulated raw knowledge (with MySQL/ES caching to dedup repeated queries). No explicit forgetting/pruning mechanism described.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No. Retrieval and tool-selection are NOT a trained/RL-optimized policy. The retriever is off-the-shelf BGE-m3 hybrid top-k; the tool router is a fixed LLM matching requests to descriptions; help-request emission is the central LLM's in-context decision. The adaptation is via in-context experience accumulation, explicitly without changing model parameters or post-training. Contrasts with M-MDP/soft-Q learned-retrieval works.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Single-agent private memory. The experience ℰ and in-house knowledge base 𝒞 belong to one MetaAgent instance; there is no sharing of memory/experience across multiple distinct agents or heterogeneous frameworks. (Internally there are role-separated modules — central reasoning agent, tool router agent, auxiliary summarizer — but they are part of one system, not a memory-sharing collective.)

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> GAIA (General AI Assistant; 103 questions from the text-only validation subset, 3 difficulty levels), WebWalkerQA (680 queries; Easy/Medium/Hard), BrowseComp (1,266 hard-to-find questions total; evaluated on two topics — Art and History — totaling 257 questions). Backbone: QwQ-32B (also Gemini-2.5-Flash in a separate study).
- **benchmark family**: Web / agentic-browsing + tool-use knowledge discovery: GAIA = tool-use + multi-step general-assistant agent benchmark; WebWalkerQA = web traversal; BrowseComp = long-horizon creative web browsing. All in the web/tool-use information-seeking family.
- **baselines**:
> Four categories: (1) Direct Reasoning w/o retrieval: Qwen2.5-32B, QwQ-32B, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1-671B; (2) Direct Reasoning w/ Retrieval: RAG (Qwen2.5-32B), RAG (QwQ-32B); (3) Expert-Designed Workflows: Query Planning, Iterative RAG, ReAct (Qwen2.5-32B / QwQ-32B / GPT-4o), Search-o1-32B; (4) End-to-End Trained Agents: WebThinker-32B-Base and WebThinker-32B-RL. QwQ-32B and Qwen2.5-32B are the shared backbones for most baselines.
- **key metrics**: Exact Match (EM) for GAIA and BrowseComp; LLM equivalence accuracy (LLM-judged) for WebWalkerQA. Reported per difficulty level and as averages. (No intrinsic retrieval metrics reported.)
- **headline result**:
> With the same QwQ-32B backbone, MetaAgent reaches GAIA avg 47.6 (Level 1 61.5 / Level 2 42.3 / Level 3 25.0), WebWalkerQA avg 52.1 (Easy 55.0 / Medium 49.6 / Hard 47.9), and BrowseComp avg 7.1 (Art 7.9 / History 6.4). It outperforms all workflow baselines (e.g., Search-o1-32B GAIA 39.8, WebWalkerQA 34.1, BrowseComp 1.9) and matches/exceeds the end-to-end RL-trained WebThinker-32B-RL (GAIA 48.5, WebWalkerQA 46.5, BrowseComp 2.7), best on WebWalkerQA (52.1 vs 46.5) and BrowseComp (7.1 vs 2.7) while being within ~1 point on GAIA — all without parameter updates.
- **ablations**:
> Ablation on GAIA (Figure 3) removing one component at a time: (1) w/o self reflection, (2) w/o verified reflection, (3) w/o in-house tool, (4) minimal workflow only, (5) w/ tool description (replace tool router with in-context tool descriptions). Findings: minimal workflow alone performs poorly and barely matches Search-o1; both self-reflection AND verified reflection are critical and together form the meta-tool-learning loop that substantially boosts performance; the in-house tool is essential for a global persistent view that mitigates single-pass search-and-refine information loss; replacing the router with in-context tool descriptions beats the minimal workflow but lacks the autonomous self-evolving capability. Separate study (Table 2): swapping backbone to Gemini-2.5-Flash, MetaAgent lifts GAIA from 7.8 (vanilla Gemini-2.5-Flash) to 49.5 avg, and QwQ-32B from 22.3 to 47.6, confirming backbone-agnostic gains.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No. Only end-to-end task metrics (EM / LLM-equivalence accuracy) are reported; intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k, nDCG, completeness) are not reported separately. Component contribution is probed only via the ablation study, not via intrinsic retrieval evaluation.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome metrics (final-answer EM / equivalence accuracy). Process is examined only qualitatively via a BrowseComp case study (showing the self-reflection-driven first-attempt failure then corrected second attempt) and the component ablation; no formal step-wise reasoning-faithfulness or retrieval-accuracy scoring.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k retrieval: search_topk=10 (repo default) for web and in-house cache search; max_retries=3 for re-attempts; in-house tool initialized by 3 simulation passes per benchmark. The tool router truncates/distills retrieved knowledge into a task-relevant subset before injection; distilled experience is appended as a concise text block. No explicit token-budget cap or adaptive/precision-driven k is reported.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A - this is a method/system paper, not a survey.
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A - this is a method paper, not a benchmark paper. (It uses existing benchmarks: GAIA 103 text-only validation Qs over 3 levels; WebWalkerQA 680 queries; BrowseComp 257 Qs from the Art and History topics of the full 1,266.)

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Test-time scaling / agentic reasoning (Snell et al. 2024; OpenAI deep research 2025); ReAct interleaved reasoning-acting (Yao et al. 2023); Search-o1 agentic search with Reason-in-Documents (Li et al. 2025a); WebThinker deep-research agent (Li et al. 2025b); RAG (Lewis et al. 2020); metacognitive theory / self-regulation (Schraw & Moshman 1995); BGE-m3 embeddings (Chen et al. 2023); LangGraph framework; QwQ-32B / Qwen2.5 backbones; Google Custom Search + Jina Reader tooling.
- **contrasts with**:
> Contrasts with (a) manually designed expert workflows / prompt-engineering agents (Search-o1, Query Planning, Iterative RAG, Mind-Map/Agentic Reasoning, generalist coding agent) — rigid, human-effort-heavy, poor cross-task adaptability; (b) end-to-end RL-trained agents (WebThinker, Search-R1, DeepResearcher, WebDancer) — need large annotated data, risk overfitting / distribution bias / catastrophic forgetting across tasks; (c) static single-pass RAG with fixed queries — lacks multi-step dynamic integration. MetaAgent instead self-evolves in-context from a minimal workflow without parameter updates.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use): self-evolving / experience-augmented tool-use agents. Sits in the lineage of agentic search + tool-augmented reasoning (ReAct -> Search-o1 -> WebThinker) but distinguished by 'meta tool learning' — frozen-LLM, training-free self-evolution via metacognitive self-reflection + verified reflection (dynamic context engineering) plus an autonomously built, BGE-m3-indexed in-house knowledge base and a modular NL-help-request-to-tool router, separating reasoning from tool execution.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- cost_efficiency_tradeoff
- venue

<a id="item-rag-mcp"></a>
### 113. RAG-MCP: Mitigating Prompt Bloat in LLM Tool Selection via Retrieval-Augmented Generation

2025  ·  arXiv 2505.03275  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.03275)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2505.03275, cs.AI/cs.SE); not peer-reviewed
- **authors affiliation**: Tiantian Gan and Qiyao Sun. Affiliations listed as Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications (Beijing, China) and Queen Mary University of London (London, UK); contact emails are QMUL (jp2022213034@qmul.ac.uk, jp2022213402@qmul.ac.uk).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.03275
- **code url**:
> N/A (no official code repository released by the authors; the paper relies on the publicly released MCPBench / 'Evaluation Report on MCP Servers' (arXiv:2504.11094) framework and WebSearch dataset, which it credits in the acknowledgements. Third-party GitHub repos named 'rag-mcp' are unrelated.)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: tool-use (LLM external tool / MCP-server selection and invocation), with web-search tasks as the evaluation setting.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive single-agent tool use: an LLM agent must, for a natural-language query, select and invoke the correct external tool from a large registry of Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. The core problem is 'prompt bloat' and decision overhead when the number of available tools scales to hundreds or thousands - including all tool schemas in the prompt saturates the context window with distractors and degrades selection accuracy. The setting is test-time / inference (no LLM fine-tuning); each trial allows up to 10 rounds of interaction with MCP servers. The toolset is large/open and can grow (new MCPs added by indexing). Supervision: a ground-truth MCP is defined per task for accuracy measurement, but the retriever itself is off-the-shelf (no task-specific training).
- **what is retrieved**: tools (MCP server schemas / function descriptions, including tool-use parameters, metadata, and usage examples).
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus: an external vector index built over MCP server metadata drawn from a registry of 4,400+ publicly listed MCP servers (mcp.so). The index can be extended by adding new MCP metadata, but it is not a growing/episodic memory the agent writes to during task execution.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Top-k ranking objective collapsed to top-1 in practice: the retriever returns top-k candidate MCPs but only the single best (top-1) MCP schema is injected into the LLM prompt for execution. The evaluation targets selecting the one ground-truth tool, not recovering a complete multi-tool set.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based reasoning method; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain case cycle - it retrieves static tool schemas, not problem-solution cases).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False - the work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner; it is framed purely as retrieval-augmented tool selection.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: tool-API: a single MCP server description / function schema (problem-relevant tool metadata including parameters and usage examples).
- **index source**: Static, offline-constructed retrievable store: an external vector index over MCP metadata from a registry of 4,400+ publicly listed MCP servers; extensible by indexing new MCPs without retraining, but not induced online/test-time.
- **index structure topology**: Flat vector index (semantic vector-space index of MCP descriptions). No graph/hierarchical organization in this work; authors note future work on hierarchical indexes for extreme scale.
- **retriever learning signal**: None (off-the-shelf): the retriever uses semantic similarity over embeddings of an existing LLM encoder (Qwen-max); no contrastive training, no LM-feedback, and no RL/preference learning of the retriever is described.
- **query construction**: Raw input: the user's natural-language task description is encoded (with Qwen-max) and used directly as the query for semantic search over the MCP index. No decomposition, expansion, or synthetic query reformulation is described.
- **query granularity**: Task-level (one-shot at t=0): the query is constructed once from the user's task description before LLM engagement.
- **when to retrieve**: One-shot: a single retrieval step is performed before engaging the LLM for execution (tool discovery is decoupled from generation and done up front).
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule: retrieval is always invoked once per query at the start of the pipeline (before the LLM), not gated by any confidence/uncertainty/reflection signal.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Selection/truncation plus optional validation: from the top-k retrieved MCPs, only the single best MCP schema is injected (focused context filtering); the optional validation step (synthetic few-shot test of each candidate) acts as a basic compatibility check. No reason-in-documents distillation or compression beyond top-1 selection.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Protocol: Model Context Protocol (MCP) - tools are MCP server schemas invoked via the function-calling interface. The index is a static external vector store extensible by manually indexing new MCP metadata; no live CRUD auto-synchronization with the MCP registry is described (index updates are manual, not automatic live sync).
- **tool dependency awareness**: No: retrieval treats each MCP independently and selects a single tool; inter-tool dependencies, shared auth, prerequisites, or dependency graphs are not modeled. Multi-tool workflows are listed as future work.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**: Prompt augmentation: only the selected (top-1) MCP's schema and tool-use parameters are injected into the LLM prompt / function-calling API, which then plans and executes the task without needing to discover tools.
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-plan (tool discovery decoupled from generation): a single up-front retrieval narrows the toolset, then the LLM performs planning and execution (up to 10 interaction rounds with the chosen MCP) using only the selected tool. Retrieval is not interleaved per step nor embedded in a tree search.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer / per-task: retrieval happens once before the reasoning/execution phase; it is not woven per-CoT-step or per-tool-call within the rollout.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (no CBR case adaptation; the retrieved tool schema is used as-is for function calling).
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw tool schema / metadata: the injected surface form is the MCP function description, parameters, and usage examples (structured tool documentation), not a distilled strategy, free-text workflow, or latent token.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Procedural tool / API specification (a single concrete tool schema). It is an actionable tool description rather than a raw trajectory, distilled strategy, or hint.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Focused context filtering (inject only the single most relevant MCP, avoiding distractor tool descriptions) plus an optional pre-invocation Validation step (synthetic few-shot test of retrieved candidates). No retriever-aware training or distractor-aware SFT; robustness comes from reducing the candidate set rather than training-time defenses.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (static external tool index; no episodic/skill/workflow memory written by the agent). The MCP index is a static, extensible knowledge store rather than a learned memory.
- **write back**: False - the system does not store new experiences/cases/skills from task execution. New MCPs can be added to the index by manual indexing of their metadata, but this is index maintenance, not agent write-back of trajectories or outcomes.
- **online growth**: No automatic online growth from deployment experience. The store is extensible (new MCP metadata can be indexed without retraining), but it does not grow from the agent's own task interactions at test time.
- **write back trigger**: Never (no experience/case write-back occurs during deployment). Index updates, when they happen, are external/manual additions of new MCP metadata, not triggered by task success or failure.
- **failure experience usage**: None: failed or negative experiences are not stored or retrieved. The framework does not maintain success vs failure cases; it only diagnoses failure via the stress test analysis (no corrective memory).
- **memory evolution update**: Append-only at the index level (new MCP metadata can be added); stored entries are not mutated, merged, refined, or pruned by the system. No experience-driven evolution.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No: retrieval is a fixed similarity-based top-k (top-1) semantic selection, not a learned/RL-optimized policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No: single-agent setting with a private/shared static tool index; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing is described.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> (1) MCP stress test on WebSearch tasks - a custom Needle-in-a-Haystack-style test varying the candidate MCP pool size N from 1 to 11100 (across 26 intervals), with one ground-truth MCP and N-1 distractors drawn from a registry of 4,400+ MCP servers (mcp.so), using 20 web-search tasks. (2) The web-search subset of MCPBench (from 'Evaluation Report on MCP Servers', arXiv:2504.11094) used as a held-out testbed, with 20 independent trials per baseline (success = >10/20 correct).
- **benchmark family**: tool (MCP tool selection/invocation; MCPBench web-search subset) plus a custom long-context-style 'MCP stress test' inspired by Needle-in-a-Haystack (NIAH).
- **baselines**:
> Three selection strategies compared: (1) Blank Conditioning ('Blank') - prompt the LLM with all N MCP descriptions at once; (2) Actual Match - keyword pre-filtering of the candidate pool on task description/MCP metadata, then prompt on the reduced set; (3) RAG-MCP (the proposed method) - vector-index semantic retriever injecting only the top candidate's schema.
- **headline result**:
> On the MCPBench web-search subset, RAG-MCP achieves 43.13% accuracy vs 13.62% for Blank Conditioning (more than triple) and 18.20% for Actual Match, while cutting average prompt tokens to 1084.00 vs 2133.84 for Blank (a >50% / roughly half reduction). Completion tokens: RAG-MCP 78.14 vs Blank 162.25 vs Actual Match 23.60.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Partial: selection Accuracy (an intrinsic tool-selection metric, fraction of trials choosing the ground-truth MCP) is reported alongside token-usage and task success. There is no separate Recall@k / nDCG / completeness reporting decoupled from end-to-end success; accuracy doubles as both selection correctness and the primary outcome.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Primarily outcome-oriented (selection accuracy and task success), with token-usage efficiency reported. The stress test adds a coarse process view (per-trial success across MCP positions / pool sizes), but no reasoning-faithfulness or step-wise process scoring.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Reranked-then-truncated to top-1: the retriever returns top-k candidates but only the single best MCP schema is injected into the prompt, capping injected-tool context to one tool description (k effectively = 1 at injection). No explicit token budget cap beyond this top-1 selection.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (this is a method paper, not a survey/taxonomy).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Lewis et al., 2020) as the core retrieve-then-generate principle; Anthropic's Model Context Protocol (MCP, 2024) as the tool-integration standard; Gorilla (Patil et al., 2024) which retrieves API documentation to improve API-call generation; the RAG survey (Gao et al., 2023). Evaluation builds directly on MCPBench / 'Evaluation Report on MCP Servers' (Luo et al., 2025, arXiv:2504.11094) code framework and WebSearch dataset. Stress test inspired by the Needle-in-a-Haystack (NIAH) test.
- **contrasts with**:
> Naive all-tools prompting / conventional MCP clients (e.g., Claude or early GPT-4 integrations) that instantiate and present all registered tools at once ('Blank Conditioning'); keyword-based pre-filtering ('Actual Match'); prompt-based tool-use methods such as ReAct and model-tuning methods such as Toolformer and WebGPT that do not address tool-discovery at scale.
- **lineage**: Group E (tool-use). Part of the tool/MCP-retrieval lineage that treats large-scale tool discovery as a retrieval subproblem (descending from Gorilla-style API-doc retrieval and classic RAG), applying it to the emerging MCP ecosystem to mitigate prompt bloat as tool counts scale.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- ablations
- benchmark_construction_and_size
- cost_efficiency_tradeoff
- index_content_separation
- key_metrics
- reranking
- retriever_type
- tool_document_engineering

<a id="item-seer"></a>
### 114. SEER: Self-Guided Function Calling in Large Language Models via Stepwise Experience Recall

2025  ·  EMNLP 2025 Findings  ·  [paper](https://aclanthology.org/2025.findings-emnlp.574.pdf)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**: EMNLP 2025 Findings (Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2025, pages 10846-10849; DBLP key conf/emnlp/CuiHXZWZWX25). Preprint arXiv:2508.15214 (submitted 21 Aug 2025).
- **authors affiliation**:
> Sijia Cui, Aiyao He, Shuai Xu, Hongming Zhang, Yanna Wang (corresponding), Qingyang Zhang, Yajing Wang, Bo Xu (corresponding). Affiliations: (1) The Key Laboratory of Cognition and Decision Intelligence for Complex Systems, Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CASIA); (2) School of Artificial Intelligence, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences (UCAS); (3) Nanjing University of Information Science & Technology; (4) Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences. Correspondence: wangyanna2013@ia.ac.cn, boxu@ia.ac.cn.
- **paper url**: https://aclanthology.org/2025.findings-emnlp.574.pdf
- **code url**: https://github.com/AI-Research-TeamX/SEER
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (the GitHub repo is the static official implementation, last commit Sep 28 2025; no continuously-updated leaderboard/paper-list).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> tool-use / function calling (multi-step and multi-turn). Specifically tool-augmented LLM agents performing multi-step function calling for tool-augmented QA (ToolQA, 8 real-world domains) and multi-turn real-world agentic tasks (tau-bench airline & retail). Falls under tool-use and decision-making.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent, training-free (no parameter updates) experience-replay setting. An LLM-based agent must achieve a user-defined goal g by interacting with a user and a set of external tools over a finite horizon of T steps, building an interaction history H_t = {o_0, a_0, ..., o_t} where observations come from both user input/feedback and tool outputs and actions are natural-language responses or tool invocations. SEER is a self-guided in-context-learning method: it retrieves prior successful trajectories from a continually-updated experience pool to guide the next decision, and accumulates new successful trajectories online during deployment. Supervision: no fine-tuning; for tasks without explicit success signals it uses an LLM-as-a-judge evaluator to decide whether a finished trajectory should be retained. Settings span one-turn multi-step QA (ToolQA) and dynamic multi-turn user-agent interaction (tau-bench, with a GPT-4o user simulator).
- **what is retrieved**:
> experiences / trajectories: past SUCCESSFUL multi-step tool-use trajectories stored in an online experience pool, retrieved as in-context fewshot exemplars to guide the LLM's next action. Each retrievable item is a complete trajectory together with a structured experience representation (trajectory embedding, first-query embedding, inferred user intent, and tool-invocation path).
- **retrieval grounding**:
> GROWING / episodic memory the agent writes itself. The experience pool is incrementally and online-augmented with the agent's own past successful trajectories during deployment (seeded with a small initial demonstration pool: 8 examples for ToolQA, 2 for tau-bench). It is not a static external corpus and not a manually curated library; it is a self-generated, continually-expanding experience store. Maximum pool size capped at 1000.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k ranking objective: SEER retrieves a fixed number k of highest-scoring trajectories (default k=4) ranked by a weighted multi-dimensional relevance score. No minimal-set-completeness objective and no precision-driven variable-size recommendation; k is a tuned hyperparameter (ablated over k in {0,2,4,6,8}, best at k=4).
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve: yes (stepwise multi-dimensional recall of successful trajectories), Reuse: yes (trajectories injected verbatim as fewshot exemplars), Revise: no (retrieved cases are not adapted/edited; the optional Reflection add-on only self-corrects the agent's own reasoning, not the cases), Retain: yes (LLM-judge gated online write-back of successful trajectories to the experience pool)].
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False. The paper frames itself as experience replay / self-guided in-context learning and self-improvement; it does NOT cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner and does not use the term 'case-based reasoning'. It realizes CBR-like Retrieve/Reuse/Retain mechanisms under an experience-recall / experience-replay framing (citing ExpeL and LLM-as-a-judge).

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> full trajectory: a complete successful multi-step tool-use trajectory tau = {o_0, a_0, o_1, a_1, ...} retrieved as a fewshot exemplar. The trajectory is described by a structured experience tuple d^tau = <E^tau, E^q, I^tau, U^tau> = (trajectory embedding, first-query/first-observation embedding, inferred discrete user intent, and the directed tool-invocation path u_1 -> u_2 -> ... -> u_n). So retrieval is at the granularity of a whole task trajectory, scored using both trajectory-level and tool-chain-level signals.
- **index source**:
> Growing memory, online/test-time-induced. The retrievable store is built incrementally during deployment from the agent's self-collected successful trajectories (continual experience accumulation), seeded by a small initial demonstration pool. Not an offline-frozen index: the pool expands online as new tasks are completed (capped at 1000 entries). Contrasts explicitly with prior static, pre-collected/offline datasets.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat vector index augmented with metadata/context keys. Each entry stores a dense trajectory embedding (and a separate first-query embedding) plus structured metadata: an inferred discrete user-intent label and the tool-invocation set/path U. Scoring combines flat cosine similarity over embeddings with metadata-keyed signals (tool-set overlap, intent equality). No explicit dependency/knowledge graph or hierarchical category->tool topology; the tool-chain is represented as a directed path within each entry but the pool itself is a flat metadata-keyed store.
- **retriever type**:
> Dense (embedding-based) retriever combined with rule/metadata scoring. Trajectory and query embeddings produced by the off-the-shelf bge-large-en-v1.5 embedding model; cosine similarity (s1) is combined with a lexical/set-overlap tool-chain coverage score (s2) and an indicator intent-match score (s3) into a single weighted relevance score. Effectively a hybrid of dense similarity + symbolic metadata matching; not BM25, not learned/generative.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> none (off-the-shelf): the retriever uses a frozen pretrained bge-large-en-v1.5 embedder and a hand-designed weighted scoring function Score = sum_i lambda_i s_i with fixed equal weights lambda_1=lambda_2=lambda_3=1/3. There is no contrastive training, LM-feedback, downstream-task or preference (Bradley-Terry) optimization, no RL/value-based learning of the retriever. The retrieval components (similarity, toolchain coverage, intent match) are selection heuristics; only the experience pool content changes online (via the LLM-judge retain decision), not the retriever parameters. The Limitations section notes the fixed weighting could be made task-aware/learned in future work.
- **query construction**:
> The query is the current interaction history H_t. SEER extracts from H_t the same structured representation used for stored items: a trajectory embedding E^{H_t} (the running interaction history), the first-query/observation embedding E^q, the inferred user intent I^{H_t} (classified by the LLM itself from the initial query against a predefined discrete intent set), and the observed tool-invocation set U^{H_t}. These are matched against each candidate experience tuple. Intent is inferred via an LLM-based intent recognizer (Appendix A.1) rather than manual annotation. A query-based ablation variant instead keys only on the first-query embedding E^q.
- **query granularity**:
> step/state-level (stepwise). Retrieval is performed from the CURRENT interaction history H_t at the agent's decision points (hence 'Stepwise Experience Recall'), conditioning on the evolving history rather than only the initial query. (Note: on ToolQA, a one-turn multi-step benchmark, the user query does not change across turns, so trajectory-level and query-only representations are less divergent; the stepwise advantage is more pronounced on tau-bench multi-turn tasks.)
- **when to retrieve**:
> iterative / stepwise: SEER performs experience recall to guide the LLM's next decision based on the current interaction history, recalling top-k examples (D_recall) at decision steps rather than only once at t=0. It is a fixed (schedule-based) stepwise recall, not uncertainty-triggered or a learned router.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> fixed schedule: stepwise recall is triggered unconditionally at decision steps, computing the multi-dimensional relevance score over the experience pool and inserting the top-k trajectories. There is no token-confidence, attention/uncertainty, learned-complexity-classifier, reflection-token, or agent-initiated trigger; retrieval is invoked on the standard schedule of the agent loop.
- **reranking**:
> None (single-stage). Candidate trajectories are scored once by the weighted multi-dimensional relevance score (trajectory similarity + toolchain coverage + intent match), sorted in descending order, and the top-k are taken directly. No second-stage cross-encoder, RRF, or instruction-tuned reranker.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> None beyond ranking/truncation: the top-k retrieved successful trajectories are injected as fewshot exemplars without compression, decomposition, distillation, or distractor filtering. (A SEER+Reflection variant adds Reflexion-style error identification/correction at inference to mitigate cumbersome/suboptimal examples that caused overthinking on simple tasks, e.g. Coffee-Easy, but this is reflection on the agent's own reasoning, not refinement of the retrieved context itself.)
- **tool document engineering**:
> N/A. SEER does not retrieve or engineer tool/skill DESCRIPTIONS; the retrievable items are past task trajectories, not tool docstrings. Tools are provided by the benchmarks (ToolQA tool set spanning SQL/DB, Python, math, text retrieval, graph; tau-bench airline 13 tools / retail 15 tools).
- **index content separation**: N/A. No separation of a lightweight retrievable index from heavy on-demand content; the structured experience tuple (embeddings + intent + tool path) is used both to score and to fetch the full trajectory, which is loaded wholesale as a fewshot exemplar.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> N/A as a tool index (SEER's growing store holds trajectories, not tools). However the EXPERIENCE pool itself is dynamic/live-synchronized: it is updated online via an insert operation after each successfully-judged task (Algorithm 2). Tool integration is via standard function-calling / tool wrappers (SQL, Python, Math, Text, Graph, Table) in ToolQA and the tau-bench tool APIs; no RapidAPI/MCP/RESTful tool-store sync.
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> Partial / implicit via toolchain coverage. SEER represents each trajectory's tool usage as a directed invocation path U = u_1 -> u_2 -> ... -> u_n and scores candidates by toolchain coverage s2 = |U^{H_t} intersect U^{tau'}| / |U^{H_t}|, rewarding overlap in tools used. The ablation shows s2 is most important on HARD questions, where the model must navigate intricate dependencies among multiple tools. However coverage is a set-overlap proportion, not an explicit inter-tool dependency graph, shared-auth model, or dependency-aware reranker; ordering/dependency edges are stored in the path but not separately scored.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> prompt augmentation: the top-k retrieved successful trajectories (D_recall) are inserted as in-context fewshot demonstrations into the LLM prompt to guide the agent's next decision (tool selection, parameter generation, tool-chain planning). No fine-tuning, no latent-token injection; pure in-context learning over a frozen LLM (Qwen2.5-7B / Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct).
- **planning integration**:
> per-step interleaved / retrieve-then-act stepwise. SEER weaves recall into the agent's decision loop: at decision points it recalls top-k trajectories from the experience pool conditioned on the current interaction history and uses them as exemplars to guide the next action; the agent then acts, observes, and continues. No MCTS/tree search and no explicit hierarchical subtask decomposition; planning is the LLM's in-context multi-step tool-use guided by recalled exemplars. On one-turn ToolQA this is effectively task-conditioned exemplar guidance; on multi-turn tau-bench it interleaves with evolving user intent.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> Verbatim ICL exemplar reuse: retrieved successful trajectories are injected as-is as fewshot demonstrations; the LLM implicitly adapts them to the current task during generation. No explicit case-rewriting, critic-guided revision, or RL reuse-finetuning at solve time. The optional SEER+Reflection variant adds execution-feedback-style self-correction (Reflexion) to the agent's reasoning, a light adaptation layer, but retrieved cases themselves are not edited.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> raw trajectory: the surface form injected into the prompt is the raw successful interaction trajectory (sequence of observations and actions / tool calls) used as a fewshot exemplar. The structured tuple (embeddings, intent label, tool path) is used internally for scoring, not injected as the demonstration content.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> raw trajectory (single concrete demonstration). SEER recalls concrete past successful trajectories rather than distilled strategies, state-aware guidelines, reusable workflows, or procedural skills; abstraction is left to the LLM's in-context generalization. (This contrasts with ExpeL, which additionally distills cross-task natural-language insights.)
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Multi-dimensional relevance scoring + LLM-judge gating on writes. (1) Quality of retrieved context is controlled by retaining only SUCCESSFUL trajectories (LLM-as-a-judge verifies task completion before a trajectory enters the pool), so noisy/failed experiences are filtered out at write time; (2) the three-component score (trajectory similarity, toolchain coverage, intent match) reduces retrieval of irrelevant exemplars; (3) a moderate k (best at 4) avoids overwhelming the model with excessive/distracting demonstrations (performance declines for k>4); (4) the optional SEER+Reflection identifies and corrects errors induced by suboptimal/cumbersome exemplars. No retriever-aware adversarial training or explicit distractor-aware SFT.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: episodic: an experience pool of past successful task trajectories (a continually-growing trajectory replay memory). Not a distilled skill-library, workflow store, knowledge graph, or latent memory.
- **write back**:
> Yes. After completing a task, SEER forms an experience tuple (tau, d^tau) and inserts the trajectory into the experience pool D <- D union {(tau,d)} if the trajectory is judged successful (continual experience accumulation, Algorithm 2). This is the central self-guided self-improvement mechanism.
- **online growth**:
> Yes. The experience pool grows online during deployment/test-time: successful trajectories are incrementally added so the pool 'continuously expands' and model performance improves over time. Explicitly contrasted with prior methods that rely on static, offline, pre-collected datasets. Pool size is capped at 1000 entries.
- **write back trigger**:
> on-success only, judged reflectively by an LLM evaluator. After a task finishes, an LLM-as-a-judge evaluator compares the agent's output to a reference answer and returns a binary success/failure judgment; only trajectories judged successful are written to the pool. The evaluator is designed to tolerate minor discrepancies (formatting variations, slight numerical differences) and still count them as success. No failures are written; writes are gated by the success judgment rather than a fixed every-task schedule.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success-only. Only successful trajectories are stored and retrieved; failed/negative trajectories are discarded (not retained, not used as contrastive or corrective examples). The LLM evaluator's role is to keep failures OUT of the pool. (The optional Reflection add-on uses within-episode error signals to self-correct, but failed trajectories are not persisted as negative memory.)
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No. Case/trajectory selection is a fixed weighted top-k heuristic (Score = 1/3 s1 + 1/3 s2 + 1/3 s3 over an off-the-shelf embedder plus metadata signals). It is not an RL/value-optimized or learned retrieval policy (no M-MDP, soft Q-learning, or learned router). What evolves online is the pool CONTENT (via LLM-judged retain decisions), not the selection policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> No. Single-agent private memory: one SEER agent maintains and reads its own experience pool. No sharing of memory/experience across multiple agents or heterogeneous agent frameworks. (A GPT-4o user simulator participates in tau-bench but is the environment/user, not a memory-sharing agent.)

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> ToolQA (Zhuang et al. 2023): 8 real-world domains (air transportation/Flight, financial/Coffee, commercial services/Yelp, lodging/Airbnb, social networks/DBLP graph, academic publications/SciREX, personal agendas/Agenda, numerical reasoning/GSM8K); easy set = 800 questions / 55 templates, hard set = 730 questions / 62 templates. tau-bench (Yao et al. 2025): multi-turn tool-agent-user interaction in two real-world domains, airline (50 tasks, 13 tools) and retail (115 tasks, 15 tools), 165 tasks total, with a GPT-4o user simulator.
- **benchmark family**: tool (ToolQA, tau-bench). ToolQA is a multi-step tool-augmented QA benchmark spanning structured DBs, graph DB, and text corpora; tau-bench is a multi-turn tool-agent-user interaction benchmark. (Both are tool-use benchmarks; ToolQA also has a QA flavor.)
- **baselines**:
> On ToolQA (foundation LLM Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct for all): Chameleon (Lu et al. 2023), CoT, ReAct (Yao et al. 2023), TUMS (He et al. 2025), ART (Paranjape et al. 2023), and ExpeL (Zhao et al. 2024) [ExpeL is the strongest/second-best overall]; full table also lists Direct and CoT-noTool. On tau-bench, reference models: closed-source Claude 3.5 Sonnet (claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022), GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-11-20), GPT-4o-mini (gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18); open-source DeepSeek-V3-0324, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct; SEER is compared against the base Qwen2.5-7B/72B (SEER-enhanced vs original).
- **key metrics**:
> ToolQA: Accuracy (%) per domain and average accuracy Acc^avg across domains (separate easy/hard averages). tau-bench: pass^k (probability an agent succeeds in all k independent dialogue trials); pass^1 reported by default (single-shot success rate / average reward across tasks). NOTE: in tau-bench, k denotes number of trials, whereas elsewhere in the paper k denotes number of demonstrations.
- **headline result**:
> On ToolQA, SEER (Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct) achieves the best average accuracy across all tasks, outperforming the second-best baseline ExpeL by +6.1% on easy (67.9 vs 61.8 avg) and +4.7% on hard (31.1 vs 26.4 avg). On tau-bench, integrating SEER yields gains of +7.44% for Qwen2.5-7B (9.34 -> 16.78 avg) and +23.38% for Qwen2.5-72B (28.46 -> 51.84 avg); SEER(72B) at 51.84% approaches GPT-4o at 54.76%.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Retrieval-strategy ablation (Fig.3): removing any of the three scoring components degrades performance vs full SEER. SEER(w/o s3 intent-match) drops most on EASY questions (intent alignment helps straightforward tasks); SEER(w/o s2 toolchain-coverage) drops most on HARD questions (toolchain coverage is crucial for complex multi-tool dependencies); SEER(query-based) (using only first-query similarity instead of full-trajectory similarity) drops only modestly, since ToolQA is a one-turn multi-step setting where the query is fixed across turns. (2) Demonstration number / top-k (Table 5, k in {0,2,4,6,8}): accuracy rises then falls, peaking at k=4 (SEER easy avg 67.88%, hard avg 31.51%); query-based SEER peaks at k=4 easy / k=6 hard. (3) Self-improvement (Fig.2): on 1,530 ToolQA questions shuffled into 10 batches of 153, batch accuracy rises from 37.7% (batch 1) to surpassing baselines by batch 5 (52.3%) and reaching 54.9% by the last batch (3-point moving average smoothed). (4) SEER+Reflection (Table 6): raises ToolQA to 69.0% easy / 32.0% hard, recovering the Coffee-Easy drop caused by cumbersome exemplars.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No. Only end-to-end task metrics are reported (ToolQA accuracy, tau-bench pass^1). No intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG / retrieval completeness) are reported separately; retrieval quality is assessed only indirectly via component-ablation effects on task accuracy.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome (final task accuracy / pass^1 success rate). The self-improvement experiment adds a process-over-time view (per-batch accuracy trajectory showing online learning), and ablations attribute outcome to specific scoring components, but there is no formal step-wise reasoning-faithfulness, retrieval-precision, or trajectory-quality metric.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Framed qualitatively as a training-free / annotation-light efficiency win: SEER requires NO additional model training (vs RL methods StepTool/SWiRL) and NO manually curated/pre-collected demonstration libraries (vs ART/ExpeL reliance), reducing offline expert effort. Efficiency-vs-accuracy is managed via the top-k sweep (best at k=4; too many demonstrations overwhelm the model and reduce accuracy) and a capped pool size (1000). No explicit token-count, latency, dollar-cost, or rollout-count figures are reported.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k, budget-managed by demonstration count. Default top-k = 4 retrieved exemplars (ablated 0-8; performance peaks at k=4 and declines beyond, indicating an implicit context budget where excess demonstrations cause confusion). Initial demonstration pool: 8 examples for ToolQA, 2 for tau-bench; experience pool capped at 1000. Max interaction steps T = 6 (ToolQA) and T = 30 (tau-bench). Scoring weights lambda_1=lambda_2=lambda_3=1/3. Selection is fixed-k retrieved-then-used (no adaptive/precision-driven k).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A (uses existing benchmarks). For reference: ToolQA easy 800 questions / 55 templates, hard 730 / 62 templates across 8 domains (structured DBs, graph DB, text corpora); tau-bench airline 50 tasks / 13 tools, retail 115 tasks / 15 tools (165 total), multi-turn with a GPT-4o user simulator. The repo includes dataset-generation notebooks to regenerate ToolQA easy/hard variants.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> ExpeL (Zhao et al. 2024, experience-pool / experiential-learning problem formulation that SEER explicitly builds its formulation upon and is the strongest baseline); ART (Paranjape et al. 2023, retrieval of similar multi-step reasoning/tool traces); ReAct (Yao et al. 2023, think-act-observe tool-use loop); in-context learning (Brown et al. 2020); LLM-as-a-judge (Li et al. 2024, used as the success evaluator for write-back); bge-large-en-v1.5 / C-Pack embeddings (Xiao et al. 2024); Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023, basis for the optional SEER+Reflection variant). Backbone LLMs: Qwen2.5-7B/72B-Instruct (Qwen et al. 2025).
- **contrasts with**:
> Coarse-grained / task-similarity-only retrieval methods (ART, ExpeL) that overlook tool-chain alignment - SEER adds fine-grained stepwise scoring (toolchain coverage + intent match); methods relying on manually curated or pre-collected task-specific demonstration libraries (Zhao et al. 2024; Xu et al. 2024) - SEER self-accumulates experiences online; RL-based tool-learning that needs additional training (StepTool, Yu et al. 2024; SWiRL, Goldie et al. 2025) - SEER is training-free experience replay; self-improvement methods using static offline datasets (ExpeL, Tian et al. 2024 MCTS) - SEER updates its pool online during deployment.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use). An experience/case-based, training-free tool-use agent in the lineage ReAct -> ART/ExpeL -> SEER: it advances experience-replay tool-use by (i) fine-grained stepwise retrieval scoring trajectory similarity + toolchain coverage + intent alignment, and (ii) online (test-time) growth of a self-judged experience pool, distinguishing it from static/offline experiential-learning predecessors and from RL-trained tool-learning.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- memory_evolution_update
- reasoning_search_interleaving_granularity

<a id="item-smith"></a>
### 115. SMITH (Shared Memory Integrated Tool Hub)

2025  ·  arXiv:2512.11303 (2025-12, verified)  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.11303)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **authors affiliation**: Jiarun Liu, Shiyue Xu, Yang Li, Shangkun Liu, Yongli Yu, Peng Cao (Caopeng). Affiliation: JD.com (author emails are @jd.com, e.g. liujiarun.1@jd.com).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.11303
- **code url**: N/A (no official code repository disclosed in the paper or found via search; the paper references manually-crafted tools and prompts only in appendices)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: tool-use / agent (dynamic tool creation) combined with general AI assistant task-solving requiring reasoning, multi-modality handling, web search, code execution, and tool-use, evaluated on the GAIA benchmark.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-task-at-inference but cross-task-accumulating setting. A multi-agent workflow (planner + developer-tester inner loop) solves GAIA tasks by iteratively writing/testing code in a Python sandbox (tool creation) and by retrieving prior successful execution experiences (experience sharing). It is training-free / cold-start (no parameter fine-tuning); memory grows online across tasks. The system addresses two coupled bottlenecks: limited predefined tool coverage and lack of systematic experience reuse. Multiple specialized sub-agents each keep their own episodic memory repository, so experience is shared across tasks and across the planner/developer roles (cross-agent within the workflow).
- **what is retrieved**: experiences (episodic trajectories of past successful tasks), agent-created tools/code (developer code memories), planner sub-plans/sub-intentions, and human-crafted tool demonstrations / few-shot style demonstrations (semantic memory).
- **retrieval grounding**:
> HYBRID: semantic memory is a (relatively static) externally-provided store of human-crafted tools and transfer-learning demonstrations, while episodic memory is a GROWING store the agents write online from their own successful executions; retrieval queries both stores with the same similarity scoring.
- **completeness vs topk objective**: Fixed top-k retrieval. The system retrieves a fixed number of items per store (semantic limit 3; episodic limit 4 for planner, 6 for developer); no explicit completeness/minimal-set objective is formulated.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: Implicitly Retrieve + Reuse (and Retain via success-gated write-back); Revise is partial via the developer-tester debug-and-refine loop on freshly generated code rather than adaptation of a retrieved case. Approx: [Retrieve: yes, Reuse: yes, Revise: partial, Retain: yes].
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The paper frames itself via cognitive architectures for language agents (Sumers et al. 2023) and episodic/semantic/procedural memory, not as case-based reasoning; it does not cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> For the developer: code memories (tool creation episodes / executable code blocks summarized before embedding). For the planner: sub-plan / sub-intention decompositions (planning trajectory chunks segmented via markdown headers). More broadly each episodic unit is a full task-solving trajectory e={task, (s0,a0)...(s_done,a_done)}; semantic memory units are human-crafted tool examples and style demonstrations.
- **index source**: Hybrid construction: semantic memory is offline/human-induced (manually crafted tools + curated WebShaper transfer samples for cold-start); episodic memory is online/test-time-induced, grown from the agent's own successful task executions during curriculum progression.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat dense+sparse vector indices, maintained as agent-specific repositories (one per sub-agent: planner repository and developer repository). Within episodic memory, t-SNE analysis shows emergent thematic clusters (e.g., search/fetch utilities, file I/O, browser automation, multimodal) but clustering is observed/analytical, not an explicit indexing topology.
- **retriever type**: Hybrid dense-sparse retrieval: dense embeddings via text-embedding-3-large plus sparse representations via Splade_PP_en_v2, combined with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF).
- **retriever learning signal**:
> none (off-the-shelf). Retrieval uses pretrained embedding models (text-embedding-3-large, Splade_PP_en_v2) with RRF fusion; the retriever itself is not trained or RL-optimized. The only 'learning signal' on the retrievable store is which trajectories succeed (success-gated write-back), not retriever parameter training.
- **query construction**:
> The query is formed by the abstraction function Phi applied to the current task and state: Phi({tau, (s_t, .)}). Action-space-specific: code-writing actions are summarized (to reduce implementation noise) before embedding; planning agents perform intention decomposition and augmentation on proposed plans before embedding. Effectively an intent/summary-conditioned query.
- **query granularity**:
> Both task-level and step/state-level: retrieval is conditioned on current task tau and current state s_t (Eq. 5-6, 8), and it is performed within the planner loop and the developer inner loop, so queries are constructed at the sub-plan / code-generation step level rather than only once at t=0.
- **when to retrieve**: iterative: retrieval is interleaved with execution: the planner retrieves at sub-plan steps and the developer retrieves within its iterative code-generation/debugging inner loop, each conditioned on the evolving state s_t.
- **reranking**: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) over dense and sparse retrieval result lists to select the final top-k candidates. No cross-encoder or hierarchy-aware reranker is used.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Pre-storage processing (abstraction/summarization of code memories and intention decomposition/augmentation of plans) plus RRF fusion; at use time, retrieved fragments are concatenated into the prompt. Markdown-header segmentation keeps chunks manageable; no explicit distractor-filtering or reason-in-documents distillation stage at retrieval time.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Human-crafted tools follow a standardized structure: a clear title/function description, a descriptive usage-scenario paragraph, and a minimalist commented Python implementation (Fig. 12 style demonstration). Agent-created code memories undergo LLM summarization before embedding to reduce implementation noise. No synthetic-query augmentation or instruction-tuned tool embeddings.
- **index content separation**:
> Partial: code memories are summarized into lightweight descriptions for indexing while the underlying implementation is the heavier content; the developer retrieves based on function description and recalls concise task-specific snippets (avoiding lengthy irrelevant code). Not a formal progressive-disclosure/index-then-content protocol.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Dynamic/live-growing tool store: the tool repository evolves online (T <- T U {T}). SMITH autonomously installs Python packages (e.g., pdfplumber, serpapi, scholarly, whisper, faster_whisper) at runtime and autonomously leverages Model Context Protocol (MCP) via fastmcp without pre-configured semantic memory. Tools are created as Python code in a sandbox (function-calling / code-execution) rather than via a fixed RapidAPI/RESTful registry; no formal CRUD auto-sync protocol.
- **tool dependency awareness**: Not explicitly modeled. Retrieval is similarity-based over individual code/tool memories; no inter-tool dependency graph, shared-auth modeling, or dependency-aware reranking is described. Tool composition is left to the agent's iterative code generation.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
