> prompt augmentation + skill/tool reuse: retrieved memories m_t are concatenated with task and state (tau (+) s_t (+) m_t) and conditioned on procedural memory, so the policy samples actions a_t ~ pi(tau (+) s_t (+) m_t | M_proc). Concretely, retrieved code memories provide reusable tool implementations for the developer and retrieved sub-plans guide the planner.
- **planning integration**:
> Per-step interleaved within a nested two-loop workflow: an outer planner loop performs task decomposition / sub-intent generation, and an inner developer-tester loop performs iterative code generation and debugging in a sandbox; retrieval feeds both loops. Retrieve-then-act at each step (planner retrieves plans, developer retrieves code). Augmented with 3-path sampling and LLM-as-a-judge consensus over the full rollout.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: per-tool-call / per-step within a rollout: retrieval and tool (code) creation occur per sub-plan (planner) and per code-generation step (developer inner loop), rather than per-token or only per final answer.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> execution-feedback-driven revision (for freshly generated code) plus verbatim/LLM-prompted reuse of retrieved code and plans: retrieved memories are injected as in-context guidance; the developer-tester inner loop revises code via sandbox error feedback until success. Not RL-reuse-finetuning and not critic-only adaptation of a retrieved case.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Surface form injected: for the developer, summarized executable code / tool snippets (program-or-skill); for the planner, free-text sub-plan/intention decompositions; plus human-crafted tool examples and style demonstrations from semantic memory. So a mix of executable-program and free-text-workflow representations.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Mixed: reusable procedural skill (developer-created tools / code), reusable workflow (planner sub-plan decompositions), and single demonstration (human-crafted tool examples in semantic memory). Code is abstracted via summarization rather than stored as raw trajectory.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Primarily relevance/consensus-based: 3-path multi-path sampling with an independent reasoning LLM-as-a-judge (o4-mini) consensus critic filters incorrect trajectories before answers/experiences are accepted; code summarization reduces implementation noise; a 5-step lookback window during trajectory summarization avoids biased critic evaluation. Only successful (critic-validated) experiences are written, implicitly filtering noisy memory. No retriever-aware/distractor-aware SFT.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: Hierarchical cognitive memory: procedural (system prompts + LLM parameters), semantic (human-crafted tools / transfer demonstrations), and episodic (online task-execution experiences = agent-created tools and sub-plans). Episodic + skill-library + procedural combined.
- **write back**: Yes. Upon successful task completion the complete execution trajectory is summarized/embedded via Phi and appended to the agent's episodic memory repository (M_ep <- M_ep U {e}); created tools likewise accumulate (T <- T U {T}).
- **online growth**: Yes. The episodic store grows during deployment/curriculum execution; the paper explicitly shows memory utilization shifting from semantic (human tools) toward episodic (agent-created tools/subplans) as the curriculum progresses (near-zero to saturation).
- **write back trigger**: on-success only: experiences are written upon successful task completion (critic/consensus-validated success); failed trajectories are not stored (the paper notes leveraging failures as negative samples only as future work).
- **failure experience usage**: success-only in the current system. Failed/negative experiences are NOT stored or retrieved; the authors explicitly list 'enhanced error utilization' treating failures as negative samples and verifier-based error attribution as future work (Sec. 6).
- **memory evolution update**:
> append-only: successful trajectories/tools are added to the repository; no dedup-merge, delta-update, refine-overwrite, or forget-prune mechanism is described. (The paper notes a concern that self-generated tools increasingly displace human demonstrations in retrieval, but this is emergent retrieval preference, not an explicit mutation/forgetting policy.)
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No. Case/experience selection is fixed similarity-based top-k (dense+sparse with RRF) over off-the-shelf embeddings; it is not an RL-optimized or learned retrieval policy. (Contrast: Memento's M-MDP soft Q-learning is cited as related, but SMITH does not use a learned retrieval policy.)
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Cross-task and cross-agent within one workflow: each sub-agent (planner, developer) keeps its own agent-specific episodic repository, and experiences are shared across tasks (cross-task experience sharing is the core claim). Sharing is across roles/agents inside the SMITH workflow rather than across heterogeneous external agent frameworks.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: GAIA benchmark (165 validation tasks with human-annotated difficulty Levels 1/2/3; 300 i.i.d. test samples mentioned for final evaluation). WebShaper dataset used as curated cold-start/transfer source for semantic memory (not as an evaluation benchmark).
- **benchmark family**: general AI assistant / agentic tool-use benchmark (GAIA) — spans QA, multi-hop reasoning, web search, file/multimodal handling, and tool-use.
- **baselines**:
> Tool creation: Alita (75.2%). Experience sharing: Memento (70.9%). Multi-agent w. tool+memory: WebShaper-32B (53.3%), AutoAgent (55.2%), OpenDeepResearch (55.2%), TapeAgents (55.8%), OWL (69.7%), Manus (73.9%), MiroFlow (74.5%), AWorld (77.6%). Python-interpreter w/o tool reuse: SmolAgents (49.7%), OAgents (66.7%). Also internal base-model baselines: claude-4-sonnet (78.8%), claude-3.7-sonnet (70.9%), gpt-4.1 (67.9%).
- **key metrics**: Pass@1 (primary) and Pass@3 accuracy on GAIA, broken down by difficulty Level 1/2/3.
- **headline result**: 81.8% Pass@1 on the GAIA validation set (new SOTA), vs Alita 75.2% (+6.6) and Memento 70.9% (+10.9); Level 1 94.3%, Level 2 80.2%, Level 3 61.5%.
- **ablations**:
> Component-removal ablations (Table 3 / Fig. 3): removing curriculum learning -10.3% (81.8 -> 71.5); removing episodic memory sharing -13.9% (-> 67.9); removing cold-start demonstration -21.8% (-> 60.0). Multi-path/self-critic ablation (Table 2): self-critic ensemble 81.8% vs best single model claude-4-sonnet 78.8% (+3.0), with consistent gains across levels (+1.8 L1, +3.5 L2, +3.8 L3). Curriculum re-estimation transforms the 3-level GAIA distribution into a balanced 4-level (L'=4) linearly-declining distribution.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> No. Only end-to-end task metrics (Pass@1/Pass@3 by level) are reported; no intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG / completeness) are reported separately. Memory behavior is analyzed qualitatively (memory-utilization trend, t-SNE clustering, 165x165 cross-task sharing correlation matrix) but not as quantitative retrieval scores.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Predominantly outcome-only (final-answer Pass@1/Pass@3). Process is examined qualitatively: memory-utilization evolution across curriculum, episodic-memory t-SNE clustering, cross-task experience-sharing correlation matrix, and failure-case analysis (OCR, Google Maps, repetitive scripting, oversized PDFs) — but not via quantitative step-wise/process metrics.
- **context budget and selection count**: Fixed-k selection: semantic memory search limit = 3; episodic memory limit = 4 for the planner and 6 for the developer (m=4 planner, n=6 developer fragments). RRF selects the final top-k candidates. No adaptive-k or explicit token budget is reported.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (this is a method paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (uses existing GAIA: 165 validation tasks, 3 human-annotated difficulty levels, 300 i.i.d. test samples; SMITH re-estimates difficulty into L'=4 levels but does not construct a new benchmark).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (Sumers et al. 2023, episodic/semantic/procedural memory); retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al. 2020); tool creation lines Alita, CRAFT, CREATOR, LATM, ToolMaker, SmolAgents (save/cache generated tools); experience-sharing/memory lines Memento (M-MDP), MAEL, CoPS, Mem0, MemGPT, Generative Agents, ReAct; workflow-agent designs OWL and OAgents; multi-path sampling + LLM-as-a-judge from AWorld and SciMaster; WebShaper used for cold-start transfer.
- **contrasts with**:
> Alita (tool creation from scratch without systematic experience reuse), Memento (cross-task experience sharing without integrated tool creation), Toolformer/predefined-tool learning (limited coverage), and parameter-based experience methods (AWorld, WebShaper SFT+RL) that lack clear memory hierarchies and continual inference-time learning. SMITH's claimed novelty is unifying tool creation + experience sharing in one cognitive memory architecture.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use): tool-creation + cross-task experience sharing line. Sits at the intersection of dynamic tool creation (Alita / CRAFT / CREATOR / LATM / SmolAgents) and episodic experience-sharing memory agents (Memento / MAEL / CoPS), unified under a cognitive (procedural/semantic/episodic) memory architecture for general AI assistants on GAIA.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- cost_efficiency_tradeoff
- retrieval_trigger_signal
- venue

<a id="item-swe-exp"></a>
### 116. SWE-Exp: Experience-Driven Software Issue Resolution

2025  ·  arXiv 2507.23361  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.23361)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **authors affiliation**: Silin Chen, Yuling Shi, Xiaodong Gu (corresponding) (Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Shaoxin Lin, Dong Chen, Lin Cao, Jiyang Liu, Nu Xia, Qianxiang Wang (Huawei); Heng Lian (Xidian University); Longfei Yun (UC San Diego).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.23361
- **code url**: https://github.com/cslsolow/SWE-Exp (linked in paper as https://github.com/YerbaPage/SWE-Exp, redirects to cslsolow/SWE-Exp); anonymous replication: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SWE-Exp-6FEA
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/cslsolow/SWE-Exp

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: code (repository-level / GitHub software issue resolution; automated program repair by LLM agents).
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, multi-step repository-level issue resolution on SWE-Bench-Verified: the agent reads a natural-language issue, navigates the codebase, localizes faults, and generates a patch verified by test execution. Supervision is available offline (ground-truth golden patches used to annotate success/failure trajectories during experience collection). It is multi-agent (dual-agent Instructor/Assistant on top of MCTS / SWE-Search) with a growing cross-repository experience bank built before test-time. Cross-issue continual learning is the core goal: knowledge distilled from prior agent trajectories is reused across different issues and repositories. Data-leakage controls exclude same-repository and temporally-posterior experiences.
- **what is retrieved**:
> Distilled, reusable 'experiences' mined from prior agent repair trajectories. Two facets: Comprehension experiences (perspective: abstract understanding/diagnostic reasoning patterns for the problem) and Modification experiences (generalized code-modification strategies/safety patterns). Both successful and failed trajectories are distilled; failed ones yield reflections/corrective insights.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> GROWING/episodic memory the agent writes (the Experience Bank), induced offline from past agent trajectories rather than a static external corpus of docs/APIs. The bank is constructed before test-time on SWE-Bench-Verified trajectories; it is not updated during a single online resolution.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Precision-driven, very small selection. Phase 1 retrieves a fixed top-N=10 candidates by error-type/description similarity; an LLM rerank agent then selects k=1 most-applicable experience. The paper finds 1 experience is optimal (more degrades performance), so the objective is precision/quality over completeness or large top-k recall.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The paper frames itself as 'experience-driven' / 'experience-enhanced' continual learning and memory-augmented agents; it does not cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner or use case-based reasoning terminology, though it realizes CBR-like Retrieve/Reuse/Adapt mechanisms.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Distilled experience entry = a (perspective, modification) dictionary derived from a past trajectory, indexed by metadata (issue_type, description). Effectively a distilled case/guideline pair rather than a raw trajectory; comprehension experiences are diagnostic insights, modification experiences are repair-strategy rules.
- **index source**:
> Growing memory built offline / before test-time: trajectories are collected by running SWE-Search on SWE-Bench-Verified, then distilled into experiences stored in a vector database (the Experience Bank). Frozen during a given online resolution run (no per-instance write-back at inference).
- **index structure topology**: Flat dense vector index (vector database) with metadata keying. Each experience is embedded and indexed by two metadata attributes (issue_type label and a generalized description); also organized into two facet categories (comprehension vs modification).
- **retriever type**: Hybrid two-stage: (1) dense embedding similarity (Multilingual-E5-Large-Instruct, cosine similarity) over issue_type+description, then (2) LLM-as-reranker (a rerank/select agent picks the most applicable experience).
- **retriever learning signal**: None for the embedding retriever (off-the-shelf pre-trained Multilingual-E5-Large-Instruct, no fine-tuning). Final selection is LLM-judgment-based (prompted reranking agent), not a trained policy; no contrastive or RL training of the retriever is reported.
- **query construction**:
> Query is the new issue's extracted issue_type label plus a generalized description (an issue agent classifies the problem statement into an error type and description). For reuse, the agent compares the current problem_statement and code-exploration history with retrieved past issue descriptions/experiences and rewrites/adapts them.
- **query granularity**: Two-level. Task-level: issue_type/description query for the initial similarity retrieval. Step/decision-level: experiences are also retrieved/integrated at critical MCTS decision nodes during tree expansion (per-decision contextual guidance).
- **when to retrieve**: Iterative within the MCTS search: relevant experiences are dynamically retrieved at critical decision points during tree expansion, not just one-shot at t=0. Retrieval is on a fixed schedule tied to decision nodes (not uncertainty-triggered or learned-router).
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule tied to MCTS decision points: before each decision / at decision nodes during tree expansion the agent retrieves the N most relevant experiences. No token-confidence, attention, or learned-complexity trigger; integration is keyed to the search-tree expansion steps.
- **reranking**: Yes. A dedicated LLM rerank agent (RerankAgent / select agent) takes the top N=10 similarity candidates and selects k=1 most-applicable experience. Ablation shows replacing LLM reranking with plain similarity selection drops Pass@1 from 42.0% to 38.2% (-3.8%).
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Adapt/generalize-then-inject. The reuse agent contextualizes the retrieved experience to the current issue (compares similarities/differences, produces a 'new_experience' tailored to the current problem) and rewrites the Assistant's next-step instruction ('enhanced_instruction') using modification experience. Comprehension experience is added as message context rather than forcibly cited (to avoid over-reliance).
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (this work retrieves distilled experiences/cases, not tools or tool/API documents).
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no live tool index or external tool integration protocol; integration is with the SWE-Search/moatless MCTS framework and a vector DB).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no inter-tool dependency modeling; retrieval is over experiences, not tools).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation + case adaptation. Retrieved comprehension experience is injected into the Instructor's context to guide high-level diagnosis/strategy; retrieved modification experience is used to rewrite/enhance the Assistant's next-step instruction. No model fine-tuning; experience is used in-context to steer MCTS action selection and value assessment.
- **planning integration**:
> Inside MCTS / tree search. Built on SWE-Search MCTS: experiences are retrieved at decision nodes and integrated into the Selection, Expansion, Evaluation, and Discrimination stages (experience-guided node selection, experience-informed action generation, experience-enhanced value assessment, experience-informed consensus). A hierarchical dual-agent (Instructor planner + Assistant executor) maps experiences to strategic planning vs tactical execution across the three-stage workflow (Issue Understanding, Fault Localization, Patch Generation).
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-decision-step within an MCTS rollout: experiences are woven in at decision nodes / per next-step instruction (Instructor decides a strategic action, Assistant's instruction is experience-enhanced), i.e. finer than per-answer; effectively per MCTS action/instruction.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> LLM-prompted adaptation: a Reuser agent generalizes the retrieved past experience into a 'new_experience' tailored to the current problem statement and rewrites the next-step instruction ('enhanced_instruction'). Comprehension experience is provided as soft message context (not forced) to avoid inflexible over-reliance; no RL-reuse-finetuning.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Distilled strategy/guideline in free text: comprehension experiences are natural-language diagnostic insights/perspectives; modification experiences are natural-language repair-strategy rules. Stored structurally as a (perspective, modification[]) dictionary with issue_type/description metadata. Not raw trajectories and not executable programs.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Distilled strategy/insight and state-aware guideline/rule: high-level problem-comprehension perspectives plus generalized code-modification strategies abstracted across repositories. Explicitly multi-level (from high-level problem comprehension to specific code-change strategies), but abstracted rather than raw trajectories.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> (1) LLM reranking to filter to the single most-relevant experience; (2) empirically capping k=1 (more experiences introduce conflicting/misleading info and degrade performance); (3) providing comprehension experience as non-forced message context to prevent over-reliance; (4) facet separation so modification experience is vetted by the Assistant against the Instructor's decided direction; (5) data-leakage exclusion (same-repo and temporally-posterior experiences removed). No retriever-aware training or distractor-aware SFT.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: episodic / experience bank (distilled-experience memory) realized as a vector database; organized into two facet categories (comprehension, modification). Not a skill-library of executable skills, not a graph.
- **write back**: True (offline). The system distills new experiences from collected success and failure trajectories and stores them in the Experience Bank vector DB. However, this happens in the offline extraction stage, not as online write-back during a single test-time resolution run.
- **online growth**:
> No (as evaluated). The Experience Bank is induced offline before test-time and frozen during online resolution; the paper does not perform per-instance write-back at inference. The RQ3 'experience bank size' study grows the bank in chronological increments (offline simulation of growth), not live streaming growth during deployment.
- **write back trigger**:
> On-success-and-failure (offline): both successful trajectories (correct patches validated against ground truth) and failed trajectories are distilled into experiences; failure trajectories get additional failure-cause metadata (incorrect localization / flawed modification strategy / insufficient comprehension). Triggered by the offline extraction pipeline using ground-truth validation, not by online self-critique at test time.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success + failure. Failure trajectories are explicitly distilled into corrective 'reflections' insights and annotated with failure cause; the bank captures both successful repair patterns and failed-attempt lessons. For success extraction the shortest path is used; for failure the longest. Comprehension reuse can draw on either a success perspective or failure reflections.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No. Retrieval is fixed similarity top-N=10 plus an LLM-prompted reranking agent selecting k=1; it is not an RL-/value-trained selection policy (no M-MDP, soft Q-learning, or learned retrieval policy).
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Cross-issue and cross-repository experience sharing within a single agent framework: experiences distilled from heterogeneous external repositories are aggregated and reused across issues/repositories (a key differentiator vs SAGE's within-instance experience). It is not framed as sharing across heterogeneous agent frameworks or multiple distinct agents; the Instructor/Assistant share one experience bank.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: SWE-Bench-Verified (500 human-verified issues from SWE-bench). Hyperparameter studies use a 75-instance subset (25 each from Django, SymPy, Sphinx).
- **benchmark family**: code (SWE-bench family).
- **baselines**: Agentless; SWE-Agent; SWE-Search (MCTS; the framework SWE-Exp extends); OpenHands; EvoCoder (experience-driven continual learning); SAGE (experience/plan-abstraction framework on OpenHands). Models: DeepSeek-V3-0324 (open-source) and Claude-4-Sonnet (20250514, closed-source).
- **key metrics**: Pass@1 resolution rate (proportion of issues correctly fixed on first attempt). Cost metrics: average token cost, average API cost (USD), average wall-clock time, average retrieval+rerank time.
- **headline result**:
> 73.0% Pass@1 on SWE-Bench-Verified with Claude-4-Sonnet (vs SWE-Search 70.8%, SAGE 71.6%, OpenHands 70.4%, EvoCoder 67.8%, Agentless 66.6% on the same model). With DeepSeek-V3-0324: 42.0% Pass@1 (vs SWE-Search 35.4%, OpenHands/SWE-Agent/EvoCoder 38.8%/38.8%/38.0%, Agentless 36.6%).
- **ablations**:
> On DeepSeek-V3-0324 (base SWE-Exp 42.0%): w/o Comprehension Experience 38.8% (-3.2%); w/o Modification Experience 39.4% (-2.6%); w/o Dual-Agent 39.8% (-2.2%); w/o Experiences Extraction (use raw problem statement + golden patch as in-context demos) 36.0% (-6.0%, largest drop); w/o LLM Reranking (plain similarity selection) 38.2% (-3.8%). RQ3 hyperparameters: number of experiences peaks at 1 (42.0%; 0 experiences = 37.8%/37.2%, declines to 39.8% at 2 and ~39.0% at 4); experience-bank size shows steady gains up to ~300 experiences then saturation.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No. Only end-to-end task metrics (Pass@1) and cost metrics are reported; no intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG / experience-retrieval accuracy) are reported separately.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Primarily outcome (Pass@1). Process is examined qualitatively via a case study (django-11964) and a manual quality verification of extracted experiences on 75 instances, plus cost/runtime; no quantitative step-wise retrieval/planning-accuracy or trajectory-quality metric.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Modest overhead vs SWE-Search (DeepSeek-V3-0324): avg token cost 203.3K vs 189.1K; avg API cost $0.13 vs $0.12; avg wall time 15min49s vs 12min37s; experience retrieval+rerank adds ~37.5s/instance (0s for SWE-Search). Authors conclude large accuracy gains come at minimal extra compute/cost.
- **context budget and selection count**: Reranked-then-truncated to a very small k: N=10 similarity candidates reranked by an LLM agent down to k=1 experience injected per instance. Empirically k=1 is optimal; larger k degrades performance. No explicit token budget cap reported for injected experiences.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (this is a method paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (uses existing SWE-Bench-Verified, not a newly constructed benchmark; 500 human-verified issues, human-curated ground-truth patches, test-execution-verifiable).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> SWE-Search (Antoniades et al., 2024) MCTS framework / moatless-tree-search (Albert Orwall) as the base; SWE-bench / SWE-Bench-Verified (Jimenez et al., 2024; OpenAI 2024) as the testbed; experience-enhanced agent line such as ExpeL (experiential learners), AutoGuide (context-aware guidelines), ExACT (Reflective-MCTS + vector DB), EvoCoder, SAGE.
- **contrasts with**:
> Memoryless / single-instance agents: SWE-Agent, OpenHands, Agentless (no cross-issue experience reuse); SWE-Search (MCTS without experience). Among experience-driven methods, contrasts with SAGE (within-instance plan abstraction, experience localized to current instance) and EvoCoder (reproduction-focused continual learning), arguing SWE-Exp uniquely abstracts and reuses experience across trajectories from different repositories with a multi-facet (comprehension+modification) bank and dual-agent reuse.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use / agentic) — experience/memory-augmented coding agents: extends the MCTS-based SWE issue-resolution line (SWE-Search) with a growing, distilled cross-repository experience bank, positioned in the experiential-learning lineage (ExpeL -> AutoGuide -> ExACT / EvoCoder / SAGE -> SWE-Exp), specialized for repository-level software issue resolution.

<a id="item-scalemcp"></a>
### 117. ScaleMCP: Dynamic and Auto-Synchronizing Model Context Protocol Tools for LLM Agents

2025  ·  arXiv 2505.06416  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06416)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **authors affiliation**:
> Elias Lumer, Anmol Gulati, Vamse Kumar Subbiah, Pradeep Honaganahalli Basavaraju, James A. Burke. Primary (single) affiliation: PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC), U.S.A. Correspondence: elias.lumer@pwc.com, anmol.b.gulati@pwc.com. The same lead author (Elias Lumer) authored the prior Toolshed / Graph RAG-Tool Fusion work this paper builds on.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06416

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> tool-use (MCP tool/server selection, retrieval, and invocation for tool-augmented LLM agents); financial-metric tool-calling is the concrete instantiation. The retrieved MCP servers (tools) are consumed by a downstream LLM agent that plans tool calls and reasons over their outputs.
- **problem setting**:
> Online/interactive, single-agent, training-free (plug-and-play, out-of-the-box LLMs and embeddings) tool selection at scale over thousands of MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers. The setting targets three stated limitations of prior tool-selection frameworks: (1) they do not integrate MCP servers; (2) they rely on error-prone MANUAL synchronization of a monolithic local tool repository (duplication, inconsistency, inefficiency); and (3) they abstract tool selection BEFORE the LLM is invoked, removing agent autonomy and preventing dynamic re-querying during multi-turn interactions. ScaleMCP instead (a) builds an auto-synchronizing tool storage system that treats live MCP servers as the single source of truth (CRUD-based indexing), and (b) equips the LLM agent itself with an MCP-retrieval tool so it autonomously decides when to search for and add tools to its context/memory and can re-query mid-conversation. Model-provider tool-count limits (e.g., 128 tools) motivate RAG-style tool retrieval. Evaluation is supervised in the sense that user-query instances carry expected (golden) tool calls (3-12 golden tools per query), but the retriever/agent are not fine-tuned.
- **what is retrieved**: tools (MCP servers exposed as tools / tool-API documents). Each retrievable item is an MCP tool document comprising tool name, description, and parameter/argument schema, optionally augmented with LLM-generated synthetic questions.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> HYBRID leaning STATIC-corpus-with-live-sync: the retrievable store is an external corpus of MCP tool documents (5,000 financial MCP servers), NOT an episodic memory of the agent's own experience. However, the store is auto-synchronized to the live MCP servers (single source of truth) via CRUD operations, so the external corpus itself can change as servers are created/updated/deleted. Separately, at inference the agent can 'add tools into its memory' (load retrieved MCP tools into context), a per-session working memory rather than a persistent experiential store.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Completeness-oriented multi-tool recovery layered on top-k retrieval. Queries are predominantly multi-hop and reference multiple golden MCP tools (typically 3-12, sometimes 12 in a single turn), so the objective is to recover the COMPLETE set of needed tools, not just a single best match. The paper explicitly notes a single query embedding cannot capture multiple distinct tool intents (a known multi-hop dense-retrieval failure), motivating agentic query decomposition: the agent calls the MCP Retrieval Tool in parallel (e.g., 5 times, one keyword set per targeted tool) to assemble the full tool set. Retrieval metrics are still reported at fixed K=1/5/10.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based reasoning method; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain case cycle over problem-solution cases)
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is positioned within tool selection, tool-applied RAG / Graph-RAG, agentic RAG, and the Model Context Protocol literature.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> tool-API / MCP tool document. The unit is a single MCP server's tool document = tool name || tool description || tool arguments(parameter schema), optionally with 0/5/10 appended synthetic questions. For TDWA embedding, this document is decomposed into N weighted components (name, description, parameters, synthetic questions).
- **index source**:
> Static external corpus that is LIVE-SYNCHRONIZED rather than offline-frozen. The store is built by an auto-synchronization indexing pipeline (Algorithm 1) that reads the current MCP server tool list (single source of truth), computes a SHA-256 hash over name+description+arguments per tool, diffs against existing storage hashes, and applies CRUD: create/index new tools, delete outdated/removed tools, update changed tools. It is offline-induced from tool definitions (no LLMs were used to create the tools themselves; tools generated deterministically from Fortune 1000 companies + yfinance). It is NOT induced from the agent's own test-time trajectories.
- **index structure topology**:
> Storage-system-agnostic; primarily a FLAT vector index in the experiments. The pipeline supports vector database (flat dense vectors, used in all reported experiments), graph database / hybrid Graph-RAG (mentioned for inter-dependent MCP servers, citing the authors' own Graph RAG-Tool Fusion), or a lexical/keyword (BM25) index, chosen by use case. Reported runs use a flat vector store (no graph/hierarchy actually evaluated).
- **retriever type**:
> Hybrid / configurable: dense vector search (off-the-shelf embeddings: OpenAI text-embedding-3-large/-3-small/-ada-002, Amazon titan-embed-text-v1, VertexAI text-embedding-005), sparse BM25 lexical search, and hybrid search, all combined with optional reranking. An LLM is used (a) as the agent that issues MCP-retrieval-tool keyword queries (LLM-as-query-issuer / agentic RAG) and (b) as an LLM reranker (GPT-4o, Claude 3.7 Sonnet). Matching itself is embedding/lexical similarity, not a trained retriever and not generative tool-as-token.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> none (off-the-shelf / training-free). The paper deliberately uses out-of-the-box embeddings and LLMs from OpenAI/Google/Amazon/Anthropic/Meta with no retriever fine-tuning (explicitly contrasting with prior work that fine-tunes retrievers, e.g., ToolLLM, Seal-Tools). The only 'learned' weighting is the manually-set TDWA component weights (var-1=[0.2,0.2,0.2,0.4], var-2=[0.2,0.3,0,0.5]); these are hand-specified, not learned. Future-work mentions LLM fine-tuning for tool discovery but it is not done here.
- **query construction**:
> Agent-issued keyword search queries. The LLM agent is equipped with a 'get_mcp_servers' / MCP Retrieval tool and, per the system prompt, decomposes the user request and passes in keyword query strings to search for specific tools, using PARALLEL tool calling (one search call per tool it wants), e.g., 5 keyword sets for 5 targeted financial metrics. On the index side, tool documents are enriched with LLM-generated synthetic questions (document expansion). Retrieval-experiment queries are the standalone user-query instances (often multi-hop / multi-company).
- **query granularity**:
> Two-level / both: task-level user query that the agent decomposes into multiple per-tool (sub-)queries issued in parallel; effectively per-targeted-tool query granularity within a single agent turn, and the agent can re-query across turns. Indexing-side keys are also multi-view (multiple synthetic questions per tool).
- **when to retrieve**:
> active / agent-initiated (adaptive). Retrieval is not a fixed pre-LLM pipeline stage; the LLM agent autonomously decides when to call the MCP Retrieval tool, can call it multiple times in parallel, and can RE-QUERY the storage system if no successful matches are found or across multi-turn conversation. (The retrieval-only Experiment 1 and the agent Experiment 2 also include a static one-shot top-k=5 retrieval as a baseline/comparison point.)
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> agent-initiated request: the LLM, guided by its system prompt ('the only way to use the tool knowledge base is to use get_mcp_servers'), decides to invoke the MCP Retrieval tool, how many parallel searches to issue, and whether to re-query when matches are insufficient during multi-turn interactions. There is no fixed schedule, token-confidence, or learned-classifier trigger; the trigger is the LLM's own function-calling decision.
- **reranking**:
> Yes, evaluated extensively. Reranking stages compared: Cohere cross-encoder reranker (rerank-v3-english), and LLM rerankers GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet 3.7. Reranking is the single most impactful lever, especially LLM rerankers, which give the strongest retrieval scores (patching low vector-only recall in the multi-hop setting). Hybrid search (vector+BM25 fusion) is also evaluated as a configuration.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Primarily rerank (cross-encoder or LLM reranking over the candidate pool) plus index-side document enrichment via synthetic-question augmentation and TDWA component weighting. The agentic loop adds query decomposition (multiple parallel sub-queries) and the ability to re-query. No explicit reason-in-documents distillation or compression of retrieved tool documents is applied.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Synthetic-question augmentation + weighted-field embedding (TDWA). Each tool document is enriched with 0, 5, or 10 LLM-generated synthetic natural-language questions (conditioned on a {company} template filled with company name/ticker/alias). SQ=10 consistently improves retrieval. The novel Tool Document Weighted Average (TDWA) embeds each component (name, description, parameters, synthetic questions) separately and takes an L2-normalized weighted average (weights sum to 1), rather than concatenation or unweighted averaging, to control each component's contribution in vector space.
- **index content separation**:
> Partial / progressive disclosure at invocation time: the lightweight tool index (embedded tool documents) is retrieved first; only the retrieved (top-k=5) MCP servers' full tool definitions are then loaded into the LLM context and 'bound' to the LLM via function calling for actual execution, separating the searchable index from the heavier bound tool set used on demand. Within an index entry there is no further index-vs-content split.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Core contribution: LIVE auto-synchronized tool index with the Model Context Protocol (MCP) as the integration protocol. MCP servers are the single source of truth; an auto-synchronization pipeline performs CRUD (create, read, update, delete) on the storage index based on SHA-256 hash diffs of tool name+description+arguments, eliminating manual updates to a monolithic local repository. Tools are served via MCP-compliant servers (fast-mcp / FastMCP framework). Retrieved tools are bound and invoked through OpenAI-compatible function calling over the bidirectional MCP connection. This contrasts with prior static RapidAPI/RESTful tool stores.
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> Limited / optional. The default reported setup treats MCP servers as independent (scaled via a vector database). The paper notes that if MCP servers are dependent on each other, a graph database / hybrid Graph-RAG approach (citing the authors' own Graph RAG-Tool Fusion) can encode dependency information for retrieval, but no inter-tool dependency graph is actually constructed or evaluated in this paper's experiments.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> prompt/tool-space augmentation via agentic function calling: retrieved MCP servers are loaded into the LLM's context and bound as callable tools; the agent then calls them (in parallel) to obtain tool responses and reasons over those responses to produce the final answer. No fine-tuning; retrieved tools enter the agent's action space and can be re-queried across turns (added to the agent's working tool memory).
- **planning integration**:
> Agentic retrieve-act loop / interleaved within the agent invocation: rather than retrieve-then-plan as a fixed pre-LLM stage, the LLM agent autonomously searches (MCP Retrieval tool, parallel calls), receives candidate tools, binds and invokes them, observes responses, and can re-query/search again, forming a retrieval-augmented planning loop over multiple steps. The paper frames this as moving beyond static top-k single-shot retrieval toward iterative agent-driven tool discovery and invocation.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> per-tool-call within an agent turn (and across multi-turn conversation): the agent issues multiple parallel MCP-search calls (one per targeted tool) and multiple parallel tool invocations within a turn, and may re-search in later turns. It is coarser than per-CoT-step/per-token interleaving; retrieval is woven in at the granularity of (parallel) tool-search and tool-invocation actions.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not a CBR method; no retrieved case is adapted/revised). The closest analog is the agent re-querying with new keywords when matches are insufficient.
- **retrieved item representation**: raw structured tool/API documents (MCP tool name, description, JSON-style parameter/argument schema) injected into the agent's context and bound as function-calling tools; on the index side these are dense vectors (optionally TDWA-weighted) over the tool-document components.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: tool-level descriptive documentation / single tool-API capability description (name + description + parameter schema, optionally with synthetic questions), i.e., a tool-API document rather than a raw trajectory, distilled strategy, reusable workflow, or procedural skill.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Mainly reranking-based relevance refinement (cross-encoder / LLM rerankers re-score candidates to suppress weak vector matches) plus agentic re-querying (the agent can search again if no successful matches are found). Synthetic-question enrichment and TDWA weighting aim to improve representation quality. There is no retriever-aware adversarial training, no learned relevance evaluator/self-reflection module (the paper proposes Anthropic's 'think' reflective tool as FUTURE work to mitigate low tool-correctness).

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: Configurable external tool store (vector/graph/lexical) treated as a synchronized tool index, plus a transient per-session agent working memory of bound tools. Not an episodic/experiential or skill/workflow/procedural memory of past task outcomes.
- **write back**:
> Partial / not experiential. The system writes to the tool STORAGE INDEX, but only to keep it synchronized with live MCP servers (CRUD create/update/delete on tool definitions), not to store the agent's own task experiences/cases/skills. The agent 'adds tools into its memory' (loads retrieved tools into context) within a session, but this is working memory, not persisted experience.
- **online growth**:
> Yes for the tool index, in the sense of auto-synchronization: the store automatically grows/shrinks/updates as MCP servers are created, updated, or deleted (single source of truth), via the CRUD pipeline. No for experiential growth: the store does not accumulate the agent's trajectories or learned cases during deployment.
- **write back trigger**:
> tool-definition change driven (single-source-of-truth sync), not experience-driven. A write/update/delete to the storage index occurs when the SHA-256 hash of a live MCP server's tool (name+description+arguments) does not match the stored hash (create or update) or when a stored tool is no longer present among live servers (delete); matching hashes trigger no operation. The agent never writes its own task experiences back; write-back of agent experience = never.
- **failure experience usage**: N/A (no storage/retrieval of successful or failed agent trajectories). Failed retrievals lead the agent to re-query with new keywords within the session, but no failure cases are persisted or later retrieved.
- **memory evolution update**:
> Index entries are mutated only to track the source of truth: refine-overwrite on tool change (delete old hash/entry, re-index new definition), delete/prune on tool removal, create on new tool. There is no merging, delta-accumulation of experience, or link-and-evolve of experiential memory; it is a hash-diff-driven refresh of tool definitions.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No. Retrieval/selection is not a trained or RL-optimized policy. It is similarity-based top-k (dense/BM25/hybrid) with optional cross-encoder/LLM reranking, while the WHEN/WHAT-to-search decisions are made by an off-the-shelf LLM via function calling (in-context, untrained for this objective). TDWA weights are hand-set, not learned.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent setting with a private (per-session) bound-tool memory. The MCP tool store is a shared external resource but not a shared experiential memory. The paper discusses Google's Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol and multi-agent ecosystems only as future work.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> A newly created (self-constructed) dataset of 5,000 real-world financial-metric MCP servers (tools) plus ~140,000 user-query instances (avg 5.0 tool calls per instance; some queries reference 3-12, up to 15-company, golden tools). Tools were built from Fortune 1000 companies x 5 deterministic templates (current_stock_price, stock_price_history, analyst_price_targets, revenue, net_income) using yfinance and the fast-mcp/FastMCP framework. Evaluations: Experiment 1 (vector-DB retrieval), Experiment 2 (end-to-end LLM agent), Experiment 3 (TDWA weighting). No external/public tool benchmark (e.g., ToolBench, API-Bank) is used for the main experiments.
- **benchmark family**: tool (tool/MCP-server retrieval and end-to-end tool invocation) -- a self-constructed financial-metric MCP benchmark, not a standard public tool benchmark family (cited related families: ToolBench/ToolLLM, API-Bank, Seal-Tools).
- **baselines**:
> Internal comparisons across configurations rather than competing external systems. Retrieval methods compared: vector-only search, hybrid search, BM25 lexical search, Cohere cross-encoder reranking (rerank-v3-english), and LLM reranking (GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 3.7); five embedding models (OpenAI text-embedding-3-large/-3-small/-ada-002, Amazon titan-embed-text-v1, VertexAI text-embedding-005); synthetic-question counts SQ=0/5/10. Storage/embedding strategies: simple Concat (baseline) vs TDWA var-1 [0.2,0.2,0.2,0.4] vs TDWA var-2 [0.2,0.3,0,0.5]. End-to-end: 10 LLM agents (gpt-4.1, gpt-4.1-mini, gpt-4.1-nano, gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini, gpt-o4-mini, gpt-o3, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3.3 70B) x three retrieval strategies (BM25 text search, vector search, vector + Cohere reranker).
- **key metrics**:
> Retrieval (Experiments 1 & 3): NDCG, Recall, MAP at K=1/5/10. End-to-end agent (Experiment 2, via the DeepEval framework): Tool Correctness (= correct tool calls / total tool calls, incl. valid args and correct output interpretation) and Task Completion Score (alignment score between expected and generated outputs).
- **headline result**:
> End-to-end: gpt-o3 with vector search + Cohere reranking achieved the highest Task Completion of 94.4% (but only 36.1% Tool Correctness); gpt-4o-mini was the most balanced at 54.0% Tool Correctness and 86.7% Task Completion (vector + Cohere reranker). Retrieval: best Recall@10 = 0.94 (VertexAI text-embedding-005 + GPT-4o reranking, SQ=10) and best MAP@10 = 0.59 (same embedding + Claude reranking). A key reported finding is the large gap between high Task Completion and low Tool Correctness on complex multi-hop queries.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Embedding-model and search-config sweep (Exp 1): vector-only retrieval is weak (MAP ~0.50) under multi-hop supervision; reranking, especially LLM reranking (GPT-4o, Claude 3.7), substantially improves results; BM25 is weakest; SQ=10 synthetic questions consistently beats SQ=0/5. (2) TDWA vs Concat (Exp 3, SQ=10, text-embedding-3-large): in plain vector search Concat slightly wins (NDCG 0.634 / Recall 0.912 / MAP 0.499 vs TDWA var-1 0.631/0.886/0.504 and var-2 0.620/0.891/0.485); gaps narrow under reranking and TDWA var-2 sometimes wins reranked MAP@5 (e.g., Cohere TDWA var-1 MAP 0.528 > Concat 0.510); authors attribute Concat's edge to keyword-heavy tickers and synthetic-query/eval-query co-generation bias, arguing TDWA may generalize better on human queries. (3) Agent retrieval-strategy ablation (Exp 2): cross-encoder reranking consistently improved both Tool Correctness and Task Completion over vector-only/BM25; Llama 3.3 70B failed tool calling entirely (0.0% Tool Correctness); Claude models underperformed on Tool Correctness.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Yes. Intrinsic retrieval metrics (NDCG/Recall/MAP @K) are reported separately (Experiments 1 and 3) from end-to-end agent metrics (Tool Correctness and Task Completion, Experiment 2), explicitly decoupling retrieval quality from downstream task success. The paper highlights the divergence (high Task Completion can mask low Tool Correctness).
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both. Process-level: retrieval ranking metrics (NDCG/Recall/MAP) and Tool Correctness (whether correct tools were invoked with valid args and outputs interpreted). Outcome-level: Task Completion Score (whether the final response fulfills the user query regardless of tools used). The paper stresses the gap between the two.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Discussed qualitatively. LLM reranking gives the strongest recall but is noted as computationally expensive (a 'patch' over weak vector recall); future work aims to show agent-driven ScaleMCP retrieval can match/exceed reranked performance at lower inference cost and higher transparency. The dataset design (templating ~100 base queries per tool across companies; deterministic tool generation) is emphasized as cost-efficient and reproducible. Agentic parallel tool-search/invocation is used to scale beyond the 128-tool provider cap. No concrete latency, dollar-cost, or token-count numbers are reported.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed top-k retrieval at k=5 for the agent experiments (retrieved MCP tools passed in via OpenAI function calling). Retrieval metrics reported at K=1/5/10. The agent issues parallel searches (e.g., 5 search calls, one per targeted tool) and can re-query, so the effective number of equipped tools is agent-driven. The motivating constraint is the model-provider limit of <=128 tools per request. No explicit token budget for the bound-tool prompt is given.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (empirical method/system paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Self-constructed, LLM-assisted but largely deterministic: 5,000 MCP servers (Fortune 1000 companies x 5 deterministic financial-metric tool templates; tools generated programmatically from structured metadata via yfinance + fast-mcp, NO LLM used for tool creation). Tool documents enriched with 0/5/10 LLM-generated synthetic questions. ~140,000 user-query instances created by writing ~100 base queries per tool and templating across companies (avg 5.0 golden tool calls/instance; complex queries reference 3-12, up to 15 companies). Answers are verifiable against expected tool calls (Tool Correctness) and via alignment scoring (Task Completion via DeepEval). Difficulty signal: even best models hit only 36-54% Tool Correctness despite up to 94.4% Task Completion. No public release link found.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Authors' own prior tool-RAG work -- Toolshed: Scale Tool-Equipped Agents with Advanced RAG-Tool Fusion and Tool Knowledge Bases (Lumer et al., 2024/2025a) and Graph RAG-Tool Fusion (Lumer et al., 2025b); Re-Invoke (Chen et al., 2024) for tool-document augmentation; the Model Context Protocol (Anthropic, 2024) and FastMCP (jlowin, 2025) as the protocol/serving substrate; agentic RAG (Singh et al., 2025), API-Bank (Li et al., 2023) and AnyTool (Du et al., 2024) for agent-driven dynamic tool discovery; BM25 (Robertson & Zaragoza, 2009) and RAG/Graph-RAG surveys (Gao et al., 2024; Peng et al., 2024); off-the-shelf embeddings/LLMs (OpenAI, Google, Amazon Titan, Anthropic, Meta) and function calling (OpenAI, 2024); DeepEval (Confident AI, 2025) for evaluation; Seal-Tools (Wu et al., 2024) for the multi-hop dense-retrieval limitation.
- **contrasts with**:
> Static, pre-LLM tool-selection pipelines that abstract retrieval before invocation and remove agent autonomy (incl. the authors' own Toolshed and Re-Invoke as static retrieval pipelines); monolithic local tool repositories requiring manual synchronization (duplication/inconsistency); non-MCP tool frameworks (RapidAPI/RESTful, e.g., ToolLLM/ToolBench, Gorilla); simple embedding concatenation or unweighted averaging of tool-document components (Chen et al., 2024; Lumer et al., 2025a/b) which TDWA replaces with weighted-component embedding; fine-tuned tool retrievers (ToolLLM, Seal-Tools, CRAFT, ToolRerank) which ScaleMCP avoids in favor of out-of-the-box, plug-and-play components.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use). A 2025 MCP-native tool-selection/retrieval system in the direct lineage of the authors' Toolshed (RAG-Tool Fusion) and Graph RAG-Tool Fusion, advancing tool retrieval from static, manually-synchronized, pre-LLM pipelines toward (a) a live CRUD auto-synchronized tool store with MCP as the single source of truth and integration protocol, (b) agentic RAG where the LLM autonomously searches/re-queries/binds MCP tools via function calling, and (c) a TDWA weighted-component tool-document embedding refining prior concatenation/averaging tool-document engineering (Re-Invoke, EasyTool). Positioned within the 2024-2025 tool-retrieval sea-change toward dynamic tool stores, MCP/function-calling protocols, and agent-driven tool discovery.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- code_url
- venue

<a id="item-tgr"></a>
### 118. Tool Graph Retriever (TGR)

2025  ·  arXiv 2508.05152  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05152)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **authors affiliation**: Linfeng Gao, Yaoxiang Wang, Yuzhe Shang, Jinsong Su (School of Informatics, Xiamen University, China); Minlong Peng, Mingming Sun (Baidu, Beijing, China); Jialong Tang (Alibaba). Corresponding/lead: Linfeng Gao and Jinsong Su (Xiamen University).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05152

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: tool-use (tool retrieval for LLM agents): retrieving relevant tools/APIs from a large tool set so an LLM can plan and invoke them.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline-trained, single-agent tool retrieval for LLM agents. Given a user query and a large equipped tool/API set, retrieve the relevant tools (including non-obvious prerequisite tools) before the LLM plans and invokes them. Supervision is available: a BERT discriminator is trained on the constructed TDI300K dataset (pretraining on LLM-generated CodeSearchNet-derived pairs + finetuning on manually annotated pairs) to identify pairwise tool dependencies; the retriever itself reuses off-the-shelf / previously-finetuned text embedding models (PMLM-L3-v2, ToolBench-IR) augmented with a parameter-free graph convolution over the tool dependency graph. Retrieval is a one-shot, task-level ranking step; the LLM planning/invocation loop is downstream and not the contribution.
- **what is retrieved**: tools / APIs (tool documents containing name, description, parameters for ToolBench; tool descriptions for API-Bank).
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus (a fixed candidate tool/API set indexed offline). The tool dependency graph and tool embeddings are induced offline and frozen; no growing/episodic agent-written memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Completeness-oriented within a top-k framing: the core motivation is recovering the complete minimal set of needed tools including prerequisite tools that have low semantic similarity to the query. Evaluated via Pass Rate@k (pass@k = fraction of queries whose ALL ground-truth tools fall within top-k), alongside Recall@k and NDCG@k. k is fixed (top-5, top-10).
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based reasoning method).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: false; the work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is dependency-graph-based tool retrieval.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: tool-API. Each node is a single tool/API represented by its tool document/description embedding.
- **index source**:
> Static corpus, offline-induced. Candidate tools are encoded offline; a tool dependency graph is constructed offline via a trained discriminator; graph convolution updates embeddings offline; the resulting tool representations are used for online query-time retrieval but the store is frozen (not grown at test time).
- **index structure topology**:
> Dependency GRAPH: tools are nodes, identified pairwise dependencies are edges. For ToolBench, APIs are first grouped by category and a separate dependency graph is built within each category group; for API-Bank a single graph over the tool set is built. (Connected-node proportion: 0.420 for API-Bank, 0.824 for ToolBench.)
- **retriever type**:
> dense (text-embedding based) retriever augmented with graph convolution. Base retrievers are dense text embedding models (Paraphrase MiniLM-L3-v2, ToolBench-IR); TGR refines their tool embeddings via GCN over the dependency graph. Word-frequency baselines (BM25, TF-IDF) are compared but not the proposed retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Two-part: (a) the dependency discriminator is trained with supervised contrastive/classification signal (3-class cross-entropy: a->b, no-dependency, a<-b) on similarity-style dependency labels, via 2-stage pretraining (LLM-generated balanced data) + finetuning (manually annotated imbalanced data with a category-specific average loss); (b) the retriever embeddings come from off-the-shelf or previously-task-finetuned encoders, and the graph convolution itself is PARAMETER-FREE (GCN trainable weights removed for efficiency). So TGR adds no new retriever-training signal beyond the dependency discriminator; it propagates dependency structure into embeddings without learning retrieval weights.
- **query construction**: Raw user query encoded into an embedding by the base text encoder; no decomposition, expansion, or thought-conditioning. Query-tool similarity over the dependency-updated tool embeddings yields the retrieval score.
- **query granularity**: task-level (one-shot at t=0): a single query embedding is matched against the candidate tool set per task.
- **when to retrieve**: one-shot (single retrieval pass per query, returning top-k tools before LLM planning).
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule (retrieve once per query at the start). No confidence/uncertainty/learned-router trigger.
- **reranking**:
> No separate learned reranking stage in the conventional sense. The dependency-aware effect is realized via graph convolution that updates tool embeddings before similarity ranking (i.e., dependency information is injected into representations, then a single descending similarity ranking is applied). This functions as a dependency-aware representation update rather than a post-hoc cross-encoder reranker.
- **retrieved context refinement**: none (retrieved tools are returned as a top-k list; no decompose/distill/compress/distractor-filtering step on the retrieved set). The refinement happens at the index/representation level (GCN over dependencies), not on the retrieved context.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Tool descriptions/documents are embedded by the base encoder: for ToolBench a structured document format (name, description, parameters) is used following Qin et al. (ToolBench); for API-Bank only the tool description is encoded (to mitigate query/tool-document domain mismatch). The key engineering is structural: dependency edges are added via a discriminator and folded into embeddings through graph convolution (not synthetic-query augmentation or weighted-field embeddings).
- **index content separation**: N/A (no progressive-disclosure / lightweight-index-then-content separation; tool embeddings are computed directly).
- **dynamic index and protocol**: Static tool index (offline-constructed dependency graph and embeddings). Tools/APIs originate from ToolBench (RapidAPI-derived) and API-Bank; no live MCP/RapidAPI auto-sync or CRUD synchronization is implemented. Graph construction is O(N^2), noted as a scalability limitation.
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> Yes -- this is the central contribution. Inter-tool dependencies are explicitly modeled: tool a depends on tool b if (1) a needs b's output as input, or (2) a needs b for prior verification (e.g., UpdateInfo depends on Login depends on Validate). A trained 3-class discriminator identifies directed pairwise dependencies, forming a tool dependency graph; graph convolution (parameter-free GCN, Kipf & Welling 2017) propagates dependency information so prerequisite tools with low query similarity get retrieved.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation: the retrieved top-k tools are provided to the LLM so it can build a tool-invoking plan and execute tool calls. TGR's own contribution stops at producing the top-k retrieval list; the downstream agent loop (plan -> invoke -> feedback -> respond) is standard and not modified.
- **planning integration**: retrieve-then-plan: a one-shot tool retrieval precedes LLM planning. The retrieved tools (now including prerequisite tools surfaced via dependency-aware retrieval) are passed to the LLM, which then creates and executes a tool-invoking plan. No interleaving with search/MCTS.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: per-answer (retrieval is a single up-front step per query; not interleaved per reasoning step or per tool-call).
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not a CBR/case-adaptation method).
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw tool documents/descriptions (tool name, description, parameters) returned as a ranked list of tools/APIs for prompt injection; underlying representation is a dense embedding refined by graph convolution.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Single tool/API (raw tool document level), not a distilled strategy, workflow, or trajectory. Dependency structure is captured at the representation level but the retrieved unit remains an individual tool.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Indirect: (1) a category-specific average training loss handles the severe class imbalance (dependencies are sparse) to avoid overfitting and reduce spurious dependency edges; (2) a 3-step validate-and-filter pipeline during pretraining-data construction discards tool pairs not meeting dependency criteria. There is no retrieved-context relevance evaluator or self-reflection at inference time; robustness against an inaccurate graph is limited by discriminator quality (acknowledged in Limitations).

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: graph (a static tool dependency graph). No episodic/skill/workflow/latent agent memory.
- **write back**: false; the system does not store new experiences/cases/skills at deployment. The dependency graph and embeddings are built offline and frozen.
- **online growth**: false; the retrievable store does not grow at test time. Graphs and tool embeddings are induced offline.
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back / no online memory writes).
- **failure experience usage**: N/A; no storage of success/failure trajectories. (The discriminator does learn from a 'no-dependency' negative class during training, but this is training-data balancing, not experiential failure memory.)
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (static graph; no post-write mutation, dedup, pruning, or evolution).
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No. Retrieval is similarity top-k over dependency-updated embeddings; it is not an RL/learned selection policy. The only learned component is the dependency discriminator (a classifier), and the graph convolution is parameter-free.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No; single-retriever / single-agent setting. The dependency graph is global over the tool set but is not described as shared across multiple agents or heterogeneous frameworks.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: API-Bank (311 test samples across 3 levels) and ToolBench (I1 level subset; I2/I3 left to future work due to cross-category graph complexity). TDI300K (constructed) is used to train the dependency discriminator; the discriminator test set is derived from API-Bank tools.
- **benchmark family**: tool (ToolBench, API-Bank).
- **baselines**:
> Word-frequency retrievers: BM25 (Robertson et al. 2009), TF-IDF (Ramos et al. 2003). Text-embedding retrievers: Paraphrase MiniLM-L3-v2 / PMLM-L3-v2 (Reimers & Gurevych 2019, API-Bank's retriever) and ToolBench-IR (Qin et al. 2023, ToolBench's finetuned retriever). TGR is applied on top of the two embedding retrievers (PMLM-L3-v2+TGR, ToolBench-IR+TGR).
- **key metrics**: Recall@5, Recall@10, NDCG@5, NDCG@10, Pass Rate@5, Pass Rate@10 (pass@k = fraction of queries whose full ground-truth tool set is within top-k). Discriminator quality also reported via Precision/Recall/F1.
- **headline result**:
> TGR consistently improves base retrievers and reaches SOTA. Strongest single result: on API-Bank, ToolBench-IR+TGR raises Recall@10 from 0.790 to 0.878 and Pass Rate@10 from 0.624 to 0.788 over ToolBench-IR; on ToolBench-I1, ToolBench-IR+TGR raises Recall@5 0.709->0.742, NDCG@5 0.791->0.811, Pass Rate@10 0.690->0.730.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Discriminator-built graph vs manually-annotated graph: +TGR-m outperforms +TGR-d on API-Bank for both encoders (e.g., ToolBench-IR+TGR-m Recall@10 0.893 vs +TGR-d 0.878; Pass Rate@10 0.817 vs 0.788), indicating graph quality bounds TGR and discriminator improvement is the key lever. (2) Graph density effect: recall increment (top-5) rises with tool dependency graph density across ToolBench categories, confirming dependencies drive gains and TGR is most effective for dependency-intensive tool sets. (3) Discriminator performance: Precision/Recall/F1 reported (valid 0.775/0.814/0.792; test 0.893/0.760/0.817). (4) Connected-node proportion analysis (API-Bank 0.420 vs ToolBench 0.824). (5) Case studies on API-Bank (GetUserToken prerequisite surfaced for DeleteAccount) and ToolBench (Get Today's Prediction surfaced).
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Yes -- intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k, NDCG@k) and a completeness metric (Pass Rate@k) are reported; the discriminator is separately evaluated with Precision/Recall/F1 and graph connectivity/density analyses. Evaluation is at the retrieval level (not full agent task-success end-to-end), so retrieval quality is effectively decoupled from downstream LLM execution.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Process/retrieval-quality oriented: metrics score retrieval correctness (recall, ranking via NDCG, completeness via Pass Rate) rather than final agent task completion. No end-to-end agent outcome (e.g., final answer success) is the primary metric; Pass Rate captures whether the full required tool set is retrieved, an intermediate-process proxy.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Efficiency-conscious design: graph convolution is made parameter-free (GCN trainable weights removed) to accelerate online retrieval; tool embeddings are precomputed offline so online cost is a similarity ranking. Main cost concern is graph construction at O(N^2) pairwise dependency checks (noted as a limitation, mitigable by prior filtering rules). No latency/throughput numbers or API-cost figures are reported.
- **context budget and selection count**: Fixed-k top-k selection: top-5 and top-10 settings evaluated. No adaptive/precision-driven k and no explicit token-budget cap on injected tools is reported.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> TDI300K (constructed dataset for tool dependency identification): format {<t_a,t_b>, y} with 3 classes (a->b, no-dependency, a<-b). Pretraining split is category-balanced 92,000 per class (~276K pairs), built via a 3-step LLM (gpt-3.5-turbo, 3 agents) pipeline over CodeSearchNet function implementations (extract tool document -> generate dependent tool document -> validate/filter). Finetuning split is manually constructed, category-imbalanced: 1,029 (a->b) / 33,365 (no-dependency) / 1,056 (a<-b), from open-source datasets/projects/libraries (incl. ToolBench training set, online shopping, OpenGL). Test set for the discriminator is manually annotated from API-Bank tools (60 / 500 / 60 per class). Answer verifiability: dependency labels are LLM-validated (pretraining) or human-annotated (finetuning/test). Discriminator difficulty signal: test F1 0.817.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> ToolBench / ToolLLM and its ToolBench-IR retriever (Qin et al. 2023); API-Bank (Li et al. 2023); Gorilla (Patil et al. 2023) as dominant semantic-similarity tool-retrieval baselines; GCN graph convolution (Kipf & Welling 2017); BERT-base-uncased (Devlin et al. 2019) as discriminator backbone; CodeSearchNet (Husain et al. 2019, 1.78M functions) as pretraining-data source; Sentence-BERT / Paraphrase MiniLM-L3-v2 (Reimers & Gurevych 2019); evaluation protocol following Qu et al. 2024.
- **contrasts with**:
> Dominant semantic-similarity tool retrievers that treat each tool independently (ToolBench-IR/Qin et al. 2023, Gorilla/Patil et al. 2023, API-Bank/Li et al. 2023) and thus omit low-similarity prerequisite tools; word-frequency retrievers BM25 and TF-IDF. TGR explicitly contrasts by modeling inter-tool dependencies via a graph and graph convolution.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use / tool retrieval). Sits in the tool-retrieval lineage that moves from independent semantic-similarity tool retrieval toward structure-aware retrieval, specifically introducing inter-tool dependency-graph modeling (graph-convolution-refined tool embeddings + a dependency identification dataset TDI300K) so prerequisite tools are recovered.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- venue

<a id="item-tool-de"></a>
### 119. Tool-DE (Tool-Document Expansion); with Tool-Embed and Tool-Rank. Paper title: "Tools are under-documented: Simple Document Expansion Boosts Tool Retrieval"

2025  ·  arXiv 2510.22670  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.22670)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **authors affiliation**:
> Xuan Lu, Haohang Huang, Rui Meng, Yaohui Jin, Wenjun Zeng, Xiaoyu Shen (corresponding). Affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Ningbo Key Laboratory of Spatial Intelligence and Digital Derivative; Institute of Digital Twin, Eastern Institute of Technology (EIT), Ningbo. Rui Meng noted working at Google Cloud AI Research.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.22670
- **code url**: https://github.com/EIT-NLP/Tool-DE (paper-listed; currently redirects to https://github.com/EIT-NLP/Tool-REX, the renamed maintained repo, ~10 stars, last pushed 2026-03)
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/EIT-NLP/Tool-REX (renamed maintained repo for the Tool-DE benchmark, models, and training corpora)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: tool-use (tool retrieval / tool selection for LLM tool-augmented agents); information retrieval (cs.IR)
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, single-stage tool retrieval (and second-stage reranking) over a large static tool repository given a user query. The setting is non-interactive and supervised: query-tool relevance labels from 35 unified tool-use datasets are used to train a dense retriever and an LLM reranker. The core problem is a data-centric one: tool documentation is incomplete (~41.6% of audited docs lack a clear functional statement or usage guidance) and heterogeneous (up to seven phrasings for the same function), causing a semantic gap between user queries and tool docs. The proposed fix enriches each tool document with LLM-generated structured fields (query-independent, query-agnostic) before indexing/training.
- **what is retrieved**: tools (tool/API documents). Retrieval targets enriched tool documentation (each tool doc augmented with a structured tool_profile containing function_description, when_to_use, limitations, tags; example_usage generated but excluded for retrieval after ablation).
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus: a fixed repository of ~43k tool documents (from ToolRet's 35 datasets) that is offline-expanded once with LLM-generated fields; no agent-written growing/episodic memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k ranking, but explicitly evaluated for multi-tool completeness: alongside NDCG@10 and Recall@10 they report Completeness@10 (C@K=1 only if ALL target tools for a query are in the top-K, else 0), targeting recovery of the complete needed set of tools per query rather than a single best tool.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based reasoning method): [Retrieve] partial (tool retrieval), [Reuse] N/A, [Revise] N/A, [Retain] N/A.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is a document-expansion / tool-retrieval framework.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: tool-API document (a single tool/function document), each enriched with a structured tool_profile object; the retrieval unit is the whole expanded tool document, not a sub-span.
- **index source**:
> Static corpus, offline-induced: built on ToolRet's 43k-tool corpus; tool docs are expanded once via an offline LLM pipeline (expansion -> judgement -> refinement -> human validation). Training corpora (50k for retriever, 200k for reranker) are also LLM-synthesized offline. No online/test-time index growth.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat vector index (dense embeddings) for the retriever; tool documents are structured internally into canonical/standardized fields (name, description, parameters, responses, method, category, example_usage, limitations) plus the added tool_profile, but the index itself is flat (no dependency graph or hierarchical category->tool topology used for retrieval).
- **retriever type**: hybrid coverage in experiments (sparse BM25s + dense embedding retrievers). The proposed model Tool-Embed is a dense retriever (fine-tuned Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B/4B); the second stage Tool-Rank is an LLM-based pointwise reranker (fine-tuned Qwen3-Reranker-4B).
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Contrastive on similarity labels for the dense retriever: Tool-Embed is trained with InfoNCE loss on 50k query-tool pairs, with 5 in-batch random negatives sampled from other queries (full-parameter tuning, 1 epoch, DeepSpeed ZeRO-3). Tool-Rank is trained with a cross-entropy (pointwise true/false relevance) objective on 200k query-tool pairs via LoRA (r=32, alpha=64, dropout 0.1), 1 epoch. No RL or interactive preference signal.
- **query construction**: Raw user query plus a task-specific query instruction (instruction-style query as provided by ToolRet). Queries are NOT expanded/rewritten; the novelty is document-side expansion. The query-side stays as given (raw input + instruction).
- **query granularity**: task-level (one-shot at retrieval time): a single query (with instruction) per retrieval task; no step/trajectory-level or two-level query construction.
- **when to retrieve**: one-shot (single retrieval pass per query), optionally followed by a single reranking pass over the top-100 candidates.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule / not applicable as a dynamic trigger: retrieval is performed once per query in a standard retrieve-then-rerank pipeline; there is no uncertainty- or confidence-based trigger and no agent-initiated retrieval request.
- **reranking**:
> Yes. Two-stage pipeline: a dense retriever (Tool-Embed-4B) produces an initial candidate set, then a reranker reorders the top-100 candidates. Proposed reranker Tool-Rank-4B is an LLM-based pointwise reranker that outputs true/false logits normalized into P(relevant|q,d) as the reranking score. Off-the-shelf rerankers (jina-reranker-m0, bge-reranker-v2-gemma, Qwen3-Reranker-4B) are also evaluated.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Document-side, pre-index refinement rather than post-retrieval: tool documents are enriched (document expansion) and canonicalized/standardized before indexing. Post-retrieval, a reranking stage refines ordering. No reason-in-documents distillation or distractor filtering of retrieved context is applied to the query-time results beyond reranking.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Core contribution: LLM-driven synthetic document expansion. Each raw tool doc is enriched with a structured tool_profile via Qwen3-32B (reasoning mode), generating function_description and tags (always) plus when_to_use, limitations, example_usage (only if explicitly supported by the doc; query-independent, strictly grounded, unsupported fields omitted). Faithfulness ensured by LLaMa-3.1-70B judgement, GPT-4o refinement, and human validation. After ablation, example_usage is dropped; function_description, when_to_use, limitations, tags are retained. Also includes canonicalization of heterogeneous raw field names into 8 unified fields (name, description, category, parameters, responses, method, example_usage, limitations). This is expanded-summary / synthetic-field augmentation, not raw docstring use.
- **index content separation**: No explicit lightweight-index-then-heavy-content (progressive disclosure) mechanism. The expanded document is embedded/indexed in full; there is no separation of a lightweight retrievable index from on-demand-loaded heavy content.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: Static index (offline-expanded, frozen). No live tool synchronization, no RapidAPI/RESTful/MCP/function-calling auto-sync CRUD (the paper contrasts itself with ScaleMCP's dynamic auto-synchronizing MCP tools but does not implement such live sync).
- **tool dependency awareness**: No. Retrieval does not model inter-tool dependencies (no dependency graph, bipartite KG, or dependency-aware reranking). Completeness@10 measures multi-tool coverage per query but tools are scored independently; prerequisite/output-feeds-input relations are not modeled.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Not used as in-context exemplars for downstream agent reasoning in this paper; retrieval/reranking is the end task. The enriched documents are used as (a) the indexed/retrievable content, (b) training signal for the retriever and reranker, and (c) the candidate documents scored by the reranker. Output is a ranked list of tools intended to be passed to a downstream tool-using agent (downstream agent usage is motivational, not evaluated here).
- **planning integration**: retrieve-then-(re)rank pipeline; not integrated into a multi-step planning/acting loop. Retrieval is the gateway to tool use but the paper evaluates retrieval quality in isolation (no MCTS/tree-search/per-step planning integration).
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: per-answer / per-query (single retrieval + single rerank pass per query); no per-CoT-step or per-tool-call interleaving. The reranker's prompt includes empty <think></think> tags (reasoning disabled) following Lu et al. 2025.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (no CBR case adaptation). The closest analogue is offline document refinement (GPT-4o regeneration for failing profiles), but retrieved items are not adapted to the query at inference.
- **retrieved item representation**: Structured note / enriched document: a tool document presented as the original documentation merged with a structured tool_profile (function_description, when_to_use, limitations, tags). Surface form is text JSON-style fields, not raw trajectories or executable programs.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Single tool documentation entry enriched to a standardized profile (a tool-API description with explicit functional, situational, and constraint signals). It is a document/tool-API unit, more abstract/standardized than a raw docstring but not a distilled multi-step strategy or workflow.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Pipeline-level faithfulness controls plus an emergent separability effect. (1) Construction-time: rule-based JSON validation + LLaMa-3.1-70B faithfulness judgement + GPT-4o refinement for the ~1.5% failing cases + human validation (100 sampled profiles, all passed), preventing hallucinated/unsupported fields. (2) Evaluation-time: document expansion lowers absolute similarity but asymmetrically (negatives drop more than positives), sharpening positive/negative separability and improving robustness of ranking. No retriever-aware distractor SFT beyond standard negative sampling.

**Memory & Learning**
