- **memory type**: none (static document store; no episodic / skill-library / procedural / graph / latent memory that grows from agent experience).
- **write back**: No. The system does not store new experiences/cases at deployment; the only writing is the one-time offline document expansion into the corpus and synthesis of training data.
- **online growth**: No. The retrievable store is frozen after offline document expansion; it does not grow during deployment/test time.
- **write back trigger**: Never (no runtime write-back). Document enrichment occurs once offline via the expansion->judgement->refinement->human-validation pipeline, not triggered by task success/failure or reflection at inference.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Not applicable / success-oriented only. No storage or retrieval of failed/negative agent experiences. The only failure handling is in the construction pipeline: profiles failing the judgement step (~1.5%) are regenerated/refined with GPT-4o. Training uses random negatives for contrastive learning but not stored failure trajectories.
- **memory evolution update**: Append-and-refine at construction time only: original doc is unioned with the generated tool_profile (d_expansion = d_original ∪ d_profile); failing profiles are refine-overwritten via GPT-4o. No post-deployment mutation of stored entries.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No (not an RL/learned-policy retrieval). Retrieval is similarity-based dense top-k (contrastively trained embedder) plus a pointwise relevance-classifier reranker; selection is not a sequential decision policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single static shared corpus consumed by retrievers/rerankers; no multi-agent or cross-framework experience sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> ToolRet (Shi et al. 2025) and Tool-DE (this paper's document-expanded benchmark built on ToolRet). Both span three domains: Web (APIs), Code (functions), Customized (apps). Tool-DE is built from 35 well-established tool-use datasets unified by ToolRet; ~7.6k retrieval tasks over ~43k tools. Released training corpora: Tool-Embed-Train (50k) and Tool-Rank-Train (200k).
- **benchmark family**: tool (tool retrieval): ToolRet / Tool-DE. Underlying source datasets include ToolBench, APIBank, MetaTool, ToolACE, Gorilla, CRAFT, TaskBench, ToolAlpaca, etc.
- **baselines**:
> Sparse: BM25s. Dense retrievers: GritLM-7B, NV-Embed-v1, gte-Qwen2-1.5B-instruct, e5-mistral-7b-instruct, Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B/4B/8B. LLM-based rerankers: jina-reranker-m0, bge-reranker-v2-gemma, Qwen3-Reranker-4B. Also the paper's own non-expansion-trained counterparts Tool-Embed_original-0.6B/4B and Tool-Rank_original-4B. Reference SoTA: Qwen3-Embedding-8B (MTEB open-source SoTA as of 2025-09-20).
- **key metrics**: NDCG@10 (N@10), Recall@10 (R@10), Completeness@10 (C@10, all-target-tools-in-top-K = 1 else 0). Reported per domain (Web/Code/Customized) and averaged.
- **headline result**:
> On Tool-DE, the full pipeline (Tool-Embed-4B retriever + Tool-Rank-4B reranker) achieves NDCG@10 = 56.44, Recall@10 = 67.81, Completeness@10 = 56.60 (Avg.), i.e., +10.23 / +10.29 / +9.08 over the MTEB open-source SoTA Qwen3-Embedding-8B. Tool-Rank-4B improves the first-stage Tool-Embed-4B by +4.21 NDCG@10 (52.23 -> 56.44).
- **ablations**:
> (1) Per-field Add-One vs One-Out analysis (GritLM dense + BM25s sparse, NDCG@10): example_usage gives smallest/often negative gains and even hurts GritLM; removing it (One-Out) raises N@10, so example_usage is excluded and function_description, when_to_use, limitations, tags are retained. function_description and tags are neutral-to-positive in Add-One and their removal causes notable drops in One-Out. (2) Document expansion as training signal: expansion-trained Tool-Embed-0.6B/4B gain +4.97/+6.69 over Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B baseline vs +3.69/+3.67 for non-expansion Tool-Embed_original; Tool-Rank gains +4.21 vs +2.00 for Tool-Rank_original. Gains persist even on non-expanded ToolRet test docs (generalization). (3) Evaluation-time similarity analysis (GritLM, 300 queries): expansion lowers similarities but negatives drop more than positives (e.g., Customized positives -0.0027 vs negatives -0.0152), sharpening separability. (4) Controlled toggle (fixed retrieval pool, switching expanded vs non-expanded document views) confirms removing expansions sharply attenuates reranker improvements. (5) Incompleteness audit: 41.6% of docs incomplete before expansion, dropping to 23.5% after.
- **evaluation decoupling**: Retrieval is the end task here, so all reported metrics are intrinsic IR metrics (NDCG@10, Recall@10, Completeness@10); there is no separate end-to-end downstream agent task metric. Thus retrieval quality is fully decoupled but no separate downstream task accuracy is reported.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Outcome (ranking quality) metrics only: NDCG/Recall/Completeness@10. No reasoning-faithfulness or step-wise process metrics (reranker reasoning is explicitly disabled with empty <think></think>).
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k evaluation at K=10 (NDCG/Recall/Completeness@10). Reranking operates on the top-100 retrieved candidates per query. Added context per tool is budget-light (avg +45.89 tokens via tool_profile; total avg expanded doc 177.61 tokens). Note the analysis flags truncation risk: longer expanded inputs can dilute salient signals / be truncated under retriever token budgets.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (this is a benchmark+framework+models paper, not a survey/taxonomy).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Tool-DE is LLM-synthesized document expansion applied on top of ToolRet: built from 35 well-established tool-use datasets, ~7.6k retrieval tasks over a ~43k-tool corpus, across Web/Code/Customized domains. Construction: four-stage pipeline (expansion via Qwen3-32B, judgement via LLaMa-3.1-70B, GPT-4o refinement for ~1.5%/~600 failing cases, human validation of 100 profiles all passing). Released training corpora: Tool-Embed-Train (50k retriever instances) and Tool-Rank-Train (200k reranker instances). Answer verifiability via labeled ground-truth target tools (NDCG/Recall/Completeness@10). Difficulty signal: best system (Tool-Embed-4B + Tool-Rank-4B) reaches only 56.44 NDCG@10 Avg., indicating substantial headroom.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> ToolRet benchmark (Shi et al. 2025) as the underlying corpus/datasets; Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B/4B (retriever base) and Qwen3-Reranker-4B (reranker base) (Zhang et al. 2025); InfoNCE contrastive training; ms-swift and LLaMA-Factory training frameworks; document/query expansion lineage (Query2doc, EnrichIndex). Reranking prompt follows Lu et al. 2025 (Rethinking reasoning in document ranking).
- **contrasts with**:
> Query-side / work-around approaches that do not fix documentation at the source: Re-Invoke (LLM pseudo-queries + intent extraction), EASYTOOL (restructure docs into concise instructions), MassTool (multi-task search-based retrieval with intent modeling), ScaleMCP (dynamic weighting of document segments), MCP-Zero, TURA. The paper argues these work around poor documentation, whereas Tool-DE fixes the root cause by standardizing and completing tool documentation via offline document expansion.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use): tool retrieval / tool-document engineering line. Sits in the 2024-2025 tool-retrieval sub-topic emphasizing tool_document_engineering (document expansion) and index standardization; descends from classic IR query/document expansion (Query2doc, EnrichIndex) applied to tool retrieval, contrasting with query-side expansion (Re-Invoke) and dynamic-index/MCP works (ScaleMCP, MCP-Zero).

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- cost_efficiency_tradeoff
- venue

<a id="item-tool-to-agent"></a>
### 120. Tool-to-Agent Retrieval: Bridging Tools and Agents for Scalable LLM Multi-Agent Systems

2025  ·  arXiv 2511.01854  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.01854)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2511.01854, cs.CL); not peer-reviewed. Submitted 3 Nov 2025, last revised 4 Nov 2025 (v2). DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2511.01854.
- **authors affiliation**:
> Elias Lumer, Faheem Nizar, Anmol Gulati, Pradeep Honaganahalli Basavaraju, and Vamse Kumar Subbiah. Affiliation: PricewaterhouseCoopers U.S.A. (PwC). The same author cluster (Lumer, Gulati, Subbiah, Basavaraju, Burke) authored ScaleMCP, Toolshed, Graph RAG-Tool Fusion, and MemTool, all from PwC.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.01854
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (no maintained leaderboard/paper-list released for this method; the benchmark it uses, LiveMCPBench, is maintained at https://icip-cas.github.io/LiveMCPBench by a separate group.)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: tool-use (LLM tool / MCP-server retrieval and routing) for multi-agent systems; large-scale tool / agent selection.
- **problem setting**:
> Inference-time, interactive multi-agent setting. A top-level assistant orchestrates specialized sub-agents, each of which is an MCP server bundling dozens to thousands of tools. Given a user query (or its decomposed sub-steps), the system must route to the right entity: a specific tool when the query is fine-grained, or an entire agent/MCP bundle when broader capability helps. The authors argue existing pipelines force a brittle two-stage choice: agent-first routing (match coarse agent descriptions, then operate within that agent, hiding relevant tools) vs tool-only retrieval (ignores complementary tools in the same bundle). No LLM fine-tuning; off-the-shelf embedding models are used. Supervision for evaluation is the ground-truth tool-agent mapping per (sub-)step in LiveMCPBench; the retriever itself is not trained. The tool/agent store is static (the 70-server / 527-tool LiveMCPBench catalog).
- **what is retrieved**: tools and agents: individual tool names/descriptions AND their parent agents (MCP servers), both embedded in one shared space and linked by metadata (tool -> owner agent).
- **retrieval grounding**: STATIC external corpus: a unified tool-agent catalog built offline over MCP server names/descriptions and their tool names/descriptions (LiveMCPBench: 70 MCP servers, 527 tools). It is not a growing/episodic memory the agent writes to during task execution.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Top-K ranking objective (top-K unique agents), but reformulated for completeness/coverage of the needed agents on multi-step tasks: tool-level retrieval feeds a top-N candidate list which is then traversed to parent agents and de-duplicated to top-K unique agents. The goal is to surface the correct agent(s)/MCP server(s) for each sub-step (each question averages 1.40 MCP agents and 2.82 tools across 2.68 steps), evaluated with Recall/mAP/nDCG @{1,3,5} rather than a fixed single-tool top-1.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based reasoning method; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain case cycle - it retrieves static tool/agent metadata, not problem-solution cases).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False - the work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner; it is framed as retrieval/routing for tool-and-agent selection.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: tool-API and agent: a single tool (name + description, an API call/function/action) OR an entire agent/MCP server (name + description bundling a coherent toolset). Tools are linked to their owning agent via metadata edges in a bipartite tool-agent graph G=(A,T,E).
- **index source**:
> Static, offline-constructed unified store. The tool-agent catalog C is composed of a tool corpus C_T (tool names/descriptions, each carrying owner(T)=A metadata) and an agent corpus C_A (agent names/descriptions as parent nodes). Built once over the LiveMCPBench catalog; not induced online/test-time.
- **index structure topology**:
> Bipartite graph / hierarchical (agent -> owned tools) layered on top of a joint flat vector index. Tools and agents share one vector space; explicit ownership edges (tool -> parent agent) enable traversal from a retrieved tool up to its executable agent. Modeled as a bipartite graph G=(A,T,E) with E = ownership relations.
- **retriever type**:
> Hybrid: dense vector retrieval combined with lexical BM25 over the unified tool-agent catalog (semantic + lexical matching for recall). Evaluated across 8 embedding models (Vertex AI text-embedding-005, Gemini Embedding 001, Amazon Titan embed text v1/v2, OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 / 3-small / 3-large, all-MiniLM-L6-v2).
- **retriever learning signal**: None (off-the-shelf): the retriever uses pretrained embedding models plus BM25 with no contrastive training, LM-feedback, preference learning, or RL of the retriever. The novelty is the indexing/traversal design (joint tool-agent space + metadata links), not a trained retriever.
- **query construction**:
> Two evaluated paradigms: (1) Direct Querying - the user's high-level question is used directly as the retrieval query without preprocessing; (2) Step-wise Querying - the query is decomposed into a sequence of sub-tasks, each submitted independently to the retriever (the primary setting in the evaluation). The retriever input may be the original query, the decomposed sub-steps, or a combination. Query rewriting is cited as a complementary lever.
- **query granularity**: Both task-level (Direct Querying, one query for the whole task) and step/sub-task-level (Step-wise Querying, one query per decomposed sub-step). Step-wise is the primary setting; it constructs a query per sub-step so different agents can be retrieved across a multi-step workflow.
- **when to retrieve**: Iterative (step-wise) in the primary setting: retrieval is performed once per decomposed sub-step. In the Direct Querying variant it is one-shot at the task level. Retrieval is decoupled from generation and run before equipping the chosen tool/agent.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed schedule: retrieval fires deterministically per query / per decomposed sub-step (one retrieval call per step in step-wise mode). It is not gated by token-level confidence, attention/uncertainty, a learned complexity classifier, reflection tokens, or an explicit agent-initiated request.
- **reranking**:
> Two-stage selection acting as a rerank/aggregation: retrieve top-N (N >> K) entities from the joint catalog by hybrid similarity, then map each tool hit to its parent agent (metadata traversal), aggregate, and select the top-K unique agents (Algorithm 1). This tool->agent owner-aggregation is the reranking-equivalent step; no learned cross-encoder or RRF reranker is described.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Selection/de-duplication via tool-to-agent traversal: from the top-N ranked entities, owner-map each retrieved tool to its agent, skip entries with missing/undefined owners, and keep only top-K unique agents. No reason-in-documents distillation, compression, or distractor-filtering classifier beyond this de-duplication.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Modest: tool entries are indexed from tool names + descriptions with explicit owner(T)=A parent-agent metadata; agent entries from agent names + descriptions. No synthetic-query augmentation or weighted-field embeddings are applied in this method (the related ScaleMCP's Tool Document Weighted Average / TDWA and synthetic-question augmentation are cited but not the core lever here). The key engineering is the dual tool-corpus + agent-corpus indexing and tool->agent ownership links.
- **index content separation**:
> Partial / by design: a lightweight retrievable index entry (tool/agent name + description + owner metadata) is separated from the heavier executable agent context (authentication, parameter inference, access policies) maintained at the agent level and resolved via traversal when an entity is selected. This is a progressive-disclosure-flavored separation but not explicitly framed as an SOP-index-then-content scheme.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Protocol: Model Context Protocol (MCP) - agents are MCP servers and tools are their exposed functions/API calls. The index as evaluated is a STATIC offline catalog over LiveMCPBench (no live CRUD auto-synchronization in this paper; auto-sync is the contribution of the cited sibling ScaleMCP, not of Tool-to-Agent Retrieval).
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> Partial: the method models tool->agent OWNERSHIP relations as a bipartite graph (G=(A,T,E)) and traverses them, and motivates retaining agent context (authentication, parameter inference, access policies) and cross-connected operations within a server. But it does not model inter-tool data-flow dependencies (output-of-A feeds B) or build a tool-prerequisite dependency graph; the modeled relation is tool-to-parent-agent ownership, not tool-to-tool dependency.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Routing / prompt augmentation: the retrieved top-K agents (and, where the query is fine-grained, the specific tool) are returned to equip the LLM agent for execution - deciding what to equip (a single tool vs an entire agent bundle) in one pass. The paper evaluates the retrieval stage (Recall/mAP/nDCG) rather than downstream task execution.
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-route within a hierarchical multi-agent pipeline: a unified one-pass retrieval narrows to top-K agents/tools, then the system routes (equips a tool or an agent). Under step-wise querying, retrieval interleaves with the query decomposition (one retrieval per sub-step), aligning with reasoning-based retrieval-planning. It is not embedded inside MCTS/tree search.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per sub-task / per decomposed step (step-wise querying): retrieval is woven in at the granularity of each decomposed sub-goal of the query. In the Direct Querying variant it is per-answer (one retrieval for the whole task). Not per-CoT-token.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (no CBR case adaptation; retrieved tool/agent metadata is used as-is for routing/equipping).
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Structured tool / agent metadata: the surface form is tool names + descriptions (and their owner-agent links) and agent names + descriptions. Not a distilled strategy, free-text workflow, executable program, or latent token; the retrieved entity is a tool or an executable agent reference.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Two coexisting abstraction levels in one space: fine-grained tool/API capability descriptions AND coarser agent/MCP-server bundle descriptions. The method deliberately spans both - procedural tool specification at the low level and an agent-bundle capability summary at the high level - bridged by ownership links.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Context-dilution mitigation by design: jointly indexing tools and agents (rather than chunking many tools into one coarse agent description) preserves fine-grained tool semantics while retaining agent context; metadata traversal recovers the executable agent without collapsing tools into a single diluted summary. No retriever-aware training, relevance evaluator, or distractor-aware SFT is used; robustness is structural (joint linked index) rather than learned.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (static external tool-agent catalog/index; no episodic, skill-library, workflow, procedural, or latent memory written by the agent). The store is a fixed, structured knowledge base of tools and agents.
- **write back**: False - the system does not store new experiences/cases/skills from execution. The catalog is built offline from the MCP server/tool descriptions; no agent write-back of trajectories or outcomes is described.
- **online growth**: No: the retrievable store is frozen after offline catalog construction. (The cited sibling work ScaleMCP adds CRUD auto-synchronization with MCP servers, but Tool-to-Agent Retrieval as evaluated uses the static LiveMCPBench catalog and does not grow from deployment experience.)
- **write back trigger**: Never: no experience/case write-back occurs. Any catalog change would be external re-indexing of tool/agent metadata, not triggered by task success or failure during deployment.
- **failure experience usage**: None: failed or negative experiences are not stored or retrieved; the method maintains no success-vs-failure case memory and learns no corrective rules. It is a static retrieval method, not an experience-accumulating one.
- **memory evolution update**: Append-only at the index level at most (catalog can be rebuilt/extended with new tool/agent metadata); stored entries are not mutated, merged, refined, or pruned by the system from experience. No experience-driven evolution.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No: retrieval is a fixed hybrid (BM25 + dense) similarity ranking followed by deterministic top-N -> parent-agent traversal -> top-K unique-agent selection (Algorithm 1). It is not a learned/RL-optimized retrieval/selection policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Partial / by design at the catalog level: the unified tool-agent index spans many MCP servers (agents) and is shared across the multi-agent system for routing, so all agents draw from one common linked store. However, there is no sharing of learned experience/memory across agents - the shared object is a static retrieval catalog, not accumulated episodic memory.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> LiveMCPBench (Mo et al., 2025, arXiv:2508.01780): 70 MCP servers, 527 tools, and 95 real-world questions annotated with step-by-step breakdowns and relevant tool-agent mappings (avg 2.68 steps, 2.82 tools, 1.40 MCP agents per question). An additional agent-only baseline dataset (MCP server names + descriptions only) is constructed to isolate the contribution of tool-level information.
- **benchmark family**: tool (MCP tool/agent retrieval; LiveMCPBench - 'an ocean of MCP tools'). Repurposes a multi-server tool-use benchmark for intrinsic retrieval evaluation.
- **baselines**:
> BM25; Q.Retrieval (query/agent-only dense retrieval baseline); MCPZero (MCP-Zero, Fei et al. 2025, arXiv:2506.01056, active tool discovery / agent-first routing); ScaleMCP (Lumer et al. 2025, arXiv:2505.06416, dynamic auto-synchronizing MCP tool retriever). MCPZero and ScaleMCP are the previous state-of-the-art agent retrievers compared against.
- **key metrics**: Recall@K, mean Average Precision (mAP@K), and normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (nDCG@K) for K in {1,3,5}. Retrieval accuracy = retrieved agents vs ground-truth agents per (sub-)query. No downstream task-success metric is reported (retrieval-stage evaluation only).
- **ablations**:
> Embedding-model sweep (Table 2): per-embedding comparison vs MCPZero across 8 models, all showing gains - strongest on Amazon Titan v2 (Recall@5 0.66 -> 0.85, +28% relative) and even compact all-MiniLM-L6-v2 +13%; very stable improvements (std 0.02 Recall@5, 0.01 nDCG@5 vs MCPZero), indicating architecture-agnostic gains driven by the unified indexing rather than a specific embedding. Agent-only-vs-joint analysis: an agent-only baseline dataset isolates tool-level contribution; the authors report 39.13% of retrieved top-K items came from the agent corpus C_A and 34.44% of matched top-K tools also traced back to C_A, evidencing the lift is from the joint tool+agent index, not tool retrieval alone. Query-paradigm comparison: Direct vs Step-wise Querying (step-wise is primary). No separate component-removal of BM25 vs dense is tabulated.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Fully decoupled to the intrinsic retrieval side: only intrinsic IR metrics (Recall@K, mAP@K, nDCG@K) are reported; the work evaluates the retrieval/routing stage in isolation and does NOT report end-to-end downstream task success (e.g., LiveMCPBench's LLM-as-Judge task-success). So there is no end-to-end metric to decouple from - it is retrieval-metric-only.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Process-level retrieval quality only: step-wise (sub-step-level) retrieval accuracy via Recall/mAP/nDCG. No final task-outcome metric and no reasoning-faithfulness scoring; evaluation targets step-level retrieval correctness against annotated tool-agent mappings.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (method/system paper, not a survey or taxonomy).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Not a benchmark-contribution paper. It reuses LiveMCPBench (70 MCP servers, 527 tools, 95 human-annotated real-world questions with step-by-step tool-agent mappings; avg 2.68 steps / 2.82 tools / 1.40 agents per question) and additionally derives an agent-only variant (MCP server names + descriptions only) to isolate tool-level information. Best system here (Tool-to-Agent) reaches Recall@5 0.83 / nDCG@5 0.46, leaving substantial headroom, signaling the retrieval task remains hard.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> ScaleMCP (Lumer et al. 2025, arXiv:2505.06416) and Toolshed / RAG-Tool Fusion (Lumer et al. 2024, arXiv:2410.14594) and Graph RAG-Tool Fusion (Lumer et al. 2025, arXiv:2502.07223) by the same PwC team; MCP-Zero (Fei et al. 2025) for agent-first active tool discovery; classic RAG (Gao et al. 2024 survey) and BM25 (Robertson & Zaragoza 2009) + hybrid semantic-lexical retrieval (Kuzi et al. 2020); graph/KG-augmented retrieval (Think-on-Graph, Graph CoT, HybridRAG, KG+LLM roadmap, Graph-RAG survey). Evaluated on LiveMCPBench (Mo et al. 2025).
- **contrasts with**:
> Agent-first / hierarchical pipelines that match a brief agent description then operate only within that agent (e.g., MCP-Zero, hierarchical MCP-server-then-tool routing) - which can hide relevant fine-grained tools; tool-only retrieval that treats each tool independently and ignores the surrounding agent bundle (e.g., Toolshed/ToolRet-style top-k tool retrieval); ScaleMCP and Q.Retrieval as agent-level retrievers; graph-only tool organizers (ToolNet, ControlLLM); iterative tool retrieval (ToolReAGT, ProTIP). The contrast is explicitly the brittle two-stage tool-only-vs-agent-first choice versus a single joint linked space.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use), MCP-era tool/agent retrieval lineage from the PwC team (Toolshed/RAG-Tool Fusion -> Graph RAG-Tool Fusion -> ScaleMCP / MemTool -> Tool-to-Agent Retrieval). It advances scalable tool retrieval from tool-only or agent-only routing toward a unified, metadata-linked tool+agent vector space for multi-agent orchestration, descending from Gorilla/ToolLLM-style API-doc retrieval and classic RAG, and intersecting graph-based tool organization.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- code_url
- context_budget_and_selection_count
- cost_efficiency_tradeoff
- headline_result

<a id="item-toolret"></a>
### 121. ToolRet (Tool Retrieval benchmark). Paper title: "Retrieval Models Aren't Tool-Savvy: Benchmarking Tool Retrieval for Large Language Models"

2025  ·  ACL 2025 Findings  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.01763)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2025 (ACL 2025 Findings), pp. 24497-24524. Also arXiv:2503.01763 (cs.CL/cs.AI/cs.IR), submitted 3 Mar 2025, last revised 26 May 2025.
- **authors affiliation**:
> Zhengliang Shi (Shandong University), Yuhan Wang (Shandong University), Lingyong Yan (Baidu Inc.), Pengjie Ren (Shandong University), Shuaiqiang Wang (Baidu Inc.), Dawei Yin (Baidu Inc.), Zhaochun Ren (Leiden University, corresponding author). Primary affiliations: Shandong University (Qingdao, China), Baidu Inc. (Beijing, China), Leiden University (Leiden, The Netherlands).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.01763
- **code url**: https://github.com/mangopy/tool-retrieval-benchmark (official ACL 2025 code; ~211 stars, Apache-2.0, last pushed 2025-12; evaluation + training scripts)
- **maintained repo url**:
> https://github.com/mangopy/tool-retrieval-benchmark and leaderboard at https://huggingface.co/spaces/mangopy/ToolRet-leaderboard ; demo at https://huggingface.co/spaces/mangopy/ToolRet-demo ; datasets at https://huggingface.co/collections/mangopy/tool-retrieval ; project website https://mangopy.github.io/tool-retrieval-benchmark/

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: tool-use (tool retrieval / tool selection for LLM tool-augmented agents); information retrieval (cs.IR). This is a benchmark paper evaluating IR models on the tool-retrieval step that precedes tool invocation by LLM agents.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, non-interactive, single-stage tool retrieval (plus optional reranking) over a large static tool corpus given a user query, formatted as an MTEB/BEIR-style IR task (query -> target tools as labels). Supervision: query-tool relevance labels collected and standardized from 30+ existing tool-use datasets. The paper argues that prior tool-use benchmarks unrealistically pre-annotate a small set of 10-20 candidate tools per task, whereas real toolsets are massive (e.g., RapidAPI >52k tools, PyPI >600k packages); ToolRet instead requires retrieving from a 43k-tool corpus. It also supports an instructional-IR setting where each query is paired with an LLM-generated instruction. A companion 200k-instance training set (ToolRet-train) is contributed to fine-tune IR retrievers.
- **what is retrieved**: tools (tool / API documents). Each retrieval task's labels are the target tool(s); a tool is a unique identifier paired with documentation (name, description, parameters) describing its functionality. Spans web APIs, code functions, and customized-app tools.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus: a fixed corpus of 43,215 tools (~43k) merged/deduplicated from 34 source datasets. No agent-written growing/episodic memory; the store is frozen for evaluation (authors note they will maintain/update the benchmark over time, but it is not online-growing at inference).
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k ranking objective, but explicitly evaluated for multi-tool completeness: in addition to NDCG@K / Recall@K / Precision@K they report Completeness@K (C@K, adopted from DUMP/Qu et al. 2024), which is 1 only if ALL target tools for a query appear in the top-K and 0 otherwise. ToolRet emphasizes that solving a task often needs a combination of multiple tools (avg ~ multiple targets per task), so recovering the complete needed set is a first-class objective alongside ranking.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based reasoning method). [Retrieve] N/A-as-CBR (the paper studies tool Retrieve mechanically but not as CBR), [Reuse] N/A, [Revise] N/A, [Retain] N/A.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is a tool-retrieval benchmark + training dataset.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: tool-API document (a single tool / function / app entry). Each unit is one tool identified by a unique id and paired with detailed documentation (avg tool documentation length 174.56 tokens); the retrieval unit is the whole tool document, not a sub-span.
- **index source**:
> Static corpus, offline-induced: 43k-tool corpus aggregated, cleaned (deduplication, text normalization), sampled (K-means clustering with NV-Embed-v1 embeddings for task sampling; manual merge of overlapping toolsets), and frozen. Source datasets collected Aug 2023 - Dec 2024 from AI-conference benchmarks (ACL/NeurIPS), IR/NLP resource tracks (CIKM/EMNLP, e.g., ToolLens, AppBench), and open-source platforms (HuggingFace). The ToolRet-train (200k) corpus is likewise offline-induced from ToolACE, APIGen, and ToolBench training splits. No online/test-time growth.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat (MTEB/BEIR-style) retrieval index: each task is a query against a flat corpus of tool documents; relevance is judged independently per tool. The benchmark additionally provides a format-based categorization of tools/tasks into three subsets (Web APIs, Code Functions, Customized Apps) for analysis, but this is a partitioning for reporting, not a hierarchical/graph retrieval topology. No dependency graph or category->tool tree is used for retrieval.
- **retriever type**:
> Benchmark evaluates multiple types (BM25 sparse, dense single-task retrievers, multi-task embedding models, LLM-based embedding models, and re-ranking models) -> hybrid coverage across six model categories. ToolRet itself is model-agnostic (a benchmark). The contributed fine-tuning recipe (ToolRet-train) trains dense embedding / instruction-tuned retrievers via contrastive learning.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> For the benchmark: none for off-the-shelf models (BM25, MS-MARCO-trained dense models, multi-task embedders are evaluated as-is). For the contributed ToolRet-train fine-tuning: contrastive on similarity labels - each query paired with target tools (positives) and 10 hard negatives retrieved by NV-Embed-v1; the IR model is optimized by maximizing log-likelihood of target tools over positives+negatives (InfoNCE-style softmax over sim(I (+) q, tool)), with K=10 negatives and learning rate 5e-5. Instruction is concatenated to the query with a special token during training. No RL or interactive-preference signal.
- **query construction**:
> Raw user query, optionally augmented with an LLM-generated instruction (instructional-IR setting). Instructions are produced by a target-aware strategy: 3 human experts handcraft 100 seed instructions, then GPT-4o generates an instruction per task via in-context learning (sampling seed + generated examples for diversity); the instruction bridges query intent and target-tool functionality (e.g., 'Given an <audio transcription> task, retrieve tools that process audio inputs to produce accurate textual transcriptions...'). Two evaluation settings: w/o inst. (query only) and w/ inst. (query (+) instruction). Queries are not decomposed into sub-queries.
- **query granularity**: task-level (one-shot at retrieval time): one query (optionally with one instruction) per retrieval task; no step-level, trajectory-level, or two-level query construction.
- **when to retrieve**: one-shot (single retrieval pass per query), optionally followed by a single reranking pass for the re-ranking model category.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed schedule / not applicable as a dynamic trigger: retrieval is performed exactly once per query in a standard retrieve(-then-rerank) IR protocol; there is no uncertainty/confidence-based trigger, reflection token, or agent-initiated retrieval request (the agent's end-to-end pass rate is measured downstream but retrieval timing is fixed).
- **reranking**:
> Yes - re-ranking models form one of the evaluated categories. Cross-encoder / LLM-based rerankers (MonoT5 / castorini/monot5-base-msmarco, jina-reranker-v2-base-multilingual, BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-gemma, BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3, mixedbread-ai/mxbai-rerank-large-v1) re-rank the top candidates from a first-stage retriever (e.g., NV-Embed-v1). Key finding: reranking gives limited or even negative gains (MonoT5 reranking NV-Embed-v1 candidates DROPS avg NDCG@10 from 33.83 to 28.92).
- **retrieved context refinement**: rerank only (optional). The benchmark protocol applies an optional cross-encoder / LLM reranking stage over first-stage candidates; no decompose-then-recompose, reason-in-documents distillation, distractor filtering, or compression of retrieved tools is part of the benchmark.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Minimal / raw documentation on the corpus side: tools are indexed using their original (cleaned, normalized) docstrings/parameters; no synthetic-query augmentation or expanded summaries of tool docs is applied to the corpus. The engineering effort is on the QUERY side: a GPT-4o target-aware strategy generates an instruction per task (seeded by 100 expert-handcrafted instructions) to support instructional retrieval; instructions describe target-tool functionality to bridge query intent and tools.
- **index content separation**: No. Each tool is indexed/retrieved with its full documentation; there is no lightweight-index-then-heavy-content (progressive disclosure / SOP-index-then-content) separation.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Static index (offline-built, frozen per benchmark version; authors plan periodic manual updates). No live tool synchronization and no RapidAPI/RESTful/MCP/function-calling auto-sync CRUD integration; downstream tool invocation is via the source datasets' protocols (e.g., ToolBench/RapidAPI-derived tools) but the benchmark index itself is not live-synchronized.
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> No. Retrieval scores each tool independently; no inter-tool dependency modeling (no dependency graph, bipartite KG, or dependency-aware reranking). Completeness@K measures whether all needed tools are retrieved, but prerequisite/output-feeds-input relations between tools are not modeled.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> (1) As the end task being measured (ranked list of tools, scored by intrinsic IR metrics). (2) Downstream: retrieved top tools are fed as the candidate toolset (prompt augmentation) to tool-use LLMs (GPT-3.5, ToolLLaMA) which then select/invoke tools; the paper measures how retrieval quality changes the end-to-end task pass rate. (3) The 200k ToolRet-train data is used as a training signal to fine-tune IR retrievers.
- **planning integration**:
> retrieve-then-act / retrieve-then-plan as a gateway: tool retrieval is the initial step that supplies the candidate toolset to a downstream tool-use agent; the benchmark evaluates retrieval in isolation and also measures its effect on the agent's end-to-end pass rate (pilot study on ToolBench shows replacing officially annotated tools with retrieved tools substantially drops agent performance). No MCTS/tree-search or per-step interleaved retrieval is part of the benchmark.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: per-answer / per-query (one retrieval pass per task, optionally one rerank pass); no per-CoT-step, per-sentence/token, or per-tool-call interleaving within a rollout.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (no CBR case adaptation). Retrieved tools are passed verbatim as candidate documents/toolset to the downstream agent; there is no inference-time adaptation/revision of retrieved items.
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw structured tool documentation: each retrieved item is the tool's documentation as text (name, description, parameters/JSON-style fields), e.g., the 'availability' tool doc with parameters. Not a distilled strategy, free-text workflow, executable program, or latent token.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Single tool documentation entry (a tool/API description). It is a single retrievable item (one tool), more concrete than a distilled strategy or reusable workflow; the unit is the functional documentation of one executable tool.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Benchmark-level rather than method-level. (1) Quality control of construction: human-expert review of generated instructions (5 experts, Cohen's Kappa 0.743; 90.1% relevant, 92.3% describe target-tool features, 5.9% hallucination) with revision of low-quality instructions. (2) The paper discusses the one-to-many / overlapping-functionality risk (similar tools across merged datasets) and argues evaluation remains reliable because real-world scenarios pick the single most appropriate tool and tools differ in fine-grained parameters/scope. The contributed training recipe uses hard negatives (NV-Embed-v1-mined) to teach fine-grained discrimination. No retriever-aware distractor-SFT or self-reflection relevance evaluator is proposed.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (static tool corpus; no episodic / skill-library / workflow / procedural / graph / latent memory that grows from agent experience).
- **write back**: No. ToolRet is a frozen evaluation benchmark; the system does not store new experiences/cases/skills at inference. (The only 'writing' is offline corpus/training-set construction and the authors' stated intent to manually update the benchmark over future versions.)
- **online growth**: No. The retrievable corpus is frozen after offline construction; it does not grow during deployment/test time (the authors note manual maintenance/updates across benchmark versions, but not automatic online growth).
- **write back trigger**: Never (no runtime write-back). Corpus and training data are built once offline (collection -> cleaning -> sampling -> instruction generation -> human validation); no task-success/failure/reflection event triggers a write at inference.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success-oriented / not applicable for memory. No storage or retrieval of failed agent trajectories. In the ToolRet-train fine-tuning recipe, hard NEGATIVE tools (mined by NV-Embed-v1) are used as contrastive negatives, but these are negative documents for contrastive learning, not stored failure experiences.
- **memory evolution update**: Append-only at construction time (datasets merged, deduplicated, normalized into the corpus; benchmark intended to be appended/updated across versions). No post-deployment mutation, dedup-merge at runtime, delta-update, or forget-prune of stored entries.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No (not an RL / learned-policy retrieval). Retrieval is standard similarity-based top-k (off-the-shelf or contrastively fine-tuned dense/sparse retrievers) with optional cross-encoder reranking; selection is not a sequential decision policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. A single shared static corpus is consumed by individual retrievers/agents; no multi-agent or cross-framework experience sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> ToolRet (this paper): 7,615 retrieval tasks (Web API 4,916; Code Function 950; Customized App 1,749) over a 43,215-tool corpus (Web API 36,978; Code Function 3,794; Customized App 2,443); avg query/instruction length 46.87/43.43 tokens, avg tool doc length 174.56 tokens. Aggregated from 30+ (34 merged) existing tool-use datasets, e.g., ToolBench, ToolACE, APIGen, COLT, ToolEyes, AppBench, ToolLens, etc. Companion training set ToolRet-train: 205,826 tasks (avg 2.31 target tools, 5 negatives/query). Downstream agent eval on ToolBench (pass rate). Comparison/reference IR benchmarks: MTEB, BEIR, HotpotQA, MS-MARCO, Natural Questions.
- **benchmark family**: tool (tool retrieval): ToolRet. Built on tool-use source datasets including ToolBench, ToolACE, APIGen, COLT, ToolEyes, AppBench, ToolLens. Downstream agent benchmark family: tool (ToolBench).
- **baselines**:
> Six types of IR models. Sparse: BM25s. Single-task dense (MS-MARCO-trained): gtr (gtr-t5-base/large), contriever (contriever-msmarco), colbertv2.0, plus COLT (an ad-hoc tool-retrieval-trained model). Multi-task embedding models: all-MiniLM-L6-v2, e5-small/base/large-v2, bge-base/large-en-v1.5, gte-base/large-en-v1.5. LLM-based / instruction-tuned embedding models: e5-mistral-7b-instruct, gte-Qwen2-1.5B-instruct, NV-Embed-v1, GritLM-7B. Re-ranking models: MonoT5 (monot5-base-msmarco), jina-reranker-v2-base-multilingual, bge-reranker-v2-gemma, bge-reranker-v2-m3, mxbai-rerank-large-v1. Downstream tool-use LLMs: GPT-3.5, ToolLLaMA.
- **key metrics**:
> Intrinsic IR metrics at K (mainly K=10): NDCG@K (N@K, ranking quality), Recall@K (R@K), Precision@K (P@K), and Completeness@K (C@K from DUMP; 1 iff all target tools are in top-K else 0). Reported per subset (Web / Code / Customized) and averaged, under w/o inst. and w/ inst. settings. Downstream: end-to-end task pass rate of tool-use LLMs (GPT-3.5, ToolLLaMA) on ToolBench.
- **headline result**:
> Even the best model NV-Embed-v1 - strong on conventional IR benchmarks - achieves only NDCG@10 = 33.83 (Avg.) on ToolRet, revealing that retrieval models are not 'tool-savvy'. Low retrieval quality degrades the downstream tool-use LLM pass rate (positive correlation between Recall@10 and agent pass rate). Reranking helps little or hurts (MonoT5 re-ranking NV-Embed-v1 drops avg NDCG@10 33.83 -> 28.92). Fine-tuning IR models on the contributed 200k ToolRet-train substantially improves NDCG@10 and lifts downstream pass rate for both GPT-3.5 and ToolLLaMA.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Two settings w/o inst. vs w/ inst.: all IR models improve when the query is paired with the generated instruction; instruction-tuned embedders (NV-Embed-v1, e5-mistral) gain the most, evidencing the value of instructions + instruction-following capability. (2) Reranking ablation: cross-encoder/LLM rerankers give limited or negative gains - MonoT5 lowers avg NDCG@10 from 33.83 to 28.92; mxbai-rerank shows a similar trend; bge-reranker-v2-gemma yields only +4.7% Completeness@10. (3) ToolRet vs conventional IR (MTEB) correlation analysis (Fig. 5): the two benchmarks share a trend but ToolRet is harder, attributed to lower query-tool lexical (ROUGE-L) overlap and a task shift from information-seeking to tool retrieval. (4) Training ablation: removing the instruction I from the contrastive loss still beats non-tuned counterparts but underperforms the instruction-tuned version, validating instructional training data. (5) Complexity analysis: ToolRet requires recalling more target tools and has lower query-target lexical overlap than HotpotQA/MTEB, demanding stronger semantic representation.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Yes - strongly decoupled. Intrinsic retrieval metrics (NDCG@10, Recall@10, Precision@10, Completeness@10) are reported separately, and the impact of retrieval on the end-to-end tool-use task pass rate (GPT-3.5, ToolLLaMA on ToolBench) is analyzed separately, with the correlation between retrieval quality (e.g., Recall@10) and downstream pass rate explicitly studied (Figure 1).
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome metrics: ranking-quality IR metrics (NDCG/Recall/Precision/Completeness@10) for the retrieval task and end-to-end task pass rate for the downstream agent. No step-wise reasoning-faithfulness or intermediate trajectory-quality metric (the 'process' studied is the retrieval step's effect on the final agent outcome, not per-step reasoning quality).
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k evaluation, primarily K=10 (N@10/P@10/R@10/C@10). Motivated by the limited context length of tool-use LLMs, which cannot fit the full 43k toolset, hence the need to retrieve a small top-k candidate set for the agent. Avg query/instruction length 46.87/43.43 tokens; avg tool doc 174.56 tokens. ToolRet-train uses K=10 mined negatives during fine-tuning. No adaptive/precision-driven variable-size selection is proposed.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (this is a benchmark + training-dataset paper, not a survey/taxonomy).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Transformed/aggregated + LLM-augmented construction. ToolRet is built by collecting 30+ (34 merged) existing tool-use datasets (released Aug 2023-Dec 2024) from AI conferences (ACL/NeurIPS), IR/NLP resource tracks (CIKM/EMNLP: ToolLens, AppBench), and open platforms (HuggingFace); standardizing them into MTEB/BEIR-style query->target-tool IR tasks; cleaning (dedup, normalization); data sampling (K-means clustering on NV-Embed-v1 embeddings, one task per cluster, cluster count = min(#queries, toolset size); manual toolset merge to remove overlap); and instruction construction via a target-aware GPT-4o strategy seeded by 100 human-crafted instructions. Final size: 7,615 tasks over 43,215 tools (Web/Code/Customized). Answer verifiability: labeled ground-truth target tool ids per task. Instruction quality validated by 5 human experts (Kappa 0.743). Companion ToolRet-train: 205,826 tasks (avg 2.31 targets, 5 negatives each) from ToolACE/APIGen/ToolBench. Difficulty signal: best model NV-Embed-v1 reaches only NDCG@10 = 33.83 (Avg.), indicating large headroom.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Standardizes onto IR benchmark conventions BEIR and MTEB (task format) and instructional-IR work (FollowIR / Weller et al. 2024, MAIR/Sun et al. 2024, Asai et al. 2022 task instructions). Uses Completeness@K from DUMP (Qu et al. 2024). Aggregates and reuses source tool-use datasets: ToolBench (Qin et al. 2023), ToolACE (Liu et al. 2024), APIGen (Liu et al. 2024), COLT (Qu et al. 2024), ToolEyes, AppBench, ToolLens, etc. Evaluated retrievers build on NV-Embed-v1, GritLM, e5-mistral, gte-Qwen2, BM25s, ColBERTv2, GTR, Contriever; instruction generation via GPT-4o.
- **contrasts with**:
> Prior tool-use benchmarks that simplify retrieval by manually pre-annotating a small (10-20) candidate toolset per task (ToolBench, ToolACE, StableToolBench, Toolink) - ToolRet instead retrieves from a 43k-tool corpus. Also contrasts with ad-hoc tool retrievers trained on narrow tool-use datasets (COLT) lacking systematic cross-scenario evaluation, and with conventional information-seeking IR benchmarks (MS-MARCO, Natural Questions, HotpotQA, MTEB/BEIR) which have higher lexical overlap and single-document targets.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use): tool-retrieval benchmark line. It is the first large-scale, MTEB/BEIR-style tool-retrieval benchmark and a foundational evaluation/training resource for the 2024-2025 tool-retrieval sub-topic; downstream work (e.g., Tool-DE / Tool-Embed / Tool-Rank, document-expansion methods) builds directly on the ToolRet corpus and metrics. Lineage: classic IR benchmarks (BEIR/MTEB) + instructional IR (FollowIR/MAIR) applied to tool retrieval, sitting upstream of tool_document_engineering and dynamic-index/MCP tool-retrieval works.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- cost_efficiency_tradeoff

<a id="item-toolweaver"></a>
### 122. ToolWeaver: Weaving Collaborative Semantics for Scalable Tool Use in Large Language Models

2026  ·  arXiv:2601.21947 (2026-01, verified)  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21947)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2026
- **venue**: ICLR 2026 (accepted; preprint arXiv:2601.21947, cs.AI, submitted 2026-01-29; DBLP: journals/corr/abs-2601-21947)
- **authors affiliation**:
> Bowen Fang, Wen Ye, Yunyue Su, Jinghao Zhang, Qiang Liu, Yesheng Liu, Jiabing Yang, Xin Sun, Shu Wu (corresponding), Baole Wei (corresponding), Liang Wang. Primary affiliation: New Laboratory of Pattern Recognition (NLPR), Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CASIA); also School of Artificial Intelligence, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences; Zhongguancun Academy; Zhongguancun Institute of Artificial Intelligence.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21947
- **code url**: https://github.com/Fwibo/ToolWeaver (stated in paper footnote: 'Data and code are available at')

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Tool-use: generative tool learning for large-scale tool selection and end-to-end tool-augmented agent task completion over ~47k real-world APIs (ToolBench/RapidAPI).
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent tool use with supervised fine-tuning. Given a user query and a massive tool corpus D (46,985 APIs from ToolBench), an LLM agent must iteratively (1) plan a step, (2) select a tool, (3) generate its parameters, and (4) observe execution feedback, forming an interaction trajectory until the task is solved. Unlike retrieval-pipeline methods, ToolWeaver unifies selection and execution inside one fine-tuned LLM (Llama-3-8B primary; Qwen series in appendix) that natively generates hierarchical code-token sequences for tools, removing the external retriever. Supervision is available: query-tool pairs for retrieval alignment and full ToolBench trajectories for trajectory alignment.
- **what is retrieved**: Tools / APIs. Each tool is represented and 'retrieved' as a generated hierarchical sequence of discrete code-tokens (e.g., <T1_1><T2_2>) rather than a flat tool ID; the LLM generates the code sequence identifying the tool to invoke.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus: the frozen ToolBench/RapidAPI pool of 46,985 APIs encoded once (offline) into a fixed compositional code space (L=2 codebooks x K=1024 codes). No growing/episodic memory is written at test time; the codebook and trie of valid tool codes are fixed after offline tokenization and fine-tuning.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Hybrid. For tool retrieval evaluation the objective is a top-k generative ranking (reported via NDCG@{1,3,5}). For end-to-end multi-tool tasks (I2/I3) the agent must recover and orchestrate the complete set of tools needed across a trajectory, so completeness of the multi-tool selection matters; selection per step is generative (one tool code sequence at a time via constrained beam search).
- **cbr cycle coverage**: Not a CBR work. If forced to map: [Retrieve: partial - generates tool identities, not prior cases; Reuse: no; Revise: no; Retain: no]. N/A.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is framed as generative tool learning with collaborative-aware structured tokenization (RQ-VAE) inspired by generative recommendation (LC-Rec) and residual quantization.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> tool-API, but represented as a compositional sequence of L discrete codes (a hierarchical code path through L=2 codebooks, e.g., <T1_*><T2_*>). The retrievable unit is the structured code sequence uniquely identifying one ToolBench API; shared parent codes group functionally/collaboratively related tools.
- **index source**:
> Static corpus, offline-induced: the 46,985-API ToolBench corpus is encoded offline by collaborative-aware residual quantization (RQ-VAE) into a fixed set of L*K=2048 code-tokens. The co-occurrence/similarity matrix used during codebook learning is mined offline from ToolBench usage trajectories. Not online/test-time-induced; the store is frozen after offline training.
- **index structure topology**:
> Hierarchical / compositional code tree: each tool maps to a length-L code path over L=2 codebooks (each K=1024), forming a prefix-tree (trie) of valid code sequences. Functionally/collaboratively related tools share higher-level (parent) codes (e.g., Realtime Weather=<T1_1><T2_1> and Air Quality=<T1_1><T2_2> share <T1_1>), giving a category->finer-distinction hierarchy emerging from residual quantization rather than a flat vector index.
- **retriever type**:
> Generative (tool-as-token / tool-as-code-sequence): the LLM itself generates the hierarchical code sequence for the target tool (no separate dense/sparse retriever). Baselines span BM25, dense embedding similarity (EmbSim), supervised dense retriever (ToolRetriever), and atomic-token generative (ToolGen).
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Two-part learned signal. (1) Codebook/tokenizer learning: unsupervised RQ-VAE objective combining reconstruction + quantization (commitment) loss with an additional graph-Laplacian collaborative regularization L_collab driven by a tool-tool co-occurrence similarity matrix A (lambda=1.0 optimal), plus Sinkhorn-Knopp optimal-transport uniform-mapping constraint on the final codebook for conflict mitigation. (2) Generative alignment: supervised next-token cross-entropy fine-tuning of the LLM to produce tool code sequences (Stage 1 retrieval alignment) and full trajectories (Stage 2). No RL (RL is named only as future work).
- **query construction**:
> Raw user query q is used directly as the conditioning input; the fine-tuned LLM generates the tool's code sequence P(iota_d | q) (Stage 1) or interleaves reasoning, tool code-tokens, and parameters within a trajectory (Stage 2). No explicit query decomposition or synthetic-query expansion of the query at inference.
- **query granularity**: Both task-level and step-level. Stage-1 retrieval alignment is query-level (q -> tool code sequence). Stage-2 trajectory alignment is step/state-level: at each agent step the model conditions on the running context to generate the next tool's code sequence and parameters.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Iterative within a trajectory: tool selection (code-sequence generation) occurs at each action step of the agent's reasoning-acting loop. There is no separate uncertainty-triggered or learned router; tool generation is woven into autoregressive decoding whenever an action/tool call is produced.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed/structural: tool selection is triggered by the autoregressive generation reaching an action/tool-call position in the trajectory; at that point constrained (trie-guided) beam search forces a valid tool code sequence. No token-confidence, attention-uncertainty, learned complexity classifier, or reflection-token trigger.
- **reranking**: No explicit reranking stage. Selection is done by constrained beam search over the hierarchical code trie (masking logits of invalid next code-tokens) rather than scoring and reranking a candidate list.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> None in the classic sense (no rerank/distill/compress of retrieved documents). The relevant processing is on the index side: collaborative-aware residual quantization plus Sinkhorn-Knopp uniform-mapping to mitigate code collisions; at inference, trie-constrained decoding ensures only valid tool codes are produced.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Tool name + description documentation is encoded by a pretrained text encoder (all-mpnet-base-v2, 768-d) into an initial semantic embedding, then projected (MLP to 64-d) and quantized via collaborative-aware RQ-VAE. The codes thus 'weave' intrinsic semantics (text embedding) with extrinsic co-usage (co-occurrence similarity matrix A). No synthetic-query augmentation; instead structured-tokenization with collaborative regularization.
- **index content separation**:
> Partial: a lightweight compositional code identifier (L*K=2048 added tokens; logarithmic vs linear vocab growth) stands in for the heavy per-tool documentation. The trie of valid code sequences is the retrievable index; full tool docs are not loaded into the LLM context at selection time (the tool is generated as codes). Not a progressive SOP-index-then-content scheme.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Static tool index (frozen ToolBench/RapidAPI pool of 46,985 APIs encoded once into codebooks). Integration/execution protocol is RapidAPI via the StableToolBench framework; no live CRUD auto-sync and no MCP. Adding new tools would require re-running/extending tokenization (logarithmic vocab growth makes this cheaper than atomic methods, but it is not live-synchronized).
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> Yes, implicitly via collaborative co-usage. A tool-tool co-occurrence matrix C (counts of tools appearing together in usage trajectories) yields a cosine similarity matrix A used in a graph-Laplacian collaborative regularization L_collab, so frequently co-used tools share parent codes and the model learns collaborative patterns from dense shared-code co-occurrence. This models co-usage / collaborative relationships rather than an explicit output-of-A-feeds-B dependency graph or shared-auth prerequisites.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Generative selection + execution: the LLM natively generates the tool's hierarchical code-token sequence (decoded back to the tool/API) plus its parameters within reasoning trajectories, then the tool is invoked (RapidAPI via StableToolBench). Tool knowledge is injected as new vocabulary code-tokens learned during generative alignment, not as prompt-context tool documents.
- **planning integration**:
> Per-step interleaved generative tool calling within the agent's reasoning-acting trajectory: the model produces reasoning, then a tool call (code-tokens + parameters), observes feedback, and repeats. Trained via Stage-2 trajectory alignment on full ToolBench trajectories; tool selection is fused into autoregressive planning rather than a separate retrieve-then-plan pipeline. No explicit MCTS/tree search over plans (constrained beam search is only over the tool-code trie at selection).
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-tool-call within a rollout: each action step in the trajectory emits a tool code sequence interleaved with reasoning and parameters; not per-CoT-token retrieval.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not a case-adaptation / CBR method).
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Latent-soft / structured code-tokens: tools are injected as hierarchical sequences of newly added vocabulary tokens (L*K=2048 codes) with randomly initialized, then fine-tuned embeddings. The surface form generated is the code sequence (e.g., <T1_1><T2_2>) standing for an executable API, not raw trajectories or free-text workflows.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Procedural tool / executable API, but represented at a structured compositional abstraction: a hierarchical code path where higher-level codes denote coarse functional/collaborative groupings and lower-level codes denote finer distinctions on the residual.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Index-side structural robustness rather than retrieved-context filtering: (1) collaborative-aware regularization balances intrinsic semantics vs co-usage (lambda=1.0 optimal; too large distorts representations); (2) Sinkhorn-Knopp uniform-mapping mitigates index collisions; (3) trie-constrained beam search guarantees only valid tool codes are generated, preventing hallucinated/invalid tool identifiers. No retriever-aware distractor SFT or self-reflection relevance evaluator.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: None (no persistent/episodic memory). Tool knowledge is amortized into fixed codebook embeddings and LLM weights; there is no test-time-growing experience store.
- **write back**: False: the system does not write new experiences/cases/skills into a growing memory during deployment. The codebooks and tool-code vocabulary are fixed after offline tokenization and fine-tuning.
- **online growth**: No: the retrievable store (tool-code space / trie) is frozen after offline induction; it does not grow at test time. (The compositional design makes future offline expansion logarithmic, but this is not online growth.)
- **write back trigger**: Never (no write-back). Learning is entirely offline: codebook training plus two-stage supervised fine-tuning; nothing is written to a durable store at inference.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Not used at inference for memory. Failures are only analyzed post-hoc (Appendix B.8 failure taxonomy: Wrong Tool dominant, rising 71%->95% from I1->I3; Wrong Parameters, Incomplete/Redundant Process). No success/failure experiences are stored or retrieved; co-usage signal is mined from (presumably successful) usage trajectories offline.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A / append-only-offline: codebook entries are learned once offline and not mutated during deployment; no delta-update, forgetting, or link-and-evolve at test time.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Partially: tool selection is a learned generative model (LLM fine-tuned to generate tool code sequences) plus a learned tokenizer (RQ-VAE with collaborative regularization), so it is not a fixed similarity top-k. However it is NOT an RL/value-based policy (no M-MDP/soft-Q/RL); selection is supervised next-token generation with trie-constrained decoding. RL is named only as future work.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No: single-model, single-agent. Tool knowledge is private to the fine-tuned LLM's weights/codebook; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> ToolBench (Qin et al., 2023; 46,985 APIs, 129 tool collections, 49 functional categories; standardized 641-query test set; scenarios I1 single-tool, I2 intra-category multi-tool, I3 intra-collection multi-tool; generalization splits I1-Tool, I1-Cat, I2-Cat). End-to-end via StableToolBench framework. General-capability evaluation: WikiText-2 (perplexity), CNN/DailyMail and XSum (summarization BERTScore), plus MMLU and additional benchmarks in Appendix B.4. Qwen2.5 results in Appendix B.3.
- **benchmark family**: tool (ToolBench / RapidAPI tool-use; StableToolBench evaluation). Auxiliary: general-LM benchmarks (WikiText-2 LM perplexity; CNN/DM, XSum summarization; MMLU understanding).
- **baselines**:
> Retrieval: BM25, Embedding Similarity (EmbSim, OpenAI text-embedding-3-large), ToolRetriever (supervised BERT dense retriever), ToolGen (atomic-token generative). End-to-end: GPT-4o-mini (retrieval setting; also SoWR reference model), ToolLlama-2 (retrieval setting), ToolGen, ToolWeaver. Additional retrieval baselines in appendix: Re-Invoke, IterFeedback. Tokenization-strategy ablation baselines: Atomic (as ToolGen), Numerical, Hierarchical (clustering-based), Semantic (lexicon-based).
- **key metrics**:
> Tool retrieval: NDCG@{1,3,5}. End-to-end agent: Solvable Pass Rate (SoPR) and Solvable Win Rate (SoWR, computed against GPT-4o-mini reference) under StableToolBench. General capability: Perplexity (WikiText-2), Summarization BERTScore F1 (CNN/DM, XSum), and average drop. Efficiency: avg/P95 latency (ms), throughput (Tok/s), peak GPU memory (GB).
- **headline result**:
> On ToolBench, ToolWeaver outperforms SOTA across tool retrieval and end-to-end tasks with ~46,985 tools. Retrieval: I3 NDCG@1 = 88.00 vs ToolGen 81.00 (and I1 NDCG@1 91.16, I2 89.76). End-to-end I3 SoPR = 52.19 vs ToolGen 36.34, and I3 SoWR = 59.02 vs ToolGen 49.18. It also preserves general language ability far better: WikiText-2 PPL 25.36 vs ToolGen 104.54 (base 6.34), summarization avg drop 0.57 vs ToolGen 2.47.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Collaborative regularization weight lambda: avg NDCG@k across I1-I3 peaks at lambda=1 (improves from 0.01->1, declines at 10), validating intrinsic-vs-collaborative balance. (2) Component ablation (cumulative): w/o semantic initialization (baseline) -> adding semantic initialization gives >20 NDCG-point jump -> adding collaborative guidance gives a further gain that scales with task complexity (largest for I3). (3) Tokenization strategy comparison: ToolWeaver > Atomic (ToolGen), Numerical, Hierarchical (clustering), Semantic (lexicon) on both retrieval and SoPR/SoWR; naive structured methods (Hierarchical/Semantic) fail to beat the Atomic baseline end-to-end. (4) General-capability impact: ToolWeaver vastly less degradation than ToolGen (PPL 25.36 vs 104.54). (5) Appendix: codebook vocab/code-length sensitivity (B.5), Sinkhorn-Knopp efficiency/entropy-eps ablation (B.6), inference latency/memory by depth L (B.7), failure analysis (B.8).
- **evaluation decoupling**: Yes: intrinsic retrieval ranking metrics (NDCG@{1,3,5}, Tables 1) are reported separately from end-to-end agent task metrics (SoPR/SoWR, Table 2), and general-LM metrics are reported separately (Table 3).
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Both. Outcome: SoPR (task completion) and SoWR (answer quality). Process: intrinsic retrieval NDCG@k (selection quality), plus a failure-mode taxonomy over trajectories (Process Consistency: Redundant/Incomplete Process; Wrong Tool; Wrong Parameters) in Appendix B.8.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Inference efficiency analyzed (Appendix B.7, A100-80GB, K=1024): vs ToolGen atomic (avg latency 108.16 ms, throughput 19.54 Tok/s, peak mem 15.77 GB), ToolWeaver L=2 = 128.21 ms (~20 ms overhead), 24.53 Tok/s, 15.08 GB; L=3 = 157.65 ms, 26.34 Tok/s, 15.10 GB; L=4 = 183.14 ms (<200 ms), 28.26 Tok/s, 15.11 GB. Latency grows linearly with depth L but absolute overhead (~20-75 ms) is negligible vs external API call times; higher token throughput at larger L; memory ~constant and ~0.67 GB lower than ToolGen (logarithmic L*K=2048 vs ~47k atomic tokens). Sinkhorn-Knopp cost analyzed in B.6.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Tool selection uses constrained beam search over the code trie; each tool decoded as an L-length code sequence (L=2 main, L*K=2048 added tokens). Training input context truncated to 6,144 tokens. Retrieval reported at fixed k for NDCG@{1,3,5}; per-step a single tool code sequence is generated (not a large candidate list injected into context), avoiding the input-length pressure of retrieval-pipeline baselines.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Uses existing ToolBench (Qin et al., 2023), not a new benchmark: 46,985 real-world RapidAPI APIs, 129 tool collections, 49 functional categories; standardized 641-query test set across I1/I2/I3 with generalization splits (I1-Tool, I1-Cat, I2-Cat). Training data adapted to generative codes: 489,702 query-tool pairs (Stage 1) and 183,336 full trajectories (Stage 2). Answer verifiability via StableToolBench (SoPR/SoWR vs GPT-4o-mini reference). Difficulty signal: best system (ToolWeaver) I3 SoPR 52.19, I3 SoWR 59.02.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> ToolGen (Wang et al., 2024b; atomic-token generative tool calling, which ToolWeaver directly extends/replaces with compositional codes); ToolLLM/ToolBench and ToolRetriever (Qin et al., 2023; corpus, retriever, ToolLlama, evaluation); StableToolBench (Guo et al., 2024; SoPR/SoWR evaluation). Tokenization machinery: RQ-VAE residual quantization (Lee et al., 2022), LC-Rec collaborative-semantic generative IDs and uniform mapping (Zheng et al., 2024), Sinkhorn-Knopp optimal transport (Cuturi, 2013); ToolkenGPT (Hao et al., 2023) tool-as-token precursor; Llama-3-8B (Dubey et al., 2024) and Qwen2.5 (Yang et al., 2025) backbones; all-mpnet-base-v2 / Sentence-Transformers encoder.
- **contrasts with**:
> Retrieval-pipeline tool selection (BM25, EmbSim, ToolRetriever, Re-Invoke, IterFeedback, Gorilla, ToolLLM) which suffer latency/complexity and context-length limits; atomic one-token-per-tool generative methods (ToolGen, ToolkenGPT) which cause linear vocab explosion (~47k OOV tokens), catastrophic general-LM degradation, and a semantic bottleneck from sparse monolithic-ID co-occurrence; and naive structured tokenizations (Numerical, clustering-based Hierarchical, lexicon-based Semantic) that fail to beat the Atomic baseline. Also contrasts with post-hoc collaborative-alignment methods (SeLLa-Rec, LC-Rec, GAL-Rec, CFRAG) by weaving collaborative semantics into the tokenization itself rather than aligning isolated IDs afterward.
- **lineage**:
> Group E (tool-use). Lineage: generative tool calling (ToolkenGPT -> ToolGen tool-as-token) evolved to compositional/hierarchical tool-as-code-sequence; ToolWeaver fuses generative-recommendation-style collaborative-aware RQ-VAE tokenization (LC-Rec, RQ-VAE, Sinkhorn-Knopp) with LLM tool learning, targeting extreme-scale (~47k tools) logarithmic vocab growth and collaborative multi-tool orchestration. Concurrent/related: ToolScaler (Su et al., 2025; structure-aware semantic tokenization for scalable generative tool calling).
