## F — Context Retrieval for Decision-Making / Agent Memory / RL

<a id="item-dpt"></a>
### 123. Decision-Pretrained Transformer (DPT) — Supervised Pretraining Can Learn In-Context Reinforcement Learning

2023  ·  NeurIPS 2023  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.14892)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2023
- **venue**: NeurIPS 2023 (Thirty-seventh Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems). DBLP: conf/nips/0002XPCFNB23. Also arXiv:2306.14892 (cs.LG), submitted 26 Jun 2023.
- **authors affiliation**:
> Jonathan N. Lee (co-first), Annie Xie (co-first), Aldo Pacchiano, Yash Chandak, Chelsea Finn, Ofir Nachum, Emma Brunskill. Primary affiliation: Stanford University. The arXiv v1 lists Aldo Pacchiano at Microsoft Research and Ofir Nachum at Google DeepMind; the NeurIPS camera-ready instead lists Pacchiano at Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard / Boston University. Correspondence: jnl@stanford.edu, anniexie@stanford.edu.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.14892
- **code url**: https://github.com/jon--lee/decision-pretrained-transformer (official, Python/PyTorch, GPT-2 backbone via HuggingFace transformers)
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (single-paper code repository, not a continuously-maintained leaderboard or paper list).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Decision-making / reinforcement learning: in-context RL for multi-armed bandits (incl. linear bandits) and finite-horizon Markov Decision Processes (gridworld navigation 'Dark Room', image-based navigation 'Miniworld'). Embodied/control-flavored but the core contribution is a meta-RL / in-context-learning method for sequential decision-making, not language QA.
- **problem setting**:
> Meta-RL style in-context decision-making. A diverse distribution of tasks (bandits / MDPs) is available at pretraining; for each task an 'in-context dataset' D of (s,a,s',r) interaction tuples is sampled (random, expert, or algorithm-generated), a query state s_query is sampled, and an OPTIMAL action label a* (from the optimal policy of that task, or from an RL-trained agent when the optimum is unavailable) is the supervision target. A causal GPT-2 transformer M_theta is trained purely by supervised learning (negative log-likelihood / softmax classification) to predict a* given (s_query, D). At test time NO parameter updates occur: the frozen model is deployed as either an OFFLINE RL algorithm (argmax over actions conditioned on a fixed dataset D) or an ONLINE RL algorithm (sample actions, append the resulting interactions to D, repeat across episodes). Single-agent. Supervision (optimal-action labels) is required at pretraining; this is the key assumption and stated limitation.
- **what is retrieved**:
> Not classical document/demo retrieval. The functional analog of 'retrieved context' is the in-context interaction dataset D = {(s_j, a_j, s'_j, r_j)} of transition tuples from the unknown current task, placed in the transformer's context window. There is no similarity search; D is supplied (offline) or accumulated online by the model's own rollouts. Pretraining additionally 'retrieves'/samples (query-state, optimal-action) supervision pairs, but at deployment the conditioning context is the task's own interaction history.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> Closest to a GROWING/episodic in-context store in the ONLINE setting (the in-context dataset D starts empty and is grown by the agent's own interactions across episodes), and a STATIC per-task dataset in the OFFLINE setting (a fixed prompt D ~ D_test). There is NO external static corpus / knowledge base / API store being searched; conditioning is on the agent's own task interactions. Best summarized as: in-context (test-time) interaction context, episodically grown online vs fixed offline — not a persistent cross-task retrieval memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> N/A in the retrieval sense — no top-k ranking and no minimal-set recovery objective. The whole in-context dataset (up to context length n, e.g. n=500 for basic bandits, 200 for linear bandits, H-length / cross-episode windows for MDPs) is conditioned on; the learning objective is predicting the single optimal action a* per query state via supervised classification, not selecting/ranking retrieved items.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> N/A — not case-based reasoning. If forced to map: only a weak Retrieve-analog (conditioning on the task's in-context interaction dataset) and an implicit Reuse (forward-pass inference of the optimal action from that context). No explicit Revise or persistent Retain across tasks. Flags: [Retrieve=partial, Reuse=partial, Revise=no, Retain=no].
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is framed as meta-learning / in-context learning / Bayesian posterior sampling.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> (state, action, next-state, reward) transition tuple — i.e., a single interaction step is the atomic context element. Each tuple xi_j=(s_j,a_j,s'_j,r_j) is embedded as one token-like vector (notably DPT does NOT split s/a/s'/r into separate tokens, unlike Decision Transformer / Algorithm Distillation); the query state s_query is a separate leading element. So the retrieved/conditioning unit is a (state,reward,action) transition tuple, aggregated into a dataset/sub-trajectory.
- **index source**:
> No retrieval index. The conditioning context is constructed per task: OFFLINE it is a static sampled dataset D ~ D_test (random or expert or algorithm-generated); ONLINE it is grown at test time from the model's own episode rollouts (online/test-time-induced). Pretraining datasets B of (s_query, D, a*) triples are induced offline by sampling tasks from T_pre and generating D via random interaction / expert demos / algorithm rollouts (e.g. TS, PPO).
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat in-context sequence (set) of transition tuples fed to a causal transformer; because dataset order is treated as exchangeable, NO positional encoding is used for the dataset elements (order-invariance is exploited; the dataset is shuffled except in linear bandits where order matters). No vector index, no graph, no hierarchy — the 'structure' is just the transformer attention over the unordered set of transition tuples plus the query token.
- **retriever type**: N/A / none — there is no retriever module. Selection of relevant context is done implicitly by the transformer's self-attention over the supplied in-context dataset (LLM-as-implicit-context-processor). No BM25/dense/learned retriever performs similarity search.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> N/A for an explicit retriever. The model as a whole is trained by SUPERVISED learning (negative log-likelihood of the optimal action a*, i.e. softmax classification over discrete actions), not by similarity labels, RL, or LM-feedback. The supervision signal is the optimal-action label a* ~ pi*_tau(.|s_query); when the optimum is unknown it can come from any (possibly inefficient) minimax-optimal regret algorithm or another RL-trained agent. The emergent in-context decision policy is therefore distilled from optimal-action prediction, NOT from a learned retrieval/value policy.
- **query construction**:
> The query/key is the raw current query state s_query (offline) or the current visited state s_h (online), concatenated as a leading element v=(s_query, 0) with the in-context dataset X=(v, xi_1, ..., xi_n). In the history-dependent theoretical variant, the conditioning also includes the within-episode history xi_{h-1}=(s_{1:h-1}, a_{1:h-1}). No query decomposition, expansion, or intent extraction.
- **query granularity**:
> Step/state-level: a prediction (and thus an action choice) is produced per query state s_h at each step h, conditioned on the (fixed or grown) dataset D (and, in the history-dependent variant, the current episode's history). In bandits (H=1) this collapses to a single per-task query. So effectively step/state-level querying within a task whose context dataset is fixed (offline) or accreted across episodes (online).
- **when to retrieve**:
> N/A in the retrieve-or-not sense. Conditioning happens every forward pass: offline the static dataset is conditioned on at each step; online the in-context dataset is grown once per episode (after each episode the full episode's interactions are appended to D) and conditioned on at every step. So it is best described as iterative/episodic context accumulation on a fixed schedule, not uncertainty-triggered or learned-router retrieval.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed schedule (no learned trigger): online, context grows by appending each completed episode's trajectory to D; offline, the full dataset is always present. No token-confidence, attention-uncertainty, complexity classifier, reflection-token, or agent-initiated retrieval trigger. (Exploration vs exploitation emerges from sampling actions a_h ~ M_theta(.|s_h,D) online vs taking argmax offline, not from a retrieval trigger.)
- **reranking**: None. No reranking stage over context items.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> None. The in-context dataset is used as-is (optionally shuffled to exploit order-invariance). No rerank/distill/compress/decompose/distractor-filtering of the conditioning context. Robustness to imperfect context is handled by training-distribution diversity, not by a refinement module.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tools/APIs; not a tool-use method).
- **index content separation**: N/A (no lightweight-index-then-content separation; the entire in-context dataset is loaded directly into the transformer context).
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index or integration protocol).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Training signal + prompt/context conditioning. (1) Pretraining: supervised next-optimal-action prediction conditioned on the in-context dataset — the dataset is used as model input and the optimal action as the label (a training signal turning interaction context into a posterior over optimal actions). (2) Deployment: the in-context dataset is injected into the transformer context; a single forward pass yields a distribution over actions M_theta(.|s_h,D), from which the agent takes argmax (offline) or samples (online). The context conditions decision-making without any gradient updates at test time (in-context learning).
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-act in a single forward pass rather than explicit search/planning. There is NO tree search, MCTS, or explicit planner. The transformer maps (state, in-context dataset) -> action distribution; online it interleaves act-then-append-experience across episodes. The paper shows this emergent in-context algorithm is theoretically equivalent (under a history-dependent pretraining variant and consistency assumptions) to Bayesian POSTERIOR SAMPLING (Thompson-Sampling generalization): the forward pass implicitly samples from a learned posterior over optimal actions / tasks. So 'planning' is implicit Bayesian posterior sampling realized by the network's forward pass, not an external search loop.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Per-action / per-step (and per-episode for context growth). Online, the model emits one action per state via a forward pass over the current context; after each episode the full trajectory is appended to D and the process repeats. No per-CoT-step or per-token interleaving of an external retriever.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> N/A in the CBR sense. The closest mechanism is in-context adaptation via a forward pass: the frozen model conditions on the (fixed offline or online-grown) interaction dataset and produces an adapted action distribution with NO gradient updates — adaptation is latent/implicit (emergent posterior sampling), not LLM-prompted case rewriting, execution-feedback revision, or RL fine-tuning at test time.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Raw interaction tuples: each (s,a,s',r) transition is embedded (linear layer over the stacked tuple vector of dimension 2*d_S + d_A + 1) and attended over; the query state is embedded as a leading token. So the injected context is a raw trajectory / set of raw transitions (not distilled strategies, guidelines, programs, or natural-language workflows). The model's OUTPUT is a softmax distribution over optimal actions (latent posterior over actions).
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Raw trajectory / raw transition tuples (lowest abstraction). The conditioning units are raw (s,a,s',r) interactions of the current task, not distilled insights, state-aware guidelines, reusable workflows, or procedural skills. Abstraction (a learned posterior / surrogate task representation, e.g. an implicit linear-bandit feature map) emerges inside the network, not in the stored unit.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Distribution-diversity / coverage-based robustness baked into pretraining: in-context datasets are deliberately diversified (Dirichlet-sampled action frequencies mixed with point-mass-on-one-arm; random/expert/algorithm-generated sources) so the model is robust to test-time distribution mismatch (the paper explicitly enumerates 3 sources of mismatch: induced state distribution, T_pre vs T_test, and online self-collected prompts). Demonstrated OOD robustness: trained on Gaussian bandits but generalizes to Bernoulli rewards and to unseen noise standard deviations; generalizes to held-out goals/dynamics/action-permutations. No explicit relevance evaluator, self-reflection, distractor filtering, or retriever-aware training module.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> episodic (in-context, transient). The only 'memory' is the in-context dataset D held in the transformer context: online it is an episodic buffer grown across episodes within a single task; offline it is a fixed prompt. It is reset per task and there is NO persistent cross-task learned/parametric memory updated at test time (parameters are frozen). Not a skill-library, workflow, graph, or persistent latent memory.
- **write back**:
> Partial/online-only, within-task: in the ONLINE setting the system appends each completed episode's interactions (s1,a1,r1,...) to the in-context dataset D, i.e. it writes its own experience into the conditioning context (in-context, non-parametric). It does NOT write back into a persistent retrievable store across tasks, and there is no parameter update. Offline: no write-back. So write_back = True only in the weak sense of growing the per-task in-context buffer online.
- **online growth**:
> Yes, but only within a single deployed task/episode-sequence (online setting): D starts empty and grows as the agent interacts across episodes of the SAME task. There is NO growth of a cross-task store and NO change to model parameters; once the task ends the context is reset. Offline: the dataset is fixed (no growth).
- **write back trigger**:
> Per-episode (online): after each completed episode the full trajectory is appended to the in-context dataset (a fixed-schedule write, on both successful and unsuccessful episodes — all collected interactions are added regardless of outcome). Offline: never. No reflective / human-validated / success-only gating; appends are unconditional.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Both success and failure interactions are kept in the in-context dataset (online, all episode interactions are appended regardless of return; offline datasets can be random/suboptimal). Failures are not separately labeled or contrastively used — the supervision is always the OPTIMAL action, and the model learns to infer optimality even from suboptimal/random context (it can outperform the data-generating algorithm). So failure data is used implicitly as informative context, not via explicit failure-only corrective rules or success-vs-failure contrastive storage.
- **memory evolution update**: Append-only (online in-context buffer grows by appending each episode's interactions; no dedup/merge/refine/forget). Parameters are never updated at test time. No mutation of stored entries.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No explicit learned retrieval policy. However, the deployed in-context decision policy IS effectively a learned (supervised-pretrained) policy that the paper proves is equivalent to Bayesian posterior sampling: action selection is governed by a learned posterior over optimal actions, not by fixed similarity top-k retrieval. So while there is no retriever-as-policy, the context-conditioned decision rule is a learned policy (emergent PS) rather than a hand-coded rule.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent, single-model setting; no sharing of memory/experience across multiple agents or heterogeneous frameworks. (Pretraining aggregates many tasks into one model, but deployment is single-agent with private per-task context.)

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> Multi-armed bandits: 5-armed Gaussian bandits (means ~ Unif[0,1], sigma=0.3); out-of-distribution Bernoulli bandits; out-of-distribution reward-shift (varying noise std 0.0/0.3/0.5); expert-biased bandits (varying expert fraction). Linear bandits (|A|=10, latent dim d=2, fixed feature map phi). MDPs: Dark Room (10x10 grid navigation, H=100, 5 actions, sparse reward; 80 train goals / 20 held-out goals), Dark Room (Three Tasks) for trajectory stitching, Dark Room (Permuted) for novel-dynamics/action-permutation generalization (20 held-out permutations), and Miniworld (25x25 RGB image-based navigation to a colored box, 4 tasks, H=50).
- **benchmark family**: decision-RL (bandits + MDPs / meta-RL); embodied-style gridworld + image navigation (Dark Room, Miniworld). NOT D4RL and NOT QA/web/tool/code benchmarks — these are custom meta-RL bandit/MDP environments.
- **baselines**:
> Bandits: Empirical-mean (Emp), Upper Confidence Bound (UCB), Lower Confidence Bound (LCB), Thompson Sampling (TS), LinUCB and LinReg (linear-bandit, given the true feature map phi). MDPs: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO, single-task from scratch, Stable-Baselines3), Algorithm Distillation (AD, Laskin et al. 2022 — distills RL learning histories), and RL^2 (Duan et al. — recurrent online meta-RL). DPT variants compared internally: DPT, DPT-Exp (expert-biased pretraining), DPT (Rand, PPO) and DPT trained on PPO action labels.
- **key metrics**:
> Bandits — offline suboptimality (mu_{a*} - mu_{a_hat}) and online cumulative regret (sum_k mu_{a*} - mu_{a_hat_k}). MDPs — episodic return / success at reaching the goal (offline performance given random vs expert datasets; online performance / cumulative return over episodes). All reported as mean +/- standard error over 200 test tasks (bandits) or 100 offline datasets / 20 online trials (MDPs).
- **headline result**:
> Despite being trained ONLY to predict optimal actions (never to explore), DPT emergently matches classical near-optimal RL algorithms in-context with no test-time parameter updates: online it matches UCB and Thompson Sampling on bandit cumulative regret; offline it hedges like (but distinct from) LCB; on latent linear bandits DPT pretrained on Thompson-Sampling data (which ignores the linear structure) approaches LinUCB (which is given phi) and substantially beats its own data-generating source TS — i.e. DPT provably/empirically improves over the algorithm that produced its pretraining data. Theoretically, DPT (under a history-dependent pretraining variant) is exactly equivalent to Bayesian posterior sampling, yielding regret O~(C H^{3/2} S sqrt(A K)) for finite MDPs and O~(d sqrt(K)) for latent linear bandits (vs O~(sqrt(|A| K)) for the TS source).
- **ablations**:
> (1) Pretraining-data source / label source: DPT trained with random in-context datasets and OPTIMAL labels generalizes best; relaxing the optimal-action requirement by using PPO-generated action labels (DPT trained on PPO labels) and/or PPO-collected datasets, DPT (Rand, PPO), gives only a slight, marginal performance loss — showing the optimal-label requirement can be relaxed. (2) Expert-bias of pretraining distribution: DPT-Exp (pretrained on expert-biased datasets) behaves like LCB at test time, whereas standard DPT behaves like TS — demonstrating the pretraining in-context-data prior controls offline conservatism (and, per Proposition 6.4, only NON-compliant expert-bias changes the learned model). (3) Structure exploitation: pretraining on linear bandits lets DPT learn an implicit surrogate for phi and explore like LinUCB even though the source data (TS) ignores structure. (4) Stitching: Dark Room (Three Tasks) shows DPT stitches expert demos of two tasks to solve an unseen third. (5) Generalization to new dynamics: Dark Room (Permuted) — recovers optimal policy offline from only 100 samples on 20 held-out permutations, snaps to near-optimal online in one episode. (6) Sensitivity (Appendix B): robust to #layers, #attention-heads (slightly worse at 8 heads due to overfitting), embedding size; performance degrades only when pretraining data is cut to 10% (10k samples).
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> No intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k/nDCG) — not a retrieval system. Evaluation is decoupled instead along RL axes: intrinsic decision-quality metrics (regret, suboptimality) are reported separately from / alongside task return, and behavior is compared head-to-head with hand-designed algorithms (UCB/TS/LCB/LinUCB) whose theoretical optimality is known. Theory (regret bounds, PS-equivalence) complements empirics.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both outcome and process. Outcome: final cumulative regret / suboptimality / episodic return. Process: full online learning curves (regret vs number of interactions / episodes — measuring exploration efficiency and sample-efficiency), demonstrated exploration behavior, conservatism, stitching, and rapid adaptation (e.g. one-episode adaptation on permuted dynamics). The PS-equivalence theorem itself is a process-level characterization of the in-context algorithm's trajectory distribution.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed context length (no adaptive selection): basic bandits context up to n=500 transition tuples, linear bandits n=200, Dark Room/Miniworld context length 100 steps; query is a single leading element. The whole available in-context dataset (up to the fixed context length) is used — there is no top-k selection, reranking, or truncation policy. Pretraining sample counts: 100k samples (basic bandit, 300 epochs), 1,000,000 (linear bandit, 200 epochs), 100k datasets for Dark Room (80k train / 20k val), 40k for Miniworld (32k/8k).
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (this is a method + theory paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A as a benchmark contribution. For context, environments are synthetic/procedurally generated: bandit tasks sampled from explicit reward distributions; Dark Room is a 10x10 gridworld with 100 goal positions (80 train/20 test) and a known optimal navigation policy used to generate labels; Miniworld has 4 image-based box-navigation tasks; pretraining datasets generated by random/expert/algorithm (TS, PPO) rollouts. Answer/label verifiability is exact in synthetic tasks (optimal actions computable).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> In-context learning of LLMs (Brown et al. GPT-3); GPT-2 architecture (Radford et al.) via HuggingFace transformers; autoregressive transformers for decision-making — Decision Transformer (Chen et al. 2021) and Algorithm Distillation (Laskin et al. 2022) (which DPT explicitly differentiates from: DPT predicts optimal actions rather than distilling an RL algorithm's learning history); meta-RL / learning-to-learn (RL^2 Duan et al., Wang et al.); Bayesian posterior sampling / Thompson Sampling for RL (Thompson 1933; Osband, Russo & Van Roy 2013; Russo & Van Roy 2014) for the theoretical equivalence and regret analysis; the in-context-learning-as-Bayesian-inference view (Xie et al. 2021); MLE generalization bound (Agarwal et al. FLAMBE).
- **contrasts with**:
> Decision Transformer (return-conditioned supervised learning — provably and unboundedly sub-optimal in common cases, cannot improve over the dataset; DPT instead improves over its data-generating algorithm); Algorithm Distillation (distills a specific RL algorithm's learning trace to imitate HOW to learn, and is trained to infer a better-than-data policy but not necessarily the optimal one — AD does worse than DPT with random in-context data); RL^2 (recurrent online meta-RL with an RL objective); single-task PPO from scratch; value/policy-based offline meta-RL methods that must handle distribution shift via pessimism/regularization or extra online interaction (DPT avoids these). Also contrasts hand-designed bandit/RL algorithms (UCB/TS/LCB/LinUCB) by matching or exceeding them emergently and amortizing posterior sampling's compute.
- **lineage**:
> Group F (decision/memory/RL) — in-context reinforcement learning lineage. Sits between Algorithm Distillation (Laskin et al. 2022, distillation-of-RL-algorithm in-context RL) and later in-context-RL / sequence-model-RL work; pioneers the 'predict-the-optimal-action via supervised pretraining' route to emergent in-context RL and ties it to Bayesian posterior sampling theory. Within the survey's retrieval lens it represents the extreme where the 'retrieved context' is the agent's own in-context interaction dataset (episodic, non-parametric, no external corpus or similarity search), contrasting with classic RAG planners that retrieve from a static external corpus and with experience/case-memory agents that maintain a persistent growing store.

### 124. MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems

2023  ·  arXiv 2310.08560  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.08560)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2023
- **venue**:
> arXiv preprint arXiv:2310.08560 (cs.AI); v1 submitted 12 Oct 2023, v2 12 Feb 2024. DBLP: journals/corr/abs-2310-08560. DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2310.08560. No formal peer-reviewed venue is recorded; the work circulated as an arXiv technical report (its commercial successor is the Letta framework).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.08560 (PDF: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.08560; DOI: https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2310.08560)
- **code url**:
> https://research.memgpt.ai (project page redirecting to the released code/data). The original repository was github.com/cpacker/MemGPT, now github.com/letta-ai/letta (renamed/rebranded as Letta, 'formerly MemGPT'). Released artifacts: augmented MSC/DMR dataset, nested KV retrieval dataset, and embeddings for 20M Wikipedia articles.
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/letta-ai/letta (continuously maintained successor framework, 'Letta, formerly MemGPT'; far more current than the frozen 2023/2024 PDF). The research-specific page is https://research.memgpt.ai.

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Long-context LLM agent / memory management. Evaluated in two domains: (1) conversational agents (multi-session chat — long-term dialogue memory, consistency, engagement) and (2) document analysis (multi-document question answering and synthetic key-value retrieval over corpora that exceed the LLM context window). Broadly a QA + interactive-agent memory-management setting.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent setting with a FROZEN, off-the-shelf LLM (no model training/fine-tuning; supervision absent). The LLM's fixed context window is treated as a constrained 'main memory' resource and is augmented with an OS-inspired hierarchical memory system. The agent is given function-call tools (via system-prompt instructions and a function schema) to self-direct paging of data between its in-context main memory and out-of-context external storage. Control flow is event-driven: events (user messages, system memory-pressure warnings, timed events) trigger LLM inference, and the LLM can chain function calls via a request_heartbeat flag. Two evaluation domains: multi-session chat (DMR consistency + conversation-opener engagement on an augmented MSC dataset) and document analysis (multi-document QA over Wikipedia + nested KV retrieval). Base LLMs are GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613), and GPT-4 Turbo (gpt-4-1106-preview).
- **what is retrieved**:
> experiences / memories: out-of-context conversational history and stored facts (recall storage = full message history; working context = key user/persona facts), and, in document analysis, documents/passages (Wikipedia articles) and synthetic key-value records loaded into archival storage. Retrieval brings these out-of-context items back into the LLM main context via self-issued function calls (e.g. conversation/recall search, archival memory search).
- **retrieval grounding**:
> HYBRID, leaning toward a GROWING/episodic memory the agent writes. In conversational settings the retrievable store is the agent's own growing memory (recall storage of the full conversation history plus a self-edited working context), i.e. episodic memory the agent writes to during interaction. In document analysis the store is a (largely static) external corpus (e.g. a precomputed 20M-article Wikipedia embedding database, or a fixed set of synthetic KV pairs) loaded into archival storage. Both are accessed through the same self-directed function-call retrieval interface.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Top-k similarity ranking executed iteratively rather than a one-shot fixed-k cut: each retrieval function call returns paginated top-K results (vector cosine-similarity top-K), and the LLM can repeatedly page/re-query to assemble the information it needs (multi-hop collation). There is no learned ranking objective (no Recall@k/nDCG optimized) and no explicit minimal-set completeness objective; instead, function chaining + pagination lets the agent approximate complete recovery by issuing additional retrieval calls until it decides it has the answer (e.g. 'do not stop until you verify the value is not a key' in nested KV).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. MemGPT does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is framed as OS-inspired virtual context management / hierarchical memory paging.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Mixed by domain: (a) conversational message/history snippet and stored fact (a message in the FIFO queue / recall storage, or a free-text fact block in working context); (b) document/passage (a Wikipedia article retrieved by vector search in archival storage); (c) a synthetic key-value record (128-bit UUID pair) in the nested KV task. Retrieval is at the granularity of paginated database records (messages, documents, or KV entries) brought into main context.
- **index source**:
> Hybrid. Conversational recall storage is a growing, online/test-time-induced store (the full message history accumulates as the conversation proceeds, with recursive summaries written on eviction). Working context is a self-edited in-context store the agent writes online. Document-analysis archival storage is a (largely offline/precomputed) static external corpus (e.g. 20M-article Wikipedia embeddings precomputed and loaded into PostgreSQL/pgvector, or a fixed synthetic KV set).
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat vector index over external storage. Implementation: PostgreSQL archival memory with vector search via the pgvector extension, using an HNSW index for approximate sub-second similarity queries. Recall storage holds the rolling message history (time-ordered, searchable). Main context itself is partitioned into three contiguous sections (system instructions / working context / FIFO queue), a tiered RAM-vs-disk hierarchy rather than a graph/hierarchical-category index. No knowledge graph or category->tool hierarchy.
- **retriever type**:
> Dense, off-the-shelf. Vector similarity search (cosine distance) over OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 embeddings. The same retriever is used by both MemGPT (exposed as a function the LLM can call against archival/recall storage) and the fixed-context baselines (a standard retriever-reader top-K fetch). No BM25, no learned/trained retriever; the 'retriever' in MemGPT effectively emerges from the archival-storage search function. The LLM acts as a controller that decides query terms and when to call the retriever (LLM-orchestrated retrieval over a dense index).
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None (off-the-shelf). The retriever uses frozen pretrained text-embedding-ada-002 embeddings with cosine-similarity vector search; it is not trained with contrastive, LM-feedback, downstream-effectiveness, RL, or value-based signals. The novelty is in how the frozen LLM self-directs (when/what to retrieve via function calls), not in learning the retriever. The base LLM is likewise not fine-tuned for MemGPT (it is prompted via system instructions).
- **query construction**:
> LLM-synthesized search queries issued as function-call arguments. The MemGPT LLM processor, guided by system-prompt instructions, formulates natural-language/keyword search queries (e.g. recall_storage.search('...'), archival memory search) based on the current situation/question, and can refine/repeat queries (paginate, reformulate) across a function-chain. In document QA the query derives from the user's question; in nested KV it is the current UUID key being looked up.
- **query granularity**:
> Step/state-level: queries are constructed dynamically at each inference cycle / function-call step as the agent reasons, not a single one-shot query at t=0. The agent issues multiple successive queries within one task (paginated / multi-hop), so retrieval is interleaved at step granularity.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Iterative / agent-initiated (self-directed). Retrieval is not on a fixed schedule; the frozen LLM decides when to call a memory-search function based on the current context and the system instructions. Function chaining (request_heartbeat=true) lets it perform multiple retrieval steps in sequence before yielding control to the user. Event-driven control flow (user/system/timed events) triggers LLM inference, after which the agent may choose to retrieve.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Agent-initiated request: the LLM emits a memory-retrieval function call when it judges (from system-prompt guidance and current context) that needed information is out of context. Complementary system signals shape behavior — 'memory pressure' warnings when prompt tokens exceed a warning threshold (~70% of context) and an impending FIFO-queue eviction, plus explicit instructions (e.g. 'keep searching until you verify the value is not a key'). No token-level confidence, attention-uncertainty score, learned complexity classifier, or reflection tokens.
- **reranking**:
> No dedicated reranking stage (no cross-encoder, RRF, or instruction-tuned reranker). Items are ordered purely by vector cosine similarity from the archival/recall search and returned in paginated pages; the LLM controller decides whether to page further or re-query rather than reranking results.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Minimal/none as an automated post-retrieval module. Retrieved records are paginated to avoid overflowing the context window, and the LLM may iteratively page/re-query and select which results to keep in main context. There is no learned distillation, decompose-then-recompose, distractor-filtering, or compression of retrieved items; the only compression in the system is the recursive summarization applied to evicted FIFO-queue messages (a memory-management step, not a retrieval-refinement step).
- **tool document engineering**: N/A. MemGPT does not index tool/skill descriptions; its function set (memory read/write/search functions) is described to the LLM via raw natural-language schemas in the system prompt, but it does not retrieve over a tool corpus.
- **index content separation**:
> Partial / implicit. MemGPT explicitly separates a small in-context 'main memory' (system instructions + working context + FIFO queue) from heavy out-of-context content in external storage (archival + recall databases) that is loaded on demand via function calls and pagination — an OS-style RAM/disk progressive-disclosure pattern. It is not the SOP-index-then-content or lightweight-tool-index pattern of tool-retrieval works; the separation is between a fixed-size context window and unbounded external storage.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A. Not a tool-retrieval system; no RapidAPI/RESTful/MCP/function-calling tool registry with CRUD auto-sync. (MemGPT does use LLM function calling, but to operate its own memory functions, not to integrate a live external tool store.)
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A. No inter-tool dependency modeling (no tools/APIs are retrieved).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation. Retrieved out-of-context items (messages, facts, documents, KV records) are paged into the LLM main context (prompt tokens) as text, where the frozen LLM reads them to answer or to ground its next action. The agent also self-edits its working context (writing/updating key facts) and consults working context inline. No training signal, no skill reuse, no latent-token injection — retrieved content is consumed as in-context text.
- **planning integration**:
> Inside a self-directed function-call loop (retrieve-within-a-search-loop). MemGPT interleaves retrieval with 'planning out loud' and acting: the LLM reasons, calls a memory function, reads the returned page into context, and can chain further calls (request_heartbeat=true) before yielding. This enables multi-step retrieval / multi-hop collation (e.g. nested KV lookups, collating across documents). There is no explicit task planner, MCTS, or hierarchical subtask decomposition; planning is the emergent control flow of the agentic function-chaining loop.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Per-tool-call within a rollout: retrieval is woven in at the granularity of individual function calls during the agent's inference cycles (the LLM can reason, call a search function, observe results, and call again), i.e. per-step/per-function-call rather than per-CoT-token or only per-final-answer.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> N/A (not a CBR case-adaptation system). Retrieved content is injected as in-context text and the frozen LLM synthesizes responses from it; there is no verbatim-case-reuse-with-adaptation, execution-feedback case revision, critic-guided revision, or RL reuse-finetuning. The closest 'adaptation' is the LLM self-editing its working-context memory block over time.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Raw natural-language text: retrieved messages, stored fact blocks, document passages, or KV records are injected into the prompt as plain text (paginated). Working context is free-text unstructured memory the agent maintains. No executable program/skill, structured schema, or latent/soft tokens.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Mostly raw/low-abstraction units (raw message history, raw documents, raw KV records) retrieved by similarity. A higher-abstraction layer exists but is generated, not the retrieval target: recursive summaries of evicted messages and the self-curated working-context fact block (distilled key facts/preferences). So retrieval targets raw records while the agent separately maintains distilled summaries/facts in main context.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Implicit / prompt-driven only. Because MemGPT can issue multiple retrieval calls and page through results, it is robust to a noisy embedding ranking as long as the gold item is somewhere in the ranking (it can keep paging until found). System instructions (e.g. 'keep searching', 'verify the value is not a key', baselines told to reply 'INSUFFICIENT INFORMATION' / 'NO ANSWER') and an LLM-judge that requires the answer be derived from retrieved text guard against hallucination. There is no retriever-aware training, learned relevance evaluator, reason-in-documents refinement, or distractor-aware SFT.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> Episodic + working/procedural memory in an OS-inspired hierarchy. Main context = system instructions (read-only) + working context (fixed-size read/write fact block) + FIFO queue (rolling message history with a recursive-summary head). External context = archival storage (read/write, arbitrary-length text, vector-searchable) + recall storage (full message-history database, searchable). Long-term, persistent, self-managed; single-agent private.
- **write back**:
> True. MemGPT self-directs writes: it stores important information from the FIFO queue into working context or archival storage on memory-pressure warnings; evicted messages are written to recall storage indefinitely; and a recursive summary is generated and stored on each queue flush. The agent also continually edits its working-context fact block.
- **online growth**:
> Yes (for conversational/recall memory). The recall-storage message history and recursive summaries grow continuously during interaction (test/deployment time), and the working context evolves. The document-analysis archival corpus (e.g. 20M-article Wikipedia, fixed synthetic KV set) is largely precomputed/static for those benchmarks, though archival storage is in principle read/write and can grow.
- **write back trigger**:
> Multiple triggers: (1) per-step / continuous — every message and function call is appended to the FIFO queue and, once evicted, to recall storage; (2) threshold-driven memory management — when prompt tokens exceed the 'warning token count' (~70% of context) MemGPT issues a memory-pressure warning prompting the LLM to save key info to working context/archival storage, and when they exceed the 'flush token count' (~100%) the queue manager evicts a chunk and writes a new recursive summary; (3) agent-initiated — the LLM can write to working context / archival storage whenever it deems information important. Writes are NOT conditioned on task success/failure (no task reward).
- **failure experience usage**:
> N/A in the success/failure sense: there is no task-level success/failure label, and the system does not store failed vs successful experiences contrastively or maintain failure-only corrective rules. All interaction history is stored uniformly in recall storage. (Runtime function errors, e.g. writing to a full main context, are fed back to the processor as immediate feedback within an episode, but are not persisted as labeled failure experiences for later retrieval.)
- **memory evolution update**:
> Mixed: append-only for the message history/recall storage and archival storage (records accumulate; evicted messages stored indefinitely), with refine-overwrite dynamics for the head-of-queue recursive summary (regenerated on each flush from the prior summary + newly evicted messages) and for working context (the agent edits/overwrites its fact block as understanding evolves). FIFO eviction provides a forget-from-context (but-retain-in-recall) behavior. No dedup-merge of stored records.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No. Retrieval/memory-management is driven by a FROZEN, prompt-instructed LLM controller plus fixed heuristic thresholds (warning/flush token counts) — not a learned/RL-optimized retrieval policy (no M-MDP, soft Q-learning, or trained selection policy). The decision of when/what to retrieve emerges from in-context instructions and the LLM's function-calling ability, not from training.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent private memory: each MemGPT agent manages its own main/external context. No shared memory store or cross-agent/cross-framework experience sharing is proposed.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> (1) Multi-session chat: an augmented version of the Multi-Session Chat (MSC) dataset (Xu et al., 2021) — Deep Memory Retrieval (DMR) consistency task (new self-instruct-generated QA over sessions 1-5 with an added session 6) and a Conversation Opener engagement task. (2) Document analysis: a multi-document question-answering task built on the 'Lost in the Middle' setup (Liu et al., 2023a) over a late-2018 Wikipedia dump (50 sampled questions), and a new Nested Key-Value (KV) retrieval task extending the synthetic KV task of Liu et al. (2023a) to multi-hop nested lookups (140 UUID pairs ~8k tokens, 0-4 nesting levels, 30 ordering configurations).
- **benchmark family**:
> memory / long-context agent (LoCoMo/LongMemEval-style long-term-conversation memory, here via augmented MSC + DMR) and QA / multi-hop (multi-document Wikipedia QA and synthetic nested key-value retrieval, i.e. 'Lost in the Middle'-derived long-context retrieval tasks). Not web/embodied/tool/code/decision-RL families.
- **baselines**:
> Fixed-context (limited-context-window) versions of the same underlying LLMs: GPT-3.5 Turbo (gpt-3.5-turbo-1106, 16k), GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613, 8k), and GPT-4 Turbo (gpt-4-1106-preview, 128k), each WITHOUT MemGPT. For conversational tasks the baselines receive a lossy recursive summarization of the prior five sessions; for document QA the baselines use the same text-embedding-ada-002 retriever in a standard retriever-reader top-K setup (à la Liu et al., 2023a). A Human baseline is reported for the conversation-opener task. Truncation is shown as a context-extension comparison for document QA.
- **key metrics**:
> DMR: Accuracy (LLM-judge correctness) and ROUGE-L recall (R). Conversation opener: CSIM similarity scores to gold persona labels (SIM-1, SIM-3) and to the human-written opener (SIM-H). Document QA: accuracy (LLM-judge) as a function of effective context length / number of retrieved documents. Nested KV: accuracy as a function of nesting level (0-4).
- **headline result**:
> On the Deep Memory Retrieval (DMR) consistency task, GPT-4 + MemGPT reaches 92.5% accuracy and 0.814 ROUGE-L(R) vs 32.1% / 0.296 for the GPT-4 fixed-context baseline; GPT-4 Turbo + MemGPT reaches 93.4% / 0.827 vs 35.3% / 0.359; GPT-3.5 Turbo + MemGPT reaches 66.9% / 0.629 vs 38.7% / 0.394. MemGPT thus dramatically improves long-term-conversation consistency over fixed-context baselines (e.g. GPT-4: 32.1% -> 92.5% accuracy).
- **ablations**:
> The main comparisons function as ablations of the MemGPT memory layer: with-MemGPT vs without-MemGPT (fixed-context) on the same base LLM across DMR, conversation opener, document QA, and nested KV. Findings: (a) DMR — MemGPT yields large accuracy/ROUGE gains for every base model (clear drop when MemGPT is removed); (b) Conversation opener — storing information in working context is identified as KEY to generating engaging openers; (c) Document QA — fixed-context baseline performance is capped near the retriever's single-shot quality, whereas MemGPT's iterative paged retrieval makes performance roughly invariant to context length / document count (and MemGPT often stops paging before exhausting the database); (d) Nested KV — MemGPT with GPT-4 is unaffected by nesting depth (multi-hop via repeated function queries) while all fixed-context baselines drop to 0% by 2-3 nesting levels; notably MemGPT+GPT-4 Turbo performs worse than MemGPT+GPT-4 on nested KV. No intrinsic Recall@k retrieval-only ablation.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> No. Intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG) are not reported separately. Evaluation is end-to-end task quality (DMR accuracy/ROUGE, opener similarity, doc-QA accuracy, nested-KV accuracy). The paper discusses retriever quality qualitatively (e.g. fixed-context baselines are capped by single-shot retriever recall; MemGPT can recover the gold doc via repeated paging) but does not tabulate Recall@k.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome metrics (final-answer accuracy / ROUGE / similarity). Some process-flavored signal: nested KV accuracy as a function of nesting depth reflects multi-hop reasoning quality, and document-QA accuracy vs effective context length probes whether the agent collates across retrieved pages; but there is no reasoning-faithfulness or step-wise retrieval-accuracy metric.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Discussed qualitatively rather than fully tabulated. MemGPT's core efficiency argument: it provides the illusion of unbounded context without paying the quadratic cost of extending the LLM context window, by paging data in/out and issuing extra retrieval calls. It can make multiple paged retriever calls (more LLM inferences/function calls than a single-shot baseline) but in practice often stops paging before exhausting the database. The pgvector HNSW index gives approximate sub-second query times. No explicit per-task token-cost, dollar-cost, or latency table comparing MemGPT vs baselines is reported.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Budget-capped, iterative top-K with pagination. Main context is a fixed-size resource partitioned into system instructions + fixed-size working-context block + FIFO queue; memory-pressure (~70%) and flush (~100%) token thresholds govern eviction, with a flush evicting ~50% of the context window's messages and replacing them with a recursive summary. Retrieval returns paginated top-K results; the agent pages further as needed rather than fixing a single k, and retrieval is designed to be token-aware to avoid context overflow.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> DMR: self-instruct-generated memory-challenge QA pairs over the MSC dataset (each MSC conversation has 5 sessions of ~a dozen messages; a 6th single-QA session was added), with answers scored by an LLM judge against gold answers (LLM-judge correctness + ROUGE-L). Document QA: 50 questions sampled over a late-2018 Wikipedia dump; 20M-article embeddings released; LLM-judge grading requiring the answer be derived from retrieved text. Nested KV: synthetic, 140 128-bit-UUID key-value pairs (~8k tokens), nesting levels 0-4, 30 ordering configurations, answer-verifiable by exact UUID lookup. Datasets (augmented MSC/DMR, nested KV, Wikipedia embeddings) are publicly released. Difficulty signal: fixed-context GPT-4 collapses to 0% nested KV by 3 nesting levels and to ~32% DMR accuracy.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Operating-systems virtual memory / hierarchical memory and paging (Patterson et al. 1988 — RAID/storage-tier analogy); LLM function-calling / tool-use agents (Toolformer, Schick et al. 2023; AgentBench, Liu et al. 2023b); retrieval-augmented LLMs (RAG, REALM, RETRO, Atlas/Izacard & Grave, DPR, in-context RALM); 'Lost in the Middle' long-context analysis and the synthetic KV / multi-doc QA setup (Liu et al. 2023a); ReAct-style reason-and-act 'plan out loud' (Yao et al. 2022); WebGPT pagination for context control (Nakano et al. 2021); Generative Agents memory+reflection for LLM agents (Park et al. 2023); Multi-Session Chat dataset (Xu et al. 2021); off-the-shelf OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 + PostgreSQL/pgvector/HNSW for the external store.
- **contrasts with**:
> Long-context architectures / context-window-extension approaches that pay quadratic attention cost or train longer models (sparse/efficient transformers — Longformer, Reformer, Sparse Transformers; Linformer; positional-interpolation/ALiBi context extension), and naive context-scaling — which MemGPT argues suffers diminishing returns and the 'lost in the middle' degradation; truncation/recursive-summarization fixed-context baselines that lose information; and standard single-shot retriever-reader RAG whose performance is capped by one-shot retriever recall (MemGPT instead lets the LLM iteratively page/re-query). Also distinct from Generative Agents (focuses on long-term memory of user inputs / OS-style self-managed paging rather than emergent social simulation).
- **lineage**:
> Foundational work in the experience/episodic-memory + long-term-memory lineage of retrieval-augmented LLM agents (Group F: decision/memory/RL — memory-management for agents). MemGPT introduced OS-inspired tiered memory (main vs external context) with self-directed, function-call-based paging and a memory-pressure/eviction + recursive-summary control flow; it became the basis of the Letta framework and influenced many subsequent long-term-memory and agentic-memory systems (e.g. memory-augmented conversational agents, LongMemEval/LoCoMo-style memory benchmarks).

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- authors_affiliation
- cbr_cycle_coverage

<a id="item-reflexion"></a>
### 125. Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning

2023  ·  NeurIPS 2023  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11366)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2023
- **venue**: NeurIPS 2023 (Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36); first posted arXiv:2303.11366, Mar 2023
- **authors affiliation**: Noah Shinn, Federico Cassano, Edward Berman (Northeastern University); Ashwin Gopinath (MIT); Karthik Narasimhan, Shunyu Yao (Princeton University). Lead author: Noah Shinn (Northeastern University).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11366
- **code url**: https://github.com/noahshinn024/reflexion

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: decision-making / agents (sequential decision-making, knowledge-intensive reasoning QA, and code generation). Covers embodied text-world (AlfWorld), multi-hop QA (HotPotQA), and code (HumanEval/MBPP/LeetcodeHard).
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, online, single-agent setting where an LLM acts as a goal-driven agent in external environments (games/TextWorld, compilers/interpreters, Wikipedia API). The agent learns from trial-and-error across multiple episodes without any weight updates or fine-tuning; instead it relies on verbal (linguistic) reinforcement. Supervision is sparse: a binary/scalar success signal comes from the environment, ground-truth match (EM), self-generated unit tests, or an LLM/heuristic self-evaluator. The same task is retried over a bounded number of trials until the Evaluator deems the trajectory correct or max trials is reached.
- **what is retrieved**: experiences: the agent's own verbal self-reflections (free-text lessons distilled from prior failed trials) stored in an episodic long-term memory buffer, conditioned on in subsequent trials of the SAME task.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> GROWING/episodic memory the agent writes itself (self-reflection text accumulated across trials). It is not a static external corpus; the agent generates and stores its own reflective notes, then re-reads them. (The ReAct-based variant additionally queries a Wikipedia API for external context, but the Reflexion-specific 'retrieval' is from self-written episodic memory.)
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve: partial - all stored reflections re-loaded each trial rather than similarity-retrieved; Reuse: yes - past reflections condition the next trial; Revise: yes - the agent generates a new reflection / revised plan; Retain: yes - new reflection appended to memory]. Realizes a CBR-like trial-revise-retain loop but over self-reflections, not problem-solution cases.
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False. The paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner; it is framed as 'verbal reinforcement learning' / policy optimization in natural language, drawing on RL (Sutton & Barto) and in-context policy iteration (Brooks et al., 2022).

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: thought-step / experience: a free-text self-reflection summarizing what went wrong in the prior trajectory and an improved plan (verbal experience feedback sr_t). Short-term memory additionally holds the full current/recent trajectory.
- **index source**: Growing episodic memory induced online at test time: built by the agent during the retry loop for each task; frozen across tasks (no cross-task memory transfer). Bounded by a maximum capacity Omega (typically 1-3 stored experiences).
- **index structure topology**: Flat append-only list (memory buffer mem = [sr_0, sr_1, ...]) truncated to the most recent 1-3 entries (sliding window). No vector index or graph; the paper explicitly suggests future work could add vector-embedding or SQL databases.
- **retriever type**: None / trivial: there is no learned or similarity-based retriever. The full (truncated) memory buffer is concatenated into the prompt. Effectively recency-windowed read-all rather than a ranked retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**: none (off-the-shelf): no retriever is trained. The signal that shapes memory CONTENT is the environment reward amplified into verbal feedback by the Self-Reflection LLM, but the read/selection mechanism itself is not learned.
- **query construction**: No explicit query is constructed for retrieval; the agent simply conditions the next trial's generation on its stored reflections plus the current task/state observation. The verbal self-reflection is generated from {trajectory tau_t, scalar reward r_t, prior memory}.
- **query granularity**: task-level / trajectory-level: reflections are generated once per trial (after a full trajectory) and re-injected at the start of the next trial; there is no per-step retrieval query.
- **when to retrieve**: iterative across trials: the accumulated memory is re-read at the start of every new trial of the same task. Writing a reflection is triggered after each failed/evaluated trial (or, for AlfWorld heuristic, when stuck >3 repeats or >30 actions).
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed schedule per trial for reading memory; for writing, the trigger is the Evaluator's failure signal (binary success/fail from environment, exact-match grading, self-generated unit-test results, LLM self-evaluation, or hand-written heuristics detecting repeated actions / inefficient planning).
- **reranking**: None. No reranking stage; the bounded memory is used as-is.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Distillation at write time rather than at read time: the Self-Reflection LLM compresses a long failed trajectory + sparse reward into a concise actionable verbal lesson before storing. At read time, the buffer is truncated to the last 1-3 experiences (window-based pruning). No rerank/distractor-filtering of retrieved items.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tool/skill descriptions are indexed).
- **index content separation**: N/A. Short-term memory holds full trajectory detail while long-term memory holds distilled reflections, a loose separation, but not a lightweight-index-then-load-content design.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**: prompt augmentation: stored self-reflections are concatenated into the LLM Actor's context as additional 'self-hint' guidance, acting as a semantic gradient that steers the next trial's actions/answers. No weight updates.
- **planning integration**:
> Per-trial conditioning / retrieve-then-act: at the start of each new episode the agent reads its long-term reflective memory plus short-term trajectory, then re-plans and re-acts (via CoT or ReAct). Memory influences the whole next rollout rather than being injected at individual planning sub-steps.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: per-trial / per-answer: reflection is woven in once per episode (between trials), not per CoT-step or per-tool-call. Within a trial the underlying Actor may be ReAct (per-step thought-action), but the Reflexion memory mechanism operates at the episode boundary.
- **adaptation mechanism**: execution-feedback-driven revision: the retrieved verbal reflection prompts the LLM Actor to adapt its plan/actions in the next trial; revision is guided by sparse reward + self-critique rather than verbatim ICL reuse of a stored solution.
- **retrieved item representation**: Distilled free-text strategy / lesson written in the first person (verbal self-reflection summarizing the failure and an improved plan). Plus the raw recent trajectory in short-term memory.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Distilled strategy/insight (an actionable lesson abstracted from a failed trajectory), more abstract than a raw trajectory but task-specific rather than a reusable cross-task skill or workflow.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Self-reflection / self-evaluation acts as the relevance/quality filter: the Self-Reflection and Evaluator LLMs (or heuristics, EM grading, self-generated unit tests) decide what feedback to store. For code, the paper analyzes false-positive/false-negative unit tests; it notes preference for false negatives. No retriever-aware training or distractor-filtering of stored items. Memory window truncation limits accumulation of stale context.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: episodic (long-term episodic memory buffer of verbal self-reflections, plus short-term trajectory memory).
- **write back**: True: after each trial the Self-Reflection model produces a new reflection sr_t that is appended to the episodic memory buffer mem.
- **online growth**: True (within a task / across trials): the memory grows during deployment as the agent retries a task, bounded by max capacity Omega (1-3). It does NOT persist/grow across different tasks (memory is per-task).
- **write back trigger**:
> Reflective, after self-critique of an evaluated (typically failed) trial: triggered by the Evaluator's sparse reward signal (environment binary success, EM grading, self-generated unit-test failure, LLM self-evaluation, or AlfWorld heuristics for repeated actions/inefficient planning). Effectively writes on failure / not-yet-passed trials.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Failure-centric corrective reflections: Reflexion explicitly learns from prior FAILINGS - verbal feedback distills what went wrong and how to improve, then conditions future trials on these corrective lessons. This failure-driven self-reflection is the core mechanism (ablation shows it adds ~8% over episodic-memory-only on HotPotQA and 60->68% on HumanEval Rust).
- **memory evolution update**: Append-only with sliding-window forgetting/pruning: new reflections are appended; the buffer is truncated to the most recent Omega (1-3) experiences. Stored entries themselves are not mutated/merged/overwritten.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No. Reflexion frames the policy as 'memory encoding + LLM parameters' and performs natural-language policy optimization, but the case/memory selection is fixed (read-all-within-window), not a learned/RL-optimized retrieval policy. Verbal reinforcement substitutes for gradient-based RL but does not learn a retriever.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent private episodic memory; no cross-agent or cross-framework experience sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> AlfWorld (134 environments, 6 task types); HotPotQA (Wikipedia multi-hop QA, 100 questions evaluated); HumanEval (Python and Rust); MBPP (Python and Rust); LeetcodeHardGym (new benchmark: 40 Leetcode hard-rated questions across 19 programming languages, released after Oct 8 2022 GPT-4 cutoff). Rust translations via MultiPL-E.
- **benchmark family**: embodied (ALFWorld); multi-hop QA (HotPotQA); code (HumanEval / MBPP / LeetcodeHard).
- **baselines**:
> ReAct (decision-making and QA); Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and CoT with ground-truth context CoT(GT) (reasoning); episodic-memory-only ablation (EPM, no self-reflection); base single-sample code generation with GPT-4; prior SOTA code methods: CodeT+GPT-3.5/Codex; reported prev-SOTA GPT-4 pass@1. Conceptually contrasted with Self-Refine, Self-Debugging, CodeRL, AlphaCode.
- **key metrics**: Task success rate / cumulative tasks solved (AlfWorld); exact-match accuracy over trials (HotPotQA); pass@1 accuracy (HumanEval/MBPP/LeetcodeHard); plus test-execution diagnostics (TP/FN/FP/TN, false-positive rate).
- **headline result**: 91.0% pass@1 on HumanEval (Python) with GPT-4 + Reflexion, surpassing the prior GPT-4 SOTA of 80.1%. Additional headline gains: AlfWorld +22% absolute (ReAct+Reflexion solves 130/134 tasks in 12 trials), HotPotQA +20% (~+14% over CoT(GT) without ground-truth answers).
- **ablations**:
> (1) HotPotQA reasoning ablation: CoT(GT) baseline -> +episodic memory (EPM, most recent trajectory) -> +self-reflection; self-reflection adds an 8% absolute boost over the episodic-memory-only advantage, showing refinement-only is weaker than self-reflection-guided refinement. (2) Code ablation on 50 hardest HumanEval-Rust problems with GPT-4: Base 0.60; test-generation-omission (reflect without unit tests) 0.52 (worse than base); self-reflection-omission (tests but no verbal reflection) 0.60 (no gain over base); full Reflexion (tests + reflection) 0.68. Shows both unit-test grounding and verbal self-reflection are necessary, and they cooperate. (3) AlfWorld: failure-type analysis showing ReAct-only converges at ~22% hallucination rate while Reflexion recovers.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No. Only end-to-end task metrics (success rate, pass@1, accuracy) are reported; no intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k/nDCG) since there is no ranked retriever. Code experiments do report unit-test confusion-matrix diagnostics (TP/FN/FP/TN) as an auxiliary process analysis.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Primarily outcome metrics (final success/accuracy across trials), but with process-level analysis: learning curves over 12 trials, failure-type classification of AlfWorld trajectories, and unit-test false-positive/false-negative rates for code.
- **context budget and selection count**: Budget-capped sliding window: long-term memory truncated to the last Omega = 1-3 self-reflections (AlfWorld and HotPotQA use 3; programming uses max 1) explicitly to respect maximum LLM context length. Code test suite capped at n<=6 self-generated unit tests.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> LeetcodeHardGym (introduced by this paper): an interactive code-generation RL gym of 40 Leetcode hard-rated questions across 19 programming languages, all released after the GPT-4 pre-training cutoff (Oct 8, 2022) to avoid leakage; answer-verifiable via execution. Best reported: GPT-4 7.5% pass@1, Reflexion 15.0% pass@1 (Python), signaling high difficulty.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> ReAct (Yao et al., 2023) as the underlying action generator; Chain-of-Thought (Wei et al., 2022) as reasoning Actor; in-context policy iteration (Brooks et al., 2022) inspiring the memory component; RL formulation (Sutton & Barto, 2018); MultiPL-E (Cassano et al., 2022) for Rust translation; self-generated unit tests akin to CodeT.
- **contrasts with**:
> Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023, single-generation, no persistent memory), Self-Debugging (Chen et al., 2023), CodeRL (Le et al., 2022), AlphaCode (Li et al., 2022), CodeT (Chen et al., 2022); gradient-based/weight-updating reinforcement learning; beam-search self-evaluation (Xie et al., 2023). Distinguished by persistent episodic memory of self-reflections + self-reflection step (vs blind retry/refine).
- **lineage**:
> Group F (decision-making / memory / RL-style agents). A foundational early (2023) work in the experience/episodic-memory lineage of LLM agents: verbal/linguistic reinforcement over self-written episodic memory, a precursor to later experience-replay, skill-library, and case-based memory agents.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- completeness_vs_topk_objective
- cost_efficiency_tradeoff

<a id="item-voyager"></a>
### 126. Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models

2023  ·  arXiv 2305.16291  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16291)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2023
- **authors affiliation**: Guanzhi Wang, Yuqi Xie, Yunfan Jiang, Ajay Mandlekar, Chaowei Xiao, Yuke Zhu, Linxi 'Jim' Fan, Anima Anandkumar. Primary affiliations: NVIDIA; with Caltech, UT Austin, Stanford, and UW Madison.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16291
- **code url**: https://github.com/MineDojo/Voyager (MIT License); project site https://voyager.minedojo.org/
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/MineDojo/Voyager (single-branch research repo, last meaningful commits 2023; not a continuously-updated leaderboard/paper-list)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Embodied agent / open-ended lifelong learning and embodied control in Minecraft (high-level code-as-action planning via the Mineflayer API).
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent, open-ended lifelong learning in the Minecraft sandbox without human intervention and without model fine-tuning. The agent (GPT-4 via blackbox queries) continuously explores, proposes its own tasks via an automatic curriculum, writes executable JavaScript skills, and reuses them. No task-success supervision is given: success is judged by a self-verification LLM critic. Setting is online/test-time: the skill library starts empty and grows during deployment. A separately learned (accumulated) skill library can also be loaded into a fresh world for zero-shot task solving.
- **what is retrieved**: Reusable skills, each represented as a self-contained executable JavaScript/code function (temporally-extended, compositional behavior) plus an LLM-generated natural-language description used as the retrieval key.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> GROWING / episodic-procedural memory written by the agent itself (an ever-growing skill library). It is not a static external corpus; the agent adds verified skills online. (Control-primitive APIs are a fixed set always available in the prompt, but the retrieved skills come from the growing library.)
- **completeness vs topk objective**: Fixed top-k ranking: a constant top-5 similarity retrieval (retrieval_top_k=5). No completeness/minimal-set objective and no precision-driven variable-size selection; k is a fixed hyperparameter (capped at the current library size when fewer than 5 skills exist).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it describes a skill library / retrieval-augmented code generation. CBR mechanisms are realized only implicitly.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: skill-or-program: a complete executable code skill (an async JavaScript function that scaffolds a temporally-extended behavior for a curriculum-proposed task), indexed by the embedding of its NL description.
- **index source**: Growing memory induced online/at test-time: the skill vector store starts empty and is populated as GPT-4 generates and self-verifies new skills during lifelong learning. Not offline-induced; not a static corpus.
- **index structure topology**: Flat vector index. Skills are stored in a Chroma vector database (collection 'skill_vectordb'); each entry's key is the embedding of the program description and the value is the program code stored on disk / in skills.json. No graph, hierarchy, or clustering over skills.
- **retriever type**: Dense embedding retriever: OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 embeddings with cosine/L2 similarity search over a Chroma vector store (similarity_search_with_score). Off-the-shelf, not learned.
- **retriever learning signal**: None (off-the-shelf). The embedding model (text-embedding-ada-002) is frozen and not trained or fine-tuned; retrieval is fixed top-k similarity with no contrastive, LM-feedback, preference, or RL signal.
- **query construction**:
> Query is a synthetic, expanded context: GPT-3.5 first generates a general suggestion / task plan for solving the new task proposed by the automatic curriculum, which is combined with environment feedback; the embedding of this self-generated plan + environment feedback is used as the retrieval query. (The skill key is itself a GPT-3.5-generated program description embedding.)
- **query granularity**: Task-level: one retrieval per newly proposed task (the automatic-curriculum objective), conditioned on a generated plan and current environment feedback; not per-step or per-token.
- **when to retrieve**: One-shot per task: skills are retrieved once when a new task is faced (before code generation), then injected into the GPT-4 prompt for that task's iterative code-generation rounds.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule tied to the task lifecycle: retrieval is triggered whenever the automatic curriculum proposes a new task (at the start of solving that task). It is not confidence-, attention-, or learned-classifier-triggered.
- **reranking**: None. A single similarity_search_with_score returns top-5; no second-stage reranker (no cross-encoder, RRF, or hierarchy-aware reranking).
- **retrieved context refinement**: None / minimal: retrieved skills are used as-is (their full code is inserted into the prompt). No decomposition, distillation, distractor filtering, or compression of retrieved skills.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Skill descriptions are LLM-engineered before indexing: a dedicated GPT-3.5 'skill' prompt summarizes each generated program into a concise NL description (synthetic-summary augmentation), and the embedding of that description (not the raw code) is the index key. The description is generated as a JS comment header for the function.
- **index content separation**: Yes (lightweight): the retrievable index stores only the description embedding (key) while the heavy content (full program code) is the value loaded on retrieval; description is separated from code, a form of progressive disclosure (embed description, load code on demand).
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Live-synchronized growing index with CRUD-like behavior: skills are added (and overwritten/rewritten if the same program_name recurs, with the old vectordb id deleted) during learning; the Chroma vectordb is kept synced with skills.json. Integration protocol is function-calling style execution via the Mineflayer JS API (not RapidAPI/REST/MCP).
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> No explicit inter-skill dependency modeling in retrieval. Compositionality is achieved at code-generation time (new skills call previously written skills/control primitives), but retrieval itself does not model a dependency graph or prerequisites; all current skill code plus control primitives are made available as reusable building blocks.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Skill reuse via prompt augmentation: the top-5 retrieved skill programs (plus fixed control-primitive APIs) are inserted into GPT-4's code-generation prompt as in-context exemplars / reusable building blocks, so GPT-4 can call or compose them when synthesizing the new skill. No fine-tuning; retrieval feeds in-context learning only.
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-generate at task time: the automatic curriculum proposes a task, GPT-3.5 generates a plan, relevant skills are retrieved, and GPT-4 then synthesizes/refines code via the iterative prompting loop. Retrieval is one-shot per task (plan-then-retrieve-then-code), not interleaved inside a tree search or per action step.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-task (per-answer/per-skill): one retrieval call per curriculum task before the code-generation rollout. The iterative self-improvement loop (up to 4 rounds) reuses the same retrieved skills; retrieval is not re-issued per CoT step or per code-execution round.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> Execution-feedback-driven adaptation under in-context reuse: retrieved skills serve as ICL exemplars/callable building blocks, and the freshly generated program is iteratively revised using environment feedback, execution errors, and a self-verification critique (not verbatim replay, not RL fine-tuning). (Voyager is not framed as CBR.)
- **retrieved item representation**: Executable program/skill: the surface form injected into the prompt is raw JavaScript skill code (async functions) plus a descriptive comment header, not a distilled strategy, free-text workflow, or latent token.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Procedural skill: a reusable, temporally-extended, compositional executable program (higher abstraction than a raw trajectory or single demonstration; lower than a free-text strategy).
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> No dedicated retrieval-noise mechanism. Robustness comes from the downstream iterative prompting loop: self-verification (GPT-4 critic), environment feedback, and execution errors let GPT-4 ignore/repair unsuitable retrieved skills; there is no retriever-aware training or relevance evaluator gating the retrieved skills.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: skill-library (procedural memory of executable code skills), implemented as a vector database; plus a lightweight event/log checkpoint. Primary retrievable memory is the skill library.
- **write back**: Yes. Each time GPT-4 generates and self-verifies a new skill, the skill (code + GPT-3.5 description + description embedding) is written into the skill library / Chroma vectordb.
- **online growth**: Yes. The skill library is 'ever-growing': it starts empty and expands continuously during deployment/lifelong learning; it is not frozen after an offline phase.
- **write back trigger**:
> On-success only (after self-verification): a skill is added to the library only once the GPT-4 self-verification critic validates the task as completed. Failed attempts are not stored as skills (the deposit/chest housekeeping skill is also explicitly excluded). If the same program_name recurs, the new version overwrites the old vectordb entry.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success-only for the persistent skill library: only verified/successful skills are retained and retrieved. Failure information (execution errors, critic critiques, environment feedback) is used transiently within the same task's iterative prompting rounds for self-improvement, but is not stored or retrieved as failure memory.
- **memory evolution update**:
> Mostly append-only with refine-overwrite on name collision: new verified skills are appended; if a skill with the same program_name is regenerated, the old entry is deleted from the vectordb and rewritten (versioned on disk as nameV2/V3...). No dedup-merge across different names, no forgetting/pruning, no delta linking.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No. Retrieval is fixed top-k cosine similarity over frozen embeddings; case/skill selection is not a learned or RL-optimized policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Single-agent private memory by design, but the learned skill library is explicitly shown to be plug-and-play across frameworks: loading Voyager's skill library into AutoGPT improves AutoGPT's zero-shot task success, demonstrating transferable/shareable skills. No multi-agent shared memory during learning.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> MineDojo-based custom Minecraft evaluation: (1) exploration performance (unique items discovered within 160 prompting iterations), (2) Minecraft tech-tree mastery (wooden -> stone -> iron -> diamond tools), (3) map coverage / distance traversed, (4) zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks in a new world (Diamond Pickaxe, Golden Sword, Lava Bucket, Compass). Built on MineDojo + Mineflayer.
- **benchmark family**: embodied (Minecraft). Custom Minecraft tasks built on MineDojo/Mineflayer rather than a standard fixed benchmark suite.
- **baselines**:
> ReAct (Yao et al. 2022), Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023), and AutoGPT (re-implemented with GPT-4 for task decomposition). All re-interpreted to run in MineDojo with environment feedback / agent state. Also internal variants: Voyager w/o Skill Library, and AutoGPT augmented with Voyager's skill library.
- **key metrics**:
