> Number of unique items discovered (exploration); prompting iterations to unlock each tech-tree level (efficiency, lower is better) with success fraction out of 3 trials; distance traversed (map coverage); zero-shot task success fraction and prompting iterations to solve unseen tasks.
- **headline result**:
> Voyager obtains 3.3x more unique items, travels 2.3x longer distances, and unlocks the wooden-tool tech-tree milestone up to 15.3x faster than prior SOTA; it discovers 63 unique items within 160 prompting iterations and is the only method to unlock the diamond tool. In zero-shot transfer to a new world it solves all 4 unseen tasks while ReAct/Reflexion/AutoGPT solve none.
- **ablations**:
> Six design choices ablated on exploration: automatic curriculum (random curriculum drops discovered-item count by 93%; manual curriculum underperforms), skill library (removing it causes performance to plateau in later stages and the agent only reaches up to iron, never diamond), environment feedback, execution errors, self-verification (most important feedback type; removal -73% discovered items), and GPT-4 vs GPT-3.5 for code generation (GPT-4 yields 5.7x more unique items). Skill library is specifically shown to drive compounding/late-stage gains and zero-shot generalization; it is also transferable (boosts AutoGPT).
- **evaluation decoupling**: No. Only end-to-end task/exploration metrics are reported; no intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k, nDCG, retrieval completeness) are measured for the skill-retrieval step.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome-oriented but with strong process/efficiency signals: besides final success it reports prompting-iteration efficiency to reach milestones, exploration trajectory (item discovery over iterations), and map traversal, which capture intermediate progress rather than only final success.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Discussed qualitatively as a limitation: GPT-4 API is ~15x more expensive than GPT-3.5 but necessary for the code-generation quality (GPT-3.5 gives 5.7x fewer items). Efficiency is reported as prompting iterations to reach milestones (e.g., diamond reached at ~102 iterations in 1/3 trials; wooden at ~6 iterations). No explicit dollar cost or latency table; embedding/retrieval cost is negligible relative to GPT-4 calls.
- **context budget and selection count**: Fixed-k selection: top-5 retrieved skills (retrieval_top_k=5), capped at the current library size. No explicit token-budget cap or adaptive/precision-driven k; retrieved skill code plus control-primitive APIs and state are concatenated into the GPT-4 prompt.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (this is a method paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (no released standalone benchmark dataset; evaluation is a custom MineDojo/Mineflayer Minecraft protocol over exploration, tech-tree, map coverage, and 4 zero-shot tasks, each averaged over 3 trials with 160 (learning) / 50 (zero-shot) max prompting iterations).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> GPT-4 (OpenAI) for blackbox code generation; MineDojo (Fan et al. 2022) and Mineflayer for the Minecraft environment and high-level control API; ReAct and Reflexion for prompting/self-reflection ideas; AutoGPT for task decomposition; DreamCoder (Ellis et al. 2020) for the program-as-skill / library-growth inspiration; chain-of-thought prompting; OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 + Chroma vector store for skill retrieval.
- **contrasts with**:
> ReAct, Reflexion, and AutoGPT (which lack a growing skill library, self-verification, and automatic curriculum); pixel-to-low-level-control Minecraft agents such as VPT, MineDojo-based RL, DEPS, and other gradient/RL approaches (positioned as orthogonal, since Voyager uses a high-level code API rather than learning sensorimotor control); self-reflection-only methods (Voyager's self-verification both checks success and reflects).
- **lineage**:
> Group F (decision-making / memory / RL agents): an early and highly influential example of a retrieval-augmented, self-growing procedural skill-library agent. Pioneers code-as-skill lifelong memory retrieved by embedding similarity, a lineage continued by works such as JARVIS-1, GITM, and later skill/workflow-memory agents (e.g., AWM, Agent Workflow Memory); contrasts with static-corpus RAG planners.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- cbr_cycle_coverage
- venue

<a id="item-awm"></a>
### 127. AWM: Agent Workflow Memory

2024  ·  ICLR 2025  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07429)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**:
> ICML 2025 (Forty-second International Conference on Machine Learning; Proceedings of the 42nd ICML, ACM DOI 10.5555/3780338.3782875). NOTE: the task metadata listed 'ICLR 2025', but the verified peer-reviewed venue is ICML 2025 (OpenReview id NTAhi2JEEE, ICML 2025 Poster). Preprint: arXiv:2409.07429 (cs.CL), v1 submitted 11 Sep 2024.
- **authors affiliation**: Zora Zhiruo Wang (Carnegie Mellon University), Jiayuan Mao (Massachusetts Institute of Technology), Daniel Fried (Carnegie Mellon University), Graham Neubig (Carnegie Mellon University). Lead author: Zora Zhiruo Wang (CMU).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07429
- **code url**: https://github.com/zorazrw/agent-workflow-memory (Apache-2.0; ~442 stars; pipelines for both webarena/ and mind2web/).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> web / decision-making: LM-based web-navigation agents that perceive web observations (accessibility tree on WebArena; filtered HTML / element candidates on Mind2Web) and emit executable actions (click, type, stop, etc.) to complete long-horizon tasks across travel, shopping, social media, software development, content management, and maps.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent sequential decision-making for web navigation. An LM-backbone agent L with a text-based memory M (base memory = built-in action docs such as CLICK/TYPE) solves a task specified by an NL instruction q in an environment with transition function T: at each step t_i, observation o_i is fed to the model to generate action a_i via L(q, M, o_i) -> a_i, executed until STOP or a max-step termination. AWM induces reusable workflows W = {w} from past experiences E = {e} via an induction module I(E) -> W, then augments memory M + W -> M_w to guide subsequent task-solving. Two settings: (1) OFFLINE — when high-quality annotated/canonical training examples are available (Mind2Web cross-task training set), workflows are induced once from training examples beforehand and used frozen at test time; (2) ONLINE / supervision-free — only test queries exist (WebArena, and Mind2Web cross-website/cross-domain); the agent processes test queries in a streaming manner, after each task it judges success with an LM evaluator (Pan et al. 2024 AutoEval) and, if success, induces workflows and appends them to memory for subsequent tasks (continual / streaming growth). Frozen LM backbone (no gradient updates); workflows are text/code injected into the prompt context. AWM is run on a per-website basis (examples grouped by website) to keep the workflow set small and relevant.
- **what is retrieved**:
> workflows (reusable routines / sub-routines induced from past agent trajectories). Each workflow = an NL description d (the high-level goal/summary) + a series of steps (p1, p2, ...) where each step has (1) an NL description of the current environment state, (2) the agent's reasoning, and (3) an executable program action. Example-specific values are abstracted out (e.g., 'dry cat food' -> '{product-name}').
- **retrieval grounding**:
> GROWING / episodic memory the agent writes (with an offline-induced variant). In the online setting the workflow memory is a growing store the agent continually writes to from its own (evaluator-verified) successful test-time trajectories. In the offline setting the store is induced once from annotated training examples and frozen at test time. Both are agent-induced experience memory, not a static external corpus/KB/API set. Overall: growing/episodic memory (online) or offline-induced experience memory (offline); not a static external corpus.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Not a top-k ranking objective. AWM does NOT rank-and-select top-k workflows per query; in the reported main results it injects ALL induced workflows for a given website into the agent memory at once (whole-memory augmentation), and lets the LM selectively attend to/apply relevant ones during generation. Selection is therefore an all-relevant-workflows-as-context scheme (kept small via per-website grouping; ~7.3-7.4 workflows/example), closer to providing the complete useful routine set than a fixed-k recommendation. The paper notes the design 'selectively providing workflows', but selection within context is done by the LM rather than an explicit retriever.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve: partial (workflows provided in context / selected implicitly by the LM, no explicit similarity retriever), Reuse: yes (workflows used as in-context guidance / callable skills to solve new tasks), Revise: partial (no per-case revision of a retrieved workflow at solve time, but workflows are induced/abstracted from experiences and complex ones are composed from simpler ones; the LM may diverge from workflow guidance), Retain: yes (induced workflows are retained in memory, online growth)]. AWM most strongly implements Reuse + Retain, with abstraction/induction at write time; explicit Retrieve and Revise are weak/implicit.
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False. The paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is presented as agent workflow memory / library learning / skill induction, motivated by cognitive-science work on expert routines (Chi et al. 1981/2014). It nonetheless realizes CBR-style Reuse+Retain over abstracted procedural routines rather than concrete cases.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> workflow-routine: a reusable sub-routine (a frequently re-appearing sub-task such as 'search for a product on Amazon' or 'find a place by its name'), represented as <description, ordered steps> where each step = (NL state description, reasoning, executable program action). Finer-grained than a full task trajectory; example-specific contexts are abstracted away. (In the AWM-AS variant a workflow is wrapped as a callable high-level function/action.)
- **index source**:
> Hybrid by setting. OFFLINE: store is offline-induced from the annotated training set (Mind2Web cross-task training examples), built once and frozen. ONLINE: store is online/test-time-induced and grows in a streaming fashion from the agent's own evaluator-verified successful test trajectories (no annotated data). An AWM-off+on integration combining both is also explored (Appendix C). The store is an induced experience/workflow memory, not a pre-existing corpus.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat textual workflow list embedded directly in the agent memory / prompt context (system prompt or auxiliary prompt context). Workflows are segmented (by double-line breaks in the LM output) and stored separately as individual entries; grouped/partitioned by website. No vector index, dependency graph, or learned hierarchy. (Implicit compositional hierarchy emerges because later complex workflows are built on top of earlier simpler ones, e.g., 'get the zip code of a place' reuses 'find a place by its name', but there is no explicit graph structure.)
- **retriever type**:
> LLM-as-selector / no explicit retriever. There is no BM25/dense/learned retrieval module: the induced workflows for a website are all placed into context, and the LM itself decides which workflows to use during generation. (The rule-based induction variant uses action-sequence deduplication, not retrieval. The compared baseline Synapse uses dense retrieval of concrete examples, but AWM replaces that with always-in-context abstract workflows.) Closest label: LLM-as-retriever / in-context selection by the generation LM.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> none (no trained retriever). Selection of which workflows to apply is performed implicitly by the frozen generation LM from the workflows present in context; there is no contrastive/LM-feedback/RL/value-based training of a retrieval component. The induction module is a frozen LM prompted to extract sub-routines (LM-based) or a deterministic rule-based dedup procedure; neither is trained. The only learning signal in the loop is the LM evaluator's binary success label gating online write-back (not a retriever-training signal).
- **query construction**:
> No explicit query is constructed for retrieval (all workflows for the website are provided in context). For workflow INDUCTION, the 'query' to the induction LM is the concatenation of one or more past experiences (NL instruction q + full action trajectory of (observation, action) steps); offline it concatenates all training examples of a website into a single prompt; online it feeds the single just-completed (evaluator-verified) experience. Induction prompts instruct the LM to extract finer-grained sub-routines and abstract out example-specific values into placeholders (e.g., {product-name}).
- **query granularity**:
> task-level (one-shot at t=0) for utilization: for each test task the full website workflow memory is provided once at the start and reused across all steps of that episode (no per-step re-query). For induction, the granularity is trajectory/experience-level (whole completed experiences are summarized into sub-routine workflows).
- **when to retrieve**:
> one-shot (per task) for utilization — the workflow memory is provided once at task start and not re-retrieved within the episode. The MEMORY itself is updated/grown on a one-task-at-a-time schedule in the online setting (induce-integrate-utilize loop after each completed test task), but there is no within-episode iterative or uncertainty-triggered retrieval.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> fixed schedule. Utilization: workflows are unconditionally included in memory at the start of each task. Memory write/update (online): triggered deterministically after every completed test task, gated by the LM evaluator's binary success judgment (write only if predicted success). Offline: workflows induced once before test time on a fixed schedule. No token-confidence/attention/reflection-token/agent-initiated retrieval trigger.
- **reranking**: None. No reranking stage; all induced website-level workflows are injected and the LM attends to relevant ones during generation.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Refinement happens at INDUCTION/WRITE time rather than at retrieval time: the LM induction module distills full trajectories into finer-grained sub-routine workflows, abstracts out example-specific values into placeholders ({product-name}), and segments outputs into separate workflow entries; the rule-based variant deduplicates by action sequence and filters invalid (non-executable) steps. At utilization time the workflows are injected as-is (no per-query rerank/compress/decompose). Optional state-abstraction explorations (Sec 4.3) describe environment states in NL vs filtered HTML, but NL descriptions worked best and HTML augmentation hurt.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (not a tool-retrieval method). In the AWM-AS variant induced workflows are wrapped as callable high-level functions (e.g., login(username,password)) added to the action space, but there is no tool-description indexing/augmentation pipeline.
- **index content separation**:
> No. Each workflow carries both its lightweight NL description and its full step content together in memory; there is no separate lightweight retrievable index pointing to on-demand heavy content (no progressive disclosure / SOP-index-then-content scheme). Workflows are kept compact via per-website grouping and abstraction instead.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no live tool index/MCP/RapidAPI/REST integration; environment interaction is via WebArena/BrowserGym and Mind2Web action APIs and executable program actions).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no inter-tool dependency modeling). Workflows do exhibit implicit compositional dependency among themselves — complex workflows reuse simpler ones — but this is not modeled as a dependency graph or dependency-aware retrieval.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> prompt augmentation / skill reuse: induced workflows are integrated into the agent's text memory (M + W -> M_w) so the agent generates actions via L(q, M+W, o) -> a, using workflows as in-context guidance / reusable routines. An additional AWM-AS variant promotes workflows to skill reuse by wrapping each workflow into a callable high-level action (e.g., find_place, login) added to the agent's action space, executing a pre-determined sequence of primitive actions when invoked.
- **planning integration**:
> retrieve(induce)-then-plan with workflows as in-context guidance: induced workflows are added to memory and used as one-shot, plan-time guidance that conditions a per-step observe-act loop (L(q, M_w, o_i) -> a_i executed by T until STOP). Workflows describe high-level goals + ordered steps that the agent follows/adapts while acting. In the online setting this is interleaved across tasks (plan task t, induce workflow, plan task t+1 with augmented memory). In AWM-AS, workflows become callable macro-actions inside the per-step action loop. No tree search/MCTS; no per-step re-retrieval.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> per-task for retrieval/memory provisioning (workflows provided once per task) combined with per-step (per-tool-call) acting within the rollout. In the online setting, the induce-integrate-utilize cycle is interleaved at the per-task granularity (after each completed task). Workflow application within an episode is woven into the per-step action generation, but no fresh retrieval occurs per CoT-step or per-token.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> LM-prompted induction/abstraction at write time + in-context guidance at solve time. Cases (experiences) are adapted into reusable form by an LM induction module that extracts finer-grained sub-routines and replaces example-specific values with placeholders; at solve time the retrieved workflow is reused as in-context guidance that the LM instantiates to the current task (filling placeholders) and may diverge from when the environment state differs. No execution-feedback-driven per-case revision loop, no critic-guided revision, no RL fine-tuning.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> free-text/code workflow: each injected workflow is an NL description d plus an ordered list of steps, each step containing (1) an NL state description (e.g., 'Order {id} is shown'), (2) the agent's NL reasoning, and (3) an executable program action (e.g., stop(), click(id), type(id, text)). Example-specific values are replaced with abstract placeholders ({product-name}, {id}). Explored alternatives: a fully textual (verbalized) workflow format (AWM-text) and HTML-augmented states — code and text forms performed comparably. In AWM-AS the workflow is an executable high-level function.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> reusable workflow / distilled procedural sub-routine: an abstracted, frequently-reused routine with example-specific contexts removed (placeholders) — explicitly NOT a raw full-trajectory exemplar (the paper contrasts this with Synapse's concrete full-example retrieval, attributing AWM's gains to the abstract, reusable nature of workflows that reduces element-selection bias). Sits between a raw trajectory and a high-level skill; described as a common sub-routine / task recipe.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> (1) LM evaluator gating: in the online setting only evaluator-verified successful trajectories are turned into workflows, filtering incorrect experiences before write-back (though imperfect — wrong workflows from mis-judged trajectories can still degrade performance); (2) abstraction of example-specific contexts into placeholders reduces over-fitting/element-selection bias from concrete exemplars; (3) rule-based induction filters invalid (non-executable) actions and deduplicates redundant trajectories; (4) per-website grouping keeps the workflow set small and relevant; (5) the agent is observed to learn to diverge from workflow guidelines when they do not match the current state (though imperfectly — slightly lower Action F1 than MindAct). No retriever-aware contrastive/distractor-aware SFT (frozen LM).

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> workflow memory (procedural / skill-library-like text memory): a continually-built text memory of reusable workflows (routines) augmenting the base action-documentation memory. Combines workflow + procedural-skill characteristics; in AWM-AS workflows additionally act as a callable skill library.
- **write back**:
> Yes (online). The system stores newly induced workflows from past (successful) experiences into the agent memory (M^t + {w^t} -> M^{t+1}). In the offline setting write-back occurs once before test time (induced from training examples); in the online setting it occurs continually at test time.
- **online growth**:
> Yes (in the online setting). The workflow memory grows during deployment/test-time in a streaming fashion as the agent induces and appends new workflows after each completed (evaluator-verified) test task, creating a snowball/continual-learning effect (e.g., +22.5 points gain over baseline after only tens of WebArena examples). In the offline-only setting the store is frozen after pre-test induction.
- **write back trigger**:
> Online: reflective / on-success-only after each task — after each completed test task an LM evaluator (Pan et al. 2024) outputs a binary success label; only if predicted success (label = 1) is the experience transformed into workflow(s) and appended to memory. Offline: induced once from the annotated training set before test time (a one-time write on a fixed schedule). No failure-triggered or human-validated writes in the main method.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success-only. Only successful experiences (offline: ground-truth annotated training examples; online: evaluator-judged-correct self-generated trajectories) are converted into workflows and stored. Failed/negative trajectories are NOT stored or retrieved; there are no contrastive success+failure entries or failure-derived corrective rules. (The paper analyzes a workflow-action failure case (book_flight pop-up airports) qualitatively but does not feed failures back as memory.)
- **memory evolution update**:
> Append-only with implicit compositional build-up. New workflows are appended to memory; the agent builds increasingly complex workflows on top of earlier simpler ones (e.g., 'get the zip code of a place' composes/extends 'find a place by its name'), so functionality grows compositionally over time. The paper does not implement explicit dedup-merge/delta-update/refine-overwrite/forget-prune of existing entries during online growth (induction quality metrics report low inter-workflow function overlap ~0.08-0.20, i.e., naturally near-non-overlapping appends). Rule-based induction deduplicates at induction time only.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No. Workflow selection/use is not a learned or RL-optimized retrieval policy; relevant workflows are chosen implicitly by the frozen generation LM from the in-context workflow set. The only learned/neural decision in the loop is the LM success-evaluator gating online write-back, which is a verification policy, not a retrieval policy. Selection is not a fixed similarity top-k either — it is whole-memory (all website workflows) in-context provisioning.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent private workflow memory; workflows are induced and used by the same agent (grouped per website). No cross-agent or cross-framework experience/memory sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> WebArena (812 web navigation tasks over 5 self-hosted websites covering e-commerce/shopping, social forum/Reddit, software development/GitLab, content management/CMS, and maps; execution-based functional-correctness evaluation; online setting only). Mind2Web (versatile real-world web navigation with cross-task, cross-website, and cross-domain test splits; offline + online settings; element accuracy / action F1 / step SR / task SR metrics). Together 1000+ tasks from 200+ domains.
- **benchmark family**: web (Mind2Web / WebArena) — agentic web-navigation benchmarks.
- **baselines**:
> WebArena: BrowserGym (Drouin et al. 2024; current SOTA autonomous, both default and accessibility-tree-only BrowserGym_ax-tree), AutoEval/AutoEval-style AutoEval (Pan et al. 2024), the original WebArena agent (Zhou et al. 2024), and SteP (Sodhi et al. 2023; uses 14 human-expert-written workflows). Mind2Web: MindAct (Deng et al. 2023; element-filtering + multi-choice format), Synapse (Zheng et al. 2024; trajectory-as-exemplar retrieval of concrete examples), and CogAgent (referenced). Backbone LLMs: GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613, temperature 0) on WebArena and Mind2Web; GPT-3.5-turbo (temperature 0) additionally on Mind2Web; same model used for workflow induction and action generation. Online success evaluator: LM-based evaluator from Pan et al. 2024.
- **key metrics**:
> WebArena: task success rate (SR, %) with per-website breakdown, plus average number of steps (efficiency). Mind2Web: element accuracy (Elem Acc / EA), action F1 (AF1), step success rate (Step SR), and whole-task success rate (SR). Workflow-quality intrinsic metrics: number of workflows, coverage, function overlap, utility rate.
- **headline result**:
> WebArena: 35.5% overall task success rate with GPT-4 (online AWM), the best published autonomous result — +12.0 absolute points / +51.1% relative over the BrowserGym baseline (23.5%), and +7.6%-7.9% relative over SteP (33.0%) despite SteP using 14 human-written workflows and AWM using no human supervision; AWM also reduces steps (5.9 vs 7.9 for BrowserGym_ax-tree, ~40.8 fewer than AutoEval). Mind2Web cross-task: +24.6% relative step-wise success rate over baseline (e.g., GPT-4 AWM_offline Step SR 45.1 vs MindAct 36.2). Online AWM generalizes by +8.9 to +14.0 absolute step-SR points as train-test distribution gaps widen. (GitHub README states 35.6% SR, matching the rule-based variant AWM_rule = 35.6, LM-based AWM_lm = 35.5.)
- **ablations**:
> (1) LM-based vs rule-based induction: comparable on WebArena (AWM_rule 35.6 / 6.3 steps vs AWM_lm 35.5 / 5.9 steps) but LM-based clearly better on Mind2Web (AWM_lm Step SR 45.1 / SR 4.8 vs AWM_rule 43.4 / 2.0), showing the abstract finer-grained sub-routine format drives the Mind2Web gain (Sec 4.1, Tables 5-6). (2) Abstract workflows vs concrete examples: vs Synapse (retrieved full examples) AWM gives +5.0 Elem Acc and +4.0 Step SR, attributed to less element-selection bias from abstraction (Sec 3.2.1). (3) Workflow format text vs code (Sec 4.2, Table 7): comparable — AWM_text slightly higher Step SR (45.4 vs 45.1) but lower task SR (3.6 vs 4.8). (4) Environment abstraction (Sec 4.3, Table 8): NL state descriptions > filtered HTML; using both NL+HTML hurts (Step SR 32.9). (5) Workflows in action space AWM-AS (Sec 5, Table 9): +1.3 Step SR (46.4) but same overall SR (3.2); workflow actions invoked in only 18.5% of tasks. (6) Online vs offline on Mind2Web generalization (Table 4): online generalizes better as domain gap widens (cross-domain Step SR online 35.5 vs offline 32.6); offline+online integration (Appendix C) gives intermediate, sub-additive results. (7) Efficient learning (Sec 3.1.2, Fig 5): a steep learning curve within ~40 WebArena map examples. (8) Workflow-quality analysis (Appendix A.3, Table 10): WebArena 7.4 workflows, utility rate 0.94, function overlap 0.08; Mind2Web 7.3 workflows, coverage 0.40, function overlap 0.20, utility rate 0.91.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Partially. The paper reports intrinsic workflow-quality metrics (number of workflows, coverage, function overlap, utility rate; Appendix A.3 Table 10) separately from end-to-end task metrics, and on Mind2Web reports element accuracy / action F1 as sub-step intrinsic-style measures. However it does NOT report standard ranked-retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG) because there is no explicit top-k retriever; workflow effectiveness is assessed mainly via downstream task gains plus the workflow-quality metrics.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both. WebArena uses outcome (task success rate) plus efficiency (number of steps). Mind2Web adds intermediate process metrics: per-step Step SR, element accuracy, and action F1, in addition to whole-task SR. Workflow-quality metrics (coverage, utility rate, function overlap) further probe process/memory quality beyond final outcome.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Efficiency is a headline benefit. WebArena: AWM uses ~5.9 steps/task vs 7.9 for BrowserGym_ax-tree (~2.0 fewer) and ~40.8 fewer steps than AutoEval (which adds evaluation+refinement loops), i.e., higher success with shorter trajectories. AWM needs no human-written workflows (vs SteP's 14) and works supervision-free online. Sample efficiency: substantial gains after only ~40 examples (Fig 5). Memory footprint is small: ~7.3-7.4 workflows per website with high utility (0.91-0.94) and low overlap (0.08-0.20). No explicit dollar/latency numbers beyond step counts; online adds one LM evaluator call + one LM induction call per task.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Whole-memory-in-context, budget-controlled by per-website grouping. All workflows induced for a given website (kept small, ~7.3-7.4 per website per the quality analysis) are concatenated into the agent memory/prompt at once rather than selecting a fixed k by similarity; per-website grouping is the explicit mechanism to keep the injected set small and relevant. No fixed-k or reranked-then-truncated retrieval; the generation LM attends to relevant workflows. Greedy decoding (temperature 0) for both GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Synapse (Zheng et al. 2024; trajectory-as-exemplar retrieval — AWM swaps concrete retrieved examples for abstract workflows) and MindAct/Mind2Web (Deng et al. 2023; element filtering + multi-choice format, reused as the agent backbone on Mind2Web); BrowserGym/WorkArena (Drouin et al. 2024) and WebArena (Zhou et al. 2024) frameworks; LM-based library-learning / skill-induction lineage (LATM/Cai et al. 2023, TroVE Wang et al. 2024c, Voyager Wang et al. 2023a skill library) and rule-based program library learning (DreamCoder/Ellis et al. 2023, Stitch/Bowers et al. 2023, LILO/Grand et al. 2023); AutoEval (Pan et al. 2024) LM success evaluator used to gate online write-back; SteP/HEAP (Sodhi et al. 2023) human-written workflows compared against; cognitive-science work on expert routines (Chi et al. 1981/2014); 'What are tools anyway?' survey (Wang et al. 2024b) for the workflow-as-action framing.
- **contrasts with**:
> Synapse and other example-demonstration-in-context methods (Zheng et al. 2024; Fu et al. 2024) that augment with concrete full examples and entangle example-specific contexts — AWM contrasts by inducing abstract, reusable sub-routine workflows (less element-selection bias, better cross-task/website/domain generalization). SteP/HEAP (Sodhi et al. 2023) which rely on human-expert-written workflows — AWM induces workflows automatically without human supervision and still surpasses SteP. Fixed/training-based agents (BAGEL Murty et al. 2024; Fu et al. 2024) that integrate a fixed example set and lack robustness to context changes; non-adapting baselines (BrowserGym, MindAct) that solve each task independently without learning from past experience. Rule-based-only induction (AWM_rule) contrasted with LM-based abstract induction.
- **lineage**:
> Group F (decision / memory / RL — experience-memory planners): a workflow-memory web agent that induces abstracted, reusable procedural routines from past trajectories and grows them online to guide future planning, in the lineage of ICL web/computer agents (ReAct -> MindAct/Synapse -> AWM) and LM library-/skill-learning (Voyager, TroVE, DreamCoder/LILO). Bridges retrieval-augmented prompting and continual experience/skill memory; distinct from concrete-trajectory CBR (Synapse) by its abstraction-to-workflow step.

<a id="item-ra-dt"></a>
### 128. RA-DT (Retrieval-Augmented Decision Transformer)

2024  ·  ICLR 2025  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.07071)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **authors affiliation**:
> Thomas Schmied, Fabian Paischer, Vihang Patil (ELLIS Unit Linz / LIT AI Lab, Institute for Machine Learning, JKU Linz, Austria); Markus Hofmarcher (Extensity AI); Razvan Pascanu (Google DeepMind / Mila / UCL); Sepp Hochreiter (JKU Linz / NXAI). Lead author Thomas Schmied (JKU Linz).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.07071
- **code url**: https://github.com/ml-jku/RA-DT (MIT License; primary language Python; maintainer thomasschmied)
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/ml-jku/RA-DT (also releases datasets for Dark-Room, Dark Key-Door, MazeRunner, and Procgen)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Decision-making / offline reinforcement learning (in-context RL). Evaluated on grid-world navigation, robotics control, and procedurally-generated video games. Not QA/tool-use/web; it is a sequence-modeling RL agent (Decision Transformer) with external memory.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline pre-training of a Decision Transformer on multi-task pre-collected trajectory datasets, followed by interactive test-time evaluation of in-context learning (ICL): after training, the frozen agent interacts with held-out tasks/environments for a fixed number of episodes (ICL trials) without weight updates, and is expected to improve across trials by storing/retrieving its own past experiences. Single-agent, supervision is next-action prediction (cross-entropy for discrete actions, MSE for continuous). No expert demonstrations are required (data comes from PPO behavioural policies); the goal is to enable ICL in long-episode, sparse-reward environments where prior in-context RL methods (which keep entire episodes in context) fail.
- **what is retrieved**: Sub-trajectories (fixed-length segments of past experience: sequences of state/action/reward/return-to-go tokens). Values stored in the index are sub-trajectories spanning t-C:t+C (the query segment plus its continuation).
- **retrieval grounding**:
> HYBRID. At training time the index is a STATIC store built offline from the pre-collected multi-task dataset D (index = D). At inference/test time the index starts EMPTY and GROWS episodically: the agent writes each completed episode of its own interaction into the retrieval buffer and retrieves only same-task experiences from this growing episodic memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k ranking via maximum inner product search (top-l then reweight to top-k). Not a completeness/minimal-set objective. k is small and fixed (k=1 retrieved sub-trajectory for grid-worlds/Procgen; top-4 concatenated for Meta-World/DMControl). It is a fixed-k similarity-driven selection, not a precision-driven variable-size set.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> N/A (not framed as CBR). If mapped loosely: Retrieve = yes (MIPS over sub-trajectory memory); Reuse = yes (cross-attention conditioning on retrieved segment); Revise = no explicit case adaptation/revision; Retain = yes (append episodes to memory at inference). Flags: [Retrieve: yes, Reuse: yes, Revise: no, Retain: yes].
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is framed as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) / episodic external memory for in-context RL.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: Sub-trajectory: a fixed-length segment of context length C of (state, action, reward, return-to-go) tuples (a (state,reward,action)-tuple sequence rather than a single transition). Keys embed the segment t-C:t; values store t-C:t+C (segment + continuation).
- **index source**: Hybrid construction. Training: offline-induced static store equal to the pre-collected training dataset D (key-value pairs of all sub-trajectories). Inference: online/test-time-induced store, initialized empty and populated by the agent's own collected episodes during ICL trials.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat vector index (Faiss). Authors note HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) graphs are supported for O(log M) search, but for their small RL datasets they use a flat GPU index. So effectively a flat dense vector index; metadata (task ID, episode return) is attached per entry for reweighting.
- **retriever type**:
> Dense, training-free / off-the-shelf. Maximum inner product search (cosine similarity) over embeddings produced by an embedding model g. Two variants: (1) domain-specific embedding = a DT pre-trained on the same domain; (2) domain-agnostic = a frozen pre-trained LM (BERT-base-uncased) accessed via the FrozenHopfield mechanism. No learned retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None (off-the-shelf / training-free). The retrieval component requires no training: it uses a frozen embedding model (either a separately pre-trained DT or a frozen BERT via FrozenHopfield) plus cosine-similarity MIPS. Retrieved items are re-ranked by hand-designed relevance + utility heuristics (task-ID match during training, episode return during inference), not a learned signal. Authors note end-to-end training of the retriever (a la Atlas/Izacard) is future work.
- **query construction**:
> The current input sub-trajectory tau_in (the agent's recent context of length C) is embedded by g to form query q = g(tau_in). Tokens are aggregated by mean over the context length, using state tokens only (found most effective). Query dropout (drop ~20% of embedded tokens) is applied during training for diversity; query-blending (interpolate query with a random index key, alpha_blend=0.5) is used for Meta-World/DMControl.
- **query granularity**:
> Step/state-level (sliding window). During inference the query is reconstructed from the current rolling context window every t environment steps (t=1 for Dark-Room/Key-Door; t=25 for MazeRunner/Meta-World/DMControl/Procgen). During training, queries are formed per sub-trajectory in the batch. Effectively trajectory-segment-level, re-issued repeatedly within an episode.
- **when to retrieve**: Iterative / fixed schedule. Retrieval is performed repeatedly during environment interaction at a fixed interval of every t steps (t=1 or t=25 depending on environment), not one-shot. There is no uncertainty/learned trigger.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule: retrieve every t environment steps (t=1 for Dark-Room and Dark Key-Door; t=25 for all other environments). t trades off inference time vs final performance. No confidence/uncertainty/learned-router trigger.
- **reranking**:
> Yes. A two-stage reweighting/reranking: first retrieve top-l (l=50) by cosine similarity, then re-score by s_ret = s_rel + alpha * s_u (relevance = normalized cosine similarity; utility = task-ID match indicator during training, total episode return during inference; alpha=1, scores normalized to [0,1]), then keep top-k. This is a heuristic, metadata-aware reranking (not a cross-encoder).
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Rerank + filtering/regularization. Retrieval regularization is applied during training: deduplication (discard entries with cosine similarity > 0.98; found the most important regularizer), similarity cut-off (discard too-similar neighbours), and query dropout. For grid-worlds, retrieved experiences are replaced with same-task random samples if the query is from very early in the episode (< timestep 10). No LLM distillation/compression of retrieved content.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tools/skills/documents are indexed; retrieved units are RL sub-trajectories).
- **index content separation**: Partial. Keys are lightweight embeddings (g(tau_{t-C:t})) while values store the heavier raw sub-trajectory with continuation (tau_{t-C:t+C}); this separates retrievable index keys from loaded content, but not a progressive-disclosure / SOP-index-then-content tool pattern.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index or integration protocol such as RapidAPI/REST/MCP; the index is a Faiss vector store of trajectory segments, static at training and grown at inference).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tools or inter-tool dependencies are modeled).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Latent-token injection via cross-attention into the policy network. Retrieved sub-trajectories are encoded by separate per-token-type embedding layers (state/action/reward/RTG) and fused into the Decision Transformer through cross-attention (CA) layers interleaved after every self-attention (SA) layer; the DT then predicts the next action conditioned on both its input trajectory and the retrieved set. It is not prompt-text augmentation and not skill reuse; it is internal-representation conditioning. Retrieval is used both during training and inference.
- **planning integration**:
> Per-step interleaved conditioning within an acting loop (no explicit planner/tree search). RA-DT is a reactive sequence-model policy: at each (or every t) timestep it retrieves relevant sub-trajectories and cross-attends to them to predict the next action. There is no MCTS, plan-then-retrieve, or hierarchical subtask decomposition; retrieval is woven into the per-step action-prediction rollout.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-step (per environment-step / per action-prediction). Retrieval+conditioning happens at each action-prediction step (or every t=25 steps for harder envs) within an episode rollout; there is no CoT/per-sentence reasoning since this is a non-language RL policy.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A for CBR-style adaptation. The retrieved sub-trajectory is used verbatim (as raw segment) and conditioned on via cross-attention; there is no LLM-prompted or execution-feedback case revision. Closest analog: latent conditioning rather than explicit adaptation.
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw sub-trajectory (the actual stored state/action/reward/RTG token sequence, including its continuation t-C:t+C), embedded and injected as latent/soft representations via cross-attention. Not a distilled strategy, free-text workflow, or executable program.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw trajectory segment (low abstraction). Retrieved units are concrete past sub-trajectories, not distilled strategies, guidelines, skills, or workflows.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Retriever-aware training plus retrieval regularization. Training with retrieval (rather than random sampling) teaches the model to use bursty, relevant context; deduplication (cosine > 0.98 removed), similarity cut-off, and query dropout prevent the model from copying near-identical retrieved trajectories (delusions/copying behaviour). Reweighting by task-ID (train) / return (inference) steers retrieval toward useful, high-reward, same-task experiences. No learned relevance evaluator / self-reflection.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: episodic (external vector-index memory of sub-trajectories). It is an episodic / experience replay-like external memory, conceptually a non-parametric complementary-learning-systems component alongside the parametric DT.
- **write back**:
> True. At inference, the agent writes each completed episode of its own environment interaction into the (initially empty) retrieval buffer/index, enabling later retrieval of its own past experiences. At training, the index is pre-built from the offline dataset (no online writes during training beyond initial construction).
- **online growth**: Yes (at test/deployment time). The inference-time vector index starts empty and grows as the agent stores each completed ICL-trial episode; subsequent retrievals draw from this accumulating same-task memory. The training-time index is frozen after offline construction.
- **write back trigger**:
> On episode completion (per-trial), unconditional. After each ICL trial/episode during inference, the whole episode trajectory is appended to the index (Algorithm 1, line 13: I <- I union tau). Writes are not gated on success/failure or self-critique; deduplication can optionally avoid storing redundant experiences. During training, writes happen once at index-construction time.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Stores all experiences regardless of outcome (both successful and unsuccessful episodes are written to the index), but does NOT use failures contrastively or as corrective rules. Instead, return-based reweighting at inference up-weights high-return (successful) sub-trajectories so the agent is steered toward high-reward behaviour; low-return experiences are de-prioritized rather than exploited as negative signal. Authors note next-action-prediction cannot distinguish positive/negative examples (a limitation).
- **memory evolution update**: Append-only with deduplication. New episodes are appended to the index; entries are not mutated, merged, or refined after writing. Deduplication (similarity > 0.98) prunes/avoids redundant entries, but stored sub-trajectories themselves are immutable.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No. Retrieval/case-selection is a fixed similarity top-l MIPS followed by heuristic reweighting (relevance + task/return utility) and top-k selection; it is not an RL- or learning-optimized retrieval policy. The authors explicitly leave end-to-end retriever training as future work.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Single-agent private memory in the experiments, but the design explicitly supports cross-agent sharing: the external memory can hold experiences from other agents (training data comes from multiple PPO agents), and the authors note the memory enables leveraging 'experiences from other agents' and distant-past experiences (e.g., continual learning). No heterogeneous multi-framework sharing is demonstrated.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> Dark-Room (10x10, 20x20, 40x20 grids); Dark Key-Door (10x10, 20x20, 40x20); MazeRunner (15x15 procedurally-generated mazes); Meta-World (ML45 train / ML5 hold-out); DMControl (DMC11 train / DMC5 hold-out); Procgen (16 games; PG12 train / PG4 hold-out; settings PG12-Seen, PG12-Unseen, PG4).
- **benchmark family**: decision-RL / in-context RL. Grid-world navigation (Dark-Room, Dark Key-Door, MazeRunner), embodied/robotics continuous control (Meta-World, DMControl), and procedurally-generated video games (Procgen). Not D4RL; these are standard in-context-RL and multi-task RL benchmarks.
- **baselines**:
> Vanilla Decision Transformer (DT, Chen et al. 2021); Algorithm Distillation (AD, Laskin et al. 2022); Decision-Pretrained Transformer (DPT, Lee et al. 2023). RA-DT itself is reported in two variants: domain-specific embedding (DT encoder) and domain-agnostic embedding (FrozenHopfield + BERT). Internal ablation baselines include random sampling (uniform / same-task) instead of retrieval.
- **key metrics**:
> Primary metric: mean episode reward / return on held-out tasks at the end of the ICL trials (with 95% confidence intervals over 3 seeds), tracked as ICL performance improvement across trials (40 trials Dark-Room/Key-Door, 30 trials MazeRunner). Also reported: data-normalized scores (Meta-World/DMControl/Procgen), context-length usage, and training/inference efficiency (samples/sec, speedup).
- **headline result**:
> On grid-worlds (Dark-Room, Dark Key-Door, MazeRunner) RA-DT outperforms AD, DPT, and vanilla DT in final ICL reward while using only a fraction of their context length (RA-DT uses ~50-transition context vs ~2-episode / up to ~2000-step context for baselines). On Dark-Room 10x10 RA-DT reaches near-optimal reward with both domain-specific and domain-agnostic (BERT) embeddings; it is the only method to improve across the 30 ICL trials on MazeRunner. On the largest grid (40x20) RA-DT is ~7x faster to train than baselines. On complex environments (Meta-World, DMControl, Procgen) RA-DT improves average hold-out performance but no method (including RA-DT) exhibits genuine in-context improvement (a reported negative result/limitation).
- **ablations**:
> All ablations on Dark-Room 10x10. (E.1) Retrieval vs sampling: training with retrieval beats both uniform and same-task random sampling (retrieval builds 'bursty' sequences important for ICL; uniform sampling yields poor ICL). (E.2) Reweighting: task-based reweighting during training is critical; no reweighting (alpha=0) drops performance sharply; sensitivity analysis shows robustness across a range of alpha. (E.3) Retrieval regularization: deduplication (sim > 0.98) is the most important regularizer; similarity cut-off and query dropout also help, preventing copying behaviour. (E.4) Query construction: mean aggregation over state tokens only is best vs actions/rewards/RTG/all/last-hidden. (E.5) Cross-attention placement. (E.6) Steps between retrievals (t) trades inference cost vs performance. (E.7) Training efficiency: ~7x faster on 40x20 due to shorter context. (E.8) Inference efficiency: slightly slower when retrieving every step, comparable when retrieving less frequently; FlashAttention important for long context. (E.9) Domain-agnostic LM choice: BERT best vs smaller LMs. (E.10) Effect of k on AD. (E.11) Convergence of baselines.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> No. Only end-to-end RL task metrics (episode reward/return, ICL improvement) are reported; intrinsic retrieval-quality metrics (Recall@k, nDCG, retrieval precision) are not reported separately. Some qualitative retrieval/attention-map analysis is provided (Appendix D.1.1) but not quantified as a decoupled retrieval metric.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome (final/cumulative episode reward and ICL improvement across trials). Some process-level analysis is qualitative: attention-map analysis showing the agent attends to the retrieved sub-trajectory, and exploration analysis (delusion/copying behaviour), but no quantitative step-wise retrieval-accuracy metric.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> RA-DT uses a much shorter context (50 transitions) vs ~2 episodes (up to ~2000 steps) for AD/DPT/DT, giving ~7x faster training on Dark-Room 40x20 (samples/sec). Retrieval adds embedding+search overhead: at inference RA-DT is slightly slower than baselines when retrieving every step (t=1) but comparable when retrieving every t=25 steps. Faiss flat/HNSW index gives O(log M) scalable search; deduplication reduces index size and speeds retrieval. FlashAttention is highlighted for handling long context efficiently.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed, small context budget. DT context length C=50 transitions (100 for 20x20/40x20 Dark variants). Retrieval: top-l=50 retrieved then reweighted to top-k; top-k after reweighting = 1 for grid-worlds/MazeRunner/Procgen, top-k = 4 (concatenated, ordered by return) for Meta-World/DMControl. Fixed-k, not adaptive/budget-capped.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (this is a primary method/empirical paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Authors release new datasets for four environments (Dark-Room, Dark Key-Door, MazeRunner, Procgen). Construction: PPO behavioural agents generate offline data (Dark-Room/Key-Door: 100K transitions per goal for 10x10/20x20, 200K for 40x20; 80 train / 20 eval goals; MazeRunner: 100K interactions per maze over 100 train mazes, 20 eval; Meta-World ML45=90M transitions, ML5 hold-out; DMControl DMC11=11M transitions, DMC5 hold-out; Procgen PG12=24M transitions (2M/task) from task-specific PPO agents trained 25M steps on 200 seeds, PG4 hold-out). Verifiability is via environment reward (programmatic).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Decision Transformer (Chen et al. 2021) as the policy backbone; Retrieval-augmented generation in LLMs, especially RETRO (Borgeaud et al. 2022) for the value=segment+continuation design and cross-attention fusion, and kNN-LM / RAG (Khandelwal 2019; Lewis 2020); FrozenHopfield mechanism (Paischer et al. 2022) for the domain-agnostic LM-based trajectory encoder; BERT (Devlin et al. 2019); Faiss (Johnson et al. 2019; Douze et al. 2024) for the vector index; multi-task DT datasets/embedding-space observations from Schmied et al. 2024; reweighting by relevance+utility following Park et al. 2023.
- **contrasts with**:
> Prior in-context RL methods that keep entire episodes in context: Algorithm Distillation (AD, Laskin et al. 2022) and Decision-Pretrained Transformer (DPT, Lee et al. 2023), and vanilla DT. RA-DT contrasts by retrieving only relevant sub-trajectories into a short context window. Also contrasts with RAG methods relying on expert demonstrations (Humphreys et al. 2022 RAG-Go) and domain-specific embedding models, since RA-DT needs neither expert demos nor a domain-specific encoder. Distinct from online in-context RL (AdA/Team et al. 2023) and in-context imitation learning (Raparthy et al. 2023).
- **lineage**:
> Group F (decision/memory RL): retrieval-augmented / external-memory in-context reinforcement learning. Sits in the lineage of episodic-memory RL and RETRO-style retrieval augmentation applied to Decision-Transformer-based in-context RL; a bridge between offline sequence-modeling RL agents and growing-memory experience retrieval, distinct from classic static-corpus RAG planners.

<a id="item-algorithm-distillation"></a>
### 129. Algorithm Distillation (AD) - In-context Reinforcement Learning with Algorithm Distillation

2022  ·  ICLR 2023  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.14215)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2022
- **venue**: ICLR 2023 (notable-top-5% / Oral). Published on OpenReview 01 Feb 2023 (id=hy0a5MMPUv). Preprint arXiv:2210.14215 (cs.LG; cs.AI), submitted 25 Oct 2022 (v1). Also presented at the NeurIPS 2022 'Foundation Models for Decision Making' workshop.
- **authors affiliation**:
> Michael Laskin, Luyu Wang, Junhyuk Oh, Emilio Parisotto, Stephen Spencer, Richie Steigerwald, DJ Strouse, Steven Hansen, Angelos Filos, Ethan Brooks, Maxime Gazeau, Himanshu Sahni, Satinder Singh, Volodymyr Mnih. All at DeepMind (now Google DeepMind). Michael Laskin is the corresponding author; equal-contribution markers are noted in the paper.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.14215

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Decision-making / reinforcement learning (sequential decision-making in partially observed environments requiring exploration, temporal credit assignment, and generalization). It is an in-context / meta-RL method realized with a causal transformer; spans bandits, 2D grid POMDPs, and pixel-based 3D navigation.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, in-context (gradient-free) meta-reinforcement learning. Two-phase setup: (Phase 1, OFFLINE data generation) for each of N tasks sampled from a task distribution, an independent single-task source RL algorithm (UCB / A3C / DQN) is trained from scratch until convergence and its FULL across-episode learning history (sequences of observation-action-reward tokens spanning policy improvement) is saved to a dataset D. (Phase 2, distillation) a causal transformer is trained by autoregressively predicting actions from multi-episodic subsequences of these histories with a negative-log-likelihood (behaviour-cloning) loss; crucially the context must be large enough (across-episodic) to capture learning progress, forcing the model to amortise the policy-improvement operator. (Phase 3, EVALUATION) on held-out test tasks the frozen transformer is unrolled in the environment, maintaining a running context queue of its own state-action-reward transitions, and improves its policy entirely IN-CONTEXT across successive episodes with NO weight updates, no demonstrations, and no return conditioning (it conditions on rewards, not desired returns). Single-agent; supervision is the source RL agent's own trajectories (no human labels); environments are partially observed, sparse/semi-sparse reward, with tasks that cannot be inferred zero-shot from observations.
- **what is retrieved**:
> Across-episode learning histories / trajectories: the transformer's context is filled with the agent's own preceding (observation, action, reward) transitions across multiple recent episodes. The 'retrieved' / conditioned-on memory is the in-context running history of the current evaluation episode(s), and at training time multi-episodic subsequences of source-RL learning histories. There is no external document/case retriever; conditioning is via the transformer's attention over its context window.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> N/A / not a ranking objective. AD does not rank or select top-k items; instead it conditions on the entire (sliding-window) across-episode context. The relevant design choice is context LENGTH (must be multi-episodic, ~2-4 episodes) rather than a top-k selection or completeness criterion.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve: partial (attention over the in-context history substitutes for explicit case retrieval), Reuse: yes (conditions on past experience to choose actions / amortises the improvement operator), Revise: no (no explicit case adaptation/critique step), Retain: partial (transient append to the rolling context only; no persistent case retention)]. AD is not a CBR system; mapping is loose.
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False. The paper frames itself as in-context reinforcement learning / offline in-context meta-RL / algorithm distillation via sequence modeling (citing RL^2, MAML, Decision Transformer, Gato, policy distillation). It does NOT cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner and does not invoke case-based reasoning.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> (state, action, reward) tuple stream, i.e. (o_t, a_t, r_t) transition tokens, organized as across-episode sub-trajectories. The conditioning unit is a multi-episodic subsequence of length c (spanning >= 1, ideally 2-4 episodes) of these transition tuples; it is reward-conditioned (not return-conditioned).
- **index source**:
> Offline-induced fixed dataset for training (the buffer D of source-RL learning histories), plus an online/test-time-induced episodic context at inference (the transformer's own rolling context of (o,a,r) tuples). No retrievable external store; the 'index' is effectively the transformer's context window populated online during evaluation.
- **index structure topology**:
> N/A in the classic sense: there is no vector index or graph. The store is a flat sequential buffer/context of (o,a,r) tokens consumed by a causal transformer via positional/causal attention. Training subsequences are sampled uniformly from histories; evaluation maintains a FIFO context queue.
- **retriever type**: N/A (no explicit retriever). Conditioning is performed implicitly by the causal transformer's self-attention over the in-context history (GPT-like decoder-only sequence model). No BM25/dense/learned retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> N/A for an external retriever. The sequence model itself (which functionally subsumes the role of selecting/attending to relevant context) is trained end-to-end by a negative-log-likelihood / behaviour-cloning loss on next-action prediction over the source-RL learning histories. So the 'attention-as-retrieval' is learned by imitation (NLL on actions), not by similarity contrastive labels, RL reward, or downstream-task preference.
- **query construction**:
> The 'query' is the current across-episode context: the most recent (o,a,r) transitions in the rolling context queue, with the current observation as the immediate conditioning input. No decomposition, intent extraction, or synthetic expansion; the raw running history is the conditioning signal.
- **query granularity**: step/state-level (autoregressive): at every timestep the model conditions on the full current across-episode context to predict the next action; effectively continuous per-step conditioning that also spans trajectory/multi-episode level via the long context window.
- **when to retrieve**: iterative / continuous: conditioning happens at every action step throughout the rollout, with the context continuously updated by the agent's own newest transitions. It is not a one-shot retrieve-then-act; in-context improvement accrues across many episodes.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> fixed schedule (every step): the model attends to its context window at each decision step automatically. There is no confidence/uncertainty/learned-classifier/reflection-token trigger and no agent-initiated retrieval request; conditioning is unconditional and continuous, governed only by the sliding context window.
- **reranking**: None. No reranking stage; the causal transformer attends over the whole context window without an explicit candidate re-scoring step.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> None / minimal: context is the raw (o,a,r) token stream truncated to the across-episodic window length c (a sliding/FIFO window because attention is quadratic in sequence length). No compression, distillation, decomposition, or distractor filtering of the context beyond windowing.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (not a tool-retrieval method).
- **index content separation**: N/A (no separated lightweight index vs heavy content; the context is the raw token stream).
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (not a tool-retrieval system; agent interacts with RL environments / DMLab, not tool APIs/MCP).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Latent / in-context conditioning for action generation: the across-episode history is fed as the transformer's context and the model autoregressively predicts the next action, implicitly inferring the (improved) policy from the conditioning history. Used as input context (in-context learning), NOT as a training signal at inference, NOT as prompt-engineered text, and NOT via fine-tuning (weights are frozen at test time).
- **planning integration**:
> Inside an autoregressive control loop (per-step interleaved): there is no explicit planner/tree-search; the transformer directly maps the across-episode context to the next action at every step, and 'planning'/exploration/credit-assignment behaviours emerge implicitly from having distilled an RL algorithm's improvement operator. Conditioning and acting are tightly interleaved per timestep across a multi-episode horizon (retrieve/condition then act, continuously).
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: per-step (per-action / per-timestep): the context is consulted and an action emitted at every environment step, with the context growing as the agent acts; improvement is realized across episodes. Not per-CoT-step (no explicit chain-of-thought) and not per-tool-call.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> N/A in the CBR sense; the closest analog is that the LEARNED in-context policy-improvement operator adapts behaviour across episodes by conditioning on accumulated experience (verbatim raw-history conditioning, not LLM-prompted case adaptation or execution-feedback revision). No explicit per-case adaptation/critique.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Raw trajectory tokens: the injected/conditioned representation is the raw sequence of (observation, action, reward) tokens of the agent's recent across-episode history (pixels/coordinates as observations, discrete actions, scalar rewards). No distilled strategy text, no executable program, no structured note; it is the raw experience stream consumed by the transformer.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Raw trajectory / raw experience tuples (the lowest abstraction level): the unit conditioned on is the concrete (o,a,r) transition history. Abstraction (the policy-improvement operator) lives in the LEARNED WEIGHTS of the transformer, not in the conditioned-on units, which remain raw.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Trained-in robustness via imitating an RL algorithm's improvement operator (the model learns to explore/exploit and ignore uninformative reward-0 transitions, e.g. in Dark Room Hard where reward is r=1 exactly once). The paper adds label-smoothing regularization for the hard-exploration variant (Dark Room Hard) to improve in-context learning. No explicit relevance evaluator, self-reflection, or distractor filter; robustness is emergent from distillation plus the across-episodic context that lets it infer goals from sparse signals.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> latent + episodic: the policy-improvement algorithm is stored latently in the transformer weights (in-weights RL algorithm amortised into an in-context one), while the operative test-time memory is an episodic across-episode context buffer of the agent's own (o,a,r) transitions. No external skill-library, workflow store, or graph.
- **write back**:
> Yes, but only into the transient in-context buffer, not a persistent external store. During evaluation the agent appends its own (o,a,r) transitions to the rolling context queue (which drives in-context improvement); these are discarded at episode/window boundaries. There is NO write-back of new cases/skills to a persistent memory and NO weight update at test time.
- **online growth**:
> Partial / context-only: the in-context history grows online during a deployment rollout (across episodes within the context window) and is what enables test-time improvement, but it is a bounded sliding window and is reset per evaluation; there is no persistent growing store and no parameter growth. The training dataset D is frozen after offline collection.
- **write back trigger**:
> per-step (into the rolling context only): each new (o,a,r) transition is automatically appended to the context queue at every timestep during a rollout (then truncated by the window). There is no success/failure-gated, reflective, or human-validated write into any persistent memory; nothing is permanently retained.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Both successes and failures are used implicitly and uniformly: training histories include the entire learning curve of the source RL algorithm (early failed/low-reward episodes through to converged success), and at test time the model conditions on its own successful AND unsuccessful (reward-0) episodes within the context, which is precisely how it explores and infers sparse goals. There is no explicit contrastive success-vs-failure mechanism or failure-only corrective rule store; failures are valuable as part of the learning-progress signal that teaches the improvement operator.
- **memory evolution update**:
> Append-and-forget (sliding window): the in-context buffer is append-only within a window and forgotten (FIFO truncation) once the across-episodic context length c is exceeded; no dedup-merge, delta-update, or refine-overwrite of stored entries. The latent algorithm (weights) is fixed after distillation.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No external learned retrieval policy. However, the in-context behaviour IS a learned (distilled) policy-improvement operator: the transformer is trained by imitation (NLL) to reproduce an RL algorithm's improvement dynamics, so 'how to use context' is learned, but it is not an RL/value-optimized retrieval/selection policy over an external store. Selection over context is implicit attention, not an explicit top-k or learned retriever.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> No. Single-agent, single-model in-context memory. (The offline training dataset is aggregated from many independent single-task source-RL runs/actors, and AD distills a multi-stream distributed algorithm into a single-stream one, but the deployed AD agent uses its own private context; there is no cross-agent memory sharing at inference.)

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> Adversarial Bandit (10-armed bandit, 100 trials, reward under odd arms 95% of the time in training vs even arms 95% at evaluation; out-of-distribution test), Dark Room (2D discrete POMDP, 9x9 room, episode length 20, dense reward r=1 each time goal reached), Dark Room (Hard) (17x17 room, sparse reward r=1 exactly once), Dark Key-to-Door (9x9, must reach an invisible key then door, semi-sparse reward, episode length 50, combinatorial task space of 81^2 = 6561 tasks), and DMLab Watermaze (partially observable 3D pixel-based navigation, observations 72x96x3, 8 actions, episode length 50, continuous/infinite goal space).
- **benchmark family**: decision-RL / meta-RL control environments (bandits + grid-world POMDPs + DMLab pixel navigation). Not in the survey's QA/web/embodied-benchmark/tool families; closest tag is decision-RL (custom RL environments, not D4RL).
- **baselines**:
> Expert Distillation (ED) - identical architecture/across-episode context to AD but trained on EXPERT (converged-policy) trajectories instead of full learning histories (closest analog to Gato but reward-conditioned); RL^2 (Duan et al. 2016) - an online meta-RL algorithm trained for 1B environment steps, used as an approximate upper bound (also compared with transformer vs LSTM backbones); the SOURCE RL algorithm run from scratch (UCB / A3C / DQN) - to compare data-efficiency of in-context RL vs the in-weights source. Decision-Transformer-style return-conditioned PD (MGDT, Gato) discussed as related work / context, with ED serving as the implemented PD-style baseline.
- **key metrics**:
> Episodic return / accumulated reward as a function of evaluation episode number (in-context learning curves), reported as mean return +/- 1 standard deviation over 5 training seeds; scores often normalized relative to UCB (bandit) and random/source. Data-efficiency is measured as episodes/environment-steps needed to reach a performance level vs the source algorithm. No retrieval-IR metrics (Recall@k / nDCG) since there is no retrieval benchmark.
- **headline result**:
> Algorithm Distillation reinforcement-learns entirely in-context (no weight updates) across all environments and is more data-efficient than the source RL algorithm it distilled. AD matches asymptotic RL^2 (an online meta-RL upper-bound trained for 1B steps) on the Dark environments and approaches it to within 13% on DMLab Watermaze, whereas Expert Distillation (ED) fails to explore/improve in-context in most settings. AD also generalizes out-of-distribution on the Adversarial Bandit better than RL^2 and ED. By distilling a multi-stream distributed source algorithm into a single-stream in-context one (and in a single-stream subsample-every-k=10 setting), AD produces a faster/more data-efficient RL algorithm than the source that generated its training data.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Context size (Fig.7, Dark Key-to-Door / Dark Room): in-context RL only emerges with multi-episodic context; ~2-4 episodes of context are needed for near-optimal in-context RL, with initial signs appearing once context >= ~1 episode length - the central ablation establishing that across-episodic context, not just learning-history data, is required. (2) AD vs ED (same architecture/context, different data): isolates that benefits come from training on LEARNING HISTORIES (showing learning progress) rather than from long context alone; ED collapses to near-random/expert-imitation without in-context improvement. (3) Single-stream Algorithm Distillation (Fig.6, App.I): subsampling every k-th (k=10) episode from a single A3C actor's history still yields a more data-efficient in-context algorithm than both the multi-stream and single-stream source. (4) Source-algorithm-agnosticism: AD distills UCB (bandit), on-policy A3C (Dark envs), and off-policy DQN (Watermaze). (5) Architecture: AD can also be realized with an LSTM (App.K) but less effectively than a causal transformer; RL^2 with transformer vs LSTM compared (App.G). (6) Label smoothing improves AD on the hard-exploration Dark Room (Hard) (App. with Fig.10).
- **evaluation decoupling**: N/A. No intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k/nDCG/completeness) are reported because there is no explicit retriever; evaluation is end-to-end in-context-RL learning curves (return vs episode).
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both outcome and process: primary metric is episodic return (outcome), but the paper also analyses the in-context LEARNING PROCESS via per-episode learning curves (how return improves across successive evaluation episodes), and probes specific capabilities - in-context exploration (Dark Room Hard), temporal credit assignment, and in-distribution / out-of-distribution generalization (Dark Key-to-Door combinatorial tasks; Adversarial Bandit OOD).
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Data-efficiency is the headline efficiency claim: AD is significantly more data-efficient (fewer episodes to reach performance) than the source RL algorithm, turning a slow gradient-based learner into a faster in-context learner. Cost caveat: transformer training and inference are quadratic in sequence length, and because environments of interest have long episodes, AD requires fitting multiple episodes into the context window, which is the main stated limitation/cost; this restricts AD to short-episode environments and motivates long-horizon sequence models as future work. No explicit dollar/latency numbers reported.
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A (introduces/uses custom RL environments rather than a curated benchmark dataset: Adversarial Bandit 10 arms/100 trials; Dark Room 9x9 ep20; Dark Room Hard 17x17 sparse; Dark Key-to-Door 9x9 ep50 with 6561 tasks; DMLab Watermaze pixel 72x96x3 ep50. Training data: 2000 A3C learning histories (100 actors) for Dark envs, 4000 distributed-DQN histories (16 actors) for Watermaze.)

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> RL^2 / fast-RL-via-slow-RL in-context meta-RL (Duan et al. 2016; Wang et al. 2016); Decision Transformer (Chen et al. 2021) and Trajectory Transformer (Janner et al. 2021) sequence-modeling-for-RL; Multi-Game Decision Transformer (Lee et al. 2022) and Gato (Reed et al. 2022) as policy-distillation predecessors; Policy Distillation (Rusu et al. 2016, here from offline data); source RL algorithms UCB (Lai & Robbins 1985), A3C (Mnih et al. 2016), DQN (Mnih et al. 2013); causal transformer / GPT-style sequence models; DMLab (Beattie et al. 2016) and Morris Watermaze (Morris 1981).
- **contrasts with**:
> Offline Policy Distillation (PD) methods - MGDT (return-conditioned, adapts by finetuning) and Gato (adapts via expert-demonstration prompting), and its own Expert Distillation (ED) baseline - all of which learn policies but NOT an RL algorithm and cannot improve in-context through trial-and-error because their contexts are within-episode (too short to capture learning progress); Decision Transformer (return-conditioned, small within-episode context); online meta-RL such as RL^2 (interacts with the env during training; used as an upper-bound proxy rather than a directly comparable method); gradient-based / optimization-based meta-RL (MAML-style) that adapts by taking gradient steps (AD is gradient-free at test time).
- **lineage**:
> Group F (decision / memory / RL). Foundational in-context-RL precursor: AD is the first method to demonstrate in-context reinforcement learning via sequence modeling of offline RL learning histories with an imitation loss, sitting in the lineage RL^2 / Decision Transformer / Gato -> Algorithm Distillation -> later in-context-RL works (e.g. Decision-Pretrained Transformer, In-Context RL from Noise Distillation, DICP). It established that conditioning a causal transformer on across-episode experience (a precursor to retrieval/experience-conditioned agents) yields gradient-free policy improvement, motivating later experience/episodic-memory-augmented decision agents.
