<a id="item-jarvis-1"></a>
### 130. JARVIS-1 (Open-World Multi-task Agents with Memory-Augmented Multimodal Language Models)

2023  ·  IEEE TPAMI 2024  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.05997)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2023
- **venue**: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence (TPAMI), vol. 47, pp. 1894-1907, 2024 (peer-reviewed journal; DOI 10.1109/TPAMI.2024.3511593; DBLP journals/pami/WangCLJHZLHZYML25). Preprint: arXiv:2311.05997 (v1 10 Nov 2023, v3 30 Nov 2023; cs.AI).
- **authors affiliation**:
> Zihao Wang (PKU, corresponding), Shaofei Cai (PKU), Anji Liu (UCLA), Yonggang Jin (BUPT), Jinbing Hou (BUPT), Bowei Zhang (PKU), Haowei Lin (PKU), Zhaofeng He (BUPT), Zilong Zheng (BIGAI), Yaodong Yang (PKU), Xiaojian Ma (BIGAI, corresponding), Yitao Liang (PKU, corresponding). 12 authors. Primary affiliations: Peking University (PKU) / Institute for Artificial Intelligence (the CraftJarvis group), Beijing Institute for General Artificial Intelligence (BIGAI), UCLA, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications (BUPT).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.05997
- **code url**:
> https://github.com/CraftJarvis/JARVIS-1 (official code, 395 stars; only offline_evaluation with fixed memory and the language-model part released; multimodal descriptor/retrieval and online learning.py with growing memory marked 'Coming Soon'). Project page: https://craftjarvis.org/JARVIS-1 (also https://craftjarvis-jarvis1.github.io/).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Embodied / open-world decision-making and long-horizon planning: an MLM-based generalist agent that perceives multimodal input (RGB visual observations + textual human instructions), generates plans, and performs human-like embodied control (mouse/keyboard) in the open-world Minecraft universe. High-level memory-augmented MLM planner + low-level goal-conditioned controller (STEVE-1). Not QA; interactive embodied agentic decision-making with life-long learning.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent embodied decision-making in Minecraft 1.16.5 survival mode (hybrid MineRL + MCP-Reborn environment), running at 20 fps. The agent uses a human-like observation space (640x360 ego-centric RGB pov plus auxiliary location/inventory/equipment/event info) and a human-like action space (keypresses, mouse yaw/pitch, plus abstracted craft/smelt/equip functional actions as in MineDojo). Default evaluation starts in survival mode with an empty inventory (some intermediate groups start with an iron_axe) and a random spawn; a task succeeds if the target object is obtained within a Max.Steps budget (12k-72k steps). Train-free / no gradient update: planning is via a frozen pre-trained MLM (GPT-3.5/GPT-4 as the language part chained with frozen MineCLIP for vision) augmented with a retrievable multimodal memory built and grown in-context. Supervision: no imitation/RL fine-tuning of the planner; the agent acquires experiences via self-instruct exploration and stores only SUCCESSFUL trajectories. Multiple JARVIS-1 instances run in parallel (speculative/distributed execution) sharing one centralized memory during the learning stage, but the deployed agent is single-agent. (The low-level controller STEVE-1 is itself pre-trained via VPT+MineCLIP; the GPT/LLM is accessed via OpenAI API.)
- **what is retrieved**:
> EXPERIENCES: past successful interactive planning experiences (multimodal trajectory entries) from the agent's own gameplay. Each retrieved entry is a key-value record whose key is multimodal (task instruction + the visual observation/situation when the entry was created) and whose value is the successfully executed plan (the goal sequence). Retrieved plans are injected as in-context demonstration references to augment current planning. (Only successful trajectories are stored.)
- **retrieval grounding**:
> GROWING / episodic memory the agent writes (with a self-instruct life-long-learning growth mechanism). The retrievable store is the agent's own multimodal memory of past successful planning experiences, built by self-exploration and continuously expanded during gameplay - not a static external document corpus. Pretrained world knowledge also informs planning, but it lives inside the frozen MLM weights, not in the retrievable index. Mildly hybrid in that situation captioning uses ~1000 internet-collected Minecraft text snippets matched by MineCLIP, but the RETRIEVAL store used for retrieval-augmented planning is the growing experience memory.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve: yes, Reuse: yes, Revise: partial, Retain: yes (success-only)]. Retrieve: multimodal-query similarity retrieval of relevant past plans. Reuse: retrieved plans injected as in-context demonstration references to produce the current plan. Revise: at the case level NO (retrieved plans are not edited); but the agent's overall plan is revised via interactive planning (self-check before execution + self-explain/re-plan on environment feedback), so plan-level revision exists. Retain: successful trajectories (task + state + plan) are written back to memory.
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False. The paper does NOT frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner. It explicitly frames the mechanism as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG; cites Lewis et al. 2020, Mao et al. 2020) over a multimodal experience memory, plus in-context life-long learning, self-instruct, and self-reflection (Reflexion/self-debugging). It nonetheless realizes Retrieve/Reuse/Retain CBR-like mechanisms (plus plan-level revise) under the RAG/memory framing.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Full trajectory / case (problem-solution). The retrieved unit is a stored experience entry = a successful planning trajectory encoded as a dict with keys {task, state, plan}: the task goal, the agent state (visual observation + symbolic info: inventory, location, etc.) at planning time, and the actual executed goal sequence (plan). The injected content is the plan (an ordered list of short-horizon goals / mine-craft-smelt steps). So the unit is a (task+situation -> plan) case.
- **index source**:
> Growing, agent-written memory; online/test-time-induced. The memory is built non-parametrically by the agent itself: during a learning stage JARVIS-1 explores via self-instruct curricula, executes plans, and stores all SUCCESSFUL trajectory experiences; the store keeps growing throughout gameplay (life-long learning) without gradient updates. Not an offline static corpus. Distributed self-improve fills a shared centralized memory in parallel.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat key-value (metadata/context-keyed) experience list. The memory is a list of dictionaries, each {task, state, plan}; keys are MULTIMODAL (task text + visual state). Retrieval is text-key filtering (CLIP text similarity above a confidence threshold) followed by visual-state similarity ranking. No knowledge graph or hierarchical category index; the implicit structure is per-sub-goal grouping at query time (retrieve top entry for each decomposed sub-goal). Same task may have multiple entries keyed by different observations/situations.
- **retriever type**:
> Dense / embedding-similarity (off-the-shelf CLIP/MineCLIP), with LLM-as-query-generator. Two stages: (1) text retrieval - CLIP text encoder embeds the textual query and each entry's task key, keeping entries above a similarity confidence threshold; (2) visual rerank - MineCLIP/CLIP visual encoder computes visual-state similarity between query observation and candidate states (Eq. 2) to sort candidates. No BM25, no trained dense retriever; the LLM/MLM reasons to GENERATE the queries (backward sub-goal search) but the matching itself is frozen-encoder cosine similarity.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None (off-the-shelf). The retriever uses frozen pre-trained encoders: CLIP text encoder for the textual task key and MineCLIP/CLIP visual encoder for the visual state, with a similarity confidence threshold. No contrastive training on similarity labels, no LM-feedback, no preference/RL training of the retriever. Improvement over time comes from a GROWING memory (more/better stored experiences), not from training the retriever. (MineCLIP is pre-trained on YouTube video-text pairs; not fine-tuned here.)
- **query construction**:
> Query generation via LLM reasoning + visual augmentation. Given the task and current observation, the MLM reasons backward (think-backward) to decompose the instruction into the needed intermediate sub-goals / related tasks (bounded search depth), e.g. 'craft 1 enchanting table' -> 'obtain book/diamond/obsidian with empty inventory'. Each sub-goal that exists in memory becomes a TEXTUAL query, which is then concatenated with the agent's current VISUAL observation to form a MULTIMODAL query (situation-aware). So queries are decomposed/synthetic sub-goal queries, not the raw instruction alone.
- **query granularity**:
> Both task-level and step/sub-goal-level (two-level). The task instruction is decomposed by reasoning into multiple sub-goal queries; retrieval is performed per sub-goal (and conditioned on the current visual state), and the current visual situation grounds the query at the state level. Effectively a two-level retrieval: reason to sub-goals (decomposition) then retrieve situation-grounded plans per sub-goal.
- **when to retrieve**:
> One-shot at the start of (re)planning, repeated across the interactive-planning loop. Retrieval is triggered when JARVIS-1 plans (and when it re-plans after a failure). It is not token-confidence/uncertainty-triggered nor a learned router; retrieval happens at each planning event. Because the interactive planner re-plans on self-check/self-explain feedback, retrieval can recur per re-plan round (typically 2-3 rounds vs DEPS's 6+).
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed/event-driven: retrieval fires at each planning and re-planning event in the control loop. A (re)plan is invoked (a) at task start, (b) on self-check finding a predicted precondition violation before execution, or (c) on a runtime execution error that triggers self-explain -> re-plan. There is no token-confidence / attention-uncertainty / learned-complexity-classifier / reflection-token trigger for retrieval; retrieval is bound to the planner being called.
- **reranking**:
> Yes - a two-stage similarity rerank (not a learned cross-encoder). Stage 1: CLIP text-key similarity filters candidates above a confidence threshold. Stage 2: the surviving candidates are re-ranked by MineCLIP/CLIP VISUAL-state similarity between the query observation and each candidate's stored state (Eq. 2), and the top-k plans are returned (only the top entry per sub-goal is kept). No cross-encoder / RRF / instruction-tuned reranker.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Rerank + selection (situation-aware filtering). Refinement is the text-threshold filter then visual-similarity rerank, plus keeping only the top entry per decomposed sub-goal so the prompt holds a small set of the most situation-relevant reference plans. No decompose-then-recompose of retrieved content, no reason-in-documents distillation, no explicit distractor-removal module, no compression of stored plans.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A - no tool/API description store is indexed. Low-level skills are executed by a single fixed controller (STEVE-1) plus environment craft/smelt/equip primitives; there are no retrievable tool docstrings to engineer.
- **index content separation**:
> Partial. The text task-key is used for a cheap first-stage filter before the heavier visual-state similarity comparison on candidates only, which separates a lightweight text index from costlier multimodal scoring. But there is no formal progressive-disclosure / SOP-index-then-content protocol; the full {task,state,plan} entry is stored together.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> N/A as a tool-retrieval system. The experience memory is a live, incrementally-growing list updated during gameplay, but there is no RapidAPI/REST/MCP/function-calling tool protocol. The agent acts via the human-like MineRL/MCP-Reborn interface (keyboard/mouse) plus abstracted craft/smelt actions; plans are emitted as Python-like mine/craft/smelt pseudo-code parsed into goals.
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> Not for tools, but craft/mine PRECONDITIONS are reasoned about (not retrieved as a dependency graph). JARVIS-1 handles item prerequisites (e.g. stone_pickaxe needed before mining iron_ore; crafting_table needed for certain recipes) via LLM self-check precondition simulation and self-explain error explanation, and via backward sub-goal decomposition - i.e. dependency awareness is implemented in the reasoning/planner, not via an explicit retrievable dependency/bipartite graph.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation (in-context). Retrieved reference plans z are inserted into the MLM planner prompt alongside the task instruction and textual situation descriptions (Eq. 1: p(y|x) ~ sum_z p_eta(z|x) p_theta(y|x,z)); the planner then produces the current plan grounded in both its pretrained knowledge and these retrieved experiences. No weight updates (train-free, in-context life-long learning). The retrieved plans serve as demonstration exemplars / reference templates the planner adapts to the current situation.
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-plan, embedded in a closed-loop interactive planning framework. Pipeline: (1) on a task+observation, the MLM generates a multimodal query (backward sub-goal reasoning) and retrieves relevant past plans; (2) the memory-augmented MLM produces a plan of K short-horizon goals g1..gK; (3) self-check simulates the plan and fixes precondition bugs before execution; (4) the controller (STEVE-1) executes goals; (5) on execution failure, self-explain reasons about the error and triggers re-planning (which retrieves again). So retrieval supplies one-shot exemplars at each (re)plan time inside an interleaved self-check / self-explain re-planning loop; no MCTS/tree search.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Per-plan / per-re-plan-round within a rollout (sub-goal-level on the query side). Retrieval and reasoning are woven in at planning events: backward reasoning decomposes the task into sub-goals (per-sub-goal retrieval), a plan is generated, then self-check / self-explain feedback triggers further re-plan-with-retrieval rounds (typically 2-3). It is NOT per-CoT-token or per-low-level-action; it is per planning round / per sub-goal query.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> LLM-prompted adaptation + execution-feedback-driven plan revision. Retrieved plans are used as in-context reference exemplars and the MLM adapts them to the current situation/inventory rather than copying verbatim; the overall plan is further revised through self-check (pre-execution precondition simulation) and self-explain (post-failure error reasoning -> re-plan). No RL-reuse-finetuning and no latent adaptation; adaptation is prompt-based plus interactive feedback.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Free-text / structured plan (goal sequence). What is injected is the stored successful PLAN - an ordered sequence of short-horizon mine/craft/smelt goals (rendered as Python-like pseudo-code with step comments, e.g. mine({'log':3}); craft({'planks':12},{'log':3})). It is a structured procedural plan, not a raw pixel trajectory, not an executable compiled program/skill, not latent tokens, and not a distilled natural-language strategy.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Reusable plan / procedure grounded to a situation - mid-level. The retrieved unit is a concrete past successful plan (ordered sub-goal sequence) keyed by a specific task+situation, i.e. a situated procedural reference, more abstract than a raw action trajectory but more concrete than a distilled free-text strategy or a generalized workflow/rule. It is a single successful demonstration plan per retrieved case.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Interactive self-verification rather than retriever-side training. Robustness against bad plans/contexts comes from: (1) success-only memory (only verified successful trajectories are stored, so retrieved references are correct plans); (2) self-check precondition simulation before execution to catch flawed plans upfront; (3) self-explain on environment feedback to detect/locate execution errors and re-plan; (4) situation-aware multimodal retrieval (visual-state rerank + confidence threshold) to keep references relevant to the current situation. No retriever-aware/distractor-aware SFT and no separate relevance evaluator over retrieved items.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> Episodic multimodal memory (key-value experience store of successful planning trajectories: keys = task+visual situation, values = executed plans). Non-parametric / in-context (no skill-library of programs, no graph, no latent memory). Pretrained semantic knowledge resides in the frozen MLM, separate from this episodic store.
- **write back**: True. Every SUCCESSFUL trajectory experience is written to memory as a dict {task, state (visual obs + symbolic info at completion), plan (executed goal sequence)}. New entries are added during both the self-instruct learning stage and ongoing gameplay.
- **online growth**:
> True. The memory grows during deployment/gameplay (life-long learning): starting from a small/seed memory, JARVIS-1 self-instructs exploration curricula and accumulates successful trajectories; success rates rise with memory size (Fig. 7) and with longer game-playing time (e.g. ObtainDiamondPickaxe 6.2% at 20 min -> 12.5% at 60 min). After 4 epochs of learning across all task sets, the memory held 425 successful trajectories. The growing memory is the only online code (online_evaluation/learning.py) not yet released as of the repo.
- **write back trigger**:
> On-success only. A trajectory is written back to memory only when the task/plan is SUCCESSFULLY executed (the memory 'records every successful trajectory experience'). Failures are used transiently for self-explain/re-planning within the episode but are NOT stored as memory entries. Writes are not human-validated; they are gated by environment-confirmed task success.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success-only storage; failures used only transiently in-loop. Failed plans are leveraged immediately via self-explain (error explanation + re-plan) to recover within the current episode, but failure/negative experiences are NOT stored or retrieved from the multimodal memory. (This success-only design is exactly what the later Optimus-1 paper contrasts against by adding failure cases to its experience pool.)
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No. Case selection is fixed similarity top-k (CLIP text-threshold filter + MineCLIP visual-similarity rerank, Eq. 2), with LLM-reasoned query generation. There is no learned/RL-optimized retrieval policy (no M-MDP soft Q-learning, no trained retriever). The MLM only generates queries; matching is frozen-encoder cosine similarity.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Yes, within the same framework (shared centralized memory across parallel homogeneous instances). During self-improve/learning, multiple JARVIS-1 agents run in parallel in different environments (speculative/distributed execution) and collect experiences into one shared centralized memory, accelerating memory growth. The memory is also backbone-swappable (ChatGPT / GPT-4 / fine-tuned LLaMA2-13B all use the same memory). It is not a cooperative multi-agent deployment nor sharing across heterogeneous agent frameworks; sharing is across parallel copies of JARVIS-1 / interchangeable LM backbones.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> Minecraft, 200+ tasks selected from the Minecraft Universe Benchmark / MCU (Lin et al. 2023a), grouped into 11 categories: Wood (34), Wood-Variants (43), Stone (10), Iron (22), Gold (9), Diamond (7), Redstone (7), Blocks (15), Armor (17), Decoration (17), Food (9); evaluated in Minecraft 1.16.5 survival mode (hybrid MineRL + MCP-Reborn), >=30 seeds per task (key items like diamond_pickaxe/diamond evaluated 300-728 times). Flagship long-horizon challenge: ObtainDiamondPickaxe (also extended to 60-minute / 72000-step gameplay).
- **benchmark family**: Embodied / open-world (Minecraft) under the survey's embodied family (ALFWorld/ScienceWorld/VirtualHome/Minecraft). Long-horizon crafting/mining decision-making with human-like low-level visuomotor control.
- **baselines**:
> LLM/MLM multi-task instruction-following planners: Instruct GPT (Huang et al. 2022a / Ouyang et al. 2022, plan-once), ReAct (Yao et al. 2022, reason-before-act), Inner Monologue (Huang et al. 2022b, feedback re-planning), and DEPS (Wang et al. 2023b, Describe-Explain-Plan-Select interactive planning, the strongest prior baseline) - all reproduced to Minecraft. For the long-horizon ObtainDiamondPickaxe challenge: VPT / VPT-RL (Baker et al. 2022, RL-finetuned over 1.4M episodes), STEVE-1 (Lifshitz et al. 2023, controller), DEPS, and a human-player baseline (10-min gameplay, ~15% diamond / ~12% diamond pickaxe). LM ablations compare ChatGPT, GPT-4, pre-trained LLaMA2-70B, and fine-tuned LLaMA2-13B.
- **key metrics**:
> Average task Success Rate (SR, %) per task group (reported as mean +/- variance), at least 30 seeds per task; for the long-horizon study, SR (% episodes) of obtaining the diamond pickaxe and intermediate milestone items over game-playing time (steps/minutes), plus efficiency proxies (rounds of re-planning, LLM tokens/thinking time). Primary headline metric is SR.
- **headline result**:
> On ObtainDiamondPickaxe, JARVIS-1 surpasses the prior state-of-the-art by ~5x: 6.22% SR within 20 minutes (24k steps) vs VPT-RL's ~2.5% (>2x VPT directly; '5x the reliability of current SOTA' in the abstract vs DEPS ~0.59-2.5%); extending gameplay to 60 minutes (72k steps) raises JARVIS-1 to 12.5% (vs human ~12% in 10 min). On the 200+ task benchmark JARVIS-1 is best in every group, e.g. group-AVG SR vs DEPS: Wood 88.84 vs 80.23, Stone 88.69 vs 69.27, Iron 34.63 vs 16.92, Gold 6.85 vs 2.20, Diamond 8.99 vs 2.42 (~3x on diamond tasks), Redstone 17.51 vs 6.02. It is described as the most general Minecraft agent, completing 200+ tasks with human-like observation/action spaces.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Architecture/challenge ablations (Fig. 2): situation-aware planning, interactive planning, and memory each substantially raise SR, with gains growing as task complexity increases (Stone->Iron->Diamond); cross-task memory transfer (Fig. 2 Right) shows experiences on related tasks (e.g. DiamondAxe) boost a target task (DiamondPickaxe). (2) LM backbone (Fig. 6 / Table 6): with memory, ChatGPT ~= GPT-4 SR; pre-trained LLaMA2-70B is poor on Minecraft, but fine-tuned LLaMA2-13B matches ChatGPT. (3) Memory size / self-improve (Fig. 7): SR on key tech-tree items rises with memory size, reaching 425 stored successful trajectories after 4 learning epochs. (4) Retrieval method (Fig. 8): Text-Memory < Text-Memory+Reasoning < Multimodal-Memory+Reasoning - reasoning before retrieval improves retrieval accuracy, and multimodal (vision+symbolic) retrieval beats text-only. (5) Long-horizon self-improve curriculum (Fig. 9): GPT-generated curriculum > human-written > random; SR keeps rising with longer gameplay (6.2%->12.5%) whereas VPT-RL is flat (2.5%->3%).
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> No. Only end-to-end task SR (and efficiency proxies) are reported. Intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG / completeness) are NOT reported separately; retrieval quality is assessed indirectly via the Fig. 8 retrieval-method ablation on downstream SR ('reasoning before retrieval improves retrieval accuracy', measured through task performance).
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome (final task SR), with some process/efficiency signals: number of re-planning rounds (JARVIS-1 ~2-3 vs DEPS 6+), LLM token / thinking-time savings, and milestone-item SR curves over time (Fig. 9 Right) that track intermediate progress on the diamond-pickaxe tech tree. No reasoning-faithfulness or step-wise retrieval-accuracy metric is scored directly.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A - JARVIS-1 is a method/agent paper, not a survey or taxonomy.
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Evaluation set of 200+ tasks selected from the Minecraft Universe Benchmark / MCU (Lin et al. 2023a), grouped into 11 recommended-category groups (sizes: Wood 34, Wood-Var 43, Stone 10, Iron 22, Gold 9, Diamond 7, Redstone 7, Blocks 15, Armor 17, Decoration 17, Food 9). Tasks target obtainable overworld items; success is auto-verifiable from Minecraft inventory/environment feedback; Max.Steps per task set to human completion time (12k-72k steps); each task run >=30 times across different seeds (diamond_pickaxe 692 times, diamond 728 times). Difficulty signaled by best-system SR collapsing along the tech tree (e.g. Diamond group AVG only 8.99% for JARVIS-1, single ObtainDiamondPickaxe 6.22%-12.5%, leaving a large gap to mastery).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> DEPS (Wang et al. 2023b, interactive Describe-Explain-Plan-Select planning - direct predecessor for the interactive planning framework); STEVE-1 (Lifshitz et al. 2023, used directly as the goal-conditioned low-level controller); MineCLIP (Fan et al. 2022 / MineDojo, chained with the LLM to form the MLM, also the frozen visual encoder/retriever); VPT (Baker et al. 2022, underlying foundation policy & action/observation interface); RAG (Lewis et al. 2020; Mao et al. 2020, retrieval-augmented generation formulation); Self-Instruct (Wang et al. 2022, curriculum generation); Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023, self-explain) and self-debugging (Chen et al. 2023, self-check); GPT-3.5/GPT-4 and LLaMA2 (planner LMs); MineRL + MCP-Reborn (environment); MCU/Minecraft Universe Benchmark (Lin et al. 2023a). Same CraftJarvis group lineage from DEPS.
- **contrasts with**:
> DEPS (Wang et al. 2023b - no memory, cannot learn from cross-task experience, limited re-planning rounds; JARVIS-1 adds multimodal memory and life-long learning, ~3x on diamond tasks with 2-3 vs 6+ re-plan rounds); GITM/Ghost-in-the-Minecraft (Zhu et al. 2023) and Voyager (Wang et al. 2023a) - text-only memory / text-based knowledge and custom non-human interfaces (MineDojo high-level APIs / code skills); JARVIS-1 uses MULTIMODAL memory + human-like raw-pixel observation and mouse/keyboard action spaces; ReAct / Inner Monologue / Instruct-GPT (no memory, weaker on long-horizon); VPT / VPT-RL (RL-finetuned, flat improvement over time, cannot follow instructions / re-plan on tool breakage). Notably success-only memory contrasts with later Optimus-1 (which adds failure cases and experience summarization).
- **lineage**:
> Group F (decision-making / memory / RL) at the intersection of retrieval-augmented planning and experiential episodic-memory agents. Lineage: video/IL+RL Minecraft policies (VPT, MineCLIP, STEVE-1) -> LLM-planner agents (Inner Monologue, DEPS, Voyager, GITM) -> JARVIS-1, which adds a GROWING multimodal episodic memory retrieved (reasoning + multimodal similarity) to augment a frozen-MLM planner for life-long open-world planning. Direct successor: Optimus-1 (Li et al. 2024, NeurIPS) which builds on and contrasts with JARVIS-1 by adding a hierarchical directed knowledge graph (HDKG) and an abstracted multimodal experience pool (AMEP) with success+failure cases; further Optimus-2/Optimus-3.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- completeness_vs_topk_objective
- context_budget_and_selection_count
- cost_efficiency_tradeoff
- maintained_repo_url
- memory_evolution_update

### 131. AriGraph: Learning Knowledge Graph World Models with Episodic Memory for LLM Agents (memory architecture: AriGraph; agent: Ariadne)

2024  ·  IJCAI 2025  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.04363)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**:
> IJCAI 2025 (34th International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Montreal, Canada). Proceedings entry https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2025/2 (pages 12-20), DOI 10.24963/ijcai.2025/2 (ACM mirror dl.acm.org/doi/10.24963/ijcai.2025/2). DBLP key conf/ijcai/AnokhinSSEK0B25. First released as arXiv:2407.04363 (v1 5 Jul 2024; v2 9 Sep 2024; v3 15 May 2025).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.04363 (DOI: https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2407.04363; IJCAI proceedings: https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2025/2, DOI https://doi.org/10.24963/ijcai.2025/2; OpenReview id WO8HLL2g1Y)
- **code url**: https://github.com/AIRI-Institute/AriGraph (official, MIT license; ~167 stars, 28 forks; primary languages Inform 7 + Python; contains agents/, envs/ TextWorld games, qa_data/ for MuSiQue & HotpotQA, graphs/ TripletGraph, prompts/, logs/ of reported runs). Last push Sep 2024.
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (single research repo, last pushed 2024-09-10; no continuously-maintained leaderboard or paper-list).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Decision-making / embodied-style interactive text-game agents (planning, exploration, navigation in partially observable text worlds) as the primary domain, plus a secondary static multi-hop QA evaluation. Environments: TextWorld text games (Treasure Hunt, Cleaning, Cooking) and NetHack (roguelike); QA on MuSiQue and HotpotQA.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, online, SINGLE-agent setting. An LLM agent (Ariadne) interacts step-by-step with an unknown Partially Observable MDP (POMDP) text environment: at each step t it receives observation o_t and emits action a_t; environment rewards r_t are used only for evaluation and are NOT visible to the agent (no gradient updates, no RL training of the LLM, frozen GPT-4-0125-preview backbone). There is no offline corpus and no ground-truth world graph given; the agent must learn a structured world model from scratch via interaction by extracting triplets from textual observations and writing them into a growing memory graph. The agent must remember long-horizon information, filter outdated facts, navigate and explore. A separate, simpler decoupled study compares against RL baselines (GATA, LTL-GATA, EXPLORER) on a 4-level Cooking variant from Adhikari et al. 2021, and a third static multi-hop QA study (MuSiQue / HotpotQA) treats document context as the source over which the same memory graph is built (here non-interactive, offline corpus).
- **what is retrieved**:
> experiences/knowledge from the agent's own learned memory graph: (1) semantic triplets / semantic edges (object1, relation, object2) representing the current structured world state, and (2) episodic vertices, i.e. full past textual observations o_t (and the episodic edges linking observations to the triplets extracted at that step). In the QA setting the same units are retrieved from a graph built over the document(s).
- **retrieval grounding**:
> GROWING / episodic memory the agent itself writes (HYBRID semantic+episodic), constructed online during interaction. For the interactive games the memory graph is built entirely from the agent's own observations (no static external KB/corpus/API). For the auxiliary multi-hop QA the same AriGraph is built over the provided document(s) before answering, so that sub-setting grounds on a (per-query) constructed graph rather than the agent's evolving experience.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Top-k retrieval with two coupled stages but no learned ranking metric: SemanticSearch returns up to width-w edges per BFS hop within depth d (a variable-size relevant subgraph), and EpisodicSearch returns the k most relevant episodic vertices (k fixed). The objective is to surface the relevant subgraph + most-relevant past observations to support decision-making, not a fixed top-k ranking optimized to Recall@k/nDCG, and not an explicit minimal-complete-set objective; effective size is driven by graph connectivity and the d/w/k hyperparameters.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve: yes, Reuse: partial, Revise: yes (of the world model, not of cases), Retain: yes]. AriGraph Retrieves relevant triplets+observations, Retains every new triplet and observation, and Revises stored knowledge by detecting and removing outdated/conflicting triplets when the world changes. 'Reuse' is partial: retrieved knowledge is fed to planning/decision-making as context rather than reusing a prior solution case. (Approximate mapping; the work is NOT framed as CBR.)
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner. It is framed as a knowledge-graph world model integrating semantic and episodic memory for LLM agents.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Two unit types from a knowledge graph: (a) KG-subgraph / semantic edge = a single semantic triplet (object1, relation, object2); and (b) episodic vertex = a full past textual observation o_t. Episodic edges (temporal 'happened at the same time' links) connect each observation vertex to the triplets extracted at that step. Retrieval returns a relevant set of triplets (the subgraph) plus the top-k episodic observations.
- **index source**:
> Growing memory, online/test-time-induced. In the interactive games the AriGraph world model is constructed and continuously updated from scratch during the agent's interaction (each observation adds an episodic vertex/edge and triggers triplet extraction + outdated-triplet removal). In the QA setting the graph is induced from the supplied documents prior to answering. No pre-existing static KB is used.
- **index structure topology**:
> Knowledge GRAPH (dependency/semantic graph) augmented with an episodic layer: semantic vertices (objects) connected by semantic edges (triplets), plus episodic vertices (observations) connected to their triplets via episodic edges ('hyper-relational'/temporal links). Spatial relations (e.g. 'hall, east of, kitchen', 'kitchen, has an unexplored exit, south') are stored as triplets enabling graph-based navigation/route inference. Edge text is embedded for similarity search. This is a structured graph index, contrasted with flat unstructured vector RAG.
- **retriever type**:
> Hybrid graph-traversal + dense retrieval. A BFS-like Memory Graph Search (Algorithm 1/2): at each hop EmbedAndRetrieve uses a pretrained dense encoder (Contriever for games; BGE-M3 for QA) to embed edges and the query and return the top-w edges by dot-product similarity, expanding to incident vertices up to depth d; episodic search then scores episodic vertices by how many retrieved triplets they contain. No trained/learned retriever, no BM25, no LLM-as-retriever, no reranker stage.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None (off-the-shelf encoders, hand-designed scoring). Semantic relevance uses frozen pretrained Contriever (games) / BGE-M3 (QA) embeddings with dot-product similarity; the episodic relevance score is a hand-crafted formula rel(v_e^i) = (n_i / max(N_i,1)) * log2(max(N_i,1)) where n_i is the number of retrieved input triplets associated with episodic vertex i and N_i is the total triplets incident, with log weighting (single-triplet observations assigned zero weight). No contrastive fine-tuning, LM-feedback, RL, or downstream-effectiveness training of the retriever.
- **query construction**:
> Query is formed from the agent's current situation. For semantic search the query set Q is derived from the current observation/state (and relevant entities); during graph traversal each newly reached semantic vertex serves as a sub-query for the next EmbedAndRetrieve hop (multi-hop query expansion across the graph). For QA, the question (decomposed into the entities/relations needed) drives the multi-hop semantic search. Episodic search uses the retrieved triplets as its query into the episodic layer.
- **query granularity**:
> Step/state-level (a fresh retrieval is performed at each interaction step before planning/decision-making), with an internal multi-hop, two-level structure: semantic search (BFS over triplets, depth d / width w) followed by episodic search (top-k observations). For QA it is task-level per question but still internally multi-hop.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Iterative / per-step. Retrieval into working memory occurs at every environment step (each new observation triggers world-model update then retrieval of relevant semantic subgraph + top-k episodic memories). Internally it is a multi-hop BFS rather than a single one-shot lookup. Not uncertainty-triggered or routed by a learned classifier.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed schedule (per-step / event-driven): every observation triggers (i) a world-model update and (ii) retrieval to repopulate working memory before planning and decision-making. An auxiliary 'exploration check' LLM prompt decides whether the current plan needs exploration (activating unexplored-exit detection that adds candidate exits to working memory), but this gates exploration mode rather than gating whether retrieval happens. No token-confidence, attention-uncertainty, reflection-token, or learned-complexity trigger.
- **reranking**: No dedicated second-stage reranker (no cross-encoder / RRF / instruction-tuned reranker). Ranking is the single similarity score (dot product) within the BFS for semantic edges, and the hand-crafted relevance formula for episodic vertices; top-w / top-k are taken directly.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Light structural selection rather than learned refinement: the BFS bounds the retrieved subgraph by depth d and width w; the episodic relevance formula down-weights low-information (single-triplet) observations; the retrieved semantic subgraph and top-k episodic observations are then placed into working memory. Outdated/conflicting triplets are removed at write time (world-model update) rather than as post-retrieval filtering. No reason-in-documents distillation or learned compression of retrieved text.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tools/APIs are indexed; the store holds learned semantic triplets and raw observations, not tool/skill documentation).
- **index content separation**:
> Partial/implicit: semantic edges (compact triplets) act as the lightweight retrievable keys and are embedded for search, while each episodic vertex stores the full observation text loaded into the prompt only when its observation is among the retrieved top-k. There is no explicit progressive-disclosure SOP-index-then-content protocol; it is the two-layer semantic(compact)/episodic(full-text) design.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (not a tool-retrieval system; no RapidAPI/RESTful/MCP/function-calling tool registry or CRUD auto-sync). The 'dynamic' aspect is that the knowledge graph is continuously updated (insert new triplets, delete outdated ones, append episodic vertices) during interaction.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tools/APIs; no inter-tool dependency modeling). Spatial/relational dependencies between locations and objects are modeled in the KG for navigation, but this is environment-state structure, not tool dependency.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation. The retrieved relevant semantic subgraph and top-k episodic observations are written into the agent's working memory (alongside goal, current observation, recent history, current plan, and unexplored exits) and injected as text into the planning prompt and the ReAct decision-making prompt, grounding plan generation/update and action selection. No training signal or latent-token injection; the frozen LLM consumes retrieved knowledge as text.
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-plan-then-act per step within an interaction loop. Pipeline at each step: update AriGraph -> retrieve semantic+episodic knowledge into working memory -> Planning module creates/updates a plan as task-relevant sub-goals (each with a reason), also evaluating outcomes of the previous action and adjusting the plan -> ReAct-based Decision-making module reads working memory and selects one valid action (articulating rationale first). Planning is separated from decision-making. A graph-specific 'go to location' macro-action lets the agent infer optimal routes from stored spatial triplets. No MCTS/tree search.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Per-step within the rollout (per environment step): retrieval, planning update, and decision-making are interleaved once per action over the long-horizon trajectory (max 60 steps Cooking, 150 steps other games). Within a single retrieval, traversal is multi-hop over the graph. Not per-CoT-token.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> N/A for classic CBR case adaptation. Retrieved knowledge is used as in-context evidence; the LLM synthesizes plans/actions from it. The closest analog is execution-feedback-driven REVISION of the world model itself (outdated triplets detected and replaced as the environment changes), not adaptation of a retrieved solution case.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Structured natural-language: semantic triplets (object1, relation, object2) rendered as text form the relevant subgraph, and full raw observation texts form the episodic items; both injected as text into working-memory prompt fields. No executable program/skill or latent/soft tokens.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Mixed: distilled structured facts (semantic triplets = compact state knowledge, a structured-note-like abstraction) coexisting with raw low-abstraction episodic observations (full past observation text). Spatial-relation triplets additionally serve a procedural/navigation role.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Several heuristic guards: (1) write-time outdated-triplet detection-and-removal keeps the semantic graph consistent with the changing world (a carefully prompted, conservative replacement rule that errs toward retaining facts); (2) the episodic relevance log-weighting assigns zero weight to single-triplet (low-information) observations to suppress distractors; (3) bounded BFS depth d / width w limits retrieval of irrelevant graph regions. No retriever-aware training, learned relevance evaluator, or self-reflection filter.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: graph memory integrating semantic memory (knowledge-graph triplets) and episodic memory (per-step observation vertices) within one memory-graph framework; long-term, persistent, single-agent, online-updated. The authors explicitly note procedural memory is left to future work.
- **write back**: True. Every observation is written back: a new episodic vertex (full observation) and episodic edges are added, new semantic triplets extracted from the observation are inserted, and outdated/conflicting triplets are removed. The graph is the agent's learned world model.
- **online growth**:
> Yes. The memory graph is built from scratch and grows/updates continuously during interaction at test time. Authors report growth saturates as the agent becomes familiar with the environment, and grows moderately for larger/harder environments; higher-quality LLM backbones produce slower graph growth (cleaner extraction).
- **write back trigger**:
> Per-step (every observation). Each environment step triggers a world-model update: append episodic vertex/edges, insert new semantic triplets, and detect+remove outdated triplets. Writes are NOT conditioned on task success/failure (no reward signal is used for writing). (The Reflexion BASELINE, by contrast, writes reflective notes on failure across trials, but that is a comparison method, not AriGraph.)
- **failure experience usage**:
> No explicit success/failure labeling in AriGraph itself: the agent stores all observations and the current factual world state regardless of outcome; there is no failure-only corrective-rule store or success-vs-failure contrastive retrieval. (Reflexion, used only as a baseline, performs cross-trial failure reflection; AriGraph operates within a single trajectory and updates state, not failure rules.)
- **memory evolution update**:
> Both append and mutate: episodic memory is append-only (new observation vertices/edges); semantic memory is dynamically mutated via delta-update / refine-overwrite, i.e. new triplets are inserted and outdated or conflicting incident triplets are detected (compared against new triplets) and deleted/replaced when the world state changes (e.g. 'item, is in, locker' -> 'item, is in, inventory'). Link-and-evolve via episodic edges connecting observations to triplets.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No. Retrieval/case-selection is a fixed graph-search + frozen-embedding similarity procedure with hand-crafted episodic scoring; it is not an RL/learned policy (no M-MDP, soft Q-learning, or trained retrieval policy). The agent's action policy is the frozen LLM with ReAct; only the world model (not the retriever) is 'learned' (constructed) online.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent private memory: one Ariadne agent builds and uses its own AriGraph. No cross-agent or cross-framework memory sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> (1) Custom TextWorld text games in three families with difficulty tiers: Treasure Hunt (Medium 12 rooms/4 keys, Hard 16 rooms/5 keys, Hardest 36 rooms/7 keys + distractors), Cleaning (9 rooms, 11 misplaced items), Cooking (Medium 9 locations/3 ingredients, Hard 12 locations/4 ingredients, Hardest adds closed doors + inventory management); (2) a 4-level Cooking variant from Adhikari et al. 2021 for RL comparison; (3) NetHack (roguelike, via NetPlay) with Room-Obs vs Level-Obs settings; (4) static multi-hop QA: MuSiQue and HotpotQA (200 random samples each, following GraphReader/Li et al. 2024a). LLM backbone gpt-4-0125-preview for games; GPT-4 and GPT-4o-mini for QA.
- **benchmark family**: Embodied/interactive text-game decision-making (TextWorld; closest to ALFWorld/ScienceWorld family) and roguelike (NetHack) for the primary tasks; multi-hop QA (MuSiQue, HotpotQA) for the secondary evaluation. Spans decision-making/RL-comparison and multi-hop QA families.
- **baselines**:
> Interactive text games (all sharing Ariadne's identical planning+decision modules, varying ONLY the memory module): Full History, Summarization, standard RAG (top-k vector retrieval), Simulacra (Generative Agents memory; recency+importance+relevance scoring with reflection), Reflexion (cross-trial verbal reflection). RL baselines on the Cooking-variant: GATA, LTL-GATA, EXPLORER (best reported numbers from Adhikari et al. 2021, Tuli et al. 2022, Basu et al. 2024); plus GPT-4 Full-History. Human players (Top-3 and All). NetHack: NetPlay [Room obs], NetPlay [Level obs] (memory-oracle). Multi-hop QA: BM25(top-3), Ada-002(top-3), GPT-4 full context, GPT-4 + supporting facts, ReadAgent(GPT-4), GraphReader(GPT-4), HOLMES(GPT-4), GraphRAG(GPT-4o-mini).
- **key metrics**:
> Text games: normalized game score (relative to max attainable points; 1.0 = task solved), reported as average of the top-3 of 5 runs, with step caps (60 Cooking, 150 others). NetHack: Score and number of dungeon Levels reached. Multi-hop QA: Exact Match (EM) and F1. Efficiency: prompt/completion token usage per step (games) and per task (QA), and cost ratio vs GraphRAG.
- **ablations**:
> Key ablations (Table 4 normalized scores): 'AriGraph w/o episodic' (semantic graph only) drops on tasks needing detailed recall: Cooking 1.0 -> 0.64 (Medium) and 1.0 -> 0.45 (Hard), Treasure Hunt Hard 1.0 -> 0.67, while it slightly IMPROVES Cleaning (0.79 -> 0.92, where filtering outdated location info matters more than long-term recall), showing episodic memory is critical for recall-heavy tasks and less so for state-filtering tasks. 'AriGraph w/o exploration' (no graph-based unexplored-exit detection / go-to macro) drops Treasure Hunt 1.0 -> 0.87 and Cooking 1.0 -> 0.87. Backbone ablation: 'AriGraph LLaMA-3-70B' is much weaker (Treasure Hunt 0.47, Cooking 0.67, Cleaning 0.5) than GPT-4, showing dependence on backbone extraction quality. NetHack ablation shows Room-Obs+AriGraph matches the Level-Obs oracle. QA: replacing Contriever with BGE-M3 for text encoding.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Partial. Intrinsic retrieval ranking metrics (Recall@k/nDCG) are NOT reported; the authors explicitly state they do not measure graph correctness against a 'true graph' (too variable), instead reporting graph growth-rate and update-rate as process diagnostics. End-to-end metrics (game score, NetHack score/levels, QA EM/F1) are the main signals; the RL-comparison and NetHack-oracle studies decouple memory contribution from the decision module.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both. Outcome metrics dominate (normalized game score, NetHack score/levels, QA EM/F1), but process-level diagnostics are reported: per-step performance dynamics (Appendix G), graph growth-rate and update-rate over time (Fig.5/6, incl. a random-walk construction experiment), and component ablations isolating semantic vs. episodic memory and exploration.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Reported (Table 3). Text games per-step token usage: Ariadne ~6,000 prompt / 500 completion tokens, vs RAG 4,000/350, Summary 3,800/350, Full History (step 150) 14,000/350, Simulacra 7,500/400, Reflexion 5,800/350 — i.e. AriGraph is far cheaper than Full History and avoids its blow-up, while richer than plain RAG. QA per-task: AriGraph 11,000 prompt / 2,500 completion vs GraphRAG 115,000 / 20,000 — AriGraph is >10x cheaper than GraphRAG at competitive accuracy.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Budget controlled by graph-search hyperparameters: SemanticSearch returns up to width w edges per BFS hop bounded by depth d; EpisodicSearch returns the top-k episodic observations (k fixed per run); working memory also holds n_prev recent observation/action pairs, the goal, current observation, plan, and unexplored exits. Selection is similarity-then-truncate within the d/w/k budget (no adaptive precision-driven k). Net per-step prompt ~6,000 tokens.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> TextWorld games are custom-authored (Inform 7 / TextWorld) with explicit difficulty tiers (Treasure Hunt 12/16/36 rooms; Cleaning 9 rooms/11 misplaced items; Cooking 9-12 locations/3-4 ingredients + Hardest with closed doors); scoring is rule-verifiable (points per key/item/recipe step). NetHack via NetPlay. QA uses 200 random samples each from MuSiQue and HotpotQA (existing datasets, answer-verifiable EM/F1). Five runs per game with top-3 averaged; difficulty signaled by baseline failure (baselines cannot find the 2nd key on Treasure Hunt Hardest).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> TextWorld text-game framework (Cote et al. 2018); NetHack Learning Environment (Kuttler et al. 2020) via NetPlay (Jeurissen et al. 2024); ReAct (Yao et al. 2023) for decision-making; Generative Agents/Simulacra (Park et al. 2023) and Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023) as memory baselines/inspiration; Contriever (Izacard et al. 2022) and BGE-M3 (Chen et al. 2024) dense encoders; cognitive-science semantic/episodic memory distinction; KG-from-text QA line (GraphReader/Li et al. 2024a, HOLMES, GraphRAG, HippoRAG, ReadAgent); RL text-game world-model line (GATA / Adhikari et al. 2021, LTL-GATA / Tuli et al. 2022, EXPLORER / Basu et al. 2024); cognitive architectures for language agents (Sumers et al. 2024).
- **contrasts with**:
> Unstructured LLM-agent memory: Full History (costly, context-limited), Summarization (lossy), plain vector RAG (scattered/unstructured retrieval), Simulacra/Generative-Agents recency-importance-relevance memory, and Reflexion cross-trial reflection — all of which lack structured semantic+episodic graph state and dynamic updating. Skill-library/episodic agents (Voyager, Ghost-in-the-Minecraft, Jarvis-1) that lack semantic graph structure and rely on external game knowledge. KG-QA methods (GraphReader, HOLMES, GraphRAG, HippoRAG) that build static document KGs but do NOT support updates in dynamic interactive environments. RL world-model agents (GATA, LTL-GATA, EXPLORER) that require training.
- **lineage**:
> Group F (decision-making / memory / RL): a knowledge-graph world-model + episodic-memory architecture for online experience-based LLM agents in interactive POMDP text games. Extends the episodic memory-stream lineage (Generative Agents/Reflexion) by adding a dynamically-updated semantic knowledge graph and graph-traversal retrieval, and connects it to the KG-from-text QA lineage (GraphRAG/HOLMES/GraphReader). Sits upstream of later structured-memory / graph-memory agent frameworks; positioned as learning a structured world model from scratch via interaction.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- authors_affiliation
- headline_result

<a id="item-hipporag"></a>
### 132. HippoRAG (Neurobiologically Inspired Long-Term Memory for Large Language Models)

2024  ·  NeurIPS 2024  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14831)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: NeurIPS 2024 (The Thirty-eighth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems; OpenReview id=hkujvAPVsg). Preprint arXiv:2405.14831 (cs.CL); v1 23 May 2024, v3 14 Jan 2025.
- **authors affiliation**: Bernal Jimenez Gutierrez, Yiheng Shu, Yu Gu, Yu Su (The Ohio State University); Michihiro Yasunaga (Stanford University). Lead/corresponding from the OSU NLP Group.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14831
- **code url**: https://github.com/OSU-NLP-Group/HippoRAG (MIT license; original HippoRAG code tagged v1.0.0 / legacy branch). OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=hkujvAPVsg
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/OSU-NLP-Group/HippoRAG (actively maintained, ~3.6k stars; the repo main branch has since evolved to HippoRAG 2 'From RAG to Memory', ICML 2025, arXiv:2502.14802; the original HippoRAG 1 is preserved under the 'legacy' branch / v1.0.0 release).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: QA: multi-hop / knowledge-integration question answering (retrieval-augmented), framed as long-term memory for LLMs.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline-indexed, single-agent, non-interactive open-domain multi-hop QA. A retrieval corpus (passages, including supporting and distractor passages following the IRCoT setup) is indexed once offline into a schemaless knowledge graph; at test time a query is answered by retrieving passages and feeding them to a frozen QA reader LLM. No task-level supervision or retriever fine-tuning is used (all components are off-the-shelf); two hyperparameters (synonymy threshold tau=0.8, PPR damping=0.5) are tuned on 100 MuSiQue training examples. The work emphasizes single-step multi-hop retrieval (vs iterative RAG) and a continually-updatable memory (new knowledge integrated by adding edges to the KG rather than re-summarizing).
- **what is retrieved**: Passages/documents (ranked via aggregated PageRank node probabilities). The underlying retrievable store is an open knowledge-graph index of noun-phrase entity nodes and relation edges (OpenIE triples) plus synonymy edges; passages are scored from the KG node probabilities.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus: an LLM-derived open KG (artificial hippocampal index) built offline over the document corpus. Authors note the KG can be incrementally updated by adding edges (continually-updating memory), but in the reported experiments it is a fixed corpus index, not a self-written episodic agent memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Both a fixed top-k ranking objective (R@2/R@5) AND an explicit completeness objective: the paper introduces an 'all-recall' metric (AR@2/AR@5) measuring the percentage of queries for which ALL supporting passages are retrieved, arguing HippoRAG's advantage is single-step recovery of the complete supporting set (gap over ColBERTv2 grows from ~20% to ~38% R@5 on 2Wiki when measured by all-recall).
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based reasoning system; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain case cycle).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The work frames itself via the hippocampal memory indexing theory (neuroscience) and KG+PageRank retrieval, not as case-based reasoning; it does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> KG-subgraph -> passage/document. The index is built from KG units (noun-phrase entity nodes and relation edges = OpenIE triples), and Personalized PageRank scores over these nodes are aggregated (via a |N|x|P| node-passage incidence matrix) to rank passages, which are the final retrieved unit.
- **index source**:
> Static corpus, offline-induced: an instruction-tuned LLM (default GPT-3.5-turbo-1106) performs OpenIE over each passage to build a schemaless open KG; off-the-shelf retrieval encoders (Contriever or ColBERTv2) add synonymy edges between similar noun phrases. The store is built offline once (though the authors highlight that new passages can be incrementally added by extending the KG with new edges).
- **index structure topology**: Knowledge GRAPH: a schemaless open KG with noun-phrase entity nodes, OpenIE relation edges, and additional synonymy edges between near-duplicate phrases (the 'artificial hippocampal index'). A node-to-passage incidence matrix links graph nodes back to source passages.
- **retriever type**: Hybrid graph-based: LLM-as-extractor (OpenIE for indexing; query NER for retrieval) + dense retrieval encoder (Contriever or ColBERTv2) for entity linking / synonymy edges + Personalized PageRank graph search for the actual ranking. No learned/trained retriever module.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None (off-the-shelf). All components (LLM for OpenIE/NER, dense encoders, PPR) are used without training or fine-tuning. Only two scalar hyperparameters (synonymy threshold tau=0.8 and PPR damping factor=0.5) are tuned on 100 MuSiQue training examples; node specificity provides an unsupervised IDF-like weighting.
- **query construction**:
> Intent/entity extraction: the LLM ('neocortex') extracts a set of salient query named entities from the raw query via 1-shot prompting; these are encoded by the retrieval encoder and linked to their most similar KG nodes (query nodes), which become the PPR seed set. No sub-query decomposition or query rewriting in the single-step setting.
- **query granularity**: Task-level (one-shot at t=0): a single query-time entity extraction + one PPR run per query. (When wrapped inside IRCoT for the multi-step variant, retrieval becomes trajectory/step-level, but core HippoRAG is single-shot.)
- **when to retrieve**:
> One-shot (single-step retrieval): a single PPR-based retrieval pass per query, performing multi-hop reasoning in one step. The paper's central claim is replacing iterative retrieval (IRCoT) with single-step retrieval; HippoRAG can also be plugged into IRCoT to enable iterative retrieval for further gains.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule: retrieval is always performed once per query (no confidence/uncertainty/learned trigger). In the IRCoT+HippoRAG variant, the trigger is IRCoT's fixed iterative reason-then-retrieve loop (2-4 rounds in their experiments).
- **reranking**:
> No explicit cross-encoder/reranking stage in HippoRAG 1. Ranking is produced directly by aggregating Personalized PageRank node probabilities over passages (weighted by node specificity, an IDF-like local signal). ColBERTv2, when used, serves as a synonymy-edge encoder, not a downstream reranker.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> None beyond passage ranking: PPR distributes probability from query nodes across the KG and the aggregated node probabilities directly rank passages; node specificity (IDF-like) reweights node contributions. No decompose-recompose, distillation, or compression of retrieved passages.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tool retrieval).
- **index content separation**:
> Partial / implicit: a lightweight graph index (entity nodes + edges, the hippocampal index) is separated from the heavy passage content, and passages are only surfaced after PPR scoring via the node-passage incidence matrix. Not a formal progressive-disclosure/SOP-index-then-content protocol.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index/protocol).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tools).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**: Prompt augmentation: the top-ranked passages are fed to a separate frozen QA reader LLM (with the same reader/prompt across methods) to generate the answer. Retrieval and generation are decoupled (HippoRAG improves QA only indirectly by improving retrieval).
- **planning integration**: Retrieve-then-read (no agentic planning in core HippoRAG): a single retrieval step feeds a QA reader. The multi-step variant interleaves HippoRAG retrieval inside IRCoT's iterative chain-of-thought reason-then-retrieve loop.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer for single-step HippoRAG (one retrieval, one read). When integrated with IRCoT, retrieval is interleaved per-CoT-reasoning-step (per IRCoT iteration).
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not a CBR system; no retrieved-case adaptation/revision). Retrieved passages are used verbatim as context for the QA reader.
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw passages/document text injected into the QA reader's prompt. The intermediate representation that drives ranking is structured (KG nodes/edges + PPR probabilities), but what is injected for generation is raw passage text.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Raw passages (single retrieval unit) ranked via structured graph associations. The retrieval signal is built on a distilled associative structure (open KG triples), but the retrieved/injected unit is the original passage, not a distilled strategy or summary (explicitly contrasted with summarization-based methods like RAPTOR/GraphRAG).
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Node specificity (an IDF-like local weighting that down-weights nodes appearing in many passages) and synonymy-edge construction (noisy entity standardization) improve robustness; PPR's restart/damping concentrates probability around query-node neighborhoods, mitigating spurious activations. No retriever-aware training or learned relevance evaluator. Error analysis attributes most errors to NER/OpenIE extraction and to PPR struggling when many passages discuss similar topics.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: graph (a schemaless open knowledge-graph 'artificial hippocampal index' that serves as long-term memory). Static corpus index in the experiments, designed to be incrementally extendable.
- **write back**:
> False (in the reported experiments): the KG index is built offline and the system does not write back query-time answers/experiences into memory. The framework is designed to support adding new knowledge by inserting new OpenIE triples/edges into the KG, but this incremental-update capability is described conceptually rather than evaluated as test-time write-back.
- **online growth**:
> Not in the evaluated setting (corpus indexed offline, frozen at test time). The paper argues HippoRAG can continuously integrate new knowledge by adding edges to its KG (vs re-summarizing as in RAPTOR/GraphRAG), positioning it as a continually-updating memory, but online growth is not empirically benchmarked in HippoRAG 1.
- **write back trigger**: Never (at query/test time in the experiments). New-knowledge integration is an offline indexing operation (add OpenIE triples/synonymy edges for new passages), not triggered by on-success/on-failure/reflective query-time events.
- **failure experience usage**: Not applicable / not used. The system stores no success/failure experiences; there is no experience memory. (A qualitative error analysis of 100 MuSiQue errors is reported but not fed back into the system.)
- **memory evolution update**: Append/extend (conceptual): new knowledge is integrated by adding nodes/edges to the KG; synonymy detection performs a form of dedup/standardization between near-duplicate phrases at indexing time. No post-write mutation, refine-overwrite, or forgetting is evaluated.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No. Retrieval is a fixed graph algorithm (Personalized PageRank seeded by similarity-linked query nodes), not a learned or RL-optimized retrieval/selection policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent, single private corpus index; no multi-agent or cross-framework memory sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> MuSiQue (answerable), 2WikiMultiHopQA (2Wiki), and HotpotQA. 1,000 questions sampled from each validation set; a retrieval corpus per dataset is formed from all candidate (supporting + distractor) passages following IRCoT (corpus sizes: MuSiQue 11,656 passages; 2Wiki 6,119; HotpotQA 9,221). A small path-finding multi-hop QA case study is also constructed.
- **benchmark family**: multi-hop QA (open-domain multi-hop question answering / knowledge integration).
- **baselines**:
> Single-step retrievers: BM25, Contriever, GTR, ColBERTv2, Propositionizer (Proposition), RAPTOR (and RAPTOR/Proposition with ColBERTv2 backbone). Multi-step: IRCoT (with BM25 / Contriever / ColBERTv2). QA readers compared: None (closed-book), ColBERTv2, IRCoT, and IRCoT+HippoRAG, all with the same reader. Ablation/alternative components: REBEL (end-to-end OpenIE), Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct (OpenIE), and PPR alternatives (query-nodes-only; query-nodes+neighbors).
- **key metrics**:
> Retrieval: Recall@2 (R@2) and Recall@5 (R@5); plus all-recall AR@2/AR@5 (fraction of queries where ALL supporting passages are retrieved). QA: Exact Match (EM) and F1. Efficiency: online retrieval API cost ($) and latency (minutes), reported as 10-30x cheaper / 6-13x faster than IRCoT.
- **headline result**:
> On 2WikiMultiHopQA, single-step HippoRAG improves single-step retrieval by ~11 points R@2 and ~20 points R@5 over the strongest baselines (e.g., HippoRAG-Contriever 71.5 R@2 / 89.5 R@5 vs ColBERTv2 59.2 / 68.2), with ~3% gains on MuSiQue and competitive results on HotpotQA; it matches or beats iterative IRCoT while being 10-30x cheaper and 6-13x faster in online retrieval. The abstract's single-number claim: outperforms state-of-the-art by up to 20%.
- **ablations**:
> Table 5 dissects HippoRAG (R@2/R@5 over the 3 datasets). OpenIE alternatives: REBEL causes large drops (avg 46.2/58.4 vs HippoRAG 57.4/72.9), showing LLM OpenIE flexibility matters; Llama-3.1-8B is competitive except on 2Wiki, Llama-3.1-70B (avg 57.1/72.5) roughly matches GPT-3.5. PPR alternatives: replacing PPR with query-nodes-only (50.7/56.2) or query-nodes+neighbors (42.2/59.2) is much worse, confirming PPR drives multi-hop association (notably, adding neighbors without PPR hurts vs nodes-only). Component ablations: removing node specificity drops avg to 54.7/70.9 (largest effect on MuSiQue/HotpotQA); removing synonymy edges drops to 56.2/70.5 (largest effect on 2Wiki). All-recall (Table 6) shows the gap over ColBERTv2 grows (e.g., 2Wiki R@5 gap ~20% -> ~38%). Intrinsic OpenIE eval (CaRB) on 239 gold MuSiQue triples corroborates extraction quality.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Yes. Intrinsic retrieval metrics (R@2/R@5, plus the all-recall AR@2/AR@5 completeness metric and a CaRB-based intrinsic OpenIE evaluation) are reported separately from end-to-end QA metrics (EM/F1); the paper explicitly attributes QA gains to retrieval improvements with a shared reader.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both. Outcome: QA EM/F1. Process/intermediate: retrieval R@k, the all-recall metric (whether ALL supporting passages, i.e. successful multi-hop reasoning, are recovered), intrinsic OpenIE precision/recall/F1, and a qualitative error analysis (NER vs OpenIE vs PPR error categories).
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Online retrieval (1,000 queries, GPT-3.5 Turbo, Table 17): HippoRAG ~$0.1 and ~3 min vs IRCoT ~$1-3 and ~20-40 min (ColBERTv2 ~$0 / ~1 min) => 10-30x cheaper, 6-13x faster than IRCoT. Tradeoff: offline indexing is heavier for HippoRAG (~$15 and ~60 min more per 10,000 passages with GPT-3.5; Llama-3.1-70B via vLLM on 4xH100 indexes 10,000 docs in ~250 min / ~4 hours at $0 API). The persistent advantage is online retrieval token count (only query NER vs reprocessing all retrieved docs).
- **context budget and selection count**: Fixed top-k passage budget: retrieval evaluated at k=2 and k=5 (R@2/R@5; QA reader fed the top retrieved passages). No adaptive/precision-driven variable-k; HippoRAG ranks all passages by aggregated PPR probability then truncates to k.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Uses existing datasets (MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA), sampling 1,000 questions per validation set and building a per-dataset retrieval corpus from all candidate passages following IRCoT (11,656 / 6,119 / 9,221 passages). Extracted KG statistics reported (e.g., MuSiQue ~91,729 nodes, ~107,448 triples). A small additional path-finding multi-hop QA case study is hand-constructed (book/movie + trait queries with Wikipedia distractors). Answers verified via EM/F1 against gold answers.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al., 2020); the hippocampal memory indexing theory (Teyler & Discenna, 1986); Personalized PageRank (Haveliwala, 2002 / Page et al.); open information extraction (OpenIE); dense retrievers Contriever (Izacard et al.), ColBERTv2 (Santhanam et al.), GTR (Ni et al.); IRCoT (Trivedi et al., 2023) for the realistic-corpus setup and as the iterative-retrieval method it both compares against and augments; LLM OpenIE via GPT-3.5 / Llama-3.1.
- **contrasts with**:
> Iterative/multi-step RAG, especially IRCoT (HippoRAG achieves comparable accuracy in a single step at far lower cost/latency, and can also augment IRCoT). Standard single-step dense retrievers (BM25, Contriever, GTR, ColBERTv2) that encode passages in isolation and cannot integrate knowledge across passage boundaries. LLM-augmented indexing-time summarization methods RAPTOR, GraphRAG, MemWalker (which must re-summarize when new data is added, whereas HippoRAG just adds KG edges). Parametric memory / model editing and long-context-as-memory approaches.
