### 133. IDT - In-Context Decision Transformer: Reinforcement Learning via Hierarchical Chain-of-Thought

2024  ·  ICML 2024  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.20692)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: ICML 2024 (Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235:19871-19885)
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.20692
- **code url**: https://github.com/SiliHuang-ai/IDT
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (single-paper code repo; not a continuously-updated leaderboard/list)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: decision-making / offline-to-online reinforcement learning (in-context RL). Continuous control (MuJoCo locomotion) and discrete navigation (Grid World) tasks.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline-trained, test-time-online in-context RL. The agent is trained by supervised sequence prediction on a fixed offline dataset of (possibly sub-optimal) trajectories, then at test time self-improves on unseen tasks purely in-context (no gradient updates) by rolling out multiple episodes and conditioning on an across-episodic context. Single-agent; supervision is the offline trajectories' low-level actions (autoregressive). Online phase involves no parameter updates, only forward passes.
- **what is retrieved**: Across-episodic experiences: multiple historical trajectories (a 'chain of experience') arranged in ascending order of returns, reconstructed by IDT into a high-level 'hierarchical chain of experience' of high-level decisions (latent vectors z) rather than low-level actions.
- **retrieval grounding**: GROWING/episodic memory the agent itself produces. The across-episodic context is the agent's own rolled-out trajectories accumulated during test-time trial-and-error (plus optionally external demonstration prompts in the case study). It is not a static external corpus/KB.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Neither a top-k ranking nor a completeness-recovery objective. The context is a fixed-size window of the most recent n=4 episodes; 'selection' is implicit via the Transformer's causal self-attention over this window. The objective is to predict a higher-return next trajectory conditioned on the ordered context (chain-of-hindsight-style return improvement).
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not framed as CBR). Loosely: Retrieve (attend over past episodes) and Reuse (condition generation on them) are present; Revise/Retain are not classic CBR operations (memory is an append-only rolling episode buffer, not a curated case base).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is framed as in-context RL / hierarchical RL / chain-of-experience / chain-of-hindsight.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Reconstructed (state/observation, high-level-decision z, reward, completion) tuples at the high-level (one per c environment steps), forming high-level sub-trajectories across episodes. Baselines (AT/AD) use per-step (return, observation, action, reward, completion) tuples; IDT's unit is the high-level decision token summarizing a c-step segment.
- **index source**: Online/test-time-induced growing memory: the across-episodic context is built from trajectories the agent itself generates during the test-time trial-and-error rollout (and at training, sampled minibatches of offline trajectories). No offline-induced static retrieval index.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat ordered sequence (context-keyed): n=4 trajectories concatenated and sorted in ascending order of total return, consumed as a single token sequence by causal self-attention. No vector index, graph, or hierarchical store; the only 'hierarchy' is temporal (high-level decision over c low-level steps).
- **retriever type**: Implicit: Transformer causal self-attention over the in-context sequence acts as the 'search/memory' mechanism (no explicit BM25/dense retriever). The paper frames self-attention as the search over memory of past experiences.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None as an explicit retriever; selection is fixed (most-recent-n episodes, return-sorted). The whole model (including the attention that does the implicit search) is trained end-to-end by supervised action-prediction loss (cross-entropy for discrete, MSE for continuous actions); there is no contrastive/RL retriever-training signal for selection itself.
- **query construction**:
> Implicit: the current observation o_t plus the past across-episodic trajectories serve as the conditioning context; the Making Decisions module predicts the next high-level decision z_t given o_t and past trajectories. No explicit query string is formed; the 'query' is the autoregressive position conditioned on the ordered experience context plus the target return token.
- **query granularity**: Two-level / both. High level: a high-level decision z is queried/generated every c steps (trajectory/segment level) by the Making Decisions module; low level: actions are generated per step within each c-step segment by the Decisions to Go module conditioned on z.
- **when to retrieve**: Iterative / fixed schedule. The across-episodic context is refreshed continuously as new episodes are rolled out; a new high-level decision is produced on a fixed schedule (every c steps). Not uncertainty-triggered or learned-router.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule: a high-level decision is generated once every c steps (c=10 for D4RL and Large Grid World, c=5 for standard Grid World), and the context window holds the most recent n=4 episodes. No confidence/attention/classifier trigger.
- **reranking**: None. No explicit reranking stage; trajectories are ordered by total return (ascending) before being placed in context, but this is a fixed sort, not a learned reranker.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Reconstruction/compression rather than rerank/distill: IDT compresses the per-step action sequence into a high-level chain of high-level decisions (one z per c steps), drastically shortening the context (smaller than one episode length). No relevance filtering or distractor removal.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tools/skills/documents).
- **index content separation**: N/A (no separate lightweight index vs heavy content; the context IS the content).
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index/integration protocol).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tools).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt/context augmentation as conditioning for autoregressive generation: the across-episodic high-level chain of experience conditions the Making Decisions module to predict the next high-level decision z; z is then a latent conditional input to the Decisions to Go module that autoregressively generates the next c low-level actions. Effectively latent-token (high-level decision) injection plus in-context experience conditioning.
- **planning integration**:
> Hierarchical, plan-then-act with interleaving: a high-level decision (sub-goal) is generated first (Making Decisions), then it guides multi-step low-level action generation (Decisions to Go), and executed actions are encoded back into high-level decisions (Reviewing Decisions) to update the across-episodic context for the next cycle. Retrieval (the across-episodic context) is woven in at the high-level subtask boundary every c steps.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-high-level-decision (every c steps): the implicit search over experience occurs at each high-level decision boundary (one high-level decision per c-step segment), not per low-level action; this is the source of the efficiency gain.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> N/A as classic CBR adaptation. Closest analogue: latent / execution-conditioned generation. Retrieved experience is reused by conditioning autoregressive generation; the Reviewing Decisions module re-encodes executed (or externally provided demonstration) actions into high-level decisions to adapt them into the agent's high-level abstraction.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Latent / soft tokens at the high level: high-level decisions are continuous vectors z sampled from a multivariate Gaussian (with reparameterization), injected as conditioning tokens; the underlying raw experience is (return, observation, decision, reward, completion) token embeddings.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Distilled/abstract: high-level decisions (latent sub-goals) abstracting c-step low-level action segments, rather than raw per-step trajectories (as in baselines AT/AD).
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Implicit robustness via return-ordered chain-of-hindsight conditioning and learning from sub-optimal data: prior (lower-return) trajectories act as negative-rated examples to predict higher-return ones; end-to-end supervised training over sub-optimal offline data. No dedicated relevance evaluator / distractor-aware module.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: episodic (across-episodic rolling context of recent trajectories) with a latent hierarchical abstraction (high-level decisions). In-context memory, not an external persistent store.
- **write back**: True (in-context only): executed actions are reviewed/encoded into high-level decisions and appended to the across-episodic context for the next trial-and-error cycle. This is in-context state growth, not persistent gradient/parameter or external-DB write-back.
- **online growth**: Yes within the rolling context window: the context grows as new episodes are rolled out during test time (capped at the most recent n=4 episodes). The model parameters are frozen at test time (no gradient updates); only the in-context experience grows/rotates.
- **write back trigger**: Per-segment/per-episode (fixed schedule): after each c-step segment the executed actions are encoded into a high-level decision (Reviewing Decisions), and completed episodes are added to the across-episodic context. Not gated by success/failure or self-critique.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success+failure mixed via return ordering: lower-return (effectively 'failed' or sub-optimal) trajectories are kept in the context as negative-rated examples (ascending-return chain of experience) to drive the model toward higher-return predictions. No explicit failure-only corrective rules.
- **memory evolution update**: Append-and-rotate within a fixed-size window (most recent n=4 episodes, return-sorted); high-level decisions are re-encoded each cycle. No dedup-merge, delta-update, or learned forgetting/pruning of stored entries.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No. Selection of context (most-recent-n, return-sorted) is fixed; it is not an RL/learned retrieval policy. The high-level decision policy is learned end-to-end by supervised sequence prediction (not a soft Q-learning / M-MDP retrieval policy).
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent private in-context memory; no cross-agent or cross-framework experience sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: Grid World (Darkroom, Darkroom Hard, Darkroom Dynamic, Dark Key-to-Door, and their Large 40x40 variants with 10x episode length); D4RL MuJoCo locomotion (HalfCheetah, Hopper, Walker) with Medium, Medium-Replay, and Medium-Expert datasets.
- **benchmark family**: decision-RL (D4RL MuJoCo) and embodied/navigation-style grid (Grid World / Darkroom family). Long-horizon decision-making benchmarks (episode lengths 20-1000 steps).
- **baselines**: In-context RL: Agentic Transformer (AT, Hao Liu 2023), Algorithm Distillation (AD, Laskin et al. 2023). TD learning: TD3+BC, TD3. Imitation learning: Behavior Cloning (BC-10%), Decision Transformer (DT). Baseline numbers for D4RL taken from the AT paper and the D4RL paper.
- **key metrics**: D4RL normalized score (100 = expert); Grid World episodic return / self-improvement curve over 50 episodes; training time per 10k gradient updates; test/evaluation time (minutes) for 10 D4RL episodes / 50 Grid World episodes; speedup factor (x) over baselines.
- **headline result**:
> Online evaluation time 36x faster than baselines on D4RL and 27x faster on (Large) Grid World, while achieving state-of-the-art / competitive task performance. D4RL Total Average normalized score 87.90 +/- 1.06 for IDT (Ours) vs AT 85.21, BC-10% 80.65, TD3+BC 84.83, AD 82.84, DT 77.49, TD3 70.28.
- **ablations**:
> Computing-cost breakdown (Table 3): on HalfCheetah (context 4000), AT testing 234.20 min (37x) and AD 173.11 min (28x) vs IDT 6.29 min; on Large Dark Key-to-Door (context 2000), AT 167.07 min (27x) vs IDT 6.18 min. Parameter sensitivity on high-level decision frequency c (c=1,5,10,15,20): stable in dense-reward D4RL, larger c better in sparse-reward Grid World. Context-size analysis: across-episodic context of ~4 episodes needed for self-improvement to emerge. Case study (Fig. 5): Reviewing Decisions module lets IDT exploit external demonstration prompts (epsilon-greedy data from random to optimal) to accelerate in-context self-improvement.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No. There are no intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k/nDCG) since retrieval is implicit self-attention over in-context experience; only end-to-end task return/score and compute/time metrics are reported.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome (final normalized score / episodic return) plus efficiency/process-cost metrics (training and testing time, speedup, context length). Self-improvement curves over episodes capture process-level improvement trajectory; no reasoning-faithfulness or step-wise retrieval-accuracy metrics.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Central contribution: IDT cuts test-time evaluation cost ~36x (D4RL) and ~27x (Large Grid World) by shortening across-episodic context to high-level decisions (context smaller than one episode). E.g., HalfCheetah test time 6.29 min (IDT) vs 234.20 min (AT); training ~21.9 h (IDT) vs ~36.2 h (AT). Lower memory requirement than AT (AT could not be trained in D4RL on the authors' hardware). Self-attention complexity is quadratic in sequence length, so context shortening yields the speedup.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed window: n=4 across-episodic trajectories (10 trajectories for some short Grid World tasks). Task horizons T range 20-1000 steps; maximum context reaches ~20000 tokens for baselines, but IDT keeps context smaller than one episode by using one high-level decision per c steps (c=10 for D4RL/Large Grid World, c=5 for standard Grid World). Selection is fixed-k (most-recent-n, return-sorted), not adaptive.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (uses existing benchmarks). Grid World data: 60 randomly-created tasks per environment, ~1M timesteps each, collected from DQN learning histories; D4RL Medium/Medium-Replay/Medium-Expert ~1-2M timesteps from medium/expert/replay policies.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Decision Transformer (Chen et al. 2021); Agentic Transformer / chain of experience (Hao Liu 2023); Algorithm Distillation (Laskin et al. 2023); Decision-Pretrained Transformer (Lee et al. 2023b); Chain of Hindsight (Liu et al. 2023); hierarchical RL with continuous sub-goals (Nachum et al. 2018, HIRO); Multi-Game Decision Transformer / Grid World (Lee et al. 2022).
- **contrasts with**:
> Agentic Transformer (AT) and Algorithm Distillation (AD): IDT contrasts by operating trial-and-error on high-level decisions instead of the smallest per-step actions, avoiding excessively long across-episodic sequences. Also contrasts with single-episode-context Decision Transformer (no self-improvement) and offline TD methods (TD3+BC) that require gradient updates / are not in-context.
- **lineage**:
> Group F (decision_memory_rl): in-context / across-episodic RL with self-improvement via in-context (episodic) memory. Sits in the Algorithm-Distillation / Agentic-Transformer lineage of treating RL as across-episodic sequence prediction, extending it with a hierarchical (high-level-decision) chain of experience for efficiency on long-horizon tasks.

### 134. RAEA (Retrieval-Augmented Embodied Agents)

2024  ·  CVPR 2024  ·  [paper](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2024/papers/Zhu_Retrieval-Augmented_Embodied_Agents_CVPR_2024_paper.pdf)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: CVPR 2024 (IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition), pp. 17985-17995, DOI 10.1109/CVPR52733.2024.01703. Preprint: arXiv:2404.11699 (v1, 17 Apr 2024). Subject: cs.RO.
- **authors affiliation**: Yichen Zhu, Zhicai Ou, Xiaofeng Mou, Jian Tang (corresponding). Affiliation: Midea Group, AI Lab. Contact: {zhuyc25, zhicai.ou, mouxf, jiantang22}@midea.com.
- **paper url**: https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2024/papers/Zhu_Retrieval-Augmented_Embodied_Agents_CVPR_2024_paper.pdf (arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.11699)
- **maintained repo url**: N/A - not a survey/benchmark; no maintained leaderboard or paper list. RAEA is listed (as an entry) in third-party trackers such as github.com/HCPLab-SYSU/Embodied_AI_Paper_List, but the authors maintain no repo.

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Embodied / robotic manipulation (decision-making via behavior cloning). RAEA is a vision-(language/audio)-action policy that maps multi-modal observations + instructions to continuous low-level robot actions for manipulation tasks (pick-and-place, contact-rich tasks). Not QA/tool-use/web; it is embodied manipulation policy learning.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline, supervised, single-agent imitation learning (behavior cloning) for robotic manipulation in low-data / few-shot regimes (10 or 25 demonstrations per task). A policy network is TRAINED to predict continuous actions; an external policy memory bank (Open X-Embodiment, large-scale cross-embodiment robot trajectories) is queried at both TRAINING and TEST time to supply analogous policies as contextual examples. The memory bank is a fixed, pre-collected external corpus (the authors explicitly ensure it contains NO data from the train/test datasets to avoid leakage). 'Shared memory' means cross-embodiment knowledge shared into the agent, not multi-agent cooperation. Supervision: human-collected demonstration trajectories with action/proprioception labels; optimized with behavior-cloning MSE loss. Evaluated in 3 simulators (Franka Kitchen, Meta-World, ManiSkill-2) and a real Franka robot (40 tasks, 70 objects, 30 trajectories + 5 instructions each).
- **what is retrieved**:
> Policies (multi-modal robot experience tuples). Each retrieved policy m = {instruction i, observation o, action a, proprioceptive state p} drawn from the external policy memory bank; i.e. demonstration trajectory fragments / video segments with their actions and robot states, used as analogous in-context examples for the current task.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus. The policy memory bank is a fixed, pre-collected large-scale robotic dataset (Open X-Embodiment) of cross-embodiment trajectories. It is NOT a growing/episodic memory the agent writes to during deployment; there is no write-back. The agent only reads from this static store at train and test time.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve: yes, Reuse: yes, Revise: no, Retain: no]. Retrieve: dense multi-modal retrieval of analogous policies from the bank. Reuse: retrieved policies are fed as contextual examples into the policy generator via cross-attention to inform action prediction. Revise: no per-case adaptation/revision step. Retain: no write-back of new experiences to the (static) memory bank.
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False - the paper does NOT frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner. It is framed as retrieval-augmented generation / retrieval-augmented models (RAG, DPR, MuRAG, Re-Imagen, RA-CLIP, REACT) extended to robotics, and likened to in-context learning. It nonetheless realizes Retrieve+Reuse mechanisms (analogous past experiences used to solve new tasks) under the RAG framing.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Full multi-modal policy tuple m = {instruction, observation, action, proprioception} - effectively a demonstration / (sub-)trajectory fragment (the authors note the action bank comprises fragments of videos). So the unit is a single demonstration / trajectory-fragment carrying its action and proprioceptive-state labels, not a token, document, tool-API, or KG-subgraph.
- **index source**:
> Static external corpus, offline-collected. The retrievable store is the recently open-sourced Open X-Embodiment (Padalkar et al. 2023), a large-scale cross-embodiment robotic dataset compiled offline from many labs. It is fixed (not induced online, not grown at test time). The authors curate it to exclude the train/test datasets to prevent leakage.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat dense vector index. All modalities are mapped by a shared mixed-modal encoder (ImageBind) into a unified latent embedding space; retrieval is Maximum Inner Product Search over this flat vector space. No graph/hierarchical/cluster topology; entries are split into instruction vs observation segments but the index itself is a flat embedding store.
- **retriever type**:
> Dense bi-encoder retriever (off-the-shelf encoders). Follows DPR-style bi-encoder r(q,m)=E_Q(q)^T E_M(m); E_Q encodes the query, E_M encodes memory policies; both are mixed-modal encoders built on ImageBind (one embedding space binding six modalities). Per-modality features are projected to a common feature plane, averaged, and L2-normalized; similarity via inner product (MIPS). Not BM25, not generative-tool-as-token, not LLM-as-retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None (off-the-shelf / frozen). The retriever uses pre-trained, off-the-shelf multi-modal encoders (ImageBind; CLIP/T5 mentioned as alternatives) without contrastive fine-tuning on similarity labels, LM-feedback, preference, or RL. Retrieval relevance is computed directly from the frozen embedding inner products; no retriever training signal is described. (The downstream policy generator is trained with behavior-cloning MSE loss, but the retriever itself is not trained.)
- **query construction**:
> Raw multi-modal input is used as the query q (the instruction-observation pair x), split into an instruction segment (text/audio) and an observation segment (image/video/point cloud), each encoded and fused. A diversity-promoting query perturbation is applied: random token dropout of ~70% of query tokens during retrieval as a regularization mechanism. No semantic query rewriting/decomposition or synthetic-query expansion.
- **query granularity**:
> Mixed: task-level at frame onset, then step/observation-level within a frame. Typically an instruction-observation pair is used at the onset of a frame, then retrieval relies solely on the observation for the remainder of the frame until the next user interaction - i.e. a one-shot instruction+observation query followed by repeated observation-conditioned queries during execution.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Iterative on a fixed schedule tied to perception, not learned/active. An instruction-observation query is issued at the onset of each frame; thereafter observation-only retrieval continues per frame until the next user interaction. Retrieval supports real-time correction. Not uncertainty-triggered, not a learned router.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed schedule keyed to input frames / user interactions. Retrieval is triggered (a) by a new instruction-observation pair at the start of a frame and (b) by ongoing observations within the frame; the schedule is determined by the perception stream and user-interaction boundaries, not by token-level confidence, attention/uncertainty, a learned complexity classifier, or reflection tokens.
- **reranking**:
> No dedicated rerank stage. After MIPS produces the ranked candidate list, candidates are ordered by relevance score and a redundancy/diversity filter is applied (skip a candidate whose relevance score is too closely aligned, e.g. >0.9, with the query or with already-retrieved policies). This is a similarity-threshold de-duplication / diversity gate rather than a cross-encoder/RRF/instruction-tuned reranker.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Diversity filtering / de-duplication: drop near-duplicate candidates (relevance score >0.9 with query or prior picks) to avoid redundant policies that hurt the generator; plus query-side random token dropout (~70%) as regularization. Within the generator, retrieved-policy tokens are down-sampled/aggregated by an MLP (SC) before cross-attention. No reason-in-documents distillation, decompose-recompose, or compression of content beyond this.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A - RAEA retrieves robot policies/demonstrations, not tool/API documents; no tool descriptions are indexed or engineered.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A - not a tool-retrieval system; the policy memory bank is a static dataset with no live tool index, RapidAPI/REST/MCP/function-calling protocol, or CRUD sync.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A - no inter-tool dependency modeling; RAEA does not retrieve tools/APIs.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Training-signal-side prompt augmentation via cross-attention (latent context injection into a trained policy). The policy generator first encodes each retrieved policy's observation, instruction, action, and proprioception into tokens (reusing retriever features; action/proprioception via MLP encoders, with a max of 9 entries each, state/policy delimiter tokens, absolute position embeddings), concatenates them by relevance score, and integrates them into the main policy network through a cross-attention module where retrieved-policy features form the query/key and the current input forms the value. The fused representation drives continuous action prediction, trained end-to-end by behavior cloning (MSE). Retrieved policies thus act as contextual examples (in-context-learning-like) baked into a trained model rather than text prepended to an LLM prompt.
- **planning integration**:
> No explicit planner/search. RAEA is a reactive retrieval-augmented policy: retrieve-then-act at each frame. Retrieved analogous policies are injected as one-shot-at-frame-onset contextual exemplars (then observation-conditioned) and fused via cross-attention to produce the next continuous action. There is no multi-step plan, MCTS/tree search, hierarchical subtask decomposition, or plan-then-retrieve loop; it is per-frame retrieve-then-predict-action.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Per-action / per-frame (per-step within a rollout). Retrieval and action prediction are interleaved at the granularity of perception frames within a rollout (instruction+observation at frame onset, observation-only thereafter), not per-CoT-step, per-token, or per-tool-call (there is no chain-of-thought; it is a continuous-control policy).
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> No CBR-style case revision. Retrieved policies are used essentially as verbatim contextual exemplars whose features are integrated through cross-attention into a trained policy network (a learned latent fusion), rather than being explicitly adapted/edited per case, revised by execution feedback, or critic-guided. Closest to verbatim ICL exemplar + learned latent integration.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Surface form injected = raw multi-modal demonstration tuple (instruction, observation, action, proprioception) tokenized into latent tokens (observation/instruction features reused from ImageBind retriever; action & proprioception via MLP encoders) and fused via cross-attention. So it is raw-trajectory-fragment content converted into latent/soft tokens, not a distilled strategy, free-text workflow, or executable program.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Raw demonstration / trajectory-fragment (low abstraction). Retrieved units are concrete past robot experiences (single analogous demonstrations / video fragments with their actions and states), not distilled strategies, state-aware guidelines, reusable workflows, or procedural skills.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Diversity/redundancy control plus query regularization rather than a relevance evaluator. (1) Skip near-duplicate candidates (relevance >0.9) so redundant/low-information policies do not dominate; (2) random token dropout (~70%) of the query during retrieval as a regularization mechanism that empirically improves the generator; (3) including cross-embodiment (different-robot) data is found to still aid learning. No retriever-aware SFT, self-reflection relevance check, or reason-in-documents distillation.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> External static knowledge store (cross-embodiment demonstration corpus) used as shared memory; effectively episodic-demonstration memory but READ-ONLY (not skill-library/workflow/graph/latent, and not agent-written). In the survey's taxonomy: a static external policy/experience corpus rather than a growing episodic memory.
- **write back**: False (boolean: no). RAEA only reads from the fixed external policy memory bank (Open X-Embodiment); it does not store new experiences/cases/skills back into memory during training or deployment.
- **online growth**: False. The retrievable store is frozen (offline-collected Open X-Embodiment, curated to exclude train/test data). It does not grow during deployment/test-time.
- **write back trigger**: Never - no write event occurs; the memory bank is static and read-only.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Not used / not applicable. The static corpus consists of (largely successful) demonstration trajectories; the method does not explicitly store or contrast FAILED/negative experiences, nor mine corrective rules from failures. Retrieval is success-demonstration-only by virtue of the demonstration dataset.
- **memory evolution update**: None (append-only is not even applicable) - stored entries are never mutated, merged, pruned, or refined; the external bank is fixed throughout.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No. Case selection is a fixed off-the-shelf dense-similarity top-k (MIPS over frozen ImageBind embeddings) plus a heuristic diversity filter and query token-dropout. It is NOT an RL/soft-Q/M-MDP-learned retrieval policy; the retriever is not trained.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Yes, cross-EMBODIMENT shared memory (not multi-agent cooperation). RAEA's central idea is 'shared memory' that lets a robot tap collective experiences from MANY different robot embodiments (Open X-Embodiment). An ablation (Table 4) shows multi-embodiment data (success rate 54) beats Franka-only data (48). This is sharing of experience across heterogeneous robot platforms feeding a single agent, not memory shared among multiple concurrently-running agents.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> Simulation: Franka Kitchen (Gupta et al.), Meta-World (Yu et al. 2020), ManiSkill-2 (Gu et al. 2023, six rigid- and soft-body tasks: PickCube, StackCube, PickSingleYCB, Fill, Hang, Excavate). Real robot: a self-collected Franka dataset of 40 tasks, 70 objects, 30 human trajectories/task, 5 instructions/task. Policy memory bank: Open X-Embodiment (cross-embodiment).
- **benchmark family**: Embodied / robotic manipulation (Franka Kitchen / Meta-World / ManiSkill-2 + real Franka). Outside the survey's named embodied set (ALFWorld/ScienceWorld/VirtualHome/Minecraft); it is the real-robot-manipulation branch of the embodied family.
- **baselines**:
> Franka Kitchen & Meta-World: R3M (Nair et al. 2022, universal visual representation), BLIP-2 (Li et al. 2023, vision-language model), EmbodiedGPT (Mu et al. 2023, embodied VLM), under 10- and 25-demonstration few-shot settings. ManiSkill-2: ResNet152 (He et al. 2016) and Swin-Base (Liu et al. 2021) (both ImageNet-pretrained), with PointNet (Qi et al. 2017) fusion for the point-cloud + image setting.
- **key metrics**: Mean success rate (%) of the behavior-cloning policy. Simulation: 30 rollouts; 100 randomized trials across 5 tasks per benchmark, 5 runs x 2 camera views, averaged. Real robot: mean success rate over 10 trials per task.
- **headline result**:
> RAEA consistently outperforms baselines, most strongly in low-data (10-demo) regimes. On ManiSkill-2 (image+point-cloud setting, Table 1) RAEA achieves PickCube 62.7, StackCube 91.0, PickSingleYCB 43.8, Fill 71.7, Hang 88.1, Excavate 24.0 - beating ResNet152+PointNet (56.6/90.7/28.4/46.9/85.7/18.4) and Swin-Base+PointNet (44.0/90.1/30.6/45.5/86.4/17.0) across all tasks; in the image-only setting RAEA (56.7/93.6/40.2/63.8/87.1/22.4) likewise tops ResNet152 and Swin-Base. On the real Franka robot, full RAEA reaches 54% success (text+image), rising to 69% with image+video+text instruction. On Franka Kitchen and Meta-World RAEA surpasses R3M, BLIP-2, and EmbodiedGPT (Figs 5-6) especially at 10 demonstrations.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Modality combination, real robot (Table 2): success rises with more modalities - Text/Image 54; Text+Audio/Image 56; Text+Audio/Image+PointCloud 65; Image/Image 58; Image+Video/Image 63; Image+Video/Image+Video 64; Image+Video+Text/Image 69 (language+visual instruction lifts 63->69; adding point cloud lifts 56->65). (2) Status information in retrieved policy (Table 3, text-image): All 54; w/o Proprioception 39; w/o Action & Proprioception 36 - action+proprioception are critical (54->36). (3) Memory-bank embodiment diversity (Table 4): All embodiments 54 vs Franka-only 48 - cross-embodiment data helps. (4) Design choices in retrieval strategy: diversity filtering (skip relevance >0.9) and ~70% random query token dropout both improve generator performance (described qualitatively).
- **evaluation decoupling**: No. Only end-to-end task success rate is reported; no intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG / completeness) are reported separately. Retrieval quality is assessed indirectly through ablations (modality, status, embodiment diversity) on downstream success rate.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Outcome only (final manipulation success rate). No intermediate process metrics (reasoning faithfulness, step-wise retrieval accuracy, trajectory quality) are reported.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A - RAEA is a method paper, not a survey/taxonomy.
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Real-robot dataset is self-constructed: 40 tasks (from simple pick-and-place to contact-rich tasks like 'open the drawer and put the pen inside' and 'sort the cube with the same color'), 70 objects, 30 human-collected trajectories per task, 5 distinct instruction annotations per task, on a Franka setup. Outcomes are success/failure of manipulation (physically verifiable). Difficulty signaled by best-system (RAEA) real-robot success of 54% (text-image) up to 69% (multi-modal). Simulation uses existing benchmarks (Franka Kitchen, Meta-World, ManiSkill-2).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Retrieval-augmented generation / dense retrieval lineage: DPR (Karpukhin et al. 2020, bi-encoder), MuRAG (Chen et al. 2022), Re-Imagen (Chen et al. 2022), RA-CLIP (Xie et al. 2023), REACT (Liu et al. 2023, retrieval-augmented customized vision models), retrieval-augmented multimodal LM (Yasunaga et al. 2023). Encoders: ImageBind (Girdhar et al. 2023). Robotics data/policy backbone: Open X-Embodiment / RT-X (Padalkar et al. 2023), R3M (Nair et al. 2022). Evaluation environments: Franka Kitchen, Meta-World (Yu et al. 2020), ManiSkill-2 (Gu et al. 2023). Trained via behavior cloning.
- **contrasts with**:
> Prior retrieval-augmented models confined to language/vision/multimodal generation (Re-Imagen, MuRAG, RA-CLIP, REACT) - RAEA instead retrieves robot POLICIES (executed analogous scenarios) for robotic action prediction. Also contrasts with foundation-model embodied agents that store knowledge implicitly in parameters and need extensive training data (R3M, BLIP-2, EmbodiedGPT, RT-1/RT-2-style models) - RAEA augments policy learning with an explicit external cross-embodiment memory, improving low-data generalization without scaling parameters/data.
- **lineage**:
> Group F (decision/memory/RL) - retrieval-augmented embodied decision-making. Lineage: text RAG / dense retrieval (DPR) -> multimodal RAG (MuRAG, Re-Imagen, RA-CLIP, REACT) -> RAEA, which transfers retrieval augmentation to robotic policy learning by retrieving cross-embodiment demonstration policies from a static external bank (Open X-Embodiment) and fusing them via cross-attention into a behavior-cloned manipulation policy. Distinct from experience/case agents (Optimus-1, ExpeL, JARVIS-1) in that its memory is a fixed read-only external corpus with no write-back or online growth.

<a id="item-rahl"></a>
### 135. RAHL (Retrieval-Augmented Hierarchical in-Context Reinforcement Learning) with Hindsight Modular Reflection (HMR)

2024  ·  arXiv 2408.06520  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.06520)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: arXiv:2408.06520 (cs.RO); published at IEEE ICRA 2025 (2025 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation), pp. 1217-1224, DOI 10.1109/ICRA55743.2025.11128105
- **authors affiliation**:
> Chuanneng Sun, Songjun Huang, Haiqiao Liu, Jie Gong, Dario Pompili. Rutgers University-New Brunswick (Dept. of Electrical and Computer Engineering; Dept. of Civil and Environmental Engineering), NJ, USA. (arXiv v1/v2 list Chuanneng Sun, Songjun Huang, Dario Pompili; the ICRA/Semantic Scholar record adds Haiqiao Liu and Jie Gong.)
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.06520

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Embodied / decision-making / task planning with LLMs; also tool-use-style web navigation and multi-hop QA. Evaluated on ALFWorld (embodied household), Webshop (web shopping), HotpotQA (multi-hop QA), plus a Boston Dynamics SPOT robot navigation demo.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, multi-episode in-context reinforcement learning with a frozen LLM as policy (no gradient updates to the LLM). The agent operates over a retrieval-augmented goal-conditioned MDP: an LLM-based high-level policy decomposes a complex task into sub-goals on-the-fly, and a low-level policy generates actions to achieve each goal; a finisher module decides goal completion. Single-agent (though the high-/low-level policies and a finisher are distinct LLM roles). Supervision is via environment success signals across repeated episodes; learning is verbal (reflections) rather than parameter updates. Few-shot full-trajectory exemplars are provided per environment.
- **what is retrieved**:
> Summarized verbal reflections (experiences) from previous sub-tasks/episodes: high-level reflections (over the sequence of proposed goals) and low-level reflections (over action sub-trajectories for each goal). Stored as key-value pairs (key = task/sub-task description, value = reflection).
- **retrieval grounding**: GROWING / episodic memory the agent writes (long-term memory of past-episode reflections), populated online at test time. Few-shot exemplars are a separate static prompt component, but the retrieval store itself is the growing reflection memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**: Fixed top-k ranking: a fixed top-2 nearest-neighbor retrieval by embedding distance for both high- and low-level memories. No completeness/minimal-set objective and no adaptive/precision-driven variable-size selection.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> Retrieve (yes, embedding top-2), Reuse (yes, reflections injected into prompt), Revise (partial: HMR revises/refines experiences into reflections at write time, not by adapting a retrieved case during solving), Retain (yes, reflections stored to long-term memory). Flags: [Retrieve, Reuse, Revise(partial), Retain].
- **explicit cbr grounding**: false. The work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it frames itself via HRL + RAG + verbal reflection (Reflexion/ExpeL lineage), realizing CBR-like retrieve/reuse/retain mechanics under different terminology.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: Distilled reflection text (one or two sentences summarizing a failed/past trial), keyed by task or sub-task (goal) description. Two granularities: high-level reflection (about the goal sequence) and low-level reflection (about a goal's action sub-trajectory).
- **index source**: Growing memory, online/test-time-induced: long-term memory accumulates reflections generated after each episode during multi-episode deployment; it starts empty and grows. (Few-shot exemplars are static and human-provided, but are not the retrieved store.)
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat vector index keyed by metadata/context: long-term memory split into two stores (high-level and low-level), each holding key-value pairs (key = task/sub-task description embedding, value = reflection text). No graph or hierarchical-category index beyond the two-level (high/low) separation.
- **retriever learning signal**: None (off-the-shelf): retrieval is fixed similarity top-2 over embedding distance; the retriever is not trained or optimized by any task/LM/RL signal.
- **query construction**: Raw task or sub-task (goal) description used as the query; its embedding is computed and matched against stored keys. High-level memory queried with the task description; low-level memory queried with the sub-task/goal description.
- **query granularity**: Both (two-level retrieval): task-level query against high-level memory and sub-task/step-level (goal) query against low-level memory.
- **when to retrieve**: Iterative / per-sub-task: reflections are retrieved and injected into the prompt as new queries arrive to the high- or low-level memory during decision-making (i.e., when a new goal/sub-task is encountered), not only once at t=0.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule tied to the hierarchical control flow: a retrieval is triggered when a new query reaches high- or low-level memory (e.g., when proposing a new goal or working on a sub-task). Not confidence/attention/learned-classifier driven.
- **reranking**: None: no reranking stage; top-2 nearest neighbors by embedding distance are used directly.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> None at retrieval time (the retrieved reflections are already distilled summaries). The key refinement is upstream at write time: HMR distills failed trials into one or two short reflection sentences per module rather than storing raw trajectories. No post-retrieval rerank/compress/filter step.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tool/skill index; retrieved items are verbal reflections, not tool descriptions).
- **index content separation**: N/A (no lightweight-index-then-content / progressive-disclosure design; reflections are short and stored/retrieved directly as key-value pairs).
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no external tool index or integration protocol such as RapidAPI/MCP/function-calling; environments are interacted with via their native text action spaces).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**: Prompt augmentation: retrieved high- and low-level reflections are concatenated with the current state/trajectory (and few-shot examples) as input context to the frozen LLM policy. This is in-context RL (verbal feedback as a substitute for policy-gradient updates).
- **planning integration**:
> Hierarchical subtask-level, online/plan-as-you-go: the high-level LLM policy proposes sub-goals step-by-step (on-the-fly, conditioned on task + current-episode history) rather than planning all sub-tasks upfront; the low-level policy acts to satisfy each goal; a finisher decides when a goal is reached and triggers the next goal. Retrieval is interleaved at both the goal-proposal (high) and action (low) levels.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-sub-task / per-goal (modular). Reflection and retrieval operate at the sub-trajectory (goal) level for the low-level policy and at the goal-sequence level for the high-level policy; within a goal, the agent uses ReAct-style [Think]/[Action] steps. Not per-token.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> Verbal in-context reuse: retrieved reflections are injected verbatim into the prompt to steer the frozen LLM's next-episode behavior. Adaptation of experience happens at write time via hindsight modular reflection (summarizing failures into corrective guidance) rather than per-query case rewriting; no execution-feedback case-rewriting or RL fine-tuning of reuse.
- **retrieved item representation**: Distilled strategy/guideline as free-text reflection (one or two natural-language sentences summarizing a past failed trial), injected verbatim into the prompt. Not raw trajectories, not programs, not latent tokens.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Distilled strategy/insight (verbal reflection) at two abstraction levels: high-level (about goal selection/sequencing) and low-level (about actions to achieve a goal). More abstract than a raw trajectory but tied to a specific task/sub-task key.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Modular reflection (HMR) itself is the main mechanism: reflecting on shorter sub-trajectories filters irrelevant information so the agent more accurately localizes errors, reducing noise from long trajectories. Tag-guided prompting injects structured prior to constrain generation. No explicit relevance evaluator, retriever-aware training, or distractor-filtering module.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: Episodic long-term memory (reflection store), split into high-level and low-level reflection memories, plus a short-term memory holding the current-episode trajectory.
- **write back**: true. After each (failed) episode, HMR summarizes the trial into short high- and low-level reflections that are written into the corresponding long-term memory as key-value pairs for use in future episodes.
- **online growth**: Yes: long-term reflection memory grows during multi-episode deployment/test-time; it is not frozen after an offline induction phase.
- **write back trigger**:
> Reflective and failure-driven: at the end of an episode, when the trial fails, the agent generates verbal reflections (summarized into one or two sentences per module) and stores them in long-term memory. Writes are essentially triggered on failure (to drive next-episode improvement) via the hindsight reflection step.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Failure-focused corrective reflections: failed trials are summarized into reflections stored in memory and retrieved to guide future trials; the framework explicitly reflects on what went wrong (no contrastive success-vs-failure pairing described; emphasis is on correcting failures).
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No: retrieval/case-selection is fixed similarity top-2, not a learned or RL-optimized retrieval policy. (RAHL is described as a deterministic decision policy with HMR acting as the analog of a policy-gradient update, but the retrieval mechanism itself is not learned.)
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No: single-agent private memory. The high-level policy, low-level policy, and finisher are roles of one agent/system; memory is not shared across multiple distinct agents or heterogeneous frameworks.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: ALFWorld (134 scenarios across six task types), Webshop, HotpotQA (Wikipedia-based multi-hop QA). Additional hardware demonstration on a Boston Dynamics SPOT robot (navigation to a person in an adjacent room) using GPT-4-turbo as image analyst and GPT-4o as decision-maker.
- **benchmark family**: embodied (ALFWorld); web (Webshop); multi-hop QA (HotpotQA). Plus a real-robot embodied navigation demo (SPOT).
- **baselines**:
> Retroformer (gradient-based, LoRA rank=4 on a separate reflection LM), ADaPT (as-needed decomposition + planning), Reflexion (full-trajectory verbal reflection over ReAct), ExpeL (experience storage/retrieval + insight rule set). Default LLM back-end GPT-3.5-turbo (with GPT-4 / GPT-4o variants studied).
- **key metrics**: Success rate (%) per environment, reported at episode 1 (Pass@1) and at 5 episodes; results averaged over ten runs with confidence intervals.
- **headline result**:
> At 5 episodes, RAHL improves success rate by 9% on ALFWorld, 42% on Webshop (new state-of-the-art), and 10% on HotpotQA over strong baselines (GPT-3.5-turbo). Table I: Webshop #Epi=5 RAHL 83% vs Retroformer 36% / ADaPT 28% / Reflexion 28% / ExpeL 41%; ALFWorld #Epi=5 RAHL 87% (Retroformer 100%); HotpotQA #Epi=5 RAHL 57%.
- **ablations**:
> Ablation variants sharing the same first episode: (1) RAHL-Retry (raw past failed full trajectories with no reflection; terminates early by exceeding LLM max sequence length); (2) RAHL-Reflexion (full-trajectory reflection instead of modular); (3) RAHL w/o Tag (LLM freely chooses next step without [Goal]/[Think]/[Action]/[Finish] tag guidance). Findings: tag guidance is helpful (w/o Tag underperforms); verbal reflection (HMR or Reflexion) beats raw-trajectory retry and is more scalable; HMR (modular sub-trajectory reflection) outperforms full-trajectory Reflexion, especially in long-trajectory / text-heavy ALFWorld and HotpotQA. LLM-backend study: GPT-4 helps ALFWorld/Webshop; GPT-3.5 with GPT-4 HMR beats GPT-3.5 and even beats GPT-4 on HotpotQA.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No: only end-to-end task success rates are reported; no intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG / completeness) are reported separately.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Primarily outcome (success rate). Process quality is addressed qualitatively/indirectly (HMR localizes errors better; tags improve interpretability; goal trajectories shown), but no quantitative step-wise retrieval/planning accuracy or trajectory-quality metric is reported.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k retrieval: top-2 reflections retrieved from each of high- and low-level memory and injected into the prompt. Few-shot exemplars: two full successful trajectories for Webshop/HotpotQA; two task-specific examples per each of six ALFWorld tasks; plus two goal-trajectory reflection examples and one full-trajectory reflection example. No adaptive-k or budget-capped selection beyond the fixed top-2 and these exemplar counts.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (primary research paper, not a survey/taxonomy).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (uses existing benchmarks: ALFWorld 134 scenarios over six task types; HotpotQA ~113K QA pairs; Webshop; not a new benchmark contribution).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Reflexion (verbal reflection / closed-loop in-context RL), ReAct (Think-then-Act reasoning traces as the low-level actor pattern), ExpeL (experience storage and embedding-based retrieval from memory), goal-conditioned Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (HRL) and Hindsight ideas (e.g., HAC 'Learning multi-level hierarchies with hindsight', option-critic), and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).
- **contrasts with**:
> Reflexion (full-trajectory reflection vs HMR modular sub-trajectory reflection), ADaPT (upfront task decomposition before execution vs RAHL's on-the-fly online goal generation, and no multi-episode policy improvement), RT-H (hierarchical but no policy improvement after first episode), Retroformer (gradient-based reflection-LM fine-tuning vs RAHL's frozen-LLM verbal in-context updates), classic HRL methods HAC and option-critic (language-integrated learning vs gradient-based hierarchies).
- **lineage**:
> Group F (decision/memory RL): goal-conditioned hierarchical in-context RL with a growing episodic reflection memory. Sits in the Reflexion/ExpeL lineage of experience-/reflection-based in-context RL agents, extending it with (a) hierarchical high-/low-level goal-conditioned policy structure and (b) modular hindsight reflection retrieved as cross-episode augmentation.

<a id="item-regent"></a>
### 136. REGENT (Retrieval-Augmented Generalist Agent)

2024  ·  ICLR 2025  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.04759)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: ICLR 2025 (Oral); preprint arXiv:2412.04759 (Dec 2024). Also presented at NeurIPS 2024 Workshops on Adaptive Foundation Models (AFM) and Open World Agents (OWA).
- **authors affiliation**: Kaustubh Sridhar, Souradeep Dutta, Dinesh Jayaraman, Insup Lee. Primary affiliation: University of Pennsylvania (Souradeep Dutta also University of British Columbia).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.04759
- **code url**: https://github.com/regent-research/regent (Apache-2.0; HuggingFace models/data at https://huggingface.co/regent-research; OpenReview https://openreview.net/forum?id=NxyfSW6mLK)
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (single-paper artifact repo at https://github.com/regent-research/regent; not a continuously-updated leaderboard/paper-list)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Decision-making / sequential control: generalist agents for robotics (Metaworld, Mujoco) and game-playing (Atari, BabyAI, ProcGen) environments. Embodied/RL control rather than text QA.
- **problem setting**:
> Pre-train a single small generalist policy on offline expert demonstration datasets from K training environments (across heterogeneous observation/action modalities), then deploy directly in held-out UNSEEN environments via in-context learning with only a few expert demonstrations and NO finetuning. Each environment is an MDP; state and action spaces of unseen environments are assumed known. Setting is offline pre-training plus interactive deployment (online rollouts in the environment); single-agent; expert demonstrations available for retrieval. The agent acts step-by-step, retrieving from the few demonstrations provided in the new environment.
- **what is retrieved**: (state, previous-reward, action) tuples drawn from expert demonstration trajectories. In R&P the nearest demonstration state's action is replayed; in REGENT the n nearest tuples form the in-context demonstrations for the transformer.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> Static external corpus of expert demonstrations: a frozen set of demonstration trajectories (a designated retrieval subset of pre-training environment datasets during training; the few provided demos in the unseen environment at deployment). Not a growing/episodic agent-written memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**: Fixed top-k (top-n) similarity ranking: retrieve the n=19 nearest states (plus the single nearest for the R&P branch). No notion of recovering a complete minimal set or precision-driven variable-size retrieval; k is a fixed hyperparameter.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: [Retrieve, Reuse] (no Revise, no Retain). REGENT Retrieves nearest (state,reward,action) tuples and Reuses them (R&P replays the nearest action; the transformer adapts/interpolates). It does not Revise retrieved cases or Retain new cases into the store.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The work frames itself as retrieval-augmented generation / semi-parametric policy and in-context learning (inspired by RAG/RETRO/REALM for language models); it does not cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner or frame itself as case-based reasoning.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: (state, reward, action) tuple. The query/key is the state (image embedding or proprioceptive vector); each retrieved unit is a single transition tuple (state, previous reward, action) from a demonstration.
- **index source**:
> Offline-induced static store. The retrievable set is built from expert demonstration datasets: during pre-training a randomly chosen subset of demonstrations per environment is designated as the retrieval set; at deployment the handful of provided demonstrations in the unseen environment. The store is frozen (does not grow during deployment).
- **index structure topology**: Flat similarity index over state vectors. In the JAT/Gato setting, FAISS-style approximate similarity-search indices over L2 state embeddings; in the ProcGen setting, a naive (GPU-parallelized) nearest-image search using SSIM distance. No graph/hierarchy.
- **retriever type**:
> Dense / nearest-neighbor (non-learned). L2 nearest-neighbor over ResNet18-ImageNet image embeddings or raw proprioceptive vectors (JAT/Gato setting); SSIM-distance nearest-image search over raw images (ProcGen setting). Off-the-shelf similarity search (FAISS), not a learned retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None (off-the-shelf, fixed similarity). The retriever is a fixed nearest-neighbor search using L2 distance (JAT/Gato) or SSIM distance (ProcGen) over frozen embeddings (ResNet18 trained only on ImageNet, or raw observations). The retriever is not trained or optimized; only the downstream transformer policy is trained.
- **query construction**:
> The raw current/query state is used directly as the query. Images are embedded with a frozen off-the-shelf ResNet18 (ImageNet) into 512-d vectors (JAT/Gato); proprioceptive vectors are used unmodified; ProcGen images are used directly with SSIM. No query decomposition, expansion, or thought-conditioning.
- **query granularity**: Step/state-level: retrieval is performed at every timestep using the current query state (one retrieval per environment step during the rollout).
- **when to retrieve**: Iterative / per-step: retrieval is triggered at every timestep of the rollout (fixed schedule, once per state).
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule: retrieval occurs deterministically at every environment step for the current query state. No confidence/uncertainty/learned-router trigger.
- **reranking**: No reranking stage. Retrieved states are simply ordered by closeness (L2 or SSIM distance) to the query, with the closest placed first in the context.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> None beyond ordering. Retrieved (state,reward,action) tuples are placed in the context in order of closeness to the query (closest first); distances are normalized and clipped to [0,1]. No decomposition, distillation, distractor filtering, or compression. (Constraint applied at training time: retrieved states for a query may not come from the same demonstration as the query.)
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tools/documents; retrieved units are state-action-reward tuples).
- **index content separation**: N/A (no separate lightweight-index-then-content scheme; the index keys are the state embeddings and the loaded content is the corresponding (state,reward,action) tuple).
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index/protocol; this is a control policy, not a tool-use agent).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tools / no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt/context augmentation plus retrieve-and-play action injection. The n=19 retrieved (state,reward,action) tuples are placed in the transformer's context (in-context demonstrations) along with the query state and previous reward; the transformer's action prediction is then combined with the nearest retrieved action via a distance-weighted interpolation. Retrieval also acts as a training signal: REGENT is pre-trained on sequences of queries and retrieved neighbors.
- **planning integration**:
> Per-step interleaved retrieve-then-act (no explicit planner or tree search). At each step the agent retrieves nearest neighbors, feeds them as in-context demonstrations to the transformer, and produces a single action via interpolation between the retrieve-and-play (R&P) action and the parametric transformer output: pi_REGENT = e^{-lambda*d}*pi_R&P + (1-e^{-lambda*d})*sigma(pi_theta), where d is the (normalized, clipped) distance from the query state to the closest retrieved state.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-step (per environment action / per state): one retrieval and one interpolated action prediction per timestep of the rollout. No CoT/token-level interleaving.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> Distance-weighted interpolation between verbatim retrieve-and-play (closest retrieved action) and the parametric transformer policy, with the transformer trained to predict the residual to the R&P action. When the query state is very close to the nearest retrieved state, REGENT essentially replays the retrieved action; as distance grows, the parametric policy takes precedence. This is the key in-context adaptation mechanism (no LLM-prompted case rewriting, no RL reuse-finetuning).
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Raw transition tuples: encoded (state, previous-reward, action) tuples placed in the transformer context as in-context demonstrations (image embeddings / proprioceptive vectors / discrete-token observations, plus reward and action). No distilled strategy or free-text workflow; surface form is the raw retrieved transitions.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw demonstration transitions (low abstraction): individual (state, reward, action) tuples from expert trajectories, not distilled strategies, guidelines, skills, or workflows.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Retrieval-augmented pre-training plus distance-weighted interpolation. The transformer is trained on sequences of queries and retrieved neighbors (so it learns to use possibly-imperfect retrieved context), and the e^{-lambda*d} weighting downweights the R&P action and relies more on the parametric policy when the nearest retrieved state is far (potentially less reliable). Distances are normalized and clipped to [0,1]; sticky-action stochasticity is added at deployment to stress-test true generalization. No explicit relevance evaluator or self-reflection module.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (static demonstration store only). The retrievable set is a fixed corpus of expert demonstrations; there is no episodic/skill/workflow memory written by the agent.
- **write back**: False. The agent never writes new experiences/cases/skills back into the retrievable store; the demonstration set is fixed.
- **online growth**: No. The retrievable store does not grow during deployment; it is the fixed set of provided demonstrations in the unseen environment.
- **write back trigger**: never (no write-back mechanism exists).
- **failure experience usage**: Not applicable / success-only. The retrievable store is composed of expert demonstrations (generated by an expert policy maximizing return); failed/negative experiences are not stored or retrieved.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (store is frozen; entries are never mutated, merged, refined, or pruned after construction).
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No. Retrieval/case-selection is a fixed similarity top-k (L2 or SSIM nearest neighbors), not a learned/RL-optimized retrieval policy. Only the downstream transformer action policy is trained (the retriever and the R&P selection rule are fixed).
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent, single-policy; the demonstration store is private to the deployed agent. No cross-agent or cross-framework memory sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> JAT/Gato setting: Metaworld (45 training + 5 unseen), Mujoco (9 training + 2 unseen embodiments), Atari (52 training + 5 unseen), BabyAI (39 training). ProcGen setting (adapted from MTT): 12 training environments, 5 held-out unseen environments, plus unseen levels of training environments (e.g., bigfish, maze). Total pre-training: ~14.5M transitions (JAT/Gato) and ~12M transitions (ProcGen).
- **benchmark family**: embodied/robotics control (Metaworld, Mujoco) and decision-RL game-playing (Atari, BabyAI, ProcGen). Gato/JAT-style multi-environment generalist-agent suites; not QA/web/tool/code benchmarks.
- **baselines**:
> JAT/Gato setting: JAT/Gato (apples-to-apples, same data as REGENT); JAT/Gato (All Data, 5x Atari / 10x other data); JAT/Gato + RAG at inference (same retrieval as REGENT); fully-finetuned and PEFT (IA3) variants of both JAT/Gato models; train-from-scratch behavior cloning; DRIL (imitation learning); plus the R&P 1-nearest-neighbor baseline. ProcGen setting: MTT (Multi-Trajectory Transformer, Meta; ~3x parameters, ~10x more pre-training levels/data). Referenced large agents include Gato (1.2B params), MGDT (Multi-Game Decision Transformer, requires 1M transitions).
- **key metrics**:
> Normalized return = (total return - random return) / (expert return - random return), reported against number of demonstrations (25/50/75/100 for Metaworld/Atari; 2/4/8/12/16/20 for ProcGen) or number of demonstration states (>=10k/15k/20k/25k for Atari). Aggregate training-environment performance reported via IQM and mean normalized return. Also reports parameter count and pre-training datapoint count as efficiency metrics.
- **headline result**:
> REGENT generalizes to unseen robotics and game-playing environments via retrieval augmentation + in-context learning with NO finetuning, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art generalist agents (JAT/Gato including its All Data variant and finetuned/PEFT variants in the JAT/Gato setting; MTT in the ProcGen setting) while using up to 3x fewer parameters (REGENT 138.6M vs JAT 192.7M in JAT/Gato; 116M vs MTT 310M in ProcGen) and up to an order-of-magnitude fewer pre-training datapoints. Notably, the simple R&P 1-nearest-neighbor baseline alone (no pre-training, no neural net) already matches or beats the SOTA generalist agents.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Interpolation ablation: WITHOUT the distance-weighted interpolation between R&P and the transformer, REGENT fails to generalize (performs like a random agent) on unseen environments -- interpolation is identified as key. (2) Context size/length: larger context improves performance but saturates quickly. (3) Context order: ordering retrieved states by closeness (closest first) is important, especially when unseen environments differ markedly from pre-training (e.g., Atari). (4) Distance metric: L2 outperforms cosine distance (JAT/Gato). (5) Inference-time / runtime ablations also reported. (6) R&P vs REGENT: R&P is a strong baseline but REGENT consistently improves on it.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No. Only end-to-end task performance (normalized return) is reported; there are no separate intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG) decoupled from task success.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome-based (normalized return / aggregate IQM). Qualitative process analysis is provided (visualizing inputs/outputs at key states in atari-pong and metaworld-bin-picking showing when REGENT matches vs improves on R&P), but no quantitative step-wise retrieval/process accuracy metric.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Efficiency is a central claim: up to 3x fewer parameters (138.6M vs 192.7M JAT; 116M vs 310M MTT) and up to ~10x fewer pre-training datapoints (14.5M vs 5-10x more for JAT All Data; ProcGen uses <=1565 levels vs 10k for MTT). Adapts to new Atari games with as little as ~10k transitions and no finetuning, vs MGDT needing 1M transitions. FAISS similarity indices and GPU-parallelized SSIM speed up retrieval; inference runtimes discussed in appendix. No per-call API cost (not an LLM agent).
- **context budget and selection count**: Fixed-k context: n=19 retrieved (state,reward,action) tuples plus the query state (and previous reward), giving n+1=20 action predictions during training. Context size is a fixed hyperparameter (ablated; larger helps but saturates). Not adaptive or precision-driven.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (primary research paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (uses existing benchmark suites; not a new benchmark paper). Data is reused/subsetted from the open-source JAT dataset (100k transitions x 145 training environments = 14.5M) and PPO-generated ProcGen rollouts (20 rollouts x 12 environments to reach 1M each = 12M).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> JAT (open-source Gato reproduction, HuggingFace) -- REGENT adapts JAT's architecture and training recipe in the JAT/Gato setting and subsets the JAT dataset; Gato (DeepMind) generalist agent; MTT (Multi-Trajectory Transformer, Meta) for the ProcGen setting and in-context comparison; retrieval-augmented language modeling (RAG (Lewis et al.), RETRO, REALM) as inspiration for semi-parametric retrieval augmentation; nearest-neighbor few-shot learning; theoretical analysis adapted from Sridhar et al. (sub-optimality bound, MixedReLU activation).
- **contrasts with**:
> Large monolithic generalist agents that scale parameters/data (Gato, JAT, RoboCat, Multi-Game Decision Transformer, RT-series, Octo, OpenVLA, Mobility VLA, BAKU, RoboAgent) which struggle to generalize to unseen environments without many finetuning transitions; MTT (positioned against as the only other in-context-adaptable agent, but with ~3x params and ~10x data); in-context RL methods that only adapt to new tasks WITHIN the same environment (Algorithm Distillation, Decision-Pretrained Transformer, Prompt Decision Transformer); plain RAG-at-inference applied to a non-retrieval-pretrained policy (JAT/Gato + RAG), which REGENT outperforms.
- **lineage**:
> Group F (decision-making / memory / RL). A semi-parametric, retrieval-augmented in-context generalist agent for sequential decision-making: retrieves (state,reward,action) tuples and interpolates a retrieve-and-play 1-NN policy with a transformer, porting RAG-style retrieval augmentation from language modeling into multi-environment RL control for fast adaptation to unseen environments without finetuning.

<a id="item-a-mem"></a>
### 137. A-Mem: Agentic Memory for LLM Agents

2025  ·  NeurIPS 2025  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.12110)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**: NeurIPS 2025 (Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems). Preprint arXiv:2502.12110 (cs.CL / cs.HC), v1 submitted 17 Feb 2025, last revised 8 Oct 2025 (v11).
- **authors affiliation**:
> Wujiang Xu (lead, Rutgers University), Zujie Liang (Independent Researcher), Kai Mei (Rutgers University), Hang Gao (Rutgers University), Juntao Tan (Rutgers University), Yongfeng Zhang (corresponding; Rutgers University and AIOS Foundation). Primary affiliation: Rutgers University; contact wujiang.xu@rutgers.edu.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.12110
- **code url**: https://github.com/WujiangXu/A-mem (reproduction/evaluation code, MIT, ~899 stars) and https://github.com/WujiangXu/A-mem-sys (official memory-system library, MIT, ChromaDB-backed; mirrored at github.com/agiresearch/A-mem)
- **maintained repo url**:
> https://github.com/WujiangXu/A-mem-sys (official maintained agentic-memory library, last push 2026-03; supports OpenAI/Ollama/SGLang/OpenRouter backends, ChromaDB vector store). Reproduction repo https://github.com/WujiangXu/A-mem actively maintained (vLLM/Ollama eval pipeline added Mar 2026).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: QA over long-term agent memory: long-range conversational question answering for LLM agents (single-hop, multi-hop, temporal-reasoning, open-domain, and adversarial QA). Framed as a memory system that LLM agents use to leverage historical experiences across extended dialogues.
- **problem setting**:
> Single-agent, online/streaming memory for LLM agents in long-term text conversations. Memory is built incrementally: as new interactions (dialogue turns/sessions) arrive, the system writes structured memory notes, links them to historical notes, and evolves existing notes. At query time the agent retrieves relevant historical memory to answer questions. No gradient training of the agent or retriever (LLM-driven, in-context); supervision is the QA answer labels of the benchmarks used only for evaluation, not for training. Backbone LLMs are swapped (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B, Llama-3.2-1B/3B, plus DeepSeek-R1-32B and Claude-3 Haiku in appendix). The setting is interactive memory construction over a single conversational agent, contrasted with static-corpus RAG and with rigid/predefined memory systems (MemGPT, MemoryBank, Mem0-style graph DB).
- **what is retrieved**:
> Structured memory notes (experiences) distilled from past interactions. Each note bundles the original interaction content plus LLM-generated keywords, tags, and a contextual description, a dense embedding, a timestamp, and a set of links to related notes. Retrieval returns the top-k most relevant such notes (and, in the system design, linked notes within the same Zettelkasten 'box' are co-accessed).
- **retrieval grounding**:
> GROWING/episodic self-written memory. A-Mem maintains no static external corpus/KB/API store; the retrievable store is an agent-written memory of past conversational interactions that grows online as new memories are added, with dynamic linking and memory evolution. (The related-work section explicitly contrasts this with static-knowledge-base agentic RAG.)
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k ranking objective. Both link generation and query-time retrieval select the top-k notes by cosine similarity (default k=10, tuned per category up to 50). There is no minimal-complete-set or variable-size precision-driven objective; the hyperparameter study shows performance rising then plateauing/declining with larger k (noise vs context tradeoff).
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve: yes (embedding-similarity top-k recall of past notes), Reuse: yes (retrieved notes injected into the prompt as historical context for answering), Revise: partial-but-on-MEMORY (no per-query adaptation of a retrieved solution; instead, on each WRITE the system evolves/rewrites existing related notes' context/keywords/tags via memory evolution), Retain: yes (every new interaction is written as a structured note and linked into the network)].
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False. The paper frames itself as an agentic memory system inspired by the Zettelkasten note-taking method and positioned against agent memory systems (MemGPT, MemoryBank, ReadAgent, SCM, Mem0) and RAG; it does NOT cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner and does not use the term 'case-based reasoning'. It realizes Retrieve/Reuse/Retain-like mechanisms under a memory-organization framing.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> case/note granularity: a structured memory note (problem-context unit) = {original interaction content, timestamp, LLM-generated keywords, LLM-generated tags, LLM-generated contextual description, dense embedding, links}. Following Zettelkasten atomicity, each note is a single self-contained unit of knowledge; it is closest to a structured note / experience item, not a token snippet, full trajectory, tool-API, or executable skill.
- **index source**: Growing memory, online/test-time-induced. The store is built incrementally as interactions arrive; notes are added, linked, and evolved continuously (no offline pre-induced static index, no external corpus). In the official library this is a persistent ChromaDB vector store.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat dense vector index augmented with an emergent LLM-generated link graph. Notes are embedded for nearest-neighbor cosine retrieval (flat vector index, O(N) storage), and on top of that the system autonomously generates links between notes, forming an interconnected Zettelkasten-style knowledge network of overlapping 'boxes' (a note can belong to multiple boxes). So topology = flat vector index + dynamic memory link graph (no predefined schema/hierarchy, deliberately unlike Mem0's predefined graph-DB schema).
- **retriever type**:
> Dense (embedding-based) retriever using cosine similarity over note embeddings produced by an off-the-shelf sentence encoder (all-MiniLM-L6-v2). An LLM is additionally used to decide which retrieved candidate notes to link/evolve, but the candidate retrieval itself is dense similarity (no BM25, no learned/generative retriever).
- **retriever learning signal**:
> none (off-the-shelf). Retrieval uses a frozen pretrained text encoder (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) with cosine similarity; there is no contrastive fine-tuning, LM-feedback retriever training, downstream-task RL, or value-based learning of the retriever. The 'agentic' learning happens in note generation, linking, and evolution via LLM prompting, not in a trained retriever.
- **query construction**:
> Raw query text. At inference the current interaction/question text q is embedded with the same encoder and matched against all note embeddings (eq = fenc(q)); no query decomposition, intent extraction, or synthetic-query expansion. (At write time the 'query' is the new note's full embedding over concat(content, keywords, tags, context) used to find nearest neighbors for linking.)
- **query granularity**:
> task/interaction-level (one-shot per query). Retrieval is performed once per current interaction/question using its embedding; not per-CoT-step or per-token. (Internally a two-step pattern exists: a write-time neighbor query when adding a memory, and a read-time query when answering, but each is a single one-shot similarity search.)
- **when to retrieve**:
> one-shot per interaction. For each query the system performs a single top-k similarity retrieval to build the answering prompt; for each new memory it performs a single top-k neighbor retrieval to drive linking/evolution. No iterative, uncertainty-triggered, or learned-router re-retrieval within a single query.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> fixed schedule. Retrieval is triggered unconditionally: once per incoming question (read path) and once per newly added memory note (write/link path). There is no token-confidence, attention/uncertainty, learned complexity classifier, reflection-token, or agent-initiated mid-step trigger; the 'agentic' decision is about linking/evolution, not about when to retrieve.
- **reranking**: None. After dense top-k retrieval the notes are used directly (the LLM linking step is a connection/evolution decision, not a relevance reranker). No cross-encoder, RRF, hierarchy-aware, or instruction-tuned reranking stage is reported.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Largely none at read time: top-k retrieved notes (and their linked notes in the same box) are injected into the prompt as historical context without compression/decomposition/distractor-filtering. The semantic enrichment (keywords/tags/context generation) and structural refinement (linking, evolution) happen at WRITE time, not as post-retrieval refinement of fetched items. The k-hyperparameter study notes large k introduces noise, motivating moderate k rather than an explicit refinement stage.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (A-Mem is a conversational memory system, not a tool/skill-retrieval method; there is no tool/API index).
- **index content separation**:
> Partial. Each note stores lightweight semantic descriptors (keywords, tags, one-line contextual description) alongside the heavier original interaction content, and embeddings fuse both. However there is no explicit progressive-disclosure mechanism that retrieves a light index first and then loads heavy content on demand; whole notes are retrieved and injected.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no external tool registry or integration protocol such as MCP/RapidAPI/RESTful/function-calling). The store is an internally managed growing note network; the official library persists it in ChromaDB and exposes CRUD (add/read/update/delete) over notes.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no inter-tool dependency modeling; not a tool-retrieval method). The system does model inter-MEMORY relations via generated links, but not tool dependencies.

**Utilization Mechanism**
