- **retriever type**: Dense embedding similarity (cosine) using OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small to embed raw input queries, then top-k nearest neighbors. Off-the-shelf; no trained retriever. (DC-Cu has no retriever.)
- **retriever learning signal**: None (off-the-shelf). The embedding model and cosine top-k are fixed; the retriever is not trained or fine-tuned on similarity labels, LM feedback, task effectiveness, or RL.
- **query construction**:
> Raw input query (the raw question text) is embedded directly as the query/key. No decomposition, sub-query generation, intent extraction, or thought-conditioning. For the Generator, the prompt is augmented with the current memory M_i (and, in DC-RS, the curator has already folded retrieved cases into M_i).
- **query granularity**: Task-level / one-shot per query. One retrieval (and one curation) is performed per incoming query x_i; there is no per-reasoning-step or trajectory-level sub-querying within a single problem.
- **when to retrieve**: One-shot per query (DC-RS / DR): a single top-k retrieval is performed once when each new query arrives, before generation. DC-Cu performs no retrieval. Not iterative/active/uncertainty-triggered within a query.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule: retrieval (when used, in DC-RS/DR) fires deterministically once per incoming query. No confidence/uncertainty/attention signal, learned router, or agent-initiated trigger decides whether to retrieve.
- **reranking**: None. Retrieved items are the raw top-k=3 by cosine similarity with no reranking stage (no cross-encoder, RRF, or hierarchy-aware reranking).
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> In DC-RS: the LLM Curator synthesizes/distills retrieved past (input, output) pairs together with the prior memory into a refined cheatsheet BEFORE generation (decompose-then-recompose / distillation). In DR baseline: none (retrieved pairs are pasted verbatim). The curation step also consolidates and prunes for clarity/compactness, acting as compression.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A. Items retrieved are past query-solution pairs, not tool/API documents; there is no tool-description engineering. (Note: stored snippets can be executable Python code the model later reuses, but these are self-generated, not indexed tool docs.)
- **index content separation**:
> No. The retrievable embedding key (query embedding) and the stored content (the past output / the cheatsheet text) are not split into a lightweight index plus on-demand heavy content; the curated memory is loaded into the prompt directly. Authors suggest a structured external database as future work.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A. No external tool index or integration protocol (no RapidAPI/REST/MCP/function-calling tool registry). The only 'tool' is a Python interpreter for executing model-written code (execute_python_code flag in the released code).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A. No inter-tool dependency modeling; the framework does not retrieve tools and has no dependency graph.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation + skill/case reuse. The current memory M_i (and, in DC-RS, the freshly synthesized cheatsheet incorporating retrieved cases) is injected into the Generator's prompt; the model reuses or adapts stored strategies/code snippets to solve the new query. No training signal and no parameter updates (black-box).
- **planning integration**:
> One-shot exemplars/strategies at solve time (plan time). For DC-Cu: generate-then-curate (solve using memory, then update memory). For DC-RS: retrieve-then-curate-then-generate (retrieve similar cases -> Curator refines memory -> Generator solves). Retrieval is woven in at the per-query level, not inside a tree search or per-reasoning-step loop. Optionally Python code execution provides a verify-by-execution step within a query (max_num_rounds, default 1).
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer / per-query. Retrieval and memory update happen once around the full solution to each query; not interleaved per-CoT-step, per-sentence/token, or per-tool-call (aside from the optional single code-execution round).
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> LLM-prompted adaptation + execution-feedback. The Curator (an LLM prompted task-agnostically) distills/revises retrieved cases and prior memory into reusable strategies; stored code snippets can be re-executed (Python interpreter) so execution feedback influences which solutions are trusted and retained. Reuse is via in-context conditioning, not RL fine-tuning.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Mixed: distilled strategies/heuristics/insights as free text, plus executable Python code snippets, plus (in DC-RS/DR) raw past (input, output) example pairs. The curated cheatsheet is a structured-ish free-text note focused on concise, transferable snippets rather than full transcripts.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Two levels: (1) distilled strategy/insight/heuristic and procedural skill (reusable Python program) in the cumulative cheatsheet; (2) raw past single demonstration (problem+solution case) in the retrieval variants. Spans from concrete code-skill to abstract guideline.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Self-curation/self-reflection by the Curator (assesses usefulness/generalizability, refines or prunes faulty entries, consolidates for compactness) without ground-truth labels; optional Python code execution to validate code-based solutions. Authors explicitly flag retrieval noise as a weakness (e.g. GPT-4o on GPQA-Diamond degraded from suboptimal retrieved cases) and note no advanced relevance filtering is used beyond cosine top-k.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: Episodic + skill-library hybrid, realized as a single non-parametric, evolving free-text memory ('cheatsheet'): stores past cases/experiences (episodic) and distilled reusable strategies + code skills (skill-library/procedural).
- **write back**: True. The Curator writes distilled strategies, code snippets, and insights back into the memory after (DC-Cu) or before (DC-RS) generation: M_{i+1} = Cur(M_i, x_i, y~_i).
- **online growth**: Yes. The memory and the retrievable pool of past (input, output) pairs grow continuously during deployment/test-time; nothing is frozen after offline induction. (Memory is also consolidated/pruned, so it grows in content but is kept compact.)
- **write back trigger**:
> Reflective, every query (after self-critique). The Curator runs once per query and decides what to add/refine/prune based on its own assessment of the solution's correctness, usefulness, and generalizability (no human validation, no ground-truth gating). It is not strictly on-success-only: it may also revise or prune entries judged faulty.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Partial / corrective. The Curator may revise or remove faulty heuristics judged incorrect or superseded, so failed/incorrect content can trigger pruning. However the framework is biased toward retaining correct/useful strategies (self-assessed without labels); it does not maintain an explicit success+failure contrastive store. Authors note faulty heuristics can slip in and be amplified.
- **memory evolution update**:
> Refine-overwrite + dedup/consolidate + forget-prune. Stored entries are mutated after writing: the Curator distills, consolidates for compactness/clarity, updates entries superseded by better strategies, and prunes incorrect ones (not append-only). FH baseline is the append-only contrast.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No. Case selection is fixed cosine top-k similarity (off-the-shelf embeddings), not a learned/RL-optimized retrieval policy. The 'learning' is in the LLM-curated memory content, not in a trained selection policy.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: AIME 2024 (30 q), AIME 2025 (30 q), AIME 2020-2024 (133 q), GPQA-Diamond (198 q), Game of 24 (100 examples from Suzgun & Kalai 2024), Math Equation Balancer (250 expressions, authors' own), MMLU-Pro Engineering (250 sampled) and MMLU-Pro Physics (250 sampled).
- **benchmark family**: QA (GPQA-Diamond, MMLU-Pro), competition-math reasoning (AIME), and heuristic-search / arithmetic puzzles (Game of 24, Math Equation Balancer). No web/embodied/tool-retrieval/code-repo/memory-dialog (LoCoMo) or decision-RL (D4RL) benchmarks.
- **baselines**:
> BL (vanilla baseline prompting, one-off inference), DC-empty (DC-0, structured problem-solving + Python tool-use instructions but memory kept empty; strong baseline), FH (Full-History Appending; all past input-output pairs verbatim, no curation), DR (Dynamic Retrieval; retrieve top-k similar past pairs pasted verbatim, no curation/synthesis), and Majority Voting (MV, 3 generations). Also zero-shot CoT was tried in preliminary experiments (no gain, not included).
- **key metrics**: Task accuracy (%): Soft Match (SM) for multiple-choice GPQA-Diamond and MMLU-Pro; Functionally Correct (FC) for Game of 24, Math Equation Balancer, and AIME. Also reports cumulative-accuracy progression curves and average output tokens (efficiency).
- **headline result**:
> GPT-4o's Game of 24 success rate rose from ~10% (baseline) to 99% under DC-RS after it discovered and reused a Python brute-force solver. Other headline gains: Claude 3.5 Sonnet AIME 2024 23.3% -> 50.0% (DC-Cu, +27 pts, more than doubled); AIME 2025 6.7% -> 36.7% (DC-Cu); GPQA-Diamond 59.6% -> 68.7% (DC-RS, +9.1); MMLU-Pro Physics 74% -> 82% (+8); Math Equation Balancer ~45-50% -> 98-100%.
- **ablations**:
> DC-empty (DC-0) isolates memory effect (Game of 24: GPT-4o 19% vs 99% DC-RS, showing memory/reuse is the driver). DR vs DC-RS isolates curation/synthesis vs raw verbatim retrieval (GPQA-Diamond Sonnet: DR 63.6% vs DC-RS 68.7%). FH vs DC isolates curation vs append-everything (AIME 2024 Sonnet: FH 26.7% vs DC-Cu 50.0%; GPT-4o FH dropped to 6.7-13.3% below baseline). MV comparison (no gain over BL). top-k sensitivity (k=3 vs 5/7 -> negligible gain). Model-scale ablation (Claude 3.5 Haiku, GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek R1/o1 show muted/inconsistent gains). Cross-model memory transfer (mixed). Example-ordering / task-similarity (curriculum) amplifies gains.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No. Only end-to-end task accuracy is reported; no intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG / retrieval completeness) are reported separately. Retrieval quality is discussed only qualitatively (e.g. suboptimal retrieved cases hurting GPQA-Diamond).
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome (final-answer accuracy). Some process-level insight is offered qualitatively (cumulative-accuracy curves over the stream, inspection of curated memory contents, token-usage trends, error/correction clustering in embedding space) but no quantitative step-wise reasoning or retrieval accuracy.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Reports average output tokens on AIME 2024 for Claude 3.5 Sonnet: BL 370, DC-0 494, DC-RS 1035, DC-Cu 1831 tokens. DC incurs per-query curation overhead and an initial discovery cost, but amortizes by avoiding re-deriving solutions (e.g. reusing a stored Python solver), reducing redundant computation over time. Sequential structure limits batch parallelism. No dollar cost or latency numbers reported.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Retrieval fixed at top-k=3 (default; k=5/7 gave negligible gain). Generation max_tokens default 2048 (released code). Memory is budget-controlled implicitly by Curator-driven consolidation/compactness rather than a hard token cap, explicitly to avoid context ballooning vs the FH (append-all) baseline.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (this is a method paper, not a survey/taxonomy).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Math Equation Balancer is authors'-constructed (250 arithmetic expressions, e.g. '1 ? 2 ? 3 = 6'); Game of 24 uses 100 examples from Suzgun & Kalai (2024); AIME subsets and GPQA-Diamond/MMLU-Pro are existing public datasets (sizes: AIME 30/30/133, GPQA-Diamond 198, MMLU-Pro 250 each subset sampled). Answers are verifiable via Functionally Correct / Soft Match metrics. The paper is method-centric, not a benchmark paper.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Retrieval-augmented generation (REALM/Guu et al. 2020; RAG-style retrieval) and in-context learning; self-reflective retrieval (Self-RAG, Asai et al. 2023); test-time/online adaptation lineage (dynamic evaluation, Krause et al. 2019; domain-adaptive pretraining, Gururangan et al. 2020); LLM reasoning/search (Tree-of-Thoughts Yao et al. 2023, Graph-of-Thoughts); STaR-style self-improvement (Zelikman et al. 2022); human retrieval-practice/cumulative-learning psychology (Karpicke & Roediger).
- **contrasts with**:
> Fine-tuning / gradient-based parameter updates; static-corpus retrieval-augmented generation (retrieving facts from a fixed external KB); naive full-history appending (FH); raw verbatim retrieval without curation (DR); and majority voting / self-consistency (passive aggregation). DC instead curates a compact, evolving, self-generated memory of strategies/code at test time, leaving black-box weights untouched.
- **lineage**:
> Group F (F_decision_memory_rl): test-time / experience-driven memory methods. Sits in the lineage of agent/LM experience-memory methods where a GROWING self-written memory of strategies/cases (rather than a static document corpus) is retrieved and reused; the DC-RS variant adds episodic case retrieval (top-k similar past (problem, solution) pairs), bridging cumulative skill-library memory and CBR-style case reuse.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing

<a id="item-evo-memory"></a>
### 142. Evo-Memory: Benchmarking LLM Agent Test-time Learning with Self-Evolving Memory

2025  ·  arXiv 2511.20857  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.20857)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **authors affiliation**:
> Tianxin Wei (lead; corresponding, twei10@illinois.edu; work done while at Google DeepMind) and Yuanchen Bei, Xuying Ning, Mengting Ai, Yunzhe Li (work done while at Google DeepMind), Jingrui He from University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (UIUC); Noveen Sachdeva, Benjamin Coleman, Zhankui He, Ed H. Chi, Chi Wang, Shuo Chen, Fernando Pereira, Wang-Cheng Kang, Derek Zhiyuan Cheng from Google DeepMind. Primary affiliations: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and Google DeepMind.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.20857
- **code url**:
> https://github.com/zhaosnw/evo_mem (MIT License; full Evo-Memory benchmark + framework with ExpRAG, ReMem, ExpRecent and baselines ReAct, A-mem, Self-RAG, Mem0, LangMem, Dynamic Cheatsheet, AWM; includes the paper PDF and dataset download scripts). The paper states code and configurations will be released for reproducibility.
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/zhaosnw/evo_mem (16 stars / 4 forks as of mid-2026; last commit Dec 2025). No separate leaderboard page found.

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> LLM-agent test-time learning across two task families: (1) single-turn reasoning and QA (multi-disciplinary MCQ MMLU-Pro, graduate science GPQA-Diamond, Olympiad math AIME-24/25, tool-use/API grounding ToolBench) and (2) multi-turn goal-oriented / embodied interactive decision-making (AlfWorld household, BabyAI navigation, ScienceWorld experimentation, PDDL symbolic planning). Spans QA, math, tool-use, planning, and embodied domains. This is a benchmark + framework paper (with two proposed methods ExpRAG and ReMem).
- **problem setting**:
> Streaming, interactive, single-agent test-time learning ('test-time evolution'). Static datasets are restructured into sequential task streams tau={(x1,y1),...,(xT,yT)}; at each step t the agent receives input x_t, retrieves from an evolving memory M_t, synthesizes a working context, produces an output y_hat_t, and updates memory M_{t+1}=U(M_t,m_t). The agent must accumulate and reuse experience across the stream WITHOUT updating model weights (memory is external; no gradient training). A correctness/feedback signal f_t is available (the ground-truth correctness of the task is used as feedback when constructing memory entries). Memory-augmented agents are formalized as a tuple (F, U, R, C): base LLM F, memory update pipeline U, retrieval module R, context construction C. Backbones are proprietary LLMs (Gemini-2.5 Flash/Flash-Lite/Pro; Claude 3.5-Haiku, 3.7-Sonnet) used inference-only via APIs. The benchmark unifies 10+ memory modules under one search-synthesize(predict)-evolve protocol.
- **what is retrieved**:
> Prior task EXPERIENCES (structured experience text S(x_i, y_hat_i, f_i) encoding past task input, the agent's solution/trajectory, and correctness feedback), plus, depending on the memory module, distilled reasoning rationales/skills, procedural workflows (AWM), or aggregated 'cheatsheets' (Dynamic Cheatsheet). For multi-turn tasks, retrieved experiences include the goal, action-sequence trajectory, and success/failure label. The core unit emphasized by ExpRAG/ReMem is the task-level experience (problem + solution + correctness).
- **retrieval grounding**:
> GROWING / episodic self-written memory. The retrievable store starts effectively empty (cold start) and is populated online during the streaming evaluation from the agent's own past task experiences; memory is retrieved, integrated, and updated continuously during deployment. No static external corpus/KB/API store is the retrieval target (ToolBench APIs are a task, not the retrieval index). Hence grounding is a growing experience memory, not a static corpus.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k ranking objective. ExpRAG retrieves the Top-k experiences m_i in M_t by retrieval score phi(x_t, m_i); the unified configuration uses a fixed retrieval budget (default k=4) of most-similar memory items appended to the prompt in order of relevance. There is no minimal-complete-set or precision-driven variable-size objective; ReMem adds an adaptive prune/refine step over the retrieved set but the base retrieval is fixed top-k.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve: yes (top-k similarity / recency retrieval of past experiences), Reuse: yes (retrieved experiences injected as in-context exemplars to solve the current task), Revise: yes (ReMem's Refine/Think-Prune meta-reasoning revises and reorganizes retrieved/stored experiences; ExpRAG reuses without per-case adaptation), Retain: yes (new experience m_t=h(x_t,y_hat_t,f_t) appended/updated via U after each task)]. The framework implements all four CBR phases (most fully in ReMem), though not framed as CBR.
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False. The paper frames itself as 'self-evolving memory', 'test-time learning/evolution', and 'experience reuse' for LLM agents; it does NOT cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner or use the term 'case-based reasoning'. It realizes CBR-like Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain mechanisms under memory/experience-learning terminology.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> case (problem-solution experience): a structured experience text m_i = S(x_i, y_hat_i, f_i) (task input + predicted solution/trajectory + correctness feedback). For multi-turn tasks the unit is a full task trajectory (goal + action sequence + success/failure); for single-turn it is a (question, rationale/answer, correctness) experience. Other unified modules use their native units (AWM = workflow-routine; Dynamic Cheatsheet = aggregated cheatsheet text; Mem0 = memory fact items).
- **index source**:
> Growing memory, online / test-time-induced. The store is built incrementally during the streaming evaluation from the agent's own task experiences (append for retrieval-based memories; summarize/compress for long-term stores; replace for bounded stores). It is not offline-induced and not a fixed external corpus; each dataset is converted into a streaming task sequence over which memory evolves.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat vector index by default: all stored memory items are embedded with BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5 and retrieved by top-k embedding similarity (cosine) against the current query. Unified modules contribute alternative organizations within the same framework: Mem0/MemOS use hierarchical/structured agent-level memory, AWM organizes reusable workflows, Dynamic Cheatsheet maintains an aggregated/curated cheatsheet; but the common retrieval substrate is a flat embedding index over memory items.
- **retriever type**:
> Dense (embedding-based) retriever using the off-the-shelf BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5 encoder to index both queries and memory items, with top-k nearest-neighbor (cosine similarity) retrieval. ExpRecent uses recency-based retrieval instead of similarity. Some modules (Self-RAG, ReMem) add LLM-based reasoning on top to decide whether/what to retrieve, but the underlying retriever is dense embedding similarity.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> none (off-the-shelf). The BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5 retriever encoder is frozen and used as-is to ensure a consistent retrieval budget and fair comparison across all methods; there is no contrastive fine-tuning, LM-feedback training, RL, or downstream-effectiveness optimization of the retriever. Adaptive behaviors (Self-RAG reflection, ReMem Think/Refine) are prompt-driven LLM decisions layered on top of the same fixed retrieval pool, not a trained retrieval policy.
- **query construction**:
> Raw input query: the current task input/question x_t is encoded by the retriever and matched against stored memory embeddings. ReMem additionally uses LLM 'Think'/'Refine' reasoning to decide whether to retrieve and which retrieved experiences to keep or prune, and Self-RAG adaptively decides whether to retrieve, but the base query is the raw current input. No systematic sub-query decomposition or synthetic query expansion in the core pipeline.
- **query granularity**:
> Primarily task-level (one query per incoming task x_t at the start of the task). For multi-turn embodied tasks the retrieved experiences are injected into the task context and the agent then runs a multi-step loop; ReMem can perform additional Think/Refine memory operations within a step, but retrieval over experiences is keyed at the task level rather than per-environment-step. Effectively task-level with an adaptive intra-task refine layer for ReMem.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Mostly one-shot per task for ExpRAG/ExpRecent (retrieve top-k experiences at the start of each task). ReMem and Self-RAG are adaptive: they introduce reasoning modules that decide whether to retrieve and what to retrieve, so retrieval can be triggered/refined adaptively within the agent loop. Overall the framework supports one-shot (ExpRAG) through adaptive (ReMem) retrieval.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> ExpRAG/ExpRecent: fixed schedule (retrieve at the start of every task). ReMem: agent-initiated / reasoning-driven trigger - the agent chooses among {Think, Act, Refine} operations, and the Refine (and Think) steps perform meta-reasoning over memory deciding whether to exploit, prune, or reorganize retrieved experiences before acting (a step terminates once Act is selected). Self-RAG uses reflection-style decisions about whether to retrieve. No token-confidence or attention-entropy signal.
- **reranking**:
> No dedicated cross-encoder/RRF reranking stage. Retrieved items are appended to the prompt ordered by embedding similarity (most to least similar). ReMem instead applies an LLM-driven Refine/Think-Prune operation that selects/prunes which retrieved experiences are kept (an interpretable LLM-based filtering rather than a learned reranker).
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> For ExpRAG: minimal (similarity-ordered append, truncated to prompt budget). For ReMem: explicit Refine-Memory module performs meta-reasoning over retrieved memory - exploiting useful experiences, pruning noise (Think-Prune: remove unhelpful experiences by ID), and reorganizing M_t to better support reasoning and action; Dynamic Cheatsheet merges retrieved content into a short curated summary. So refinement ranges from none/truncation (ExpRAG) to active prune-and-reorganize distillation (ReMem).
- **tool document engineering**:
> N/A. ToolBench is used as a task (API selection/configuration), not as a retrievable tool index with engineered tool descriptions. Memory items are task experiences, not tool docstrings, so no tool-document engineering (synthetic-query augmentation, weighted-field embeddings, etc.).
- **index content separation**:
> Partial. Multi-turn experiences are stored with lightweight identifiers (goal + correctness label) alongside heavier trajectory content, and ReMem references experiences by ID for pruning (Think-Prune: <IDs>). However there is no formal progressive-disclosure / index-then-load-content mechanism; retrieved experiences are injected as whole items (truncated to the prompt budget).
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A. No live external tool registry or integration protocol (MCP/RapidAPI/RESTful/function-calling) is synchronized; the memory store is an internally-managed growing pool of experiences. LLM access is via official vendor SDKs/APIs, but that is not a tool-index protocol.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no inter-tool dependency modeling; tools are not the retrieval unit).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation (in-context learning). Retrieved experiences are inserted into a structured prompt (e.g., a 'RELEVANT EXPERIENCE FROM SIMILAR TASKS' section with goal/trajectory/correctness for multi-turn, or 'LOCAL EXPERIENCE MEMORY' rationales/skills for single-turn) and the base LLM conditions on them: y_hat_t = F(x_t, R_t). No weight updates or latent-token injection; memory is external and consumed via context. ReMem additionally lets the model reason about and update its own memory during problem solving.
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-plan with an interleaved refine loop. ExpRAG performs one-shot retrieve-then-act in-context. ReMem expands the ReAct action space into {Think, Act, Refine}: the agent interleaves internal reasoning (Think), environment actions (Act), and memory meta-reasoning (Refine) within a Markov decision process where state s_t^n = (x_t, M_t, o_t^{1:n-1}); multiple Think/Refine rounds can occur before an Act terminates the step. Memory thus becomes an adaptive component woven into the act-think loop rather than static context. No explicit MCTS/tree search.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> ExpRAG: per-task / per-answer (retrieve once, then solve). ReMem: per-step within a rollout for multi-turn tasks (Think/Act/Refine operations interleaved across environment steps), and per-operation memory reasoning within a step. So interleaving granularity is per-task for the retrieval baseline and per-action/per-step (with intra-step memory refine) for ReMem.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> ExpRAG: verbatim in-context exemplar reuse (retrieved experiences used as ICL examples without per-case editing). ReMem: LLM-prompted adaptation + meta-reasoning - the Think/Refine operations exploit useful experiences, prune noise, and reorganize memory before/while acting, effectively revising the working memory rather than copy-editing a single retrieved solution; feedback (correctness) informs what is retained. No RL reuse-finetuning or latent adaptation.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Structured experience text / note: each memory entry is a templated experience S(x_i, y_hat_i, f_i) recording past task, solution/trajectory, and correctness, surfaced as free-text in the prompt (e.g., Goal / Trajectory / Correctness for multi-turn; rationale/domain/skill notes for single-turn). AWM contributes free-text workflows and Dynamic Cheatsheet a distilled cheatsheet; the proposed methods inject raw-to-lightly-distilled experience text, not executable programs or latent tokens.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Spans raw-to-distilled. ExpRAG/ExpRecent retrieve near-raw task experiences/trajectories with correctness labels (single demonstration / raw trajectory level). ReMem operates over the same experiences but distills/prunes them via Refine into a more useful working memory. Unified baselines cover more abstract forms: AWM (reusable workflow routines), Dynamic Cheatsheet (distilled strategy aggregate). The paper finds explicit task-level (experience) utilization is both promising and underexplored.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> ReMem's Refine-Memory module is the central noise-robustness mechanism: it actively prunes unhelpful/noisy experiences (Think-Prune by ID) and reorganizes memory, making it robust when both successful AND failed experiences are stored (Table 3) whereas baselines degrade under unfiltered failures. Keeping a small retrieval budget (default k=4, truncated to prompt length) and similarity-ordered injection also limits noise. Memory pruning analysis (Appendix B.2) shows higher pruning for diverse datasets (GPQA 36.8%) vs concentrated ones (AIME 17.5%/10.8%), evidencing selective discarding of domain-irrelevant experiences.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> episodic experience memory (with procedural/workflow variants among the unified modules). The proposed ExpRAG/ExpRecent/ReMem maintain a growing pool of episodic task experiences (trajectories + correctness); baselines instantiate skill/workflow memory (AWM), curated procedural cheatsheets (Dynamic Cheatsheet), and structured/hierarchical agent memory (Mem0, MemOS, LangMem). The framework abstracts all as evolving memory M_t.
- **write back**:
> Yes. After each task the agent constructs a new memory entry m_t = h(x_t, y_hat_t, f_t) capturing the experience and feedback, and updates memory via M_{t+1} = U(M_t, m_t). For ExpRAG, U is a direct append: M_{t+1} = M_t union {(x_t, y_hat_t, f_t)}. Different modules use append (retrieval-based), summarize/compress (long-term), or replace (bounded-capacity).
- **online growth**:
> Yes. Memory grows continuously during the streaming test-time deployment; the entire premise of 'test-time evolution' is that the store accumulates and evolves after every interaction across the task stream (starting from a cold start). Cumulative-accuracy curves (Appendix B.3) show ReMem surpassing the History baseline as more tasks accumulate.
- **write back trigger**:
> Per-task (after every interaction), using the correctness feedback f_t. The agent writes a new experience entry after each completed task regardless of outcome (both successful and failed experiences can be stored, as analyzed in RQ4/Table 3). ReMem additionally performs reflective Refine operations that reorganize/prune existing memory during problem solving, so writing/updating is per-task with reflective in-loop refinement.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success + failure stored, with selective refinement. Experiences carry a correctness label (success/failure), and RQ4 (Table 3) explicitly evaluates storing BOTH successful and failed experiences on AlfWorld/ScienceWorld: naive baselines degrade under unfiltered failures (noise), while ReMem stays robust by actively refining/pruning stored experiences, achieving the best success/progress. The paper motivates future work on failure-aware memory evolution. So failures are retained and used, but require ReMem-style filtering to be beneficial.
- **memory evolution update**:
> Depends on module: append-only (ExpRAG direct union), summarization/compression (long-term stores), or replacement (bounded-capacity stores). ReMem adds delta-update + forget-prune + reorganize: its Refine operation prunes noisy entries (Think-Prune by ID) and reorganizes M_t over time. Reported memory pruning rates vary by dataset (e.g., GPQA 36.8% pruned vs AIME 10.8%-17.5%), demonstrating active forgetting/curation rather than pure append.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No (not a trained/RL retrieval policy). Retrieval is fixed top-k embedding similarity over a frozen bge-base encoder. ReMem's decision to retrieve/refine/prune is an LLM-prompted (in-context) meta-reasoning policy framed as a Markov decision process, but it is NOT optimized via RL or value learning - the LLM weights are not updated. So memory control is reasoning-driven but not a learned/parameter-optimized policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> No. Single-agent private memory: each agent maintains and evolves its own memory across its task stream. The benchmark UNIFIES many memory frameworks under one protocol for comparison, but memory/experience is not shared across multiple agents or across heterogeneous frameworks at run time.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> Single-turn: MMLU-Pro (Engineering 969q, Economics 844q, Philosophy 499q domains used; ~12K total across 14 areas), GPQA-Diamond (198 graduate-level science MCQ), AIME-24 and AIME-25 (30 Olympiad math problems each, exact-match), ToolBench/Gorilla (750 tool-use/API-grounding tasks). Multi-turn embodied/interactive: AlfWorld (134 text household tasks), BabyAI (112 grid navigation/manipulation tasks), ScienceWorld (90 interactive science tasks), PDDL (60 symbolic planning problems). 10 datasets total.
- **benchmark family**:
> Mixed: QA / multi-disciplinary reasoning (MMLU-Pro, GPQA-Diamond), math (AIME-24/25), tool (ToolBench), and embodied/interactive decision-making (AlfWorld, BabyAI, ScienceWorld - embodied; PDDL - symbolic planning). No LoCoMo/LongMemEval-style conversational-memory benchmarks (the paper positions itself against those static-recall settings) and no D4RL decision-RL.
- **baselines**:
> Grouped into four families. (1) Agent pipelines without procedural memory: ReAct, A-mem (Amem); also a 'Baseline' (zero-shot) and 'History' (raw history context). (2) Adaptive agentic memory: Self-RAG (SelfRAG), MemOS, Mem0, LangMem. (3) Procedural-memory agents: Dynamic Cheatsheet (DC-Cu = Cumulative/curated, DC-RS = Retrieval-Synthesis), Agent Workflow Memory (AWM). (4) Proposed evolving-memory framework: ExpRecent, ExpRAG, ReMem. MemoryBank/MemoryGPT excluded (factual recall only); MemOS and LangMem excluded from multi-turn embodied evaluation as incompatible.
- **key metrics**:
> Single-turn: Exact Match (AIME, GPQA, MMLU-Pro) and API/Accuracy for ToolBench (reported as API/Acc., e.g., 0.85/0.71), plus an average. Multi-turn: Success rate (S) and Progress rate (P) per environment, plus averages. Also Step efficiency (average steps to complete a task; lower is better), Sequence robustness (consistency across Easy->Hard vs Hard->Easy orderings), and cumulative accuracy/success over the task stream. Pearson correlation r used to relate ReMem gains to within-dataset task similarity.
- **headline result**:
> Across single-turn and multi-turn tasks, evolving-memory methods (ExpRAG, ReMem) consistently outperform baselines; gains are largest in multi-turn settings. On multi-turn (Claude-3.7-Sonnet) ReMem reaches average S/P = 0.78/0.91 vs Baseline 0.24/0.52 and ReAct 0.57/0.79, with AlfWorld 0.92/0.96, BabyAI 0.73/0.83, PDDL 0.83/0.95, ScienceWorld 0.62/0.89. On Gemini-2.5-Flash multi-turn, ReMem averages 0.50/0.64 vs Baseline 0.27/0.46. On single-turn (Gemini-2.5-Flash) ReMem achieves 0.65 average exact match with ToolBench API/Acc 0.85/0.71, the best in its column. ReMem also cuts steps substantially (e.g., AlfWorld 22.6 -> 11.5 steps).
- **ablations**:
> (1) RQ2 memory-improvement vs task similarity (Fig.3): ReMem's gain over History correlates with within-dataset task similarity (Pearson r=0.717 Gemini-2.5-Flash, r=0.563 Claude-3.7-Sonnet); high-similarity datasets (PDDL, AlfWorld) gain most, diverse ones (AIME-25, GPQA) gain least. (2) RQ3 sequence difficulty (Table 2): evolving-memory robust to Easy->Hard vs Hard->Easy ordering; ReMem reaches up to 0.94/0.97 (Hard->Easy), and harder-task experiences transfer better. (3) RQ4 feedback / success+failure storage (Table 3): baselines degrade under unfiltered failures; ReMem stays robust via refinement (Claude AlfWorld 0.92/0.96, ScienceWorld 0.69/0.91). (4) Step efficiency (Fig.4): ReMem largest, most stable step reductions. (5) Memory pruning rates (Fig.5/App B.2): GPQA 36.8% pruned vs AIME 10.8%-17.5%. (6) Cross-model (App B.1, Tables 4-5): trends hold across Gemini-2.5 Flash/Flash-Lite/Pro and Claude-3.5-Haiku/3.7-Sonnet; smaller models benefit most. (7) Cumulative accuracy curves (App B.3): ReMem surpasses History as tasks accumulate.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> No. Only end-to-end task metrics (exact match, success/progress rate, API accuracy) plus efficiency (steps), robustness, and cumulative accuracy are reported. No intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG / retrieval completeness) are reported separately; the closest decoupled memory-quality signal is the memory pruning-rate analysis and the task-similarity correlation.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Mixed. Outcome metrics (exact match, success rate, API accuracy) are primary, but the framework explicitly adds process/efficiency signals: Progress rate (partial completion in multi-turn), Step efficiency (number of steps), Sequence robustness (cross-ordering consistency), cumulative accuracy/success over the stream, and memory pruning/selectivity analysis. So intermediate process quality (progress, steps, adaptation curves) is evaluated alongside final outcome.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Reported via step efficiency and qualitative compute notes. Evolving-memory methods need fewer steps to complete multi-turn tasks; ReMem gives the largest, most stable reductions (e.g., AlfWorld 22.6 -> 11.5 steps; Fig.4). Smaller/lightweight LLMs benefit most from test-time refinement (App B.1). A fixed retrieval budget (default k=4, prompt-length truncation) is enforced for fair comparison. Total API compute cost for the study was 'on the order of tens of thousands of US dollars' (App G.1); exact per-method token/latency costs are not tabulated.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k, budget-capped. Default top-k = 4 most-relevant memory items retrieved per task via bge-base similarity, appended in similarity order and truncated so retrieved texts + task input fit within the same prompt-length constraint across all methods (ensuring a consistent retrieval budget). ReMem may further prune the retrieved set adaptively. Memory store size configurable (e.g., memory_size 1000 in the released config).
- **survey scope and axes**:
> N/A (this is a benchmark/framework paper, not a survey). It does, however, organize evaluated methods along four families: (1) agent pipelines without procedural memory, (2) adaptive agentic memory, (3) procedural-memory agents, (4) the proposed evolving-memory framework; and evaluates along four dimensions: answer accuracy, success rate, step efficiency, sequence robustness.
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Construction: Evo-Memory TRANSFORMS existing static datasets into streaming task sequences tau={(x1,y1),...,(xT,yT)} with a unified, fixed task ordering per dataset, so earlier tasks supply information/strategies for later ones; evaluated under the unified search-synthesize-evolve loop with correctness as feedback. Size: 10 datasets - single-turn (MMLU-Pro using Eng 969q/Eco 844q/Philo 499q domains, GPQA-Diamond 198q, AIME-24 30q, AIME-25 30q, ToolBench 750 tasks) and multi-turn (AlfWorld 134, BabyAI 112, ScienceWorld 90, PDDL 60). Answers verifiable via exact match (math/QA), API/execution-based accuracy (ToolBench), and success/progress rates (embodied). Difficulty signaled by low baseline scores (e.g., AIME exact match ~0.13-0.47; multi-turn baseline averages ~0.24-0.27 success) vs ReMem reaching 0.78 avg success on Claude-3.7-Sonnet multi-turn. 10+ memory modules unified and implemented.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> ReAct (Yao et al. 2023) as the reasoning-acting backbone that ReMem extends with a Refine/memory-reasoning action; retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al. 2020) and Self-RAG (Asai et al. 2024) for adaptive retrieval; unified memory baselines A-mem (Xu et al. 2025), Mem0, MemOS (Li et al. 2025), LangMem, Dynamic Cheatsheet (Suzgun et al. 2025), and Agent Workflow Memory / AWM (Wang et al. 2024); BAAI bge-base-en-v1.5 (Chen et al. 2024) retriever. Benchmark datasets: MMLU-Pro, GPQA-Diamond, AIME-24/25, ToolBench/Gorilla, AlfWorld, BabyAI, ScienceWorld, PDDLbench. Prior streaming/lifelong benchmarks StreamBench (Wu et al. 2024) and LifelongAgentBench (Zheng et al. 2025) are the closest predecessors it extends.
- **contrasts with**:
> Static conversational-memory benchmarks and methods that test recall rather than experience reuse (LongMemEval, LoCoMo-style evaluations, Maharana et al. 2024; MemoryBank/MemoryGPT - excluded as factual-recall only). Also contrasts with StreamBench (sequential learning but mainly factual retention, no trajectory reuse) and LifelongAgentBench (retention without modeling memory structure/updates). Within methods, it positions ExpRAG/ReMem against procedural-only (AWM, Dynamic Cheatsheet) and adaptive-retrieval-only (Self-RAG, Mem0, MemOS, LangMem) memories, arguing for tightly integrating reasoning + action + memory refinement (test-time evolution).
- **lineage**:
> Group F (decision/memory/RL - self-evolving agent memory & test-time learning). A 2025-2026 streaming BENCHMARK + framework that operationalizes 'test-time evolution', advancing the lifelong/streaming-agent line (StreamBench, LifelongAgentBench) and the self-evolving agent-memory line (ExpeL/Synapse/AWM/Reflexion/ReasoningBank/Dynamic Cheatsheet). Distinctive contributions: (a) restructuring static datasets into streaming task streams to test experience reuse vs conversational recall; (b) a unified (F,U,R,C) search-synthesize-evolve formulation unifying 10+ memory modules; (c) ExpRAG (simple but strong task-level experience-retrieval baseline) and ReMem (an action-think-memory-refine pipeline extending ReAct with explicit memory reasoning).

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- venue

<a id="item-graph-memory-trainable"></a>
### 143. From Experience to Strategy: Empowering LLM Agents with Trainable Graph Memory (trainable multi-layered graph memory of decision paths + meta-cognition; sometimes referred to internally as 'Graph Memory / strategy graph')

2025  ·  arXiv 2511.07800  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.07800)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **authors affiliation**:
> Siyu Xia (co-first; Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CASIA) & School of AI, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences), Zekun Xu (co-first; Meituan), Jiajun Chai (Meituan), Wentian Fan (Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications), Yan Song (AI Centre, Dept. of Computer Science, University College London), Xiaohan Wang (Meituan), Guojun Yin (Meituan; corresponding-affiliated), Wei Lin (Meituan), Haifeng Zhang (corresponding; CASIA & UCAS, haifeng.zhang@ia.ac.cn), Jun Wang (corresponding; UCL, jun.wang@cs.ucl.ac.uk). Primary affiliations: Chinese Academy of Sciences / UCAS, Meituan, and University College London.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.07800

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Tool-augmented / agentic question answering and decision-making: open-domain factoid QA and multi-hop QA solved by an LLM agent that interleaves reasoning (<think>) with retrieval tool calls (<tool_call> over a Wikipedia RAG MCP tool) and answer generation (<answer>). Framed as long-horizon strategic tool-use / decision-making for LLM agents.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent, multi-turn tool-integrated decision process formalized as s_t=(q, h_{1:t-1}), a_t ~ pi_theta(a_t|s_t), with actions being internal reasoning, a tool (RAG search) call, or answer generation, up to K=6 tool invocations. Two regimes are studied: (1) Direct/zero-training inference (the memory workflow is plugged into a frozen Qwen3 backbone), and (2) RL training, where the structured memory is injected into the GRPO training loop (Search-R1 style) to guide policy optimization. Supervision: outcome reward via Exact Match against ground-truth QA answers (used both to label success/failure trajectories during memory construction and as the RL/counterfactual reward). The central research question is whether dynamic structured EXPLICIT memory can actively guide and enhance IMPLICIT (parametric) policy learning, combining the interpretability of prompting with the generalization of training. Memory is built exclusively from in-domain HotpotQA (1,000 examples for memory construction + 5,000 for graph-weight training; remaining HotpotQA training split used as the RL corpus); evaluation spans 7 QA datasets (HotpotQA in-domain, six out-of-domain). Hardware: 8x A100; vLLM v1; GRPO with n=8 rollouts, batch 512, temperature 1.0.
- **what is retrieved**:
> High-level, human-interpretable strategic 'meta-cognition' nodes (generalized heuristics / decision principles, e.g. 'early recognition of KnowledgeSufficient state and structured validation help prevent synthesis inaccuracies'), distilled from abstracted decision paths. Retrieval is keyed by query similarity and traverses the trainable graph (query -> transition-path -> meta-cognition); the retrieved/injected unit is the top-k meta-cognition strategies (not raw trajectories). Underneath, the graph also stores raw query nodes (with trajectories and outcome labels) and canonical FSM decision-path nodes, but only meta-cognitions are verbalized into the prompt.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> GROWING / experience-induced memory: the retrievable store is a heterogeneous graph the agent builds from its OWN sampled trajectories on HotpotQA (successful and failed), abstracted via an FSM and distilled into meta-cognitions, with a separate Wikipedia RAG corpus used only as the agent's external tool at solve time. So the STRATEGY memory is a self-written/induced experiential store (constructed offline from training rollouts, then frozen for downstream evaluation/RL), while the factual knowledge access (the search tool over the 2018 Wikipedia dump) is a static external corpus. Net: HYBRID (self-induced strategy graph + static external Wikipedia knowledge tool), with the studied/learned memory being the growing-experience graph.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k ranking objective: a query activates a similarity-based subgraph and the top-k highest-relevance-score meta-cognitions are selected (selection-probability via softmax over learned-weight-aggregated path scores). k is a fixed small hyperparameter (k=3 reported as the best balance in the main text; appendix Table 3 finds top_k=5 marginally best on the 4B average). No minimal-complete-set or variable-size precision-driven objective.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve: yes (similarity-activated subgraph + learned-weight top-k meta-cognition selection), Reuse: yes (selected strategies verbalized and prepended to guide acting and RL), Revise: partial (meta-cognitions are induced/updated by contrasting success vs failure FSM paths and confidence updates; no per-instance verbatim-then-edit case adaptation), Retain: yes (new/updated meta-cognition nodes and reinforced edge weights retained in the graph during construction; redundant/low-confidence paths pruned)].
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False. The work frames itself as agent memory / experiential learning / meta-cognition + RL, and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner or use the term 'case-based reasoning'. It realizes CBR-like Retrieve/Reuse/Retain mechanisms under a trainable-graph-memory and implicit-vs-explicit-memory framing (related to Reflexion, ExpeL, A-MEM, G-Memory).

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> guideline-rule / distilled strategic meta-cognition node (a high-level, human-readable problem-solving principle). The graph has three node types: query nodes (task instance + trajectory + outcome), transition-path nodes (canonical FSM decision pathways abstracting raw traces), and meta-cognition nodes (distilled heuristics); the injected retrieval unit is the meta-cognition node.
- **index source**:
> Growing memory, offline-induced from training rollouts then frozen for downstream use (hybrid in the broader sense). The strategy graph is constructed before evaluation by sampling N trajectories per query from the policy on HotpotQA, grounding each to an FSM path, and inducing meta-cognitions; graph EDGE WEIGHTS are then trained (Stage 2). At downstream inference/RL the graph is fixed and queried. A static external Wikipedia (2018 dump, E5 retriever) serves as the agent's search tool but is not the strategy index.
- **index structure topology**:
> Dependency / knowledge GRAPH with a hierarchical (multi-layered) topology: a heterogeneous directed acyclic graph G=(V,E,O_V,R_E,C) with three layers Q (query) -> T (transition path) -> M (meta-cognition), connected by bipartite adjacency matrices A^{q->t} and A^{t->m}, each augmented with learnable weights w_qt and w_tm. Transition-path nodes are canonical paths over a finite state machine (FSM) of abstract cognitive states (e.g. StrategyPlanning, InformationAnalysis, ToolExecution, DecisionMaking, DiagnosisHub). Query similarity (cosine over embeddings) activates task-specific subgraphs.
- **retriever type**:
> Hybrid: dense embedding similarity (cosine over query embeddings, Sim(q_new,q_i)=cos(e_qnew,e_qi)) to activate the relevant subgraph / find similar historical queries, combined with a LEARNED graph-weight relevance score rho(m_k|q_new)=sum_{q_i,t_j: q_i->t_j->m_k} Sim(q_new,q_i)*w_qt^{(i,j)}*w_tm^{(j,k)} and softmax selection. The graph edge weights are trained by policy gradient (REINFORCE), so the retriever is partly a learned scoring function over a graph, not pure off-the-shelf top-k. (The external factual search tool is a separate E5 dense retriever over Wikipedia.)
- **retriever learning signal**:
> RL / learned-policy via downstream-task effectiveness (counterfactual reward). Stage 2 trains the graph edge weights with REINFORCE: for a sampled meta-cognition m_k, it runs the agent WITH guidance m_k (reward R_with) and WITHOUT (R_w/o), forms the reward gap Delta R_k = R_with - R_w/o (utility signal), and updates weights via L_RL = -E_{m_k~p}[Delta R_k * log p(m_k|q_new)]. Positive Delta R_k strengthens supporting q->t->m paths, negative weakens them. The base query-similarity uses off-the-shelf embeddings, but the utility/relevance calibration is RL-trained on task reward (Exact Match), making this a value/utility-driven learned selection signal.
- **query construction**:
> Raw query context: a new query q_new is represented by its embedding similarity to historical query nodes in the graph; the top-k most similar neighbors activate a task-specific subgraph G(q_new)=(Q',T',M'). No query decomposition, intent extraction, or synthetic expansion; the agent additionally issues raw-text search-tool queries during solving (e.g. 'George D. Maziarz state').
- **query granularity**:
> task-level (one-shot at t=0): retrieval of meta-cognitions from the graph is performed per incoming query, and the selected strategies are prepended to the query for the whole episode (q_tilde = [m_1,...,m_k; q_train]). The agent's separate factual tool calls happen per-step during the rollout, but the strategy-memory retrieval that this method contributes is task-level.
- **when to retrieve**: one-shot (per task): the top-k meta-cognitions are retrieved once from the (optimized) memory graph and prepended to the query before the agent acts; they remain fixed context throughout that episode's reasoning/tool loop.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> fixed schedule: strategy retrieval is triggered unconditionally for every query (compute relevance scores for all activated meta-cognitions, take top-k). Within the rollout, the agent itself decides when to call the factual RAG tool (agent-initiated, reasoning-conditioned) but that is the underlying tool-use, not the contributed memory-retrieval trigger.
- **reranking**:
> Effectively a learned-weight relevance scoring/ranking rather than a separate cross-encoder reranking stage: meta-cognitions are scored by aggregated learned graph-path weights (rho), softmax-normalized, and the top-k are selected. No external cross-encoder, RRF, or instruction-tuned reranker is reported.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> None beyond selection: retrieved meta-cognitions are verbalized and prepended to the query without post-retrieval compression, decomposition, or distractor filtering. Abstraction/distillation happens at WRITE time (FSM grounding + meta-cognition induction), and the trainable weights act to suppress low-utility strategies; the appendix notes too many strategies can introduce noise/overlap, motivating a small k rather than a refinement module.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (not a tool-retrieval method; the agent uses a single Wikipedia RAG MCP tool, not a retrievable tool/API index. Memory items are distilled strategy text, not tool docstrings.)
- **index content separation**:
> Partial: the multi-layer graph separates a lightweight high-level meta-cognition layer (retrieved/injected) from heavier underlying query nodes (full trajectories/outcomes) and FSM transition-path nodes (kept for analysis/induction but not injected). However, this is hierarchical abstraction rather than an explicit progressive-disclosure 'index-then-load-content' retrieval mechanism.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> The factual retrieval is wrapped as a modular MCP tool (search-query_rag) the LLM invokes autonomously (function-calling protocol via <tool_call>/<tool_response> tags over the 2018 Wikipedia dump with E5). The strategy memory graph itself is an internally-managed store, not a live external tool registry; no RapidAPI/RESTful CRUD auto-sync. So: function-calling/MCP for the knowledge tool, internal graph for strategy memory.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (single search tool; no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Both prompt augmentation AND training signal. (1) Prompt augmentation: top-k meta-cognitions are prepended to the query (q_tilde=[m_1,...,m_k; q]) as an explicit strategic policy prior at inference and during RL rollouts. (2) Training signal: the augmented context is fed to the policy which is then optimized with GRPO (L_{RL+Mem} = -E_{a~pi_theta(.|q_tilde)}[R(a)]), so the memory directly shapes implicit policy learning. The memory graph's own edge weights are also trained via REINFORCE on counterfactual reward. This dual integration into the RL training loop (not inference-only) is the paper's distinguishing claim.
- **planning integration**:
> retrieve-then-plan, integrated into the RL training loop: for each training instance, top-k meta-cognitions are retrieved from the optimized graph and prepended to the query; the GRPO policy then plans and acts (multi-turn reasoning + RAG tool calls up to 6) conditioned on these strategic priors, and gradients update the policy. Memory is thus a per-task strategic prior at the start of planning that is woven into RL optimization, rather than per-step interleaving inside a tree search.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> per-answer / per-task for the contributed strategy memory (meta-cognitions injected once and held fixed across the episode's reasoning). The underlying agent reasoning interleaves with factual tool calls per-tool-call within the rollout (ReAct-style think/tool_call/tool_response), but the memory-retrieval contribution operates at the per-task level.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> LLM-prompted distillation + RL utility calibration rather than per-case verbatim reuse: retrieved meta-cognitions are reused as injected guidance (not copied solutions to edit). New strategies are produced by an LLM that contrasts success vs failure FSM paths (intra-query), borrows from similar successful queries (inter-query speculative), or distills from positive examples; the graph's edge weights are then adapted by REINFORCE on counterfactual reward, and the downstream policy is fine-tuned via GRPO under the augmented context.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Distilled strategy / free-text guideline: a concise, human-readable strategic principle (meta-cognition) with cautious-language phrasing ('consider', 'may help', 'tends to'), e.g. structured-validation and confidence-awareness heuristics. Internally each meta-cognition node carries summary, strategy_principles with confidence scores (30-85), overall_confidence, evidence_paths count, and an uncertainty_note; the verbalized item prepended to the prompt is the natural-language strategy text. Not a raw trajectory, executable program, or latent token.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Distilled high-level strategy / meta-cognition (the most abstract layer). The pipeline deliberately abstracts raw trajectories -> canonical FSM decision paths (intermediate) -> generalizable meta-cognitive principles (top layer), filtering execution-level noise to preserve only semantically meaningful, transferable decision strategies; these are what get retrieved and injected.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> (1) Trainable utility weighting: REINFORCE on counterfactual reward gaps strengthens broadly useful meta-cognitions and suppresses ineffective/overly-specific ones (ablation: freezing weights to uniform significantly degrades performance, especially on 2WikiMultiHopQA). (2) FSM grounding filters execution-level noise so only semantically meaningful decision points are stored. (3) Selective memory update (reinforce/create/skip; discard redundant or low-confidence paths; cap ~30 meta-cognitions, preferring updates over creation). (4) Small k (k=3) to avoid prompt overload / conflicting strategies. (5) Cautious-language prompting and explicit uncertainty acknowledgment in induced strategies to avoid over-confident, misleading heuristics.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> graph (trainable, multi-layered heterogeneous graph memory) over distilled procedural/strategic knowledge: query layer + canonical-FSM transition-path layer + meta-cognition layer, with learnable edge weights. Combines episodic provenance (query/trajectory nodes) with a procedural/strategy abstraction (meta-cognitions).
- **write back**:
> Yes (during memory construction). Algorithm 1 (UpdateMemoryGraph) adds the new query node, samples N trajectories, grounds each to an FSM path node, adds query->path edges, induces meta-cognitions (intra-query contrast of success vs failure, inter-query speculative from similar queries, or positive-example distillation), and creates/updates meta-cognition nodes plus path->meta edges. Writing is part of the (offline) memory-formation phase from training rollouts; the graph is then frozen for downstream evaluation/RL (no further online growth reported at deployment).
- **online growth**:
> No (not during downstream deployment/RL): the strategy graph is constructed and weight-trained on HotpotQA rollouts in a dedicated phase, then used as a fixed/optimized memory for evaluation and as a fixed prior during RL training. The construction algorithm itself is incremental/append-and-update per query, but the paper does not grow the graph during the downstream test-time stream.
- **write back trigger**:
> on-success-and-failure, reflective per-query during construction: for each construction query, N trajectories are sampled and labeled success/failure (by Exact Match), then meta-cognitions are induced and the graph updated. Three induction triggers: (Case 1) both success and failure paths exist -> high-confidence causal meta-cognition by contrasting their FSM paths; (Case 2) only failures -> speculative meta-cognitions borrowed from successful paths of top-K semantically similar queries; (else, e.g. only successes / no rollouts in Alg.1) skip, though appendix also describes Positive Example Distillation from successful paths. A new meta-cognition is created if no match exists, else an existing one's confidence is updated.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Success + failure used contrastively (a core design point): high-confidence meta-cognitions are derived by CONTRASTING successful vs failed FSM paths of the same query to explain outcome divergence; failure-only queries trigger speculative heuristics from similar successful queries. Failed paths thus directly drive strategy induction (failure-cause summary / errors-to-avoid), not just success patterns. Note: EXPEL baseline (which also uses experiential insights) underperforms here, and the paper attributes its method's gains partly to the trainable utility weighting over these success/failure-contrasted strategies.
- **memory evolution update**:
> link-and-evolve with dedup-merge and prune: when a new path is generated the agent reinforces existing principles (UpdateConfidence), creates new meta-cognition nodes for novel patterns (FindMatchingMetaCognition then CreateNewMetaCognitionNode), and discards redundant/low-confidence paths; a quantity cap (~30 meta-cognitions) makes the system prefer UPDATE over CREATE and target low-confidence nodes once the budget is exceeded. Separately, edge weights are continuously refined by REINFORCE (delta-update of utility). So the store is curated/evolving (not purely append-only).
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Yes. Meta-cognition selection is a learned, RL-optimized policy over the graph: a stochastic selection p(m_k|q_new) proportional to exp(rho) where rho aggregates trainable edge weights w_qt, w_tm; these weights are optimized by REINFORCE using counterfactual reward gaps (Delta R_k). This is explicitly a policy-gradient-trained retrieval/selection mechanism, not a fixed similarity-only top-k (the no-weight-update ablation confirms the learned weighting is crucial).
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Single-agent private memory (no multi-agent sharing). However, the memory graph is shown to be model-agnostic / portable across LLM backends and APIs: a graph constructed with one builder LLM (GPT-4o) transfers to another (Gemini-2.5-pro) and to different downstream policies (Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B) with minor performance differences (Cross-API Robustness, Table 4). This is plug-and-play across frameworks/backbones rather than collective multi-agent memory.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> Seven QA datasets. General/open-domain factoid QA: Natural Questions (NQ), TriviaQA, PopQA. Multi-hop QA: HotpotQA (the single in-domain dataset; used for memory construction, graph-weight training, and RL training), 2WikiMultiHopQA (2wiki), MuSiQue, Bamboogle. External knowledge source: 2018 Wikipedia dump with the E5 retriever (exposed as an MCP RAG tool, max 6 tool calls). Backbones: Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B; memory-builder LLMs: GPT-4o (default) and Gemini-2.5-pro (robustness).
- **benchmark family**: QA and multi-hop QA (single-turn factoid + multi-hop reasoning). No web/embodied/tool-retrieval-leaderboard/code/decision-RL benchmarks; all evaluation is tool-augmented open-domain QA over Wikipedia.
- **baselines**:
> Inference (zero-training) baselines: ITR/TIR (Tool-Integrated Reasoning, the no-memory tool-use base from RL-Factory/Chai et al. 2025; also written 'ITR' in tables), Direct Inference, CoT (Chain-of-Thought), Direct Trajectory (past trajectories used directly as memory), A-MEM (Xu et al. 2025, dynamic agentic memory notes / graph), EXPEL (Zhao et al. 2024, high-level experiential insights). RL-training baselines: Search-R1 (Jin et al. 2025, multi-turn tool-use RL with no memory) and Search-R1 + memory variants (Direct Trajectory, A-MEM, EXPEL). Cross-API robustness compares the method built with GPT-4o vs Gemini-2.5-pro.
- **key metrics**:
> Exact Match (EM) accuracy is the single primary metric, reported per dataset and as a seven-dataset average, plus relative improvement (%) over the relevant base (ITR for inference, Search-R1 for RL). RL training also reports convergence/training curves (Figure 3). No Recall@k/nDCG/F1/latency metrics for the strategy memory itself.
- **headline result**:
> The trainable graph memory consistently improves over all memory and no-memory baselines, with gains largest on smaller models. Inference (Table 1): average EM 0.365 on Qwen3-8B (+9.3% rel. over ITR 0.334, best among all methods) and 0.351 on Qwen3-4B (+25.8% rel. over ITR 0.279). RL training (Table 2): average EM 0.408 on Qwen3-8B (+3.29% over Search-R1 0.395) and 0.426 on Qwen3-4B (+13.60% over Search-R1 0.375); notably the trained Qwen3-4B (0.426) exceeds the baseline Qwen3-8B (0.395). Strong out-of-domain generalization despite memory built ONLY from in-domain HotpotQA. Most-cited single number: +25.8% relative average improvement over ITR on Qwen3-4B at inference.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Disabling weight optimization (Fig.4a/b): freezing edges to uniform weight and retrieving by structural presence only causes a significant performance drop, especially on 2WikiMultiHopQA, validating the REINFORCE-based utility learning. (2) Number of meta-cognitions k (Fig.4c, Table 3, Qwen3-4B avg over 7 datasets): ITR(k=0)=0.279 -> top_k=1=0.344 -> top_k=3=0.351 -> top_k=5=0.355; even a single strategy helps markedly (Bamboogle +11.6%, HotpotQA +2.9%); diminishing returns / noise beyond moderate k, main text recommends k=3 (appendix marginally favors k=5). (3) Cross-API memory robustness (Table 4): memory built with GPT-4o vs Gemini-2.5-pro yields near-identical downstream EM (e.g. Qwen3-8B avg 0.365 vs 0.369; Gemini slightly better, +0.043 on Bamboogle for 8B), showing the framework is largely model-agnostic. (Stated three ablation dimensions: weight updates, number of meta-cognitions, and memory composition granularity/API-call structure.)
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> No. Only end-to-end task EM (and relative improvements) are reported; there are no intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k, nDCG, retrieval completeness) for the meta-cognition selection. The closest decoupled signal is the k-ablation on number of injected meta-cognitions and the weight-freezing ablation.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Predominantly outcome-only (Exact Match). Some process-oriented signals are reported qualitatively/indirectly: RL training/convergence curves (Figure 3) indicate faster/better convergence, the FSM decision-path abstraction and case studies illustrate trajectory/reasoning quality (e.g. self-checking correcting 'National Security Law' -> 'Macau National Security Law'), but no quantitative step-wise process metrics (e.g. step success rate, faithfulness scores) are given.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed small-k selection: top-k meta-cognitions prepended to the query, k a tuned hyperparameter (k=3 recommended in main text; top_k in {0,1,3,5} ablated, 5 marginally best on 4B average). Meta-cognition pool capped at ~30 nodes (quantity-management in the induction prompt). Agent factual tool calls capped at 6 per query; RAG returns top-3 documents by default. No adaptive/precision-driven k beyond the fixed top-k with the ~30-node memory cap.
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A (uses seven existing QA benchmarks: NQ, TriviaQA, PopQA, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, Bamboogle. Memory built from 1,000 HotpotQA examples; graph weights trained on 5,000 HotpotQA examples; remaining HotpotQA training split used as RL corpus. No new benchmark constructed.)

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> RL-Factory (Chai et al. 2025) plug-and-play multi-turn tool-use RL framework and its TIR/ITR base; Search-R1 (Jin et al. 2025) as the RL search-agent baseline extended; GRPO for policy optimization; ReAct (Yao et al. 2022) think/act tool interleaving; experiential-memory line — Reflexion (Zhang/Shinn et al. 2023), ExpeL (Zhao et al. 2024), A-MEM (Xu et al. 2025); graph-memory line — G-Memory (Zhang et al. 2025), Zep (Rasmussen et al. 2025), HopRAG (Liu et al. 2025); heterogeneous graph neural networks (Zhang et al. 2019) for the weighted-graph formalism; E5 embeddings (Wang et al. 2024) and DPR/2018 Wikipedia (Karpukhin et al. 2020) for the search tool; long-horizon memory agents MEM1 (Zhou et al. 2025), MemAgent (Yu et al. 2025).
- **contrasts with**:
> Implicit memory via training (RL-only, e.g. Search-R1) — generalizes but is black-box, lossy, and prone to catastrophic forgetting; and explicit memory via static prompting (Direct Trajectory, A-MEM, EXPEL, Mem0, and static/logic-aware graph memories like Zep/HopRAG/G-Memory) — interpretable but non-adaptive and poorly generalizing, with no mechanism to evaluate/refine strategy utility. EXPEL in particular (raw experiential insights, inference-only) underperforms and even degrades RL training in their tables (-6.08% on 8B, -10.13% on 4B vs Search-R1). The paper positions its trainable, utility-aware graph injected INTO the RL training loop against all of these inference-only or static-weight approaches.
- **lineage**:
> Group F (decision/memory + RL): a 2025 method that fuses experiential graph memory with RL training for tool-augmented decision-making. It advances the Reflexion -> ExpeL -> A-MEM / G-Memory experiential- and graph-memory lineage by (a) abstracting trajectories into canonical FSM decision paths and distilling human-interpretable meta-cognitions in a multi-layer heterogeneous graph, (b) making memory TRAINABLE via REINFORCE on counterfactual reward gaps (utility-aware edge weights / learned selection policy), and (c) integrating the retrieved strategies into the GRPO RL training loop as an explicit policy prior (not inference-only), thereby unifying explicit (interpretable) and implicit (parametric) memory.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- code_url
- cost_efficiency_tradeoff
- venue

<a id="item-muse"></a>
### 144. MUSE: A Memory-Utilizing and Self-Evolving Agent (Learning on the Job: An Experience-Driven, Self-Evolving Agent for Long-Horizon Tasks)

2025  ·  arXiv 2510.08002  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08002)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **authors affiliation**:
> Cheng Yang (Central South University & Shanghai AI Laboratory), Xuemeng Yang, Licheng Wen (equal contribution; Shanghai AI Lab & Shanghai Innovation Institute), Daocheng Fu (Fudan University & Shanghai AI Lab), Jianbiao Mei, Rong Wu (Zhejiang University & Shanghai AI Lab), Pinlong Cai, Yufan Shen, Nianchen Deng, Botian Shi (corresponding; Shanghai AI Lab), Yu Qiao (Shanghai AI Lab), Haifeng Li (corresponding; Central South University). Primary affiliations: Central South University, Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, Fudan University, Shanghai Innovation Institute, Zhejiang University.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08002
- **code url**: https://github.com/KnowledgeXLab/MUSE (MIT license; benchmark harness at https://github.com/KnowledgeXLab/TheAgentCompanyForMuse)
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/KnowledgeXLab/MUSE (ranks #1 on TheAgentCompany leaderboard https://the-agent-company.com/#/leaderboard; last updated Oct 16 2025, ~91 stars)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> LLM-agent decision-making on long-horizon real-world productivity tasks: cross-application computer-use (web browsing, code editing, shell, file/spreadsheet/PDF manipulation, chat/project-management tools). Spans web + code + general OS tool-use within a simulated software-company environment.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, multi-application, single primary agent operating in a fixed environment E (chat clients, cloud storage, project management, code editors, browsers, OS) executing actions via a minimal general-purpose toolset. Tasks are long-horizon productivity tasks (often >40 and up to >100 action steps, spanning two or more apps). The core challenge is gradient-free test-time learning ('learning on the job'): the backbone LLM (Gemini-2.5 Flash by default, also DeepSeek-V3) is NOT fine-tuned; instead a natural-language Memory Module is incrementally built from the agent's own trajectories so performance R(t) improves over repeated trials. The framework is multi-agent internally (a Planning-Execution PE Agent and a separate third-party Reflect Agent supervisor, both sharing the same toolset). Supervision is autonomous/self-supervised: the Reflect Agent self-judges sub-task success/failure (no human labels) via truthfulness, deliverable, and data-fidelity checks; TAC's official protocol provides scoring only for final evaluation, not as a training signal.
- **what is retrieved**:
> Self-distilled, hierarchically organized experience at three abstraction levels: (1) Strategic Memory = high-level <Dilemma, Strategy/Resolution-Pattern> behavioral principles; (2) Procedural Memory = Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for sub-tasks, indexed by application then by SOP, capturing key analyses/precautions/core parameters/operational steps; (3) Tool Memory = per-tool static descriptions + dynamic post-use instructions ('muscle memory'). The agent actively retrieves Procedural-Memory SOP content on demand; Strategic and Tool memories are always loaded into the prompt rather than retrieved.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> GROWING/episodic self-written memory. The retrievable store (the Memory Module M = {M_strat, M_proc, M_tool}) is entirely self-generated from the agent's own past trajectories and grows across tasks/iterations; there is no static external corpus/KB/API doc store being retrieved. (Memory can be frozen for the final TAC full-benchmark evaluation after 3 continual-learning iterations, but it is grown online during learning.)
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Neither a fixed top-k ranking nor an explicit minimal-complete-set objective. Procedural-Memory retrieval is agent-initiated, on-demand fetching of specific SOP contents (the agent queries relevant SOPs by application/item when uncertain), so it is a precision-driven, variable-size lookup rather than a ranked top-k; the goal is to recover the relevant procedural guidance for the current sub-task, not to optimize a Recall@k metric.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve: yes (on-demand SOP/procedural lookup by application/item via a memory tool), Reuse: yes (retrieved SOPs/strategies/tool-notes injected to guide ReAct execution), Revise: yes (Reflect Agent verifies/replans; retry disables memory to discover novel methods; post-task global refinement generalizes/merges experiences), Retain: yes (successful sub-task trajectories distilled into new SOPs immediately, plus post-task Strategic/Tool memory writes and integration)].
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False. The paper frames itself as experience-driven, self-evolving agent memory / test-time learning ('learn on the job'), drawing on cognitive-science memory taxonomies; it does NOT cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner or use the term 'case-based reasoning'. It does analogize Procedural-Memory consultation to 'how human experts consult past cases', realizing CBR-like Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain under a memory framing (lineage near ExpeL/AWM/Memp).

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> workflow-routine / procedural SOP (problem-solution-style 'case' for a sub-task) is the primary retrieved unit (full content of an SOP: preconditions, steps, notes for a given application function). Secondary always-loaded units are guideline-rules (Strategic Memory <Dilemma,Strategy> principles) and tool-API usage notes (Tool Memory descriptions + dynamic instructions).
- **index source**:
> Growing memory, online/test-time-induced (hybrid two-stage construction). SOPs and other memories are induced at test time from the agent's own successful sub-task trajectories: added immediately after a successful sub-task for instant reuse, then globally refined (dedup/generalization) after the whole task. No offline pretraining of the store; it is built and refined during deployment.
- **index structure topology**:
> Hierarchical for Procedural Memory: indexed first by application (related platforms/APIs), then a second-level SOP index per sub-task (application -> function -> SOP). Crucially, a lightweight SOP INDEX is separated from heavy SOP CONTENT (p = (index_p, content_p)). Strategic Memory is a flat concise set of <Dilemma,Strategy> key-value principles; Tool Memory is keyed per tool. No dense vector index or knowledge graph is used for the SOPs; retrieval is via an application/item-keyed lookup tool (access_guide / a_mem).
- **retriever type**:
> LLM-as-retriever / agent-initiated tool-based lookup. The PE Agent invokes a dedicated memory-retrieval tool (access_guide, a_mem) with a batch request of application/item names to fetch the relevant SOP content; selection is driven by the agent's reasoning over the lightweight SOP index rather than by BM25/dense embedding similarity. Strategic and Tool memories are not retrieved (always prompt-loaded).
- **retriever learning signal**:
> none (no trained retriever). Retrieval/selection is performed by the off-the-shelf backbone LLM reasoning over the loaded SOP index and choosing which SOP content to fetch via a tool call; there is no contrastive training, LM-feedback retriever, preference/Bradley-Terry, RL, or value-based retrieval policy. (What IS learned online is the memory CONTENT, not the retriever.)
- **query construction**:
> Agent-formed intent query: the PE Agent, given the current sub-task st_i = (desc_i, goal_i) and the loaded SOP index, formulates a batch request naming the relevant application(s) and item(s) (e.g., batch_requests={'RocketChat': ['Login','Create Channel']}) to pull SOP content. Prompt engineering encourages the agent to query for relevant experience at the start of each sub-task and whenever uncertain. No embedding-based query vector; query = LLM-selected app/item keys.
- **query granularity**:
> sub-task / step-level (proactive, on-demand). Procedural retrieval is keyed to the current sub-task and can be issued at any point during execution when the agent faces uncertainty (not a single one-shot at t=0 for the whole task, and not a fixed per-step schedule). Strategic/Tool memory injection is task-level (loaded once at initialization).
- **when to retrieve**:
> active / agent-initiated (uncertainty-triggered, on-demand) for Procedural Memory: the agent proactively queries detailed SOPs 'when facing uncertainty', mimicking a human expert consulting past cases; prompt-encouraged at sub-task start. By contrast Strategic and Tool memories are one-shot loaded at initialization (always-on, not retrieved).
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> agent-initiated request driven by the agent's own assessment of uncertainty: the PE Agent decides within its ReAct (Thought-Action-Observation) loop to emit a memory-retrieval action (a_mem / access_guide) when it needs decision support, and is prompted to prioritize querying at the beginning of each sub-task. Not token-confidence, attention/uncertainty scores, a learned complexity classifier, or reflection tokens.
- **reranking**: None. There is no cross-encoder, RRF, hierarchy-aware, or instruction-tuned reranking stage; the agent directly fetches the SOP content(s) it selects from the index via the lookup tool.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Index-content separation as the main efficiency mechanism: only the lightweight SOP index is loaded at startup; full SOP content is loaded on demand (progressive disclosure), keeping context small. Beyond this, retrieved SOP content is used largely as-is; refinement (dedup, generalization, merging) is applied at WRITE/consolidation time (post-task global refinement) rather than as a post-retrieval distillation of fetched items. Tool Memory's dynamic instruction is appended with the observation to guide the next action.
- **tool document engineering**:
