> Tool descriptions are learned/engineered as Tool Memory: each tool has a Static Description (loaded at init explaining core functionality) and a Dynamic Instruction (returned with the observation after use, guiding the next action), and Tool Memory is updated/refined by the Reflect Agent after each task from successful usage (i.e., experience-augmented tool docs with usage caveats), rather than raw docstrings or synthetic-query-augmented embeddings.
- **index content separation**:
> Yes - this is a defining feature. Procedural Memory SOPs are stored as p = (index_p, content_p); only the lightweight index of all SOPs is loaded into context at sub-task start, and the full content is fetched on demand via a dedicated tool (a_mem / access_guide). This SOP-index-then-content progressive disclosure minimizes context overhead while enabling low-cost experience reuse within the LLM's context limit.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Partially applicable: the agent uses a minimal general-purpose toolset (browser operator built on the browser-use framework, code interpreter / run_python_code, shell / run_cmd, GPT-4o vision extractor, memory retriever access_guide) rather than a large live external API registry; there is no RapidAPI/RESTful/MCP tool-store with CRUD auto-sync. The Procedural-Memory SOP store IS dynamically updated (added/refined) during operation, but it indexes self-induced procedures, not third-party tools.
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> Partial/implicit. Procedural SOPs and Tool dynamic instructions encode operational sequencing (e.g., 'always follow a click with browser_update', 'after input locate and click Save/Submit'), capturing prerequisite/next-action dependencies between tool calls; but there is no explicit inter-tool dependency graph, bipartite KG, or dependency-aware reranking.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> prompt augmentation + procedural guidance reuse. Retrieved SOP content is injected into the PE Agent's ReAct context to guide composing primitive tool actions into the workflow for the sub-task (case/SOP reuse). Strategic Memory principles are loaded into the system prompt to steer global strategy; Tool Memory static descriptions are in the system prompt and dynamic instructions are returned with each observation to guide the next action. No fine-tuning or latent-token injection; all knowledge is natural-language in-context (making it LLM-agnostic/transferable).
- **planning integration**:
> retrieve-then-plan/act at the sub-task level inside a 'Plan-Execute-Reflect-Memorize' loop. The PE Agent decomposes the task into an ordered sub-task queue Q, and for each sub-task first queries Procedural Memory for relevant SOP guidance, then runs a memory-enhanced ReAct loop; after each sub-task the Reflect Agent evaluates and the PE Agent adaptively replans/updates Q. Retrieval is interleaved within sub-task execution (the agent can re-query mid-execution). Not MCTS/tree-search; planning is iterative queue maintenance with reflect-driven replanning and a retry that explicitly disables Procedural Memory to encourage exploration of novel methods.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> per-tool-call within a sub-task rollout: memory retrieval is one possible action in the agent's (Thought, Action, Observation) ReAct iteration, issued on demand (typically at sub-task start and when uncertain). It is therefore finer than per-answer/per-task but coarser than a fixed per-token schedule; the natural unit is the sub-task and the individual tool-call step.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> LLM-prompted adaptation + execution-feedback-driven revision. Retrieved SOPs are not copied verbatim: tool notes explicitly tell the agent guides 'may not match current UI; adapt as needed' and to prioritize adaptive exploration on discrepancies. The Reflect Agent's verification drives replanning, and a memory-free retry lets the agent discover novel methods when stored knowledge is wrong/inapplicable. Post-task distillation generalizes the adapted solution back into refined memory.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Structured natural-language notes. Procedural Memory SOPs are free-text structured guides (Application | Function | Preconditions/Steps/Notes). Strategic Memory is <Dilemma/Principle, Description/Strategy> pairs. Tool Memory is per-tool Description + Instruction text. Everything is human-readable natural language (not raw trajectories injected verbatim, not executable programs, not latent/soft tokens).
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Multi-level by design: (1) distilled high-level strategy/principle (Strategic Memory, macro behavioral paradigms); (2) reusable procedural workflow/SOP for tool-sequence combinations (Procedural Memory); (3) single-tool usage guidance ('muscle memory', Tool Memory). Raw action trajectories are explicitly converted into these structured abstractions to enhance reusability and reduce redundant exploration.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> (1) Independent third-party Reflect Agent supervises execution to suppress hallucinations (e.g., false 'task complete' beliefs) via an ordered checklist: Truthfulness Verification (ground conclusions in real environmental feedback), Deliverable Verification, Data Fidelity; using trajectory referencing + active verification (proactively re-interacting with the environment to cross-check). (2) Only SUCCESSFUL trajectories become SOPs, and post-task global refinement deduplicates/generalizes/merges to maintain quality and prevent context bloat. (3) The retry mechanism disables Procedural Memory when existing knowledge is 'erroneous or inapplicable', guarding against stale/incorrect retrieved guidance. (4) Tool-memory notes warn the agent that guides may not match current UI and to prioritize adaptive exploration on discrepancies.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> Procedural + workflow + strategic experiential memory (hierarchical, natural-language, long-term). Composite M = {Strategic (semantic/strategic guidelines), Procedural (SOP workflows), Tool (per-tool procedural notes)}; not a vector-embedding store, not a knowledge graph, not latent.
- **write back**:
> Yes. After each successful sub-task the Reflect Agent distills the trajectory into a new SOP (p_new) added to Procedural Memory; after the whole task it distills higher-level Strategic Memory (<Dilemma,Resolution-Pattern>) and Tool Memory, then performs a global refinement/integration of all three memory types.
- **online growth**:
> Yes (during learning). The Memory Module grows continuously across sub-tasks/tasks/iterations at test time (3 continual-learning iterations over an 18-task set, carrying knowledge forward). For the final TAC full-175-task evaluation the memory is FROZEN after those 3 iterations, demonstrating zero-shot generalization, but the mechanism is online-growing by construction.
- **write back trigger**:
> Two-stage, reflective and outcome-gated: (a) immediately after a sub-task, on success the Reflect Agent writes a new SOP to Procedural Memory (and on failure generates a failure-cause report R_fail that triggers replanning, not a stored memory item); (b) after the entire task completes, a post-task distillation writes/updates Strategic and Tool memories from the full trajectory and globally refines all memory. Writing is autonomous/self-judged (no human validation in the default fully-autonomous setting; the architecture also permits optional human add/delete/modify/query).
- **failure experience usage**:
> Largely success-only for persistent memory: SOPs are summarized only from SUCCESSFUL sub-task trajectories. Failures are used transiently/diagnostically (failure-cause analysis R_fail feeds immediate replanning and a memory-free retry to encourage exploration) and inform the distilled Strategic <Dilemma, Resolution-Pattern> principles (which encode how dilemmas were overcome), but failed trajectories are not stored as standalone negative/contrastive memory items. The Discussion notes contrasting successful vs failed trajectories as future work.
- **memory evolution update**:
> Refine-and-merge, not pure append-only. Procedural Memory: SOPs are added immediately, then post-task global refinement performs deduplication and generalization. Strategic Memory: 'updated, merged, and refined after each task, always maintaining a concise size'. Tool Memory: updated by the Reflect Agent after each task. The whole module undergoes a periodic 'integrate new and old knowledge, eliminate redundancy, generalize common patterns' upgrade (dedup-merge + generalize + refine-overwrite), keeping size bounded.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No. Retrieval/selection is performed by the off-the-shelf LLM reasoning (prompt-encouraged tool calls), not an RL-/value-optimized or otherwise trained retrieval policy. There is no M-MDP soft Q-learning or learned ranker; the learning happens in the memory content, not in a retrieval policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Cross-MODEL sharing rather than cross-agent. Because memory is stored in natural language, it is explicitly LLM-agnostic: experience accumulated by one model can be transferred to another (validated by transferring Gemini-2.5-Flash-accumulated memory to DeepSeek-V3). Internally it is a two-agent system (PE + Reflect) sharing one Memory Module, not a population of agents with shared memory; there is no multi-agent collective memory across heterogeneous frameworks.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> TheAgentCompany (TAC) (Xu et al. 2024): 175 tasks across six employee roles (HR, PM, SDE, DS/Data Science, Finance, Admin/BizMaster) in a simulated software company (RocketChat, GitLab, Plane, ownCloud, etc.). Subsets used: T_cl (18 tasks, continual learning, all six roles); T_hard (12 hard tasks where strong models near-zero). NPCs powered by GPT-4o; visual extractor uses GPT-4o.
- **benchmark family**:
> web + code + decision-making productivity / computer-use agent benchmark (TheAgentCompany family). Closest to web (WebArena-style) and code (SWE-style) but specifically a long-horizon cross-application productivity benchmark; not QA/multi-hop, embodied, tool-retrieval (ToolBench), memory (LoCoMo), or decision-RL (D4RL).
- **baselines**:
> On TAC full 175: OWL-RolePlay (GPT-4o + o3-mini); OpenHands (Gemini-1.5-Pro, Gemini-2.0-Flash, Gemini-2.5-Pro); OpenHands-Versa (Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Claude-4-Sonnet, the previous SOTA). On T_hard: OpenHands-Versa (Claude-4-Sonnet), OpenHands (Gemini-2.5-Pro), plus MUSE w/o memory. Open-source comparison (T_cl): OpenHands with Llama-3.1-405B, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen-2.5-72B vs MUSE+DeepSeek-V3. Internal baselines: MUSE w/o Memory Module, and No-Reflection variant.
- **key metrics**:
> TAC official protocol: partial completion score S_partial = 0.5*(Completed_ckpt/Total_ckpt) + 0.5*S_full (S_full in {0,1}); aggregate checkpoint score S_ckpt (completed checkpoints / total checkpoints across all tasks); PCR = Perfect Completion Rate (fraction fully solved). Reported as averages over tasks (5 runs averaged for continual-learning).
- **headline result**:
> New SOTA on TAC full 175-task benchmark with a lightweight Gemini-2.5-Flash: Avg S_partial = 51.78% (S_ckpt = 59.92%, 465/776 checkpoints, PCR = 41.14%), the first agent to exceed 50% S_partial on TAC and ~20% relative improvement over the previous SOTA OpenHands-Versa + Claude-4-Sonnet (S_partial 43.19%, S_ckpt 50.52%, PCR 33.14%). Memory was learned from only ~10% of tasks (the 18-task T_cl set) and frozen for evaluation.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Continual learning (T_cl, 18 tasks, 5 runs): both S_ckpt and S_partial grow monotonically over 3 iterations; final round beats the memory-less baseline by >10%. (2) Generalization (T_hard, 12 tasks): MUSE+Gemini-2.5-Flash w/o memory already S_partial 23.65% (S_ckpt 30.51%, 18/59 ckpt) vs OpenHands-Versa+Claude-4-Sonnet 2.00% and OpenHands+Gemini-2.5-Pro 3.00%; adding pre-learned (frozen) memory raises MUSE to S_partial 33.41% (S_ckpt 40.68%, 24/59) -> zero-shot transfer of memory. (3) Reflect Agent ablation (T_cl, both w/o memory): No-Reflection 43.21% S_partial (S_ckpt 63.53%) vs MUSE 55.85% (S_ckpt 66.12%) -> reflection is indispensable. (4) Cross-model / open-source (T_cl): MUSE+DeepSeek-V3 w/o memory 28.01% S_partial (beats OpenHands open-source: Llama-3.1-405B 9.78%, Llama-3.3-70B 5.84%, Qwen-2.5-72B 6.50%); MUSE+DeepSeek-V3 w/ (Gemini-learned) memory 36.75% -> memory is model-agnostic and transferable.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No. Only end-to-end task metrics (S_partial, S_ckpt, PCR) are reported; no intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k/nDCG/completeness) are reported separately, since retrieval here is agent-initiated on-demand memory lookup rather than a ranked-retrieval benchmark.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Mostly outcome, with process granularity via checkpoints. S_partial and S_ckpt give partial-progress (intermediate checkpoint) credit beyond binary full completion, so intermediate progress is scored. The paper also gives qualitative process analysis (two case studies on adaptive multi-step strategies, ~20 sub-tasks / >100 actions), but does not report quantitative reasoning-faithfulness or step-wise retrieval-accuracy metrics. Step counts/latency/token cost are not tabulated.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Qualitatively strong but not quantified in money/tokens/latency. The central efficiency claim is matching/beating much stronger models (Claude-4-Sonnet, Gemini-2.5-Pro) using only the lightweight Gemini-2.5-Flash, and reducing redundant exploration by reusing structured memory (pruning the decision space, focusing on effective solutions). Context efficiency is achieved by index-content separation (load only the SOP index; fetch content on demand) and a concise, refined memory. The paper does not report retrieval-call counts, API cost, latency/speedup, or token-savings numbers (max N=20 actions per sub-task attempt; one retry).
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Budget-conscious via progressive disclosure: only the lightweight SOP index is loaded at startup; full SOP content is fetched on demand by the agent (no fixed-k or reranked-then-truncated cap). Strategic Memory is deliberately kept concise (merged/refined to a small size) and Tool static descriptions are loaded at init. Per-sub-task attempt action budget N=20 (with one retry). No explicit token cap or fixed top-k for memory items reported.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (primary research paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A (uses the existing TheAgentCompany benchmark, 175 Docker-image tasks; partial-credit checkpoint grading with LLM-assisted graders). Authors curate two subsets from TAC (T_cl 18 moderate-difficulty tasks; T_hard 12 near-zero-score tasks), manually inspected for correctness and balanced across the six roles, but construct no new benchmark.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> ReAct (Yao et al. 2023) for the Thought-Action-Observation loop; procedural/experience-memory line ExpeL (Zhao et al. 2024, trajectory->NL insights/rules), Agent Workflow Memory (Wang et al. 2024, reusable workflows), Memp (Fang et al. 2025, learnable lifelong procedural memory); memory-management work Mem0 (Chhikara et al. 2025) and MemInsight (Salama et al. 2025); Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023) and SAGE (Liang et al. 2025) for self-reflection; skill/toolset self-evolution (Voyager, OS-Copilot, Iterative Experience Refinement, Agent-KB, Alita). Built on the browser-use framework for browser actions; evaluated on TheAgentCompany (Xu et al. 2024); backbone Gemini-2.5 (Comanici et al. 2025) and DeepSeek-V3.
- **contrasts with**:
> Static, test-time-frozen LLM agents (cannot learn from experience); massive-API tool agents like ToolLLM (Qin et al. 2023) and Gorilla (Patil et al. 2024) - MUSE instead uses a minimal toolset and learns to compose primitives; embedding/vector-DB or knowledge-graph memory stores (e.g., FAISS-, Neo4j-based) - MUSE uses natural-language, application-keyed SOP index with index-content separation; prior procedural-memory methods (ExpeL, AWM, Memp) validated mainly on short-horizon text/web benchmarks (HotpotQA, ALFWorld, WebShop, WebArena, Mind2Web) that lack TAC's long-horizon cross-application complexity; fine-tuning and sparse-reward RL approaches (deemed intractable / hard to reward for >100-step productivity tasks).
- **lineage**:
> Group F (decision/memory/experience-driven self-evolving agents). A 2025 procedural/strategic experience-memory framework extending the ExpeL -> Agent Workflow Memory -> Memp lineage of self-distilled, test-time-learned agent memory. Distinctive contributions: (a) a hierarchical three-level Memory Module (Strategic / Procedural / Tool) at differing abstraction levels; (b) SOP index-content separation enabling low-cost, agent-initiated on-demand procedural retrieval; (c) a PE + independent Reflect dual-agent 'Plan-Execute-Reflect-Memorize' loop with autonomous self-verification; (d) natural-language, LLM-agnostic memory enabling cross-model experience transfer; (e) new SOTA on the long-horizon cross-application productivity benchmark TheAgentCompany with a lightweight backbone.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- venue

<a id="item-mem0"></a>
### 145. Mem0: Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory

2025  ·  arXiv 2504.19413  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.19413)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **authors affiliation**: Prateek Chhikara, Dev Khant, Saket Aryan, Taranjeet Singh, Deshraj Yadav — all at Mem0 (mem0.ai; correspondence research@mem0.ai).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.19413
- **code url**: https://github.com/mem0ai/mem0
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/mem0ai/mem0 (continuously-maintained open-source 'universal memory layer for AI Agents'; the paper's Mem0/Mem0g architectures are productized in this repo and at https://mem0.ai)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Long-term conversational memory for LLM-driven AI agents; long-context multi-session dialogue question answering (QA over prior conversation history).
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, online, multi-session single-agent assistant setting: fixed LLM context windows cannot retain consistency over prolonged dialogues. Memory is built incrementally as conversation turns arrive (message pairs ingested one at a time, with an asynchronously-refreshed running summary), and queried at test time to answer questions about earlier sessions. No task supervision / no training of the underlying LLM; all memory operations are LLM-prompted with GPT-4o-mini. Evaluated offline on the LoCoMo benchmark (10 multi-session conversations, ~600 dialogues / ~26k tokens each, ~200 QA pairs each).
- **what is retrieved**: Salient natural-language memory facts (Mem0) extracted/consolidated from dialogue; in Mem0g, entity nodes and relationship triplets (subject, relation, object) from a knowledge graph. These are agent-written experiences/facts about the conversation, not external documents.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> GROWING / episodic memory the agent writes: memory is dynamically extracted from the ongoing conversation and consolidated into a persistent store (vector DB for Mem0, Neo4j graph for Mem0g). Not a static external corpus; the conversation history itself is the source from which the growing memory is induced.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k similarity ranking at query time (top-s for the update step, threshold-ranked triplets for the graph variant). Not framed as recovering a complete minimal set; objective is precise salient-fact retrieval under a small token budget. Mem0 retrieves only the most salient memories rather than fixed-size chunks.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False — the paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it frames itself as a memory-centric architecture (extract / consolidate / retrieve).

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Mem0: a single consolidated natural-language memory fact (dense memory) per item. Mem0g: KG entities (nodes with type + embedding + timestamp) and relationship triplets (vs, r, vd) / KG-subgraph. So the retrievable unit is a memory fact (Mem0) or a (entity, relation, entity) triplet / subgraph (Mem0g).
- **index source**: Growing memory built online/incrementally at ingestion time from the conversation (online/test-time-induced). The store is populated as message pairs arrive and is queried later; it is not a frozen offline corpus.
- **index structure topology**: Mem0: flat dense vector index over natural-language memory facts (similarity search in a vector database). Mem0g: directed labeled knowledge GRAPH G=(V,E,L) (entities as nodes, relations as edges) stored in Neo4j, with per-entity embeddings enabling semantic node lookup.
- **retriever type**:
> Dense embedding retrieval (semantic similarity over OpenAI text-embedding-3-small / dense embeddings). Mem0g adds dual graph retrieval: entity-centric node lookup (embedding similarity then graph traversal) plus semantic-triplet matching (query embedding vs triplet text encodings). No BM25; retriever is off-the-shelf dense embeddings, not learned.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None (off-the-shelf). The retriever uses fixed pretrained dense embeddings (text-embedding-3-small) with cosine similarity; no contrastive training, no RL, no LM-feedback fine-tuning of the retriever. The 'intelligence' is in LLM-based extraction/consolidation, not in a trained retriever.
- **query construction**:
> Raw user query is embedded for similarity search. In Mem0g, the query is also processed two ways: (1) entity extraction from the query to anchor graph nodes, and (2) encoding the whole query as a dense vector matched against triplet text. During memory writing, the extraction prompt is constructed from the running conversation summary S, the last m recent messages, and the new message pair.
- **query granularity**: Task-/query-level (one retrieval per incoming question at answer time). Memory writing operates at the message-pair (turn) level. Mem0g uses a two-level query (entity-centric + semantic-triplet) but still at the per-question granularity.
- **when to retrieve**: One-shot at query time (single retrieval per question to fetch relevant memories before answer generation). Memory updates happen iteratively/incrementally during ingestion, but retrieval-for-answering is one-shot.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule: retrieval is triggered once per user query (answer time). During ingestion, the update-phase similarity retrieval (top-s) is triggered per extracted candidate fact. No uncertainty/confidence/learned-router trigger.
- **reranking**: No dedicated learned reranking stage. Mem0g ranks candidate triplets by decreasing similarity and applies a configurable relevance threshold; results are similarity-ordered. No cross-encoder / RRF / instruction-tuned reranker reported.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Refinement happens primarily at write time, not at read time: the LLM consolidates raw turns into concise salient facts (compression/distillation) and dedups/updates via ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP so the store contains denoised facts. At read time it is essentially similarity top-k with (for Mem0g) threshold filtering; the key noise reduction is the upfront fact distillation that surfaces precise cues to the LLM.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A — no tool/skill retrieval; memory items are not tool documents.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A — no external tool index / RapidAPI / MCP integration in the paper; the memory store is updated dynamically via the LLM tool-call (function-calling) ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP CRUD operations on the memory DB.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A — no inter-tool dependency modeling (not a tool-retrieval method).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**: Prompt augmentation: retrieved memory facts (Mem0) or graph triplets/subgraph (Mem0g) are injected as context into the LLM prompt to ground answer generation for the user query. No training signal, no skill execution.
- **planning integration**: Retrieve-then-answer (one-shot exemplar/context injection at answer time); there is no multi-step planning, MCTS, or tree search. Memory writing is a separate incremental extract-then-update pipeline decoupled from answering.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer: a single retrieval feeds the full answer generation for each question. Retrieval is not interleaved per-CoT-step or per-token. (At ingestion, the consolidation tool-call operates per-extracted-fact, but that is memory maintenance, not reasoning-time search.)
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> N/A — not a CBR case-adaptation method; retrieved memories are injected verbatim as prompt context (no LLM-prompted case revision of past solutions). The closest mechanism is LLM-driven memory consolidation (ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP) applied to stored facts, not to retrieved answers.
- **retrieved item representation**: Mem0: distilled/structured natural-language memory facts (concise consolidated statements, ~7k tokens per conversation). Mem0g: structured graph entities + relationship triplets / subgraph (~14k tokens per conversation). Injected as text into the prompt.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Distilled fact / structured note rather than raw trajectory: Mem0 stores consolidated salient facts (not raw dialogue); Mem0g stores state-aware relational triplets (entity-relation-entity) with timestamps. Higher abstraction than raw chunks but lower than reusable workflows/skills.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Write-time consolidation is the main mechanism: the LLM extracts only salient facts and the update phase (ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP, conflict detection + LLM update-resolver in Mem0g) removes contradictions and redundancy, so the indexed store is low-noise. Mem0g marks obsolete relationships invalid (rather than deleting) for temporal consistency. No retriever-aware adversarial training or read-time relevance self-reflection module.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: episodic + graph: Mem0 is an episodic natural-language fact memory; Mem0g is a graph (knowledge-graph) memory of entities and relationships. Persistent long-term memory across multi-session dialogues.
- **write back**: True — the system stores new memories. Mem0 extracts salient facts from each message pair and writes them via ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP tool calls; Mem0g writes entities and relationship triplets into the Neo4j graph with conflict resolution.
- **online growth**: True — the retrievable store grows during deployment/ingestion: memories are added incrementally as the conversation proceeds (incremental processing paradigm), not frozen after an offline induction pass.
- **write back trigger**:
> Per-turn (per message pair): each new (m_{t-1}, m_t) pair triggers extraction of candidate facts, then per-candidate the update phase selects ADD / UPDATE / DELETE / NOOP against the top-s similar existing memories. Writes are continuous during ingestion, not gated on task success or human validation.
- **failure experience usage**: N/A / not applicable — the memory stores conversational facts, not success/failure problem-solving experiences. There is no success-vs-failure contrastive storage; DELETE/UPDATE handle contradicted or outdated facts but this is fact correction, not failure-experience reuse.
- **memory evolution update**:
> Stored entries are mutated after writing: dedup-merge and delta/refine-overwrite via UPDATE (augment existing memory), DELETE (remove contradicted memory), NOOP (no change). Mem0g additionally does conflict detection + an LLM update-resolver that marks obsolete relationships invalid (soft-delete) rather than physically removing them, preserving temporal reasoning. So: dedup-merge + delta-update + refine-overwrite + (graph) link-and-evolve with soft-invalidation.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: False — retrieval/selection is fixed dense-similarity top-k (and threshold filtering for the graph), not a learned/RL-optimized policy. The LLM does choose memory-edit operations (ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP) via reasoning, but selection of what to retrieve is not a trained policy.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> LoCoMo (LOCOMO) long-term conversational memory benchmark (Maharana et al., 2024): 10 multi-session conversations, ~600 dialogues and ~26k tokens each, ~200 QA pairs each; question types: single-hop, multi-hop, temporal, open-domain (adversarial category excluded for lack of ground-truth answers).
- **benchmark family**: memory (LoCoMo) — long-term conversational memory QA; conceptually multi-session multi-hop dialogue QA.
- **baselines**:
> Six categories: (i) established LoCoMo benchmark methods — LoCoMo, ReadAgent, MemoryBank, MemGPT, A-Mem (and A-Mem* re-run for J score); (ii) open-source memory — LangMem (Hot Path); (iii) RAG with chunk sizes {128,256,512,1024,2048,4096,8192} and k in {1,2}; (iv) full-context (entire ~26k-token conversation in context); (v) proprietary model — OpenAI ChatGPT memory feature (gpt-4o-mini); (vi) memory provider platform — Zep.
- **key metrics**: Performance: F1 score (F1), BLEU-1 (B1), and LLM-as-a-Judge score (J, mean over 10 runs +/-1 std). Deployment: token consumption (tiktoken cl100k_base), search latency and total latency at p50/p95 (seconds). All run with GPT-4o-mini, temperature 0.
- **headline result**:
> On LoCoMo with LLM-as-a-Judge (J): Mem0 achieves ~26% relative improvement in J over OpenAI's memory; Mem0g ~2% higher overall than base Mem0. Overall J: Mem0 66.88%, Mem0g 68.44% (best non-full-context). Mem0 cuts p95 total latency ~91% (1.44s vs full-context ~17.1s) and saves >90% token cost. Per-category best J: single-hop Mem0 67.13, multi-hop Mem0 51.15, open-domain Zep 76.60 (Mem0g 75.71), temporal Mem0g 58.13.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No — intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG) are not reported separately; evaluation is end-to-end answer quality (F1, B1, J) plus deployment metrics (latency, tokens). Retrieval quality is measured only via downstream answer accuracy.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Primarily outcome metrics (final answer F1/B1/J). Deployment/process efficiency (search vs total latency at p50/p95, token consumption, memory construction time) is reported, but reasoning-faithfulness / step-wise retrieval accuracy is not.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Strong efficiency emphasis: Mem0 lowest search latency (p50 0.148s, p95 0.200s) and total (p50 0.708s, p95 1.440s); ~91% lower p95 total latency vs full-context (~17.117s p95) and >90% token-cost savings; memory footprint ~7k tokens (Mem0) / ~14k (Mem0g) per conversation vs Zep >600k and full-context ~26k. Mem0g costs more latency (p50 1.091s, p95 2.590s) for +1.56 overall J. Full-context is most accurate (~73% overall J) but computationally prohibitive.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k selection: m=10 recent messages for extraction context and s=10 similar memories compared during the update phase. Retrieval at query time returns top similarity-ranked memories/triplets (Mem0g threshold-filtered). RAG baselines use k in {1,2}; full-context uses ~26k tokens. Memory injected as context is compact (~7k/14k tokens per conversation store).
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A — not a survey.
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A — Mem0 is a method, not a benchmark; it evaluates on the existing LoCoMo benchmark (10 conversations, ~600 dialogues / ~26k tokens each, ~200 QA pairs each, human-curated multi-session dialogues with ground-truth answers; adversarial category excluded).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Builds on memory-augmented LLM agents and RAG: MemGPT, MemoryBank, ReadAgent, A-Mem, the LoCoMo benchmark (Maharana et al., 2024); dense embedding retrieval (OpenAI text-embedding-3-small); LLM function-calling / tool-call for memory operations (GPT-4o-mini); graph-memory ideas (Zhang et al., 2022) realized in Neo4j.
- **contrasts with**:
> Explicitly positioned against full-context processing (entire conversation in context), naive RAG over conversation chunks, the OpenAI ChatGPT memory feature, LangMem, A-Mem, MemGPT/MemoryBank/ReadAgent, and the Zep memory platform (argues Zep over-stores ~600k tokens and has slow async graph construction).
- **lineage**: Group F (decision/memory) — long-term agent memory / experience-memory lineage: growing episodic + graph memory that the agent writes and retrieves, contrasting classic static-corpus RAG planners; productionized memory layer for conversational agents.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- ablations
- cbr_cycle_coverage
- cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing
- index_content_separation
- venue

<a id="item-memgen"></a>
### 146. MemGen: Weaving Generative Latent Memory for Self-Evolving Agents

2025  ·  arXiv 2509.24704  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.24704)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**: arXiv:2509.24704 (cs.CL); accepted at ICLR 2026 (per official GitHub README)
- **authors affiliation**: Guibin Zhang (co-first), Muxin Fu (co-first), Shuicheng Yan; National University of Singapore
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.24704
- **code url**: https://github.com/bingreeky/MemGen (also reachable via https://github.com/KANABOON1/MemGen); checkpoints at https://huggingface.co/Kana-s/MemGen
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (single-paper code repo, not a maintained leaderboard/paper-list)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Multi-domain LLM-agent decision-making and reasoning: web/open-domain QA (TriviaQA, PopQA), embodied action (ALFWorld), math reasoning (AQuA, GSM8K, MATH), scientific reasoning (GPQA), and code generation (KodCode, BigCodeBench).
- **problem setting**:
> Agent memory for self-evolving LLM agents. An agent powered by a frozen core LLM (the 'reasoner') interacts with an environment, producing trajectories tau=(s0,a0,...,sT) whose success is scored by a reward R(tau). Given a history of past experiences H={(x_i,tau_i)}, the goal is to jointly leverage memory M and policy pi_theta to maximize expected reward on new tasks. Setting is single-agent; supervision comes from official training splits of the evaluated datasets (task reward / answer correctness). MemGen trains lightweight memory modules (LoRA adapters) on these experiences while keeping the reasoner frozen; both offline training and test-time autoregressive generation are interactive at the token level. Positioned against parametric memory (which alters reasoner weights) and retrieval-based memory (which externalizes experience to a database).
- **what is retrieved**:
> Machine-native latent memory: a fixed-length sequence of K latent token embeddings (M_t in R^{K x d_model}) generated on the fly by a learned 'memory weaver' from the agent's current hidden cognitive state. It is generated/synthesized rather than retrieved from a text store; optionally textual experiences can be retrieved from an external memory system (e.g., MemoryBank, ExpeL) and fused into the weaver's input (Appendix E).
- **retrieval grounding**:
> Primarily GROWING/internalized parametric memory: experiences are internalized into the weaver's LoRA parameters (a generative, not database, store). Can be HYBRID: an external retrieval system can supply textual memory that is merged with the hook and fed to the weaver. Default mode does not query a static external corpus.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Neither top-k ranking nor completeness recovery. There is no ranked candidate set; the weaver generates a fixed-length latent memory M_t of K tokens (K in {2,4,8}, ablated 2->32) at each invocation. The 'selection' decision is binary INVOKE/SKIP per sentence boundary, learned to be sparse and strategically placed.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> Not framed as CBR. Loosely: Retrieve = generative recall of latent memory (no discrete case retrieval); Reuse = latent tokens woven into reasoning; Revise = N/A (no explicit case adaptation); Retain = experiences internalized into weaver LoRA parameters during training. Flags: [Retrieve(generative), Reuse, no-Revise, Retain(parametric)].
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is framed via human cognitive neuroscience analogy (hippocampus/prefrontal cortex, working/procedural/planning memory).

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: Latent token sequence / soft tokens: a fixed-length K-by-d_model matrix of continuous hidden-state embeddings ('machine-native latent memory'), generated per invocation. Not a discrete demo, trajectory, document, or tool.
- **index source**:
> Growing/online-induced parametric store: experiential knowledge from offline training trajectories is internalized exclusively into the memory weaver's LoRA parameters (reasoner left frozen). No discrete external index by default; an optional hybrid mode can attach a retrieval database. The latent memory itself is regenerated at inference (test-time) conditioned on the current state.
- **index structure topology**:
> No explicit index structure (the 'store' is the weaver's parameters). Emergent organization: post-hoc t-SNE/K-means analysis shows generated latent memories self-cluster by domain and by functional role (planning / procedural / working memory), i.e., an implicit, unsupervised hierarchical organization rather than an engineered topology.
- **retriever type**: Generative neural module ('memory weaver'): a LoRA adapter on the frozen reasoner that maps the current hidden-state context H_{t,<j} to a latent memory matrix M_t. This is generation-as-retrieval (no BM25/dense/index lookup in the default setting).
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Learned via downstream task reward. The weaver is trained to maximize expected reward R over past trajectories, with two variants: MemGen-SFT (supervised/SFT-style updates) and MemGen-GRPO (RL with GRPO). The memory trigger is trained separately by reinforcement learning with a reward-adaptive sparsity penalty. Both modules optimized for task effectiveness, not similarity labels.
- **query construction**:
> The 'query'/stimulus is the reasoner's current internal cognitive state: the sequence of hidden-state vectors H_{t,<j}=(h_{t,1},...,h_{t,j-1}) accumulated up to the current token j. This same hook is consumed by both the trigger (to decide INVOKE/SKIP) and the weaver (to synthesize M_t). No textual query is formed by default.
- **query granularity**: Token/sentence-level (fine-grained, within-step). The trigger evaluates at delimiter tokens (commas, periods) during action generation, so memory is invoked at sentence granularity within each reasoning step, far finer than task-level (Expel) or step-level (AgentKB) invocation.
- **when to retrieve**: Active / adaptive: a learned memory trigger decides on-demand, at sentence boundaries during token-by-token generation, whether to invoke memory (INVOKE vs SKIP). Frequency self-adapts to task difficulty (more invocations on harder/familiar domains, fewer in unfamiliar ones).
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Learned trigger over the reasoner's hidden states. A LoRA-based trigger T_trigger reads H_{t,<j} and outputs an invocation probability p_j=sigma(T_trigger(...)); d_j ~ Bernoulli(p_j) in {INVOKE,SKIP}. Gated to fire only at a predefined delimiter token set D (sentence-granularity activation). Trained by RL with a reward-adaptive penalty using mean activation probability of high-reward trajectories as the reference threshold p-bar.
- **reranking**: None. No candidate set is produced or reranked; memory is generated directly as latent tokens.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> None in the conventional sense. The latent memory is itself a 'selective reconstruction' synthesized by the weaver (analogized to hippocampal consolidation) rather than a verbatim restatement; no rerank/compress/distill stage over retrieved text. Optional hybrid mode fuses external textual memory into the weaver input before latent synthesis.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tools/documents are indexed).
- **index content separation**: N/A (no separated lightweight index vs heavy content; memory is generated from weaver parameters).
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no external tool index or integration protocol).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no tool retrieval; no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Latent-token injection. The generated latent memory M_t is prepended to the reasoner's current hidden states H_{t,<j}; the frozen reasoner then resumes autoregressive generation conditioned on this enriched context (a_t ~ pi_theta(.|s_t, z_{t,<j}, M_t)). Memory directly conditions the model's internal computation rather than being appended as prompt text.
- **planning integration**:
> Per-step / per-token interleaved within reasoning. Memory is woven into the ongoing generation autoregressively (generate -> monitor -> invoke -> weave -> reintegrate), turning linear decoding into a 'recursive dialogue with memory'. Not plan-then-retrieve or one-shot exemplars; invocation can occur many times within a single action/step.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-sentence / per-token within a rollout: the trigger evaluates at delimiter (sentence-boundary) tokens during each action's token generation, finer than per-CoT-step and far finer than per-answer.
- **adaptation mechanism**: Latent. Retrieved/generated memory is not adapted as a discrete case; instead the weaver synthesizes a state-conditioned latent representation that is injected into hidden states. Experiential adaptation lives in the weaver's trained LoRA parameters (SFT or GRPO).
- **retrieved item representation**: Latent / soft tokens: continuous hidden-state embeddings (K x d_model), machine-native and human-unreadable (forced decoding yields non-natural-language but structurally regular token patterns). Not raw text, trajectory, program, or structured note.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Distilled latent strategy/insight at sub-symbolic level. Post-hoc analysis maps clusters to abstract functional roles (planning memory for high-level strategy, procedural memory for tool-use/formatting operations, working memory for context retention) rather than raw trajectories or single demonstrations.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Learned selective invocation as the main guard: the RL-trained trigger with reward-adaptive sparsity penalty avoids spurious/unnecessary memory insertions that could disrupt reasoning; sentence-granularity gating aligns injection with semantic boundaries. Ablations show trained-trigger > all-delimiter activation > random insertion, evidencing interference control. The frozen reasoner also preserves base capabilities.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: Latent (generative latent memory). Self-organizes into an emergent human-like hierarchy of planning, procedural, and working memory; distinct from episodic database, skill-library, workflow, or graph memory.
- **write back**:
> True (at training time, parametric). Experiences are internalized into the memory weaver's LoRA parameters during SFT/GRPO training; the reasoner is never modified. There is no discrete episodic database write; 'write-back' is parameter consolidation rather than appending records.
- **write back trigger**:
> On training over experiences (reward-driven). Weaver/trigger parameters are updated from batches of past trajectories using their rewards (SFT or GRPO). Not per-step episodic appends; not reflective text writes; no human validation. In continual learning, each new task stage triggers a parameter update.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Reward-graded (implicit success+failure). Training uses full reward signals over trajectories (GRPO/REINFORCE-style and SFT), so low-reward (failed) trajectories shape the gradient; the trigger's reward-adaptive penalty uses high-reward trajectories (reward >= batch median) to set the sparsity reference. No explicit separate failure-only corrective-rule store.
- **memory evolution update**: Refine/overwrite via gradient updates to weaver and trigger LoRA parameters (parametric refinement), not append/dedup/prune over discrete entries. Continual sequential training progressively updates parameters while mitigating catastrophic forgetting.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: Yes. Both the WHEN (memory trigger, trained by RL with a reward-adaptive sparsity penalty) and the WHAT (memory weaver, trained by SFT or GRPO toward task reward) are learned policies, not fixed similarity top-k. The trigger is an explicit learned invocation policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent private memory; the weaver/trigger are tied to a specific frozen reasoner. No multi-agent or cross-framework memory sharing is proposed.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: ALFWorld, TriviaQA, PopQA, KodCode, BigCodeBench, GPQA, GSM8K, MATH, AQuA; plus out-of-domain generalization tests on ScienceWorld and FEVER. (Abstract cites 'eight benchmarks'; setup text lists nine datasets across five domains.)
- **benchmark family**: embodied (ALFWorld; out-of-domain ScienceWorld), QA / open-domain (TriviaQA, PopQA; out-of-domain FEVER fact-verification), math (AQuA, GSM8K, MATH), scientific reasoning (GPQA), code (KodCode, BigCodeBench).
- **baselines**: Twelve baselines in four groups: (I) Prompt-based: Vanilla, CoT; (II) Parametric memory: SFT, GRPO, REINFORCE, REINFORCE++, Agent-FLAN; (III) Retrieval-based memory: MemoryBank, ExpeL, Agent Workflow Memory (AWM); (IV) Latent computation: SoftCoT, Co-processor.
- **key metrics**:
> Task performance per dataset (accuracy / success rate %), e.g., ALFWorld success rate, QA accuracy, math accuracy, code pass rate. Also relative improvement (%) over baselines, cross-domain transfer accuracy, continual-learning retention, and inference latency (relative to vanilla).
- **headline result**: Across eight benchmarks MemGen surpasses leading external memory systems (ExpeL, AWM) by up to 38.22% and exceeds GRPO by up to 13.44%. Concrete example: on ALFWorld+SmolLM3-3B, MemGen-GRPO reaches 63.60% (vs vanilla 18.96%, +44.64%); MemGen-SFT 50.60%.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Latent memory length K sensitivity: performance rises monotonically as K grows 2->32 (more memory capacity). (2) Memory invocation strategy (Table 5): trained Trigger > all-delimiter activation > random insertion (e.g., on GPQA/KodCode/TriviaQA trained trigger 18.28/58.16/65.02 vs all-delimiter 17.34/56.20/64.15 vs random p=0.5 16.66/52.95/57.28), showing selective when/where invocation matters. (3) Weaver parameterization (Table 6): full-parameter SFT > LoRA, but LoRA is competitive and parameter-efficient. (4) Cross-domain generalization (train on one dataset, test on others incl. ScienceWorld/FEVER) and continual learning (Table 4) showing reduced forgetting vs SFT/ExpeL. (5) Post-hoc cluster-removal intervention mapping clusters to planning/procedural/working memory failure modes.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> No. Only end-to-end task metrics are reported; there are no intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k/nDCG) because memory is generated, not retrieved from a labeled corpus. Auxiliary diagnostic analyses (invocation frequency, t-SNE clustering, cluster-removal failure-mode shifts) are reported but are not standard intrinsic retrieval metrics.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Mostly outcome (task accuracy/success). Some process-level analysis is provided: memory invocation frequency across percentile positions, failure-mode breakdown under cluster removal (planning/tool/parsing/formatting errors per Song et al. 2025 taxonomy), and inference latency, giving partial process insight.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Reported as favorable. Despite up to 57.66% performance improvement over vanilla, per-query inference latency stays below the vanilla baseline, ranging from 24% to 94% of vanilla LLM latency (fewer tokens needed to reach correct answers; e.g., MemGen-SFT completes KodCode tasks in 2.94s on Qwen2.5-1.5B). Memory modules are lightweight LoRA adapters (r=16). Trigger sparsity penalty limits unnecessary invocations.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed latent budget per invocation: K latent tokens, K in {2,4,8} in main experiments (ablated 2->32). Number of invocations is adaptive (learned trigger, sentence-granularity, self-scaled to task difficulty). No prompt-token top-k truncation since memory is injected in hidden-state space, not as text.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (primary method paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A (uses existing benchmarks via their official training/eval splits; does not construct a new benchmark). Training uses official train splits of all datasets except PopQA, which has no train set and is evaluated with the TriviaQA-trained model to probe cross-dataset generalization.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Latent/soft-token reasoning and memory: SoftCoT (Xu et al. 2025), Coconut-style latent reasoning, Co-processor (Liu et al. 2024), LatentSeek, R3Mem (acknowledged in repo). RL fine-tuning: GRPO (DeepSeek), REINFORCE/REINFORCE++. LoRA parameter-efficient adaptation. Search environment from Search-R1. Code framework adapted from LAVIS. Conceptually contrasts with parametric tuning (Agent-FLAN) and retrieval memory (ExpeL, MemoryBank, AWM, G-Memory, AgentKB).
- **contrasts with**:
> Parametric memory that modifies reasoner weights (SFT, GRPO, REINFORCE, REINFORCE++, Agent-FLAN); retrieval/text-database memory that externalizes experience (ExpeL, MemoryBank, Agent Workflow Memory/AWM, and by reference G-Memory, AgentKB); other latent-computation methods (SoftCoT, Co-processor). MemGen argues neither parametric nor retrieval memory captures the fluid interweaving of reasoning and memory.
- **lineage**:
> Group F (decision/experience memory + RL): self-evolving agent memory. Sits in the lineage of experience/case memory for agents (ExpeL, AWM, AgentKB, G-Memory) but pivots from text-retrieval memory to generative latent (machine-native) memory interwoven with reasoning, with RL-learned invocation and weaving policies; bridges latent-reasoning and agent-memory lines.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- online_growth

<a id="item-memp"></a>
### 147. Memp (Mem^p): Exploring Agent Procedural Memory

2025  ·  arXiv 2508.06433  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.06433)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **authors affiliation**: Runnan Fang, Yuan Liang, Xiaobin Wang, Jialong Wu, Shuofei Qiao, Pengjun Xie, Fei Huang, Huajun Chen, Ningyu Zhang. Affiliations: Zhejiang University; Alibaba Group; State Key Lab. for Novel Software Technology, Nanjing University. (Corresponding author: Ningyu Zhang, ZJU.)
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.06433
- **code url**: https://github.com/zjunlp/MemP (MIT License; supports offline and online procedural-memory building; references LangChain and ETO codebases)
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/zjunlp/MemP

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: LLM-agent long-horizon planning, tool-use, and embodied decision-making. Evaluated on long-horizon housework (ALFWorld) and long-term constraint-based information-seeking/planning (TravelPlanner).
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent, long-horizon task solving modeled as an MDP where the agent invokes tools/actions over many rounds. The work studies how to endow an agent with a learnable, updatable, lifelong PROCEDURAL memory that is distilled from past trajectories and reused on analogous tasks. Setting shifts from parallel/isolated task completion to SEQUENTIAL task completion so the agent can distill and reuse experience. Supervision: benchmark-supplied binary/scalar reward signals R(env, s_T, tau) in [0,1] (gold trajectories from the training set are used offline to seed memory; online setting builds memory from scratch at test time). Both an offline mode (memory built from training-set gold trajectories) and an online mode (memory grown during test-time execution) are supported.
- **what is retrieved**:
> Procedural memory entries distilled from past agent trajectories: (1) full verbatim trajectories ('Trajectory'), (2) high-level script-like abstractions/guidelines ('Script'), and (3) their combination ('Proceduralization' = retrieved trajectories + model-generated high-level script). Retrieved memory is appended as prior context before task execution.
- **retrieval grounding**: GROWING / episodic memory the agent writes (procedural-memory repository built from the agent's own past trajectories), with an offline-seeded variant; not a static external doc/API corpus. Classified as growing-memory (hybrid offline-seed + online-growth).
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k similarity ranking: at inference the system retrieves the top-k procedural memories whose query/keyword vectors are most cosine-similar to the current task. Not framed as completeness of a minimal needed set; an analysis varies k and shows performance rises then plateaus and finally declines if too many memories are retrieved.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> Retrieve: yes; Reuse: yes (append retrieved procedural memory as context / prior knowledge); Revise: yes (the 'Adjustment' update combines an erroneous trajectory with the original memory and revises it in place; reflexion-based error correction); Retain: yes (Build/Update writes distilled memories back into the bank). Effectively [Retrieve, Reuse, Revise, Retain] all present, though not framed as CBR.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The paper frames itself around 'procedural memory' (cognitive-science grounding: Cohen & Squire 1980; Gupta & Cohen 2002) and the Build/Retrieve/Update life-cycle, not as case-based reasoning; it does not cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: Full trajectory (verbatim round-by-round trajectory) and/or workflow-routine/script-like abstraction (distilled step-by-step instructions and higher-level script). Retrieval unit granularity = full trajectory or distilled procedural script (task-level memory entry).
- **index source**: Growing memory. Offline-induced from gold training-set trajectories (offline mode) AND online/test-time-induced (online mode builds and refreshes memory from test-set task execution every t tasks). Hybrid offline-seed + online-growth construction.
- **index structure topology**: Flat vector index (cosine-similarity over embedded keys). Each memory entry is keyed by an embedding (query embedding, keyword/AveFact embedding, or random for the no-key baseline); no graph or hierarchical topology.
- **retriever type**: Dense (off-the-shelf embedding model phi with cosine similarity). The AveFact variant uses an LLM to extract keywords, then averages keyword-vector similarities. No BM25/sparse retriever (explicitly noted as future/missing in Limitations).
- **retriever learning signal**: None (off-the-shelf). Retrieval is fixed cosine-similarity top-k over a pretrained embedding model; the retriever is not trained. Different fixed key-construction strategies (Query vs AveFact vs Random) are compared but no learned retrieval signal or RL policy is used.
- **query construction**:
> Two compared key-building strategies: (1) Query = use the task query description as the storage/retrieval key, leveraging semantic similarity of queries; (2) AveFact = an LLM extracts keywords from the task query, then retrieval averages cosine similarity across matched keywords; plus a Random Sample baseline that uses no key. The new-task query is embedded and matched to stored keys.
- **query granularity**: Task-level (one-shot at t=0): a single retrieval is performed at the start of a new task using the task query/keywords; retrieved memory is appended before execution rather than re-queried per step.
- **when to retrieve**: One-shot (retrieval performed once before task execution; retrieved procedural memory is supplied as prior context for the whole task).
- **retrieval trigger signal**: Fixed schedule: retrieval is triggered once at task onset (no token-confidence, attention, learned classifier, or reflection-token trigger). Memory UPDATE (a separate operation) is triggered on a fixed schedule (after every t tasks) and on failure (Adjustment).
- **reranking**: None. Retrieval is direct cosine-similarity top-k with no separate reranking stage.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Compression/abstraction at BUILD time (trajectories distilled into compact script-like procedural memories), but no post-retrieval rerank/decompose/distractor-filtering at query time. At retrieval time the chosen top-k is appended verbatim (Trajectory) or as script (Script) or both (Proceduralization).
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (not a tool-retrieval method; memory entries are trajectories/scripts, not tool docs).
- **index content separation**: Partial: a lightweight key (query embedding or AveFact keyword embedding) is separated from the heavier memory content (full trajectory / script) that is loaded on demand after a key match. Not a formal SOP-index-then-content progressive-disclosure scheme.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no external tool index or live tool-sync protocol; memory store is internal and refreshed every t tasks in the online setting).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**: Prompt augmentation / skill reuse: the retrieved procedural memory (trajectory and/or distilled script) is appended to the task as part of the context, serving as prior knowledge to guide the agent (transforming policy pi(a|s) into pi_{m^p}(a|s)).
- **planning integration**: Retrieve-then-plan / one-shot exemplars at plan time: a similar procedural memory is retrieved once before execution and prepended as prior knowledge; the agent then runs in a ReAct fashion using that procedural memory. Not interleaved per-step, not inside MCTS/tree search.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer / per-task: retrieval is woven in once at the task level (one retrieval per task episode), not per-CoT-step or per-tool-call.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> Verbatim ICL exemplar for the Trajectory/Proceduralization conditions (retrieved trajectory/script injected as context). For UPDATE, execution-feedback-driven revision: the 'Adjustment' strategy combines a failed/erroneous trajectory with the original memory and revises it in place; the best-performing update is reflexion-based (error-correction) revision.
- **retrieved item representation**: Two surface forms (and their combination): raw trajectory (verbatim round-by-round) and distilled script/guideline (free-text step-by-step instructions plus higher-level script-like abstraction). Proceduralization injects both concrete trajectory + abstract script.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Spans raw trajectory (Trajectory) to distilled procedural script/workflow (Script), with Proceduralization combining both. Script = higher-level reusable workflow/guideline abstraction; Trajectory = raw demonstration.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Validation update (only successful trajectories are consolidated; failed/redundant/noisy trajectories discarded) and reflexion-based Adjustment (error-correction revision of memory after a failed retrieval-guided execution); dynamic discarding/deprecation of outdated memory. Also notes that retrieving too many memories introduces less-accurate entries and hurts performance, motivating bounded k.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: Procedural memory (also described as long-term/episodic-refreshed); a skill-library/workflow-like repository of distilled procedures. memory_type = procedural (with skill-library/workflow characteristics).
- **write back**: True. The Builder B(tau_t, r_t) writes distilled procedural memories (trajectories and/or scripts) into the memory bank Mem; online mode continuously writes/refreshes after every t tasks.
- **online growth**: True (in the online/test-time mode): the repository grows and is refreshed during deployment after every t test-set tasks via Vanilla/Validation/Adjustment update strategies. The offline mode freezes memory after offline induction from training trajectories.
- **write back trigger**:
> Scheduled (after every t tasks) for Vanilla and Validation updates; on-failure (reflective/error-correction) for Adjustment, which revises memory in place when a retrieved memory leads to a failed execution. Validation writes on-success-only (success-filtered consolidation). So: on-success-and-failure combined across strategies; Validation = success-only, Adjustment = failure-triggered reflective revision.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Both: Validation discards failed/noisy trajectories (success-only consolidation), whereas Adjustment explicitly USES failed trajectories correctively—combining the erroneous trajectory with the original memory and revising it (reflexion-based error correction). So failures are used as corrective signal in the reflexion/Adjustment update.
- **memory evolution update**:
> Stored entries are mutated after writing: the update mechanism U = Add(M_new) (-) Del(M_obs) (+) Update(M_est) supports add (append new), delete/deprecate (forget-prune outdated/obsolete entries), and refine/overwrite (in-place revision via reflexion/Adjustment). Includes dynamic discarding/deprecation and delta/refine-overwrite updates.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> False. Retrieval/case-selection is fixed cosine-similarity top-k (with hand-crafted Query/AveFact keys), not a learned/RL-optimized policy. The MDP framing is for the agent's task policy, not for the retriever; the paper explicitly notes only vector-similarity with manually crafted keys is used.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: Single-agent private memory, BUT supports cross-MODEL transfer: procedural memory built by a stronger model (GPT-4o) is transferred to and reused by a weaker model (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct), yielding gains. No multi-agent/heterogeneous-framework shared memory.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: TravelPlanner (Xie et al., 2024); ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021, with dev and test splits).
- **benchmark family**: TravelPlanner = planning/tool-use under constraints (long-horizon information-seeking planning); ALFWorld = embodied (text-based household tasks). Families: planning/tool (TravelPlanner) and embodied (ALFWorld).
- **baselines**:
> No Memory (ReAct-style, no external memory); Build-policy variants Script / Trajectory / Proceduralization; Retrieve-policy variants Random Sample / Key=Query / Key=AveFact; Update variants Vanilla / Validation / Adjustment(reflexion). Cross-method comparison (ALFWorld, GPT-4o) vs ReAct, Expel, and AWM (Agent Workflow Memory).
- **key metrics**:
> TravelPlanner: #CS (Commonsense constraint pass rate %), #HC (Hard Constraint pass rate %), Steps (lower better). ALFWorld: Dev success rate (%), Test success rate (%), Steps (lower better). Also token consumption savings. Plus reward gain and step reduction across sequential trajectory groups.
- **headline result**:
> On ALFWorld with GPT-4o, the Proceduralization build policy reaches 87.14 (dev) / 77.86 (test) success vs 39.28 / 42.14 for No Memory, while cutting steps from 23.76 to 15.01. On TravelPlanner (GPT-4o) Proceduralization reaches #CS 79.94 vs 71.93 No Memory with steps 14.62 vs 17.84. Memp also beats ReAct, Expel, and AWM on ALFWorld (best dev/test success, fewest steps).
- **ablations**:
> Build policy ablation (No Memory vs Script vs Trajectory vs Proceduralization across GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Qwen2.5-72B): Proceduralization best overall; Script generalizes better to ALFWorld test, Trajectory better on dev (similar tasks). Retrieve-key ablation (Random vs Query vs AveFact on TravelPlanner): Query and AveFact both beat Random; AveFact best on most settings. Update-strategy ablation (Vanilla vs Validation vs Adjustment over sequential task groups): reflexion-based Adjustment best, surpassing the second-best by +0.7 points and reducing 14 steps by the final group. Transfer ablation: GPT-4o memory transferred to Qwen2.5-14B raises completion +5% and cuts ~1.6 steps on TravelPlanner. Scaling-k ablation: performance rises then plateaus with more retrieved memories, and declines if too many are retrieved.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No. Intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k/nDCG) are NOT reported separately; evaluation is end-to-end task metrics (success/constraint pass rates, steps, tokens). Retrieval-strategy quality is judged only via downstream task performance.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both outcome and process: outcome via success/constraint-pass rates; process/efficiency via step count (Steps) and token consumption, plus per-group reward gain and step reduction over sequential tasks (a case study shows 9 fewer steps and 685 tokens saved). No reasoning-faithfulness metric.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Strong efficiency emphasis: procedural memory reduces step counts (e.g., ALFWorld GPT-4o 23.76 -> 15.01 steps) and token consumption (case study: -9 steps, -685 tokens), eliminating fruitless exploration. Trade-off noted: retrieving too many memories increases context length and injects noisy memories, degrading performance (an optimal k exists).
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k top-k retrieval appended as context; a scaling analysis varies the number of retrieved procedural memories and finds an upward-then-plateau curve with decline when k is too large (excessive retrieval inflates context length and adds inaccurate entries). No explicit token-budget cap reported beyond this observation.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (uses existing benchmarks TravelPlanner and ALFWorld rather than constructing a new one).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Procedural-memory / experience-learning agents: Voyager (Wang et al., 2023), AWM / Agent Workflow Memory (Wang et al., 2024b), AutoManual (Chen et al., 2024), Expel; ReAct as the base no-memory agent; cognitive-architecture/memory grounding (Soar, MemoryBank, CoALA cognitive architectures for language agents). MDP formulation (Puterman 1990). Code adapted from LangChain and ETO (uses ETO-provided train-set trajectories).
- **contrasts with**:
> Manually engineered / brittle prompt-template procedural knowledge and parameter-entangled skills; coarse memory frameworks (LangGraph/LangChain, AutoGPT, MemoryBank, Soar) that leave memory life-cycle optimization unexamined; prior experience-learning methods with rudimentary merge-only memory updates. Directly compared against ReAct, Expel, and AWM on ALFWorld.
- **lineage**:
> Group F (decision-making / memory / RL-style experience learning): procedural/experience memory for LLM agents. Positioned as a systematic study elevating procedural memory (Build/Retrieve/Update life-cycle) to a first-class optimization object, extending the Voyager/AWM/AutoManual/Expel line toward learnable, updatable, lifelong, and transferable procedural memory.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):
