<a id="item-memory-r1"></a>
### 148. Memory-R1: Enhancing Large Language Model Agents to Manage and Utilize Memories via Reinforcement Learning

2025  ·  arXiv 2508.19828  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.19828)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2508.19828, cs.CL / cs.MA); submitted 27 Aug 2025, last revised 14 Jan 2026 (v5); no peer-reviewed venue confirmed as of this writing
- **authors affiliation**:
> Sikuan Yan, Xiufeng Yang (co-first authors), Zuchao Huang, Ercong Nie, Zifeng Ding, Zonggen Li, Xiaowen Ma, Jinhe Bi, Kristian Kersting, Jeff Z. Pan, Hinrich Schuetze, Volker Tresp, Yunpu Ma (corresponding). Primary affiliations: Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU) and Munich Center for Machine Learning; also Technical University of Munich, University of Cambridge, University of Hong Kong, Technical University of Darmstadt, University of Edinburgh.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.19828

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: QA / decision-making over long-horizon multi-session dialogue memory (memory management + memory-augmented question answering); framed as a multi-agent system (cs.MA). Memory operations are cast as RL decision-making.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive multi-session dialogue setting where each dialogue contains multiple sessions and turns, and answering a question requires synthesizing information spread across sessions. Two specialized agents (a Memory Manager and an Answer Agent) are fine-tuned with outcome-driven RL. Supervision is minimal: no per-operation labels are provided; only final-answer correctness (Exact Match against gold QA) acts as the learning signal, with only 152 training QA pairs. The two agents are trained separately (decoupled) for stability under sparse rewards; when training one agent the other is frozen.
- **what is retrieved**: Episodic memory entries (natural-language fact statements / consolidated memories) distilled from prior dialogue turns and stored in an external memory bank; at QA time a set of candidate memory entries is retrieved via similarity-based RAG.
- **retrieval grounding**: GROWING/episodic memory the agent writes and evolves over the dialogue (the Memory Manager constructs and maintains the bank via ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP); retrieval at QA time runs over this self-written growing memory bank, not a static external corpus.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> At QA time a fixed top-k is retrieved (60 candidate memories, 30 per participant), then a learned Memory Distillation policy selects a variable-size relevant subset before reasoning, so the effective objective is precision-driven variable-size selection of relevant entries out of a fixed top-k retrieval pool rather than a fixed final-k ranking.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it adopts a CRUD-style {ADD, UPDATE, DELETE, NOOP} memory-operation framing (following Mem0) rather than CBR.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: Single memory entry (a natural-language fact / consolidated statement, e.g. 'Andrew adopted 2 dogs named Buddy and Scout'); these are episodic memory items derived from dialogue turns, not raw token snippets or full trajectories.
- **index source**:
> Growing memory bank constructed online over the dialogue stream: at each turn an LLM extracts key info, retrieves related entries, and the RL-fine-tuned Memory Manager updates the store. Training-data construction uses GPT-4o-mini to build temporal memory-bank snapshots from preceding turns. The bank evolves during processing rather than being a frozen offline corpus.
- **index structure topology**: Flat memory bank of fact entries keyed by ID, retrieved via similarity-based (vector) RAG; entries are maintained per-participant (memories segmented by speaker/user). No knowledge-graph or hierarchical index is used (contrasts with graph-based memory systems like A-Mem/Zep).
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None for the retriever itself (the RAG retriever is off-the-shelf and not trained). The learned components are the Memory Manager and Answer Agent policies, trained with outcome-driven RL (downstream answer Exact Match reward). The Answer Agent's Memory Distillation acts as a learned post-retrieval selection policy, but the underlying similarity retriever is fixed.
- **query construction**:
> At QA time the raw question is used as the query to retrieve candidate memories (top-30 per participant). During memory construction, the newly extracted/summarized information from the current dialogue turn serves as the query/key to retrieve related existing memories for the Memory Manager.
- **query granularity**: Two levels: (1) turn/step-level during memory construction (extracted info from the current turn queries the bank to drive ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP), and (2) task/question-level at QA time (the question retrieves candidate memories once before answering).
- **when to retrieve**: Memory-construction retrieval is per-turn (iterative, fixed schedule as each dialogue turn arrives). QA-time retrieval is one-shot per question (retrieve 60 candidates once, then distill and answer).
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed schedule: retrieval is triggered deterministically at every dialogue turn (for memory management) and once per question (for answering). There is no learned/uncertainty-based trigger for WHEN to retrieve; the learned policies decide WHAT operation to apply and WHICH retrieved memories to use, not whether to retrieve.
- **reranking**:
> No dedicated reranker stage in the main pipeline. The paper explicitly compares against a Base+Reranker pipeline as an ablation and argues its learned Memory Distillation achieves higher accuracy with lower latency than reranker-based pipelines, positioning distillation as a substitute for reranking.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Learned Memory Distillation: the Answer Agent pre-selects (filters) the most relevant entries from the 60 retrieved candidates before reasoning, discarding distractors/noise. This is an LLM-driven, RL-fine-tuned relevance-filtering / distillation step (not classic rerank or compression).
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tool/skill retrieval; memory entries are LLM-generated fact summaries, not tool docstrings).
- **index content separation**: N/A / No explicit progressive-disclosure index-then-content separation; memory entries themselves are lightweight fact statements stored and retrieved directly.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index / external API protocol; memory store is the agent's own evolving bank).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no inter-tool dependency modeling).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation with distilled memories: retrieved memories are filtered by the Memory Distillation policy and the selected relevant entries are concatenated with the question to form a memory-augmented prompt over which the Answer Agent reasons to produce the answer. RL outcome reward (answer EM) also serves as a training signal for both the manager and answer policies.
- **planning integration**:
> Two-stage pipeline: Stage 1 (retrieve-then-manage) maintains/evolves the memory bank turn-by-turn via the Memory Manager; Stage 2 (retrieve-then-distill-then-answer) is plan-then-act at QA time, where memories are retrieved once, distilled, then reasoned over to answer. No tree search / MCTS; integration is sequential per question.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer at QA time (single retrieval + distillation + reasoning pass per question, with the Answer Agent first outputting selected memories then the answer). Memory-management retrieval/operations are per-turn during bank construction.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> N/A (not a CBR case-adaptation method). The closest analog is RL-fine-tuned reuse: the Memory Manager learns to consolidate overlapping info via UPDATE rather than DELETE+ADD, and the Answer Agent learns to distill and reason; both adapted via outcome-driven RL (PPO/GRPO), not case revision.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Structured natural-language note / fact statement (e.g. JSON-tagged memory entries with id, text, and an operation event field such as ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NONE during management); at answer time the injected form is the distilled set of relevant free-text memory statements with timestamps.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Distilled fact/statement-level memory (consolidated natural-language summaries of dialogue content), higher abstraction than raw dialogue turns but not a procedural skill or reusable workflow.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Learned Memory Distillation in the RL-fine-tuned Answer Agent: it filters out irrelevant/distractor memories from the 60 retrieved candidates before reasoning, reducing 'lost in the middle' style distraction. Trained via outcome-driven RL so that selecting/reasoning over noisy retrieval still yields correct answers. Ablation shows distillation improves all metrics.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: episodic (external memory bank of dialogue-derived fact entries), actively managed via CRUD-style operations.
- **write back**: True. The Memory Manager writes new experiences into memory via structured operations ADD (insert new entry), UPDATE (consolidate/merge into an existing entry, keeping ID), DELETE (prune contradictory entry), or NOOP (no change).
- **online growth**: Yes. The memory bank is incrementally built and evolved as new dialogue turns arrive (per-turn ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP). The store grows/changes during processing rather than being frozen after offline induction.
- **write back trigger**:
> Per-turn: at every new dialogue turn the Memory Manager evaluates the extracted information against retrieved existing memories and issues one of ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP. Writes are not gated on success/failure of QA; they happen continuously as the dialogue stream is processed (operations are learned via downstream answer-correctness reward, but the trigger to act is per-turn/scheduled).
- **memory evolution update**:
> Mutable with consolidation: append (ADD), dedup-merge / refine-overwrite (UPDATE consolidates overlapping or more-detailed info while keeping the same ID), and forget-prune (DELETE removes contradictory entries); NOOP leaves entries unchanged. A key behavior learned by RL is to favor UPDATE-style consolidation over fragmenting DELETE+ADD.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Partly. The candidate retrieval (top-k similarity RAG) is a fixed, non-learned step; but the downstream memory-USE policy (Answer Agent's Memory Distillation = which retrieved memories to select/reason over) and the memory-management operation policy are learned/RL-optimized (PPO/GRPO with outcome-driven reward). So memory selection/use is a learned policy while initial retrieval is fixed top-k.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent private memory per dialogue; the two agents (Memory Manager, Answer Agent) operate within one framework and the memory bank is not shared across multiple heterogeneous agents/frameworks.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> LoCoMo (primary; long multi-session dialogues, ~600 turns / 26k tokens reported in main text, with single-hop, multi-hop, open-domain, temporal questions; adversarial subset excluded; 1:1:8 train/val/test split = 152/81/1307 questions), MSC (Multi-Session Chat, MemGPT-modified version), and LongMemEval (long-term interactive memory benchmark). Models trained only on LoCoMo and evaluated zero-shot on MSC and LongMemEval.
- **benchmark family**: memory / long-term conversational QA (LoCoMo, MSC, LongMemEval) with multi-hop and temporal reasoning subtypes.
- **baselines**:
> (1) LoCoMo (RAG) chunk-retrieval baseline; (2) A-Mem (agentic structured memory); (3) Mem0 (modular memory with in-context CRUD operations, the most competitive prior baseline); (4) MemoryOS (memory-as-OS framework, strongest non-RL baseline); (5) Memory-SFT (supervised fine-tuning ablation: same architecture/data as Memory-R1 but behavior-cloned from GPT-5-generated trajectories instead of RL). All re-implemented on LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct backbones (temperature 0, max 2048 tokens).
- **key metrics**: Token-level F1 (F1), BLEU-1 (B1) for lexical overlap, and LLM-as-a-Judge (J) for semantic correctness (CORRECT/WRONG labeling). Also reports inference latency (median and tail) in the distillation-vs-reranking comparison.
- **headline result**:
> On LoCoMo with LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, Memory-R1-GRPO sets a new state of the art, with relative improvements over the strongest baseline (MemoryOS) of +28.5% F1, +34.0% BLEU-1, and +30.2% LLM-as-a-Judge (overall scores 45.02 F1 / 37.51 B1 / 62.74 J), achieved with only 152 training QA pairs. (Note: abstract/intro phrase the gain over 'Mem0' as ~28% F1 / 34% BLEU-1 / 30% J; main-results text attributes the same percentages to MemoryOS as the strongest baseline.)
- **ablations**:
> Component ablations (Figure 5) removing each piece on LLaMA-3.1-8B: (a) without RL-fine-tuned Memory Manager, PPO drops from 41.0/32.9/57.5 to 34.5/28.1/49.0 (GRPO to 37.5/30.6/52.9); (b) without RL-fine-tuned Answer Agent, PPO is 32.5/24.6/59.4 and GRPO 33.0/24.9/59.9 vs full 41.0/32.9/57.5 (PPO) and 45.0/37.5/62.7 (GRPO); (c) without Memory Distillation, PPO 39.3/30.9/57.4 -> 41.0/32.9/57.5, GRPO 41.0/34.4/60.1 -> 45.0/37.5/62.7. Stronger Memory Manager compounds Answer Agent gains (GPT-4o-mini manager vs LLaMA manager: F1 +19.72 vs +10.10, B1 +18.19 vs +10.81, J +15.76 vs +5.05). Reward-design ablation (Table 2): PPO with J-based reward yields highest J (63.58) but lower F1/B1 (33.69/23.36) due to verbose answers, while EM-based reward gives balanced 41.05/32.91/57.54; EM reward chosen. PPO vs GRPO: GRPO converges faster initially, both reach comparable final reward.
- **evaluation decoupling**: No. Only end-to-end QA metrics (F1/BLEU-1/LLM-as-a-Judge) are reported; intrinsic retrieval metrics such as Recall@k or nDCG for the memory retrieval/distillation are not reported separately.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome (final-answer) metrics. Process quality is illustrated qualitatively via case studies (correct UPDATE vs erroneous DELETE+ADD operations; distilled-memory selection) and component ablations, but there are no quantitative step-wise memory-operation-accuracy or retrieval-faithfulness metrics.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Data efficiency is the headline: strong gains with only 152 training QA pairs. Memory Distillation vs reranking comparison (Figure 8) shows Memory-R1 (GRPO) achieves higher accuracy with lower median and tail latency than a Base+Reranker pipeline, which adds substantial latency for modest accuracy gains. Training: 4x NVIDIA H100 80GB GPUs (8 for Qwen-2.5-14B), total batch size 128, micro-batch 2/GPU, max prompt/response 4096/2048 tokens. No explicit API-cost or per-query retrieval-call counts beyond the fixed 60-candidate retrieval.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (not a benchmark paper). Uses existing benchmarks; LoCoMo evaluation split is 152/81/1307 (train/val/test) questions after excluding the adversarial subset.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025) memory-operation set {ADD, UPDATE, DELETE, NOOP} and RAG-style 60-candidate retrieval setup; PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) and GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) RL algorithms; VERL / HybridFlow RLHF framework (Sheng et al., 2025) for training; LoCoMo benchmark (Maharana et al., 2024); RL-for-LLM-behavior line including Search-R1 (Jin et al., 2025), ToolRL (Qian et al., 2025), R1-Searcher (Song et al., 2025). Backbones: LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen-2.5-3B/7B/14B-Instruct.
- **contrasts with**:
> Static, heuristic-driven memory pipelines that use vanilla in-context LLMs to choose memory operations without a correctness-tied learning signal: Mem0, MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023), A-Mem (Xu et al., 2025), MemoryOS, MemLLM (Modarressi et al., 2024); and reranker-based retrieval pipelines (Base+Reranker). Also contrasts with supervised imitation (Memory-SFT distilled from GPT-5) by showing outcome-driven RL outperforms behavior cloning.
- **lineage**:
> Belongs to the decision/experience-memory + RL sub-topic (group F, decision_memory_rl): casts external-memory management and memory utilization as RL-optimized policies (PPO/GRPO) over a growing episodic memory bank, extending the RL-for-LLM-agents lineage (Search-R1, ToolRL, R1-Searcher, WebAgent-R1) to the memory-management problem; among the first to frame memory operation selection and relevant-memory utilization as an RL problem.

### 149. MemoryOS - Memory Operating System of AI Agents (paper title: 'Memory OS of AI Agent')

2025  ·  EMNLP 2025  ·  [paper](https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-main.1318.pdf)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**:
> EMNLP 2025 (Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, Main track, pages 25961-25970; November 4-9, 2025; (c)2025 ACL). DBLP: conf/emnlp/KangJZB25. Also available as arXiv preprint arXiv:2506.06326 (submitted 30 May 2025; cs.CL/cs.AI). DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2506.06326.
- **authors affiliation**:
> Jiazheng Kang (Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, BUPT; kjz@bupt.edu.cn), Mingming Ji (Tencent AI Lab), Zhe Zhao (Tencent AI Lab), Ting Bai (Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, BUPT; corresponding author; baiting@bupt.edu.cn). Two primary affiliations: BUPT and Tencent AI Lab. The open-source repository lives under the 'BAI-LAB' GitHub org (Ting Bai's lab at BUPT). Sponsored by CCF-Tencent (RAGR20240108), NSFC No. 62236003, and the Tencent Rhino-Bird Focused Research Program.
- **paper url**: https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-main.1318.pdf (ACL Anthology). arXiv abstract: https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.06326; DOI: https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2506.06326.
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/BAI-LAB/MemoryOS (continuously maintained implementation repo from the authors' lab; includes a MemoryOS-MCP server integration; more current than the frozen EMNLP/arXiv PDF).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Long-term conversational memory management for LLM-based AI agents / personalized dialogue agents (a QA + interactive personal-assistant setting). Evaluated on long multi-session dialogue QA, not on tool-use/embodied/code/decision-RL.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent setting with a FROZEN, off-the-shelf LLM (e.g. GPT-4o-mini; the LLM is prompted, not fine-tuned). The LLM's fixed context window is augmented by an OS-inspired hierarchical memory management system layered on top of the model. No task reward/supervision is used to train any component; all 'learning' is via LLM-prompted summarization/extraction plus off-the-shelf embedding similarity and heuristic heat scores. Memory is built up online over extended multi-session dialogues (LoCoMo conversations average ~300 turns / ~9K tokens; GVD spans simulated 10-day interactions). The agent must (a) retain dialogue history coherently across large temporal gaps and (b) maintain a persistent, evolving persona (user profile/traits/knowledge base + agent profile/traits) to give personalized, consistent answers. The four modules (Storage, Updating, Retrieval, Generation) run as a fixed pipeline; experiments use 8x H20 GPUs (only for serving/embeddings).
- **what is retrieved**:
> experiences / memories: past dialogue pages (user query Q + model response R + timestamp T), LLM-summarized topic-segment summaries (mid-term), and persona/profile information (user profile, user traits across 90 dimensions, user knowledge base, agent profile, agent traits). These are retrieved from the agent's own growing memory store and injected into the generation prompt.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> GROWING / episodic memory the agent writes. The retrievable store is built entirely from the ongoing conversation (short-term dialogue pages -> mid-term topic segments -> long-term persona memory); there is no static external corpus/KB/API being queried. It is a self-written, online-growing personal memory (hence 'memory' rather than classic static-corpus RAG).
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k ranking (with a two-stage top-m then top-k cut), not a completeness/minimal-set objective. MTM retrieval selects top-m candidate segments then top-k dialogue pages within them; LPM retrieves top-10 entries from the User KB and Assistant Traits; STM returns all current dialogue pages. k is a fixed hyperparameter (top-m segments=5; top-k pages=5 on GVD, 10 on LoCoMo). No explicit minimal-needed-set or precision-driven variable-size objective.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve: yes, Reuse: partial, Revise: no, Retain: yes]. MemoryOS Retrieves relevant memory tiers and Retains new dialogue/persona information (write-back across STM->MTM->LPM). 'Reuse' is only the injection of retrieved memory into the prompt (not case-solution adaptation); there is no CBR-style solution Revise step. (Approximate mapping; the work is not framed as CBR.)
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. MemoryOS does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is explicitly framed as an OS-inspired memory operating system (segment-paging, FIFO, heat/LRU-style eviction, working-set models).

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Multi-granular by tier: (a) STM = a 'dialogue page' = {Q_i, R_i, T_i, meta_chain_i} (one user-turn + model-response pair with timestamp and a chain meta-summary); (b) MTM = a 'segment' (an LLM-summarized topic cluster of multiple dialogue pages) at the first stage, then individual dialogue pages within the chosen segments at the second stage; (c) LPM = persona/profile entries (user profile fields, user-trait dimensions, User KB facts, agent profile/traits). The core retrievable units are dialogue pages and topic segments, plus persona entries.
- **index source**:
> Growing memory, online/test-time-induced. The store is constructed incrementally during the dialogue: STM pages are appended live, FIFO-migrated to MTM, clustered into LLM-summarized segments, and (when hot enough) distilled into LPM persona memory. Nothing is offline-induced from an external corpus; the entire index is built from the agent's own interaction stream.
- **index structure topology**:
> Hierarchical, OS-style segment-paging. Three tiers: STM (fixed-length FIFO queue of dialogue pages, length 7) -> MTM (Segmented Paging: topic 'segments' each holding multiple dialogue 'pages'; max segment capacity 2000; each segment carries an embedding, keyword set, and heat score) -> LPM (structured persona store: User Profile/Static + User Traits [90 dims across 3 categories] + User KB [FIFO size 100] + Agent Profile + Agent Traits [FIFO size 100]). Within each tier retrieval uses flat embedding/Jaccard similarity; the topology across tiers is hierarchical (category->segment->page) plus heat-prioritized eviction, not a knowledge graph.
- **retriever type**:
> Dense embedding similarity + lexical (hybrid within MTM). Segment selection uses a combined score F_score = cos(e_s, e_p) + Jaccard(K_s, K_p) (semantic embedding cosine + keyword-set Jaccard). Page-level and LPM retrieval use semantic embedding (cosine) similarity / top-k semantic relevance. Off-the-shelf embeddings; no BM25 index per se, no learned/trained retriever, no generative tool-as-token retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None (off-the-shelf / heuristic). Retrieval relies on frozen pretrained text-embedding similarity, LLM-generated keyword sets for Jaccard, fixed thresholds (segment similarity theta=0.6), and a hand-weighted heat score (alpha=beta=gamma=1). No contrastive training, no LM-feedback fine-tuning of the retriever, no downstream-task/preference optimization, no RL/value-based learning of the retrieval policy.
- **query construction**:
> Raw user query is the query/key. Given the current user query Q, MemoryOS embeds it and matches against segment/page/persona embeddings (and LLM-summarized keyword sets for MTM segment scoring). No sub-query decomposition, synthetic query expansion, or thought-conditioned query rewriting is described; the query is the user's current utterance.
- **query granularity**:
> Task/turn-level (one query per user turn, executed once per response), with a two-LEVEL retrieval within that turn for MTM (segment-level then page-level). It is not step/state-level inside a multi-step reasoning rollout; retrieval is performed once per dialogue turn before generation.
- **when to retrieve**:
> One-shot per dialogue turn (fixed schedule). For every incoming user query the retrieval module is invoked once to gather STM + MTM (two-stage) + LPM context, then the generation module produces the response. No iterative/active/uncertainty-triggered or learned-router retrieval within a turn.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed schedule: retrieval fires deterministically on each user turn (every query triggers a full STM/MTM/LPM retrieval pass before generation). There is no token-level confidence, attention/uncertainty signal, learned complexity classifier, reflection token, or agent-initiated request gating retrieval.
- **reranking**:
> Two-stage hierarchical selection rather than a learned reranker. MTM first ranks segments by F_score (cosine + Jaccard) to pick top-m, then ranks dialogue pages within those segments by semantic similarity to pick top-k (a coarse-to-fine, hierarchy-aware selection). No cross-encoder, RRF, or instruction-tuned reranking model is used.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Summarization/compression at storage time plus selection at query time; no query-time distillation/distractor-filtering module. Refinement is built into the storage hierarchy: dialogue chains are LLM-summarized into meta_chain; segments are LLM-summarized topic summaries; LPM stores distilled persona traits/facts. At retrieval, results are simply selected (top-m/top-k/top-10) and concatenated into the prompt; there is no separate reason-in-documents distillation or compression of the retrieved set beyond the per-tier selection cap.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A. MemoryOS does not retrieve over tools/skills; no tool/skill descriptions are indexed.
- **index content separation**:
> Partial / implicit. The MTM uses segment-level summaries/embeddings as a lightweight index that is matched first (top-m segments) before drilling into the heavier dialogue-page content (top-k pages within selected segments) - an index-then-content, progressive-disclosure pattern across the two-stage retrieval. It is not the SOP-index-then-content tool pattern, but the segment-summary-then-page-content design plays an analogous lightweight-index role.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A. Not a tool-retrieval system (the repo ships a separate MemoryOS-MCP server to expose the memory system via MCP, but the paper itself does not retrieve over a live tool registry / RapidAPI / RESTful API store).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A. No inter-tool dependency modeling (no tools/APIs are retrieved).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation. The Response Generation module integrates the retrieved STM (recent dialogue), MTM (relevant segment summaries + dialogue pages), and LPM (user profile/traits/KB + agent profile/traits) together with the current user query into a single final prompt fed to the frozen LLM, which generates a contextually coherent, personalized response. No training signal, skill execution, case adaptation, or latent-token injection - retrieved memory is consumed as in-context text.
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-generate (no explicit planning/search). MemoryOS is a fixed retrieve->prompt-assemble->generate pipeline per turn; there is no task planner, tree search/MCTS, hierarchical subtask decomposition, or interleaved plan-act loop. Retrieval interfaces with response generation, not with a planner.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer (per dialogue turn). Retrieval is performed once and the result is used to produce the single response for that turn; retrieval is not woven per-CoT-step, per-sentence/token, or per-tool-call.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> N/A (not a CBR case-adaptation system). Retrieved memory is injected verbatim/as-summarized into the prompt and the frozen LLM synthesizes the answer; there is no case-solution adaptation, execution-feedback revision, critic-guided revision, or RL reuse-finetuning. The closest 'adaptation' is the LLM-driven re-summarization/trait-extraction that happens when memory is promoted across tiers (a storage-side operation, not query-time case adaptation).
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Mixed natural-language text: raw dialogue pages (Q/R/T), LLM-distilled chain meta-summaries and segment topic summaries, and structured persona fields/traits (User Profile fixed attributes, 90-dimension User Traits, User KB facts, Agent Profile/Traits). Injected as plain text into the prompt. No executable program/skill or latent/soft tokens.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Multi-level: raw dialogue turns (STM) -> distilled per-topic segment summaries (MTM) -> highly distilled, state-aware persona traits/profile/knowledge (LPM). So retrieval spans raw trajectory-like dialogue, distilled topic summaries, and distilled persona 'insight'/preference representations simultaneously.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Topic-coherent segmentation + capped retrieval breadth, rather than a learned relevance filter. Pages are merged into a segment only if F_score exceeds threshold theta=0.6, keeping segments topically coherent and reducing cross-topic contamination (the paper criticizes MemGPT's flat FIFO for 'topic mixing'). The two-stage segment-then-page retrieval narrows the candidate pool. The hyperparameter analysis explicitly notes that retrieving too many pages 'may introduce noise, adversely affecting performance', motivating k=10. No retriever-aware training, self-reflection relevance evaluator, reason-in-documents refinement, or distractor-aware SFT.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> Episodic + procedural/persona memory in an OS-inspired three-tier hierarchy: Short-Term Memory (STM, FIFO queue of dialogue pages), Mid-Term Memory (MTM, segment-paging topic store), and Long-term Personal Memory (LPM, structured user/agent persona = profile + traits + knowledge base). Long-term, persistent, self-managed, single-agent private.
- **write back**:
> True. MemoryOS continuously writes new experiences into memory: every dialogue turn is appended as an STM page (with LLM-generated chain meta); FIFO-evicted STM pages are written into MTM segments (with LLM topic summarization); hot MTM segments are distilled into LPM (User Traits/User KB/Agent Traits). Write-back is core to the system.
- **online growth**:
> Yes. The memory store grows continuously during deployment/test time across the multi-session dialogue: STM appends turns, MTM accumulates and re-summarizes segments, and LPM evolves persona traits/knowledge. Capacity is bounded by FIFO/heat eviction rather than frozen after an offline induction phase.
- **write back trigger**:
> Per-step / scheduled cascade, not success/failure-conditioned. (1) STM write: every dialogue turn is appended as a page (per-step). (2) STM->MTM: triggered when the STM FIFO queue (length 7) overflows - the oldest page migrates to MTM. (3) MTM eviction: segments exceeding capacity (max 2000) are evicted by lowest heat (heat = alpha*N_visit + beta*L_interaction + gamma*R_recency, with R_recency an exponential time decay). (4) MTM->LPM: segments whose heat exceeds threshold F=5 are promoted to LPM (persona trait/KB extraction; then L_interaction reset to 0 to decay heat and avoid redundancy). No task-reward / on-success-vs-failure gating; writes are driven by FIFO position, heat, and recency.
- **failure experience usage**:
> N/A in the success/failure sense. There is no task-level success/failure label; all dialogue turns are stored uniformly. The system does not store failed vs successful experiences contrastively or maintain failure-only corrective rules - it is a conversational memory store, not an experience-of-failures learner.
- **memory evolution update**:
> Mixed: append-then-summarize / dedup-by-merge / refine-overwrite / forget-prune. STM is append-only within its FIFO window (then forget-from-STM via FIFO eviction to MTM). MTM merges topically similar pages into the same segment (dedup/cluster-merge, threshold theta=0.6) and re-summarizes segment content via LLM; segments are forget-pruned by lowest-heat eviction at capacity. LPM persona traits/KB are incrementally extracted and updated (refine/overwrite of evolving traits), with User KB and Agent Traits maintained as fixed-size FIFO queues (size 100). After MTM->LPM promotion, the segment's L_interaction is reset to 0 (heat decay) to prevent repeated promotion/redundancy. The paper's Limitations note the lack of dynamic segment-merging to resolve overlapping/evolving topics.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No. Retrieval and memory promotion/eviction are governed by fixed similarity thresholds, top-m/top-k cutoffs, and a hand-weighted heat/recency heuristic (alpha=beta=gamma=1; F=5; theta=0.6) - not a learned or RL-optimized retrieval/selection policy (no M-MDP, soft Q-learning, or trained selector).
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent private memory: each MemoryOS instance maintains its own user/agent persona and dialogue memory. No cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing is proposed.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> (1) LoCoMo benchmark (Maharana et al., 2024) - very long-term conversational memory, ultra-long dialogues averaging ~300 turns / ~9K tokens; questions in four categories: Single-hop, Multi-hop, Temporal, Open-domain; scored by F1 and BLEU-1. (2) GVD dataset (Zhong et al., 2024, the MemoryBank evaluation set) - multi-turn dialogues simulated between 15 virtual users and an assistant over a 10-day period, >=2 topics/day; scored by Memory Retrieval Accuracy (binary), Response Correctness, and Contextual Coherence (3-point scale), auto-judged by DeepSeek-R1.
- **benchmark family**: memory / long-term conversational memory (LoCoMo, the canonical LoCoMo/LongMemEval-style family) plus a personalized-dialogue memory set (GVD from MemoryBank). QA-flavored multi-session dialogue memory; not web/embodied/tool/code/decision-RL families.
- **baselines**:
> TiM (Think-in-Memory; Liu et al., 2023), MemoryBank (Zhong et al., 2024), MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023), A-Mem (Agentic Memory; Xu et al., 2025), and a plain base LLM (GPT-4o-mini, no memory). On LoCoMo, A-Mem is reported both as the original paper's numbers and as a re-implementation (A-Mem*) under the same environment.
- **key metrics**: LoCoMo: F1 and BLEU-1 (per-category Single-hop / Multi-hop / Temporal / Open-domain, plus average ranks). GVD: Memory Retrieval Accuracy (Acc., binary 0/1), Response Correctness (Corr., 0/0.5/1), Contextual Coherence (Cohe., 0/0.5/1), auto-scored by DeepSeek-R1.
- **ablations**:
> Component ablations (Figure 2) remove: the Persona/Long-Term module (-LPM), the Dialogue-page Chain (-Chain), the Mid-Term Memory (-MTM), and the entire system (-MemoryOS). Findings: removing the memory system entirely (-MemoryOS) causes the largest performance drop; among components, MTM has the most significant impact, followed by LPM, while the dialogue-page Chain has the least impact. Hyperparameter analysis (Figure 3) on LoCoMo varies top-k MTM dialogue pages over k in {5,10,20,30,40}: performance rises with k but with diminishing returns and eventual noise; k=10 chosen as the favorable accuracy/cost trade-off.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Partial. On GVD an intrinsic memory metric (Memory Retrieval Accuracy, binary) is reported separately from the end-to-end response-quality metrics (Correctness, Coherence). On LoCoMo only end-to-end QA metrics (F1, BLEU-1) are reported - no separate Recall@k/nDCG retrieval metric. So intrinsic-vs-end-to-end decoupling exists only on GVD and is coarse (binary retrieval accuracy, not Recall@k/nDCG).
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Mostly outcome metrics (F1, BLEU-1, response correctness). Some process/quality signal is captured: GVD's Memory Retrieval Accuracy probes whether the right memory was recalled, and Contextual Coherence judges dialogue-flow quality beyond raw answer correctness; the LoCoMo per-category breakdown (single/multi-hop/temporal/open-domain) gives reasoning-type-resolved outcome scores. No step-wise retrieval-accuracy or reasoning-faithfulness metric within a turn.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Discussed qualitatively / via k-sweep rather than a full cost table. The hierarchical segment-paging + heat-based eviction is argued to be more efficient than alternatives (the paper notes A-Mem's heavy multi-step link generation 'inflates latency and error accumulation', and MemGPT's flat FIFO causes topic mixing). The top-k analysis picks k=10 to 'minimize computational overhead' while retaining most of the accuracy gain (larger k adds noise and cost). No explicit per-query token-cost, dollar-cost, or latency-vs-accuracy table is reported.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k, budget-capped selection. STM is a length-7 FIFO of dialogue pages (all returned). MTM retrieval is two-stage with fixed cutoffs: top-m segments=5, then top-k dialogue pages=5 (GVD) / 10 (LoCoMo). LPM returns top-10 entries each from User KB and Assistant Traits plus all profile/trait fields. Memory capacities are capped (MTM segment max 2000; User KB / Agent Traits FIFO size 100) with heat/FIFO eviction governing what stays. k is a tuned constant (k=10 on LoCoMo), not adaptive/precision-driven.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A (MemoryOS is a method, not a benchmark). For context on the datasets it uses: LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024) is a human/LLM-curated very-long-term-conversation benchmark (~300 turns, ~9K tokens per conversation; four QA categories); GVD (Zhong et al., 2024) is an LLM-simulated dialogue set (15 virtual users x ~10 days, >=2 topics/day), answer quality auto-judged by DeepSeek-R1.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Operating-systems segment-paging and virtual-memory management (Multics segment-page memory, Bensoussan et al. 1972; virtual memory / working-set & LRU eviction, Denning 1970; segment-page management on many-core processors, Zheng et al. 2020); MemGPT's OS-style hierarchical read/write memory (Packer et al. 2023); prior LLM-agent memory systems for long dialogue - MemoryBank's vector memory + Ebbinghaus forgetting curve and the GVD dataset (Zhong et al. 2024), Think-in-Memory (Liu et al. 2023), A-Mem agentic note network (Xu et al. 2025), Generative Agents memory+reflection (Park et al. 2023), Self-Controlled Memory (Wang et al. 2025); psychological memory-recall-inspired two-stage retrieval (Yuan et al. 2024); 90-dimension user-trait personalization (Li et al. 2025); LoCoMo evaluation (Maharana et al. 2024).
- **contrasts with**:
> MemGPT (OS-style paging but a FLAT FIFO queue that causes topic mixing as dialogue grows - MemoryOS adds topic-segment paging + hierarchy); A-Mem (interconnected note graph that enriches semantics but whose heavy multi-step link generation inflates latency and error accumulation); MemoryBank (forgetting-curve decay alone, found insufficient and weakest baseline); Think-in-Memory (single-stage LSH hash retrieval that cannot preserve cross-topic dependencies). More broadly, MemoryOS positions itself against single-dimension memory methods (knowledge-organization vs retrieval-mechanism vs architecture-driven) by unifying storage + updating + retrieval + generation into one system.
- **lineage**:
> Group F (decision / memory / RL): the long-term / episodic-memory-management lineage of retrieval-augmented LLM agents. Directly extends the OS-inspired hierarchical-memory line opened by MemGPT, adding a three-tier STM/MTM/LPM architecture with topic segment-paging, dialogue-chain FIFO, heat/recency (LRU-style) eviction, and an evolving persona module. Sits alongside MemoryBank, A-Mem, Think-in-Memory, and Generative Agents as a long-term conversational/personalized-memory system, and has itself become a baseline/target in subsequent memory-retrieval work (e.g., HiNS, 2026).

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- code_url
- headline_result
