## Surveys, Taxonomies & Benchmarks

<a id="item-rag-survey-gao"></a>
### 152. Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey (Gao et al.)

2023  ·  arXiv 2312.10997  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.10997)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2023
- **authors affiliation**:
> Yunfan Gao (Shanghai Research Institute for Intelligent Autonomous Systems, Tongji University); Yun Xiong, Xinyu Gao, Kangxiang Jia, Jinliu Pan (Shanghai Key Laboratory of Data Science, School of Computer Science, Fudan University); Yuxi Bi, Meng Wang (College of Design and Innovation, Tongji University); Yi Dai, Jiawei Sun (Shanghai Research Institute for Intelligent Autonomous Systems, Tongji University); Haofen Wang (corresponding author; Shanghai Research Institute for Intelligent Autonomous Systems & College of Design and Innovation, Tongji University). 10 authors across Tongji University and Fudan University, China.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.10997
- **code url**: https://github.com/Tongji-KGLLM/RAG-Survey (maintained companion repository of RAG papers; the survey itself has no method code).
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/Tongji-KGLLM/RAG-Survey (Tongji-KGLLM RAG-Survey GitHub paper list maintained alongside the survey, organizing academic RAG papers under the LLM context; more current than the frozen PDF).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Survey of RAG for LLMs. Primary task surveyed is knowledge-intensive QA (single-hop, multi-hop, long-form, multiple-choice, domain-specific), but the survey explicitly catalogs 26 downstream tasks including dialogue generation, information extraction, reasoning, fact verification, text summarization/classification, code search, machine translation, and recommendation. Not specifically about planning/agents/tool-use, though it touches agentic adaptive retrieval (WebGPT, Toolformer, Self-RAG) at the inference stage.
- **problem setting**:
> A comprehensive literature review (not a method). It synthesizes 100+ RAG studies and ~50 datasets into a paradigm taxonomy (Naive RAG -> Advanced RAG -> Modular RAG), analyzes the three core stages of every RAG pipeline (Retrieval, Generation, Augmentation), and reviews the evaluation landscape (targets, aspects, benchmarks, tools). The setting surveyed is predominantly offline, single-agent, non-interactive RAG over external knowledge bases for knowledge-intensive generation; supervision ranges from off-the-shelf (training-free ICL/inference) to fine-tuned retrievers/generators and end-to-end/collaborative training. The survey organizes RAG along the LLM lifecycle stages of pre-training, fine-tuning, and inference (the 'technology tree').
- **what is retrieved**:
> Predominantly docs/text chunks from external knowledge bases. The survey's Table I enumerates retrieved units across surveyed methods: text (phrase, proposition, sentence, sentence-pair, chunk, document, item), knowledge-graph elements (entity, triplet, sub-graph), tabular data, code, and cross-lingual text. Also discusses LLM-internal/parametric 'retrieval' (RECITE, GenRead) and memory-pool retrieval (Self-Mem). Not focused on demos/cases/trajectories/skills/tools as in agentic-experience retrieval.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> Predominantly STATIC external corpus (Wikipedia, search engines, datasets, knowledge graphs like Freebase/CMeKG, pre-training corpora, BEIR, Common Crawl, arXiv/PubMed). The survey also covers HYBRID/generated-knowledge variants where the LLM generates context (Generate-Read, Recite-Read, PKG) and a 'Memory module' that builds an unbounded, iteratively self-enhanced memory pool (Self-Mem, Selfmem) - a growing store. Overall the dominant grounding surveyed is static external knowledge, with some hybrid/generative and memory-pool exceptions.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> The canonical RAG objective surveyed is a fixed top-k chunk ranking by semantic similarity (Naive RAG retrieves the Top K most-similar chunks). Advanced/Modular RAG add reranking and context selection/compression but still operate on a top-k-then-curate paradigm; the survey does not frame the objective as recovering a complete minimal set or as precision-driven variable-size recommendation. Multi-hop/iterative retrieval expands coverage across steps rather than enforcing per-call set completeness.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based-reasoning work; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain case cycle. It is a knowledge-RAG survey.)
- **explicit cbr grounding**: false. The survey does not frame RAG as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it treats RAG as retrieval-augmented generation over external knowledge.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Surveyed as a spectrum of granularities (the survey devotes section III-A2 to 'Retrieval Granularity'). Table I lists: Phrase (CoG), Proposition (DenseX), Sentence, Sentence Pair, Item (TIGER/LM-Indexer recommendation items), Chunk (the dominant unit), Document/Doc, Multi (UniMS-RAG), plus KG units: Triplet, Entity, Entity Sequence, Sub-Graph (SURGE, G-Retriever). The default Naive-RAG unit is the text chunk (vectorized segment of a document).
- **index source**:
> Surveyed across the spectrum: predominantly static offline-built corpora (Wikipedia, datasets, KGs, pre-training corpora indexed in vector databases). The survey notes the 'augmentation stage' axis (Pre-training / Fine-tuning / Inference) for when the index/method is constructed. Also covers inference-time generated context (LLMs as a knowledge source: GenRead, RECITE, PKG) and self-enhanced growing memory pools (Self-Mem). So index source is mostly static external; some hybrid offline+online/generated variants.
- **index structure topology**:
> The survey's section III-B (Indexing Optimization) and III-A (Retrieval Source / Data Structure) cover: flat vector indices (the Naive-RAG default vector database over chunks), metadata-attached indices (III-B2: metadata filtering, time-aware), structural/hierarchical indices (III-B3: hierarchical structural index, tree/summary structures e.g. RAPTOR, document trees), and knowledge-GRAPH indices (KGs/sub-graphs: SURGE, RoG, G-Retriever, HyKGE, KnowledGPT). So flat vector, metadata-keyed, hierarchical/tree, and graph topologies are all surveyed.
- **retriever type**:
> Surveyed broadly: dense embedding retrievers (the default; section III-D Embedding), sparse/keyword (BM25), mix/hybrid retrieval (III-D1, combining keyword+semantic+vector), fine-tuned/learned embedding models (III-D2), LLM-as-retriever / generative approaches (GenRead, RECITE generating context from model weights; LM-Indexer/TIGER generative item retrieval), and KG/graph retrievers. Adapter-based retrieval (III-E) is also covered. No single retriever is endorsed; the survey catalogs all types.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Surveyed across the full range: none/off-the-shelf (frozen dense or BM25 embeddings, training-free ICL), contrastive similarity training (fine-tuning embedding models, III-D2), LM-feedback signals (e.g. Rewrite-Retrieve-Read uses an LM-feedback mechanism to update the rewriting model; AAR uses LLM preferences; UPRISE, LLM-R train retrievers from LM signal), downstream-task-effectiveness, and end-to-end / collaborative fine-tuning of retriever+generator (RA-DIT, Atlas, RePLUG, BGM bridge model). Reinforcement learning is surveyed for adaptive retrieval/agents (WebGPT trains GPT-3 with RL to use a search engine). The survey frames retriever training along an Adapter/embedding-fine-tuning/RL spectrum.
- **query construction**:
> Surveyed in section III-C (Query Optimization): raw query (Naive RAG), query expansion (III-C1: multi-query, sub-queries, Chain-of-Verification), query transformation (III-C2: query rewriting via RRR/Rewrite-Retrieve-Read, HyDE hypothetical document embeddings, step-back prompting), and query routing (III-C3: routing to data sources/sub-pipelines). Iterative/recursive augmentation reconstructs queries from generated CoT/intermediate text (IRCoT, ITER-RETGEN, ToC clarification tree). So raw, expanded, rewritten/transformed, decomposed, and thought-conditioned query construction are all covered.
- **query granularity**:
> Surveyed at multiple levels. Default is task-level (one query at t=0 -> top-k). The augmentation chapter (V) covers trajectory/step-level query construction: iterative retrieval re-queries based on accumulated generation; recursive retrieval refines queries and decomposes into sub-problems (IRCoT uses CoT to guide each retrieval step); adaptive retrieval issues retrieval mid-generation (FLARE per upcoming-sentence, Self-RAG per segment). So task-level, trajectory-level, and step/state-level query granularities are all surveyed.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Surveyed as four modes (the organizing axis of section V and Table I's 'Retrieval process' column): Once (single retrieval before generation, the Naive-RAG default), Iterative (alternating retrieval and generation), Recursive (progressive query refinement / problem decomposition; also multi-hop on graphs), and Adaptive (the system autonomously decides whether/when to retrieve, e.g. FLARE, Self-RAG, SKR). Some entries are 'Multi-time'.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Surveyed concrete WHEN-to-retrieve signals in section V-C (Adaptive Retrieval): (a) fixed schedule (Once/Iterative-RETGEN fixed rounds); (b) token-level generation confidence/probability (FLARE monitors the probability of generated terms and triggers retrieval when below a threshold); (c) reflection/special tokens (Self-RAG emits 'retrieve' and 'critic' reflection tokens; WebGPT emits special action tokens for search/browse/cite); (d) learned classifier of self-knowledge (SKR judges whether the model already knows). The survey frames adaptive retrieval as the LLM exercising active judgment like an agent (AutoGPT, Toolformer, Graph-Toolformer).
- **reranking**:
> Yes - reranking is a first-class topic. Section IV-A1 (Reranking, under Context Curation in Generation) and the Advanced-RAG post-retrieval process cover relocating the most-relevant content to prompt edges, cross-encoder/rule-based and model-based rerankers, and RAG-Fusion's intelligent re-ranking after multi-query parallel search. Reranking is presented as a core post-retrieval / Advanced-RAG strategy implemented in LlamaIndex/LangChain/Haystack.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Surveyed extensively in section IV-A (Context Curation): reranking (IV-A1) and context selection/compression (IV-A2). Covered operations include reranking, context compression (RECOMP, PRCA, Token-Elimination/Long-context token reduction), selecting/emphasizing essential information to avoid information overload, noise filtering (FILCO, FILTER-rerank, CoN/Chain-of-Note), and the Predict module (GenRead generating context to reduce redundancy/noise). So none/rerank/decompose/distill/filter/compress are all surveyed.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (the survey is not about tool/skill retrieval; it focuses on document/knowledge retrieval. It touches tool-use only via agentic adaptive-retrieval examples like Toolformer/WebGPT, without analyzing tool-description engineering for indexing.)
- **index content separation**:
> N/A as a method, but the survey covers the related pattern under hierarchical/structural indexing (III-B3) and recursive retrieval (V-B): a lightweight summary/structural index can be searched first, then the heavier underlying document content retrieved on demand (e.g. summarize sections, then retrieve within the document; RAPTOR's tree of summaries). Not framed as progressive-disclosure SOP-index-then-content.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> N/A (no tool API / RapidAPI / MCP / function-calling tool index; static document/KG vector indices. The 'Search module' in Modular RAG can issue queries to search engines/databases/KGs via LLM-generated code/query languages, but this is not a synchronized tool registry with CRUD auto-sync.)
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no inter-tool dependency modeling; the survey covers document/KG retrieval, not multi-tool dependency graphs).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Predominantly prompt augmentation: retrieved chunks are synthesized with the query into a prompt for the LLM (the Naive/Advanced-RAG default). The survey also covers training-signal uses - retrieval integrated at the pre-training stage (Atlas, RETRO++, RAVEN), fine-tuning stage (RA-DIT, generator fine-tuning), and via adapters/intermediate modules (III-E Adapter, BGM bridge model) and latent integration. The 'how' is organized along the augmentation stage axis (pre-training / fine-tuning / inference).
- **planning integration**:
> As a RAG (not planning/agent) survey, planning integration is mostly out of scope; the closest analog is the augmentation-process taxonomy (section V): plan-then-retrieve and retrieve-then-plan analogs appear as recursive retrieval with problem decomposition into sub-problems (IRCoT chain-of-thought-guided retrieval, ToC clarification tree, DSP Demonstrate-Search-Predict) and iterative retrieve-read loops (ITER-RETGEN). Adaptive retrieval embeds the retrieve decision inside generation. There is no MCTS/tree-search planner or explicit hierarchical subtask planner surveyed.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Surveyed at several granularities: per-answer (Once retrieval), per-CoT-step (recursive retrieval, IRCoT interleaves a reasoning step with a retrieval step; ITER-RETGEN alternates retrieval-augmented-generation and generation-augmented-retrieval each round), and per-sentence/per-token (adaptive retrieval: FLARE triggers retrieval per upcoming sentence based on token confidence; Self-RAG operates per segment with fragment-level beam search). Per-tool-call is touched via WebGPT/agentic special tokens.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> N/A (no case adaptation/revision cycle - knowledge RAG injects retrieved text as context rather than adapting a retrieved case. The closest analog is post-retrieval context curation/compression and corrective retrieval, but that is refinement of context, not CBR-style case adaptation.)
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Predominantly raw retrieved text (chunks/documents/passages) injected as prompt context. The survey also covers distilled/compressed representations (context compression, summaries in hierarchical/recursive retrieval, RAPTOR summary nodes), generated/predicted context (GenRead, PKG), structured KG triples/sub-graphs (SURGE, RoG, G-Retriever), and notes (Chain-of-Note). The dominant surface form is raw text; refinement produces compressed/summarized/structured variants.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Mostly raw retrieved passages/chunks (no distilled strategy or procedural skill - this is classic knowledge RAG, not experience/skill retrieval). Higher-abstraction units surveyed include summaries (RAPTOR recursive summarization, hierarchical structural index), propositions (DenseX), and KG sub-graphs/triples (structured relational abstraction). The survey does not retrieve strategies/workflows/skills in the agentic-experience sense.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> A central evaluation aspect and discussion topic. Methods surveyed for guarding against irrelevant/incorrect context: relevance evaluation / self-reflection (Self-RAG critic tokens, CRAG corrective retrieval), reason-in-documents / note-taking (CoN Chain-of-Note), distractor filtering and context compression (FILCO, FILTER-rerank, RECOMP, NoiseRAG study), and retriever-aware / robustness-targeted training (RAG-Robust, NoMIRACL for negative/no-relevant-doc rejection). Section VII-B (RAG Robustness) discusses how noise and even counterfactual/adversarial documents affect RAG, and evaluation aspect 'Noise Robustness', 'Negative Rejection', and 'Counterfactual Robustness' formalize it.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> Mostly none (classic RAG over static external knowledge). The survey does cover a 'Memory module' in Modular RAG (II-C1): leveraging the LLM's memory to guide retrieval, creating an unbounded memory pool aligned to data distribution through iterative self-enhancement (Self-Mem). So an episodic/self-enhancing memory-pool type is surveyed as one module, but it is not the dominant paradigm.
- **write back**:
> Mostly false for canonical RAG (the external index is static). Exception surveyed: the Memory module (Self-Mem) writes back self-generated/selected memories into an unbounded, iteratively self-enhanced memory pool. As a survey it documents both static (no write-back) and self-enhancing (write-back) variants; write-back is the minority case.
- **online growth**:
> Predominantly false (the vector index is frozen after offline construction; retrieval is read-only at inference). The surveyed Memory module / Self-Mem is the exception where the memory pool grows via iterative self-enhancement at inference. The dominant surveyed paradigm has no online growth.
- **write back trigger**:
> Mostly never (static external corpus, read-only retrieval). For the minority Memory-module / Self-Mem case surveyed, writes are reflective/self-enhancement-triggered (the model iteratively generates candidate memories and selects/retains the better ones to align the pool with the data distribution). No on-success/on-failure experience-logging trigger is a focus, since this is knowledge RAG not experience RAG.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Not a focus (knowledge RAG does not store success/failure experiences). The closest related ideas surveyed are negative/distractor handling at training time (RAG-Robust, NoMIRACL negative-rejection, FILCO filtering) and counterfactual-robustness evaluation - i.e. handling incorrect retrieved documents, not storing the agent's own failed trajectories. No success-vs-failure contrastive experience memory is surveyed as a paradigm.
- **memory evolution update**:
> Mostly N/A (static external index; no stored experiential entries to mutate). For the Self-Mem memory-pool exception the dynamic is iterative refine/self-enhancement (regenerate-and-select to improve the pool). Indexing optimization (re-chunking, metadata, hierarchical re-structuring, RAPTOR summarization) is an offline index-construction operation rather than online entry mutation.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Surveyed as a spectrum but the dominant paradigm is fixed similarity top-k, not a learned policy. Learned/optimized variants covered: RL-trained retrieval/search action selection (WebGPT trains GPT-3 with reinforcement learning to use a search engine), learned query routing (III-C3), learned adaptive-retrieval triggers (Self-RAG reflection tokens, SKR self-knowledge classifier), and end-to-end trained retriever-generator (RePLUG, RA-DIT, Atlas, BGM). No M-MDP / soft-Q case-selection policy (out of scope for a knowledge-RAG survey).
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Not a focus / largely N/A. The survey covers single-system RAG pipelines; it does not center collective or cross-agent shared memory. It does note that the Modular-RAG flexible architecture can integrate other technologies and that adaptive retrieval mirrors agent tool-use (AutoGPT, Toolformer), but no explicit cross-agent or cross-framework experience sharing is surveyed.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> Catalogs ~50 datasets across 26 tasks (Table II). QA: Natural Questions (NQ), TriviaQA, SQuAD, WebQuestions, PopQA, MS MARCO (single-hop); HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue (multi-hop); ELI5, NarrativeQA, ASQA, QMSum (long-form); Qasper, COVID-QA, CMB, MMCU_Medical (domain); QuALITY, ARC, CommonsenseQA (multiple-choice); GraphQA. Dialogue: Wizard of Wikipedia, KBP, DuLeMon, CamRest, Amazon (recommendation). IE: WikiEvent, RAMS, T-REx, ZsRE. Reasoning: HellaSwag, CoT, CSQA, StrategyQA. Others: MMLU, WikiText-103, FEVER, PubHealth, Biography, WikiASP, XSum, VioLens, TREC, SST-2, CodeSearchNet, NoMIRACL, GSM8K, JRC-Acquis. RAG-specific evaluation benchmarks: RGB, RECALL, CRUD; tools: RAGAS, ARES, TruLens, RALLE.
- **benchmark family**:
> QA (single-hop NQ/TriviaQA/SQuAD/WebQ/PopQA/MS MARCO), multi-hop QA (HotpotQA/2WikiMultiHopQA/MuSiQue), long-form QA (ELI5/NarrativeQA/ASQA/QMSum), domain QA (Qasper/COVID-QA/CMB), multiple-choice QA (QuALITY/ARC/CommonsenseQA), dialogue, information extraction, reasoning (StrategyQA/CSQA/HellaSwag/GSM8K), fact-checking (FEVER/PubHealth), summarization, classification/sentiment, code search (CodeSearchNet), machine translation, recommendation, and RAG-robustness (NoMIRACL). Plus dedicated RAG evaluation families: RGB/RECALL/CRUD benchmarks and RAGAS/ARES/TruLens tools. Not the agent/web/embodied/tool benchmark families (Mind2Web/WebArena/ALFWorld/ToolBench) of the agentic-RAG literature.
- **baselines**:
> N/A (a survey, not a method - it runs no head-to-head experiments and reports no baseline comparison table of its own). It compares RAG conceptually against Fine-tuning (FT) and Prompt Engineering along the axes of 'External Knowledge Required' vs 'Model Adaptation Required' (Figure 4), and against Long-Context LLMs (section VII-A), citing that RAG consistently outperforms unsupervised fine-tuning on knowledge-intensive tasks.
- **key metrics**:
> Surveys the metrics rather than reporting its own. Task metrics: EM, F1, Accuracy, BLEU, ROUGE/ROUGE-L (Table III). Retrieval-quality metrics: Hit Rate, MRR, NDCG, Recall, Precision. RAG-specific aspect metrics: R-Rate (Reappearance Rate, for counterfactual robustness), Cosine Similarity, BertScore, RAGQuestEval, plus the RAGAS/ARES triad scores (Context Relevance, Faithfulness, Answer Relevance). Table III maps each metric to the seven evaluation aspects.
- **headline result**:
> N/A (no single experimental headline number - it is a review). Its headline conceptual contribution is the three-paradigm taxonomy Naive RAG -> Advanced RAG -> Modular RAG plus the tripartite 'Retrieval / Generation / Augmentation' decomposition, and an evaluation framework of 3 quality scores (Context Relevance, Faithfulness, Answer Relevance) and 4 abilities (Noise Robustness, Negative Rejection, Information Integration, Counterfactual Robustness), synthesized from 100+ RAG studies, 26 tasks, and ~50 datasets.
- **ablations**:
> N/A (no experiments, hence no ablations). The analytical equivalent is the comparative framing: (1) the paradigm comparison (Naive vs Advanced vs Modular RAG, Figure 3) showing which components/strategies address which Naive-RAG failure modes; (2) the RAG-vs-Fine-tuning-vs-Prompt-Engineering quadrant (Figure 4); (3) the augmentation-process comparison (Once vs Iterative vs Recursive vs Adaptive, Figure 5); (4) the RAG-vs-Long-Context discussion (VII-A).
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Yes - the survey explicitly separates Retrieval Quality (intrinsic IR metrics: Hit Rate, MRR, NDCG, Context Relevance) from Generation Quality (Faithfulness, Answer Relevance, Accuracy, BLEU/ROUGE) as the two 'Evaluation Targets' (section VI-B), and maps metrics/abilities to each (Table III, Table IV). It advocates measuring retrieval and generation separately, which is precisely the decoupling principle.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both, and the survey argues process quality matters. Outcome: task accuracy/EM/F1/BLEU/ROUGE. Process: Context Relevance and retrieval IR metrics (Hit Rate/MRR/NDCG) score the retrieval step; Faithfulness scores whether generation is grounded in retrieved context (a process-faithfulness measure); the four 'required abilities' (Noise Robustness, Negative Rejection, Information Integration, Counterfactual Robustness) probe intermediate behavior beyond final-answer correctness.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Discussed qualitatively rather than measured. The survey notes RAG is cost-effective vs native LLMs and vs retraining (FT), but incurs higher inference latency and retrieval overhead; context compression/selection (IV-A2) and token elimination are surveyed to cut prompt length/cost; the RAG-vs-Long-Context discussion (VII-A) weighs retrieval cost against feeding long context; 'Scaling laws of RAG' (VII-D) and 'Production-Ready RAG' (VII-E) raise efficiency/engineering tradeoffs. No quantitative latency/token/API-cost numbers are reported by the survey itself.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> The canonical RAG budget lever surveyed is Top-K chunk selection by similarity, then post-retrieval reranking-then-truncation and context compression (IV-A2) to fit the LLM context window and avoid information overload / 'lost in the middle'. The survey discusses chunking strategy (III-B1, chunk size/overlap, sliding window) as the granularity-vs-budget tradeoff. k is typically fixed but adaptive/iterative variants change the effective number of retrieved items across steps. No single numeric budget is prescribed.
- **survey scope and axes**:
> Explicit organizing axes: (1) the three-paradigm evolution Naive RAG / Advanced RAG / Modular RAG; (2) the tripartite RAG foundation Retrieval / Generation / Augmentation; (3) the LLM-lifecycle 'technology tree' axis: pre-training / fine-tuning / inference; (4) Table I axes per method: Retrieval Source, Retrieval Data Type, Retrieval Granularity, Augmentation Stage, Retrieval Process (Once/Iterative/Recursive/Adaptive); (5) evaluation axes: 2 targets, 3 quality scores, 4 abilities. Coverage: 100+ RAG studies, 26 downstream tasks, ~50 datasets; reference count ~169 (numbered citations to bib169); time window roughly 2020-2023 with v5 revised March 2024.
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A (this is a survey, not a benchmark paper - it does not construct a new dataset). It instead catalogs existing benchmarks/tools (RGB, RECALL, CRUD benchmarks; RAGAS, ARES, TruLens, RALLE tools) and ~50 task datasets, summarizing each framework's evaluation targets, aspects, and metrics in Table IV.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Foundational pre-LLM RAG and retrieval-augmented LM work: the original RAG (Lewis et al. 2020), REALM, RETRO/RETRO++, Atlas, kNN-LM, DPR; in-context learning with ChatGPT/GPT-3.5. Builds conceptually on the Retrieve-Read framework and on prior component lines: query optimization (HyDE, query rewriting), reranking, context compression (RECOMP), iterative/recursive retrieval (IRCoT, ITER-RETGEN, DSP), and adaptive retrieval (FLARE, Self-RAG, WebGPT). Evaluation framework builds on RGB, RECALL, CRUD, RAGAS, ARES, TruLens.
- **contrasts with**:
> Positions RAG against (1) Fine-tuning (FT) and (2) Prompt Engineering as alternative LLM-optimization strategies (Figure 4 quadrant: External Knowledge vs Model Adaptation), arguing RAG consistently outperforms unsupervised fine-tuning for knowledge injection; (3) Long-Context LLMs (VII-A), arguing RAG remains valuable for efficiency/updatability despite growing context windows; and (4) within RAG, contrasts Naive vs Advanced vs Modular paradigms and Once vs Iterative/Recursive/Adaptive augmentation. Also contrasts with concurrent RAG surveys (e.g. by being the most-cited foundational RAG paradigm survey).
- **lineage**:
> Surveys lineage. This is the canonical, most-cited foundational RAG survey (Group: Surveys), defining the Naive->Advanced->Modular RAG vocabulary widely adopted thereafter. It anchors the RAG-for-LLMs literature and is a precursor to later, more specialized surveys (agentic RAG, graph RAG, multimodal RAG, RAG evaluation). It sits upstream of the agentic/experience-retrieval works in this collection by establishing the static-corpus knowledge-RAG baseline that adaptive/iterative methods (FLARE, Self-RAG, IRCoT, Adaptive-RAG) extend.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- venue

### 153. The Rise and Potential of Large Language Model Based Agents: A Survey (LLM-Agent Survey / Xi et al.)

2023  ·  arXiv 2309.07864  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.07864)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2023
- **venue**:
> arXiv preprint (arXiv:2309.07864, cs.AI/cs.CL); submitted 14 Sep 2023, v3 19 Sep 2023, 86 pages. Later formally published (peer-reviewed) as a REVIEW in Science China Information Sciences (SCIS), Feb 2025, Vol. 68, Iss. 2, 121101 (44 pages), DOI 10.1007/s11432-024-4222-0 (received 7 Sep 2024 / accepted 11 Nov 2024 / published online 17 Jan 2025).
- **authors affiliation**:
> Zhiheng Xi, Wenxiang Chen, Xin Guo, Wei He, Yiwen Ding, Boyang Hong, Ming Zhang, Junzhe Wang, Senjie Jin, Enyu Zhou (10 co-first authors), Rui Zheng, ... Xipeng Qiu, Xuanjing Huang, Qi Zhang (corresponding) and Tao Gui (corresponding), et al. (29 authors). Primary affiliation: School of Computer Science, Fudan University, Shanghai, China (with Fudan College of Foreign Languages & Literature, Institute of Modern Languages and Linguistics, and Meituan).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.07864
- **code url**: https://github.com/WooooDyy/LLM-Agent-Paper-List (curated paper list / reading list accompanying the survey; not a runnable method implementation since this is a survey).
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/WooooDyy/LLM-Agent-Paper-List (continuously-updated GitHub paper list maintained by the authors; describes itself as the paper list of the 86-page SCIS cover paper).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Survey / taxonomy. Broad survey of LLM-based agents spanning planning, tool-use, embodied, web, multi-agent, decision-making, and human-agent cooperation; not restricted to a single task domain.
- **problem setting**:
> This is a comprehensive literature survey (not a method/system with experiments). It traces the concept of agents from philosophical origins to AI, argues why LLMs are suitable agent foundations, and proposes a conceptual framework for LLM-based agents with three components: brain, perception, and action. It then organizes applications into single-agent scenarios, multi-agent scenarios, and human-agent cooperation, and discusses agent society (behavior/personality, emergent social phenomena) and open problems. It covers both offline and interactive settings and both single- and multi-agent systems as surveyed sub-areas, but the survey itself defines no controlled experimental protocol, supervision, or benchmark of its own.
- **what is retrieved**:
> N/A for the survey as an artifact (it does not itself retrieve). As a surveyed topic, it covers agent memory retrieval (retrieving past experiences/dialogue history/observations from agent memory) and tool-related knowledge (tool descriptions/manuals, demonstrations). The brain module discussion includes knowledge, memory (recall of prior interactions), and tool descriptions as content an agent draws upon.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> Survey-level: covers BOTH a GROWING/episodic agent memory (the surveyed 'memory capability' where agents store and later retrieve past interactions/experiences) and access to STATIC external knowledge/tools (knowledge, tool manuals/APIs). The survey itself is not grounded in any single corpus.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> N/A (survey, no retrieval objective of its own). The surveyed memory-retrieval discussion describes top-scoring selection via a weighted recency+relevance+importance memory score (i.e., a ranked top-k style selection in the generative-agents line it cites), not a completeness objective.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (the survey is not a case-based reasoning system; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain cycle is implemented).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The survey does not frame LLM-based agents as case-based reasoning and does not center Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it organizes the field around a brain/perception/action framework (with memory, knowledge, reasoning/planning, tool-use, etc.).

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: N/A (survey defines no retrieval unit of its own). Surveyed memory units include past dialogue/interaction history and stored experiences/observations (episodic memory entries); surveyed tool-use units include tool descriptions/manuals and usage demonstrations.
- **index source**: N/A for the survey. Surveyed memory is a growing store that agents write during interaction (online/test-time-induced episodic memory); surveyed tool/knowledge access is from static external resources. The survey itself builds no index.
- **index structure topology**:
> N/A (survey has no index of its own). It reviews memory storage substrates used by agents (e.g., natural-language memory in context, external vector/embedding stores, and structured databases such as SQL/ChatDB/DB-GPT), i.e., it surveys both flat and structured/database memory organizations rather than prescribing one.
- **retriever type**:
> N/A (survey; no retriever implemented). The surveyed memory-retrieval methods include embedding/similarity-based retrieval plus heuristic scoring (recency/relevance/importance weighting), and database-query retrieval (SQL). Tool selection is described as LLM-driven (prompt/feedback based).
- **retriever learning signal**: N/A (survey; no retriever is trained). It surveys agents that learn tool use from zero-shot/few-shot prompts and from environmental/human feedback, and memory retrieval driven by hand-designed scoring (recency+relevance+importance) rather than a trained retriever.
- **query construction**: N/A (survey). For surveyed memory retrieval, the current interaction/state acts as the query that is matched against stored memories; no query-construction method is proposed by the survey itself.
- **query granularity**: N/A (survey). Surveyed agents retrieve from memory at the step/interaction level during a task (when the agent needs relevant content to make a decision), but the survey prescribes no single granularity.
- **when to retrieve**: N/A (survey). Surveyed memory retrieval occurs interactively (when the agent must access relevant memory content to make a decision during environment interaction); the survey does not standardize a trigger.
- **retrieval trigger signal**: N/A (survey defines no trigger). Surveyed agent-initiated retrieval is driven by the agent's need for relevant memory during decision-making (agent-initiated / per-interaction), and tool invocation is agent-initiated within reasoning loops.
- **reranking**: N/A (survey; no reranking stage of its own). It notes memory-score-based prioritization (weighted recency/relevance/importance) as a selection/ranking heuristic in the generative-agents line it cites.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> N/A (survey). It discusses memory reflection/summarization (e.g., summarizing or editing dialogue history, interactive memory objects that can be moved/edited/deleted/combined via summarization) as post-storage processing in surveyed systems, but proposes no refinement pipeline itself.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Surveyed (not a method contribution): the survey describes agents learning tools via zero-shot prompts containing tool functionality and parameter descriptions and few-shot prompts providing usage demonstrations (analogous to consulting tool manuals or observing usage), plus learning tools from environmental and human feedback. It does not propose its own tool-document-engineering technique.
- **index content separation**: N/A (survey; no index-vs-content separation mechanism of its own).
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (survey). It predates and does not cover MCP; it surveys tool use via prompting/API-calling and feedback-based learning rather than a live-synchronized tool index/protocol.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (survey). It discusses single-tool and multi-tool use and tool-creation/learning at a high level but does not center an inter-tool dependency-graph retrieval formalism.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> N/A as a method. The survey describes how agents use retrieved/recalled content: prompt augmentation (recalled memory and tool descriptions/demos placed in the LLM context to inform reasoning, planning, and action), tool invocation, and reflection. No method is implemented by the survey.
- **planning integration**:
> N/A as a method. The survey reviews planning as a brain/reasoning capability with two stages: plan formulation (decompose an overarching task into sub-tasks) and plan reflection. It catalogs planning-without-feedback styles (single-step full-plan-then-execute; adaptive CoT-series one-sub-task-at-a-time; hierarchical planning; tree-structured search over candidate paths) and planning-with-feedback (environment/human/model feedback), but proposes no single integration.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: N/A (survey). It contrasts decompose-first (one-shot full plan) vs adaptive/interleaved per-step planning (CoT-series, ReAct-style) as surveyed paradigms rather than committing to one interleaving granularity.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not a CBR method; no retrieved-case adaptation mechanism of its own).
- **retrieved item representation**: N/A (survey). Surveyed memory/knowledge is mostly represented as natural-language (free-text) entries (past interactions, observations, reflections) or stored in databases; the survey injects nothing itself.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: N/A (survey). Surveyed memory ranges from raw interaction/dialogue history to distilled/summarized reflections; the survey reviews this spectrum rather than fixing an abstraction level.
- **noise robustness mechanism**: N/A (survey). It discusses memory reflection/summarization and feedback-driven correction in surveyed agents and notes general robustness/hallucination challenges, but contributes no specific noise-robustness mechanism.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> Survey-level: the brain/perception/action framework explicitly includes a Memory capability (episodic agent memory of past interactions/experiences), alongside knowledge. It reviews short-term (in-context) and long-term memory and various storage substrates (natural language, embeddings/vector stores, structured databases). As an artifact the survey itself has no memory.
- **write back**: N/A as a method. Surveyed agents DO write back experiences/dialogue into memory (the memory capability stores past interactions for later retrieval), and the survey covers memory reading, writing, and reflection as core operations; but the survey itself stores nothing.
- **online growth**: N/A as a method. Surveyed agent memory grows online during interaction/deployment (the agent continually stores new interactions/experiences); the survey itself has no growing store.
- **write back trigger**: N/A (survey; no write-back trigger of its own). Surveyed memory writing is generally per-interaction / per-step during environment interaction, with reflective summarization/editing of stored memory in some cited systems; the survey does not standardize a trigger.
- **failure experience usage**: N/A (survey). It discusses agents learning from environmental feedback (including whether actions succeeded or failed) and self-reflection, implying use of both success and failure signals in surveyed systems, but contributes no specific failure-experience storage scheme.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (survey). It notes memory operations such as editing, deleting, combining via summarization, and reflection (i.e., post-write mutation in cited systems like interactive memory objects, ChatDB/DB-GPT SQL deletion), but proposes no single update policy.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: N/A (survey). Surveyed memory retrieval is largely heuristic (recency/relevance/importance scoring) or similarity/database-query based, not a learned RL retrieval policy; the survey does not center retrieval-as-learned-policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Surveyed (not a method contribution): the survey devotes major sections to multi-agent scenarios (cooperative and adversarial), agent communication, and agent societies, which include shared/collective information and experience across multiple agents; it reviews rather than implements cross-agent sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**: N/A (survey; runs no experiments and reports no benchmark results of its own). It references and discusses many agent benchmarks/environments used by surveyed works (e.g., embodied/game environments, web/tool/QA settings) but presents no controlled evaluation.
- **benchmark family**: N/A (survey). Surveyed sub-areas span embodied (e.g., Minecraft/Voyager-style, ALFWorld-type), web, tool-use, QA, code, and multi-agent/social-simulation families, but the survey itself reports no benchmark family results.
- **baselines**: N/A (survey; no method comparison or baselines of its own).
- **key metrics**: N/A (survey; reports no quantitative metrics of its own).
- **headline result**:
> N/A (survey; no headline number). Its 'headline' contribution is the conceptual brain/perception/action framework for LLM-based agents plus a comprehensive, widely-cited organization of the field (highly cited: >1,700 citations on the arXiv version; the SCIS journal version reports 512 references).
- **ablations**: N/A (survey; no ablations). As a literature survey it conducts no experiments and therefore reports no component ablations.
- **evaluation decoupling**: N/A (survey reports no retrieval or end-to-end metrics). It does include a dedicated discussion of evaluating LLM-based agents (utility, sociability, values, etc.) as an open topic, but no intrinsic-vs-end-to-end metric decoupling is performed.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: N/A (survey; performs no scoring). It discusses, at the field level, evaluation dimensions for agents (capabilities and behaviors) but does not itself score process or outcome.
- **context budget and selection count**: N/A (survey; no token budget or k of its own). It discusses agents' limited context windows and the role of memory in extending effective context as a surveyed challenge.
- **survey scope and axes**:
> Primary organizing axes: (1) a general LLM-based-agent framework with three components -- brain (knowledge, memory, reasoning/planning, transferability/generalization), perception (multimodal inputs: text, visual, auditory, etc.), and action (text output, tool use, embodied/physical action); (2) agents in practice -- single-agent scenarios, multi-agent scenarios (cooperative/adversarial), and human-agent cooperation; (3) agent society -- behavior & personality, social environment, emergent social phenomena; plus open problems/future directions. Coverage: ~2023 snapshot (v3 Sep 2023). Reference count: the SCIS journal version (2025) lists 512 references (the arXiv v3 is 86 pages / 12 figures).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (this is a survey, not a benchmark; it constructs no dataset and reports no dataset size or best-system score of its own).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Builds conceptually on the classical AI notion of agents (perception-decision-action) and on LLMs as agent foundations; synthesizes prior agent capabilities literature on planning/reasoning (CoT, ReAct, Tree-of-Thoughts-style search), memory (generative-agents-style recency/relevance/importance memory; long-term memory stores incl. databases like ChatDB/DB-GPT), tool use (tool-learning via prompts/demonstrations and feedback), multi-agent systems, and embodied agents. It aggregates and organizes these as a survey rather than extending a single predecessor method.
- **contrasts with**:
> Positions itself against task-specific or capability-specific prior agent work (algorithm/training-strategy advances for particular tasks) that lacks a general, powerful foundation model; argues LLM-based agents provide a general starting point. As a survey it contrasts with, and complements, other contemporaneous LLM-agent surveys (e.g., Wang et al. 2023 'A Survey on Large Language Model based Autonomous Agents') by emphasizing the brain/perception/action framework and agent-society perspective.
- **lineage**:
> Surveys group: a foundational, broad 2023 survey of LLM-based agents (brain/perception/action; single-/multi-agent; agent society). It is an umbrella reference for the agent-memory, planning, and tool-use sub-topics that the retrieval-augmented-agent lineage (Groups A-F) specializes, rather than a method within any single sub-topic.

### 154. A Survey on the Memory Mechanism of Large Language Model based Agents (Zhang et al.)

2024  ·  ACM TOIS 2024  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.13501)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**:
> ACM Transactions on Information Systems (TOIS); accepted 2025-07-02 (DOI 10.1145/3748302). First released as arXiv:2404.13501 [cs.AI] on 2024-04-21. The task label 'ACM TOIS 2024' refers to the same TOIS publication; the arXiv preprint is dated 2024 and the journal acceptance is 2025.
- **authors affiliation**: Zeyu Zhang, Xiaohe Bo, Chen Ma, Rui Li, Xu Chen (corresponding), Ji-Rong Wen — Gaoling School of Artificial Intelligence, Renmin University of China, Beijing; Quanyu Dai, Jieming Zhu, Zhenhua Dong — Huawei Noah's Ark Lab, China.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.13501
- **code url**: N/A (a survey; no method code. A curated paper-list repository is maintained instead.)
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/nuster1128/LLM_Agent_Memory_Survey (curated paper list, ~495 stars; README last updated 2025-07-27; tracks works on memory sources/forms/operations/evaluation/applications).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Survey/taxonomy of the memory mechanism of LLM-based agents, spanning conversation, role-playing/social simulation, multi-source QA, long-context applications, recommendation, code generation, embodied/open-world (e.g., Minecraft via Voyager/GITM), and decision-making agents (anchor memory survey, not a single task method).
- **problem setting**:
> A holistic survey that defines what agent memory is and why it is needed (cognitive psychology, self-evolution, applications), then systematically reviews HOW memory is designed and evaluated for LLM-based agents. Settings covered are predominantly interactive and long-horizon agent-environment loops (single- and multi-agent), where memory enables self-evolution via experience accumulation, environment exploration, and knowledge abstraction. Supervision varies by surveyed work; the survey itself proposes no new method, dataset, or experiments and offers a unified framework abstracting common design patterns. It explicitly notes that, at the time, there were no open-sourced benchmarks tailored specifically for evaluating agent memory modules.
- **what is retrieved**:
> Across surveyed systems: experiences / trajectories (inside-trial and cross-trial information), summaries/insights, external knowledge (docs/KB/APIs), and dialogue/episodic records. The survey frames retrieval as the 'memory reading' operation that pulls relevant stored memory entries (raw histories, summaries, retrieved memory pieces, external knowledge) for the current state.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> HYBRID — the survey's memory-sources taxonomy spans inside-trial information and cross-trial information (a GROWING/episodic memory the agent writes during interaction) plus External Knowledge (a STATIC external corpus such as docs/KB). It explicitly distinguishes dynamically generated in-loop memory from static out-of-loop external knowledge.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (a survey, not a CBR method). However, the surveyed memory-operation framework (Writing / Management / Reading) plus experience-accumulation maps loosely onto CBR's Retain/Revise/Retrieve, though the survey does not use CBR phase terminology.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False — the survey frames memory via cognitive psychology (sensory/short-term/long-term memory analogies) and a sources/forms/operations taxonomy; it does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Survey taxonomy of memory units rather than one unit: inside-trial steps (observations, thoughts, actions), cross-trial trajectories/experiences, distilled summaries/insights, dialogue segments (topic-keyed), structured relations (e.g., entity relations in TiM), and external knowledge documents. Retrieved 'reading' units are memory entries at these granularities (full trajectory / sub-trajectory / summary / document).
- **index source**:
> Hybrid construction. Memory store is built from (a) dynamically generated in-loop information (inside-trial and cross-trial, written online during agent-environment interaction) and (b) static external knowledge induced offline. The survey explicitly contrasts dynamically generated memory with static external information.
- **index structure topology**:
> Surveyed stores span multiple topologies: flat vector index (e.g., ExpeL using FAISS), structured/relational database (ChatDB SQL, TiM structured relation DB grouping similar contents), topic-keyed segment indices (MemoChat), hierarchical/virtual-context memory (MemGPT), and parametric stores (encoded into model parameters). No single topology is prescribed; the survey organizes by source/form/operation rather than index topology.
- **retriever type**:
> Survey-level: surveyed memory-reading methods use mainly text-similarity dense retrieval (e.g., ExpeL FAISS top-K similarity), LLM-generated query/SQL retrieval (ChatDB Chain-of-Memory SQL), and rule/agent-directed reading; for parametric memory, 'reading' is implicit forward-pass use of encoded parameters. Hybrid across works; no canonical retriever is proposed.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Survey-level: most reviewed reading mechanisms are off-the-shelf (text similarity, auxiliary scoring such as recency/relevance/importance as in Generative Agents). Some are LM-/agent-directed (LLM generates SQL or decides what to read). The survey does not propose a learned retriever; learning signals discussed are mainly heuristic relevance/recency/importance rather than trained ranking models.
- **query construction**:
> Survey-level: queries to memory are formed from the current state/task (raw current query), agent-generated structured queries (ChatDB generates SQL as a Chain-of-Memory in advance), and Chain-of-Thought-guided selection (MPC provides CoT examples to ignore certain memory). Construction is method-dependent; the survey abstracts it as state-conditioned memory reading.
- **query granularity**: Survey-level: predominantly step/state-level reading (memory is read for the current state during reasoning/decision-making), with task-level reads also present; the survey does not standardize a query granularity.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Survey-level: both one-shot and iterative reading appear across surveyed works; memory reading is invoked when the agent needs information for reasoning/decision-making (often per step/turn). Some works use a controller to decide when to operate on memory (e.g., SCM memory controller). No single trigger policy is prescribed.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Survey-level: triggers across works include fixed schedule (read each step/turn), agent-initiated/self-directed access (MemGPT self-directed memory ops; ChatDB agent-generated SQL reads), and controller-decided operations (SCM memory controller deciding when to write/manage/read). The survey does not adopt token-confidence or attention-based triggers as a unifying signal.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Survey-level: refinement is treated under 'Memory Management' (reflection, summarization, abstraction, merging of stored entries) and at write time (storing summaries/insights vs raw info). At read time most works do similarity top-K with light auxiliary scoring. Distractor filtering/compression are discussed mainly as management/summarization, not as a separate post-retrieval module.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (memory survey; tool/skill-description engineering is out of scope, though external-knowledge and skill-library memory such as Voyager's skill code are mentioned).
- **index content separation**:
> Partially covered: hierarchical/virtual-context memory (e.g., MemGPT) separates a small in-context working memory from a larger external store paged in on demand; topic-keyed indexing (MemoChat) stores topic keys for indexing fuller memory pieces. The survey discusses this as a memory-management/forms pattern rather than a formal index-vs-content separation principle.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index / integration protocol; memory stores grow via in-loop writing rather than tool-API CRUD sync).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (inter-tool dependency modeling is out of scope for this memory survey).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Survey-level: retrieved memory is used as prompt augmentation (injecting recalled context/experiences into the LLM prompt for reasoning and decision-making), as experience reuse for self-evolution, and—in parametric form—as a training signal/parameter encoding that implicitly influences actions (fine-tuning, model editing). The survey frames usage as providing information for LLM inference via the reading operation.
- **planning integration**:
> Survey-level: memory supports planning/acting by supplying past experiences/observations at plan and act time (e.g., Reflexion/ExpeL reuse cross-trial reflections; Voyager/GITM use skill/experience memory for open-world planning). The survey abstracts this as memory enabling experience accumulation, exploration guidance, and knowledge abstraction rather than prescribing a specific plan-time integration.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Survey-level: reviewed works interleave memory reading at per-turn / per-step granularity during reasoning and decision-making; the survey does not impose a single interleaving granularity.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (a survey, not a CBR adaptation method). Surveyed 'memory management' (reflection/abstraction/summarization) and write-time summarization are the closest analogues to case revision/adaptation.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Survey-level: two top-level forms — Textual form (raw histories, recent/complete context, retrieved memory pieces, summaries/insights, external knowledge as natural language) and Parametric form (memory encoded into model parameters via fine-tuning or model editing, latent/soft representation). Surface forms thus range from raw trajectory to distilled summary to structured relation to latent parameters.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Survey-level spectrum: raw inside-trial steps/observations, cross-trial trajectories, distilled summaries/insights/abstracted knowledge (knowledge abstraction), and structured relations. The survey explicitly highlights moving from raw observations to higher-level abstracted concepts as a key memory function.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Survey-level: discussed via write-time information extraction/summarization (original info is 'lengthy and noisy', so extraction strategy is vital), memory management (reflection/merging to consolidate), and CoT-guided ignoring of irrelevant memory (MPC). No retriever-aware training or distractor-aware SFT is proposed by the survey itself.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> Survey/taxonomy — covers all listed types: episodic (in-loop dialogue/observation histories), skill-library (e.g., Voyager skills), workflow/procedural experiences, structured/graph-like relational memory (TiM), and latent/parametric memory (fine-tuning, model editing). It does not pick one; it taxonomizes textual vs parametric forms over inside-trial/cross-trial/external sources.
- **write back**:
> True (survey-level) — 'Memory Writing' is one of the three core operations: agents store perceived information (raw and/or summarized) for future use; many surveyed systems (MemGPT, MemoChat, TiM, Reflexion/ExpeL) write back experiences/summaries. The survey describes write-back as central, not a single implementation.
- **online growth**:
> Yes (survey-level) — inside-trial and cross-trial memory grow dynamically during agent-environment interaction (written online), while external-knowledge memory may be static. The survey explicitly distinguishes dynamically generated in-loop memory from static out-of-loop information.
- **write back trigger**:
> Survey-level: triggers vary across works — self-directed/autonomous writing (MemGPT updates memory based on context), controller-decided writing (SCM memory controller decides when to execute operations), per-segment summarization (MemoChat summarizes each conversation segment), and reflective writing after trials (Reflexion/ExpeL store reflections/experiences). The survey notes designing the information-extraction (write) strategy is vital but prescribes no single trigger.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Survey-level: explicitly highlighted — a key memory function is to remember past error plannings, inappropriate behaviors, and failed experiences so the agent handles similar future tasks better (self-evolution via experience accumulation). Surveyed systems (e.g., Reflexion/Retroformer/ExpeL) store both successful and failed/negative trial experiences for reuse.
- **memory evolution update**:
> Survey-level: covered under 'Memory Management' — stored entries can be processed/abstracted over time via reflection, summarization/abstraction, and merging of similar contents (e.g., TiM groups similar contents; reflection/merging consolidate memory). So beyond append-only, dedup-merge and refine/abstract dynamics are surveyed; the survey notes parametric memory needs no manual merging rules unlike textual memory.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Survey-level: largely single-agent private memory, but the survey explicitly flags 'Memory in LLM-based Multi-agent Applications' as a future direction (memory shared/coordinated across agents, e.g., MetaGPT/ChatDev multi-agent settings) and reviews multi-agent systems where memory is exchanged. Cross-framework shared experience is identified as an open direction rather than a solved mechanism.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> No new benchmark is introduced. The survey reviews indirect-evaluation tasks/datasets used by other works (conversation, multi-source question-answering, long-context applications, and other tasks) and direct-evaluation question sets constructed from agent histories. It explicitly states there are no open-sourced benchmarks tailored for LLM-agent memory modules. Surveyed open-world/embodied settings include Minecraft (Voyager, GITM).
- **benchmark family**:
> memory (agent-memory evaluation survey) — primarily QA / conversation / long-context / multi-source-QA task families used for indirect memory evaluation, plus embodied/open-world (Minecraft) among reviewed applications. Predates dedicated memory benchmarks like LoCoMo/LongMemEval.
- **baselines**:
> N/A — a survey with no experiments; it compares and tabulates representative memory systems (MemoryBank, RET-LLM, ChatDB, TiM, SCM, Voyager, MemGPT, MemoChat, MPC, Generative Agents, RecMind, Retroformer, ExpeL, Synapse, GITM, ReAct, Reflexion, RecAgent, Character-LLM, MetaGPT, ChatDev, etc.) along the sources/forms/operations axes (Tables 1-3) rather than benchmarking baselines.
- **key metrics**:
> Survey-level taxonomy of evaluation metrics. Direct: subjective (Coherence, Rationality via human/GPT-4 judgment) and objective (Result Correctness = accuracy of memory-based answers; Reference Accuracy = whether the retrieved/recalled memory matches ground-truth references; plus efficiency metrics). Indirect: task-completion metrics for conversation (consistency, engagement), multi-source QA accuracy, long-context performance, etc.
- **headline result**:
> N/A (no empirical headline number; it is a survey). Its headline contribution is a unified framework: a memory taxonomy along Sources (inside-trial / cross-trial / external knowledge), Forms (textual vs parametric), and Operations (writing / management / reading), plus a Direct vs Indirect evaluation framework.
- **ablations**: N/A (no experiments/ablations). The survey's comparative tables (Table 1 memory sources, Table 2 memory forms, Table 3 memory operations) function as a structured cross-system comparison clarifying which design choices each system adopts.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Yes (conceptually) — the survey's central evaluation contribution is exactly this decoupling: Direct Evaluation measures the memory module as a stand-alone component (intrinsic: coherence/rationality, result correctness, reference accuracy) separately from Indirect Evaluation via end-to-end agent task success. It argues direct evaluation improves reliability since task performance conflates many factors.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both, as a taxonomy: outcome metrics via indirect end-to-end task completion; process/intermediate metrics via direct evaluation (Reference Accuracy targets the intermediate recalled-memory quality, not just the final answer; coherence/rationality assess recalled-memory quality). The survey advocates measuring intermediate memory quality, not only final outcome.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Discussed qualitatively: textual memory is interpretable and easy to expand/edit but less storage- and efficiency-optimal; parametric memory is more storage-efficient (knowledge compression) and robust but harder to edit/interpret. Objective evaluation is noted to include efficiency metrics. No concrete latency/cost numbers (it is a survey).
- **survey scope and axes**:
> Organizing axes: (Why) cognitive psychology / self-evolution / applications; (How to design) Memory Sources {inside-trial, cross-trial, external knowledge} x Memory Forms {textual: complete/recent/retrieved/external; parametric: fine-tuning, model editing} x Memory Operations {writing, management, reading}; (How to evaluate) Direct {subjective: coherence, rationality; objective: result correctness, reference accuracy} vs Indirect {conversation, multi-source QA, long-context, other}; plus memory-enhanced applications and future directions (parametric memory, multi-agent memory, lifelong learning, humanoid agents). ~174 references; coverage window through early 2024 (v1, April 2024).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (proposes no benchmark). It notably observes the absence of open-sourced benchmarks dedicated to LLM-agent memory at the time, and reviews how others construct direct-evaluation questions from agent histories with annotated ground-truth answers/references.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Cognitive-psychology memory theory (sensory/short-term/long-term memory) as an organizing analogy; foundational LLM-agent and memory systems it taxonomizes — Generative Agents (memory stream with recency/relevance/importance), MemGPT (virtual context management), Reflexion / Retroformer (verbal reflection memory), ExpeL (experiential learning, FAISS trajectory retrieval), Voyager / GITM (skill/experience memory for open-world agents), MemoryBank, RET-LLM, ChatDB, TiM, SCM, MemoChat, MPC, RecAgent.
- **contrasts with**:
> Positions itself against prior surveys that treated LLM-agent memory only in passing or in scattered papers without a holistic source/form/operation framework, and against general LLM-agent surveys (e.g., Wang et al. agent survey, Xi et al.) that do not center memory. It contrasts textual vs parametric memory forms and direct vs indirect evaluation as design dichotomies.
- **lineage**:
> Surveys group — an anchor/foundational memory survey for LLM-based agents. It sits upstream of later, more granular memory and experience surveys (e.g., 2026 'From Storage to Experience', 'Memory for Autonomous LLM Agents') and underpins the experience/case-memory planner lineage by formalizing sources (inside/cross-trial/external), textual-vs-parametric forms, and the writing/management/reading operation cycle plus direct/indirect evaluation.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- completeness_vs_topk_objective
- context_budget_and_selection_count
- reranking
- retrieval_as_learned_policy

<a id="item-paradigms-survey-li"></a>
### 155. A Review of Prominent Paradigms for LLM-Based Agents: Tool Use (Including RAG), Planning, and Feedback Learning

2024  ·  arXiv 2406.05804  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.05804)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: CoLing 2025 (Proceedings of the 31st International Conference on Computational Linguistics, pp. 9760-9779); preprint arXiv:2406.05804 (submitted Jun 2024, v6 Nov 2024)
- **authors affiliation**: Xinzhe Li (single author). Independent Researcher; part of the work conducted while affiliated with Deakin University, Australia.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.05804 (ACL Anthology: https://aclanthology.org/2025.coling-main.652/)
- **code url**: N/A (no executable code; this is a survey. A maintained reading-list repository is provided instead, see maintained_repo_url)
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/xinzhel/LLM-Agent-Survey (reading list / paper list; ~505 stars; last major update 14 Mar 2025; author announced inactive maintenance from Apr 2025, redirecting to https://github.com/xinzhel/LLM-Search)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Survey/taxonomy of LLM-based agents spanning tool use (including RAG), planning, and feedback learning. Covers task domains: QA / NLP-as-agent (NLIE-QA), planning, tool-use, embodied, web, code, and decision-making.
- **problem setting**:
> A unified conceptual taxonomy paper (no new empirical method). It defines task environments (decision-making vs Natural Language Interaction Environments/NLIEs), three task-agnostic LLM-Profiled Roles (LMPRs): policy models (actor/planner), evaluators, and dynamic models, and four universal LMPR-based workflows (base, tool-use, search, feedback-learning). Covers single-agent settings, both offline/static (RAG over a corpus) and interactive (search/feedback) workflows. Supervision-wise it discusses prompting (zero-/few-shot) profiling rather than training. RAG is framed as the canonical 'passive tool use' case where a retrieval mechanism collects relevant information to assist the policy model.
- **what is retrieved**:
> As a taxonomy: docs/passages (for RAG-style passive tool use), tools/APIs (for autonomous tool use), and few-shot demonstrations (for prompting LMPRs). The survey treats RAG-retrieved documents/passages as the primary retrieval target; no single retrieved unit is the paper's own contribution.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (the survey does not adopt a case-based-reasoning framing; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain cycle is discussed)
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False. The work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. Its organizing concepts are LLM-Profiled Roles (policy/evaluator/dynamic) and universal workflows; feedback-learning workflows (Reflexion, Self-Refine, CRITIC) realize revise-like mechanisms but are not described as CBR.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> document/passage (for the RAG-style passive tool-use category) and tool/API (for the autonomous tool-use category). At the prompting level, the few-shot demonstration is also a retrievable/selectable unit. The survey does not commit to a single granularity; it describes RAG as retrieving 'relevant information' to assist the policy model.
- **query construction**:
> The query is the user input/question for RAG-style passive tool use ('given a query, a retrieval mechanism collects relevant information'). For autonomous tool use, tool invocation is triggered by in-generation triggers, the reasoning-acting strategy, or confidence-based invocation rather than an explicit query construction step.
- **query granularity**:
> Task-level / one-shot for passive RAG (retrieve from the query). For autonomous tool use (e.g., Active RAG / ReAct), retrieval/tool-calls can occur at the step level during reasoning. The survey distinguishes passive (one-shot at the policy input) from autonomous (interleaved) but does not formalize query granularity beyond this.
- **when to retrieve**:
> The survey distinguishes passive (one-shot: RAG-style, retrieve-then-generate) from autonomous (iterative/active: tool/retrieval invocation triggered during reasoning). It explicitly cites confidence-based invocation (Active RAG, Jiang et al. 2023) as an uncertainty-triggered/active variant.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> For RAG-style passive tool use: fixed (retrieve given the query). For autonomous tool use the survey enumerates three concrete trigger mechanisms: (1) in-generation triggers (agent program monitors token generation and pauses on a detected tool trigger), (2) reasoning-acting strategy (ReAct: each reasoning/acting step is a full inference cycle ending with a stop token), and (3) confidence-based invocation (token-confidence-triggered retrieval, used by Active RAG; noted as unable to specify which tool to invoke).
- **tool document engineering**:
> Partially noted: for autonomous tool use, the survey states LLMs 'must be aware of the available tools, which requires including tool information during LLM profiling,' and that triggers are defined through tool descriptions and/or few-shot demonstrations. It does not taxonomize tool-document engineering (synthetic-query augmentation / weighted-field embeddings / instruction-tuned tool embeddings).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation: retrieved information/tool outputs are integrated into the policy model's context to assist response/decision generation. For passive RAG the retrieved info conditions a single generation; for autonomous tool use, tool outputs are 'integrated into the reasoning process' step by step. No training-signal or latent-token injection is part of the framing.
- **planning integration**:
> The survey's central contribution is positioning retrieval/tool-use relative to planning via LMPR-based workflows: (a) RAG-style passive tool use = retrieve-then-generate at the policy input; (b) autonomous tool use = per-step interleaved (in-generation triggers / reasoning-acting / confidence-based) within the policy's rollout; (c) separately, planning is handled by search workflows (Traversal/Heuristic and Simulation-based/MCTS) using policy + evaluator (+ dynamic model). Retrieval is classified under the tool-use paradigm rather than embedded inside the search tree.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Two modes are distinguished: per-answer (passive RAG: one retrieval then generation) vs per-reasoning/acting-step or per-tool-call within a rollout (autonomous tool use: ReAct-style step cycles, in-generation token-monitored triggers, confidence-based per-step invocation).
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (no CBR case-adaptation framing). For feedback-learning workflows the analogous mechanism is LLM revision conditioned on evaluator/tool/human feedback (e.g., Reflexion, Self-Refine, CRITIC), but the survey describes this as feedback learning, not case adaptation.
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw retrieved text/information injected into the prompt (for RAG) and raw tool outputs integrated into reasoning (for autonomous tool use). The survey does not analyze distilled-strategy / executable-skill / latent-token representations.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: For RAG-style passive tool use: raw retrieved information/document content (low abstraction). For prompting LMPRs: single demonstrations (few-shot). The survey does not analyze higher-abstraction retrieved units (distilled strategy / workflow / procedural skill).

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (workflow/role taxonomy). The survey organizes agents by LLM-Profiled Roles and workflows, not by a memory store. Feedback-learning workflows (e.g., Reflexion) maintain self-reflection text across trials, but the survey does not formalize this as a retrievable memory type.
- **write back**: False at the survey level. No memory write-back is an organizing dimension. (Reflexion-style verbal feedback retained across trials is mentioned within the feedback-learning paradigm but not framed as memory write-back.)
- **write back trigger**: N/A (no memory write-back framing in this taxonomy). Within feedback-learning workflows the analogous trigger is reflective (after evaluator self-critique) and can use both success and failure signals, but the survey does not formalize a write-back trigger.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: False. The survey treats retrieval (RAG) as an external/off-the-shelf mechanism and tool invocation as prompt-driven (trigger/reasoning-acting/confidence); it does not frame retrieval/case-selection as a learned or RL-optimized policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: N/A. The survey focuses on single-agent, task-agnostic workflows (its unifying value is cross-FRAMEWORK comparison of LMPRs/workflows, but not shared memory/experience across agents). No cross-agent memory sharing is discussed.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> No experiments are run by this survey. It catalogs environments/benchmarks used by reviewed frameworks, including: Game of 24 / CrossWords, Blocksworld (BlocksWorld), AlfWorld, VirtualHome, Minecraft, Webshop, WebArena, AppWorld, GSM8K, HotpotQA. (Repo benchmark section also lists MetaTool, TaskBench, PlanBench.)
- **benchmark family**: Mixed (catalog only): embodied (ALFWorld/VirtualHome/Minecraft), web (Webshop/WebArena/AppWorld), QA / multi-hop (GSM8K/HotpotQA), rule-based games/planning (Game of 24/Blocksworld). The survey reports no metrics of its own.
- **baselines**: N/A (survey; no empirical comparison). It compares COVERAGE against four highly-cited surveys (Guo et al. 2024; Xi et al. 2023; Huang et al. 2024; Wang et al. 2024a) along tool-use / planning / feedback-learning / universal-LMPR axes (Table 1), not method baselines.
- **key metrics**: N/A (survey; reports no quantitative metrics). The only quantitative comparison is a qualitative coverage matrix (checkmarks/crosses with section pointers) against prior surveys.
- **headline result**:
> N/A (no empirical headline number). The headline contribution is the unified taxonomy: three task-agnostic LLM-Profiled Roles (policy/evaluator/dynamic models) and four universal workflows (base, tool-use, search, feedback-learning) enabling cross-paradigm comparison, plus identification of three limitations of existing workflow designs.
- **evaluation decoupling**: N/A. No retrieval or task metrics are reported; the survey reports neither intrinsic retrieval metrics nor end-to-end task metrics.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: N/A (no metrics reported). Conceptually the survey emphasizes process/workflow structure (how LMPRs interact) over outcomes, but it does not score either.
- **survey scope and axes**:
> Organizing axes: (1) task universality (decision-making environments: rule-based games, embodied; vs information-processing environments: web, NLIEs); (2) three task-agnostic LLM-Profiled Roles (LMPRs): policy models (actor/planner), evaluators, dynamic models; (3) four universal LMPR-based workflows: base, tool-use (RAG-style passive / passive validation / autonomous / autonomous validation), search (traversal & heuristic / simulation-based MCTS), feedback-learning (from evaluator only / evaluator+task-env / humans); (4) cross-paradigm discussion and three identified limitations. Reference count: 59 references. Coverage window: work through ~2024 (CoLing 2025 camera-ready, extended to 9 pages); maintained repo extends to ~Mar 2025.
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (this is a survey, not a benchmark; it constructs no dataset).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Foundational frameworks it unifies: ReAct (Yao et al. 2023b), CoT (Wei et al. 2022), Tree-of-Thoughts (Yao et al. 2023a), RAP (Hao et al. 2023), Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023), Self-Refine (Madaan et al. 2023), CRITIC (Gou et al. 2024), RAG (Lewis et al. 2020), Active RAG (Jiang et al. 2023), LLM-MCTS, AgentQ. Conceptually builds on RL formalisms (policy/evaluator/dynamic model; MDP).
- **contrasts with**:
> Explicitly positioned against four prior surveys (Table 1): Guo et al. (2024), Xi et al. (2023), Huang et al. (2024, planning-focused), and Wang et al. (2024a) -- criticizing them for focusing on a single paradigm/domain or lacking a unified comparison basis; notes Wang et al. (2024a) discuss LLM profiling only as personas, not as general roles. Also contrasts task-agnostic 'workflows' against task-specific 'frameworks'.
- **lineage**:
> Surveys group. A cross-cutting taxonomy survey that bridges tool use (with RAG framed as passive tool use), planning, and feedback learning under unified LLM-Profiled Roles -- bridging groups B (planning/search), C (tool use/RAG), and E (feedback learning / self-correction). Companion to the author's later TMLR 2025 search survey (LLM Test-Time Compute via Search).

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):
