<a id="item-reticl-survey"></a>
### 156. In-context Learning with Retrieved Demonstrations for Language Models: A Survey (RetICL survey)

2024  ·  TMLR 2024  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.11624)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: TMLR 2024 (Transactions on Machine Learning Research). DBLP: journals/tmlr/0003XLPK24. Also arXiv:2401.11624 (submitted 21 Jan 2024, last revised v5 23 Mar 2024); subjects cs.CL/cs.AI/cs.IR.
- **authors affiliation**: Man Luo (Arizona State University; lead author), Xin Xu, Yue Liu, Panupong Pasupat, Mehran Kazemi (Google Research). Primary affiliations: Arizona State University and Google Research.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.11624
- **code url**: N/A (this is a survey; no method code repository is associated. No official accompanying code/repo found.)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> QA and broader NLP via in-context learning (ICL). The survey reviews retrieval-based ICL (RetICL) across natural language understanding (sentiment analysis, paraphrase detection, reading comprehension, NLI), reasoning (math/commonsense/ethical reasoning), knowledge-based QA, and text generation (code generation, summarization, data-to-text, semantic parsing). Not planning/agents/tool-use specific.
- **problem setting**:
> A survey (literature review) of retrieval-augmented in-context learning. The reviewed setting: given a test query q* and a retrieval corpus C of candidate demonstrations d_i=(q_i,a_i), a demonstration retriever DR selects a set {d_1,...,d_k} from C to prepend to q* so the frozen LLM maximizes the probability of the correct answer a*. The LLM parameters are not fine-tuned (training-free adaptation); only the (optional) retriever is trained. Single-model, offline-corpus setting (retrieval corpus is typically a static labeled training set, in-domain / mix-domain / cross-domain / unlabelled-with-generated-answers / free-form). The survey organizes the design space along three axes: retrieval models (off-the-shelf vs fine-tuned retrievers), retriever training procedures (training-data collection + objectives), and inference algorithms (one-shot / clustering / iterative retrieval). It is not interactive/agentic and not multi-agent.
- **what is retrieved**: demos / ICL demonstrations: input-output exemplars d_i=(q_i,a_i) (e.g. (query, label) or (question, answer/reasoning chain)) tailored per query. The survey is exclusively about retrieving few-shot demonstrations (not tools, docs-as-evidence, skills, or trajectories).
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus: the surveyed methods retrieve from a fixed demonstration corpus (most commonly a labeled training set, optionally a subset, mixed-task pool, cross-domain set, or free-form/unlabelled corpus with auto-generated answers). The survey notes that nearly all current work uses a static, constant retrieval corpus; it flags 'Active Demonstration Retrieval' (a growing corpus updated with new incoming queries) only as an open future direction, not as established practice.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Predominantly fixed top-k ranking, but the survey explicitly contrasts independent top-k selection with set-level composition. It distinguishes 'one-hoc' (one-shot) retrieval where each of the top-k demonstrations is chosen independently (risking homogeneity) versus clustering retrieval and iterative retrieval that aim for diversity/coverage and selecting demonstrations that complement each other (a set-composition / coverage objective). It also covers diversity objectives (e.g. DPP) that model negative interactions among selected demonstrations. The selection count k is still a fixed budget in practice.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (the survey is not framed as case-based reasoning; in CBR terms only the Retrieve phase is covered - demonstrations are retrieved and reused verbatim as ICL exemplars, with no Revise/Retain of cases).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False - the survey does not frame retrieval-based ICL as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is framed as demonstration retrieval / RetICL (retrieval models, training, inference algorithms).

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> single demonstration (one ICL exemplar = an input-output pair d_i=(q_i,a_i)); the retrieved object as a whole is a set of k such demonstrations. Demonstrations may include chain-of-thought reasoning chains where applicable, but the indexed/retrieved unit is the demonstration (snippet-level exemplar), not a trajectory, tool, or KG-subgraph.
- **index source**:
> Static corpus, built offline: the retrieval corpus is typically the task's labeled training set (in-domain IID), or a representative subset, or a combination of multiple tasks (mix-domain), or cross-domain annotated data, or unlabelled queries with LLM-auto-generated answers, or a free-form text corpus (e.g. Wikipedia for pseudo-demonstrations). Demonstrations are encoded and indexed once; the store is frozen at test time. Online/test-time-growing corpora are only discussed as a future direction (active demonstration retrieval).
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat dense/sparse vector index: candidate demonstrations are encoded (BM25 term vectors, SBERT/sentence embeddings, or dual-encoder dense vectors) and retrieved by similarity (cosine / inner product / BM25 score). Clustering-retrieval methods add k-means sub-grouping over the embeddings (a shallow partition for diversity), but there is no graph or deep hierarchy. No knowledge-graph or dependency-graph index.
- **retriever type**:
> Surveys multiple types: (1) off-the-shelf - term-based sparse (BM25), sentence-embedding similarity (SBERT, RoBERTa, optionally NLI/STS-finetuned), and pretrained dual encoders (DPR-style); (2) fine-tuned learned dense retrievers (dual-encoder, contrastively/list-wise/distillation trained); plus optional cross-encoder rerankers. Covers heuristic/off-the-shelf, learned-dense, and learned-with-LM-feedback retrievers. Generative tool-as-token retrievers are out of scope.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Spans the full spectrum the survey organizes in Section 5: (a) none / off-the-shelf (BM25, SBERT, dual encoders used as-is); (b) LM-feedback supervision - a scoring LLM (ideally the inference LLM, often a smaller same-family proxy) scores candidates by s(d)=p(a|d,q); top/bottom ranked become positive/negative training pairs; (c) contrastive InfoNCE, list-wise ranking loss (LambdaRank-inspired), KL-divergence distillation from a cross-encoder/reward teacher, and multi-objective combinations; (d) model-free label-similarity heuristics (e.g. average F1 between query and demonstration labels); (e) iterative/RL training of the retriever (e.g. Scarlatos & Lan train an LSTM retriever with reinforcement learning; Lu et al. train an RL reranker). Iterative training mines harder negatives across rounds. Diversity training via Determinantal Point Processes (DPP).
- **query construction**:
> Primarily the raw test query is encoded as the search key. Variants surveyed: (i) one-shot - encode the raw query once and take top-k; (ii) clustering - query matched to one representative per cluster; (iii) iterative - the query is augmented with already-retrieved demonstration(s) before retrieving the next, so the effective query becomes history-conditioned. Some structural-similarity methods construct queries from the query's syntactic/reasoning structure. For unlabelled/free-form corpora, pseudo-demonstrations or LLM-generated answers may be created first.
- **query granularity**:
> Mostly task/query-level (one-shot retrieval at inference using the input query). Iterative-retrieval methods are step-level: a new query is formed at each of the k retrieval steps conditioned on previously selected demonstrations (a two-level / history-aware retrieval). Clustering retrieval is also query-level but enforces per-cluster selection.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Survey covers one-shot (top-k in a single pass; the dominant 'one-hoc' strategy), clustering (single-pass but cluster-constrained), and iterative (k sequential retrieval steps conditioned on prior selections). Active/uncertainty-triggered retrieval and continually-updated corpora are discussed only as future directions, not as established practice.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed schedule in the reviewed methods: retrieval is performed once (one-shot) or for a predetermined number of iterations to assemble k demonstrations; the trigger is the need for the few-shot prompt, not a learned/confidence-based signal. The survey identifies learned/active triggering (selecting which new examples to annotate-and-add as input distribution shifts, akin to active learning) as an explicitly open future direction ('Active Demonstration Retrieval').
- **reranking**:
> Yes - the survey reviews a two-stage retriever-reranker architecture (Section 5.2 'Re-ranker Training'): a fast dual-encoder retriever first selects top-N candidates, then a slower cross-encoder reranker (capturing token-level interactions) reranks them and the top-K are used to build the prompt. Reranker training uses sigmoid cross-entropy; one variant (Lu et al.) trains the reranker via reinforcement learning. Reranking is presented as an optional enhancement, not universal.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Mostly none - retrieved demonstrations are inserted into the prompt as exemplars. The main post-retrieval operations the survey discusses are (a) reranking (cross-encoder two-stage) and (b) set-level diversity selection (clustering / DPP) to reduce homogeneity/redundancy. There is no decompose-then-recompose, reason-in-documents distillation, or compression of demonstration content; demonstrations are used in raw exemplar form.
- **tool document engineering**:
> N/A (no tools/skills; demonstrations are raw input-output text pairs encoded by the retriever. For free-form/unlabelled corpora, pseudo-labels or LLM-generated answers may be attached to candidate text before indexing, but this is corpus construction, not tool-description engineering.)
- **index content separation**: N/A - a demonstration is both the indexed unit (via its embedding) and the content injected into the prompt; no lightweight-index-then-heavy-content (progressive-disclosure) separation.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool APIs / live tool stores; the corpus is a static demonstration pool. Continually-updated corpora are only a future direction.)
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no inter-tool dependencies; demonstrations are independent exemplars, though clustering/DPP model inter-demonstration redundancy/diversity rather than dependency.)

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> prompt augmentation: the selected k demonstrations are concatenated before the test query as the few-shot ICL context (d_1,...,d_k,q*) and fed to the frozen LLM, whose parameters are unchanged. Retrieved demonstrations also serve as a training signal in the retriever-training pipeline (a scoring LLM's p(a|d,q) labels which demonstrations are positive/negative for retriever learning). No case adaptation or latent-token injection.
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-generate (one-shot exemplars at inference time): demonstrations are retrieved and assembled into a single ICL prompt before one LLM generation; there is no planning, MCTS/tree-search, or per-step interleaving with the LLM's reasoning. Iterative-retrieval methods run a retrieval-side loop to compose the demonstration set, but the LLM still performs a single answer generation afterward. (RetICL is orthogonal to agent planning.)
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> per-answer: the retrieval (whether one-shot or k-step iterative composition) happens before a single LLM answer/generation. Retrieval is not woven into per-CoT-step, per-token, or per-tool-call reasoning of the LLM; the iterative steps, when present, are over demonstration selection, not over the LLM's reasoning trace.
- **adaptation mechanism**: verbatim ICL exemplar - retrieved demonstrations are used as-is in the prompt; the survey does not cover LLM-prompted or feedback-driven revision of retrieved demonstrations (no CBR-style case adaptation).
- **retrieved item representation**: raw demonstration (a natural-language input paired with its output/label, optionally including a chain-of-thought reasoning chain), injected as a verbatim few-shot example in the prompt. No distillation into strategies/guidelines, workflows, programs, or latent tokens.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: single demonstration (raw input-output exemplar), the lowest abstraction level. The survey does not retrieve distilled strategies, workflows, skills, or guideline-rules; CoT-augmented demonstrations are still concrete exemplars, not abstracted insights.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Mainly retriever-training-based and set-diversity-based: training the retriever on LM-feedback signals (positive demonstrations raise p(a|d,q), negatives mislead it) so it learns to avoid unhelpful exemplars; contrastive/list-wise objectives with hard-negative mining (and iterative training to mine better negatives); two-stage reranking to filter top-N down to high-quality top-K; clustering/DPP diversity to avoid homogeneous/redundant demonstrations. The survey also notes a robustness finding: retrieved demonstrations can HARM commonsense-reasoning and coreference tasks (random can be better), a cautionary noise observation. No explicit self-reflection or reason-in-documents distillation module.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none - no episodic/skill/workflow memory; the only persistent store is the static demonstration corpus (the labeled training set). No growing memory is maintained by the reviewed methods (active/growing corpora are a future direction only).
- **write back**: False - the surveyed RetICL methods do not write new experiences/cases/skills into memory during deployment; the retrieval corpus is fixed. (The survey raises corpus-growth/active demonstration retrieval as an open problem, not an implemented mechanism.)
- **online growth**:
> False - the retrieval corpus is static/frozen after offline construction in essentially all reviewed work; the survey explicitly notes 'Much of the current research is based on a static framework where the retrieval corpus remains constant' and proposes online corpus updating only as future work.
- **write back trigger**:
> never (at deployment) for the reviewed methods - nothing is written to the corpus during/after inference. The survey's future-direction 'Active Demonstration Retrieval' would add a human-validated / annotation-gated write (select a representative subset of incoming unlabelled queries for annotation, then add to the corpus), but this is proposed, not realized.
- **failure experience usage**:
> No persistent storage of failed experiences. However, in retriever TRAINING the survey describes using both positive (LLM-helpful) and negative (LLM-misleading) demonstrations contrastively (InfoNCE / list-wise / hard-negative mining), so 'failure' signals inform retriever training - but failures are not stored as retrievable corrective items at inference. Success-only at deployment.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A / none - no deployed memory to mutate (static corpus). Iterative retriever TRAINING re-mines positives/negatives across rounds (a training-time refinement of the retriever, not a mutation of stored memory entries).
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Partially / surveyed as one option: most reviewed methods use fixed similarity-based top-k or contrastively-trained dense retrievers (not RL policies), but the survey explicitly covers learned-policy / RL approaches for iterative retrieval (Scarlatos & Lan's LSTM retriever trained with reinforcement learning) and an RL-trained reranker (Lu et al.). So retrieval-as-learned-policy is included in the taxonomy but is not the dominant paradigm.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> No - single-model demonstration retrieval; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory sharing. The survey does note transferability across inference LLMs (a retriever trained with one scoring LLM can serve a different/larger inference LLM, since smaller same-family scorers are often used for labeling), i.e. cross-model retriever reuse, but not multi-agent sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> As a survey it catalogs datasets used across the reviewed RetICL literature rather than running its own. Examples cited by application category: NLU - SST/SST-5 (sentiment), MRPC/PAWS (paraphrase), SQuAD/BoolQ/OpenBookQA (reading comprehension), MNLI/SNLI/RTE/CB (NLI); Reasoning - GSM8K/MathQA/AQuA (math), CommonsenseQA (CMSQA)/HellaSwag/PIQA/COPA (commonsense), ethical-reasoning sets; Knowledge-based QA - WebQuestions, Natural Questions, TriviaQA, ARC; Text generation - code generation (GeoQuery/semantic parsing), summarization, data-to-text. (Specific dataset-to-method pairings are in Section 6 and the appendix tables.)
- **benchmark family**:
> QA (open-domain and knowledge-based QA), plus general NLU/GLUE-style classification, reasoning (math GSM8K-style; commonsense CommonsenseQA/HellaSwag), and text generation (code generation / semantic parsing). Not in the agentic web/embodied/tool/code-agent/memory-dialogue benchmark families; it predates and is orthogonal to ALFWorld/WebArena/ToolBench/SWE-bench/LoCoMo.
- **baselines**:
> As comparison points within the surveyed design space: zero-shot, random few-shot, and fixed/manually-curated demonstrations as the lower-bound baselines; off-the-shelf retrievers (BM25, SBERT/sentence embeddings, pretrained dual encoders) vs fine-tuned/learned retrievers (EPR-style InfoNCE, list-wise/LambdaRank, DPP diversity, KL-distillation, iterative, RL). The survey contrasts off-the-shelf vs fine-tuned retrievers and one-shot vs clustering vs iterative inference rather than reporting a single head-to-head leaderboard.
- **key metrics**:
> Downstream task metrics of the reviewed work: accuracy / F1 (classification, NLI, commonsense), exact match and answer accuracy (QA, math reasoning), and generation metrics (e.g. exact match / execution accuracy for code-generation & semantic parsing, ROUGE/BLEU for summarization & data-to-text). The survey reports qualitative comparisons (e.g. retrieval vs random) rather than a unified metric. Retrieval-intrinsic metrics (Recall@k/nDCG) are largely not the focus.
- **headline result**:
> Survey-level takeaway: retrieving query-tailored demonstrations substantially and consistently improves ICL over fixed/random demonstrations across most NLU, reasoning, QA, and generation tasks, and reduces sensitivity to demonstration ordering. A concrete cited number: Ye et al. (2023) report 10+% improvement on open-domain QA using BM25-retrieved demonstrations. An important caveat: on commonsense reasoning and coreference tasks, random demonstrations can outperform retrieval-based selection.
- **ablations**:
> As a survey it aggregates findings rather than running ablations, but it synthesizes component-level evidence: (1) off-the-shelf vs fine-tuned retrievers - fine-tuned/learned retrievers generally outperform off-the-shelf ones by tailoring to the task, though off-the-shelf already beats random; (2) similarity vs diversity - diversity (clustering/DPP) matters notably for mathematical reasoning (Zhang et al. 2022), and DPP fine-tuning improves over pure similarity (Ye et al. 2023); (3) one-shot vs iterative - iterative retrieval gives the most significant gains on math reasoning (Scarlatos & Lan 2023); (4) scoring-LLM choice - using the inference LLM (or a smaller same-family proxy) as scorer best reflects its preferences; (5) corpus subset vs full - retrieving from a carefully selected representative subset can match retrieving from the full training set (Hongjin et al. 2022 vs Ye et al. 2023); (6) task-dependence - retrieval can hurt commonsense/coreference tasks.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Largely No / not standardized - the survey reports end-to-end downstream task metrics from the reviewed papers; it does not impose or systematically report decoupled intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k/nDCG) separated from task performance. It notes the limited understanding of WHY retrieved demonstrations help (calling for theory), implicitly highlighting the lack of decoupled retrieval-quality evaluation.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Outcome-focused: the reviewed evaluations score final task outputs (accuracy/EM/F1/generation metrics). Intermediate/process metrics (retrieval-step accuracy, reasoning faithfulness) are generally not reported; the survey itself flags the missing theoretical/process understanding of demonstration retrieval as an open problem.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k demonstration budget in the reviewed methods: a retriever selects k demonstrations (one-shot top-k, one-per-cluster for k clusters, or k iterative steps). Two-stage methods retrieve top-N then rerank-and-truncate to top-K. The survey discusses k as a tunable budget and reviews work studying performance vs number of demonstrations, but k is generally fixed per experiment rather than adaptively/precision-driven. No explicit token-budget cap framework.
- **survey scope and axes**:
> Explicit organizing axes: (1) Retrieval-based ICL design choices - retrieval objectives (similarity vs diversity), inference/retrieval strategy (one-shot 'one-hoc' / clustering / iterative), and retrieval corpus (in-domain / mix-domain / cross-domain / unlabelled-with-generated-answers / free-form); (2) Off-the-shelf retrievers (term-based BM25 / sentence-embedding SBERT / pretrained dual encoder); (3) Fine-tuned retrievers - training-data collection (LLM-signal-based vs model-free) and training objectives (list-wise ranking / InfoNCE / KL-distillation / multi-objective / iterative / diversity-DPP / reranker); plus Applications and Future Directions. Reference count: 175 references (Semantic Scholar). Coverage window: ICL-with-retrieved-demonstrations literature through early 2024 (survey v5 March 2024).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (not a benchmark-construction paper; it surveys methods and aggregates existing datasets across reviewed works rather than building a new benchmark).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Synthesizes and builds on the foundational RetICL line: KATE (Liu et al. 2022, semantic-similarity demonstration retrieval), EPR (Rubin et al. 2022, LM-scored InfoNCE-trained retriever), CEIL (Ye et al. 2023, DPP set selection), Li et al. 2023b (unified/list-wise demonstration retriever), Luo et al. 2023 (Dr.ICL / retriever training), Cheng et al. 2023; off-the-shelf encoders BM25 (Robertson), SBERT (Reimers & Gurevych), DPR/dual-encoder (Karpukhin et al.), and ICL foundations (Brown et al. 2020 GPT-3; Min et al. 2022). Builds on retrieval (DPR, Contriever) and ICL literature.
- **contrasts with**:
> Positioned against fixed/manually-curated and random-few-shot ICL (context-insensitive demonstrations), and against non-retrieval advanced selection by complexity/diversity/difficulty/perplexity that still selects a static set. Within RetICL it contrasts off-the-shelf vs fine-tuned retrievers, similarity-only vs diversity-aware selection, and one-shot independent top-k vs clustering/iterative set composition. As a survey it is distinguished from broader RAG / LLM-agent surveys by its narrow, dedicated focus on demonstration retrieval for ICL.
- **lineage**:
> Surveys group; anchors Group A (ICL demonstration retrieval). It is the dedicated survey of retrieval-based in-context learning, organizing the lineage from off-the-shelf similarity retrieval (BM25/SBERT) -> LM-feedback-trained dense retrievers (KATE -> EPR -> CEIL -> list-wise/iterative/RL retrievers) and along the inference-strategy axis (one-shot -> clustering -> iterative). It serves as the taxonomic anchor for the demonstration-retrieval (Group A) sub-topic of the broader retrieval-augmented LLM agents survey.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- cost_efficiency_tradeoff
- maintained_repo_url

<a id="item-locomo"></a>
### 157. LoCoMo: Evaluating Very Long-Term Conversational Memory of LLM Agents

2024  ·  ACL 2024  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17753)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2024
- **venue**: ACL 2024 (Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, Volume 1: Long Papers; ACL Anthology 2024.acl-long.747, Bangkok, Thailand, August 2024). Preprint arXiv:2402.17753 (cs.CL), submitted 27 Feb 2024.
- **authors affiliation**:
> Adyasha Maharana (University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill); Dong-Ho Lee (University of Southern California); Sergey Tulyakov (Snap Inc.); Mohit Bansal (UNC Chapel Hill, equal advising); Francesco Barbieri (Snap Inc., equal advising); Yuwei Fang (Snap Inc., equal advising). Primary affiliations: UNC Chapel Hill, USC, and Snap Inc.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17753
- **code url**: https://github.com/snap-research/locomo
- **maintained repo url**:
> https://github.com/snap-research/locomo (official Snap Research repo hosting the LoCoMo dataset data/locomo10.json and evaluation scripts; project page https://snap-research.github.io/locomo/). No live leaderboard is maintained by the authors, though LoCoMo has been widely adopted as a standard long-term-memory benchmark by later systems (e.g. Mem0, MemGPT, A-MEM, Memory-R1).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> memory / QA (very long-term conversational memory benchmark): evaluates an LLM agent's long-term memory over multi-session open-domain dialogues via three tasks: question answering, event-graph summarization, and multi-modal dialogue generation. Touches retrieval (RAG over conversation history) and temporal/causal reasoning.
- **problem setting**:
> Offline benchmark for measuring long-term memory of LLM agents over very long, multi-session, multi-modal open-domain dialogues. The authors first build a machine-human GENERATIVE PIPELINE: two LLM-based generative agents (each a gpt-3.5-turbo agent with a unique persona, a temporal event graph of causally-linked life events, and a Park et al. 2023 generative-agent memory/reflection module plus image-sharing/image-reaction behaviors) converse over up to 35 sessions; human annotators then verify and edit ~15% of turns and remove/substitute ~19% of images for long-range consistency and grounding to the event graphs. The resulting LoCoMo dataset (originally 50 conversations on arXiv v1; the released benchmark is a curated 10-conversation subset locomo10.json with the longest, highest-quality conversations) averages ~300 turns, ~9.2K tokens, and ~19 sessions per conversation. The EVALUATION setting is then offline, single-turn-at-a-time inference over a frozen, fully-observed conversation: given the (truncated, full, or retrieved) conversation history, a model must (a) answer annotated questions in five reasoning categories (single-hop, multi-hop, temporal, open-domain knowledge, adversarial), (b) summarize each speaker's event graph, and (c) generate the next multi-modal dialogue turn. It compares three model classes: short-context base LLMs (history truncated), long-context LLMs, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) over a database of dialogs / observations / session summaries. Human upper-bound performance is reported for QA. Supervision: QA/event annotations are human-curated; for multimodal dialogue, three MiniGPT-5 variants are trained on 50 auto-generated (un-filtered) conversations.
- **what is retrieved**:
> For the RAG QA setting, retrieved units are past CONVERSATION CONTENT in one of three database forms: (a) raw dialog turns (utterances), (b) observations (atomic assertions/facts about each speaker's life and persona extracted per turn), or (c) session-level summaries. The retrieved context is then fed to a reader LLM to answer the question. (Note: retrieval also appears inside the data-GENERATION pipeline, where each agent retrieves relevant observations from its long-term memory to condition the next response; but the headline benchmark evaluates RAG over dialog history at inference.)
- **retrieval grounding**:
> GROWING/episodic memory of the conversation itself, treated as a per-conversation static store at evaluation time. The retrievable store is the agent's/conversation's own dialogue history (and derived observations/summaries), i.e. an episodic conversational memory rather than an external static KB/doc corpus or API library. Within a single evaluation it is fixed (the full conversation is known); conceptually it represents the growing memory of a long-running dialogue.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Fixed top-k retrieval objective: RAG retrieves the top-k items (dialogs/observations/summaries) by similarity for a query, with k swept over {5,10,25,50} for dialog/observation and {2,5,10} for summary. The paper reports Recall@k of the gold answer-containing context. The key empirical finding is that more is not better: QA F1 with observations peaks at top-5 and DEGRADES as k grows (signal-to-noise ratio), so although high k yields high recall, a smaller precision-oriented k gives better answers; the objective is effectively precision-driven top-k rather than recovering a complete minimal set.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: [Retrieve: yes (dense top-k retrieval of past dialog/observations in the RAG setting), Reuse: partial (retrieved context is reused as prompt evidence to answer, not as a prior solved case), Revise: no, Retain: no (at eval time)]. Not a case-based-reasoning system.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False: the paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is a long-term conversational-memory benchmark with episodic-memory RAG.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Variable by database: (a) a single dialog turn/utterance, (b) a single observation = an atomic assertion (fact) about a speaker derived from one turn, or (c) a session-level summary. Granularity ranges from snippet/single-turn (dialog), to distilled fact (observation), to summary (session). The most effective unit reported is the observation.
- **index source**:
> Growing/episodic conversational memory built per conversation: the retrievable store is derived from the LoCoMo dialogue itself. Observations and session summaries are generated offline with gpt-3.5-turbo from the conversation (and released with the dataset). At evaluation each conversation's store is fixed/fully observed; it is not a cross-corpus external KB and is not induced from the model's own test-time trajectories.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat vector index: each database (dialogs, observations, or session summaries) is embedded and retrieved by dense similarity (DRAGON), with no graph or hierarchical topology over the retrievable units. (The dataset itself is grounded on per-speaker temporal EVENT GRAPHS with causal links, but those event graphs are ground-truth annotations / generation scaffolding, not the retrieval index used by the RAG reader.)
- **retriever type**:
> Dense retriever: DRAGON (Lin et al., 2023, 'How to train your DRAGON: Diverse augmentation towards generalizable dense retrieval') is used as the retriever, with gpt-3.5-turbo-16k as the reader. Off-the-shelf dense bi-encoder retrieval; no BM25/learned-for-task/generative retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> None for the benchmark task (off-the-shelf): DRAGON is used as a pre-trained generalizable dense retriever without task-specific fine-tuning on LoCoMo. The paper explicitly notes a limitation that retrieval models are trained on generic semantic-similarity tasks rather than on dialogue, which hurts retrieval of co-referential/anaphoric dialogue content; no contrastive/LM-feedback/RL retraining of the retriever is performed.
- **query construction**:
> Raw question as query: in the QA RAG setting the question is used (as-is) to retrieve relevant dialogs/observations/summaries from the conversation database; there is no query decomposition, expansion, or thought-conditioning at inference. (In the separate data-generation pipeline, the agent retrieves observations relevant to the ongoing dialogue context to condition its next response.)
- **query granularity**: Task/turn-level: one retrieval per QA question (one-shot per query). Not step-decomposed or two-level. In the generative pipeline retrieval is per dialogue turn/session.
- **when to retrieve**: One-shot: a single retrieval is issued per QA question before the reader answers. No iterative/active/adaptive re-retrieval loop is used in the benchmark.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed schedule: retrieval is always performed once per QA question (RAG condition), with a preset top-k. There is no confidence/uncertainty/learned-router/reflection-token trigger; whether to retrieve is determined by the experimental condition (Base vs Long-context vs RAG), not by the model at runtime.
- **reranking**: None: top-k items are taken directly from the DRAGON dense-similarity ranking and fed to the reader; no cross-encoder, RRF, or hierarchy-aware reranking stage is applied.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Pre-indexing transformation rather than post-retrieval refinement: the main lever is the FORM of the retrievable unit (raw dialog vs distilled observations vs session summaries). Converting dialogs into observations (atomic assertions) acts as a distillation/denoising step that improves QA. The paper notes reducing top-k improves signal-to-noise ratio (implicit truncation), but there is no explicit post-retrieval reranking, distractor-filtering, or compression module at inference.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A: no tools/APIs are retrieved; retrieval is over conversation content (dialogs/observations/summaries).
- **index content separation**:
> Partial / by-construction: the retrievable index is a derived, lighter representation (observations = atomic assertions, or session summaries) separated from the full raw dialog; the reader is then given only the retrieved subset rather than the whole conversation. This is closer to a representation-choice ablation than an explicit progressive-disclosure/index-then-content protocol.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A: no tool index or integration protocol (RapidAPI/REST/MCP/function-calling); retrieval is over a static per-conversation text store.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A: no inter-tool dependency modeling (no tools).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation: the top-k retrieved dialogs/observations/summaries are concatenated into the reader LLM's (gpt-3.5-turbo-16k) context to answer the question (QA) or, for multimodal generation, retrieved observations are supplied as additional training/inference context to MiniGPT-5. No skill reuse, case adaptation, or latent-token injection.
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-read (no planning): for QA, a single retrieval step precedes a single answer generation; there is no multi-step planning, tree search, or interleaved act/observe loop in the benchmark evaluation. (The generative pipeline embeds retrieval inside a reflect-and-respond agent loop, but that is for data creation, not the evaluated task.)
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer: retrieval happens once and the model produces the answer; retrieval is not interleaved per CoT step, per sentence, or per tool call.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not framed as CBR): retrieved context is used verbatim as in-context evidence for the reader to answer; there is no case-adaptation/revision step.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Surface forms: (a) raw dialog turns (verbatim utterances with speaker), (b) observations rendered as natural-language atomic assertions/facts about a speaker, or (c) free-text session summaries. Injected as text into the reader context; no executable program, structured note, or latent-soft tokens.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Spans the abstraction axis: raw dialogue turn (lowest), distilled atomic fact/assertion (observation, mid), and session summary (higher). The observation form (distilled per-speaker assertions) is the most effective for QA, indicating mid-level distillation beats both raw turns (noisy) and summaries (lossy).
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Implicit, via unit choice and small k: distilling dialogs into observations (assertions) and using a small top-k improves the signal-to-noise ratio of retrieved context. The paper shows performance DEGRADES with more retrieved observations and that improper retrieved context can hurt (especially open-domain knowledge questions), but there is no dedicated relevance-evaluator, self-reflection, or distractor-aware-training mechanism; robustness is a measured weakness rather than an engineered defense.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> episodic (conversational): the evaluated 'memory' is the agent's episodic memory of the prior multi-session conversation. The data-generation agents additionally use a reflection-based long-term memory of observations plus short-term session summaries (Park et al. 2023 generative-agent architecture). No skill-library/workflow/procedural/latent memory.
- **write back**:
> true (in the generative pipeline; N/A for the benchmark-eval RAG): during data generation, each agent writes per-turn observations to long-term memory and per-session summaries to short-term memory after each session, then retrieves them to condition future responses. In the benchmark EVALUATION the conversation store is precomputed and frozen, so no test-time write-back occurs while answering questions.
- **online growth**: Mixed: during conversation GENERATION the memory grows turn-by-turn / session-by-session as the dialogue proceeds. During benchmark EVALUATION the per-conversation store (dialogs/observations/summaries) is fixed and fully observed; it does not grow from the reader's own outputs.
- **write back trigger**:
> Per-turn and per-session (generation pipeline): a single dialogue turn is converted into an observation and stored in long-term memory each turn, and a session summary is produced and stored after each session. There is no success/failure-conditioned or reflective-critique write-back; for the evaluated QA/summarization tasks the trigger is effectively 'never' (precomputed store).
- **failure experience usage**:
> N/A / none: the memory stores observations/summaries of the conversation, not success-vs-failure experiences; no negative/failed experiences are stored or contrastively retrieved. (The benchmark instead probes failure indirectly via adversarial questions that should be answered 'unanswerable'.)
- **memory evolution update**:
> Append-with-running-summarization (generation pipeline): observations are appended to long-term memory per turn (append-only); the session summary w_k is produced by conditioning on the latest session history h_k and the previous summary w_{k-1}, i.e. an incrementally-refined running summary. Stored observations are not later mutated/dedup-merged/pruned. For the benchmark eval, the store is static (no evolution).
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No: retrieval/selection is fixed dense top-k similarity (DRAGON), not an RL- or value-learned retrieval policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No: each conversation has its own private per-speaker/per-conversation memory; there is no cross-agent or cross-framework shared retrievable memory. (Two agents converse during generation, but each maintains its own private memory.)

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> LoCoMo (introduced by this paper): the released benchmark (data/locomo10.json) contains 10 very long-term conversations (a curated subset of the original 50 on arXiv v1), each ~300 turns, ~9.2K tokens, up to 35 sessions (avg ~19.3 sessions, ~304.9 turns, ~9,209.2 tokens per conversation), spanning a few months, multi-modal (image-sharing). Three evaluation tasks: (1) Question Answering with 5 reasoning categories (single-hop, multi-hop, temporal, open-domain, adversarial), F1; (2) Event-graph Summarization, FactScore precision/recall/F1 + ROUGE; (3) Multi-modal Dialogue Generation, MM-Relevance + NLG metrics. Compared in Table 1 against MPChat, MMDialog, DailyDialog, SODA, MSC, Conversation Chronicles (LoCoMo is ~9x longer per conversation than MSC).
- **benchmark family**: memory (LoCoMo) - this paper IS the LoCoMo long-term conversational-memory benchmark, a canonical entry in the memory benchmark family alongside LongMemEval. Also touches QA (multi-hop, temporal) and multi-modal dialogue.
- **baselines**:
> Three model classes on QA: (1) Base short-context LLMs with truncated history: Mistral-Instruct-7B (8K), Llama-2-Chat-70B (4,096), GPT-3.5-turbo (4,096), GPT-4-turbo (4,096); (2) Long-context: GPT-3.5-turbo-16K (context swept 4K/8K/12K/16K); (3) RAG: DRAGON retriever + GPT-3.5-turbo-16K reader over Dialog / Observation / Summary databases at various top-k. Human performance is the upper bound. Event summarization baselines: Mistral-Instruct-7B, Llama-2-Chat-70B, GPT-4-turbo, GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-3.5-turbo-16K (incremental summarization; no RAG). Multimodal generation: three MiniGPT-5 variants (Base / +summary / +observation), initialized from a MiniGPT-5 checkpoint fine-tuned on MMDialog.
- **key metrics**:
> QA: F1 (partial/exact-match F1 after normalization), per reasoning category and Overall; Recall@k (R@k) for retrieval accuracy of the gold answer-containing context (RAG). Event summarization: FactScore-based Precision/Recall/F1 (atomic-fact decomposition) plus ROUGE-1/2/L. Multi-modal dialogue generation: MM-Relevance plus standard NLG metrics. Human upper bound reported for QA.
- **headline result**:
> On LoCoMo QA, all models lag far behind the human F1 of 87.9 Overall. Best base/long-context model GPT-4-turbo (4K) reaches 32.1 Overall; GPT-3.5-turbo-16K (16K) reaches 37.8 Overall. RAG (DRAGON + GPT-3.5-turbo-16K) with top-5 OBSERVATIONS reaches 41.4 Overall F1 (the best configuration), but observation-RAG F1 degrades as k grows beyond 5 (signal-to-noise). Long-context LLMs collapse on adversarial questions (GPT-3.5-turbo-16K adversarial F1 = 2.1 vs 70.2 for 4K GPT-4-turbo). Temporal reasoning is the hardest category (models ~17-26 F1 vs human 92.6). Summarized: long-context/RAG improve memory by 22-66% over base but still lag human by ~56% overall and ~73% on temporal reasoning.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Context-length sweep for GPT-3.5-turbo-16K (4K/8K/12K/16K): single-hop/multi-hop F1 rise sharply with more context (single-hop 31.7->56.4) but adversarial F1 COLLAPSES (13.1->2.1), showing long context induces hallucination/misattribution. (2) Retrieval-unit ablation (Table 3): Dialog vs Observation vs Summary databases - observations give the best QA F1 (top-5 obs = 41.4 Overall) and especially help temporal (~42) and adversarial (44.7 at top-5); summaries help recall but not F1 (information loss in dialog->summary conversion); raw dialogs improve over no-retrieval but plateau. (3) Top-k sweep: observation-RAG F1 peaks at k=5 and decreases at k=10/25/50 (SNR effect) while Recall@k keeps rising - decoupling recall from answer quality. (4) Event-summarization: long-context GPT-3.5-turbo-16K is WORSE than 4K GPT-3.5-turbo (precision -3.0, recall -8.7), and lags base by ~14%, showing long-context models do not use context well; incremental summarization with GPT-3.5-turbo gives best F1. (5) Multimodal generation: MiniGPT-5 +observation > +summary > Base; MM-Relevance drops as dialog-history length grows, and RAG (observations) partially alleviates the drop. (6) Manual error taxonomy for QA (temporal/open-domain hardest) and 5 event-summary error types (missing info, hallucination, dialog-cue misunderstanding, speaker misattribution, salience errors).
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Yes: intrinsic retrieval quality (Recall@k of the gold answer context) is reported in Table 3 SEPARATELY from end-to-end QA answer-prediction F1. The paper explicitly shows recall and F1 decouple - e.g. summary-RAG attains high recall but low F1, and observation-RAG F1 drops as k (and recall) increases.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both: outcome metrics are QA F1, summarization FactScore-F1/ROUGE, and MM-Relevance; process/intermediate metrics include retrieval Recall@k (was the right context retrieved), per-reasoning-category breakdown (single/multi/temporal/open-domain/adversarial), and qualitative error taxonomies for QA and event summarization. FactScore decomposes summaries into atomic facts (fine-grained factuality rather than only final overlap).
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Reported as the recall-vs-precision / context-length-vs-accuracy tradeoff rather than wall-clock cost: longer context and larger top-k raise retrieval recall but can hurt QA F1 (SNR), so a small top-k (=5) observation-RAG is both cheaper (fewer/shorter retrieved items) and more accurate than dumping the whole 16K context or top-50. RAG is positioned as a balanced compromise between cheap short-context accuracy and expensive long-context comprehension. No explicit API-cost/latency/token-savings numbers are tabulated. Dataset curation cost is noted (release trimmed 50 -> 10 conversations for cost-effective closed-source evaluation).
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (this is a benchmark/dataset paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Construction: machine-human pipeline. (a) Personas expanded from MSC seeds via gpt-3.5-turbo; (b) per-agent temporal event graph (up to 25 causally-linked events over 6-12 months) generated by text-davinci-003 iteratively (batches of k=3); (c) two generative agents (Park et al. 2023 architecture: reflect-and-respond with long-term observation memory + short-term session summaries) converse, with image-sharing (caption->keywords->icrawler web search) and image-reaction (BLIP-2 caption then react); (d) human annotators edit ~15% of dialog turns, remove/substitute ~19% of images, and verify event-graph grounding. Size: original arXiv v1 = 50 conversations; RELEASED benchmark = 10 conversations (locomo10.json), each ~300 turns / ~9.2K tokens / up to 35 sessions (avg 19.3 sessions, 304.9 turns, 9,209.2 tokens), multi-modal, spanning a few months - ~9x longer per conversation than MSC. Answer verifiability: QA answers are taken verbatim from the conversation where possible and annotated with evidence turn IDs, enabling F1 partial-match and Recall@k scoring; event-summary ground truth = annotated per-speaker event lists scored by FactScore. Difficulty: best system (top-5 observation RAG) ~41.4 QA F1 vs human 87.9; long-context adversarial F1 as low as 2.1, signaling a hard benchmark.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Generative Agents (Park et al., 2023) memory/reflection architecture for the dialogue-generating agents; MSC / 'Beyond Goldfish Memory' (Xu et al., 2022) for seed personas and as the prior multi-session benchmark it extends; DRAGON (Lin et al., 2023) as the dense retriever; FactScore (Min et al., 2023) for summarization factuality; MM-Relevance / MMDialog (Feng et al., 2023) and MiniGPT-5 (Zheng et al., 2023) for multimodal dialogue; BLIP-2 (Li et al., 2023b) for image captioning; SODA/Conversation Chronicles (Kim et al. 2023; Jang et al. 2023) for LLM-generated dialogue datasets.
- **contrasts with**:
> Prior long-term dialogue benchmarks limited to <=5 sessions / ~1K tokens (MSC - Xu et al. 2022; Conversation Chronicles - Jang et al. 2023; Zhang et al. 2023), and shorter multimodal dialogue datasets (MPChat, MMDialog, DailyDialog, SODA) - LoCoMo is far longer (300 turns, 9K tokens, up to 35 sessions). Methodologically it contrasts long-context LLMs vs RAG vs short-context base LLMs, finding long-context models hallucinate (adversarial collapse, weak event summarization) while distilled-observation RAG is the best balance.
- **lineage**:
> Surveys/benchmarks group: a foundational very-long-term conversational-MEMORY benchmark (LoCoMo). It established the standard testbed for evaluating long-context vs RAG memory in dialogue agents and is cited as the canonical 'memory' benchmark (alongside LongMemEval) for later agent-memory systems (Mem0, MemGPT, A-MEM, Memory-R1, etc.). Sits in the lineage of multi-session dialogue benchmarks (MSC -> Conversation Chronicles -> LoCoMo) with added scale, multimodality, temporal event-graph grounding, and a three-task evaluation framework.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- context_budget_and_selection_count

<a id="item-context-engineering-survey"></a>
### 158. A Survey of Context Engineering for Large Language Models

2025  ·  arXiv 2507.13334  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.13334)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2507.13334) [cs.CL]. Submitted 17 Jul 2025 (v1), last revised 21 Jul 2025 (v2). Marked 'ongoing work; 166 pages, 1411 citations'. No peer-reviewed venue found as of the survey date; arXiv-only.
- **authors affiliation**:
> Lingrui Mei (lead, corresponding contact), Jiayu Yao, Yuyao Ge, Baolong Bi, Jiazhi Liu, Mingyu Li, Jiafeng Guo, Shenghua Liu (corresponding) - Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences (ICT, CAS) and University of Chinese Academy of Sciences (UCAS); also Key Laboratory of Network Data Science and Technology (ICT, CAS) and State Key Laboratory of AI Safety. Co-authors: Yiwei Wang (University of California, Merced), Yujun Cai (The University of Queensland), Zhong-Zhi Li, Duzhen Zhang, Tianze Xia (UCAS), Chenlin Zhou (Peking University), Jiayi Mao (Tsinghua University). Primary affiliation: ICT, Chinese Academy of Sciences. Contact: meilingrui25b@ict.ac.cn, liushenghua@ict.ac.cn.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.13334
- **code url**: N/A (no method code; this is a survey). The associated curated paper list is the maintained_repo below.
- **maintained repo url**:
> https://github.com/Meirtz/Awesome-Context-Engineering (the authors' continuously-updated 'Awesome Context Engineering' curated list, ~3.2k stars; actively maintained and as of March 2026 expanded beyond the frozen PDF to cover agent harnesses, runtime memory, protocols MCP/A2A/AG-UI/ACP/ANP, coding agents, and observability - therefore more current than the July 2025 PDF).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Survey / taxonomy spanning the full LLM 'context engineering' landscape: prompt-based generation, in-context learning / CoT reasoning, external knowledge acquisition and RAG (QA, multi-hop, graph), long-sequence processing, self-refinement, structured-information (knowledge-graph) integration, memory systems, tool-integrated reasoning / function calling, and multi-agent systems. Not a single task; it unifies QA, reasoning, tool-use, agentic, and decision-making settings under one framework.
- **problem setting**:
> This is a horizontal survey (not a method paper). It formalizes 'Context Engineering' as the systematic optimization of the information payload C supplied to an autoregressive LLM at inference, decomposing C into a set of structured components (instructions, knowledge, tools, memory, state, query) assembled by formatting/concatenation functions, and framing the goal as maximizing expected output quality subject to a context-length budget |C| <= L_max (an information-theoretic / optimization view replacing the single static prompt string with a dynamic, multi-component stream). It covers offline and interactive, single- and multi-agent regimes. Supervision varies by surveyed method (none/frozen prompting, SFT, RL). The survey analyzes over 1400 research papers and is organized into Foundational Components (Context Retrieval & Generation; Context Processing; Context Management) and System Implementations (RAG; Memory Systems; Tool-Integrated Reasoning; Multi-Agent Systems), plus Evaluation and Future Directions. It contributes no new method or experiments of its own.
- **what is retrieved**:
> Survey-level: covers retrieval/acquisition of all major context types - retrieved documents/knowledge (RAG), knowledge-graph subgraphs/structured data, demonstrations/exemplars (ICL/CoT), tools/APIs (tool-integrated reasoning), and memory entries (episodic/long-term agent memory). The survey treats 'context retrieval and generation' broadly: both retrieving external knowledge and generating context (prompts, CoT).
- **retrieval grounding**:
> HYBRID (survey-wide). The taxonomy explicitly spans STATIC external corpora/KBs/APIs (classic RAG, knowledge-graph integration, tool documentation) and GROWING/episodic agent memory the system writes (Memory Systems section: MemoryBank, MemGPT, A-MEM, memory hierarchies, persistent interactions). Tool-integrated reasoning and multi-agent memory add further hybrid grounding.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A. The survey is not a case-based-reasoning method; it does not implement Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain itself. (It catalogs memory and experience-reuse systems, but CBR cycle coverage is a per-method property not applicable to the survey.) [N/A]
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The survey does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not center Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it frames the field as 'Context Engineering' (retrieval/generation, processing, management) integrated into RAG/memory/tool/multi-agent systems.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Survey-level: the taxonomy spans many retrievable units - token/snippet and document (RAG), demonstration/exemplar (ICL/CoT), knowledge-graph subgraph and structured records (GraphRAG/KG integration, e.g. HippoRAG, LightRAG, RAPTOR), tool/API specifications (Toolformer, Gorilla, ToolLLM, function-calling), and memory entries (MemoryBank, MemGPT, A-MEM). No single retrieval unit; it is a multi-granularity catalog.
- **index source**:
> Survey-wide HYBRID: it reviews static offline-built corpora/KBs and tool registries as well as online/test-time-growing agent memory (memory hierarchies, persistent storage written during interaction). Construction is described as both offline-induced (document indices, KG construction in graph-RAG) and online (memory write-back in agent memory systems).
- **index structure topology**:
> Survey-level: covers flat vector indices (modular RAG), knowledge/dependency GRAPH indices (Graph-Enhanced RAG, GraphRAG, LightRAG, HippoRAG, RAPTOR hierarchical trees), hierarchical memory structures (MemGPT/OS-style memory hierarchies, hierarchical memory), and structured/KG topologies for structured-information integration. It explicitly organizes RAG into 'modular, agentic, and graph-enhanced' architectures.
- **retriever type**:
> Survey-level (not one retriever): reviews sparse and dense retrievers, learned retrievers, graph-based retrieval (GraphRAG/HippoRAG), agentic/LLM-driven retrieval (Agentic RAG, Self-RAG, RAG-Gym), and tool retrieval (generative/function-calling). It does not propose a single retriever.
- **query construction**:
> Survey-level: discusses query forms across methods - raw input queries, decomposed sub-queries (multi-hop / agentic RAG), self-refined/clarified queries, CoT-conditioned queries, and dynamic context assembly. Context Retrieval & Generation includes prompt-based generation and 'Dynamic Assembly' as a way of constructing the context payload. No single query-construction recipe.
- **query granularity**: Survey-level: spans task-level one-shot retrieval (classic RAG/ICL), iterative/step-level retrieval (agentic and iterative RAG, tool-integrated reasoning per step), and trajectory/session-level memory queries. Presented as a design spectrum, not a fixed choice.
- **when to retrieve**: Survey-level: covers one-shot (modular RAG), iterative/agentic (Agentic RAG, RAG-Gym, ReAct-style tool loops), active/adaptive/self-reflective triggering (Self-RAG, CDF-RAG), and memory-driven on-demand retrieval. The survey frames these as the modular->agentic evolution of RAG.
- **reranking**:
> Survey-level: reranking and post-retrieval refinement are discussed as part of modular/advanced RAG and context processing (self-refinement, structured information integration), but the survey does not commit to a single reranker. It treats reranking/refinement as a stage in the RAG pipeline taxonomy.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Survey-level: a central theme of 'Context Processing' and 'Context Management' - covers self-refinement (Self-Refine, Reflexion), structured-information integration (StructGPT, KG integration, GraphFormers), context compression (Recurrent Context Compression, Activation Refilling, KV-cache management, Heavy-Hitter Oracle), and long-sequence processing (StreamingLLM, InfLLM, Infini-attention, YaRN). Refinement/compression is one of the survey's three foundational components.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Survey-level: tool-integrated reasoning is a dedicated section (Toolformer, Gorilla, ToolLLM, Granite-Function-Calling, ToRA, ReTool, Chameleon, API-Bank, MCP-RADAR). It discusses tool documentation/description handling and function-calling interfaces, but as a literature survey it does not prescribe a single tool-document-engineering recipe.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Survey-level: the Multi-Agent Systems and Tool-Integrated Reasoning sections explicitly cover integration protocols - MCP, A2A, ACP, ANP, KQML, FIPA ACL, function-calling - and the maintained repo's 2026 update emphasizes live MCP/A2A/AG-UI protocol coverage and CRUD-style runtime tool/memory management. Static-vs-live tool index is discussed at the ecosystem level, not as one method.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Survey-level: covers the full spectrum - prompt augmentation (RAG, ICL), context assembly/formatting into the payload, self-refinement feeding back into generation, memory injection for persistence, tool outputs fed back into reasoning (tool-integrated reasoning), and orchestration across agents. The unifying view is that all of these populate/optimize the inference-time context C.
- **planning integration**:
> Survey-level: planning/acting integration is covered via Tool-Integrated Reasoning (ReAct, Program-Aided Language Models, ToRA, Chameleon - interleaved reason-act-retrieve loops), Agentic RAG (retrieve-within-a-loop, RAG-Gym), and Multi-Agent orchestration/coordination (MetaGPT, AutoGen, CAMEL, CrewAI, CoA, SagaLLM). It catalogs per-step interleaved, plan-then-act, and orchestrated multi-agent integration patterns.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Survey-level: spans per-answer (single-shot RAG), per-CoT-step (CoT/ToT/GoT, iterative retrieval), and per-tool-call within a rollout (ReAct, tool-integrated reasoning). Presented as the modular->agentic spectrum rather than a fixed granularity.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (the survey itself adapts no retrieved case). At the catalog level it discusses self-refinement (Self-Refine, Reflexion) and agentic revision as adaptation strategies of surveyed systems, but adaptation_mechanism is a per-method CBR property not applicable to a survey. [N/A]
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Survey-level: covers raw documents/snippets, structured/KG representations (StructGPT, GraphFormers, KG integration), distilled/compressed context (context compression, summarization), workflow/agent memory entries, and tool/function specifications. Surface form varies by surveyed system; no single representation.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Survey-level: ranges from concrete documents/demonstrations (RAG, ICL) to structured knowledge subgraphs (GraphRAG/KG), compressed/distilled context (context management), persistent memory abstractions (memory hierarchies), and tool/skill abstractions (tool-integrated reasoning). Multi-level by design.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Survey-level: discusses self-reflection / self-refinement (Self-RAG, Self-Refine, Reflexion), contextual calibration, brittleness assessment, corrective/decision-flow RAG (CDF-RAG), and context-handling-failure analysis as robustness themes; it analyzes these as challenges (e.g. 'Context Handling Failures', 'Brittleness Assessment') rather than proposing one mechanism.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> Survey-level: a full dedicated 'Memory Systems' section covering episodic/long-term memory, memory hierarchies, and procedural/persistent memory (MemoryBank, MemGPT, MemOS, A-MEM, Self-Controlled Memory, REMEMBERER, Short-term & Long-term memory, Memory-Enhanced Agents). Also covers graph and latent memory under structured integration. The survey treats all memory types as a taxonomy, not a single type.
- **write back**:
> Survey-level: True as a covered theme - the Memory Systems section centers on writing/storing experiences for persistent interactions (MemoryBank, MemGPT paging, A-MEM agentic memory, REMEMBERER). The survey itself stores nothing; it catalogs write-back as a memory-system capability.
- **online growth**: Survey-level: Yes as a covered theme - persistent, growing agent memory during deployment is a defining property of the Memory Systems section (and the repo's 2026 'runtime memory / project memory' update). Not a property of the survey artifact itself.
- **memory evolution update**: Survey-level: covered as memory management - append, consolidation/compression, hierarchical paging (MemGPT/MemOS), agentic linking/evolution (A-MEM 'agentic memory' linking and evolving notes). The survey catalogs these update dynamics rather than committing to one.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Survey-level: covered - agentic/RL-driven retrieval and decision policies are reviewed (Agentic RAG, RAG-Gym, Self-RAG's learned reflection, RL for tool/retrieval decisions), contrasted with fixed similarity top-k modular RAG. The survey presents learned-policy retrieval as the agentic end of the RAG spectrum, not its own contribution.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Survey-level: a dedicated 'Multi-Agent Systems' section covers cross-agent communication, shared context/memory, orchestration, and interoperability protocols (KQML, FIPA ACL, MCP, A2A, ACP, ANP; AutoGen, MetaGPT, CAMEL, CrewAI, Swarm, SagaLLM, CoA). Cross-agent/cross-framework context sharing is explicitly treated as a first-class concern.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> The survey's Evaluation section catalogs many benchmarks (it does not run experiments). Named examples include GAIA, GTA, WebArena, VideoWebArena, Deep Research Bench, StableToolBench, NesTools, ToolHop, T-Eval, BFCL (Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard), NarrativeQA, MEMENTO, API-Bank, Mind2Web, SWE-Bench, LongMemEval, MADail-Bench, MCP-RADAR.
- **benchmark family**:
> Survey-wide coverage across families: agentic/general (GAIA, GTA, Deep Research Bench), web (WebArena, VideoWebArena, Mind2Web), tool/function-calling (StableToolBench, NesTools, ToolHop, T-Eval, BFCL, API-Bank, MCP-RADAR), memory (LongMemEval, MEMENTO, MADail-Bench), QA/long-context (NarrativeQA), and code (SWE-Bench). It is a multi-family catalog, not a single benchmark family.
- **baselines**: N/A. As a survey it reports no head-to-head baselines or new experimental comparisons; it reviews and contrasts methods qualitatively rather than benchmarking a proposed system against baselines.
- **key metrics**: N/A as own results. The survey discusses, at the meta level, the metrics used across the field (task success/pass rate, accuracy, tool-call correctness, retrieval/answer quality, memory recall over long horizons) and critiques evaluation; it reports no metric numbers of its own.
- **headline result**:
> No quantitative headline number (survey, not a method). The qualitative headline finding: across 1400+ analyzed papers, a fundamental asymmetry exists - LLMs augmented by advanced context engineering are highly proficient at UNDERSTANDING complex contexts but exhibit pronounced limitations in GENERATING equally sophisticated, long-form outputs; closing this comprehension-generation gap is named the defining future priority.
- **ablations**: N/A. A survey performs no ablation studies. (Its analytical equivalent is the decomposition into Foundational Components vs System Implementations and the identification of the comprehension-generation asymmetry and evaluation challenges.)
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Survey-level: it explicitly distinguishes Component-Level Assessment from System-Level Integration evaluation (Evaluation Frameworks section), i.e. it argues for decoupling intrinsic component metrics from end-to-end system metrics, and flags 'Memory System Isolation Problems' as an evaluation challenge. It does not itself report intrinsic-vs-end-to-end numbers.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Survey-level: discusses both, advocating beyond outcome-only scoring - it raises process-oriented concerns (reasoning faithfulness, multi-tool coordination, transactional integrity, self-validation dependencies, attribution challenges) alongside final-task outcome metrics, as part of its Evaluation Challenges.
- **survey scope and axes**:
> Organizing axes (Figure 1 taxonomy): (A) Foundational Components - (4.1) Context Retrieval & Generation, (4.2) Context Processing, (4.3) Context Management; (B) System Implementations - (5.1) Retrieval-Augmented Generation (modular / agentic / graph-enhanced), (5.2) Memory Systems, (5.3) Tool-Integrated Reasoning, (5.4) Multi-Agent Systems; plus (6) Evaluation (frameworks, benchmark datasets, challenges) and (7) Future Directions (foundational research, technical innovation, application-driven). Coverage: 'over 1400 research papers' analyzed; 166 pages; 1411 citations/references in the bibliography; evolution timeline spans 2020-2025 (maintained repo extended to ~March 2026).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A. The survey introduces no new benchmark/dataset of its own; it reviews and categorizes existing ones (see benchmarks/benchmark_family). [N/A]

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Positions itself relative to and builds upon prior vertical surveys it cites: prompt-engineering surveys, knowledge-graph/structured-knowledge-integration surveys, long-context surveys, RAG surveys (including modular/agentic/graph-enhanced RAG surveys), LLM-agent surveys, tool-learning/function-calling surveys, and multi-agent-systems surveys. Conceptually builds on the autoregressive LLM probabilistic model to define context optimization.
- **contrasts with**:
> Explicitly contrasts itself with (a) 'prompt engineering' as too narrow (a single static string) and (b) prior surveys that treat individual verticals (RAG, memory, tool use, multi-agent, long context) in isolation; its differentiator is a horizontal, unifying taxonomy that separates foundational components from their integration into systems and surfaces the cross-domain connections those vertical surveys leave implicit.
- **lineage**:
> Surveys group: a unifying meta-survey of the retrieval-/context-augmented LLM landscape. It sits above and stitches together the per-topic lineages (ICL/demonstration retrieval, RAG and agentic/graph RAG, agent memory, tool retrieval/use, multi-agent orchestration), providing the umbrella 'Context Engineering' framework under which the other works in this collection (RAG, memory, tool, CBR, multi-agent methods) can be located.
