### 159. A Survey of Self-Evolving Agents: What, When, How, and Where to Evolve

2025  ·  arXiv 2507.21046  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21046)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2507.21046, submitted Jul 2025); accepted to Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), Jan 2026
- **authors affiliation**:
> Huan-ang Gao, Jiayi Geng, Wenyue Hua, Mengkang Hu, Xinzhe Juan, ... Cheng Qian, Qingyun Wu, Heng Ji, Mengdi Wang (27 authors, equal-contribution alphabetical order; corresponding: Hongru Wang and Mengdi Wang). Lead/primary affiliations: Princeton University & Princeton AI Lab; Tsinghua University; CMU; University of Sydney; Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Penn State; University of Michigan; Oregon State; CUHK; Fudan; HKUST(GZ); HKU; UC Santa Barbara; UC San Diego; University of Edinburgh; UIUC.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21046
- **code url**: N/A (no method code; this is a survey)
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/CharlesQ9/Self-Evolving-Agents (official maintained awesome-list / paper collection, Apache-2.0, ~1.2k stars; last updated Oct 2025)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Survey spanning agentic task domains: QA/reasoning, coding (SWE-bench, MLE-Bench), web/GUI navigation (WebArena, WebShop, Mind2Web, OSWorld, mobile), tool-use (ToolBench, API-Bank, T-Eval), embodied (Voyager/Minecraft), multi-agent, and specialized domains (education, healthcare, finance/quant trading, scientific discovery).
- **problem setting**:
> Survey of self-evolving LLM agents: systems that autonomously modify their internal parameters, contextual state, toolset, or architectural topology based on their own trajectories or feedback to improve future performance. Formalizes the agent system as a (multi-)agent tuple over a POMDP environment, with a self-evolving strategy f that recurrently maps (agent, trajectory, feedback) -> new agent to maximize cumulative utility over a task sequence. Covers offline and online/test-time settings, single- and multi-agent systems, with supervision ranging from scalar rewards to textual feedback; explicitly distinguishes passive (externally scheduled) vs active (self-initiated exploration/reflection) evolution and proto-evolution vs strong self-evolution.
- **what is retrieved**:
> As a survey, it reviews what self-evolving components store/retrieve/reuse: long-term memory entries (episodic experiences, facts), distilled experiences/insights/guidelines/rules (Expel, AutoGuide, ReasoningBank), demonstrations/trajectories (cross-agent and self-generated), skills/tools/executable programs (Voyager, Alita), prompts/instructions, and retrieved cases (Memento case bank). Retrieval-augmented memory is one evolutionary locus among models, context, tools, architecture.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> HYBRID across the surveyed field: emphasizes a GROWING/episodic memory the agent writes back to (Mem0, A-mem, SAGE, Memory-R1, Memento, ReasoningBank, Agent Workflow Memory) but also covers static external corpora/tools and tool indices; the survey's central axis is precisely the static-to-growing (online-growth/write-back) distinction.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (survey, not a CBR method). It does review CBR-style methods within memory evolution (e.g., Memento's Retrieve-Reuse over an evolving case bank), but does not itself implement a CBR cycle.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: No. The survey does not frame itself as case-based reasoning nor systematically cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; CBR mechanisms appear only implicitly via surveyed case-bank methods (e.g., Memento).

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Surveyed across granularities: single memory record/fact, full trajectory and sub-trajectory, distilled insight/guideline/rule, free-text workflow/routine, executable skill/program, tool/API, prompt/instruction, and retrieved case (problem-solution). No single canonical unit since it is a survey.
- **index source**:
> Survey covers all three: offline-induced stores (STaR/bootstrapped data, ExpeL rules), online/test-time-induced growing memory (WebRL self-evolving curriculum, Mobile-Agent-E, Alita, Memento), and hybrid. The 'when to evolve' taxonomy (intra-test-time vs inter-test-time/offline vs online) directly organizes index-source timing.
- **index structure topology**:
> Survey reviews flat vector memory, metadata/context-keyed memory, interconnected knowledge networks (A-mem Zettelkasten dynamic linking), hierarchical memory (G-Memory for multi-agent systems), and graph/workflow structures; architecture evolution covers graph/code topologies of agent systems.
- **retriever type**: Survey-level: covers off-the-shelf dense/similarity retrieval over memory, generative tool retrieval (ToolGen tool-as-token), LLM-as-retriever, and learned/RL retrieval policies (Memento, Memory-R1). No single retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Survey reviews the spectrum: none/similarity top-k, RL/learned policy for memory and case selection (Memento online RL case-retrieval policy; Memory-R1 RL-trained Memory Manager; REMEMBER RL-updated experience memory), and reward/feedback-driven selection. A key surveyed shift is from fixed similarity retrieval to RL-optimized retrieval/memory-management policies.
- **query construction**: Not unified (survey). Reviews methods using raw task input, reflection/self-critique-conditioned queries, and learned memory triggers (MemGen learned memory trigger deciding when to invoke memory; Mem0 fact extraction from recent dialogue).
- **query granularity**: Survey covers task-level, trajectory-level, and step/state-level retrieval; the intra-test-time vs inter-test-time temporal taxonomy spans within-task (step-level) and across-task (trajectory/task-level) granularities.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Survey-level: covers one-shot, iterative, and adaptive/learned triggers. The 'When to Evolve' chapter is a core axis: Intra-Test-Time (during task execution, real-time/active) vs Inter-Test-Time (between tasks, offline or online); learned memory triggers (MemGen) decide invocation.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Survey reviews fixed schedule, self-confidence/uncertainty, reflection/self-critique signals, environment feedback (scalar reward or textual), and learned triggers (MemGen memory trigger). The intra-test-time mode is characterized by the agent recognizing its own limitations and self-initiating learning.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Survey covers post-retrieval refinement via experience distillation (raw trajectories -> insights/rules in ExpeL, AutoGuide, ReasoningBank), summarization/tagging (MemInsight), and memory consolidation (ADD/MERGE/UPDATE/DELETE in Mem0). Distillation into general guidance rather than retrieving exact instances is highlighted as a key memory-evolution aspect.
- **tool document engineering**: Survey reviews tool evolution (creation/mastery/management) and tool retrieval/representation (ToolGen tool-as-token generation, ToolLLM, COLT completeness-oriented tool retrieval, ToolRet benchmark) but does not prescribe a single document-engineering recipe.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: Survey covers dynamic/live tool ecosystems and protocols, including MCP (MCP-Universe benchmark) and RapidAPI-based tool stores (ToolBench/ToolLLM 16000+ APIs), and discusses self-directed tool discovery/integration lifecycle (Alita) as an under-evaluated capability.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Survey-level: prompt augmentation (ICL with retrieved experiences/demos), skill reuse (Voyager skill library), case adaptation (Memento), latent-token injection (MemGen generative latent memory), and as training signal (RL/SFT on self-generated trajectories). Memory and experience are reused to shape future decision-making.
- **planning integration**:
> Survey reviews retrieval/experience integrated as one-shot exemplars at plan time, per-step interleaved reflection (Reflexion, AdaPlanner, Self-Refine), retrieve-then-plan over memory, and inside online RL loops (WebRL, RAGEN). Planning is one of the internal agent capabilities evaluated.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Survey spans per-answer, per-CoT-step (Self-Refine, Reflexion iterative refinement), and per-rollout interleaving; intra-test-time evolution couples adaptation tightly with each step of task execution.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> Survey covers adaptation/reuse mechanisms across methods: verbatim ICL exemplars, LLM-prompted/reflective revision (Reflexion, Self-Refine, AdaPlanner), execution-feedback-driven revision, RL reuse/fine-tuning (Memento, RAGEN), and latent adaptation (MemGen). Not a single mechanism (survey).
- **retrieved item representation**: Survey covers raw trajectories, distilled strategies/guidelines/rules (free text), free-text workflows (Agent Workflow Memory), executable skills/programs (Voyager, Alita), structured/tagged notes (MemInsight, A-mem), and latent/soft tokens (MemGen).
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Survey explicitly contrasts retrieving raw past instances vs distilling experiences into more general guidance (insights, state-aware guidelines/rules in ExpeL/AutoGuide/ReasoningBank), reusable workflows, and procedural skills; this raw-vs-distilled abstraction spectrum is a discussed memory-evolution theme.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> Survey taxonomy of memory/context as an evolutionary locus: episodic/long-term memory, skill-library, workflow/procedural memory, graph/interconnected memory (A-mem, G-Memory), and latent generative memory (MemGen). Context is one of four 'what-to-evolve' pillars (Models, Context, Tools, Architecture).
- **write back**:
> Yes (central theme). The survey frames self-evolving agents as systems that write back experiences/cases/skills: memory evolution where agents store, forget, and retrieve; Mem0 ADD/MERGE/UPDATE/DELETE; Memory-R1 RL Memory Manager; Memento evolving case bank; skill libraries (Voyager). Write-back/online-growth is an explicit organizing axis.
- **online growth**:
> Yes. The 'When to Evolve' chapter distinguishes inter-test-time online learning (continuous adaptation from streaming interaction data: WebRL self-evolving online curriculum, Mobile-Agent-E, Alita, DigiRL) and intra-test-time adaptation, vs frozen offline-induced stores. Online growth of the store during deployment is a first-class surveyed dimension.
- **write back trigger**:
> Survey covers the spectrum: reflective writes after self-critique (Reflexion, ExpeL), on-success and on-failure storage, per-step/per-episode updates (REMEMBER updates memory after each episode), learned/RL-decided writes (Memory-R1, MemGen trigger), and human-validated. No single trigger.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Survey notes both success and failure experiences are leveraged: agents reflect on failed trajectories (Reflexion verbal reinforcement from failures), distill corrective insights/rules, and consolidate/delete contradictory memories (Mem0). Contrastive use of success+failure is discussed within reflection/experiential-learning methods.
- **memory evolution update**:
> Survey explicitly covers post-write dynamics: append-only accumulation, dedup-merge and delta-update (Mem0 ADD/MERGE/UPDATE/DELETE), forget-prune (SAGE Ebbinghaus forgetting curve), and link-and-evolve (A-mem dynamic indexing and linking forming knowledge networks). Memory mutation after writing is a discussed axis.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Yes (surveyed). The survey highlights works where retrieval/case-selection/memory-management is a learned RL policy rather than fixed top-k: Memento (online RL case-retrieval policy, fine-tuning agents without fine-tuning the LLM), Memory-R1 (RL-trained Memory Manager selecting ADD/UPDATE/DELETE), REMEMBER (RL signals to update experience memory).
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Yes (surveyed). Covers cross-agent demonstration learning (Sec 5.2.2), multi-agent shared/hierarchical memory (G-Memory for multi-agent systems), self-evolving multi-agent collaboration networks, and the 'Ecosystems of Multi-Agents' future-direction chapter discussing co-evolution and shared experience across agents.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> Catalogs many: SWE-bench, MLE-Bench, ScienceAgentBench, DSBench, WebArena, WebShop, Mind2Web/Mind2Web 2, OSWorld, WebWalker, BrowseComp, GAIA, AgentBench, LifelongAgentBench, TheAgentCompany, xbench, ToolBench/ToolLLM, API-Bank, T-Eval, ACEBench, Seal-Tools, MCP-Universe, MultiAgentBench, SwarmBench, Collab-Overcooked, Agent-SafetyBench, ST-WebAgentBench, AgentDAM, LTMBenchmark, PlanBench, ACPBench, StoryBench.
- **benchmark family**:
> Spans QA/reasoning, code (SWE-bench/MLE-Bench/ScienceAgentBench), web & GUI (WebArena/WebShop/Mind2Web/OSWorld/mobile), tool (ToolBench/API-Bank/T-Eval/MCP-Universe), embodied (Voyager/Minecraft), memory/lifelong (LifelongAgentBench/LTMBenchmark), multi-agent (MultiAgentBench/SwarmBench), and safety (Agent-SafetyBench/ST-WebAgentBench).
- **baselines**:
> N/A as a survey (no head-to-head method baselines). It instead positions itself against prior surveys (e.g., 'A survey on self-evolution of large language models', 'Advances and challenges in foundation agents', 'Lifelong learning of LLM-based agents: a roadmap') and contrasts self-evolving agents with curriculum learning, lifelong/continual learning, model editing, and unlearning.
- **key metrics**:
> Survey proposes a five-goal evaluation framework with associated metrics: Adaptivity (e.g., Success Rate by Iteration Steps / learning curve), Retention (catastrophic-forgetting / knowledge stability), Generalization (in-domain-evolve / out-of-domain-evaluate transfer), Efficiency (cost-aware: tokens/latency/compute), and Safety. Notes shift from single-shot scoring to longitudinal, cost-aware trajectory metrics.
- **headline result**:
> N/A (survey, no single empirical headline number). Its headline contribution is the first systematic taxonomy organizing self-evolving agents along What / When / How / Where to evolve, plus a five-dimension (Adaptivity, Retention, Generalization, Efficiency, Safety) evaluation framework. 77 pages, 9 figures, ~455 references.
- **ablations**:
> N/A (survey; no controlled ablations). Provides comparative tables instead: Table 2 (methods x four evolutionary pillars Model/Context/Tool/Architecture), Table 3 (How-to-evolve: feedback type/source, learning method, updated components, update timing), and evaluation coverage/gap tables (Tables 6-11).
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Survey advocates decoupling: distinguishes Internal/Component-level evaluation (planning, tool use, memory management, multi-agent coordination) from External end-to-end task-solving evaluation, and separates static, short-horizon adaptive, and long-horizon lifelong assessment paradigms.
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Survey argues for both: beyond final-outcome scoring it calls for trajectory-centric, process-aware, longitudinal assessment (adaptation over time, retention, step-wise component quality), criticizing single-shot outcome-only evaluation as insufficient for self-evolving agents.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**: Survey elevates Efficiency to one of five core evaluation goals (cost-aware assessment: token/compute/latency budgets, per-query token budgets, millisecond response constraints) and flags that current benchmarks under-evaluate adaptation under hard resource limits.
- **survey scope and axes**:
> Explicit organizing axes: What to evolve (Models, Context [memory + prompt], Tools, Architecture [single/multi-agent]); When to evolve (Intra-test-time vs Inter-test-time, offline vs online); How to evolve (reward-based, imitation/demonstration learning, population-based/evolutionary, plus cross-cutting dimensions); Where to evolve (general vs specialized domains: coding, education, healthcare, finance, science). Plus Evaluation (5 goals) and Future Directions. ~455 references; coverage window through 2025 (v4 revised Jan 2026). First systematic survey of self-evolving agents.
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (survey, not a benchmark). It catalogs and analyzes benchmark coverage gaps (Tables 7-8) rather than constructing a dataset.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Builds on prior agent and self-evolution literature: surveys on LLM agents and foundation agents; 'A survey on self-evolution of LLMs' (Tao et al. 2024); 'Lifelong learning of LLM-based agents: a roadmap'; and foundational methods it organizes (Reflexion, Self-Refine, ExpeL, Voyager, STaR, AFlow/ADAS, Mem0, AgentBench).
- **contrasts with**:
> Explicitly contrasted (Table 1) with related learning paradigms: curriculum learning, lifelong/continual learning, model editing, and unlearning, emphasizing self-evolving agents' adaptive, dynamic, and autonomous (active self-initiated) nature. Also distinguished from prior LLM-self-evolution surveys by focusing on agent-system-level evolution across components/timing/methods/domains.
- **lineage**: Surveys lineage. A foundational taxonomy/roadmap survey for the self-evolving / experience-growing agent line; relevant to the write-back / online-growth axis separating experience-/memory-evolving agents from static RAG planners.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- completeness_vs_topk_objective
- context_budget_and_selection_count
- index_content_separation
- noise_robustness_mechanism
- reranking
- tool_dependency_awareness

<a id="item-adaptation-agentic-survey"></a>
### 160. Adaptation of Agentic AI: A Survey of Post-Training, Memory, and Skills

2025  ·  arXiv 2512.16301  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.16301)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **authors affiliation**:
> Pengcheng Jiang, Jiacheng Lin, Zhiyi Shi (co-first authors), Zifeng Wang, Luxi He, Yichen Wu, Ming Zhong, Peiyang Song, Qizheng Zhang, Heng Wang, Xueqiang Xu, Hanwen Xu, Pengrui Han, Dylan Zhang, Jiashuo Sun, Chaoqi Yang, Kun Qian, Tian Wang, Changran Hu, Manling Li, Quanzheng Li, Hao Peng, Sheng Wang, Jingbo Shang, Chao Zhang, Jiaxuan You, Liyuan Liu, Pan Lu, Yu Zhang, Heng Ji, Yejin Choi, Dawn Song, Jimeng Sun, Jiawei Han (senior author, corresponding). Primary affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (UIUC); other affiliations span Stanford, Princeton, Harvard, UC Berkeley, Caltech, University of Washington, UCSD, Georgia Tech, Northwestern, Texas A&M (TAMU), MGH, Keiji AI, and Unity.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.16301

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Survey of agentic AI adaptation spanning multiple task domains: tool-use, retrieval/RAG, planning, code/software development, web/computer use, QA/multi-hop reasoning, embodied (Minecraft), and decision-making. Evaluation applications surveyed: deep research, software development, computer use, and drug discovery.
- **problem setting**:
> A survey (taxonomy/framework paper) that unifies post-training, retrieval, memory, and skill systems under a single notion of 'adaptation' (improving an agent, its tools, or their interaction after pretraining). It introduces a four-paradigm framework split by optimization target (agent vs. tool) and signal source: A1 (tool-execution-signaled agent adaptation), A2 (agent-output-signaled agent adaptation), T1 (agent-agnostic tool adaptation, including pre-trained reusable modules and 'graduated' subagents-as-tools), and T2 (agent-supervised tool adaptation, where a frozen agent's outputs supervise the training of memory systems, skill libraries, or lightweight subagents). Settings covered include offline SFT/off-policy and online/interactive RL (RLVR); single-agent and multi-agent/subagent pipelines; supervised, preference-based, and verifiable-reward signals. The survey situates adaptive memory and skill libraries primarily as T2 tool-adaptation mechanisms, contrasted with agent fine-tuning (A1/A2).
- **what is retrieved**:
> As a survey, it catalogs what various adapted systems retrieve/store: memories (episodic/case-based, strategy-based, skill-based), skills (executable code, API/MCP protocols, programs, synthesized tools), trajectories, distilled strategies/heuristics, guidelines/rules, documents (RAG), and tools/APIs. Memory and skills are framed as 'two facets of the same adaptation mechanism': memory provides the storage substrate; skills provide executable, composable content.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> HYBRID across the surveyed space. The survey explicitly distinguishes static/agent-agnostic stores (T1: pre-trained tools, classic RAG corpora, embedding models) from GROWING/agent-written memory and skill libraries (T2: dynamic memory stores, skill libraries curated by frozen-agent success/failure). It notes skill-based memory bridges T2 (agent-feedback-curated skill libraries) and T1 (pre-trained, agent-agnostic tool APIs).
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Not a single objective; the survey discusses both. For retrieval/RAG tools it references fixed top-k ranking and intrinsic ranking metrics (nDCG, Recall@K). It frames adaptation objectives more broadly as maximizing tool-execution quality (A1, e.g., retrieval scores/success rate) or holistic final-output utility (A2/T2), rather than committing to a single completeness-vs-topk objective.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> N/A (survey). The survey does not implement a CBR cycle, but it characterizes the surveyed memory/skill systems using a closely analogous lifecycle: skill acquisition (learn) / representation (store) / invocation (retrieve+reuse) / refinement (revise/retain via reflection, RL, or sharing); and memory formation / evolution / retrieval. These map loosely onto Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain across the works it reviews.
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False. The survey does not explicitly frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not foreground Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner CBR terminology. It uses 'case-based memory' (raw trajectory storage) as one abstraction level within an experiential-memory hierarchy (case-based / strategy-based / skill-based, borrowed from Hu et al.), and grounds memory taxonomy in cognitive-science / CoALA (Sumers et al.) rather than the CBR literature.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Surveys multiple granularities of the retrievable/stored unit: full trajectories (case-based memory), distilled strategies/heuristics/workflows (strategy-based memory), executable skills/programs/code snippets and API/MCP protocols (skill-based memory), documents and (query,document) pairs (RAG), tools/APIs, specialist subagents (subagent-as-tool), and (for RL-optimized memory) state/case representations used by a learned policy.
- **index source**:
> HYBRID/both. The survey contrasts static or offline-induced stores (T1 pre-trained modules; classic RAG corpora) with online/test-time-induced growing stores (T2 dynamic memory and skill libraries that the frozen agent writes during deployment, e.g., Voyager's growing skill library, ReasoningBank's test-time memory curation).
- **index structure topology**:
> Surveys multiple topologies. For T2 dynamic memory stores it identifies three design families: (1) hierarchical/OS-inspired tiers with page-eviction/garbage-collection (MemGPT, MemoryOS); (2) reflection-based consolidation (Generative Agents, A-MEM); (3) graph/structured indices keyed by relational/semantic structure (HippoRAG, SHIMI). Skill libraries are indexed by natural-language descriptions (Voyager); RAG uses flat vector indices.
- **retriever type**:
> Surveys all types: BM25/sparse and dense retrievers (RAG/T1), learned/trained retrievers optimized under frozen-LM feedback (T2, e.g., REPLUG), LLM-as-retriever/agent-initiated retrieval, and similarity-based retrieval over skill/memory stores. As a survey it does not adopt a single retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Surveys the full spectrum and emphasizes a shift from similarity-only to learned signals. T1 tools are trained agent-agnostically (off-the-shelf or pre-trained, e.g., SAM, AlphaFold2, dense retrievers). T2 tools are trained under frozen-agent supervision via: proxy signals (REPLUG's perplexity-reduction / KL alignment), structured preferences, downstream-task effectiveness (s3's Gain-Beyond-RAG), and RL/learned policies (PPO, GRPO, soft Q-learning) where the frozen agent's downstream success is the reward.
- **query construction**:
> Survey covers several: raw query (classic RAG), agent-generated/reformulated search queries (learned searchers like s3, Search-R1), task descriptions used to retrieve skills (Voyager indexes by NL skill descriptions), and reflective summaries used to retrieve experiential memory. No single canonical query construction is adopted.
- **query granularity**:
> Surveys both task-level (one-shot retrieval of relevant skills/memories at task start, e.g., skill-library lookup) and step/trajectory-level (per-step interleaved retrieval in interactive tool-use and search loops). The four-paradigm framework formalizes multi-turn tool use as iterated single-step interactions.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Surveys one-shot and iterative/interactive retrieval. Interactive RL-based methods (A1/A2 with tools, T2 searchers) retrieve iteratively within multi-turn rollouts; skill/memory retrieval is typically invoked when a new task arrives and refined across steps. Active/adaptive triggering is discussed in the broader memory-utilization literature it cites.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Survey-level: no single trigger. It describes agent-initiated tool/memory calls within interactive loops, fixed-schedule retrieval in classic RAG, and reflection-driven consolidation/retrieval in memory systems. Trigger signals are discussed as part of the memory 'dynamics' axis (formation, evolution, retrieval) rather than prescribed.
- **reranking**: Survey acknowledges reranking as a component in surveyed RAG/retrieval pipelines (it cites retrieval benchmarks reporting nDCG/Recall@K), but the survey itself does not propose a reranking method. No paradigm-specific reranking is mandated.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Surveys multiple post-retrieval/processing operations: distillation of trajectories into strategies/skills (case->strategy->skill abstraction), reflective consolidation deciding what to retain, progressive/lazy context loading for skills (SKILL.md, MCP, progressive context loading per Xu and Yan), and pruning/forgetting in memory management. As a survey it describes rather than implements a single refinement pipeline.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (survey does not propose tool-description engineering). It does note skill/tool representation standards (SKILL.md, MCP protocols, API specifications) and progressive context loading as ways surveyed systems package tool/skill descriptions before invocation.
- **index content separation**:
> Surveys this pattern: progressive/lazy context loading and SKILL.md/MCP interface standards (Xu and Yan) separate a lightweight skill index from heavy on-demand content; hierarchical/OS-inspired memory (MemGPT, MemoryOS) separates a small working context from large long-term storage with paging.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Surveys MCP (Model Context Protocol) and function-calling as integration protocols for skills/tools, and discusses dynamic/growing skill libraries (live-updated by the frozen agent) vs. static pre-trained T1 modules. SKILL.md and MCP are highlighted as emerging interface standards.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Surveys all uses: prompt augmentation (RAG, retrieved exemplars/guidelines), skill reuse (retrieve-and-compose executable skills, e.g., Voyager), case adaptation (experiential memory guiding future tasks), and training signal (frozen-agent feedback used to train T2 tools/retrievers/memory writers). It positions adaptive memory and skill libraries as adaptation mechanisms that are an alternative/complement to agent fine-tuning.
- **planning integration**:
> Survey covers a range: one-shot exemplars at plan time, per-step interleaved tool/retrieval calls inside interactive rollouts, plan-then-retrieve and retrieve-then-plan, hierarchical subtask decomposition (e.g., GITM/DEPS in embodied settings), and skill retrieval-and-composition within planning loops. Planner subagents themselves are framed as T2-adapted tools (e.g., AgentFlow's learned planner over a frozen backbone).
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Surveys per-answer (A2 final-output evaluation), per-tool-call within a rollout (A1 tool-execution signals; multi-turn tool use), and per-step interleaving in interactive search/RL methods (Search-R1, s3). The four-paradigm formalism treats each tool invocation as a discrete interleaving point.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> Core organizing concept. 'Adaptation' = improving an agent, its tools, or their interaction after pretraining. Mechanisms surveyed: agent adaptation via SFT, preference optimization, and RLVR (A1 tool-execution-signaled, A2 agent-output-signaled); tool adaptation via pre-trained agent-agnostic modules and graduated subagents-as-tools (T1) and via frozen-agent-supervised training of retrievers, memory writers, skill libraries, planners/advisors, and lightweight subagents (T2). The survey's distinctive claim is that adaptive memory and reusable skill libraries are themselves adaptation mechanisms (predominantly T2), complementary to fine-tuning.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Surveys the surface forms injected/stored: raw trajectories (case-based), distilled strategies/heuristics/free-text workflows (strategy-based), executable programs/code/skills and API/MCP specifications (skill-based), structured notes, and parametric/latent memory. It explicitly organizes these along an abstraction continuum.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Explicitly central axis. The survey adopts (from Hu et al.) a three-level experiential-memory hierarchy: case-based memory (raw trajectory), strategy-based memory (distilled workflows/heuristics), and skill-based memory (executable code/APIs/MCP). It also references the broader spectrum from raw trajectory to procedural skill to single demonstration/hint across the works reviewed.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Survey-level: discusses generalization and robustness as an evaluation dimension (Sec 7.3.2) and notes failure-aware curation (ReasoningBank extracting preventative lessons from failures) and counterfactual/controlled evaluation to isolate tool contribution. It does not propose a single noise-robustness mechanism; it surveys robustness as an open evaluation concern (benchmark saturation, metric validity, backbone dependence).

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> Surveys all: episodic, skill-library, workflow/procedural, graph/structured, hierarchical/OS-inspired, parametric, and latent memory. It adopts a tripartite forms/functions/dynamics lens (Hu et al.) and CoALA's working/episodic/semantic/procedural memory decomposition. Skills are framed as procedural memory.
- **write back**:
> True (for the T2 memory/skill systems surveyed). The survey's defining T2 characterization is that a frozen agent's outputs/downstream performance supervise how a memory module writes, retrieves, reflects, and forgets, and skill libraries grow by storing successful (verified) programs/skills.
- **online growth**: Yes for the T2 dynamic-memory and skill-library systems surveyed (e.g., Voyager's growing skill library, ReasoningBank's test-time memory curation, dynamic procedural memory). The survey contrasts these growing/test-time-induced stores with frozen T1 pre-trained modules.
- **write back trigger**:
> Surveys multiple triggers across systems: on-success only (Voyager stores verified successful programs), on-success-and-failure (ReasoningBank distills lessons from both successful and self-judged failed experiences; EXPEL extracts rules from success and failure), reflective consolidation (Generative Agents, A-MEM decide what to consolidate), and OS-style eviction/garbage-collection (MemGPT, MemoryOS). No single trigger is prescribed.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Surveys both success-only and success+failure usage. It explicitly highlights ReasoningBank (distills generalizable reasoning strategies from successful AND self-judged failed experiences, extracting 'crucial preventative lessons') and EXPEL (extracts rules from success and failure) as advances over success-only/raw-trajectory storage.
- **memory evolution update**:
> Surveys the full range as a 'dynamics'/update-policy axis: append-only (Voyager adds skills without modifying existing ones, avoiding catastrophic forgetting), reflective consolidation/refine (Generative Agents, A-MEM), delta/refine-overwrite via iterative refinement (Cao et al.'s dynamic procedural memory; RL-optimized memory), and forget/prune via eviction or garbage-collection (MemGPT, MemoryOS).
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Surveys this explicitly as a distinct T2 trend. It tabulates RL-optimized memory/tool policies including Memento (M-MDP / Q-function via soft Q-learning, GPT-4.1 frozen agent), Mem-alpha (GRPO), MAE (REINFORCE++), AgentFlow (Flow-GRPO planner), Advisor Models, QAgent, AI-SearchPlanner (PPO), and s3 (learned searcher via Gain-Beyond-RAG) -- contrasted with fixed similarity top-k retrieval.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Surveys both. It notes community-shared/collective skills (SkillWeaver's community-shared API-level skills; agent skills as shareable, executable artifacts via SKILL.md/MCP per Xu and Yan; 'Agent Skills in the Wild' marketplace audit), alongside single-agent private memory. Co-adaptation and collective sharing are flagged as open problems (Sec 9).

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> Survey catalogs many benchmarks mapped to A1/A2/T1/T2. A1 (verifiable tool execution): HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench, SWE-Bench, MTEB Retrieval. A2 (agent final output): multi-hop QA (as used by Search-R1, ReSearch), GSM8K, GPQA Diamond, IFEval, Arena-Hard, GAIA, AgentBench. T1: MTEB / standalone retriever and model evaluations. T2 (memory/skill): LongMemEval, Skill-Inject, Agent Skills in the Wild. Integrated/long-horizon agent environments: WebArena, and others (Mind2Web/Online-Mind2Web, ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, Minecraft per surveyed systems). Application domains: deep research, software development, computer use, drug discovery.
- **benchmark family**:
> QA / multi-hop (GSM8K, GPQA, multi-hop QA); code (HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench, SWE-Bench); retrieval/embedding (MTEB Retrieval); web (WebArena, Mind2Web/Online-Mind2Web); embodied (Minecraft/Voyager, ALFWorld, ScienceWorld); tool/agent (GAIA, AgentBench); memory (LongMemEval); instruction-following/chat (IFEval, Arena-Hard); skill-security (Skill-Inject, Agent Skills in the Wild).
- **baselines**:
> N/A as a survey (it does not run experiments with baselines). Instead it cites cross-paradigm empirical comparisons drawn from the surveyed papers, e.g., Search-R1 (A2) vs. s3 (T2) on RAG/QA, and DeepRetrieval's recall gains as A1 illustrations. The compared 'methods' are the surveyed systems themselves organized under A1/A2/T1/T2.
- **key metrics**:
> Survey distinguishes verifiable execution metrics (A1 & T1: pass@k, test-suite pass rate, retrieval Recall@K / nDCG, SQL correctness, formal-proof verification) from holistic utility metrics (A2 & T2: final-answer accuracy, win rate, GAIA score, task success rate of the frozen agent). It also emphasizes adaptation-dynamics metrics (sample/interaction efficiency, generalization/robustness, continual/co-adaptation stability) and systemic metrics (cost/inference-time compute, safety, alignment).
- **headline result**:
> Survey (no single experimental headline). Its most-cited illustrative comparison: in the RAG/QA case study, the T2 approach s3 trains only a lightweight ~7B searcher with frozen-generator feedback using ~2.4k training samples to reach 58.9% average accuracy (and 76.6% on specialized medical QA), comparable to or exceeding the A2 approach Search-R1 (~170k examples; 71.8% on medical QA) -- presented as evidence that T2's narrower optimization target yields high data efficiency, with explicit caveats that this is not a controlled comparison.
- **ablations**:
> N/A as a survey (no controlled ablations of its own). It instead performs comparative analysis across paradigms (A1 vs A2; T1 vs T2; A2 vs T2 data-efficiency synthesis) and uses the Search-R1 vs s3 contrast as a quasi-ablation of optimization target, while explicitly noting confounds (backbone composition, training-data distribution, architecture) that prevent attributing the efficiency gap to paradigm choice alone.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Yes -- a central methodological point. The survey argues A1/T1 verifiable-execution metrics (intrinsic, e.g., Recall@K, pass@k) should be reported separately from A2/T2 holistic end-to-end metrics, and exposes the 'A1-A2 evaluation gap' (high recall but low synthesis, or high final accuracy with shortcut reasoning) to motivate decoupled, both-family evaluation.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Survey advocates evaluating both. Beyond final outcomes it calls for process/dynamics metrics: sample and interaction efficiency, generalization and robustness, continual/co-adaptation stability, and intermediate skill-lifecycle quality (whether a skill library improves through reuse or degrades through drift) -- noting no current T2 benchmark measures these intermediate stages.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Explicitly treated (Sec 6.4, 7.4.1). It contrasts A2's monolithic, high-compute retraining (~170k examples for Search-R1) with T2's data efficiency (~2.4k samples for s3) and discusses cost and inference-time compute as a systemic evaluation axis. Trade-offs across paradigms (cost, flexibility, generalization, catastrophic forgetting, orchestration complexity, error compounding) are a core comparison theme.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Survey-level: discusses progressive/lazy context loading for skills (SKILL.md, MCP, progressive context loading per Xu and Yan) and hierarchical memory tiering (working vs. long-term, page-eviction in MemGPT/MemoryOS) as mechanisms to manage prompt/context budget. It does not prescribe a fixed k; it describes budget-management strategies across surveyed systems.
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A (survey, not a benchmark). It catalogs and critiques existing benchmarks (Table of benchmarks mapped to A1/A2/T1/T2) and identifies a gap: dedicated T2 benchmarks that hold the agent fixed and measure marginal tool/memory value remain scarce; LongMemEval is highlighted as a dedicated memory benchmark testing five capabilities (information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, abstention).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Builds on / synthesizes prior post-training and RL works (DeepSeek RLVR, Search-R1, ReSearch, s3, REPLUG, AgentFlow), memory surveys and frameworks (Hu et al. forms/functions/dynamics; Zhang et al. memory surveys; CoALA / Sumers et al.; Huang et al. foundation-agent memory), skill/procedural-memory works (Wu and Zhang; Xu and Yan; Fang et al.; Cao et al.; Voyager, JARVIS-1, EXPEL, Synapse, SkillWeaver, ASI, CREATOR, LATM, AgentStore), and dynamic memory stores (MemGPT, MemoryOS, Generative Agents, A-MEM, HippoRAG).
- **contrasts with**:
> Positions the four paradigms against one another: A1 (verifiable mechanistic mastery, expensive, poor cross-task transfer) vs. A2 (holistic orchestration, monolithic retraining, catastrophic forgetting) vs. T1 (agent-agnostic, reusable, possibly under-optimized for a host) vs. T2 (data-efficient modular tool/memory/skill adaptation under a frozen agent, bounded by backbone quality). It contrasts adaptive memory/skill libraries (mostly T2) as an alternative to agent fine-tuning (A1/A2), and contrasts narrower per-mechanism memory surveys with its broader adaptation-centric synthesis.
- **lineage**:
> Surveys group. A unifying taxonomy/survey of agentic-AI adaptation that situates retrieval, adaptive memory, and skill libraries (T2 tool adaptation) alongside post-training (A1/A2 agent adaptation) and agent-agnostic tools (T1), bridging the RAG/retrieval, agent-memory, agent-skill, and RL post-training literatures under one 'adaptation' framework.
