- **retriever learning signal**:
> N/A (survey; trains no retriever). It reviews systems where retrieval is controlled by LLM agents using prompting, query reformulation, reflection, and learned query-complexity classifiers (Adaptive RAG uses a classifier to route queries), and relevance-evaluation agents (Corrective RAG) rather than a contrastively trained retriever; it proposes no learning signal of its own.
- **query construction**:
> N/A (survey). Surveyed Agentic RAG constructs queries via agent-driven query reformulation/refinement (Corrective RAG's Query Refinement Agent), self-query, decomposition for multi-hop reasoning, and routing by a coordinating/master retrieval agent that selects knowledge sources based on query type; the survey prescribes no single query-construction method.
- **query granularity**:
> N/A (survey). Surveyed systems range from task-level routing (single-agent router at intake) to iterative step/sub-query-level construction (multi-step reasoning, corrective re-querying); Adaptive RAG selects granularity by query complexity. The survey commits to no single granularity.
- **when to retrieve**:
> N/A (survey). Surveyed Agentic RAG spans one-shot, iterative, and adaptive retrieval: Corrective RAG retrieves iteratively/correctively when document relevance is low; Adaptive RAG uses a learned query-complexity classifier to decide between no-retrieval, single-step, and multi-step retrieval (adaptive/learned router); single-agent router decides per query.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> N/A (survey defines no single trigger). Surveyed triggers include: a learned query-complexity classifier (Adaptive RAG), a relevance-evaluation agent comparing retrieved documents to a relevance threshold (Corrective RAG), and agent-initiated reflection/planning loops. The survey reviews these rather than standardizing one.
- **reranking**: N/A (survey; no reranking stage of its own). It situates reranking within the Advanced RAG paradigm (pre-/post-retrieval optimization including re-ranking) and within Corrective RAG's relevance evaluation, but contributes no reranking method itself.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> N/A (survey). It reviews refinement operations used by Agentic RAG: relevance evaluation and filtering of retrieved documents, query refinement/reformulation, corrective re-retrieval from external sources when context is insufficient (Corrective RAG), and iterative refinement of context across reflection loops; it implements no refinement pipeline itself.
- **tool document engineering**:
> N/A (survey contributes no tool-document-engineering technique). It discusses tool use as a core agentic pattern and reviews frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, CrewAI, AG2/AutoGen, Semantic Kernel, OpenAI Swarm, Vertex AI, Amazon Bedrock) that integrate retrievers, generators, and external tools/APIs, but does not propose how tool/skill descriptions are indexed.
- **index content separation**: N/A (survey; no index-vs-content separation mechanism of its own). It notes LlamaIndex's Agentic Document Workflows use a meta-agent with sub-agents managing smaller document sets coordinated by a top-level agent, but this is reviewed, not a contribution.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> N/A (survey). It reviews tool/framework integration (LangChain/LangGraph, LlamaIndex, CrewAI, AG2/AutoGen, OpenAI Swarm, Semantic Kernel, Vertex AI, Amazon Bedrock) and function-calling/tool-use patterns, but does not center a live-synchronized tool index or a specific integration protocol such as MCP/RapidAPI (the v4 revision predates deep MCP coverage in its taxonomy).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (survey). It discusses tool use and orchestrator-workers/multi-agent task delegation at a high level but does not center an inter-tool dependency-graph retrieval formalism.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> N/A as a method. The survey describes how Agentic RAG uses retrieved content: prompt/context augmentation for LLM synthesis (data integration and LLM synthesis into a coherent response), iterative refinement of context across reflection loops, and feeding validated/refined information to a response-synthesis agent. No utilization method is implemented by the survey.
- **planning integration**:
> N/A as a method. Planning is reviewed as one of the four core agentic design patterns. The survey catalogs how retrieval interfaces with planning/acting via agentic workflow patterns: prompt chaining (sequential steps), routing (directing inputs to specialized processes), parallelization (concurrent execution), orchestrator-workers (dynamic task delegation), and evaluator-optimizer (iterative refinement). It also reviews single-agent router, multi-agent, hierarchical (tiered), corrective, adaptive, and graph-based integrations rather than committing to one.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: N/A (survey). It contrasts single-step/sequential pipelines, iterative corrective loops (per-evaluation re-retrieval), per-step multi-agent delegation, and reflection-driven refinement as surveyed interleaving styles rather than fixing one granularity.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not a CBR method; no retrieved-case adaptation mechanism of its own).
- **retrieved item representation**: N/A (survey). Surveyed Agentic RAG injects retrieved content as natural-language documents/passages, structured query results (SQL), web snippets, and knowledge-graph subgraphs/relational structures (graph-based variants); the survey injects nothing itself.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: N/A (survey). Surveyed units range from raw documents/passages and structured records to relational graph structures; in graph-based Agentic RAG the unit is a more abstract relational/symbolic subgraph. The survey reviews this spectrum rather than fixing an abstraction level.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> N/A (survey contributes none). It reviews noise/robustness mechanisms in surveyed systems: Corrective RAG's relevance-evaluation agent that filters low-relevance documents and triggers corrective re-retrieval, reflection/self-correction loops, and notes 'robustness under noisy retrieval' as a needed evaluation axis and 'retrieval quality remains the primary bottleneck' as a key lesson.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> Survey-level: it treats memory as a distinguishing capability of Agentic RAG vs Traditional RAG -- context maintenance 'enabled through memory modules' and state maintained across multi-step workflows (episodic/workflow memory). It reviews short-term context plus longer-term agent memory (e.g., CrewAI's 'robust memory systems') but, as an artifact, the survey itself has no memory. Memory management/long-term adaptation is flagged as an open research challenge.
- **write back**: N/A as a method. Surveyed Agentic RAG systems DO maintain/update memory and state across multi-step workflows (memory modules; CrewAI memory systems; LlamaIndex ADW maintaining state), but the survey itself stores nothing.
- **online growth**: N/A as a method. Surveyed agent memory grows/updates online during multi-step workflows and deployment, but the survey itself has no growing store; it raises long-term memory growth (persistence vs adaptability, knowledge drift) as an open challenge.
- **write back trigger**:
> N/A (survey; no write-back trigger of its own). Surveyed memory updates occur per-step/per-workflow as agents maintain context; the survey discusses the open question of when to update (frequent updates can amplify hallucinations; persistent memory risks knowledge drift) without standardizing a trigger.
- **failure experience usage**:
> N/A (survey). It reviews reflection and corrective/evaluator-optimizer patterns that act on poor or failed retrieval/outputs (relevance-evaluation triggering corrective steps), implying use of failure signals in surveyed systems, but contributes no explicit failure-experience storage scheme.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (survey). It discusses memory persistence vs. updating as an open challenge (selective retention, reconciling external knowledge with stored agent experiences, avoiding bias reinforcement/knowledge drift) but proposes no single post-write update policy.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: N/A (survey). Surveyed retrieval control is mostly agent/LLM-driven or classifier-based (Adaptive RAG's query-complexity classifier; Corrective RAG's relevance evaluator) rather than an RL-optimized retrieval policy; the survey does not center retrieval-as-learned-policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Surveyed (not a method contribution): multi-agent and hierarchical Agentic RAG, orchestrator-workers, and multi-agent frameworks (CrewAI, AG2/AutoGen, OpenAI Swarm) involve coordination and shared context/state across multiple agents; it reviews rather than implements cross-agent sharing, and flags agent coordination/control and emergent behavior as an open challenge.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> N/A as original experiments (survey reports no results of its own). It catalogs benchmarks/datasets used to evaluate RAG systems: BEIR, MS MARCO, TREC (Deep Learning Track), MuSiQue, 2WikiMultihopQA, HotpotQA, Natural Questions (NQ), TriviaQA, SQuAD, WebQ, PopQA, ELI5, NarrativeQA, ASQA, QMSum, Qasper, COVID-QA, plus Agentic/graph-RAG-specific benchmarks AgentG (Agent-G knowledge fusion) and GNN-RAG, and evaluation toolkits/benchmarks RAGBench (100,000 examples, TRACe framework), BERGEN, and FlashRAG.
- **benchmark family**:
> Survey-level grouping (Table 4 'Downstream Tasks and Datasets'): QA -- single-hop (NQ, TriviaQA, SQuAD, WebQ, PopQA, MS MARCO), multi-hop (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue), long-form (ELI5, NarrativeQA, ASQA, QMSum), domain-specific (Qasper, COVID-QA); information retrieval (BEIR, MS MARCO, TREC); graph/knowledge-graph QA (Agent-G/AgentG, GNN-RAG); plus RAG evaluation frameworks/toolkits (RAGBench, BERGEN, FlashRAG). It does not use the agentic-trajectory benchmark families (web/embodied/tool/code/memory/decision-RL) as a primary axis.
- **baselines**:
> N/A (survey; no method comparison/baselines of its own). Its qualitative comparison contrasts paradigm classes -- Traditional/Naive RAG vs Advanced RAG vs Modular RAG vs Graph RAG vs Agentic RAG -- and architecture classes (single-agent router, multi-agent, hierarchical/tiered, corrective, adaptive, graph-based, agentic document workflows), but runs no head-to-head experiments.
- **key metrics**:
> N/A (survey; reports no quantitative metrics of its own). It discusses that evaluation should move beyond output-level metrics (answer correctness, retrieval accuracy) toward process-aware metrics (reasoning trajectories, planning depth, adaptability, robustness under noisy retrieval, cost efficiency, tool-usage patterns).
- **headline result**:
> N/A (survey; no headline number). Its central contributions are conceptual: a principled taxonomy of Agentic RAG architectures organized by agent cardinality, control structure, knowledge representation, knowledge dependency, reasoning mode/depth, retrieval adaptivity, scalability, latency, and engineering complexity (Table 3), plus the RAG-evolution narrative (Naive -> Advanced -> Modular -> Graph -> Agentic RAG) and a Traditional-RAG vs Agentic-RAG vs Agentic-Document-Workflows comparison (Table 2). It is a widely cited preprint (Semantic Scholar: 311 citations).
- **ablations**:
> N/A (survey; conducts no experiments and therefore reports no component ablations). Its closest analogue is a qualitative taxonomy-driven trade-off analysis (Table 3) mapping architecture classes to dimensions/trade-offs (e.g., single-agent = low latency but limited multi-domain reasoning; multi-agent = high scalability but coordination overhead; hierarchical/corrective = higher reliability at higher latency; graph-based = strong relational reasoning but sensitive to graph quality).
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> N/A as original measurement (survey performs no evaluation). It explicitly catalogs retrieval-focused benchmarks (BEIR, MS MARCO, TREC) separately from end-to-end RAG/QA benchmarks and toolkits (RAGBench/TRACe, BERGEN, FlashRAG), and argues intrinsic retrieval accuracy alone is insufficient, recommending decoupled process- vs outcome-level evaluation.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Survey-level: a recurring thesis (Lesson 10.5 and Challenge 12.2) is that evaluation must account for PROCESS, not just outcomes -- output-level metrics (answer correctness, retrieval accuracy) are insufficient, and process-aware metrics (reasoning efficiency/trajectories, planning depth, tool-usage patterns, adaptability to changing context, robustness under noisy retrieval) are needed. The survey itself scores nothing.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> N/A as original measurement (no cost numbers of its own). It repeatedly discusses cost/efficiency qualitatively: Agentic RAG introduces coordination complexity, latency, and computational cost (Lesson 10.1); Table 3 maps latency/scalability/engineering-complexity per architecture (single-agent = low latency; hierarchical/corrective = high latency; multi-agent = moderate latency, high scalability); and Challenge 12.4 calls for cost-aware planning, adaptive inference, selective tool invocation, and dynamic adjustment of active agents and retrieval depth.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> N/A (survey; no token budget or k of its own). It discusses adaptive retrieval depth (Adaptive RAG selecting no-retrieval/single-step/multi-step by query complexity; optimizing retrieval depth based on task complexity in Challenge 12.4) as a budget lever, but prescribes no fixed-k or token budget.
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (this is a survey, not a benchmark; it constructs no dataset). It does report sizes for benchmarks it catalogs, e.g., RAGBench is described as a large-scale explainable benchmark with 100,000 examples using the TRACe framework, and BEIR as spanning 17 datasets.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Builds on and synthesizes the RAG literature (Lewis et al. RAG; Gao et al. 'Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLMs: A Survey' for the Naive/Advanced/Modular taxonomy and the downstream-task/dataset table) and the Graph RAG line; on agentic-pattern literature (reflection, planning, tool use, multi-agent collaboration) and Anthropic-style agentic workflow patterns (prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer); on specific Agentic RAG variants it reviews (Corrective RAG/CRAG, Adaptive-RAG by query complexity, Agent-G and GeAR for graph-based, GNN-RAG); and on frameworks (LangChain/LangGraph, LlamaIndex ADW, CrewAI, AG2/AutoGen, OpenAI Swarm, Semantic Kernel, Vertex AI, Amazon Bedrock). It aggregates these rather than extending a single predecessor method.
- **contrasts with**:
> Positions Agentic RAG explicitly against Traditional/Naive RAG (static workflows, limited context, poor multi-step reasoning), Advanced RAG, Modular RAG, and Graph RAG, arguing agents add adaptability, multi-step reasoning, and dynamic retrieval management (Table 2). Notably it tempers this (Lesson 10.1): Agentic RAG is NOT always the right default -- for simple fact retrieval, modular RAG is sufficient with lower overhead. As a survey it complements other RAG/agent surveys (e.g., Gao et al.'s RAG survey, which it adapts for its dataset table).
- **lineage**:
> Surveys group. A flagship 2025 Agentic RAG survey providing a principled architecture taxonomy (agent cardinality, control structure, autonomy, knowledge representation) and a RAG-evolution narrative. It serves as an umbrella reference for the retrieval-augmented-agent sub-topics -- particularly multi-agent/agentic retrieval, corrective/adaptive retrieval, and graph-based retrieval (relevant to groups B, C, and E in this collection) -- rather than being a method within any single sub-topic.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- survey_scope_and_axes

<a id="item-browsecomp-zh"></a>
### 163. BrowseComp-ZH: Benchmarking Web Browsing Ability of Large Language Models in Chinese

2025  ·  arXiv 2504.19314  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.19314)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **authors affiliation**:
> Peilin Zhou and Bruce Leon (co-first authors); other authors: Xiang Ying, Can Zhang, Yifan Shao, Qichen Ye, Dading Chong, Zhiling Jin, Chenxuan Xie, Meng Cao, Yuxin Gu, Sixin Hong, Jing Ren, Jian Chen, Chao Liu, Yining Hua (corresponding). Affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou), Peking University, Mindverse AI, Alibaba Group, Zhejiang University, Zhejiang University of Technology, MBZUAI, NIO, HSBC, and Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.19314
- **code url**:
> https://github.com/PALIN2018/BrowseComp-ZH (official; ~153 stars, ~7 forks at time of access; MIT License). Hosts the encrypted 289-question dataset (browsecomp-zh-encrypted.xlsx with a canary-token decryption script to prevent pretraining leakage), construction guidelines, prompts, and evaluation/scoring code (run.sh, run_acc_calibration_error.py).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> web (Chinese-web browsing / agentic search) + multi-hop QA. A high-difficulty benchmark evaluating LLMs and agentic search systems on their ability to retrieve, filter, and reason over live information from the Chinese web to answer multi-constraint, multi-hop factual questions. Spans 11 topic domains (Film & TV, Technology, Art, History, Sports, Music, Geography, Policy & Law, Medicine, Video Games, Academic Research). It is a benchmark/evaluation paper, not a retrieval method.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent (or single-system) evaluation of web-browsing / information-seeking ability in Chinese, with no training/supervision provided to the evaluated systems (off-the-shelf evaluation of >20 SOTA systems). Each task is a reverse-engineered multi-hop question whose answer is a short, objective, easily verifiable fact (date, number, proper noun) with a unique answer. Three system categories are evaluated: (a) open-source LLMs and (b) closed-source APIs queried in direct-answer (often no web access) mode where they rely on internal knowledge, and (c) AI search products (agentic systems with live retrieval). For open/closed LLMs, decoding follows DeepSeek-R1 settings (temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95) where configurable; for fixed-config models (O1, Claude-3.7) defaults are used; AI search products are exercised via human GUI interaction and their outputs recorded. Answers from open/closed models are extracted via regex and graded by GPT-4o using BrowseComp-style grading prompts; AI-search-product answers are manually extracted and verified by human annotators. Metrics are accuracy and Expected Calibration Error (ECE). The Chinese web (fragmented platforms such as Baidu Baike / Zhihu / government portals, inconsistent naming, censorship, implicit linguistic referents) is emphasized as a uniquely hard retrieval environment that English benchmarks (BrowseComp) and naive translations fail to capture.
- **what is retrieved**:
> docs / live web content (for the web-enabled systems): search-engine results and web pages from the Chinese web (Baidu, Bing China, Google, and platform content such as Baidu Baike, Zhihu, government portals). For non-browsing LLMs, no external retrieval occurs; they answer from parametric knowledge. The benchmark itself does not prescribe a retrieval corpus - it measures whether a system can successfully retrieve and reconcile the supporting evidence chain for each reverse-designed question. Each ground-truth item also carries at least one authoritative source URL used during construction.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus (the live open Chinese web / search engines) for the agentic-search systems; NOT an agent-written growing/episodic memory. Each question is anchored to verifiable web evidence (>=1 authoritative source URL collected at construction time). For pure LLMs evaluated without browsing, there is effectively no retrieval grounding (parametric-only). Overall the benchmark probes grounding against the open web rather than any persistent memory store.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Neither a fixed top-k ranking nor a recall metric. The benchmark scores end-to-end answer ACCURACY (exact factual correctness of a unique short answer), so success implicitly requires recovering the COMPLETE evidence chain needed to satisfy all multi-hop constraints, but the paper reports no Recall@k / nDCG / completeness retrieval metric. Each question is constructed to have a single unique correct answer (answer-uniqueness validation), making it an outcome-completeness objective at the answer level rather than a candidate-list ranking objective.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: [Retrieve: no, Reuse: no, Revise: no, Retain: no] - not a case-based-reasoning system; it is an evaluation benchmark.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False: the paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. (It does cite CBR-RAG (Wiratunga et al., 2024) once in Related Work as an example RAG-for-QA application, but BrowseComp-ZH itself is not a CBR method.)

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> document / web page + search result (for browsing systems): the unit a system must locate is the web evidence (page/snippet) that satisfies each constraint of a multi-hop question. There is no method-defined fine-grained retrieval unit (the paper is a benchmark, not a retriever); the de facto unit is whatever the evaluated system retrieves from search engines / web pages. The ground-truth answer unit is a short objective fact (date / number / proper noun, typically 5-10 Chinese characters).
- **index source**:
> Static, externally-defined: the live Chinese web accessed via three search engines (Baidu, Bing China, Google) for browsing systems; for non-browsing models, the model's frozen parametric knowledge. The benchmark dataset itself (289 questions) is offline, human-curated, and frozen; it is not induced from agent trajectories. Each item is grounded by >=1 authoritative source URL collected by annotators.
- **retriever type**:
> Determined by each evaluated system, not by the benchmark. AI search products use their own proprietary retrieval/search pipelines (single-round retrieval: Kimi, Yuanbao/Hunyuan, DeepSeek; multi-round iterative retrieval: OpenAI DeepResearch, Perplexity Research, Doubao Deep Search). Pure LLMs use no retriever (LLM-as-parametric-knowledge). The benchmark is retriever-agnostic and treats systems as black boxes; it does not implement a BM25/dense/learned retriever of its own.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> none from the benchmark (off-the-shelf). No retriever is trained by the authors; systems are evaluated as-is. Any learning signal lives inside the proprietary AI search products and is not controlled or specified by BrowseComp-ZH. The paper proposes (as future work) post-training such as reinforcement learning to improve browsing/reasoning, but does none itself.
- **query construction**:
> From the benchmark perspective, the query is the fixed reverse-designed natural-language Chinese question given to each system; systems then construct their own internal search queries from it. During DATASET CONSTRUCTION, annotators reverse-engineer each question from a known factual answer by combining multiple constraints (temporal, spatial, categorical, descriptive; >=2 dimensions typically), then test it on Baidu/Bing/Google with three distinct keyword combinations per engine to ensure non-trivial retrievability, and obfuscate lexical signals / add implicit constraints if GPT-4o and DeepSeek (web-enabled) solve it too easily.
- **query granularity**:
> task-level (one question per task, given once at t=0). The benchmark issues a single multi-hop question per item; how that decomposes into step/state-level sub-queries is left to each evaluated system (multi-round-retrieval products effectively perform trajectory/step-level sub-querying, single-round products do task-level retrieval). The benchmark does not prescribe query granularity.
- **when to retrieve**:
> System-dependent, not prescribed by the benchmark. The analysis distinguishes single-retrieval systems (one round: Kimi, Yuanbao, DeepSeek) from iterative / multi-round-retrieval systems (DeepResearch, Perplexity, Doubao Deep Search), and shows multi-round (iterative/adaptive) retrieval yields substantially higher accuracy. Pure LLMs perform no retrieval (direct answer). The benchmark itself imposes no schedule.
- **reranking**: Not defined by the benchmark; any reranking happens inside the proprietary AI search products and is not specified or measured. No benchmark-level reranking stage exists.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Not defined by the benchmark. The paper notes (qualitatively) that systems struggle to reconcile retrieved evidence with internal knowledge - e.g., enabling web search for DeepSeek-R1 DROPS accuracy from 23.2% to 7.6% because unreliable retrieved content overrides correct internal knowledge - implying weak/absent post-retrieval distillation/filtering in some systems. The benchmark itself applies no refinement; it measures the consequences of (in)adequate refinement in the evaluated systems.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A: not a tool-retrieval method; no tool/skill descriptions are processed or indexed.
- **index content separation**: N/A: no lightweight-index-then-content design; the benchmark dataset is a flat record set and the retrievable surface is the open Chinese web.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A: the benchmark does not define a tool index or integration protocol. Browsing systems use their own search-engine / web access; the benchmark notes the live web's temporal volatility as a reproducibility caveat.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A: no inter-tool dependency modeling; not a tool-use benchmark in the function-calling sense (it is a web-browsing / search benchmark).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> For browsing systems: prompt augmentation / answer synthesis - retrieved web evidence is used to produce a final short factual answer, requiring multi-hop reasoning and information reconciliation. For non-browsing LLMs: parametric-only answering. There is no training signal; usage is purely inference-time. The benchmark grades only the final extracted answer (plus a confidence estimate for calibration).
- **planning integration**:
> Not a method; the benchmark evaluates systems whose planning is internal. The key finding is that retrieve-then-reason pipelines with ITERATIVE (multi-round) retrieval (plan-search-refine loops, e.g., DeepResearch/Perplexity/Doubao Deep Search) substantially outperform single-shot retrieval and pure parametric answering on these multi-faceted queries. BrowseComp-ZH thus measures, rather than prescribes, planning-retrieval integration quality.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not framed as CBR; no retrieved-case adaptation).
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Raw web content / search snippets and pages (for browsing systems), surfaced in whatever form the proprietary product injects them; no distilled strategy, workflow, executable skill, or latent-token representation is defined by the benchmark. The benchmark's own stored items are plain-text Chinese question + short factual answer + authoritative source URL(s) + domain label.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Low abstraction: raw web documents / search results and concrete factual evidence (the literal answer is a single concrete fact such as a date, number, or proper noun). No distilled strategy, guideline, reusable workflow, or procedural skill is involved.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> None built into the benchmark; robustness is instead MEASURED and shown to be a weakness. The paper documents that naively integrating retrieval without robust post-retrieval reasoning/alignment can HURT performance (DeepSeek-R1: 23.2% -> 7.6% when web search is enabled; calibration error also rises from 59% to 65%), attributing this to the model trusting less-reliable retrieved content over correct internal knowledge. Thus the benchmark exposes the absence of effective noise-robustness / evidence-reconciliation in current systems rather than providing a mechanism.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none. BrowseComp-ZH is a static evaluation benchmark with no episodic/skill/workflow/procedural/graph/latent memory; evaluated systems are treated as black boxes and each question is answered independently.
- **write back**: false: the benchmark stores no new experiences/cases/skills; it is a frozen, human-curated test set. (Any internal memory of an evaluated product is out of scope and not measured.)
- **online growth**:
> false: the 289-question dataset is fixed and does not grow from agent outputs at test time. The dataset is released encrypted with a canary token to prevent pretraining contamination; the authors note future work to expand size/diversity (offline human curation, not online growth).
- **write back trigger**: never: no memory write-back exists in the benchmark. Dataset items are created and validated entirely offline by human annotators through the two-stage quality-control protocol.
- **failure experience usage**:
> N/A / none: the benchmark does not store or retrieve failed experiences as memory. It performs qualitative analysis of failure modes (e.g., the DeepSeek-R1 search-degradation phenomenon, single-round vs multi-round retrieval gaps), and proposes future failure-case studies, but persists no negative cases for retrieval or learning.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A: there is no model-written memory to mutate. The benchmark set is updated only by human curation; the authors note answers may drift over time given the dynamic web (a reproducibility caveat), but no automatic append/dedup/refine/forget mechanism exists.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No: the benchmark does not learn or optimize any retrieval policy; it evaluates fixed off-the-shelf systems. No M-MDP / soft Q-learning / RL retrieval is involved (RL is mentioned only as future work to improve browsing/reasoning).
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> No shared memory across agents. Each system is evaluated independently and in isolation; there is no cross-agent or cross-framework experience/memory sharing. The benchmark does, however, enable cross-SYSTEM comparison (open-source LLMs vs closed-source APIs vs agentic search products) over the same task set.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> BrowseComp-ZH (introduced by this paper): 289 reverse-engineered multi-hop Chinese questions across 11 topic domains, each with a short unique verifiable answer and >=1 authoritative source URL. Topic distribution (approx.): Film & TV 15.6%, Art 13.8%, Geography 12.8%, Music 11.1%, History 10.0%, Medicine 9.0%, plus Technology, Sports, Video Games, Policy & Law (3.5%), and Academic Research/Papers (2.4%). Question length mostly 60-90 characters; answer length mostly 5-10 characters. Inspired by and contrasted with the English BrowseComp (Wei et al., 2025).
- **benchmark family**:
> web (Chinese-web browsing / agentic search), closely paralleling BrowseComp; also a multi-hop knowledge-intensive QA benchmark. Positioned within the web-browsing/agent evaluation family alongside BrowseComp (English), GAIA, and the QA/multi-hop lineage (TriviaQA, HotpotQA, FEVER, KILT). Distinct from prior Chinese retrieval benchmarks (Level-Navi Agent, Chinese dynamic QA, CRUD-RAG, medical QA datasets CMExam / Huatuo-26M).
- **baselines**:
> 23 evaluated systems in three categories. Open-source LLMs: DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, Qwen3-235B-A22B (Non-Thinking and Thinking), QwQ-32B, LlaMa4 (Maverick-instruct-basic). Closed-source APIs: GPT-4o, O1, O4-mini, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Claude-3.7-Sonnet (20250219), Gemini-2.0-Flash, Gemini-2.5-Pro (preview-03-25), Qwen2.5-MAX. AI search products: OpenAI DeepResearch, Grok-3 (Research), Perplexity (Research), Doubao (Deep Search and Standard), Kimi (Deep Think), Yuanbao (Hunyuan), DeepSeek (Deep Think and Standard). Reasoning-vs-non-reasoning pairs (DeepSeek-V3 vs R1; Claude-3.5 vs 3.7; Gemini-2.0-Flash vs 2.5-Pro) serve as internal comparisons.
- **key metrics**:
> (1) Accuracy (%): fraction of questions answered with the correct unique short fact, graded by GPT-4o (BrowseComp-style prompt) for open/closed models and by human verification for AI search products. (2) Calibration Error - Expected Calibration Error (ECE, %): weighted average over 5 confidence bins ([0-0.2),[0.2-0.4),[0.4-0.6),[0.6-0.8),[0.8-1.0]) of |accuracy - confidence|, requiring models to emit confidence estimates. No Recall@k/nDCG, latency, or dollar-cost metrics are reported.
- **headline result**:
> Even the best system, OpenAI's DeepResearch, reaches only 42.9% accuracy (with the lowest calibration error, 9%). Most systems perform far worse: many below 10% (e.g., LlaMa4 4.8%, Claude-3.5-Sonnet 5.5%, GPT-4o 6.2%, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct 6.6%), and only a handful exceed 20% (O1 29.1%, Gemini-2.5-Pro 27.3%, Doubao Deep Search 26.0%, DeepSeek-R1 23.2%, Perplexity Research 22.6%). The low ceiling (<43%) is the central difficulty signal.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Reasoning vs non-reasoning (Sec 4.5): reasoning-augmented models consistently improve - DeepSeek-R1 23.2% vs DeepSeek-V3 8.7% (+14.5pp); Claude-3.7-Sonnet 17.7% vs Claude-3.5-Sonnet 5.5% (+12.2pp); Gemini-2.5-Pro 27.3% vs Gemini-2.0-Flash 6.9%; Doubao Deep Search 26.0% vs Standard 18.7% (~+8pp). (2) Single-round vs multi-round retrieval (Sec 4.6): multi-round/iterative systems (DeepResearch 42.9%, Doubao Deep Search 26.0%, Perplexity 22.6%) far exceed single-round ones (Yuanbao 12.2%, Kimi 8.0%, DeepSeek 7.6%); DeepSeek's deep-think search shows little gain because it does only a single retrieval round. (3) Counterintuitive retrieval harm: enabling web search for DeepSeek-R1 drops accuracy 23.2% -> 7.6% and raises ECE 59% -> 65%, indicating unreliable retrieved content overriding correct internal knowledge. (4) Calibration (Sec 4.7): adding search generally increases calibration error; DeepResearch is notably well-calibrated (ECE 9%).
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> No. The benchmark reports only end-to-end answer accuracy (plus calibration error); it does NOT report intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k/nDCG/retrieval completeness) decoupled from task accuracy. Retrieval quality is inferred indirectly via system-category comparisons (browsing vs non-browsing, single- vs multi-round) rather than measured standalone.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome-based (final answer accuracy). The only additional axis is Expected Calibration Error (alignment of stated confidence with correctness), which is a meta-outcome rather than a process-quality metric. No step-wise retrieval/reasoning faithfulness or trajectory-quality scoring is reported; failure modes are examined qualitatively, and detailed process/failure analysis is deferred to future work.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Not quantified in dollar/latency/token terms. The paper qualitatively links higher accuracy to more expensive test-time compute - multi-round (iterative) retrieval and explicit reasoning improve accuracy ('test-time scaling through iterative retrieval'), while single-round retrieval is cheaper but markedly weaker. No explicit retrieval-call counts, API cost, latency, or token-budget tables are provided.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Not specified by the benchmark. No fixed token budget or fixed-k retrieval count is imposed; the number of retrieval rounds and amount of injected context are determined by each evaluated system (single-round vs multi-round). For open/closed LLMs, decoding follows DeepSeek-R1 settings (temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95) where configurable; AI search products are run via their native GUIs.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (benchmark paper, not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Size: 289 validated questions across 11 domains, distilled from 480 preliminary samples. Construction: REVERSE-ENGINEERED by 10 expert annotators (Master's/PhD, with LLM and topical expertise) - start from a single objective verifiable answer (date/number/proper noun), craft a multi-constraint (>=2 dimensions: temporal/spatial/categorical/descriptive) Chinese question, verify non-trivial retrievability on Baidu/Bing/Google (rejected if the answer appears on any engine's first page using 3 keyword combos per engine), and obfuscate if GPT-4o + DeepSeek (web-enabled) solve it too easily. Two-stage quality control: Stage 1 difficulty validation - peer cross-checking using search engines only (no LLMs) under a strict 10-minute limit, removing 76 easy samples (404 remain); Stage 2 answer-uniqueness validation - top systems (OpenAI DeepSearch, Perplexity, Doubao deep-reasoning, OpenAI O1, Gemini-2.5-Pro) generate candidate answers, annotators reject any question for which an alternative answer also satisfies all constraints, removing 115 ambiguous samples (289 remain). Answer verifiability: HIGH - short, objective, unique answers grounded by >=1 authoritative source URL; graded by GPT-4o (BrowseComp prompt) for LLMs and human-verified for AI search products. Dataset released ENCRYPTED with a canary token to prevent pretraining contamination. Difficulty signal: best system (DeepResearch) only 42.9%; most systems <10%.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> BrowseComp (Wei et al., 2025, arXiv:2504.12516) - directly adopts its reverse-design philosophy, multi-constraint hard-to-retrieve / easy-to-verify question format, grading prompts (GPT-4o grader), and calibration-error methodology, extending it to the Chinese web. Conceptually builds on web-browsing/tool-use agent work (WebGPT, Toolformer, ReAct), RAG (Guu et al. 2020; Lewis et al. 2020), and the multi-hop / knowledge-intensive QA lineage (TriviaQA, HotpotQA, FEVER, KILT, GAIA).
- **contrasts with**:
> (1) English BrowseComp (Wei et al., 2025) - argues direct translation fails (structural/idiomatic mismatch, missing Chinese equivalents of Wikipedia/IMDb, queries collapsing into keyword matches), motivating native Chinese construction. (2) Prior Chinese retrieval/QA benchmarks shown to be insufficient: Level-Navi Agent (Hu et al., 2024, lacks difficulty/accessibility control), Chinese dynamic QA (Xu et al., 2024, no multi-hop emphasis), CRUD-RAG (Lyu et al., 2025, generation-quality focus over retrieval-path validation), and medical-domain QA (CMExam / Huatuo-26M, domain-specific, no open-ended browsing). (3) Keyword-retrievable classic QA benchmarks (TriviaQA/HotpotQA/FEVER/KILT/GAIA) that fail to test complex search-trajectory planning.
- **lineage**:
> Surveys/Benchmarks group: a benchmark (not a method) in the web-browsing / agentic-search evaluation lineage. It is the Chinese-web counterpart of BrowseComp (English), extending reverse-engineered, evidence-grounded, hard-to-retrieve / easy-to-verify multi-hop question design into the fragmented Chinese information ecosystem, and serves as a difficulty-defining testbed (best system 42.9%) for diagnosing the retrieval-plus-reasoning and evidence-reconciliation limits of contemporary LLMs and AI search products.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- index_structure_topology
- maintained_repo_url
- reasoning_search_interleaving_granularity
- retrieval_trigger_signal

<a id="item-cbr-meets-llm-roadmap"></a>
### 164. Case-Based Reasoning Meets Large Language Models: A Research Manifesto For Open Challenges and Research Directions (Bach, Bergmann, Wiratunga et al.) [NOTE: the task title used the shorthand 'A Research Directions Roadmap'; the paper's actual subtitle is 'A Research Manifesto For Open Challenges and Research Directions'.]

2025  ·  ICCBR-adjacent 2025  ·  [paper](https://www.mirkolenz.com/assets/Bach2025CaseBasedReasoningMeets.KHCYdg9G.pdf)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **authors affiliation**:
> 16 authors listed in alphabetical order with equal contribution; corresponding author Lukas Malburg (malburgl@uni-trier.de). Kerstin Bach (Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Trondheim, Norway); Ralph Bergmann, Florian Brand, Lukas Malburg (University of Trier & German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence (DFKI), Germany); Marta Caro-Martinez (cited as a CBR/XAI researcher, Spain); Viktor Eisenstadt (DFKI, Smart Data & Knowledge Services, Kaiserslautern, Germany); Michael W. Floyd (Knexus Research LLC, National Harbor, MD, USA); Lasal Jayawardena, Nirmalie Wiratunga (School of Computing, Engineering and Technology, Robert Gordon University, Aberdeen, UK); David Leake, Kaitlynne Wilkerson, Brian Schack (Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA); Mirko Lenz (University of Trier & DFKI, Germany); David H. Menager (AI and Autonomy Group, Parallax Advanced Research, Beavercreek, OH, USA); Mirjam Minor (Department of Computer Science, Goethe University, Frankfurt am Main, Germany); Ian Watson (School of Computer Science, University of Auckland, New Zealand).
- **paper url**: https://hal.science/hal-05006761v1 (canonical HAL deposit; PDF at https://hal.science/hal-05006761v1/file/main.pdf). Author-hosted copy: https://www.mirkolenz.com/assets/Bach2025CaseBasedReasoningMeets.KHCYdg9G.pdf. Semantic Scholar CorpusId:282717922.
- **code url**: N/A (a position/manifesto paper; no method implementation or code release). It references concrete companion systems that have code, notably CBR-RAG (https://github.com/rgu-iit-bt/cbr-for-legal-rag).
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (no maintained paper list / leaderboard accompanies this manifesto). Related community venue: the recurring CBR-LLM workshop proceedings on CEUR-WS (e.g. ICCBR 2025 CBR-LLM workshop, CEUR-WS Vol-3993).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Cross-cutting position / roadmap spanning many task domains rather than one. The manifesto surveys the synergy of Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) and LLMs across QA (legal/medical/numerical reasoning QA), planning (case-based planning, agentic workflows), tool/agent use (supervisory multi-agent CBR-LLM roles), explainability/XAI, knowledge engineering, and decision-making. It is framed around CBR's four knowledge containers (vocabulary, similarity, case base, adaptation) mapped onto LLM mechanisms (episodic memory, case-based RAG, case-based planning).
- **problem setting**:
> A position / research-manifesto / roadmap paper (not a method and not an empirical study). It synthesizes a comprehensive literature review plus author expertise to (1) identify 13 open challenges grouped into four thematic areas (Guided Generation; Accuracy & Dehallucination; Explainability & Trust; Operational Efficiency) afflicting LLMs and CBR systems, and (2) propose 17 research directions/opportunities for combining CBR and LLMs bidirectionally (CBR-for-LLM and LLM-for-CBR). The setting discussed ranges across offline knowledge-engineering and interactive/agentic deployments, single- and multi-agent (supervisory agent roles), with no fixed supervision regime; the paper proposes directions rather than committing to one experimental setting.
- **what is retrieved**:
> Cases (problem-solution episodes) are the central retrieved unit in the CBR view, used to enrich LLM prompts via case-based RAG. The manifesto also discusses retrieving/leveraging the four CBR knowledge containers: vocabulary, similarity knowledge, the case base, and adaptation knowledge; plus episodic memories (past prompts and their completions), guidelines/best practices stored as cases, and structured representations (workflows, graphs, plans). It contrasts these with generic docs retrieved by standard RAG.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> HYBRID as discussed. The classic CBR case base is treated as a curated/maintained store (which LLMs can also help acquire and maintain), while the manifesto promotes case-based episodic MEMORY that the system writes to over time (prompts and their completions as cases) and case-based RAG over a structured case base. So the proposed grounding spans a static/curated case corpus and a growing episodic memory, rather than a single fixed external corpus.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> ['Retrieve', 'Reuse', 'Revise', 'Retain'] -- the full canonical 4R cycle is discussed (the paper repeatedly references the '4R cycle' of CBR1). As a manifesto it does not implement the cycle but proposes LLM roles across all four phases: Retrieve (case-based RAG, LLMs in the retrieval step), Reuse/Revise (adaptation rules/cases, LLM-prompted adaptation, supervisory adaptation advisors), and Retain (continuously updating the case base, LLM-assisted maintenance/curation).
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> true. The paper is authored by core CBR researchers and is explicitly and centrally grounded in case-based reasoning: it cites Aamodt & Plaza 1994 (ref 1), Richter's knowledge containers (refs 26-27), Schank's Dynamic Memory Theory / MOPs (ref 29), Kolodner-lineage CBR, Hammond's case-based planning (ref 10), and Watson 1999 'CBR is a methodology not a technology' (ref 33). CBR's 4R cycle and four knowledge containers are the organizing frame of the entire manifesto.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> case (problem-solution episode) is the primary unit. The manifesto explicitly notes case representation formalisms range from plain text and attribute-value pairs to structured forms such as workflows, graphs, and plans. Other discussed units: episodic-memory items (prompt + completion), guideline/best-practice cases, vocabulary/domain-knowledge elements, similarity knowledge, and adaptation rules/cases. Cases are compared at multiple levels (local individual facts vs global overall context).
- **index source**:
> Mixed/hybrid as proposed: a curated case base (whose construction the manifesto proposes to accelerate via LLM-based knowledge acquisition to address the cold-start problem) plus a growing/online episodic memory of past prompts-and-completions that the system accrues. No single fixed offline-vs-online commitment is made; it is a roadmap advocating both maintained and self-growing case stores.
- **index structure topology**:
> Discussed as structured/hierarchical and graph-capable rather than flat-only. The manifesto highlights structured case representations (workflows, graphs, plans), Schank's hierarchically organized Memory Organization Packages (MOPs) that index cases across multiple contexts and are assembled dynamically, taxonomy/knowledge-graph-derived similarity, and embedding-based (vector) similarity as one special form among many. So it spans flat vector indices, taxonomy/KG-backed indices, and hierarchical MOP-style memory organization.
- **retriever type**:
> Discussed as a spectrum centered on CBR similarity functions, not a single retriever. Embedding-based (dense) similarity is called out as one special form, complemented by classical CBR similarity measures (Euclidean distance, symbolic value tables, graph/text edit distances) and taxonomy/knowledge-graph-derived similarity. CBR-RAG (the cited concrete instance) uses general and domain-specific embeddings (BERT/LegalBERT/AnglEBERT) with inter/intra/hybrid similarity. LLMs are also proposed as agents in the retrieval step (LLM-as-retriever / fact weighting).
- **retriever learning signal**:
> No retriever is trained in this paper (it is a manifesto). It surveys/proposes signals: classical CBR similarity is largely knowledge-engineered (manually defined measures), off-the-shelf embeddings are used in CBR-RAG, and the manifesto proposes LLM-assisted refinement of similarity measures -- learning latent features from past cases, dynamically revising attribute weights based on context, and integrating structured + unstructured descriptions. So proposed signals span none/off-the-shelf, knowledge-engineered, and LLM-feedback-driven similarity adaptation; no contrastive/RL retriever training is implemented.
- **query construction**:
> Discussed conceptually: in case-based RAG the structured case (its containers) is used to enrich/augment the LLM prompt, providing a richer query than the raw input (CBR-RAG augments the original query with contextually relevant cases). The manifesto also proposes filling prompt templates with case data via episodic memory, and using LLMs to extract/weight the relevant facts to retrieve (fact-weighting). No single query-construction algorithm is specified.
- **query granularity**:
> Discussed at multiple levels rather than fixed. Prompt-level (task) query augmentation via case-based RAG, multi-level comparison (local individual facts and global overall context), and step-level reasoning support via case-based planning / process-oriented CBR workflows that formalize sequential LLM calls. As a roadmap it does not commit to one granularity.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Discussed as both one-shot (case-based RAG augmenting the prompt before generation) and iterative/adaptive (iterative RAG-style filtering, augmentation and refinement, where CBR is proposed to decide the optimal number of refinement iterations via abort conditions or similarity thresholds, and adaptive retrieval pipelines that adjust similarity thresholds). No single trigger regime is implemented.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Discussed conceptually under 'Reasoning for Filtering, Augmentation, and Refinement' (O2.3): CBR-LLM methods to filter, augment, and refine iterative-RAG context, using case-based planning to decompose generation tasks and compose results, LLMs as candidate plan generators that a case-based planner reviews/filters/augments, and CBR-controlled iteration counts. Structured case knowledge is proposed to validate and ground outputs (de-hallucination). No single refinement operator is fixed.
- **tool document engineering**:
> N/A (the manifesto is about case/knowledge retrieval, not tool/skill-description engineering for a tool index). It does discuss serialization of structured case knowledge (e.g. JSON/XML) into prompts and the resulting context-size/cost tradeoffs (Challenge C2), but not tool-docstring augmentation.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index / API protocol; not a tool-retrieval system). It mentions agentic workflows and supervisory multi-agent roles conceptually but specifies no RapidAPI/REST/MCP/function-calling integration.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no inter-tool dependency modeling; the paper concerns CBR cases and knowledge containers, not tool dependency graphs).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Primarily prompt augmentation / case adaptation. Retrieved structured cases enrich the LLM prompt with context-specific details (case-based RAG), grounding generation in verifiable evidence to reduce hallucination; the case container structure is reused to help the LLM produce more robust, well-structured answers. The manifesto also proposes case reuse with LLM-assisted adaptation (adaptation rules/cases), and a training-signal use: fine-tuning LLMs on structured cases (e.g. for JSON-schema-conformant structured outputs) and case-based distillation of LLMs.
- **planning integration**:
> Discussed prominently as retrieve/plan integration directions: case-based planning to guide the LLM reasoning chain (decompose a generation task, compose results following a case-based plan), LLMs as candidate plan generators inside a case-based planner that reviews/filters/augments, and process-oriented CBR (POCBR) representing sequential LLM calls as a workflow that formalizes system-LLM interactions (linked to 'agentic workflows'). It cites Hammond's case-based planning (ref 10), Bergmann et al. CBR-applied-to-planning (ref 3), Munoz-Avila & Cox case-based plan adaptation (ref 23), and the LLM-Modulo framing. No concrete MCTS/tree-search integration is implemented.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Discussed at the per-step / per-iteration and workflow level (decompose-then-compose under a case-based plan; CBR-controlled iteration counts in RAG refinement; POCBR workflows formalizing sequential LLM calls) as well as per-answer (one-shot case-based RAG augmentation). Not fixed to one granularity; a roadmap rather than a concrete interleaving schedule.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> Discussed (CBR Reuse/Revise): the manifesto proposes LLM-prompted adaptation (LLMs propose adaptation rules or adaptation cases), supervisory LLM agents in roles such as output generators, reviewers, and adaptation advisors, and notes that plain prompt-instruction adaptation gave low accuracy in a classification scenario (citing Wilkerson & Leake, ref 34) -- motivating structured/knowledge-guided adaptation. It also proposes LLMs to refine adaptation strategies during maintenance. Spans LLM-prompted adaptation, critic/reviewer-guided revision, and adaptation-rule learning; nothing is implemented here.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Structured cases injected as context: structured case knowledge (attribute-value pairs, workflows, graphs, plans) and the case-container structure are surfaced to the LLM to produce robust, well-structured (e.g. schema-conformant) outputs; cases can also be turned into human-readable unstructured text by the LLM (O6.3). So both structured-note and raw/free-text representations are discussed, with emphasis on structured case knowledge for grounding and de-hallucination.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Discussed across abstraction levels: concrete past cases (problem-solution episodes / examples), distilled guidelines/best-practices stored as cases, structured procedural knowledge (workflows, plans via case-based planning and POCBR), adaptation rules/cases, and episodic memories of prior prompts+completions. The manifesto spans raw-case, distilled-guideline, and reusable-workflow/plan abstractions.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Discussed conceptually: structured case knowledge and the four knowledge containers are proposed to validate outputs and reduce hallucination (de-hallucination through structured knowledge, O3.2), structured outputs enable correctness checking, evidence-based fine-grained retrieval grounds answers in real cases/factual data (O3.3), and supervisory reviewer/adaptation-advisor agents check generations. No trained noise-robustness mechanism is implemented (roadmap).

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> Episodic (the paper's primary lens). It argues episodic memory is 'the missing piece' for long-term LLM agents (citing Pink et al. 2025, ref 24) and that episodic memory is the primary focus of CBR; it grounds this in Schank's Dynamic Memory Theory and hierarchical MOPs. Also discusses procedural/long-term memory and case-based long-term memory (LTM). So: episodic + (CBR) case-library / skill-and-workflow memory.
- **write back**:
> true (proposed). The manifesto advocates storing experiences as cases and continuously updating the case base; e.g. episodic memory of prompts and their completions, retaining best practices/lessons as cases, and LLM-assisted continuous case-base updating during the Retain phase. As a roadmap it proposes write-back rather than benchmarking a specific implementation.
- **online growth**:
> true (proposed). It promotes case-based episodic memory that accrues over time (prompts+completions), continuous case-base updating, and dynamic MOP-style memory whose structures change to reflect new understanding -- i.e. a store that grows/evolves during use rather than a frozen offline index.
- **memory evolution update**:
> Discussed conceptually via Schank's Dynamic Memory Theory: memory structures (MOPs) and the memories they reconstruct can change to reflect new understanding, and learning can change a MOP used later to assemble a memory -- i.e. link-and-evolve / refine dynamics. Also proposes continuous case-base updating, refining similarity assessments, and enhancing adaptation strategies (maintenance). Concrete mutation policy (append vs dedup-merge vs prune) is not specified.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Touched conceptually: the manifesto envisions multi-agent / supervisory CBR-LLM systems with agents in distinct roles (output generators, reviewers, adaptation advisors), references MetaGPT (ref 12) and agentic-workflow/agent surveys (refs 31-32), and the iSee platform for defining, sharing, and reusing explanation experiences. So shared/reusable experience across roles/agents is discussed, but no concrete cross-framework memory-sharing protocol is implemented.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> N/A -- no benchmarks are run (this is a position/manifesto paper with no experiments). It references empirical results from companion works it cites (e.g. CBR-RAG on legal QA; Wilkerson & Leake on implementing CBR with LLMs; Brand et al. LLMs as Knowledge Engineers; DS-Agent), but reports no datasets/environments of its own.
- **benchmark family**: N/A (no benchmark family; no empirical evaluation). The application domains discussed map loosely to QA (legal/medical/numerical reasoning), planning, XAI/explanation, and knowledge engineering, but the paper itself evaluates nothing.
- **baselines**:
> N/A (no method, no head-to-head comparison). Conceptually it positions hybrid CBR+LLM systems against (a) standalone LLMs (which lack long-term memory, are opaque, and hallucinate) and (b) standalone classical CBR systems (which suffer the knowledge-acquisition bottleneck, cold-start, and limited algorithm transferability), and against plain RAG (argued less precise than case-based RAG).
- **key metrics**: N/A (no metrics reported -- no experiments). The paper's 'deliverables' are qualitative: 13 open challenges, 17 research directions/opportunities, and 4 thematic research areas (summarized in Table 1 mapping each challenge to its proposed research directions).
- **headline result**:
> N/A (no experimental headline). The headline contribution is the first systematic analysis of challenges and opportunities for bidirectional CBR-LLM integration: 13 open challenges grouped into 4 thematic areas (Guided Generation; Accuracy & Dehallucination; Explainability & Trust; Operational Efficiency) and 17 research directions, organized around mapping CBR's four knowledge containers (vocabulary, similarity, case base, adaptation) and the 4R cycle onto LLM mechanisms (episodic memory, case-based RAG, case-based planning, structured-output de-hallucination).
- **ablations**: N/A (no experiments, hence no ablations). The analytical equivalent is Table 1, which decomposes which research directions address which challenges, and the two-way framing (CBR-for-LLM vs LLM-for-CBR) clarifying which integration lever targets which weakness.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> N/A (no evaluation conducted). It does argue conceptually for transparent retrieval whose case-similarity decisions are inspectable (explaining which features/attributes drove a retrieval), i.e. a qualitative interest in the retrieval step's quality separate from final output, but reports no intrinsic-vs-end-to-end metric split.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> N/A (no metrics). Conceptually the manifesto stresses process transparency: explainable, similarity-based retrieval decisions and reasoning traces (turning structured cases/reasoning traces into human-readable explanations), reflecting interest in process quality beyond final-answer correctness -- but nothing is measured.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Discussed qualitatively as a core theme (Operational Efficiency). Challenges: high computational complexity/size of LLMs (C9), context-window limits and large serialized structured inputs increasing input size, latency, and inference cost (C2). Proposed efficiency directions: case-based distillation of LLMs (O5.1), fine-tuning smaller models on structured cases to speed inference (O5.2), and efficient case selection extracting only critical facts within limited context windows with adaptive similarity thresholds (O5.4). No quantitative cost/latency numbers are reported by the paper.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Discussed conceptually rather than numerically: context-window limitation is a named challenge (C2 -- structured serializations bloat tokens, cost, and latency), and the proposed lever is precision-/budget-driven efficient case selection that extracts critical facts and dynamically adjusts similarity thresholds to fit within limited LLM context windows (O5.4). No fixed k or token budget is prescribed.
- **survey scope and axes**:
> Explicit organizing axes: (1) two top-level research directions -- CBR-for-LLM (improving LLM utility) and LLM-for-CBR (LLMs supporting/advancing CBR); (2) four thematic research areas -- Guided Generation, Accuracy & Dehallucination, Explainability & Trust, Operational Efficiency; (3) CBR's four knowledge containers (vocabulary, similarity, case base, adaptation) and the 4R cycle (Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain) as the mapping frame onto LLM mechanisms (episodic memory, case-based RAG, case-based planning); (4) a foundations section (case-based memory, knowledge structures, case-based retrieval, LLM-based knowledge acquisition/maintainability/explainability). Coverage: 13 challenges, 17 research directions, ~32 references; recent-window literature review (predominantly 2023-2025 works alongside foundational CBR references from the 1980s-2010s).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (not a benchmark paper; constructs no dataset).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Foundational CBR: Aamodt & Plaza 1994 (4R cycle, ref 1); Richter's knowledge containers (refs 26-27); Schank's Dynamic Memory Theory / MOPs (ref 29); Hammond's Case-Based Planning (ref 10); Hanney & Keane adaptation-knowledge bottleneck (ref 11); Munoz-Avila & Cox case-based plan adaptation (ref 23); Watson 1999 (CBR methodology, ref 33); Bergmann et al. CBR for planning (ref 3); process-oriented CBR (refs 20/22). LLM/RAG side: Lewis et al. RAG (ref 16/18); the 'episodic memory is the missing piece for long-term LLM agents' position (Pink et al. 2025, ref 24); DSPy (Khattab et al., ref 14); the Prompt Report (ref 30); LLM-Modulo / 'LLMs Can't Plan but can help planning' (Kambhampati et al.); MetaGPT (ref 12); structured-output works (refs 17-19). Companion CBR-LLM systems: CBR-RAG (Wiratunga et al. 2024, ref 35), Wilkerson & Leake (implementing CBR with LLMs, ref 34), Brand et al. (LLMs as Knowledge Engineers, ref 4), DS-Agent (Guo et al. 2024, ref 9), CBR-Ren (Feng et al., ref 7), iSee platform (Caro-Martinez et al., ref 5).
- **contrasts with**:
> Contrasts hybrid CBR+LLM systems against the limitations of each pure paradigm: standalone LLMs (limited/no long-term memory, opaqueness/black-box, hallucination, non-deterministic outputs, context-window limits, high compute) and standalone classical CBR (knowledge-acquisition bottleneck, cold-start problem, limited cross-domain transferability of 4R algorithms). Also contrasts case-based RAG against plain RAG, arguing standard RAG retrieves overly broad/generic context whereas structured multi-level case comparison yields higher precision/specificity. Echoes the LLM-Modulo stance that LLMs can't plan alone but can help within structured frameworks.
- **lineage**:
> Surveys / position papers lineage (Group: Surveys). It is a community manifesto sitting at the CBR <-> LLM intersection, downstream of foundational CBR (Aamodt & Plaza, Richter, Schank, Hammond) and of the RAG/agentic-LLM lineage, and serving as an umbrella that frames and motivates the concrete CBR-LLM works in this collection (e.g. CBR-RAG, case-based planning, episodic-memory agents, structured-output de-hallucination). Companion follow-ups elaborate its themes (e.g. Leake et al.'s 'Levels of AI Memory' extends its memory opportunities). Distinct from generic RAG surveys (e.g. Gao et al.) by being explicitly CBR-grounded and bidirectional (CBR-for-LLM and LLM-for-CBR).

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):
