### 165. Deep Research: A Systematic Survey (Shi et al.)

2025  ·  arXiv 2512.02038  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.02038)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **authors affiliation**:
> Zhengliang Shi (Shandong University; corresponding, zhengliang.shii@gmail.com) and Yiqun Chen, Haitao Li, Weiwei Sun, Shiyu Ni, Yougang Lyu, Run-Ze Fan, Bowen Jin, Yixuan Weng, Minjun Zhu, Qiujie Xie, Xinyu Guo, Qu Yang, Jiayi Wu, Jujia Zhao, Xiaqiang Tang, Xinbei Ma, Cunxiang Wang, Jiaxin Mao, Qingyao Ai, Jen-Tse Huang, Wenxuan Wang, Yue Zhang, Yiming Yang, Zhaopeng Tu, Zhaochun Ren (corresponding, z.ren@liacs.leidenuniv.nl). 26 authors. Affiliations span Shandong University, Renmin University of China, Tsinghua University, Carnegie Mellon University, UCAS, University of Amsterdam, University of Massachusetts Amherst, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Westlake University, University of Arizona, and Tencent.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.02038
- **code url**: https://github.com/mangopy/Deep-Research-Survey (companion paper-list repository; no method code since this is a survey).
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/mangopy/Deep-Research-Survey (continuously-updated GitHub paper list, ~319 stars / 54 commits, last README update Jan 2026; organizes Deep Research papers by the four key components, training paradigms, and benchmarks/resources).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Survey of Deep Research (DR) systems: LLM agents that combine reasoning with external tools (search engines, web browsing, code execution) to solve complex, open-ended research tasks. Surveyed task families span agentic information seeking (open-domain QA, multi-hop QA, live web navigation), integrated/comprehensive report generation (survey/long-form report/poster/slides generation), AI-for-research (idea generation, experimental execution, academic writing, peer review), and software engineering. Spans QA, web, tool-use, decision-making, and long-form generation domains.
- **problem setting**:
> A comprehensive literature review (not a method). It formalizes DR as a closed-loop, interactive, single- or multi-agent workflow that takes a complex research question and produces a structured, citation-grounded long-form answer (e.g., a report). The setting is predominantly online/interactive (live web, tools, APIs, code executors), long-horizon, and multi-turn, with minimal human supervision; it contrasts this with offline static-corpus RAG. Supervision spans training-free workflow prompting, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) cold-start, and end-to-end agentic reinforcement learning (RL). The survey introduces a three-stage capability roadmap (Phase I Agentic Search; Phase II Integrated Research; Phase III Full-stack AI Scientist) and four foundational components (query planning, information acquisition, memory management, answer generation).
- **what is retrieved**:
> Predominantly documents/web pages/evidence acquired via search engines, web browsing, tools, APIs, and local files, plus multimodal content (tables, charts, figures with grounded pointers for citation). The survey also surveys memory retrieval: consolidated experiences/episodic memories, structured graphs/knowledge bases, skills (skill libraries), workflows/procedural memory, and user profiles/preferences. So the retrieved units span docs, tools/API calls, structured graph entities, and stored experiences/memories rather than only static text.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> HYBRID. The dominant DR grounding surveyed is interaction with a DYNAMIC external world (live commercial web search like Google/Bing, web APIs, tools, code executors) rather than a frozen pre-indexed corpus, which the survey explicitly cites as the key limitation of standard RAG ('static retrieval loop, relying solely on pre-indexed corpora'). It also surveys a GROWING/episodic agent memory (memory management component: consolidation, indexing, updating, forgetting) that the agent writes during deployment, plus classic static-corpus lexical/dense retrieval. Overall grounding is hybrid: real-time external tools/web + growing agent memory + static corpora.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Mixed across the surveyed spectrum. Classic information-filtering still uses fixed top-k document selection by relevance. But the survey emphasizes a shift toward completeness-driven objectives for DR: WideSearch is highlighted as requiring agents to 'thoroughly and accurately acquire all large-scale atomic information that meets a set of criteria' (set completeness), and report-generation evaluation uses key-point coverage / recall. Adaptive retrieval reframes the objective as variable, precision/cost-driven (retrieve only when knowledge is insufficient) rather than a fixed top-k. So both fixed top-k ranking and completeness/coverage objectives are surveyed, with DR pushing toward completeness and coverage.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based-reasoning work; the survey does not organize DR around a Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain case cycle. Its memory-management loop - consolidation/indexing/updating/forgetting - is functionally adjacent but framed in cognitive-memory rather than CBR terms.)
- **explicit cbr grounding**: false. The survey does not frame Deep Research as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it draws on cognitive-neuroscience memory analogies (consolidation, engrams, Ebbinghaus forgetting curve) rather than the CBR ontology.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Surveyed as a spectrum. Information-acquisition units: document/passage/chunk (lexical BM25/TF-IDF, dense, commercial web search), multimodal units (text-with-layout, figures/chart thumbnails via CLIP/SigLIP/BLIP, parsed table cells/chart data marks with grounded pointers), and tool/API calls. Memory units: consolidated summaries/event logs, structured graph entities/triples/sub-graphs (knowledge graphs), tree nodes (MemTree), skills (skill library), procedural workflows, and timestamped episodic memories. Query-planning units: sub-queries/sub-tasks. So units range from token/snippet and document to KG-subgraph, tool-API, skill, workflow, and case/experience.
- **index source**:
> Hybrid. Static corpora (Wikipedia, local resources for BM25/dense retrieval) coexist with live external sources (commercial web search APIs, web pages, tools) accessed at test time, and with a growing agent memory built online via consolidation/indexing/updating/forgetting. The survey explicitly distinguishes DR's dynamic, online-induced, real-world information access from RAG's offline-frozen pre-indexed corpus. Memory indexing uses LSH/HNSW/FAISS, signal-enhanced (temporal+semantic metadata), graph-based (HippoRAG, A-Mem), and timeline-based (Theanine, Zep bi-temporal) structures built over consolidated experiences.
- **index structure topology**:
> Surveyed across all topologies. Retrieval indices: flat vector / inverted-index (BM25, dense ANN via FAISS/HNSW), reciprocal-rank-fusion over multimodal indices. Memory indices: (i) signal-enhanced (metadata: temporal, topic, keyword, emotional context pivots; LongMemEval, MMS); (ii) graph-based (knowledge graphs as index, HippoRAG, A-Mem dynamic links, AriGraph, ChatDB, TiM tuples); (iii) timeline-based (chronological/causal sequences; Theanine, Zep bi-temporal valid/invalid timestamps); plus hierarchical tree structures (MemTree, ChatGPT-RSum recursive summary, hierarchical compression). So flat-vector, metadata-keyed, knowledge-GRAPH, timeline, and hierarchical/tree topologies are all surveyed.
- **retriever type**:
> Surveyed broadly: (i) lexical retrieval (TF-IDF, BM25, neural sparse models with learned query/doc expansion); (ii) semantic/dense retrieval (encode query+doc into vectors); (iii) commercial web search (Google/Bing APIs providing real-time, ranked, freshness-/authority-aware results); plus multimodal retrievers (CLIP/SigLIP/BLIP text-image similarity, LayoutLM/Donut layout-aware, ChartReader/Chartformer structure-aware). For memory, LLM-driven managers (Mem0, Memory-R1) and graph retrievers. Document selection/reranking uses cross-encoders, LLM-as-retriever (special True/relevance tokens), and reasoning rerankers (Rank-R1, ReasonRank). Hybrid fusion (RRF) is common.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Surveyed across the full range. Off-the-shelf (frozen BM25/dense). Contrastive similarity training (BGE point-wise embeddings). LM-feedback / distillation (RECOMP, Chain-of-Note summarizers trained on GPT-4 labels). Downstream-task-effectiveness / preference (BIDER optimized with PPO on answer-correctness gains; RankCoT via DPO; ReasonRank/Rank-R1 via GRPO on ranking reward). RL / learned policy is a central theme: Search-R1 frames retrieval as part of an MDP and uses RL to learn when+what to retrieve; R1-Searcher uses outcome rewards; Memory-R1 trains a Memory Manager via RL. So the survey traces a shift from similarity-only to LM-feedback, task-effectiveness/preference, and RL-trained retrieval/selection.
- **query construction**:
> Surveyed as query planning (Section 3.1): transforming a complex question into a structured sequence of executable sub-queries via (i) parallel planning (independent sub-queries resolved concurrently), (ii) sequential planning (linear, each step conditioned on intermediate outcomes; DRAGIN reformulates attention-selected tokens into focused queries; ReSP targets identified information gaps; LLatrieval generates a new question/pseudo-passage when verification fails), and (iii) tree-based planning (RAG-Star MCTS+UCT, DeepRAG binary-tree, DeepSieve/DTA DAG, MAO-ARAG orchestrated reformulation modules). So raw input, decomposed sub-queries, thought/attention-conditioned queries, and synthetic pseudo-passages are all surveyed.
- **query granularity**:
> Surveyed at multiple levels: task-level decomposition into sub-queries at planning time (parallel planning), trajectory/sequential-level (sequential planning where each sub-query depends on accumulated evidence; iterative QA), and step/state-level (per-step query reformulation conditioned on global+local memory state, e.g., ReSP, DRAGIN attention-driven; adaptive per-step retrieval). Tree-based planning constructs queries across branching decision nodes. So task-level, trajectory-level, and step/state-level query construction are all covered.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Surveyed as 'retrieval timing' / adaptive retrieval (Section 3.2.2), tracing an evolution: fixed/per-step retrieval (IR-CoT retrieves after every reasoning step) -> dynamically triggered retrieval as a model-issued action (ReAct, Self-RAG, Search-o1) -> RL-trained retrieval policies (Search-R1 jointly optimizes when and what to retrieve). Modes covered: one-shot, iterative, active (uncertainty/knowledge-boundary triggered), and adaptive/learned-router. The survey lists retrieval timing as an open challenge (over- vs under-retrieval).
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Surveyed as four adaptive-retrieval paradigms keyed to knowledge-boundary perception: (i) Probabilistic Strategy (trigger on low token-generation confidence; FLARE-style, DRAGIN); (ii) Consistency-based Strategy (Rowen triggers retrieval when cross-model/cross-lingual agreement is low); (iii) Internal-States Probing (CtrlA, UAR, SEAKR use the model's internal states as a faithful confidence signal); (iv) Verbalized Strategy (special action/reflection tokens: ReAct generates action text, Self-RAG emits a 'retrieve' token). Reasoning-driven timing (Search-o1 Reason-in-Documents) and RL-trained policies (Search-R1) are the recent frontier. Underpinned by confidence estimation: probabilistic, consistency-based, internal-state, and verbalized confidence.
- **reranking**:
> Yes - a first-class topic under Information Filtering / Document Selection (Section 3.2.3). Surveyed reranking families: point-wise (cross-encoder binary relevance, BGE embedding similarity, LLM relevance tokens), pair-wise (PRP pairwise-ranking-prompting with heapsort and order-swap debiasing), and list-wise (RankGPT global ranking, TourRank tournament, ListT5 FiD-based parallel m-ary tournament, InstructRAG rationale-based, Rank-R1 and ReasonRank GRPO-trained reasoning rerankers). Multimodal results are fused via reciprocal-rank fusion (RRF) or cross-modal reranking.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Surveyed extensively as Information Filtering with three approaches: (i) Document Selection (point/pair/list-wise reranking and top-k selection to drop noise); (ii) Context Compression - lexical-based (RECOMP summarization, Chain-of-Note reading notes, BIDER key supporting evidence, information-bottleneck noise filtering, RankCoT implicit-rerank-then-summarize) and embedding-based (ICAE, COCOM, xRAG single-token compression, ACC-RAG/QGC query-adaptive compression rates); (iii) Rule-based Cleaning (HtmlRAG removes HTML boilerplate). Motivated by LLM sensitivity to retrieval noise. So rerank, decompose/distill, distractor filtering, and compression are all covered.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Partially surveyed under retrieval tools and multimodal retrieval rather than as explicit tool-description engineering. The survey discusses indexing/search techniques for retrieval tools (lexical inverted indices with learned query/doc term expansion, dense embeddings, commercial web-search ranking) and multimodal indexing of titles/captions/layout/chart schemas, but does not center a dedicated taxonomy of tool/skill docstring augmentation (synthetic-query expansion, weighted-field embeddings, instruction-tuned tool embeddings) the way tool-retrieval-specific papers do.
- **index content separation**:
> Partially surveyed. Memory indexing is explicitly distinguished from memory consolidation: indexing builds a lightweight navigational map (vector embeddings, summaries, entity tags, LSH/HNSW/FAISS access structures) over already-consolidated heavier memory content - a lightweight-index-then-content pattern. Hierarchical/tree structures (MemTree, recursive summaries) and signal-enhanced metadata indices support searching a compact index before loading full content. Not framed explicitly as SOP-index-then-content progressive disclosure.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Partially surveyed. The survey emphasizes DR's shift from static, closed-corpus retrieval to live commercial web search (Google/Bing APIs) and real-time tool/web-API interaction with up-to-date information, and notes web-fetch / PDF-parsing / calculator tool registries (Anthropic-style central tool registry). Memory stores are live-synchronized via updating/forgetting (Mem0 ADD/UPDATE/DELETE, Zep bi-temporal). However, it does not provide a dedicated MCP / RapidAPI / function-calling protocol taxonomy with CRUD auto-sync the way tool-retrieval-specific papers do.
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> Largely N/A as a focused axis. The survey covers tool use and multi-tool scenarios (Tool-Star, ARPO, AEPO, multi-agent tool callers) and graph-based memory of inter-entity relationships, but it does not center an explicit inter-tool dependency-modeling taxonomy (output-of-A-feeds-B, shared auth, prerequisite/dependency graphs, dependency-aware reranking) for tool retrieval.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Surveyed across uses: prompt augmentation (feeding ranked/compressed evidence into the generator), latent-token injection (embedding-based compression projects documents into soft tokens, e.g., xRAG single token, ICAE/COCOM embedding sequences), training signal (SFT cold-start on distilled trajectories; end-to-end RL where retrieved tokens are masked in the policy-gradient loss, Search-R1), skill reuse (Voyager/GITM skill libraries), and case/experience reuse (episodic memory recall). In answer generation, retrieved evidence is integrated for grounded, citation-attributed synthesis (Self-RAG reflection-token-gated integration; Stateful Query Planning couples plan with evolving memory state, e.g., Plan-on-Graph, MCTS-OPS).
- **planning integration**:
> Surveyed as a dedicated component (Query Planning) tightly interleaved with retrieval/acting in a closed-loop research workflow. Integration patterns: parallel planning (decompose then retrieve in parallel), sequential/iterative plan-then-retrieve-then-replan (each sub-query conditioned on accumulated evidence; iterative QA, S3, AI-SearchPlanner decide when to stop), tree-search planning (RAG-Star MCTS+UCT with a retrieval-based reward and back-propagation; DeepRAG binary-tree; DeepSieve/DTA DAG aggregation), and end-to-end RL pipelines where planning, retrieval, tool use, and answer extraction are jointly optimized (Search-R1 as a fully observable MDP, R1-Searcher, Tool-Star/ARPO/AEPO). Multi-agent orchestration (Anthropic-style orchestrator + worker agents) coordinates planning, gathering, and synthesis.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Surveyed at several granularities: per-answer (one-shot retrieval before answering), per-CoT-step / per-reasoning-step (IR-CoT retrieves after every reasoning step; sequential planning re-queries per step on information gaps), per-token/per-sentence (probabilistic adaptive retrieval triggered by low-confidence tokens), and per-tool-call within a rollout (ReAct action text, Search-R1/Tool-Star multi-turn tool invocations in an RL rollout). MCTS-based planners interleave retrieval at each node expansion.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> N/A in the CBR sense (no verbatim-case adaptation/revision cycle). The functionally related mechanisms surveyed are self-reflection updating of memory (Reflexion verbal self-correction, A-Mem memory evolution, Voyager skill refinement), execution/environment-feedback-driven memory updates (Mem0, Memory-R1 RL manager), and answer-generation reconciliation of conflicting evidence (Self-RAG reflection tokens, Plan-on-Graph reflection-guided self-correction) - i.e., experience/memory revision rather than CBR case adaptation.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Surveyed surface forms: raw retrieved text/passages/web content; distilled/compressed summaries and reading notes (RECOMP, Chain-of-Note); latent/soft compressed embeddings (xRAG single token, ICAE/COCOM embedding sequences); structured notes / knowledge-graph triples and sub-graphs (HippoRAG, AriGraph, TiM tuples, ChatDB relational, Zep temporal KG); free-text workflows and skills (Voyager/GITM skill libraries, MIRIX procedural memory); and multimodal grounded pointers (table cells, chart coordinates) for citation. So raw text, distilled summaries, structured graphs/notes, executable skills, and latent-soft tokens are all surveyed.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Surveyed across abstraction levels: raw retrieved passages/web content (information acquisition); distilled summaries / event logs / high-level abstractions (unstructured memory consolidation: MemoryBank, MemoChat, ChatGPT-RSum, Generative Agents reflections); state-aware structured representations (knowledge graphs, trees - structured consolidation); reusable workflows / procedural skills (GITM common-reference memory, Voyager skill library, MIRIX procedural memory); and single demonstrations/notes. The memory component explicitly distills transient experiences into durable, higher-abstraction engrams.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Surveyed as a central concern: LLMs are highly sensitive to retrieval noise. Mechanisms covered: relevance evaluation / self-reflection (Self-RAG critic/reflection tokens; reasoning rerankers Rank-R1/ReasonRank/InstructRAG that judge document usefulness with rationales); reason-in-documents / reading-notes distillation (Search-o1 Reason-in-Documents, Chain-of-Note); information-bottleneck and KSE-based filtering (Zhu et al., BIDER); context compression to raise useful-content density; rule-based cleaning (HtmlRAG); and confidence/knowledge-boundary perception to avoid retrieving (or trusting) low-quality evidence. Consistency-based and internal-state probing further guard against unreliable context.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> Surveyed comprehensively as a distinct component (Memory Management): episodic (timestamped interaction histories), semantic (consolidated user traits/facts), graph (knowledge-graph memory: AriGraph, HippoRAG, Zep, ChatDB), tree/hierarchical (MemTree), skill-library/procedural (Voyager, GITM, MIRIX procedural memory), and parametric/latent (memory encoded in weights, modular memory). Distinguished from standard RAG by maintaining and revising a working memory across long horizons.
- **write back**:
> Yes (true) for the DR memory paradigm. The survey defines memory management with four core operations - Consolidation (transform short-term experiences into durable long-term representations), Indexing, Updating, and Forgetting - i.e., the agent actively writes back and maintains experiences/findings. Examples: MemGPT FIFO paging to long-term store, MemoryBank daily-event summaries, Mem0 ADD/UPDATE/DELETE, A-Mem dynamic linking. (Standard RAG, the contrast paradigm, does not write back.)
- **online growth**:
> Yes - the memory store grows and evolves during deployment/test-time. Memory consolidation converts ongoing interactions into durable memories, indexing creates new retrieval pathways, updating refines stored knowledge, and the store can prune via forgetting. A-Mem progressively grows a flexible access network; Generative Agents accumulate reflections; MEM1 maintains a constant-size evolving state. The survey contrasts this online-growing memory with RAG's frozen pre-indexed corpus.
- **write back trigger**:
> Surveyed across triggers: per-step / use-and-discard (MEM1 synthesizes a compact state and discards raw context after each interaction; MemGPT FIFO eviction); reflective/after-self-critique (Generative Agents trigger reflection after sufficient event accumulation; Reflexion verbal self-correction; A-Mem Memory Evolution re-evaluates linked memories); on-success (GITM summarizes key actions from successful plans into reference memory; Voyager adds verified skills); and conflict-/contradiction-triggered (Mem0 UPDATE/DELETE, Zep edge-invalidation on superseding facts, TiM MERGE/FORGET). RL-trained managers (Memory-R1) learn when to ADD/UPDATE/DELETE.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Surveyed mainly via self-reflection updating where agents reflect on past experiences (including failures) to refine knowledge (Reflexion verbal self-correction, Voyager skill-library updates, A-Mem memory evolution). The survey does not center an explicit success-vs-failure contrastive memory taxonomy; experiences are reactivated and modified based on new information or environmental feedback. Forgetting actively removes outdated/erroneous content (Mem0 DELETE, TiM FORGET, MEOW machine-unlearning of contradictory facts). So failure/correction signals are used chiefly through reflective updating and active forgetting rather than a dedicated negative-experience retrieval store.
- **memory evolution update**:
> Surveyed in detail (Memory Updating + Forgetting). Update dynamics: integration & conflict resolution (Mem0 ADD/UPDATE, Zep effective-time-range modification, TiM MERGE), self-reflection reconsolidation (Reflexion, Voyager, A-Mem autonomous re-evaluation of linked memories), and parametric updating (global continued training, localized locate-and-edit, modular). Forgetting: passive decay (MemGPT FIFO, MemoryBank Ebbinghaus curve, MEM1 use-and-discard) and active removal (Mem0 DELETE, TiM FORGET, AriGraph vertex/edge removal, Zep non-destructive edge invalidation, MEOW unlearning). So append, dedup-merge, delta-update, refine-overwrite, forget-prune, and link-and-evolve are all surveyed.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Yes - a major surveyed axis. Retrieval/search is increasingly a learned/RL-optimized policy rather than fixed top-k: Search-R1 formulates search-augmented reasoning as a fully observable MDP and optimizes when+what to retrieve via RL (masking retrieved tokens in the policy-gradient loss); R1-Searcher learns search invocation via outcome rewards; Tool-Star/ARPO/AEPO optimize tool-use pipelines with GRPO. Reranking is also RL-learned (Rank-R1, ReasonRank GRPO). Memory management is cast as an RL decision problem (Memory-R1 Memory Manager; goal-driven reinforced memory evolution as a future direction with long-term credit-assignment challenge).
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Partially surveyed. The workflow-prompting paradigm centers multi-agent orchestration (e.g., Anthropic's orchestrator + parallel worker agents sharing an evidence ledger; multi-agent distillation with planner/tool-caller/verifier; Chain-of-Agents distilling multi-agent capability into one model; OAgents/OWL). Memory in these settings can be shared via a common evidence ledger / orchestrator. However, the survey does not foreground a dedicated cross-framework shared-memory taxonomy; most memory work surveyed is single-agent private memory, with multi-agent collaboration handled at the workflow/orchestration level.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> Catalogs many benchmarks in Tables 4-5. Agentic information seeking / QA: Natural Questions (NQ), TriviaQA, SimpleQA, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue, Bamboogle, MultiHop-RAG, FRAMES, GPQA, GAIA, HLE (Humanity's Last Exam), BrowseComp, BrowseComp-Plus. Interaction environments: InfoDeepSeek, AssistantBench, Mind2Web, Mind2Web 2, WebArena, WebWalkerQA, WideSearch, MMInA, DeepResearchBench, DeepResearchGym. Report generation: AutoSurvey, ReportBench, SurveyGen, Deep Research Comparator, DeepResearch Bench, ResearcherBench, LiveDRBench, PROXYQA, SCHOLARQABENCH. Poster/Slides: Paper2Poster, PosterGen, P2PInstruct, Doc2PPT, SLIDESBENCH, Zenodo10K, TSBench. AI-for-research: AI Idea Bench, Scientist-Bench, PaperBench, ASAP-Review.
- **benchmark family**:
> QA / multi-hop (NQ, TriviaQA, SimpleQA, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue, Bamboogle, MultiHop-RAG, FRAMES); knowledge-intensive reasoning (GPQA, GAIA, HLE); web / live-browsing (Mind2Web, Mind2Web 2, WebArena, WebWalkerQA, BrowseComp, BrowseComp-Plus, InfoDeepSeek, AssistantBench, WideSearch, MMInA, DeepResearchBench, DeepResearchGym); long-form report & survey generation (AutoSurvey, ReportBench, SurveyGen, ResearcherBench, LiveDRBench, PROXYQA, SCHOLARQABENCH, Deep Research Comparator); presentation generation (Paper2Poster, PosterGen, Doc2PPT, SLIDESBENCH, Zenodo10K, TSBench); AI-for-research (AI Idea Bench, Scientist-Bench, PaperBench, ASAP-Review). Not the embodied (ALFWorld) or decision-RL (D4RL) families.
- **baselines**:
> N/A (a survey, not a method - it runs no head-to-head experiments of its own and reports no baseline comparison table). Conceptually it positions standard RAG as the baseline against the three Deep Research stages (Agentic Search, Integrated Research, Full-stack AI Scientist) in Table 1, and compares optimization paradigms (workflow prompting vs SFT vs end-to-end RL) and data-synthesis approaches (strong-to-weak distillation vs multi-agent distillation vs iterative self-evolving) qualitatively. It cites representative systems (Search-R1, R1-Searcher, WebDancer, WebSailor, WebThinker, Chain-of-Agents, OpenAI/Gemini/Perplexity DeepResearch) as the landscape rather than running comparisons.
- **key metrics**:
> Surveys metrics rather than reporting its own (Tables 4-5). QA/seeking: Exact Match, F1, Accuracy, Recall, Recall@k, Step Success Rate, Action Count, Search Call, Calibration Error, Similarity. Web/agent: Correctness, Success Rate, Agent-as-a-Judge. Report/long-form: Citation Quality, Content Quality, key-point coverage, Report Relevance / Retrieval Faithfulness / Report Quality, Precision/Recall/F1, Rubric/Factual Assessment, Bradley-Terry score, LLM-as-Judge. Presentation: Visual Quality, Textual Coherence, ROUGE, BERTScore, layout/design scores. Phase I prioritizes retrieval recall@k + answer exact match + citation correctness + latency; Phase II shifts to fine-grained factuality, verified citations, structural coherence, and key-point coverage.
- **headline result**:
> N/A (no single experimental headline number - it is a survey). Its headline conceptual contributions are: (i) a three-stage capability roadmap distinguishing DR from RAG (Standard RAG -> Agentic Search -> Integrated Research -> Full-stack AI Scientist, Table 1); (ii) four foundational components each with fine-grained sub-taxonomies - Query Planning (parallel/sequential/tree-based), Information Acquisition (retrieval tools/timing/filtering), Memory Management (consolidation/indexing/updating/forgetting), Answer Generation (integration/synthesis/structuring/presentation); (iii) three optimization paradigms (workflow prompting, SFT, end-to-end agentic RL); and (iv) a consolidated evaluation landscape across information-seeking and long-form generation with 30+ benchmarks.
- **ablations**:
> N/A (no experiments, hence no ablations). The analytical equivalents are comparative analyses: (1) capability comparison of Standard RAG vs the three DR stages across 11 feature axes (Table 1: search-engine access, tool use, code execution, reflection, memory management, hypothesis proposal, long-form generation, action space, reasoning horizon, workflow organization, output form); (2) output-capability comparison of contemporary DR systems (Table 2: text/image/audio/video/presentation/table/JSON/code/chart/GUI/citation across Gemini/OpenAI/Grok/H2O.ai/Skywork/Perplexity/Manus/Alita etc.); (3) comparison of single-agent vs multi-agent distillation vs iterative self-evolving data synthesis (Figure 7); (4) RL training-stability analyses (void-turn filtering / SimpleTIR, Echo-Trap / StarPO-S).
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Yes - the survey frames evaluation as two complementary aspects: (i) evaluation of agentic information-seeking capabilities (intrinsic: retrieval recall@k, search call count, accuracy, EM) and (ii) evaluation of long-form generation (report quality, citation faithfulness, coherence). Several surveyed benchmarks report intrinsic retrieval/process metrics separately from end-to-end outcome (e.g., BrowseComp-Plus reports Accuracy/Recall/Search Call/Calibration Error; DeepResearchGym reports Report Relevance / Retrieval Faithfulness / Report Quality; InfoDeepSeek reports Accuracy/Utilization/Compactness). So intrinsic retrieval metrics are decoupled from end-task metrics in the surveyed landscape.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both, and the survey advocates process-aware evaluation. Outcome: EM/F1/Accuracy/Success Rate/Correctness for short-form and Content Quality/Rubric/LLM-Judge for long-form. Process: Step Success Rate, Action Count, Search Call count, Retrieval Faithfulness, citation correctness/verified citations, key-point coverage, calibration error, and logical-coherence assessment (proposed multi-granularity sentence/paragraph/document coherence). Section 6.4 raises logical evaluation, the novelty-vs-hallucination boundary, and LLM-as-Judge bias/efficiency as open process-evaluation challenges.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Discussed qualitatively and as a challenge. The survey repeatedly weighs retrieval/inference cost vs accuracy: adaptive retrieval is motivated by the cost/overhead of blind per-step retrieval (over-retrieval vs under-retrieval); context compression (xRAG single-token, ACC-RAG/QGC query-adaptive rates) cuts token/context cost; Chain-of-Agents reduces compute vs multi-agent systems while preserving accuracy; AEPO/ARPO improve rollout efficiency; multi-agent distillation incurs substantial inference cost and infrastructure overhead. Benchmark metrics include Search Call count, Action Count, end-to-end latency, and editing efficiency. LLM-as-Judge efficiency (cost of large-scale pairwise evaluation) is flagged as an open issue. No single quantitative headline cost number (it is a survey).
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Surveyed budget levers: top-k document selection then reranking-then-truncation (Document Selection); context compression to fit/raise density within the LLM context window (lexical summarization and embedding-based, with query-adaptive compression rates in ACC-RAG/QGC); rule-based cleaning (HtmlRAG) to remove boilerplate; and memory forgetting / FIFO paging (MemGPT) plus use-and-discard constant-size state (MEM1) to cap working-memory budget. Anthropic-style orchestration allocates explicit budgets of agents, tool calls, and synthesis passes scaled to query complexity (1-2 agents for factual lookups up to more for complex queries). So budgets are fixed-k, query-adaptive/precision-driven, and budget-capped.
- **survey scope and axes**:
> Explicit organizing axes: (1) three-stage capability roadmap - Phase I Agentic Search, Phase II Integrated Research, Phase III Full-stack AI Scientist - vs Standard RAG (Table 1); (2) four foundational components, each with fine-grained sub-taxonomies: Query Planning (parallel / sequential / tree-based), Information Acquisition (retrieval tools [lexical/semantic/web/multimodal] / retrieval timing [adaptive: probabilistic/consistency/internal-state/verbalized] / information filtering [document selection / context compression / rule-based cleaning]), Memory Management (consolidation / indexing / updating / forgetting), Answer Generation (integrating upstream / synthesizing & coherence / structuring reasoning & narrative / presentation generation); (3) three optimization paradigms (workflow prompting, SFT [strong-to-weak / multi-agent distillation / iterative self-evolving], end-to-end agentic RL); (4) evaluation across information-seeking and long-form generation; (5) challenges (retrieval timing, memory evolution, training instability, evaluation) and open discussion (creativity, fairness, safety). Coverage: 8 sections, 30+ benchmarks tabulated, 500+ references; time window roughly 2019-2025 (v1 Nov 2025), with a continuously-updated companion repo.
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A as an authored benchmark (this is a survey, not a benchmark paper). It instead tabulates 30+ existing benchmarks with dates, aspects, data sizes, and metrics (Tables 4-5), e.g., HotpotQA (90124/5617/5813; EM/F1/Acc), 2WikiMultihopQA (167454/12576/12576), GPQA (448; Accuracy), GAIA (450/466; Exact Match), BrowseComp (1266; EM), BrowseComp-Plus (830; Accuracy/Recall/Search Call/Calibration Error), HLE (2500; EM/Accuracy), FRAMES (824), Mind2Web (2350), Mind2Web 2 (130; Agent-as-a-Judge), WebArena (812; Correctness), WebWalkerQA (680), WideSearch (200; LLM Judge), AutoSurvey (530000; Citation/Content Quality), SCHOLARQABENCH (2967), DeepResearchGym (96000). Construction methods span human-curated, multi-hop-composed (MuSiQue bottom-up), and closed academic (HLE - not answerable via quick online search), with difficulty signaled by low best-system scores on BrowseComp/HLE/GAIA.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Synthesizes and builds conceptually on: standard RAG (Lewis et al.; surveyed as the static-corpus predecessor it distinguishes DR from); iterative/adaptive retrieval (IR-CoT, FLARE, Self-RAG, DRAGIN, Search-o1); agentic reasoning-acting (ReAct, WebGPT/SearchGPT); RL-trained search agents (Search-R1, R1-Searcher/++, Tool-Star, ARPO, AEPO); web agents (WebDancer, WebSailor, WebThinker, WebShaper, Chain-of-Agents); memory systems (MemGPT, MemoryBank, Generative Agents, Reflexion, Voyager, GITM, HippoRAG, A-Mem, Mem0, Zep, TiM, AriGraph, Memory-R1); planning/tree-search (RAG-Star MCTS, DeepRAG, DeepSieve); compression (RECOMP, Chain-of-Note, xRAG, ICAE/COCOM); and commercial DR systems (OpenAI/Gemini/Perplexity/Grok/Anthropic DeepResearch, Manus, Skywork, H2O.ai).
- **contrasts with**:
> Primarily positions Deep Research against conventional/standard RAG, arguing RAG operates in a static retrieval loop over pre-indexed corpora and treats retrieval as a heuristic augmentation step without a flexible research workflow or broad action space, whereas DR enables flexible interaction with the dynamic digital world, long-horizon autonomous planning, dynamic memory management, and verifiable long-form generation (Table 1; Section 2.3). Also contrasts with prior surveys that only cover RAG or web agents in isolation, with single-shot prompting / static parametric knowledge, and internally contrasts the three optimization paradigms and the single- vs multi-agent distillation vs iterative self-evolving data-synthesis approaches.
- **lineage**:
> Surveys lineage. Positioned as a foundational, systematic survey of the Deep Research (DR) paradigm - the agentic, tool-augmented, long-horizon successor to RAG and web agents. It sits in the Surveys group alongside RAG surveys (Gao et al.), agentic-RAG surveys, agent/memory surveys, and context-engineering surveys, but uniquely consolidates the DR-specific workflow (query planning + information acquisition + memory management + answer generation) and its optimization (prompting/SFT/RL) and evaluation. It is upstream of and frequently cited by subsequent DR benchmark/method papers (e.g., Knowledgeable Deep Research, structural-evaluation work, FinDeepForecast).

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- venue

### 166. Evaluating LLM-based Agents for Multi-Turn Conversations: A Survey (Guan et al.)

2025  ·  ACM TIST 2025  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.22458)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**: ACM Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Technology (ACM TIST) 2025; DOI 10.1145/3793671. First posted arXiv:2503.22458 (28 Mar 2025; v2 revised 5 Jan 2026).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.22458
- **code url**: N/A (this survey has no associated official code repository or released artifact; it is a literature review)
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (no maintained GitHub paper list / leaderboard is associated with this survey; the similarly named repo yubol-bobo/Awesome-Multi-Turn-LLMs belongs to a different survey, 'Beyond Single-Turn')

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Survey of evaluation methods for LLM-based multi-turn conversational agents; spans dialogue/conversation, tool-use/action, memory and context retention, and planning. Not a single-domain method but a meta-level survey covering QA, tool-use, planning, embodied/web agent benchmarks under the multi-turn dialogue umbrella.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, multi-turn (multi-round) conversational setting where an LLM-based agent integrates dynamic tool use, persistent memory, and sequential planning across turns and sessions, as opposed to isolated single-turn queries. The survey itself is an offline literature analysis (PRISMA-inspired systematic review) rather than an interactive system; it studies how to evaluate such agents. It covers both single- and multi-agent systems and both supervised (annotation-based) and unsupervised (annotation-free / self-judging) evaluation regimes. Literature window 2017-2025 (Transformer era onward), reviewing nearly 250 sources.
- **what is retrieved**:
> N/A as a retrieval method. As a survey, it organizes the literature and (within the surveyed agents) discusses what conversational agents retrieve/recall: dialogue history, retrieved past interactions, tool/API documents, and long-term user preferences/memories. The survey's own 'units' are ~250-350 scholarly papers, benchmarks, metrics, and evaluation methods.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> N/A for the survey itself (not a retrieval system). Within surveyed agents, the discussed memory grounding is HYBRID: a static external corpus/tools (docs, APIs) plus a GROWING/episodic memory the agent writes (turn / conversation / permanent memory), with textual forms (complete/recent/retrieved/external interaction) and parametric forms.
- **completeness vs topk objective**: N/A. The survey is not optimizing a retrieval ranking objective. Its evaluation-oriented analog is comprehensiveness: it aims for holistic coverage of evaluation dimensions (what-to-evaluate) and methodologies (how-to-evaluate) rather than a fixed top-k ranking of methods.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based reasoning work).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: false - the survey does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> N/A (survey, not a retrieval method). The survey's units of analysis are scholarly papers, benchmarks/datasets, metrics, and evaluation methods. Within surveyed agents it discusses retrieval units such as dialogue turns, retrieved past interaction segments (cosine/semantic similarity), and tool/API documents.
- **index source**: N/A. The survey's 'store' is the curated literature corpus assembled via a PRISMA-inspired search (Google Scholar plus venue searches over ICLR, NeurIPS, AAAI, NAACL, EMNLP, ACL, 2022-2024); offline, fixed at review time.
- **index structure topology**:
> N/A as a retrieval index. The survey organizes its corpus via two interrelated taxonomies (hierarchical / tree-structured): a 'what to evaluate' taxonomy (end-to-end experience; action & tool-use; memory; planning) and a 'how to evaluate' taxonomy (annotation-based vs annotation-free, incl. automated metrics, hybrid, and self-judging LLM methods).
- **retriever type**: N/A (survey performs manual PRISMA-style keyword search + screening, not an automated retriever). Keyword/Boolean search via Google Scholar and venue databases followed by human screening for eligibility.
- **retriever learning signal**: N/A (none; off-the-shelf literature search engines plus manual human inclusion/exclusion screening, no learned retriever).
- **query construction**: N/A. The survey's literature-search 'query' is a fixed set of keywords (e.g. 'evaluation', 'performance assessment', 'benchmark', 'multi-turn/multi-round conversation/dialogue', 'Large Language Model (LLM)', 'LLM-powered/based/agent') applied to Google Scholar and named venues.
- **query granularity**: N/A. Literature search is one-shot at the corpus level (topic-level keyword query); not a per-step or trajectory-level retrieval.
- **when to retrieve**: N/A (one-shot literature collection during the systematic review; the survey itself does not perform iterative or active retrieval).
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> N/A (fixed schedule: a single PRISMA-inspired collection/screening pass). Within surveyed agents, the survey discusses when-to-retrieve signals for memory (e.g. semantic/contextual relevance, recency thresholds, thought-based retrieval), but this is descriptive of the literature, not the survey's own mechanism.
- **reranking**: N/A. No reranking stage; literature was filtered by manual relevance screening (duplicates removed, then excluded for not focusing on evaluation/agents/benchmarks, then full-text eligibility assessment).
- **retrieved context refinement**: N/A. The survey's analog is its multi-stage PRISMA screening/filtering pipeline (dedup, abstract screening, full-text eligibility) that distills 1,123 unique records down to 276 for meta-analysis; not retrieval-context refinement in the RAG sense.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (survey, not a tool-retrieval method). It reviews tool-use evaluation benchmarks (ToolBench, MetaTool, MTU-Bench, ToolDial, API-Bank, GAIA) but does not engineer tool documents/embeddings.
- **index content separation**: N/A.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A. The survey discusses dynamic/real-time tool use and document retrieval (e.g., Gorilla-style real-time API documentation retrieval, ToolBench/RapidAPI) as evaluation subjects, but implements no live tool index or protocol itself.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A as a mechanism. The survey notes the importance of multi-step tool chaining and sequential ordering of tools across turns (chain of execution) as an evaluation dimension, but does not model inter-tool dependencies itself.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**: N/A as a method. As a survey, surveyed evidence is used for qualitative synthesis and taxonomy construction (organizing evaluation goals and methodologies, summarizing metrics/benchmarks, and identifying gaps and future directions).
- **planning integration**:
> N/A for the survey itself. The survey reviews planning as one of the four 'what to evaluate' components, covering Task Modeling, Task Decomposition (e.g., ADaPT, MLDT, LLM-DP, TDAG), Adaptation and Control, and Reflection (Plan Verification and Plan Selection, e.g., ReAct, Critic-CoT, Self-Refine, MultiESC, DAT, DMPO). It does not itself integrate retrieval with planning.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: N/A (survey does not interleave retrieval with reasoning). It discusses, descriptively, per-turn and per-step evaluation granularity for planning/tool-use within surveyed agents.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not a CBR work).
- **retrieved item representation**: N/A. The synthesized outputs are taxonomies, comparison tables (Table 1 annotation-based vs annotation-free; Tables 2-3 benchmark listings), a PRISMA flow diagram, and a roadmap figure; not injected context.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: N/A. The survey abstracts the literature into high-level taxonomic categories and evaluation dimensions (distilled organizing axes) rather than retrieving raw trajectories or demonstrations.
- **noise robustness mechanism**: N/A. The survey's analog is PRISMA-style inclusion/exclusion criteria and human relevance screening to filter out irrelevant/low-quality sources (333 excluded as irrelevant, 267 excluded for lacking focus on LLM-based agent evaluation).

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> N/A for the survey itself. The survey devotes a dimension to evaluating agent memory, taxonomized by Memory Span (turn / conversational / permanent memory) and Memory Forms (textual: complete / recent / retrieved / external interaction; and parametric: fine-tuning and memory-editing). Episodic, retrieval-augmented (e.g., MemoryBank+FAISS), and parametric memory are all covered as subjects of evaluation.
- **write back**:
> N/A (survey produces no growing store). Within surveyed agents, write-back to memory (storing new interactions, preferences, insights) is discussed as a capability to evaluate (e.g., Memory Sandbox, experience/insight selectors), but the survey itself does not implement write-back.
- **online growth**: N/A. The surveyed corpus is fixed after the review. The survey discusses online memory growth (test-time accumulation of context across sessions, e.g., long-term conversation datasets spanning hours to years) as an agent property to evaluate.
- **write back trigger**: N/A (never, for the survey itself; it writes no memory). Within surveyed agents, write triggers (per-turn updates, reflective/insight-based storage, recency-based discarding) are described as evaluation targets.
- **failure experience usage**: N/A. The survey notes that several reviewed works lack analysis of failure causes and calls for better failure/error-propagation evaluation, but it does not itself store failure experiences.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A for the survey. It reviews memory-editing/update techniques (targeted parameter modification, memory management like Memory Sandbox) as agent capabilities to be evaluated.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: N/A (the survey's literature selection is manual PRISMA screening, not a learned/RL policy). It does, however, discuss learned reward models and self-judging LLM evaluators as evaluation methods.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: N/A for the survey. It reviews single-agent and multi-agent dialogue/debate evaluation (e.g., multi-agent data generation, multi-agent task decomposition like TDAG, parliamentary/structured debate benchmarks) but does not itself share memory across agents.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> Surveyed (not run by the authors). Representative benchmarks/datasets discussed include: MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 57 tasks), MT-Bench, the LMSYS million-conversation/Chatbot Arena dataset (25 LLMs), MMDU (27 turns), HUMOD (~28,500 dialogues), TopicChat, DailyDialog, MultiWOZ, BotChat, ConvBench, AgentBench, GAIA, ToolBench, MetaTool/ToolE, MTU-Bench, ToolDial, HuggingGPT, API-Bank, MT-Mind2Web, CoSafe (safety/coreference attacks), LoCoMo (long-term memory), LongEval, SocialBench, MemoryBank (with FAISS), DialFact (22k claims), Factcheck-Bench, BELIEF, WikiFactCheck-English.
- **benchmark family**:

The survey groups these by its 'what to evaluate' axes (end-to-end experience, tool-use/action, memory, planning) rather than by RAG benchmark family.
- **baselines**:
> N/A (a survey reports no head-to-head experimental baselines of its own). For positioning, it contrasts itself against prior surveys: Arora et al., Chang et al. (LLM evaluation), Li (LLM-agent capabilities), Zhang et al. (LLM-as-evaluator/GPT-4), and other dialogue-system surveys, arguing none jointly cover what-to-evaluate and how-to-evaluate for multi-turn agents with agentic-component interactions.
- **key metrics**:
> Surveyed evaluation metrics rather than the survey's own results. Covers traditional reference-based metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, perplexity, F1, exact match, accuracy), embedding/model-based metrics (BERTScore), task-completion/success rate, interaction-pattern recognition, memory retention/recall, tool-selection/API-call success rate, hallucination-detection accuracy, and annotation-free / self-judging metrics (LLM-as-a-judge pointwise/pairwise scoring, learned reward-model scores). Categorized into annotation-based vs annotation-free (automated metrics, hybrid human+quantitative, self-judging LLM).
- **headline result**:
> N/A (survey, no single experimental headline number). Closest quantitative facts: PRISMA-inspired systematic review of nearly 250 sources (264 references); collected 479 (Google Scholar) + 1,081 (venue) records, 1,123 unique after dedup, 351 included in qualitative synthesis and 276 in meta-analysis; two complementary taxonomies (what-to-evaluate / how-to-evaluate).
- **ablations**:
> N/A. As a literature survey, it presents no controlled ablations. Its structural analyses instead include the qualitative comparison of annotation-based vs annotation-free evaluation (Table 1) and the PRISMA selection breakdown showing how exclusion criteria reduce the candidate pool.
- **evaluation decoupling**: N/A for the survey. It does, however, advocate decoupling component-level evaluation (tool-use accuracy, memory retention, planning/decomposition quality) from end-to-end experience evaluation, organizing the field along exactly this intrinsic-vs-end-to-end split.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> N/A as own results. Thematically, the survey argues strongly for process (not just outcome) evaluation: it emphasizes per-turn and interaction-process quality, error propagation across turns, reasoning faithfulness, and intermediate planning/tool-use steps, criticizing benchmarks that score only final outcomes.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> N/A as own measurements. The survey discusses cost/efficiency trade-offs as a theme: annotation-based evaluation is costly/slow (human effort) while annotation-free/self-judging is scalable but incurs per-query LLM API latency/cost and bias; it calls for scalable, real-time, hierarchical evaluation pipelines (fast filters + deeper evaluation) to reduce cost.
- **context budget and selection count**: N/A. Not applicable to a survey (no injected-context token budget). Related theme: the survey discusses agent memory budget trade-offs (retaining everything vs discarding) and complete-vs-recent-vs-retrieved interaction strategies as evaluation concerns.
- **survey scope and axes**:
> Two interrelated taxonomies: (1) WHAT to evaluate - end-to-end experience (task completion, multitask capabilities, interaction patterns, user experience & safety), action & tool-use (API interaction/dynamic tool-use, multi-step tool selection & reasoning, reliability/hallucination), memory (memory spans: turn/conversation/permanent; memory forms: textual complete/recent/retrieved/external and parametric), and planning (task modeling, decomposition, adaptation & control, reflection). (2) HOW to evaluate - annotation-based vs annotation-free, including automated metrics, hybrid human+quantitative, and self-judging LLM methods. PRISMA-inspired methodology over literature from 2017-2025; ~264 references (cited as 'nearly 250 sources'); collected 1,560 records -> 1,123 unique -> 351 qualitative-synthesis -> 276 meta-analysis. Sources span peer-reviewed conference (~40%), journal (~25%), preprint (~20%), industry reports (~15%).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (this is a survey, not a benchmark). It catalogs others' benchmarks in Tables 2-3 (multitask/interaction/temporal/safety/tool-use, and reliability/next-turn/query-rewrite/memory/task-representation/decomposition/plan-selection) but constructs no new dataset.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Methodologically builds on the PRISMA systematic-review protocol (Page et al. / Moher et al.). Conceptually grounded in the agent paradigm (planning, tool-use, memory) and standard NLG/dialogue evaluation (BLEU, ROUGE, perplexity, BERTScore) and LLM-as-a-judge / reward-model evaluation literature (e.g., MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena).
- **contrasts with**:

(brief dialogue-system overview), task-oriented vs non-task-oriented dialogue classifications that overlook agent-system interaction, Li (LLM-agent capabilities without multi-turn focus), Chang et al. (broad LLM evaluation without multi-turn specifics), Zhang et al. (LLM-as-evaluator without detailed annotation-based vs annotation-free treatment), and several recent perspective surveys that ignore inter-component interactions and multi-turn-specific challenges.

> Surveys lineage: a meta-level survey of evaluation methodology for LLM-based multi-turn conversational agents. It sits alongside other agent/RAG/evaluation surveys, uniquely organizing the field via dual what-to-evaluate / how-to-evaluate taxonomies and covering memory, tool-use, and planning components jointly within the multi-turn dialogue setting.
