### 167. Evaluation and Benchmarking of LLM Agents: A Survey (Mohammadi et al.; sometimes mislabeled 'Yehudai et al.')

2025  ·  arXiv 2507.21504  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21504)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**:
> Peer-reviewed: KDD '25 (Proceedings of the 31st ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining), Aug 3-7 2025, Toronto, ON, Canada, DOI 10.1145/3711896.3736570 (survey/lecture-style paper). Preprint: arXiv:2507.21504 [cs.LG, cs.AI], submitted 29 Jul 2025 (v1), CC BY 4.0.
- **authors affiliation**:
> Mahmoud Mohammadi, Yipeng Li, Jane Lo, Wendy Yip -- all SAP Labs (Bellevue, WA and Palo Alto, CA, USA). NOTE: the task brief attributed this to 'Yehudai et al.'; that is a different agent-evaluation survey (Yehudai et al., 'Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents', arXiv:2503.16416). The paper at the given URL (2507.21504) is authored by Mohammadi, Li, Lo, Yip (SAP Labs).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21504

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Survey / taxonomy of LLM-agent EVALUATION. Cross-domain: covers tool-use, planning/reasoning, memory/context-retention, multi-agent collaboration, web/app agents, software-engineering, scientific, healthcare and finance agents, plus reliability and safety/alignment evaluation; not restricted to one task domain.
- **problem setting**:
> This is a literature survey (no method, no experiments of its own). It addresses how to evaluate LLM-based agents and proposes a two-dimensional taxonomy: (1) Evaluation Objectives = WHAT to evaluate (Agent Behavior: task completion, output quality, latency&cost; Agent Capabilities: tool use, planning&reasoning, memory&context retention, multi-agent collaboration; Reliability: consistency, robustness; Safety&Alignment: fairness, harm/toxicity/bias, compliance&privacy) and (2) Evaluation Process = HOW to evaluate (Interaction Mode: static&offline vs dynamic&online; Evaluation Data: synthetic/real-world datasets, domain benchmarks; Metrics Computation Methods: code-based, LLM-as-a-Judge / Agent-as-a-Judge, human-in-the-loop; Evaluation Tooling: instrumentation frameworks and leaderboards; Evaluation Contexts: simulation to open-world web/API). It also raises enterprise-specific challenges (role-based data access, reliability guarantees, dynamic/long-horizon interactions, compliance) and future directions (holistic, more realistic, scalable evaluation). It surveys both static/offline and interactive/online and both single- and multi-agent settings, but defines no controlled experimental protocol, supervision, or benchmark of its own.
- **what is retrieved**:
> N/A as an artifact (the survey itself retrieves nothing). As a surveyed topic it discusses agents that retrieve TOOLS from large tool repositories (tool retrieval over candidate toolsets) and that retain/recall MEMORY/context across long dialogues; tool descriptions, prior conversation turns, and intermediate working-memory results are the surveyed retrieved/recalled content.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> N/A for the survey (no grounding corpus of its own). The surveyed evaluation landscape spans BOTH retrieval over STATIC external tool/API repositories (tool retrieval, function-calling over candidate sets) and GROWING/episodic agent MEMORY (context retention over 40+ to 600+ turn dialogues; working memory of intermediate results), i.e. it reviews both static-corpus retrieval and growing-memory settings.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> N/A (survey, no retrieval objective of its own). It NOTES the relevant evaluation distinction: tool retrieval is scored with top-k rank accuracy, MRR and NDCG (ranking objective), while planning/multi-tool tasks are scored against a complete reference tool SET/sequence via Node F1, Edge F1 and Normalized Edit Distance (completeness-of-the-needed-set framing). The survey itself prescribes no single objective.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (the survey is not a case-based reasoning system; it implements no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain cycle).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The survey does not frame agent evaluation as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is organized around the WHAT/HOW (objectives/process) evaluation taxonomy.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**: N/A (survey defines no retrieval unit of its own). Surveyed units include: tool-API (single function/tool retrieved from a repository for function calling) and memory entries (prior dialogue turns, intermediate working-memory results) recalled during long-horizon interaction.
- **index source**: N/A for the survey (it builds no index). Surveyed tool retrieval is over static external tool/API repositories (e.g., large API sets in ToolBench/API-Bank/TaskBench); surveyed memory is a growing/online store the agent accumulates during multi-turn interaction.
- **index structure topology**:
> N/A (survey has no index of its own). It notes that some surveyed planning/tool benchmarks adopt GRAPH-based representations of tools (dependency/ordering graphs, scored with Node F1 / Edge F1 / Normalized Edit Distance), alongside flat candidate tool lists -- i.e. it reviews both flat and graph-structured tool organizations rather than prescribing one.
- **retriever type**:
> N/A (survey; no retriever implemented). It references retrieval of the correct tool from a large toolset based on a natural-language task description and ranking-based evaluation (rank accuracy@k, MRR, NDCG), implying dense/similarity tool retrievers in surveyed systems, but contributes no retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**: N/A (survey; trains no retriever). It catalogs how tool-retrieval QUALITY is measured (Retrieval Accuracy, MRR, NDCG) rather than how a retriever is trained.
- **query construction**:
> N/A (survey). For surveyed tool retrieval the query is the natural-language task/intent description matched against tool descriptions; for surveyed memory recall the current request/turn acts as the query against stored conversation history. The survey proposes no query-construction method.
- **query granularity**: N/A (survey). Surveyed agents query at the step/decision level (per tool-call decision; per-turn memory recall) and at the task level (multi-tool plan over a task); the survey reviews both rather than fixing one.
- **when to retrieve**: N/A (survey). It frames the relevant evaluation question 'can the agent correctly determine WHETHER tool invocation is necessary' (Invocation Accuracy) and contrasts plan-ahead vs interleaved ReAct-style retrieve/act-during-execution paradigms; it standardizes no single timing.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> N/A (survey defines no trigger). Surveyed agent-initiated tool invocation is decided by the model itself (native function-calling: the model autonomously decides whether to invoke a function), and memory recall is agent-initiated per request; evaluation of this decision is captured by Invocation Accuracy.
- **reranking**: N/A (survey; no reranking stage of its own). It mentions ranking-based tool-retrieval evaluation (rank accuracy@k, MRR, NDCG) as a measurement, not a reranking pipeline it contributes.
- **retrieved context refinement**: N/A (survey). It discusses memory operations such as appropriate forgetting of irrelevant details and tracking intermediate (working-memory) results in surveyed agents, but proposes no refinement pipeline of its own.
- **tool document engineering**:
> N/A as a contribution. It notes (surveyed) that, when the candidate toolset is extensive, an agent must retrieve the correct tool from a repository based on a natural-language task description, and that tool descriptions/parameter schemas are matched -- but it proposes no tool-document-engineering technique.
- **index content separation**: N/A (survey; no lightweight-index-then-content mechanism of its own).
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> N/A as a contribution. It surveys native function-calling/function invocation and large API repositories (ToolBench/API-Bank/TaskBench, Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard) and dynamic/online agent-environment interaction (web browsers, APIs), but does not center a live-synchronized tool index or a specific protocol (e.g., MCP) of its own.
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> N/A as a contribution. It NOTES that tool order and inter-tool dependency matter and that some surveyed benchmarks use graph-based tool representations with Node F1 (selection) and Edge F1 / Normalized Edit Distance (sequence/structure) to capture dependencies -- but contributes no dependency-aware retriever itself.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> N/A as a method. The survey describes how agents USE retrieved/recalled content (tools invoked for actions/grounding; memory recalled to maintain consistency across long-horizon tasks; ReAct-style interleaving of reasoning and tool use), and how EVALUATION consumes agent outputs (code-based checks, LLM-as-a-Judge / Agent-as-a-Judge, human-in-the-loop). It implements nothing.
- **planning integration**:
> N/A as a method. It reviews planning/reasoning evaluation: static plan comparison against a reference tool set/sequence (T-Eval set-based planning; graph-based Node F1 / Edge F1 / Normalized Edit Distance per TaskBench), interleaved plan-and-execute (ReAct) with step-wise reasoning metrics (T-Eval reasoning metric; AgentBoard Progress Rate), program-style multi-step plans scored with code-generation/program-similarity metrics (ScienceAgentBench), and Step Success Rate. It proposes no single integration.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> N/A (survey). It contrasts plan-ahead (static full plan vs reference) with per-step interleaved reasoning+tool-use (ReAct), and notes step-level reasoning metrics (T-Eval next-tool-call alignment per step; AgentBoard Progress Rate per trajectory step) -- reviewing per-step vs per-trajectory evaluation rather than committing to one.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not a CBR method; no retrieved-case adaptation of its own).
- **retrieved item representation**: N/A (survey). Surveyed retrieved/recalled content is represented as tool/API descriptions and call signatures (with parameter schemas) and as natural-language conversation memory / intermediate results; the survey injects nothing itself.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: N/A (survey). Surveyed units range from raw conversation turns (episodic memory) to single tool/API calls and to multi-step plans/programs; the survey reviews this spectrum rather than fixing an abstraction level.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> N/A as a contribution. Robustness is a first-class EVALUATION TARGET in the taxonomy (Reliability -> Robustness; Safety -> resilience to prompt-injection via AgentDojo; harmful-behavior testing via AgentHarm), so the survey reviews how robustness is MEASURED, but contributes no robustness mechanism of its own.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> N/A as an artifact. As a surveyed evaluation target, Memory and Context Retention is an explicit capability category (Section 3.2.3): episodic conversation memory (Memory Span / Memory Forms per Guan et al. 2024), long-dialogue context retention (40+ to 600+ turns), and working memory for tool-using agents (tracking intermediate results) plus forgetting strategies. The survey itself has no memory.
- **write back**: N/A as a method. Surveyed long-running agents accumulate/retain memory across turns and track intermediate results, but the survey stores nothing itself (boolean: False for the artifact).
- **online growth**: N/A as a method. Surveyed agent memory grows online during multi-turn/long-horizon interaction; the survey itself has no growing store.
- **write back trigger**: N/A (survey; no write-back trigger of its own). Surveyed memory accumulation is per-turn/per-interaction during deployment; the survey standardizes no trigger.
- **failure experience usage**:
> N/A (survey). It evaluates robustness/error handling (whether agents behave robustly when the system encounters errors) and execution-based outcomes (Gorilla-style running of tool calls to catch failures), implying use of failure signals in surveyed evaluation, but contributes no failure-experience storage scheme.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (survey). It notes forgetting strategies (appropriately forgetting irrelevant details) and consistency tracking across turns as surveyed memory dynamics, but proposes no single update/evolution policy.
- **retrieval as learned policy**: N/A (survey). It does not center retrieval/case-selection as a learned RL policy; surveyed tool retrieval is described via ranking metrics (rank@k/MRR/NDCG) and native function-calling decisions, not a trained retrieval policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> N/A as a method. Multi-Agent Collaboration is an explicit surveyed evaluation CAPABILITY (Section 3.2.4), and Agent-as-a-Judge (multiple AI agents interacting to refine assessment) is surveyed as a metric-computation method; the survey reviews multi-agent settings but implements no cross-agent memory sharing itself.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> N/A (survey; runs no experiments of its own). It CATALOGS many agent-evaluation benchmarks/datasets/leaderboards, including: Tool use / function-calling: TaskBench (Shen et al. 2024), ToolBench (Huang et al. 2024b), API-Bank (Li et al. 2023), T-Eval (Chen et al. 2024b), Gorilla/Gorilla-APIBench (Patil et al. 2023), Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard (BFCL, Yan et al. 2024). Memory/context retention: LongEval (Krishna et al. 2023), SocialBench (Chen et al. 2024a), LoCoMo (Maharana et al. 2024, 600+ turns), Optimus-1 (Li et al. 2024d, NeurIPS 2024). Planning/reasoning & science: ScienceAgentBench (Chen et al. 2025), AAAR-1.0 (Lou et al. 2025), AgentBoard (Ma et al. 2024), FlowBench (Xiao et al. 2024). Web/app interactive: AssistantBench (Yoran et al. 2024), AppWorld (Trivedi et al. 2024), WebArena (Zhou et al. 2023). Safety/robustness: AgentHarm (Andriushchenko et al. 2025), AgentDojo (Debenedetti et al. 2024). Leaderboards: BFCL, Holistic Agent Leaderboard (Stroebl et al. 2025).
- **benchmark family**:
> N/A (survey reports no benchmark family results of its own). Surveyed families: tool/function-calling (TaskBench, ToolBench, API-Bank, T-Eval, BFCL, Gorilla), memory (LongEval, SocialBench, LoCoMo, Optimus-1), planning/science (ScienceAgentBench, AAAR-1.0, AgentBoard, FlowBench), web/app interactive (WebArena, AppWorld, AssistantBench), and safety/robustness (AgentHarm, AgentDojo).
- **baselines**: N/A (survey; no method comparison or baselines of its own).
- **key metrics**:
> N/A (survey reports no metrics of its own). It CATALOGS agent-evaluation metrics it surveys: Task Success Rate; Invocation Accuracy; Tool Selection Accuracy; Retrieval Accuracy (rank accuracy@k), MRR, NDCG; parameter name F1; AST correctness and execution-based correctness (Gorilla); Node F1 / Edge F1 / Normalized Edit Distance (graph-structured plans, TaskBench); T-Eval reasoning metric; AgentBoard Progress Rate; Step Success Rate; Win Rate; factual recall accuracy and consistency score (memory); plus latency & cost, fairness/toxicity/bias, and robustness measures.
- **headline result**:
> N/A (survey; no headline number). Its central contribution is the two-dimensional WHAT/HOW taxonomy (Evaluation Objectives x Evaluation Process) for LLM-agent evaluation, plus the enterprise-challenge framing (role-based access, reliability guarantees, long-horizon interactions, compliance) and future directions (holistic, realistic, scalable evaluation).
- **ablations**: N/A (survey; conducts no experiments and therefore reports no ablations).
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> N/A (the survey reports no metrics of its own). It DOES analytically separate intrinsic capability/retrieval metrics (e.g., tool Retrieval Accuracy, MRR, NDCG, Node/Edge F1, parameter F1, Progress Rate, Step Success Rate) from end-to-end Task Completion / Task Success Rate within its Metrics discussion, i.e. it surveys both intrinsic and end-to-end metrics as distinct layers.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Surveyed (a core organizing theme): the taxonomy explicitly distinguishes outcome-oriented Agent Behavior (task completion, output quality) from process-oriented Agent Capabilities (tool use, planning/reasoning, memory, multi-agent), and surveys step-wise/process metrics (T-Eval reasoning metric, AgentBoard Progress Rate, Step Success Rate, trajectory comparison) alongside final-outcome metrics. The survey itself scores nothing.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Surveyed: Latency & Cost is an explicit Agent-Behavior evaluation sub-category (Section 3.1.3), and scalability/cost of evaluation (LLM-as-a-Judge scalability vs human-in-the-loop reliability; Evaluation-driven Development tooling for scalable continuous evaluation) is discussed throughout. The survey reports no cost/efficiency numbers of its own.
- **context budget and selection count**: N/A (survey; no token budget or k of its own). Long-context/long-horizon retention (40+ to 600+ turn dialogues) and context-window limits are surveyed as evaluation challenges, but no fixed-k or token budget is prescribed.
- **survey scope and axes**:
> Primary organizing axes: a TWO-DIMENSIONAL taxonomy -- (A) Evaluation Objectives (WHAT to evaluate): Agent Behavior (task completion, output quality, latency&cost), Agent Capabilities (tool use, planning&reasoning, memory&context retention, multi-agent collaboration), Reliability (consistency, robustness), Safety & Alignment (fairness, harm/toxicity/bias, compliance&privacy); and (B) Evaluation Process (HOW to evaluate): Interaction Mode (static&offline vs dynamic&online), Evaluation Data (synthetic/real-world datasets, domain benchmarks), Metrics Computation Methods (code-based, LLM-as-a-Judge / Agent-as-a-Judge, human-in-the-loop), Evaluation Tooling (LangSmith, Arize/Phoenix, DeepEval, InspectAI, GALILEO, OpenAI Evals, Azure AI Foundry, Google Vertex AI, LangGraph, Amazon Bedrock; leaderboards: BFCL, Holistic Agent Leaderboard), Evaluation Contexts. Plus enterprise-specific challenges and future directions. Coverage window: through ~2025 (v1 submitted Jul 2025). Reference count: approximately 128 references (max in-text bib index 128).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A (this is a survey, not a benchmark; it constructs no dataset and reports no dataset size or best-system score of its own). It does survey benchmark CONSTRUCTION practices (human-annotated, synthetic, and interaction-generated data; gold tool sequences with expected parameter structures; execution-based verification a la Gorilla).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Builds on prior LLM-evaluation methodology (LLM-as-a-Judge, Zheng et al. 2023) extended to agents (Agent-as-a-Judge, Zhuge et al. 2024), and synthesizes agent-capability and benchmark literature: ReAct (Yao et al. 2023), tool-use/function-calling benchmarks (Gorilla/Patil 2023, API-Bank/Li 2023, ToolBench, TaskBench/Shen 2024, T-Eval/Chen 2024b, BFCL/Yan 2024), planning benchmarks (AgentBoard/Ma 2024, ScienceAgentBench/Chen 2025), memory benchmarks (LongEval, SocialBench, LoCoMo/Maharana 2024, Optimus-1/Li 2024d), web/app benchmarks (WebArena/Zhou 2023, AppWorld/Trivedi 2024, AssistantBench/Yoran 2024), and safety benchmarks (AgentHarm/Andriushchenko 2025, AgentDojo/Debenedetti 2024). Aggregates rather than extends a single predecessor.
- **contrasts with**:
> Positions itself against the fragmented, capability-narrow prior evaluation landscape that lacks a unifying framework, and against research that overlooks enterprise deployment concerns (role-based data access, reliability guarantees, dynamic/long-horizon interaction, compliance). As a survey it complements and is distinct from other contemporaneous agent-evaluation surveys, notably Yehudai et al. 'Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents' (arXiv:2503.16416) -- which the task brief appears to have conflated with this paper -- by emphasizing the WHAT/HOW (objectives/process) two-axis taxonomy and enterprise challenges.
- **lineage**:
> Surveys group: a 2025 survey specializing in EVALUATION & BENCHMARKING of LLM agents (WHAT/HOW two-dimensional taxonomy with enterprise focus). It is an umbrella reference for the evaluation/benchmark sub-topics that the retrieval-augmented-agent lineage relies on -- in particular it catalogs the memory benchmarks (LoCoMo, SocialBench, LongEval, Optimus-1) and tool-use benchmarks (ToolBench, API-Bank, TaskBench, T-Eval, BFCL) used to evaluate the memory/tool-retrieval methods in Groups A-F -- rather than being a method within any single sub-topic.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- code_url
- maintained_repo_url

<a id="item-compound-ai-survey"></a>
### 168. From Standalone LLMs to Integrated Intelligence: A Survey of Compound AI Systems (CAIS)

2025  ·  arXiv 2506.04565  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.04565)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2506.04565, cs.MA/cs.CL; v1 Jun 2025, v2 May 2026). Indexed by Semantic Scholar/DBLP as a Review/JournalArticle; no peer-reviewed venue identified.
- **authors affiliation**: Jiayi Chen, Junyi Ye, Guiling Wang -- all at New Jersey Institute of Technology (NJIT), Newark, NJ, USA.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.04565
- **code url**: N/A (literature survey; no official code repository associated)
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (no maintained GitHub paper list / leaderboard found; the survey is a frozen PDF with no companion living repo)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Survey spanning QA, tool-use, decision-making/agents, multimodal (vision/audio/video), code, and web; organizes the field of LLM-augmented compound systems rather than solving a single task.
- **problem setting**:
> A systematic literature survey (not an empirical method). It defines Compound AI Systems (CAIS) as a framework integrating one or more LLMs (L), external components (C: retrievers, tools, agents, multimodal encoders, prompt-engineering, self-optimization), and a system design (D: orchestration/topology), formalized as f(L,C,D). Settings covered include offline RAG pipelines, interactive single- and multi-agent loops, multimodal perception, and orchestrated multi-component pipelines. Supervision varies by surveyed work. Search ran Dec 2024-May 2026 over ACM DL, arXiv, IEEE Xplore, Semantic Scholar covering 2020-early 2026; ~400 candidates screened to 220+ papers retained (227 references).
- **what is retrieved**:
> Primarily documents/passages and external knowledge (open-domain corpora, knowledge-graph triples, KBs) in the RAG axis; tools/APIs in the agent and orchestration axes; and multimodal context (encoded image/audio/video tokens) in the MLLM axis. As a survey it catalogs these retrieval targets rather than retrieving itself.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> Predominantly STATIC external corpus (docs/KB/APIs) for the RAG axis; the survey also covers HYBRID grounding where orchestration adds memory management (e.g., KV-cache via PagedAttention) and agents draw on tool registries. Growing/episodic agent memory is acknowledged but is not the survey's central retrieval framing.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (the survey does not frame any axis as case-based reasoning; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain cycle is discussed)
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False -- the survey does not frame itself or surveyed systems as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Heterogeneous across axes as catalogued: token/snippet and document/passage (RAG dense/sparse retrieval), knowledge-graph triples / KG-subgraph (graph retriever, e.g., KAPING, GraphRAG), tool-API schemas (agent/orchestration tool use, MCP tools), and multimodal token embeddings (MLLM encoders). Document/passage is the dominant RAG retrieval unit.
- **index source**:
> Mainly static offline-built corpora/vector indices for RAG (pre-retrieval: chunking, embedding, indexing). The survey also covers live/dynamic tool indices via MCP and active tool discovery (Fei et al. 2025) and KV-cache memory (PagedAttention), i.e., hybrid static-plus-runtime stores. No single induced store -- it is a meta-level catalog.
- **index structure topology**:
> Catalogs multiple topologies: flat vector index (dense retrieval), sparse term index (BM25), knowledge GRAPH index (graph retrievers / GraphRAG / KAPING), and hierarchical/modular component organization in orchestration (structural layer: hierarchical and centralized structures). Tool registries are organized for retrieval/discovery (MCP servers).
- **retriever type**:
> Survey explicitly classifies retrievers into five types: Sparse (BM25), Dense (BERT-style embeddings), Graph (KG traversal), Hybrid (sparse+dense), and LLM-as-Retriever. Also a two-dimension framing (Phase: pre-retrieval/retrieval/post-retrieval; Approach: the five functional types).
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Spans the spectrum across surveyed work: off-the-shelf (BM25), contrastive/dense similarity training, LM-feedback and downstream-effectiveness co-training/dual fine-tuning of retriever+generator (e.g., RAG-end2end, Atlas/T5, REPLUG), and query-rewriting learned via trainable rewriters (Ma et al. 2023). No single signal -- the survey enumerates them.
- **query construction**:
> Catalogs raw query, query rewriting (trainable rewriter), query preprocessing/expansion, docid-based mapping (DSI), thought-conditioned queries in iterative/recursive RAG (IRCoT, ITER-RETGEN), and self-reflection-driven decisions (SELF-RAG). Multimodal queries are encoded into vectors that drive the RAG retriever in the unified pipeline.
- **query granularity**: Both task-level (one-shot retrieval at query time, classic RAG) and step/iteration-level (iterative ITER-RETGEN, recursive IRCoT chain-of-thought, adaptive SELF-RAG) are covered. The survey contrasts one-shot vs iterative/recursive/adaptive patterns.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Survey contrasts one-shot retrieval, iterative (repeated retrieve-generate cycles), recursive (nested decomposition), and adaptive (dynamically decide when to retrieve, e.g., SELF-RAG self-reflection). Covers the full one-shot/iterative/active/adaptive space as a RAG-design taxonomy axis.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Catalogs fixed-schedule retrieval (standard RAG), iteration-driven triggers (ITER-RETGEN/IRCoT), and learned/self-reflective triggers (SELF-RAG reflection tokens deciding when to retrieve and critique). In agents, retrieval/tool calls are agent-initiated within ReAct-style loops; orchestration may trigger additional retrieval via feedback arcs.
- **reranking**:
> Yes -- explicitly part of the Post-Retrieval phase: reranking reorders/reassesses retrieved results to maximize relevance (cites Lazaridou et al. 2022, Glass et al. 2022, Ram et al. 2023). Also lists knowledge filtering and refinement as post-retrieval steps. Specific reranker architectures (cross-encoder etc.) are referenced rather than prescribed.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Survey enumerates post-retrieval refinement: knowledge filtering (constraint-based search-space reduction), knowledge refinement (coherence/usability improvement), and reranking. Generator-side filtering (fine-tuned to keep relevant docs and discard irrelevant ones, e.g., Yoran et al. 2023) is also covered as distractor filtering.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Covered at a survey level: tool schemas standardized via function-calling / OpenAPI and MCP (resources, prompts, tools, sampling). Mastouri et al. 2025 auto-compile OpenAPI REST APIs into MCP servers; Fei et al. 2025 add active tool discovery so agents retrieve relevant tools from large registries instead of dumping static schemas into the context window.
- **index content separation**: Discussed implicitly: Fei et al. 2025 (active tool discovery over MCP) retrieves relevant tools from registries rather than loading all schemas into context -- a lightweight-index-then-load pattern. Not framed as a formal SOP-index-then-content principle for RAG.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Yes, a notable theme in Section 8.5 (Standardization). Covers static schema layer (structured tool interfaces / function-calling / OpenAPI), the Model Context Protocol (MCP, Anthropic Nov 2024; host/client/server over JSON-RPC 2.0; resources/prompts/tools/sampling) as a live tool-access protocol with active discovery, and agent-interoperability protocols (A2A, ACP, ANP).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Catalogs prompt augmentation (injecting retrieved context into the generator), training-signal use (co-training / dual fine-tuning of retriever+generator, RL-trained generators), modular augmentation (REPLUG keeps LLM frozen), and tool-result injection in agent/orchestration loops. Multimodal tokens are fused into the LLM context.
- **planning integration**:
> Surveyed across patterns: retrieve-then-generate (one-shot RAG), iterative/recursive interleaving of retrieval with chain-of-thought reasoning (IRCoT, ITER-RETGEN), adaptive self-reflective retrieval (SELF-RAG), per-step tool calls inside ReAct-style agent loops, and orchestration-scheduled retrieval/tool triggers in a feedback loop (the unified CAIS pipeline, Figure 1).
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Survey spans per-answer (vanilla RAG), per-CoT-step / per-iteration (IRCoT recursive, ITER-RETGEN iterative), reflection-token-gated (SELF-RAG), and per-tool-call within an agent rollout (ReAct loops, orchestration feedback). No single granularity -- it is a taxonomy axis.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (no CBR framing; the survey does not discuss case adaptation/revision mechanisms)
- **retrieved item representation**: Catalogs raw retrieved passages/documents injected into prompts, KG triples (graph retrieval), tool/API call results, and multimodal token embeddings. The survey treats surface form descriptively rather than proposing a distilled/latent representation.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Mostly raw retrieved passages/documents and KG triples (low abstraction); also tool-API descriptions and multimodal embeddings. The survey does not emphasize distilled strategies/skills as retrieved units (that is more an agent-memory framing outside its central RAG taxonomy).
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Covers generator-side filtering fine-tuned to discard irrelevant retrieved docs (Yoran et al. 2023, Zhang et al. 2024, Luo et al. 2023), post-retrieval knowledge filtering, self-reflection/critique (SELF-RAG a priori/a posteriori judgment, Ren et al. 2023), and reranking to demote distractors. Faithfulness/Context-Precision metrics (Ragas) used to measure robustness.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> Catalogs several: none (stateless RAG), KV-cache/working memory managed at the system level (PagedAttention), and orchestration-level memory management; multi-agent shared state. Episodic/skill-library agent memory is acknowledged but not a deeply developed dedicated taxonomy axis in this survey.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Partially: the survey covers learned/trainable retrievers and query rewriters and RL-trained generators (co-training, dual fine-tuning, RL frameworks), and adaptive retrieval policies (SELF-RAG). It does not frame retrieval as a formal RL policy (e.g., M-MDP soft Q-learning) -- it catalogs the shift from similarity-only to learned/adaptive retrieval.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Yes -- a distinctive contribution: Section 8.5 treats cross-framework/cross-agent interoperability protocols (Agent-to-Agent A2A, Agent Communication Protocol ACP, Agent Network Protocol ANP) and the 'convergence-by-layering' thesis, plus multi-agent collaboration/debate frameworks and model communication in orchestration. Shared memory across heterogeneous agents is framed as an open standardization concern.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> RAG: Natural Questions, TriviaQA, WebQuestions, RealTimeQA, MS MARCO, BEIR, TREC-DL, OpenBookQA, PopQA, TruthfulQA, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue, StrategyQA, SQuAD, DROP, WikiAsp, Multi-News, NarrativeQA, UniEval, Ragas, KILT. MLLM: MM-Vet, ALLaVA, SEED-Bench, ChartQA, MMC-Benchmark, DocVQA, TextVQA, MM-SafetyBench, MME, MultiBench. Orchestration: BigDataBench, AIBench Training, AISBench, WebArena, Long Range Arena, ZeroSCROLLS, AI Fairness 360. LLM Agents: RoleLLM, AgentBench, AgentBoard, AgentQuest, InfiAgent-DABench, CriticBench, ML-Bench, Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL).
- **benchmark family**:
> QA (NQ, TriviaQA, WebQuestions, SQuAD, DROP, OpenBookQA, PopQA, TruthfulQA, RealTimeQA); multi-hop (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue, StrategyQA); passage retrieval (MS MARCO, BEIR, TREC-DL); RAG-pipeline (Ragas, KILT); summarization/long-form (WikiAsp, Multi-News, NarrativeQA, UniEval); multimodal (MM-Vet, SEED-Bench, ChartQA, DocVQA, TextVQA, MME, MultiBench, MM-SafetyBench); web/agent (WebArena, AgentBench, AgentBoard, AgentQuest); tool (ML-Bench, BFCL); long-context (Long Range Arena, ZeroSCROLLS); systems/orchestration (BigDataBench, AIBench, AISBench); fairness (AI Fairness 360).
- **baselines**:
> N/A as a single comparison -- being a survey, it does not run head-to-head baselines. It positions itself (Table 1) against prior surveys: Lin et al. 2024, Lee et al. 2025, Bhagat et al. 2025, Li 2025, Guo et al. 2024, Yan et al. 2025, Xi et al. 2025, claiming the first full cross-axis (RAG+Agents+MLLM+Orchestration+Evaluation+Standardization) coverage.
- **key metrics**:
> Catalogs per-axis metrics: RAG -- Accuracy, F1, EM, MRR, nDCG, Precision, Recall, ROUGE, BLEU, Faithfulness, Context Precision, Context Recall. MLLM -- Accuracy, F1, EM, Perplexity, BLEU, ROUGE, custom safety metrics. Agents -- Role-Consistency Score, Self-Correction Rate, Reasoning Trace Accuracy, Generalization Score, Tool Call Accuracy, Token Efficiency. Orchestration -- Throughput, Latency Overhead, Bandwidth Utilization, Mean Task Completion Time, Avg. API Response Time, Cache Hit Rate, fairness metrics.
- **headline result**:
> As a survey there is no single empirical headline number. Headline contribution: the first unified multi-dimensional CAIS taxonomy across four axes (RAG, LLM Agents, MLLMs, Orchestration) plus evaluation and standardization (MCP/A2A/ACP/ANP), synthesizing 227 references / 220+ papers (2020-early 2026), positioned (Table 1) as the only prior work providing full cross-axis coverage.
- **ablations**:
> N/A -- a survey does not run ablations. It instead provides comparative analyses: RAG retriever paradigms (sparse/dense/graph/hybrid) across latency, recall, scalability dimensions (Table 2); LLM agent reasoning-framework comparison; MLLM architecture comparison; and orchestration-framework comparison tables, which serve an analogous design-tradeoff role.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Yes -- the survey explicitly notes RAG evaluation targets both retrieval quality (MRR, nDCG) and generation factuality (EM, F1, ROUGE, BLEU) as separate concerns, and Ragas/KILT for end-to-end pipeline evaluation, thereby distinguishing intrinsic retrieval metrics from end-to-end task metrics.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both. Beyond outcome metrics (Accuracy/EM/F1), it highlights process/intermediate metrics: Reasoning Trace Accuracy, Self-Correction Rate, Role-Consistency Score, Faithfulness/Context-Precision/Context-Recall (Ragas), and orchestration process metrics (task completion time, cache hit rate). It flags lack of unified system-level metrics as a gap.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Discussed qualitatively: RAG retriever comparison weighs retrieval latency, recall quality, and scalability (Table 2); orchestration metrics include throughput, latency overhead, API response time, cache hit rate; agent metrics include Token Efficiency; PagedAttention is cited for memory/throughput efficiency. Sustainable/efficient deployment is named as an open opportunity (Sec 10.2.6).
- **survey scope and axes**:
> Four organizing axes: (1) RAG, (2) LLM Agents, (3) Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), (4) Orchestration; plus cross-cutting Evaluation and Standardization (MCP/A2A/ACP/ANP). Formalism: CAIS = f(L, C, D). Coverage: literature search Dec 2024-May 2026 over ACM DL, arXiv, IEEE Xplore, Semantic Scholar; window 2020-early 2026; ~400 candidates screened to 220+ retained; 227 references.
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A -- the survey does not construct a new benchmark; it aggregates and catalogs existing benchmarks (Table 8) and identifies the absence of unified system-level CAIS benchmarks and robust multimodal benchmarks as a key gap.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Builds on the Berkeley AI Research (BAIR/Zaharia et al. 2024) 'Compound AI Systems' framing; foundational works it organizes include Lewis et al. 2020 (RAG), Brown et al. 2020 (GPT-3), ReAct (Yao et al. 2023), SELF-RAG (Asai et al. 2023), IRCoT (Trivedi et al. 2022), ITER-RETGEN (Shao et al. 2023), REPLUG (Shi et al. 2023), Atlas (Izacard et al. 2023), and the MCP specification (Anthropic 2024).
- **contrasts with**:
> Prior surveys with narrower scope (Table 1): Lin et al. 2024 and Lee et al. 2025 (optimization-only), Bhagat et al. 2025 (info-seeking QA only), Li 2025 (agent paradigms), Guo et al. 2024 (multi-agent), Yan et al. 2025 (agent communication), Xi et al. 2025 (agent systems). It claims to be the first with full cross-axis CAIS coverage including standardization.
- **lineage**:
> Surveys group. A cross-cutting CAIS taxonomy survey that links the RAG (group B), Agents/tool-use (group C), and Orchestration/multi-agent (group E) sub-topics under one f(L,C,D) framework, also covering MLLMs; positioned as an umbrella/integration survey across the retrieval-augmented LLM-agents landscape.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- completeness_vs_topk_objective

### 169. InfoDeepSeek: Benchmarking Agentic Information Seeking for Retrieval-Augmented Generation

2025  ·  arXiv 2505.15872  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15872)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **authors affiliation**:
> Yunjia Xi, Jianghao Lin (corresponding), Yongzhao Xiao, Zhuoying Ou, Jiaqi Liu, Tong Wan, Weiwen Liu, Weinan Zhang (corresponding), Yong Yu - Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Menghui Zhu, Bo Chen, Yasheng Wang, Ruiming Tang - Huawei Noah's Ark Lab. Contact: {xiyunjia,chiangel,wnzhang}@sjtu.edu.cn. Primary affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Huawei Noah's Ark Lab.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15872
- **code url**: https://github.com/YunjiaXi/InfoDeepSeek (the InfoSeekAgents agentic-RAG harness + eval scripts; CC BY-NC 4.0). Dataset on HuggingFace: https://huggingface.co/datasets/yoga334/InfoDeekSeek (also data/InfoDeepSeek_v1.json in the repo). Project page: https://infodeepseek.github.io/
- **maintained repo url**:
> https://github.com/YunjiaXi/InfoDeepSeek (project page https://infodeepseek.github.io/). The authors do not maintain a public live leaderboard; the repo (5 commits, ~18 stars as of mid-2026) and the HuggingFace dataset (InfoDeepSeek_v1, 245 queries) are the canonical sources. The work is listed in third-party trackers such as github.com/qhjqhj00/awesome-agentic-search.

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> web / QA / decision-making: a benchmark for agentic information seeking (Agentic RAG) in open, dynamic real-world web environments. Factual open-domain QA requiring multi-turn web search and browsing, planning, disambiguation, and cross-lingual retrieval; touches tool-use (search engines, browser, time utilities) and multi-step decision-making.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, single-agent, test-time online setting in the live open web (no fixed corpus). Given a query q, an Agentic RAG agent iteratively plans, acts (search engine / Selenium browser / time tool / terminate), observes, and reflects for up to T steps (default T=5) to acquire an evidence set C (size n_q, capped at n=5) from the real web, then generates an answer. The environment is dynamic (web content is volatile and multi-source), so ground-truth retrieval documents cannot be pre-fixed; only ground-truth answers and a human-annotated standard set of supporting source webpages S_q are recorded. No training/supervision is provided to the agent: the benchmark evaluates off-the-shelf LLMs zero-shot under a unified plan-reflect-act framework. Questions are deliberately filtered so neither GPT-4o nor DeepSeek-R1 can solve them with a single-turn web search, forcing genuine multi-round agentic behavior. Dataset: 245 validated queries, each carrying >=2 of six difficulty attributes, 14 domains, 19 predominant languages, all provided in both English and Chinese.
- **what is retrieved**:
> docs (live web content): web search results / snippets / page titles and full webpage contents fetched from real search engines (Google, Bing, Yahoo, DuckDuckGo) and a Selenium browser. The agent distills these into an ordered evidence set C of up to n=5 webpages (URL + extracted relevant content). It is open-web documents/evidence, not demos/cases/tools/skills.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus in the loose sense of querying the open, live web (a dynamic external information source the agent does NOT write to). It is NOT a growing/episodic agent memory: the agent has a per-query working memory (its own trajectory) used for planning, but retrieval targets the external web, and nothing is persisted back into a retrievable store across queries. Best described as retrieval over a dynamic external corpus (the live web) rather than over a fixed offline KB or an agent-written memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Completeness-and-precision oriented with a variable-size, capped recommendation: the agent must recover the complete minimal set of supporting sources needed to answer (multi-hop questions need multiple sources; annotated |S_q| typically 1-3). The agent dynamically chooses the evidence-set size n_q up to a cap n=5 and ranks evidence by importance. Evaluation rewards both having sufficient top-k evidence (IA@k) and keeping the set compact (Information Compactness penalizes over-retrieval), i.e., a precision-driven variable-size objective rather than a fixed top-k ranking.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A: not a case-based-reasoning system. No Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain over a case library; retrieval targets the live web, not prior solved cases.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False: the paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is an Agentic RAG information-seeking benchmark.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> document / webpage (and snippet): the retrievable observation is a web search result snippet, page title, or full webpage content; the curated evidence unit c_i is a webpage represented as (URL, query-relevant extracted content). Selection operates at both document-level and span-level.
- **index source**:
> Dynamic external corpus = the live, open web, queried online at test time through commercial/free search-engine APIs and a Selenium browser. There is no offline-induced index and no agent-written store; the 'index' is whatever the real-time search engine and the web return for each query, making it volatile and source-multiplicitous by design.
- **index structure topology**:
> No constructed index structure: retrieval is delegated to external general-purpose search engines (Google/Bing/Yahoo/DuckDuckGo) whose internal indexes are opaque, plus direct Selenium browsing of live URLs. On the agent side the retrieved content is held as a flat, chronologically-appended trajectory memory (plans + actions + observations); the curated evidence set C is a flat importance-sorted list of <=5 webpages. No vector index, dependency graph, or hierarchical topology is built by the benchmark.
- **retriever type**:
> LLM-as-retriever orchestrating external search-engine tools: the LLM agent forms search keyword queries and decides which tool to call (search engine or browser); the actual lexical/semantic matching is performed by the black-box commercial search engines (BM25/dense hybrid internally, not controlled by the benchmark). For the augmentation stage, the LLM also acts as a relevance selector/ranker over retrieved content. So: hybrid = LLM-driven query formulation + tool/search-engine backend + LLM-based relevance selection.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> none (off-the-shelf): neither the search engines nor the LLM agent are trained or fine-tuned for retrieval in this benchmark. All LLMs are evaluated zero-shot under a fixed unified plan-reflect-act prompt; query construction and evidence selection rely on the LLM's pretrained capabilities. The benchmark studies behavior, not a learned retriever; no contrastive/LM-feedback/preference/RL retrieval signal is introduced.
- **query construction**:
> LLM-generated search keywords conditioned on the query, current plan, observations, and trajectory memory. The agent decomposes complex queries into sub-problems during planning and issues per-step search keyword queries (the paper notes search keywords are strongly aligned with the input language; a language-aware prompt can force use of a predominant language). Thus queries are thought/plan-conditioned, decomposed sub-queries, not raw verbatim input.
- **query granularity**:
> step/state-level (iterative): a fresh search query is constructed at each of the up to T reasoning steps based on the evolving plan and prior observations, rather than a single one-shot task-level query at t=0. Initial planning happens at t=0 but retrieval queries are issued and refined per step.
- **when to retrieve**:
> iterative / agent-initiated (active): the agent retrieves across multiple steps (up to T, default 5; ablated 1-20) and decides at each step whether to search/browse again or invoke the termination tool when it judges the gathered information sufficient. Retrieval is interleaved with planning and reflection; it is not one-shot.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Agent-initiated request driven by self-assessed sufficiency: at each step the LLM plans/reflects and either issues another search/browse action or calls the explicit termination tool once it deems the information sufficient (subject to the hard step cap T). The trigger is the agent's own reasoning ('call the tool for questions you are not sure about'; 'if you have sufficient information ... invoke the termination tool'), not a learned router, token-confidence, attention, or reflection-token mechanism.
- **reranking**:
> Yes, LLM-based importance ranking in the augmentation stage: the agent consolidates retrieved content, merges duplicate-URL pieces, selects the <=n (=5) most relevant webpages, and sorts them by importance/contribution to answering the query (the first-ranked page contributes most). This is an LLM relevance-and-coverage reranker over raw observations, not a trained cross-encoder or RRF.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Distillation + selection + dedup: the augmentation stage applies document-level and span-level selection, summarizes/extracts query-relevant content from each webpage, removes redundancy by merging identical-URL evidence, ranks by relevance/coverage/redundancy, and truncates to <=5 evidence items. Effectively a reason-in-documents distillation plus distractor-filtering/compression step performed by the LLM.
- **tool document engineering**:
> N/A: the agent's tools (search engines, Selenium browser, time utility, termination) are exposed via a tool_specification in the prompt, but the benchmark does not engineer/index tool documentation for retrieval (tools are few and fixed, selected by the LLM during planning, not retrieved by similarity).
- **index content separation**:
> Partial / implicit: search returns lightweight snippets/titles first, and the agent uses the Selenium browser to fetch heavier full webpage content on demand (progressive disclosure from snippet to full page). This is a property of the web/search backend rather than a designed lightweight-index-then-content store built by the benchmark.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Live/dynamic external retrieval over real search-engine and browser tools: Google (via Serper API), Bing and Yahoo (via SerpApi), DuckDuckGo (free API with Selenium fallback), plus a Selenium-based live-webpage browser and a time utility. Integration is via each engine's API with Selenium scraping fallback; supports OpenAI/Gemini/DeepSeek/Qwen LLM clients. Not MCP; not a synchronized tool index with CRUD - the 'index' is the live web itself, queried in real time.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A: with only a small fixed toolset (search engines, browser, time tool, terminate), the benchmark does not model inter-tool dependencies, dependency graphs, or dependency-aware tool reranking; tool sequencing is left to the LLM's step-by-step planning.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> prompt augmentation: the curated, importance-sorted evidence set C (and, for ACC, the full observation sequence O) is provided to the LLM in the generation stage to produce the final answer y_hat = Generate(q, C). The retrieved web evidence grounds the answer; there is no skill reuse, case adaptation, training signal, or latent-token injection.
- **planning integration**:
> Per-step interleaved retrieve-while-planning inside an iterative agent loop: initial plan at t=0, then a plan-act-reflect cycle (Plan -> Act with a tool -> Observe -> Reflect/replan) for up to T steps, followed by a separate augmentation (select-and-rank) stage and then generation. It is neither one-shot retrieve-then-plan nor tree-search/MCTS; retrieval and planning are tightly interleaved step by step, with explicit reflection on accumulated trajectory memory.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: per-step within a rollout: retrieval (a search-engine or browser tool call) is woven into reasoning at the granularity of each planning step (up to T steps), with reflection between steps. Not per-token/per-sentence; closer to per-tool-call / per-reasoning-step interleaving.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> N/A (not CBR): no retrieved-case adaptation. The closest analogue is the augmentation stage's LLM-based selection, summarization, and importance ranking of retrieved web evidence, plus iterative replanning/reflection over the trajectory - but this adapts a search strategy to observations, not a prior solved case to a new problem.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Structured note per webpage: each evidence item is injected as a (URL, query-relevant extracted/summarized content) record, sorted by importance. It is distilled free-text web content with provenance (URL), not raw full pages, executable programs, latent tokens, or abstract strategies.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw/lightly-distilled factual web evidence: the unit is concrete document/webpage content (snippets and extracted spans relevant to the query), optionally summarized. It is reference evidence, not a distilled strategy, guideline/rule, reusable workflow, or procedural skill.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Built into the framework and measured by the benchmark: (1) the augmentation stage's relevance selection + summarization + dedup + importance ranking is the primary noise-filtering mechanism; (2) the planning prompt instructs the agent to verify truthfulness and cross-check; (3) the benchmark explicitly quantifies failure to filter noise via Effective Evidence Utilization (EEU) and Information Compactness (IC), and surfaces a 'retrieval interference' phenomenon (model answers correctly without retrieval but wrongly after noisy retrieval) with a defined interference-rate metric. No trained retriever-aware/distractor-aware SFT module; robustness relies on the LLM's in-context filtering, which the paper shows is weak (EEU mostly <1).

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> episodic (per-query working memory only): the agent maintains a within-episode memory of all past plans, actions/queries, and observations (~4,000-char short-term memory) used for planning and reflection. There is no persistent skill-library, workflow, graph, or latent memory and no cross-query memory.
- **write back**: false: nothing is written to a persistent/retrievable store. The per-query trajectory memory is updated during an episode for planning/reflection but is discarded after the query; no cases/skills/experiences are saved for reuse on later queries.
- **online growth**: false: there is no retrievable store that grows during deployment. The external 'corpus' is the live web (changes independently of the agent, but the agent does not add to a controlled index), and the agent's episodic memory does not persist or accumulate across queries.
- **write back trigger**:
> never: the benchmark/framework performs no write-back of experiences. Within an episode the working memory is appended every step (plans, actions, observations) purely as transient context for the next planning/reflection step, but this is not persisted as a learned memory after the query, so there is no success/failure/reflective write-back to a durable store.
- **failure experience usage**:
> N/A / none: failed trajectories or wrong answers are not stored or retrieved as negative experiences. The paper analyzes failure phenomena (e.g., retrieval interference, fail cases for the unified prompting strategy) for scientific insight, but does not persist failures for contrastive or corrective retrieval.
- **memory evolution update**:
> Append-only within an episode (transient): the per-query trajectory memory is appended with each new plan/action/observation and used for reflection; no dedup-merge, delta-update, refine-overwrite, forget-prune, or link-and-evolve of a persistent store occurs (the augmentation stage does merge identical-URL evidence, but that is one-shot evidence-set construction, not memory evolution).
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No: retrieval/search and evidence selection are driven by a fixed, prompted LLM policy (plan-act-reflect) plus black-box search engines; there is no RL- or value-learned retrieval policy. The benchmark is designed to evaluate emergent agentic behavior of off-the-shelf LLMs, not to train a retrieval policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> No: single-agent, single-framework evaluation with private per-query memory. No memory/experience sharing across multiple agents or heterogeneous frameworks. (The benchmark does compare many different LLMs and search engines plugged into the same unified framework, but they do not share memory.)

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> InfoDeepSeek (introduced by this paper): 245 human-validated, challenging factual queries for agentic information seeking in the live web, each with >=2 of six difficulty attributes (Multi-Hop 188, Long-Tail 187, Time-Sensitive 162, Freshness 48, Distracting Information 76, False Premise 27), 14 domains, 19 predominant languages, provided in English and Chinese. Comparison table (Table 1) positions it against NQ, MultiHop-RAG, FreshLLM, RGB, CRAG, BrowseComp, and BrowseComp-ZH. Evaluated under the authors' InfoSeekAgents Agentic-RAG framework with four search engines (Google, Bing, Yahoo, DuckDuckGo).
- **benchmark family**:
> web / agentic search benchmark (open-web information seeking / Agentic RAG factual QA). Sits in the family of real-world web QA / browsing benchmarks (alongside BrowseComp, BrowseComp-ZH, FreshLLM/FreshQA, CRAG), distinguished by dynamic-environment evaluation rather than a static fixed corpus.
- **baselines**:
> No prior 'method' baselines (it is a benchmark); instead it benchmarks many LLM agents under a unified framework: Llama-4-Maverick-17B-128E-Instruct, Qwen3-32B (with/without thinking), DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-R1, GPT-4o, o3-mini, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Gemini-2.5-Pro. It also varies the search-engine backend (Google, Bing, Yahoo, DuckDuckGo) as a controlled factor and contrasts retrieval-augmented vs no-retrieval (parametric-only) behavior (retrieval interference).
- **key metrics**:
> Four core metrics: (1) Answer Accuracy (ACC) - LLM-judged correctness of the answer generated from all observations O; (2) Information Accuracy IA@k - correctness of an answer regenerated from only the top-k curated evidence C_{1:k}, a dynamic, gold-document-free measure of evidence quality (utility), reported for k=1..5; (3) Effective Evidence Utilization (EEU) = max_k IA@k / ACC, measuring how well the agent extracts/orders useful evidence (utility); (4) Information Compactness (IC) - evidence-set size relative to the human-annotated supporting-source count |S_q|, with a penalty for answer failures, measuring compactness/redundancy. Accuracy is via LLM-as-judge (DeepSeek-V3 + Gemini-2.0-Flash, GPT-4o-mini/human arbiter), achieving 99.29% agreement with human-eval after false-premise handling.
- **headline result**:
> Even SOTA LLMs perform poorly: the best model, Gemini-2.5-Pro, reaches only 22.45% ACC and 21.63% IA@5 under the default DuckDuckGo search engine (T=5, n=5). Search-engine quality dominates: switching Gemini-2.5-Flash from DuckDuckGo (14.29% ACC) to Google raises ACC to 34.29% (IA@3 37.55%), and DeepSeek-V3 jumps from 8.98% (DuckDuckGo) to 28.57% ACC with Google. EEU is mostly below 1 (agents fail to fully exploit retrieved evidence).
- **ablations**:
> (1) LLM comparison (Table 3): reasoning/search-optimized models lead (DeepSeek-R1 > DeepSeek-V3; o3-mini > GPT-4o; Gemini-2.5-Pro best at 22.45% ACC); IA@k rises then falls with k (later sources add distractors); EEU mostly <1; IC shows large redundancy (~3.7-4.0). (2) Search-engine ablation (Table 4): Google/Yahoo >> Bing > DuckDuckGo; a strong engine partly compensates for a weaker model. (3) Question-attribute breakdown (Fig 3): easier on false-premise/time-sensitive/freshness, hardest on multi-hop/long-tail/distracting-information; reasoning gains concentrate on easy attributes. (4) Test-time scaling (Fig 4): increasing max steps T from 1 to 20 monotonically improves ACC, IA@k, and IC. (5) Retrieval interference (Fig 5a): a measurable fraction of questions answered correctly from parametric knowledge become wrong after noisy retrieval. (6) Language impact (Fig 5b): English > Chinese; predominant-language-aware prompting best. (7) Impact of answer LLM (App D.6) and evaluation-prompt strategy for false premises (95.57% -> 99.29% agreement with humans).
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Yes - a central contribution: intrinsic information-seeking quality (IA@k evidence sufficiency, EEU utilization, IC compactness) is reported separately from end-to-end answer correctness (ACC). Crucially, because the web is dynamic, IA@k replaces static Recall@k/nDCG with a gold-document-free, answer-regeneration-based evidence-quality measure, explicitly decoupling retrieval/augmentation quality from final-answer accuracy.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both: outcome = ACC (final answer correctness). Process = IA@k (quality/sufficiency of the curated evidence), EEU (how well evidence is utilized/ordered), IC (compactness/redundancy of the seeking process), plus analyses of test-time scaling, retrieval interference, and per-attribute behavior. The framework is explicitly designed to assess the information-seeking process, not just the outcome.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Compute is studied as test-time scaling: varying max retrieval steps T from 1 to 20 trades more search compute for higher ACC/IA@k/IC (clear scaling effect). Information Compactness (IC) directly captures the retrieval-cost-vs-quality tradeoff (over-retrieval is penalized; IC values ~3.3-4.0 indicate substantial redundancy relative to the 1-3 truly needed sources). Default budget: T<=5 steps, evidence set <=5 webpages, ~4,000-char working memory. No dollar/latency/token-count figures are reported per query; dataset construction cost is noted as manual/expensive but not quantified in dollars.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Adaptive, budget-capped selection: the agent dynamically chooses evidence-set size n_q up to a hard cap n=5 (chosen because human-annotated supporting sources |S_q| typically range 1-3), and ranks-then-truncates the candidate webpages by importance. Working memory is capped at ~4,000 characters; retrieval is capped at T<=5 steps by default (ablated 1-20). So selection count is variable but bounded, with reranked-then-truncated context.
- **survey scope and axes**: N/A (not a survey).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> Size: 245 high-quality validated queries (HuggingFace InfoDeepSeek_v1), 14 domains, 19 predominant languages (English + Chinese dominant; 17 others incl. Japanese 11, Russian 9, Korean 8, Italian 6, Arabic 6, French 5, etc.), each query >=2 of six difficulty attributes (Multi-Hop 188, Long-Tail 187, Time-Sensitive 162, Freshness 48, Distracting-Info 76, False-Premise 27). Construction: human-curated via reverse construction (start from authoritative/multilingual web knowledge, write a uniquely-answerable question), 'expand from anchor knowledge' (compose long-tail/distracting anchors with extra hops/attributes), and diversification; two filters (determinacy/verifiability check + difficulty filter discarding any question both GPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1 solve via single-turn web search); multi-stage validation by two verifiers + a third adjudicator; 7 annotators. Each query stores ground-truth answer y_q, supporting source webpages S_q, and metadata. Answer verifiability: high - deterministic, time-invariant, uniquely-answerable factual answers, scored by LLM-as-judge (99.29% agreement with humans). Difficulty signal: best system (Gemini-2.5-Pro) only 22.45% ACC under DuckDuckGo (and ~34% with Google), confirming the benchmark is hard.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Builds on the standard three-stage RAG formulation (retrieval/augmentation/generation; Gao et al. RAG survey, ref 42) extended into Agentic RAG by inserting an autonomous plan-act-reflect LLM agent (ReAct-style planning/reflection). Uses real-world web-QA difficulty notions from FreshLLM/FreshQA, CRAG, RGB, MultiHop-RAG and the browsing-benchmark line BrowseComp / BrowseComp-ZH. Inspired by deployed agentic deep-research products (OpenAI Deep Research, Gemini, Perplexity). Evaluates contemporary LLM agents (GPT-4o, o3-mini, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, DeepSeek-V3/R1, Gemini-2.5-Flash/Pro, Llama-4-Maverick, Qwen3-32B).
- **contrasts with**:
> Explicitly contrasts with static, fixed-corpus RAG/QA benchmarks and gold-document retrieval metrics: NQ, TriviaQA, MS MARCO, MultiHop-RAG, RGB, CRAG, FreshLLM/FreshQA (Table 1). Versus real-web browsing benchmarks BrowseComp and BrowseComp-ZH, InfoDeepSeek adds dynamic-environment information-seeking evaluation (Dyna.Eval.), LLM-based difficulty filtering, and the full set of six difficulty attributes (freshness, time-sensitivity, distracting info, false premise) that those lack. It contrasts gold-set Recall@k/nDCG (infeasible in dynamic web) with its IA@k / EEU / IC framework.
- **lineage**:
> Surveys/benchmarks line (evaluation infrastructure for retrieval-augmented agents): a benchmark + evaluation-framework contribution for Agentic RAG / agentic information seeking. It extends the RAG-benchmark lineage (NQ/TriviaQA -> RGB/CRAG/MultiHop-RAG/FreshQA -> BrowseComp/BrowseComp-ZH) into dynamic open-web, agent-driven, gold-document-free evaluation, and provides process-level metrics (IA@k/EEU/IC) for the retrieval+augmentation stages of agentic RAG systems.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- venue

<a id="item-tool-learning-survey-springer"></a>
### 170. LLM-Based Agents for Tool Learning: A Survey (Xu et al.)

2025  ·  Data Science and Engineering (Springer)  ·  [paper](https://doi.org/10.1007/s41019-025-00296-9)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**: Data Science and Engineering (Springer), Volume 10, pages 533-563, published 26 June 2025; open access; DBLP journals/dase/XuHGS25
- **authors affiliation**: Weikai Xu, Chengrui Huang, Shen Gao, Shuo Shang. All authors: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China (UESTC), Chengdu, China.
- **paper url**: https://doi.org/10.1007/s41019-025-00296-9

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: tool-use (tool learning by LLM-based agents): the survey covers tool invocation timing, tool retrieval/selection, tool planning, multimodal tools, downstream applications (data science, software engineering, web/mobile, robotics), benchmarks/metrics, and safety/ethics.
- **problem setting**:
> Survey/taxonomy of LLM-based tool-learning agents. The problem is framed via the 'Three Ws': Whether to invoke a tool, Which tool(s) to retrieve, and HoW to use them. Settings span single-agent and multi-agent frameworks, interactive (environment-feedback / reflection loops) and offline-trained pipelines, with both training-based (supervised fine-tuning on open-source LLMs) and non-training (in-context / prompting on closed-source LLMs such as GPT-4) approaches. A canonical agent framework is defined with five components (executor, perceiver, validator, controller, retriever) operating iteratively over a toolset and environment until subtasks are resolved.
- **what is retrieved**: tools / APIs (and their documentation: tool background knowledge + query-tool-invocation-response demonstration triplets). Secondarily, demonstrations/exemplars for in-context tool use are retrieved for non-fine-tuned LLMs.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus of user-defined tools/APIs (e.g., RapidAPI hub, HuggingFace/TensorFlow/Torch Hub model APIs, RESTful APIs). The survey notes tool documentation grows outdated and discusses methods to integrate new tools, but the dominant grounding is a static/user-defined tool repository rather than agent-written growing memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Mixed/both. The survey describes top-k structured retrieval (greedy/staged search, rerank-then-truncate) and emphasizes cross-category then in-category comparative screening to recover the correct (possibly multiple) tools for multi-tool tasks; it discusses one-to-many API mapping where Recall (completeness of the needed set) matters beyond single-instance accuracy.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The survey does not frame tool learning as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; reflection and demonstration reuse are discussed under their own terminology.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> tool-API (the primary retrievable unit), together with tool documentation (background description + demonstration triplets). For non-trained LLMs, single demonstrations/exemplars are also retrieved. ToolkenGPT treats tools as special tokens ('toolkens') predicted in the generation stream (tool-as-token granularity).
- **index source**:
> Static external tool corpora: virtual API servers (StableToolBench cache+simulator) and real APIs (RapidAPI hub with 16k+ APIs, HuggingFace/TensorFlow/Torch Hub, RESTful services, OpenAI plugin lists). The survey notes documentation can become outdated and discusses auto-integration of new tools, but the store is predominantly offline/user-defined rather than agent-grown.
- **index structure topology**:
> Mostly hierarchical/category-keyed: ToolLLM structures RapidAPI into hierarchical tree (coarse-grained category -> fine-grained sub-category -> tool/API) enabling tree-search retrieval (DFSDT, MCTS). Flat dense vector indices are also used (dual-encoder retrievers). Tool dependency / invocation-sequence structures are noted (ToolChain* stores invocation sequences).
- **retriever type**:
> Hybrid across the surveyed works: dense dual-encoder retrievers, classification/generative tool prediction (ToolkenGPT tool-as-token via toolken embeddings), tree/graph search-based retrieval (DFSDT, MCTS, A* in ToolChain*), and LLM-as-retriever/selector via prompting (AutoGPT, HuggingGPT). Cross-encoder rerankers are used downstream (ToolRerank).
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Multiple, organized by the survey's training-based vs non-training-based split: (1) none / off-the-shelf in-context (closed-source LLMs prompted with documentation+demonstrations); (2) supervised fine-tuning with coarse/fine-grained classification + API classification losses (ToolLLM); (3) curriculum / introspective-feedback iterative data construction (Confucius ISIF, easy-to-difficult); (4) self-play / data-augmentation bootstrapping (TALM); (5) knowledge distillation from teacher LLMs (ToRA); (6) toolken-embedding training on contextual examples (ToolkenGPT).
- **query construction**:
> Intent extraction from the user command (intent distribution model / semantic analysis), then task decomposition into subtasks; each subtask becomes a structured retrieval query within the toolset. Documentation may be expanded/standardized (EASYTOOL compression) and retrieved API docs are concatenated into the prompt (Gorilla) to condition subsequent reasoning.
- **query granularity**: Both task-level and subtask/step-level: the controller decomposes the user query into multi-step subtasks, and retrieval is performed per subtask (one tool per subtask in the ideal decomposition), so queries are constructed at trajectory/step granularity over the iterative loop.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Both one-shot and iterative depending on the method. The canonical framework is iterative: the controller/retriever progressively narrows the candidate tool pool over rounds based on perceiver feedback and validator reflection until all subtasks are resolved. The 'Whether' (tool invocation timing) decision governs whether retrieval is triggered at all.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Tool-invocation necessity judgment ('Whether'): Toolformer's criterion is whether the model can answer correctly without a tool; AnyTool/Du extends this to first check whether the current toolset even contains a useful tool, weighing invocation cost vs task-resolution efficiency. In the iterative framework, the controller re-triggers retrieval based on perceiver feedback and validator reflection (agent-initiated, feedback-conditioned).
- **reranking**:
> Yes. ToolRerank (ToolReranker) performs adaptive and hierarchy-aware reranking: a dual-encoder retriever produces coarse-grained candidates, Adaptive Truncation cuts the list, then a cross-encoder reranker reranks the truncated set; it is reported to outperform ToolLLM in search efficiency by avoiding multi-round feedback evaluation. Functional reranking by the controller is also noted.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Documentation engineering and reranking: EASYTOOL compresses/standardizes heterogeneous tool documentation (addressing inconsistency/redundancy) and auto-fills/validates parameters; rerank-then-truncate (ToolRerank Adaptive Truncation); Hsieh et al. show tool documentation enables zero-shot usage. The survey explicitly catalogs documentation issues: inconsistency, redundancy, incompleteness, impracticality.
- **tool document engineering**:
> Central theme. Tool documentation = (1) background knowledge (functionality + parameter definitions) and (2) demonstration examples (query-invocation-response triplets). Engineering levers surveyed: text compression/standardization (EASYTOOL), retrieved-doc concatenation into prompts (Gorilla), auto-integration of new tools (Hsieh et al.), and toolken-embedding learning (ToolkenGPT). Four documentation pathologies are named: inconsistency, redundancy, incompleteness, impracticality.
- **index content separation**:
> Partially: the hierarchical category->subcategory->tool index (ToolLLM) and coarse-retrieve-then-rerank-then-truncate (ToolRerank) effectively separate a lightweight candidate index from heavier per-tool documentation/invocation loaded on demand; ToolChain* stores invocation sequences for evaluation. Not framed as explicit progressive-disclosure but the pattern is present.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> The survey discusses multiple integration protocols across surveyed works: RapidAPI hub, RESTful APIs (RestGPT/RestBench), HuggingFace model invocation (HuggingGPT), and function/token-level invocation (ToolkenGPT). It flags that static documentation becomes outdated and that real APIs fluctuate (motivating StableToolBench's virtual API server with cache+simulator). MCP is not discussed (predates/outside the 2022.6-2024.5 coverage window). No CRUD auto-sync mechanism is standardized.
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> Yes, acknowledged: the survey stresses inter-tool dependencies and invocation order (e.g., latitude/longitude must be obtained before elevation), and notes cross-category then in-category comparison; ToolChain* stores and compares tool invocation sequences (maximum common subsequence) to capture dependency/ordering, and tree-search planners (ToolLLM DFSDT/MCTS, ToolChain* A*) navigate dependency-laden action spaces.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation (retrieved API documentation concatenated into the prompt, Gorilla; demonstration triplets for in-context tool use), latent-token injection (ToolkenGPT toolken embeddings predicted inline then replaced by invocation results), and as a training signal (fine-tuning on retrieved/augmented tool-use corpora). Retrieved tools are then executed by the executor against the environment with parsed feedback.
- **planning integration**:
> Both retrieve-then-plan and plan-then-retrieve, and retrieval embedded inside search loops. Internal planners use decomposition (CoT, ReAct, CoA), selection (CoT-SC, ToT, GoT, ToolChain* tree/A* search), and clustering; external planners formalize tasks for symbolic solvers (LLM+P/PDDL, LLM-DP with BFS, AutoGPT+P) or neural planners. ToolLLM interleaves retrieval with MCTS/DFSDT over the hierarchical API tree.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Per-tool-call / per-subtask within the iterative controller-perceiver-validator-retriever loop; ReAct interleaves reasoning+action per step; CoA fills abstract placeholders with tool calls per reasoning chain. Tree/graph-of-thought methods interleave at the per-thought/per-branch level.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Surface forms surveyed: raw/standardized tool documentation text (description + demonstration triplets) injected into the prompt; executable API calls / function tokens (ToolkenGPT toolkens; Toolformer <API>...</API> translated calls embedded in text); reasoning chains with abstract placeholders reified by tool outputs (CoA).
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Predominantly single tool/API + its documentation (a concrete callable unit) and single demonstrations; ToolkenGPT abstracts tools to special tokens; CoA abstracts to placeholder-and-reify reasoning chains. Not distilled strategies/skills in the experience-memory sense.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Validator/self-reflection (unsupervised and supervised-external) to catch wrong parameters/returns; documentation standardization (EASYTOOL) to reduce noisy/redundant docs; staged curriculum training (Confucius) to distinguish similar tools; and dedicated robustness benchmarks (RoTBench five noise levels: Clean/Slight/Medium/Heavy/Union across tool selection, parameter recognition, content generation; Noisy-ToolBench for ambiguous instructions; InjecAgent for indirect prompt-injection attacks).

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> none / not a memory-centric framework. The surveyed canonical framework keeps an invocation history H_t within the controller loop and uses reflection, but it is not organized as episodic/skill-library/graph long-term memory; the retrievable store is a static tool repository, not an agent-written experience memory.
- **write back**:
> False (no general experience write-back to a growing memory). Exceptions noted in cited works: TALM self-play and Confucius ISIF dynamically construct/augment training data; ToRA reintegrates corrected outputs into the training set; GitAgent (cited) autonomously extends its toolset from GitHub. These are training-data/toolset growth, not test-time experience memory.
- **online growth**:
> Largely no for the retrievable store at deployment; the survey emphasizes that toolsets and documentation become outdated and discusses auto-integration of new tools (Hsieh et al.) and toolset extension (GitAgent), but the dominant setting is a frozen offline tool corpus. StableToolBench freezes API behavior via a cache+simulator for stable evaluation.
- **write back trigger**:
> never (for experience memory) in the canonical framework. Where data/toolset growth occurs in cited works it is training-time and reflective/iterative: Confucius ISIF updates training data based on model introspective feedback; TALM bootstraps via self-play; ToRA reintegrates after error detection/correction (success-and-failure-aware correction). No standardized per-step/human-validated experience write rule.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Partially via output-space correction at training time: ToRA systematically detects errors in generated tool-invocation outputs and corrects (manual/automatic) them before reintegration, mitigating error propagation; reflection deletes/updates incorrect tools at inference. Failures are corrective signals rather than stored failure cases for retrieval.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Mixed: many surveyed retrievers are learned (supervised classification-based tool retrieval in ToolLLM, toolken prediction in ToolkenGPT, curriculum-trained Confucius), and tree-search planners (DFSDT/MCTS, ToolChain* A*) use learned/heuristic value evaluation, but a substantial portion is fixed similarity top-k (dense dual-encoder) or prompt-based selection. No RL-as-retrieval-policy (e.g., soft Q-learning M-MDP) is centrally featured; online RL environments are flagged only as future work.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Discussed mainly via multi-agent frameworks where specialized agents (planner/caller/summarizer in Shen et al.; code-writer/executor in MechAgents) collaborate and a stronger agent provides external reflection. This is role-specialized collaboration rather than shared retrievable experience memory across heterogeneous frameworks; cross-framework experience sharing is not a focus.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> API-Bank; APIBench (Gorilla, 16,460 instructions); ToolBench/ToolLLM (16,464 RapidAPI APIs); ToolAlpaca (400+ APIs, 3938 instances); RestBench (IMDB, Spotify); UltraTool (2032 tools, 22 domains); ToolTalk (7 plugins, 28 tools, 78 dialogues/178 turns); StableToolBench; ToolEyes (~600 tools, 7 scenarios, 5 dimensions); MLLM-Tool / Tool-LMM (932 model APIs from HuggingFace); RoTBench (5 noise levels); InjecAgent (1054 cases, 17 user + 62 attack tools); Noisy-ToolBench (100 RESTful APIs, 1000 ambiguous instructions); ToolQA (8 fields, easy/hard); MetaTool/TOOLE (390 tools); MenatQA (2853 temporal samples); T-eval; plus general datasets (GSM8K). Safety: AdvBench, ToolSword.
- **benchmark family**:
> tool (ToolBench/ToolLLM, StableToolBench, API-Bank, APIBench/Gorilla, ToolAlpaca, RestBench, UltraTool, ToolTalk, ToolEyes, T-eval, MetaTool, ToolQA); multimodal-tool (MLLM-Tool/Tool-LMM); robustness/safety-tool (RoTBench, InjecAgent, Noisy-ToolBench, AdvBench, ToolSword); QA/reasoning auxiliaries (GSM8K, MenatQA).
- **baselines**:
> N/A as a survey (no single set of methods is run head-to-head).
