The reviewed/compared method families include: ToolLLM, Confucius, ToolRerank, Gorilla, TALM, ToRA, ToolkenGPT, CoA, Toolformer, HuggingGPT, RestGPT, AutoGPT, EASYTOOL, ToolChain*, AnyTool, ReAct, CoT/CoT-SC, ToT, GoT, LLM+P/LLM-DP/AutoGPT+P, and multi-agent frameworks (Shen et al., MechAgents). Backbone LLMs referenced include GPT-4 / ChatGPT and open-source models.
- **key metrics**:
> Pass Rate and Pass Rate* (ToolLLM/ToolBench); Win Rate; Accuracy and Recall (one-to-many API mapping); ROUGE-L and Plan Score (T-eval) and MD Point-Wise (UltraTool, 6 dimensions) for plan quality; AST sub-tree matching and Levenshtein Distance for parameter filling; Correct Selection Rate (CSR, MetaTool); Hallucination Rate (MLLM-Tool). Manual, advanced-model (LLM-as-judge), and objective indicators are all catalogued.
- **ablations**:
> N/A (survey runs no experiments/ablations of its own). It instead analytically contrasts component choices: training-based vs non-training tool retrieval; greedy vs staged-curriculum search; rerank-then-truncate vs multi-round feedback (ToolRerank reported more search-efficient than ToolLLM); internal vs external (symbolic/neural) planners; single-agent vs multi-agent reflection; virtual vs real toolsets.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Yes, conceptually. The survey separates metric categories: (1) task completion (Pass Rate, Win Rate, Accuracy, Recall), (2) output quality (plan quality: ROUGE-L/Plan Score/MD Point-Wise; parameter filling: AST matching/Levenshtein), (3) tool selection/invocation (CSR), and (4) robustness/error-handling (Hallucination Rate). Intrinsic selection/retrieval quality (CSR, Recall) is thus distinguished from end-to-end completion.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both. Beyond final-outcome Pass/Win Rate, the survey highlights process/intermediate metrics: step-wise Plan Score and ROUGE-L for plan quality, AST/Levenshtein for per-parameter correctness, CSR for tool-selection correctness, and MD Point-Wise scoring across accuracy/completeness/executability/syntactic soundness/structural rationality/efficiency.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Discussed qualitatively: tool-invocation cost vs task efficiency drives the 'Whether-to-invoke' decision (AnyTool/Du); ToolRerank reduces search cost by avoiding multi-round feedback evaluation; StableToolBench cache/simulator reduces real-API cost/instability; documentation redundancy (RapidAPI) inflates token consumption; ToolChain* navigates action space more efficiently with A* search. No standardized cost numbers across works.
- **survey scope and axes**:
> Organizing axes: (1) the 'Three Ws' task definition (Whether / Which / HoW); (2) a 5-component agent framework (executor, perceiver, validator, controller, retriever); (3) Learning to Use Tools split into training-based (calculation / translation / retrieval, with greedy/staged/rerank/data-augmentation) vs non-training (in-context / documentation); (4) Tool Planning split into internal (decomposition/selection/clustering) vs external (symbolic/neural) planners; (5) multimodal tools; (6) applications; (7) benchmarks (by task complexity, toolset type, special scenarios) and metrics (4 categories); (8) safety/ethics + future directions. Reference count: 166 references; coverage window for the work-summary tree diagram: 2022.6 to 2024.5.
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> The survey catalogs construction methods/sizes of others' benchmarks rather than building one: e.g., APIBench 16,460 LLM-generated API instructions; ToolBench 16,464 real RapidAPI APIs with ChatGPT-generated instructions; ToolAlpaca 3938 instances over 400+ APIs (simulated); UltraTool 2032 tools across 22 domains; ToolTalk 78 dialogues/178 turns; InjecAgent 1054 cases; Noisy-ToolBench 100 APIs/1000 expert-written ambiguous instructions; MLLM-Tool 932 filtered model APIs; ToolQA spanning 8 fields. Answer verifiability ranges from LLM-generated-then-human-annotated (API-Bank) to virtual-server-stabilized (StableToolBench).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Foundational tool-learning and reasoning works it synthesizes: Toolformer (self-supervised tool-call insertion), ToolLLM/ToolBench (16k+ API retrieval with DFSDT), Gorilla/APIBench, HuggingGPT, RestGPT, ReAct, Chain-of-Thought, Tree/Graph-of-Thoughts, ToolkenGPT, CoA, Confucius, ToolRerank, EASYTOOL, ToolChain*, LLM+P/PDDL planners. It positions itself relative to prior tool-learning surveys (e.g., Qin et al. 'Tool learning with foundation models').
- **contrasts with**:
> Prior LLM-agent / tool-learning surveys it complements/distinguishes from: Qin et al. 'Tool learning with foundation models' (ACM CSUR); Xinzhe Li's 'A Review of Prominent Paradigms for LLM-Based Agents: Tool Use, Planning (incl. RAG), and Feedback Learning'; planning surveys (Huang et al. 'Understanding the planning of LLM agents'); multimodal-agent surveys. This survey is distinguished by its 'Three Ws' framing, the explicit five-component agent framework, the training-based vs non-training retrieval dichotomy, and a dedicated benchmarks+metrics compilation.
- **lineage**:
> Surveys group (anchors group E: tool retrieval, selection, and the benchmark landscape). It is a peer-reviewed (Data Science and Engineering) anchor for the tool-learning / tool-retrieval sub-topic, providing taxonomy and benchmark/metric scaffolding that situates method papers on tool retrieval, reranking, dependency-aware selection, and tool benchmarks.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- adaptation_mechanism
- cbr_cycle_coverage
- code_url
- context_budget_and_selection_count
- headline_result
- maintained_repo_url
- memory_evolution_update

<a id="item-memory-in-age-of-agents"></a>
### 171. Memory in the Age of AI Agents (Hu et al.)

2025  ·  arXiv 2512.13564  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13564)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**: arXiv preprint, arXiv:2512.13564 [cs.CL] (also cs.AI). v1 submitted 2025-12-15; v2 revised 2026-01-13. CoRR/DBLP record DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2512-13564. Not peer-reviewed at time of writing (preprint).
- **authors affiliation**:
> Yuyang Hu, Shichun Liu, Yanwei Yue, Guibin Zhang (the four daggered/listed-alphabetically core contributors; Guibin Zhang is the project organizer), Boyang Liu, Fangyi Zhu, Jiahang Lin, Honglin Guo, Shihan Dou, Zhiheng Xi, ... and 47 authors total, with core supervisors Tao Gui, Yan Zhang, and senior authors including Wangchunshu Zhou, Yixin Liu, Dawei Cheng, Qi Zhang, Shirui Pan, Philip Torr, Zhicheng Dou, Ji-Rong Wen, Xuanjing Huang, Yu-Gang Jiang, Shuicheng Yan. Affiliations: National University of Singapore, Renmin University of China, Fudan University, Peking University, Nanyang Technological University, Tongji University, University of California San Diego, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou), Griffith University, Georgia Institute of Technology, OPPO, Oxford University.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13564
- **code url**: N/A (a survey; no method code). Curated paper-list repository is maintained instead (see maintained_repo_url).
- **maintained repo url**:
> https://github.com/Shichun-Liu/Agent-Memory-Paper-List (official 'Agent-Memory-Paper-List', ~2.1k stars, MIT license; organizes papers by the forms x functions x dynamics taxonomy under Factual / Experiential / Working Memory each split into Token-level / Parametric / Latent; last major commit 2026-03-03, README updated through 2026-02-10).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Survey/taxonomy of memory for foundation-model-based (LLM) agents, spanning conversation/long-term dialogue, personalization, multi-source/multi-hop QA, deep research, web navigation, desktop/mobile GUI agents, embodied/game environments, code/software engineering, recommendation, role-playing, and multi-agent systems (an anchor agent-memory survey, not a single-task method).
- **problem setting**:
> An up-to-date, comprehensive survey aiming to de-fragment the rapidly expanding agent-memory field. It first delineates the SCOPE of agent memory and explicitly distinguishes it from LLM memory, RAG, and context engineering, then organizes the literature through the unified 'Forms-Functions-Dynamics' triangle. Settings covered are predominantly interactive, multi-turn, long-horizon agent-environment loops (single- and multi-agent), where memory enables long-horizon reasoning, continual adaptation, personalization, and self-evolution. It formalizes a memory state M_t updated by three lifecycle operators Formation F, Evolution E, Retrieval R within the agent loop (policy a_t = pi(o_t, m_t, Q)). The survey proposes no new method, dataset, or experiments; it offers a unified conceptual framework, a benchmark/framework compilation (Tables 8-9), and a forward-looking positions/frontiers section.
- **what is retrieved**:
> Across surveyed systems: factual knowledge (dialogue facts, user profiles, KG triples, documents), experiential traces (raw trajectories, reflections, distilled insights/workflows/rule-templates, procedural skills), and working-memory content (active context, intermediate states, tool outputs, summaries). The survey frames retrieval (operator R) as returning a context-dependent memory signal m_t for the LLM policy.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> HYBRID / primarily GROWING memory. The survey's defining position is that agent memory is a persistent, evolving store the agent writes and updates over multi-turn, multi-task interaction (vs RAG's static external corpus for single-task invocation). It explicitly notes graph-based agent memory 'constructs, extends, or reorganizes' itself throughout operation, treating the store as a 'living, evolving representation of experience'; static external knowledge (docs/KB) is covered but framed as the RAG boundary case.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (a survey, not a CBR method). The surveyed lifecycle (Formation / Evolution / Retrieval) plus experiential reuse maps loosely onto CBR Retain/Revise/Retrieve/Reuse, but the survey does not use CBR phase terminology.
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False - the survey frames memory via cognitive science (declarative memory: episodic vs semantic; multicomponent / embedded-processes working-memory models) and its own forms/functions/dynamics taxonomy. It does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Survey taxonomy of memory units rather than one unit. By FORM: token-level discrete units (chunks, dialogue logs, experience pools, tree/graph nodes, KG triples/subgraphs, hierarchical pyramids), parametric units (weight edits, adapters/LoRA modules), latent units (KV-cache, soft/continuous memory tokens, hidden states). By FUNCTION: factual entries (facts, profiles, documents), experiential entries (trajectories, reflections, workflows, rules, skills), working-memory entries (active context, intermediate states). Retrieved 'reading' units span snippet / dialogue segment / full trajectory / distilled insight / KG-subgraph / document / latent token.
- **index source**:
> Hybrid construction. The store is primarily a GROWING memory written/evolved online during multi-turn, multi-task interaction (formation + evolution operators), optionally seeded with cross-trial information distilled from prior trajectories; static external knowledge (RAG-style corpora) is covered as the boundary case. Short-term vs long-term memory phenomena are framed as emerging from temporal invocation patterns of F/E/R rather than fixed modules.
- **index structure topology**:
> Survey taxonomizes token-level topology by complexity/dimensionality: Flat (1D: chunk sets, dialogue logs, experience pools), Planar (2D: single-layer Tree or Graph structures), and Hierarchical (3D: Pyramids and Multi-layer graphs for vertical abstraction). Concrete topologies reviewed: flat vector stores, knowledge/temporal-knowledge graphs (Zep, AriGraph, HippoRAG, EMG-RAG, G-Memory three-tier hierarchy), structured profiles/relational DBs, hierarchical OS-style memory (MemGPT main/external; MemoryOS S/M/LTM), and tree/community-graph indices (GraphRAG). Parametric and latent forms have their own (non-index) organizations.
- **retriever type**:
> Survey-level taxonomy of retrieval strategies: Lexical (TF-IDF, BM25), Semantic/dense (Sentence-BERT, CLIP; 'default choice in most agentic memory frameworks'), Graph retrieval (node/triple seeding + K-hop ego-graph expansion, personalized PageRank in HippoRAG, LLM-steered subgraph exploration, temporal-graph retrieval), Generative retrieval (DSI/tool-as-token; noted as under-explored in agent memory), and Hybrid (lexical+semantic, e.g., Agent KB, MIRIX; multi-factor scoring as in Generative Agents' recency/importance/relevance). No single canonical retriever is proposed.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Survey-level: most reviewed retrieval is off-the-shelf (lexical/dense similarity, heuristic recency/importance/relevance scoring). Trainable/learned variants are surveyed: Rewrite-Retrieve-Read trains a small RL rewriter; the survey's Frontiers section (RL integration) charts a progression from RL-free heuristic/prompt pipelines, to partially RL-involved designs governing selected memory operations (e.g., Memory-R1, MemSearcher, MemAgent, Mem-alpha), to envisioned fully RL-driven memory where architectures and control policies are learned end-to-end. The survey itself proposes no learned retriever.
- **query construction**:
> Survey-level: query construction is treated as a 'translation layer' between the user's surface utterance and the memory index, via (a) direct raw-query retrieval (simple baseline), (b) Query Decomposition into sub-queries (Visconde, ChemAgent; planner-driven in PRIME/MA-RAG; failure-aware fine-grained sub-queries in Agent KB), and (c) Query Rewriting / hypothetical-document generation (HyDE; MemoRAG conditions on compressed global memory; MemGuide produces command-like intent phrases; ToC tree-of-clarifications; RL-trained rewriter).
- **query granularity**:
> Survey-level: spans task-level (one-shot retrieval at t=0), step/state-level (intermittent or continuous retrieval on contextual triggers during reasoning), and decomposed sub-query level (multiple sub-queries per task). The survey formalizes this with a piecewise retrieval schedule and does not standardize a single granularity.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Survey-level: ranges from always-on retrieval (e.g., MIRIX retrieves from all six memory stores per query) to selectively/agent-triggered retrieval. The survey's 'Retrieval Timing and Intent' section reviews one-shot (t=0 only), intermittent/continuous, and adaptive (model- or controller-decided) triggering; no single policy is prescribed.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Survey-level taxonomy under 'Automated Retrieval Timing and Intent': (a) LLM/controller-decided from the query alone (MemGPT, MemTool invoke retrieval functions OS-style), (b) fast-slow / cognitive-state-aware triggering that integrates the model's evolving reasoning state (to fix the limitation of query-only static judgments), and (c) automated retrieval INTENT selecting WHICH store to access (AgentRR switches between low-level procedural templates and high-level experiential abstractions on environmental feedback). The survey warns of a 'silent failure mode' when the agent over-trusts internal knowledge and fails to trigger retrieval, causing hallucination.
- **reranking**:
> Survey-level: reranking is identified as one of the four phases of the retrieval pipeline (Post-Retrieval Processing: re-ranking, filtering, aggregation) and as a key lever in modular RAG and in mitigating semantic-drift/forced-top-K noise. Multi-factor scoring (recency+importance+relevance in Generative Agents; mixed-utility in MAICC) and two-stage graph reranking (semantic node retrieval then topology expansion) are surveyed. No single reranker is proposed.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Survey-level: Post-Retrieval Processing is an explicit pipeline phase covering re-ranking, filtering (distractor/noise suppression, token pruning, importance-based selection), and aggregation of decomposed sub-query results; compression/summarization and reason-in-documents-style draft generation (MemoRAG) are also covered. Refinement is framed as filtering noise while providing essential information 'at the right moments.'
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (memory survey; tool/skill-description engineering is largely out of scope, though tool-use experience, ToolMem learnable tool-capability memory, and tool-output memory are mentioned as experiential memory and as memory-relevant signals in tool benchmarks like ToolBench).
- **index content separation**:
> Covered: OS/virtual-context memory separates a small active/working context from a larger external store paged on demand (MemGPT main vs external context; MemoryOS short/mid/long-term; MemOS tree memory + memcube). Hierarchical/pyramid forms keep detailed traces for the active subgoal while compressing completed subgoals into higher-level summaries that are selectively retrieved (HAgent, ILM-TR). Treated as a forms/working-memory pattern rather than a formal index-vs-content principle.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (inter-tool dependency modeling is out of scope for this memory survey).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Survey-level: retrieved memory signal m_t is formatted for direct consumption by the LLM policy (prompt augmentation as textual snippets or structured summary), and across forms is also used as latent-token injection (latent memory interfering with/augmenting the forward pass; KV-cache reuse), parametric internalization (weight edits/adapters as implicit memory), experiential reuse (workflows/skills/rules guiding new tasks), and training signal (RL-optimized memory control in the frontiers section).
- **planning integration**:
> Survey-level: memory supplies context for planning/acting at varied points - one-shot at task initialization, intermittent/continuous per-step retrieval, planner-agent-driven global retrieval plans before sub-query decomposition (PRIME, MA-RAG inspired by ReAct), subgoal-level hierarchical working memory (HAgent), and beam-search planning over KG memory (D-SMART). The survey abstracts this via the agent loop a_t = pi(o_t, m_t, Q) with flexible memory-agent coupling rather than one integration scheme.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Survey-level: spans per-answer (single retrieval at t=0), per-step/per-turn (intermittent or continuous retrieval triggered by contextual/cognitive state), per-sub-query (decomposed retrieval-then-aggregate), and iterative refinement loops (ILM-TR inner loop until evidence/answer stabilize). Not standardized to one granularity.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (a survey, not a CBR adaptation method). The closest analogues surveyed are Evolution-operator mechanisms (consolidation, conflict resolution, refinement) and experiential abstraction of trajectories into reflections/workflows/rules, plus RL-driven memory updating.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Survey-level: organized by FORM into Token-level (explicit, discrete, human-readable text: raw dialogue, summaries, reflections, workflows, rule-templates, KG triples, executable skills), Parametric (information encoded into model weights via fine-tuning, model editing, or attached adapters/LoRA - implicit), and Latent (hidden-state / soft continuous memory tokens / KV-cache - operating in the model's internal representational space). Surface forms thus range from raw trajectory to distilled strategy/workflow to executable program/skill to latent soft tokens.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Survey-level spectrum, explicitly highlighted: raw observations/dialogue at the lowest level; distilled reflections/insights and high-level 'thought-templates', universal workflows, and rule templates (e.g., Reflexion's self-reflection long-term memory; AWM workflows); procedural skills; and structured semantic/relational abstractions (KG world models, hierarchical schemata). The survey frames a progressive raw -> abstracted continuum, especially for experiential memory.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Survey-level: noise robustness is addressed via Post-Retrieval Processing (filtering distractors, token pruning, importance-based selection, reranking), external evaluators that filter redundant/inconclusive content during summarization (convolutional consistency discriminator; DeBERTa filtering), conflict resolution and consolidation in the Evolution operator, online LLM filtering (HippoRAG 2), and balancing retrieval timing to avoid both knowledge gaps (silent-failure hallucination) and excessive-retrieval noise. RL-trained summarization (PPO/GRPO in Mem1, MemAgent) is also surveyed.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> Survey/taxonomy covering all listed types via the FORM x FUNCTION matrix. Functions: Factual (knowledge/facts/profiles ~ semantic), Experiential (insights, workflows, skills, reflections ~ episodic+procedural), and Working memory (active context management). Forms: Token-level (episodic/skill-library/workflow/graph realizations), Parametric, and Latent. It deliberately moves beyond the coarse long/short-term temporal split.
- **write back**:
> True (survey-level) - the Formation operator (F: M_t, phi_t -> M^form) creates new memory artifacts and the Evolution operator (E) integrates/consolidates them; write-back of facts, experiences, profiles, workflows, and skills is central across surveyed systems (Mem0, MemGPT, A-MEM, Reflexion/ExpeL, AWM, ReasoningBank, etc.).
- **online growth**:
> Yes (survey-level) - a defining property distinguishing agent memory from single-task RAG: memory grows and is reorganized online during multi-turn, multi-task deployment (long-term memory updated episodically at task boundaries or continuously throughout operation). Graph memory is explicitly described as a 'living, evolving representation of experience.'
- **write back trigger**:
> Survey-level taxonomy: per-step accumulation (minimal logging M_{t+1} = M_t U {o_t}), at task boundaries (episodic long-term updates), reflective/self-critique writing (Reflexion, reflection mechanisms), incremental semantic summarization (chunk-by-chunk fusion in MemGPT/Mem0; RL-enhanced in Mem1/MemAgent), and learned/RL-governed memory construction (Memory-R1, Mem-alpha). No single trigger is prescribed; the survey notes triggers range from always-on to selectively/agent-decided.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Survey-level: experiential memory explicitly abstracts 'procedural knowledge from past successes AND failures'; failure-driven mechanisms are surveyed (e.g., Agent KB's teacher model observing the student's failures to generate corrective fine-grained sub-queries; reflection on failed trials in Reflexion/Retroformer; hindsight reflection). Both success and failure experiences are treated as reusable, not success-only.
- **memory evolution update**:
> Survey-level: a dedicated 'Memory Evolution' taxonomy with three branches - (a) Consolidation (local consolidation, cluster fusion, global integration; incremental semantic summarization), (b) Updating (external-DB conflict resolution: rule-based replace/delete -> temporally-aware soft deletion/invalid-timestamps in Zep -> delayed-consistency -> fully learned update policies; plus internal parametric updates), and (c) Forgetting (pruning by time expiration, low access frequency, low informational value; soft weight decay e.g. MAICC; stochastic token replacement). Goes well beyond append-only to dedup-merge, conflict-resolve, soft/decay-forget, and refine-overwrite.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Survey-level: increasingly yes, and the survey dedicates a Frontiers subsection to it. It charts RL-free heuristic/prompt pipelines -> partially RL-involved designs governing selected memory operations (retrieval/construction/management as RL-optimized, e.g., Memory-R1, MemSearcher, Mem-alpha, RL-trained Rewrite-Retrieve-Read; Mem1/MemAgent for summarization) -> envisioned fully RL-driven, model-native self-optimizing memory. The survey positions fully-RL-driven memory as 'the next major stage.' Most current systems still use fixed similarity top-k, however.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Survey-level: explicitly covered. Multi-agent memory is a Frontiers topic; surveyed shared-memory mechanisms include Memory Sharing (centralized repository of past queries/responses for asynchronous reuse across agents), G-Memory (three-tier insight/query/interaction graph hierarchy for multi-agent systems), MIRIX (multi-agent memory system), LEGOMem (modular procedural memory for multi-agent workflow automation), and RCR-Router (role-aware context routing with structured shared memory). Both single-agent private and cross-agent shared memory are taxonomized.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> No new benchmark is introduced. The survey compiles two categories (Table 8): (1) memory/lifelong/self-evolving-oriented: MemBench, MemoryAgentBench, LoCoMo, WebChoreArena, MT-Mind2Web, PersonaMem, LongMemEval, PerLTQA, MemoryBank, MPR, PrefEval, LOCCO, StoryBench, MemoryBench, Madial-Bench, Evo-Memory, LifelongAgentBench, StreamBench, DialSim, LongBench / LongBench v2, RULER, BABILong, MM-Needle, HaluMem, HotpotQA; (2) other agent-oriented but memory-relevant: ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, AgentGym, BabyAI, WebShop, WebArena, MMInA, ToolBench. Also references GAIA, XBench, BrowseComp, SWE-bench Verified, 2WikiMQA, MuSiQue in the RAG-vs-memory discussion.
- **benchmark family**:
> memory (agent-memory / lifelong-learning / self-evolving evaluation survey). Sub-families spanned: memory (LoCoMo, LongMemEval, MemoryBank, MemBench, PerLTQA, PersonaMem, HaluMem), long-context (LongBench/v2, RULER, BABILong, MM-Needle), multi-hop/QA (HotpotQA, 2WikiMQA, MuSiQue), web (MT-Mind2Web, WebChoreArena, WebShop, WebArena, MMInA, Online-Mind2Web-style), embodied/game (ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, BabyAI, StoryBench), tool (ToolBench), code (SWE-bench Verified), deep-research (GAIA, XBench, BrowseComp), and lifelong/streaming (StreamBench, LifelongAgentBench, MemoryBench, Evo-Memory).
- **baselines**:
> N/A - a survey with no experiments. It instead tabulates and compares representative memory systems (e.g., MemGPT, Mem0, A-MEM, Zep, HippoRAG/HippoRAG 2, GraphRAG, AriGraph, EMG-RAG, G-Memory, Memory-R1, MIRIX, MemoryOS, MemOS, Reflexion, ExpeL, AWM, ReasoningBank, Memento, Memp, MemGen, MEM1, MemAgent) along forms/functions/dynamics axes (Tables 1, 8, 9).
- **key metrics**:
> Survey-level: no single metric is proposed; it surveys metrics used across benchmarks - QA/dialogue accuracy and F1, memory recall/reference accuracy, retrieval precision/recall, task success/pass rate (web/embodied/code, e.g., SWE-bench Verified resolved %), long-context retrieval accuracy, lifelong-learning measures (catastrophic forgetting, forward/backward transfer, test-time adaptation), hallucination metrics (HaluMem), and efficiency/cost (token budget, latency). It emphasizes precision and recall in retrieval plus continual-learning transfer metrics.
- **headline result**:
> N/A (no empirical headline number; it is a survey). Its headline contribution is the unified 'Forms (token-level / parametric / latent) x Functions (factual / experiential / working) x Dynamics (formation / evolution / retrieval)' taxonomy, plus a clear conceptual delineation of agent memory from LLM memory, RAG, and context engineering, and compilations of memory benchmarks (Table 8) and open-source frameworks (Table 9). It was Hugging Face Daily Paper #1 (2025-12-16).
- **ablations**:
> N/A (no experiments/ablations). The survey's comparative tables (Table 1 token-level methods by 1D/2D/3D topology and factual/experiential/working type; Table 8 benchmarks; Table 9 open-source frameworks) and lifecycle formalization (F/E/R) function as the structured cross-system comparison clarifying which design choices each system adopts.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Conceptually yes - the survey distinguishes isolated memory-retrieval evaluation (intrinsic: retrieval precision/recall, reference/memory accuracy, hallucination) from end-to-end lifelong/agentic task performance, and explicitly separates benchmarks 'explicitly designed for memory' from 'other benchmarks that implicitly stress memory through long-horizon interaction.' It notes lifelong benchmarks track performance on current AND previously seen tasks (decoupling retention from immediate task success). The survey itself reports no numbers.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both, as a taxonomy: outcome metrics via end-to-end task success across web/embodied/code/QA benchmarks; process/intermediate metrics via memory reference accuracy, retrieval precision/recall, memory hallucination (HaluMem), forgetting/transfer measures, and trajectory/consistency quality. The survey advocates measuring intermediate memory quality and continual-learning dynamics, not only final outcomes.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Discussed qualitatively and as a theme: token-budget management and context-window cost (working memory / context engineering overlap), compression-vs-fidelity trade-offs in latent memory, O(n^2) full-sequence cost vs incremental summarization, I/O/compute burden of real-time memory updates under high-frequency interaction (motivating delayed-consistency strategies like MOOM/LightMem), efficiency gains from autonomous retrieval timing/intent (reducing unnecessary retrieval noise), and frameworks like LightMem targeting lightweight/efficient memory. No single concrete latency/cost number is the focus (it is a survey).
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Survey-level: the finite context window is a core motivation; working memory and context engineering manage a bounded token budget via compression, importance-based selection/token pruning, rolling summaries, and OS-style paging (MemGPT main vs external context; MemoryOS/MemOS tiered stores). Selection count ranges from fixed top-K (default) to comprehensive 'retrieve-from-all-stores' (MIRIX) to dynamic/budget-capped policies; the survey critiques forced-top-K and advocates adaptive selection. No single k value is prescribed.
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A as a proposed benchmark, but the survey reports sizes/features for compiled benchmarks in Table 8, e.g., MemBench 53,000 samples (interactive scenarios), LoCoMo 300 samples (conversational memory, multimodal, real), LongMemEval 5 tasks/500 samples (interactive memory), MemoryBank 194 samples, MPR 108,000 samples, PrefEval 3,000, PerLTQA 8,593, StreamBench 9,702 (continuous online learning), MM-Needle ~280,000 (multimodal long-context retrieval), HaluMem 3,467 (memory hallucinations), ALFWorld 3,353 tasks, AgentGym 89 tasks/20,509 samples. It distinguishes simulated vs real environments and factual vs experiential evaluation.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Cognitive-science foundations: declarative memory theory (episodic vs semantic; Tulving, Squire) and multicomponent / embedded-processes working-memory models. RAG taxonomy of Mei et al. 2025 (modular / graph / agentic RAG) for the agent-memory-vs-RAG analysis. Foundational systems it taxonomizes: MemGPT, MemoryBank, RET-LLM, Generative Agents, Reflexion/Retroformer, ExpeL, HippoRAG/HippoRAG 2, GraphRAG, AriGraph, Zep, Mem0, A-MEM, AWM, JARVIS-1, Voyager-style skill memory, ReasoningBank, Memento, Memp, MemGen, MEM1, MemAgent.
- **contrasts with**:
> Explicitly contrasts agent memory with (1) LLM memory (which agent memory 'almost fully subsumes' - architectural optimizations of representational capacity), (2) RAG (static knowledge access for single-task invocation, evaluated on HotpotQA/2WikiMQA/MuSiQue, vs persistent evolving multi-turn memory), and (3) Context Engineering (transient resource management of the finite context window vs cognitive modeling of a persistent evolving identity). It also positions against traditional long/short-term-memory taxonomies as 'insufficient', and against prior fragmented/loosely-defined agent-memory terminology and earlier memory surveys.
- **lineage**:
> Surveys group - a late-2025/early-2026 anchor agent-memory survey. It explicitly extends and sharpens the lineage of prior LLM-agent memory surveys (e.g., Zhang et al. 2024 'A Survey on the Memory Mechanism of LLM-based Agents' sources/forms/operations framework) by reorganizing the field around Forms x Functions x Dynamics and by carefully delineating agent memory from RAG and context engineering. It sits alongside and is contemporaneous with other 2026 memory surveys (e.g., 'Rethinking Memory Mechanisms of Foundation Agents', graph-based agent-memory taxonomies, 4W memory taxonomy) and underpins the experience/memory-augmented agent and self-evolving-agent lineage.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- completeness_vs_topk_objective
- dynamic_index_and_protocol
- survey_scope_and_axes

<a id="item-memoryagentbench"></a>
### 172. MemoryAgentBench (Evaluating Memory in LLM Agents via Incremental Multi-Turn Interactions)

2025  ·  arXiv 2507.05257  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.05257)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**: arXiv preprint 2507.05257 (cs.CL); accepted as ICLR 2026 Poster (OpenReview forum id=DT7JyQC3MR)
- **authors affiliation**: Yuanzhe Hu*, Yu Wang* (equal contribution), Julian McAuley. University of California, San Diego (UCSD). Joint corresponding authors: Yuanzhe Hu and Yu Wang.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.05257
- **code url**: https://github.com/HUST-AI-HYZ/MemoryAgentBench
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/HUST-AI-HYZ/MemoryAgentBench (datasets on HuggingFace: https://huggingface.co/datasets/ai-hyz/MemoryAgentBench and https://huggingface.co/datasets/Kakezh/MemoryAgentBench)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Memory evaluation for LLM agents over multi-turn interactions; spans QA (single-/multi-hop document QA, dialogue-based QA, novel event QA), classification/recommendation (test-time learning), long-document summarization and detective-novel reasoning (long-range understanding), and counterfactual fact updating (selective forgetting). A benchmark + unified evaluation framework rather than a single method.
- **problem setting**:
> Interactive, incremental, single-agent (single-user) memory evaluation. Agents receive textual inputs as a sequence of chunks wrapped in a simulated User-Assistant dialogue, each preceded by a memorization instruction; they must absorb and incrementally update memory chunk by chunk, then answer questions only after all chunks are ingested. Contexts range 103K-1.44M tokens, far exceeding typical context windows, forcing genuine memory mechanisms. No task-specific training/supervision is provided (test-time/deployment setting); the benchmark identifies four core competencies (Accurate Retrieval, Test-Time Learning, Long-Range Understanding, Selective Forgetting) and evaluates whether existing memory-agent architectures master them.
- **what is retrieved**:
> Past textual context the agent has ingested: raw input chunks (documents, dialogue turns, labeled in-context examples, novel passages, counterfactual fact-edit pairs) stored in episodic/external memory; for structure-augmented agents, entities/relations in a knowledge graph or tree. This is what the evaluated agents retrieve; the benchmark itself does not retrieve.
- **retrieval grounding**: GROWING/episodic memory the agent writes incrementally during the interaction (chunks absorbed one by one and consolidated). It is not a static external corpus; the store is built online from the streamed conversation. (Benchmark evaluates agents over this growing memory.)
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Mixed by competency. RAG/agentic-memory agents use a fixed top-k retrieval objective (k=10 chunks by default; ablated at 2/5/10). The benchmark's design philosophy critiques pure top-k: Long-Range Understanding and Test-Time Learning require holistic/complete-set integration across the entire history that top-k retrieval cannot recover, while Accurate Retrieval needs recovery of the correct (possibly multi-hop) snippet(s). Selective Forgetting requires recovering the single most recent (correct) fact among contradictory edits.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based reasoning method; it is a benchmark). The evaluated agentic-memory agents loosely realize Retrieve/Reuse but the benchmark does not frame itself in CBR terms.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is grounded instead in memory science and cognitive science (James 1890; McClelland et al. 1995; Anderson & Neely 1996; Wimber et al. 2015).

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Primarily text chunk / passage (chunk size 512 tokens for SH-Doc QA, MH-Doc QA, LME(S*) and all Selective-Forgetting tasks; 4096 tokens for other tasks and uniformly 4096 for Mem0/Cognee/Zep/MIRIX). Structure-augmented agents additionally retrieve KG-subgraph / tree-node / event-timeline units; long-context agents use the whole context buffer (no retrieval unit).
- **index source**:
> Growing memory induced online/test-time: built by segmenting reconstructed long-context datasets into chunks and feeding them incrementally in time order. The benchmark transforms existing long-context datasets (NIAH-style Doc QA, LongMemEval, infinity-Bench Sum, DetectiveQA, classification datasets, MQUAKE edit pairs) and adds two newly constructed datasets (EventQA, FactConsolidation) into the incremental multi-turn format.
- **index structure topology**:
> Depends on the evaluated agent: flat raw-text store (Simple RAG / BM25), flat dense vector index (embedding RAG), knowledge GRAPH (GraphRAG, HippoRAG-v2, Cognee, Zep temporal KG), tree (RAPTOR recursive abstractive tree), event timeline, or hierarchical/multi-agent memory (MemGPT paging, MIRIX multi-component memory). Long-context agents use a FIFO context buffer (no structured index).
- **retriever type**:
> Heterogeneous across evaluated agents: lexical/non-neural (BM25), dense/embedding (Contriever, OpenAI text-embedding-3-small/large, Qwen3-Embedding-4B), structure-augmented (GraphRAG, RAPTOR, HippoRAG-v2, MemoRAG), commercial/agentic memory (Mem0, Cognee, Zep, MemGPT, MIRIX, Self-RAG). Long-context agents do not retrieve (full context as memory).
- **retriever learning signal**: None / off-the-shelf for the core comparison: retrievers are used as-is (pretrained BM25/embedding models, off-the-shelf graph/commercial memory systems). No retriever is trained or RL-optimized within the benchmark; selection is fixed similarity top-k.
- **query construction**:
> Raw user question is used as the query at test time. Agentic memory agents (e.g., Self-RAG, MemGPT) may reformulate the question internally across iterative reasoning cycles; structure-augmented systems may translate queries against a KG/tree. The benchmark itself supplies the raw question.
- **query granularity**:
> Task-level (one query per question issued after the full incremental context is ingested). Multiple questions follow a single ingested context (e.g., 5 contexts paired with 300 questions in LongMemEval(S*)) to amortize memory-construction cost. Agentic agents may issue step/iteration-level sub-queries internally.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Two-phase protocol: a memory-construction phase (incremental chunk ingestion, build/update memory) followed by a query-execution phase where retrieval happens at answer time. For most RAG agents this is one-shot retrieval per question; agentic memory agents (MemGPT, Self-RAG) perform iterative/active retrieval loops.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Fixed schedule for RAG agents (retrieve top-k at each question). For agentic memory agents, retrieval is agent-initiated / reflection-driven within iterative reasoning cycles (self-reflection tokens in Self-RAG; function-call/paging decisions in MemGPT). The benchmark does not impose a single trigger; it depends on each agent's design.
- **reranking**: No reranking stage is imposed by the benchmark; RAG agents use plain similarity top-k (default k=10). Some structure-augmented/commercial systems may apply internal ranking, but no dedicated cross-encoder/RRF reranking is reported as a benchmark component.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Depends on agent: Simple/embedding RAG inject retrieved chunks verbatim (no refinement). Structure-augmented agents perform summarization/abstraction (RAPTOR recursive summaries, GraphRAG community summaries, MemoRAG global memory draft). Agentic agents (Self-RAG) apply self-reflection/critique filtering. The benchmark itself does not prescribe refinement.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (no tool-retrieval engineering; not a tool-use benchmark).
- **index content separation**: N/A. No lightweight-index-then-content / progressive-disclosure separation is prescribed; RAG agents store and retrieve full chunks. (Structure-augmented agents implicitly separate KG/summary indices from source text, but this is per-agent, not a benchmark design.)
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A. Memory is built from a streamed conversation, not from a live/external tool index; no RapidAPI/REST/MCP tool protocol involved. Some agents use function-calling internally (e.g., MemGPT memory operations), but no tool-API store is benchmarked.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no inter-tool dependency modeling; not a tool-use benchmark).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation: retrieved chunks / KG-subgraphs / summaries are concatenated into the LLM prompt to answer the question. Long-context agents place the entire (windowed) history in-context. With chunk size 4096 and top-k=10 the injected context is ~40K tokens. No training-signal or latent-token usage.
- **planning integration**:
> Mostly retrieve-then-answer (one-shot retrieval at query time, not interleaved with multi-step planning) for RAG agents. Agentic memory agents use an iterative retrieve-reflect-update loop (per-iteration interleaving). No MCTS/tree-search planning is involved; the benchmark targets memorization rather than action planning.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**: Per-answer for long-context and standard RAG agents (single retrieval then generate the answer). Per-iteration / per-reasoning-cycle for agentic memory agents (MemGPT, Self-RAG, MemoRAG) that reformulate, look up memory, and update working memory across cycles.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (not a CBR method). Retrieved content is used as verbatim in-context evidence (RAG) or, for test-time learning tasks, as labeled in-context exemplars from which the agent must induce the labeling rule; no explicit case revision/critic mechanism is prescribed by the benchmark.
- **retrieved item representation**: Raw text chunks (RAG/long-context); for structure-augmented agents, distilled summaries / structured KG facts / tree-node abstractions / event timelines. For Test-Time Learning, raw labeled (input, label) demonstrations. For Selective Forgetting, serial-numbered fact statements.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Spans the spectrum: raw trajectory/passage (RAG, long-context), single demonstration (TTL labeled examples), distilled summary/insight (RAPTOR, GraphRAG, MemoRAG), and structured fact/rule (KG-based Cognee/Zep/HippoRAG, FactConsolidation serial-numbered facts). The benchmark deliberately spans abstraction levels to test whether retrieval-only abstraction suffices.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Not a built-in mechanism but a tested property: the benchmark stresses robustness to distractors (NIAH-style multi-document QA, multi-hop retrieval) and to stale/contradictory information (Selective Forgetting via FactConsolidation). For SF, explicit prompt guardrails are added (facts indexed by serial numbers; 'newer facts have larger serial numbers'; agents mandated to resolve conflicts by selecting the newest fact). Agentic agents may use self-reflection for noise filtering.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> The benchmark evaluates multiple memory types: none/full-context buffer (long-context agents, FIFO eviction), episodic external store (RAG agents), graph memory (GraphRAG/HippoRAG-v2/Cognee/Zep), tree memory (RAPTOR), and agentic/multi-component memory (MemGPT, MIRIX, MemoRAG, Self-RAG). It primarily focuses on textual-history and external-database memory (not parametric).
- **write back**:
> True (for the evaluated agents). Each ingested chunk is written into the agent's memory during the incremental construction phase (stored as raw text, embeddings, KG nodes/edges, tree nodes, or agentic memory entries). The benchmark mandates that all agents take chunks one by one, absorb them into memory, and incrementally update memory.
- **online growth**: True. The retrievable store grows during deployment/test-time as chunks are streamed in time order; this incremental accumulation (vs single-block static context) is the central design principle distinguishing memory agents from long-context LLMs.
- **write back trigger**:
> Per-chunk during the memory-construction phase: every incoming chunk triggers a memory write/update. For structure-augmented and agentic systems the write may involve abstraction/consolidation (summarization, KG extraction). Triggers are agent-internal; the benchmark only mandates incremental ingestion of every chunk.
- **failure experience usage**:
> N/A / not modeled. There are no agent task trajectories with success/failure labels stored; the stored content is the ingested context, not the agent's own success/failure experiences. The Selective Forgetting task instead stores both old (now-incorrect) and new (correct) facts, requiring the agent to override outdated information.
- **memory evolution update**:
> Depends on agent: append-only for raw/embedding RAG and long-context (FIFO eviction once window exceeded); refine/consolidate for structure-augmented (RAPTOR recursive summaries, GraphRAG/Zep graph updates) and agentic memory (MemGPT paging, MIRIX). The Selective Forgetting competency specifically probes refine/overwrite/forget behavior, which the benchmark finds all methods handle poorly (multi-hop <=7% accuracy).
- **retrieval as learned policy**: No. Retrieval/case-selection is fixed similarity top-k (or off-the-shelf agent logic); no RL-optimized or learned retrieval policy is introduced or required by the benchmark.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: No. Single-agent (single-user) private memory; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory sharing is evaluated. (MIRIX is internally multi-component/multi-agent memory for one user, but memory is not shared across distinct agents/users in the benchmark.)

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> MemoryAgentBench (2071 questions, context depth 103K-1.44M tokens). Datasets: Accurate Retrieval - SH-Doc QA (~197K), MH-Doc QA (~421K), LongMemEval(S*) (~355K, reformulated to 5 dialogues/300 questions), EventQA (new, ~534K); Test-Time Learning - BANKING77 (~103K, 77 labels), CLINC150 (151 labels), NLU (68 labels), TREC-Coarse (6 labels), TREC-Fine (50 labels), Movie Recommendation (~1.44M); Long-Range Understanding - infinity-Bench Sum/En.Sum (~172K), Detective QA (~124K, 10 novels/71 questions); Selective Forgetting - FactConsolidation-SH and FactConsolidation-MH (new, ~262K, built from MQUAKE counterfactual edit pairs, context lengths 6K/32K/64K/262K).
- **benchmark family**:
> memory (LongMemEval-derived dialogue QA, FactConsolidation) + long-context/QA (infinity-Bench Sum, DetectiveQA, NIAH-style Doc QA) + test-time-learning classification (BANKING77/CLINC150/NLU/TREC) + recommendation (ReDial/movie). It is itself a new memory-agent benchmark family unifying these sources.
- **baselines**:
> Long-Context Agents: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini (reference backbone), GPT-4.1-mini, Gemini-2.0-Flash, Claude-3.7-Sonnet. Simple RAG: BM25. Embedding RAG: Contriever, OpenAI text-embedding-3-small, text-embedding-3-large, Qwen3-Embedding-4B. Structure-Augmented RAG: RAPTOR, GraphRAG, MemoRAG, HippoRAG-v2, Mem0, Cognee, Zep. Agentic Memory: Self-RAG, MemGPT, MIRIX (and MIRIX with GPT-4.1-mini backbone). Reasoning-model validation: GPT-4o and o4-mini on FactConsolidation. (RAG and commercial memory agents use GPT-4o-mini as default backbone.)
- **key metrics**:
> Accuracy (SH-QA, MH-QA, LME(S*), EventQA, MCC classification, Detective QA, FactConsolidation-SH/MH); Recall@5 (Movie Recommendation); F1-Score (infinity-Bench Sum novel summarization). Per-competency averages (AR/TTL/LRU/SF) and an Overall score. Appendix also reports computational latency, GPU memory usage, and cost-performance analysis.
- **headline result**:
> No existing memory agent masters all four competencies. Best overall scores are modest: Claude-3.7-Sonnet 49.6 and GPT-4o 48.8 (long-context agents) lead overall. Key splits: RAG agents excel at Accurate Retrieval (HippoRAG-v2 AR Avg 65.1, matching/ beating GPT-4o-mini's 49.2), but long-context models dominate Test-Time Learning and Long-Range Understanding. Selective Forgetting is a universal failure: all methods achieve at most ~7% on multi-hop FactConsolidation (FC-MH), and only long-context agents reach reasonable single-hop scores (GPT-4o 60.0 FC-SH). Even o4-mini drops from 80.0 to 14.0 on FC-MH as context grows from 6K to 32K.
- **ablations**:
> (1) Input chunk size: smaller chunks + more retrieval calls help Accurate Retrieval (especially embedding RAG) but hurt Long-Range Understanding (RAG ill-suited to coherent global context). (2) Retrieval top-k (2/5/10): larger k generally improves performance; k=10 at 4096 chunk size already ~40K tokens, so k=20 not evaluated. (3) Backbone model (GPT-4o-mini / GPT-4.1-mini / Gemini-2.0-Flash): for RAG agents a sufficiently strong backbone is no longer the bottleneck (marginal gains), but for agentic memory (MIRIX) a stronger backbone gives large gains (Avg 15.9 -> 25.6, +9.7; overall 26.2 -> 37.7). (4) FactConsolidation validation with reasoning models (GPT-4o, o4-mini) shows the dataset is solvable in short context (o4-mini FC-MH 6K = 80.0) but breaks at longer context (32K = 14.0), confirming task validity and that the bottleneck is long-range reasoning over memory.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Largely coupled to end-to-end task metrics (accuracy/F1/Recall@5 per competency). Intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k/nDCG over chunks) are not the primary reported scores; the benchmark measures downstream answer correctness, though chunk-size and top-k ablations indirectly probe retrieval quality. Recall@5 is used as the recommendation task metric rather than as a retriever-intrinsic metric.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Primarily outcome metrics (final-answer accuracy/F1/Recall@5). Process quality is examined indirectly via ablations (chunk size, top-k, backbone, context-length scaling) and the FactConsolidation validation, but no per-step reasoning-faithfulness or trajectory-quality score is reported.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Fixed-k retrieval: default top-k=10 chunks (ablated 2/5/10). Chunk size 512 for AR (SH/MH-Doc QA, LME(S*)) and all SF tasks; 4096 for other tasks and uniformly for commercial memory agents. With 4096-token chunks and k=10, injected context ~40K tokens. Long-context agents use a FIFO buffer capped at the model's window (128K-1M+), evicting earliest chunks when exceeded.
- **survey scope and axes**:
> N/A (benchmark, not a survey). Organizing axes are the four memory competencies (Accurate Retrieval, Test-Time Learning, Long-Range Understanding, Selective Forgetting) crossed with three agent categories (Long-Context Agents, RAG Agents [Simple/Embedding/Structure-Augmented], Agentic Memory Agents). References: 84.
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> 2071 questions; context depth 103K-1.44M tokens. Construction: reconstructs existing long-context datasets into incremental multi-turn chunk streams, plus two new LLM/automated-pipeline datasets - EventQA (fully automated pipeline over novels; multiple-choice event selection) and FactConsolidation (built from MQUAKE counterfactual edit pairs ordered old->new). LongMemEval reformulated to LME(S*) = 5 dialogues / 300 questions. Answer verifiability: mostly exact-match/multiple-choice accuracy, Recall@5 for recommendation, F1 for summarization. Difficulty signal: best overall system ~49.6 (Claude-3.7-Sonnet); Selective Forgetting multi-hop maxes at ~7% for evaluated memory agents (validated as solvable in short context by o4-mini at 80.0 on FC-MH 6K).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Reconstructs / builds on prior datasets: LongMemEval, infinity-Bench (En.Sum), DetectiveQA, MQUAKE (counterfactual edits for FactConsolidation), BANKING77/CLINC150/NLU/TREC (test-time-learning classification), ReDial / conversational movie recommendation, NIAH-style document QA. Conceptually grounded in memory/cognitive science (James 1890; McClelland et al. 1995; Anderson & Neely 1996; Wimber et al. 2015) and the in-context-learning-as-test-time-learning line (Bertsch et al. 2024; HELMET/Yen et al. 2024).
- **contrasts with**:
> Positioned against prior memory/long-context benchmarks that cover only subsets of competencies and use shorter/static contexts: MemoryBank, LoCoMo (~9-10K), PerLTQA, RealTalk, LongMemEval, StoryBench, and long-context benchmarks (LongBench, LooGLE, infinity-Bench, RULER, HELMET, NOCHA, NoLiMa, NovelQA, Loong) and RAG benchmarks (KILT, BEIR, RAGBench, etc.). MemoryAgentBench is the only one covering all four competencies (AR/TTL/LRU/SF) and all three agent categories (LCA/RAG/AM) with incremental multi-turn injection.
- **lineage**:
> Surveys/benchmarks line of the retrieval-augmented agents map: a memory-agent evaluation benchmark (group: surveys). Sits alongside memory benchmarks like LongMemEval and LoCoMo, extending them to a unified four-competency, incremental-multi-turn protocol spanning long-context, RAG, and agentic-memory architectures.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- cost_efficiency_tradeoff

<a id="item-reasoning-agentic-rag-survey"></a>
### 173. Reasoning RAG via System 1 or System 2: A Survey on Reasoning Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Industry Challenges (Liang et al.)

2025  ·  arXiv 2506.10408  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10408)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **authors affiliation**:
> Jintao Liang (Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Gang Su (University of Georgia); Huifeng Lin, You Wu (South China University of Technology); Rui Zhao (SenseTime Research & Qingyuan Research Institute, Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Ziyue Li (corresponding author; Technical University of Munich & University of Cologne). 6 authors across Chinese, German and US institutions.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10408
- **code url**: N/A (survey, no method code). Companion paper list: https://github.com/ByebyeMonica/Reasoning-Agentic-RAG
- **maintained repo url**:
> https://github.com/ByebyeMonica/Reasoning-Agentic-RAG (companion GitHub paper list curating representative Predefined-Reasoning and Agentic-Reasoning papers plus open-source Agentic RAG projects; ~28 stars, last updated around May 2025, so only lightly maintained vs the frozen PDF).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Survey of Reasoning Agentic RAG. Primary surveyed task is knowledge-intensive / open-domain QA and multi-hop reasoning, framed for industry challenges; explicitly motivated by multi-document synthesis, legal/biomedical QA, multi-modal (tables/charts/images) enterprise intelligence, scientific reporting, technical support, deep research, and strategic/multi-step decision-making. Spans QA, retrieval, tool-use and web search rather than embodied/robotics.
- **problem setting**:
> A literature review (not a method). It synthesizes the shift from static/basic RAG pipelines to Reasoning Agentic RAG, where decision-making and adaptive tool use are embedded directly into the retrieval process. It defines two top-level paradigms - (1) Predefined Reasoning: fixed, modular, rule-based pipelines (query reformulation, retrieval, re-ranking, generation under static control logic), aligned with cognitive System 1 (fast, structured); and (2) Agentic Reasoning: the LLM acts as an autonomous agent that dynamically decides when/what/how to retrieve and interact with tools during inference, aligned with System 2 (slow, deliberate, model-driven). The surveyed setting is predominantly single-agent (one LLM agent orchestrating retrieval/tools), interactive/iterative at inference time, over external corpora or live search engines; supervision ranges from training-free prompting (off-the-shelf LRMs/function-calling) to RL-trained search agents. DeepResearcher is noted as a multi-agent (reasoning + browsing agents) exception.
- **what is retrieved**:
> Predominantly external documents / passages / chunks from knowledge bases and live search engines. The survey also covers retrieving via tool/API calls (function calling, search APIs, structured database queries) and, for tree-based methods, hierarchical document summaries (RAPTOR). It is a document/tool-retrieval survey, not an experience/case/skill-memory survey; demos/trajectories/skills are not the retrieval target.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> Predominantly STATIC external corpus (local document collections, knowledge bases) and live external search engines (web/PubMed). The dominant grounding is a fixed external knowledge source queried at inference; there is no agent-written growing episodic memory as the central object (no experience write-back store). So grounding = static external corpus / live search engine, not growing memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> The canonical objective surveyed is top-k retrieval by relevance (BM25/dense top-k), refined by re-ranking, corrective filtering (CRAG), and iterative/agentic multi-turn retrieval that progressively expands coverage across reasoning steps. Training-based agents optimize retrieval-quality metrics (recall@k, NDCG, Hits@N for DeepRetrieval) and final-answer correctness rather than recovering a fixed complete minimal set. Multi-hop/agentic loops pursue sufficiency-of-evidence across turns rather than per-call set completeness; not framed as precision-driven variable-size recommendation.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based-reasoning work; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain case cycle. It surveys document/tool retrieval with reasoning, not CBR).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: false. The survey does not frame Reasoning Agentic RAG as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; its cognitive grounding is dual-process System 1 / System 2 theory, not CBR.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Surveyed as a spectrum: document / passage / text chunk (the dominant unit for both predefined and agentic methods); hierarchical document-summary nodes in tree-based RAPTOR; tool/search-API call as a retrieval action in agentic reasoning (search query encapsulated in special <search> tokens for RL agents); and structured-database query results. The default unit is the retrieved document/chunk; agentic methods add the tool-call/search-query as the operative unit.
- **index source**:
> Surveyed across the spectrum but dominantly static offline-built corpora indexed for retrieval (local retrieval systems for Search-R1/R1-Searcher/ReZero) and live external/real-world search engines (restricted PubMed for DeepRetrieval; open web search APIs for DeepResearcher). The store is read-only/external; there is no online experience-induced growing memory. So index source = static external corpus or live web search engine, constructed offline / queried online, not agent-grown.
- **index structure topology**:
> Surveyed: flat retrieval indices (BM25 sparse / dense semantic vector indices, the basic-RAG default); refined indexing with fine-grained chunking and metadata-aware retrieval (Advanced RAG); hierarchical / recursive TREE structures (RAPTOR's recursive summary tree); and modular/LEGO-like configurable pipelines (Modular-RAG) rather than a single index topology. Agentic methods treat the search engine/API as an external black-box index. No knowledge-graph index is a focus.
- **retriever type**:
> Surveyed broadly: sparse keyword retrieval (BM25, the Naive-RAG default), dense semantic retrievers (Advanced RAG), and live search engines / search APIs invoked as tools (function calling, web search). Agentic training-based methods add LLM-as-query-generator / LLM-as-policy that reformulates queries (DeepRetrieval) or decides when to call a fixed retriever (Search-R1). No single retriever is endorsed; the survey catalogs sparse, dense, and tool/search-engine retrievers.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Surveyed across the full range and this is a central axis. Predefined-reasoning / prompt-based methods use off-the-shelf retrievers (none / frozen BM25 or dense). Training-based agentic methods learn retrieval/query behavior via REINFORCEMENT LEARNING (PPO / GRPO): Search-R1 and R1-Searcher use outcome-based answer reward (+ format/retrieval rewards) to learn when/what to search; DeepRetrieval rewards retrieval metrics (recall@k, NDCG, Hits@N) of the executed query; ReZero adds a retry reward for productive persistence; DeepResearcher uses F1-based answer reward in live web environments. So signal spans none/off-the-shelf to RL-trained search/query policies.
- **query construction**:
> Surveyed: raw query (basic RAG); query reformulation / rewriting (Modular-RAG module; DeepRetrieval learns to rewrite queries via RL to maximize retrieval metrics); sub-question decomposition (Self-Ask generates and answers follow-up questions); thought-conditioned mid-generation queries (ReAct's Thought->Action->Search; Search-o1 triggers search on self-assessed knowledge gaps); and learned search-token emission (<search>...</search> in Search-R1/ReZero). Spans raw, reformulated, decomposed, and reasoning-state-conditioned query construction.
- **query granularity**:
> Surveyed at multiple levels. Predefined route-based methods decide retrieval at the task/turn level (RAGate per dialogue turn; Self-Route per query). Loop/agentic methods construct queries at the reasoning-step level (Self-RAG mid-generation; ReAct per Thought-Action step; Search-R1 emits search queries interleaved with <think> steps across a multi-turn trajectory). So task-level, turn-level, and step/trajectory-level query granularity are all covered.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Surveyed as the organizing distinction. Predefined reasoning: route-based conditional triggering (one-shot decision on whether to retrieve), loop-based iterative refinement, tree-based recursive/hierarchical, and hybrid-modular routing. Agentic reasoning: active/adaptive, agent-initiated retrieval where the LLM autonomously decides WHEN and WHAT to retrieve during its reasoning trajectory (ReAct, Search-o1, Search-R1). Overall spans one-shot/route -> iterative/loop -> active agent-initiated -> learned RL policy.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Surveyed concrete WHEN-to-retrieve signals: model confidence / uncertainty estimation and conversation context (RAGate route-based; Self-Route confidence-based routing between RAG and Long-Context); retrieval-quality evaluator scores categorizing chunks as correct/incorrect/ambiguous (CRAG); reflection / self-critique decisions mid-generation (Self-RAG); learned query-complexity routing (Adaptive-RAG); self-assessed knowledge gaps in a reasoning chain (ReAct Thought, Search-o1); and learned policy emitting special <search> tokens (Search-R1, ReZero, with retry-triggered re-search in ReZero). So signal spans confidence/uncertainty, evaluator scores, reflection, learned complexity classifier, and agent-initiated/learned-policy triggers.
- **reranking**:
> Yes - re-ranking is surveyed as a core component of Advanced/Modular RAG (a dedicated module for ranking/filtering retrieved results in the Modular-RAG pipeline; dense re-ranking and multi-hop querying in Advanced RAG). CRAG's lightweight retrieval evaluator acts as a corrective relevance assessor. Re-ranking is presented as one of the swappable modules rather than a single prescribed reranker type.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Surveyed across operations: corrective filtering and query rewriting / web-search fallback when retrieved chunks are low quality (CRAG); recursive abstractive summarization of retrieved content into a tree (RAPTOR); a Reason-in-Documents module that distills retrieved content into a refined, denoised format to preserve reasoning integrity (Search-o1); retrieved-token masking during RL loss to stabilize training (Search-R1); and module-level filtering/ranking in Modular-RAG. The survey explicitly flags the lost-in-the-middle problem and need for adaptive context management. So refinement spans rerank/filter, distill/reason-in-documents, summarize, and compress.
- **tool document engineering**:
> N/A / lightly touched. The survey is about reasoning over retrieved documents and search tools, not tool-description indexing. Function calling exposes predefined tool/API interfaces integrated into model training/prompt design, and a future direction calls for richer tool configurations (result filtering, sorting, domain specification, structured DB queries), but tool-description embedding/engineering for retrieval is not analyzed.
- **index content separation**:
> N/A as a method, but the related pattern appears via RAPTOR's hierarchical summary tree (search lightweight summaries first, descend to heavier content) and via distillation of retrieved content (Search-o1 Reason-in-Documents). Not framed as a progressive-disclosure / index-then-content efficiency mechanism.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> Partially relevant. Agentic reasoning surveys live tool/search-engine interaction via function calling / built-in tool interfaces (GPT/Gemini) and live web search APIs (DeepResearcher), as opposed to a static document index. However, the survey does not discuss MCP, RapidAPI registries, or CRUD auto-sync of a tool index; the integration protocol is function-calling / search-API invocation. So: live search-engine/API tool use is covered, but not a synchronized tool-registry protocol like MCP.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A. The survey does not model inter-tool dependencies (output-of-A feeds B, shared auth, prerequisites) or dependency-aware tool retrieval; tool use is primarily single search-engine/API invocation interleaved with reasoning.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Predominantly prompt augmentation: retrieved documents are injected into the LLM context for grounded generation (basic/predefined RAG). Agentic reasoning interleaves retrieval as an action within the reasoning trajectory (ReAct Observation feeds subsequent Thought; Search-R1 places retrieved content in <information> tags consumed by further reasoning). Training-based methods additionally use retrieval outcomes as the RL TRAINING SIGNAL (reward) to shape the search policy. So usage spans prompt augmentation, interleaved tool-result consumption, and retrieval-as-reward-signal.
- **planning integration**:
> Surveyed across the predefined/agentic split. Predefined: retrieve-then-reason within fixed pipelines, route-then-retrieve (RAGate/Adaptive-RAG router selects path), loop/iterative refine (Self-RAG/CRAG), and tree/MCTS search (RAPTOR recursive tree; MCTS-RAG embeds retrieval inside a Monte Carlo Tree Search loop). Agentic: reasoning and retrieval are tightly interleaved per step (ReAct Thought-Action-Observation; Search-o1; Search-R1 interleaves <think>/<search>/<information>); DeepResearcher plans and dynamically adjusts plans during web research. So integration spans retrieve-then-plan, plan-then-retrieve, per-step interleaved, and inside-tree-search (MCTS-RAG).
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Surveyed at several granularities: per-answer / per-turn (route-based predefined methods retrieve once per query/turn); per-reasoning-step / per-CoT-step (loop-based Self-RAG, ReAct interleaves reasoning steps with retrieval actions, Search-R1 interleaves <think> and <search> across a multi-turn trajectory); and per-tool-call within a rollout (function calling, RL search agents emit search calls inside the reasoning rollout). The agentic paradigm is characterized by tight per-step / per-tool-call interleaving of reasoning and search.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> N/A (no CBR case adaptation/revision cycle). The closest analogs are corrective/iterative refinement of retrieval+generation (CRAG query rewriting / web-search fallback, Self-RAG self-critique) and RL fine-tuning of the search policy (Search-R1/ReZero/DeepRetrieval/DeepResearcher), but these refine behavior/context rather than adapt a retrieved case.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Predominantly raw retrieved document/passage text injected into context. Higher-abstraction surface forms surveyed: recursive document summaries (RAPTOR tree nodes); a distilled/denoised representation produced by Search-o1's Reason-in-Documents module; and structured tool/API call results. The dominant injected form is raw retrieved text, with summarized/distilled variants for tree-based and reason-in-documents methods.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Mostly raw retrieved passages/documents (this is document RAG, not strategy/skill retrieval). Higher-abstraction units surveyed: hierarchical summary nodes (RAPTOR recursive abstractive summaries) and distilled refined evidence (Search-o1 Reason-in-Documents). No distilled strategies, reusable workflows, or procedural skills are retrieved in the agentic-experience sense; abstraction tops out at document summaries.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Surveyed explicitly: a retrieval evaluator that scores chunk quality (correct/incorrect/ambiguous) and triggers corrective query rewriting or web search (CRAG); self-reflection / critique during generation (Self-RAG); a Reason-in-Documents distillation module that filters verbose/noisy/contradictory retrieved content to preserve reasoning integrity, addressing the lost-in-the-middle problem (Search-o1); cross-validation across multiple web sources and self-reflection on contradictory evidence as emergent behaviors (DeepResearcher); and retrieved-token masking to stabilize RL training (Search-R1). So robustness spans relevance evaluation, self-reflection, reason-in-documents refinement, and cross-validation.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> Mostly none in the classic experiential-memory sense (the survey centers retrieval over external corpora/search engines, not an agent-written memory store). Structural 'memory' analogs surveyed are the hierarchical document-summary tree (RAPTOR) and the multi-turn reasoning context (interleaved <think>/<information> trajectory). No episodic experience memory, skill library, or workflow memory is a central object. So memory_type = none/external-corpus-centric (with a document-summary tree as the closest structured store).
- **write back**:
> Mostly false. The surveyed paradigm retrieves from a fixed external corpus or live search engine and does not write experiences/cases/skills back into a persistent memory. RL training updates the agent's policy weights (a form of learning), but there is no experiential memory write-back store. So write_back = false for the surveyed methods (no episodic/case/skill write-back).
- **online growth**:
> Predominantly false. The retrievable store is a static external corpus or a live (externally maintained) search engine; the agent does not grow its own retrievable memory at test time. Live web search reflects external content changes but is not agent-authored growth. So online_growth = no (no agent-driven test-time store growth).
- **write back trigger**:
> Never (for an agent-written experience store). The surveyed methods do not log success/failure experiences into a retrievable memory; there is no on-success/on-failure/reflective write trigger. The only analog is offline construction of document summary trees (RAPTOR), built once, not triggered by deployment events. So write_back_trigger = never / N/A.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Not a focus as stored experience. The survey covers handling failed RETRIEVALS within a trajectory rather than storing failed experiences: CRAG corrects when retrieval is judged incorrect/ambiguous; ReZero adds a retry reward incentivizing 'trying one more time' after an unsuccessful initial search (conditioned on eventual task success); DeepResearcher self-reflects and refines search strategies when evidence is contradictory/insufficient. These shape in-trajectory behavior / RL reward, not a success-vs-failure experience memory.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A / append-only-offline. No stored experiential entries are mutated over deployment (no episodic memory). The closest analog is RAPTOR's offline recursive summarization that builds the tree once. So memory_evolution_update = N/A (no online entry mutation).
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Surveyed as a major axis and the defining feature of training-based agentic reasoning: retrieval/search IS a learned RL-optimized policy in Search-R1 (outcome reward, PPO/GRPO), R1-Searcher (two-stage outcome-based RL), ReZero (adds retry reward, GRPO), DeepRetrieval (query rewriting rewarded by retrieval metrics, PPO), and DeepResearcher (GRPO with F1 answer reward in live web). In contrast, predefined-reasoning and prompt-based agentic methods use fixed/heuristic top-k or prompt-driven retrieval rather than a learned policy. So the survey explicitly contrasts fixed-retrieval vs learned-retrieval-policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Largely N/A / single-agent. Most surveyed methods are single-agent (one LLM orchestrating retrieval/tools). DeepResearcher uses a multi-agent architecture (a reasoning module plus dedicated browsing agents) within one framework, but this is intra-framework task division, not cross-agent or cross-framework experience/memory sharing. No shared collective memory across heterogeneous frameworks is surveyed.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmark family**:
> Primarily QA and multi-hop QA (open-domain, knowledge-intensive, deep-research). Tool/search-engine interaction is evaluated via retrieval metrics on a restricted real search engine (PubMed-style) for query-rewriting (DeepRetrieval) and via live web search for open-web research (DeepResearcher). Families touched: QA / multi-hop QA / web-search / deep-research; not embodied (ALFWorld) or code (SWE-bench) families.
- **baselines**:
> N/A as a survey (no head-to-head experiments of its own). Conceptually it contrasts paradigms: basic/Naive RAG and Advanced/Modular RAG vs Reasoning Agentic RAG; predefined reasoning vs agentic reasoning; prompt-based vs training-based agentic; RAG vs Long-Context LLMs (Self-Route); and Chain-of-Thought vs ReAct (grounded vs purely internal reasoning). It cites that training-based agents (Search-R1, DeepResearcher) outperform RAG baselines and prompt-engineering / static-corpus RL baselines per their source papers.
- **key metrics**:
> The survey reports the metrics used by surveyed methods rather than its own. Mentioned: final-answer correctness / exact match and F1 (Search-R1 outcome reward; DeepResearcher F1-based reward); retrieval-quality metrics recall@k, NDCG, and evidence-seeking accuracy Hits@N (DeepRetrieval reward). Reasoning Complexity (Low/Medium/High) and Control Type (Fixed/Adaptive/Agentic) are the survey's own comparison descriptors in Table 2 rather than quantitative metrics.
- **headline result**:
> N/A (no single experimental headline number - it is a review). The headline contribution is the two-paradigm taxonomy of Reasoning Agentic RAG: Predefined Reasoning (= cognitive System 1: route-based, loop-based, tree-based, hybrid-modular) vs Agentic Reasoning (= System 2: prompt-based and training-based/RL), summarized in Figure 3 and Table 2, with a cognitive-science dual-process (System 1 / System 2) alignment and an industry-challenge framing.
- **ablations**:
> N/A (no experiments, hence no ablations). The analytical equivalents are: (1) the predefined-vs-agentic and System-1-vs-System-2 contrast (Table 1); (2) the Control-Type x Reasoning-Complexity comparison across predefined methods (Table 2: Fixed/Adaptive/Agentic; Low/Medium/High); (3) the reward-design comparison across training-based agents (answer reward only for Search-R1; +retrieval/+format/+retry for R1-Searcher/ReZero; retrieval+format for DeepRetrieval; format+answer for DeepResearcher); and (4) training-environment comparison (local retrieval vs restricted vs real-world search engine).
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Partially / surveyed. The survey notes that some methods optimize/report intrinsic retrieval-quality metrics separately (DeepRetrieval rewards recall@k / NDCG / Hits@N) while others use end-to-end outcome metrics only (Search-R1 answer reward; DeepResearcher F1). It does not impose its own decoupled evaluation protocol but documents both intrinsic-retrieval and end-to-end task evaluation across the cited works; it advocates finer-grained process-oriented metrics as future work.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Surveyed as a tension and an explicit future direction. Most training-based agents use outcome-only rewards (final-answer correctness / EM / F1). The survey argues for finer-grained, PROCESS-oriented reward/evaluation that assesses intermediate steps - document relevance, reasoning coherence, information cross-validation, and effective problem decomposition - because simple outcome rewards under-guide complex multi-step RAG. So it covers both but flags outcome-only as a limitation.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Discussed qualitatively and flagged as a key future direction. Self-Route reduces computation cost vs Long-Context models while maintaining performance; RAGate skips unnecessary retrieval for simple turns; route-based/adaptive control avoids redundant operations. The survey calls out 'Improving Efficiency in Retrieval' as a research direction: agents should avoid excessive/unnecessary searches, select promising sources, know when enough has been gathered, and avoid unproductive search loops. No quantitative latency/token/cost numbers are reported by the survey itself.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Surveyed qualitatively. The survey raises the lost-in-the-middle problem for long contexts and the need for adaptive context management; Search-o1's Reason-in-Documents module compresses/distills retrieved content to fit and denoise the reasoning context; fine-grained chunking is noted under Advanced RAG. Selection count k is method-dependent (basic top-k; agentic multi-turn accumulates information across <information> blocks). No single numeric budget or fixed-k policy is prescribed by the survey.
- **survey scope and axes**:
