> Explicit organizing axes: (1) two top-level paradigms - Predefined Reasoning vs Agentic Reasoning (Figure 3 taxonomy); (2) cognitive dual-process alignment System 1 (predefined) vs System 2 (agentic) (Table 1); (3) within Predefined Reasoning, four sub-types: Route-based, Loop-based, Tree-based, Hybrid-modular; (4) within Agentic Reasoning, Prompt-based (function-calling/ReAct, Self-Ask, LRM-based/Search-o1) vs Training-based (RL: local-retrieval, restricted, real-world search engines); (5) comparison descriptors: Control Type (Fixed/Adaptive/Agentic), Reasoning Complexity (Low/Medium/High), Training Environment, Reward Design (Table 2). Coverage: 50 references; time window roughly 2020-2025 (heavy 2024-2025 emphasis), with an explicit industry / enterprise open-source-project lens (DeepSearcher, RAGFlow, Haystack, LightRAG, R2R, FlashRAG, Langchain-Chatchat).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (a survey, not a benchmark paper; it constructs no dataset). It instead curates a paper list and a comparison of ~18 representative methods/projects (Table 2) split across predefined and agentic reasoning.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Builds on the foundational RAG line (Lewis et al. 2020) and the Naive->Advanced->Modular RAG framing of Gao et al. (2023, 2024). Predefined-reasoning lineage: RAGate, Self-Route (route-based), Self-RAG, CRAG (loop-based), RAPTOR, MCTS-RAG (tree-based), Adaptive-RAG, Modular-RAG (hybrid-modular). Agentic-reasoning lineage: ReAct, Self-Ask, OpenAI function calling, Search-o1 (prompt-based); Search-R1, R1-Searcher, ReZero, DeepRetrieval, DeepResearcher (RL training-based), themselves built on DeepSeek-R1 / o1-style RL reasoning and PPO/GRPO. Cognitive framing builds on dual-process System 1 / System 2 theory.
- **contrasts with**:
> Positions Reasoning Agentic RAG against static/basic RAG pipelines (limited by fixed control logic, no reflection/adaptation). Internally contrasts Predefined Reasoning (System 1, fixed orchestration) vs Agentic Reasoning (System 2, autonomous decision-making); prompt-based vs training-based agentic methods; ReAct's thought-action-observation cycle vs the more direct function-calling style; RAG vs Long-Context LLMs (Self-Route); grounded ReAct vs purely-internal Chain-of-Thought; and DeepRetrieval (optimize a single refined query) vs ReZero (value of multiple retrieval attempts). Distinct from broader RAG surveys (Gao et al.) by focusing specifically on reasoning + agentic tool-use and an industry-challenge lens.
- **lineage**:
> Surveys group. A focused 2025 survey of Reasoning Agentic RAG, sitting downstream of the foundational RAG survey (Gao et al. 2023) and adjacent to agentic-RAG and reasoning-LLM surveys. It is the canonical reference for the Predefined-Reasoning (System 1) vs Agentic-Reasoning (System 2) dichotomy and for organizing RL-trained search agents (Search-R1/DeepResearcher) alongside prompt-based agentic methods (ReAct/Search-o1); it anchors the reasoning-and-tool-use sub-topic within the broader agentic-RAG / experience-retrieval literature.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- benchmarks
- venue

<a id="item-foundation-agent-memory-survey"></a>
### 174. Rethinking Memory Mechanisms of Foundation Agents in the Second Half: A Survey

2025  ·  arXiv (Awesome-Agent-Memory repo)  ·  [paper](https://github.com/AgentMemoryWorld/Awesome-Agent-Memory)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2026
- **venue**:
> arXiv preprint (arXiv:2602.06052 [cs.CL]; cross-listed cs.AI). Submitted 2026-01-14 (v1); current v3 revised 2026-02-10. No peer-reviewed venue yet. NOTE: the task card listed the short title 'Rethinking Memory Mechanisms of Foundation Agents: A Survey' and year 2025; the verified paper's full title includes 'in the Second Half' and its first arXiv submission is dated 2026-01-14, so year is recorded as 2026. The companion living paper-list repo is github.com/AgentMemoryWorld/Awesome-Agent-Memory.
- **authors affiliation**:
> Wei-Chieh Huang, Weizhi Zhang (co-first authors), Yueqing Liang and ~57 other authors; senior/supervisors include Philip S. Yu and Kai Shu (corresponding). 60 authors total. Primarily academic: University of Illinois Chicago (UIC), Illinois Institute of Technology (IIT), UIUC, UW-Madison, ASU, Emory, Northwestern, NTU, UCF, Rutgers, Cambridge, Harvard, UTokyo, UCSD, UCSC, TAMU, UCSB, MBZUAI, McGill, UCLA, Stanford; plus industry: Salesforce (AI Research), Google, Meta, Roblox, Cisco, Capital One.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.06052
- **code url**: N/A (a survey; no method code). Companion curated paper-list repository instead.
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/AgentMemoryWorld/Awesome-Agent-Memory ('Awesome-Agent-Memory', [Up-To-Date] paper resource; ~156 stars; last commit 2026-02-11; README mirrors the survey taxonomy: memory substrates, cognitive mechanisms, subjects, operations, learning policy, benchmarks).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Survey/taxonomy of memory mechanisms for foundation (LLM-based) agents, spanning user-centric personalization/dialogue (conversation, recommendation, role-play, user simulation) and agent-centric task execution (QA/multi-hop, web/GUI, OS/desktop, tool/API, code/software engineering, embodied robotics/games, long video, scientific research) under long-horizon, dynamic, user-dependent environments. Anchor memory survey, not a single-task method.
- **problem setting**:
> A unifying survey arguing that as AI enters its 'second half' (problem definition + real-world utility over benchmark chasing), the central bottleneck is real utility in long-horizon, dynamic, user-dependent settings where agents face context explosion and must continuously accumulate, manage, and selectively reuse large volumes of information. It organizes foundation-agent memory along three orthogonal axes — (1) memory substrate (external vs internal), (2) cognitive mechanism (sensory, working, episodic, semantic, procedural), (3) memory subject (user-centric vs agent-centric) — then analyzes memory OPERATIONS under single- and multi-agent topologies, surveys LEARNING POLICIES over memory operations (prompting, fine-tuning, RL), discusses scaling (interaction horizon, environment complexity, environment quantity), and reviews evaluation metrics/benchmarks plus open challenges. Settings covered are predominantly interactive, long-context, single- and multi-agent; supervision varies by surveyed work. The survey proposes no new method, dataset, or experiments.
- **what is retrieved**:
> Across surveyed systems: stored memory entries at multiple granularities — episodic interaction trajectories/events, semantic facts/concepts/entity-relations, procedural skills/workflows/reasoning patterns, user facts/preferences/persona, dialogue/session records, external documents/knowledge, and (for internal memory) parametric knowledge / latent hidden states / KV-cache. The survey frames retrieval as the 'Loading and Retrieval' memory operation that surfaces task-relevant memories for the current context.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> HYBRID (survey-level). External memory is grounded in a GROWING/episodic agent-written store (vector index, text-record, structural store, hierarchical store) that the agent reads from and writes to, and may also wrap a STATIC external corpus (RAG over docs/KB). Internal memory (weights, latent-state, KV-cache) is parametric/transient. The survey explicitly distinguishes external (separated computation vs knowledge, scalable, editable) from internal (parametric, fast, hard to update) substrates, and argues effective systems use hybrid architectures.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> N/A (a survey, not a CBR method). However, the surveyed agent-centric experience-memory loop (store experience -> retrieve relevant episodes -> reuse/adapt at decision time -> revise/update memory) maps loosely onto CBR Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain, and the memory-operations framework (storage/index, loading/retrieval, updates/refresh, compression, forgetting) covers Retain/Revise dynamics. The survey does not use CBR phase terminology.
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False — the survey is grounded in cognitive-psychology memory theory (Tulving episodic/semantic; sensory/working/procedural memory; Atkinson-Shiffrin-style multi-store analogies) rather than case-based reasoning; it does not frame itself as CBR and does not center Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Survey taxonomy of units rather than one: episodic events/interaction trajectories (sub-trajectory, action+feedback), semantic facts/concepts/entity-relations/KG-subgraphs, procedural skills/workflow-routines/reasoning patterns, user facts/preferences/persona records, dialogue/session segments, external documents, and (internal) parametric knowledge / latent hidden-state tokens / KV pairs. Retrieved 'reading' units are memory entries at these granularities organized in vector / text-record / relational-table / graph / tree / hierarchical stores.
- **index source**:
> Hybrid (survey-level). The retrievable store is mostly a GROWING memory written online during agent-environment/user interaction (indexed at write time with semantic embeddings + metadata: timestamps, task IDs, entities, tool usage), optionally combined with a STATIC external corpus (RAG). Internal substrates (weights via pre/post-training/editing/distillation; latent states; KV-cache) are induced parametrically/at inference. No single construction is prescribed; the survey contrasts external (online-grown, editable) vs internal (parametric) sources.
- **index structure topology**:
> Survey-level: organizes external-memory stores into four substrate topologies — (1) flat vector index (HNSW/IVF/PQ ANN), (2) text-record (human-readable core summary + episodic/semantic lists), (3) structural store (relational tables via SQL / graph-based knowledge graph / tree-structured e.g. RAPTOR), and (4) hierarchical store (multi-store: core/episodic/semantic/procedural/resource/knowledge modules coordinated by a meta-memory manager). Multi-agent adds private-only / shared-workspace / hybrid / orchestrated memory layouts.
- **retriever type**:
> Survey-level (heterogeneous across works): predominantly dense embedding ANN retrieval over vector indices; plus BM25 / keyword / string match (text-record and hierarchical stores), symbolic SQL queries and graph traversal (structural stores), and LLM/agent-directed selection (memory-driven routing, meta-memory managers). Hybrid; no canonical retriever is proposed.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Survey-level spectrum, explicitly framed as a Memory Learning Policy along three paradigms: (1) Prompt-based (off-the-shelf retrieval + static/dynamic prompt-controlled selection, no training); (2) Fine-tuning (parameterized memory policies internalized into weights, retrieval refinement); (3) Reinforcement Learning (memory operations as a learned policy optimized by downstream task reward — step-level memory edits, trajectory-level compact-state learning, cross-episode/multi-agent). The survey highlights the shift from heuristic similarity to RL-optimized memory read/write/prune policies (e.g., Memory-R1, Mem-alpha, MemAgent, MemSearcher).
- **query construction**:
> Survey-level: queries to memory are formed from current state/task (raw current query/sub-trajectory for similarity retrieval), with metadata pre-filtering (recency, task scope, memory type) before similarity ranking; agent- or LLM-generated structured queries (SQL, graph traversal); reflection/self-evaluation-conditioned retrieval; and state-matching against structured trajectory representations (e.g., SIT-graph episodic retrieval matches current execution state). Construction is method-dependent; abstracted as state-conditioned memory reading.
- **query granularity**:
> Survey-level: both task/session-level reads (recall user profile or relevant episodes at the start) and step/state-level reads during reasoning/acting (per-step retrieval in interactive agents, per-sub-trajectory matching). Multi-agent adds role-specific per-call memory views. No single granularity is standardized.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Survey-level: spans one-shot (load relevant memory at task start), iterative/per-step (interactive agents read memory each step/turn), active (agent-/reflection-initiated reads, e.g., Talker-Reasoner deciding when to read; Self-Validator requesting more retrieval if evidence is insufficient), and adaptive (learned/RL memory-read policies, e.g., revisitable/look-back retrieval). No single trigger policy is prescribed.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Survey-level: triggers across works include fixed schedule (read each step/turn), metadata/loading filters (recency, task scope, memory type), agent-initiated/self-directed access, reflective/self-evaluative signals that trigger updating-and-refresh-and-read, orchestrator/controller routing decisions in multi-agent systems, and learned RL memory-read policies (reflective retrieval in Retroformer/Memento, revisitable memory in ReMemR1). The survey does not adopt token-confidence/attention triggers as a unifying signal.
- **reranking**:
> Survey-level: after loading, memories are 'ranked or refined using semantic similarity, heuristic constraints, or budget-aware selection' before injection; multi-agent memory-driven routing performs explicit 'retrieval, scoring and reranking, selection' (e.g., S3 scores items by forgetting/relevance/source-credibility; G-Memory expands then compresses to a core subgraph then trims to role views). No single cross-encoder reranker is prescribed; reranking/scoring is treated as part of loading/retrieval and routing.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Survey-level: refinement covered under operations — Compression and Summarization (condense episodic records into compact/abstract or hierarchical/tree representations; Dynamic Cheatsheets maintain a compact task-adaptive summary; ReSum/IterResearch summarization-based context management), Updates and Refresh (rewrite/merge/re-rank salient entries), and budget-aware selection/truncation to fit context. Distractor avoidance is discussed (over-retrieval injects noise; 'lost in the middle'). Refinement is a central operation, but no single post-retrieval module is prescribed.
- **tool document engineering**:
> N/A (memory survey). Tool/skill-description engineering is largely out of scope, though procedural-memory skill/tool induction (e.g., TroVE verifiable toolboxes, ToolLibGen tool creation/aggregation) and resource-memory for documents/media are mentioned within the substrate taxonomy.
- **index content separation**:
> Covered as a recurring pattern: hierarchical/virtual-context memory (MemGPT-style OS memory hierarchy) separates a small in-context working memory from a larger external store paged in on demand; text-record memory keeps a compact core summary indexing fuller episodic/semantic lists; hierarchical store uses a lightweight meta-memory-manager index routing to heavy per-module content; structural/tree stores keep node summaries+embeddings as a lightweight index over detailed leaves. Discussed as a substrate/management efficiency pattern, not a formal principle.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (inter-tool dependency modeling is out of scope for this memory survey; procedural memory covers skill composition/sequencing but not tool-dependency graphs/bipartite KGs).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Survey-level: retrieved memory is primarily used as prompt/context augmentation (inject recalled snippets/summaries/experiences into the LLM context for reasoning and decision-making); plus skill/workflow reuse (procedural memory invoked as routines), experience reuse for self-evolution and test-time learning (TTL without parameter updates), guideline reuse (CRMWeaver injects best-matching workflow guideline), and — for internal memory — implicit parametric recall (weights) or carried-forward latent states/KV-cache. RL-based policies also use memory as a learnable Markov state.
- **planning integration**:
> Survey-level: memory supports planning/acting by supplying relevant episodes/skills/state at plan and act time across agent topologies — single-agent per-step interleaved retrieval during reasoning; multi-agent orchestrated routing where a planner/controller selects which history to retrieve and inject at each step (MGA Planner, AgentFlow shared memory, LEGOMem task/subtask memory routing); shared experience pools queried by current sub-trajectory for in-context reuse (MAICC). The survey abstracts this as memory enabling long-horizon planning, skill reuse, and cross-session continuity rather than prescribing a single integration.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Survey-level: interleaving spans per-answer (one-shot recall then answer in QA), per-step/per-turn (interactive agents read/write memory each step), per-sub-trajectory (state-matching retrieval), and per-tool-call within rollouts (tool/API agents). RL trajectory-level work folds summarization/compression into the policy across multi-turn rollouts. No single granularity is imposed.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> N/A (a survey, not a CBR adaptation method). The closest analogues surveyed are Updates-and-Refresh (rewrite/merge/correct entries), Compression/Summarization (abstract episodes), and RL/fine-tuning policies that internalize or revise reused experience; for retrieved skills/guidelines, LLM-prompted reuse and execution-feedback-driven revision are described.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Survey-level: surface forms span raw episodic trajectories/event records, distilled semantic facts/concepts/entity-relations, free-text core summaries + episodic/semantic lists (text-record), executable/JSON-encoded procedural workflows/skills, structured KG nodes/edges and tree-node summaries, user-profile/preference records, and latent/parametric forms (weights, hidden-state 'memory tokens' as in MemGen, KV pairs). The survey explicitly contrasts non-parametric explicit memory with parametric/latent neural memory.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Survey-level spectrum: raw episodic interaction records -> distilled semantic facts/concepts (decontextualized from episodes) -> reusable procedural workflows/skills and abstracted strategies/reasoning patterns -> state-aware guidelines/rules. The survey explicitly describes an abstraction gradient: episodic experiences are 'semanticized' into stable semantic knowledge, and procedural memory evolves from explicit non-parametric templates toward implicit parametric neural policies.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Survey-level: discussed via the over-retrieval problem (excessive/low-quality memory injects noise and 'lost in the middle' degradation) addressed by budget-aware selection, summarization/compression, pruning/forgetting (recency decay, importance thresholds, learned removal e.g. BudgetMem/Mem-alpha), deduplication, write-control isolation (Memory-R1 ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP; WebCoach episode-completion writes), conflict resolution / consistency feedback loops (EvoMem constraint memory + verifier), and hallucination-oriented evaluation (HaluMem Memory Integrity / False Memory Rate). No single retriever-aware-training mechanism is prescribed by the survey itself.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> Survey/taxonomy — covers all listed types. By cognitive mechanism: sensory, working, episodic, semantic, procedural memory. By substrate: external (vector / text-record / structural-graph / hierarchical) and internal (parametric weights, latent-state, KV-cache). By subject: user-centric vs agent-centric. It does not pick one; it provides a three-axis taxonomy (substrate x cognitive mechanism x subject).
- **write back**:
> True (survey-level) — memory writing/storage-and-index is a core operation; agents store new experiences/facts/skills (indexed with embeddings + metadata at write time). Surveyed systems (Generative Agents, MemGPT, Mem0, A-Mem, Memory-R1, ReasoningBank, etc.) write back episodes/summaries/edits. The survey treats write-back, plus updates/refresh/compression/forgetting, as central operations rather than one implementation.
- **online growth**:
> Yes (survey-level) — external memory grows online during deployment/interaction (the survey's whole 'context explosion / scaling with interactions, environment complexity, environment quantity' framing); the store is written/updated across sessions. Internal parametric memory grows only via (costly) weight updates; latent/KV memory is transient per-session. The survey explicitly contrasts scalable online-growing external memory with hard-to-update internal memory.
- **write back trigger**:
> Survey-level: triggers vary — per-step/per-turn writing, on-task-completion (WebCoach writes only after an episode completes; periodic/after-task summarization), reflective/self-evaluative writing (Reflexion/ReasoningBank store reflections), evaluation-signal- or conflict-triggered updates (rewrite when new evidence contradicts old), controlled write-time editing (Memory-R1 manager decides ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP), and human/system-validated writes (ChatGPT memory user control). The survey notes write strategy design (what/when to store) is vital but prescribes no single trigger.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Survey-level: explicitly important — agents recall trajectories of previous failures and fixes to improve (e.g., coding agents recall failure trajectories to raise unit-test pass rates; cross-episode memory distills self-correction rules; EvoMem keeps a growing feedback memory of failures from earlier rounds; Reflexion/Retroformer store reflective/negative experience). The survey frames learning from both successful and failed experiences as central to agent-centric memory and self-evolution.
- **memory evolution update**:
> Survey-level: covered under Updates-and-Refresh, Compression/Summarization, and Forgetting/Retention — beyond append-only, stored entries are mutated via rewrite/merge of overlapping episodic records, delta UPDATE/DELETE (Memory-R1), refine-overwrite of semantic summaries, importance re-ranking/refresh, dedup, recency-decay/importance-threshold forgetting, learned pruning, and graph link-and-evolve (e.g., temporal KG Zep, A-Mem entry linking). The survey stresses memory must 'evolve rather than merely accumulate' in non-stationary environments.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Yes (survey-level, highlighted) — Section 5 ('Memory Learning Policy') centers RL/learned memory policies: step-level memory-edit policies (Memory-R1 ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP, MemAct, MemAgent, RMM, Mem-alpha), trajectory-level compact memory-state learning (IterResearch, ReSum, MemSearcher, context-folding/summarization-as-policy), and cross-episode/multi-agent memory policies (Retroformer/Memento reflective retrieval, MAICC, SRMT). The survey explicitly contrasts these learned policies with fixed similarity top-k heuristics.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Yes (survey-level) — Section 4.2 dedicates the multi-agent setting: private-only vs shared-workspace vs hybrid vs orchestrated memory architectures; memory routing (orchestrator-based, agent-initiated, memory-driven); and isolation/conflict handling. Shared experience pools (MAICC, Spark, CRMWeaver shared guidelines), shared memory vectors (SRMT), hierarchical multi-agent memory (G-Memory), meta-memory managers (MIRIX), and collaborative/multi-user memory with access control (Collaborative Memory). Cross-framework sharing and 'agentic communities of practice' are surveyed and flagged as a key direction.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> No new benchmark is introduced; the survey compiles two benchmark tables. User-centric (Table 3): MSC, DuLeMon, MemoryBank, PerLTQA, LoCoMo, DialSim, LOCCO, MemoryAgentBench, LongMemEval, HaluMem, PersonaMem, PrefEval, MemBench, MemoryBench, ConvoMem. Agent-centric (Table 4): HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, HLE, BrowseComp, Mind2Web, WebArena, WebShop, GAIA, OSWorld, AppWorld, tau-Bench, tau-Bench2, HumanEval, SWE-Bench, LoCoBench, LoCoBench-Agent, PaperBench, RECODE-H, ALFRED, ALFWorld, MineDojo, EgoSchema, Video-MME, LongVideoBench, MT-Mind2Web, MPR, StoryBench, Evo-Memory, LifelongAgentBench, OdysseyBench.
- **benchmark family**:
> memory (agent-memory evaluation survey) cross-cutting many families: QA / multi-hop (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, HLE, MPR), memory/long-term-conversation (LoCoMo, LongMemEval, MemoryAgentBench, MemBench, HaluMem, PersonaMem, PrefEval, ConvoMem, MSC, DuLeMon, MemoryBank, PerLTQA, DialSim), web/GUI (Mind2Web, WebArena, WebShop, GAIA, BrowseComp, MT-Mind2Web), OS/desktop (OSWorld), tool/API (AppWorld, tau-Bench/tau-Bench2), code (HumanEval, SWE-Bench, LoCoBench/-Agent, PaperBench, RECODE-H), embodied (ALFRED, ALFWorld, MineDojo), long video (EgoSchema, Video-MME, LongVideoBench), and lifelong/test-time-learning agent (LifelongAgentBench, Evo-Memory, OdysseyBench, StoryBench).
- **baselines**:
> N/A — a survey with no experiments. It tabulates and compares representative memory systems along its taxonomy (e.g., MemGPT, Mem0, MIRIX, A-Mem, Generative Agents, MemoryBank, Reflexion, Retroformer, ExpeL, Voyager, ARIGraph, RAPTOR, Titans, MEMORYLLM, HippoRAG, Zep, ReasoningBank, Memory-R1, Mem-alpha, MemAgent, MemSearcher, G-Memory, AWM/Agent Workflow Memory, LEGOMem, MetaGPT, ChatDev, Collaborative Memory) rather than benchmarking baselines.
- **key metrics**:
> Survey-level metric taxonomy (Table 2) in three categories. Accuracy-based: Accuracy/Memory Accuracy, F1, Recall@K, MAP, NDCG@K, Success Rate (SR)/Goal Completion (GC), Pass@K/Resolved Rate (RR), Memory Integrity (MI), False Memory Rate (FMR). Similarity-based: ROUGE, BLEU, Distinct-n, BERTScore, FactScore, Perplexity. LLM-as-a-judge: Response Correctness, Faithfulness/Groundedness, Preference Following. Plus capacity/efficiency (MemBench).
- **headline result**:
> N/A (no empirical headline number; it is a survey). Headline contribution: a unified three-axis taxonomy of foundation-agent memory — substrate (external vs internal) x cognitive mechanism (sensory/working/episodic/semantic/procedural) x subject (user- vs agent-centric) — plus a memory-operations framework (storage/index, loading/retrieval, updates/refresh, compression/summarization, forgetting/retention; single- and multi-agent), a learning-policy taxonomy (prompting / fine-tuning / RL), and curated metric + benchmark tables, synthesizing 218 papers from 2023 Q1 to 2025 Q4.
- **ablations**:
> N/A (no experiments/ablations). The survey's comparative benchmark tables (Table 3 user-centric memory abilities FE/MR/TR/UR/CS/FR/UP/AS/IC/AB coverage; Table 4 agent-centric env/interact/abilities) and the metric table function as structured cross-system comparisons clarifying which design choices and abilities each benchmark/system covers.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Yes (conceptually, a key argument). The survey repeatedly stresses making evaluation 'attributable to the memory mechanism' by separating retrieval/selection from generation: retrieval/ranking metrics (Recall@K, MAP, NDCG@K) assess whether the memory interface surfaces the right items, while integrity/hallucination metrics (Memory Integrity, False Memory Rate) and operation-level scoring (e.g., HaluMem, LongMemEval question-type categorization) expose memory failure modes separately from end-task accuracy. It explicitly calls for next-gen benchmarks to add memory-sensitive metrics beyond single end-to-end success.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both, as a taxonomy. Outcome: answer-level Accuracy/F1, SR/GC, Pass@K/RR. Process/intermediate: retrieval faithfulness/coverage, Recall@K/MAP/NDCG@K, Memory Integrity, False Memory Rate, Memory Retention Score, state-tracking error modes (drift/omission/contradiction), persistence under interruptions, and judge-based faithfulness/groundedness. The survey advocates complementing end-to-end success with memory-attributable process metrics.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Discussed qualitatively and as a metric dimension: external memory adds retrieval latency and storage/indexing cost that grows with horizon; internal/parametric memory is fast but costly to update; latent/KV memory scales linearly with sequence length. The survey calls for reporting computational/storage trade-offs (capacity & efficiency, e.g., MemBench; BudgetMem cost-efficient policies; efficiency trade-offs: memory size, update frequency, retrieval cost). No single quantitative speedup/cost number (it is a survey).
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Survey-level: finite context window / 'context explosion' is the core motivation; memory externalizes state so agents do not retain all context in-prompt. Retrieval is typically top-k by similarity with budget-aware selection and reranked-then-truncated injection; fixed-size memory buffers under capacity constraints (MemAgent, BudgetMem) and adaptive forgetting/retention regulate budget. Benchmarks span max-context from ~1K to ~3M tokens (Table 3). No single budget/k value is prescribed.
- **survey scope and axes**:
> Organizing axes: (3) Taxonomy = Memory Substrates {external: vector index, text-record, structural store [relational/graph/tree], hierarchical store; internal: weights, latent-state, KV-cache} x Cognitive Mechanisms {sensory, working, episodic, semantic, procedural} x Subjects {user-centric, agent-centric}; (4) Memory Operations {storage/index, loading/retrieval, updates/refresh, compression/summarization, forgetting/retention} for single-agent, and multi-agent {architecture: private-only/shared-workspace/hybrid/orchestrated; routing: orchestrator-based/agent-initiated/memory-driven; isolation & conflicts}; (5) Learning Policy {prompt-based [static/dynamic], fine-tuning [parameterized policies], reinforcement learning [step/trajectory/cross-episode-multi-agent]}; (6) Scaling {interaction horizon, environment complexity, environment quantity}; (7) Evaluation {metrics: accuracy/similarity/LLM-judge; benchmarks: user- vs agent-centric}; (8) Applications; (9) Future Directions. Coverage: 218 key articles, 2023 Q1 to 2025 Q4 (curated from several hundred via Google Scholar + top-venue screening).
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A as a proposed benchmark (it is a survey), but it tabulates construction details for surveyed benchmarks: user-centric (Table 3) with #Sessions, #Questions, Max Tokens, data source Real/SIM/MIX, and ten memory-ability coverage flags (FE/MR/TR/UR/CS/FR/UP/AS/IC/AB) — e.g., LongMemEval 50K sessions / 500 Q / 1.5M tokens (MIX), LoCoMo 1K / 7,512 (MIX), ConvoMem 300 / 75,335 / 3M (SIM), MemBench 65K / 53K (MIX); agent-centric (Table 4) with #Data, Env, Interact, Resource (REAL/SIM/MIX), core abilities, and evaluation metric — e.g., SWE-Bench 2.3K (REAL, RR), WebArena 812 (SIM, SR), GAIA 466 (REAL).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Cognitive-psychology memory theory (Tulving episodic/semantic memory; Atkinson-Shiffrin / sensory-working-long-term multi-store; procedural memory) as the organizing analogy; foundational LLM-agent memory systems it taxonomizes — Generative Agents, MemGPT/MemOS, Mem0, MIRIX, MemoryBank, RET-LLM, A-Mem, ARIGraph, Zep, RAPTOR, HippoRAG, Titans, MEMORYLLM; experience/self-evolving systems Reflexion, Retroformer, ExpeL, Voyager, ReasoningBank, Agent Workflow Memory; RL memory policies Memory-R1, Mem-alpha, MemAgent, MemSearcher; multi-agent MetaGPT, ChatDev, G-Memory, LEGOMem, Collaborative Memory.
- **contrasts with**:
> Positions itself against prior memory surveys that used a single classification axis (e.g., Zhang et al. 2024 'A Survey on the Memory Mechanism of LLM-based Agents' [sources/forms/operations]; Du et al. 'Rethinking Memory in AI: taxonomy, operations, topics'; human-inspired long-term-memory surveys) by adding the orthogonal three-axis view (substrate x cognitive mechanism x subject) and emphasizing learning policies and 'second-half' real-utility evaluation. Within the taxonomy it contrasts external vs internal substrates, user- vs agent-centric subjects, and heuristic vs learned (RL) memory policies.
- **lineage**:
> Surveys group — a 2026 comprehensive memory survey for foundation agents. It builds on and extends earlier anchor memory surveys (e.g., Zhang et al. 2024 LLM-agent memory survey; cognitive-architectures-for-language-agents) and sits alongside other 2025-2026 agent-memory/experience surveys, formalizing substrate/cognitive/subject axes, the memory-operation cycle, and the prompting/fine-tuning/RL learning-policy spectrum; downstream it frames the agent-memory research roadmap (continual/self-evolving agents, multi-human-agent organization, memory infrastructure/efficiency, lifelong personalization & trustworthy memory, multimodal/embodied/world-model agents, real-world benchmarking).

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- completeness_vs_topk_objective
- dynamic_index_and_protocol

<a id="item-rethinking-memory-survey-du"></a>
### 175. Rethinking Memory in AI: Taxonomy, Operations, Topics, and Future Directions (a.k.a. v3 title: Rethinking Memory in LLM based Agents: Representations, Operations, and Emerging Topics) (Du et al.)

2025  ·  arXiv 2505.00675  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00675)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2505.00675, cs.CL); submitted 1 May 2025, last revised 24 Dec 2025 (v3). No peer-reviewed venue identified as of mid-2026.
- **authors affiliation**:
> Yiming Du, Wenyu Huang, Danna Zheng, Zhaowei Wang, Sebastien Montella, Mirella Lapata, Kam-Fai Wong, Jeff Z. Pan. Affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong; The University of Edinburgh; HKUST; Poisson Lab, CSI, Huawei UK R&D Ltd. (work done during Yiming Du's visit to University of Edinburgh).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00675
- **code url**: https://github.com/Elvin-Yiming-Du/Survey_Memory_in_AI
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/Elvin-Yiming-Du/Survey_Memory_in_AI (the 'Memory Compass' continuously-updated paper/dataset/tools list; ~350 stars, last push Dec 2025, MIT license, includes a 'Week Papers' rolling update section)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**: Survey/taxonomy of memory in LLM-based agents, spanning QA, long-term conversational/personalized dialogue, long-context modeling, knowledge editing (parametric modification), and multi-source/multi-agent memory; not a single task method.
- **problem setting**:
> A survey that reframes memory in AI/LLM-based agents through atomic operations and representation types. Setting is conceptual/organizational rather than experimental: it argues prior surveys emphasize application-level memory use (e.g., personalized dialogue) while overlooking the atomic operations governing memory dynamics. It covers both offline (parametric/pretrained memory, knowledge editing) and interactive/online (episodic, multi-session, agentic) settings, and both single-agent and multi-agent/multi-source memory. Supervision availability varies by surveyed sub-topic; the survey itself provides taxonomy, dataset tables, and a tools landscape rather than new supervised training.
- **what is retrieved**:
> Across surveyed systems: external contextual memory items including documents, dialogue/episodic histories, personas, knowledge-graph nodes/relations, multimodal content (text/image/audio/video), and structured KB entries; Retrieval is one of the six defined atomic operations. Parametric memory is 'accessed' via feedforward computation rather than explicit retrieval.
- **retrieval grounding**: HYBRID at the survey level: the taxonomy explicitly spans STATIC external corpora/KBs/documents, GROWING/episodic memory the agent writes (long-term, multi-session), and parametric (in-weights) memory, plus multi-source memory that fuses several stores.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A — not a case-based reasoning work; the survey does not frame itself around CBR Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain phases (though its Retrieval/Updating/Consolidation/Forgetting operations partially parallel CBR mechanisms).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False — the survey does not explicitly frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; its operations are grounded in cognitive memory science and LLM-agent literature instead.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Heterogeneous across the survey: documents/passages, dialogue turns and multi-session histories, episodic experiences/trajectories, knowledge-graph subgraphs/triples, persona facts, and multimodal segments. Retrieval is defined formally as selecting relevant memory entries from the contextual memory store conditioned on a query.
- **index source**: Both: static corpora and offline-induced parametric memory, plus online/test-time-induced growing memory (Consolidation writes short-term experiences into persistent memory; Indexing organizes the contextual store). Hybrid construction is explicitly covered (multi-source memory).
- **index structure topology**:
> Surveyed across topologies: flat vector indices (FAISS, Chroma, Milvus, Qdrant, Weaviate), knowledge/temporal GRAPH stores (Neo4j, Graphiti, knowledge-graph memory), and hierarchical/structured organizations. Indexing is defined as a distinct operation that builds structures (e.g., indices, graphs) over stored memory for efficient access.
- **retriever type**: Surveys the full spectrum: sparse BM25, dense retrievers (Contriever, embedding models), graph-based retrieval, and LLM-driven retrieval; hybrid retrieval is discussed. No single retriever is proposed.
- **query construction**: Varies by surveyed system: raw user query, dialogue-context-conditioned query, decomposed sub-queries for multi-hop QA, and temporally-conditioned queries; the survey formalizes Retrieval as conditioned on a query but does not prescribe a single construction method.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Compression/Condensation is one of the six defined operations: it summarizes/distills retrieved or stored memory before use (reducing redundancy while preserving salient information). The survey thus frames post-retrieval refinement primarily as compression/condensation, alongside indexing-based filtering.
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A — inter-tool dependency modeling is not within the survey's memory-operations scope.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Across surveyed systems: prompt/context augmentation (memory-grounded generation), parametric injection via knowledge editing/fine-tuning (parametric modification topic), and graph/structured grounding. The survey's Utilization category covers Retrieval + Compression feeding generation.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A — no CBR case-adaptation mechanism; the closest surveyed mechanisms are Updating (refine stored memory) and Compression/Condensation (distill memory), described across surveyed systems rather than as a single adaptation method.
- **retrieved item representation**: Surface forms surveyed include raw text/dialogue, distilled summaries (via Compression/Condensation), structured knowledge-graph notes, and parametric (latent, in-weights) representations. The survey's representation taxonomy is parametric vs contextual (unstructured/structured).
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Spans raw episodic experiences/trajectories, distilled/condensed summaries, structured guidelines/KB entries, and parametric knowledge; the survey's organizing abstraction is the parametric-vs-contextual representation split rather than a single abstraction level.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: All types in scope: parametric (in-weights), episodic/long-term, graph (knowledge-graph/temporal), workflow/procedural, and latent — the survey explicitly unifies these under parametric vs contextual (unstructured/structured) representations.
- **write back**: Yes (as a surveyed capability): Consolidation writes short-term experiences into persistent memory and Updating modifies stored entries; these are two of the six defined operations. The survey itself does not implement write-back but catalogs it.
- **online growth**: Yes (covered): long-term and multi-source memory systems grow the store during deployment via Consolidation/Updating; parametric memory grows via parametric modification (knowledge editing). The survey treats online memory growth as central.
- **memory evolution update**: Explicitly covered: Updating (delta/refine-overwrite of existing entries) and Forgetting (prune) are defined operations; Consolidation appends/encodes new entries; the survey describes memory as temporally evolving (link-and-evolve via temporal knowledge graphs such as Graphiti).
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**: Yes — Multi-source Memory is one of the four key topics, covering integration/sharing of memory across sources and (in part) across agents/frameworks; this is explicitly highlighted as an emerging direction.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> Survey catalogs benchmark/dataset tables rather than running them. Long-term memory: PersonaMem-v2, MemoryBench, HaluMem, BFCL V4, LongMemEval, LoCoMo, MemoryBank, PerLTQA, MaLP/MALP, DialSim, MovieChat-1K, Conversation-Chronicles (CC), LaMP, MSC, DuLeMon, 2WikiMultiHopQA, NQ, HotpotQA. Long-context: MMLongBench, WikiText-103, PG-19, LRA, and others. Plus parametric-memory-modification (knowledge editing) and multi-source memory evaluation tables.
- **benchmark family**:
> memory (LoCoMo, LongMemEval, PersonaMem, MemoryBench, HaluMem, MemoryBank, PerLTQA, MSC, DuLeMon); QA / multi-hop (NQ, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA); long-context (PG-19, WikiText-103, LRA, MMLongBench); tool/function-calling (BFCL V4); multimodal/long-video (MovieChat-1K); personalization (LaMP, MaLP).
- **baselines**: N/A — as a survey it does not run head-to-head baseline comparisons; it organizes prior methods (e.g., MemoryBank, knowledge-editing methods, RAG systems, long-context models) within the operation/topic taxonomy.
- **key metrics**:
> Reports the metrics used by catalogued benchmarks: Accuracy, Recall@K, NDCG@K, EM, F1, ROUGE, BLEU, MAP, Precision/Recall, PPL, GPT-4 score, Persona Score, Hallucination/Omission Rate, Retention Rate, AST Accuracy / Execution Success (BFCL). No single headline metric is computed by the survey.
- **headline result**:
> N/A — no experimental headline number; the survey's contribution is the taxonomy of two memory representations (parametric vs contextual) and six atomic operations (Consolidation, Updating, Indexing, Forgetting, Retrieval, Compression/Condensation) mapped to four topics (long-term, long-context, parametric modification, multi-source). Most-cited framing number: 6 operations x 2 representations -> 4 topics.
- **ablations**: N/A — no empirical ablations are run; the survey instead maps which operations each topic and each benchmark exercises (e.g., dataset tables tag the operations evaluated, such as 'Indexing, Retrieval, Compression' for LongMemEval/LoCoMo).
- **evaluation decoupling**: Reports, via catalogued benchmarks, that intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@K, NDCG@K, MAP) and end-to-end task metrics (Accuracy, F1, ROUGE) are sometimes reported separately (e.g., LongMemEval, PerLTQA), but the survey does not enforce decoupling itself.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Mixed across catalogued benchmarks: most score final outcomes (Accuracy/F1), while some add process-oriented signals (Retention Rate for continual learning, Hallucination/Omission Rate for memory faithfulness, temporal-reasoning subsets). The survey itself reports no process metrics.
- **survey scope and axes**:
> Two organizing axes: (1) Memory representation — Parametric vs Contextual (Contextual split into Unstructured and Structured); (2) Six atomic memory operations grouped into Memory Management (Consolidation, Indexing, Updating, Forgetting) and Memory Utilization (Retrieval, Compression; renamed Condensation in v3). These map to four key research topics: long-term memory, long-context memory, parametric memory modification, and multi-source memory. The survey also catalogs benchmark datasets and a four-level tools landscape (Components / Framework / Application-Layer / Product) and a Human-vs-AI memory comparison plus future directions. Reference coverage: ~310 bibliography entries (v2); coverage window through 2025 (continuously updated repo through Dec 2025).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A — the survey does not construct a benchmark; it aggregates existing datasets in comparison tables annotated with modality, supported operations, dataset type (QA vs multi-session), persona presence, temporal-reasoning presence, metrics, purpose, and year.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Prior memory surveys it extends/critiques, e.g., Zhang et al. 2024 (operational view: writing/management/reading, but missing indexing), long-context surveys (Huang et al. 2023b), long-term memory surveys (He et al. 2024d; Jiang et al. 2024b), personalization (Liu et al. 2025a), and knowledge-editing surveys (Wang et al. 2024h). Grounds memory operations in cognitive-science notions (e.g., Consolidation: Squire et al. 2015).
- **contrasts with**:
> Application-centric memory surveys that emphasize use cases (e.g., personalized conversational memory) without a unified operational framework; and subtopic-narrow surveys (long-context-only, long-term-only, editing-only). Du et al. argue these miss atomic operations such as Indexing and lack cohesive architectural/operational views plus practical benchmark/tool foundations.
- **lineage**:
> Surveys group. A foundational taxonomy/operations survey for memory in LLM-based agents; provides the parametric-vs-contextual representation split and six-operation lifecycle that situates RAG (Retrieval), memory consolidation/updating, and knowledge editing (parametric modification) within one framework — a reference map for memory-augmented and retrieval-augmented agent lines of work.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- completeness_vs_topk_objective
- context_budget_and_selection_count
- cost_efficiency_tradeoff
- dynamic_index_and_protocol
- failure_experience_usage
- index_content_separation
- noise_robustness_mechanism
- planning_integration
- query_granularity
- reasoning_search_interleaving_granularity
- reranking
- retrieval_as_learned_policy
- retrieval_trigger_signal
- retriever_learning_signal
- tool_document_engineering
- when_to_retrieve
- write_back_trigger

<a id="item-rag-eval-survey"></a>
### 176. Retrieval Augmented Generation Evaluation in the Era of Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Survey (Gan et al.)

2025  ·  arXiv 2504.14891  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.14891)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **authors affiliation**:
> Aoran Gan, Hao Yu, Kai Zhang, Qi Liu, Wenyu Yan, Zhenya Huang, Shiwei Tong, Guoping Hu (8 authors on the arXiv abstract page; the HTML body also lists Enhong Chen). Primary affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China (USTC), Hefei, China. Additional affiliations: McGill University, Montreal, Canada (Hao Yu); Tencent Company, Shenzhen, China; Artificial Intelligence Research Institute, iFLYTEK Co., Ltd, Hefei, China.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.14891
- **code url**: N/A (a survey, not a method; no method code). It is associated with the maintained 'Awesome-RAG-Evaluation' paper-list/benchmark-list repo (see maintained_repo_url).
- **maintained repo url**:
> https://github.com/YHPeter/Awesome-RAG-Evaluation (the official GitHub repository whose citation block explicitly cites this paper, arXiv:2504.14891; it catalogs RAG evaluation frameworks/benchmarks with code and paper links and was updated 2025-04-21 to 'Add new benchmarks for RAG system'. The repo was originally created for the predecessor CCF Big Data 2024 survey 'Evaluation of RAG: A Survey'/Auepora, which this work extends; ~198 stars).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Survey of RAG evaluation. The surveyed systems target knowledge-intensive QA as the prevailing operationalization (RAG assessments are typically converted into a QA/conversational format of question + ground-truth answer + candidate docs), plus downstream domains catalogued via benchmarks: medical, legal, finance, telecom, multilingual, multi-turn, long-context. Not about planning/agents/tool-use/embodied; it explicitly scopes to the narrow training-free RAG framework over unstructured documents and excludes knowledge-graph and multimodal RAG evaluation.
- **problem setting**:
> A comprehensive literature survey (not a method) of how to evaluate RAG systems in the LLM era. It deconstructs a RAG system into retriever and generator components and organizes evaluation into Internal Evaluation (component-level: retrieval and generation, conventional IR/NLG metrics, and LLM-based metrics) versus External Evaluation (system-level utility: Safety and Efficiency), framed via a systems-theory internal/external lens that extends the authors' earlier Auepora unified evaluation process. The surveyed setting is predominantly offline, single-agent, non-interactive, training-free RAG over unstructured external documents; supervision ranges from off-the-shelf metrics to LLM-as-judge. It also performs a meta-analysis (research-oriented meta-evaluation) over 582 peer-reviewed RAG papers crawled from high-level NLP/AI venues since autumn 2022 to quantify which evaluation methods are actually used.
- **what is retrieved**:
> docs (unstructured text documents / chunks). The survey scopes to unstructured text retrieval as the prevailing paradigm and explicitly excludes knowledge-graph and multimodal retrieval; only datasets that contain retrieved ground-truth documents are included in its dataset table. It does not survey retrieval of demos/cases/trajectories/skills/tools/experiences/guidelines (that agentic-experience family is out of scope).
- **retrieval grounding**:
> STATIC external corpus is the dominant grounding surveyed (a corpus is constructed offline via chunking + embedding; sources include Wikipedia, specialized corpora such as scientific articles and financial reports). The survey also notes real-time / dynamic knowledge sources (web scraping, search engines, live news) and time-sensitive benchmarks (FreshLLMs/FreshQA, MultiHop-RAG, CDQA, CRAG) that depend on rapidly updated documents - i.e. dynamic-but-external grounding, not an agent-written growing memory. So: predominantly static external corpus, with a notable dynamic/real-time-corpus dimension; not episodic agent memory.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> The default retrieval objective surveyed is a fixed top-k document ranking (Recall@K / Precision@K / NDCG@K / Hit@K over top-k retrieved docs). The survey additionally elevates 'Comprehensiveness' (Relevant Documents <-> Relevant Documents) as an explicit retrieval evaluation target measuring diversity and coverage so that retrieved docs give a comprehensive view of the topic - a coverage/completeness-flavored objective distinct from precision-only top-k. It does not frame the goal as a precision-driven variable-size recommendation.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (not a case-based-reasoning work; no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain case cycle - it is a RAG-evaluation survey over unstructured documents).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: false. The survey does not frame RAG as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it treats RAG as retriever+generator over external knowledge and focuses on its evaluation.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Document / text chunk. The survey describes offline chunking that segments large documents into smaller manageable units, then embedding for retrieval; the retrieved unit evaluated is the relevant document/passage/chunk (it scopes to unstructured documents and excludes KG-subgraph and multimodal units).
- **index source**:
> Static, offline-constructed retrievable store is the dominant case (corpus built before retrieval via offline chunking + embedding into a vector index). The survey also covers dynamic/online sources (search-engine queries, real-time web/news scraping) used by time-sensitive benchmarks. As a survey it is not itself inducing an index; it catalogs static-corpus and dynamic-external-corpus construction. Not an online/test-time agent-induced memory.
- **index structure topology**:
> Flat vector index over embedded chunks is the surveyed default (text vectorized into a high-dimensional dense semantic space for efficient retrieval). The survey notes online-RAG add-ons (intent recognition, query rewriting, routing) and multiple retrieval strategies (sparse/dense/graph/hybrid), but it explicitly scopes the main paradigm to unstructured-document flat-index retrieval and excludes graph/structured indices from its evaluation focus.
- **retriever type**:
> Surveyed across types: sparse retrieval (BM25-style), dense retrieval (embedding-based, the default), graph retrieval, and hybrid methods. Some commercialized systems perform additional dynamic search-engine queries. The survey does not endorse one retriever; for its evaluation scope dense/sparse/hybrid over unstructured text is the prevailing setting.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> N/A as a contribution - this is an evaluation survey, not a retriever-training method, so it does not train a retriever. It scopes to the training-free RAG framework. Where relevant it notes retrievers are typically off-the-shelf dense/sparse embedding models within the surveyed systems; the survey's focus is on how to score retrieval quality (Relevance/Comprehensiveness/Correctness via IR metrics and LLM-based judges), not on retriever optimization signals.
- **query construction**:
> Surveyed as part of the online RAG workflow: raw query plus optional pre-retrieval components - intent recognition, query rewriting, and routing - introduced before retrieval. RAG assessments commonly convert the task into a QA/conversational format (question + ground-truth answer + candidate docs). The survey catalogs query construction as a pipeline stage rather than proposing one.
- **query granularity**:
> Task-level / query-level is the prevailing granularity surveyed (one user query mapped to retrieved docs then a response), with the QA-format conversion of question -> answer. Multi-turn and bridging-query benchmarks (MTRAG) and multi-hop cross-document benchmarks (MultiHop-RAG) are catalogued, which involve trajectory/turn-level querying, but the dominant evaluated unit is the single query.
- **when to retrieve**:
> One-shot retrieve-then-generate is the prevailing surveyed paradigm (retrieve documents, then the LLM synthesizes a response). The survey notes online workflows with pre-retrieval routing and post-retrieval reranking/fusion and discusses multi-hop/multi-turn benchmarks, but iterative/active/adaptive retrieval is not the organizing axis of this evaluation survey (it inherits the standard retriever->generator pipeline).
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> N/A / fixed schedule. As an evaluation survey over the standard retriever->generator pipeline, retrieval is triggered once per query by the pipeline; the survey does not center an adaptive WHEN-to-retrieve signal (token confidence, learned classifier, reflection tokens). Robustness/safety evaluation does probe whether the system should keep vs discard retrieved context (Chen et al.'s answerable/unanswerable x keep/discard Risk/Carefulness/Alignment/Coverage metrics), which is closest to a retrieval-use decision.
- **reranking**:
> Yes - reranking is surveyed as an optional post-retrieval step where some systems rerank documents or fuse data across sources before generation. A 'Diversity Reranker' framework (using Cosine Distances) is catalogued in the frameworks table (Table 2). Reranking is treated as a pipeline component whose effect is evaluated, not as the survey's own contribution.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Surveyed as pipeline stages: post-retrieval reranking and cross-source data fusion before generation, and (on the generation side) prompt-engineering scaffolds applied to retrieved context such as CoT, Tree-of-Thoughts (ToT), Self-Note, and RaR (Rephrase-and-Respond). Post-processing after generation (e.g. entity recognition for multiple-choice/classification, translation for multilingual tasks) is also noted. The survey catalogs these refinements rather than proposing a single one.
- **tool document engineering**:
> N/A (not about tool/skill retrieval; focuses on document/knowledge retrieval evaluation. It touches API-call accuracy only via the AST-based hallucination metric (Patil et al./Gorilla) used to evaluate correctness of external API calls, but does not analyze tool-description engineering for indexing).
- **index content separation**: N/A (the survey does not center a lightweight-index-then-content / progressive-disclosure pattern). It discusses offline chunking + embedding into a vector index and top-k retrieval, but not an SOP-index-then-content separation.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> N/A (no tool API / RapidAPI / MCP / function-calling tool registry; the surveyed indices are document/vector stores. It notes some systems issue dynamic search-engine queries and that the corpus can draw on real-time web data, but this is not a synchronized tool index with CRUD auto-sync).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (no inter-tool dependency modeling; the survey covers document retrieval evaluation, not multi-tool dependency graphs).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Prompt augmentation: retrieved relevant documents are passed to the LLM, which acts as a decision-maker/reasoner that synthesizes the retrieved information into a coherent response (rather than generating knowledge independently), thereby reducing hallucination. The survey's focus is on evaluating whether that synthesis is Relevant, Faithful (grounded in the docs), and Correct (matches the gold answer).
- **planning integration**:
> N/A / out of scope. This is a RAG-evaluation survey over the retriever->generator pipeline; it does not cover planning, MCTS/tree-search, or hierarchical subtask planning. The closest analog is the standard retrieve-then-generate flow plus prompt-engineering reasoning scaffolds (CoT/ToT) inside the generator.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Per-answer (single retrieve-then-generate per query is the prevailing evaluated unit). The survey notes generation-side reasoning scaffolds (CoT/ToT/Self-Note) and multi-hop/multi-turn benchmarks, and flags evaluating deep-thinking models (e.g. OpenAI o1) interleaved with RAG retrieval/generation as an under-explored future direction - implying finer-grained interleaving is not yet standard in surveyed evaluations.
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A (no CBR-style case adaptation/revision; retrieved documents are injected verbatim as prompt context, and the survey's concern is evaluating the resulting generation, not adapting a retrieved case).
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Raw retrieved text documents/passages injected as prompt context for the generator. The survey evaluates the surface response against the retrieved documents (Faithfulness) and against the gold answer (Correctness); it does not survey distilled-strategy/workflow/program/latent representations (out of scope for unstructured-document RAG).
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**: Raw retrieved documents/passages (single retrieved document/chunk granularity). No distilled strategy, workflow, skill, or hint abstraction - the survey scopes to unstructured-text knowledge retrieval, not experience/skill retrieval.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Central evaluation theme rather than a method. The survey catalogs how RAG robustness to irrelevant/misleading/counterfactual retrieved context is measured and benchmarked: RGB (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness with Accuracy); RECALL (reliable vs counterfactual knowledge via BLEU/ROUGE-L and Misleading Rate); Wu et al. Misrepresentation Ratio / Uncertainty Ratio for semantically-related-but-irrelevant info; SafeRAG (inter-context conflict); C-RAG (conformal risk analysis / theoretical risk guarantees); Cheng et al. Resilience Rate and Boost Rate; and Chen et al.'s Risk/Carefulness/Alignment/Coverage for keep-vs-discard decisions. These are evaluation/diagnostic mechanisms, not a training-time defense the survey itself proposes.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**: none (classic RAG over static/dynamic external documents; the survey scopes to training-free unstructured-document RAG and does not center episodic/skill/workflow/graph/latent agent memory).
- **write back**: false. The surveyed RAG paradigm reads from an external corpus and does not write new experiences/cases back into a memory store. The survey is about evaluating retrieval+generation quality, not memory accumulation.
- **online growth**:
> Mostly false (the corpus/index is constructed offline and read at inference). The survey does note dynamic external knowledge sources (real-time news/web scraping, search engines) and time-varying benchmarks (FreshQA, CDQA, CRAG) whose underlying corpora update over time - external corpus dynamism rather than an agent-written growing memory.
- **write back trigger**: never (no experience/case write-back in the surveyed training-free document-RAG paradigm; retrieval is read-only over an external corpus).
- **failure experience usage**:
> Not a focus / N/A. The survey does not store the system's own success/failure trajectories. The closest related ideas it catalogs are robustness/safety evaluations of how the system handles incorrect or adversarial retrieved documents (RECALL counterfactuals, PoisonedRAG corpus poisoning, hallucination-rate measurement), i.e. evaluating responses to bad context, not storing failed experiences.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (no stored experiential entries to mutate in the surveyed document-RAG paradigm). External-corpus updates (live news, dynamic QA benchmarks) are offline data refreshes rather than online entry-level memory evolution.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No / N/A. Retrieval is treated as standard similarity-based top-k over a document index in the surveyed training-free framework; the survey does not present retrieval/case-selection as a learned or RL-optimized policy (its contribution is evaluation methodology, not retrieval optimization).
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> N/A / not a focus. The survey covers single-system RAG pipelines and does not center cross-agent or cross-framework shared memory. It does compile cross-framework evaluation resources (Table 2) so practitioners can compare evaluation frameworks, but that is a catalog of evaluation tools, not shared agent memory.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> Catalogs RAG-specific benchmarks/datasets (Table 1) and evaluation frameworks (Table 2). Benchmarks/datasets include: WikiEval (RAGAS), FreshQA (FreshLLMs), RECALL (EventKG/UJ), ARES (reusing NQ, HotpotQA, FEVER, WoW, MultiRC, ReCoRD from KILT and SuperGLUE), RGB, MultiHop-RAG, CRUD-RAG (with UHGEval), MedRAG (MIRAGE), FeB4RAG (with BEIR), RAGBench (PubMedQA, CovidQA, HotpotQA, MS MARCO, CUAD, DelucionQA, EManual, TechQA, FinQA, TAT-QA; TRACe), ReEval (NQ-MRQA + RealTimeQA), DomainRAG, Telecom RAG Eval (TeleQuAD, 3GPP), LegalBench-RAG (PrivacyQA, CUAD, MAUD, ContractNLI), RAGEval (DragonBall: finance/law/medical), CoURAGE (RealTimeQA + NQ), RAG Unfairness (TREC22 FairRank, BBQ), CoFE-RAG, OCR-Hinders-RAG (1,261 PDFs + 8,561 images / OHR-Bench), OmniEval (finance), CRAG (KG + web), RAG Playground (319 QA pairs), MTRAG (CLAPNQ, FiQA, Govt, Cloud), CDQA (Chinese Dynamic QA), U-NIAH (Starlight Academy long-context needle-in-haystack), SCARF, Arabic RAG Eval. Frameworks/tools (Table 2): RAGAS, ARES, RGB, TruEra/TruLens RAG Triad, LangChain Benchmarks, Databricks Eval, FiD-Light, Diversity Reranker, RECALL, FreshLLMs/FRESHEVAL, RAGBench/TRACe, eRAG, RAGChecker-style, SafeRAG, RAGTruth-style, etc. Underlying classic QA/IR datasets referenced: NQ, HotpotQA, FEVER, MS MARCO, BEIR, KILT, SuperGLUE.
- **benchmark family**:
> QA-centric: general/single-hop QA (NQ, MS MARCO, RealTimeQA), multi-hop QA (HotpotQA, MultiHop-RAG, 2Wiki-style), long-form/needle long-context (U-NIAH), fact-checking (FEVER), domain QA (medical MedRAG/MIRAGE/PubMedQA/CovidQA, legal LegalBench-RAG/CUAD/MAUD/ContractNLI, finance OmniEval/FinQA/TAT-QA/FiQA, telecom TeleQuAD/3GPP), multilingual (Arabic RAG Eval, Chinese CRUD-RAG/CDQA), multi-turn (MTRAG), dynamic/time-sensitive (FreshQA, CDQA, CRAG), robustness/counterfactual (RGB, RECALL, ReEval), safety (SafeRAG, PoisonedRAG, RECALL), fairness (RAG Unfairness/BBQ/TREC FairRank), OCR-noise (OHR-Bench). Standard IR collections: BEIR, KILT, SuperGLUE. This is the RAG-evaluation benchmark family - NOT the agent/web/embodied/tool families (Mind2Web/WebArena/ALFWorld/ToolBench).
- **baselines**:
> N/A (a survey, not a method; it runs no head-to-head method comparison). Its comparative work is (1) comparing evaluation targets/metrics for retrieval (Relevance/Comprehensiveness/Correctness) vs generation (Relevance/Faithfulness/Correctness); (2) comparing conventional IR/NLG metrics vs LLM-based (output-based and representation-based) metrics; (3) comparing evaluation frameworks side-by-side in Table 2; and (4) a meta-analysis comparing the actual usage frequency of traditional vs LLM-based metrics across 582 peer-reviewed RAG papers. It positions itself against prior RAG surveys, especially the authors' own predecessor Auepora (Yu et al.).
- **key metrics**:
> Surveys (does not report its own) the metric landscape. IR metrics: non-rank-based Accuracy/Hit@K, Recall@K, Precision@K, F1; rank-based MRR, NDCG@k (DCG/IDCG), MAP. NLG metrics: EM, ROUGE (ROUGE-N/L/W/S), BLEU, METEOR (plus BertScore). LLM-based output metrics: RAGAS/Databricks LLM-as-judge prompts, GPT-4 few-shot match, AST-based hallucination (Gorilla/Patil), SePer (Semantic Perplexity), KPR (Key Point Recall), MRWR/MRLR, FactScore and D-FActScore, and risk-aware Risk/Carefulness/Alignment/Coverage. LLM-representation metrics: GPTScore, ARES (classifier + LLM embeddings), RAGAS answer-relevance cosine, Thrust. Safety metrics: Misleading Rate, Misrepresentation/Uncertainty Ratio, Attack Success Rate (ASR), Retrieval Failure Rate, Citation Precision/Recall, Hallucination Rate, Extraction Success Rate, PII Leakage Rate, Membership-Inference success, Resilience Rate, Boost Rate. Efficiency metrics: Time-to-First-Token (TTFT), total/end-to-end latency, Single Query Latency, token-based cost, Cost-Effectiveness Ratio.
- **headline result**:
> N/A (no single experimental headline number - it is a survey). Its headline contributions are (1) the internal-vs-external evaluation taxonomy for RAG and the dual evaluation-target framework (retrieval: Relevance/Comprehensiveness/Correctness; generation: Relevance/Faithfulness/Correctness); and (2) a meta-analysis over 582 peer-reviewed RAG papers (crawled from high-level NLP/AI venues since autumn 2022) finding that traditional metrics still predominate over LLM-based evaluation methods, while LLM-based evaluation usage is rising (peaking in 2024 H2 and 2025 H1) and that internal (retrieval/generation) evaluation vastly outweighs external (safety/efficiency), with safety the most neglected.
- **ablations**:
> N/A (no experiments, hence no ablations). The analytical equivalents are the meta-analysis breakdowns: (1) distribution of evaluation methods across the four segments Retrieval / Generation / Safety / Efficiency (Figure 3), showing internal >> external and safety least covered; (2) word-frequency word-cloud of metrics (Figure 4) showing traditional metrics dominate over LLM-based (-LLM-suffixed) metrics; (3) per-half-year count of papers explicitly using LLM-based RAG evaluation (Figure 5), rising with 2024 H2 and 2025 H1 highest.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> Yes - decoupling is a core organizing principle. The survey explicitly separates retrieval-component evaluation (intrinsic IR metrics: Recall@K/Precision@K/NDCG/MRR/MAP, and targets Relevance/Comprehensiveness/Correctness) from generation-component evaluation (Faithfulness/Correctness/Relevance, NLG and LLM-based metrics), and further separates internal (component) from external (system safety/efficiency) evaluation. This component-decoupled view is the central distinction from end-to-end-only RAG evaluation.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both, and the survey argues for going beyond outcome-only scoring. Outcome: final-answer EM/F1/Accuracy/ROUGE/BLEU. Process/intermediate: retrieval-quality IR metrics (Recall@K/NDCG/MRR) score the retrieval step; Faithfulness scores whether generation is grounded in retrieved docs; KPR scores incorporation of key points from retrieved docs; SePer/Thrust probe internal belief/knowledgeability. The survey critiques that many components are still evaluated only via end-to-end RAG-ontology metrics and calls for more functional-decomposition and reasoning-process (e.g. deep-thinking-model) evaluation.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> A first-class external-evaluation dimension (Section 4.2). Latency: Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) and complete/end-to-end response time (retrieval + processing + generation), plus Hofstatter et al.'s Single Query Latency. Cost: categorized into infrastructure, token-based API expenses, storage, operational overhead, and development costs; LLM-provider token-usage metrics multiplied by pricing rates; and a Cost-Effectiveness Ratio (performance improvement per unit cost). The survey flags the high cost of thorough RAG evaluation itself (vast scale of tools/datasets) and balancing cost vs effectiveness as an open challenge. No single numeric headline is given.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> Discussed via chunking strategy (segmenting documents into manageable units guided by original structure/context) and top-k retrieval (Recall@K/Precision@K with a chosen k), with optional reranking/fusion to curate which retrieved docs reach the generator's prompt. Long-context handling is benchmarked separately (U-NIAH needle-in-haystack for extremely long contexts). The survey does not prescribe a single token budget; k and chunk size are treated as configurable pipeline choices whose effects are evaluated.
- **survey scope and axes**:
> Explicit organizing axes: (1) Internal vs External evaluation (systems-theory framing); (2) within Internal: Evaluation Target (retrieval: Relevance/Comprehensiveness/Correctness; generation: Relevance/Faithfulness/Correctness), Conventional methods (IR metrics: non-rank-based + rank-based; NLG metrics) vs LLM-based methods (Output-based vs Representation-based); (3) within External: Safety (robustness, factuality, adversarial attacks, privacy, fairness, transparency/accountability) and Efficiency (latency, cost); (4) Resources: a dataset/benchmark catalog (Table 1) and an evaluation-framework catalog (Table 2, categorized as Research/Tool/Benchmark with retrieval/generation/safety/efficiency targets). Scope is explicitly limited to training-free RAG over unstructured documents, excluding KG and multimodal RAG. Coverage: 124 references; meta-analysis over 582 peer-reviewed RAG papers since autumn 2022 through 31 March 2025.
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A as a new benchmark (this is a survey, not a benchmark paper - it constructs no new dataset). It catalogs existing RAG-evaluation benchmarks with their construction methods in Table 1 (e.g. real-time-news sourcing for FreshQA/MultiHop-RAG/CDQA; domain-corpus curation for MedRAG/LegalBench-RAG/OmniEval; LLM-synthesized/schema-based generation with false-premise/counterfactual elements for RAGEval/RECALL; OCR-noise from 1,261 PDFs + 8,561 images). Its own empirical artifact is the meta-analysis corpus of 582 peer-reviewed RAG manuscripts crawled from high-level NLP/AI venues.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Directly extends the authors' own predecessor survey 'Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey' (Yu et al., the Auepora unified evaluation process; CCF Big Data 2024 / arXiv 2405.07437, reference [21]), broadening it with internal/external systems framing, LLM-based evaluation methods, safety/efficiency, and a 582-paper meta-analysis. Builds on foundational RAG formulations (retriever+generator) and the broader RAG survey lineage (e.g. Gao et al.), classic IR/NLG metrics (BLEU/ROUGE/METEOR; Recall/Precision/NDCG/MRR/MAP), and established RAG evaluation frameworks/benchmarks (RAGAS, ARES, RGB, RECALL, TruLens RAG Triad, FactScore).
- **contrasts with**:
> Positions itself against prior RAG surveys that mainly collect methods/applications but lack systematic evaluation discussion (e.g. Gao et al. and multimodal-RAG surveys), and especially against its own earlier Auepora review (Yu et al. [21]), which it says was largely confined to mainstream frameworks; this work claims to be the most comprehensive RAG-evaluation survey, bridging traditional and LLM-driven methods. Methodologically it contrasts conventional metrics (favored for simplicity/reliability) vs LLM-based metrics (more flexible but harder to standardize across LLM versions/prompts), and internal component evaluation vs external system (safety/efficiency) evaluation.
- **lineage**:
> Surveys lineage. A RAG-evaluation-focused survey within the Surveys group, sitting downstream of foundational RAG surveys (e.g. Gao et al. 'RAG for LLMs: A Survey') and directly extending the authors' Auepora evaluation survey. It is orthogonal/complementary to the agentic-RAG, graph-RAG, and memory surveys in this collection: rather than cataloging RAG methods, it catalogs how RAG is measured (faithfulness, factual accuracy/correctness, relevance, comprehensiveness, safety, efficiency) and meta-analyzes evaluation practice, providing the evaluation vocabulary that method papers in this collection are scored against.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- venue

<a id="item-cbr-llm-survey-hatalis"></a>
### 177. Review of Case-Based Reasoning for LLM Agents: Theoretical Foundations, Architectural Components, and Cognitive Integration (Hatalis et al.)

2025  ·  arXiv 2504.06943  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.06943)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**:
> arXiv preprint (arXiv:2504.06943, cs.AI / cs.MA). Submitted 9 Apr 2025 (v1), last revised 11 Apr 2025 (v2). Not a peer-reviewed venue; arXiv-issued DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2504.06943. As of indexing, Semantic Scholar reports referenceCount 44 (the bibliography numbers entries up to [44]); citationCount was low/near-single-digit at indexing time (cited by e.g. AgentFly arXiv:2508.16153).
- **authors affiliation**:
> Kostas Hatalis (corresponding, kostas@gocharlie.ai), Despina Christou, and Vyshnavi Kondapalli. Primary affiliation: GoCharlie.ai (all three list GoCharlie.ai); Kondapalli's email is lehigh.edu (Lehigh University), indicating a Lehigh affiliation as well. Three authors; industry-led (GoCharlie.ai).
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.06943
- **code url**:
> N/A (this is a theoretical/conceptual review with no original experiments; the authors release no code or implementation repository. GitHub/framework references in the text are citations to third-party CBR-LLM systems such as DS-Agent, CaseGPT, and CBR-RAG, not an artifact of this paper.)
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (no continuously-updated authors' paper list or leaderboard repository; the work is a frozen arXiv PDF, last revised to v2 on 11 Apr 2025).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Survey / review (decision-making and agent reasoning). Reviews how Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) can be integrated into LLM-agent frameworks for planning, structured/specialized-knowledge tasks, and accountable decision-making. Surveyed application domains of the cited CBR-LLM systems span automated data science (DS-Agent), healthcare and legal QA (CaseGPT, CBR-RAG), triage classification, logical fallacy detection, code generation, and multiagent gaming/goal reasoning, rather than a single task domain.
- **problem setting**:
> Analytical literature review plus a proposed theoretical/mathematical framework -- not a method with original experiments. It (1) reviews the theoretical foundations of CBR-augmented LLM agents, (2) identifies critical architectural components, (3) formulates a mathematical model of the CBR processes of case retrieval, adaptation, and learning (mapping the classic Aamodt & Plaza 4R cycle Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain onto LLM agents), (4) gives a qualitative comparative analysis of CBR-LLM vs Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning vs vanilla RAG, and (5) explores cognitive dimensions (self-reflection, introspection, curiosity) integrated with Goal-Driven Autonomy (GDA). It covers both single-agent and multi-agent (multiagent gaming GDA) settings and interactive/online learning settings as surveyed sub-areas, but defines no controlled experimental protocol or benchmark of its own; all quantitative numbers are drawn from cited works.
- **what is retrieved**:
> Cases (problem-solution-outcome episodes). In the proposed framework a case is the unit; surveyed CBR-LLM systems retrieve past cases / problem-solution pairs / exemplars / nearest-neighbor precedent cases (e.g., DS-Agent retrieves expert case insights; Dannenhauer et al. retrieve NL-task/Python-code problem-solution pairs; CBR-RAG retrieves contextually relevant legal cases).
- **retrieval grounding**:
> HYBRID / GROWING (episodic) memory. The defining framing is a GROWING agent-owned case library L that the agent writes to via the Retain phase (L_{t+1} = L_t U {c_new} when utility >= delta), as opposed to a static external corpus. CBR is explicitly contrasted with vanilla RAG's reference-based corpus retrieval; the case library evolves over time, making it a growing/episodic store (HYBRID where seeded from an offline expert case base as in DS-Agent's development stage).
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> Threshold/top-k similarity retrieval. The proposed retrieval function returns the subset C_q = R(q,L) = {c_i in L | sim(q,P_i) >= tau}, i.e., a similarity-threshold (tau) selection rather than a fixed-completeness-set or precision-driven variable-size objective. As a review it does not define a completeness metric; surveyed systems mostly use top-k / nearest-neighbor case retrieval.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> [Retrieve, Reuse, Revise, Retain] -- all four. The paper explicitly defines and models the full Aamodt & Plaza 4R cycle: Retrieve (case retrieval, Eqs. 2-4), Reuse/Revise (solution adaptation A = A_compose o A_transform o A_select, Eqs. 5-6, 10-12), and Retain (case learning/retention via utility-thresholded library update, Eqs. 7-8). It frames itself entirely around this cycle.
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> True. The work explicitly frames itself as Case-Based Reasoning and grounds in the canonical CBR literature -- it cites Aamodt & Plaza (1994) for the 4R cycle and lazy learning, Kolodner (1992) for human expert reasoning, plus Craw & Aamodt (2018) and CBR knowledge-container theory. The entire paper is about integrating classic CBR into LLM agents.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Case (a structured problem-solution tuple).
