Formally a case c = (P, S, O, M): P = problem space (features p_1..p_n), S = solution space (actions s_1..s_m), O = outcome space (success metrics o_1..o_k), M = metadata (temporal markers, environmental conditions, provenance). Surveyed instantiations include problem-solution pairs (NL task -> Python code), expert insight cases, and precedent legal/medical cases.
- **index source**:
> Growing case library L = {c_1,...,c_l}, constructed both offline (seeded from expert/historical cases, e.g., DS-Agent development stage) and online/test-time-induced via the Retain phase that appends successful new problem-solution episodes. HYBRID: an initial offline case base that grows during deployment.
- **index structure topology**:
> Hierarchical + hybrid index. Each case is indexed with BOTH a dense semantic embedding E_i (from the foundation LLM's latent space) AND sparse feature-based indices I_i capturing domain-specific attributes (Algorithm 1). The library is then organized via a hierarchical structure (OrganizeHierarchy) enabling coarse-to-fine search; a structural-similarity retrieval channel (R_structural) also matches problem-structure / solution-pattern topology.
- **retriever type**:
> Hybrid. The proposed hybrid retrieval combines three channels: R_semantic (dense embedding/cosine similarity in the LLM latent space, Eq. 4), R_feature (explicit feature matching), and R_structural (problem-structure / solution-pattern matching), fused by weights lambda_1, lambda_2, lambda_3 (Eq. 9). It is therefore a dense+feature+structural hybrid retriever rather than a single BM25/dense/learned retriever.
- **query construction**:
> Raw query problem q is matched against the problem component P_i of stored cases; query/key formed from the current problem features (problem-space representation). In the GDA extension, queries are also keyed on (state, goal) for the Plan Case Base and on detected discrepancies/mismatches m for the Mismatch Case Base. No synthetic-query expansion is prescribed.
- **query granularity**:
> Both task-level and step/state-level. Base CBR retrieval is task-level (retrieve cases for the query problem q at problem-solving time). The CBR-GDA extension adds step/state-level retrieval: Retrieve_PCB: S x G -> S x P (plan cases keyed on state+goal) and Retrieve_MCB: M -> G (goal cases keyed on discrepancy), invoked during execution monitoring -- a two-level scheme.
- **when to retrieve**:
> One-shot at problem-solving time for the core CBR cycle (retrieve relevant cases for query q, then adapt). In the CBR-GDA cognitive extension retrieval becomes active/iterative: triggered during execution by discrepancy detection (mismatch m between expected and actual state) to retrieve new goals (online monitoring loop).
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> For core CBR: fixed/once-per-query (retrieve when a new problem q arrives, gated by similarity threshold tau). For CBR-GDA: discrepancy-triggered -- a detected mismatch m = Discrepancy(s_c, e_c, s_actual) between expected and actual states triggers retrieval from the Mismatch Case Base to formulate a new goal (agent-/event-initiated, uncertainty/expectation-violation signal).
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Selection/transformation as part of adaptation rather than a separate refinement pipeline: A_select identifies the most relevant components from retrieved solutions, A_transform modifies them to target constraints, A_compose integrates them (Eq. 6). A meta-cognitive process selects the adaptation approach based on problem characteristics and retrieval results. No explicit distractor-filtering or compression module is described.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Case adaptation / reuse (and prompt augmentation). Retrieved cases C_q are passed to the LLM adaptation function s_hat = A(q, C_q) = f_LLM(q, C_q, Theta); the LLM adapts retrieved solutions into a context-appropriate answer via transformational (substitution/deletion/insertion, Eq. 10), compositional (weighted combination of k solutions, Eq. 11), and generative (LLM-synthesized, Eq. 12) adaptation. Retrieved cases also serve as explicit precedent exemplars for explainability and (surveyed) dynamic few-shot prompting.
- **planning integration**:
> Retrieve-then-adapt (case-based plan/solution synthesis), extended to per-execution interleaving in the GDA loop. Core: retrieve cases at plan/solve time, then adapt into a solution. Cognitive extension integrates CBR into a Goal-Driven Autonomy controller (discrepancy detection -> explanation -> goal formulation -> goal management), with two case bases (Plan Case Base mapping state+goal->expectations, Mismatch Case Base mapping discrepancy->new goal) consulted during execution monitoring -- i.e., retrieval woven into a plan-monitor-replan loop.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Per-answer for the core CBR cycle (retrieve-adapt-answer once per problem). In the CBR-GDA extension it becomes per-step / per-monitoring-cycle: retrieval is invoked each time a discrepancy is detected during execution to reformulate goals. The framework also proposes a weighted blend of reasoning pathways f_reasoning(q) = omega_1 f_CBR + omega_2 f_CoT + omega_3 f_parametric (Eq. 13).
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> LLM-prompted adaptation (the LLM is the adaptation engine), formalized as A(q,C_q) = A_compose o A_transform o A_select (Eq. 6) with three sub-types: transformational adaptation (substitution/deletion/insertion operations to fit target constraints, Eq. 10), compositional adaptation (weighted combination of components from k retrieved solutions, Eq. 11), and generative adaptation (LLM synthesizes a novel solution conditioned on retrieved cases, s_adapted = f_LLM(q,{S_1..S_k},Theta), Eq. 12). A meta-cognitive process selects the adaptation strategy by problem characteristics and retrieval results; not execution-feedback or RL-reuse-finetuning based.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Structured case (problem-solution-outcome-metadata tuple) injected as explicit precedent/exemplar; the solution component S is adapted into the final answer. Surface forms across surveyed systems include raw problem-solution pairs (NL task + executable Python code), expert insight cases, and nearest-neighbor precedent cases presented alongside difference statements for explainability.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Single concrete case / precedent (a problem-solution episode), not a distilled abstract strategy. Cases retain concrete problem features, solution actions, and outcome metrics; CBR is characterized as lazy learning where generalization is delayed until a specific problem is encountered, so retrieved units stay at the concrete-precedent level (with metadata).
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Similarity-threshold gating (tau) for retrieval selectivity, plus meta-cognitive / self-reflective adaptation-strategy selection and (in GDA) discrepancy detection that flags expectation violations. The proposed cognitive dimensions (self-reflection, introspection) are positioned as a robustness mechanism. No retriever-aware training or distractor-aware SFT is described (it is a conceptual framework).

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> Episodic case-library memory (skill/case base). The agent maintains a case library L of past problem-solution-outcome episodes; the GDA extension adds two specialized case bases (Plan Case Base, Mismatch Case Base). Framed as experiential / episodic knowledge that mirrors human episodic memory.
- **write back**: True. The Retain phase stores new problem-solution episodes into the case library: L_{t+1} = L_t U {c_new} if U(c_new, L_t) >= delta, else L_t (Eq. 7). The CBR-GDA variant similarly appends to the Plan and Mismatch Case Bases (Eqs. 18-19).
- **online growth**:
> True. The case library grows during deployment/test-time as successful new cases are retained (continuous learning / knowledge evolution); this online growth is presented as a core CBR advantage for domain adaptation (accelerated adaptation trajectories, storing previously unseen scenarios for future reuse).
- **write back trigger**:
> Utility-thresholded retention (selective, quality/effectiveness-gated): a new case is added only if its utility U(c_new, L_t) >= delta (Eq. 7), where U = alpha*novelty + beta*effectiveness + gamma*generalizability (Eq. 8). In CBR-GDA, plan/goal cases are retained only if their Quality exceeds thresholds theta_P / theta_M (Eqs. 18-19). Effectively on-success / high-utility retention with novelty and generalizability considered.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> No. Case selection is a fixed similarity-threshold retrieval (sim >= tau) with heuristic weights, not a learned/RL-optimized retrieval policy. The GDA controller learns by updating its case bases (storing high-quality plans/goals), but retrieval/case-selection itself is similarity-based, not an M-MDP or RL retrieval policy.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Mostly single-agent private case memory, but the cognitive/GDA section reviews a multiagent setting: Munoz-Avila et al.'s CB-GDA used in a multiagent gaming domain with two shared case bases. The proposed framework is largely single-agent; multi-agent/shared-memory CBR is discussed via cited work rather than as a central contribution.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> N/A as original experiments (the review runs no benchmarks of its own). It cites empirical results from prior CBR-LLM works: automated data science (DS-Agent, Guo et al. 2024), legal question answering (CBR-RAG / CaseGPT, Wiratunga et al. 2024), triage classification (Wilkerson 2024), logical fallacy detection (Sourati et al. 2023), code generation via dynamic few-shot prompting (Dannenhauer et al. 2024), and multiagent gaming GDA (Munoz-Avila et al. 2010).
- **benchmark family**:
> N/A as a primary axis (no benchmark suite of its own). The cited evaluations span: tool/code & automated data science (DS-Agent code-generation tasks), domain-specific QA (legal/healthcare QA for CBR-RAG/CaseGPT), classification (triage classification, logical fallacy detection), and decision/planning in games (multiagent gaming GDA). It does not adopt the standard agentic-trajectory benchmark families (Web/Embodied/Tool/Code/Memory/Decision-RL) as an organizing axis.
- **baselines**:
> N/A as original comparisons (no head-to-head experiments). Its qualitative comparative analysis (Section 7, Table 1) contrasts three reasoning-approach classes: CBR-LLM vs Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning vs vanilla/standard RAG. Cited works compare their CBR systems against zero-shot, static few-shot prompting (Dannenhauer et al.), baseline LLM agents / other SOTA agents (DS-Agent), and rule-based GDA / non-GDA replanning (CB-GDA).
- **key metrics**:
> N/A as original measurement. The review enumerates the metrics used across the surveyed evaluations: accuracy, generalizability, user trust, task completion rate, mean rank, best rank, one-pass rate, cost efficiency, and various explainability metrics. It also proposes conceptual metrics: an explainability score E(a) (Eq. 20), an adaptation rate A(a,d) (Eq. 21), compute time / memory cost (Eqs. 22-23), and a composite solution-quality Q(a) (Eq. 24).
- **headline result**:
> Cited (not produced by this review): the DS-Agent CBR framework (Guo et al. 2024) achieved a 100% success rate in the development stage and a 99% one-pass rate in the deployment stage with GPT-4, outperforming other state-of-the-art LLM agents while demonstrating cost efficiency. The review uses this and Wilkerson's triage-trust result and Sourati's fallacy-detection accuracy/generalizability gains as evidence for CBR-LLM advantages; its own central contributions are the 4R mathematical model and the CBR vs CoT vs vanilla-RAG comparison (Table 1).
- **ablations**:
> N/A (the review conducts no experiments and reports no component ablations of its own). Its closest analogue is the qualitative dimension-by-dimension comparison in Table 1 (Knowledge Utilization, Reasoning Transparency, Adaptation Capacity, Domain Specificity, Learning Mechanism, Cognitive Capabilities, Goal Reasoning) attributing distinct strengths to CBR-LLM vs CoT vs vanilla RAG.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> N/A as original measurement. It conceptually separates an intrinsic explainability metric E(a) (Eq. 20) and adaptation-rate A(a,d) (Eq. 21) from end-task solution quality Q(a) (Eq. 24) and from compute/memory cost (Eqs. 22-23), but reports no measured retrieval-vs-task decoupling (Recall@k/nDCG are not used; it is not an empirical study).
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Both are discussed conceptually. Beyond outcome metrics (accuracy, success/one-pass rate, task completion), the review emphasizes process/transparency metrics -- precedent-based reasoning transparency, an explainability score E(a) = (1/n) sum trace(r_i)/complexity(r_i), user-trust scores, and adaptation rate over time -- arguing CBR's explicit precedent traces give superior explainability vs CoT and vanilla RAG. It measures none of these itself.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Discussed qualitatively/formally, not measured. It formalizes total compute time T(a,q) = T_retrieval + T_processing + T_generation (Eq. 22) and memory M(a) = M_model + M_knowledge + M_working (Eq. 23), arguing CBR incurs extra retrieval cost but benefits from reduced processing for well-matched cases and more efficient knowledge management (selective retention) than corpus-based vanilla RAG. The one cited efficiency claim is DS-Agent's reported cost efficiency with GPT-4.
- **survey scope and axes**:
> Organizing axes: (1) theoretical foundations of CBR-augmented LLM agents (formal case definition c=(P,S,O,M), and a mathematical model of Retrieve/Adapt/Retain); (2) architectural components (case representation & indexing, hybrid retrieval, adaptation mechanisms, integration with LLM reasoning); (3) cognitive dimensions (self-reflection, meta-cognition/introspection, curiosity/extrospection, CBR knowledge-container interactions); (4) Goal-Driven Autonomy (GDA) integration with a CBR-GDA mathematical model and learning; and (5) comparative analysis CBR vs CoT vs vanilla RAG across seven dimensions (Table 1). Reference count: 44 entries (Semantic Scholar referenceCount = 44; bibliography numbered to [44]); coverage window classic CBR (1992-1994) through 2024 CBR-LLM work, with the survey itself published April 2025.
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (this is a review, not a benchmark; it constructs no dataset). It cites others' results (e.g., DS-Agent's 100% development success / 99% one-pass deployment with GPT-4) as difficulty/quality signals rather than building or sizing any benchmark.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Builds on the classic CBR literature -- Aamodt & Plaza (1994) 4R cycle and lazy learning, Kolodner (1992), Craw & Aamodt (2018) cognitive CBR / knowledge containers -- and on Goal-Driven Autonomy (Munoz-Avila et al. 2010; Langley 2012 cognitive systems). It synthesizes recent CBR-LLM systems it reviews: DS-Agent (Guo et al. 2024), CaseGPT and CBR-RAG (Wiratunga et al. 2024), CBR for code generation (Dannenhauer et al. 2024), logical-fallacy CBR-LLM (Sourati et al. 2023), triage CBR (Wilkerson 2024), and cognitive-architecture/LLM work (Sumers et al. 2023).
- **contrasts with**:
> Positions CBR-augmented LLM agents explicitly against Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning and standard/vanilla Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): CBR uses experiential, precedent-based, transparent reasoning with high adaptation capacity, explicit domain modeling, case-acquisition learning, and dynamic goal reasoning, whereas CoT relies on parametric knowledge and static step-based reasoning, and vanilla RAG on reference-based corpus retrieval with corpus-expansion learning (Table 1). It also contrasts CBR-GDA with rule-based GDA and non-GDA replanning (cited).
- **lineage**:
> Surveys group. A 2025 conceptual/theoretical review that maps the canonical CBR 4R cycle (Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain) onto LLM agents with an explicit mathematical model and a CBR vs CoT vs vanilla-RAG comparison; it anchors group D (case-based / experiential-memory agents) by providing the CBR ontology (explicit Aamodt & Plaza grounding, case = (P,S,O,M), growing case library, retain-driven online learning) that distinguishes true case-based reasoning from plain retrieval-augmentation, complementing method papers such as DS-Agent and CBR-RAG.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- context_budget_and_selection_count
- failure_experience_usage
- memory_evolution_update
- reranking
- retriever_learning_signal

### 178. The Landscape of Agentic Reinforcement Learning for LLMs: A Survey

2025  ·  arXiv 2509.02547  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.02547)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2025
- **venue**: arXiv:2509.02547 (submitted 2 Sep 2025, v5 17 Apr 2026); accepted to / published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), OpenReview forum RY19y2RI1O.
- **authors affiliation**:
> Guibin Zhang, Hejia Geng, Xiaohang Yu (equal contribution) ... Zhenfei Yin, Lei Bai (corresponding); 25 authors total. Primary affiliations: University of Oxford; Shanghai AI Laboratory; National University of Singapore; UIUC; Brown University; University College London; USTC; Imperial College London; Dalian University of Technology; Chinese Academy of Sciences; CUHK; University of Georgia; UC San Diego; UC Santa Barbara; University of Bristol.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.02547
- **code url**: N/A (survey; no method code). Companion OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=RY19y2RI1O
- **maintained repo url**: https://github.com/xhyumiracle/Awesome-AgenticLLM-RL-Papers (official maintained paper list, ~1.8k stars / 79 forks, actively updated)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Survey of agentic reinforcement learning (Agentic RL) for LLMs. Spans a twofold taxonomy: (a) core agentic capabilities (planning, tool use, memory, reasoning, self-improvement, perception), and (b) task domains: search/research agents, code agents, mathematical agents, GUI agents, vision agents, embodied agents, and multi-agent systems. Retrieval/tool-use/memory are treated as RL-controlled agentic capabilities rather than static modules.
- **problem setting**:
> Survey synthesizing 500+ works. Formalizes the conceptual shift from PBRFT/LLM-RL (modeled as a degenerate single-step MDP over a prompt -> response) to Agentic RL, which is cast as a temporally extended, partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) with multi-step interaction, environment state, action space (text actions + structured agentic actions such as tool calls), stochastic transition dynamics, and (often sparse / verifiable) rewards. Settings covered are interactive and long-horizon, single- and multi-agent, with supervision ranging from verifiable outcome rewards (RLVR) to preference/process rewards. The central thesis: RL is the mechanism that turns heuristic static capability modules (planning, tool use, memory, reasoning) into adaptive, robust agentic behavior.
- **what is retrieved**:
> As a survey it reviews what RL-controlled agentic memory/tool subsystems store and retrieve: external documents/web pages (RAG-style search agents), tools/APIs, episodic memory entries, natural-language memory tokens (explicit) and latent memory tokens (implicit), structured/graph memory (temporal KG), skills, and prior experiences/trajectories. Retrieval is framed as an RL-learnable decision (what to store, when to retrieve, how to forget).
- **retrieval grounding**:
> HYBRID across the surveyed field. Covers retrieval over STATIC external corpora/web/tools (RL-based search agents like Search-R1, R1-Searcher; tool retrieval) AND over GROWING/episodic memory the agent writes and manages with an RL policy (MemAgent, MEM1, ReSum, MemoryLLM/M+, MemGen, structured/graph memory). The RAG-style-vs-token-level-vs-structured memory taxonomy directly spans the static-corpus vs growing-memory distinction.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (survey, not a CBR method). Does not implement a Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain cycle; experience reuse appears via RL self-improvement and memory rather than explicit CBR.
- **explicit cbr grounding**: No. The survey does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not center Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; experience reuse is framed through RL, memory, and self-improvement rather than the CBR ontology.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Reviewed across granularities (survey): document/web page (search agents), tool/API call, natural-language memory token/segment (explicit memory), latent memory token/embedding (implicit memory), knowledge-graph node/subgraph (structured memory), full trajectory/experience, and skill. No single canonical unit.
- **index source**:
> Survey covers all: static external corpora/web/tool sets (RAG-style search agents, TIR tool stores) and online/test-time growing memory written and pruned by the agent during interaction (MemAgent natural-language memory pool, MEM1, ReSum context summarization, MemoryLLM/M+ self-updatable latent memory). Hybrid is the dominant picture; the memory chapter explicitly traces evolution from RAG-style external memory to trainable token-level and structured memory.
- **index structure topology**:
> Survey reviews flat external corpora/vector stores (RAG-style), natural-language memory pools, fixed-size latent memory-token banks (MemoryLLM/M+), and structured/graph memory (temporal knowledge graph in Zep; structured memory as a 'prospective' direction). No single topology; structured/graph memory is highlighted as an emerging trend.
- **retriever type**:
> Survey-level: covers off-the-shelf dense retrieval over external corpora (search agents), generative/agent-issued retrieval where the LLM emits search/tool calls, and RL-controlled memory controllers that decide retrieval/retention. Emphasis is on retrieval/memory access becoming an RL-learned decision rather than a fixed retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Central surveyed shift: from off-the-shelf similarity retrieval toward RL-optimized retrieval/memory-management policies trained with outcome/verifiable rewards (RLVR). Search agents (Search-R1, R1-Searcher, ZeroSearch, ReSearch) learn when/what to retrieve via RL on final-answer reward; memory agents (MemAgent, MEM1, ReSum) train an RL policy controlling what to store/retrieve/overwrite. Also covers SFT/imitation and process/preference signals as alternatives.
- **query construction**:
> Not unified (survey). Reviews agent-issued queries: the LLM generates explicit search/tool-call queries interleaved with reasoning (TIR), reasoning-conditioned queries, and learned memory-trigger decisions. Query construction is itself part of the RL-trained policy in agentic search.
- **query granularity**: Survey spans task-level (one-shot retrieval), trajectory-level, and step/turn-level retrieval. The multi-turn TIR and RAG-style memory discussions emphasize per-step/per-turn retrieval decisions interleaved across a long-horizon rollout.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Survey-level: covers one-shot, iterative, and adaptive/learned (agent-initiated) retrieval. A core theme is that Agentic RL lets the agent autonomously learn WHEN to retrieve / invoke tools / access memory, moving from fixed schedules to RL-learned, agent-initiated retrieval decisions.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Survey reviews fixed schedules, model/agent-initiated requests (the policy emits a retrieve/tool/memory token), and RL-learned triggers (memory controllers deciding per-segment what to retain/overwrite, e.g. MemAgent; learned memory triggers, e.g. MemGen). The WHEN-to-retrieve decision is framed as part of the learned agentic policy rather than a single hand-set signal.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Survey covers post-retrieval / context-management refinement, especially context compression and summarization for long-horizon memory: ReSum (context summarization), context folding, MemAgent (compress long context into concise natural-language summaries), and MEM1 (synergize memory and reasoning). Refinement is framed as RL-controlled what-to-retain/overwrite/compress rather than classic rerank-then-distill.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Survey-level: prompt/context augmentation (RAG-style search agents inject retrieved docs), tool-integrated reasoning (retrieved tool outputs woven into the reasoning loop), memory injection (natural-language or latent memory tokens fed into the forward pass), skill reuse, and as RL training signal (outcome reward shapes when/how retrieval is used). Latent-token injection (MemoryLLM/M+, MemGen) is explicitly covered.
- **planning integration**:
> Survey distinguishes two RL-planning paradigms: (i) RL as an EXTERNAL GUIDE to a structured planning/search process (e.g. RL-scored nodes inside tree/MCTS-style planning), and (ii) RL as an INTERNAL DRIVER that directly evolves the LLM's intrinsic planning policy via outcome reward. Retrieval/tool use is interleaved per-step within these planning loops (TIR), and plan-then-act / retrieve-then-reason patterns are reviewed.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Survey emphasizes deep interleaving: from post-hoc ReAct-style tool calling to Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) that embeds tool/retrieval calls within the cognitive/reasoning loop, up to multi-turn TIR with temporal credit assignment. Granularity spans per-CoT-step and per-tool-call within a rollout (interleaved reasoning + acting).
- **adaptation mechanism**: N/A as a single mechanism (survey). Reviews adaptation via RL fine-tuning of the agentic policy (RLVR/PPO/GRPO), self-improvement/reflection, and RL-controlled memory update; no single CBR-style case-adaptation mechanism.
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Survey covers raw retrieved documents/tool outputs, distilled/summarized context (ReSum, MemAgent summaries), explicit human-readable natural-language memory tokens, latent/soft memory tokens (MemoryLLM/M+, MemGen, IMM), and structured/graph memory (temporal KG). Spans surface text to machine-native latent representations.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Survey spans the spectrum: raw retrieved documents/trajectories, compressed/summarized context, distilled experiential/latent memory (MemGen generative latent memory carrying experiential knowledge), and structured graph memory. Notes the move from flat token memory toward more abstract structured/latent representations.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> Survey memory taxonomy (Table 3) organizes agent memory into three classic categories with RL-marked variants: (1) RAG-style / external memory, (2) token-level memory (explicit natural-language tokens, e.g. MemAgent/MEM1/Memory Token; and implicit latent tokens, e.g. MemoryLLM/M+/IMM/MemGen), and (3) (prospective) structured memory (temporal knowledge graph, e.g. Zep). So: episodic + latent + graph + RAG-style.
- **write back**:
> Yes (central theme of the memory chapter). The survey frames RL-controlled memory as deciding what to store, when to retrieve, and how to forget; memory controllers write/overwrite natural-language or latent memory during interaction (MemAgent retain/overwrite per segment; MemoryLLM/M+ self-updatable latent memory; MemGen generating experiential memory).
- **online growth**:
> Yes. Token-level and RAG-style memory grow/update during deployment: MemAgent maintains and updates a natural-language memory pool per segment; ReSum/context-folding compress accumulating context online; MemoryLLM/M+ are self-updatable at test time. Online growth/management of memory is a first-class surveyed dimension (vs frozen offline stores).
- **write back trigger**:
> Survey covers RL-learned/per-segment writes (MemAgent decides per segment which tokens to retain/overwrite), summarization-triggered writes (ReSum, context folding), and continual latent updates (MemoryLLM/M+ update memory tokens as context evolves). No single trigger; writes are increasingly RL-policy-decided rather than fixed.
- **memory evolution update**:
> Survey reviews post-write dynamics: overwrite/retain decisions (MemAgent), compression/summarization-based consolidation (ReSum, context folding), continual update of fixed latent memory tokens (MemoryLLM/M+ repeatedly retrieved, integrated, and updated, with strong resistance to forgetting), and prospective structured/graph memory evolution (temporal KG). Update is framed as RL-controlled retain/overwrite/compress.
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> Yes (a defining surveyed theme). The survey's thesis is precisely that retrieval/tool/memory access becomes an RL-learned policy: search agents learn when/what to retrieve via RL (Search-R1, R1-Searcher), and memory controllers are RL policies deciding store/retrieve/forget (MemAgent, MEM1). Marked with daggers in Table 3 for works directly employing RL.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> Yes (surveyed). Section 4.7 covers Multi-Agent Systems and RL for multi-agent collaboration, and MARTI is reviewed as a framework for reinforced training/inference of multi-agent LLM systems. Shared/collective experience across agents is discussed as part of the multi-agent and self-improvement directions.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> Consolidated compendium (Table 10) of environments/benchmarks by capability and domain: Web (WebShop, Mind2Web/Mind2Web 2, WebArena, VisualWebArena, AppWorld); GUI (AndroidWorld, OSWorld, MiniWoB++); Coding/SWE (SWE-bench, Debug-Gym, and interactive SWE environments); Math; Search/Research (search-agent benchmarks); Embodied (ALFWorld/ScienceWorld-style, Minecraft); Tool (tool-use benchmarks); Multi-agent. Plus a frameworks table (Table 11).
- **benchmark family**:
> Spans web (Mind2Web/WebArena/WebShop/AppWorld/VisualWebArena), GUI/computer-use (OSWorld/AndroidWorld/MiniWoB++), code/SWE (SWE-bench/Debug-Gym), math, search/deep-research, embodied (Minecraft/ALFWorld-style), tool-use, and multi-agent. Organized by agent capability (Reasoning/Planning/Tool Use/Memory/Collaboration/Self-Improve) x task domain x modality.
- **baselines**: N/A as a survey (no head-to-head method baselines). It contrasts itself conceptually with prior LLM-RL / agent surveys (e.g. 'A Survey of Frontiers in LLM Reasoning' Ke et al. 2025; LLM/VLM-integrated RL surveys) and positions Agentic RL against PBRFT/conventional LLM-RL.
- **key metrics**:
> N/A as a survey (no single empirical metric). Discusses RL learning objectives and reward functions (verifiable/outcome rewards, process rewards, preference rewards) and capability/task success as the relevant evaluation signals; tabulates environments by capability rather than reporting numbers.
- **headline result**:
> N/A (survey, no empirical headline number). Headline contribution: a formalization of Agentic RL as a POMDP (vs degenerate single-step MDP of LLM-RL) and a comprehensive twofold taxonomy (six agentic capabilities x task domains), synthesizing 500+ works, plus a consolidated compendium of open-source environments (Table 10) and RL frameworks (Table 11).
- **ablations**: N/A (survey; no controlled ablations). Provides structured comparison tables instead: RL-algorithm variant comparison (Table 2: REINFORCE/PPO/GRPO/DPO families), agent-memory categories (Table 3, RL-marked), environments/benchmarks (Table 10), and RL frameworks (Table 11).
- **process vs outcome metrics**: Survey discusses both outcome rewards (RLVR / verifiable final-answer rewards) and process/intermediate signals (process reward models, step-wise / temporal credit assignment for multi-turn TIR), noting the challenge of credit assignment over long horizons as a key open problem.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> Survey discusses efficiency at the training-systems level (Sec 5.2 / Sec 6.2): asynchronous/distributed RL frameworks and rollout/experience-generation bottlenecks (e.g. AWorld reports a 14.6x speedup over single-node execution by parallelizing rollouts). Memory works target context-length/efficiency (ReSum, MemAgent compress long context). Not a single cost-vs-accuracy curve.
- **survey scope and axes**:
> Explicit organizing axes: (1) Preliminary formalization LLM-RL (single-step MDP) vs Agentic RL (POMDP), covering environment state, action space, transition dynamics, reward, learning objective, and RL algorithms (REINFORCE/PPO/GRPO/DPO). (2) Capability perspective: Planning, Tool Use, Memory, Self-Improvement, Reasoning, Perception, Others. (3) Task perspective: Search/Research, Code, Math, GUI, Vision, Embodied, Multi-Agent, Others. (4) Environments & Frameworks compendium (Table 10 environments, Table 11 frameworks). (5) Open challenges (trustworthiness, scaling training, scaling environments, mechanistic debate, deployment, social impact). Synthesizes 500+ works; coverage window through 2025 (v5 revised Apr 2026).
- **benchmark construction and size**: N/A (survey, not a benchmark). It catalogs environments/benchmarks (Table 10) and frameworks (Table 11) with their domains/modalities/resource links rather than constructing a dataset.

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Builds on and organizes LLM-RL / RLHF foundations (PPO, GRPO, DPO, REINFORCE, RLVR a la DeepSeek-R1) and agentic methods it taxonomizes (ReAct, Toolformer, Search-R1/R1-Searcher, MemAgent/MEM1/ReSum, MemoryLLM/M+, MemGen, Reflexion-style self-improvement, Voyager-style skills). Relates to prior surveys on LLM reasoning and LLM/VLM-integrated RL.
- **contrasts with**:
> Explicitly contrasts Agentic RL with conventional LLM-RL / Preference-Based RL Fine-Tuning (PBRFT), framed as a degenerate single-step MDP, and with prompt-engineering/SFT-only agent pipelines (static, imitation-based) that lack adaptation through experience. Also positioned relative to other recent surveys (LLM reasoning; LLM/VLM-integrated RL; agentic systems).
- **lineage**:
> Surveys lineage. A foundational taxonomy/compendium survey for the Agentic-RL line, organizing RL-trained agentic capabilities (planning, tool use, memory, reasoning, self-improvement, perception). Relevant to the retrieval-as-learned-policy and write-back/online-growth axes that separate RL-controlled experience/memory agents from static RAG planners.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- completeness_vs_topk_objective
- context_budget_and_selection_count
- dynamic_index_and_protocol
- evaluation_decoupling
- failure_experience_usage
- index_content_separation
- noise_robustness_mechanism
- reranking
- tool_dependency_awareness
- tool_document_engineering

<a id="item-agentic-tool-use-survey"></a>
### 179. Agentic Tool Use in Large Language Models (Hu et al.)

2026  ·  arXiv:2604.00835 (2026-04, verified)  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.00835)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2026
- **venue**: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2604.00835, cs.CL). Submitted 1 Apr 2026 (v1). Not a peer-reviewed venue; arXiv-issued DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2604.00835. (Verified from the arXiv abstract page; submission history shows [v1] Wed, 1 Apr 2026, 976 KB.)
- **authors affiliation**:
> Jinchao Hu (School of Computer Science and Technology, Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen, China); Meizhi Zhong (TikTok Inc, Beijing, China); Kehai Chen (HIT Shenzhen, China; corresponding-style senior author); Xuefeng Bai (HIT Shenzhen, China); Min Zhang (HIT Shenzhen, China). Lead institution: Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen), with one author at TikTok Inc.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.00835
- **code url**:
> N/A (survey; no official code/implementation or paper-list repository is announced in the abstract page or paper. The many citations to GitHub-hosted frameworks such as ReAct, ToolLLM, Search-R1, VerlTool, OpenAI Swarm, AgentKit are third-party works, not artifacts of this survey.)
- **maintained repo url**: N/A (no continuously-updated authors' paper list or leaderboard is associated with this survey; it is a frozen v1 arXiv PDF/HTML as of indexing.)

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Survey / taxonomy of agentic tool use (function calling) in LLMs. Spans tool-use across QA/knowledge retrieval, mathematical and program-aided reasoning, code/software engineering, web and computer/GUI agents, embodied/robotic action, and safety. Tool use is framed as the mechanism that operationalizes action for LLM agents (search, computation, external system control).
- **problem setting**:
> This is an analytical literature survey, not a method or system with original experiments. It organizes the agentic-tool-use literature into three methodological paradigms distinguished by their optimization signal: (I) Prompting as Plug-and-Play (frozen weights, in-context control), (II) Supervised Tool Learning (SFT on labeled/synthetic tool-use data), and (III) Reward-Driven Tool Policy Learning (RL over multi-turn tool interaction). It treats evaluation as a cross-cutting fourth dimension. Settings covered range from offline single-call function calling to interactive, stateful, multi-turn single-agent and multi-agent deployments; supervision availability is precisely the organizing axis (none/in-context -> supervised -> reward). The survey itself defines no controlled experimental protocol, training run, or benchmark of its own; it offers a six-dimension comparison of prior surveys (chronological evolution, paradigm taxonomy, tool coverage, training data, evaluation landscape, open challenges) and qualitative benchmark tables.
- **what is retrieved**:
> N/A as an artifact (the survey itself retrieves nothing). As surveyed content: tools/APIs and tool documentation (the central retrieved object, e.g., AnyTool hierarchical API retrieval, Gorilla retrieval over evolving API docs); reasoning-action programs/templates from external task libraries (ART); search/web evidence and knowledge documents (WebGPT, Search-R1, HotpotQA-style retrieval); and reusable synthesized tools/skills from an evolving tool library (TroVE, LATM). The survey's evaluation section devotes an explicit category to 'Tool Retrieval and Selection.'
- **retrieval grounding**:
> Survey-level: covers BOTH access to STATIC/dynamic external tool corpora (curated function pools, large real-world API collections such as ToolLLM's 16000+ APIs, evolving API documentation in Gorilla, MCP-served tool marketplaces) and GROWING agent-curated stores (TroVE/LATM tool libraries, Titans test-time long-term memory). HYBRID overall; the survey itself is grounded in no single corpus.
- **completeness vs topk objective**:
> N/A (survey; defines no retrieval objective of its own). Surveyed tool-retrieval work spans top-k selection from large candidate pools (StableToolBench, API-Bank), hierarchical narrowing of the candidate space before invocation (AnyTool), and whether-or-not / when-to-call decisions (When2Call, WTU-Eval) that emphasize precision-driven necessity rather than fixed top-k. No completeness metric is standardized.
- **cbr cycle coverage**: N/A (the survey is not a case-based reasoning system and implements no Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain cycle; CBR is not an organizing concept of this survey).
- **explicit cbr grounding**: False. The survey does not frame agentic tool use as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it organizes the field around the optimization signal (in-context control, supervised signals, reward feedback).

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> N/A (survey defines no single retrieval unit). Surveyed units: tool-API / function signature (the dominant unit, with its docstring/specification), reasoning-action program or template (ART task library), retrieved document/passage or web snippet (search-augmented QA, Search-R1), and reusable synthesized tool/program (TroVE, LATM). At evaluation time the relevant unit is the candidate function plus its specification.
- **index source**:
> N/A for the survey. Surveyed Agentic tool-use systems draw on static curated function pools and large real-world API collections (ToolLLM, StableToolBench), live/evolving API documentation (Gorilla; the future MCP-served dynamic tool marketplaces), and growing agent-curated tool libraries (TroVE continuous tool-library evolution; LATM tool making). The survey builds no index itself.
- **index structure topology**:
> N/A (survey has no index of its own). It reviews multiple organizations: flat candidate function pools (BFCL, ToolEyes), HIERARCHICAL retrieval over large API libraries (AnyTool's hierarchical agents narrowing the candidate space; ToolLLM's depth-first/tree-style API exploration), dependency-aware computation graphs over tool calls (LLMCompiler organizes tool calls as a dependency-aware graph for parallel execution), and protocol-served dynamic tool catalogs (envisioned MCP marketplaces).
- **retriever type**:
> N/A (survey; no retriever implemented). Surveyed retrievers include dense/embedding-based tool retrieval over documentation (Gorilla retrieval), hierarchical LLM-agent-driven retrieval (AnyTool), and search-engine/web APIs as retrievers in RL-trained settings (Search-R1, DeepResearcher). The LLM frequently acts as router/selector over candidate tools rather than as the retriever.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> N/A (survey; trains no retriever). It reviews the spectrum it explicitly champions: from in-context/prompted tool selection (no retriever training; Paradigm I) to supervised/API-aware fine-tuning for accurate selection and calling (Gorilla combines retrieval with API-aware fine-tuning; NexusRaven; APIGen), to reward-driven policies that learn when and which tool to call from environmental feedback (ReTool, ToolRL, Search-R1). The survey itself proposes no learning signal.
- **query construction**:
> N/A (survey). Surveyed query/key construction includes raw task instruction matched against tool docstrings (function-calling benchmarks), decomposed sub-questions (Self-Ask, Least-to-Most), thought-conditioned reasoning steps that decide the next action (ReAct), and explicit plans whose subtasks are dispatched to tools (ReWOO planner-worker, LLMCompiler). The survey prescribes no single construction method.
- **query granularity**:
> N/A (survey). Surveyed systems range from task-level one-shot tool selection (decoupled planning, ReWOO/HuggingGPT plan-then-execute), to step/state-level per-turn action selection (ReAct interleaved loop, RL multi-turn policies). The survey commits to no single granularity, instead organizing by control flow (interleaved vs decoupled vs program-aided).
- **when to retrieve**:
> N/A (survey). Surveyed control spans one-shot/plan-then-execute (ReWOO, HuggingGPT, LLMCompiler), iterative per-step interleaving (ReAct, Reflexion, LATS tree search), and learned/adaptive decisions about whether to invoke a tool at all (ReTool RL distinguishes tool-needed vs internal-knowledge cases; When2Call/WTU-Eval evaluate this decision boundary).
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> N/A (survey defines no single trigger). Surveyed triggers: the model's own thought/decision in the Thought-Action-Observation loop (ReAct), verbal self-reflection on failure (Reflexion), external-tool-grounded verification (CRITIC, Chain-of-Verification), tree-search expansion (LATS), and learned RL policies that decide when a tool is necessary (ReTool). Evaluation benchmarks When2Call and WTU-Eval target the whether-or-not-to-call signal explicitly.
- **reranking**: N/A (survey; no reranking stage of its own). Reranking/selection over large tool pools is reviewed implicitly via hierarchical candidate narrowing (AnyTool) and tool-selection benchmarks (StableToolBench, API-Bank), but the survey contributes no reranking method.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> N/A (survey). It reviews refinement operations in surveyed systems: self-reflection/self-refinement over trajectories (Reflexion, Self-Refine), tool-grounded verification and critique (CRITIC, Chain-of-Verification), and System-2-Attention-style context regeneration plus TroVE tool-library curation flagged as future directions. The survey implements no refinement pipeline.
- **tool document engineering**:
> N/A as a contribution (survey). It discusses that accurate tool use depends on understanding tool specifications/docstrings, that Gorilla uses up-to-date documentation at inference time (retrieval + API-aware fine-tuning), that NexusRaven emphasizes zero-shot function calling from tool descriptions, and that APIGen produces verifiable synthetic function-calling data; it proposes no new tool-document-indexing technique itself.
- **index content separation**:
> N/A (survey; no index-vs-content separation mechanism of its own). It notes hierarchical retrieval that narrows a large candidate space before loading/invoking specific tools (AnyTool) and the envisioned MCP model where a lightweight protocol-served catalog is queried before binding a tool, but these are reviewed, not contributed.
- **dynamic index and protocol**:
> N/A as a contribution, but a central FUTURE-DIRECTION theme. The survey's first future direction is 'Standardization and the MCP Revolution': the Model Context Protocol (Hou et al., 2025) as a standardized interface decoupling agents from tool implementations, turning integration from quadratic to linear complexity, and enabling dynamic, protocol-compliant tool marketplaces that agents query and subscribe to in real time. It also reviews RESTful API interaction (RestGPT) and large real-world API ecosystems (ToolLLM, Gorilla). The survey itself maintains no live tool index.
- **tool dependency awareness**:
> N/A as a contribution (survey). It reviews dependency modeling in surveyed systems: LLMCompiler organizes tool calls as a dependency-aware computation graph enabling parallel execution of independent subtasks, ReWOO's planner emits subtasks with variable assignments passed between steps, and NESTFUL evaluates nested API calls where one call's output feeds the next. The survey contributes no dependency-graph retrieval formalism of its own.

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> N/A as a method. The survey describes how surveyed systems use tools/retrieved content: prompt/context augmentation and in-context interaction in Paradigm I; internalization into model weights via SFT in Paradigm II (teaching tool-call syntax and logic); and reward-driven policy optimization in Paradigm III where tool-call outcomes provide training signal. Code/program execution is used as an externalized computation backend (PAL, PoT) and as an action space (CodeAct, Code as Policies).
- **planning integration**:
> N/A as a method. The survey explicitly organizes Paradigm I by how reasoning/planning interfaces with tool execution: (a) Interleaved Reasoning and Action (per-step thought-action-observation loops; ReAct, Reflexion, CRITIC, LATS tree search); (b) Decoupled Planning and Execution (plan-then-execute; ReWOO planner-worker, LLMCompiler dependency graph + parallel calls, AdaPlanner feedback-revised plans, HuggingGPT/TaskMatrix.AI central planner over experts); and (c) Program-Aided Reasoning (code as the planning/execution medium; PAL, PoT, ViperGPT, Code as Policies, LATM/CREATOR tool creation). Paradigm III integrates planning into RL over multi-turn rollouts (Search-R1, SimpleTIR end-to-end).
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> N/A (survey). It contrasts per-step interleaving (per thought-action-observation cycle in ReAct/Reflexion), plan-level / per-answer decoupling (ReWOO, LLMCompiler issuing batched/parallel calls), and per-tool-call-within-a-rollout interleaving in RL multi-turn tool-integrated reasoning (SimpleTIR, Search-R1, ReTool). The survey reviews these styles rather than fixing one granularity.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> N/A (not a CBR method; the survey contributes no retrieved-case adaptation mechanism). Adjacent surveyed mechanisms include verbal-reflection-driven revision (Reflexion), execution-feedback-driven plan revision (AdaPlanner, TRICE execution feedback, Retroformer retrospective policy gradient).
- **retrieved item representation**:
> N/A (survey). Surveyed surface forms injected/used: free-text tool documentation and function schemas (function calling), executable code/programs (PAL, PoT, CodeAct, TroVE/LATM synthesized tools), reasoning-action programs/templates (ART), and natural-language reasoning traces interleaved with tool outputs (ReAct trajectories). The survey injects nothing itself.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> N/A (survey). Surveyed units range from a single concrete tool/API call and its arguments, to reusable procedural skills/programs (LATM, TroVE, CREATOR tool creation), to higher-level reasoning-action templates retrieved from a task library (ART). The survey reviews this spectrum rather than fixing an abstraction level.
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> N/A (survey contributes none of its own). It reviews robustness mechanisms in surveyed systems: self-reflection and iterative refinement (Reflexion, Self-Refine), external-tool-grounded verification/critique (CRITIC, Chain-of-Verification), and a dedicated Safety-and-Reliability evaluation layer covering indirect prompt injection (ToolSword, InjecAgent), sandboxed risk emulation (ToolEmu), and risk-awareness judgment (R-Judge, SafetyBench, PsySafe). Future directions add NeMo Guardrails and PromptArmor as defenses.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> N/A as an artifact. Surveyed memory spans episodic/long-context memory (Generative Agents, MemGPT memory management), skill/tool libraries (Voyager skill acquisition, TroVE/LATM tool libraries), and test-time neural long-term memory (Titans, flagged as a future direction). The survey treats memory as part of the agentic architecture (reasoning core + planning + memory + action) rather than implementing one.
- **write back**:
> N/A as a method. Surveyed systems DO write back: Voyager stores acquired skills, TroVE continuously evolves an agent's tool library, LATM creates and stores reusable tools, MemGPT manages long-context memory, and Titans memorizes historical context at test time. The survey itself stores nothing.
- **online growth**:
> N/A as a method. Surveyed agent stores grow online/at test time (TroVE continuous tool-library evolution; Titans test-time memorization; Voyager incremental skill acquisition), and the survey's 'Agentic Self-Consistency and Continuous Evolution' future direction foresees agents curating their own internal libraries of synthesized tools and usage patterns instead of resetting after each session. The survey itself has no growing store.
- **write back trigger**:
> N/A (survey; no write-back trigger of its own). Surveyed triggers include reflective writes after self-critique (Reflexion), on-success skill/tool acquisition (Voyager, TroVE, LATM creating verified reusable tools), and test-time memorization of salient context (Titans). The survey discusses continuous self-extension as a future goal without standardizing a trigger.
- **failure experience usage**:
> N/A (survey). It highlights learning from failed executions as a key challenge and reviews several approaches: Reflexion's verbal self-reflection over failed trajectories reused in later attempts, Retroformer's retrospective learning over past tool-use trajectories, and TRICE's credit assignment that strengthens steps contributing to correct answers while suppressing noisy/unhelpful actions. The survey contributes no failure-storage scheme of its own.
- **memory evolution update**: N/A (survey). It frames continuous tool-library curation and self-evolution (TroVE, agents curating internal libraries) and test-time memory updates (Titans) as future directions, but proposes no single post-write update policy (append/merge/refine/prune).
- **retrieval as learned policy**:
> N/A (survey). Paradigm III explicitly covers tool use as a learned/RL-optimized policy: ReTool learns when external tools are needed vs internal knowledge, ToolRL treats reward as central to tool learning, Search-R1 trains the reasoning-retrieval interaction via RL, and SimpleTIR unifies reasoning and tool execution in one end-to-end RL loop. The survey reviews (does not implement) retrieval/tool-selection-as-learned-policy and identifies multi-tool credit assignment in long tool chains as a core open problem.
- **cross agent or cross framework sharing**:
> N/A as a method. Surveyed and future-direction theme: multi-agent orchestration and standardized interoperability are highlighted (OpenAI Swarm lightweight handoffs between specialized agents, AgentKit structured reasoning with dynamic graphs, MetaGPT/AutoGen/OpenDevin multi-agent collaboration), and MCP is positioned as enabling a tool built once to be usable by any compliant agent/framework (cross-framework sharing). The survey reviews rather than implements cross-agent/cross-framework sharing.

**Evaluation**

- **benchmarks**:
> N/A as original experiments (survey reports no results of its own). It catalogs benchmarks across three evaluation levels. Tool Usage Correctness: BFCL (Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard), ToolEyes, T-Eval, API-Bank, StableToolBench, Gorilla, When2Call, WTU-Eval, NexusRaven, NESTFUL. Task Completion: AIME(25), MATH/MATH-500, GSM8K, TabMWP, FreshQA, ToolQA, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, Natural Questions, TriviaQA, MMLU, StrategyQA, HumanEval, MBPP, BigCodeBench, SWE-bench, BIRD, Spider 2.0, DSBench, DS-1000, InterCode, SheetBench/SpreadsheetBench, FinQA, SciBench, SciCode, BioPlanner, ChemCrow, MedAgent-Bench. Tool-Driven Interaction: WebArena, VisualWebArena, WebVoyager, Mind2Web, GAIA, TravelPlanner, WorldSense, OSWorld, OS-Copilot, OmniACT, AndroidWorld, AppWorld, AppAgent, ScreenAgent, GUI-World, OfficeBench, WorkArena, tau-bench, TheAgentCompany, CodeAct; plus Safety: ToolSword, InjecAgent, ToolEmu, SafetyBench, R-Judge, PsySafe.
- **benchmark family**:
> Survey-level grouping into three evolving levels: (1) Tool Usage Correctness -- function-call validity (BFCL/ToolEyes/T-Eval), tool retrieval and selection (API-Bank/StableToolBench/Gorilla), tool-use decisions (When2Call/WTU-Eval), compositional invocation (NexusRaven/NESTFUL); (2) Task Completion -- math/knowledge QA (GSM8K, MATH, AIME, HotpotQA, ToolQA, FreshQA), programming/data (HumanEval, MBPP, BigCodeBench, SWE-bench, BIRD/Spider 2.0, DSBench, InterCode), scientific/professional (SciBench, SciCode, BioPlanner, ChemCrow, MedAgent-Bench); (3) Tool-Driven Interaction -- web (WebArena/VisualWebArena/WebVoyager/Mind2Web/GAIA), computer/GUI/OS and mobile (OSWorld/OmniACT/AndroidWorld/AppWorld), workplace (OfficeBench/WorkArena/tau-bench/TheAgentCompany), and safety/reliability (ToolSword/InjecAgent/ToolEmu/R-Judge/SafetyBench/PsySafe). Maps onto the collection families: tool (ToolBench/API-Bank/BFCL), web (Mind2Web/WebArena), code (SWE-bench), QA/multi-hop (HotpotQA).
- **baselines**:
> N/A (survey; runs no head-to-head experiments and reports no baselines of its own). Its comparative analysis is qualitative: a Table-1 comparison of representative prior surveys (Zhao et al. 2023; Wang et al. 2024; Mialon et al. 2023; Qu et al. 2025; Shen 2024; Chen et al. 2025) along six dimensions, showing only 'Ours' covers all six (chronological evolution + paradigm taxonomy + tool coverage + training data + evaluation landscape + open challenges); and a paradigm-vs-paradigm contrast (Prompting vs Supervised vs Reward-Driven) by strengths and failure modes.
- **key metrics**:
> N/A (survey; reports no quantitative metrics of its own). It catalogs the evaluation signals used across levels: function-call validity / schema-constrained correctness and fine-grained error diagnosis (BFCL, ToolEyes, T-Eval), tool retrieval/selection accuracy, whether-or-not / when-to-call decision accuracy (When2Call, WTU-Eval), end-to-end task success / pass rate (math accuracy, code pass@k, QA accuracy, SWE-bench resolved rate), interactive task-success and trajectory match (WebArena task success, Mind2Web trajectory match, tau-bench state outcome / policy compliance), and safety/attack-resistance and risk-judgment signals (ToolSword, InjecAgent, R-Judge).
- **headline result**:
> N/A (survey; no headline number). Its central contribution is conceptual: a unified three-paradigm evolutionary taxonomy of agentic tool use -- (I) Prompting as Plug-and-Play, (II) Supervised Tool Learning, (III) Reward-Driven Tool Policy Learning -- distinguished by optimization signal (in-context control / supervised signals / reward feedback), plus a cross-cutting three-level evaluation landscape (tool usage correctness -> task completion -> tool-driven interaction). It argues the three paradigms are complementary and that production-grade systems will likely combine all three.
- **ablations**:
> N/A (survey; conducts no experiments and reports no component ablations). Its closest analogue is the qualitative per-paradigm strengths/failure-mode analysis: Prompting is flexible, interpretable, low deployment cost but suffers high latency/token cost and brittleness on complex multi-step tasks; Supervised internalizes tool-use behavior into weights (efficiency/reliability) but is bottlenecked by large-scale high-quality data construction and risks degrading generalist ability (motivating AgentTuning/Lemur balance); Reward-driven enables exploration, error recovery, and long-horizon adaptation but faces multi-tool credit assignment over long tool-call chains.
- **evaluation decoupling**:
> N/A as original measurement (survey performs no evaluation). It explicitly DECOUPLES diagnostic intrinsic correctness (function-call validity, tool retrieval/selection, fine-grained error diagnosis via ToolEyes/T-Eval) from end-to-end task-completion success and from interactive task success/state outcomes, treating these as three distinct, progressively higher evaluation levels.
- **process vs outcome metrics**:
> Survey-level: it argues evaluation must capture both. It highlights step-wise/process-oriented diagnostic benchmarks (T-Eval decomposing tool use into intermediate steps; ToolEyes separating intent-understanding, format-alignment, and tool-selection errors) alongside end-to-end outcome benchmarks (task success), and notes interaction-level evaluation must also assess process properties like error recovery, policy compliance (tau-bench), and safety, not only final outcomes.
- **cost efficiency tradeoff**:
> N/A as original measurement (no cost numbers of its own). It discusses efficiency/cost qualitatively as a primary axis: Prompting incurs high latency and token overhead from repeated prompting; decoupled planning (ReWOO) and parallel function calling (LLMCompiler) reduce interaction overhead; Supervised learning internalizes tool use to cut prompting cost; Reward-driven methods (ReTool) reduce unnecessary tool calls; and the MCP future direction reframes integration cost from quadratic to linear complexity.
- **context budget and selection count**:
> N/A (survey; no token budget or k of its own). It reviews mechanisms that manage budget/selection in surveyed systems -- hierarchical retrieval narrowing a large candidate tool space before invocation (AnyTool), long-context memory management (MemGPT), and UI-guided visual token selection for high-resolution screens (ShowUI, future direction) -- but prescribes no fixed-k or token budget.
- **benchmark construction and size**:
> N/A (this is a survey, not a benchmark; it constructs no dataset of its own). It does annotate cataloged benchmarks by attributes in its tables (Year, Primary Focus, Executable, Compositional, Tool Source for correctness benchmarks; Task Type, Tool Role, Executable, Open-Ended for task-completion; Trajectory, Target, Challenge, Signal for interaction), e.g., ToolLLM is described as covering 16000+ real-world APIs and ToolAlpaca as 3000 simulated cases (in Sec.2 prose).

**Relations**

- **builds on**:
> Builds on and synthesizes the agentic-LLM and tool-learning literature it reviews: prompting foundations (Chain-of-Thought, ReAct, Reflexion, Tree of Thoughts; PAL/PoT program-aided reasoning), supervised tool learning (TALM, WebCPM, Toolformer, ToolAlpaca, ToolLLM, Gorilla, APIGen, FireAct, AgentTuning, Lemur), and reward-driven policy learning (ReTool, Retroformer, TRICE, Search-R1, SimpleTIR, RLFactory, VerlTool). It positions itself relative to prior surveys it tabulates: Zhao et al. (2023) and Wang et al. (2024a) agent-architecture surveys, Mialon et al. (2023) augmented-LM survey, Qu et al. (2025) tool-learning survey, Shen (2024), and Chen et al. (2025b).
- **contrasts with**:
> Explicitly contrasts itself with prior surveys (Table 1) that provide a largely static snapshot and lack a methodological-evolution view: Zhao et al. (2023), Wang et al. (2024a), Mialon et al. (2023) emphasize agent architecture but no paradigm taxonomy/tool coverage/training-data axis; Qu et al. (2025), Shen (2024), Chen et al. (2025b) cover taxonomy/tool/data but (variously) lack the chronological-evolution axis or evaluation landscape. The survey's distinguishing claim is the evolutionary three-paradigm synthesis (in-context -> supervised -> reward) with evaluation as a co-evolving cross-cutting dimension. It also internally contrasts the three paradigms against one another by strengths and failure modes.
- **lineage**:
> Surveys group. A 2026 evolutionary survey of agentic tool use / function calling that organizes the field by optimization signal (prompting -> supervised tool learning -> reward-driven tool policy learning) and adds a tool-retrieval/selection evaluation category. It serves as an umbrella reference linking the tool-use sub-topics in this collection -- tool retrieval/selection (relevant to Group D tool-retrieval works such as ToolLLM, Gorilla, AnyTool, ToolRet) and reward-driven/agentic-RL methods -- rather than being a method within any single sub-topic.

**Uncertain fields** (not researched / unverifiable):

- survey_scope_and_axes

<a id="item-agent-memory-survey-2026"></a>
### 180. From Storage to Experience: A Survey on the Evolution of LLM Agent Memory Mechanisms (Luo et al.)

2026  ·  arXiv:2605.06716 (2026-05, verified)  ·  [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06716)


**Basic Info**

- **year**: 2026
- **venue**: ACL 2026 Findings (Accepted). First released as arXiv:2605.06716 [cs.AI] on 2026-05-07 (submitted 7 May 2026, v1). Subjects: cs.AI; cs.CL. The 'arXiv:2605.06716 (2026-05)' label refers to this same preprint; the peer-reviewed venue is ACL 2026 Findings.
- **authors affiliation**:
> Jinghao Luo (South China Normal University; equal contribution / project leader), Yuchen Tian (Hong Kong Baptist University; equal contribution), Chuxue Cao (Hong Kong University of Science and Technology), Ziyang Luo, Hongzhan Lin, Chuyi Kong (Hong Kong Baptist University), Kaixin Li (National University of Singapore), Ruichao Yang (University of Science and Technology Beijing), Jing Ma (Hong Kong Baptist University; corresponding author). Primary affiliation: Hong Kong Baptist University. Contact: FeishuEcho@outlook.com, {yctian, majing}@comp.hkbu.edu.hk.
- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06716
- **code url**: N/A (a survey; no method code).
- **maintained repo url**:
> https://github.com/FeishuLuo/Evolving-LLM-Agent-Memory-Survey (continuously updated paper/resource list announced in the paper; README organized as Overview / Evolution Path / Paper List with Storage 33 papers, Reflection 28 papers, Experience 42 papers, and Benchmarks & Datasets 43 entries).

**Problem Definition**

- **task domain**:
> Survey/taxonomy of memory mechanisms for LLM-based agents, spanning planning, tool-use, multi-step reasoning, long-context QA/dialogue, web navigation, embodied/open-world, code, recommendation/personalization, role-playing/social simulation, and multimodal/embodied settings (anchor evolutionary memory survey, not a single-task method).
- **problem setting**:
> A survey that reframes LLM-agent memory research, which it argues is fragmented between operating-system engineering and cognitive-science paradigms, into a single evolutionary perspective. It formalizes an LLM agent as a policy pi_theta(a_t | I, o_t, m_t) where m_t = Retrieve(M, o_t) is context-specific memory pulled from a global externalized repository M, and defines a trajectory tau = <(o_1,a_1),...,(o_T,a_T)>. It proposes a three-stage evolutionary framework (Storage -> Reflection -> Experience) based on the degree to which past interaction trajectories are utilized/abstracted. Settings covered are predominantly interactive, long-horizon, single- and multi-agent agent-environment loops; supervision varies by surveyed work. The survey proposes no new method, dataset, or experiments; it offers design principles and a roadmap. It explicitly notes that benchmarks for the Experience stage (abstraction/generalization) are scarce, and that current benchmarks mostly assess storage/retrieval of static data.
- **what is retrieved**:
> Across surveyed systems: raw interaction trajectories / observation-action logs (Storage), refined/critiqued trajectory units and corrective insights (Reflection), and abstracted experiences -- natural-language heuristic guidelines/rules, reusable procedural skills/program functions, experience graphs, latent variables, and parameter-internalized priors (Experience). The survey frames retrieval as m_t = Retrieve(M, o_t): pulling context-specific memory from the global repository M for the current observation.
- **retrieval grounding**:
> GROWING/episodic memory the agent writes is the central object (M is defined as an externalized repository bridging frozen parametric knowledge theta and evolving environmental dynamics, populated by Storage, Reflection, and Experience operations during interaction). It is HYBRID in that static external knowledge/long-context corpora and parametric/latent (internalized) memory are also covered, but the survey's organizing axis is the dynamically written, evolving trajectory store rather than a static external corpus.
- **cbr cycle coverage**:
> N/A (a survey, not a CBR method). The three-stage workflow maps loosely onto a case lifecycle: Storage/Retrieve (preserve and recall trajectories), Reflection/Revise (critique, denoise, repair, dynamic maintenance), Experience/Retain+Reuse (abstract generalizable rules/skills reused as policy priors), but the survey does not use CBR Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain terminology.
- **explicit cbr grounding**:
> False -- the survey frames memory via an evolutionary/cognitive lens (Storage->Reflection->Experience; statelessness, long-term consistency, dynamic environments, continual learning) and contrasts OS-engineering vs cognitive-science paradigms. It does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner.

**Retrieval Mechanism**

- **retrieval unit**:
> Survey taxonomy of units rather than one: token/snippet (linear FIFO context streams), full/sub trajectories and observation-action logs (raw Storage), vector-encoded trajectory chunks (Vector storage), tabular rows / tiered-context entries / entity-relation triples and KG-subgraphs (Structured storage), refined memory units m'_i (Reflection), and abstracted experience units -- heuristic guidelines/rules, experience-graph nodes, reusable program functions/skills, latent token sequences, and internalized parameters (Experience). Defined by the degree of abstraction/cognitive processing.
- **index source**:
> Hybrid construction, but emphasizing online/test-time-induced growing memory: M is written during interaction (Storage appends raw trajectories M_raw = {tau_i}; Reflection injects refined units M <- M U {m'_i}; Experience extracts a separate rule set K). Storage also covers static long-context handling, and Experience covers offline-induced parameter internalization. The survey contrasts static-storage paradigms with active-management and abstraction paradigms.
- **index structure topology**:
> Survey spans multiple topologies, explicitly enumerated in the Storage taxonomy: Linear (chronological token stream, FIFO; context-window adaptation + information sparsification), Vector (flat high-dimensional embedding index; semantic + weighted retrieval), and Structured (tabular relational databases e.g. ChatDB/DB-GPT/MAC-SQL; tiered/hierarchical architectures e.g. MemGPT/MemoChat/MemOS; and semantic/entity-relation GRAPHS e.g. MemLLM/AriGraph/GraphReader). No single topology prescribed.
- **retriever type**:
> Survey-level / hybrid across works: dense semantic retrieval (embedding proximity), weighted retrieval (relevance+recency+importance, temporal decay), BM25/lexical and visual channels (in multimodal parallel-fusion), LLM/SQL-generated structured queries (ChatDB/DB-GPT), graph traversal (semantic graphs), agent-driven/autonomous retrieval controllers, and -- in implicit/hybrid Experience -- parameter-/latent-based 'reading' via forward pass (no explicit retriever). No canonical retriever proposed.
- **retriever learning signal**:
> Survey-level: storage/reflection-stage reading is predominantly off-the-shelf (text similarity, heuristic relevance/recency/importance, temporal-decay weighting). The survey highlights a shift toward learned/RL-optimized signals chiefly in the Experience stage (RL on reflections, group-based policy optimization, RL-aligned tool invocation, early-experience/implicit-world-model paradigms, soft-Q / value-style internalization) and toward agent-learned retrieval controllers (active memory perception). It proposes no retriever itself; learning signals discussed range from none (similarity) to environment-feedback and RL.
- **query construction**:
> Survey-level: queries to memory are formed from the current observation/state (m_t = Retrieve(M, o_t)); via agent-generated structured queries (LLM-to-SQL in ChatDB/DB-GPT); via query-key similarity over memory blocks; via multi-channel queries (semantic/lexical/visual) in multimodal retrieval; and via agent-driven multi-turn intent-conditioned queries. Construction is method-dependent; abstracted as observation-conditioned memory reading.
- **query granularity**:
> Survey-level: predominantly step/state-level reading (memory retrieved per observation o_t during reasoning/acting), with task-level/session-level reads also present and, in the Experience stage, abstracted rules used as priors without trajectory-level matching. The survey does not standardize a query granularity.
- **when to retrieve**:
> Survey-level: both one-shot and iterative reading appear; an explicit future direction ('Active Memory Perception') argues for adaptive, learned/autonomous triggering -- agents should evaluate on-demand whether and what type of memory is needed -- moving beyond passive, indiscriminate retrieval. Some surveyed systems already use autonomous retrieval controllers; no single trigger policy is prescribed.
- **retrieval trigger signal**:
> Survey-level: triggers across works include fixed schedule (read per step/turn), similarity/weighted thresholds, agent-initiated/self-directed access (MemGPT-style OS controllers; LLM-generated SQL reads), and -- as a flagged future direction -- learned autonomous retrieval controllers that decide whether/what memory to introduce on demand. The survey critiques passive triggering and indiscriminate retrieval (irrelevant/obsolete memories disrupt reasoning coherence). No token-confidence/attention trigger is adopted as a unifying signal.
- **retrieved context refinement**:
> Survey-level: refinement is a defining axis. Storage uses information sparsification / compression (attention-score eviction H2O, query-key salient-block retrieval Quest, perplexity-based redundancy removal LLMLingua). Reflection performs semantic refinement: error rectification (self-critique/repair), dynamic maintenance (lifecycle update/dedup), and knowledge compression/distillation (structured reflections, modular procedural decomposition, multi-granularity abstraction, context-folding e.g. AgentFold). Experience performs cross-trajectory abstraction/induction. So: rerank/decompose-then-recompose/distill/compress/filter all appear, organized by stage.
- **tool document engineering**: N/A (memory survey; tool/skill-description indexing engineering is largely out of scope, though procedural-skill libraries and tool-use experience internalization are discussed in the Experience stage).
- **index content separation**:
> Partially covered: tiered/hierarchical storage architectures (e.g., MemGPT dual-layer main vs external context with virtual context expansion; MemoChat topic-keyed segments; MemOS) separate a small in-context working memory from a larger external store paged/retrieved on demand; SWIFT-SAGE dynamically adjusts retrieval intensity. Discussed as a storage-management pattern rather than a formal lightweight-index-then-content principle.
- **dynamic index and protocol**: N/A (no tool index / integration protocol such as RapidAPI/MCP; memory stores grow via in-loop trajectory writing and OS-style controller updates rather than tool-API CRUD sync).
- **tool dependency awareness**: N/A (inter-tool dependency modeling is out of scope; the survey's structured/graph storage models entity-relation dependencies of the environment, and Experience models causal/cross-step dependencies, but not tool-to-tool dependency graphs).

**Utilization Mechanism**

- **how retrieved used**:
> Survey-level: retrieved memory is used as prompt/context augmentation (injecting recalled trajectories/insights into pi_theta(a_t | I, o_t, m_t)); as refined references for similar future tasks (Reflection units m'_i); as reusable skills/program functions invoked as atomic actions and natural-language heuristic guidelines/rules used as policy priors for unseen tasks (explicit Experience); as latent token injection / activation modulation (latent Experience, e.g., MemGen 'Memory Weaver'); and as a training signal -- internalizing experience into model parameters via fine-tuning/RL (implicit and hybrid Experience).
- **planning integration**:
> Survey-level: memory supports planning/acting by supplying past observations/experiences at decision time (per-step interleaved retrieval m_t = Retrieve(M, o_t)); by providing persistent high-level goals to prevent goal drift in long-horizon and multi-agent planning; by guiding active exploration (reward/curriculum/reuse-driven) whose outcomes are abstracted back into memory; and -- in Experience -- by elevating pi_theta to decision-making at a higher level of abstraction via rule/skill priors that enable zero-shot transfer to unseen scenarios. The survey abstracts integration as a Storage->Reflection->Experience evolution rather than prescribing one plan-time scheme.
- **reasoning search interleaving granularity**:
> Survey-level: reviewed works interleave memory reading at per-step / per-turn granularity during reasoning and acting (m_t per observation o_t), with per-answer/session reads also present and Experience priors applied without per-step trajectory matching. The survey does not impose a single interleaving granularity.
- **adaptation mechanism**:
> N/A (a survey, not a CBR adaptation method). The closest analogues it surveys are Reflection's revision/refinement (self-critique error rectification, dynamic maintenance, distillation) and Experience's adaptation/reuse (LLM-prompted heuristic-rule reuse, skill composition/cascading, RL/fine-tuning internalization, latent modulation).
- **retrieved item representation**:
> Survey-level spectrum tied to the three stages: (Storage) raw trajectory token streams, vector embeddings, tabular rows, tiered-context entries, entity-relation graphs; (Reflection) distilled/critiqued free-text memory units m'_i, structured profiles, compressed procedural memories, folded context; (Experience) human-readable natural-language guidelines/rules, experience graphs, executable program functions/skills, latent/soft token sequences (MemGen), and internalized model parameters. Surface forms thus range from raw trajectory to distilled rule to executable skill to latent/parametric.
- **abstraction level of retrieved unit**:
> Survey-level the central axis: classification is explicitly by 'degree of utilization/abstraction of past trajectories.' Storage = raw trajectory fidelity (one-to-one with execution traces); Reflection = intra-trajectory refined units (quality density, context-tied); Experience = inter-trajectory inductive abstraction into universal rules/skills K detached from any specific scenario (policy prior). Experience abstraction is further graded shallow (NL rules) -> intermediate (modular executable skeletons/skills) -> deep (parameter-internalized intuition).
- **noise robustness mechanism**:
> Survey-level: a core motivation. Reflection is the principal robustness mechanism -- it acts as a 'semantic filter' against hallucinations/logic errors/invalid attempts via introspective self-critique (error rectification, post-reasoning verification, consistency checks), environmental feedback grounding, and coordinative/consensus calibration. Storage uses sparsification/denoising; Experience uses contrastive induction over success/failure trajectories to sharpen policy boundaries and abstraction to avoid context-shift errors from following raw successful trajectories. Active Memory Perception (future) targets filtering irrelevant/obsolete retrievals.

**Memory & Learning**

- **memory type**:
> Survey/taxonomy -- covers all listed types organized by the Storage/Reflection/Experience evolution: linear/episodic context streams, vector memory, structured (tabular/tiered/graph) memory, skill-library and workflow/procedural memory (explicit Experience), and latent/parametric memory (implicit Experience: latent modulation, parameter internalization). It does not pick one.
- **write back**:
> True (survey-level) -- writing to M is foundational: Storage appends raw trajectories (M_raw = {tau_i}_{i=1}^N), Reflection injects refined units (M <- M U {m'_i}), and Experience extracts/accumulates an abstracted rule/skill set K (and, in hybrid, internalizes it into parameters). Write-back is described as central across stages, not a single implementation.
- **online growth**:
> Yes (survey-level) -- M grows during interaction across all three stages; a key continual-learning driver is that long-horizon real-world interaction causes linear memory expansion, and the survey explicitly warns that unrestricted growth degrades performance (errors propagate and contaminate learning), motivating strategic add/delete policies, decay, pruning, and abstraction-based compression.
- **write back trigger**:
> Survey-level: triggers vary by stage/work -- per-step/turn appending (Storage); reflective writing after a completed trajectory (m'_i = F_ref(tau_i | phi); Reflexion-style post-trial reflection); on-success-and-failure storage for contrastive abstraction (Experience); OS-controller / lifecycle-managed updates (MemGPT/Mem0/Zep dynamic maintenance); and periodic parameter-update internalization (hybrid Accumulate-Internalize cycle). No single trigger prescribed; the survey advocates more strategic, possibly learned, add/delete policies.
- **failure experience usage**:
> Survey-level: explicitly important. Reflexion-style Reflection distills corrective feedback from FAILED trajectories into textual memory; the Experience stage uses contrastive induction over successful AND failed trajectories to delineate policy boundaries precisely (Forouzandeh et al. 2025; He et al. 2024c).
